https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Russia expels Moldovan diplomat in tit-for-tat move
Relations between Moscow and Chisinau have worsened since the 2022 Ukraine war.
Russia has expelled a Moldovan diplomat in retaliation for Chisinau’s expulsion of a Russian embassy employee over the crash of a drone in Moldova.
Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Tuesday that it had summoned Moldova’s ambassador, Lilian Darii, and informed him that a member of the Moldovan embassy’s staff had been declared unacceptable “on the basis of the principle of reciprocity”.
“A strong protest was lodged with the ambassador after the Moldovan authorities on October 23 declared an employee of the Russian embassy in Chisinau persona non grata,” the ministry said in a statement.
It said Moldova’s decision was made “under the formal pretext of the alleged discovery on the territory of the republic of debris of an unmanned aerial vehicle carrying explosives”, calling it “another unfriendly step”.
The ministry said the “true goal” of the move was “to further undermine the centuries-long history of Russian-Moldovan relations”.
‘Crashed near homes’
Last month, Moldovan President Maia Sandu said a “Russian attack drone” had violated the country’s airspace and “crashed near homes and an energy facility”.
Moldova then declared a staff member of the Russian embassy “persona non grata”.
Drones have penetrated Moldovan territory on multiple occasions since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Since then, Russia’s relations with former Soviet states, such as Moldova, have hit an all-time low, compounded by the push by some of those states to join the European Union.
On Sunday, Moldova officially launched a new power line connecting the country to neighbouring Romania and the European grid to reduce its dependence on Russian energy.
The 400-kilovolt extra-high-voltage line, which runs from the city of Vulcanesti to Chisinau, allows Moldova to cut reliance on the Cuciurgan thermal power plant in Transnistria.
Other European-aligned states in the Black Sea region say they are experiencing renewed attacks allegedly carried out by Moscow, such as a drone strike that sank a cargo ship off Romania’s Black Sea coast in October.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: US House Republicans block Pete Hegseth impeachment effort
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
US House Republicans block Pete Hegseth impeachment effort
Defence Secretary has been accused of spearheading war on Iran without required congressional approval.
Republicans in the United States House of Representatives have nixed an effort to advance the impeachment of Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, following a midterm election in which voters vented frustrations over the Iran war Hegseth has helped spearhead.
The lower house of the US Congress voted in favour of a motion to refer the impeachment charges to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee in a procedural vote on Tuesday, effectively killing an effort to remove Hegseth from his position led by Republican Representative Thomas Massie.
That push also won support from Democratic representatives, setting up a test of whether Republican lawmakers would break with the Trump administration and distance themselves from the unpopular war after a rebuke at the polls.
The final vote on Tuesday was 211 in favour and 204 against, with Massie the lone Republican to vote against it. The result means that Republicans will be able to slow-walk the process and can avoid a direct vote on the eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, which cover issues such as the Iran war.
“The Democrats’ attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED!” Trump said in a social media post following the vote. “Every single Republican, except Thomas Massie, a major LOSER, voted in favour of Pete.”
Regardless of the outcome of Tuesday’s vote, an impeachment conviction in the US Senate, where it would require a two-thirds vote and Republicans have a 53-seat majority, was seen as unlikely.
‘Farce’
Massie’s resolution included eight separate articles of impeachment, accusing the combative Pentagon chief of launching an illegal war against Iran without congressional approval and overseeing a campaign of strikes targeting alleged drug trafficking vessels that legal scholars say are extrajudicial killings.
Hegseth has denounced the resolution as “sabotage” and a “farce”, while US President Donald Trump and prominent members of his administration expressed their continued support for him.
Speculation about Hegseth’s position within the administration has circulated as polls suggest that voters partly blame the war for surging prices of goods such as gasoline and groceries, and has grown stronger after Republicans faced punishing losses in the midterm elections.
“Is he being truthful in the way the war is going?” outgoing Republican Senator Joni Ernst said of Hegseth on Tuesday.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: UNIFIL patrol comes under fire in southern Lebanon
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
UNIFIL patrol comes under fire in southern Lebanon
UNIFIL said on Tuesday that ‘about a dozen rounds’ were fired at one of its patrols, without identifying the assailants.
A United Nations peacekeeping force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) patrol has come under fire in southern Lebanon, the force said.
UNIFIL said on Tuesday that “about a dozen rounds” were fired at one of its patrols near Wadi Jilu, in Lebanon’s Tyre district, without specifying the entity behind the shooting.
The patrol returned fire, after which the shooting stopped. UNIFIL reported no casualties and called for an investigation.
“We reiterate the obligation under international law for all actors to ensure the safety and security of UN personnel and property at all times. Deliberate attacks on peacekeepers are violations of Security Council resolution 1701 and international humanitarian law,” UNIFIL said.
Security limbo
UNIFIL is a peacekeeping mission established by the UN Security Council in March 1978, days after Israel invaded Lebanon.
The force has acted as a buffer between Israel and Lebanon ever since, but its presence has been unable to prevent several rounds of conflict, including the latest between Israel and Hezbollah.
Israel continues to occupy swaths of southern Lebanon, despite a so-called ceasefire and a US-brokered framework agreement through which the Israeli military would withdraw from those areas and the Lebanese army would move in to disarm Hezbollah.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Tuesday that the G7 foreign ministers agreed on “the need to avoid a security void” in Lebanon after the UNIFIL mandate expires at the end of 2026.
The foreign ministers backed “the need to move quickly toward a new security architecture”, Barrot said after the group met in Paris.
However, the French foreign minister acknowledged that there had been no breakthrough regarding replacing UNIFIL, which comprises some 7,500 personnel from nearly 50 countries.
The UN Security Council last year voted, under US pressure, to end UNIFIL’s mandate on December 31, 2026. Lebanese officials have called for the mandate to be extended.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: US poll shows death penalty lost majority support for first time since 1971
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
US poll shows death penalty lost majority support for first time since 1971
Support for capital punishment has been declining in the US for years over concerns such as fairness and racial bias.
A new Gallup poll has found that support for the death penalty in the United States has fallen below 50 percent, marking the first time that the controversial practice has lost majority support since 1971.
The poll released on Tuesday found that 49 percent of people said they are in favour of capital punishment for those convicted of murder, the lowest level since 1966, while 45 percent say they are opposed.
“While statistically similar to last year’s 52 percent, the latest update marks the first time support has been below the majority level since 1971, when it was also at 49 percent,” Gallup said in a statement.
Support for the death penalty has been declining for decades amid concerns about issues of fairness, racial bias, high costs, botched executions and the possibility of innocent people being put to death. Decades of scholarship have also cast doubt on the argument that capital punishment deters crime.
Age, party divide
The latest Gallup poll found stark divides by age and partisan affiliation. While 54 percent of people aged 50 and older support the death penalty, that figure drops to just 39 percent for those younger the age of 30.
About 73 percent of Republicans are in favour, compared with 50 percent for independents and 28 percent for Democrats.
But all of those groups have seen support decline over the last three decades, dropping by 11 points for Republicans, 29 points for independents, and 47 points for Democrats since 1994, during the heyday of tough-on-crime politics in the US.
In that period, a punitive approach to criminal justice embraced by both parties transformed the US into one of the most prolific jailers on the planet and saw an increase in the number of crimes that qualified for execution.
A debate about the legacy of the policies championed during that era, including the death penalty, has been pushed forward by protests for racial justice in recent years.
While 27 US states still have the death penalty, 23 have done away with the practice and four have paused it through executive action, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit research group.
Rise in federal executions
Many states that still have capital punishment on the books have gone years without carrying out an execution, and lengthy appeals processes have meant that many prisoners spend years or even decades on death row.
President Donald Trump has been an exception to the move away from capital punishment, overseeing a massive increase in federal executions during his first term in office and promising to continue using it during his second.
The prevalence of botched executions, such as that of Christa Pike via failed lethal injection in the state of Tennessee last month, has also raised questions about whether the practice violates the constitutional prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment.

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: Jon Stewart on Trump’s testy 60 Minutes interview: ‘Was that sass?’
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Guardian staff
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
Late-night hosts reacted to Donald Trump’s strange interview with 60 Minutes and his unpopular promotion of Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff.
Jon Stewart
A week after Democrats’ decisive victories in the US midterm elections, widely seen as a repudiation of Trump, Jon Stewart checked in with the beleaguered president. “Donald Trump headed over to the newly Maga-fied CBS for a little self-soothing with one of 60 Minutes’s new correspondents, a religious conservative by the name of Ross Douthat,” he said on Monday’s Daily Show.
On the once-storied news program, Trump claimed that “we have created wealth at a level that our country has never seen before” – “including for yourself,” Douthat cut in.
“Young man, was that sass?” Stewart laughed. “Did the new Maga-fied CBS 60 Minutes just deliver sass to Donald Trump? I think you’re supposed to ‘yes, and … ’ not ‘yes, but … ’.”
Trump tried to defend himself, claiming that “everyone’s” wealth increased, but Douthat again countered: “My net worth did not go up by $3bn.”
“I think I’m going to enjoy this,” Stewart relished. “I did not come into this interview thinking: ‘Uh, I’m going to enjoy this.’ But now, as I am watching this, I am thinking to myself: ‘I am going to enjoy this.’ Let me prepare the table for the feast we are all about to enjoy. As regular viewers of our program know, Donald Trump has a somewhat high regard for his own financial acumen. In fact, not 20 minutes prior, in this very same interview we are watching, Donald Trump said this: ‘I’m really good at money and finances.’”
And yet in the same interview, Trump said of his own fortune: “I guess it’s gone up. I don’t even know.”
“My frustration with reporters is, I wish someone would, like, hammer down on this,” said Stewart. “Trump acts like he’s got all this money squirreled away in some index fund, and it just magically grew. Meanwhile, since the guy has returned to office, he’s made $125m from foreign golf and real-estate schemes, $117m from legal settlements, $636m from selling that bullshit novelty meme coin. He’s gotten $800m from his World Liberty Financial crypto company. Why can’t someone just bring this up to his face?”
Douthat did, in fact, ask Trump about World Liberty Financial, which is partly owned by investors connected to the government of the United Arab Emirates. “I think if I told you that story,” he said, “and it was about the Biden family, if I said Joe Biden is the part-owner of a company and it has all of these investments from the Middle East, you would say that sounds corrupt.”
“I’ll have what he’s having,” Stewart cheered, referencing the famous scene from When Harry Met Sally. “I love that Douthat is forcing Trump to compare himself to the Biden crime family.”
In response to that comparison, Trump claimed the difference was he knew “nothing about” his son’s business.
“My god, Ross, you beautiful bearded bastard,” Stewart cheered. “Do you know what you’ve just done here? Do you have any idea what you just did here? You have made Donald Trump admit that the difference between him and Joe Biden is that Joe Biden is more aware of his surroundings.”
Jimmy Kimmel
On Jimmy Kimmel Live!, the host kept track of Trump’s reaction to the midterms landslide, which quickly morphed from accepting the results to questioning the legitimacy of the results. Over the weekend, Trump posted on Truth Social: “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong???”
“This is how it starts,” Kimmel said. “This is how he does a little taste of conspiracy. Nothing too intense, just enough to whet your appetite. And then he feeds it a little more. It grows. The lie gets bigger. He keeps repeating it.
“And then he starts talking about people talking about him claiming the election was rigged, as if there are people other than him claiming the election was rigged,. And before you know it, someone in a Viking helmet is making a toilet out of Nancy Pelosi’s desk. God bless America!”
“I don’t think we’re prepared for the amount of insanity that this drama queen president is about to pump on us,” Kimmel added. “Donald Trump right now is a raccoon in a duffel bag. He’s been cut off at the cankles. And there are two possible paths he can take. The first one is to check out. No more meetings. Lots of trips to Mar-a-Lago. Lots of golf with Natalie running behind the cart. Every once in a while he’ll host a Super Bowl team. That’s the best case scenario.”
But the host also saw a different, much darker future on the horizon. “Scenario number two is he goes nuts. Like Jack Nicholson in The Shining nuts. Everybody who works for him gets the axe. He turns on anybody who might possibly want to succeed him, whether that be Lil Marco or JD Vance. Even his own son. Even if Don Jr decides to run for president, his father will say and do anything he can to destroy him. Because he wants to make sure no one but him will ever live in the White House again. He might knock down the rest of it for all we know.”
Seth Meyers
And on Late Night, Seth Meyers post-gamed the midterms. “The GOP is furious with Trump and blaming him for their historic drubbing, which might be why Trump is suddenly pretending to strike a more conciliatory tone,” he noted.
In that 60 Minutes interview, Douthat asked Trump: “If it took six months of not insulting the Democrats to get a deal done, do you think you could do it?” Trump, who had just called the Democrats “dumb-ocrats,” answered: “Very easily.”
“Very easily?!” Meyers marveled. “You couldn’t even get through the question without insulting Democrats. He’s like a guilty dog who also offers up more things he did.”
But despite his gesturing at conciliation, Trump this weekend promoted Stephen Miller, the hardline architect of the president’s unpopular immigration crackdown, to be the new White House chief of staff. “It’s especially absurd that Trump would promote the most unhinged member of his staff, given that he also specifically cited immigration as an area where he could like to compromise with Democrats,” Meyers said.
In the 60 Minutes interview, Trump conceded that his hardline immigration policy “might be too tough”.
“Stephen Miller is the guy who created that policy!” Meyers exclaimed. “Why are you promoting the guy responsible for the thing you admit people hate! It’s like if Subway made Jared Fogle their CEO.”
“How can Trump say that he wants to work with Democrats on immigration while promoting Stephen Miller at the same time?” he concluded. “It may seem contradictory, but there’s actually a very simple answer: he doesn’t give a shit. He has no idea what his own government is doing and he doesn’t care. His biggest priorities right now are making money and building his ballroom.”

https://www.propublica.org/article/borde.title: Tribal Leaders Warned Border Wall Construction Would Disturb Native American Remains. They Were Right.
https://www.propublica.org/article/borde.author: Ryan Devereaux
https://www.propublica.org/article/borde.text:
Lorraine Eiler stood in the blazing August sun, surrounded by reporters, to offer a warning. The Trump administration was racing to erect a second border wall across Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, southwest of Tucson. If the bulldozers came, she said, they were bound to disturb the final resting places of her family and Hia-Ced O’odham tribal ancestors.
“People used to live here,” the 89-year-old said.
Fifteen days later, her fears were realized.
ProPublica has confirmed that Native American remains were unearthed in Organ Pipe amid soil overturned by border wall contractors.
The discovery, unreported until now, was made on Sept. 8, the National Park Service said in a statement. “Following established protocols, the University of Arizona conducted an assessment and confirmed that the remains are human and align with tribal cremation practices,” the agency said.
The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act governs the steps agencies must take following an inadvertent discovery of Native American remains on federal land. Those steps include halting any activity that contributed to the discovery until tribal communities are consulted.
“The National Park Service is committed to respecting tribal rights and traditions,” the agency went on to say, adding that it was “working diligently to identify the culturally affiliated tribe and ensure the respectful return of the remains, so the tribe may observe their religious and cultural practices.”
Eiler was alerted to the discovery by a cultural affairs specialist with the Tohono O’odham Nation, a larger tribe whose reservation is east of Organ Pipe, and later by the Organ Pipe superintendent’s office. Her family discussed what to do next. Ultimately, they decided to hold off on reburying the newly unearthed remains until construction in the area stops, fearing the work will disturb more sites.
“Who knows what more will come up,” Eiler said in an interview. “They’re going to find remains wherever they dig.”
Customs and Border Protection contractors have bulldozed a wide swath of vegetation parallel to the international divide. The agency has fashioned staging areas for heavy equipment by knocking down, uprooting and attempting to transplant select specimens of the monument’s native plants. Eiler was told the remains were found by a park service archaeologist near the base of a saguaro cactus that was still standing.
In a statement, CBP said it was advised of the discovery six days after it was made, that its cultural resource specialists examined the area and found no other remains, and that “no additional construction has occurred at this location to date.”
The discovery comes amid tensions between the Department of Homeland Security and tribal communities in the Sonoran Desert. In April, border wall contractors bulldozed through a large, well-marked earthen etching, known as the Las Playas Intaglio, that was believed to be at least 6,500 years old. (CBP said the incident was accidental.)
Soon after, the department awarded a $1.3 billion contract for construction of a 62-mile border wall across the entirety of the Tohono O’odham Nation. The tribe is fighting the project in federal court and has erected “no trespassing” signs to keep border wall contractors off its land. As ProPublica recently reported, DHS has responded by deploying masked federal agents as escorts for its work crews and conducting aerial surveillance of tribal members. The head of CBP has justified the need for a wall by describing the reservation as “one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border.”
Verlon M. Jose, the tribe’s chairman, expressed gratitude that the park service had notified his office of the discovery, but mourned the fact that it was necessary.
“When you have mass destruction and disturbance of land taking place where there are clearly sacred sites, cemeteries and other areas of cultural importance, these types of discoveries are bound to happen,” Jose said in a statement. “Every time this happens it is a wound to the heart of all members of the Tohono O’odham Nation — these are our ancestors, our family members — whose remains are being desecrated.”
U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, who appeared with Eiler and the chairman at the August news conference, blasted the government for failing to heed their warnings. “Tribal leaders and elders have warned DHS about the devastating consequences of bulldozing through their ancestral lands, beginning with the destruction of the Las Playas Intaglio,” she said in a statement. “For months, those warnings have fallen on deaf ears. Now, we are seeing exactly what they feared: sacred sites destroyed and ancestral burial grounds desecrated.”
James T. Watson, curator of bioarcheology in the Arizona State Museum at the University of Arizona, analyzed the remains recovered in Organ Pipe in the field.
While he was not authorized to discuss the details of his findings without park service approval, Watson said in an email that he confirmed the remains were human. The evidence suggested they were cremated in a manner consistent with precolonial practices in the region dating back 1,500 years, he wrote.
Under NAGPRA, the graves protection act, Native American remains inadvertently uncovered on park service lands must be immediately secured, Watson explained, and the superintendent of the jurisdiction must notify “all relevant lineal descendants” with “potential cultural affiliation or ancestral ties to the land.”
“Work in the immediate discovery area must remain suspended for at least 30 calendar days,” he wrote, while the park service consults with tribal representatives “to determine the disposition and physical treatment of the remains.”
In a region as rich with archaeological sites as the American Southwest, the inadvertent disturbance of Native American remains occurs with some regularity. What sets the discovery in Organ Pipe apart are the extraordinary powers the Department of Homeland Security wields to expedite wall construction in the borderlands.
Following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Congress passed the Real ID Act, which included a provision empowering the secretary of DHS to waive any law that might slow border wall construction. In the two decades since, DHS has invoked its powers 66 times, with 60 of those instances occurring under President Donald Trump’s two administrations.
When DHS uses this authority, it typically waives dozens of laws at a time. That was the case in 2019 when the department set its sights on Organ Pipe. A waiver issued by then-acting Secretary Kevin K. McAleenan set aside more than 40 of the nation’s most stringent environmental and cultural resource protection laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act and others. Also on that list was the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act, the landmark 1990 law that acknowledged the nation’s long history of desecrating Native American burials and required that ancestral remains and cultural objects be returned to tribes.
In an internal 2019 report obtained by The Washington Post, park service officials identified nearly two dozen archaeological sites in Organ Pipe as at risk of damage or total destruction by government contractors.
Of particular significance is a desert oasis known as Quitobaquito Springs. Less than 200 feet from the international border, the springs provide one of the only reliable sources of groundwater and shade for miles around, and they were a longtime gathering place, grazing site and home for O’odham families.
“Archaeological evidence of human presence at Quitobaquito extends back thousands of years, at least to Archaic times,” the survey found, adding that the springs represent the “only known Hia C-ed O’odham village site in the United States.”
A park service report in 2024 noted that a cemetery at Quitobaquito holds the remains of at least two families, including Eiler’s, and 34 graves. Throughout the region, remains of 5,500 ancestors that were displaced have been made available for return to the Tohono O’odham Nation, according to ProPublica’s NAGPRA database.
“This sort of incident has happened numerous times across our homeland, and it’s always alarming to hear about a case from an O’odham point of view,” said David Martínez, a professor of American Indian and transborder studies at the University of Arizona and a member of the Hia-Ced O’odham and Akimel O’odham tribes, as well as the Gila River Indian Community.
“Those remains shouldn’t have been disturbed in the first place,” he said. “While there are protocols existing today to properly care for these remains, ultimately, whatever either the government or the corporate world is pursuing to build, we know that at some juncture that construction will continue, and it always leaves us feeling, I think, a little hollow.”
Today, Quitobaquito lies in the shadow of the border wall erected during Trump’s first term. Its construction required detonating explosives in the national monument, blasting apart an area called Monument Hill and outraging tribal leaders. According to Eiler, the remains recovered in September were not found at the springs, though government work crews are working in close proximity to the site.
This year, DHS hired Sundt Construction, an Arizona-based company, to build a second wall in the monument. The $443 million contract was finalized in May. (Sundt directed questions concerning the discovery of human remains on its job site to CBP.)
According to CBP, the 2019 waiver for Organ Pipe is still in effect, years after completion of the project that prompted it. A second waiver, exempting DHS from many of the same laws and applying to the national monument as well as a wildlife refuge to the west, was issued by Homeland Security’s then-Secretary Kristi Noem last year.
“Unfortunately, there is no end date to the effectiveness of the waivers,” said Dinah Bear, a Tucson-based lawyer who served for 25 years as a senior attorney in the White House’s Council on Environmental Quality under both Democratic and Republican administrations. What’s more, she added, “there’s nothing in the statutory language that ties the waivers to a particular project.”
The Department of Homeland Security’s waiver powers have been central to a high-profile legal fight over the department’s efforts to build a border wall through Big Bend National Park in West Texas, with a federal judge overseeing the case recently ordering a temporary halt to the project.
Borderlands advocates in Arizona are hoping for similar interventions. In Congress, Grijalva is preparing legislation to void existing waivers that have allowed DHS to disregard laws designed to protect tribal sovereignty, sacred sites and environmentally sensitive lands.
In the meantime, construction on the border continues. For Eiler, it’s not just the destruction in Organ Pipe that’s troubling. She sees the disturbance of tribal graves resulting from wall construction as reflective of a wider pattern of destruction across the border.
“It’s sad because it’s not only happening down there,” she said. “It’s happening all over the United States, and nobody’s saying much about it.”

https://www.propublica.org/article/ameri.title: After ProPublica Investigation, House Democrats Demand Answers on U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
https://www.propublica.org/article/ameri.author: Nicole Foy
https://www.propublica.org/article/ameri.text:
What Happened: Citing ProPublica’s recent investigation, House Democrats are again asking the Trump administration to explain why hundreds of U.S. citizens have been held by immigration agents and how the government verifies citizenship during immigration operations.
In an October letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, California Rep. Lou Correa and 39 other legislators demanded the administration share the number of citizens that immigration agents have detained and how the government is tracking such encounters. They also asked for more information about how agents are trained to verify citizenship and legal status.
Why It Matters: ProPublica counted more than 500 Americans detained by immigration agents — almost certainly an undercount since the government is not transparently tracking the cases.
Experts told us the cases collectively show federal agents running roughshod over the constitutional rights of citizens. We found more than 100 Americans who were questioned about their citizenship, 63 Americans detained while recording, 36 Americans held for at least a day without being able to contact a lawyer or their family and roughly a dozen citizens deported, mostly children.
What They Said: “We remain concerned that the Department’s actions are violating American citizens’ constitutional rights to due process, equal protection, and freedom from unreasonable search and seizure, and request transparency regarding the Department’s actions,” the representatives wrote in their letter to DHS.
DHS has long insisted it is not arresting U.S. citizens, and it defended its immigration operations as “highly targeted.”
“These members of Congress have shown more concern for criminal illegal aliens who’ve broken our laws and destroyed any possibility of ever remaining in our country than they ever have for Rachel Morin, Laken Riley, Jocelyn Nungaray, and the true victims of illegal alien crimes in America,” a spokesperson wrote to ProPublica.
Background: Democrats have been pushing the second Trump administration for more details about how immigration agents are interacting with U.S. citizens since early 2025. Last year, congressional Democrats announced a wide-ranging investigation into immigration agents’ detention of U.S. citizens in response to our earlier reporting that found that more than 170 citizens were detained by immigration agents.
Last month, Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, a New Mexico Democrat, introduced a bill, Justice for Citizens Wrongfully Detained by ICE Act, that would make it easier for citizens to sue immigration agents for wrongful arrests.

https://www.propublica.org/article/five-.title: “Chaos” in the Air: Five Ways Voting Could Be Disrupted on Election Day
https://www.propublica.org/article/five-.author: Jen Fifield, Peter Elkind
https://www.propublica.org/article/five-.text:
As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out.
Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting. The Department of Homeland Security has used its resources to identify and prosecute noncitizen voters, an effort that has unfolded alongside the agency’s massive crackdown on immigrants.
The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats.
Help Us Report on Key Election Issues
ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something?
Courts have thwarted most of the administration’s plans to date, but Trump and his top deputies have kept up the pressure. Most recently, they’ve threatened to prosecute election officials who don’t reject ballots from people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens.
The administration hasn’t explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to the polls or seizing ballots or voting machines.
Election experts say the cumulative effect has been to ramp up anxiety about the midterms and to erode voters’ trust in the system.
“The administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a lot of doubt,” said Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he worries that this will make voters “sit it out” and “throw their hands up.”
“Paper Trail” Podcast
Learn more about this story on ProPublica’s podcast “Paper Trail.”
In an emailed response to questions, a DHS spokesperson said Immigration and Customs Enforcement “is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” adding that the agency would only arrest people at the polls to address a safety threat as part of “intelligence-driven targeted enforcement.”
The DHS and the Justice Department “are laser focused on identifying, prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,” the spokesperson added. “Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation.”
Before and on Election Day, it’s typical for the major political parties to mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans say they’ve expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm.
Republicans will focus on issues such as voter eligibility and voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National Committee’s election integrity communications director. Democrats will concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, Angelo Fernández Hernández, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson, said.
Here are five issues that voting rights experts say they’re watching as this year’s election unfolds:
1. Will There Be Federal Interference?
An incident in Leon County, in the Florida Panhandle, illustrates the widespread anxiety about law enforcement at the polls.
Mark Earley, the county’s supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was “furious” when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked outside the county’s busiest early voting location last month, after he’d been repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this.
He reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The episode generated a flurry of news coverage.
“Given the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it shows pretty bad judgment that they showed up in their official vehicles,” Earley said.
It’s against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places.
Nick Brown, Washington’s attorney general, leads a group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates who have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has “war-gamed” how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots.
“We’ve seen the tension and chaos that’s in the air,” Brown said. He called the federal government “the biggest challenge to smooth elections right now, which is not the way it’s supposed to be.”
A DOJ spokesperson said “the best preparation for any election official is following federal law.”
It’s routine for DOJ monitors to watch over polling places, and the agency has assured states that, in the midterms, its observers will follow the law and not interfere with voting or election administration. Still, state officials remain concerned. During Wyoming’s primary election, poll workers said they felt uneasy when DOJ monitors asked about their training and to inspect voting systems. The state’s governor criticized these actions as “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.”
2. What Effect Will Noncitizen Voter Challenges Have?
The Trump administration’s multipronged effort targeting alleged noncitizen voters has already led to eligible voters being improperly removed from the rolls. Voting rights groups fear this will block some U.S. citizens from being able to vote when they show up on Tuesday.
Federal officials have made clear they plan to go after anyone they think is committing voter fraud.
On the first day of early voting in Texas, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, posted a YouTube video announcing his intentions. “If you violate federal election law,” he warned, “I will hunt you down and prosecute you.”
This threat came days after the DOJ sued California, seeking to block the state from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are “likely” noncitizens. The administration had obtained the state’s public voter rolls, which the DHS had blended with its own immigration information and third-party data.
In a court filing, California called the claim that there are 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls “specious.” Los Angeles County analyzed a sampling of the likely noncitizen voters that the federal government claimed were registered there. Many weren’t registered in the county or had never voted, the analysis showed. Some said on their voter registration forms that they were born in the United States.
Asked about the case, the DOJ told ProPublica, “Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and the Department has a duty to enforce it.”
A federal judge has rejected the DOJ’s motion for an emergency order that would have barred California from counting the 20,000 voters’ ballots. (A federal appeals panel later backed that decision.) On Thursday, the administration sent grand jury subpoenas to California officials demanding records about their response to allegations of noncitizens on the state’s rolls. Late Friday, a federal judge issued a restraining order blocking the DOJ’s demands, calling them an “intimidation plan” that would interfere with legal voting.
Last week, the DOJ wrote a letter threatening to sue Washington state if officials there refused to review a list of 400 voters it believes to be noncitizens within 24 hours. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters late last month that the department was considering additional actions, saying there were “a number of states that we’re looking at.”
In a letter responding to the DOJ, Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs called the government list of 400 names “not reliable,” saying it included U.S. citizens, people who aren’t registered to vote and duplicate entries. “Time and time again,” Hobbs wrote, “DHS claims about noncitizen voter registration turn out to be greatly exaggerated or false.”
Sam Trepel is Rule of Law program director at States United Democracy Center and a former attorney for the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division. She said the agency’s actions involving California and Washington were a “disturbing use of prosecutorial authority.”
Trepel worries that the DOJ may try to seize ballots cast by voters identified as likely noncitizens, before or after the election, which would “put their votes at risk and undermine trust more broadly.”
Voting rights advocates also worry that the government’s efforts to target noncitizen voters could frighten eligible voters to the point that they won’t show up.
A federal judge recently put limits on a multistate effort by the DHS to go door-to-door in search of suspected noncitizen voters, at least through Election Day, saying it was illegally intimidating legal voters.
“A voter could say, ‘Well, maybe I don’t want to put myself on the target list here, maybe I won’t register, or maybe I won’t vote,’” said David Janovsky, acting director of The Constitution Project at the watchdog group Project on Government Oversight.
3. Will There Be Problems at the Polls?
States often change laws and rules related to voting.
Since 2024, Republican-led states have taken a number of steps that experts say will make it more difficult for some of their residents to cast ballots and have them count.
A North Carolina law, for example, requires voters to provide proof of identification when sending mail-in ballots. Under new rules, ballots now come with two envelopes, both of which must be sealed. Ballot rejections have skyrocketed, Democracy Docket reported, because voters aren’t sealing the inner envelope.
Texas and other states have cut back on the number and location of polling places, especially in areas favoring Democrats. In hotly contested Tarrant County, which includes Fort Worth, the number of polling sites was slashed by almost a third. This could increase the risk of long lines and voter confusion on Election Day.
Voting rights groups such as the Texas Civil Rights Project are tracking two issues involving the state’s voter registration systems. A software error at the Texas Department of Public Safety stopped several hundred thousand new voter registrations from being forwarded to local election officials, preventing them from being added to the rolls. A separate state system for updating registration information wasn’t processing changes for several weeks, leading to more backlogs. Counties say they’ve been able to address these problems.
Every election features some issues with voting equipment.
So far, there have been isolated complaints involving touch-screen voting machines — including one from Dolly Parton’s sister in Tennessee — spawning fears that machines have been “rigged” to switch votes.
ES&S, the company that makes the machines garnering the complaints, told ProPublica that the company hadn’t received widespread reports. Election experts say occasional problems with touch-screen machines don’t signify tampering or manipulation. Any attempt to tamper with programming would surface during testing by election officials and be corrected, they said.
4. How Secure Will the Election Be?
Incidents in the run-up to the midterms have ratcheted up election officials’ concerns about the potential for both cyber and physical attacks.
Last month, officials in several states, including Arizona, received envelopes with an unknown white powder. Arizona eventually deemed the material nontoxic, but Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said “the fear it caused was real.”
In 2024, false bomb threats, thought to be from foreign actors, caused widespread evacuations of vote-counting sites across the country. The disruptions were brief, however, in part because a message board funded by the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, alerted election officials that the FBI had deemed the threats not credible.
Trump, however, has dismantled CISA since retaking the presidency, leaving states and local election officials to grapple with both physical and cyber threats on their own. Election nonprofits have stepped up to try to fill the gap, and states, with CISA’s help, have enhanced their own cyber defenses.
Derek Tisler, counsel and manager for the elections and government program at the Brennan Center for Justice, said the federal government’s absence has weakened the defenses.
“States acting on their own just do not have the same power,” he said.
5. Where Will Postelection Challenges Come From?
Election lawyers fear that actions by the Trump administration in the run-up to the midterms suggest the government will aggressively pursue postelection challenges if the results are not to the president’s liking.
Late last month, the DOJ sued Alaska, seeking to block the state from certifying the result of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent doesn’t win. A federal judge threw out that lawsuit on Sunday, but the administration is expected to appeal.
Trump has said he personally ordered the lawsuit to be filed. It claims the system is unfairly rigged against Sen. Dan Sullivan, because another Alaska man named Dan Sullivan also qualified for the general election ballot. The New York Times reported last week that campaign aides to Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola orchestrated the candidacy of the second Dan Sullivan after a monthslong, statewide search to recruit someone with the same name.
Nonetheless, the DOJ’s case is unusual, both because federal law prohibits the government from interfering with an active election and because challenges typically come after voting is complete. Postelection challenges are most often brought by losing candidates in state courts.
“This is using the federal government to interfere with our election process in a way that I think is pretty troubling on multiple levels,” said Brown, the Washington attorney general.
In response to ProPublica’s questions, the DOJ pointed to Blanche’s statement about the lawsuit on social media, which said the agency “does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska’s election.” (The lawsuit calls it “vital” that the state not certify “any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion” and asks the judge to prevent Alaska from doing this.)
Some election lawyers have suggested that if the GOP suffers significant losses, Trump could try to pressure Republicans in Congress to block new members from being seated. Several lawyers, including Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, say that the incoming Democratic majority would be able to fend off such an effort; courts, too, are likely to stymie it, though it might cause a short delay, according to Muller.
Brown said he and other attorneys general are also planning how to respond if local election officials or boards refuse to certify election results, based on their own claims of fraud or claims by the administration.
“I worry tremendously about what they might do,” Brown said.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Sydney's new $641m Powerhouse arts and science museum to open amid crisis
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Elizabeth Fortescue
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Sydney’s Powerhouse, a new arts, design, science and technology museum that the New South Wales government describes as its biggest cultural investment since the city’s Opera House, is due to open on 7 November amid controversy and uncertainty.
The most recent crisis is the departure of Lisa Havilah, the museum’s chief executive, who stepped down in August over allegations of misconduct. Havilah had been the figurehead of the Powerhouse development at Parramatta, located in Sydney’s multicultural western suburbs, since 2019.
Some of Australia’s most powerful and influential arts identities have since signed a petition calling for Havilah to be reinstated immediately. The petition was launched on 27 October by Kon Gouriotis, the editor of Artist Profile magazine.
Among the more than 750 signatories so far are the prominent artist Ben Quilty, the architect and arts patron Penelope Seidler, the commercial gallery owner Anna Schwartz, and Lucy Turnbull, the former lord mayor of Sydney (2003-04) whose husband Malcolm Turnbull was Australia's prime minister (2015-18).
John Graham, the state’s arts minister, also announced that Powerhouse’s chief operating officer, Mark Wilsdon, is on leave while a Sydney law firm, Lander & Rogers, investigates the allegations. Those allegations have not been publicly detailed, but Graham has said they were brought forward by a whistleblower and touch on “governance and procurement”. Graham’s office did not respond before we went to press to a question about whether the inquiry’s findings will be made public.
Powerhouse is part of the broader Museum of Applied Arts and Sciences, which also encompasses a large site in Ultimo, a storage area and discovery centre in Castle Hill, and the Sydney Observatory.
The Ultimo site was the location of the Powerhouse Museum and its half a million objects from 1893 until the state government decided to distribute the city’s cultural assets more equitably across the population base. In 2015, Parramatta, about 20km west of central Sydney, was selected as the new site.
The Ultimo building was closed in 2024 and is now undergoing a A$300m ($210m) heritage revitalisation by the state government.
But a public petition has been launched to save the site following a newspaper report that the government is secretly considering selling part of the Ultimo site to cover the cost of the new Powerhouse.
The closure of the Ultimo site is a cultural “tragedy”, heritage expert and former Powerhouse trustee Kylie Winkworth tells The Art Newspaper. “It’s a globally unprecedented museum demolition,” explains the vocal member of the Powerhouse Museum Alliance pressure group. Located on the banks of the Parramatta River, the new Powerhouse was designed by the Franco-
Japanese architectural practice Moreau Kusunoki in collaboration with the Australian firm Genton. Its exhibition spaces cover more than 18,000 sq. m across seven vast, column-free galleries. It also has a rooftop terrace and garden, and temporary accommodation for students, artists and scientists.
Meccano monolith
Dubbed by some “the milk crate” because of its steel criss-cross design, the Powerhouse is in good company in earning an irreverent nickname: the Sydney Opera House was called a “scrum of nuns” in the 1970s because its sails resembled wimples. While the Opera House was made a Unesco World Heritage Site in 2007, a similarly illustrious future for the Powerhouse, which cost A$915m ($641m) to build, is far from assured.
Even before construction began, experts told a parliamentary inquiry that the museum’s riverfront undercroft would flood in heavy rain. This led to changes in the building’s design.
During a tour around the site in June, before her departure, Havilah told The Art Newspaper that “the whole of Parramatta would be under water” before the Powerhouse flooded. However, Winkworth says she fears people within the building would still be at risk in the event of overland flooding.
Already widely viewed as having consumed a disproportionate share of the state’s arts budget, the Powerhouse has in recent months been the focus of a new funding scandal—the backdrop to Havilah’s departure. The Sydney Morning Herald reported in August that more than A$70m ($46.2m) had been spent in the run-up to the museum’s grand opening, including A$10m ($7m) for LED screens, staging and backdrop for an immersive experience created by the British artist Es Devlin.
Another point of contention was Havilah’s introduction of a five-year “artistic associates” programme, costing A$2.6m ($1.8m), in which external experts were employed to help bring the Powerhouse to fruition. The Public Service Association, a trade union, claimed this sidelined long-serving and knowledgeable Powerhouse curators in favour of outsider non-specialists. The programme was scrapped in May following a review by the state treasury.
After Havilah’s dismissal, Abbie Galvin, the New South Wales government’s architect, took over as interim chief executive. At the same time, the state appointed former Sydney Opera House CEO Louise Herron as a “strategic adviser”. Cassandra Wilkinson, a New South Wales treasury executive, took over Wilsdon’s role in July, in an environment of constant media reports about apparent cost blowouts in the lead-up to the launch.
Minus its famed machines
Campaigners are unhappy that key treasures of the Powerhouse collection will not be on display in the new building. The 1785 Boulton & Watt steam engine, the 1855 Locomotive No.1 and the Strasburg Clock model—along with most of the rest of the collection—are stored off-site in a discovery centre that is open to the public only on weekends.
Winkworth says the Ultimo site was “uniquely resonant and appropriate for the display of the Powerhouse Museum’s internationally significant power and transport collections. Now the collections are dismembered at Castle Hill and never to be seen together again.”
She argues that the new Powerhouse was “never intended to be a museum” at all but rather a function and performance centre, helping boost the local nighttime economy.
Five inaugural shows are all scheduled to open on 7 November. Task Eternal, the main draw, traces the history of aviation and space exploration in partnership with the Smithsonian and the British Museum. Es Devlin: The Turning features five major works by the artist and stage designer. The Dark, for children, turns darkness into a “playground of curiosity” through interactive storytelling, a crystal tunnel and 100 borrowed childhood toys.
The fourth show, Overflow, explores the care of salt and freshwater ecosystems around Australia. Finally, The Mall centres on western Sydney’s pioneering role in the global development of shopping malls as part of modern culture and lifestyle.
General admission to the Powerhouse will be free. Over-16s will pay A$30 ($21) for a ticket to Task Eternal. All visitors will pay from A$10 ($7) for James Turrell’s light-based installation, Shangri La (Over the Hump). A 23-day opening festival will feature 179 events including Space Shuttle astronaut Charles Bolden reflecting on leadership in space exploration. Most of the opening events are free.
- Powerhouse, Sydney, opens on 7 November

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Deathbed portrait of Vanessa Bell by Duncan Grant discovered
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Maev Kennedy
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A poignant portrait of the artist Vanessa Bell, made within days of her death in 1961 by her sometime lover and lifelong friend Duncan Grant, has been rediscovered among family papers and donated to the famous home of the Bloomsbury Group, Charleston farmhouse in East Sussex.
The drawing in soft pencil and biro, from an angle suggesting Grant was sitting by her bedside, was rediscovered among family papers during research for a forthcoming exhibition of the work of both artists at Tate Britain. It may have been made just after Bell’s death, though she could just be resting peacefully with eyes closed.
Although Grant has dated the drawing “Friday April 14”, Bell actually died at the farmhouse on a week prior. In a statement from Charleston, now a museum and archive, Darren Clarke, head of collections and research, says that in later years, Grant and his friends went through masses of the work in his studio identifying and labelling pictures, so the date may have been added in error years later.
“What seems very likely here is that Duncan knew this drawing had been made around Vanessa’s death and later added a date from memory. He got remarkably close, but apparently not quite close enough. Everything about the drawing itself – its viewpoint, its intimacy and its extraordinary economy – suggests someone sitting quietly beside Vanessa’s bed and drawing the face he had known for half a century.”
The friendship and artistic partnership of Grant and Bell was one of the happiest and longest lasting of the tangled affairs of the group. Although Grant was gay and a former lover of Bell’s brother Adrian, they were lovers for a time and in 1918 had a child, Angelica—who went on to marry David Garnett, another of Grant’s lovers. Grant and Bell lived and worked at the 17th-century farmhouse for decades, covering many of the interiors with striking painted decoration. He outlived her by 17 years, and in 1978 was buried beside her in the churchyard of St Peter’s in Firle, near their home.
Grant was long regarded as the most talented artist of the group, and the first major solo exhibition of Bell’s work came only in 2017 at the Dulwich Picture Gallery. At that time most of her paintings in the Tate collection were languishing in storage, but her reputation has been growing steadily in recent years. The Tate is making amends with a major exhibition of work by both artists, Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury (12 November 2026 - 11 April 2027) at Tate Britain.
Although Charleston is the largest lender to the Tate exhibition, including the entire contents of Grant’s studio, the drawing will only be included in the exhibition catalogue. It will go on public display for the first time at Charleston in May 2027, when the studio reopens after major conservation work.
The drawing has been donated to Charleston as part of the 50 for 50 campaign which aims to bring 50 major works by the group back to the farmhouse in time for 2030, the 50th anniversary of the founding of the Charleston Trust, which runs and maintains the museum.
Nathaniel Hepburn, the director and CEO of Charleston, says in a statement on the discovery: “I found this drawing deeply moving when I first saw it. We know Duncan’s drawings of Vanessa so intimately, made over the course of their long friendship, that the discovery of a previously unknown work is remarkable in itself. But there is something incredibly poignant about imagining Duncan sitting beside Vanessa, drawing her after her death.“

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Hong Kong artists create a poetic moment in Venice
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
For Fermata: Hong Kong in Venice, the Hong Kong-born artists Kingsley Ng and Angel Hui are training visitors’ attention on the quiet moments and subtle details connecting both cities. The exhibition, marking the 25th anniversary of Hong Kong’s first participation in the Venice Biennale, is curated by the Hong Kong Museum of Art (HKMoA) and continues until 22 November. It is housed in a historic Venetian residential building in the floating city’s Campo della Tana neighbourhood, a setting that underlines the meditative, lived-in quality to the works.
“What we hope visitors take away from the exhibition is a moment of reflection,” says Dr Maria Mok, the director of the HKMoA. “Through Kingsley and Angel’s attention to everyday details, we hope visitors feel invited to slow down and become more attentive to their surroundings, even within the hustle and intensity of urban life.”
One of Kingsley Ng’s installations, for instance, Laundry Nocturne (2026), consists of a projection and soundscape that evoke the play of light across laundry hung between buildings. It was inspired by the artist’s experience visiting Venice, where billowing laundry on clotheslines is still common, though for Ng it also evoked memories of Hong Kong.
“The laundry becomes a point of entry into a wider soundscape of nighttime labour: recordings from a wastewater treatment plant, a newspaper-printing facility and a postal sorting centre evoke the work that continues while much of the city sleeps,” Ng says. “These modest, often overlooked processes that keep a city alive do not only connect Venice and Hong Kong. They are like a low hum in almost every city, to be picked up by an ear that doesn’t only listen to loud grandeur.”
For her installations, Angel Hui shines a spotlight on humble features of Hong Kong’s everyday life, including goldfish in plastic bags and a neighbour’s ornate but faded window frame. In her magical rendering, glowing plastic bags embroidered with goldfish motifs are suspended overhead, while a handwrought iron window made by Hui and traditional metalsmiths rotates slowly in the gallery.
“In Hong Kong, a goldfish bag is an everyday object; in Venice, it seemed almost precious—delicate and exposed,” Hui says. “The experience reminded me that a work does not need to be grand to hold meaning. Sometimes, its poetry lies in inviting us to look more attentively, and to meet the familiar with tenderness.”
Both artists, through their site-specific installations, encourage visitors to mark a pause while heightening their attention to details of light, sound, colour and texture. This invitation to contemplation is echoed in the exhibition’s title, Fermata, which is a type of musical symbol instructing a performer to hold a note or a pause for an extra moment, and the term for the places where Venetian vaporettos stop to let off and pick up passengers. For Hui, this title and its dual meanings resonate across the exhibition’s disparate locales.
“The difference in pace is pronounced: Hong Kong often presses forward, while Venice seems to make room for pause,” she says. “This is why Fermata—a moment of stopping, of stillness—felt so resonant. In both cities, the ordinary endures, and in that endurance, everyday objects acquire a quiet radiance.”
The exhibition’s title and installations also complement the theme of this year’s Venice Biennale, In Minor Keys, set by the late curator Koyo Kouoh.
“I come to see the works as experiences to return to and live alongside,” Ng says. “For me, that is one meaning of In Minor Keys: making time for the ordinary and immediate—the air, light and weather around us—and becoming more attentive to our presence within them.”
The artists’ ability to turn familiar objects and moments into tableaux where time pauses and senses are heightened is key to the exhibition’s power. It allows their installations to resonate across localities, from the Venetian Lagoon to Hong Kong’s cityscape.
“The artworks merge into the Venetian neighbourhood, from laundry hanging across nearby alleys and above our courtyard exhibition space to the view of the neighbourhood outside Kingsley’s Laundry Nocturne gallery, to wrought-iron windows that echo Angel’s work,” Dr Mok says. “All these details are blurring the boundary between the exhibition and its surroundings. They also show how small moments of daily life can quietly synchronise across different cities and audiences.”
- Fermata: Hong Kong in Venice, Campo della Tana, Castello 2126, 30122, Venice, until 22 November 2026

https://hellgatenyc.com/anthony-constant.title: Why Did We Just Listen to NY Congressmember-Elect Anthony Constantino’s MAGA Rap Album?
https://hellgatenyc.com/anthony-constant.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/anthony-constant.text:
Amidst the blue wave, few across the country will notice that a YouTube rapper was elected to Congress last night. Republican Anthony Constantino will represent New York's 21st district in Congress in January, a seat formerly represented by one-time gubernatorial candidate Elise Stefanik before her mysterious flame-out in 2025, finally giving federal representation to white boys with bars.
But this previous January, Constantino's full-length rap album "Thank You President Trump" was released. "Thank You President Trump" is a project with a concept, organized around nine voice notes issuing personal thank yous to President Trump, including from Constantino himself, golfer John Daly, former NFL star with an increasingly alarming TikTok account Antonio Brown, and other people who I assume are famous, but who I just wouldn't know about for lifestyle reasons.
In the wake of Constantino's victory, the Hell Gate staff took it upon ourselves to once again collectively review a piece of art, and our opinions were as complicated and diverse as the great state of New York itself.
