https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Rare Altdorfer landscape previously unknown to scholars to be auctioned next month
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Catherine Hickley
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A rare landscape by the German Renaissance artist Albrecht Altdorfer will be offered at auction at Sotheby’s Old Masters Evening Sale in London on 9 December, with an estimated price of between £3m and £5m.
The painting of a thickly wooded landscape and a rainbow against a densely clouded sky, dating from around 1520, surfaced in a Swiss private collection. It was previously unknown to Altdorfer scholars and does not feature in the artist’s catalogue raisonné. It is one of only three known oil landscapes by Altdorfer, who is considered one of the first landscape artists. The other two are both in museums—one is in Munich’s Alte Pinakothek, and the other in London’s National Gallery.
“To add to the known body of work of one of the great masters of the Northern Renaissance is one of the most exciting discoveries imaginable in our field,” says George Gordon, the chairman of Sotheby’s Worldwide Old Masters Department.
The current owner of the painting inherited it from his father, who purchased it in 1957 from the collection of a noble Austrian family, the House of Harrach. Painted on parchment, it was later glued to a wooden panel support. It is the smallest of Altdorfer’s known landscapes. A distant castle perches on a rocky outcrop beyond the rain-wettened forest and undergrowth that dominates the painting, which is signed.
Altdorfer was born in 1480 in Regensburg in southern Germany, spent most of his career there, also working as a politician, and died in the city in 1538. His densely wooded landscapes are drawn from the mixed deciduous and evergreen forests either side of the Danube downstream from Regensburg, Gordon says.
He says it was difficult to give a price estimate for the painting because no Altdorfer work has been offered on the market since 1980, when the National Gallery paid the reported sum of £2.4m for Christ Taking Leave of His Mother (around 1520). It was one of the highest prices ever paid for a work of art at that time.
“We don’t really know what it’s worth because it’s many decades since an Altdorfer last came to the market,” Gordon says. “It could fetch more than our estimate. I think it’s quite likely that museums will be interested.”
Sotheby’s will exhibit the painting in New York from 7-19 November and in London from 4-9 December.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Charles Dickens’s writing chalet and Hastings Castle added to list of English heritage sites at risk
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Maev Kennedy
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The cabin where Charles Dickens spent the last day of his life, the home in Stratford-upon-Avon of William Shakespeare’s daughter Susanna and the castle built by William the Conqueror high on the cliffs above the town of Hastings are among 197 buildings and sites added to Historic England’s Heritage at Risk Register today (5 November).
The list identifies sites such as buildings, parks, battlefields and shipwrecks that are threatened by decay, neglect or inappropriate development. There are now 4,991 entries on the register, all of which are labelled as of national importance. This encompasses 197 sites that were added this year.
The miniature Swiss chalet which became the writing retreat of Charles Dickens was a Christmas gift to the author in 1864, arrived flat packed in 94 pieces, and was put together by a theatre carpenter after Dickens and his house guests failed. Dickens placed it at the furthest end of the garden, reached by a tunnel he built under the road at his last home, Gad’s Hill, near Rochester in Kent. He spent much of 9 June 1870 working in the chalet on The Mystery of Edwin Drood, before returning to the house where he died that night, aged just 58.The house, now a school, and tunnel survive, but the chalet was moved in the 1960s to the garden of Eastgate House in Rochester, where it is now too fragile for public access.
Hall’s Croft, an imposing timber-framed building dating from 1613, was the home of Susanna Shakespeare and her husband John Hall. After many uses, and residents including the playwright George Bernard Shaw and the bestselling Victorian romantic novelist Marie Corelli, it was acquired by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust and opened to the public in 1951. It had already been closed for several years for extensive conservation work when, in October 2025, a car reversed into the facade and caused further serious damage. The playwright Ken Ludwig has donated £1m to the work but major fundraising will still be needed.
Hastings Castle was one of the first three such sites built by William the Conqueror after his victory in the famous battle—and is depicted in the Bayeux Tapestry. The site, with a sweeping view across a stretch of the coast, has a long history, with remains of an Iron Age fort having been discovered there. The castle’s commanding site has made it very vulnerable to storms and coastal erosion and there have already been urgent works to stabilise its ruins. Future plans for the site include the creation of a new visitor centre and cafe.
Along with the sites that have been added this year there is good news: 85 sites for which solutions have been found, and which have now been removed from the register. They include the storm-lashed Newlyn Harbour in Cornwall and a little hut in the Gloucestershire garden of Edward Jenner, in which, in 1796, he performed the first-ever vaccinations.
A pair of elegant Georgian houses in east London, built around 1715 and Grade II* listed, had an unusual saviour: Tottenham Hotspur Football Club, which has converted them—with help from the Lottery Heritage Fund—into artists studios, gallery spaces, and a cafe. The space is run by Sarabande Foundation, which was founded by the late fashion designer Lee Alexander McQueen.
Rescue grants available include the Heritage at Risk Capital Fund and the Places of Worship Renewal Fund, both funded by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport and administered by Historic England, and the Countryside Stewardship Heritage Service.
The UK’s heritage minister Baroness Twycross said in a statement that the register has a crucial role in identifying historic places in need of support. “Every part of the UK is bursting with history, so it is vital we protect the heritage sites at the heart of communities which help tell the stories of our nation.”
Claudia Kenyatta and Emma Squire, the joint chief executives of Historic England, said the most effective way of protecting the sites was to bring them back into use.“The sites saved and removed from the Register this year show what can be achieved when partners and communities work together to deliver positive lasting change.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: How Southern Brooklyn Democrats Flipped State Seats in Immigrant-Heavy Areas
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: April Xu
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Documented. Sign up for their newsletter here.
It was around 9:30 p.m., when the loud chants began.
“La-rry, La-rry!” “Joyce, Joyce!”
Inside the two-story house in Bensonhurst, it felt as though the roof could come off. Dozens of community members and campaign volunteers for State Senate District 17 and State Assembly District 49 candidates gathered inside Tuesday night to watch the election results pour in.
Standing in the center of the crowd was Larry He, the Democratic challenger to incumbent Republican state senator Steve Chan. Beside him was Joyce Xiaoqiong Xie, the Democratic challenger to incumbent Republican Assembly member Lester Chang.
By 10 p.m., the updated vote counts flashed across a large TV screen with more cheers following from the crowd. Both He and Xie were victorious, unseating the incumbents in previously Republican-held districts — part of a wave of shifts toward Democrats that happened all over the country on Tuesday.
The following morning, WeChat groups run by local Chinese residents in Bensonhurst were buzzing with the news.
In this part of South Brooklyn, the Republican and Democratic tickets were each represented by Chinese American candidates. After leaning increasingly Republican in recent years — driven in part by local voters’ concerns about public safety and the placement of homeless shelters in the neighborhood — the neighborhood had turned blue.
Like many Democrats, Xie, the budget director and community liaison for City Council member Susan Zhuang, and He, the chief of staff to Assembly member William Colton, had campaigned on issues such as housing, affordability, supporting local families and small businesses with essential resources and improving public safety.
He handily trounced the incumbent Chan by over 14 percentage points to secure a seat in the state Senate. In the state Assembly race, Xie beat Chang by nearly six percentage points, according to the latest results from the New York State Board of Elections.
On Election Day, several Chinese voters told Documented they were concerned about public safety, citing the recent fatal stabbing of a runner in Bath Beach and a proposed homeless shelter in South Brooklyn as reasons for their concern. But more important were issues that directly affected their daily lives, such as affordability and broader economic conditions under the Trump administration that have taken precedence over broader political debates, voters told Documented. Some specifically mentioned the administration’s immigration enforcement policies.
Dan Chen, 44, cast her ballot at P.S. 97 The Highlawn in Bensonhurst before 7:30 a.m. on Tuesday, hoping to finish voting before heading to work.
“Exercising our rights as citizens is important,” said Chen, an immigrant from Fujian, China, who became a U.S. citizen in 2016.
Chen voted for Donald Trump and Republican candidates in 2024. But over the past two years, rising living costs and concerns about public safety have shifted her support toward Democrats.
“I hope Democrats can do a better job,” she said in Mandarin. “Trump did a good job maintaining border security and improving safety when many immigrants came into the country in recent years. But the cost of everything in our daily lives has gone up — rent, food, utilities, you name it. At the end of the day, what matters is our own lives.”
Kenneth Lee, 74, who has lived in Bensonhurst for more than three decades, said that while he hopes Democrats will do more to improve public safety and address immigration issues, he still voted for Democrats because he believes the party cares more about low-income residents, particularly as inflation continues to squeeze many New Yorkers.
“Food prices are so high now. Twenty years ago, you could buy several apples for $1. Now, a single apple costs more than $1, while our incomes haven’t increased at the same pace,” he said. “Many people have to rely on food stamps to get by.”
Another voter, Li, who requested to only use his last name for privacy reasons, cast his ballot for Democratic candidates at P.S. 101 in Bensonhurst. Li, who is 70 years old, said that he has voted in every election since becoming a U.S. citizen four years ago.
Li said rising prices and inflation over the past few years have made life particularly difficult for low-income residents, like him, especially after the federal government stopped reimbursing stolen SNAP [food stamp] benefits in December 2024. “Life has been very difficult,” he said.
For Li, supporting Democrats was an obvious choice.
“The simplest way to look at it is that inflation has been high under Republican leadership, and life has become more difficult for low-income people,” he said. “I hope things will get better. We ordinary people don’t know that much about policy. These are just our simple thoughts,” he added.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Actually, Democrats Don’t Have to Sacrifice Trans People or Immigrants to Win
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Elie Mystal
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Actually, Democrats Don’t Have to Sacrifice Trans People or Immigrants to Win
For two years, leading Democratic factions have insisted that the party must abandon key populations to win. Tuesday proved them wrong.
In Muncie, Indiana, Republican Representative Victoria Spartz lost her deep-red district to J.D. Ford, an openly gay Democrat who loudly and proudly supports trans rights. In Maine, Republican Senator Susan Collins lost to Democrat Troy Jackson, a logger who does not have Nazi tattoos or a history of violence toward women or a backlog of homophobic comments on Reddit. In Michigan, Muslim doctor Abdul El-Sayed defeated a Republican who was endorsed by a pro-Israel Democrat who lost the primary to him, while never wavering from his defense of Palestinian rights. In Minnesota, Peggy Flanagan, a citizen of the White Earth Nation, defeated a former NFL reporter while running explicitly on “dismantling ICE,” the paramilitary organization that is responsible for the murder of some of her neighbors and constituents. And in Alabama, Allison Montgomery won a state House race, becoming the first transgender legislator in Alabama.
For the past two years, we have been repeatedly told that to win elections, Democrats must abandon their principles. We’ve been told to throw certain groups under the bus. We’ve been told that AIPAC is an insurmountable force. We’ve been told to demonize immigrants. We’ve been told to embrace a form of masculinity that is toxic. We’ve been told that if we don’t do these things, Democrats cannot win anywhere outside New York and California.
No, no, no, and no. Tuesday night showed that having principles is a feature, not a bug. Tuesday night illustrated that Democrats can win anywhere. Tuesday night proved that no group needs to be left behind in order for the coalition to rise.
The Democrats are not the Republicans: There’s no ring you have to kiss or cult leader you have to praise to be part of the group. While the Democrats certainly had a national legislative agenda (that they’ll now be expected to deliver), I’d say the things that bind the current party together are not policies so much as principles. Decency, accountability, fairness, dignity. Donald Trump has debased the Republican Party to the point that the thing that marks you as a “liberal” is not where you stand on the marginal tax rate on incomes over $1,000,000 but where you stand on whether rape is a crime that should be prosecuted.
Having strong principles helped Democrats everywhere. Authentically standing up for those principles helped Democrats everywhere. Standing 10-toes down for what you believe helped Democrats even in races they lost. Just look at Angie Nixon, the DSA-backed candidate who came within striking distance of winning her Senate race in Florida. Nixon received almost no support from the Democratic National Committee, which wrote Florida off as a lost cause, and yet she almost pulled it out. She didn’t have to campaign on policing where kids go to the bathroom or promise to send bombs to Israel to get this close to the upset of the night. The difference between Nixon winning and Nixon losing was establishment Democrats seeing her potential earlier and giving her some money, not Nixon selling out her ideals to the first tech-bro billionaire willing to cut her a check.
Tuesday was a historically good night for candidates of color and women, but I must admit that the victory that was most gratifying to me was Jackson’s up in Maine. I’m one of those people who jumped off the Graham Platner bandwagon so hard when I saw his “Totenkopf” tattoo that I sprained several ankle ligaments. My tolerance for Nazi-aligned body art… does not exist. I got into a lot of fights with the lefty-boy commentariat who told me to overlook the tattoo, and essentially assured me that Platner embossed himself with Nazi insignia as a youthful indiscretion. I got into even more fights with people as Platner’s disgusting history of Reddit homophobia came out. By the time the allegations of sexual assault showed up, I was telling my Maine friends to write in “literally any black bear” instead of voting for Platner.
Through it all, I was told that Platner’s Marine-honed masculinity was the key to defeating Susan Collins and winning the Senate. I was told that I was being elitist for expecting a “perfect” candidate, as if my request of “maybe don’t nominate the guy who posts homophobic slurs and gets a Nazi tattoo” was some sort of impossible purity test from the egghead left. I was told I was out of touch with regular Maine voters, as if any of these pundits were in touch with rural Mainers who have to shovel snow off their roofs to keep their ceilings from caving in.
All of those political know-it-alls were dead wrong. Troy Jackson, it turns out, is every bit as “manly” as Platner without having committed assault. He’s every bit as “salt-of-the-earth” without being a bigot online. He’s not a guy I will probably agree with on a lot of things, but, by all accounts, he seems to be a decent person. And this year, in this election, that was enough.
I hope the pollster-industrial-complex learns that lesson from this election. No, Democrats don’t have to sacrifice trans children on the altar of the megachurch because J.C. (James Carville) told them to. No, Democrats don’t have to take testosterone supplements and treat consent as optional to prove they can win the locker room. No, Democrats don’t have to ignore suffering in Gaza. No, Democrats don’t have to mass deport their neighbors. No, Democrats don’t have to act like Republicans to win Republican districts.
Democrats won this election by having principles. If they also govern that way, things will work out just fine.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: The Midterms Are Over, and We Won. Now It’s Time to Till the Democratic Soil
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Zephyr Teachout
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The Midterms Are Over, and We Won. Now It’s Time to Till the Democratic Soil
To renew the promise of self-government, we must create a politics beyond opposing Trump.
With the midterms over, we must now turn to the hard work of tending the democratic soil. Such work is not easy, and it will be tempting to train our attention instead on the polling about 2028, on Trump’s latest atrocities, on worrying about whether our country will survive.
These temptations are old ones. Thousands of years ago, the Greek statesman Demosthenes scolded Athenians for being “content to run round and ask one another, ‘Is there any news today?’” about Philip, King of Macedon, the great threat. He mocked the daily dialogue: “‘Is Philip dead?’ you ask. ‘No, indeed; but he is ill.’” Demosthenes begged the Athenians to see that “this Philip has not grown great through his own unaided strength so much as through our carelessness.” If Athenians kept up at this anxious gossip, he cautioned, they “will soon raise up a second Philip.”
Trump has become our modern-day Philip. His gross destruction of institutions and almost gleeful corruption, his desire to slander opponents and his naked venality, make his actions different in kind from those of other presidents. He flaunts his abuses like a peacock displaying its feathers. “Drain the swamp,” he crows, while accepting a jet from Qatar. “Leakers should be shot,” he shouts at a campaign rally.
“Is he ill?” we ask. “Are his poll numbers down?” Even if you are not embedded in Kalshi and Polymarket, you are likely tempted by the prognostications. But this obsession risks distracting us. Trump’s extremity only means we have greater responsibilities than we might want. As Wendell Berry said to Bill Moyers in 2013, “We don’t have a right to ask whether we’re going to succeed or not. The only question we have a right to ask is: ‘What’s the right thing to do? What does this earth require of us if we want to continue to live on it?’” If we don’t want to raise up a second Philip, there are at least three things people who believe in the promise of self-government should be doing today to till the democratic soil.
First, we must engage in local politics. We can yell at an inert Congress all we want, but if we are careless about our local democratic institutions, congresspeople will only become more untethered from our concerns—after all, the average representative theoretically hears from more than 700,000 people. From Arendt to Brandeis to Tocqueville, the greatest theorists of American democracy have pointed to the townships and local and regional politics as the places where the art of collective action amid difference is learned. It is where we develop the ability to laugh and feel compassion even as we fiercely disagree, tolerating opposing—even hated—ideas without breaking apart. In cities and towns, the public creates democracy tethered to human life.
The most riveting and inspiring actions today are happening locally, with local resistance against ICE and true left-right, MAGA-socialist-independent alliances forming in opposition to AI companies and surveillance tools like Flock cameras. Amid the decay, we see an extraordinary—and successful—uprising of political courage. In the first quarter of 2026, local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 AI data-center projects, and the number of grassroots anti-data-center groups has been growing exponentially, from under 150 in spring 2025 to over 800 now. People are setting aside their differences to fight against a dictated industrial policy of building sprawling water-and-energy-gobbling server farms that communities don’t want.
Second, we need to build a national anti-corruption movement, one that is separate from the political parties. That anti-corruption movement must demand to investigate Trump’s corrupt deals with law firms and big companies, to be sure, but it must do far more. It must fight to overturn Buckley v. Valeo and Citizens United, the Supreme Court’s catastrophic rulings on campaign finances, as well as the court’s decision to bless lobbyists giving Rolex watches to governors. And it must reclaim our understanding of human nature from the view of it that has dominated American politics for half a century.
The economics revolution of the 1970s taught judges, policymakers, and politicians that to be human is to be Homo economicus—essentially, profit-maximizers whose behavior should be “nudged” in certain directions by laws that appeal to our self-interest. This vision of the person as inherently devoid of empathy feeds a politics of paranoia and mistrust of others. A society with a thin and suspicious understanding of the person will collapse on itself. We must expect courage and compassion from each other, and ourselves. When Aristotle warned against corrupt constitutions, he feared the radical breaking of a shared public life. He described the fundamental threat of corruption as that of the selfishness of rulers. We must renew from within.
Finally, we should use both national and local tools to take on the pinnacle of antidemocratic power: corporate monopolies. Not only are they destroying our food, land, and farmers, but the huge tech companies—the biggest monopolies today—are embedding isolation in every action we take, feeding each of us different content and, increasingly, assigning us different prices and different wages. Megacorporations like UnitedHealthcare are gobbling up independent medical practices and corrupting doctor’s offices by taking decisions away from primary-care providers. Massive monopolies have sucked the soul out of cities and rural areas across America and are driving the epidemic of loneliness and powerlessness.
What does the future require of us if we want to continue to live in it together? Our country is teetering between possibilities. To truly fight corruption, we need to recover democratic power and, with it, democratic responsibility. We cannot renew ourselves unless we build local institutions, learn to love each other through our bitterness, and, instead of asking which Democrat will save us in 2028, ask what the soil needs, and whether we are willing to get blisters on our hands to tend it.

https://gothamist.com/news/amtraks-penn-.title: Amtrak's Penn Station plan could funnel taxpayer money to new venue for James Dolan
https://gothamist.com/news/amtraks-penn-.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/amtraks-penn-.text:
Amtrak’s proposal to rebuild Penn Station could lead to heaps of taxpayer money being used to subsidize a new entertainment venue for the Madison Square Garden Company.
The plan to overhaul the station calls for Amtrak to purchase the Infosys Theater at MSG, demolish it and convert the site into a grand light-filled entrance on Eighth Avenue. Previous estimates have put the cost of purchasing the theater at hundreds of millions of dollars.
During an investor’s call Wednesday, MSG’s chief financial executive David Collins fielded questions about the potential sale of the theater, which has a capacity for roughly 5,600 people. He noted the move would take away a revenue source for the company — but said the money from the sale could be used to fund a new venue, potentially in the five boroughs.
“The primary way for us to minimize the tax leakage would be to reinvest all of the potential proceeds in another domestic venue. … I would say that we are not limited to just the New York City market,” Collins said. “However, I would also say that New York City is our core operating market and with us having one less theater here, we would definitely most likely look to the New York market first.”
He did not say whether the Garden would look to buy an existing venue or build a new one.
In recent years James Dolan, the billionaire owner of MSG and the New York Knicks, has struck gold with his Las Vegas Sphere. That cutting-edge venue has a capacity for 20,000 people and has been so successful that Dolan is building another sphere at National Harbor on the Potomac River, just outside of Washington, D.C.
Amtrak special adviser Andy Byford, who is leading the redesign effort of Penn Station, has repeatedly said that the national railroad is looking to get us much money in federal grants and before potentially seeking funding from New York and New Jersey. That means if Amtrak's plan goes through, taxpayers would likely be on the hook to purchase the Infosys Theater — and in turn to fund MSG’s new theater elsewhere.
Representatives for MSG and Amtrak did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
MTA Chair Janno Lieber has repeatedly criticized Amtrak’s plan and has declined to sign on as an official partner for the rebuild, stating the work could interrupt Long Island Rail Road service at the station. Lieber has said Amtrak has refused to disclose the full details of its plan unless the New York transit agency agrees to join the project.
The MTA was planning its own rebuild of Penn Station — which is owned by Amtrak — until President Donald Trump took over the project last year. Lieber in 2023 said he did not want taxpayer money to be used to purchase the theater, saying he thought “the Dolans have gotten a pretty good deal from New Yorkers so far.”
While the MTA’s plan was under consideration that year, a private developer with ASTM Group estimated at a public hearing that the cost of purchasing Infosys was “substantially less” than $1 billion. The estimate came from Peter Cipriano, who is now CEO of Penn Transformation Partners, which was selected by the federal government to redevelop the rail hub.
Dolan supported Trump’s 2024 election campaign and this year backed Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman, who lost this week to Gov. Kathy Hochul.
MSG’s latest Securities and Exchange Commission filing lists the redevelopment of Penn Station as having a potential impact on its financial outlook, including the “potential transfer” of the Infosys Theater.
The Trump administration has set a tight deadline to begin work on the redevelopment of Penn Station. Officials said they expect shovels in the ground by the end of 2027.
Collins said during MSG’s investor call that executives “expect ample time to determine the appropriate path forward” on selling the theater.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/israel-democ.title: Israel’s Shaky Democracy Continues to Crumble
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/israel-democ.author: Jared Hillel
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/israel-democ.text:
Israel’s Shaky Democracy Continues to Crumble
From military rule over Palestinians to apartheid in the occupied territories, Israel has never been a democracy for Palestinians. Efforts to restrict expat voting ahead of the elections showed how barriers to democracy can reach Jewish citizens, too.
In July 1950, speaking at the annual Zionist Organization of America convention, US Vice President Alben W. Barkley asserted that Israel was “an oasis of liberty in the desert of despotism,” articulating a precursor to the oft-repeated adage “Israel is the only democracy in the Middle East.” While the expression cannot be traced to a singular person, the sentiment that Israel — a nation with free elections and civil liberties — stands alone amid a sea of authoritarian regimes has been cultivated by Western institutions and Israeli leaders since the state was founded.
From the outset, Israel’s earliest laws legalizing persecution against Palestinians showed the incompatibility between Jewish supremacy and democracy. But the subjugation of one group is rarely self-contained, and throughout history, illiberal nations have almost always turned against a portion of their citizens, often as violence against the outgroup reaches its peak.
In the midst of the bloodiest three years in the country’s history, and particularly during the election campaign, this tendency began to play out. Israel has disenfranchised voters, at times even contradicting its own discriminatory laws, in efforts to marginalize Jews perceived as a threat to Benjamin Netanyahu and his increasingly violent political agenda.
Barriers to the Ballot
In the past three years, emigration from Israel has reached record heights. According to a study published by Tel Aviv University, 270,000 citizens have left the country in the past three years. Between 2013 and 2015, the corresponding period in the previous decade, the number sat at 183,000. Like much of the American Jewish diaspora, those who have left in recent years have become deeply critical of Benjamin Netanyahu.
While Israel guarantees every citizen over the age of eighteen the right to vote, it has never permitted absentee ballots. With the exception of diplomats, emissaries, and Israel Defense Forces (IDF) soldiers occupying territory in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria, voters must be in the country on Election Day. With this election largely seen as one of the most consequential in the nation’s history, a survey taken before the election estimated that up to 67,000 expats could be returning home to vote.
On October 27, Likud won twenty-seven seats, and Gad Eisenkot’s Yashar party won twenty-one. Netanyahu’s bloc took fifty-three seats, against forty-eight for the Jewish opposition bloc and nineteen for the Arab-led parties. No bloc won the sixty-one seats needed for a majority. The results have left the country facing uncertain coalition negotiations.
Leading up to the vote, Likud tried to stop Israelis outside the country from coming back. In September, Likud petitioned the Central Election Committee, demanding it block Fly & Vote, an initiative by the nonpartisan American-Israel Democracy (AID) Coalition, which sought to help Israelis abroad return and cast a vote.
Offering logistical help, including eligibility checks and passport renewals, the organization also coordinated six group flights and helped search for commercial flights. While participants were still required to pay their airfare, Likud argued the initiative violated financing laws and constituted election bribery.
While the petition was ultimately dismissed, the AID Coalition agreed to not subsidize tickets, organize any additional group flights, or provide transportation and accommodation.
This summer, a second spat broke out when hundreds of Israelis living abroad discovered they had been stripped of their voting rights after being classified by the Interior Ministry as nonresidents. The designation, known as Code 51, excluded citizens from the voter registry altogether.
Petitioning the Supreme Court, the expats argued that they were not notified of their status change, with several only realizing when checking their electoral eligibility. The courts dismissed the case on procedural grounds, stating the claim was filed too late.
While there is no definitive proof linking Likud to the Code 51 scandal, it is clear that the party has repeatedly tried to curtail the expat vote. Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that informal discussions were held between senior Transport Ministry officials about the possibility of restricting designated landing slots at airports, making it more difficult to fly into the country.
Similar to the proposed judicial reforms of 2023, where Netanyahu sought to weaken the power of the Supreme Court, this democratic backsliding has prompted furor among the Israeli left. But as is often the case with liberal Zionists, the far greater repression affecting Palestinians remains largely ignored.
Defending the Ethnocracy
The AID Coalition describes itself as a group “strengthening, and preserving the democratic foundations of the State of Israel.” While a valiant objective, a more honest statement would be about preserving an ethnocracy. Israeli Professor Oren Yiftachel describes this form of governance as one that “promotes the expansion of the dominant group in contested territory and its domination of power structures while maintaining a democratic facade.” This dynamic has been present since the state’s founding.
While the 150,000 Palestinians who remained in their homeland after the Nakba were declared citizens and granted the right to vote from the beginning, the community also faced systematic discrimination from the outset. From 1948 until 1966, Palestinian citizens of Israel were placed under military rule, which included measures that restricted their movement, prohibited political organizing, and imposed arbitrary curfews. Simultaneously, the government confiscated hundreds of thousands of dunams of land, uprooting farmers from their livelihood and forcing many to turn to low-wage labor to survive.
In 1967, a year after lifting the military administration, Israel would turn their attention toward Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza after occupying both territories in the Six-Day War.
Assuming control of around one million Palestinians, residents of the newly occupied territory were placed under military rule. This time citizenship and the right to vote were withheld from them, since such incorporation would threaten the Jewish demographic majority.
As Jewish settlers moved into the occupied territories, aided by generous Israeli government subsidies, an apartheid regime took shape, as authorities applied separate laws, courts, and democratic rights to Palestinians and Israelis living in neighboring areas.
Although Israel disengaged from Gaza in 2005, it lay siege to the Strip two years later, imposing a crushing blockade. After the October 7 attacks, it returned yet again as the occupying power, this time unleashing a genocide that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. In the West Bank, the apartheid regime continues, as roughly 500,000 settlers, excluding those in East Jerusalem, live with full rights outside of Israel’s internationally recognized border, beside Palestinians who cannot vote, travel freely, or even build on their ancestral land.
Amid the dire situation in the West Bank and Gaza, the plight of Palestinians living inside Israel is largely forgotten. Yet these 2.1 million residents continue to live as second-class citizens.
In 2018, the Israeli Knesset passed the quasi-constitutional Nation-State Law, stipulating that self-determination is unique to the Jewish people, without guaranteeing equality for its other citizens. Furthermore, Palestinian citizens of Israel continue to face entrenched discrimination in urban planning, economic development, and educational opportunities.
The Authoritarian Turn
In 2024, the Varieties of Democracy Institute downgraded Israel from a liberal to an electoral democracy. The demotion followed Netanyahu and his coalition’s attempt to overhaul the judiciary, their accusations the Supreme Court was “left-leaning,” and deterioration in protections against torture. This classification did not take into account the active atrocities that Israel was perpetrating in Gaza and the West Bank at the time.
Yet since this reclassification, Netanyahu has shed more of the democratic facade he has long sought to uphold.
More than five hundred humanitarian workers have been killed since the war in Gaza began. In December 2025, Israel attempted to bar thirty-seven nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) from operating in the West Bank and Gaza. The Supreme Court froze the ban, allowing the organizations to continue operating pending a final ruling.
More recently, numerous foreign journalists have been turned away at the border during the election campaign, with others facing arduous interrogations and detention before being allowed entry.
Perhaps most revealing is the government’s willingness to break long-standing supremacist laws, which uphold Jews as a privileged class in Israel.
Starting in 2025, several Jewish activists were detained and deported for engaging in protective presence, a form of nonviolent solidarity work in which civilians deter violent settlers from harassing Palestinian communities. Earlier this year, a Jewish American academic on a three-year residency visa was denied entry after being accused of being a “left-wing anarchist.”
After the backlash prompted by the film NAZA, in which IDF soldiers admitted to knowingly killing innocent civilians in Gaza, Netanyahu announced plans to introduce a bill that would strip those who defame the IDF of their Israeli citizenship.
Last month, it was reported that two Jews were denied citizenship for having previously partaken in anti-occupation activism in the West Bank. This was the first known case of the state violating the Law of Return, which stipulates that every Jew is entitled to immigrate to Israel.
Many saw Gad Eisenkot as the last chance to halt the country’s authoritarian drift. The election has left open the possibility that he could still lead the government, but he has no clear path to power. While he might reverse the emerging trend of discriminating against Jews and Israelis deemed insufficiently patriotic, none of his proposed policies address the core issues that make Israel an ethnostate.
The election has not changed the reality for Palestinians, with or without Israeli citizenship, or the refusal of every major party to address these injustices. What Eisenkot may offer is merely a return to the illusion of democracy.

https://gothamist.com/news/intoxicated-q.title: Intoxicated Queens driver killed baby after running stop sign, indictment says
https://gothamist.com/news/intoxicated-q.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/intoxicated-q.text:
A Flushing man has been indicted on charges including manslaughter after he allegedly sped past a stop sign while on cocaine and THC, then struck and killed a 1-year-old boy in a stroller.
Elvin Rivera, 57, was driving in a residential area of Flushing around 8:35 a.m. on Oct. 11 when he ran through a stop sign on 32nd Avenue, traveling northbound on Murray Street, according to the indictment.
He then sped through the intersection and struck the stroller, which was being pushed by the 1-year-old’s nanny, authorities say.
The Queens District Attorney’s Office said Rivera remained on the scene, where he failed drug sobriety and field tests. A blood test later confirmed the presence of THC and cocaine, the DA’s office said. Rivera had also been driving in violation of restrictions resulting from a DWI case in April, according to the DA’s office.
The child, 1-year-old Justin Hu, was rushed to the hospital, where he was later pronounced dead, according to Queens District Attorney Melinda Katz.
“Our thoughts are with Justin’s family as they mourn this unimaginable loss,” Katz said in a statement Friday.
The indictment charges Rivera with 12 counts, including manslaughter, vehicular manslaughter, assault, driving while impaired, failure to exercise due care and failing to stop at a sign.
He could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted of the top charge, and is scheduled to return back to court on Jan. 7.
Attorney information for Rivera was not immediately available.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/brazil-lula-.title: Austerity Is Now the Central Conflict in Brazilian Politics
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/brazil-lula-.author: André Singer, Catarina Príncipe, Aldo Cordeiro Sauda
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/brazil-lula-.text:
Austerity Is Now the Central Conflict in Brazilian Politics
Lula da Silva beat Flávio Bolsonaro to win a fourth term as Brazil’s president. Political scientist André Singer says the hardest fight is still ahead: Brazil’s bourgeoisie wants harsh austerity, and Lula’s coalition is split over it.
- Interview by
- Catarina Príncipe
- Aldo Cordeiro Sauda
On October 4, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, finished the first round of Brazil’s presidential election nearly two points ahead of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Three weeks later, Lula turned the result around and won a fourth term in the October 25 runoff. In between, left-led demonstrations filled the streets of hundreds of Brazilian cities. The government also banned online betting, backed a forty-hour workweek, and raised the benefit of Bolsa Família, the cash-transfer program for poor families that Lula created in 2003.
Few analysts know Lula’s political project better than André Singer. A professor of political science at the University of São Paulo, Singer served as Lula’s spokesperson from 2003 to 2007 and press secretary from 2005 to 2007. He developed the concept of Lulism in Os sentidos do lulismo (2012) and O lulismo em crise (2018), and his new book, Impasse: O Brasil diante da onda reacionária, came out in August.
After the runoff, Singer spoke with Catarina Príncipe and Aldo Cordeiro Sauda for Jacobin about Bolsonarism as autocracy with a fascist bias, the Brazilian bourgeoisie’s silence during the campaign, and why the second-round mobilization was not populism. He also discussed the fight over austerity that awaits Lula’s fourth term.
- Catarina Príncipe You’ve written about the idea of an “autocracy with a fascist bias” to understand the phenomena of Donald Trump in the United States and Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil. Could you explain this idea further?
- André Singer Honestly, I can’t speak directly about Trumpism, because I don’t have enough expertise. So I’ll talk about Bolsonarism, the experience from which I formulated the idea of an autocratic tendency with a fascist bias. Studying the Bolsonaro presidency of 2019–2022, one can show empirically that he tried to reshape Brazil’s institutions in the direction of an autocratic regime. One of the major conflicts during his term was over the independence of the Federal Police. For an American audience: The Federal Police is equivalent to the FBI. It is a national police force for the country’s major security problems, because everyday problems fall to the state governments. But the big questions of corruption, organized crime, drug trafficking, and arms trafficking are all the Federal Police’s business. That is why a convention that successive presidents have observed since the return to democracy in the 1980s is so important: guaranteeing the Federal Police’s independence. The president of the republic appoints the director, but presidents have made a practice of appointing directors who have a certain independence from themselves. Bolsonaro made a point of violating that convention and appointing a Federal Police leadership at the service of his own political interests. I’m describing this because it is the most evident case of all: he tried to manipulate the Federal Police to concentrate power. Why do I say this autocratic tendency has a fascist bias? Because I find in it certain elements in common with historical fascism. Why don’t I say it’s fascist tout court? Because there are many elements that don’t correspond. Let me give one element in common: the activation, through propaganda, of the unconscious of the masses. It is a kind of advertising that aims to hook the voter, the citizen, and the supporter through unconscious identification rather than rational argument. That doesn’t mean there aren’t also arguments of a material nature, material interests; I’m not saying it is merely a technique aimed at the unconscious. But I think this is very typical of fascism and not of the nonfascist right. What isn’t in common with fascism? For example, there is no political party organized into militias, as in Italian fascism and then German Nazism. There is also no warlike rhetoric, in the sense of external war: Bolsonarism has a very strange nationalism of submission to the United States — something hard to understand. But it has no rhetoric of confrontation with other countries or of territorial expansion, an important element of historical fascism. Since some elements are in common and many are not, I proposed a way of understanding the Bolsonaro phenomenon. We are facing an autocratic tendency — that is proven — with a fascist tendency that we still need to test. Meanwhile, there is a more general theoretical problem: the concept of fascism isn’t well defined. Strange as it may seem, that is the problem we have to face: arriving at a concept of fascism that lets us understand the present situation. Obviously we are interested in understanding history, but with a view to the present and the future.
- Catarina Príncipe In an interview, I heard you distinguish between fascism from below and fascism from above. Which class does this autocracy with a fascist bias mobilize most?
- André Singer Marxist-inspired thought has already made clear the characteristics of historical fascism, and one stands out: fascism is a movement that comes from below, not from above. Leon Trotsky first made that contribution, in his writings on Germany, and it still holds; it is a fundamental distinction. Bolsonarism has this characteristic: it comes from below; it is not a movement of the ruling class. It draws in the middle strata, but it quickly spreads to intermediate popular layers, which form its backbone. So in Brazil today, the far right penetrates from below.
- Catarina Príncipe How do you analyze the relationship between the ruling class and politics, given the existence of what you call two cross-class coalitions: the Bolsonarist “confederacy” and the Lulist “concertación”? What is the composition of these two coalitions?
- André Singer I call one the “confederacy,” by a certain analogy with the nineteenth-century American case, and the other the “concertación,” by analogy with Chile after Augusto Pinochet. I developed these two hypotheses to understand the 2022 election. So I’ll answer with 2022 in mind, then briefly go through the changes in 2026. The idea of the confederacy was that a coalition of agribusiness entrepreneurs and service sector entrepreneurs in the cities formed. Certain evangelical denominations, which represent a kind of Brazilian Bible Belt, joined them. These denominations account for about 30 percent of the Brazilian electorate, and Bolsonarism has repeatedly won 70 percent of their vote. In the 2022 election, the whole of the security forces joined these two components, the entrepreneurs and the evangelical Bible Belt, from the armed forces down to the regional (state) police forces. These forces represent a large contingent. Besides everyone formally engaged in security work, Brazil has an enormous army of private security guards, because public security can’t cope with the very serious crime problem. These three tracks of the confederacy, so to speak, created an enormous corridor through the interior of the country. It runs from the north of Rio Grande do Sul to the south of the North Region, through the interior of São Paulo and Minas Gerais, the country’s most industrialized states. That corridor aligned with Bolsonarism, which largely explains its significant electoral power. In addition, the evangelical Bible Belt gives Bolsonarism a very strong bridgehead in Brazil’s large metropolitan regions. In 2026, there was a change: because of the failed coup attempt, the armed forces pulled back. They had been very important because Bolsonaro, a former army captain, went through the military academy with the men who, by coincidence, made up the high command when he took office. He brought them into the government, and so the armed forces were deeply committed to the Bolsonaro government. That is no longer the case. You can’t identify anyone of note from the armed forces in the campaign of his son Flávio Bolsonaro. But we know that the police forces backed that candidacy discreetly, rather than explicitly, as they had with Jair Bolsonaro’s government. I call it a confederacy, although it has no connection with slavery. But it does have this connection: it divided Brazil. It united the interior, as if against the big cities, even though, I repeat, the evangelical denominations have influence in the big cities. You also notice a certain prejudice against the Northeast and an underlying ideology that a more modern Brazil would be better off rid of a more backward Brazil. It is a kind of implicit ideology, which sometimes shows up more, sometimes less. As for the concertación: the name came to me because, to build the coalition that sustained him, President Lula made an alliance with sectors of the old Brazilian Social Democracy Party (PSDB). Until 2018, the PSDB had been the main rival of Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT). The current vice president, Geraldo Alckmin, headed the sectors willing to join. The PSDB as a whole has shrunk to a small party, and it stayed neutral: it backed Lula neither in 2022 nor now. But the alliance with Alckmin represented a union with former PSDB sectors willing to form the democratic front. So, as in Chile, the two great adversaries came together: in Chile, the Socialist Party and the Christian Democratic Party; in Brazil, the PT and the PSDB. Along with this party coalition, there was an important class coalition. Lulism represents the base of the Brazilian social pyramid, as everyone knows. But the alliance with this faction of the PSDB also brought in what I call the cosmopolitan bourgeoisie, the most modern sector of the Brazilian bourgeoisie, which backed President Lula in the second round of 2022, not the first. That was very important both for his victory and for the future of the government. In this 2026 election, that sector of the bourgeoisie did not speak out; it stayed neutral and backed neither Flávio Bolsonaro nor President Lula. João Moreira Salles — founder of Piauí magazine, an important filmmaker, and an heir to one of Brazil’s biggest banking families — wrote a very powerful article on the importance of that silence. The consequence of that silence was the acceptance, practically until the last minute, of a Flávio Bolsonaro victory. An extraordinary movement reversed that in this year’s second round. To conclude for now: the cosmopolitan sector of the Brazilian bourgeoisie, which stayed silent, is no longer explicitly present in the concertación.
- Catarina Príncipe You define Latin American populism as a mass phenomenon: in certain circumstances, classes take the form of multitudes with little or no class organization, connecting people and leader directly. Was this type of populism what secured Lula’s victory? And how can we reconnect this expression of the multitude with more sustained class organization?
- André Singer I think the concept of populism doesn’t apply to the second-round victory. It’s a very interesting question, and it’s going to give me some work, because I’ll have to develop something more sophisticated to account for the phenomenon. But at first sight, I think we had a social explosion — let’s call it that — without the characteristics of populism. It was more organized and more conscious of its aims than the populist phenomenon implies. To be clear, my theoretical framework is Ernesto Laclau’s old definition, from 1978, not that of the so-called second Laclau. It is a good one for thinking about populism in Latin America and, of course, in Brazil too. Why do I say the explosion is more conscious and more organized? More conscious because it aimed, first, to stop the far right. Flávio Bolsonaro won [the first round] by 2 percentage points and immediately began putting together his government and saying he would change the Constitution. That was a tactical error, even from his own standpoint: it had such an impact that the democratic sectors of Brazilian society immediately began to speak out and organize. That is one side of the phenomena. The other is a feeling that President Lula needed a fourth term, because the government itself began to change during the campaign. It isn’t obvious, but President Lula changed the campaign in mid-September without saying so: he began to take measures. One event seems revealing to me. On September 11, at a rally in Porto Alegre, he said, “I know you are finding products expensive at the supermarket,” referring to coffee and beef. That is very significant, because until then the government had not addressed the population’s material needs directly. From then on, the president not only spoke to those needs but began taking measures. For example, he raised the Bolsa Família benefit, which the government had not adjusted in four years, and he banned online betting, the “bets.” Remember that Brazil is living through a triple crisis: a cost-of-living crisis, a crisis of household indebtedness, and, on top of it, an epidemic of bets. People began gambling wildly, partly to earn extra income to pay off debts. Since betting companies design bets so that the great majority lose, people ended up worse off. President Lula faced great resistance to the ban. First, many companies are involved, and long-term legal contracts were already in place; second, soccer clubs, which are very popular and important in Brazil, depended to some extent on sponsorship from those companies. The other very important decision was the switch from six workdays and one day off (6x1) to five and two (5x2), cutting the workweek from forty-four to forty hours: probably the greatest labor victory since the 1988 Constitution. Congress passed it, but everyone knows it was the president’s initiative and that he committed himself to it. Structurally, of course, it is even more important than the betting ban. But the ban has symbolic meaning, because the president decided on it during the campaign: an act of boldness and courage in defense of the popular economy. Alongside it, the government took two measures to restructure the debts of the popular classes, and others such as free public transit on weekends, which speaks directly to the young people who took to the streets. What I mean is that all this is not populist rhetoric; these are actions. It is what I call a change in the character of the government. Finally, these sectors that took to the streets are not completely disorganized. The demonstrations took place in hundreds of cities, but the largest, and most unprecedented, were in São Paulo, the country’s biggest metropolis. I have been comparing the two October demonstrations in São Paulo, on October 11 and 24, with the great right-wing demonstration for the impeachment of President Dilma Rousseff in March 2016. There had been no demonstration of this kind for at least ten years. The Left led these demonstrations, although they were not only of the Left. They formed a democratic front, with centrist sectors and possibly even a democratic right: individually, people may have gone out to defend democracy. But the leadership clearly belonged to the Left, and these are possibly the largest left-wing demonstrations in Brazil’s history. The Brazilian left has organizations: the PT, the Socialism and Liberty Party (PSOL), the Communist Party of Brazil (PCdoB), the student organizations, the cultural associations, the unions, the neighborhood associations, and the popular movements, especially the Landless Workers’ Movement (MST) and the Homeless Workers’ Movement (MTST). On the center left, you have the Socialist Party of Brazil (PSB) and the Labour Democratic Party (PDT). In short, Brazil has an organizational structure, and it mobilized. So, from these two angles, I wouldn’t describe this as a populist phenomenon; something different happened.
- Aldo Cordeiro Sauda This year, you observed a pendular movement by the cosmopolitan wing of the bourgeoisie toward the far-right candidacy, the opposite of its support for Lula’s election in 2022. Internationally, US foreign policy shows the same pendular movement: sympathy for Lula under Joe Biden in 2022, explicit support for Bolsonarism under Trump in 2026. To what extent does the Brazilian ruling class’s shift toward Bolsonarism express mere deference to Washington?
- André Singer As far as I understand, the sector I call cosmopolitan — in the American case, the big technology companies — backed Biden in 2020. In 2024, it wasn’t very clear to me what they were doing, but they didn’t seem to back Trump either, with the exception of Elon Musk. Yet when Trump took office, all of them were there. In the Brazilian case, though, it seems plausible that a conversion of the American cosmopolitan bourgeoisie to the far right influenced the Brazilian bourgeoisie. Until the last minute, there was a certain expectation that this sector might speak out in favor of President Lula. That sector committed itself to democracy in 2022, in a movement broader than support for President Lula. In August 2022, at a demonstration in São Paulo, those business leaders issued a letter. They said they would not accept, under any circumstances, a refusal to recognize the election result — exactly what the White House said. Those two positions were very important in keeping most of the armed forces from joining the coup, because the military knew it could not govern without that support. So you see: there is a Brazilian phenomenon. A link to a transformation in the United States is a possible hypothesis.
- Catarina Príncipe Our understanding of the question is that the Brazilian cosmopolitan bourgeoisie is staying neutral now because of the political change in the United States from Biden to Trump. At the time of the coup attempt, the Biden presidency was very important in stopping it from going forward. Now, with Trump, there might be some attempt at direct intervention in Brazilian politics. So, part of the cosmopolitan bourgeoisie doesn’t want to take a position today, to avoid a falling-out with US policy and with a possible Bolsonaro victory. It’s less a direct mirror between fractions of the bourgeoisie.
- André Singer Then I’ll take advantage of your interpretation to add something that makes the problem more complex. The major point of division between that sector of the Brazilian bourgeoisie and Lula’s third government is the fiscal deficit. That sector demands a big cut in public spending, which in its view would have to fall on pension benefits, and it wants to delink them from the minimum wage. The Brazilian Constitution links the two, so raising the minimum wage in real terms also raises all benefits. The other target is the constitutional floor for health and education: the Brazilian Constitution requires that a certain share of annual tax revenue go to health and education, and this cannot go down. The bourgeoisie’s aim is to remove that floor from the Constitution, so that this spending falls. So, we have a very serious issue: on one side the pension system, all the retirees; on the other, the two main social policies that form the social core of the 1988 Constitution, health and education. That is the main problem. We still don’t know whether there is also a certain caution or a desire to align with the American cosmopolitan bourgeoisie.
- Aldo Cordeiro Sauda National sovereignty took center stage in the campaign, perhaps for the first time since the return to democracy. What role did this issue play in the second-round turnaround against Flávio Bolsonaro?
- André Singer The Trump administration’s offensive against Brazil — the tariffs and its direct or indirect intervention in the elections — has put national sovereignty on the agenda. Trump justified the first tariffs by saying that Brazil was persecuting his preferred candidate, Jair Bolsonaro. Brazil today does not have a very strong nationalist current. A nationalism is now starting to grow, because the global situation has changed and the country faces political-economic aggression — let’s call it that. So nationalism has come onto the agenda, but in my opinion — and I may be wrong — it has still not become a central issue.
- Catarina Príncipe Lula wants to transform the Brazilian economy by investing in the green economy, infrastructure, and artificial intelligence (data centers) and by using Brazil’s resources in rare metals and minerals. How much room for maneuver does he have to do this, given the New Fiscal Framework, the Lula government’s 2023 fiscal rule capping annual spending growth at 70 percent of revenue growth? How should we think about his government’s relationship with the bourgeoisie in this fourth term and the new balance of forces? Do you believe the bourgeoisie will tend to deepen its conflict with the PT, intensifying the pendular movement? And in this context, what happens to the mass mobilization from below that we saw in the second round?
- André Singer I think this is the central point regarding the fourth term: what the outcome of this conflict will be. The stock market fell nearly 14 percent the day after the election. As I have been saying, the market has no vote, but it has money, and its message is clear: if you don’t cut public spending, we’re leaving. The question of fiscal adjustment is truly central, because the bourgeoisie is demanding harsh austerity. In my opinion, the demand for austerity is the fundamental issue in Brazilian politics today, but in general nobody puts it openly: it remains an implicit debate. That is partly because we are not managing to politicize the problem, to make the popular classes, the working class, aware that this is what is at stake. This is the main confrontation. This organizes Brazilian politics. In my recent book, Impasse: O Brasil diante da onda reacionária, I tried to show that this issue splits the democratic front in two. It is, as Americans say, an elephant in the room: everyone treats it as if it didn’t exist. I felt that my role was to bring it to the surface; obviously I can’t do that alone, but I can contribute to some extent. The conflict is immediate, because the transformation Brazil needs, which runs through reindustrialization, is a gigantic task. Brazil is an enormous country, and you don’t change a structure of this order without major investment. This transformation can’t rely on public investment alone; there must also be private investment. But we have to think with the instruments we have. Perry Anderson says Keynesianism no longer works, so we need to create new mechanisms; but until we have them, I’ll use the old ones. The state will have to induce this development process, although it also has to bring in other investors. There is, therefore, an incompatibility between the country’s needs and this radical cut in public spending, which goes in the opposite direction. This is the central point. Even if the terms of the debate were not clear, I think the large demonstrations in hundreds of Brazilian cities point toward the government having this commitment. We’ll have to follow events to see how it unfolds.
- Catarina Príncipe Your earlier book defined Lulism as “combating poverty without confronting capital.” Can Lulism go beyond itself, and does it want to? Is there room to do so today, given the current party arithmetic in Congress? And how can the Brazilian left organize to force it to take measures that go beyond welfarism?
- André Singer I’ll start with Congress, which I think is simpler. In the Congress that takes office in 2027, the far right has grown, not at the expense of the Left but of other forces on the Right. In the Chamber of Deputies, it went from 91 to 121 deputies, out of 513 seats. That is significant: since the return to democracy, we would hardly find such a large single-party caucus. But it decides nothing on its own. What we will have is permanent negotiation, which is already happening: Lula’s third government already negotiated permanently with what we in Brazil call the Centrão. To be clear, the Centrão is the established right, the traditional right, so to speak. It generally holds the majority in Brazil’s National Congress, because the Brazilian electoral system reproduces small local oligarchies that tend to dominate legislative elections. This is structural in Brazil, and it will continue. President Lula has specialized in negotiating with those sectors. The third term was the most difficult in this respect, because Congress gained power from what we in Brazil call the “secret budget” (orçamento secreto) [budget amendments through which lawmakers steer federal funds without disclosing who requested them]. Even so, the president managed to pass his two boldest proposals. The first was the income-tax exemption for those who earn up to R$5,000 (about US$940) a month, offset by a levy on those who earn more than R$50,000 (about US$9,400). The Chamber of Deputies approved it unanimously. The second was the change of the work schedule from 6x1 to 5x2, which we have already discussed. The Chamber had already approved it unanimously, and the Senate has just passed it by an overwhelming majority. This shows that such negotiation is possible. The traditional right makes concessions on one side and concessions on the other. Its concession to the far right is an effort to reduce the sentences the courts imposed on Jair Bolsonaro and on everyone they convicted of taking part in the 2022 coup attempt, and that effort will expand. It will probably have real consequences: the far right will try to make it possible for Bolsonaro to run in 2030. I think that is its outlook. I repeat, it won’t achieve this without the support of the Right, but depending on the back-and-forth negotiations, it could happen. I now turn to the problem of the Left. The Left should not leave the democratic front. The central problem in Brazil, as in many countries around the world, is to isolate the far right and reverse its advance toward power everywhere. Looking at the long term, we are witnessing a gradual, slow, but constant advance of the far right, sometimes faster, sometimes slower. If the far right comes to power and consolidates itself around the whole world, the working class will suffer a tremendous setback in every respect. Our task, then, is to avoid this by isolating the far right and defeating it as an alternative for power in Brazil. For that, we have to stay in the democratic front. But two incompatible economic programs divide the democratic front. We have to fight explicitly inside this democratic front for our position to win a majority. I’m convinced that democracy depends on the majority of the population recognizing in it an answer to their problems; if it doesn’t, it won’t last. That is the best contribution the Left can and must make to the defense of democracy. Lulism, as I characterized it, is a movement that seeks to combat poverty, which is fundamental in Brazil, without confronting capital. I stand by that definition. But political reality is dynamic. We and all the other actors are facing new situations, so new things are bound to happen. As you know, we can’t predict the future; we can only see tendencies. I would end by saying that a popular commitment is in Lulism’s nature: it depends on a popular base; it is a popular movement. Beyond that, only the political process will tell.
