Police found a deceased person with multiple stab wounds inside a building in Queens on Friday, officials said.
The NYPD said officers entered a building at 3617 164 St. in Flushing around 4:30 p.m. on Friday and found an unconscious and unresponsive female individual.
Emergency responders pronounced her dead at the scene.
There were no arrests as of Friday night, and police hadn't yet described any suspects. Police also had not identified the woman or provided an estimate of her age. Police said the incident was still under investigation.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/finland-ai-g.title: In Finland, the Left Can Lead on Fair AI Policy
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/finland-ai-g.author: Mike Watson
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/finland-ai-g.text:
In Finland, the Left Can Lead on Fair AI Policy
Finnish authorities have instructed Google to stop work on two data centers after the firm flouted environmental rules. Ahead of the country’s election, the Left is calling for a wider plan to ensure AI doesn’t cause further devastation.
Finland’s next general election has been set for next April 18, hopefully bringing an end to the National Coalition Party’s current slash-and-burn coalition, in which the far-right Finns Party plays a key role. Recent polls have, however, seen the latter worryingly rise to second position, becoming the main right-wing force for the first time ever. Trailing Antti Lindtman’s Social Democrats (SDP) by 6 percentage points, the Finns Party is placing its hope in polarizing the election over immigration. But as the SDP and other left-of-center parties like the Left Alliance and the Greens seek to fend off a far-right surge, a new key battleground has emerged: artificial intelligence.
Crossing over into the perennial issues of education, employment, and the environment, AI is already becoming a key issue for voters wherever elections are held globally. In Finland, a narrative is emerging that relates to the specific local terrain, culture, and economy. Unemployment is currently at 10 percent nationwide, the worst in the European Union, which makes the country particularly vulnerable to further AI-induced job loss. The Left Alliance’s leader Minja Koskela released a statement in October insisting that “The data center boom must be reflected in increasing tax revenues, jobs, and expertise, not in municipal residents’ electricity bills or the destruction of forest nature.” In doing so, she signaled that the Left Alliance, which has polled at over 12 percent for the first time ever, can be trusted to navigate the tricky terrain of ethical AI use.
This statement seems to have a major recent data center controversy in its sights. Google has been instructed by Finnish authorities to stop work on two data centers in Finland, located in Muhos and Kajaani. This followed news that the tech giant had flouted regulations by clearing hundreds of acres of forest across both sites prior to performing obligatory environmental impact assessments or ensuring that felled trees would be replaced. The extent of Google’s wrongdoing is still unclear, as recriminations pass between the firm and local authorities. In any case, the act has caused a media storm in a country defined by its relationship to nature, and particularly to its abundant forests, while drawing attention to the clear dangers AI poses for the environment. Public discontent led to a hundred protesters gathering outside Google’s Finnish headquarters in Helsinki on October 12 to demand environmental accountability. The protest signaled dismay at a foreign goliath hacking away at Finland’s natural resources.
Both conservative Prime Minister Petteri Orpo and Finns Party leader and Finance Minister Riikka Purra have welcomed Google’s €13 billion investment in the country, which will result in a total of four data centers (one already completed in Hamina, the two mentioned above and one more planned in Vaala). Yet they are walking a tightrope between seeking to embrace new and vital technology and disregarding the public interest in the name of profit. Finland’s right-wing parties universally caution — along with the Left — that assurances need to be made to prevent rising electricity consumption impacting energy costs. Yet the Finns Party’s nationalist rhetoric stands in stark contrast with its actions. As the second- biggest party in the governing coalition, it too must take some responsibility for permitting a foreign tech giant to run roughshod over Finnish sensibilities. They may as well have allowed Google to destroy Moominvalley, the fictional home of Finland’s much-loved unofficial mascot, the Moomins.
Juha-Matti Mustonen, a Left Alliance candidate in Oulu (the district where Muhos and Kajaani are situated, and where I live) wrote to me in email that, “It seems Google will face no sanctions for these logging activities. In fact, it appears the company will get away scot-free with the environmental devastation it has caused. An ordinary citizen would be heading straight to prison for such actions.” Police have since launched an investigation into Google’s actions, though the episode raises major questions about the governing parties’ seriousness in defending local interests, and it gets worse if we consider the actual financial benefits. As Mustonen continues: “The government was overjoyed by Google’s €13 billion investment. However, closer examination reveals that only a small fraction of the total investment will actually remain in Finland.” This latter point was backed up by Lassi Linnanen, professor of environmental economics and management at the Lappeenranta-Lahti University of Technology, on the national broadcaster’s politics show A-talk in mid-October. Linnanen stated that Finland offers land and infrastructure, while the profits will go elsewhere.
Left-Wing Solutions
Against this backdrop, AI will likely be a key election issue nationally, and particularly in Oulu. The Left will need to show it has the public interest at heart, while the Right merely pays lip service to the desire for a fair and equitable AI future. One politician who is well-placed to focus on this topic is the Oulu Left Alliance MP Jessi Jokelainen, who is running to maintain her parliamentary seat. This spring, Jokelainen published a policy paper called “Left-Wing Solutions to the Artificial-Intelligence Revolution,” arguing that AI productivity gains should be distributed to employees as shorter working hours instead of merely amounting to more profit for business owners.
Jokelainen also cites education as an area in need of overhaul, with lifelong learning necessary to ensure people aren’t left behind by AI advances. She argues for degree studies to be made more flexible for the unemployed. I am a teacher of academic writing in a Finnish university and can attest that AI is seen as an inevitability — for good and bad. It clearly brings great potential in the right hands. Yet it also brings considerable uncertainty for the sector. Finnish student numbers are in decline due to demographics. Along with the potential for the automation of teaching, this clearly threatens the sector, especially in nonvocational subjects. Lifelong training could breathe new life into Finland’s tertiary education sector.
What is clear is that tech giants see Finland as fertile ground for AI expansion. It is seen as the “Texas of Europe” for its level of data center investment and planning, and a pushover for capitalists: After all, the government recently proposed to cut corporate income tax from 20 to 18 percent, effective from early 2027. Given austerity measures, it might understandably be seen as gung ho in its courting of capitalist projects that have little consideration for the local environment or workers. Such austerity is arguably responsible for a slowdown of the economy through its negative impact on spending. Finland’s leaders mustn’t seek to compensate by giving hasty permissions for foreign AI companies who ignore ordinary Finns’ interests.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/turkey-gokta.title: In Turkey, When Does a Joke Become a Crime?
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/turkey-gokta.author: Dora Mengüç
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/turkey-gokta.text:
In Turkey, When Does a Joke Become a Crime?
Comedian Deniz Göktaş spent 88 days in a high-security prison for insulting Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. He turned his sentence into a punch line, but the chilling consequences of the case extend far beyond one comedian.
Have you ever made a joke that offended someone? Maybe they took it personally or stopped speaking to you. A joke can put strain on a relationship or leave someone feeling isolated. But what if the consequences for a joke go far beyond social fallout? What if a comedy performance lands you in a high-security prison cell? For Deniz Göktaş, this question is no longer hypothetical.
Until recently, Göktaş performed for relatively small audiences, playing bars in Kadıköy, an Istanbul district known for political satire, and occasionally in university halls elsewhere in Turkey. He was part of a niche comedy scene.
Things changed when he took his show to one of Istanbul’s most prominent stages and uploaded the performance to YouTube, opening it to a much wider audience. He knew the show might attract attention. Not just because of the words he spoke onstage, but also because the title and stage image played on a grisly visual gag. Ölü Deniz (“Dead Sea”) was a dark play on his first name, Deniz (“Sea”), while an enormous, sculpted image of his face lay on its side as if decapitated.
What began as a night of laughter would end with Göktaş spending eighty-eight days behind bars in a high-security prison. His case exposed not only the limits of free expression in Turkey but also the fraught relationship between political satire and political power.
The Charges
The thirty-two-year-old comedian was detained at Istanbul airport on July 2, after his ninety-minute special was released on YouTube. Prosecutors cited passages from the performance in bringing charges: insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, inciting public hatred and hostility, and praising crime or criminals.
At his first hearing, on September 28, 2026, Göktaş addressed the court:
“As a comedian, seeing that sentences can have such a powerful impact makes me proud. But as a citizen, I am saddened by my country’s record on freedom of expression.”
He said he worried the case would discourage others from performing and lead them to censor themselves.
The court ordered his release after sentencing. By then, he had spent eighty-eight days in pretrial detention. He told the court he had been held in a cell without sunlight or contact with other prisoners at Çorlu Karatepe High Security Prison, a facility known in Turkey as a well-type prison.
The court acquitted him of praising crime or criminals. It convicted him of insulting the president and, because public hatred and hostility were not established, reclassified the incitement charge as insulting religious values. The sentences were eleven months and twenty days and seven months and fifteen days, respectively.
The case raised a question beyond the sentences themselves: How had a comedy performance been transformed into a criminal prosecution? Göktaş’s defense argued that prosecutors had removed the alleged offenses from their original context onstage, but the heart of the matter was a dispute over how a comedian’s words should be interpreted.
Jokes About Politicians Are Not the Same as Political Comedy
While Göktaş was still in prison, I spoke with his friend and fellow stand-up comedian Emre Günsal.
Günsal distinguishes Göktaş’s comedy from much of what passes for “political humor” in Turkey. A comedian can get an easy laugh simply by mentioning a politician, referring to a current scandal, or repeating a political cliché the audience already agrees with. In Turkey, Günsal says, that is the least risky kind of political comedy.
Göktaş’s work is more deliberate. He combines political satire with social observation, using comedy to say something about the political climate, social tensions, and the shrinking space for free expression. The result can be both funny and cathartic for those who feel alienated or frustrated by the society in which they live. Günsal considers Göktaş one of the leading figures of this tradition in Turkey today.
This may help explain Göktaş’s appeal among young people and audiences opposed to the government. Günsal describes Göktaş’s work as a form of emotional release, then trails off: “Seeing someone stand onstage, knowing millions of people will watch, and say the things that others are afraid to say openly because of what might happen to them. . . . ”
Göktaş made a similar point in an interview with The New York Times after his release. He recalled a viewer writing beneath his performance that watching it made them feel as though they lived in a free country. The comment, he said, captured exactly what he had hoped to achieve.
But he was modest about comedy’s political power. Humor, he suggested, can help people feel understood, given them motivation and the courage to speak, and offer psychological support.
Plus Ça Change
Political satire and state power has a long and vexed history in Turkey.
In 1946, two of the country’s best-known writers, Sabahattin Ali and Aziz Nesin, founded Markopaşa, a socialist-leaning satirical newspaper that sharply criticized class inequality and the government of the day. The paper faced distribution restrictions, pressure on printing houses, confiscations, closures, and criminal prosecutions. Its writers and cartoonists were arrested or forced into exile. Markopaşa remains one of the most important examples of socialist and oppositional humor in Turkey.
In later decades, political satire found new forms in cabaret theater and humor magazines, including the work of Ferhan Şensoy and the satirical magazines of the 1990s and 2000s. By the time of the 2013 Gezi Park protests, irony and satire had become prominent forms of political expression.
The protests began with opposition to plans to redevelop Gezi Park near Istanbul’s Taksim Square. The government framed the unrest in terms of hooliganism and terrorism. Many protesters, meanwhile, used humor and irony to defy the government’s account of the movement. Researchers have documented how humor and satire became a form of dissent in an environment where traditional media were subject to tight control.
In his courtroom defense, Göktaş placed himself in this tradition, invoking Aziz Nesin, Rıfat Ilgaz, Ferhan Şensoy, and Turkey’s major satirical magazines. Then he reached back to Nasreddin Hodja, the legendary Anatolian folk figure whose stories have circulated for centuries. Traditionally dated to 1208–1284, Hodja occupies a place in Anatolian culture somewhat comparable to the traditions of folk wisdom and social satire in American humor.
Göktaş distilled the connection between that tradition and contemporary Turkey into a single sentence: “If Nasreddin Hodja were doing stand-up today, half his show would be about President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.”
Göktaş argued that calling Erdoğan, who has governed Turkey for more than two decades, a “dictator” was political characterization, not an insult. As the country’s most powerful political figure, Erdoğan should be expected to face satire and harsh criticism, he said. He argued that politicians must be open to ridicule as well as praise.
The language of this debate is not new in Turkey.
A few days ago, I came across a street bookseller on the narrow Kadıköy street where Deniz Göktaş had performed stand-up for years. Among the books on the shelves was Görülmüştür, a collection by journalist and writer İlhan Selçuk, published in the 1980s.
Leafing through it, I found an essay titled “Freedom of Thought and Tolerance.” One sentence stood out: “Where freedom of thought does not exist, tolerance is nothing more than an empty word.”
Selçuk’s point resonates in the Göktaş case. If political or religious satire is tolerated only as long as it offends no one, can that be called freedom of expression?
How Does a Court Interpret a Joke?
One of the clearest examples of this problem was Göktaş’s joke about “divers.”
Prosecutors treated it as an insult to women who wear modest swimwear because of their religious beliefs. In court, Göktaş said he used the audience’s expectations to set up the joke. He described people emerging from the sea with their hair concealed and their bodies covered in black clothing. The audience, he said, assumed that he was describing women wearing modest Islamic swimwear. Then came the punch line: “f–king divers.”
The case raised a basic question: Can a stand-up performance be judged solely by a written transcript, stripped of its context onstage?
Göktaş invoked American comedian Lenny Bruce, who had faced similar problems. Bruce satirized the courts with the line, “In the Halls of Justice the only justice is in the halls.” He was repeatedly arrested and prosecuted on obscenity charges during the 1960s. In 1964, a New York court sentenced him to four months in a workhouse. He remained free while his appeal was pending and died in 1966 without serving the sentence. Thirty-seven years after his death, in 2003, New York governor George Pataki granted him a posthumous pardon.
Bruce’s trials showed how words spoken by a comedian onstage should not be evaluated independently of their delivery, facial expressions, timing, and relationship with the audience.
Göktaş argued that tone of voice, pauses, physical performance, audience reactions, and the surprise of the punch line all help make up a joke’s meaning. He compared evaluating a stand-up performance by its transcript to understanding a film by listening only to its soundtrack.
Clear and Present Danger
To better understand how Turkish law treats the line between satire and incitement, I spoke with Professor Tolga Şirin. Göktaş was still being held in a high-security prison.
For Şirin, any legal assessment had to begin with context.
“What does it mean within a stand-up performance?” he asked. A legal assessment, he said, must account for irony, exaggeration, satire, and the possibility that a comedian will deliberately lead an audience in one direction before reversing its expectations. Evaluating a few sentences only according to their literal meaning can exclude other reasonable interpretations and privilege the harshest possible criminal reading.
Şirin stressed that this was not merely an aesthetic question: “The fact that a statement offends or disturbs some people is not sufficient in itself.” Context matters particularly to the charge of inciting public hatred and hostility. Under the Turkish Penal Code, the offense requires more than a statement that people find offensive. It also requires the emergence of a clear and imminent danger to public safety.
Prosecutors cited complaints submitted through CİMER, Turkey’s online public petition and complaints system operating under Turkey’s presidency.
In his defense, Göktaş addressed the 185 complaints submitted against him. He argued that the overwhelming majority of complainants had never watched his full performance but had instead reacted to selectively edited clips circulated on social media. He described the backlash as an artificially orchestrated campaign.
For Şirin, the complaint count alone could not establish a legally significant danger. Otherwise, organized groups could make speech they disliked into a punishable offense simply by launching petition campaigns.
“Public peace is not measured by the number of people who are offended,” he said.
Göktaş said he performed Ölü Deniz 198 times over approximately three years, before more than a hundred thousand people in cities across Turkey, without receiving complaints about the statements in question. According to him, the controversy began only after the performance was uploaded to YouTube and short clips started circulating on social media.
“What development has caused a statement made and made accessible months ago to suddenly create a clear and imminent danger today?” Şirin asked.
When I asked whether the prosecution could affect other comedians and artists, Şirin’s answer was unequivocal: “This is absolutely an act of intimidation.”
According to Şirin, Göktaş had pushed against the fear surrounding political figures and sensitive subjects that many people hesitate to joke about. In Şirin’s view, the proceedings could deter other comedians and artists from crossing the same boundaries.
“We Have Cancel Culture — and Jail”
Günsal’s account shows how the chilling effect described by Şirin can manifest itself on the stand-up stage.
Small comedy venues in Istanbul have long provided spaces where comedians can speak relatively freely. The risk changes when a performance circulates on the internet. Jokes lose their original context and reach a much larger audience.
After Göktaş’s arrest, Günsal saw comedians grow more reluctant to post political sets.
He believes the greater problem is not simply censorship but the inability to tell where the line lies. “There is no clear line telling you, ‘Say this and you go to prison, but you can say that,’” he explained. Even careful comedians cannot know how their words will later be interpreted. The uncertainty can result in performers ruling out jokes before they have even written them.
Günsal knows that risk firsthand. In April 2020, he was arrested after a clip from one of his performances circulated on social media. The case involved comments about Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder of the Turkish Republic, and the historical religious figures Rumi and Shams of Tabriz.
He spent eleven days in prison. In 2021, he was sentenced to three years and five months; the sentence was suspended. Six years later, while Deniz Göktaş was behind bars, Günsal tells me that political comedy had become both more difficult and more necessary.
After his release, Göktaş told The New York Times that he never regretted releasing the performance during his time in prison, not even for a second. As his popularity grew, he said, he had more to lose and began censoring his own material even before his arrest.
Asked about American comedians’ complaints about cancel culture and online backlash, he replied: “I don’t want to brag, but we have cancel culture — and jail.”
Choosing to Stay
There is another revealing detail in the Göktaş case.
When the investigation began, he was abroad. According to his courtroom defense, he cut his vacation short and returned to Turkey rather than fleeing.
He said that most of his close friends had moved abroad because they no longer saw a future in the country. He had been trying to persuade them to come back.
Günsal described this decision as one of the qualities he most admired in his friend. Günsal believes Göktaş could perform stand-up in English and appear regularly on stages abroad. But Göktaş does not want to build a new home somewhere else. That determination to keep calling Turkey home is something Günsal admires.
Deniz Göktaş is no longer in prison. But the impact of his case cannot be measured solely by his release on September 28. Perhaps the more telling measure will be the jokes not written, the performances never uploaded to the internet, and the comedians who censor themselves before finishing a sentence because they cannot predict where the legal boundaries lie.
The Göktaş case is not merely about whether one comedian crossed the limits of free expression. It is also a struggle over who gets to draw those limits in Turkey.

https://hyperallergic.com/mona-chalabi-p.title: Mona Chalabi Paints a Picture of Class Inequality
https://hyperallergic.com/mona-chalabi-p.author: Lakshmi Rivera Amin
https://hyperallergic.com/mona-chalabi-p.text:
Mona Chalabi Paints a Picture of Class Inequality
“The crisis is the system that we’re in,” the Pulitzer Prize-winning data journalist and artist says in an interview with Hyperallegic about her first book, “Ten Lives.”
“As an adult and as a journalist, I have stared shamelessly.” That refusal to look away is precisely what data journalist, writer, and artist Mona Chalabi has built her deeply principled career on. Known best for her indelible data visualizations, from the obscenity of Jeff Bezos’s wealth to the Israeli government’s starvation of Palestinians in Gaza and the racial and gender biases in museum collections, the Pulitzer Prize-winning Iraqi-British journalist tackles the subject of wealth and economic inequality in America in her first book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026).
When I met her in the West Village in September, she’d just come from recording its accompanying audiobook, a delicate process given the visuals on its pages. Chalabi organized meticulous interviews conducted with anonymous subjects across income levels over the course of six years into 10 vividly fleshed-out characters. Each represents a particular economic class, illustrated in her signature hand-drawn style and punctuated by reflections on her own financial struggles as a young journalist and, more recently, in the wake of her mother’s illness. Chalabi carries a long tradition of data visualization — W.E.B. Du Bois’s The Exhibit of American Negroes comes to mind — into her refreshing candor about class and the stifling silence around it, particularly in journalism and the art world.
That insistence on specificity and honesty in her reporting goes hand-in-hand with her political advocacy; Chalabi donated her $15,000 Pulitzer Prize award to the Palestinian Journalists Syndicate and has been fighting for Palestinian rights since she was a teenager. Her drive to seek out and represent truth, in Ten Lives and in her social media posts, is anchored in a sensitivity and profound sense of responsibility. In this way, she restores some of the humanity and dignity to the statistics that capture the brutality of genocide, exploitation, and economic inequality, one brushstroke at a time. In an interview, we spoke about the financial realities of journalism, the value of collaboration in an era of isolation, and the art and literature that sustains her. Our conversation has been lightly edited for clarity and length.
Hyperallergic: In the intro to Ten Lives, you recall getting scolded for not observing “the etiquette of looking away” as a child. And it’s so striking that you have made a career of doing the opposite. How did you decide to make class, something we’re taught to overlook from a young age, the subject of this book?
Mona Chalabi: The first line of the original manuscript said, “I wrote this book because I was paid a shitload of money to write it.”
H: Ha!
MC: And my editor was like, “Yeah, you can't do that. No one's gonna want to read a book that you wrote simply for money.” But I also knew that this was a commercial idea, and that did inform it. I have been quite shameless about the fact that I want my work to reach a wide audience. That has always, always mattered to me. It was the beginning of the pandemic, and part of the way that I pitched it was this idea that there's gonna be a big financial crisis and the dynamics are more nuanced than simply talking about the one percent. There's this idea of a coming economic collapse or a coming financial crisis. But as soon as we're in it, it's not this cyclical model. The crisis is the system that we're in that is so broken.
H: That gradation of class that usually doesn't get talked about is such a crucial contribution of this book. What led you to stratify these stories based on subcategories that often just get collapsed into “working class, middle class, upper class”?
MC: Class is really informative about who I am and how I move through the world and my relationships. And I felt like it was really, really lacking in our discourse. I feel a bit hesitant to use the word “discourse,” but it's just true. And it's not just about discourse, it's more mundane than that. It's the way that someone like me can say, “I'm an Arab, cis, heterosexual woman,” with total ease, but class doesn't really come into it. There's a dishonesty there. Actually, class is really, really important. And many of us aren't really talking about that in accurate and fruitful ways.

https://hyperallergic.com/clouds-were-on.title: Clouds Were Once Photography’s Greatest Challenge
https://hyperallergic.com/clouds-were-on.author: Julia Curl
https://hyperallergic.com/clouds-were-on.text:
Clouds Were Once Photography’s Greatest Challenge
The Met Museum’s “Chasing Clouds” is a pleasing romp through the technical problem of capturing clouds at photography’s beginning.
The original 1996 Windows XP default background is arguably the most viewed photo of all time; its cumulus puffs drifting across a way-too-blue sky are seared into my and countless others’ Y2K childhoods. Such images of fluffy clouds are so ubiquitous that it’s hard to believe they once presented one of photography’s greatest technological challenges. The Met exhibition Chasing Clouds is a pleasing romp through the history of this problem through a union of art and science, spanning the early 1800s to 1929 — roughly photography’s first century. While the medium showed promise as “the pencil of nature,” its first processes were overly sensitive to blue light, registering the sky as a blank white space, impossibly overexposed.
While this lent some images a minimalist mystique, like John Beasley Greene’s “The Nile in Front of the Theban Hills” (1853–54), other photographers resorted to painting clouds into their landscapes by hand. An initial breakthrough came when French photographer Gustave Le Gray figured out how to stitch together two pictures — one calibrated to sky, and the other to land and sea. (Photographic fakery is as old as the medium itself.)
Though the exhibition begins with painted cloud studies and ends with photographic modernism, visual discoveries unfold in a dialogue between painting and technology rather than as a scientific march from one to the other. This makes for a much more interesting story; obsolescence is often a capitalist public relations trick.

https://hyperallergic.com/is-sexy-art-ba.title: Is Sexy Art Back, or Is It Just Me?
https://hyperallergic.com/is-sexy-art-ba.author: Lori Waxman
https://hyperallergic.com/is-sexy-art-ba.text:
Is Sexy Art Back, or Is It Just Me?
From Willem de Kooning’s miserable nudes to Alexandra Barth’s hot and bothered architecture, sex is in the air in Chicago.
CHICAGO — I see a lot of exhibitions in Chicago, and lately, I have been noticing more than a few that feel almost ridiculously erotic. I mean, I get it, there's always been plenty of eros in art, but I haven't observed it much lately at the school where I teach nor in the shows that I view. Is sex back? Or it could just be me. I turned 50 this past year, and popular culture suggests that this might be what happens around my age, à la Sharon Horgan's Youth and Olivia Colman's Wicker, both recent screen-based explorations of lusty midlife ladyhood.
For those who have never had one or maybe never will, female middle-age libido sets at either zero or 1,000, on a scale of one to 100. It is not an easy ride. Shifting from one state to the other causes severe whiplash for driver and passengers alike. That’s based on an admittedly minuscule survey, though fear not, this will not be a personal essay about my own sexuality or that of my acquaintances. God, no. Maybe after everyone’s dead. What proceeds, instead, is a round-up of exhibitions that, for me, have a strong connecting thread, obviously red, and not discussed much if at all in the various associated didactics.
What shows? Last spring, Alice Tippit’s sly, meticulous paintings at the DePaul Art Museum had me thinking I probably needed to start talking to a therapist again, because what was going on in my head was not articulated anywhere in the otherwise delightful catalogue. Not even close. During the summer, SHADOW at tête-à-tête-à-tête, a wicked little curatorial project of Shannon Stratton, included Holly Murkerson’s sensuous photographs of a stone passageway worth entering and two dark leather-and-wood stools by David Sprecher and Neiva Mulhearn that required straddling and peering into.
What wasn’t a turn-on was the Art Institute of Chicago’s summer blockbuster, Willem de Kooning Drawing. You wouldn’t know from the glowing reviews or polite museum text that miserable naked women filled the walls. I like a good nude as much as anyone, but at some point, maybe it was the third room — definitely by the time I got to the giant rowboat charcoals of the mid-60s — de Kooning’s subjects started to look like crime victims.

https://hyperallergic.com/the-zen-mona-l.title: The Zen Mona Lisa
https://hyperallergic.com/the-zen-mona-l.author: Will Heinrich

The Zen Mona Lisa
A review of an ancient Chinese ink painting takes an art critic on a journey through his own past.
Editor’s Note: The following article is a chapter titled “Six Persimmons” that has been excerpted from From Darkness to Darkness by Will Heinrich, published by Thousand Horsemen Press in the summer of 2026 and available online and through independent booksellers. (Copyright © 2026 by Will Heinrich. Published by permission. All rights reserved.)
Every summer Jonah compiled a list of about a hundred upcoming museum shows for the newspaper’s special fall preview section. The first time he did it they were visiting Nadia’s college friend at her parents’ house in Pasadena, where he had to share a queen-size bed with Nadia and eight-month-old Orly. Fording hundreds of press releases, making decisions, and writing one-to-two-sentence synopses of complex shows he hadn’t seen while exhausted and sleepless was a trial. But the next year found him more confident, and ultimately the process became so automatic that it made no impression on him at all. If someone asked him in August, after he had filed his piece, what fall shows he was looking forward to, he would have to refer back to the document to come up with an answer.
One exhibit that did stick in his mind, though, the year Orly was six, was of a famous Chinese ink painting, a still life of persimmons, making a brief visit to the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. It would be coming from the Japanese monastery which had acquired it when it was already nearly 300 years old and which had then kept it mostly rolled up and hidden away since the early 1500s. Jonah mentioned the show to his editor as one he’d like to cover, emphasising how unprecedented it was for the piece to travel and reminding her that he was her only freelancer with any affinity for, or knowledge of, Asian art.
She was amenable to his writing about it, she told him, but said that, because of the expense of covering the war in Ukraine, the art section had no travel budget left for the year.
“Do you really have to see it in person?” she asked.
Jonah hesitated.
“I mean,” he said, “for a review.”
Then cannily, or guilelessly, he added that he planned to go see it regardless. He figured that after more than a decade as an art critic, it was time to admit that art was important to him, and that so long as she did pay him to write something, he would at least break even on the experience. She offered to pay for a night in a hotel and he replied that he was planning to stay with his cousin.
“Well,” she said noncommittally, “see if you can find a cheap flight.”
Using credit card points, he found one for a couple of hundred dollars. He checked with his cousin and made plans to stay for two nights; it would be the longest he had been alone since Orly was born. Then he forgot about it, mostly. But he would mention his upcoming trip now and then to this or that person, amused to cut the figure of an adult whose job let him travel. Downtown to take notes about a conceptual art show, he met his father for coffee.
“Wow!” Alan exclaimed when Jonah told him about the ink painting. “I always wanted to see that but your mother and I were never in Kyoto on the right day.”
When the time came to go and Jonah found himself alone with a backpack on the E train, bound for Kennedy Airport, he was bemused again. As a younger man, he had travelled to escape his ordinary life, to fling himself without boundaries into unfamiliar locales. His last visit to San Francisco had been to visit a girl he’d briefly dated in New York, and he could still summon up the Pacific smell of the air when he first stepped out of the airport, the dark luxury of the apartment she was borrowing, the softness of her freckled, paper-white skin as they made love and fell asleep in a narrow guest-room bed. She had reminded him of a doe. Now, as he passed through the airport security line in New York, endured a two-hour delay caused by San Francisco air traffic related to the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference, read the London Review of Books, crammed himself into an economy seat, watched half a movie on his iPad, and took a cab, at his cousin’s suggestion, to Bernal Heights, it all felt more like an errand, albeit a pleasant one, than an adventure. The air smelled of nothing. His own company felt like a childhood friend he was glad to see again, but with whom, because it had been so long, he felt shy.
First thing the following morning, Jonah accompanied his cousin, an accomplished video game designer, as he walked his dog in a nearby park. They hadn’t met in years, and Jonah felt shy with him, too — as well as rebuked in his own aimless financial irresponsibility by the cousin’s comfortably furnished 3-bedroom house with basement rental apartment attached. Looking for something to talk about, he asked whether there had been many protests about Israel’s response to the attacks of October 7.
“Not really,” his cousin said. “I did drive past one group of people with signs that said ‘Stop the Genocide.’”
His tone made clear what he thought of the protestors’ use of the word “genocide.” Not seeing any benefit in starting an argument with his host at 7:30 in the morning, Jonah changed the subject. He went and climbed a nearby hill for its view of the city; returned to the house, where his cousin fed him breakfast; and rode the bus to a still awakening Chinatown to see a show someone had told him about, work by an artist he liked at a gallery he had encountered at art fairs but never visited in person. He chatted with the young man behind the desk, asking what else there was to see in the neighbourhood and sharing his concern that the artist, a Native American ceramicist who had gotten very popular, might get boxed into grinding out the same thing over and over. Because the young man asked, Jonah also shared his name. There was a photography gallery a few blocks away, another one Jonah knew by reputation; walking there he saw a large protest of the summit that had delayed his flight.
He got past the desk and into the show — tasteful, boring photography by a successful Japanese artist, what he privately thought of as “rich people art” — with only a brief hello, but then turned around, just when he would have walked out again, to see that the gallery founder and two directors had emerged to greet him.
“They told us you were coming,” explained one of the directors, a pretty young woman in a severe business suit. Once the founder had shaken his hand and gone back to his office, Jonah let the pretty young director show him around the exhibit he’d already dismissed as well as the gallery’s back office and viewing room. He took his usual approach in such situations, making small talk as if at a cocktail party and biding his time. He admired the unique design of the display racks in the viewing room. He inquired after her family and asked where she liked to eat in the neighbourhood. As soon as he could he slipped out and hurried over to City Lights, where he bought two paperbacks by the Sicilian writer Leonardo Sciascia, whom he’d never read before.
The restaurant she recommended turned out to be an ornate Szechuan spot, deserted at that hour, whose prices he could not possibly afford. Slinking out again after looking at the menu he felt foolish to have expected anything else. Fortunately he’d overheard the clerk at City Lights mention another place, an old-school Hunanese lunch counter where there was a television playing the local news and they did not offend Jonah’s sensibilities by charging for tea. Later he rode out to the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive to see the exhibition of a grad school friend, another conceptual artist who made work about North American settler colonialism; the next morning, he visited a sculptor who had gone to college with Nadia and had just spent six months carving the impurities out of an enormous chunk of quartz salvaged from a commercial rock quarry.
This sculptor’s New York gallery had just closed and he had a new baby in a carrier on his chest. Jonah’s heart was in his mouth every time the sculptor leaned over his opus, bringing the baby’s head within an inch of a corner; he remembered the dirty looks he used to get from old women in Jackson Heights when they saw him carrying his own newborn infant under one arm like a football. He and the sculptor went out for dim sum and to a bookstore and the sculptor shared the advice another artist had given him about making money.
“‘Use archival material,’” he said, “‘and get used to doing the same thing over and over.’”
Then Jonah walked a mile and a half to the Asian Art Museum, which had been closed to the public to host a grand lunch for the spouses of the heads of state in town for APEC.
“Jill Biden was standing right here two hours ago,” the museum’s press chief told him, grinning and squeezing his arm, once he’d gotten past security and been led into the dim and empty gallery. “I’ll leave you alone.”
Publicists liked to talk, and curators liked to lecture, but Jonah had learned to be forthright about his need for solitude. This time they had agreed ahead of time that he would have 45 minutes to himself before the curator arrived to explain what he was supposed to think of the painting. When he was starting out, he had sometimes spent many hours over multiple days confronting a work that perplexed him. In this case, having already seen many images of what turned out to be a very easily photographed black and white art work, and having already begun to write down ideas earlier in the day, he could probably have made do with a glance. He was unlikely to experience any transcendence in such a tightly choreographed encounter, anyway. He was just too contrary. But showing up felt like a matter of principle, and after all, it couldn’t hurt.
When the press contact, a former dancer type who later surprised Jonah by mentioning his wife and two children, returned with the curator, a trim older woman in an embroidered jacket, Jonah prepared to joust. She was perfectly nice and had interesting things to say. But he needed her to understand that he was no mere journalist, to whom the Zen esthetic was news, while she, as an academic, had to demonstrate her mastery of the material. Once he felt they had both made their points, he looked at his watch, and they continued next door to a Japanese pop art exhibit. Then the curator excused herself, but the former dancer offered Jonah a tour of the rest of the museum, and Jonah couldn’t see how to refuse, even though his feet hurt and his eyes were exhausted. He hadn’t ever been there before and, as the dancer pointed out, there was no way of knowing if he’d ever be back.
When finally he left, with many thanks and professions of good will, he got on a train to a gentrified section of Oakland for dinner with a close college friend who had, after an interval in academia, become a corporate lawyer. Jonah held the friend’s new baby and then, leaving the baby and his older brother with either the night nurse or the mother in law — she wasn’t introduced — he, his friend, and his friend’s wife, also a corporate lawyer, walked to a nearby French restaurant. Jonah had been surprised, because his friend always seemed worried about money, by how nice his house was, but he supposed it made sense. The first thing his friend said, once they had been seated and had ordered some appetizers, was, “Flying across the country to see one painting is completely ridiculous.”
Jonah wasn’t sure whether he was meant to litigate this question, for entertainment’s sake, or to agree that he had wandered into an unbelievable life. He suspected the latter, but either way he didn’t feel up to it.
“Well,” he said mildly, “art is important to some people.”
“No, of course,” his friend replied, and Jonah stopped listening. In the morning he discovered that a train ran directly to the airport from quite close to his cousin’s house. There had been no reason to take a cab when he arrived. He began transcribing his notes on the airplane, and then began writing, and when this flight, too, was delayed, and they were all forced to deplane for several hours, he was delighted. The airline gave them food vouchers, there was a decent enough sushi counter, and this way he could finish his piece and finish watching Parasite on his iPad before returning to family life. It was a beautiful experience. He was engaged in what he was doing, but with something deeper than his anxious ordinary mind; he could feel himself pirouette around the ink painting’s formal qualities and Buddhist subtext like an ice skater. “The point of this minimalism isn’t to make anything simple,” he concluded, after about 1000 words, “but to cut away distractions and reveal how complicated the world actually is.”
He filed that evening from Kennedy Airport, and when there was no reply the following day, he wondered if he should call. But then the assistant art editor sent an edit, and he dared hope he could get through the whole process without talking on the phone at all. He did end up speaking to the assistant editor, because she would need a synopsis of his piece for a meeting the following week and called to ask him to write one for her. In the course of their exchange, he mentioned that some people called “Six Persimmons” the “Zen Mona Lisa.” She suggested putting this phrase in the subheadline, and to make this intelligible, he agreed to add the fact that some people called “Six Persimmons” the “Zen Mona Lisa” to his story.
When the piece was published, he got vastly more response than he usually did, which is to say that as many as three or four people emailed him about it. One was a former college professor, who said that he wasn’t sure either of them had brought their best to the class they had shared, but that he congratulated Jonah on conserving his energies for such top-flight art writing. The next week Jonah went to Chinatown to visit an artist he might profile for a museum catalogue, a renowned older Japanese woman who had lived like a squatter in an unfurnished loft for 40 years. The gallerist who would be paying him for this, if she decided to spend what he was asking, sat between them as they chatted, interrupting their rapport from time to time to underline the parts of the artist’s life that she felt were important art historically. When she got up to use the bathroom, the artist followed her with her eyes.
“She’s okay,” the artist said. “But I think something weird about her. Like whenever we travel, she insist on getting one room with king size bed.”
“To share?” Jonah exclaimed.
On his way to Tribeca, where he was meeting his father for coffee, Jonah ran into a different art dealer, the one whose conceptual art show he had just reviewed, and she invited him into her office for a chat. They talked about marriage and their children, as they usually did, and she thanked him for the review, which he shrugged off.
“No,” she said, “it’s huge.”
She had worked at a mega gallery before opening her own space, and she told him that reviews in his paper had been the only ones the mega gallerist cared about. They appeared in sales presentations. They played a key role in what she called the mega gallerist’s “ongoing pissing contest” with his peers.
“Yeah,” Jonah laughed, “and then I get $250.”
The dealer’s jaw dropped, and he in turn stared right back at her. He couldn’t remember having ever surprised her before.
“Yeah,” he repeated. “Two-fifty for the short ones.”
“But you have so much power!” she exclaimed.
He didn’t know what to say.
“How was the piece?” Alan asked him, once they were sitting side by side in the little cafe that now occupied the former boarding house where Frederick Douglass had first slept when he came to New York.
“To be honest,” Jonah said, “I think it comes through pretty well in reproduction.” He made a deprecating gesture. “You know, it’s black and white.”
“It’s still good you went,” Alan said.
“Oh, yeah, no,” Jonah said, “it was a great trip. I’m glad I went.”
He walked Alan back to the loft and went upstairs to say hello to his mother, to whom he couldn’t help boasting that he’d gotten some nice emails about his latest review.
“Oh, I’m so glad!” she exclaimed. “Because I saw someone on Facebook making fun of you for calling it the Zen Mona Lisa.”

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120377.author: Thekla Sickinger
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120377.text:
- Kultur
- Literatur
Ilse Aichinger wollte sich ihre Renitenz bewahren
Wo die Wirklichkeit versagt, beginnt das Schreiben: »Kontern« war das Motto von Ilse Aichinger, die vor zehn Jahren in Wien starb.
Am 11. November 2016 stirbt Ilse Aichinger in Wien. Die österreichisch-jüdische Schriftstellerin wurde 95 Jahre alt. »Ich gebrauche jetzt die besseren Wörter nicht mehr«, beginnt der schmale, 1976 erschienene Band »Schlechte Wörter«, der manchen als Höhepunkt ihres Werkes gilt. Lapidar erteilt der Eröffnungstext guten, besseren oder gar besten Redewendungen eine Absage, um sich stattdessen zu zweit-, drittbesseren oder eben »schlechten« Wörtern zu bekennen. Die Begründung: »Das Beste ist geboten.« Aber: »Gebote jagen mir Angst ein.«
Aichinger wurde 1921 in Wien geboren und erlebt dort den Aufstieg der Nationalsozialisten. Sie hat allen Grund, Gebote zu fürchten. Nach dem »Anschluss« Österreichs im März 1938 wird die Mutter, die als eine der ersten Frauen in Österreich Medizin studiert hat, gemäß den Nürnberger Gesetzen als »Volljude« deklariert, entlassen und zwangsumquartiert.
Aichinger, die wegen ihres »deutschblütigen« Vaters als »Mischling 1. Grades« gilt, darf nicht studieren und muss Zwangsarbeit leisten. Ihrer Zwillingsschwester, die später bildende Künstlerin wird, gelingt mit einem der letzten Kindertransporte im Juli 1939 die Flucht nach England. Die zurückgebliebene Familie kann nach Kriegsbeginn nicht mehr ausreisen. Aichinger, deren »Mischling«-Status der Mutter vorübergehend Schutz bietet, muss im Mai 1942 die Deportation ihrer geliebten Großmutter, ihres Onkels und einer Tante mitansehen.
Der Widerstand, auch der Widerstand gegen sprachliche Normen, der sich als roter Faden durch Aichingers Schreiben zieht, ist biografisch motiviert. Aichinger hat erlebt, was im äußersten Fall passieren kann, wenn Worte zu starren Bedeutungen gerinnen, die diejenigen, die damit bezeichnet werden, fixieren. Ihre Kritik an der Welt ist immer auch Sprachkritik: Kritik an einer Sprache, die unbedacht benennt und einteilt oder, wie in der Nachkriegszeit, Tradiertes fortführt, ohne unhintergehbare Brüche anzuerkennen.
Mit ihrem Gedicht »Winterantwort« schreibt sie 1963 den Höhepunkt des Rotkäppchen-Märchens, einen der bekanntesten deutschen Texte, neu, um an den Zivilisationsbruch der Judenvernichtung zu erinnern: »Großmutter, wo sind deine Lippen hin, / um die Gräser zu schmecken«.
Schon in ihrem Roman »Die größere Hoffnung«, der als eine der ersten literarischen Auseinandersetzungen mit der Judenverfolgung gilt, heißt es: »Großmutter, warum hast du so kalte Hände?« Auch das vermag Literatur: Das Kind kann in der Fiktion der Sterbenden die Hände halten. In der Realität sieht Aichinger ihre in das Vernichtungslager Maly Trostinec bei Minsk verschleppten Verwandten niemals wieder. Vergeblich wartet sie noch lange nach Kriegsende auf deren Rückkehr.
Wo die Wirklichkeit versagt, beginnt das Schreiben. Aichingers Werkherausgeber, der früh verstorbene Journalist Richard Reichensperger, bezeichnet die Literatur der Autorin als »Bergung der Opfer in der Sprache«. Wo Menschen vernichtet wurden, setzt Aichingers Sprache ein Denkmal, das sich gegen das von den Nationalsozialisten intendierte Vergessen stemmt. »Ich erinnere mich der Küche meiner Großmutter«, fängt der Titeltext des 1987 veröffentlichten Buches »Kleist, Moos, Fasane« an, der in das späte Werk vorausweist, in dem Aichinger die ihrem Schreiben zugrunde liegenden Erlebnisse explizit benennt.
Im Spätwerk, das sich großteils aus Zeitungskolumnen zusammensetzt, die ab 2001 in Buchform erscheinen, taucht etwa wieder eine »Brücke« auf, wie sie zum Schluss des frühen Romans symbolisch am Ort des Suizids der Protagonistin steht. In den späten Texten handelt es sich um die Schwedenbrücke, also die Stelle in Wien, die Innenstadt und Leopoldstadt verbindet: In der Leopoldstadt befindet sich im 17. Jahrhundert das Ghetto, von dort fahren 1942 mit Menschen beladene Viehwagen zu den Deportationszügen.
Aichingers Texte des frühen und mittleren Werkes, ihre Prosastücke, Szenen, Hörspiele, Gedichte, die bis in die 90er Jahre erscheinen, werden mehrfach als hermetisch, unverständlich, gar esoterisch tituliert, auch wenn sie der Autorin zahlreiche Literaturpreise einbringen. Aichingers sporadische Interviews, ihr Rückzug aufs Land nach dem Erfolg der »Spiegelgeschichte«, für die sie 1952 Preis der Gruppe 47 bekommt, und der Heirat mit Günter Eich, verfestigen den Ruf der stillen, schwer zugänglichen Schriftstellerin.
Erst nach dem Tod Eichs 1972, mehreren Umzügen und Jahren ohne Publikationen tritt Aichinger im achten und neunten Lebensjahrzehnt verstärkt in die Öffentlichkeit: Sie spricht in Interviews über ihr Leben, das ihrer Verwandten und Freunde und verflicht in Zeitungsbeiträgen Beobachtungen aus dem Kaffeehaus oder einem der mehrmals täglich frequentierten Wiener Kinos mit Erinnerungen zu einer eigenen Art Autobiografie.
Ihr Antrieb bleibt, Realität und Sprache zu »kontern«. Noch im letzten großen Interview aus dem Jahr 2005 spricht sie von ihrem »Zorn über die Welt«, von ihrer Freude am »Anarchischen« und der Notwendigkeit von Rebellion.
