https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: White supremacist Nick Fuentes linked to college Republican group, records show
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jason Wilson
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A college Republican coalition claiming 31 affiliated student groups in 14 states that attacked the Trump administration from the right routed its email through the same Microsoft 365 account as a company controlled by white nationalist Nick Fuentes.
Until Monday morning, Microsoft’s public sign-in records put the College Republican Patriot Coalition (CRPC)’s web domain in an account registered to NJF LLC, a Fuentes-managed company that also runs his personal website and online store.
By Monday evening, hours after the Guardian sent questions to Fuentes and the coalition, the domain no longer appeared in that account, and a Microsoft verification code had been deleted from its settings. Fuentes’s own domains remained in the account.
The organization has hinted at ties with Fuentes in the past, but no operational link has been definitively shown until now.
The revelation of an operational link between Fuentes and the highlights the inroads that Fuentes and his white nationalist “Groyper” movement have made among younger Republican activists and student organizations.
“[Fuentes] advises his young followers to join organizations that are closer to the conservative establishment, and he tells them to ‘hide their power level’ and maybe downplay their kind of most radical ideas,” said Ben Lorber, a senior research analyst at Political Research Associates, a non-profit that researches extremist groups.
The CRPC has not publicly named its leaders and is not associated with any known registered legal or organizational entity.
The Guardian contacted Nick Fuentes and the CRPC for comment.
In social media posts on Wednesday, CRPC blamed Tuesday’s midterm defeats on the Trump administration and the Republican party, saying young voters had received “a war on behalf of Israel, stunted deportations, and a flailing economy”. The statement listed 31 college Republicans groups, including chapters at the University of Florida, Clemson and Iowa State University, and state-level federations in Georgia, Maryland, New York, Tennessee and Virginia.
The coalition’s post-election messaging echoed attacks Fuentes made on Donald Trump before the vote. Fuentes posted on 26 October that Trump had “started a war with Iran that we are not only losing but which also destroyed the economy”. He also reportedly accused Trump of starting the war at Benjamin Netanyahu’s bidding, criticised his failure to deport millions and told viewers of his stream: “Normies don’t like war with Iran. Normies don’t like 3.7% inflation!”
But the group has never admitted the apparent affiliation with the far-right podcaster disclosed by the email link. Simon Dickerman, a former Fuentes associate, said in a 2022 live stream that the coalition “has to pretend like it has nothing to do with Nick Fuentes because Nick has made himself so radioactive to other people”, but the shared Microsoft account is the first confirmed operational link between Fuentes and the coalition.
The Guardian contacted Simon Dickerson for comment.
Many of the groups on the CRPC statement also belong to College Republicans of America (CRA), which is seeking recognition as the Republican party’s official student wing and has publicly contended with the more established College Republican National Committee over who should represent college activists. CRA’s political director, Kai Schwemmer, appears in the coalition’s Instagram posts this year.
The Guardian reported on Schwemmer’s appointment and his history of bigoted statements on live streams in March. (He claims he has abandoned his extremist views.)
The Guardian contacted CRA and Schwemmer for comment on CPRC’s shared email infrastructure with Fuentes’ company.
Lorber, the extremism expert, said of Fuentes’s so-called “America first” movement: “From the very beginning, Fuentes positioned America First as an alternative to Turning Point USA, and so it makes sense that he has a toehold in alternative campus conservative groups that position themselves as more radical than the mainstream GOP campus groups”.
‘A recent antisemitic gesture’
Student groups closely affiliated to CRPC have encountered local controversies, often over their promotion of white nationalist ideas, links to white nationalist activists, and endorsement of political candidates who have themselves voiced views similar to Fuentes’s.
The University of Florida’s College Republicans chapter has co-authored eight Instagram posts with CRPC this year, and was deactivated by the university in March after photographs reportedly appeared to show members flashing Nazi salutes and posing with Fuentes and Myron Gaines, the antisemitic influencer and podcaster.
The university said on social media that the Florida Federation of College Republicans had told it that the state group had “disbanded the local chapter of College Republicans”. The Guardian reported in March that the chapter’s state leadership had cited “a pattern of conduct that violated its rules and values, including a recent antisemitic gesture”.
The chapter sued for reinstatement, and was represented by Anthony Sabatini, the lawyer and former Republican state representative. A federal judge dismissed the Florida case in June after a bench trial, and the CRPC reportedly co-hosted the chapter’s first meeting after the ruling.
Sabatini, a Lake county commissioner who served in the Florida House from 2018 to 2022, headlined a 2022 conference in Tampa that was reportedly organized by former members of Fuentes’s America First Foundation, and reportedly called for a moratorium on immigration, the abolition of the Juneteenth national holiday that celebrates the end of slavery, and telling the crowd: “God bless the nationalist populist movement.”
The Guardian contacted Sabatini, UF College Republicans and the Florida Federation of College Republicans for comment.
‘Who cares about the lying media?’
The Florida chapter’s complaint argued that the university had acted in part because they had hosted the Republican “gubernatorial candidate James Fishback, a critic of Israel”. In a post co-authored with the CRPC, the chapter had called the Fishback event the “Largest Candidate event at UF in almost 10 years”.
Fishback, a 31-year-old investor, finished third in August’s Republican primary for governor. His campaign was peppered with controversies arising from his racist remarks.
He repeatedly referred to Byron Donalds, the Republican congressman who on Tuesday was elected Florida’s first Black governor, as a “slave”. In July, he wrote in a statement that a dispute had led Donalds “to chimp out on a 5’0 blonde woman in a Naples grocery store”, using a slur that likens Black people to apes. Fishback has reportedly said he was “not aware of the history” of the comparison.
On 28 October, Fishback floated a run for president in 2028. The College Republican chapters at Clemson and Georgia State, both on the CRPC’s list, hosted him on 29 and 30 October. On Wednesday, Fishback quote-posted the coalition’s election statement with the words “Great statement”.
The Guardian contacted Fishback for comment.
At the chapter’s first meeting after its return, the speakers included Marshall Rawson, the Republican nominee for a north Florida seat in the state house, who reportedly marched with the neo-Confederate League of the South at the 2017 Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, Virginia. In a statement, Rawson said he had been “very active defending historical monuments” throughout his adult life.
“Who cares about the lying media when the largest and most active College Republican chapter in the United States is behind you!” Rawson posted on X that week, alongside a photo of himself with chapter members. The chapter’s post about the meeting, co-authored with the coalition, also thanked Tim Marden, the chair of the Alachua county Republican party and mayor of Newberry, who has publicly backed Rawson.
The Guardian contacted Rawson for comment.
In an email, Marden wrote: “I prefer to use my relationships as an opportunity to influence people in what I believe is a more positive direction. Life is not an all or nothing scenario.”
‘A non-English-speaking hellscape’
The Maryland Federation of College Republicans, which is on the coalition’s list and co-authored the Instagram version of Wednesday’s statement, invited the white nationalist Jared Taylor to speak at Salisbury University this spring.
Salisbury postponed the talk in March “based on public safety considerations”, saying that anticipated attendance, “counter-demonstrations, and related security needs” had “increased significantly”. It noted that the federation was “not an SU organization” but an outside group renting space on campus. The university’s College Democrats group had planned a protest for the day of the talk. The chair of the Maryland Republican party, Nicole Beus Harris, reportedly said the party had not been involved and condemned “the advertised event and the speaker’s despicable views”.
The talk went ahead on 29 April under heavy security, as dozens of protesters gathered outside at a demonstration organised by the Salisbury College Democrats. Taylor reportedly called the protesters “a bunch of big babies”.
The federation’s then chair, Colin McEvers, at that time a Salisbury student, reportedly introduced Taylor as someone who might have the key to “save our country, to keep it from becoming a non-English-speaking hellscape where white people are spit at, despised and persecuted”. College Republicans of America, which the Maryland federation joined in 2025, said it “did not endorse or sanction the Maryland event”, the Guardian reported in July.
A Facebook account with McEvers’ name in its URL now posts under the name Maryland White Republican Council. On Wednesday, it said: “It is time for the pro-White flank of the right wing that has been censored, suppressed, and cast aside by the establishment to legitimately take the reins of the GOP.”
The Guardian contacted the Maryland Federation of College Republicans for comment.
Asked about his call for “white advocacy” in the Republican party, McEvers responded in an email that despite a failed effort from the Maryland GOP to censure him, he was able “to secure the Republican nomination for Delegate in Maryland Legislative District 32, become a member of the Anne Arundel County Republican Central Committee, and there have been many people within the party, of all age groups, who have come to accept that White advocacy is both acceptable and necessary for Republican success”.
On the Maryland White Republican Council page, he wrote: “White people of all age groups failed to show up for the GOP this year, mostly among young voters. This proves that White people, namely young White men, are a legitimate voting bloc that the Republican Party must explicity advocate for; hence, the White Republican Council, which fundamentally promotes White Advocacy within the GOP in order to get Whites out to vote Republican.”
He denied any direct relationship with the CRPC.
‘A spectacular failure and a disaster’
One of the main public outlets for CRPC is its Instagram account, which features photos of faceless members carrying out flyer drops around the country, memes including racist depictions of Trump administration officials, and retrospective albums of face-to-face meet-ups, many of which redact the faces of members who presumably do not wish to be identified as adherents of Fuentes’s movement.
On the blacked-out faces, Political Research Associates’ Lorber said: “It makes it clear that they [are] associated with a radical right politics that they don’t necessarily want traced to their names and faces right now.”
Fuentes dropped out of Boston University after he was seen at the 2017 Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, and built a following of young men, known as “Groypers,” through his livestreamed show, America First.
He was present at the riot at the US Capitol on 6 January 2021, though he did not enter the building, and in 2022 dined with Trump and the rapper Kanye West at Mar-a-Lago. Trump later said he did not know who Fuentes was.
After being banned from YouTube and many other platforms for hate speech, Fuentes was allowed back on X by Elon Musk in 2024. In October 2025 his podcast briefly became the highest-trending on Spotify, and Tucker Carlson gave him a friendly two-hour interview that the Guardian reported in November had set off “a bitter and widening civil war within the American right”. The president of the Heritage Foundation, Kevin Roberts, apologized after initially defending Carlson’s interview.
Fuentes backed Trump in 2016 and 2020, but has increasingly attacked him from the right over Israel and what he sees as the insufficient radicalism of the Republican party, especially on immigration.
Growing disillusionment has seen Fuentes urge his followers in recent months to disengage from elections or even to vote for Democrats. In February he reportedly told his audience: “Do not vote in the midterms. The Republicans have to lose.” When Trump went to war with Iran, Fuentes condemned the war and mocked people who had voted for Trump believing he represented a break with US foreign policy. On election day he posted: “Get out and vote Democrat today.” On election night, he reportedly said: “This is literally the worst case scenario for Republicans playing out tonight. And honestly, I could not be happier.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Trump-era lawlessness must be prosecuted. Our new group is working to end the impunity | Kenneth Roth
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Kenneth Roth
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The Democrats’ midterm victory was resounding, but it will not be enough to re-establish the rule of law in the United States.
The basic principle that even the president and his officials and cronies are subject to the law has been profoundly undermined by Donald Trump through unchecked ICE violence, apparently large-scale official corruption, and frequent defiance of the law.
Democratic-run congressional committees can investigate and expose lawlessness but cannot prosecute the criminality they uncover. More is needed.
Many people equate democracy with elections, but they are not enough. A president can be elected, his policies can be publicized by the media and debated by the public, his legislative proposals can require the assent of a majority of lawmakers, but if the president holds himself above the law, a nation ceases to be a democracy. That is what has been at stake in Trump’s second term.
The American system delegates many of the responsibilities for upholding the rule of law to an independent judiciary. If a president violates our rights, we can file a civil suit in court and hope a judge orders the president to stop.
But if the president or his allies engage in criminality, the American system has a built-in weakness. Some countries empower prosecutors to be independent, akin to a judge. But in the United States, the prosecutor for any federal crime is an employee of the Department of Justice. It is headed by the attorney general, who is nominated by and serves at the pleasure of the president.
In other words, the president can decide which criminal conduct in his administration will be prosecuted – and which will not.
Because the president’s ability to control the Department of Justice could put him and his friends above the law, presidents traditionally have exercised that power with restraint. While setting broad priorities, most presidents deferred to the judgment of their attorney general. But not Trump.
Trump has weaponized his justice department, pursuing his perceived political enemies while neglecting crimes by his allies, who have often enjoyed effective impunity. They have little to fear from Trump’s politicized prosecutors.
The result has been increasingly brazen behavior – seemingly corrupt deals that few past officials would have dared to make, and arbitrary violence by ICE and others that is excused rather than investigated.
The Rule of Law Project, a new civic group of which I am a founding board member, seeks to end that impunity. We are hiring former federal prosecutors and FBI agents to investigate allegations of corruption and abuse by government officials and their accomplices that the current justice department is ignoring.
We have attracted an extraordinary set of past public servants. Many have served in the justice department, which has been decimated in the second Trump administration. We don’t know their political views and haven’t asked. What we know is that they are eager to continue their work in a different capacity.
The Rule of Law Project operates from the premise that criminal cases are more likely to be pursued if a prosecutor can be handed a case file that is largely ready for action. We will do the legwork of interviewing witnesses, collecting documents, and analyzing the results, with the aim of putting cases together while the evidence is fresh.
We won’t have subpoena power, wiretaps, or a grand jury, but many cases can be built with witnesses who voluntarily cooperate. Indeed, in the most sensitive cases, cooperating witnesses are essential.
Until we have a president and attorney general who believe in the rule of law, we plan to present these ready-made cases to state and local prosecutors, who are not subject to federal control. Many would like to uphold the law but lack the investigative resources to take on these cases on their own.
I have seen the power of such investigations in my global work. For the mass atrocities under Syria’s former president Bashar al-Assad, for example, the international criminal court did not have jurisdiction, and Syrian prosecutors took instructions from the dictator.
The only option was national courts around the world exercising what is known as universal jurisdiction. But a typical prosecutor there would have no clue about how to prosecute torture, executions, or forced disappearances in Syria, let alone the resources to advance such a case.
That’s why, with the encouragement of Human Rights Watch, the UN general assembly established the International, Impartial and Independent Mechanism (IIIM) for Syria. A similar mechanism has been established to address atrocities by the military junta in Myanmar.
The IIIM, based in Geneva, is essentially a prosecutorial team without a court. They have no capacity to bring prosecutions, but they prepare them. That way, when an abusive Syrian official shows up in a national jurisdiction, local prosecutors have a place to turn for the evidence they need.
That happened in the German city of Koblenz, where a former Syrian intelligence officer was convicted of crimes against humanity for overseeing a detention facility where torture was pervasive. He was sentenced to life in prison. The IIIM has contributed to 269 distinct investigations and prosecutions in 16 different jurisdictions, including in France, Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands and the United States.
The Rule of Law Project will play a similar role in the United States. It will develop the prosecution-ready cases that make it harder for available prosecutors to say they are too busy to take on Trump officials’ illegality.
The project will also make it harder to look forward, not back, as Barack Obama erroneously did with respect to the torture and abuse of the George W Bush administration’s “war on terrorism”. In May 2009, I met with Obama to make the case that the failure to hold perpetrators accountable would lead to future abuses. He thought it would be too divisive.
Sadly, that precedent of impunity is contributing to Trump’s lawlessness today, such as the summary execution of people in alleged drug boats that he has ordered in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific.
This is not a vindictive exercise. The project seeks not to even scores but to uphold the law. It will apply an “ordinary times” test – what would a prosecutor do, regardless of the party holding the White House, if they simply analyzed the facts and applied the law free of the politicized limitations of the Trump administration?
What if Trump pardons the culpable before he steps down? That is unlikely to save his accomplices, because the president’s pardon power does not extend to state crimes. Much of the criminality that merits investigation can be characterized as an offense under either federal or state law.
It is extraordinary that the United States needs a group like the Rule of Law Project. But these are extraordinary, even unprecedented, times.
To salvage America’s democracy, it is not enough to vote out corrupt and abusive officials. They should also be prosecuted to re-establish the rule of law.
We cannot count on the federal government under Trump to perform this role. We as citizens must take it on.
- Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120377.title: Repression | Mexiko: Offensive gegen Zapatisten-Gemeinden
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120377.author: Luz Kerkeling
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120377.text:
- Politik
- Repression
Mexiko: Offensive gegen Zapatisten-Gemeinden
Der Staat und die Eliten versuchen, den indigenen Widerstand gegen die umstrittene Autobahn »Route der Maya-Kulturen« zu brechen.
Das renommierte Menschenrechtszentrum Fray Bartolomé de las Casas (Frayba) aus dem südmexikanischen Bundesstaat Chiapas schlägt Alarm: »Wir prangern öffentlich die schwerwiegende Gefahrensituation an, mit der Gemeinden von EZLN-Unterstützer*innen auf ihren wiedergewonnenen Territorien konfrontiert sind«, heißt in einem aktuellen Kommuniqué.
Mehrfach wurden in den vergangenen Tagen Basisgemeinden der sozialrevolutionären Bewegung um die Zapatistische Armee zur nationalen Befreiung (EZLN) bedroht und schikaniert. Teile ihrer Ländereien wurden okkupiert, gemeinschaftlich angebaute Maisfelder und Waldstücke zerstört sowie Rinder geraubt. Es kam auch zu Geldstrafen oder Verhaftungen von Personen, die ihre Kinder in die autonomen zapatistischen Schulen geschickt oder die das unabhängige Gesundheitssystem der EZLN genutzt haben.
All diese Praktiken stehen laut Frayba »im Widerspruch zur Regierungsrhetorik, da es sich um eine Reihe von Maßnahmen zur Aufstandsbekämpfung handelt, die zu einem schwerwiegenden Vorfall wie dem Massaker von Acteal führen könnten.« 1997 wurden in diesem Dorf 45 – explizit pazifistische – pro-zapatistische Bewohner*innen von paramilitärischen Kräften ermordet. Sie hatten direkte Kontakte zu Bundesarmee und -polizei. Die in Sichtweite stationierten staatlichen Sicherheitskräfte griffen nicht ein.
Regierung will freie Bahn für die Autobahn
»Diese Angriffe implizieren eine direkte Bedrohung der Unversehrtheit der Gemeinden, ihres Territoriums und der Ausübung ihrer Autonomie«, so das Zentrum weiter. Sie »finden im Kontext des voranschreitenden Baus der Autobahn San Cristóbal-Palenque – offiziell bekannt als ›Route der Maya-Kulturen‹ – statt, sowie im Zusammenhang mit den fortwährenden Angriffen, die bereits die Vollversammlung der Kollektive der zapatistischen autonomen Regierungen (ACGAZ) öffentlich gemacht haben«.
Aktuell liegen Berichte vor, nach denen der Bau dieser auf Tourismus und Extraktivismus ausgelegten Schnellstraßentrasse intakten Regenwald zerstört und den kleinbäuerlichen Gemeinden durch Korruption, Desinformation und Gewaltandrohung aufgezwungen wird. Selbst eigene staatliche Umweltgesetze wurden laut Frayba nicht ausreichend befolgt. Auch die von Mexiko unterzeichnete ILO-Konvention 169 über indigene Rechte wird demnach permanent verletzt. Vermessungs- und Bauarbeiten mit schwerem Gerät werden auch auf Flächen der Zapatistas weitergeführt.
Spiel mit dem Feuer
Für diese sind das Provokationen der Eliten in einem größeren Kontext: »Dieses Jahr im Juli haben wir unsere Absicht bekanntgegeben, nach Mexiko-Stadt zu reisen, um uns mit den Gruppen, Kollektiven oder Gruppenlosen aus den suchenden Familien zu treffen. Um ihrer Geschichte und der Geschichte ihrer Vermissten zuzuhören: Gruppe für Gruppe, Familie für Familie.«
In ihrem Kommuniqué vom 3. November stellt die Vollversammlung der Zapatistischen Autonomen Regierungen ACGAZ klar: »Die Regierenden spielen mit dem Feuer. Wir wollen keinen Aufruhr machen, wir können es aber. Diese Provokationen zwingen uns nicht, die Reise abzusagen.«
Die Zapatistas werfen der Regierung vor, die Menschenrechtsverletzungen zu dulden und teilweise sogar zu protegieren: »Diejenigen, die provozieren, sind Mitglieder des Kartells um Mario Delgado, Staatsminister für öffentliche Bildung. Der Haupt-Auftragskiller ist Eusebio Cruz Ruiz, der sich als Lehrer präsentiert und sagt, er erhält von Delgado direkte Anordnungen.«
Die »Reise für das Leben« geht weiter
Frayba fordert angesichts der Ereignisse von der Regierung die sofortige Einstellung aller Angriffe auf die zapatistischen Gemeinden sowie die uneingeschränkte Achtung ihres Rechts auf Autonomie und Selbstbestimmung. Ein klares Zeichen für die Bedeutung der aktuellen Mobilisierung der EZLN ist die Solidarität der unabhängigen Gewerkschaft »Nationalkoordination der Bildungsarbeiter*innen« (CNTE) mit »unseren Geschwistern Zapatistas«. In der CNTE sind rund 500.000 Aktivist*innen, hauptsächlich Lehrkräfte, organisiert.
Bei den geplanten zapatistischen Aktivitäten handelt es sich um die zweite Etappe der »Reise für das Leben«, das »Kapitel Mexiko«. Im Rahmen des »ersten Kapitels« der »Reise für das Leben« hatten 2021 über 170 Delegierte der EZLN und des Nationalen Indigenen Kongresses CNI über 250 Städte im »widerständigen Europa« besucht und sich intensiv mit anti-systemischen linken Gruppen ausgetauscht. Zum aktuellen Vorhaben in Mexiko-Stadt ab Dezember stellte Subcomandante Moisés von der EZLN klar: »Wir werden kommen, ob sie es wollen oder nicht.«
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: This small Alaska town is swamped by cruise ship visitors every summer. But what happens when they all go home?
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Molly McCluskey in Skagway, Alaska
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
October comes to the small Alaska coastal town of Skagway like a sigh. The shops that were bustling throughout the crazed tourist season are reducing their opening hours or beginning to close. The hordes of employees sleeping in overcrowded bunkhouses are leaving or have left.
The crowds of cruise passengers who have filled the streets since April, wearing lanyards emblazoned with the names of their ships, have dwindled to a trickle. Soon, they will all be gone. Snow is visible on the nearby mountains.
What is left after the season has ended and the last ship has disappeared from sight is a year-round community of about 1,100 people – on paper, at least – and the concern that, as the demands of the cruise ship industry grow, life in this small town is becoming more and more difficult.
“The year-round economy, the year-round population is one of my bigger concerns as someone who lives here,” says Skagway’s mayor, Orion Hanson. “What does Skagway do without a coffee shop to congregate in or without a restaurant open all the time? We don’t have a diner any more.”
Two local restaurants stay open, albeit with limited hours outside the cruise ship season. But the Sweet Tooth cafe, once a longstanding year-round diner, is gone. It is now a storefront for Diamonds International, a tax-free jewellery store that partners with cruise lines for onboard retail and shops in ports that open seasonally.
At the height of the Klondike gold rush, Skagway was the largest town in Alaska, with a population of about 10,000 people. In 1900, it became Alaska’s first official city. But by 1910, as the gold rush subsided, the population had dwindled to about 600 people.
It took a decade for that dramatic swing. Now, as one of the most popular cruise ship destinations in the world, it can happen in a single day, when thousands can flood on to Skagway’s streets from cruise ships, only to leave again when the sun sets. The most recent figures available show that more than 1.35 million tourists arrived in Skagway by cruise ship in 2025, alongside more than half a million crew – and the numbers are growing each year.
That means housing, services and infrastructure designed for a town of about 1,000 people having to accommodate an influx of thousands of workers who arrive in late winter and stay until early autumn.
“Part of the complication of Skagway is that you have such a boom in the summer and such a lull in the winter,” says Hanson. “In terms of revenue that’s not directly related to cruise ships there is not a lot.
“As we saw during the pandemic, we’re at risk,” he says. “If all your eggs are in one basket, it leaves you very vulnerable.”
Like many tourist towns, Skagway has a housing shortage. Unlike other towns, however, it is squeezed into a narrow valley set at the northern end of Alaska’s Inside Passage, a 500-mile maritime route that hugs the coast along Alaska and British Columbia. It is known for its rugged mountains, forests, glaciers and abundant wildlife; there are no realistic commuting options and no room to expand – the only road leads to Canada.
The Skagway Development Corporation commissioned a report in 2023 that found there were 644 housing units in town. In the years since, more have been added, but not enough for the town to accommodate the cruise ship industry and the businesses that support it, its permanent residents, seasonal employees and the workers and families who keep Skagway’s essential services running.
As a result, everything from warehouses to single-family homes, from tents to recreational vehicles or motorhomes, are accommodating the increasing numbers of seasonal workers each year.
“There’s a lot of congregate living and couch surfing,” says Al Wall, director of the town’s Dahl Memorial Clinic. “There are quite a few people that sleep in hammocks in the woods. And frankly, some would prefer to sleep in a hammock in a tree than stay in a crowded place with a bunch of people.”
In years past, many seasonal workers slept in camp sites. But a change in the town’s law forbidding season-long camping pushed them into traditional homes that previously housed the town’s established population.
Janilyn Heger, a longtime Skagwegian, owns the town’s distillery, Skagway Spirits. She and her husband Gary, who owns a construction company, once managed the town-owned camp sites.
“The city made the decision for whatever reason to abandon that type of housing, and that created a domino effect that has been a disaster for the community,” she says.
“Employers started buying buildings and displacing year-round housing and so now we’re at an absolute standstill. There’s none to be had.”
Skagway’s housing shortage has become so severe that many of the town’s limited hotels have been converted into accommodation for seasonal employees.
Longtime resident Mike Healy bought Sergeant Preston’s hotel from friends when he was unable to find land to build enough employee housing to meet his businesses’ needs.
“I didn’t want to purchase Sergeant Preston’s … I approached the city and said, hey, Municipality of Skagway, I am going to purchase the only year-round hotel in this community if you don’t free up some land for housing.”
Healy, not receiving an answer, duly converted the hotel into seasonal housing, part of a portfolio that provides off-season accommodation to visiting workers and contractors.
Jonathan Hillis, a town assembly member who owns the local Mountain Shop outdoor gear store, says that pattern is playing out across town.
“We have very few places now for independent travellers to stay, which is fostering this kind of cycle of more and more cruise ship tourists and fewer independent travellers.”
The scale of cruise tourism is a frequent topic of debate in towns throughout the Inside Passage. As the 2026 season winds down, these towns are consulting the docking schedules for 2027 and 2028, making note of the projected increase in tourism, and asking how much they can realistically handle.
One hundred miles south of Skagway in Alaska’s capital, Juneau, there have been repeated attempts to limit cruise ship tourism. After a ballot measure for “ship-free Saturdays” failed in 2024, the city introduced a voluntary limit on the number of ships that could dock daily.
Farther south in the Inside Passage, Ketchikan has reported more ships as a result of cruises adhering to Juneau’s limitations, while Sitka, also on the cruise ship destination trail, is reviewing its agreements with the industry after an anticipated increase in visitor numbers in 2027.
A survey conducted by Oregon State University reveals a nuanced position when it comes to the cruise sector in Skagway. Just over 40% of people who responded thought that the benefits of tourism outweighed the costs, compared with 25% who put it the other way round. Another 33% viewed the relationship as roughly balanced.
Whatever the sentiment, for a small town that is economically dependent on one industry for its livelihood, options are limited.
“There’s only so much we can do, even if we wanted to,” Hanson says. “We need to be incredibly careful about not rocking the boat.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: ‘The many v the money’ should frame the next US Congress
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Naomi Klein
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Welcome back to How We Win, a Guardian opinion series with leading thinkers, offering bold ideas for America’s political future. Last week, Judd Legum shined a spotlight on the role of dark money in US elections. Today’s edition was written by Naomi Klein, Guardian US columnist and author of End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World, co-written with Astra Taylor.
To see the battle lines of the post-midterm era in sharp relief, look to Texas.
Just two days after her earthquake victory as the governor-elect, Gina informed reporters that she had already asked the parks and wildlife department to freeze a proposal to sell 1,300 acres (525 hectares) in a state park to SpaceX until she is sworn into her new office. The department complied with her request.
The Boca Chica state park is next door to Starbase, Elon Musk’s rocket launch facility and company town. That makes the park’s beaches and protected lands – a refuge for shore birds and sea turtles – the ideal location for SpaceX to expand.
“These are our beaches we’re talking about. I mean, selling our beach to Elon Musk is just something that is almost unimaginable,” Hinojosa told CNN’s Jake Tapper. “It’s unacceptable. Our beaches are enshrined in our Texas constitution as being free and open to the people of Texas.”
This was not about shutting down “Elon Musk and his companies”, she went on, “but it has to be on our terms. It cannot be just running over the people of Texas. And that’s what changes now that I will be governor.”
When Hinojosa’s clips circulated on X, she was roundly mocked by Musk’s many fans: imagine valuing some “empty beaches” more than the need for ocean-front launchpads to the stars! Imagine caring more about some lowly birds than Musk’s hulking, phallic, silver rockets! She must be a [insert vomitorium of misogynistic, racist and ableist slurs here]. Musk, his boys and bots predicted, will just pick up his expensive toys and move them to still-Republican Louisiana or Florida, leaving economic carnage in his wake.
So far, Hinojosa seems unmoved. In Texas, she and Senator-elect James Talarico shaped their campaigns as battles of the many v the money, a vertical struggle pitting the vast majority of Texans, struggling to get by, against the increasingly concentrated wealth at the top – perfectly embodied by the man flooding their democracy with cash. As Talarico reminded an audience of supporters in Austin last month: “Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator.”
The richest man in the world didn’t get his senator, or his governor, as the early clash over Boca Chica state park makes clear. What he did get – or rather, help produce – is an America polarized around a new political axis. On one side are ultrarich tech oligarchs, whose wealth is tethered to dreams of merging with machines and becoming multiplanetary, no matter the cost to our multispecies planet. On the other side are regular people, with human needs for things such as clean air, fresh water and healthcare – maybe even a day off at a public park – and who increasingly find themselves competing over these basics with sprawling datacentres and rocket launchers.
The oligarchs in this battle have no loyalty to the nations, states and cities that helped them grow their enormous wealth, thus the threats that Musk will soon ditch Texas if its newly elected representatives dare to keep their promises to voters (just as he dumped California and Canada before that). If all else fails, maybe he will join his friend Peter Thiel in Argentina, which Javier Milei is rapidly turning into techno-libertarian laboratory (Interestingly, Tesla just launched an Argentine division.)
 The oligarchs in this battle seem to have no loyalty to the nations, states and cities that helped them grow their enormous wealth.
In sharp contrast, the masses of people in this battle, regardless of their political leanings, tend to be attached to where they live – to its cities, towns, public lands and to the only planet that we know of suited to human life. This is as true in Texas as it is in Tirana, Albania, where, under the banner of the “flamingo revolution” citizens have been in revolt for months against a different set of oligarchs who laid claim to a different beloved wildlife refuge for their private benefit.
In our book End Times Fascism, Astra Taylor and I characterize these as fights between “the leavers v the stayers” – and we make the case that they increasingly define our age. You can see these fault lines running through a great many of the hot-button issues that animated and energized this election cycle. There were the many ballot measures to tax the super-rich to pay for basic services, and entirely predictable tantrums from billionaires who threatened to pick and leave rather than pay up. There was the muscular, national backlash against artificial intelligence and datacenters, which focused on the ways this latest (final?) capitalist stage is devouring art, literature, incomes, lands, energy and wellbeing. (As the Guardian reported, “Voters approved nearly every datacenter moratorium that was on the ballot, dozens in total.”)
The commitment to place, and to one another, was equally evident in the rage at the US war-of-choice in Iran, and at Israel’s genocide in Gaza, with many winning candidates including Abdul El-Sayed consistently stressing that the money being spent to kill children far away should be used to care for children at home, and that all children are equally deserving of life and opportunities.
Similar dynamics were there, too, in the revolt against ICE: As Minnesota’s Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan said in her victory speech, the movement that lifted her to power all began when Minnesotans decided to stand up to “masked goons shooting our neighbors”. And the faultlines were clearest of all in the white-hot anger at the legalized corruption at the heart of the US political system, now widely understood as the wellspring producing all the other depravities.
Writing in this space one month ago, Rebecca Solnit astutely characterized the midterms as “a referendum on the GOP’s alignment with tech overlords over the public they’re meant to serve”. Well, the results are in and they could scarcely be more decisive. The complicating factor, however, is that it is not only the GOP that is aligned with the tech overlords and their anti-human, anti-Earth agenda. Plenty of powerful Democrats have chosen to underwrite their political campaigns and their personal wealth portfolios by entangling themselves with the very individuals and corporations their voters just roundly and unequivocally rejected.
Shamefully, the campaign to defeat a California ballot measure that would have imposed a much-needed, one-time 5% tax on billionaires – one of few places where tech oligarchs clocked a victory last week – was only successful because powerful Democrats including outgoing governor (and presidential hopeful) Gavin Newsom sided with the billionaires (as did the incoming governor). Meanwhile, several Senate Democrats have joined with Republicans to push through a sweeping bill in the current lame-duck Congress that would dismantle a host of environmental protections and be a bonanza for fossil fuel companies and the datacentres that burn them.
This kind of betrayal is the surest path for Democrats to turn their historic midterm victories into entirely predictable defeats before the highly consequential 2028 presidential election.
In Texas, Hinojosa is showing a better way. By picking an early fight pitting public beaches against Musk’s private rockets, she is telling voters which side she is on – the side of life, not machines; the side of staying, not leaving. That is how the Democrats just won, and it is their path to continue winning.
Want to hear more from our contributors?
Follow them on Substack and elsewhere: Stacey Abrams, Robert Reich, Paul Krugman, Naomi Klein, Mehdi Hasan, Bernie Sanders, Rebecca Solnit, Katie Phang, Judd Legum, Wajahat Ali, Margaret Sullivan and Charles Blow.

https://www.humanite.fr/societe/mouvemen.title: « Le rapport de force est de notre côté, il faut continuer » : après avoir claqué la porte de Matignon, lycéens et étudiants dans la rue ce mardi
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/mouvemen.author: La rédaction
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/mouvemen.text:
Lycéens, étudiants et enseignants appellent à une nouvelle journée de mobilisation et de manifestations ce mardi 10 novembre. La veille, les organisations de jeunesses ont claqué la porte du comité de réforme de Parcoursup pour dénoncer la présence de l’extrême droite alors que, de son côté, le gouvernement n’avait rien de neuf à mettre sur la table.
Pas plus que les syndicats de travailleurs (avec son maigre « coup de pouce » au Smic), Sébastien Lecornu n’a convaincu les lycéens et étudiants qu’ils recevaient lundi, dans la foulée de la Conférence sociale. Face à l’absence de réponses du gouvernement à la hauteur des exigences défendues depuis bientôt deux mois, leurs différentes organisations – de même qu’une intersyndicale de l’Éducation nationale – appellent à redescendre dans la rue dès ce mardi 10 novembre.
« Le rapport de force est de notre côté, il faut continuer. Je ne dis pas qu’on a des victoires, mais je dis qu’on tient le bon bout », a jugé lundi soir Ryad Rani, président de l’Union syndicale lycéenne (USL), après la rencontre avec le premier ministre.
Après avoir rencontré le locataire de Matignon, étudiants et lycéens ont claqué la porte du comité de réforme de Parcoursup en raison de la présence de l’extrême droite (des membres de l’Uni et du RN) et du Medef. Tous sont cependant restés assez longtemps pour constater que le gouvernement n’avait rien de neuf à leur annoncer. La transformation progressive de Parcoursup dès 2027, avant son remplacement complet en 2028, déjà promise il y a 15 jours, a tout du ripolinage.
« C’est le moment d’amplifier la mobilisation »
« Le gouvernement ne prend toujours pas au sérieux nos revendications. Ce ne sont pas des annonces sur la transparence des algorithmes locaux et sur la lisibilité de Parcoursup grâce à des vidéos faites par l’IA pour mieux expliquer comment on est sélectionnés entre le lycée et l’université qui vont répondre à nos revendications », a dénoncé auprès du Monde Éloïse Lefebvre-Milon, secrétaire générale de l’Union étudiante.
Seule innovation de la journée : « des cours de rattrapage » qui pourront être organisés pendant les vacances scolaires, « en février » ou « à Pâques », selon le ministre de l’Éducation nationale qui n’a pas précisé quels moyens seraient dégagés pour les mettre en place. Édouard Geffray a, en revanche, de nouveau menacé de sanctions les élèves mobilisés sur les blocages – faute de répondre à leurs revendications.
Face à l’inertie savamment entretenue de l’exécutif, « l’idée, c’est d’avoir une journée de mobilisation au sens large, avec des grèves, des manifestations et des rassemblements » pour « offrir un rebond à la mobilisation de la jeunesse avec des cortèges encadrés, sécurisés alors que devant les lycées, ça commence à pas mal se tendre », a de son côté expliqué à l’AFP Sophie Vénétitay, secrétaire générale du Snes-FSU, premier syndicat dans le second degré.
« C’est le moment d’amplifier la mobilisation en continuant à mettre le gouvernement sous pression », avait fait valoir dans un communiqué l’intersyndicale CGT, FSU, FO, Solidaires, Union syndicale lycéenne, Unef, Union étudiante, Fage et FSE, après le 5 novembre où 1,6 million de personnes ont manifesté.
Dans l’Éducation nationale, la grève « s’annonce suivie à certains endroits », a estimé la responsable syndicale, tout en reconnaissant que la mobilisation devrait être moins importante que celle du 5 novembre, où près de 16 % des enseignants s’étaient mis en grève selon le ministère. Des manifestations sont prévues dans la plupart des grandes villes de France. À Paris, un cortège partira à 14 heures de Panthéon en direction de la Place d’Italie.
Aux côtés de celles et ceux qui luttent !
L’urgence sociale, c’est chaque jour la priorité de l’Humanité.
- En exposant la violence patronale.
- En montrant ce que vivent celles et ceux qui travaillent et ceux qui aspirent à le faire.
- En donnant des clés de compréhension et des outils aux salarié.es pour se défendre contre les politiques ultralibérales qui dégradent leur qualité de vie.
Vous connaissez d’autres médias qui font ça ?  
Je veux en savoir plus !

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/am.title: American Alliance of Museums Makes Case for Policy Proposals Following Democrats’ Landslide Election Win
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/am.author: Harrison Jacobs
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/am.text:
Since President Donald Trump returned to office last year, his administration has made reining in the cultural sphere a core plank of his agenda.
Those efforts have included slashing federal funding for the National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH) and the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA); attempting to remake the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., in his image; and unleashing a relentless barrage of executive orders, attempted firings, and investigations targeting the Smithsonian Institution and its affiliated museums. The campaign reached a fever pitch in July, when the White House released a 162-page report detailing supposed “ideological capture” at the National Museum of American History. Two congressional hearings followed, in which lawmakers grilled the museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, over her perceived failure to uphold the institution’s mission.
The American Alliance of Museums (AAM), a leading industry group for museums, has steadfastly defended cultural institutions facing Trump’s wrath, rebuking the administration’s efforts in public statements.
Now, with the political winds shifting and Democrats having secured their biggest midterm election victory in decades, AAM isn’t wasting time. In a statement released November 4, the day after the election, the organization said it plans to push the newly elected Congress to restore or increase funding for the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS), as well as for the NEA and NEH. (Trump’s proposed 2025 budget would have decimated IMLS, but following an advocacy campaign led by AAM, and legal challenges from the American Library Association and the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, its budget was largely restored.) AAM also called for lifting the House Appropriations Committee’s current ban on earmark funding for museums.
Asked about the organization’s priorities for the incoming Congress, an AAM spokesperson told ARTnews, “We’re focused on continuing to build strong bipartisan support for museums, protecting federal funding for museums, and ensuring museums can fulfill their educational missions without political interference which is an important part of the conversation for the entire field.”
AAM did not offer details on how Congress might prevent political interference in the museum field. In late September, a group of Democratic lawmakers led by Representative Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico introduced a bill to protect the independence of the Smithsonian Institution, a measure AAM endorsed. At the time, Devon Akmon, chair of AAM’s board, said of the bill, “Protecting the Smithsonian’s scholarly independence honors that public trust and affirms a principle fundamental to all museums: scholarship and interpretation must be guided by evidence, expertise, and professional standards, not political influence.” The bill has not advanced since its introduction and will need to be reintroduced when the new Congress convenes in January.
On December 2, AAM will host a live webinar with Brandy Dillingham, its director of advocacy, and Nichole Westin, its senior director of government and field relations, on how the election results may affect museums.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.title: The Secret Handshake’s Latest Statue Mocks President Trump for Toe-Related Deferment to Avoid Vietnam War Draft
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.text:
One of the five deferments President Donald Trump received to avoid being drafted for the Vietnam War is now the subject of a new statue mocking him by the Secret Handshake, an anonymous artist collective. On Monday, a gold statue appeared on the National Mall depicting Trump sitting down and holding his right foot, reports the Washington Post.
The plaque at the base of the statue says, “We honor the service and sacrifice of our Commander in Chief, Donald J. Trump. He’s a soldier in spirit, who marched to the front lines of dodging the draft, armed with a perfect diagnosis of bone spurs,” a reference to the deferment in question.
The inscription adds, “We salute a leader who knows you can’t spell sacrifice without ‘I,’ and a warrior who reminds us that sometimes when you’re called to stand up, it’s best to just sit down and rest your feet.” The statue has been named The Foot Soldier.
The statue was accompanied by a mascot, a masked individual in a big-toe costume that had nine hairs and their name “TOEY” printed in block letters. “I’m the biggest toe. The hugest toe. Huge. Hugest toe. Largest toe that anyone’s ever seen,” says Toey, concealing their identity and repeating things such as “Draft dodger? I hardly know her.”
In a statement on Monday responding to the work’s installation, White House spokesman Davis Ingle said, “Trump Derangement Syndrome is a sick and incurable disease that has rotted the brains of these Democrat activists. President Trump will never waver in fighting for and protecting the American people.” During the Vietnam War, Trump received deferments, four of them being for his studies in college.
The Foot Soldier is the latest work by the Secret Handshake, whose work has been taunting the president since 2024. They include a pile of feces; an 8-foot-tall sculpture of a gold-painted hand squashing the green crown of the Statue of Liberty; and a statue of Trump holding hands with disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein, which has repeatedly been reinstalled throughout D.C.
On Monday, the group said that as Trump “continues to wage a war and threaten new ones, it’s time to harken back to a time when Donald Trump would do whatever it takes to stay out of combat.”

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/zo.title: Zohran Mamdani Visited MoMA’s West African Modern Architecture Survey and Loved It
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/zo.author: Alex Greenberger
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/zo.text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has continued his social media campaign to stump for exhibitions staged by the city’s museums, this time focusing on a survey of West African modernist architecture at the Museum of Modern Art, whose praises he sang on Instagram early this morning.
Titled “Architects of Liberation: Modernism in Western Africa,” the 400-work show surveys architectural projects in Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Togo, Benin, Nigeria, and Cameroon produced during a period of decolonization that began in some countries in the late 1950s. Curated by Martino Stierli and Ikem Stanley Okoye, the show features architectural models and archival imagery, as well as some contemporary artworks.
“visited @themuseumofmodernart this weekend and am still thinking about their exhibition ‘architects of liberation: modernism in western africa,’” wrote Mamdani in his post.
He specifically singled out Kader Attia’s 2014 sculpture Indépendence Tchao, a sculpture composed of rows of rusting index card boxes that the Algerian French artist obtained from a French colonial police headquarters. They are topped with a sign reading “HOTEL INDÉPENDENCE,” a reference to a similarly named hotel in Dakar, Senegal.
Mamdani wrote that the sculpture asks the question: “to what extent were the visions of the independence era achieved?”
It’s the second museum presentation Mamdani has posted about in the past month. In October, to celebrate his birthday, Mamdani visited the Studio Museum in Harlem, where he took in Taylor Simmons’s painting The Hypnotist (2026). Mamdani called the work by Simmons, a current participant in the museum’s storied artists-in-residence program, “just incredible.”

https://taz.de/Nach-der-Parlamentswahl-i.author: Marina Klimchuk
https://taz.de/Nach-der-Parlamentswahl-i.text:
Nach der Parlamentswahl in Israel: Der Anfang vom Ende?
Die neue israelische Knesset tritt zum ersten Mal zusammen. Eine Regierung ist noch nicht gebildet, doch handlungsunfähig ist die Opposition nicht.
Es könnte das sein, worauf viele Israelis kaum noch zu hoffen wagen: der Anfang vom Ende der Ära Netanjahu. Oder auch ein weiterer vergeblicher Versuch, den Regierungschef abzulösen, der seit 2009 mit nur einer Unterbrechung an der Macht ist. Am Sonntag hat Israels Präsident Itzhak Herzog den Chef des Oppositionsblocks, Gadi Eisenkot, mit der Regierungsbildung beauftragt. Dafür hat er zunächst 28 Tage Zeit. Am Dienstag ist nun die 26. Knesset, das neu gewählte israelische Parlament, zu ihrer konstituierenden Sitzung zusammengekommen.
46 der 120 Abgeordneten ziehen erstmals ins Parlament ein. Viele dieser Neuen haben eine direkte Verbindung zum Massaker des 7. Oktobers 2023 – als Angehörige von Opfern oder Armeereservist:innen etwa. Mehr als drei Jahre danach prägt dieser Tag die israelische Gesellschaft und Politik.
Zwar gibt es in der neuen Knesset eine Mehrheit gegen Netanjahu. Doch die Parteien, die ihn ablösen wollen, müssen sich erst auf eine gemeinsame Regierung einigen. Scheitert die Regierungsbildung, könnten erneut Wahlen anstehen. Und Neuwahlen, das lehrt die Geschichte, enden fast immer mit Netanjahus Machterhalt.
Auch ohne neue Regierung ist die Knesset jedoch handlungsfähig. Sie kann Ausschüsse bilden und Gesetze verabschieden, während Netanjahus bisherige Regierung die Amtsgeschäfte weiterführt.
Erster Amtsakt der Opposition: Knesset-Sprecher ablösen
Der oppositionelle Block des Wandels will den bisherigen Knesset-Sprechers Amir Ohana ablösen. Ohana ist ein enger Verbündeter Netanjahus. In die Kritik geriet er unter anderem wegen seines erniedrigenden Umgangs mit Angehörigen der Opfer des 7. Oktobers. 2025 hinderten Parlamentswachen Angehörige gewaltsam am Zugang zur Besuchertribüne. Ohana entschuldigte sich anschließend bei den Betroffenen.
Am Dienstag gab das Oppositionsbündnis seinen Kandidaten für Ohanas Nachfolge bekannt: Matan Kahana von Eisenkots Partei Jaschar. Der Einigung gingen tagelange Verhandlungen voraus. Nach einem Bericht des israelischen Nachrichtenportals Ynet soll Kahana das Amt zunächst während der Regierungsbildung übernehmen.
Die Wahl des Knesset-Sprechers ist die erste Bewährungsprobe für die Zusammenarbeit der Opposition. Auch deshalb ist dieser Posten so umkämpft. Wer ihn besetzt, bestimmt Tagesordnung und Ausschussbesetzung, kann Gesetzesinitiativen vorantreiben und aufhalten.
Kahana ist 54 Jahre alt. Schon in frühen Jahren schloss er sich als Jugendbetreuer der nationalreligiösen Bewegung Bnei Akiva an. Vor seiner politischen Karriere diente er in einer Spezialeinheit und als Kampfpilot der Luftwaffe. 2019 zog er für das rechte Bündnis Jamina in die Knesset ein. In der großen Koalition unter der Führung von Naftali Bennett und Yair Lapid, die nur ein Jahr hielt, von 2021 bis 2022, war er Religionsminister. Später wechselte er zu Benny Gantz’ Nationaler Einheit; 2025 verließ es die Knesset. Jetzt kehrt er zurück.
Kreative Wege zur Koalition
Weder Netanjahus Bündnis noch Eisenkots Block verfügt allein über eine Mehrheit. Gemeinsam mit der arabisch geführten Gemeinsamen Liste und der Partei Ra’am käme Eisenkots Bündnis jedoch auf 67 Sitze – genug, um einen Nachfolger für Ohana zu wählen. Beide unterstützen seine Ablösung. Für die Gemeinsame Liste sagte Ahmad Tibi heute zu, für Kahana zu stimmen. Ob Eisenkots Bündnis sich auf eine Koalition mit den mehrheitlich arabisch geprägten Parteien einlässt, ist allerdings fraglich. Als weitere Option steht eine Koalition mit der Partei Vereinigtes Torah-Judentum im Raum.
Netanjahu klammert sich derweil wie an ein sinkendes Boot an die Erzählung, die Wahl sei von den arabischen Parteien „gestohlen“ worden. Er ruft zu einer großen Koalition auf. Mit einer solchen würde Gadi Eisenkot gegen sein Wahlversprechen, Bibi abzulösen, verstoßen.
Auch auf Kandidaten für weitere Schlüsselposten hat sich das Eisenkot-Bündnis derweil verständigt: Der rechte und säkulare Avigdor Liberman soll den Außen- und Verteidigungsausschuss leiten, Liran Avisar Ben-Horin von B’Yachad den Finanzausschuss und Roy Folkman von Jaschar den vorläufigen Organisationsausschuss. Mit den Nominierungen demonstriert das Bündnis: Wir können auch ohne fertige Regierung handeln.
Innenpolitisch brodelt es in Israel. Eine zentrale politische Priorität der Wähler:innen ist das Versprechen der Opposition, eine unabhängige, staatliche Untersuchungskommission zu den Versäumnissen rund um den 7. Oktober 2023 einzurichten, die Netanjahu bisher ablehnt.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: UK counter-terrorism police arrest senior US soldier with alleged links to Russia
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Nadeem Badshah
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
A US soldier with alleged links to Russia has been arrested by British counter-terrorism police.
The man, 41, was arrested as part of an investigation by counter terrorism policing, working closely with US authorities, the US military and the FBI, counter terrorism policing London said.
US army counterintelligence command said the allegations related to a “senior soldier”.
The man was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday on suspicion of offences under section one and section three of the National Security Act and remains in custody at a London police station.
As part of the investigation, officers were carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire, the Metropolitan police said.
The BBC reported that the soldier was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire. The barracks serve as the headquarters of Nato’s allied rapid reaction corps.
The FBI director, Kash Patel, said in a statement the arrest “involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies”.
He added: “While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message – this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners.
“This includes 167 counterintelligence and espionage arrests from this FBI over the last 21 months – a 53% increase.
“This matter shows that partnerships are essential to protect our countries and I want to express my thanks to UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence, and the U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command for their outstanding work.”
The investigation is not linked to any other ongoing counter-terrorism policing investigations.
Deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for counter terrorism policing, said: “The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing.
“This activity demonstrates the strength of our UK and US law enforcement and national security partnerships, and I commend the work of all the teams involved.
“We will work together to take robust action against those we suspect of any criminal activity that could undermine our national security.”
Brig Gen Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US army counterintelligence command, said the alleged conduct “of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent”.
He added: “I encourage anyone who thinks they’ve witnessed something suspicious to report it to their local counterintelligence office.”

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.title: Only Known Handwritten Draft of Martin Luther King Jr.’s ‘I Have a Dream’ Speech Could Top $10 M. at Christie’s
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.author: Harrison Jacobs
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.text:
Christie’s announced Monday that it will offer the only known handwritten manuscript of Martin Luther King Jr.‘s 1963 speech at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, better known as the “I Have a Dream” speech.
The manuscript has seven yellow pages of King’s handwriting, including edits and cross-outs. It will be offered in a single-lot sale on January 22, 2027. The lot will carry an estimate on request, though Christie’s said it expects the manuscript to sell for more than $10 million.
In a statement, Peter Klarnet, a manuscripts specialist at Christie’s, called the piece “a treasure of American history.”
“When I first saw these pages, and realized what they were, I was astounded,” Klarnet said. “It gives you chills to look at it. Reading along, you’re there in the moment with Dr. King, watching him compose it and making edits in real time. It captures a moment that literally changed the course of our nation and makes it very real and very human. It’s an honor and privilege that Christie’s has an opportunity to present it to the world.”
According to Christie’s, the pages were found in a desk drawer that belonged to Edward T. Clayton, head of public relations for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC), the civil rights organization King led until his assassination in 1968. Clayton was also a speechwriter and editor for King and helped write the speech. His wife, Xernona Clayton, a civil rights leader and philanthropist, found the manuscript in the late 1990s. She recognized the speech but didn’t know it was the only handwritten final draft, so she put it back in her late husband’s desk. In 2024, she and her adviser, Eddie Bridgeman, brought the manuscript to Christie’s.
“I’m just glad I looked in the drawer,” Xernona Clayton said in a statement. “The two of them gelled with writing and words. They would go back and forth and there was such respect. Dr. King, who was a great thinker, said Ed was so good at getting his words on paper and putting them in the right place at the right time. I enjoyed watching them. I was privileged, and now the world will have the opportunity to see those words of wisdom that continue to inspire hope, freedom, and the pursuit of equality.”
The handwritten manuscript doesn’t include the words “I have a dream,” because King famously improvised that part of the speech. It does include his famous conclusion: “Free at last, free at last; thank God almighty, we are free at last.”
Christie’s said proceeds from the sale will go to charities “furthering the legacies of Ms. Clayton and Dr. King,” including the Xernona Clayton Foundation and the King Center in Atlanta.
“We are also grateful to join with Ms. Clayton to ensure that the sale of this draft helps support the great work of The King Center and our mother, Mrs. Coretta Scott King, who would be 100 this upcoming year,” Bernice A. King, the Kings‘ daughter, said in a statement.
	The manuscript will be on view at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta from November 16–22. It will then be shown at Christie’s New York from January 15–21.

https://taz.de/Geraeuschlose-Regierungsb.text:
Linksbündnis in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern : Kein Modell, aber eine Chance
Geräuschlos wurden in Schwerin die Koalitionsverhandlungen für eine Rot-Rot-Grüne Landesregierung abgeschlossen. Einfach nachzuahmen ist das nicht.
S tell dir vor, es ist Rot-Rot-Grün – und keiner dreht durch. Kaum vorstellbar bei der teils irren Debatte über eine mögliche Regierung in Berlin, aber genau das ist Manuela Schwesig in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern nun gelungen. Ist der Nordosten eine Ausnahme – oder ein Vorbild für den Bund?
Zunächst fallen die Unterschiede ins Auge. Im Schweriner Landtag ist Rot-Rot-Grün alternativlos, die Parteien sind zum Regieren verdammt. Zudem sind die Kräfteverhältnisse klar. Die SPD ist fast dreimal so groß wie Linke und Grüne zusammen. Um es mit Gerhard Schröder zu sagen: Es ist klar, wer Köchin ist und wer ihre Kellner.
Das schlägt sich im Koalitionsvertrag nieder. Der ist im Ton wohltuend menschenfreundlich und enthält kleine Fortschritte: Bahnfahren soll für Jugendliche günstiger, Abschiebungen aus Schulen sollen „vermieden“ werden. Andere grüne und linke Forderungen, etwa ein ambitionierteres Ziel für die Klimaneutralität, fehlen. Wie überall gilt: Es muss gespart werden.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Wer Schwerin nun zum Leuchtturm erhebt, tut das womöglich aus politischer Nostalgie: Hach, wenn die SPD noch Volkspartei wäre, wenn Linke und Grüne nur ohne Murren mitmachen würden, dann wäre ein Bündnis ja kein Problem. Aber so einfach wird es wohl nirgendwo anders. Welche der drei Parteien nach der nächsten Bundestagswahl am stärksten sein wird, ist offen. Wenn es dann etwas werden soll mit einem Linksbündnis, müssten sich drei Köche einigen.
Auch inhaltlich sind die Hindernisse größer. Bei der Unterstützung der Ukraine ist aktuell kein Kompromiss vorstellbar. Auf Umverteilung könnte man sich dagegen wohl einigen. Der Zeitgeist ist eben nicht nur rechts, in dieser Frage haben sich die Parteien angenähert.
Ansonsten dürften die Parteien unterschiedliche Schlüsse ziehen: Für die Linke eignet sich Schwerin kaum als Modell. So günstig wie dort kann sie sich anderswo nicht verkaufen. Ihren Wahlsieg in Berlin etwa hat sie radikaleren Forderungen zu verdanken. Für SPD und Grüne dagegen ist jedes rot-grün-rote Bündnis eine Chance: Sie können beweisen, dass sie sich nicht auf Gedeih und Verderb an die Union klammern. In aktuellen Umfragen ist ein Linksbündnis die einzige Alternative. Selbst wenn die politischen Differenzen am Ende doch zu groß sind, sollten SPD und Grüne daran arbeiten, diese Möglichkeit offen zu halten. Sonst verlieren sie Wähler, die ein „Weiter so“ mit der Union nicht wollen.
Denn auch das zeigt die neue Koalition in Schwerin: Wenn die sogenannte Mitte schrumpft, kann ein Linksbündnis Stabilität bedeuten. Für die Union ist das, siehe Sachsen-Anhalt, noch nicht ausgemacht.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ju.title: Julia Stoschek Collection to Celebrate 20 Years with ‘Selfish in Bed’ Exhibition and Düsseldorf Reopening
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ju.author: Daniel Cassady
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ju.text:
Sarah Lucas doesn’t appear particularly apologetic in her 2000 self-portrait Selfish in Bed II. Standing with her hands on her hips, the British artist wears a black T-shirt with the words “SELFISH IN BED” printed across the front. Next April, that cheeky photograph will set the tone for a major group exhibition celebrating the 20th anniversary of the Julia Stoschek Collection in Düsseldorf, Germany.
Aptly titled Selfish in Bed, the exhibition opens on April 10, 2027, and will bring together 52 works by 43 artists, including Tracey Emin, Bill Viola, Wolfgang Tillmans, and Bruce Nauman. Selfish in Bed marks the inaugural exhibition of the reopened Julia Stoschek Foundation’s Düsseldorf headquarters, which closed for renovations in April 2025.
Curated by Krist Gruijthuijsen, the director of Finland’s EMMA – Espoo Museum of Modern Art and former director of Berlin’s KW Institute for Contemporary Art, the show looks at how we construct our identities, express our sexuality, and present ourselves to the world.
The exhibition takes the bed as its starting point. It’s a place increasingly of contradictions: It’s private and vulnerable, yet inter-connected, where we spend hours scrolling through the images and opinions that shape how we see ourselves. The show explores that tension through works spanning the late 1960s to the present, including several that the foundation has never exhibited before.
There are more than a few highlights. Emin’s Why I Never Became a Dancer (1995), Simon Fujiwara‘s Joanne (2016/2018), and Hannah Wilke’s Through the Large Glass (1976), all explore women’s relationships with their bodies, sexuality, and public image. Meanwhile Monica Bonvicini‘s Destroy She Said (1998) challenges traditional domestic roles, and Ed Atkins’s Us Dead Talk Love (2012) examines questions of identity and authenticity in the digital age.
The exhibition is set to span two floors, and include video projections, mirrored surfaces, glass walls, and television monitors creating an immersive environment. Works by Viola, Tillmans, and Rosemarie Trockel will be presented together in a grouping that explores the human experience from birth onward.
For Stoschek, whose collection now includes more than 1,000 works by over 300 artists, the anniversary is also an opportunity to reflect on two decades of collecting.
“I am a very emotional collector,” Stoschek said in a statement. “An artwork has to get under my skin. I need images that stay with me.”
The Düsseldorf headquarters, housed in a converted industrial building dating to 1907, has undergone an extensive renovation by Berlin architecture firm Kuehn Malvezzi, which originally adapted the space for exhibitions in 2007. In Berlin, the foundation closed its exhibition space at the end of October after a decade of programming, shifting its attention toward Düsseldorf and international projects.
A publication marking the collection’s 20th anniversary will accompany the exhibition, with contributions from writers and critics including Rachel Cusk, Chris Kraus, Dean Kissick, and McKenzie Wark.
Selfish in Bed will run from April 10 through December 19, 2027, with an opening reception on April 9.

https://taz.de/Ansturm-auf-Elektroautos/.title: Ansturm auf Elektroautos: Mehr Förderung und längere Förderzeiten
https://taz.de/Ansturm-auf-Elektroautos/.author: Bernward Janzing
https://taz.de/Ansturm-auf-Elektroautos/.text:
Ansturm auf Elektroautos: Mehr Förderung und längere Förderzeiten
Der Bund will nächstes Jahr mehr Geld für die Förderung der Elektromobilität geben. Ein spezieller Fördertopf ist bereits leer.
Die hohen Spritpreise zeigen Wirkung: Immer mehr Menschen wollen ein E-Auto haben, die Hersteller kommen deswegen mit der Produktion nicht mehr nach. Im Oktober waren 37 Prozent aller Neuzulassungen von Pkws in Deutschland reine Elektroautos. Zählt man die Hybrid-Modelle noch hinzu, hatten im Oktober sogar 75 Prozent der Neufahrzeuge Elektroantrieb.
Die Nachfrage nach Elektroautos sei so groß, dass es „bei einzelnen Modellen aktuell zu einer Verlängerung der Lieferzeiten“ kommen könne, räumt auch der Verband der Automobilindustrie ein. Die Unternehmen passten aber „ihre Produktionskapazitäten entsprechend der Nachfrage an, um Lieferzeiten möglichst gering zu halten“. Das Branchenportal Carwow benennt Lieferzeiten, die bei einzelnen Modellen bei einem Jahr und mehr liegen.
Angesichts der unerwartet hohen Nachfrage will die Bundesregierung nach einem Bericht der Nachrichtenagentur Reuters im kommenden Jahr deutlich mehr Geld für die Förderung von Elektroautos bereitstellen als ursprünglich geplant. Statt der vorgesehenen 803 Millionen Euro sollen nun für die Kaufprämie im Jahr 2027 sogar 1,72 Milliarden Euro veranschlagt werden.
Das gesamte Programmvolumen soll aber offenbar nicht erhöht werden. Das kann dazu führen, dass der vorgesehene Etat deutlich vor dem geplanten Ende 2029 ausgeschöpft ist. Seit dem Programmstart im Mai wurden bisher im Mittel rund 4.400 Euro pro Fahrzeug bezahlt. Bei einer angesetzten Fördersumme von 3 Milliarden Euro dürfte das Geld somit für rund 680.000 Fahrzeuge reichen. Zum 1. Oktober waren bereits fast 98.000 Zuschussanträge bewilligt und 432 Millionen Euro ausbezahlt, davon gut 200 Millionen allein im vorangegangenen Monat.
Tesla Model Y am häufigsten gefördert
Laut Zahlen des Bundesamts für Wirtschaft und Ausfuhrkontrolle entfielen die meisten Förderzusagen auf Modelle des Volkswagen-Konzerns, gefolgt von Stellantis und Tesla. Betrachtet man die Marken der Konzerne separat – also zum Beispiel VW und Audi –, steht Tesla an der Spitze der geförderten Hersteller. Der Tesla Model Y ist mit fast 8.300 geförderten Exemplaren das beliebteste Modell überhaupt.
Zugleich boomte der Bau von geförderten Ladeboxen. Die entsprechenden Fördermittel sind deswegen bereits ausgeschöpft. Am Dienstag schloss das Bundesverkehrsministerium das Programm „Ladeinfrastruktur in und an Mehrparteienhäusern“. Für Wohnungseigentümergemeinschaften war das Programm bereits am 2. November beendet worden.
Auslöser des Elektrofahrzeug-Booms sind neben der staatlichen Förderung und der ausgeweiteten Modellpalette – allein von deutschen Herstellern gibt es inzwischen mehr als 110 Modelle – die hohen Treibstoffpreise. Diese lagen nach Zahlen des Wirtschaftsverbands Fuels und Energie im September für Benzin bei durchschnittlich 2,31 Euro und für Diesel bei 2,37 Euro. Andererseits ist das Laden eines E-Fahrzeugs auch nicht jederzeit günstig: Kunden, die für ihre heimische Ladesäule einen dynamischen Strompreis gebucht haben, bezahlten in diesen Tagen in der Spitze fast 1 Euro pro Kilowattstunde – in jenen Stunden nämlich, in denen bei fehlender Sonne und wenig Wind ein Drittel der deutschen Stromerzeugung aus Erdgas stammte.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/abu-dhabi/.title: Guerre en Ukraine : un groupe de hackers biélorusse affirme que 400 000 Russes sont morts depuis 2022
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/abu-dhabi/.author: Vadim Kamenka
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/abu-dhabi/.text:
À Abu Dhabi, les négociations ont débuté ce mardi 10 novembre entre les États-Unis, la Russie et l’Ukraine pour tenter d’avancer sur un processus diplomatique. Si certains évoquent la possibilité de cessez-le-feu locaux, la bataille autour du nombre de morts se poursuit. Des groupes de hackers évoquent un bilan de 400 000 morts russes entre février 2022 et l’été 2026.
En pleine négociation diplomatique à Abu Dhabi, entre Washington, Kiev et Moscou, un chiffre met en avant la réalité de la guerre. Plus de 400 000 Russes auraient trouvé la mort au combat en Ukraine depuis l’invasion, le 24 février 2022. Ces informations ont été obtenues par le groupe de hackers biélorusse « Cyber Partisans », lié à l’opposition, et par le collectif ukrainien « Silent Crow », qui ont piraté l’agence nationale des statistiques Rosstat le 1er novembre.
Ils ont eu « accès à plus de 11 millions d’actes de décès, comprenant notamment l’âge des défunts, leur lieu de résidence et le lieu de leur décès », explique le journal du Guardian qui a récupéré une partie des données.
