https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Republicans elect Jim Jordan as House minority leader after midterm defeats
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Chris Stein in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Republicans have elected veteran congressman Jim Jordan as their new leader in the House of Representatives, putting a strident defender of Donald Trump at the helm of their conference as they navigate the fallout from sweeping losses in last week’s midterm elections.
Jordan will serve as minority leader under the new Congress that begins next year, where Democrats will have their largest margins in both the House and Senate in years. He will be responsible for shaping the party’s strategy against the waves of investigations Democrats have promised to open into Trump’s second administration, as well as their vows of an ambitious legislative agenda, regardless of whether it has the president’s support.
“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families,” Jordan said in brief remarks to reporters after his elections. “When Democrats offer more government, we’ll offer more freedom, and we will bring that fight in committee, on the floor, and on the stump every single day.”
The Ohio lawmaker is a longtime leader of the right wing in the US House, and gained national renown for standing up for Trump against earlier efforts by Democrats to hold him to account. In 2023, Jordan was briefly a candidate for speaker after dissident Republicans removed Kevin McCarthy as the chamber’s leader, but his bid collapsed after it became clear he did not have enough support.
House Republicans elected Jordan over Steve Scalise, who serves as majority leader in the current Congress. Following comprehensive defeats last week in the midterm elections, the current House speaker, Mike Johnson, announced he would not remain in leadership, and has thus far not committed to serving out the rest of his term.
“Jim was a mentor of mine when I first came to Congress 10 years ago, and we worked alongside one another all these years,” Johnson said. “He’s always been regarded as a leader by the conference, and he’s going to do an extraordinary job.”
Jordan will serve alongside John Thune, the Republican Senate leader who also won re-election from his conference on Tuesday.
“I’m proud of what this Republican team has accomplished together, and we remain united in our commitment to advancing conservative priorities, working with President Trump and our colleagues in the House, and holding the line against Democrats’ efforts to enact their far-left, liberal agenda,” Thune said in a statement.
Elections for both roles were held in behind-closed-door meetings.
Ahead of the House GOP’s meeting, several spoke of the need for a change in strategy, after two years spent trying to answer Trump’s demands with one of the smallest majorities in history, only to have voters decisively remove them from power.
“I want somebody that’s going to message and admit that … we made mistakes,” said Tim Burchett, a conservative lawmaker from Tennessee, who declined to say who he would be voting for.
Florida congresswoman Anna Paulina Luna said she was backing Jordan, and blamed Scalise for not fighting hard enough to get rightwing priorities through the chamber.
“If you have a play and you get destroyed, you don’t put the same people back in charge that were part of running that failed play,” she said.
First elected in 2006, Jordan helped found the rightwing House Freedom Caucus in 2015, and served as its first chair. Seen almost always in shirtsleeves, his profile rose during Trump’s first term, particularly after Democrats regained control of Congress’s lower chamber in the 2018 midterms. As the top Republican on the oversight and then the judiciary committees, Jordan made energetic stands against efforts by Democrats to investigate Trump, and served as a member of the president’s defense team during his first impeachment.
Jordan echoed Trump’s false claims of fraud in the 2020 election, and championed the investigation of Hunter Biden during Joe Biden’s final two years in office. Since Trump returned to the White House, Jordan has used his role as judiciary committee chair to pursue allegations of “weaponization” by prosecutors who investigated Trump, including Jack Smith, the special counsel who oversaw the federal cases.
Democrats decried Jordan’s appointment as sign that the party was doubling down on extremism, with Virginia congressman Don Beyer noting that Jordan’s election came days after Trump had named immigration hardliner Stephen Miller as his chief of staff.
“Republicans learned absolutely nothing from what happened a week ago, and are responding by elevating their most extreme voices to positions of power,” he said.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Em mais um adiamento de obra, Tarcísio de Freitas culpa chuva por atraso no Rodoanel Norte
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O governador de São Paulo, Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos), culpou a chuva pelo descumprimento da promessa de entregar a obra finalizada do trecho norte do Rodoanel até o final de 2026.
“Não foi possível, choveu muito. Você sabe que você não faz obra de terraplanagem com chuva, você não faz obra de pavimentação com chuva. A gente realmente depende do tempo para poder avançar e avançar com qualidade, porque, obviamente, você tem que fazer uma obra que vai durar”, disse o governador em coletiva nesta terça-feira (10).
Com isso, o trecho norte do Rodoanel deve ser entregue somente em abril de 2027, como estava previsto antes de Tarcísio prometer a obra para 2026, durante a campanha eleitoral. Segundo a Agência Reguladora de Transporte do Estado de São Paulo (Artesp), a obra está 80% concluída.
O trecho faltante do Rodoanel Norte tem cerca de 20 quilômetros e vai ligar a Rodovia Fernão Dias à região de Perus. São quatro faixas de rolamento em cada sentido, dez túneis, que somam aproximadamente dez quilômetros de extensão, além de 43 pontes e viadutos.
A construção do Rodoanel começou em 1998, durante o governo de Mário Covas (PSDB). As obras do trecho Norte foram iniciadas em 2013, mas ficaram paralisadas por seis anos devido a investigações de um esquema de corrupção.
Adiamento do Metrô
Na semana passada, Tarcísio de Freitas também adiou a entrega das estações Brasilândia e Itaberaba-Hospital Vila Penteado, que compõem o segundo trecho da Linha 6-Laranja do Metrô na zona norte da capital paulista.
As duas paradas haviam sido prometidas pelo governador para o mês de outubro, durante a inauguração do primeiro segmento da linha, realizada em 2 de julho, no limite do prazo estipulado pela legislação eleitoral para a participação de candidatos à reeleição em entregas de obras públicas.
Apesar do descumprimento do prazo anunciado, a concessionária Linha Uni e a Artesp não definiram uma nova data para a abertura das estações.

https://taz.de/Prozess-gegen-Patricia-Sc.title: Prozess gegen Patricia Schlesinger: Dit kann dauern
https://taz.de/Prozess-gegen-Patricia-Sc.author: Anne Fromm
https://taz.de/Prozess-gegen-Patricia-Sc.text:
Prozess gegen Patricia Schlesinger: Dit kann dauern
In Berlin hat der Prozess um die ehemalige RBB-Intendantin Patricia Schlesinger begonnen. Der Vorwurf lautet Untreue. Die Verteidiger widersprechen.
Patricia Schlesinger lächelt. Mit schnellen Schritten bahnt sie sich am Dienstagmorgen mit ihren zwei Anwälten den Weg durch eine Menschentraube. Journalisten stehen da, Kameras, Besucher und Unterstützer von Schlesinger. Einem Besucher winkte sie zu, einem anderen wirft sie eine Kusshand zu. Entspannt sieht sie aus, siegesgewiss. So betritt sie um kurz nach halb 10 einen der größten Säle im Berliner Landgericht.
Ab heute wird hier verhandelt, was als einer der größten Skandale des öffentlich-rechtlichen Rundfunk gilt. Die Generalstaatsanwaltschaft wirft Schlesinger und drei Mitangeklagten vor, das Vermögen des RBB geschädigt zu haben.
Insgesamt sollen die vier den Sender um 1,8 Millionen Euro gebracht haben, es geht um Untreue und Betrug. Im Zentrum der Anklage steht dabei nicht mehr all das, was den Skandal vor vier Jahren so juicy gemacht hatte: italienisches Edelparkett in der Chefetage, Massagesessel für die Mitarbeiter und ein protziger Dienstwagen. Die Berliner Generalstaatsanwaltschaft klagt in erster Linie ein System aus Gehaltszuschlägen an, das unter Schlesinger ausgebaut wurde und die Gehälter der Führungsriege aufgebessert hat.
Angeklagt ist Schlesinger nicht allein, mit ihr stehen der ehemalige Verwaltungsdirektor des Senders Hagen B., die ehemalige Justiziarin Susanne L. und der ehemalige Vorsitzende des Verwaltungsrats Wolf-Dieter W. vor Gericht.
Sieben besonders schwere Fälle
Die Angeklagten haben zum Teil schon mehrere Prozesse hinter sich – arbeits- und zivilrechtliche. Auch Schlesinger hat bereits vor einem Berliner Gericht mit dem RBB gestritten, unter anderem um ihre Ruhegeldzahlung und um die Frage, ob sie ihrem ehemaligen Sender Schadenersatz zahlen muss. Das, was das Berliner Landgericht nun, vier Jahre nach Schlesingers Abberufung als RBB-Intendantin verhandelt, ist die Strafsache.
Die Berliner Generalstaatsanwaltschaft wirft Patricia Schlesinger vor, zwischen 2018 und 2022 in 26 Fällen das RBB-Vermögen geschädigt zu haben, bei den anderen Angeklagten geht es um weniger Fälle. Siebenmal soll es dabei um besonders schwere Fälle gegangen sein.
Ab April 2019 sollen sechs Mitglieder der Geschäftsleitung, darunter Schlesinger selbst, die angeklagte Justiziarin und der Verwaltungsdirektor jährlich Zielvereinbarungen getroffen haben. Hatten sie diese voll oder teilweise erreicht, gab es einen Jahresbonus.
Kleinteilig dröselt die Oberstaatsanwältin am Dienstagmorgen auf, wer wann wie viel Bonus bekommen haben soll. Es sind Summen zwischen 27.000 und 56.000 Euro, die die Führungsriege vier Jahre hintereinander zusätzlich zum Jahresgehalt erhalten haben soll. Insgesamt seien dabei 933.505 Euro brutto gezahlt worden, 223.722 Euro allein an Schlesinger, so die Anklage.
Verteidiger attackieren
Unzulässig seien auch die Zulagen gewesen, die Schlesinger und der Verwaltungsratschef für die Übernahme des ARD-Vorsitzes ausgehandelt haben. Turnusgemäß hatte der RBB 2022 den Vorsitz der ARD übernommen. Dafür gewährte der Sender den Mitgliedern der Geschäftsleitung jeweils 1.700 Euro brutto monatlich zusätzlich.
Das Pikante daran: Der Verwaltungsrat, der für die Kontrolle und Aufsicht der RBB-Finanzen zuständig ist, soll weder von diesem neuen Vergütungssystem noch von den tatsächlich ausgezahlten Boni gewusst haben. Damit hätten Schlesinger und der Verwaltungsratschef W. gegen das Gebot der Wirtschaftlichkeit und Sparsamkeit des Senders verstoßen. Schlesinger, argumentiert die Staatsanwaltschaft, habe sich damit „eine nicht unerhebliche weitere Einnahmequelle verschaffen“ wollen.
Die Anklage umfasst 498 Seiten, 46 davon werden im Gerichtssaal verlesen. Danach ergreifen die Verteidiger der Angeklagten das Wort und attackieren die Generalstaatsanwaltschaft. Alle Verteidiger weisen die Vorwürfe vehement zurück.
Dabei bestreitet niemand, dass das Bonussystem eingeführt und Zulagen für den ARD-Vorsitz gezahlt worden seien. Nur sei es falsch, dass die entscheidenden Aufsichtsgremien dem nicht zugestimmt hätten. Die Staatsanwaltschaft habe in ihrer dreijährigen Ermittlung nicht einmal Mitglieder des Verwaltungsrats vernommen. Diese hätten bestätigen können, dass der Verwaltungsrat dem Zulagenwesen zugestimmt hatte.
Den RBB zu einem modernen Sender machen
Schlesingers Anwalt Oliver Sahan wirft der Generalstaatsanwaltschaft „gezielte Einseitigkeit“ in den Ermittlungen vor. Die Verteidiger von Wolf-Dieter W. und Hagen B. zitieren aus Protokollen von Verwaltungsratssitzungen aus dem Jahr 2018, aus denen hervorgehe, dass nicht nur der Verwaltungsrat, sondern auch der Rundfunkrat mit der Zahlung der Boni einverstanden gewesen sein müssen.
Leistungsbezogene Vergütung, sagt der Verteidiger von Wolf-Dieter W., sei ein anerkanntes Instrument in öffentlichen Unternehmen. Deren Einführung beim RBB habe dazu gedient, den RBB zu einem modernen Sender umzubauen.
Fast läppisch wirken im Gegensatz zu dem Bonussystem zwei weitere Teile der Anklage gegen Patricia Schlesinger. Dabei geht es um Abendessen mit der Berliner Hauptstadtprominenz und um eine London-Reise mit ihrem Ehemann. Schlesinger hatte regelmäßig in ihrer Wohnung Dinner in kleiner Runde veranstaltet. Mit dabei war zum Beispiel der Leiter der Münchner Sicherheitskonferenz, ein anderes Mal die Berliner Polizeipräsidentin oder der Vorstandsvorsitzende der Charité.
Schlesinger hat diese Essen, bei denen nicht für alle Teilnehmer immer klar gewesen sein soll, dass es sich um berufliche Essen gehandelt habe, über den Sender abgerechnet. Minutiös trägt die Staatsanwältin vor, um welche Essen es gehe: Datum, Uhrzeit, Ort und Bestellungen von Schlesinger („Tischwäsche, Geschirr und Gläser“, in einem Fall „gehobenes Essen“), was es zu trinken gab – hier stolpert die Staatsanwältin, als sie die Namen der Weine vorträgt, jedenfalls: „Alkohol in nicht unerheblichen Maße“. Insgesamt habe Schlesinger den Sender mit diesen Essen um 4.871 Euro gebracht. Eine London-Reise mit ihrem Ehemann, die den Sender 1.650,62 Euro gekostet haben soll, soll privat gewesen sein.
Warum so lange verhandelt wird
Aber auch hier widerspricht Schlesingers Anwalt: Die Abendessen hätten dem Auftrag einer Intendantin entsprochen, ihren Sender nach außen zu repräsentieren und sich in der Stadt zu vernetzen. Die London-Reise sei nicht privat gewesen, sondern hatte das Ziel, dass sich Schlesinger mit Kollegen der BBC vernetzt. In beiden Fällen sei es legitim gewesen, über den Sender abzurechnen.
Das Gericht hat 56 Verhandlungstage angesetzt, sie reichen bis in den Sommer 2027 hinein. Eine Gerichtssprecherin erklärte die lange Verhandlung damit, dass das Verfahren mit seinen vier Angeklagten, vielen Zeugen und Dokumenten, die zu hören und sichten sein werden, sehr komplex sei.
Für die Verteidiger von Schlesinger und der anderen Angeklagten hingegen ist klar: Die Verhandlung werde deswegen so lange dauern, weil die Generalstaatsanwaltschaft ihre Ermittlungsaufgaben im Vorfeld der Verhandlung nicht gründlich geführt habe.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.propublica.org/article/ruido.title: I Was There to Document the Aftermath of Deadly Flooding. Then, It Started Raining.
https://www.propublica.org/article/ruido.author: Cengiz Yar
https://www.propublica.org/article/ruido.text:
Three summers ago, over Father’s Day weekend, my family and I went camping in the Lincoln National Forest, just a few hours drive north of our home in El Paso, Texas. It’s a beautiful area that’s long served as a getaway for the region, with skiing in the winter, and golf and hiking in the summer. My daughter played under the trees, and I rode my bike down mountain trails that, I noticed, seemed concerningly dry.
The next evening, after we left to drive home, two fires started in forests surrounding the town of Ruidoso, New Mexico, around 25 miles away from where we’d been. I watched horrifying videos online of fire lapping the mountains behind the village’s strip malls and parking lots. The fires were eventually suppressed by a combination of human effort and the late summer monsoon season. But when the downpour of rain hit the burnt landscape around Ruidoso, it created another problem: Recurring floods then ripped through town, damaging homes and infrastructure, and leading to emergency rescues.
The following summer, the scene repeated. On July 8, 2025, monsoon rain hit a burn scar and quickly swelled the Rio Ruidoso and its tributaries. Three people — two of them children — lost their lives.
Reporter Abe Streep, a member of ProPublica’s Southwest office, and I met in Ruidoso to report on what happened. Ruidoso is a place built on tourism, with a paid (rather than volunteer) fire department staff and its own disaster manager. How could two children and a man be swept to their deaths in a place that appeared equipped to handle such disasters?
In two stories ProPublica recently published, Abe answered those questions. He found that, after the 2024 fires, experts warned the town of increased flash flooding risks. Initially, local and state leaders considered a relocation plan for some homes and businesses that would get people out of harm’s way, but the project faltered. Instead, village leaders continued promoting tourism to the town, and the mayor even chastised residents for warning of floods on social media. Abe also reported that, while local and state officials insisted the emergency response to the flood was admirable, first responders say the three deaths could have been avoided. The responders told Abe that village leadership left them understaffed and inadequately equipped to contend with the flooding.
The Village of Ruidoso did not respond to detailed written questions about its emergency response, and it has not publicly released a report on rescue efforts during the flood. Reached by phone, the fire chief, Cade Hall, disputed our reporting but declined to provide specifics. Mayor Lynn Crawford has said protecting the village includes balancing public safety with tourism, the lifeblood of its economy. But in an interview last year, Crawford said to Abe and me: “Who’s to blame? I didn’t start the fire.”
My role as a photographer was to document Ruidoso as the story unfolded — to visualize the people and place at the center of it. It’s a role I’ve had countless times in my career, but this story hit unexpectedly close to home. I could imagine my own family caught unaware in a similar situation, trying to escape the El Paso summer heat but instead navigating an unfathomable disaster.
When Abe and I started reporting, we met people from the community and out of town who tried to help. I watched as New Mexico National Guard service members loaded sand bags into families’ cars, people prepared hot meals for those who had been displaced and volunteers handed out donated supplies from collection centers.
While we were reporting one afternoon, it started raining. Fear swept through me. Our phones lit up with flood warnings from the National Weather Service. We knew we should take them seriously.
Abe and I sought refuge in a local brewery perched high above the river basin. Before we knew it, the water from that thin little creek of Rio Ruidoso became a torrent. The rushing water rose quickly. It swept through the river valley right under the brewery, carrying what looked like trees and debris with it.
Still, I wanted to photograph the river up close. I left the safety of the brewery and let the heavy rain cover me as I moved closer to the river. As I made photos that afternoon and throughout the rest of the trip, questions about my own safety ran through my mind: Would the water keep rising? If it did, could I get to high ground? And, notably, would I have enough warning?
In hindsight, I realize these questions were largely about whether I could trust the systems in place to keep me and others safe. And as Abe kept reporting over the next year, the more those questions felt valid.
Last month, Abe and I traveled again to Ruidoso. The town felt lighter and less ominous. Much of the ruin had been removed or rebuilt. Grass and sagebrush sprouted on a burn scar. Tourists wandered around a lively downtown on a Friday afternoon. People seemed to be moving on from the terror of the previous year.
But Stephanie and Sebastian Trotter still carry the scars of the day. They lost their two children, Sebastian Rowan, 7, and Charlotte, 4, in the Ruidoso flooding.
There is now a memorial for them and Benjamin “Tim” Feagin, the third person who died, at the RV park where they had been camped. But I wanted to see for myself the places where each of them was found. I felt that making photos of those places could help people connect with the reality of their deaths as well as their lives. So, early one morning, I walked along the floodplain trying to find the locations Abe had shared with me.
I got to the bridge where a firefighter found Sebastian Rowan. There was no marker, no indication that anyone’s body had been found there.
Then I went looking for the area where Charlotte was found. I wandered under pine and cottonwood, through knee-deep grasses and wild sunflowers. Crows cawed overhead, and the early morning sun broke through the trees. I stood there for a while, admiring the beauty, awed by the sadness of the river’s trickle.

https://hellgatenyc.com/barn-owls-upper-.title: Evicted Upper West Side Barn Owls Are Doing OK—For Now
https://hellgatenyc.com/barn-owls-upper-.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/barn-owls-upper-.text:
Despite an unceremonious, sudden, and possibly illegal eviction, it seems like the young barn owls of upper Manhattan will be OK.   
A parliament of barn owls had been nested in a hole in the roof of the rickety water tower of an Upper West Side apartment building—but late last week, birders noticed workers doing construction on the roof of the water tower, destroying the nest that the owls had built.  
Birder David Lei told Hell Gate that the fledglings being raised in the disrupted nest began roosting out in the open on nearby buildings last week, which was unusual, he explained. 
"That owl should have been roosting in a more sheltered location, like on an air conditioner windowsill, something like that," Lei said. "But it was out in the open, fully exposed. Songbirds had been bothering it during the day, just natural behavior. But you know, a hawk could have seen it and attacked it."
Lei said that management at 15 West 75th Street had told the residents that they were doing "scheduled maintenance" on the water tower. The building's management did not respond to Hell Gate's request for comment by publication time, but we will update this story if they do.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Guillaume Cerutti named president of the Palace of Versailles
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Alexandre Crochet
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
After eight months without a president, the Palace of Versailles finally has a new leader. Guillaume Cerutti, 60, has been named the president of the prestigious institution, according to the newspaper Politico. A graduate of France’s elite École nationale d’administration (ENA) and a former senior civil servant in the finance ministry, he succeeds Christophe Leribault, who was appointed president and director of the Louvre in February following the abrupt departure of Laurence des Cars.
The appointment marks Cerutti’s return to public service after two decades in the private sector. In a twist of fate, he is following in the footsteps of his former mentor, Jean-Jacques Aillagon, who headed the Palace and National Estate of Versailles from 2007 to 2011. Cerutti worked closely with Aillagon for many years, first at the Centre Pompidou, where Aillagon was the president from 1996 to 2002, and later as his chief of staff when Aillagon became France’s culture minister in 2002. “Having worked alongside Guillaume [Cerutti] for decades, I know he has all the experience and qualities needed to lead Versailles,” Aillagon told Le Monde.
Cerutti went on to put his management skills to work in the art market, becoming head of Sotheby’s France in 2007. In 2015, he was poached by François Pinault, who appointed him president of Christie’s operations in Europe, the Middle East, Russia and India. Just months later, he was promoted to global chief executive of the auction house. At both Sotheby’s and Christie’s, Cerutti built a reputation as a formidable cost-cutter. He also proved adept at steering Christie’s through difficult market conditions.
His next move within the Pinault empire, however, was less successful. In January 2025, Cerutti was appointed president of the Pinault Collection, which oversees the Palazzo Grassi and Punta della Dogana in Venice, as well as the Bourse de Commerce in Paris. Once again, he was following in the footsteps of Aillagon, who had held the same position in the 2010s. But, as Le Monde reports, Cerutti’s efforts to impose the kind of financial discipline he had introduced at Christie’s, coupled with his wish to slow the pace of acquisitions, brought him into conflict with Pinault, who was used to running his collection on his own terms. Barely a year later, Cerutti was forced to step down.
He now assumes one of the most coveted positions in French cultural life, taking charge of a historic palace, museum and gardens that welcomed 8.4 million visitors in 2025 and employ around 1,000 people. His extensive connections in the worlds of business, culture and politics could prove particularly valuable as Versailles faces mounting budgetary pressures and an ever-greater need to secure support from wealthy patrons.
- This article was originally published in The Art Newspaper France

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Hochul Made Big Gains in NYC’s Blue Wave — Except in These Neighborhoods
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Kennedy Sessions, Haidee Chu
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Almost 2 million New Yorkers cast their ballots in this year’s gubernatorial election, 218,453 more than in 2022. The increase in voters helped Democratic incumbent Gov. Kathy Hochul safely secure another term, as she trounced Republican Bruce Blakeman in New York City, 76% to 24% with 97% of scanners counted.
Nationwide, Democrats rode an historic blue tsunami to control of the House and Senate. That lifted the party in New York City too, as many of its blue neighborhoods got bluer — and some of its red ones went blue too. Hochul gained votes in 92% of neighborhoods in the city compared with her 2022 effort.
In that election, Hochul beat Republican Lee Zeldin, 69% to 30% in New York City, but lost some 675,000 votes compared with Andrew Cuomo’s haul in 2018 — hemorrhaging voters in many neighborhoods.
Hochul’s biggest advance in 2026 was in South Williamsburg. There, she gained 45 percentage points over the 2022 election. Other notable neighborhoods that saw a blue swing were Borough Park, Bronx Park, Queensboro Hill and Sunset Park.
Hochul did lose ground in a handful of neighborhoods, however — nearly all of them in Manhattan, in areas among the most exposed to the new pied-a-terre tax. The contentious city tax targeting luxury second homes was announced by Hochul and Mayor Zohran Mamdani in April, signed into law in May and has since faced multiple legal challenges.
The governor lost seven percentage points in Carnegie Hill in Manhattan’s Upper East Side compared to her last showing in 2022 — the most of any neighborhood. Tribeca followed with a five percentage point decrease. The vast majority of these neighborhoods that inched toward the right nonetheless turned out overwhelmingly for Hochul overall.
Here are four more takeaways from the gubernatorial general election data:
Hochul Flipped These Neighborhoods
Hochul flipped 22 neighborhoods from red to blue from 2022, according to Board of Elections data. Besides South Williamsburg, some of the biggest leftward shifts came in Queensboro Hill, Sunset Park and Bensonhurst, where Hochul saw a 20 percentage point jump from 2022.
Not one neighborhood in the city flipped from Democrat to Republican.
Did Mamdani Voters Turn Out?
Ahead of the 2025 mayoral primary, then-candidate Zohran Mamdani urged New Yorkers to register to vote, drawing thousands of new voters to the polls. According to the Board of Election records, those same voters who registered last year came out in droves to cast their ballots in this year’s general election at a rate that almost matched the number of voters who registered in 2024, a presidential election year.
Voters who registered as part of Mamdani’s 2025 wave were just as likely, or more likely, to turn out this year as voters who registered ahead of the last three presidential elections. They were 6% of the overall 2026 electorate.
Millennials Beat Gen X in Voter Turnout
Millennials, born between 1981 and 1996, made up the second-largest voting group this election — beating Gen Xers, born between 1965 and 1980, voter records show. Younger neighborhoods also overwhelmingly voted for Hochul, according to CUNY’s Center for Urban Research. Overall, Hochul gained seven percentage-points compared to the 2022 election in districts where more than a quarter of voters are under 30.
Millennials accounted for 27% of the general election voters, or 528,809 votes, while Baby Boomers, born between 1946 and 1964, were the largest voting group, edging out millennials by just two percentage points. Gen Xers cast 25% of the total ballots.
Hochul Gained Most in Asian and Latino Neighborhoods
Hochul made inroads across all racial and ethnic groups — but especially in Asian and Latino neighborhoods. Compared with the 2022 gubernatorial race, the governor picked up 11 and seven percentage points in election districts where at least 40% of the vote-eligible population is Asian and Latino respectively, according to the Center for Urban Research.
Notably, nearly all the Latino neighborhoods that made a strong showing for Trump in 2024 voted for Hochul, and many of the Asian neighborhoods trending that way did the same. Overall, Hochul won 73.08% of votes in neighborhoods where more than half the population is foreign-born, according to Documented.

https://hellgatenyc.com/the-real-housewi.title: 'The Real Housewives of New York City' Act…Normal?!
https://hellgatenyc.com/the-real-housewi.author: Katie Way
https://hellgatenyc.com/the-real-housewi.text:
In case you haven't noticed, it's fall. Daylight has been saved; full dark hits before the workday ends. In just a few days, the idyllic stretch of weather we basked in all October will be nothing but a distant memory, little comfort in the face of November's chill. This week's RHONY episode, Season 16, Episode 9, was filmed sometime in the spring. But because it features the cast members wearing scarves and light jackets as they make their windswept way across the city, it feels, somehow, seasonally appropriate. 
And I don't know if it's just the approaching holiday season making me more charitable, but this week's episode was also surprisingly nice to watch, given how little actually happened in terms of moving the "plot" of the season forward. 
RHONY S16 has been about constructing a plausible friend group of cast members, something the previous two seasons failed at spectacularly. In that regard, despite my grousing, I think this week proved that the project was a success. Finally, after two pretty excruciating years of franchise triaging, it doesn't feel totally random that these women are gossiping with each other over lunch, or attending each others' birthday parties, because most of them seem to have some kind of actual connection to each other.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Democrats Would Be Insane Not to Break With Israel Now
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Hamid Bendaas
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Democrats Would Be Insane Not to Break With Israel Now
The party has an unequivocal mandate to fundamentally change the US-Israel relationship.
The definition of insanity, famously, is doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results. This should certainly be what Republican strategists are thinking to themselves after launching a needless, illegal, failed, and wildly unpopular war in the Middle East that, just like in 2006, has handed the Democratic Party control of the Senate and a commanding majority in the House in this week’s midterm elections.
Vice President JD Vance released a statement Wednesday morning that served as a rapid autopsy, naming the war with Iran and resultant rising prices as top reasons for Republicans’ generational wipeout. He also cited the United States’ relationship with Israel. These, of course, are not separate issues. In March, the State Department wrote that it had launched the Iran War in large part at Israel’s request (Benjamin Netanyahu having finally found a president foolish enough to fulfill his decades-long desire for this exact war). And the impunity that the US granted Israel for its ongoing genocide of Palestinians in Gaza, its invasion of Lebanon, and its aggressive strikes against its neighbors—including US allies like Syria and Qatar—fueled the arrogance that led to the Iran conflict.
Vice President Vance’s pointed statement was surprising in its seeming disloyalty to his boss. But in saying that voters wanted to, in his words, “change our relationship to Israel,” Vance was only reflecting a truth that millions of people have known for years—even if some within the Democratic Party still might not want to admit it.
In fact, the most glaring issue with Vance’s comments might be that they’re two years late. Americans didn’t just want a fundamental break with Israel in 2026. They wanted one in 2024, and they punished Democrats for refusing to reflect their revulsion at Israel’s actions. It’s worth remembering where we were two years ago: As polls showed a majority of swing-state voters opposing further US funding for Israel, President Biden sent Israel tens of billions of dollars in weapons to continue the slaughter in Gaza.
The Israeli government had announced in August 2024 that it had received 50,000 tons of weapons from Biden in 607 shipments over the preceding 11 months—a weapons shipment every 12 hours. At the same time, Save the Children estimated that Israel was killing a Palestinian child in Gaza every hour. By the end of Biden’s term, the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics estimated that Israel had dropped 100,000 tons of bombs on Gaza—the equivalent of seven Hiroshima atomic bombs on an area of land smaller than Detroit. Millions of Americans watched this horror livestreamed, day after day after day.
Biden even made a surprise appearance at the White House Press Briefing Room on October 4, 2024, to say that “no administration has helped Israel more than I have. None.” Meanwhile, the voters Democrats needed to turn out were calling Biden “Genocide Joe.”
We all know what happened next.
In the wake of the Democrats’ 2024 loss, our polling at the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project found that “ending Israel’s violence in Gaza” was the top-cited factor among Biden 2020 voters who defected from Kamala Harris, especially in the crucial swing states of Arizona, Wisconsin, and Michigan. President Biden’s response to the election results was to announce another $8 billion weapons package to Israel as one of his final acts as president.
And we weren’t the only ones picking up on this pattern. Earlier this year, Axiosreported that the author of the Democratic National Committee’s (DNC) 2024 autopsy report also “concluded the war in Gaza hurt Kamala Harris politically.” Concerningly, a version of the report released by DNC Chair Ken Martin made zero mention of either Israel or Gaza.
Nevertheless, many establishment Democrats continued to deny what was staring them in the face. The New York Times reported last year that Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer justified his refusal to endorse Zohran Mamdani on the belief that being “deeply critical of Israel” would be a liability in swing states in 2026. This was not reflected in polling at the time, and certainly did not bear out in polling as we approached this election, with most voters in key states including Texas, Maine, Ohio, Iowa, and North Carolina—all states Democrats ultimately flipped—saying they support blocking the transfer of bombs to Israel.
Throughout the 2026 primaries, candidates who recognized Israel’s genocide and called for a weapons embargo against Israel won with the odds stacked against them—including in New Jersey, Pennsylvania, New York, Colorado, Florida, and California. Nowhere was this clearer than in the critical swing state of Michigan, where the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spent over $30 million—a record amount for one organization to spend in a single Democratic primary in US history—to defeat Dr. Abdul El-Sayed. El-Sayed was able to overcome that record spending because of his moral clarity in recognizing Israel’s genocide, a position that 80 percent of Michigan Democratic primary voters agree with.
El-Sayed also won by refusing to allow AIPAC’s money and political power to intimidate him into silence. For years, advocates for Palestinian rights have tried to warn Democrats about the dangers of candidates backed by AIPAC—an organization largely funded by Republicans and whose agenda contradicts the core values of human equality that the Democratic Party is supposed to represent at its best. That warning was fully realized in Representative Haley Stevens, Senator Schumer’s recruit for the seat.
Her bizarre turncoat act in the last weeks of the election was a historic embarrassment for the Democratic Party, but it was just as much an embarrassment for the claim, so popular in the media, that there is a bitter Democratic voter divide when it comes to what the future of US-Israel policy should be. As the results in Michigan showed, there simply isn’t one.
El-Sayed coasted to a seven-point victory, just as he predicted in May, because Democratic voters fully consolidated behind him and independents broke his way. Stevens’s shenanigans and the millions spent against him by AIPAC couldn’t overcome the majority of Michigan voters—including 66 percent of Michigan independents—who say they want to end US funding to Israel. And despite endless warnings that Jewish Michiganders were set to abandon El-Sayed en masse, early exit polls showed him winning 60 percent of the Jewish vote.
It could not be clearer: Unyielding support for Israel is electoral poison, and candidates who back Palestinian rights, oppose genocide, and call for a decisive break with Israel will win. Democrats—the honest ones, anyway—know this. The question then becomes: What are they going to do about it, now that they have so much more political power?
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Unbelievably, some observers are suggesting that Democrats should elide the questions over their position on Palestinian rights, and holding Israel accountable for its ongoing genocide, that have roiled their voters for over three years. That would be a severe betrayal of the clearly stated wishes of the Democratic base that delivered this week’s historic victory.
Others might want to follow AIPAC’s lead. In October, the lobby group announced, in an admission of its own toxicity, that it would stop endorsing candidates going forward, while still continuing to spend millions of dollars in our elections through its super PAC, and presumably more untraceably through shell super PACs, as it has throughout this year.
AIPAC’s new strategy mirrors what some supporters of a close US-Israel relationship foresee for themselves as well. At the 11th hour on election morning, President Trump dubiously claimed in a Fox & Friends phone interview that he would end annual taxpayer funding for Israel’s military at year’s end. Given Trump’s penchant for lying, this is more important for its recognition of this ritual’s unpopularity than it is as a reliable indicator that such a policy change will actually come about under his watch. Regardless, his allies in Congress are, at this moment, advancing legislation to rapidly integrate Israeli weapons companies into the Pentagon procurement process—a method of providing taxpayer funding for Israeli companies at even higher levels than today, and without congressional oversight. Any Democrat who joins them will be walking down a political path they will almost certainly regret.
With the mandate voters have given them, Democrats have every ounce of leverage to strip those measures out of this year’s National Defense Authorization Act. They have every ability to strip funding for Israel’s military out of next year’s budget and send it to Trump’s desk to call his bluff. And they have every ability to bring the Block the Bombs Act for a vote and test how much their Republican counterparts have really learned from this election.
They not only have this ability; they also have every reason to become a party that is a full-throated defender of Palestinian rights—and human rights for every person. They have a mandate to stand against endless war in the Middle East, and to stand up to megadonors and super PACs that have distorted our democracy for too long.
To do anything else is the definition of insanity.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: The real race at the NYC Marathon is getting to the front of the toilet line
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Samantha Max
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
The New York City marathon was the culmination of months, or even years, of physical and mental preparation for more than 60,000 runners who dashed across the five boroughs on Sunday.
But before the run, participants had another important race to complete: the race to the bathroom.
Rows upon rows of purple, plastic portable toilets were stationed around the starting villages on Staten Island, where tens of thousands of runners waited for the race to begin. Doors constantly slammed shut as long lines of people in running shoes and cozy warm-up gear passed in and out of the stalls.
“It’s like the porta-potty company’s Super Bowl,” said Paola Yepez, 26, as she waited for the toilet before running her first marathon.
I was doing the same. My stomach twists in knots when I think about a half marathon I ran a few years ago. I needed the toilet before the race. But the line was so long I had to jump over the gates to get to the start. This time in the toilet line, I wanted to know how other runners were managing their uneasy stomachs and full bladders.
Using the facilities before the race is essential. Urinating or defecating outside of sanctioned toilets can lead to disqualification from the marathon and suspension from future races, according to New York Road Runners, which organizes the event.
One elite athlete went viral earlier this year when she kept competing after soiling herself at a HYROX race in Beijing, prompting outrage, disgust and vicarious humiliation. The pressure was on as runners queued up in front of the portable toilets on Sunday.
“We have a big responsibility on our plate,” said Angelo Martinez, CEO of John To Go, which provided more than 2,000 portable toilets and 46 hand washing stations for spectators and runners.
“When it's game time, [we’re] making sure that they can get ready to run the whole 26 miles and not have to worry about making a pit stop,” he said.
Martinez said John To Go started to prepare for the New York City marathon almost a year in advance. The company spent months investing in more toilets, making staffing plans and mapping out the transportation route. Deliveries started around 10 on Saturday night, he said.
“While the city's sleeping, we're delivering portable toilets and getting ready for the event, where it can be a seamless launch when they start running the race,” he said.
As a longtime runner, going to the bathroom before a race is one of the biggest sources of anxiety for me. I’m always paranoid that I’ll need to go mid-run and either suffer for miles or lose time using a toilet on the course.
As I waited with other runners, they told me about their training, their racing strategies, their goals and all the pre-race fuel sloshing around in their stomachs: gnocchi with pesto, pizza, coffee, bananas, sandwiches, sushi rice.
“After all the carb loading, I'm seriously considering going Keto, because I'm over it,” said Brian Dagliere, 36. “It sounds great, the carb load, but one way to describe it is, to me, it's disgusting. It's just a lot.”
Jodi Renert said her full bladder provided a welcome distraction.
“Waiting in the bathroom to pee is taking away my anxiety to run 26.2 miles,” she said, clutching a big bottle filled with a nutrition-packed drink and resisting the urge to cut to the front of the line.
“ I have to pee so bad,” Renert said. “Like, I shouldn't be drinking this, but it's got, like, all my carbs and electrolytes.”
The whole scene was a little ridiculous. While many New Yorkers were still in bed, we were lining up to flush the nerves — and the waste — out of our systems before we voluntarily ran an absurd distance.
The toilet line leaves a lot of time to marinate on every ache, pain and tummy rumble that could get in the way of achieving a hard-fought goal. Lisa Endrodi said she felt “awful.”
“Scared. Nervous. Yeah, all those emotions. Anxious,” she said.
Marathons have become a mid-life obsession for the 53-year-old, who traveled from the U.K. for her third 26.2-mile race.
“ My husband thinks I'm mad,” she said as she waited in line for the loo.
Going to the bathroom before a race is essential, she said.
“Especially for a female,” she said. “Most definitely. Yes.”
Running 26.2 miles is not a normal thing to put a body through. In my quiet moment of solitude inside the stinky stall, clutching my packet of tissues and bottle hand sanitizer, I remembered I was merely a human with basic biological needs that no amount of training could overcome.
Every person in the toilet line has their reason for running the race. Getting sober. Recovering from cancer. Checking a goal off the bucket list. I was there with my fiance, preparing to run my first marathon. We were racing together three weeks before our wedding, and we had committed to crossing the finish line together.
After multiple trips to the toilet, our starting time arrived, and we had to trust that our bodies were ready. Frank Sinatra’s “New York, New York” serenaded us as we ran side by side across the Verrazano Bridge. That’s when I began to lose a different fluid from my body: tears of joy.

https://gothamist.com/news/work-is-under.title: Work is underway to replace deteriorating Newark Bay Bridge, a major NY-NJ route
https://gothamist.com/news/work-is-under.author: Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/work-is-under.text:
Work is underway to replace the outdated Newark Bay Bridge, which carries the New Jersey Turnpike extension into Hudson County and serves as one of the main connecting roads between the Garden State and New York City.
That bridge, also known as the Casciano Memorial Bridge, opened in 1956 and carries about 95,000 cars and trucks daily. The New Jersey Turnpike Authority has warned that it is at the end of its usable life. The project to replace it is scheduled to be complete in 2031. Officials say there will be no disruption for commuters and minimal impact to local residents during construction, as the existing bridge will remain open during construction.
“All that traffic brings wear and tear,” Gov. Mikie Sherrill said at a groundbreaking ceremony Thursday. “After 70 years of service, the bridge is in dire need of replacement.”
The new cable-stayed bridge will be built just north of the existing bridge across Newark Bay. It will have two lanes for traffic in both directions as well as full shoulders, addressing a safety concern plaguing the existing bridge.
“Because of the constant repair work on it, we have to shut down the shoulder routinely. Or if there is a downed vehicle, that shuts off a lane and we have to use the shoulder,” Sherrill said. “We can't get safety vehicles on the bridge.”
It cost about $40 million to build the existing bridge in the 1950s, said Kris Kolluri, the executive director of the New Jersey Turnpike Authority. That figure works out to be a little shy of $500 million in 2026 dollars.
The new bridge is expected to cost more than $6.7 billion, making it the most expensive single effort pursued by the Turnpike Authority. It’ll be paid for with toll revenue. Turnpike tolls have increased 3% annually since 2020. Sherrill did not directly say whether or not those annual increases will continue.
"We are going to make sure that we're not kicking the can down the road on anything,” Sherrill said. “So we'll be ensuring that we have the funding to continue to invest in infrastructure, which over time is going to ensure that every tax dollar is spent wisely.”
Kolluri noted that work in the river has already begun, with temporary construction trestles expected to be finished by the end of this year. The Turnpike Authority expects to award a contract for the actual bridge construction in March.
Sherrill compared the bridge to a pair of other major projects underway in the state — the new Hudson River rail tunnels currently being dug, and the new Portal Bridge currently being completed.
“ Unfortunately, in too many cases, it has been politically expedient for people to kick the can down the road, to do little patchwork repairs and not actually make sure we are making sound structural improvements,” Sherrill said. “So we are taking this on at every level, and making sure we're building for the future, and that New Jersey, once again, will be the crown jewel in infrastructure and improvement.”
The new Newark Bay Bridge will be a scaled back version of a $10.7 billion proposal, advanced by then-Gov. Phil Murphy’s administration, that called for building two new bridges and widening the part of the extension that weaves through Jersey City to the Holland Tunnel.
That original plan drew fierce pushback from environmentalists and Jersey City community groups, who warned it would bring unnecessary air and noise pollution to already overburdened neighborhoods.
Murphy later walked back the extension widening in Jersey City, but still pushed for a two-bridge replacement. Sherrill announced in March that the extra lanes would be dropped from the plan. Her decision was praised by the mayors of Newark and Jersey City and environmental advocates.
The groundbreaking for the new bridge was held on the 75th anniversary of the New Jersey Turnpike opening. Mid-century Gov. Alfred Driscoll championed the turnpike, Kolluri said, with a vision of an efficient system for moving freight and passengers without burdening local roads in a growing state.
Kolluri said the whole turnpike system now serves about 260 million vehicles annually.
“That is a volume that I don't think even Gov. Driscoll thought was possible,” Kolluri said.

https://gothamist.com/news/quest-diagnos.title: Quest Diagnostics pays $13M to settle kickback allegations involving NY Giants tickets
https://gothamist.com/news/quest-diagnos.author: Kaya Laterman
https://gothamist.com/news/quest-diagnos.text:
Quest Diagnostics paid over $13 million to resolve allegations that it provided health care providers and executives illegal kickbacks in the form of New York Giants tickets and access to exclusive events, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office of New Jersey.
U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer on Friday said the clinical lab operator, based in Secaucus, NJ, offered clients Giants suite seats and access to training camp in exchange for business referrals.
Frazer said Quest violated the Anti-Kickback Statute, which prohibits offering, soliciting, or taking payment to encourage the use of services or items covered by Medicare, Medicaid and other federally funded healthcare programs.
“Kickbacks to referring providers, especially by lab companies, corrupt medical judgment, lead to unnecessary lab testing, cause providers to steer patients to labs that offer inducements, and squander taxpayer money,” Frazer said in a statement.
The settlement resolves allegations that, between July 25, 2013 and Aug. 3, 2022, Quest violated the kickback statute and that the firm submitted false claims for lab services that Medicare and New York and New Jersey Medicaid paid for, officials said.
In 2013, Quest entered into a naming rights and sponsorship agreement with the New York Giants. As part of this agreement, the Giants provided suites to Quest for home games at MetLife Stadium. The firm also gained various marketing, commercial programming and hospitality benefits, according to prosecutors.
Quest then provided clients access to Giants home game suite seats, VIP training camp, draft “chalk-talk” presentations, and NFL scouting events for free, according to officials.
After inviting clients to the games and events, Quest calculated the revenue it received from them for up to one year after entertaining them, officials said. In addition, the company then billed Medicare, as well as New York and New Jersey Medicaid for claims for lab testing that were referred from the clients that they entertained, prosecutors said.
The New York Giants organization, which is based in New Jersey, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Under the settlement Quest is also required to enter into a five-year corporate integrity agreement with the Department of Health and Human Services-Office of Inspector General, requiring the firm to obtain an independent review organization to audit the company.
A spokesperson for Quest said the firm denies any allegations of wrongdoing or violation of the law, but agreed to the settlement to “put the matter behind us.”
“We adhere to a policy of strict compliance with the laws and regulations governing our business,” spokesperson Amanda Rivera said in a statement. “Since last year, we have shared information about this settlement, which includes a Corporate Integrity Agreement, with the public through our regulatory filings. In many respects, the CIA mirrors our existing rigorous compliance program, and we have been complying with its requirements.”

Sweden will return 40 sacred Benin artifacts to Nigeria. It will be one of the largest repatriations of Benin work to date. The artworks were set to return to Lagos yesterday. Oba Ewuare II, the monarch of Benin, has described the return of work as long in the making. “We have been trying, through my grandfather’s efforts, to bring back our artifacts,” he said in a statement. “My grandfather succeeded, my father succeeded more, and I think now history is obvious to everybody. We are doing our best to triple and triple all those efforts of our forefathers”
The Benin Bronzes, as they are called, are a collection of bronze sculptures, ceremonial objects, and ivory carvings. The Kingdom of Benin, in what is now Nigeria, was looted of roughly 5,000 religious objects by the British in 1897. The works were dispersed among museums and private collections throughout the world. There has been an increase in repatriations as public sympathies have shifted towards the formerly colonized. Museums in the US, the Netherlands, Germany, and Switzerland, have returned Benin Bronzes and other significant artworks to their countries of origin.
The Swedish government will also return 77 Kallawaya objects, including human remains, to the Archaeological Museum in La Paz, Bolivia. The objects were taken illegally from Bolivia, and were held in Gothenburg’s World Culture Museum until 2023, when the Swedish government began their transfer of ownership.

On November 5, U.S. President Donald Trump signed a proclamation declaring the White House’s Oval Office and Cabinet Room as a national monument—a designation that protects the spaces from major alterations in the future.
The proclamation, which is not legally binding, does not prohibit any forthcoming president from redecorating, adding new furniture, or making security and operational modifications, as long as they do not affect the monument’s architectural and historic character. The proclamation was accompanied by a fact sheet that noted that the Oval Office deserves greater recognition and protection. The White House and its grounds are already a National Historic Landmark administered by the National Park Service, having been designated as such in 1960.
Trump told the New York Times that he wants “to make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space.” The proclamation followed a midterm election where Trump’s Republican Party suffered historic losses in both houses of Congress. Trump’s first interaction with reporters after receiving election results was during a visit to the construction site of the new 90,000-square-foot White House ballroom, built on the former site of the East Wing.
In his second term, Trump has commenced several renovation and building projects in the White House: paving over the Rose Garden; gilding the Oval Office; and the controversial demolition of the East Wing to make way for a new ballroom.
He has also undertaken similar ventures across Washington D.C., including the botched repair of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, the contested remodeling of the Kennedy Center, and a planned 250-foot-tall triumphal arch. These projects are estimated to cost over $1 billion in total, with funds collected from both public and private sources.

The Art Gallery of Ontario, Toronto, has announced September 25, 2027, as the date it will open its forthcoming Dani Reiss Contemporary and Modern Gallery to the public. Begun in 2022, the project is being collaboratively overseen by Diamond Schmitt, Selldorf Architects, and Two Row Architect. Indigenous leaders and communities were also involved in the development of the wing. It is named for Dani Reiss, the CEO and chair of Canada Goose, who supplied $35 million in funding, with private donors and the governments of Ontario and Canada supplying the rest.
The new wing marks the gallery’s seventh expansion since opening in 1900. It will comprise 40,000 square feet distributed across five floors overlooking Grange Park and connecting to the museum’s Frank Gehry–renovated main building. Featuring 5,000-square-foot galleries with 23-foot-high ceilings, it will increase the institution’s gallery space by 30 percent. When completed, it will display nearly four hundred works from AGO’s collection of contemporary and modern art, with a focus on works by Canadian and Indigenous artists, as well as their international counterparts.
Of note, the building is designed to operate without burning fossil fuel and has received CAGBC Zero Carbon Building Design certification.
“The Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery is more than an expansion project—it is Toronto and Canada announcing its global position,” said AGO director and CEO Stephan Jost in a statement. “When this gallery opens in September 2027, the world will be made aware of the strength of the AGO collection and the degree to which it has evolved to be truly global.”
Jost will not be around to christen the new wing: He announced his departure from the institution earlier this year.

Sheldon and Marianne Lubar have committed $10 million to the Milwaukee Art Museum to establish the Lubar Family Center for Drawings and Prints. The gift provides long-term support for researching and maintaining works on paper, which comprise more than half of the museum’s collection of some 35,000 objects.
Both Sheldon and Marianne Lubar serve as “Life Trustees” of the museum, and have been involved with the administration of the institution for more than fifty years. Previously, Sheldon has served as president of the museum’s board, and spearheaded the fundraising campaign that helped complete funding for the Santiago Calatrava-designed Quadracci Pavilion, which opened in 2001. Their daughter Joan is also a trustee.
“Great cities need great institutions,” Sheldon Lubar said in a statement. “We’re proud to support the Milwaukee Art Museum as Milwaukee’s great institution!”
The gift also endows several positions at the museum—the Lubar Family Curator of Drawings and Prints, the Lubar Family Paper Conservator, and the Lubar Family Fellow in Drawings and Prints—as well as the Lubar Family Drawings and Prints Exhibition Program.
“Behind every exhibition are people who study the art, care for it, and help us see it in new ways,” said Susan Lubar. “It’s exciting to support that work and to know this collection will continue to be a source of discovery for Milwaukee.”
Chicago Gallery News reports that Nikki Otten will lead the center as the Lubar Family Curator. She joined the museum in 2018 and is an expert in drawings and prints.
“Because works on paper are sensitive to light, they can only be on view for limited periods before returning to storage to rest,” Otten said. “Each exhibition offers an opportunity to share different selections and explore new connections across the collection. This gift supports the research and specialized care that make those experiences possible.

Five oil sketches by Peter Paul Rubens were removed from Ducal Museum in Gotha, Germany, during World War II. Three were returned since then, and now the remaining two have been recovered and restituted to the museum. All will go on view together for the first since in eighty years.
The Art Newspaper reports that the five sketches are part of a group of twenty-two that Rubens composed on wood between 1620 and 1621 as studies for his commission to paint the ceiling of the newly built Jesuit Church in Antwerp (now Saint Charles Borromeo’s Church). Rubens created thirty-nine paintings for the ceiling, in what was then his largest commission; the upper level focused on stories from the Old and New Testaments, and the lower level depicted saints.
The preparatory sketches are particularly significant because the paintings themselves were destroyed in a fire that swept through the church in 1718, caused by a lightning-bolt strike. According to The Art Newspaper, the sketches were among the most valuable works in the collections at the museum, whose holdings once belonged to the former Duchy of Saxe-Gotha. Representatives of the duchy, which hadn’t owned the work since 1918, removed a considerable amount of art from the castle in the closing weeks of World War II.
Two of the sketches were looted by the Soviet army but were returned to the museum in 1959. Three others ended up in Coburg, were illegally sold, and turned up in the US market. In 2024, one of them was returned by a museum in Buffalo, New York. Now a fourth has been located in a private collection in the US and returned through private settlement, funded by the Ernst von Siemens Art Foundation.
The fifth sketch resides in the Foundation E. G. Bührle Collection at the Kunsthaus Zurich. The foundation has agreed to loan the work to the Ducal Museum for an exhibition of the complete series.
Tobias Pfeifer-Helke, the director of the Friedenstein Foundation Gotha, called the reassembled works “nothing short of a miracle.” He added, “They are not only five unique masterpieces by the Flemish painter and the jewels of the Gotha art collection, but also bear witness to European and international history.”

A conversation with the artist on his series of high school-inspired photos from Artforum's October 2000 issue
For Artforum’s October 2000 issue, Dennis Cooper interviewed Mike Kelley at the start of his “Extracurricular Activity Projective Reconstruction” series, a twelve-year project in which Kelley re-created found images of Halloween costumes, religious events, and oddball student portraits from high school yearbooks. These facsimiles of mundane extracurricular activity were shown as diptychs along with their original referent, and presented alongside intricately designed sets replicating the surroundings of the pupils in the photos.
In their conversation, Kelley speaks with Cooper about Extracurricular Activity Projective Reconstruction #1 (A Domestic Scene), 2000, a work that transformed a photo of a haunting “Tennessee Williams kind” of high school play into a “full-scale production” comprising a “crudely furnished studio apartment” stage set and “a twenty-two-minute video documenting a one-act play performed on that set.” After nearly twenty years of feeling that the critical response to his work primarily focused on themes of “nostalgia and trauma,” Kelley “gave the people what they want,” and leaned into a multiyear psychodrama dredging the American high school experience.
The sculptural element of the “EAPR” works was of increased importance to Kelley, who constructed them to be inspected in “close proximity,” inverting the tradition of shoddily built stage props meant to be seen by faraway audiences. This, along with Kelley’s concern for the “conundrum” of translating an image into a physical object, then back into a reproduction of the initial image, foregrounded a formalism that Kelley saw as otherwise underrecognized in his work. Speaking on his worries that the recorded play would outshine his set, Kelley lamented that people “always glom right on to [my work’s] abject nature, or blah blah blah blah . . . I’ve been typecast as some kind of mindfucker or something.”
Read “Trauma Club: Dennis Cooper Talks with Mike Kelley” in Artforum’s October 2000 issue.
–Theo Belci

Mona Chalabi on Money and Art
An interview with the Pulitzer Prize winner, Lori Waxman on bringing sexy back in Chicago, stolen Picasso prints found, and the problem with clouds.
“I wrote this book because I was paid a shitload of money to write it,” Mona Chalabi says in her new book Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are — or tried to, anyway, before her editor stopped her. The Iraqi-British, Pulitzer-winning artist and illustrator has made a career saying what nobody else can, or will — calling out fellow journalists for their refusal to report on Palestine, for instance. Today, she talks to Associate Editor Laskhmi Rivera Amin about her data-driven, hand-drawn process, as well as how class and inequality shape journalism, art, and our lives.
Funny — as an editor, my favorite thing is not stopping my writers. That’s precisely how Lori Waxman’s piece on the return of sexy art in Chicago was born. No, this is not a personal essay about her or her acquaintances’ sexuality (“Maybe after everyone’s dead,” she says). It’s much better — loaded with art historical judgments (has anyone referred to Willem de Kooning’s drawings as “slasher sketches” before? We ought to); discussion of glory holes and sexy architecture; and gems about life (“female middle-age libido sets at either zero or 1,000, on a scale of one to 100”). God, I love my job.
—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor
Mona Chalabi Paints a Picture of Class Inequality
“As an adult and as a journalist, I have stared shamelessly.” That refusal to look away is precisely what data journalist, writer, and artist Mona Chalabi has built her deeply principled career on. Known best for her indelible data visualizations, from the obscenity of Jeff Bezos’s wealth to the Israeli government’s starvation of Palestinians in Gaza and the racial and gender biases in museum collections, the Pulitzer Prize-winning Iraqi-British journalist tackles the subject of wealth and economic inequality in America in her first book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026). | Lakshmi Rivera Amin
