Russian negotiator rejects territorial swaps with Ukraine as Abu Dhabi talks end
After two days of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi, Russia's chief negotiator said there was no possibility of exchanging territory with Ukraine as part of any peace deal, Russia's Tass news agency reported on Wednesday.
Vladimir Medinsky and Ukrainian negotiators had earlier reported some progress in the talks, which ended on Wednesday. But US mediators said there was a lack of trust between the warring sides and differences remained on a number of issues, including territory.
Medinsky was also cited as saying that if what he called a fair security system for Europe could be created, it would help ensure peace on the continent for decades, and possibly centuries, to come.
He added that Russia's buffer zone along its border with Ukraine was already substantial and would keep expanding, according to the Interfax news agency, as cited by Reuters.

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: ‘They see me as non-Western’: Top court to rule on Denmark’s housing law
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
‘They see me as non-Western’: Top court to rule on Denmark’s housing law
Residents say Denmark’s ‘ghetto law’ is breaking up strong communities, as the Supreme Court prepares to rule.
Copenhagen, Denmark – Under a graffiti-covered bridge in Norrebro, a multicultural, trendy district of the Danish capital, Sara touches her hijab.
“I am Muslim. The way the government and the media speak, they see me as not Western,” says the 46-year-old, born and raised in Denmark, who has asked not to use her real name.
She believes the country’s so-called “ghetto law” is a way of cracking down on Muslims, who account for little more than 4 percent of the population.
On November 23, Denmark’s Supreme Court is due to rule on a case that could shape the future of that law, which can force the sale, demolition or conversion of nonprofit homes in areas where more than half of residents are classed as “non-Western”.
In Denmark, nonprofit housing accommodates more than one million people and is open to all.
Seven families from the Nojsomhed estate in Helsingor, north of Copenhagen, are challenging their former landlord, Boliggarden, after the estate was put on the “ghetto list” in January 2020.
They argue that they were forced out because of where they or their parents come from.
‘A proxy for ethnic origin’
In his warmly lit, cosy office space in central Copenhagen, Eddie Khawaja, the families’ lawyer, told Al Jazeera that the case boils down to whether the evaluation is “neutral” and “detached from ethnicity elements or not”.
It is the first case to reach the Supreme Court since the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) ruled last December, in cases from Mjolnerparken, an estate in Norrebro, and another estate, that the “non-Western” categorisation could amount to ethnic discrimination, and left Danish judges to decide.
Lower courts had ruled against the families, finding that “non-Western” does not describe an ethnic group.
The Supreme Court, which heard the case over two days, must now weigh that against the EU ruling.
Khawaja, who presented his closing arguments to the court on Monday, said the EU ruling opened the way for judges to look beyond the law’s wording to how politicians talked about it. In his view, “non-Western” is “a proxy for ethnic origin”.
His clients are almost all employed, well educated, and none are criminals, he said. “They are part of the community with the wrong ethnicity.”
Even if the families lose against their landlord, Khawaja said, the court must still decide whether the criterion is neutral, which could affect every estate on the lists.
The law works through lists updated by the government on December 1 every year of what were once referred to as “ghettos” but are now named “parallel societies”.
‘We are not a ghetto’
When Denmark published its first official “ghetto list” in 2010, being on it felt “stigmatising” but it did bring money for social projects, said Helle Hansen, a gregarious night-shift care worker from Gellerup in Aarhus, one of the country’s largest nonprofit housing estates.
When the annual list was published, residents of newly named estates appeared on the evening news. “We are not a ghetto,” she recalled them saying.
Under the 2018 “parallel society” law, nonprofit housing areas with at least 1,000 residents, more than half of them “non-Western”, go on the list. They must also meet two of four criteria on unemployment, crime, education and income.
After five consecutive years on the list, the areas must cut nonprofit family housing to 40 percent by 2030, through sales, demolition or conversion.
In 2021, the Social Democrat-led government removed the word “ghetto” from the law.
“Ghetto areas” became “parallel societies” and “hard ghettos” became “transformation areas”, while a new list of “prevention areas” added estates where the “non-Western” threshold is 30 percent.
An estate with the same social problems, where half or fewer residents are “non-Western”, faces no such obligation.
Khawaja said that cutting crime and raising education, incomes and employment were good aims, “but we are just saying, fine, regulate on that”.
Instead, he argued, politicians had made ethnicity “a decisive factor”.
In Gellerup, seven blocks with 408 flats were marked for demolition, said Hansen, who is part of Almen Modstand, a grassroots movement against the “ghetto law”.
Residents voted against the plan, but the wider housing association overruled them.
‘A racial category in real time’
Under Statistics Denmark’s definition, “non-Western” covers anyone outside the EU and a short list of countries, including the United States, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.
Amani Hassani, a Danish urban ethnographer and lecturer in politics and history at Brunel University London, said the criterion does something the social measures alone do not.
“What ‘non-Western’ does in Denmark is actually creating a racial category in real time,” she told Al Jazeera. “It is a question of ancestry,” she said, not citizenship.
What the category captures, she added, is “people who originate in non-white majority countries”.
‘Descendants of descendants’
Since 2020, Statistics Denmark has also published figures that separate out a third generation, which Hassani calls “descendants of descendants”.
Her grandparents came to Denmark as migrants.
“My family has been here for half a century,” she said. “The political class can speak all they want about how I am not Danish.”
Under the bridge in Copenhagen’s Norrebro district, traders work at a bustling market while students speed past on bicycles.
Sara believes religion is at the heart of the issue. “I am Muslim, and that is really what they see as non-Western,” she said.
Many people Al Jazeera spoke to said that the rhetoric used by politicians is ultimately directed at Islam.
Days after the housing law took effect, parliament adopted a resolution during a debate on the integration of Muslims, describing “parallel societies” where attempts are made to enforce Islamic customs at “the expense of Danish values”.
Ester Anker, a 27-year-old psychology student who lives in Norrebro, called the law “straight up racist” and said it was clearly aimed at Muslims. Politicians “haven’t even done a good job at hiding that fact”, she said.
‘A community of care’
Majken Felle, a 52-year-old teacher, has loved Mjolnerparken since she moved there in 2014.
For years, the list was little more than a label, she said. Then, from 2019, letters began landing in residents’ mailboxes urging them to accept “voluntary” rehousing.
Eviction notices followed, and she has since moved three times.
Yet the pressure also pulled neighbours together. Residents bound by a common cause got to know each other and met in the laundry rooms to swap what they knew about their rights, she said.
Felle speaks warmly of her former neighbours, many of them women from the Middle East who fled their countries young, raised children, and learned Danish, demonstrating, she said, resourcefulness and tenacity.
The government and housing associations underestimated many of those women, Felle said. They were supposed to just move away, but they ended up taking on the Danish state.
Hassani described the emergence of “a community of care”, where earlier arrivals help refugees navigate schools and public services.
“That’s what’s at risk. That’s what’s being dismantled here,” she said.
The estate has changed in character now, Felle said.
Most newcomers are young, mainly ethnically Danish students and expats, many from Argentina and France.
People stay for a couple of years, meaning the area has a more transitory nature. Residents do not invest in the community in the same way. Where neighbours once said hello, people now look at the ground, she said.
Mjolnerparken itself came off the list in 2023 after its population fell below 1,000, but it still has to complete its plan by the end of 2029, the housing ministry told parliament.
‘Remove the label’
A four-party coalition led by Mette Frederiksen’s Social Democrats has governed Denmark since early June.
Housing is now in the hands of Jacob Mark of the Socialist People’s Party, which voted for the law in 2018.
Even a win in court may not end it, Hassani warned.
The government could use “political acrobatics”, she said, to keep targeting the same communities without the category. “They’ll just remove the label, right?” she said.
Felle has the same fear.
“People cannot change who they are,” she said. “And if these estates are the target today,” she asked, “who is next?”

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/reviews.title: New Richard Avedon Documentary Shows That Fashion Isn’t All Style—It’s Substance, Too
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/reviews.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/reviews.text:
When The Devil Wears Prada 2 hit theaters this past spring, it painted an accurate and depressing picture of how fashion publishing has dwindled, its creative juices squeezed. Miranda Priestly, is no longer calling on her assistants to ring Patrick, a reference to the fashion photographer Patrick Demarchelier, or anyone of that caliber.
As someone who spent a majority of their career in that industry and had a short stint at Vogue, the publication the “Devil Wears Prada” films were based on, it’s fair to say everyone goes in with a dream of what it means to work at a fashion magazine. Often, those fantasies are informed by the photographs of Herb Ritts, Helmut Newton, and Richard Avedon, the latter of which is the subject of a new documentary by filmmaker Ron Howard. Titled Avedon, it releases on Netflix today.
As far as fashion documentaries go, it’s full of style and substance, backed up with anecdotes from Larry Gagosian, Tina Brown, Twiggy, Hilton Als, Samira Nasr, Isabella Rossellini, Calvin Klein, Avedon’s son John, and James Martin, the executive director of the Richard Avedon Foundation. Gagosian, who represents the Richard Avedon Foundation and has just opened an Avedon show in Beverly Hills, recalls going to brunch with the photographer, where all that was served was hard-boiled eggs and champagne. “I thought it was super elegant,” says Gagosian.
Using a combination of archival footage and interviews, Howard echoes the glitz and extravagance of fashion publishing’s bygone era of hefty budgets and creative freedom: Avedon’s photoshoots for Harper’s Bazaar and Vogue would last four days, and often featured models such as Lauren Hutton, Beverly Johnson, and Penelope Tree. Avedon managed to capture not just pretty faces, but the souls and secrets behind them.
Avedon grew up reading magazines such as Harper’s Bazaar, Vanity Fair, and Vogue at his father’s women’s retail business on Fifth Avenue. In them, he found the photographs by Martin Munkácsi, Edward Steichen, and Anton Bruehl.
He got his start in the 1940s, during World War II, working as a staff photographer for the United States Maritime Service, for which photographed around 100,000 faces on plain white backgrounds for ID cards with his Rolleiflex camera. “It’s existential white, the only thing you see is the geography of the face,” Avedon says in an old interview used in the film, referring to the way he spotlit his subjects against a white background.
After the war, he took courses in graphic design and photography at the New School, where he met Harper’s Bazaar’s art director, Alexey Brodovitch, who encouraged him to go to Paris in 1947 as part of the magazine’s mandate of “bringing back the glamor of pre-war Paris.”
At that publication, Avedon bore witness to a fashion revolution. In 1947, Christian Dior presented his New Look collection, an antidote to the rationed fabrics of the war, with full pleated skirts falling below mid-calf length. Avedon, who extravagantly captured five girls swirling in their full-length skirts, says that he lit each photograph he took in Paris as though he were reconstructing a Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers film.
He recalls photographing a model crying at a railway station. The picture was met with some acerbic feedback from Carmel Snow, the renowned editor-in-chief of Harper’s Bazaar, who coined the term the New Look: “Nobody cries in a Dior hat, Dick.”
Avedon’s work for Harper’s Bazaar shaped his career, paving the way for him to become a star beyond the fashion world. In 1955, he photographed one of his most famous images, Dovima with elephants; Gagosian reveals he once sold it for $2 million. By 1957, Avedon had shot to fame like Picasso (he photographed the artist in 1958) and had become the inspiration behind Stanley Donen’s film Funny Face, in which an Avedon-like photographer is played by Astaire. In a nod to the film’s inspiration, Avedon was brought on to shoot the stills used for the film’s opening credits.
Fundamentally, Avedon was always on a mission to capture the human condition. He firstly did so with stars and starlets to illustrate that nothing is really so perfect. Howard’s documentary seems to suggest that this was all related to Avedon’s own imperfect upbringing.
In Howard’s documentary, Avedon, who died in 2004, says that his parents always presented an idealized family in their scrapbooks and often borrowed a dog as a prop to exaggerate the image they cultivated. He grew up in a stern household with a father that was emotionally absent for a big chunk of his life until they reconciled later in life.
His sister Louise, was his first muse. Avedon says in the film that her “beauty affected me,” and that all the models he chose resembled his sister with their oval faces, high cheekbones, and brunette hair. Louise was catatonic and spent more than 15 years living in a psychiatric hospital, where she died in 1968 at age 42.
“One of the great themes in his work is alienation and isolation. He wants to know what’s going on inside human beings,” says John, Avedon’s son. In times of heartache, Avedon reveled in his work—such as when his first wife, the actress Doe Avedon, left him for another man that was blonde and tall, or when his second wife, Evelyn Franklin, fell into depression, leading Avedon to start living out of his studio. “Everything diminishes,” Avedon says here. “Work does not. It’s the one thing that doesn’t turn on you.”
Maybe because his life wasn’t so pretty, Avedon’s photographs didn’t always flatter. When he shot Nancy Reagan, for example, he abided by all of her handler’s guidelines. Then, in the final image, he focused on her claw-like hands, a contrast to her perfectly, smooth face.
Sometimes to get the image he wanted, he would manipulate his subjects, as he did when he shot the Duke and Duchess of Windsor (formerly King Edward VIII and Wallis Simpson). Avedon told them that, on the way to the photoshoot, his taxi ran over a dog. This was a lie, but they seemed to believe it, and Avedon captured the droop in their smile. Simpson told Avedon that she would destroy him when the photos were published, but Avedon, who was Jewish, described the couple as “compassionate,” despite the fact that they sympathized with the Nazis during World War II.
It’s evident through Avedon’s line of work that the photographer saw the world beyond the pages of Harper’s Bazaar and Vogue. He waited seven weeks in Vietnam to photograph the American generals of the war; the residents of the American West and the Chicago 7 also counted among his subjects. The film portrays Avedon as a complicated figure, one whose contributions exceed the field of fashion photography.
It also portrays him as a complicated person, but it could’ve gone even further. Howard shies away from claims about Avedon’s sexuality that have been voiced in books such as Avedon: Something Personal, by Norma Stevens and Steven M. L. Aronson, and Michael Gross’s Focus: The Secret, Sexy, Sometimes Sordid World of Fashion Photographers. Gross reports that Avedon had an affair with his high school classmate, the writer James Baldwin, who even worked on a book with Avedon called Nothing Personal. That isn’t addressed here. (Avedon’s foundation vigorously disputed certain episodes described in Something Personal upon the book’s release, but it did not outright deny the descriptions of the photographer’s sexual identity.)
Howard also glosses over the fact that Avedon stopped working for Vogue when Anna Wintour replaced Grace Mirabella as editor-in-chief, moving away from his cropped headshot covers. This is also skipped over entirely.
Howard is instead more focused on the glamorous ghosts of a vanished era. The fashion industry has been consumed by capitalism, and fashion magazines have lost their ability to influence. All we’re left with is tales of the good old days and a graveyard of nostalgic images. You don’t have to look too closely to see that the devil is in the picture. For proof, just look at one of the photographs featured here: Avedon’s 1952 portrait of the actor Charlie Chaplin, who raises two fingers to his head, as though he were Satan himself.

Netanyahu draws calls of 'hate speech' in the newly elected Israeli parliament
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was accused of giving a "hate-filled speech" against the Palestinian-led parties in the newly elected parliament on Tuesday.
On Tuesday, two weeks after Netanyahu's far-right bloc lost the elections following an historic voter turnout from Palestinian citizens of Israel, the parliament was sworn in in Jerusalem, with an unprecedented 19 members from the Palestinian-led Joint List alliance and Ra'am party.
Marking the ceremonial day, Netanyahu initially told the new Knesset members that Israel was facing "great threats" from Iran's nuclear programme, stating that "the only way to remove this existential threat permanently is by toppling the regime of the ayatollahs".
However, after boasting about Israeli military achievements in the occupied Palestinian territories, Syria, Lebanon and Iran, Netanyahu began lashing out at the Palestinian-led parties.
The Israeli premier said that Israel must "set aside every other consideration and form a national unity government" with his main challenger Gadi Eisenkot.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
"Only such a government will be able to meet challenges of this magnitude," he said, accusing Eisenkot's broad bloc of otherwise wanting to form "a government that includes within it terror supporters, haters of Israel".
Netanyahu clarified he was not referring to Palestinian citizens of Israel as a whole - some of whom, he said, voted for his Likud party.
'Are you prepared to be dependent on those whose purpose is the destruction of the Jewish state?'
- Benjamin Netanyahu
"I am talking about people whose ideology is hatred of Israel and the destruction of the Jewish state. People who say Hamas is just a charitable organisation," he said, referring to Ra'am and the Joint List.
"To those who are thinking of establishing a government with these people, I say: Are you prepared to be dependent on those whose purpose is the destruction of the Jewish state?"
He continued, claiming - falsely - that both Ra'am and the Joint List "agree that the Jewish state must be destroyed".
The Palestinian-led parties, who have Jewish MPs, have repeatedly called for a two-state solution in which Israel is an independent state alongside Palestine.
During the speech, Netanyahu cited past comments by Palestinian MPs, arguing that "a government that depends in any way on Ra’am or the Joint List must not be formed", and that a unity government would ensure the Jewish state would "stand for eternity".
Reactions to Netanyahu
The speech garnered condemnation from much of Eisenkot's bloc, with former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett from the centre-right Together alliance interrupting Netanyahu during the speech, while centre-left Democrats leader Yair Golan stormed out mid-speech.
"What about a State Commission of Inquiry? Why don’t you declare Qatar an enemy state? What about your Qatari advisers?" Bennett reportedly said.
Haaretz recently reported that Netanyahu and his allies in the Israeli media had prepared the ground for an attack on the Palestinian vote, which sharply intensified following the elections, with loyalist Shin Bet chief David Zini opening investigations into election fraud and foreign interference in the last two weeks.
Meanwhile, Netanyahu called to form a Jewish-only government under his leadership, despite his bloc having only 53 seats.
"I sat and listened to the delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful speech of the outgoing prime minister, in which he exploited a state occasion at the swearing-in of the 26th Knesset," Eisenkot, who earlier this week was tasked with forming a governing coalition, said on X.
"I became even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one minute more," the former army chief stated, adding that Netanyahu's rule was "dividing Israel and endangering its security".
Following the speech, Eisenkot cancelled coalition talks with Netanyahu's Likud party, the Israel Hayom newspaper reported.
According to Ynet's report, Netanyahu said the word "Jewish" 20 times during his speech, while the word "unity" was said only four times, and he didn't mention any of the leaders of his opposition bloc.
On the other hand, words that relates to Palestinians, which include "Palestinians, Arabs, terrorism and Caliphate", among others, were said by Netanyahu 36 times, according to Ynet's analysis.
Mansour Abbas, leader of the conservative Ra'am party, said on Tuesday that he was "astounded that the prime minister would exploit a state occasion to lie, to incite and to spread blood libel about the Arab parties".
"We don’t want to establish an Islamist state or an Arab state. This is where the State of Israel was established," he told Israel's Channel 12, adding that "we stand for peace and for ending the conflict with a two-state solution".
The left-wing Joint List described Netanyahu's speech as "deranged, inciting and racist".
"The bloodthirsty and criminal prime minister is in a state of complete hysteria," the party stated, adding that they were "committed to doing everything in our power" to remove Netanyahu from power and send his government "to the dustbin of history".

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Qatar Grand Prix was ‘right decision’ despite regional tensions: MotoGP
MotoGP chief says ‘it was normal that the riders showed their concerns’ but was surprised at Yamaha’s withdrawal.
MotoGP’s deputy chief Carlos Ezpeleta says the championship was right to go ahead with the Qatar Grand Prix despite rider concerns about travelling to the Gulf amid the United States-Israel war on Iran, but added that Yamaha’s withdrawal came as a surprise.
MotoGP had based its decision on official information from the Qatari government and from embassies with a large presence in the paddock, Ezpeleta revealed on Wednesday.
The race was postponed from April to November 6–8 due to the regional conflict, and Ezpeleta said the event would have been cancelled or postponed again if the situation had escalated.
“We can unequivocally say that it was the right decision,” Ezpeleta told the Reuters news agency.
“Obviously, it was normal that the riders showed their concerns, and I think that we mitigated those and confronted them to the best that we possibly could.”
“It’s just important in today’s day and age to follow official information and real intelligence versus speculation in the media and disinformation, which I think ultimately was what brought a lot of noise around the event itself.”
Several Saudi Arabian sporting events – including football, tennis, golf and cycling – were cancelled or postponed in recent weeks after attacks by Yemen’s Houthis on Riyadh’s international airport last month killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300.
But Ezpeleta said Qatar had not been affected in the same way as its Gulf neighbours and that planning for the race had accelerated after conditions improved in June and July.
Yamaha withdrawal surprised MotoGP
However, Yamaha withdrew from the Qatar Grand Prix citing “company-wide travel restrictions” for the Middle East, with the factory team and the satellite team Prima Pramac not lining up on the grid, reducing the field to 18 riders.
“I can say that the decision surprised us, given the level of detail that was put into the assessment and all the planning,” Ezpeleta said.
“All the questions that Yamaha had were answered. Ultimately, Yamaha is a great partner of the championship historically, and I’m sure they will continue to be,” he added.
“We understand that it wasn’t a decision that was taken easily from their side, but it is a decision that was surprising to us for sure.”
MotoGP leaves sanctions to FIM
MotoGP had said Yamaha’s non-participation carried sporting implications, with any consequences to be managed by FIM, the governing body of motorcycle racing.
But Ezpeleta declined to speculate on penalties.
“We just said that we would manage any contractual matters with Yamaha directly and any sporting conversations would be handled by FIM,” he said.
“We continue to say that it’s a disappointment because I think one of the strengths of MotoGP as a championship is that all the riders, all the teams are committed for the full season,” Ezpeleta added.
“I would say as a rights holder that the teams are committed and obliged to show up at all the events and all races.”
Yamaha and FIM did not respond to Reuters requests for comment. Yamaha’s Moto2 team travelled to Qatar, with Izan Guevara in a close title fight and sitting second in the championship. He had a technical issue and did not finish.
‘Improve communication’
The episode has also raised questions about how well MotoGP’s management communicates with riders, and Ezpeleta acknowledged the need to improve that relationship with all stakeholders.
“We have to proactively push to improve communication, especially with the teams and the riders because they are obviously the most important part of the championship,” he said.
“We’ve been managing the sport for 35 years and we’ve had situations like this before,” Ezpeleta added, pointing to the 2011 race in Japan held after the Fukushima nuclear disaster.
“There was a lot of controversy at the time, as was now with Qatar, guided by misinformation and speculation, rather than facts,” he said. “We continue to say that this was the right decision.”
Aprilia’s Marco Bezzecchi won the Qatar Grand Prix, but Ducati’s sprint winner Marc Marquez finished second to establish a 60-point lead in the championship with two rounds left.

Good Morning!
- Art Basel Paris has pledged a 20 percent reduction on the final invoices of all exhibitors who participated in the last edition, which was cut short because of protests.
- Tracey Emin has gotten the green light to turn a dilapidated building thought to have once been an Edwardian bathing house in Margate into an arts and community space.
- The Kennedy family has joined a legal suit to stop the building of President Trump’s massive triumphal arch, arguing it would cast a shadow on the graves of their relatives.
The Headlines
PARIS DISCOUNT. Art Basel Paris has pledged a 20 percent reduction on the final invoices of all exhibitors who participated in the fair’s last edition, which was cut short because of protests, ARTnews has learned. In recognition of the costs incurred from having to close on the fair’s final two days, Saturday, October 24 and Sunday, October 25. “We will exceptionally be extending a 20 percent reduction on booth fees to all galleries,” Art Basel chief executive Noah Horowitz told ARTnews in an exclusive interview. Tickets purchased for that weekend have already been refunded. Smaller and emerging dealers have been hit hardest by the loss of crucial business for which they spent months preparing and investing, and galleries have been eagerly awaiting news of compensation. Some have put pressure on the art fair. The French galleries association Comité Professionnel des Galeries d’Art addressed a strongly worded letter to Art Basel Paris director Karim Crippa on October 28 demanding financial redress, but also complaining they had been treated with “contempt,” or “disregard,” (the original French term used was “mépris”) because they were not consulted prior to the decision to shut for the fair’s final weekend. Protests were planned for that Saturday, but not for the next day. “This is a highly dynamic situation we were responding to,” Horowitz explained in the fair’s defense. He also acknowledged where there is room for improvement. “We had many conversations with many galleries during the fair and certainly in the weeks following, and I think we learned a lot of lessons coming through this. And as all businesses do, we’ll continue to improve our processes and make adjustments for the future.”
MEET YA AT MARGATE. Artist Tracey Emin has gotten the green light to turn a dilapidated building and former Edwardian bathing house on the seafront in Margate into an arts and community space, with a sauna, shower facilities, and restaurant, reports Kent Online. “The proposal will ensure a vacant building of some historic merit is brought back into use, and the proposed external changes are considered to result in the creation of a high-quality building that is an asset to the surrounding area,” wrote a local planning officer in their approval of the scheme. Emin, who was born in Croydon and grew up in Margate, a seaside town located on the north coast of Kent, southeast England, left London about a decade ago to settle there, and has been boosting the local arts scene, notably by founding and 2023-opening of TKE Studios, which offers affordable studios, exhibition spaces and a residency program.
The Digest
The Kennedy family has joined a legal suit to stop the building of President Trump’s massive triumphal arch, arguing it would cast a shadow on the graves of their relatives and obstruct the sightline from President John F. Kennedy’s gravesite. [The New York Times]
UAE collector Elie Khouri is building a newly renovated and redesigned space for his eponymous art foundation in Dubai’s coastal district of Jumeirah 1, with planned public exhibitions and educational programs due to open in 2028. [The Art Newspaper]
A senator in Peru has requested the removal of giant erotic sculptures, known as huacos eróticos, from a public park near the northern city of Trujillo, which are replicas of pre-Incan Moche ceramics and were initially installed to promote tourism. [The Art Newspaper]
Who can resist an exhibition co-curated by a K-pop superstar, “RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me”? Over 66,000 people have bought tickets since last month’s opening, as advance sales run six times higher than for any previous San Francisco Museum of Modern Art exhibition. [ARTnews]
The Liverpool Biennial has announced its theme—The Age of Magical Thinking—and artists for the edition scheduled for 5 June to 19 September, curated by Aimee Harrison and Lucía Sanromán. [ArtReview]
The Kicker
FOREVER PHOTO. “I think photography will never die. It’s like painting,” German photographer Thomas Ruff told the Financial Times. He was speaking ahead of a solo exhibition of his photographs at Paris Photo, the international fair opening to the public November 12-15 at the Grand Palais. This edition celebrates the 200th anniversary of photography and looks closely at how the medium has evolved over the centuries. Ruff’s major presentation on a large wall at the fair entrance is a highlight, produced by five galleries (David Zwirner, Konrad Fischer, Mai 36, Lia Rumma, Sprüth Magers). Speaking about how his practice took a key turn around the late 1980s, Ruff remembers: “I said to myself, ‘If I insist on authorship [of the photograph], I cannot make this work. And if I give it up, I can.’ And so I decided in this case I have to give up authorship to create the work.” From there grew his celebrated “Sterne (Stars)” series from 1989 to 1992, which he made by enlarging negatives depicting outer space, photographed by the European Southern Observatory.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/revea.author: Simon Hooper
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/revea.text:
Revealed: West Bank petrol station chain faces $325m claim in PA fuel-smuggling probe
A petrol station chain owned by one of the West Bank’s wealthiest businessmen is facing accusations of alleged fuel smuggling, financial misconduct and tax evasion totalling more than 1bn shekels ($325m), according to a leaked report seen by Middle East Eye.
The investigation, which has unfolded against a backdrop of worsening fuel shortages in the occupied Palestinian territory, has led to the arrest and weeks-long detention of Tarek al-Natsheh, the chairman of Al-Huda Group, as well as raids by security forces on his company’s offices and the confiscation of computers and financial records.
Lawyers for Natsheh, who is accused in the report of profiting from smuggling activities, say he denies wrongdoing and stands ready to pay any taxes he may legally owe.
They say the company and Natsheh are cooperating with legal proceedings, but have criticised his detention, commenting that “personal freedom should not be used as a means of pressure to accept figures whose accuracy has not been established”.
MEE sent a detailed list of questions and a request for comment to Malek al-Awri, legal adviser for the defence team, ahead of publication of this article. Awri referred MEE to a previous statement he had given to the Palestinian Watan newspaper last month.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
MEE has also asked the Palestinian Authority’s Ministry of Finance, which commissioned the report, for comment.
Tanker seized
Al-Huda Group controls a number of businesses in the West Bank, including Al-Huda Fuel Group, which operates a network of 28 petrol stations across the territory.
On 10 July, one of its fuel tankers was seized in Jericho on suspicion of transporting smuggled petrol, prompting PA Finance Minister Estephan Anton Salameh to appoint an audit committee to investigate the company’s operations.
In a report seen by MEE, which is understood to date from early September, the committee called for Al-Huda to pay 1,003,189,811 shekels ($322.5m) to the public treasury, which it said was owed as a result of alleged financial misconduct, tax evasion and smuggling dating back to 2020.
This consisted of 712,736,591 shekels owed in VAT, unpaid fuel duty and other taxes based on the company’s own records and accounting figures, and 290,453,220 shekels covering a further amount the committee estimated it owed for shipments in which it had been unable to establish how much fuel was smuggled.
The committee said this figure did not include interest or fines that might be imposed as a result of its findings. It also called for further investigation and access to the bank accounts of a number of individuals and companies linked to Al-Huda.
Fuel supplies in the West Bank are tightly controlled by Israel and the PA.
Under an agreement in place since 1994, the PA-run General Petroleum Authority (GPA) is the only body permitted to import petrol into the territory. Almost all of it is purchased from Israeli fuel companies - at Israeli prices - and transported through Israeli-controlled checkpoints.
Private companies such as Al-Huda then buy petrol from the GPA. Nonetheless, up to a third of petrol sold in the West Bank is estimated to be smuggled fuel.
According to the 35-page report, the files seized from Al-Huda included a number of GPA delivery notes that did not match the GPA’s own records.
The driver of the fuel tanker seized on 10 July, whose name was the same as a driver named in the documents, had admitted involvement in previous deliveries of smuggled petrol earlier in 2026, the report said.
The driver told investigators these deliveries had been arranged under the direct command of Mazen al-Natsheh, Tarek al-Natsheh’s brother, who serves as the general manager of Al-Huda Fuel Group.
Mazen al-Natsheh was detained for questioning in August and initially denied any involvement in, or knowledge of, fuel smuggling.
But he later admitted he had organised some deliveries to a petrol station in Jericho because of the seriousness of fuel shortages in the West Bank, according to the report.
These deliveries had been arranged through a Palestinian with Israeli identification documents, Mazen al-Natsheh is reported to have told investigators.
Tarek al-Natsheh is currently in detention in Ramallah. He handed himself in on 9 September, weeks after prosecutors issued a warrant for his arrest in July. At a court hearing on 22 October, his detention was extended for 45 days, according to local news reports.
Tarek al-Natsheh faces accusations of sharing in profits from alleged smuggling operations at Abu Khalil petrol station in Anata in the central West Bank.
According to a statement made to prosecutors by the owner of the petrol station, Natsheh was a partner in a scheme which started shortly after the start of the war in Gaza and involved smuggling 30,000 to 40,000 litres of petrol a month.
The report also cited what it described as a “close and extensive financial relationship” between Tarek al-Natsheh and Al-Huda Fuel Group and others involved in alleged fuel smuggling.
Lawyers for Tarek al-Natsheh and Al-Huda have repeatedly stressed in public statements that they deny wrongdoing and are cooperating with the financial investigation and stand ready to pay any money that they may legally owe.
'Legal and accounting principles'
When contacted, Malek al-Awri, legal advisor for the defence team, referred MEE to statements made to Watan in early October.
Watan reported, citing “informed sources”, that the investigation into the company was complete and had estimated the amount it owed at more than 1bn shekels.
Awri said the figure did not constitute an official financial claim or a settled debt and said the case remained under investigation.
He said that the defence team had not received the official report or any details of the legal or accounting grounds on which the figure was based.
He said its alleged conclusions remained subject to “examination, debate, challenge, and judicial oversight”, Watan reported.
Awri said figures and data on which the investigation was based were still under review and scrutiny and that the defence team had “substantial legal, technical, and accounting-based arguments and objections regarding them”.
“Awri affirmed that the defence team’s position is clear: they seek to establish the financial truth - documented and based on sound, fair legal and accounting principles - that ensures the recovery of any funds rightfully owed to the public treasury, while simultaneously protecting the rights of the company and the individuals involved,” Watan reported.
Commenting on Natsheh’s detention, Awri said that “personal liberty should not be used as leverage to compel the acceptance of figures whose accuracy has yet to be determined”.
He said that assets already seized from the company were “sufficient to cover any claims ultimately proven valid through proper judicial proceedings”.
'Personal liberty should not be used as leverage to compel the acceptance of figures whose accuracy has yet to be determined'
- Malek al-Awri, legal advisor for Tarek al-Natsheh and Al-Huda Group
Awri reiterated the defence team’s respect for the public prosecution, the judiciary, and the finance ministry, and said it was committed to “cooperating with the established legal procedures aimed at uncovering the truth and protecting public funds”, Watan reported.
Palestinian security forces, along with customs officers, raided Al-Huda petrol stations at the end of July, confiscating fuel reserves and seizing documents and financial records.
On 5 August, the company’s headquarters in Ramallah was raided, with investigators seizing accounting records and equipment, including Tarek Al-Natsheh’s laptop computer.
The investigation into Al-Huda has taken place at a time of acute fuel shortages in the West Bank, prompted by factors including tighter Israeli economic restrictions and a deteriorating security situation.
The crisis has left Palestinians queuing for hours at petrol stations, and cars stranded on the streets, with Majdi Hasan, the head of the GPA, blaming shortages on panic buying caused by “the lack of stability in the region” in an interview with Voice of Palestine Radio.
Hani al-Masri, a Palestinian political analyst and the director general of Masarat, the Palestinian Centre for Policy Research and Strategic Studies, told MEE that fuel smuggling was nothing new and was necessary for Palestinian daily life because Israel exported far less fuel into the West Bank than was needed.
“There’s a daily shortage, so there’s bound to be smuggling,” said Masri.
“It seems that there is a dispute regarding who benefits from it and how to organise it.”
Masri said it remained unclear why Natsheh had been detained, and that there were many unanswered questions about the case.
“Clearly there are stories that still aren’t known,” he added.
Some reports have sought to link the PA’s crackdown on fuel smuggling to its own dire financial straits, prompted largely by Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s withholding of funds, including customs and excise revenues, it collects on behalf of the PA under the terms of the Oslo Accords.
In October, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas signed a decree for the creation of a new PA-controlled “national petroleum company” to control the import, transport, storage and sale of fuel in the West Bank.
Speaking to An-Najah Broadcasting Channel in early October, Jawad Obeidat, another lawyer on Natsheh’s defence team, rejected speculation about political interference in the case.
“The public prosecution, with all due respect, is performing its role with full transparency and without any outside interference,” he said.

Italy vs France: UEFA Nations League – preview, team news, predictions
Kylian Mbappe ‘under treatment’ as Group A1 leaders France travel to Italy for a game at the San Siro, Milan.
Who: Italy vs France
What: UEFA Nations League, Group A1
Where: San Siro, Milan, Italy
When: Thursday, November 12, at 8:45pm (19:45 GMT).
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 16:45 GMT ahead of our live text commentary stream
Italy host France for a heavyweight Nations League clash as they meet in the penultimate group stage game.
Under Roberto Mancini, who is back in his second stint in charge of the Azzurri, Italy lost their first group game 2-0 to Belgium but subsequently recorded thumping wins over Turkiye and got an impressive draw in Paris.
Italy, who travel to Belgium for their final group game on Sunday, sit second in the group – one point ahead of the Belgians but three adrift of France.
Zinedine Zidane, who took over as France coach from Didier Deschamps after the 2026 World Cup, led Les Bleus to a 1-0 win in Turkiye, and victories over Belgium home and away – including a 4-1 thrashing in Paris.
Zidane certainly has plenty of history with Italy as a player; he spent five seasons with Juventus and famously got a red card after headbutting Italy’s Marco Materazzi in the 2006 World Cup final.
France, who host Turkiye in their final group game on Sunday, can secure their quarterfinal spot with victory over Italy.
Mbappe misses France training ahead of Italy clash
France captain Kylian Mbappe did not take part in team training on Wednesday and remained “under treatment” ahead of his country’s Nations League match against Italy, Les Bleus’ coaching staff said.
The French staff did not provide any further details regarding the 27-year-old’s physical condition.
The Real Madrid forward is back in the France squad for this camp after missing their last three matches through injury.
Mbappe scored the winning goal in Zidane’s first match as coach against Turkiye in September, but had to leave the pitch shortly afterwards due to pain in his left knee.
Mancini injects youth into the Italy setup
AC Milan forward Alphadjo Cisse earned his first Italy call-up after an impressive start to the season. The 20-year-old has scored seven goals in 12 games in his first season with Milan, including a hat-trick in the Europa League win over Red Bull Salzburg last month.
Cisse is one of four new faces among the 31 players selected by Italy coach Roberto Mancini. Parma midfielder Simone Lontani, 18, is included along with Como teenagers Mattia Liberali and Riccardo Cassano.
Liberali, 19, scored in Como’s record-equalling 9-1 win over Lens in the Champions League on Wednesday.
Cassano, 17, has yet to make his Como first-team debut. He and Lontani will train with the senior squad from Sunday before rejoining Italy’s under-18 and under-19 teams.
What happened in the last Italy vs France game?
Michael Olise scored a superb goal but France were held to a 1-1 draw by Italy on October 2, 2026 in Zinedine Zidane’s first home game since being appointed coach of Les Bleus.
Four days after coming off the bench to score a stunning solo effort to give France a 1-0 win in Belgium, Bayern Munich star Olise again showcased his spectacular talent by smashing a shot in off the crossbar from a free kick early in the second half.
However, Inter Milan defender Alessandro Bastoni equalised for Italy midway through the second half to prevent Zidane from making it three wins out of three in charge of his country.
What have the coaches said?
Mancini: “In football, results change everything, but we still need to work, raise the bar and improve as a team; results are not enough.”
“I like that we are building a group of young players, along with some experienced ones who aren’t here now because they have issues. We played some good games and they are building a nice bond.”
Zidane: [on the death of Tenerife’s Jesus de Miguel after an on-pitch collision] “I’m saddened by what happened, deeply affected. It even gives me goosebumps, because you never want to see something like that on a football pitch.
“Above all, I feel sad for the family. I hope I never see anything like that again on a football pitch for the rest of my life.”
Predictions
The Opta supercomputer has made France the favourites, with a win probability of 47.4 percent.
Italy were given a 28.3 percent chance of winning, while a draw was estimated at a 24.3 percent likelihood.
Head-to-head
- Previous matches: 42
- Italy wins: 20
- Draws: 10
- France wins: 12
Last five encounters:
- October 2, 2026: France 1-1 Italy (Nations League)
- November 17, 2024: Italy 1-3 France (Nations League)
- September 6, 2024: France 1-3 Italy (Nations League)
- June 1, 2018: France 3-1 Italy (Friendly)
- September 1, 2016: Italy 1-3 France (Friendly)
Italy’s team news
Roma defender Gianluca Mancini has withdrawn from the squad with a muscular injury, so Juventus’s Federico Gatti has been called up to replace him.
Italy are also missing Giovanni Di Lorenzo, Giacomo Raspadori and Moise Kean due to injuries.
Predicted starting XI:
Donnarumma (goalkeeper); Kayode, Scalvini, Bastoni, Calafiori; Barella, Tonali, Doumbia; Vergara, Pio Esposito, Sebastiano Esposito
France’s team news
Mbappe is the big concern for France as he undergoes treatment for an unspecified problem.
William Saliba, Maghnes Akliouche, Ousmane Dembele, Manu Kone, Pierre Kalulu and Esteban Lepaul have all been ruled out with injuries.
However, Les Bleus will welcome back Real Madrid’s Ibrahima Konate and Aurelien Tchouameni, who missed out on the last round of games due to injuries. Dayot Upamecano returns from suspension to bolster the defence.
Predicted starting XI:
Maignan (goalkeeper); Gusto, Jacquet, Upamecano, Truffert; Cherki, Tchouameni, Rabiot; Olise, Doue, Mbappe

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.title: Art Basel to Reduce Galleries’ Invoices by 20 Percent Due to Early Closure of Paris Fair
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.author: Devorah Lauter
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.text:
All exhibitors who participated in the most recent edition of Art Basel Paris, which closed two days early because of planned protests, will get a 20 percent reduction on their final invoices.
“We will exceptionally be extending a 20 percent reduction on booth fees to all galleries that participated in the Paris fair, in recognition of the closure,” on October 24–25, Art Basel chief executive Noah Horowitz told ARTnews in an interview.
Additionally, tickets purchased for that weekend have already been refunded. Galleries typically pay up front for most of their participation, but the final invoices come within 30 days of a fair’s closure, and they will reflect the new discount. The reduction will not apply to so-called “special orders” (lights, booth customisation, etc.), as the latter represent a third-party expense that Art Basel does not control. For example, if a gallery’s booth fee were $10,000, and the additional special order service fees accrued during the fair’s installation, such as lighting costs and any customization to the booth, were $10,000, for a total of $20,000, the exhibitor would receive a discount of $2,000.
Since Art Basel Paris announced it would shut early for security reasons ahead of a new wave of protests, participating exhibitors, particularly smaller and emerging galleries, have been eagerly awaiting to hear whether they will be compensated for the lost time.
The fair opened to its “Avant Première” preview to VVIP guests on Tuesday, October 20, with its Wednesday and Thursday openings also being exclusive to invited guests. The fair was only open to the public for one day, Friday, instead of extending to Saturday and Sunday as originally planned.
“[I’m] conscious that it’s taken about two and a half weeks to get here, but we wanted to bring this all together comprehensively and ensure that we engaged our gallery community properly before implementing and rolling all this out,” said Horowotiz.
Art Basel, which is in the midst of preparing its Miami Beach edition (running December 2–6), also sent a letter about the discount to all participating galleries Wednesday, signed by Art Basel Paris director Karim Crippa. “While we appreciate that the closure impacted galleries in different ways, we believe this approach offers a fair and considered way forward, reflecting our appreciation of the partnership we share and our commitment to strengthening it further,” it states.
The Letter
The news comes following a strongly worded letter from the French galleries association Comité Professionnel des Galeries d’Art (CPGA) addressed to Crippa, dated October 28, demanding “fair compensation” for the shortened event, as first reported by Monopol.
In its letter, the CPGA, which counts over 340 members and represents 57 of the 211 galleries who exhibited at Art Basel Paris, complained that the fair had shown “contempt” or “disregard” (the original French term used was “mépris”) for not consulting exhibitors before announcing the early closure.
There was “a lot of anger and incomprehension” about the extent of communication between the fair and its exhibitors on the discussion of when to close, according to one leading CPGA member speaking to ARTnews anonymously to protect their relationships. They added: “We understand it was a difficult decision to make, but we don’t understand why no one was consulted, not even for a few minutes!”
In an October 29 email update from the CPGA to its members, the group stated further: “Such a decision called for opening a dialogue with the exhibitors’ representatives; it was the subject of no prior discussion.”
The fair’s Saturday closure has been widely accepted as necessary because of protests scheduled that day, including one that called for people to gather outside the Grand Palais, the venue for Art Basel Paris. Many exhibitors, however, were surprised that the fair would not reopen on Sunday. Protests were not planned for that day, and a major Cezanne exhibition located in another part of the Grand Palais reopened Sunday.
“We fully support the Saturday closure. As a measure of precaution, it seemed to us absolutely essential after the security failure of the previous weekend and the extremely serious unrest that followed. But we would have liked to argue for reopening on Sunday,” CPGA president Philippe Charpentier told the Art Newspaper, France last month.
In response to the CPGA’s remonstrance, Horowitz told ARTnews: “This is a highly dynamic situation we were responding to. We had many conversations with many galleries during the fair and certainly in the weeks following, and I think we learned a lot of lessons coming through this. And as all businesses do, we’ll continue to improve our processes and make adjustments for the future.”
About staying closed through Sunday, he added that, “Given the uncertainty surrounding the potential impact and duration of the planned demonstrations, as well as access to the Grand Palais, we couldn’t be confident at the time that conditions would allow for a safe reopening on Sunday. Several exhibitors also expressed serious concerns about leaving the artworks in the Grand Palais unattended on the Saturday. In recognition of all of that, we concluded that closing early and beginning the dismantling on Friday evening was the most responsible course of action, and ultimately in the best interest of safeguarding the artworks themselves, but also the gallerists, teams, all the workers, and, of course, the visitors as well.”
Horowitz also confirmed a December 14 meeting is planned between Art Basel Paris and CPGA, to talk more broadly about the “overarching situation [and] the broader relationship” between various parties. Though Horowitz said such meetings regularly take place, the forthcoming one follows the CPGA’s specific request to convene with Art Basel leadership about redress for the shortened fair.
Representatives of France’s Ministry of Culture and the Grand Palais RMN venue are also expected to attend, but both told ARTnews they have not been involved with the question of discounts for the shortened fair. (Horowitz said he could not comment on Art Basel’s contract with the venue, French authorities, or its insurance arrangements.)
“Our role is to ensure a space for constructive dialogue: to understand the impact on the galleries, the organizer and the host venue, and to learn lessons from this situation,” a Culture Ministry spokesperson told ARTnews in a statement.
What the Dealers Say
The CPGA is not the only one that has formally requested compensation. ARTnews reached out to dozens of smaller galleries outside of France to ask how they think the fair handled the closure, whether they agree some reimbursement is in order (they all said yes), and if so, what kind. To the latter question, answers ranged from suggesting the fair prioritize reimbursements for smaller galleries to proposing the fair pay back one third of the booth fair price, since that was the amount of time the fair was cut short. Vouchers toward next year’s application and booth fees were also suggested.
Horowitz said that unlike some sort of credit scheme for future Art Basel fairs, “we thought the most important thing was to directly tie it to and provide immediate relief now for those that showed with us at the fair in October.”
“We felt that a 20 percent reduction was a fair and reasonable place to land,” he added. He also explained the fair has “concerns for the success of all galleries across all sectors of our fairs,” no matter their size or prominence.
Many of the dealers interviewed for this article said they trusted Art Basel had made the best decision, given the information they had at the time, in regard to the closure. They also said they agreed with CPGA’s demands and appreciated its lobbying on behalf of participating galleries. But the dealers often shied away from the harsher language used in the CPGA’s letter, including that exhibitors had been treated with “contempt.”
“We all feel that our interests are well-defended, and personally I feel like the French gallery association, and Philippe Charpentier from Mor Charpentier, [the CPGA’s president], will advocate for all of us, not just the French galleries. They are the best equipped to deal with it,” said Los Angeles– and New York–based dealer François Ghebaly. “Because of that letter [from the CPGA], we felt no need to press forward,” with further claims, he added.
The CPGA has also successfully led lobbying efforts in the past to the French government, notably on issues such as lowering art sales tax to 5.5 percent.
Ghebaly’s prominent mid-sized gallery did well at the fair, largely thanks to advanced planning, rather than relying on chance encounters to make key sales. “It was a pretty extreme and unprecedented situation, and in a way, I think [the fair] did okay,” Ghebaly said. “I’m glad most of the event was able to move forward as planned for the beginning of the week, and then they made a call, which I’m sure was a complicated decision.”
However, he said, “Conversations were a little different with younger dealers who are starting out and are upstairs in the alleys [of the Grand Palais]. They may have a loss of income that is more difficult to absorb.”
Though the fair reported selling 306 artworks for $148 million by Wednesday, much of that business was done by major galleries, who typically complete their sales after the first few days. Smaller and emerging galleries were hit hardest by the shortened schedule, because they rely on those final days to close deals. Visitors also tend to use the rest of the week to see booths along the venue’s periphery and upstairs level, while smaller-budgeted collectors from the region visit more affordable galleries over the weekend, when they’re off work.
Aron Gent, owner of Document, a gallery with spaces in Chicago and Lisbon, told ARTnews he formally requested a partial refund from Art Basel; His booth was located in the fair’s upstairs corridors.
“The closure affected us greatly, being 1/3 shorter, as we sell mostly works under [$]10k that a great deal of weekend attendees can afford,” Gent wrote in an email. “Also, most of the artists in our booth are unknown to a majority of the people who enter our booth, so the main goal is to educate them on their practices and hope for additional exhibition opportunities and the possibilities of future sales.”
He added that, on further reflection, the fair should have announced earlier, on Tuesday, that they would close early, and then extended daily opening hours for the remaining days, “to accommodate as many people as possible.”
Other dealers said they had also been waiting to hear about reimbursement, but felt they lacked the power to do much about it. Ellen de Bruijne, who runs the eponymous gallery in Amsterdam, said that being a small gallery from the Netherlands, she was “not in a position to demand” compensation from Art Basel Paris. An associate at LC Queisser, which has spaces in Tbilisi, Georgia, and Cologne, Germany, said the gallery is “simply waiting for Art Basel to come up with a proposed solution, whether that involves compensation or, for example, a reduction in the application fee. We are not requesting any specific form of compensation, but some form of compensation.”
The associate continued, “Even just considering hotel costs and staff who had already travelled to Paris, galleries have lost money. … We don’t necessarily think anything would have happened, but the public anticipation and concern were already so intense that many people decided not to come to Paris over the weekend. We think it was reasonable to take these precautions.”
Going forward, dealers observed that disturbances to large art-world gatherings on a similar scale may become the new normal. “We are living through a turbulent moment across the world,” said Ghebaly. “There may be more disruptions of these kinds of massive events, and we should get used to it.”

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.title: Dua Lipa, Tame Impala and SZA set to headline Coachella 2027
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.author: Owen Myers
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.text:
The lineup for the 2027 Coachella festival has been revealed after months of speculation, with Dua Lipa, SZA and Tame Impala set to headline the California event.
The festival will also see Madonna headlining the dance tent with Zara Larsson, Robyn, Phoebe Bridgers, Weezer and Daddy Yankee set to perform. The festival will take place in the Empire Polo Club in Indio on 9-11 April and 16-18 April.
In recent weeks, rumors have swirled surrounding the 2027 lineup. SZA seemingly confirmed her booking earlier this week with an Instagram story teasing “SZAChella” as well as a new album and tour coming next year.
The event marks Tame Impala’s return to the desert after the group previously headlined in 2019, while SZA guested during Justin Bieber’s headline set earlier this year. Dua Lipa previously popped out during Martin Garrix’s 2017 appearance; her 2027 slot marks the first time a British female solo artist has headlined the festival.
This year’s Coachella was headlined by Bieber, Karol G and Sabrina Carpenter, with the latter’s performance praised by the Guardian’s Adrian Horton as “a dizzying full-scale hybrid production of undaunted vision … and immaculate performance”.
As well as US names, the 2027 festival also showcases global talent including Adéla, Becky G, Jisoo, Drain Gang, NCT and Måneskin.
In addition to Dua Lipa, British artists are well represented with Jorja Smith, EsDeeKid, Underworld, Shygirl and Lambrini Girls all set to perform.
Breakout talent on the lineup includes the young pop artist Underscores, rapper Nettspend, showgaze duo After and hyperpop artist Tiffany Day.
Madonna’s slot comes 21 years after she first headlined the dance tent around the release of her 2005 album Confessions on a Dance Floor; earlier this year, she released a sequel titled Confessions II which hit number one on the US and UK charts.
In August, Emily Eavis denied rumors that Madonna was set to play Glastonbury next year.
Passes for the 2027 Coachella festival go on sale on 13 November at 12pm pacific time. For the fifteenth year, YouTube will return as Coachella’s livestream partner for both weekends.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Rubio backs blockade, Vance wants deal: Is Trump’s team split on Iran war?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Rubio backs blockade, Vance wants deal: Is Trump’s team split on Iran war?
Torn between more military action and diplomacy, US appears to settle for drawn-out economic pressure campaign, blockade.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said that Washington’s economic pressure campaign against Iran is proving so effective that a resumption of large-scale military operations is unnecessary.
His remarks are the latest in an often-evolving series of messages from US President Donald Trump’s administration on the conflict with Iran. They also come after a crushing midterm defeat for Trump’s Republican Party, which the president acknowledged was likely partly driven by public opposition to the war.
So how do Rubio’s latest remarks compare with the positions of other administration officials, and what do they say about the state of the conflict?
What have Trump, Rubio and Vance said about the conflict?
Rubio made his latest comments on Tuesday after meeting with foreign ministers from the Group of Seven (G7) forum in Paris.
He said he told G7 allies that “the economic campaign [against Iran] is so devastating that right now there is no need for major combat operations”.
“We don’t need to conduct military strikes if we’re achieving the same objective through economic means and economic pressure. That’s not stalemate,” Rubio said.
“The economic pressure on Iran is going to get even worse,” he added.
Rubio also pushed G7 allies to help “protect shipping” around the embattled Strait of Hormuz, where he said US forces would stay.
The secretary of state’s remarks were largely in line with Trump’s comments on Monday, when the president said further strikes against Iran were “quite unlikely”.
Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump said the US’s Gulf allies preferred a continuation of the “status quo”, referring to the US’s blockade of Iranian ports. Trump added that there appears to be “positive momentum” towards ending the conflict, but that the US remains “locked and loaded” should circumstances change.
Vice President JD Vance, who has been more critical of the war and recently wrote a lengthy social media post blaming the Republican Party’s midterm defeat on the conflict, favours a deal with Iran, which Trump does not believe is possible right now, the Reuters news agency cited an informed source as saying.
Between sanctions and diplomacy: What are the divisions on Iran war strategy?
Negotiations to end the US-Iran conflict have been largely stalled for months, as Iran continues to target vessels it claims are violating its conditions for transit through the Strait of Hormuz and the US ramps up sanctions against Iran and continues to blockade Iranian ports, with plans to block Iran’s land-based supply routes as well.
Back in September, Iran proposed a seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart talks. Tehran has since said that timeline could be brought down to two days. Tehran’s demands for the US include lifting sanctions Washington imposed after the collapse of a June memorandum of understanding (MoU), reducing the US military presence in the region, reinstating oil waivers and releasing frozen Iranian funds.
Trump, torn between restarting an unpopular war or pushing harder for a deal with Tehran, has for now settled on a middle ground: doubling down on the pressure campaign against Iran while avoiding a return to full-scale military action, according to officials quoted by Axios.
That strategy is backed by several key administration officials, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and CIA Director John Ratcliffe, as well as Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, Axios cited US officials as saying.
However, several US allies in the region, including Pakistan, Iraq and Turkiye, are concerned that a drawn-out US pressure campaign against Iran could hurt their own business interests, said one official cited by the news outlet.
Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, said that a long-term US policy of intensive sanctions and a blockade against Iran would only prolong an “unstable status quo” that would eventually escalate into more military confrontation.
However, he said one “walk-away” option for Trump could be to quietly relax the sanctions and blockade while maintaining them “on paper”.
In this case, “Trump walks away and claims to retain the blockade and sanctions infrastructure, but in reality, allows it to imperceptibly wither away,” Parsi told Al Jazeera. “The blockade begins to loosen, sanctions enforcement begins to decay, and slowly but surely, Asian and Middle Eastern countries begin trading with and investing in Iran.”
“A new equilibrium emerges in which sanctions enforcement is strong enough for the US to claim the restrictions are still in place, yet weak enough to prevent Tehran from challenging the new status quo,” Parsi said.
Have the midterm election results impacted Trump’s strategy?
Yes, according to analysts.
Negar Mortazavi, senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy in Washington, DC, said the Republicans’ resounding election defeat “dramatically raised the political cost of more escalation” and gave the Democrats a stronger mandate to challenge the war.
“If Democrats unite and use their new power aggressively, they can make it increasingly difficult for Trump to continue the war, pressuring him to end it,” Mortazavi told Al Jazeera.
“A diplomatic breakthrough is not guaranteed, but the political and strategic costs of escalation keep growing, making another round of war less likely,” she added.
Both Trump and Vance have acknowledged that the Iran war was partly to blame for the Republicans’ loss, with Trump saying voters were not ready for petrol prices to rise.
According to a poll by Reuters/Ipsos completed on Monday, 71 percent of Americans – including 93 percent of Democrats and 51 percent of Republicans – favour congressional legislation that would halt the Iran war.
What is Iran saying?
Iranian officials have upped their rhetoric even as Washington appears to be moving away from military escalation.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Tuesday said the war will “not end either through military means or by increasing sanctions”, but only through “using the language of respect”.
In comments carried by Iran’s IRNA news agency, he urged the US “to act on Iran’s demands and conditions”, adding that Trump “should have realised much earlier that he has not achieved, and will not achieve, any of his goals in the war with Iran”.
Iran’s top security chief Mohsen Rezaei, in a social media post on Monday, said the US government had been “wrecked” by the war and that it was time for it to “surrender” to Iran’s demands.
Al Jazeera’s Mohamed Vall, reporting from Tehran, noted that Iran’s language has become “more confident than ever before”.
“They’re trying to convey to the public, internally, and also to the Americans, that there is no way this war can be declared over without responding to those conditions presented by Iran during the negotiations,” said Vall.
What is the current status of diplomacy?
There are mixed messages.
The Qatari Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Tuesday said that Doha is “working tirelessly” in its ongoing mediation efforts, and has received positive reactions from both sides.
Trump, the day before, after hosting Qatar’s prime minister at the White House, also spoke of “momentum towards the end of this conflict”, adding that “Iran is talking to us, and they’re talking very politely”.
Rubio, for his part, said the US remains “open to diplomacy”, but called Iran’s current demands “totally unrealistic”.
“We expect that could change – and if it does, we’re prepared for diplomacy,” he said.
Iranian officials, meanwhile, have appeared more sceptical of the latest reports of mediation, insisting that the US must accept their demands.
Rezaei on Tuesday said there were no negotiations taking place between Tehran and Washington and that Iran would retaliate against any new US attack by targeting US bases “far away”. He also said Iran would not let any of its enriched nuclear material leave the country, ruling out a concession the US has sought in potential nuclear talks.
In a social media post, Rezaei went on to accuse the US of “manufacturing FAKE NEWS about imaginary talks”.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/an.title: Anonymous Was A Woman 2026 Recipients Include Kay WalkingStick, Trisha Baga, and Beatriz Cortez
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/an.author: Maximilíano Durón
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/an.text:
The New York–based Anonymous Was A Woman has announced the 2026 recipients of its annual awards, which come with $50,000 each for this year’s 15 winners.
The 2026 cohort includes Kay WalkingStick, a painter whose work examines the American landscape from the point of view of Indigenous people, and Trisha Baga, whose video installations look at the relationship between the physical and digital worlds. Born in 1935, WalkingStick is this year’s oldest winner, while Baga, who was born in 1985, is the youngest recipient.
Other winners include Beatriz Cortez, whose sculptures engage speculative futures and multiple temporalities; Elisabeth Kley, who is known for her ceramic installations that feature geometric and plant motifs; and Candace Hill-Montgomery, whose experimental practice since the 1970s has synthesized “her experience of post-war segregation in New York and the revolutionary activism of the time,” per a release, and was recently showcased in MoMA PS1’s Greater New York quinquennial.
“At a time when artists face mounting uncertainty within a fast-changing world, the need for direct, unrestricted support is as urgent as ever,” AWAW founder Susan Unterberg said in a statement. “The artists that we recognize this year are extraordinary. The range, ambition, and originality of their work is a reminder of just how vital artists are for our world.”
In addition to the awards, the organization also announced the launch of the second edition of its Artists Speaks Survey, in partnership with SMU DataArts and journalist Charlotte Burns. The 2024 edition collected responses from some 1,200 artists, and the new edition seeks to “examine what has changed—and what has not—while addressing emerging challenges including artificial intelligence, changes in policy and funding, and the conditions artists need to sustain their practices.” The survey is open to women, trans, and nonbinary artists of any age; responses will be accepted until January 3.
Since 1996, the AWAW awards have disbursed over $10 million in funds to more than 400 artists. Last year’s winners included Candida Alvarez, Park McArthur, and Lola Flash. The awards are meant to support the careers of mid-career women, trans, and nonbinary artists “at a significant junction in their lives or careers to continue to grow and pursue their work,” according to a release.
“Receiving this award was incredible news. I was literally calculating the astronomical cost of hard drives to back up my digital archive when I received the call,” Baga told ARTnews in an email. “As you might know, hard drive prices these days are insane because of AI data centers driving up the demand, and I am a video artist with about 80 terabytes of very important, very tenuously stored video files I’ve gathered and metabolized over the past 20 years.”
Textile artist Elaine Reichek echoed Baga’s sentiment about the rising cost of making art, saying, “The amount is significant enough to make a real difference in my day-to-day practice. I’m truly grateful to be able to afford the cost of my materials, which have risen due to tariffs and supply chain difficulties. A burden has been lifted!”
Baga added that she will also use the funds to continue focusing on her “recently revived 3D video installation practice, providing an income so I can focus on the several institutional shows I have scheduled this year.”
“This award comes at the end of a long year, a year of big works with very limited resources,” choreographer nora chipaumire told ARTnews. “Receiving this individual award validates my life in the arts. It means recognition of an artist who wants to continue to shift frames and push over the edges. This award says to me: people matter. Massive joy and gratitude.”
The full list of winners follows below.
	Laylah Ali (b. 1968, Buffalo, New York; based in western Massachusetts) 
Trisha Baga (b. 1985, Venice, Florida; based in Queens, New York)
nora chipaumire (b. 1965, Rhodesia, now Zimbabwe; based in New York)
Beatriz Cortez (b. 1970, San Salvador, El Salvador; based in Los Angeles and Davis, California)
Ellie Ga (b. 1976, New York; based in Lisbon)
Andrea Geyer (b. 1971, Freiburg im Breisgau, Germany; based in New York)
Candace Hill-Montgomery (b. 1945, New York; based in Bridgehampton, New York)
Elisabeth Kley (b. 1956, New York; based in New York)
Laura Parnes (b. 1968, Buffalo, New York; based in New York)
Marsha Pels (b. 1950, Brooklyn; based in Brooklyn)
Elaine Reichek (b. 1943, Brooklyn; based in New York)
Katherine Sherwood (b. 1952, New Orleans, LA; based in San Francisco Bay Area)
Sara Siestreem (Hanis Coos, b. 1976, Springfield, Oregon; based in Portland, Oregon)
Rea Tajiri (b. 1958, Chicago, IL; based in Philadelphia)
Kay WalkingStick (b. 1935, Syracuse, NY; based in Pennsylvania)

Retrial of Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah suspended
An Egyptian court on Wednesday adjourned the retrial of Mada Masr editor-in-chief Lina Attalah until 18 November to consider a defence request for the judge’s removal, the independent news outlet said.
Attalah faces charges of publishing false news and operating a website without a licence in a case in which she was sentenced to a year in prison in her absence in 2024.
Mada Masr’s lawyer, Hassan al-Azhari, said the defence would submit its grounds for seeking the judge’s removal ahead of the next hearing, arguing that he had “already formed a view against the defendant”.
The presiding judge, Mohamed Mubarak, also issued a ruling on 27 October in a separate case fining Attalah three million Egyptian pounds (about $56,000) and ordering Mada Masr’s closure.
The proceedings come amid a wider crackdown on independent media, including the detention in September of all six journalists working for fact-checking outlet Matsadaash.
