https://www.artnews.com/art-news/reviews.title: RM’s SFMOMA Show Changed My Mind About Celebrity Curators
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/reviews.author: Alex Greenberger
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/reviews.text:
An exhibition co-curated by a K-pop superstar isn’t the kind of show most art critics rush to review. But I couldn’t resist. Call it curiosity, or perhaps a little FOMO. Even my preparation for writing this review felt different: Instead of poring over essays by art historians and curators, I scrolled through fan-made reels, virtual walkthroughs, and videos featuring excerpts from RM’s audio guide. By the time I arrived, the show already felt strangely familiar.
The numbers alone make it a sensation. Since “RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me” opened in San Francisco last month, more than 66,000 tickets have sold, advance sales ran six times higher than for any previous San Francisco Museum of Modern Art exhibition, and merchandise vanished within hours. In Korea, the show has become a major cultural story. Yet when I pitched this review, the art press had given the exhibition surprisingly little critical attention. Everyone was counting the crowds. Who was looking at the walls?
I understand the reluctance. Celebrity sells, and famous names increasingly anchor exhibitions through their collections, their art, their merch. When fame becomes the main draw, what happens to the art?
RM, born Kim Namjoon, is harder to dismiss. After a 2018 visit to the Art Institute of Chicago exposed how little he knew about Korean artists, he began looking, learning, and collecting. His museum visits, shared through vlogs and social media, have sent fans on their own “RM Tours” around the world. Now, with SFMOMA curators América Castillo and Hyoeun Kim, he has arranged nearly 180 works from his collection and the museum’s holdings across eight rooms organized around color, home, friends, and people. Can personal taste carry a museum exhibition?
The exhibition starts strong. The first gallery, “Bluewater,” opens with Kim Whanki’s 1970 field of tiny blue dots, a painting that the artist’s widow donated to SFMOMA. Around it, blue keeps changing shape: Yves Klein’s saturated pigment, Kim Tschang-yeul’s water drops, Tony Feher’s plastic bottles, Roni Horn’s thick glass, uncannily like water or ice. Color is a loose, even obvious, curatorial thread, but it works on the eye: The same blue reads as weightless, liquid, dense, or impossibly still. In his audio guide, RM marvels that a painting by a Korean artist who died in New York could bring together him, the museum, and strangers from around the world.
“Friendscape” trades serenity for charm. Ugo Rondinone’s rough-hewn bronze fish hang overhead; below, old Korean wooden geese sit on a rippling, water-patterned floor, each bird differently carved, like an eccentric relative. Tiny objects perch on tiled pedestals resembling Korean floor cushions. In the exhibition’s audio guide, RM speaks fondly of the geese, traditionally associated with weddings, as objects that make him feel at home. Tigers and other animals populate the surrounding paintings and ceramics, while Lee Daiwon’s speckled Bugaksan Mountain (1976), RM’s first acquisition, recalls the Pointillist paintings of Seurat that had enchanted him.
In “PhotoBuddha,” visitors take selfies beside Nam June Paik’s television-watching Buddha, a cheeky mirror for our screen-obsessed lives, while a solitary Buddha by Kwon Jinkyu keeps to its corner. RM’s hand is everywhere: handwritten Korean wall texts, polite “please do not touch” signs, an audio track full of laughter and the occasional ramble. One gallery is titled, simply, “I Don’t Know But I Like It.”
That title is either the show’s weakness or its manifesto. I suspect it’s both. Critics are trained to look beyond mere liking. But fandom begins there: you fall for something first and study it later. RM’s audience will learn the story of a wooden goose the way they learned the lore behind an album, because someone they trust cared first. As a critic, I found that oddly nostalgic. It’s how most of us started.
The show is at its best when RM turns that openness on himself. “Home” resembles a living room: worn wooden furniture, shelves of ceramics, a sofa, small paintings, a suspended light by Minjae Kim. Chang Ucchin and Park Soo Keun keep domestic company with Giorgio Morandi. Then comes Son Sangki’s Artificial City–Irony (1987), a lavish living room with a painting hanging on its wall. Son, who lived with a disability and endured considerable hardship, often painted Seoul neighborhoods facing redevelopment. Now his canvas hangs in an interior much like the one it depicts. “Am I being a boring rich person?” RM asks, questioning his own privilege. “It makes me really uncomfortable, and I like it.” The display’s comfort suddenly becomes its critique.
In “Passion,” that discomfort deepens. A spare Park Rehyun abstraction, its floating form resembling a sail or moon, looks effortless. It wasn’t. Park raised four children, helped her deaf husband, the painter Kim Kichang, communicate with others, and painted after everyone slept. Rhee Seundja, who left three sons in wartime Korea to pursue painting in Paris, imagined each brushstroke as a spoonful of rice for her children. Suddenly, her repeated marks suggest separation, labor, and longing. Biography risks flattening complex practices into inspirational stories. Yet listening to RM reflect on his privilege in light of their perseverance, I understood why visitors were moved. The exhibition’s curators told me some visitors had cried, and that more than 700 post-visit comments had been submitted to the museum’s digital mural.
The exhibition begins in blue and ends in umber. In the final room, Yun Hyong-keun’s dark vertical bands bleed into the canvas beside a Rothko. Yun has long been introduced as the “Korean Rothko,” a convenient Western shorthand that RM challenges simply by hanging the two side by side: Rothko’s color hovers and dissolves at the edges, while Yun’s sinks into the cloth, dense and earthbound. The histories differ, too. Yun survived war, imprisonment, and the threat of execution, and his paintings carry that weight. RM admits he cannot fully grasp what those dark stains have swallowed. After the geese and the selfies, it’s an unexpectedly grave farewell, and proof that a fan’s taste can do critical work.
The timing is striking. The show opened days after Ha Chong-Hyun’s retrospective at the Asian Art Museum and the Samsung-backed “Korea” exhibition at the British Museum, and a week before Haegue Yang’s Dia Beacon commission. Korean art’s moment rests on decades of scholarship, institutional effort, and corporate and government backing. RM brings what none of that could guarantee: an audience ready to follow him.
Of course, BTS fans come first, and that should give us pause. A collector’s taste is no substitute for art history. Once it enters a museum, private taste gains public authority, shaping which artists get seen and, potentially, how their work is valued. Star-driven exhibitions shouldn’t become a museum habit. Yet the usual objection, that fame eclipses the art, misses what works here.
RM isn’t standing in front of the paintings. He’s pointing at them. His personal voice brings viewers close enough to form attachments of their own. We don’t always know why we like something. Sometimes that’s where looking begins.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Why did it take so long to unmask Brand and Walliams? Because noughties culture told girls like me abuse was normal | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Mr Justice Bennathan’s sentencing remarks in the trial of Russell Brand hit me like a train, and I know I’m not the only one. This week my Instagram feed has been full of female friends, colleagues and acquaintances sharing his words: “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent.” Those same women are now sharing the Guardian and ITV’s investigation into David Walliams, who is accused of preying on young women for sex, with the same fury and fervour (Walliams has denied the allegations against him).
Both of these stories concerning predatory male behaviour took place in an era when I was a young woman: the “lad culture” era. It dated from about the mid-to-late 90s until the beginning of the #MeToo movement in 2016, and those of us who came of age during it sometimes joke bleakly that it’s a miracle we made it out in one piece. Some of us didn’t, and those victim-survivors live with the daily impact of male coercion, abuse and violence, still.
We were all, essentially, frogs in boiling water. Misogyny and female objectification were so common, so normalised, that all you could do was try to keep swimming before you were boiled alive. With Bennathan’s words I was catapulted back to being 17 years old and sitting in my boyfriend’s parents’ kitchen, where I read a tabloid newspaper column arguing that girls who wore short skirts essentially deserved to be raped. So many of us girls, as we were then, must have had a moment like that, where we realised, essentially, that we were prey, when we realised that we “deserved” it.
How to explain to young women today how it felt back then? Today’s girls face their own dark threats, not least from online grooming and harassment, deepfakes and being blackmailed over images, as well as the rape and sexual assault that remains prevalent. At the same time, their knowhow when it comes to consent and boundaries is far superior to what ours was then, when the word “safeguarding” was barely used. We were all learning on the job, essentially, while being surrounded by perverts.
I know girls who met rock stars more than twice their age at festivals who targeted them when they were still in their teens. Girls whose older male bosses shoved their tongues down their throats. Girls who were groomed and abused by their teachers, or preyed upon by older men with a preference for girls still doing their GCSEs. Girls whose boyfriends locked them in their flats. Girls who were assaulted, or anally raped, like Brand’s victim was.
You’d feel sick, strange, or shocked by a man’s behaviour towards you. You would know on some level that what had happened was wrong, and yet the overwhelming message from the culture around you was that this was normal because you were young and beautiful, and that was always going to be tempting to men, wasn’t it? When I was attacked by a stranger while walking home after a night out, a common rape myth at the time had it that I was a car who had left her doors unlocked. What did I, or any of us, expect?
And so this weird sort of splitting of the self would occur: one half comprised of the pain of it all, a trauma that lives in the body, a body that knows on a cellular level that it has been violated, and the other, well, the other a shell walking around this world set with traps, surviving. Making light of it, even, or not consciously realising that what happened to you was wrong, that it mattered. Living while embodying that disconnect does odd things to you, ultimately. Especially when you’re surrounded by fully grown adults who seem to think that it’s all fine.
You forget how different the media culture was then. It wasn’t as online, as disparate and diffuse as it is now, where there are megastars on TikTok of whom whole demographics are entirely ignorant. The landscape was much more of a monoculture, its tenets, its myths and its doctrines, its language and its cadences decided by far fewer individuals, most of them older, and often, but not always, men. It was a world of lads’ mags and tabloids and telly – and if a celebrity was king of all three then their power was immense indeed. Being able to make the nation laugh was treated as a superpower. Banter and rape jokes were par for the course. That clip that is doing the rounds of Jonathan Ross, Noel Fielding and Brand joking about rape? It seems sickening now, but in the audience’s laugh you hear the truth: it was all normal then.
In 2014, I co-wrote a book with Holly Baxter about the media landscape called The Vagenda. I picked it up this morning because I wanted to remember what the world was like then. Just a sample for you: Jimmy Carr – these days rebranded as a worldly, empathic sage of social media – joking about gang-rape. The Evening Standard having a strip club correspondent. The Telegraph glowingly reporting the fact that Gymbox ran a Playboy “bunny bootcamp”. An academic study that found members of the public struggled to differentiate between statements taken from lads’ mags and those who had committed serious sexual offences. Teenage magazines having a section for readers’ photos entitled “How Sexy Am I?”.
This book, which contained a section on rape culture and rape myths and was aimed at teenage girls, was given to older men to review, as though they knew anything about what it was like to spend your adolescence in a sexist hellscape. It was trashed both by them and by the women who took money from the women’s magazines we criticised, who were complicit. There were some adults who were on our side – our mums, our editors – but by and large any woman who tried to challenge that prevailing media culture was doing so very much alone.
That is why it does not surprise me that these stories have taken so long to come to public attention, or for any justice to be delivered. That sordid, shabby era may be over, but those who endured it as the backdrop to their girlhood are still trying to reconcile those two parts of themselves: the half that knows it has been violated, and the half walking around in a world that refused to listen.
- Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist

Egypt deployed forces to Saudi Arabia before Sisi's public pledge, sources say
Egypt deployed forces and military aircraft to Saudi Arabia and moved air defence systems to strategic locations across the country long before President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi publicly pledged Cairo's support for Riyadh, Egyptian military sources have told Middle East Eye.
The deployment included a squadron of Rafale fighter jets, eight helicopters and four large transport aircraft, an Egyptian military source said on condition of anonymity as he was not authorised to speak with the media.
Egyptian naval warships had also moved towards the southern Red Sea, near the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, the source added.
The reported naval movements came amid growing Egyptian concern over the security of Red Sea shipping lanes and the threat posed by Houthi attacks in Yemen.

https://www.humanite.fr/environnement/co.author: La rédaction avec AFP
https://www.humanite.fr/environnement/co.text:
Renforcés par le phénomène El Niño, les mégafeux qui ravagent l’Indonésie ont détruit 2,9 millions d’hectares depuis le début de l’année, selon l’organisme de surveillance Nusantara Atlas.
Ce sont des données encore non actualisées, mais qui révèlent déjà l’ampleur de la catastrophe que traverse l’Indonésie depuis plusieurs mois. Selon l’organisme indépendant de surveillance Nusantara Atlas, qui analyse les images satellites, les gigantesques incendies qui ravagent l’Indonésie ont détruit près de 2,9 millions d’hectares de terrains et de forêts. Son précédent bilan faisait état de 1,9 million d’hectares de forêts et de végétation brûlés en septembre.
Toutefois, le nombre et la taille des feux détectés lors de ces analyses, effectuées jusqu’à fin octobre, sont une estimation prudente, a averti David Gaveau, fondateur de Nusantara Atlas, en partie parce que la fumée a partiellement masqué les images satellites.
El Niño, déforestation et assèchement des tourbières
Quoi qu’il en soit, le bilan 2026 dépasse déjà celui de l’année 2019, jusqu’alors la pire pour le pays en la matière. Le phénomène El Niño, qui aggrave les effets dévastateurs du réchauffement climatique, est l’une des raisons de l’ampleur de ces feux. Mais pas seulement.
Car ces incendies sont également le résultat de décennies de déforestation et de l’assèchement des tourbières en vue de la création de plantations, estiment les experts. Résultat : de vastes étendues de terres deviennent beaucoup plus vulnérables au feu.
Fumées toxiques : des milliers de victimes
Aux impacts dramatiques sur la biodiversité et les écosystèmes s’ajoutent les conséquences sur la santé publique. Ainsi, ces incendies monstres ont dégagé une fumée toxique qui a rendu malades et tué des centaines de milliers de personnes et s’est propagée dans les pays voisins, notamment en Malaisie et à Singapour.
Si l’arrivée de la pluie a permis de maîtriser certains des pires départs de feu et si le nombre de « points chauds » commence à se stabiliser ou à diminuer, plutôt qu’à augmenter, relève Nusantara Atlas, l’ampleur de la destruction est manifeste, souligne David Gaveau qui regrette « une très mauvaise année ».
La Terre de nos batailles
La justice climatique, c’est notre bataille. Celle qui relie luttes environnementales et sociales pour contrer un système capitaliste faisant ventre de tout. Du vivant, de la planète, de notre humanité.
Il n’y a pas de fatalité.
- Nous démasquons les manipulations des lobbies.
- Nous battons en brèche les dénis climatiques mortifères.
- Nous mettons en valeur les initiatives visant à réduire les inégalités environnementales et les fractures sociales.
Soutenez-nous.

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: ‘Our neighbours are gone’: Gaza survivors recount horrors of deadly floods
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
‘Our neighbours are gone’: Gaza survivors recount horrors of deadly floods
A deadly sandbank collapse buried displaced families alive in Deir el-Balah, as survivors describe desperate rescue attempts.
Deir el-Balah, Gaza Strip – Gaza is dealing with the cleanup of catastrophic flooding after storms submerged displacement camps and war-destroyed cities.
Heavy rain has directly affected 106,000 people in Gaza, according to UNICEF, with thousands of tents for displaced Palestinians submerged under water and latrines overflowing into camps.
The floods also brought death: a sandbank under pressure from heavy rain collapsed at the Ard al-Ribat displacement camp in Deir el-Balah, central Gaza, on Sunday evening, killing three children and a woman.
Without excavation equipment, residents had to dig through the sand with their bare hands to reach people trapped under debris. When darkness came, they used flashlights on their mobile phones to search for survivors.
Zahira al-Sahar, 58, was preparing to sleep in her tent in the camp on Sunday when she and her 28-year-old daughter were almost entombed in the collapse.
“I was lying in my bedding when something suddenly pushed me and came down on top of me,” al-Sahar told Al Jazeera. “The sand reached up to my neck. My daughter was beside me, and she was almost completely buried.”
Her sons came to the rescue. “I told them: ‘Pull your sister out first, then come back for me.’ They pulled her out, then came back and rescued me,” she said.
Meanwhile, in a neighbouring tent, members of the al-Nabhan family were also buried in the sandbank’s collapse.
“[When I realised] I started screaming and calling for people to come and help,” al-Sahar said. “I told everyone that our neighbours had been buried. We kept shouting: ‘Please, save them. Our neighbours are gone.’”
But the family did not respond to the rescuers’ calls. Eight-year-old Salah, his six-year-old sister Maryam, and their mother, Tahrir, 36, who was five months pregnant, were among the dead. Their father, Ahmed, who was only recently released from Israeli detention, is the family’s sole survivor.
“[Ahmed al-Nabhan] and his wife had been very happy after he came out of prison. They were looking forward to having another child in a few months,” said Suhaib Abu Darabi, 32, who was among neighbours who rushed to the site to help save them.
Abu Darabi said the collapse sounded like an explosion and was followed by screaming. The site was exposed to the elements and on unstable ground and collapsed after just a few minutes of rain. By the time neighbours reached the area, they found two tents completely buried under debris.
Abu Darabi said residents were digging with whatever tools they could find.
“We managed to clear some of the rubble, but we could not save the people trapped underneath. The scale of the collapse was far beyond what the residents here could handle, given the lack of resources,” Abu Darabi told Al Jazeera.
“The tents that collapsed beneath the embankment are what the world saw. But what people did not see was that all these tents fell to the ground that night. Residents had to repair whatever they could so they could continue living in them.”
In the neighbouring al-Zein family’s tent, four-year-old Habiba was killed, while her mother, Reem, and brother Ibrahim remain in intensive care.
The scale of the damage caused by this winter’s first storm, which began on November 6, was significant and has exposed the dangers faced by families living in tents with little protection from extreme weather.
This is the fourth winter since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began, in October 2023, and hundreds of thousands of people are living in tattered tents or makeshift shelters that have been exposed to the elements for years.
More than 26,000 households had reported damage to their shelters or other belongings by November 8, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported. The UN estimated that about 1.4 million people, or 65 percent of Gaza’s population, were living in tents or makeshift shelters when the storms hit.
The danger is only compounded by the extensive destruction of Gaza’s infrastructure from Israeli strikes. Drainage networks have been severely damaged, roads and access routes remain in poor condition, and municipalities lack sufficient equipment to remove accumulated rainwater and respond to emergencies.
Gaza’s Government Media Office described the Deir el-Balah sandbank collapse as a humanitarian disaster.
It said it held Israel, the United States administration and the international community responsible and the blocking of proper shelters, construction materials, mobile homes, fuel and spare parts was a factor in the deadly floods.
The media office also said the failure of the so-called Board of Peace and the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza to act in the crisis also raised “serious questions about the purpose of these bodies”, which have been accused of working with Israel to continue its siege on Gaza.
The Board of Peace said in a statement this week that it had urged Israel to allow essential supplies such as temporary shelters and drainage equipment to enter the enclave.
Aid organisations have also repeatedly called for the entry of shelter materials and equipment needed to repair damaged tents and infrastructure to avoid a repeat of this past week’s deadly events.
Shaima al-Daour, 22, a displaced woman from northern Gaza who works as a nurse in the Ard al-Ribat camp, was also among those who rushed to help the injured.
“I tried to resuscitate a young child who was pulled out from under the rubble, but he had internal bleeding. I tried, but there was no response,” she said.
Al-Daour said another boy, aged 15, was brought to her with difficulty breathing. She opened his airway and he began to breathe, but his pulse was weak. With no ambulance readily available, she called on people around her to find any means of transport to get him to the hospital.
“I was surrounded by men, shouting at them: ‘Does anyone have a tuk-tuk? A cart? Anything to carry him?’ What I saw was unbearable. I could not save the little child in front of me,” she said.
“We need shelter and land where people can live safely. We also need equipment so that, God forbid, if something happens again, there is something available to help us.”
Al-Daour said she is still in shock by what she witnessed and is terrified by the prospect of the impending winter.
“I still cannot get over what happened,” she said. “Have the people of Gaza not experienced every possible way of dying? Have some compassion for us. Just have some compassion for us, people of the world,” she said.

https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.title: Can Barack Obama be credited for the blue wave? Perhaps – but others fathered this success
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.author: Nesrine Malik
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.text:
A blue wave has surged in the United States. It has been a week since the Democrats hammered the Republicans and regained majorities in the House and the Senate, and the credit for that is, shall we say, a matter of debate.
Success has many fathers. One of them is Barack Obama, the first to break the kind of barriers a new generation of Democrats has overcome. This week, I follow what can and cannot be traced to the man who still holds a unique position in the liberal political imaginary, almost a decade after leaving the White House.
Barack Obama’s presidency and specifically his first election win, remains a formative politicising moment for many millennials. Few imagined that a Black man with an Arab Muslim middle name, and an electrifying agenda of hope, could become president of the United States. Then there were his own personal attributes: an orator for the ages, cool as ice, confident and unflappable. These qualities were sharpened by what followed – a Donald Trump presidency that wrecked political institutions and norms, fomented racial divides, led by a peevish, insecure narcissist that made the Obama years feel like a hallucination. The Trump era, and how the country swung so sharply in another direction, suggested that Obama was in fact, not the start of something, but an anomaly. But there may be more of an enduring legacy to Obama than the Trump era suggests.
A canny alliance
The question is: How much does a Dr Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s new senator and the US’s first ever Muslim senator, owe to Obama? El-Sayed answered that question himself by saying he is picking up the baton from the former president.
Obama also riffed on that note of continuity when he threw himself behind El-Sayed during the last days of the latter’s campaign, by comparing the Islamophobic attacks on El-Sayed’s name to those he faced. “I remind them his name was Barack,” El-Sayed said, of his detractors. He likened his disagreements with Obama to a son who loves his dad and “really appreciates all they’ve done, but … here are some things I would have done differently”.
But rewind a little, and this begins to look like clever campaigning. El-Sayed previously said that the Obama presidency had left the country “no better off”. He criticised Obama’s “war on terror” campaigns in Pakistan and Yemen, use of drones and for presiding over record deportations. Obama’s historic win, El-Sayed wrote, is a memory that “will serve not as a reminder of the history we made that night – but of the silly emotions of a naive young man who didn’t understand that hope and change required more than flowery prose and a winning smile”. Oof.
When questioned on these strong critiques, El-Sayed’s softer tone credited Obama with one specific and revealing achievement: being of a certain background and still believing that he could make it into high office.
A racial rather than political legacy
This suggests that Obama’s impact lies less in any radical anti-status quo politics that he pioneered – the sort that Bernie Sanders championed – but simply in breaking that psychological racial barrier for the American electorate. It is impossible to say whether successful candidates like Zohran Mamdani or El-Sayed would have prevailed in an environment steeped in Islamophobia, if Obama had not prevailed in an environment steeped with racism and Islamophobia. There is an argument that a president who was presented as radical, an “Arab”, even as a terrorist, who then spent eight years in the White House without passing sharia law, retained enough political muscle memory.
But is that all that new left-wing candidates of colour have to thank Obama for? It can be argued that Obama’s hawkish wars and conventional immigration policy, for example, preserved the sort of mainstream political capital that he could confer on people like El-Sayed. Since leaving office, Obama has remained a broadly milquetoast figure, occupying a cultural and political territory in which he has been refashioned as a curator of pop culture. From recommending literature and music, to his latest podcast, in which he hosts guests to discuss “great books”, Obama has frustratingly recused himself from the big political battles playing out since he left office, choosing to become some sort of jazz-playing uncle.
When he did make interventions, Obama’s once-moving rhetoric sounded remote and inappropriate for the moment. On Gaza, where a genocide is grinding down an entire population, Obama posted a weak statement which spoke of securing “lasting peace”, lacking the moral clarity to name the crimes that have been committed.
Cop-out or shrewd strategy?
This cop out reveals that Obama, even out of office and free to be a political engine of change without risk to his career in Washington DC, is not a cautious canny tactician. He is just that regular establishment centrist critiqued for being little more than flowery prose and winning smiles.
But when he showed up for El-Sayed, bringing his trademark humour and presence to the Michigan campaign, one could see how valuable that centrism was and that Obama does not flinch from defending and endorsing politicians with more progressive views than him. In choosing to show up, lending his imprimatur of authority to a candidate who has sharply criticised him while sitting firmly outside the Democratic party mainstream on everything from corporate power to Israel, Obama enabled El-Sayed to advance a revolutionary agenda.
But that agenda is no orphan either. It owes much to Bernie Sanders who ran for the Democratic presidential nomination twice on a left-wing platform, and since his loss, continued advancing positions such as reducing military spending, curbing corporate powers, blocking military sales to Israel and wealth taxes for billionaires. Much of the exciting politics in the blue wave is downstream from him.
Working in tandem with Obama’s backing, these legacies have paved the way for the success of the racial outsider and those who want to break the grip of ‘moderate’ establishment politics. Not many fathers, but two.

Netanyahu sought private talks with Palestinian party leader despite public attacks
The leader of the United Arab List, Mansour Abbas, said on Wednesday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had held private talks with him through a close associate, despite publicly branding Palestinian parties "terror supporters who hate Israel".
"He was interested in our position on the law barring an indicted lawmaker from serving as prime minister, and whether we really intended to enter a coalition and replace Netanyahu's government," Abbas told Kan public radio.
"When it serves his interests, Arab citizens suddenly become legitimate, he becomes 'Abu Yair', and Mansour Abbas becomes a worthy partner in his eyes."
The Palestinian-led United Arab List (Ra'am) and the Joint List won a record 19 seats combined, following a surge in turnout among Palestinian voters in Israel, giving them the balance of power.
In a speech to parliament on Tuesday evening, Netanyahu said the United Arab List and the Joint List were seeking to end Israel’s existence, adding that the two parties disagreed only on "what kind of state will arise on its ruins".

https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.title: Daniel Kretinsky met la main sur le groupe FNAC Darty et étend son empire
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.author: Michaël Mélinard
https://www.humanite.fr/culture-et-savoi.text:
En prenant le contrôle du groupe Fnac-Darty, le milliardaire tchèque, déjà propriétaire du groupe Editis, conforte sa position de poids lourd dans l’édition française. Son OPA réussie permet au magnat de l’énergie, des médias, de l’édition et de la distribution de réduire l’influence du chinois JD. com au sein du groupe et sur le marché européen.
Le milliardaire tchèque Daniel Kretinsky, déjà propriétaire d’Editis – le deuxième géant de l’édition française et de titres de presse comme Elle, Marianne et Franc-Tireur – étoffe un peu plus son empire. Il a officiellement réussi son OPA sur le groupe Fnac Darty dont il possède désormais 69,3 % des parts. Un chiffre qui pourrait encore gonfler puisque l’offre publique d’achat s’ouvre à nouveau du 12 au 25 novembre afin de permettre aux actionnaires d’apporter le maximum de titres.
L’offensive lancée le 26 janvier dernier par l’intermédiaire d’EP Group, sa société, valorise le groupe FNAC Darty à plus d’un milliard d’euros. Elle fait surtout de Kretinsky le propriétaire d’une des plus grosses librairies de France. Cette OPA visait aussi à contrer l’influence chinoise de JD. com, en passe d’acquérir le distributeur allemand Ceconomy, lui-même détenteur de plus de 20 % du capital de Fnac Darty. Ce qui ferait du géant chinois le deuxième actionnaire du groupe français. Restent les risques de monopole.
La concentration capitalistique du secteur
La commission européenne les a balayés le 20 octobre en validant le projet d’OPA, dernier verrou à faire sauter avant l’autorisation attendue pour cette opération. Elle avait « conclu » que cette dernière « ne soulèverait pas de problèmes de concurrence, compte tenu de son impact limité sur la concurrence sur les marchés où les entreprises sont présentes ». Néanmoins, les craintes demeurent avec un acteur de la filière livre qui possède désormais des parts conséquentes dans la production et la diffusion.
Oui, on s’en doute : vous en avez assez
Voir ces messages d’appel au don, ça peut être pénible. Nous le savons. Et on doit bien vous avouer que nous préférerions ne pas avoir à les écrire…
Mais voilà : c’est crucial pour l’Humanité. Si ce titre existe toujours aujourd’hui, c’est grâce au financement régulier de nos lectrices et lecteurs.
- C’est grâce à votre soutien que nous pouvons exercer notre métier avec passion. Nous ne dépendons ni des intérêts d’un propriétaire milliardaire, ni de pressions politiques : personne ne nous dicte ce que nous devons dire ou taire.
- Votre engagement nous libère aussi de la course aux clics et à l’audience. Plutôt que de chercher à capter l’attention à tout prix, nous choisissons de traiter les sujets que notre rédaction juge essentiels : parce qu’ils méritent d’être lus, compris, partagés. Parce que nous estimons qu’ils vous seront utiles
À l’heure actuelle, moins d’un quart des lectrices et lecteurs qui viennent plus de 3 fois sur le site par semaine nous aident à financer notre travail, par leur abonnement ou par leurs dons. Si vous voulez protéger le journalisme indépendant, s’il vous plaît, rejoignez-les.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Why is Pochettino the favourite to replace Carrick at Manchester United?
What would Mauricio Pochettino bring to the job if he replaces Michael Carrick in the Old Trafford hot seat?
If Michael Carrick’s departure as head coach of Manchester United is confirmed, Mauricio Pochettino is reportedly the man tasked with turning the fortunes of the Old Trafford club around.
United lie in the Premier League’s relegation zone, one point off the bottom in 18th, after winning just one of their opening 10 matches, that coming against Ipswich in August.
It’s the club’s worst start to a season in 30 years, and the expectations will be high for whoever takes the role, with their first league game coming away at bitter rivals Liverpool on November 22.
Pochettino – whose release from the contract extension he signed as USA head coach has reportedly been arranged while Carrick officially remains in position – would become the eighth permanent man in charge at Old Trafford since Sir Alex Ferguson’s departure in May 2013 after more than 26 years in the job.
Who is Mauricio Pochettino?
The 54-year-old Argentinian was known during his playing career as a no-nonsense central defender, but as a manager he has evolved into one known for attractive, attacking football, with a focus on developing young talent.
He began playing in 1989 with Newell’s Old Boys before a switch to Spain in 1994, joining La Liga side Espanyol, where he played more than 200 league games across a seven-year career and broke into the Argentina squad, winning 20 caps and starting every game in the 2002 World Cup.
He had spells with Paris Saint-Germain and Bordeaux in France’s Ligue 1 before ending his career with Espanyol, for whom he passed 300 appearances in all competitions.
His first job in management came in January 2009, when he became Espanyol’s third coach of the season and successfully guided the Barcelona-based club away from the threat of relegation and beat city rivals Barcelona at Camp Nou for the first time in 27 years along the way.
He left the club by mutual consent in November 2012 and landed his first job in the Premier League at Southampton two months later, earning plaudits as Saints climbed the table before leading them to an eighth-placed finish in his first full season and the club’s highest points tally since the Premier League’s formation in 1992.
He moved to Tottenham in 2014 and oversaw the most successful run in the club’s recent history, reaching the League Cup final in his first season and finishing in fifth. He also allowed young prospects like Harry Kane, Dele Alli and Eric Dier the chance to shine – something which has been a focus for the Argentinian during his coaching career, often watching youth games and allowing young prospects to train with first-team set-ups to help their progress.
Spurs recorded their highest league finish since 1990 in 2016 and in 2017 finished second with a club-record 86 points, their highest finish since 1963.
Pochettino guided Tottenham to the Champions League final in 2019, overcoming Man City and Ajax in dramatic style along the way before losing 2-0 to Liverpool in the final in Madrid.
He was, however, sacked five months later after a poor start to the Premier League season before becoming head coach of Paris Saint-Germain from January 2021 to July 2022, departing after winning his first league title.
He spent the 2023-24 season in charge of Chelsea but departed two days after guiding the Blues to a sixth-place finish and took over the USA national team in September 2024, guiding the cohosts to the last-16 exit at the hands of Belgium at the 2026 World Cup before extending his contract in August.
Is Pochettino’s style a good fit?
Man United have long been associated with free-flowing attacking football, and Pochettino’s style was always likely to make him a more appealing option for the club’s hierarchy than the more pragmatic approach of another of the potential frontrunners for the job, Antonio Conte.
The Italian’s style is built more around tactical discipline, high work rate and defensive stability with reliance on quick counter-attacks.
Across his coaching career, Pochettino has become known for his attacking style of play, which relies on pressing high to win the ball back, focuses on keeping possession and usually adopts a 4-2-3-1 formation – which might suit the squad he inherits, as it becomes more of a 3-2-5 when building from the back, employing one inverted full-back and allowing the other to provide width in attack.
The likes of Bruno Fernandes, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo would likely thrive in his system, but the lack of a top-class No. 9 will be a hindrance, with Benjamin Sesko sidelined through injury and Joshua Zirkzee having struggled to make an impact.
The defence will come under huge scrutiny too; United have conceded 30 goals in their 15 games in all competitions this season and Pochettino’s defence can be exposed on the counterattack with so many men committed forward.
One of the factors which Pochettino is known for is his willingness to integrate young talent into training and match day squads and help establish a club’s identity, particularly at Southampton, where he previously worked with United’s Luke Shaw, and at Tottenham. That is also something United have traditionally been associated with, with Sir Alex Ferguson taking the likes of Ryan Giggs, David Beckham, Paul Scholes and Gary Neville and turning them into global stars. The likes of Shea Lacey might benefit particularly from Pochettino’s tutelage.
Any potential pitfalls?
There might be some. One of Tottenham fans’ main gripes during Pochettino’s largely successful period at the club was that he prioritised league games over cup games, and team selections often reflected that.
United are already out of the League Cup, but a new boss appointed during the international break will face 16 games in 60 days starting with the trip to Anfield, with four Champions League games and an FA Cup third-round tie to fit in around 11 Premier League games which might prove crucial to their season.
Pochettino’s style also places a heavy reliance on fitness, intensity and discipline, something which has been somewhat lacking in large parts of the season so far at the Red Devils.
There were also issues arising from his spell at PSG. He was able to call upon some of the icons of the sport in Kylian Mbappe and Neymar in 2021, but PSG failed to win Ligue 1 for the first time in the past nine seasons, finishing a point behind Lille after losing four games down the stretch. He did win the title the following year, with Lionel Messi added to the ranks, but they failed to make even the quarterfinals of the Champions League or the Coupe de France.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120379.title: Fußballnationalmannschaft | Felix Nmecha nimmt die Bibel wörtlich
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120379.author: Christoph Ruf
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120379.text:
- Kommentare
- Fußballnationalmannschaft
Felix Nmecha nimmt die Bibel wörtlich
Religiöser Wahn: Der Fußballer Felix Nmecha ist weder katholisch noch evangelisch, er ist evangelikal. Doch den DFB interessiert das nicht.
Fußballspieler, die sich nach einem Tor bekreuzigen oder ekstatisch gen Himmel zeigen, gingen mir schon immer auf den Zeiger. Wenn es ihn gäbe, würde ich wirklich schwer hoffen, dass er Besseres zu tun hat, als irgendwelchen Trotteln beim Kicken zuzuschauen und regulatorisch einzugreifen. Aber okay, jedem seine Folklore. Es gibt schließlich auch Torhüter, die vor den Spielen in ihre Handschuhe spucken, ohne vom örtlichen Gesundheitsamt dafür auf die Ekelliste gesetzt zu werden.
Christoph Ruf ist freier Autor und beobachtet in seiner wöchentlichen nd-Kolumne »Platzverhältnisse« politische und sportliche Begebenheiten.
Der Fall von Felix Nmecha liegt allerdings anders. Der Spieler von Borussia Dortmund ist in die Kritik geraten, weil er zum x-ten Mal seine christlich-fundamentalistischen Ansichten zelebriert hat. Zweimal kniete er sich am Samstag vor die eigene Fankurve und nahm eine imaginäre Krone ab. Die Kampagne »The King’s return« (englisch für: Jesus steht morgen bei Aldi hinter dir an der Kasse) steht den evangelikalen Kickern von »Ballers in God« nah, deren berühmtester Propagandist hierzulande Nmecha ist.
BIG ist kein harmloser Betkreis und Nmecha keiner, der seinen christlichen Glauben eben nun mal etwas ernster nimmt als andere. Nmecha ist weder katholisch noch evangelisch, er ist evangelikal. Er nimmt die Bibel wörtlich. Das erklärt, warum die Kicker Abtreibung für Mord (»Satans Plan«) und Homosexualität für Sünde halten. Und das jeden von morgens bis abends wissen lassen müssen. Gott, sagt Nmecha, habe ihn beauftragt, den Fußball zu nutzen, um »die Wahrheit« zu teilen: »No way, dass ich diese Plattform bekomme und sie nur für mich selbst nutze. Damit würde ich Gott entehren.«
Schon als Nmecha von Wolfsburg nach Dortmund wechselte, wiesen BVB-Fans auf dessen Haltung zu Homosexualität hin, nachdem Nmecha ein Video des rechten Bloggers Matt Walsh (»Kindesmord (Abtreibung) zu akzeptieren, bedeutet, deine Seele preiszugeben«) geteilt hatte, der sich über trans Menschen lustig gemacht hatte. »Wenn wir nicht sehen, was falsch daran ist.« Später entschuldigte er sich – wie er es seither immer wieder tut, wenn seine Aussagen mal wieder so verstanden werden, wie sie gemeint waren.
Schon nach dessen Verpflichtung hatte der BVB die Wogen zu glätten versucht, indem er sich auf Statement Nmechas berief, das eigentlich nicht für Entwarnung steht: »Ich glaube nicht, dass ich homo- oder transphob bin«, sagte er damals und schon die ersten drei Worte müssten eigentlich jedem die Lachtränen in die Augen treiben. »Ich hasse niemanden, aber ich stehe für meinen Glauben ein.«
So und nicht anders ist das bei Evangelikalen, denn ihnen ist ihr Glaube wichtiger als staatliche Gesetze. Wie weit der religiöse Wahn bei seinen Nationalspielern geht, hat den DFB schon bei seinem radikal-muslimischen homophoben Nationalspieler Antonio Rüdiger nicht interessiert. Auch bei Nmecha dürfte es nicht schwer herauszubekommen sein, wie er wirklich denkt, wenn man ihm zu Themen wie Frauen, Homosexualität oder Atheismus die richtigen Fragen stellt. Dass das passiert, ist unwahrscheinlich. Denn das würde ein Bewusstsein für die Gefahren des religiösen Fanatismus voraussetzen. Aber wie sagte doch Sportdirektor Rudi Völler so schön, als er ein Gespräch zwischen dem Bundestrainer und Nmecha ankündigte: »Wir werden mit ihm darüber reden, weil es ein öffentliches Thema geworden ist.«
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: UN chief urges Cop31 hosts Turkey and Australia to turn fossil fuel promises into action
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Graham Readfearn in Antalya
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Turkey and Australia, the co-hosts of crucial climate talks, must urgently move from discussing the end of fossil fuels to delivering it, the UN chief has said.
“It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable,” António Guterres said, in a dramatic intervention on the second day of the conference on Tuesday.
“Now, here at Cop31, we must move from discussing the transition to organising it, financing it, and delivering it.”
The two countries hosting Cop31 are significant exporters of fossil fuels. Early on Tuesday, the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, was extolling his country’s oilfields even as he prepared for his appearance at the summit on Wednesday.
Guterres said the talks should end with “clear next steps” to advance a roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels presented to delegates on Tuesday by Brazil, which presided over last year’s talks.
During a presentation with the Brazilians, Guterres – who will step down as UN secretary general at the end of this year and has made the climate crisis a central part of his agenda, often intervening on issues with dramatic language – was energetically backed by the former US secretary of state and climate envoy John Kerry, the UN’s chief climate negotiator, Simon Stiell, and his predecessor, the Mexican diplomat Patricia Espinosa. He was met by rapturous applause as he left the stage.
Brazil announced at the close of last year’s Cop30 climate summit that it would produce the roadmap. Previewing it last week, the country said an exit from fossil fuels would boost economies and help pull people out of poverty.
Kerry said the roadmap had come “at a critical moment” but “words in conversation don’t cut a single ton of emissions – action does”.
There is growing pressure on this Cop to deliver after several years in which the summits have been criticised for a lack of progress. It took 28 years of annual UN Cop negotiations for the first mention of a transition away from fossil fuels to be included in a final decision, at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023.
Greta Thunberg, the Swedish climate activist who inspired global climate protests several years ago, attended this year’s Cop for the first time since 2021,. “Cops have become greenwashed circuses. That is the reality,” she told reporters.
The drama came on the eve of a two-day leaders’ summit at which more than 90 world leaders, including the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, his Australian counterpart, Anthony Albanese, and the newly elected Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, were expected to speak and join negotiations.
Alden Meyer, a senior associate at the climate thinktank E3G and a Cop veteran, described the presentation of the roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels as “an incredible display of collective firepower”.
“There’s clearly now an expectation that the presidencies [of Australia and Turkey] will pick up the baton from Brazil in some way,” he said. “But it won’t be agreed by consensus here. It took us 28 Cop meetings to get the need to transition away from fossil fuels into a Cop decision.
“This is what we are getting down to and it will be interesting to see how this hybrid presidency responds to this. This is the challenge to this presidency and how they pick up this baton and keep this discussion going.”
A spokesperson for Australia’s climate minister, Chris Bowen, said: “Our message had been clear: countries working together is not only the best way, it is the only way of dealing with climate change and the other crises that countries are facing.
“Before us is the opportunity to make our nations more prosperous, our energy system more secure and the climate more safe.”
The Turkish hosts were approached for comment.
The second day of the conference also saw more than 700 groups, ranging from trade unions to disability advocates, urging diplomats to prioritise a “just transition” for the people who will be hit hardest by a shift to a clean economy.
Organisations from 88 countries demanded a mechanism at Cop31 to turn promises of a just transition into action. Known as the Belém-Antalya Mechanism (BAM), it would seek to support issues including human rights, gender equality and good jobs, while respecting Indigenous rights.
Lidy Nacpil, the coordinator of the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development, said: “Workers and communities, especially in the global south, welcomed and celebrated the Cop30 decision to develop a just transition mechanism – or BAM – which has the promise of delivering real support and action for just transition on the ground.
“However, in pre-Cop, governments of the global north have once again exposed their determination to pour cold water over this promise, by limiting what a mechanism can do and delaying the process of its operationalisation.”
On Tuesday, with 100,000 people attending the talks, many delegates were stuck in traffic for hours. Tram services were crammed with attenders, while some bus journeys took more than three hours.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/will.title: Lesson From Lansing: To Win in Swing Districts, Fight Data Centers
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/will.author: Matt Sledge
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/will.text:
When progressive Will Lawrence beat two moderates in a Michigan congressional primary earlier this year, some Democrats were worried about his ability to win one of the nation’s most evenly divided districts.
Early Wednesday morning, Lawrence claimed victory over Republican Rep. Tom Barrett. (National news organizations such as The Associated Press had not called the race as of Wednesday morning.)
A national swing in favor of Democrats helped him — but so did a campaign that leaned heavily on opposition to data centers to 
situate Lawrence as a populist instead of an extremist.
Data centers were on voters’ minds everywhere, but they rarely dominated a race as much as the 7th Congressional District of Michigan. Lawrence vocally opposed data center construction almost as soon as he began running last year. A series of proposed hyperscale developments in and around Lansing pushed the issue into the limelight.
A month and a half before the election, Lawrence announced a data center platform calling for a moratorium on new development, environmental regulations, and a national jobs program to replace work taken away by artificial intelligence.
As progressives take stock of the 2026 midterms, Lawrence’s approach points one way forward for their wing of the Democratic Party. Lawrence’s opponent tried to turn his time as an environmental activist into a liability, but in an interview with The Intercept, Lawrence said his background primed him to come down on the same side as the public on a red-hot issue like data centers.
“I fought against Wall Street landlords trying to kick people out of their homes. I fought against oil companies who are polluting our air and water,” he told The Intercept in an interview last month. “So for me, this was not the first time that I’ve stood on the line against a corporate behemoth like this.”
From Sunrise to Congress
Lawrence is a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, which had one of its most famous moments when its youth activists marched into the office of then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi to push for the Green New Deal with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., by their side in 2018.
Data centers and AI were remote issues for voters then, but they were starting to bubble up in the public consciousness by the time Lawrence announced his run for Congress in August 2025.
Two months later, one of his first moves as a candidate was to visit public meetings in two small townships in Michigan to express his opposition to proposed data center developments.
As a former member of the Democratic Socialists of America, he drew skepticism from many observers over his ability to win the primary in a district that narrowly voted for Donald Trump in 2024. They were equally skeptical of his ability to beat Barrett, a Republican who tried to play up his moderate bona fides in the race’s final weeks. Barrett was one of a handful of Republicans to vote in favor of a resolution to end the Iran war, for instance.
Lawrence had some major liabilities in a purple district, including tweets where he wrote “fuck the nuclear-family home” and told then-Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin in a song to “hurry up and die.”
While Barrett leaned on those posts and Lawrence’s time with the DSA to cast his opponent as an extremist, the young progressive had a card up his sleeves in the form of the data center issue.
It is the rare cause that leaps across party lines to unite Republicans and Democrats who are just as worried about water sources drying up and ceaseless buzzing sounds.
At an October 5 city council meeting in the quaint town of Mason, where a developer has proposed a hyperscale data center on a plot of picturesque farmland, Democrats and Republicans alike said they were outraged. Some residents said they would sell their house and leave town if the development is built.
In a sign of how politically charged the issue has become, many of the speakers were candidates for office angling for votes. Lawrence had dropped by himself a few weeks before. His first television ad centered on his opposition to the Mason project.
Karl Sime, a Mason resident who crisscrossed the area on behalf of Democratic candidates, told The Intercept last month that “100 percent” of voters were angry about the data center proposed for the swath of farmland just outside city limits.
“Sometimes they’ll just say it unprovoked,” he said. “You can see the body language just dramatically change into anger.”
Republican Countermoves
Lawrence was hardly the only candidate who tried to tap into opposition to data centers. Some Republicans tried to catch the wave as well.
Barrett voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill, which included tax breaks that could benefit rural data center developers. But as the danger he faced in the election became clear, he proposed legislation in Congress that would ban local officials from signing non-disclosure agreements with developers and would allow local communities to set regulations on data centers without federal interference.
Some voters said they wanted to see candidates take a harder stance in favor of regulation, however. At the City Council meeting last month, Doug DeLind said he was left shaking his head at neighbors who had yard signs opposing data centers and supporting Barrett.
DeLind, a sculptor who lives near the proposed data center, said that Barrett’s position was that “we’re going to leave it up to the local communities, but we’re not going to provide any federal protection or any guidelines to what a data center can do.”
Although Mason faces a more imminent possibility of a massive data center, Americans across the country are worried about having one in their backyard. Multiple surveys showed a remarkable shift in public opinion on the subject over the past year. Half of Americans oppose a data center being built within 3 miles of their house, according to a recent Politico poll.
In recent months, data centers became a signature issue for Democrats with progressive pasts trying to recast themselves as populists. Sherrod Brown, the party’s Senate candidate in Ohio, and Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa also staked their campaigns on opposition to data centers. Both won.
“The playbook was listening to voters. I think voters across ideologies were speaking with one voice, and I think their opponents were some of the people most willing to silence voters and accept industry cash instead,” said Alex Bores, who became a national figure by arguing for stricter AI regulations during a failed New York congressional primary bid earlier this year.
As candidates ran away from data centers, the artificial intelligence industry’s most powerful super PAC stopped intervening in close races. An Intercept analysis found that the well-funded Leading the Future super PAC network, which is aligned with OpenAI, largely stopped spending in competitive general election races.
It lost in the one state where it did place a big bet, South Carolina. Incumbent Sen. Darline Graham, a Republican, fell to challenger Annie Andrews.
Bores, who now leads a pro-AI regulation group called Who Decides, said he was not surprised to see candidates increasingly market themselves as AI skeptics.
“I think it’s overdue. I think candidates and elected officials are catching up to where the electorate is, across parties,” Bores told The Intercept. “It is remarkable the agreement that voters have around wanting guardrails to protect us from the most powerful and fastest moving technology of our lifetime. Democracy is sometimes slow, but only so much.”
This story was supported by a grant from the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/el-s.title: Haley Stevens Destroyed Her Political Career for Absolutely Nothing
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/el-s.author: Eoin Higgins
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/el-s.text:
Eoin Higgins is the author of “Owned: How Tech Billionaires on the Right Bought the Loudest Voice on the Left.”
Abdul El-Sayed handily defeated Republican Mike Rogers for Senate in Michigan early Wednesday morning, retaining Democratic control of the seat and solidifying the party’s Senate majority. To become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, the former public health official overcame rampant, bipartisan Islamophobia and bigotry. For the country, and the Democrats, to move forward, we must cast it out of public life forever.
The Michigan Democrat’s victory felt almost like an afterthought compared to the upset Senate victories won by Democrats in South Carolina and Texas. The 2026 midterms were a referendum on President Donald Trump and his control of the GOP, and voters delivered their verdict, turning control of both houses of Congress over to the opposition party.
But we should neither forget nor forgive how we got here. El-Sayed faced an uphill battle from the beginning, which included a protracted, venomous primary, and the call was often coming from inside the house.
No detractor was as vicious as his former primary opponent Rep. Haley Stevens, whose eleventh-hour betrayal of her party’s nominee — she formally switched her endorsement to Rogers on Sunday — was a transparent attempt to turn the seat red.
Backlash was swift and harsh and came from all corners of the party. Sen. Chuck Schumer, the powerful leader of the Senate who has made little secret of his disagreements with El-Sayed on Israel, called Stevens’s actions “a despicable betrayal.” Michigan Democratic Rep. Debbie Dingell and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who finished third in the primary, went as far as to express personal concern for Stevens.
And Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., just days after implying El-Sayed and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani were antisemites for opposing ethno-supremacy in Israel, said Stevens chose “to dangerously betray Michigan families’ healthcare, freedoms, and future with her horrific endorsement of Mike Rogers.”
In the 48 hours-plus since she threw in with Rogers — which increasingly seems like it was motivated primarily out of spite when she was boxed out of a Sunday campaign event with Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., in Detroit — Stevens embarked on a media tour of justification that got weirder and weirder.
A 15-minute, rambling interview with Anderson Cooper on CNN Sunday night didn’t provide insight into her motivations, or much else; on Monday evening, Stevens followed up with a long statement posted on X owning the decision to destroy her political career with the Democratic Party. She also denied that her fiancé, political donor Jason Turkish, played any role in the endorsement: “I made this decision, and I am proud of it. Do not question my independence simply because you disagree with my conclusion.”
Congressional staffers to Stevens resigned en masse on Sunday, and former campaign aides told the Washington Post that they had to run defense to keep Turkish — who had endorsed Rogers before Stevens did — out of the spotlight and marginalize his influence.
“Any campaign staff being directly quoted in this article, I was made miserable by working with them,” Stevens told the Post in response, adding, “I have nothing else to say about the campaign at this time.”
But a singular explanation of Stevens’s decision lets Democrats off the hook far too easily for the anti-El-Sayed campaign waged by leaders in the House and Senate. For the party to move forward after the midterms, the Democrats need to take a hard look in the mirror and purge institutionalized Islamophobia from their ranks.
They can start with their friends in the media. The Atlantic’s Jonathan Chait, in a screed published Sunday, whined that “during the same period of time that El-Sayed has been winking at a political movement inflected with anti-Semitism, he has been targeted by a political message that is not merely inflected with racism but saturated with it.”
Political commentator Van Jones noted on X ahead of Election Day that “the Republicans are conducting a campaign of blatant anti-Muslim fear mongering.” But in the same post, he also argued El-Sayed’s “refusal to outright denounce” a little-seen ad produced by an outside PAC — an ad which El-Sayed distanced himself and his campaign from — tying the rise of grocery costs to U.S. support for Israel was comparable.
“Something is going horribly wrong in the Senate race in Michigan,” Jones added huffily. “And I am going to keep calling it out.”
After last night’s massive blue wave, it should be undeniable that the left was a major factor in flipping the House and Senate. That means the party’s progressive wing can now credibly claim a seat at the governing table without compromising on domestic or foreign policy. We should get ready for a long overdue, but almost certainly painful, intraparty debate on how Democrats policed dissent in their own ranks in this election, and how to disentangle leadership from unconditional support for Israel.
There’s always the possibility that the party’s centrist wing comes together with the left and repairs the damage. A good first step would be for leadership to make clear that Stevens, and anyone else who indulged in anti-Muslim arguments to score political points, has torched any possible future in the Democratic Party. Any advocacy or lobbying group that offer Stevens or her ilk safe political harbor should also be blacklisted.
Party discipline applied to the treacherous center doesn’t appear to be the top priority for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, the presumptive next speaker, who devoted his first remarks after the election to downplaying partisanship in this “patriotic moment.”
But without backup from party leadership, El-Sayed will continue to be met with hostility. On Wednesday morning, CNN asked fellow incoming Texas Sen. James Talarico if he would “stand up” to El-Sayed and other, unnamed left-wing members of his caucus. To his credit, Talarico demurred from directly challenging his fellow future senator. Still, it’s a sign of a long battle to come.
The question for “unity”-caping Democrats remains: Who will they rally around — and who will be left out in the cold?
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-arrests-.title: NYPD arrests and charges city schools employee in murder of Brooklyn jogger
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-arrests-.author: Kaya Laterman
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-arrests-.text:
A current employee of the Department of Education was arrested and charged with murder Saturday in the death of Brooklyn jogger last month, the NYPD said.
Police officials said they arrested Sayed Mohassib, 27, and charged him with murder.
Katie Suarez, 28, was stabbed in the neck as she was running on the path on Shore Parkway near Bay 17th Street on Oct. 30.
It's unclear if Mohassib had a relationship to the victim, but police said previously they believed the attack to be random. His attorney information was not immediately available.
The city Department of Education did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
On the night of the attack, Suarez was doing her usual routine, Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny told reporters during a recent briefing.
She left work at a nearby bank around 6:35 p.m., changed into athletic gear, met up with her mother who took her work outfit, and then set off for her run, he said.
Her father had also just left work and was planning to meet up with both of them at a nearby Wendy’s restaurant and give them a ride home after Suarez finished her jog, according to Kenny.
At 7:56 p.m., her father called Suarez to find out when she would arrive, and she told him she was about half a mile away and would be there soon. Kenny said when she didn’t arrive on time, the father set off to look for her on the path and at 8:16 p.m. he found her unconscious under a tree, bleeding from the neck.
The path where she was attacked is a stretch of running and biking trail that is not covered by surveillance cameras, Kenny added. The path runs along the water from a pier in Bay Ridge to a large shopping center in Bath Beach. It’s often crowded with runners, bikers and fishermen.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

https://hyperallergic.com/mexican-duo-ro.title: Mexican Duo RojoNegro Installs Colossal Work on UC San Diego Campus
https://hyperallergic.com/mexican-duo-ro.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/mexican-duo-ro.text:
Mexican Duo RojoNegro Installs Colossal Work on UC San Diego Campus
María Sosa and Noé Martínez, the Michoacán artists representing Mexico at the Venice Biennale, hand-painted 260 ceramic tiles for the installation.
Sometimes, the best lessons are taught outside the classroom. Though still embedded on a college campus, a new artwork in San Diego brings a wealth of Mesoamerican history to the public commons, imparting ancient customs and knowledge that resisted colonial extinction efforts to the next generation.
A permanent outdoor artwork by RojoNegro, the duo representing Mexico at the 61st Venice Biennale, was recently unveiled on the University of California, San Diego (UCSD) campus. Comprising 260 unique, hand-painted ceramic tiles mounted on four tree-like panels, “La asamblea del barro” (2026) probes the transmission of cultural memory across generations by drawing on the relationship between Mesoamerican and Western knowledge that is inextricably connected through colonialism.
Hailing from Michoacán and based in Mexico City, RojoNegro artists and life partners María Sosa, who has Purépecha roots, and Noé Martínez, whose family origins trace back to Mexico's Huasteca region, use their multidisciplinary practice to bring Indigenous ways of being to the foreground. Together, they disrupt dominant colonial narratives and legacies by invoking the ancestral knowledge imbued in materials and practices that have endured four centuries of violent erasure.
“In 'La asamblea del barro,' we include the four cosmic trees that sustain the universe in Mesoamerican thought, an idea that lives on among our Indigenous peoples and bears witness to a cultural and ideological resistance that reveals the profound relationship between the body, its surroundings, and the forces of nature,” RojoNegro explained in a statement on the artwork.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ar.title: Art Week NYC Kicks off at Metropolitan Museum of Art with New York Pols and Art Leaders
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ar.author: Brian Boucher
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ar.text:
Dozens of leaders from the New York art and political worlds rubbed shoulders at the Metropolitan Museum of Art on Tuesday morning at the launch of Art Week NYC, a citywide gathering celebrating New York’s leading galleries, institutions, and cultural spaces, organized by ARTnews, Art in America, and Artforum. The inaugural event takes place from November 11–14, 2026.
The distinguished roster of speakers included Julie Menin, City Council Speaker; City Council Deputy Speaker Nantasha Williams; Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal; New York State Senator Jose Serrano; and City Council member Virginia Maloney.
In attendance were VIPs like advisor Augusto Arbizo; MoMA PS1 director Connie Butler; Lisson Gallery international director Alex Logsdail; Arts Council England chairman Nicholas Serota; and Simone Subal, senior director at Paula Cooper Gallery, along with ARTnews/Art in America editor Sarah Douglas and publisher Erica Lubow Necarsulmer as well as Artforum co-editor Rachel Wetzler and publisher Danielle McConnell.
The gathering took place in the light-filled Charles Engelhard Court, anchored by the Neoclassical facade of the Second Branch Bank of the United States (1822–24) and featuring sculptures by American artists such as Daniel Chester French, Hiram Powers, and Augustus Saint-Gaudens.
All were there, said David Breslin, the museum’s curator in charge of the modern and contemporary art department, “to launch what we know will become a defining tradition in our city’s cultural landscape—and that’s saying a lot.”
Kicking off the remarks, City Council Speaker Julie Menin looked to history to set the tone, noting that it was 100 years ago when pioneering New York dealer Edith Halpert launched what would become the Downtown Gallery, which was early to show American modern art and folk art. To signal its spirit of inclusivity, Menin said, it was initially called Our Gallery, adding, “As the very first citywide contemporary art festival, that is precisely the same spirit that Art Week NYC has built here.” The City Council was proud to allocate a record $323 million in its latest budget to the Department of Cultural Affairs, she added.
Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal recalled bringing together all the city’s local community boards at the museum recently and finding that some had never before visited. “Art Week is a way to invite New Yorkers—just like we invited those community board members to the Met to experience art—to meet New Yorkers, as they say, where they are,” he said, and called New York’s hundreds of galleries, many of them participating in Art Week, “magnificent little crown jewels.”
Citing Public Theater founder Joseph Papp to the effect that art belongs to everyone, Hoylman-Sigal noted, “I’m very proud to have committed 100 percent of our capital dollars to arts and cultural institutions.” That was $50 million in discretionary funds, he noted, adding that the recipient institutions were called upon to leverage the public dollars to raise money from private donors, and the 83 cultural institutions raised an additional $52 million through what he called the “Manhattan Multiplier.”
Wrapping up the event, City Council member Virginia Maloney noted that her namesake grandmother was an artist before it was common for women to have careers. Her brother-in-law is also an artist, she noted, adding, “They both taught me that art changes the way that you view the world. As chair of the Economic Development Committee, I also know that culture and art is not a luxury in New York. It’s an economic engine for tourism, for visitors, for employers, and for businesses that surround the organizations that we’re supporting today. When we invest in the arts, we know that we recoup the benefits tenfold.”
For a full listing of member galleries and institutions and a calendar of events, head to Art Week NYC.
