https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Congresso prorroga MP que proíbe bets por mais 60 dias
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O presidente da Mesa do Congresso Nacional, senador Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), prorrogou por mais 60 dias a vigência da Medida Provisória (MP) 1.394 de 2026, que proíbe a exploração, oferta, intermediação e publicidade de apostas de quota fixa, conhecidas como bets, em todo o território nacional.
O ato foi publicado no Diário Oficial da União desta quarta-feira (11). Editada pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) em 25 de setembro, a norma encerra as autorizações previamente concedidas às operadoras, determina o bloqueio de plataformas digitais e exige a devolução dos saldos mantidos pelos apostadores.
As restrições já estão em vigor, mas dependem de aprovação na Câmara dos Deputados e no Senado Federal para se tornarem permanentes. Com a suspensão da contagem de prazos durante o recesso parlamentar de fim de ano, a medida provisória seguirá em vigor até 5 de março de 2027.
Caso deputados e senadores não concluam a votação do texto até essa data, a medida perde a eficácia e as apostas voltam a ser liberadas no país. Se a deliberação for transferida para fevereiro do próximo ano, a análise caberá aos novos parlamentares eleitos em outubro.
A proposta já recebeu 99 emendas e teve seu regime de urgência aprovado na segunda-feira (9). No entanto, a comissão parlamentar mista de deputados e senadores responsável por emitir o parecer preliminar sobre a matéria ainda aguarda instalação.
Além do trâmite legislativo, o tema é alvo de disputas jurídicas. No domingo (8), o ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) Luiz Fux atendeu a um pedido da Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) e suspendeu todos os processos judiciais em instâncias inferiores que contestavam a proibição, até que a Corte analise em definitivo a constitucionalidade da norma.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: 2º turno no RJ com Eduardo Paes e Douglas Ruas ganha fôlego com apelo popular e apoio da esquerda
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A expectativa para a realização de segundo turno para o governo do Rio de Janeiro aumentou esta semana com a adesão de políticos de esquerda e um protesto marcado para sexta-feira (13) na Cinelândia, no centro da cidade, em defesa da “democracia e da soberania popular”. A controvérsia teve início com a decisão da Justiça Eleitoral que, ao excluir os votos do terceiro colocado na disputa, elevou o percentual de Douglas Ruas (PL) contra Eduardo Paes (PSD).
A retotalização beneficiou Ruas, que atingiu 50,88%, ultrapassando o percentual necessário para vencer. Assim, o presidente da Assembleia Legislativa (Alerj) foi declarado governador eleito sem uma nova votação. O PSD de Paes recorreu ao Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) contra a exclusão dos votos de Anthony Garotinho (Republicanos) da base de cálculo, questionando violação de princípios constitucionais.
O partido solicita uma nova votação com a justificativa de que Douglas Ruas não atingiu a maioria dos votos para ser declarado eleito no primeiro turno. A ação sob relatoria do ministro Cristiano Zanin aguarda pareceres da Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) e da Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU). Nos últimos dias, advogados de Paes e de Ruas tiveram audiência com o ministro.
A defesa do segundo turno ganhou novo fôlego com um abaixo-assinado que reúne mais de 300 mil apoiadores e declarações de políticos de esquerda questionando a legitimidade do resultado. Entre eles estão deputados estaduais e federais do PT e PCdoB como Marcelo Freixo, Marina do MST, Verônica Lima, Dani Balbi, Reimont e Jandira Feghali.
“Estamos nessa luta porque a palavra final sobre quem governa o nosso estado é do povo do Rio”, publicou Marina (PT). A deputada Dani Balbi (PCdoB) afirmou que as irregularidades na candidatura de Garotinho já eram conhecidas, e mesmo assim o TSE falhou em não concluir o julgamento antes da votação.
:: Quer receber notícias do Brasil de Fato RJ no seu WhatsApp? ::
“Não se trata de defender Garotinho ou qualquer outra candidatura, mas de garantir o direito dos eleitores, a segurança jurídica e a soberania popular. A Justiça Eleitoral teve a oportunidade de resolver essa controvérsia antes da votação e não o fez”, escreveu nas redes sociais.
Em vídeo, o deputado federal eleito Marcelo Freixo (PT) defendeu o direito de decisão do povo fluminense que votou em Garotinho de escolher outro candidato no segundo turno. “A decisão de anular os votos de Garotinho depois da eleição fere o princípio do direito do eleitor”, dissse.
“Garotinho foi candidato, ele estava nas urnas. Tinha lá o seu retrato, o seu número, você digitou e apareceu ‘confirma’. Isso aconteceu. Portanto, o eleitor de Garotinho não votou nulo, não votou em branco; ele votou no Garotinho”, afirmou Freixo.
Indefinição
Douglas Ruas recebeu 49,27% dos votos, enquanto Eduardo Paes obteve 42,76% na eleição de 4 de outubro. Condenado por improbidade administrativa, o candidato Garotinho concorreu sub judice e teve 274.411 votos (3,17%). No entanto, o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) confirmou o indeferimento de seu registro em 8 de outubro, e anulou sua votação. Com a decisão, Ruas obteve 50,88% dos votos, e Paes 44,16%.
A diplomação do novo governador está marcada para 18 de dezembro, e a posse para 6 de janeiro. A ação do PSD pede novas eleições antes dessa data. A última reservada pela Justiça Eleitoral para eleições suplementares este ano, 6 de dezembro.
Depois disso, o calendário eleitoral prevê uma data a cada mês, com exceção de novembro, para disputas suplementares. A primeira seria em 10 de janeiro. A data, porém, abre outro questionamento sobre o governo interino, uma vez que Ricardo Couto ficará à frente do Palácio Guanabara até o final deste ano.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Rússia, Ucrânia e EUA concluem negociações em Abu Dhabi sem avanços concretos
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Serguei Monin
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
As negociações trilaterais entre Rússia, Ucrânia e Estados Unidos, realizadas em Abu Dhabi, foram concluídas nesta quarta-feira (11). O chefe da delegação russa, Vladimir Medinsky, afirmou que Rússia e Ucrânia concordaram com uma troca de prisioneiros em larga escala e que o tema central das reuniões foi o sistema de segurança europeu.
De acordo com Medinsky, houve entendimento mútuo sobre alguns pontos ligados à discussão sobre segurança, mas sobre outros, não. Negociadores ucranianos classificaram a reunião como “difícil” e que detalhes específicos das negociações só serão revelados após resultados concretos.
Ao mesmo tempo, a delegação da Ucrânia declarou que as partes podem chegar a uma decisão até o final do ano. A afirmação foi do chefe da bancada do partido “Servo do Povo” na Verkhovna Rada (parlamento ucraniano), David Arakhamia, durante uma coletiva de imprensa após as negociações de hoje.
Arakhamia também afirmou que esta rodada de negociações “foi uma das mais difíceis”. Segundo ele, os negociadores russos “vieram com diretrizes muito rígidas”. No entanto, expressou otimismo em relação a novas reuniões.
“Acredito que estamos em boas condições para chegar a uma decisão antes do Ano Novo”, afirmou o membro da delegação ucraniana nas conversações.
Medinsky ainda afirmou que o diálogo com Kiev e Washington terá continuidade. “Com a participação do lado estadunidense, trocamos avaliações sobre nossas posições; em algumas áreas encontramos entendimento mútuo, em outras não. E essa conversa certamente continuará”, disse.
De acordo com o vice-chefe de informação do Estado-Maior das Forças Armadas Russas, a troca de prisioneiros entre a Rússia e a Ucrânia envolverá mais de mil prisioneiros de cada lado e poderá ocorrer nas próximas duas ou três semanas.
O vice-ministro das Relações Exteriores da Rússia, Sergei Ryabkov, também afirmou, após as conversas, que existe uma base para dar continuidade ao trabalho.
Já o chefe do gabinete presidencial ucraniano, Kyrylo Budanov, afirmou que o conteúdo e o resultado das negociações não serão anunciados até que haja um resultado concreto. “Só o resultado importa. Quando conseguirmos, será anunciado publicamente”, disse ele em coletiva de imprensa.
Essas foram as primeiras negociações trilaterais entre representantes da Rússia, da Ucrânia e dos Estados Unidos desde fevereiro deste ano. As negociações em Abu Dhabi duraram 4 horas e meia no primeiro dia, 10 de novembro, e menos de duas horas no segundo, 11 de novembro.
Enviados dos EUA viajam a Moscou
Os enviados especiais do presidente dos EUA, Steve Witkoff e Jared Kushner, que participaram das negociações em Abu Dhabi, viajarão a Moscou na quinta-feira (12). A informação foi divulgada por Kushner em uma coletiva de imprensa após a conclusão das negociações trilaterais com Rússia e Ucrânia.
Foi informado também que, após a viagem a Moscou, Witkoff e Kushner se reunirão com o presidente ucraniano, Volodymyr Zelensky, em Dublin.
De acordo com Kushner, os representantes dos EUA pretendem discutir com o presidente russo, Vladimir Putin, em Moscou, a possibilidade de envolver os europeus nas negociações.
“Um dos objetivos da reunião em Moscou é tentar descobrir se podemos incluir os europeus neste formato para torná-lo multilateral”, disse Kushner.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: 17-year-old charged in fatal Bronx shooting of 15-year-old boy
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A 17-year-old boy has been arrested and charged with murder in connection with the fatal shooting of 15-year-old Javits Frimpong in the Bronx.
The teenager was taken from his Bronx home for questioning Wednesday morning and brought to the New York City police department (NYPD)’s 42nd precinct. The suspect, whose identity has not been released, faces several charges, including murder, manslaughter, criminal possession of a weapon and other firearm-related offenses.
Investigators had previously been searching for three teenage boys believed to be connected to the shooting. Authorities have not ruled out the possibility of additional arrests. It remains unclear whether the suspect and the victim knew one another.
The arrest took place just hours before attorneys representing Frimpong’s family held a news conference in Harlem.
The deadly incident occurred on 29 October near Crotona Park in the Bronx. Officers responded to a shooting report at approximately 9.24am and discovered Frimpong suffering from a gunshot wound to his abdomen, according to the NYPD.
The 15-year-old was rushed to a nearby hospital, where he was pronounced dead. Police initially reported that no arrests had been made as investigators searched for three teenage suspects.
Surveillance video reportedly showed Frimpong running while someone dressed entirely in black followed him. Footage from another camera angle appeared to capture masked individuals wearing dark clothing running away from the scene.
Frimpong’s death has deeply affected members of the Bronx’s close-knit Ghanaian community, as well as students at DreamYard Preparatory School, where he was in his sophomore year.
The teenager had moved to the US from Ghana a year earlier to reunite with his father, who works as a taxi driver. His killing occurred around the time he was marking his first anniversary of living in New York.
Frimpong’s father remembered his son as “clever” and “quiet”. He also said the teenager had been experiencing bullying at DreamYard Preparatory School.
As the investigation continues, the family has hired civil rights attorney Ben Crump to represent them.
“A juvenile suspect has reportedly been charged in connection with Javits’ killing,” Crump said in a statement. “While these charges mark an important step toward accountability, the questions remain: Why did this happen, and could it have been prevented? His family deserves answers and justice.”

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: Veteran actor Irma P Hall, star of The Ladykillers, dies aged 91
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Owen Myers
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
Actor Irma P Hall, star of Soul Food and the Coen brothers’ The Ladykillers, has died at the age of 91.
Hall died on Tuesday, her family confirmed alongside a statement that described her as “a beloved actress, author, poet, educator and public speaker whose contributions touched countless lives throughout her remarkable career”.
In an acting career that spanned six decades, Hall starred opposite Denzel Washington, Oprah Winfrey, Robin Williams and Tom Hanks, and worked with directors including Michael Mann, the Coen brothers and Jonathan Demme.
Born in Texas in 1935, Hall was raised with a passion for the arts as the daughter of saxophone player Samuel Player. For 27 years she worked as a high school teacher in Houston before pivoting to acting the early 1980s.
“I always believed I could do whatever I wanted,” she said in a 2001 interview. “I never knew there [were things] I wasn’t supposed to be able to do because I was Black or a woman.”
After roles in 1980s films including On Valentine’s Day and They Still Call Me Bruce, Hall starred alongside Hollywood A-listers such as Dolly Parton in Straight Talk and John Goodman in The Babe, before her career progressed to the next level in the mid-90s.
In the 1997 drama Soul Food, she played Big Mama Joseph, the unforgiving matriarch to three daughters (Vanessa Williams, Vivica A Fox and Nia Long). Hall won the outstanding supporting actress award at the NAACP Image awards for her portrayal. She resumed the role of Big Mama in a TV spin-off of the film which aired from 2000-2004.
She also worked with Robin Williams in 90s comedy drama Patch Adams and Clint Eastwood in the fact-based crime drama Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil.
In 2004, Hall received a Cannes special jury prize for her work in the Coen brothers’ The Ladykillers, in which she played spiky landlady Marva Munson. The same year, she played the no-nonsense mother of Jamie Foxx’s character in Mann’s thriller Collateral.
Hall’s later films include Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call New Orleans; My Son, My Son, What Have Ye Done and the Sundance TV show Hap and Leonard.
The actor consistently advocated for the arts community and helped establish the Dallas Minority Repertory Theatre. Since 2015, the Irma P Hall Black Theatre awards have been annually held to recognize artistic achievement in the Dallas-Fort Worth area.
For many years, Hall was church mother at Dallas’s Inspiring Body of Christ church and a treasured member of the local religious community.
“Our beloved Church Mother, Irma P Hall, has taken her final bow on the stage of life and stepped into eternity,” said pastor Rickie G Rush in a statement. “While we mourn her passing, we are forever grateful for the remarkable legacy she leaves behind.”
“She started as a teacher in the classroom but ended up being a teacher to the world,” her daughter, Irma Hall Crayton, said. “My mom used to always say, ‘To the world you may be one person, but to one person you may be the world.’ And she was just that to many people.”

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Complaint filed to IRS in relation to Fifa head Gianni Infantino’s housekeeper
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Paul MacInnes
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
A complaint has been filed to the United States Internal Revenue Service calling for an investigation into claims an individual on the Fifa payroll was working privately as a housekeeper for Gianni Infantino.
If the IRS investigates and finds the claims to be proven then Fifa could lose its tax-exempt status in the US. Fifa has 501(c)(4) status in the country, a category for organisations “created to promote community welfare for charitable, educational or recreational purposes”.
The complaint, which has been seen by the Guardian and is supported by a number of documents, claims an individual “performed domestic work exclusively for Fifa president Gianni Infantino and his wife, Leena Infantino, at their Miami residence, while receiving compensation or benefits through a Fifa-affiliated entity”, and argues that “senior leadership, acting in their official capacity and on behalf of Fifa, have abused the entity’s tax-exemption status”.
The complaint goes on to argue: “If organisational funds or resources were used to pay for services benefiting a leader’s household, the arrangement raises serious questions about private benefit, financial reporting, compensation, and governance. The materials also raise questions about the accuracy of representations in employment, payroll, tax, and immigration records. We ask the agencies to investigate the underlying records and determine what occurred.” The IRS has been approached for comment.
The news comes as Fifa’s activities, and specifically Infantino’s involvement in the failed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme and his relationship with the Trump White House, are to come under intensified scrutiny from Democratic politicians in the US after the “blue wave” at the midterm elections. A spokesperson for the ranking member of the House judiciary committee, representative Jamie Raskin, said the committee had not requested documents related to the housekeeper but was “looking closely at those developments”.
A Fifa spokesperson said: “Matters related to the Fifa president’s personal and home life are private; however, for the avoidance of any doubt, the costs of any domestic staff are met by the Fifa president personally.”
The complaint, if taken up, would probably take months to complete and commonly the results of IRS investigations are not published. Any action taken as a result, however, would be in the public domain. The complaint was submitted by the Washington DC lawyer Abed Ayoub, who works in immigration law and has served as the national executive director of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC). Last year the ADC was part of the campaign Game Over Israel, which called for Israeli football teams to be banned from international competition.
Fifa said: “We urge the media to act responsibly. As Fifa stated in August, it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president. Fifa welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a licence to amplify false allegations. Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading Fifa will continue to challenge it directly and vigorously.”
Infantino has been described by his predecessor, Sepp Blatter, as a “dictator” who “no longer knows any borders”. Blatter, Fifa’s president for 17 years before resigning amid a corruption scandal at the organisation, made the remarks in an interview with the German magazine Der Spiegel. He criticised the FFE scheme, the Fifa peace prize and, most significantly in his opinion, the overturning of Folarin Balogun’s suspension for a red card during the World Cup.
“Fifa is suffering,” Blatter said. “It is currently led by a person who has allowed himself to be blinded.” He described the peace prize as “embarrassing”, saying: “Why would he do something like that? Infantino awards a peace prize to someone who wages war against Iran shortly afterwards?”
In assessing the FFE scheme, which was abandoned after an international outcry, Blatter said: “Infantino no longer knows any borders. He doesn’t understand any of this.” He described the Balogun controversy as “the worst”, saying: “Statutes can be interpreted. But rules of the game must apply to everyone, you can’t interpret them.”
FIfa has been approached for comment.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: F1 champion Lewis Hamilton calls on Israel to open Gaza’s Rafah border
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
F1 champion Lewis Hamilton calls on Israel to open Gaza’s Rafah border
Hamilton visited the Egypt-Gaza border as conditions worsened for Palestinians in Gaza after heavy rains.
Lewis Hamilton visits Rafah crossing to witness Gaza aid efforts
Seven-time Formula One champion Lewis Hamilton has called on Israel to reopen the Rafah crossing to allow humanitarian supplies into Gaza from Egypt, amid worsening conditions after heavy rains and flooded makeshift camps.
The remarks came on Wednesday, a day after the British F1 driver visited Egypt’s northern city of el-Arish, which borders Gaza, touring a storage facility where the Egyptian Red Crescent had prepared boxes of aid to be sent to Palestinians in the besieged enclave.
In a post on social media, Hamilton said, “People in Gaza and Palestine are in such urgent need that they could hardly need this aid more than they do right now.”
“That’s why we really need to put pressure on Israel and work together to make sure this aid reaches them,” he said.
Hamilton said there were warehouses storing essential supplies in several locations, but the supplies were not reaching Palestinians who need them because of the border closure.
“Injustice”
A post on Hamilton’s Instagram page showed him meeting some of the volunteers and workers for the Egyptian Red Crescent, as well as stationary trucks loaded with food waiting to cross the border.
“The past three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling. It’s an injustice for people to being denied their freedom, their safety and their dignity. No human being should be treated as though their life matters less,” Hamilton said.
Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected accusations that Israel has been delaying the entry of winter supplies into the Gaza Strip.
More than 150,000 tents bought by humanitarian partners and member states are waiting outside the Gaza Strip for Israeli permission to enter, the United Nations said on Wednesday.
UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said on Wednesday that waiting for a new Israeli government to form is “not an acceptable excuse” for delays in getting essential winter supplies into Gaza.

https://apache.be/2026/10/27/schaduw-van.title: De schaduw van Didier Reynders boven een assisenproces
https://apache.be/2026/10/27/schaduw-van.author: Walter De Smedt
https://apache.be/2026/10/27/schaduw-van.text:
Wat heeft de gevallen Belgische toppoliticus Didier Reynders te maken met het assisenproces tegen Nicolas Ullens? Op 29 maart 2023 reed Nicolas Ullens de Schooten zijn stiefmoeder, barones Myriam 'Mimi' Lechien, klem en schoot vervolgens zesmaal, waarna Myriam Lechien overleed. Vader Ullens werd verwond.
Nicolas Ullens ging zich daarop aangeven bij de politie en bekende de feiten. De feiten zelf vormden op het assisenproces bijgevolg geen probleem. Wel is er de vraag of Ullens met voorbedachtheid had gehandeld, in welk geval het dus niet om doodslag maar om moord zou gaan. Een moord wordt zwaarder bestraft dan doodslag.
Op het eerste gezicht is dit een dramatische afloop van een familiale aangelegenheid. Maar de actualiteit – gelekte gesprekken tussen Reynders en een door hem benoemde topman binnen de Belgische Staatsveiligheid – leert dat er elementen spelen die mogelijk een antwoord kunnen geven op de vraag of er voorbedachtheid in het spel was dan wel of Ullens “ontplofte”.
De volgende vraag is dan of die elementen ook effectief werden onderzocht, of er op de assisenzitting over werd gepleit en of er bij de beoordeling rekening mee werd gehouden. Is het onderzoek naar de feiten voldoende gevoerd? En is het zogenoemde “moraliteitsonderzoek” – het onderzoek naar het verleden en de ingesteldheid van de verdachte – volledig gevoerd of vertoont het lacunes?
Voorbedachtheid
De jury en de beroepsrechters beslisten samen dat er sprake was van voorbedachtheid en veroordeelden Nicolas Ullens voor moord. De vaststelling dat de beroepsrechters daarbij meestemden werd initieel aangevochten, maar door het Hof van Cassatie terecht goedgekeurd. De wet voorziet immers dat bij een krappe meerderheid (zeven van de vijf stemmen) de rechters moeten tussenkomen. (Terzijde: dat neemt niet weg dat deze wettelijke voorziening eigenlijk het principe dat het volk de schuldvraag beoordeelt onderuithaalt.)
Op het proces werd voornamelijk naar de verspilling van het familiefortuin door de stiefmoeder en het gebrek aan aandacht door de vader gewezen
Voorbedachtheid (of voorbedachten rade) is in het strafrecht het plegen van een misdrijf na een kalme overweging en met een gepland besluit, in plaats van in een blinde opwelling. Als het dat laatste was, wat bracht Ullens dan tot zo’n blinde opwelling.
Op het proces werd voornamelijk naar de verspilling van het familiefortuin door de stiefmoeder en het gebrek aan aandacht door de vader gewezen. Er zijn echter heel wat andere elementen die de gewezen agent van de Staatsveiligheid in een toestand kunnen hebben gebracht die door professor Philippe de Timary, hoofd van de afdeling psychiatrie van de Cliniques Universitaires Saint-Luc, werd uiteengezet.
De arts getuigde op het proces dat Nicolas Ullens op het moment van de schietpartij vermoedelijk een “dissociatieve” episode doormaakte. Een dissociatieve periode is een toestand waarin de normale, samenhangende functies van je brein − zoals bewustzijn, geheugen, identiteit, emoties en waarneming − tijdelijk verstoord of losgekoppeld raken. Wanneer iemand een misdrijf pleegt (zoals slagen of doodslag) nadat hij zelf werd uitgelokt door zwaar, onmiddellijk en onrechtmatig fysiek of psychisch geweld dat zijn vrije wil aantast, kan dat dienen als een verschoningsgrond of leiden tot strafvermindering.
Andere elementen
Als agent van de Staatsveiligheid deed Ullens onderzoek naar mogelijk beïnvloeding en corruptie door Didier Reynders en zijn entourage, voornamelijk zijn rechterhand Jean-Claude Fontinoy. Hij maakte er ook interne nota's over. Ullens deed ook aangifte bij het Vast Comité I dat de inlichtingendiensten controleert. Hij getuigde daar binnen de Belgische Staatsveiligheid te zijn tegengewerkt en gepest.
In een interview in Humo (18/05/2021) legde Nicolas Ullens in dat verband erg bezwarende verklaringen af:
Reynders en Fontinoy hebben een putsch op de Staatsveiligheid uitgevoerd: ze benoemden een derde topman, Hugues Brulin, terwijl de Staatsveiligheid sinds 1830 werd bestuurd door een tweespan: de administrateurgeneraal en zijn adjunct. Brulin kwam rechtstreeks van het kabinet-Reynders. Daarmee overtraden ze de regel dat een staflid van de Staatsveiligheid een magistraat hoort te zijn. Mijn diensthoofd, Frank J, was ook een MR-man. Frank J. en Brulin hebben me het leven onmogelijk gemaakt en de economische afdeling van de Staatsveiligheid, waar ik werkte, opgedoekt. Frank J. heeft me ook aangemaand om op te houden met het onderzoek naar Kazachgate, het dossier van een parlementaire onderzoekscommissie. Uiteindelijk heb ik me tot het Comité I gewend, dat toezicht houdt op de inlichtingendiensten. De toenmalige voorzitter, Guy Rapaille, een man van socialistische signatuur, heeft me niet bepaald gesteund: hij heeft geprobeerd me in diskrediet te brengen. Maar de ergste was de chef van de Dienst Enquêtes van Comité I, Frank Franceus, de oud-kabinetschef van Geert Bourgeois (N-VA, red.). Toen ik mijn verklaringen ging ondertekenen, zei hij: 'Meneer Ullens, als u dit tekent, brengt u niet alleen uzelf, maar ook uw vrouw en uw vier kinderen in gevaar.'
Bedreigd
Over de mogelijke bedreiging door de chef van de enquêtedienst I aan het adres van Nicolas Ullens werd een strafonderzoek gevoerd. Daarin kwam een belangrijke getuige terug op voordien schriftelijk weergegeven elementen die de klacht ondersteunden. Het onderzoek door het comité I zelf, kreeg evenmin gevolg.
Er waren ook andere bedreigingen. Die werden duidelijk en bovendien openbaar door meerdere artikelen en een boek van onderzoeksjournalisten.
Apache bracht er, soms samen met Humo, verschillende artikelen over:
Daarnaast werd het boek van de Franstalige onderzoeksjournalist Philippe Engels, De clan Reynders, in april 2021 gepubliceerd. Het onderzoekt de nauwe banden tussen politiek en het bedrijfsleven en volgt de loopbaan van MR-politicus Didier Reynders en zijn naaste medewerker Jean-Claude Fontinoy. Engels beschrijft daarin onder meer hoe private firma's zijn bevoordeeld, hoe NMBS-personeel zou zijn ingezet voor verkiezingscampagnes, en hoe de samenwerking achter de schermen verliep.
Vooral de verwijzingen naar de mogelijke betrokkenheid van Russische spelers en spionage openen de deur naar een geheel andere wereld. De mogelijke bedreigingen door externe personen en diensten, is een opdracht van de Staatsveiligheid. De vraag of Ullens zich ook daardoor bedreigd voelde is, gezien wat er in die wereld allemaal mogelijk is, niet onbelangrijk.
Gewapend
Een ander element dat als bezwarend kan worden gezien, is de vaststelling dat Nicolas Ullens gewapend was op het moment van de feiten. Was dat om zich te verdedigen tegen mogelijke bedreigingen? Wat daarover door onderzoeksjournalisten werd geschreven ondersteunt deze stelling. Ullens had immers al geruime tijd steeds zijn wapen bij. Nadat Nicolas Ullens geschoten had, stapte vader Ullens de wagen uit en riep “Dood mij ook” of “Schiet me nu ook maar dood”.
Nicolas Ullens was gewapend op het moment van de feiten. Was dat om zich te verdedigen tegen mogelijke bedreigingen?
De gespannen verhouding tussen vader en zoon was danig aangewakkerd door het bezoek van vader Ullens aan Didier Reynders. Vader Ullens had Reynders zijn verontschuldigingen aangeboden voor de beweringen van zijn zoon aan het adres van de gevallen toppoliticus. Werd daarover gesproken tijden het gesprek onmiddellijk voorafgaand aan de feiten? Speelde ook deze frustratie mee?
Al op 19 januari 2017, jaren voor de feiten, schreef Ullens een brief aan de directeur operaties van de Staatsveiligheid, Christiane Delvoye. Daarin komt hij terug op het verwijt dat zijn chef hem maakte omdat hij een examen voor het gebruik van zijn dienstwapen niet zou hebben afgelegd. Ullens antwoordde daarop dat hij de nodige schietoefeningen wel degelijk had gevolgd.
Daarbij verwijst hij expliciet naar het gevaar dat uitgaat van het fameuze Kazachse trio – een dossier waarin ook Didier Reynders opduikt − “en de verleiding die zou kunnen bestaan om een lastige getuige in dat dossier te laten verdwijnen”.
In de brief heeft Ullens het over “het feit dat de zaak rond het ‘Kazachse trio’ – een kwestie waarover ik tussen 2008 en 2015 veertien verslagen heb geschreven – op dramatische wijze opnieuw is opgedoken” en over “de banden met de georganiseerde misdaad en buitenlandse inlichtingendiensten die bekendstaan om hun gewelddadigheid binnen onze instelling ruimschoots gedocumenteerd zijn”.
Kazachgate
De voormalige justitieministers Stefaan De Clerck (CD&V) en Koen Geens (CD&V) slaagden erin de fameuze afkoopwet door het parlement te jagen. Daardoor kon het strafonderzoek in meerdere grootschalige fraudezaken worden stil gelegd en konden de daders door een enkele betaling van een “uitgebreide minnelijke schikking” aan een veroordeling ontsnappen.
Dat gebeurde onder meer in het onderzoek naar Kazachgate en bij de fameuze diamantdossiers. Omdat parlementairen zich bij de voorbereiding van de afkoopwet bedrogen voelden, werd er een parlementaire onderzoekscommissie in het leven geroepen. Die leerde dat bij de eerder genoemde dossiers zeer ernstige “disfuncties” speelden. Er werd “gelobbyd” zowel bij ministers, parlementairen als parketmagistraten. Bovendien werd de afkoopwet toegepast nog voor hij was gestemd en ongeacht de terechte kritiek van de Hoge Raad voor de Justitie. Er waren ook ernstige en samenlopende aanwijzingen van corruptie.
De bewering van Ullens dat hij door de chef van de enquêtedienst Frank Franceus werd bedreigd roept vragen op
De bewering van Ullens dat hij door de chef van de enquêtedienst Frank Franceus werd bedreigd roept eveneens vragen op. Frank Franceus, de oud-kabinetschef van Geert Bourgeois, werd door het Comité I immers aangesteld als expert bij de audit over de werking van de Staatsveiligheid. Hoe kon een expert nadien chef van de enquêtedienst van het Comité I worden?
Soortgelijke vragen werden ook gesteld bij de benoeming van Franceus in de Hoge Raad voor Justitie. De Hoge Raad voor Justitie is een onafhankelijk orgaan dat de selectie van te benoemen magistraten doet maar ook onderzoeken voert naar mogelijke “disfuncties” binnen justitie.
Bij de oprichting van het orgaan werd voorzien dat zowel vertegenwoordigers van de magistratuur, academici als politici maar ook leden van het middenveld een plek konden krijgen.
Hoe kon Franceus benoemd worden als vertegenwoordiger van het middenveld? Hij was immers tegelijk chef van de enquêtedienst van het Vast Comité I. Dat is geen particuliere organisatie maar een overheidsinstelling.
Bij de invulling van mandaten wordt bovendien gekeken naar het beroepsverleden van de kandidaten, minstens nagegaan of er geen “onverenigbaarheden” zijn die de uitoefening van het mandaat kunnen bemoeilijken. Als chef enquêtes van het Comité I mag Franceus naar de organieke wet op het comité I geen onderzoeken doen naar de werking van de magistratuur vermits dat uitdrukkelijk uit de onderzoeksbevoegdheid van de comités is uitgesloten.
Als voorzitter van de onderzoekscommissie heeft hij daartoe uitdrukkelijk wél de opdracht en is het zelfs de essentie van zijn taak. Frank Franceus verenigde dus op het ogenblik van zijn benoeming twee bevoegdheden die volgens de wet onverenigbaar zijn. Ook feitelijk zijn de twee opdrachten niet te verzoenen. Als chef enquêtes moest hij de opdrachten van de magistraten uitvoeren. Als voorzitter van de onderzoekscommissie moet hij onderzoeken of in die opdrachten “disfuncties” te vinden zijn. Hij was dus tegelijk uitvoerder en controleur. Hoe verkreeg Franceus beide benoemingen? Voor wie reed hij?
Didier Reynders
De bewering van Nicolas Ullens dat Reynders en Fontinoy een putsch op de Staatsveiligheid hadden uitgevoerd en zij daarbij Hugues Brulin benoemden, wordt intussen bevestigd door een gelekt document. Daarin schrijft Brulin onder meer dat hij zijn “job heeft volbracht” en de “krankzinnige Ullens” werd tegengewerkt en uit de dienst werd verwijderd.
Ullens verklaarde dat door de inmenging en de bedreigingen zijn leven onmogelijk werd gemaakt
Werd daar rekening mee gehouden? Een gerechtelijk onderzoek gebeurt zowel ten laste als ter ontlasting. De onderzoeksrechter moet daarbij “alle maatregelen nemen die de rechtscolleges in staat stellen met kennis van zaken te oordelen”.
De vraag of dat wel is gebeurd is terecht. Zowel de door de politie gekraakte berichten tussen Brulin en Reynders als de brief van Ullens waarin hij op de bedreigingen wijst zitten in het dossier. De verklaringen van Ullens in Humo zijn voor iedereen leesbaar. Daarin verklaarde Ullens dat door de inmenging en de bedreigingen zijn leven onmogelijk werd gemaakt.
Vanzelfsprekend is het proces-Ullens niet het proces van Didier Reynders. Maar een verdachte heeft wel het recht om alle elementen die een verklaring kunnen geven voor zijn daad aan het onderzoek toe te voegen. Zowel het parket als de onderzoeksrechter moeten dat volgens de vereisten van het “eerlijk proces” zelfs ambtshalve doen.
Dissociatieve periode
Dat brengt ons terug bij de vraag of Nicolas Ullens met voorbedachtheid handelde of op het ogenblik van de feiten in een dissociatieve toestand verkeerde
Tijdens het proces werd vooral naar de verstoorde relatie met de stiefmoeder en de vader gekeken. Maar zoals hiervoor aangegeven zijn er heel wat andere gegevens voorhanden die aantonen dat Ullens binnen Staatsveiligheid werd tegengewerkt en gepest en dat hij sinds 2017 door zijn onderzoeken naar voornamelijk de invloed van het Russisch crimineel milieu werd bedreigd.
Die bedreigingen moeten ernstig worden genomen. Bovendien werden die bedreigingen in de eigen dienst aangewend om de onderzoeken naar in de dossiers betrokken politieke mandatarissen te stoppen.
Tijdens het proces kwamen die feiten niet voldoende aan bod. Ze zijn belangrijk om de vraag te beantwoorden of Ullens met voorbedachtheid handelde, want ze bepaalden mee de toestand waarin Ullens werd gebracht. Dat vader Ullens bij Didier Reynders bovendien zijn verontschuldigingen had aanboden voor de door zijn zoon gevoerde onderzoeken kan daarbij de druppel zijn geweest.

https://www.propublica.org/article/propu.title: We Can’t Predict What Will Happen on Election Day. But We’ll Be Here to Cover It.
https://www.propublica.org/article/propu.author: Stephen Engelberg
https://www.propublica.org/article/propu.text:
This has been a midterm election cycle unlike any other. Wealthy donors spent staggering sums. Both parties moved to redraw congressional district lines. President Donald Trump and his allies relentlessly questioned whether the results could be trusted even before a single ballot was counted. At Trump’s direction, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit that said the federal government would contest any outcome in which Sen. Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent in Alaska, was not victorious.
Newsrooms, including ours, have tried to plan how we will cover an election in which the losing side refuses to accept the will of the voters. Was the Alaska lawsuit a single data point or a harbinger?
As we prepare to write about Nov. 3 and beyond, we find ourselves in the uncomfortable position of trying to game out what might happen in the future — not our strong suit. The record shows that journalists are pretty good at telling readers what happened, particularly if we have some time and some data to sift through, and much less good at forecasting the future.
Help Us Report on Key Election Issues
ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something?
And yet we have to plan. Over the past few weeks we have prepared our reporters and editors to cover every scenario we can imagine. None of us have forgotten the chaos of 2020 when Trump was urged by advisers to send the military to seize voting machines in states he had lost. The Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol as lawmakers gathered to certify Joe Biden’s victory underscored the sense that literally anything was possible in the aftermath of elections.
We will have reporters on the ground in 11 key states covering voting, with even more in Washington, D.C., and others on standby. Our reporters have detailed what experts will be watching. But elections are no longer confined to Election Day (early voting and voting by mail constitute a huge share of the electorate). And our plans for covering voting stretch back many months.
Over the past year, we’ve tried to use the techniques of accountability journalism to add new facts to this pivotal moment in American history.
We have focused considerable attention on the mechanics of elections, a once-arcane issue that has become a central aspect of the MAGA movement’s argument that Trump’s 2020 loss was “rigged” by his opponents. We examined how the Trump administration depleted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the arm of the federal government charged with safeguarding election systems. We discovered that Department of Homeland Security officials had asked CISA to obtain a voting machine and hack it without informing the manufacturer of any vulnerabilities found. The plan wasn’t acted on, but its existence made CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference. CISA and DHS didn’t respond to our questions, but a White House spokesperson said Trump “has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections.”
Another story looked at how delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures endangered the validity of mail-in ballots in rural counties, typically Republican strongholds, during this year’s primaries. The Postal Service said such delays are less likely in the general election.
One of our most detailed election stories traced the career of Cleta Mitchell, a lawyer who spearheaded the legal attacks on the 2020 results. Mitchell leads a coalition of what she calls “election believers” — people who scour the voting results for errors that they believe point to larger conspiracies. Changes she’d hoped Trump could push through before the midterms, such as compelling states to turn over confidential voter information to the Justice Department, have been blocked by the courts. But she has nonetheless become the voice of a well-funded national movement, one which has the president’s ear. When Trump is weighing what to do in the aftermath of this week’s vote, our reporting strongly suggests that Mitchell will be among the people he listens to.
We asked to speak with Mitchell multiple times. She declined but told us in an email: “What we focus on is making sure the election process is accurate, transparent, and honest. The ONLY steps I’ve urged the Administration to take are those that will give the voters — ALL voters — confidence that the outcomes are correct.” A White House spokesperson said she has no official role in election policy but is an effective private advocate.
We have also spent time doing the traditional work of investigative reporting, looking closely at candidates’ records in public office. A newsroom like ours can’t cover every race, so we focus our resources on areas where we have particular expertise.
Our team in Texas has covered state Attorney General Ken Paxton for years, and we kept our focus once he announced he would run for the U.S. Senate. One story looked at his travels, revealing that only 1 in 6 of his nearly 1,000 out-of-state trips were linked to his official duties. Texas taxpayers paid $3.3 million for Paxton’s security detail to accompany him. (Paxton didn’t answer our questions, but his office said he “faced numerous security threats.”) That has become an issue in the Senate campaign.
Another opportunity arose from an investigation that was seemingly not related to the midterms: our examination of the Trump administration’s handling of the Justice Department. We began many months ago to look for promising cases that had been dropped and found out the FBI had been looking into pay-to-play allegations involving prominent Democratic and Republican members of Congress. The case included a bipartisan list of political figures such as Susan Collins, the Republican senator from Maine running in a closely contested race this year, and James Clyburn, a leading Democratic representative from South Carolina who’s also on the ballot this year.
Our first story revealed that Collins helped a little-known defense contractor win millions in federal contracts while the company’s CEO helped bankroll her 2020 reelection effort through a donation made via a shell company. Our second story revealed that the FBI was looking into interactions that Clyburn and Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died in July, had with the same contractor. Collins has denied all wrongdoing. “A donation would never cause Congressman Clyburn to increase his support for the donor’s request,” Clyburn’s office said. Graham’s communications director wrote that “any allegations of quid-pro-quo behavior … are simply false.” The FBI stopped examining the allegations after Trump purged the bureau. Our coverage likewise has become an issue in the Maine race.
We stand at a moment of uncertainty in our history as a democracy. Trump has made his willingness to smear news organizations an essential aspect of his appeal. He routinely insults reporters to their face and has attempted to ban some outlets from the White House and Air Force One because he didn’t like the stories they wrote about him. He has diverted hundreds of federal agents from their jobs fighting drug cartels and organized crime to search for evidence that noncitizens have illegally voted in federal elections. Hardly any were found.
I’m deeply reluctant to make any predictions about how all this will end. ProPublica prepared for an array of dire scenarios in November of 2024 that might arise from a close election. None of them came to pass as Trump decisively prevailed. A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department’s lawsuit to block the Alaska Senate race results over the weekend, and the Trump administration’s plans to appeal stand on shaky legal ground.
The one thing I know for certain is that we will keep digging into the story of what really happened in this election, whoever wins.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/ice-.title: ICE Was Secretly Ordered to Stop All Immigration Raids on Election Day
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/ice-.author: Karl Loftus
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/ice-.text:
Orders for what one official called a “national no enforcement day” began circulating on Monday inside U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement.
Handed down through ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division through internal group chats and verbal commands, the directive called for a halt to all immigration enforcement operations on Election Day, according to ICE officials across the country who spoke to The Intercept.
“We were told all operations are canceled for Election Day,” said one ICE immigration official, who operates in the south and requested anonymity to protect their livelihood. “Word of mouth from our first-line supervisors, no official email notice.”
According to multiple ICE officials who spoke to The Intercept, the orders were handed down quietly to avoid media attention.
“Yesterday was the least amount of activity observed from ICE ERO throughout the entire year so far,” said Sherman Austin, the creator of StopICE.net, a crowdsourced platform tracking reported ICE activity across the United States. “You can kind of tell like from the morning. Usually, ICE gets started really early, and there’s a huge spike in activity between 5 a.m. and 10 a.m. That spike wasn’t there on Election Day.”
Another ICE official, who works in the Great Lakes region, confirmed the orders ahead of Election Day, referring to it as “National No Enforcement Day.”
“We were told to do ‘admin’ shit,” the official said. They said that ICE deportation officers who regularly do street-level operations were diverted to administrative office work: “I’ll be drinking coffee at the office for the first time in a year.”
In total, ICE officials working in four areas of responsibility — ICE’s jurisdictional regions — coving parts of the northeastern, midwestern, northern, and south-central U.S. regions told The Intercept that they had received orders to stand down on Election Day.
“Something Unusual Was Going On”
StopICE, the tracking website, which has roughly half a million subscribers, did record some ICE activity on Election Day, according to Austin, although most of the reports stemmed from sightings unrelated to any immigration enforcement activities.
“There were a few reports that came in about ICE being at usual spots like the jails,” Austin said, “or seen driving in certain areas in in the city, but it wasn’t the same type of activity that’s usually seen on the site. It was pretty clear that something unusual was going on.”
AntiFreeze, another crowdsourced ICE-tracking platform that allows users to report and receive real-time alerts about ICE raids, also saw abnormally low levels of ICE activity on November 3, according to Josh, the creator and developer behind the site, who requested to keep his last name anonymous.
“On Election Day, our network only logged about 56 reported ICE sightings nationwide, which is one of the quietest Tuesdays we’ve ever seen,” Josh said. “We did get about three sightings that did report ICE activity near polling stations, but most of the reports were observations of vehicles associated with ICE. We barely got any reports about actual ICE arrests yesterday.”
Local activists also observed a low level of ICE activity on the street level.
“There was no evidence of street abductions,” said an activist working with the rapid-response network in Minnesota’s Twin Cities.
“ICE, in some capacity, was still out and about, but we did not see any reports of off-the-street detainments by ICE or attempts at detainments,” said the activist, who said they got word of ICE arrests at jails, but not targeted operations among the general public. “There were a lot of folks, probably more than usual, observing, and so I think we can be pretty confident that this wasn’t due to lack of observation.”
Leo Martinez, who volunteers with VC Defensa in Southern California, told The Intercept that no one in his rapid-response group reported any sightings of ICE activity on Tuesday.
It is still unclear exactly where the orders to halt immigration enforcement operations on Election Day originated from, although some ICE officials believe the orders stemmed from ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations leadership — and not directly from the White House.
“Nobody from the SDDO level” — a reference to Supervisory Detention and Deportation Officer, part of ICE’s upper management — “expected it to happen until the very last moment,” said another ICE official familiar with the matter. “But I think some of us caught on that senior leadership was making this call with fears of us being at the polls.”
The official said, “It’s crazy that The White House didn’t catch on.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.author: Akela Lacy

Now that Democrats have secured earth-shattering wins in both chambers of Congress, the party’s progressives are sending a message to their more moderate leaders: It’s time to deliver for voters who are demanding meaningful action.
“Even where the candidate wasn’t a self-described progressive, progressives won big last night,” said Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar, D-Texas, during a press call on Wednesday. “Across the country, so-called moderate candidates ran on ending forever wars,” he added, pointing out that Democrats went after the GOP for voting down congressional attempts to stop President Donald Trump’s unpopular military actions — efforts that the progressive caucus had organized.
With comfortable majorities in both chambers — 54 seats in the Senate and 237 in the House, as of 4:30 p.m. ET Wednesday — Democrats now have the legislative breathing room to deliver on their promises to reduce the cost of living, root out government corruption, and end Trump’s failed war in Iran.
But they’ll have to notch these achievements under an angry lame-duck president who vowed last night — via a Truth Social post of one of his signature red hats — to wield his veto against the new class of Democrats. The current Democratic leaders in each house of Congress, Sen. Chuck Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, both have long track records of sparring with the left. And which of their goals will progressives prioritize when their ranks swell come January?
“We will have an H.R. 1 through 10 that focuses on costs and healthcare and corruption,” Casar said Wednesday, referring to the first 10 House resolutions he wanted to see his party push. “Every single week, we should now be sending a bill to Donald Trump’s desk that is overwhelmingly popular with the American people, that cracks down on corporate greed, that cracks down on price gouging, that cracks down on big money and politics.”
To Will Lawrence, a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement and a former member of the Democratic Socialists of America who beat Republican incumbent Rep. Tom Barrett in a Michigan swing district on Tuesday, the Democrats’ historically successful night translates into a responsibility to achieve transformative change.
“It’s undoubtable that this was a sweeping mandate around the entire country,” said Lawrence, who ran a campaign focused on his opposition to data centers, a notoriously unpopular area of tech development that the left has pushed Democrats to oppose.
The outsized influence of the artificial intelligence industry is another critical area for progressives to tackle, Rep. Summer Lee, D-Pa., told The Intercept. She said that she and other progressives will push legislation to end the outside influence of billionaire and super PAC money in elections, including her bills to ban super PACs and overturn the Citizens United Supreme Court decision.
“Every year, we see record-breaking numbers for the most expensive races in history by the millions,” Lee said. “In the 120th Congress, I look forward to our party recognizing the detrimental impact of special interests and billionaire influence in our politics, whether it be from crypto or AI or AIPAC.”
Other progressive priorities include passing policies like Medicare for All, ending corporate corruption, and investing in affordable housing. The ideas are tenets of the redistributive platform popularized by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who rallied voters across the country to “fight oligarchy” earlier this year and helped elevate many of this cycle’s upstart candidates.
On Wednesday, progressives did not yet seem prepared to commit to which single issue they would push for first. Asked by The Intercept about their Day-One priorities when they return to Congress, Casar said progressives planned to keep up the legislative pressure throughout the two years of the coming congressional term.
The Working Families Party, which backed Lawrence and often works to push Democrats to the left, saw Tuesday’s results as a sign that “voters want Democrats to stop the buildout of data centers and rein in the AI industry,” said Ravi Mangla, the group’s spokesperson. Like the congressional progressives, WFP cited a range of priorities for the years to come: guaranteeing healthcare and low-cost childcare, lowering housing costs, and providing more union jobs to American workers.
In fact, candidates who signed onto a promise to push a suite of pro-labor policies organized by labor leaders in swing states were among the Democrats’ biggest winners on Tuesday night. Signatories to the “Contract with Working America” included Troy Jackson, who toppled three-decade incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins in Maine; James Talarico, who flipped the Texas seat for the first time in almost 40 years; and Gina Hinojosa, who ousted 10-year incumbent Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott.
Jackson pointed to the pledge during his victory speech in Maine on Tuesday night and thanked the union members who canvassed for him.
“On Labor Day, brothers and sisters, I stood before you and I made a pledge to working Mainers,” Jackson said to cheers at his election night party in Portland. “And I’m going to keep that promise. Because I am a union member tonight. I’ll be a union member when I walk into that Senate chamber.”
“The way things are set up in our economy right now, the money is just moving up and concentrating at the top, and squeezing the people at the bottom,” said Maine AFL-CIO President Cynthia Phinney. Her organization helped develop the labor platform Jackson signed onto, and she said they “fully anticipate that we’re going to need to continue to organize around these issues that matter to the folks who voted for him, and a lot of folks who didn’t vote for him.”
Referring to Hinojosa, Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., noted that Latino voters “delivered a gubernatorial seat in Texas,” as well as a U.S. senator. Ramirez, who has introduced a bill to abolish the Department of Homeland Security, argued that her party should not lose sight of outrage over violent immigration enforcement.
“Shame on us Democrats if we again do not meet the moment when it comes to immigration and when it comes to justice as it pertains to ICE and CBP and DHS,” Ramirez told The Intercept.
Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., pointed out that the issues that defined this cycle were often first championed by progressives.
“We were the first to fight back against the war in Iran. We were the first to call out corruption on so many levels. We were the first to push to rein in ICE and CBP, a shift that really drove a lot of Latino voters across the country that mattered in this election,” said Jayapal. “Hopefully, this puts to rest the idea that you can’t be a progressive and win with your ideas in any district in the country.”
If history is any guide, it won’t. As the wins rolled in on Tuesday night, Jeffries, the next likely speaker of the House, threw cold water on the idea that the vote marked a seismic rebuke of the Republican Party’s way of doing things, saying the results were “patriotic,” not “partisan.”
On Wednesday, Jeffries said voters had chosen Democrats “because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”
“I agree, and I’ll go one step further,” Casar said. “The American people delivered a demand for bold change.”

We Stomped All Over the Patriarchy on Tuesday Night
Almost everywhere, abortion rights initiatives won, and pro-choice candidates prevailed. Even in Idaho, where they didn’t, women are taking heart.
I’ve always wondered what smashing the patriarchy really feels like, and on Tuesday night, we found out.
Up until then, the patriarchy had been on quite the winning streak, so much so that a newly surfaced rape allegation against the sitting president was hardly a news story. Then, on Tuesday, we got to watch a child sexual abuse survivor defeat the Republican challenger who called her a liar in the Ohio governor’s race. We got to see Max Miller, an Ohio Republican whose ex-wife accused him of holding a gun to her head while she changed their toddler’s diaper, lose his seat in a former Republican stronghold. We got to see Texans elect a Democratic Latina governor from Brownsville, Gina Hinojosa, who ran an ad about her decision to carry a nonviable pregnancy to term—and used that horrific ordeal to defend the right of Texans to choose. A Tennessee woman denied an abortion under the state’s ban won a state House seat; Virginia, Missouri, and Nevada voted to protect or expand abortion rights; and Maine Senator Susan Collin was ousted in large part because of her vote to confirm accused attempted rapist Brett Kavanaugh, to the Supreme Court.
But there were exceptions to the trend, including the success of anti-trans ballot initiatives and the defeat of an abortion rights initiative in Idaho, a state that, in the midst of the blue tsunami felt, as Idaho-based reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris put it to me, like an “island of sadness.”
Related Articles
“It was a great night in this nation for a rebuke” of patriarchy, Melanie Folwell, executive director of the ballot initiative campaign Idahoans United for Women and Families, told me. “But here in Idaho, where we had two of the wealthiest, most powerful patriarchies in the world—the Catholic Church and the Mormon Church—and then the supermajority Idaho GOP, my God, patriarchy won the day.”
Proposition 1 would have enshrined in Idaho statutes a right to abortion up until viability. But 56 percent of voters chose instead to keep the state’s near-total abortion ban. It was a gutting loss in a state where more than a third of the state’s ob-gyns have left or stopped practicing since the ban took effect, and where the campaign shared harrowing stories of women traveling to terminate nonviable pregnancies, getting med-flighted to neighboring states while miscarrying, or bleeding out while doctors whose colleagues have fled the state scrambled to save them. “I feel like the women and families and doctors were so brave telling their stories,” Suzanne Gallus, a Catholic mom of seven who knocked 1,289 doors to support Prop 1, told me. “For people to just ignore all that is especially hard to take.”
Folwell said the campaign faced uniquely strong headwinds, including an influx of new Republican residents that have turned the state into one of the country’s reddest and a convoluted explanation of the meaning of a “yes” or “no” vote that was attached to the ballot by the Republican secretary of state. The Mormon and Catholic churches donated a combined $1.3 million to an anti-abortion PAC that ran a barrage of ads in the final weeks of the campaign claiming that the proposition’s “fine print” would redefine fetal viability to exclude premature newborns who needed oxygen, allow “late-term abortion on demand,” and let minors get abortions without parental consent. The claims were false; the initiative didn’t repeal the state’s existing parental consent laws, and it would have allowed the state to ban abortion after fetal viability except in medical emergencies. But the ads forced canvassers like Suzanne Gallus, a Catholic mom of seven, to have uncomfortably technical conversations about fetal viability at the doors.
“For crying out loud, I’m not a doctor; I’m not a lawyer,” Gallus told me. “I know how to explain that, but then you’re getting into the weeds, and when you get into the weeds like that, I think you do more damage than you do good.”
Folwell said the initiative also suffered crucially from a lack of support from national organizations who balked at the fact that it could be repealed by the Republican legislature. The dozen or so abortion ballot initiatives that have passed since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in states ranging from Ohio and Arizona to Virginia and Vermont have all been more enduring constitutional amendments, not statutory provisions, but Idaho does not allow voters to initiate constitutional amendments.
“There was a lot—from national groups— a lot of gnashing of teeth about, ‘Oh, well, it could just be statutorily overturned,’ before it was even won, and a lack of investment and care because of this silly gamesmanship about what’s next, rather than focusing on tangible movement-building and wins to get things done,” Folwell told me. “And I’m [feeling] pretty crappy about it.”
But Folwell felt proud of the 2,500 or so volunteers who powered her campaign.
“The most important story out of all of this is the degree to which there are thousands and thousands of women in this state who feel less alone,” Folwell said, her voice breaking. “And that’s from people who survived something terrible to people who found community in advocacy, and that all has meaning.”
“They may have been let down in myriad ways by people in the state and outside the state, but they showed up for each other.”
Among those who showed up was Whitney Montgomery, the daughter of the architect of Idaho’s abortion ban. Montgomery drew audible gasps during a Prop 1 rally when she revealed that she was the daughter of David Ripley, who has built his anti-abortion lobbyist career on an origin story about his objections to his ex-wife’s abortion. Montgomery’s childhood memories of her dad include his stint in jail for failing to pay child support to her mother—whom he divorced before later marrying the woman who had the abortion.
“I have spent years trying to understand how someone can dedicate his life to ‘saving babies’ while ignoring one of his own,” Montgomery wrote in an op-ed for the Post Register about her decision to support Prop 1. “By his own public admission, he was a cruel and abusive husband to many of his wives. As a child, I remember hiding in a bathroom with a phone nearby, ready to call 911 if things got worse.”
I interviewed Montgomery on election night, after she had just voted at her son’s elementary school; she’d brought her 3- and 6-year-olds to the polls as part of a family tradition, and that night, they were going to make Barack Obama’s chili recipe. Montgomery conceived through IVF, another reason she objects to the agenda of her father’s political party, which opposes it. When I told her that her decision to stand up to her father—who has admitted being a “jackass” to the wife who had the abortion—felt like a symbol of the stakes for this entire election, she agreed.
“It comes down to punishing women and having that control,” Montgomery said. “He feels like he was wronged by a woman, and now it’s this punishment to women’s health.
“It’s wild.”
(David Ripley didn’t respond to my calls for comment for this article. I did speak to his fourth wife, Wendy, at 10:15 am on Election Day. She told me her husband was still asleep. They’d had a late night; among other things, they were fending off teenagers from the nearby high school who kept stealing their anti–Prop 1 yard signs.)

But outside of Idaho, women won the day, and even from the island of sadness, Montgomery felt like she was part of it.
“It was a sad night for Idaho but I’m so happy for the rest of the country and the progress that is being made,” Montgomery texted me on Wednesday. “I truly believe this fight is not over. It’s just the beginning.”
Indeed, Folwell’s critique about a lack of investment from national groups who saw Idaho as a lost cause echoed what I heard in 2021 from abortion rights advocates in Texas, who felt under-resourced, isolated, and ignored as they fought a Republican legislature that banned abortion at six weeks. To see Texas turn blue on Tuesday after the most highly invested-in Senate race in history, to see a new Democratic attorney general–elect pledge to drop lawsuits against out-of-state abortion providers, while a pro-choice Latina takes the governor’s office is a reminder that all progress is incremental, until it’s not. Before a wave grows big enough to smash the patriarchy, it starts with ripples too small to detect.
Gallus said she would keep making those ripples with the women she’d met through the campaign.
“Cultivating these little seeds here and there is really important when you’re in a place that is very extreme, because this is our home,” Gallus told me in an emotional interview on Wednesday.
“If Texas can do this, then maybe we can, too; it’s just going to take longer.”

Exhibition of the week
Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires 
  
From the tulips and silks of the Ottoman court, back in time to the Emperor Constantine’s palace, this is a sumptuous and haunting mystery tour.
 
V&A South Kensington, London, 7 November to 9 May
Also showing
Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant 
  
Two modern painters, one complex relationship in an exhibition that takes you to the heart of the early 20th century Bloomsbury Group.
 
Tate Britain, London, from 12 November
Ida Applebroog 
  
Angry Birds of America, a series of animal images that updates Audubon for the Trump era, and naked portraits of people that celebrate human variety.
 
Fruitmarket Gallery, Edinburgh, until 11 February
Glenn Brown 
  
The superbly decadent contemporary painter takes on the luscious genius of Thomas Gainsborough.
 
Gainsborough’s House, Sudbury, until 18 April
Alexis Kyle Mitchell 
  
An exhibition about health inequalities and the way people’s bodies are judged.
 
Site Gallery, Sheffield, until 21 March
Image of the week
The aficionados among you will immediately recognise this screenprint: Marilyn Monroe was recreated countless times with infinite variety by Andy Warhol. Only the very keenest cognoscente, however, will recognise that pop art’s king of reproduction has himself been reproduced here. Elaine Sturtevant’s Warhol Black Marilyn (2004) is just one example of a feedback loop the conceptual forger has created with artists such as Jasper Johns, Keith Haring and her beloved Warhol, by copying their work to such a degree that it makes us reflect on how meaning is created around art. Her exhibition is at Raven Row in London until 20 December.

Comedian Andy Field drew a horse a day until he mastered it

Masterpiece of the week
The Virgin and Child by Giovanni Bellini, c1480-90
The Bellinis not only dominated Venetian art in the later 15th century but spanned east and west, linking Italy with Istanbul. Giovanni’s brother Gentile travelled to the capital of the Ottoman Empire and portrayed its Sultan – as seen in the V&A blockbuster Constantinople to Istanbul – as well as other places and people he saw in the eastern Mediterranean. Giovanni was more of a homebody but you couldn’t entirely avoid global influence in Venice, capital of a great trading empire, with its golden Byzantine mosaics in St Mark’s. Is there perhaps a hint of a Byzantine icon about this painting with its eerie spiritual calm and the subtly luxurious hanging behind the Virgin? You feel the air warming and vibrating around her, the stillness of those clouds, the rich veined purple marble of the parapet in front of her. Bellini makes you meditate with his music of colour.
