https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Hochul Wants More Power Over State Education Dept. Amid Move to End Regents Requirement
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Alex Zimmerman, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters.
New York’s slow-moving transition away from requiring Regents exams to graduate has a new critic: Gov. Kathy Hochul.
Hochul, who decisively defeated her Republican opponent Bruce Blakeman on Tuesday, has raised concerns that state education officials are moving to eliminate existing graduation exam requirements without a clear plan for what will replace them, potentially weakening the value of a New York diploma.
Those concerns have also prompted Hochul to renew her call to give the governor’s office more control of the state Education Department, which answers to a board chosen by New York lawmakers rather than the chief executive.
“People see in the articles, ‘New York State abandons Regents,’” Hochul said last week on the Max Politics Podcast. “They think I’m New York.” She added: “The buck should stop with me, given that we are the funder of education.”
Hochul’s comments come as state education officials have yet to spell out what will replace Regents exams as a graduation requirement. The class of 2027 is the last crop of students required to pass Regents exams under the state’s current timeline. The 17-member Board of Regents, which sets state education policy and selects the education commissioner, will determine what comes next.
Hochul spokesperson Jonah Allon said that the governor is concerned about “the lack of clarity about what will replace” the Regents exams. “The Board of Regents have a responsibility to preserve academic rigor and ensure clear, consistent graduation standards across the state.”
The clock is ticking. This year’s seniors generally must still pass a series of standardized Regents exams in English, math, science and social studies to graduate. But the state Education Department is developing new diploma requirements for future graduating classes. New York City officials said that for the next three years, students will only have to pass their classes to earn a diploma.
What Hochul would do with more control over state education policy remains a question mark. A spokesperson did not respond to questions about whether she thinks the Regents exams should remain in place or whether she supports alternative requirements.
Hochul has previously clashed with state education officials on other issues, including a school cellphone ban. State Education Department Commissioner Betty Rosa favored giving school districts more control to set their own policies, but Hochul pushed for a statewide approach and signed a ban into state law last year.
A spokesperson for the state Education Department did not respond to questions.
Giving the governor control could help create a stronger vision for schools across the state — and clarify who is responsible for education policymaking, supporters say.
“There is no single, clear line of accountability for the quality of education New York’s children receive,” Dan Weisberg, a former top official in New York City’s Education Department, wrote in the publication Vital City. “When a governor is clearly in charge, there’s real potential for serious leadership on education.”
There is some precedent for such a move: California Gov. Gavin Newsom recently mounted a successful push to consolidate power over state education policy.
But taking control of the Education Department comes with political challenges, too.
Hochul could face criticism of New York’s academic performance, which is middling even as the state leads the nation in education spending.
And if she moves forward with changes to graduation standards — including hands-on projects, work-based learning and dual enrollment envisioned by state officials — she would also be responsible for their consequences. Other states offer cautionary tales about how difficult such changes can be to pull off.
State lawmakers may also be reluctant to cede some of their power over state education policy to the governor.
“It’s great that the governor would like to take a more hands-on approach to education,” state Sen. John Liu told Politico. “The state Education Department is structured the way it is due to law as well as the state constitution so the governor will need to work within those confines.”
Arlen Benjamin-Gomez, executive director at the advocacy group EdTrust-New York, said it is a “big deal” that the governor is weighing in more strongly on the graduation requirement changes. Her organization recently called for a two-year pause on changes to develop a clearer vision and give schools more time to prepare.
Benjamin-Gomez emphasized that giving the governor more power could help elevate education policy issues, which received little discussion during the gubernatorial race.
“If she had control over the education system, she would be running on an education agenda that she could develop and then be held accountable to implement,” Benjamin-Gomez said.
Alex Zimmerman is a senior reporter for Chalkbeat New York, covering NYC public schools. Contact Alex at azimmerman@chalkbeat.org.

https://gothamist.com/news/federal-judge.title: Federal judge rules Mamdani administration must give ICE names of Bronx shelter residents
https://gothamist.com/news/federal-judge.author: Willow Higgins
https://gothamist.com/news/federal-judge.text:
A federal judge has ruled that the Mamdani administration has to give immigration officials the names and birthdays of certain people living in a large, city-run homeless shelter in the Bronx.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement claims they need the information as part of an investigation into residents that may be subject to deportation. But City Hall, which has barred city agencies from cooperating with ICE, has fought the subpoena in court and advocates are urging Mamdani to keep up the fight.
The mayor’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment Saturday.
“The City has not shown that producing this list would be unduly burdensome,” the ruling by U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan reads. “Under the applicable case law, the Court therefore has no choice but to compel the subpoena’s enforcement.”
The ruling requires the city to turn over a list of certain male residents that live in a shelter on Bruckner Boulevard along with their birthdays and any additional records that would help ICE identify the people who live there.
ICE had asked for the names of all the residents, but under Friday's ruling, the agency has appointed a special master to identify only residents with “serious criminal histories,” according to the ruling.
The shelter is a converted warehouse in the South Bronx that sleeps more than 2,000 and is the city’s last emergency migrant housing facility. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in February he plans to phase out the shelter by the end of the year.
Friday’s ruling comes after several failed attempts by the federal government to file similar subpoenas. Beginning in August 2025, ICE submitted four separate subpoena requests for personal information about residents of New York City shelters and the city fought them.
The city called a previous request a “fishing expedition lacking any legitimate investigative purpose,” according to the ruling.
The New York Immigration Coalition, which represents more than 200 immigrant and refugee rights groups throughout New York, is calling for the latest order to be appealed.
What “ICE has been trying to do for some time now is continuously launch these horrible campaigns of mass deportation against our community members,” said Murad Awawdeh, the president and CEO of the New York Immigration Coalition.
“ We believe that the city must appeal and that City Hall and Albany must act also on the simple principle of making sure they are also protecting everyone that's in their care.”
Awawdeh said that the city should not have to comply with the order because of the city’s sanctuary law policies, which limit cooperation between local government and ICE.
“Providing data on civil immigration enforcement…that's illegal as per our local law,” Awawdeh said.

https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-expan.title: Mamdani expands free produce programs for New Yorkers on SNAP
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-expan.author: Karen Yi
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-expan.text:
The Mamdani administration is expanding two fresh produce programs that help SNAP recipients take home free fruits and vegetables.
The additional funding for Health Bucks and Get the Good Stuff comes amid persistently high food costs and cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Program by the federal government that left at least 26,500 New Yorkers without the monthly food aid. Mayor Zohran Mamdani is also launching five city-owned grocery stores to further alleviate pricey grocery bills and slash prices by 30%.
“Every New Yorker should be able to afford a well-balanced, healthy diet,” Deputy Mayor for Health and Human Services Dr. Helen Arteaga said in a statement. “But rising grocery prices have put fresh fruits and vegetables out of reach for far too many families.”
Get the Good Stuff lets SNAP recipients get a dollar for dollar match for every dollar they spend on fresh or frozen fruits, vegetables and beans. The program offers up to $10 dollars cash back at participating grocery stores. The program is currently available at 21 supermarkets but city officials said they would fund another 12 grocery stores interested in participating. Stores can apply through Nov. 20.
The Health Bucks program allows New Yorkers on SNAP benefits to get cash back if they shop at local farmer's markets and farm stands. SNAP users can get $2 dollars for every $2 dollars they spend on fresh fruits and vegetables. But starting in January, that matching program will be increased. So instead of $10 dollars back, New Yorkers will be able to get up to $14 dollars for every dollar they spend.
The city’s health department said among adults who are at risk of food insecurity, nearly eight in 10 struggled to afford balanced meals, according to new research. And almost one in five had not eaten any fruits or vegetables the previous day.
“Fruits, vegetables, and beans are important to a balanced diet and help reduce the risk of diet-related diseases. But with the rise in grocery prices, they aren't always affordable,” said NYC Health Commissioner Dr. Alister F. Martin.
New Yorkers can look up participating grocery stores and find their nearest farmer’s market on the city’s health map.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/09/m.title: Mamdani Needs a Miracle on 34th Street Amid Mystery Delay
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/09/m.author: Dave Colon
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/09/m.text:
The M34 has still not been freed from traffic. And Mayor Mamdani (inset as Santa) is missing his window. The Streetsblog Photoshop Desk
It’s getting late early.
Mayor Mamdani may need a miracle on 34th Street if he hopes to follow-through on his pledge to put a busway on the crosstown corridor by the end of 2026 — as the end of road-striping season approaches and the street shows no evidence of construction starting “in the coming weeks” as the Department of Transportation told the Times back in September.
After criticizing former mayor Eric Adams for delaying the project last year on the campaign trail, the new mayor announced in June that the busway had “advanced” to be completed this fall. But as the calendar has flipped to November, Hizzoner is running out of time to paint the street red.
On a visit to 34th Street last Thursday evening, Streetsblog found no indication that any work had been done to transform the street into a bus-and-truck-only thoroughfare. The existing combination of offset and curbside bus lanes on the street had not changed, and no signage indicated that a busway was imminent at East 34th Street and 3rd Avenue, where the eastern gateway for the project.
It’s unclear what exactly is preventing the city from finally delivering on the project, which would ban non-local private car traffic from 34th Street between Third Avenue and Ninth Avenue. A City Hall spokesman insisted that some work would be done this year on the corridor, but declined to say if the busway itself was still on schedule.
“We are installing an overhead gantry at Ninth Avenue for future busway signage, and we are working to coordinate related street furniture installations by the end of the year,” the spokesman, Jeremy Edwards, said in a statement.
City officials first proposed the busway in May 2025, with plans to move forward on the project that same year, until then-Mayor Adams inexplicably halted it. Adams later reversed himself and allowed the busway to go forward as part of a deal to up-zone a large piece of Midtown — but only after Mamdani called him out in a video as the two men prepared for a general election match-up that never happened.
But before Adams’s DOT could actually begin the work, Trump Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and the Federal Highway Administration stepped in to stop the 34th Street busway over what it claimed were concerns about truck and emergency vehicle access on the corridor, which is technically part of the National Highway System. (New York City typically exempts trucks and emergency vehicles from most busways.)
Those same federal delays also held up implementation of the Tremont Avenue busway, which unlike 34th Street Mayor Mamdani’s administration did build in 2026.
The FHWA also publicly accused the city of failing satisfy regulations involving coordination with the New York Metropolitan Transportation Council, a body that organizes regional planning for transportation projects that will need federal funding. However, one former city planning official questioned why NYMTC had to be involved at all.
“If the busway is going to get federal aid then it has to be in the TIP,” said Jon Orcutt, a former DOT official under mayors Bloomberg and de Blasio. “But if it’s not getting federal aid then they can just do it.”
A source with knowledge of the city’s conversations about 34th Street said that after the Times article raised questions about the apparent delay, DOT told community boards and elected officials that the there was a delay getting the busway through NYMTC’s Transportation Improvement Program, the council’s list of projects which get federal assistance.
Mamdani, who campaigned to make buses “fast and free,” repeatedly attacked Adams’s delays to the busway on the 2025 campaign trail.
Last August, the then-candidate raced the bus on foot with a large gaggle of elected officials, advocates and media to make the point that the bus moved slower than walking.
Yet the snail-pace persists 11 months into Mamdani’s mayoralty.
As of September, the M34 crawled across 34th Street at an average of just 5.3 miles per hour. The slow speeds force riders to spend an average of almost two and a half minutes more waiting for a bus at the bus stop, almost two extra minutes per trip. Only 66 percent of M34 buses get where they’re going within five minutes of the scheduled arrival time.
“The M34 is one of the slowest buses in the city and neighbors, tourists, and workers deserve faster buses,” said Samir Lavigna, the 2nd vice-chair of Manhattan Community Board 5. “It is disappointing that the federal government has been delaying this project at every turn and I hope that the newly elected Democrats will let the city push forward with a busway as soon as possible.”
Ordinarily, the city’s striping season, when the weather is warm enough for DOT employees to put paint down on the streets, lasts from about May until October. But if there’s any solace to take in a rapidly warming world, and a winter that will most likely have higher than normal temperatures thanks to this year’s “super El Nino” it is that the city may have more time than usual to finish streets projects before the end of the year.
“Striping season used to end around now, but I’ve been riding around in a T-shirt all week. You’d think we’re almost to the point where we don’t have an off-season anymore,” said Orcutt.
Dave Colon is a reporter from Long Beach, a barrier island off of the coast of Long Island that you can bike to from the city. It’s a real nice ride. He’s previously been the editor of Brokelyn, a reporter at Gothamist, a freelance reporter and delivered freshly baked bread by bike.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/09/m.title: MEMO TO MAMDANI: Make Queens Boulevard the City’s First ‘Cycle Super-Highway’
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/09/m.author: John Surico
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/09/m.text:
Queens Boulevard's bike lanes were state-of-the-art when the city designed them a decade ago, but they remain far too vulnerable to illegal parking and danger. Photo: John Surico
The city has come a long way on Queens Boulevard, my home borough’s namesake stretch that runs from Long Island City to Jamaica. But now it’s time to take it up a notch.
For decades, Queens Boulevard was the notorious “Boulevard of Death.” Freeway-sized widths and speeds promoted reckless driving through residential communities that claimed the lives of too many New Yorkers over the years. That included 22-year-old Asif Rahman in 2008, who was struck by a driver while cycling home. The tragedy pushed his mother, Lizi, to do something. “For almost eight years, I fought by myself, and it was difficult,” she told me, for an article I wrote in Bloomberg in 2024.
Then the city did something — and it worked.
Advocacy from Lizi Rahman and others catalyzed Vision Zero, then-mayor Bill de Blasio’s pledge for zero traffic fatalities and injuries. Beginning in 2015, the city’s safety-first approach trimmed crossing distances and turn radiuses, while adding bike lanes along the service roads. The city lowered the speed limit on Queens Boulevard from 30 to 25 miles per hour. By the time all seven miles of the redesign wrapped up in 2024, traffic deaths had all but disappeared from the corridor, with injuries seeing a similar precipitous drop — an immense victory for the city’s efforts.
Let’s not stop there, though.
In part due to the city’s efforts, Queens Boulevard today serves as a vital connector for cyclists living in the seven neighborhoods it passes through, many of which don’t have much bike infrastructure. Yet it’s far from reaching its potential as a people-first promenade, with daily hazards that dampen usership and scare away even the most confident riders.
I bike the road regularly in my new role at Friend of the QueensWay — especially now that Citi Bike has reached Forest Hills. I experience Queens Boulevard’s shortcomings firsthand. The “protected” part of “protected bike lanes” often just means crushable bollards or stopgap barriers that invite bike lane blockages. Double-parked vehicles send cars onto green paint, which has eroded in some parts, blurring safety for road users. “Mixing zones” force drivers and cyclists to navigate the same space are abrupt. Add lots of potholes to that mix, and you’ve got a pretty substandard cycling experience.
As its recent record shows, Queens Boulevard has all the right ingredients of modern-day safer street design. But too often, it feels like a fragile baseline, where you’re still riding next to high levels of car traffic with barely an inch or two of separation to keep you safe. It’s aching for an upgrade that doubles down on the life-saving investments the city made during the first decade of Vision Zero, and readies it for the second one.
The solution? A cycle super-highway.
A refreshed, forward-thinking design could include innovative neighborhood traffic diverters, like we’re seeing spring up in Greenpoint and Astoria; non-mountable lanes separated by new greenery, like at Brooklyn Navy Yard; and a whole new sense of navigation that honors the borough’s central artery and all the incredible diversity that surrounds it, like we see on the Empire State Trail maps along the West Side Highway, America’s busiest bike path. Let’s call it Queens Boulevard 3.0.
In London, the “cycle super-highways” formed the foundation of the city’s cycling network seen today. Bike paths are either grade-level or lined with protective concrete, making it difficult for cars to encroach. The wayfinding is world-class, with directions and distances to neighborhoods and institutions at every major turn. And the lanes truly act as a spine, shuffling riders off on other routes or “quietways” that stem from it. We see similar interventions in Paris, Copenhagen and Guangzhou.
Thankfully, there are some signs of progress on Queens Boulevard to get there. In the city’s new Vision Zero plan, Queens Boulevard is listed as part of the ‘Great Streets’ initiative, with $30 million set aside in federal funding for a capital overhaul. What’s proposed to start next year looks promising: a center-running bus lane; new plantings; and an elevated pedestrian and cycle paths.
But that capital work only covers a stretch, and it’ll be a major missed opportunity if it doesn’t meet the moment in front of us. When the next road repaving is scheduled, which is ideally sooner rather than later, DOT should take that opportunity to test out new features of its street redesign toolkit that move beyond the bollard. And the city should leverage that momentum to deliver the ‘world-class streets’ that Mayor Mamdani touts to the rest of the Boulevard.
Asif Rahman’s death catalyzed his mother to take action. And no doubt, the results have been life-changing. But the city shouldn’t stop there—a Queens Boulevard that serves as the gold standard for bike infrastructure in New York City would further build upon and honor Asif’s memory, ensuring future generations never feel unsafe riding home.
John Surico (@johnsurico) lives in Astoria and teaches journalism at New York University. He is the executive director of Friends of QueensWay, and the chairperson of the 31st Avenue Open Street Collective, Inc., in Queens.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/09/m.title: Monday’s Headlines: There’s a Meeting for That Edition
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/09/m.author: David Meyer
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/09/m.text:
An increase in lithium-ion battery fires? There’s a meeting for that.
City Council Speaker Julie Menin loves an oversight hearing, and with the year’s increase in lithium-ion battery fires (first reported by Streetsblog) making major, tragic headlines in recent weeks, that’s just what she’s got in store.
Menin on Friday announced plans for an oversight hearing on Nov. 20 “to examine residential fire safety, following a concerning increase in fatal fires, including battery-related fires, across the city.”
So far this year FDNY attributes 406 fires to lithium-ion batteries — which are commonly but not exclusively used in e-bikes — compared to 241 last year. The largest increase has been in non-structural fires — meaning blazes that occur outside of a home or business. The Department of Sanitation recorded 87 lithium-ion fires in garbage trucks as of mid-October, a 58 percent increase from 2025.
The most recent high-profile blaze killed six people in a row house in Sunset Park,  just days after another fire in the Bronx that filled four. Council Member Susan Zhuang, who was at the scene in Brooklyn, told Streetsblog she planned to “look and see if we can set up some stations so people can just charge outdoors.”
Zhuang may have been referring to the city’s extra-delayed efforts to set up battery charging and swapping cabinets on curbsides and sidewalks, which the Adams administration announced in 2023 and have been stuck in bureaucratic hell ever since. The city has not approved a single application for an outdoor charging cabinet.
The Times, meanwhile, reported on Friday on an overall increase in fires — 86 this year compared to 44 last year — but focused its scrutiny on e-bike batteries, which it called “a major driving force behind the rise in fires and fire deaths” despite accounting for just nine of this year’s fatalities.
Menin will co-lead the hearing with Council Members Pierina Sanchez and Joann Ariola. Ariola, a conservative Republican from Queens, has used her bully pulpit as chair of the Committee on Fire and Emergency Management to push unsubstantiated claims that bike lanes slow emergency response times. Earlier this year, she celebrated the reopening of a park road in her district to cars by obnoxiously joy-riding down the strip while parents and kids held a protest to keep the street car-free. Don’t count on Council Member Joann Ariola to give people who rely on bikes to get around the city a fair hearing.
In other news:
- Menin seems ready to play ball on some type of Amazon regulation. (NY Times)
- amNY covered the MTA’s tin-cup funding requests for the new Democratic Congress.
- Penn Station probably won’t be named after Donald Trump after Tuesday’s election results. (Our Town)
- A driver high on cocaine and weed allegedly ran a stop sign and killed a baby in Flushing last month. (Gothamist)
- Another drunk driver allegedly struck a woman on the BQE who had exited a taxicab for unknown reasons. (Gothamist)
- This lady with the middle name “Blank” somehow ended up with tens of thousands of dollars in parking fines, and spent days in court clearing her name. (NY Times)

https://hyperallergic.com/mrs-gallery-ma.title: Mrs. Gallery Marks 10 Years of Getting Art Collectors to Queens
https://hyperallergic.com/mrs-gallery-ma.author: Aaron Short
https://hyperallergic.com/mrs-gallery-ma.text:
Mrs. Gallery Marks 10 Years of Getting Art Collectors to Queens
A decade since Sara Maria Salamone and Tyler Lafreniere found their storefront space on Craigslist, the gallery presents a rotating anniversary show that channels its evolving nature.
Maspeth has not traditionally been thought of as an arts hub like Bushwick or the East Village, but one gallery has thrived by drawing collectors from all over the world to Western Queens.
“We’ve had people stop here on the way to the airport and end up buying something,” Mrs. Associate Director Lily Frances Pendery told Hyperallergic. “We had an advisor who recently spent an hour and a half with us. Anyone who comes in the door is serious about what their visit is for.”
From its leafy one-way street near the Long Island Expressway, Mrs. has worked with dozens of emerging artists, held 72 shows, and traveled to art fairs in Paris, South Korea, and across the country. This fall, the gallery is celebrating its anniversary with DECENNIUM: Ten Years at Mrs., a rotating exhibition of 30 works by 23 artists.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Trump could be about to sell out Ukraine. Europe must get its act together, fast | Paul Taylor
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Paul Taylor
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Donald Trump has lost substantial power over domestic policy after last week’s devastating midterm losses, but his ability to cement his legacy by upending US foreign policy remains largely intact.
There is every reason to fear a ”great betrayal” of Ukraine in the coming weeks, one that would reward Vladimir Putin for Russia’s war of aggression against Kyiv, and also do lasting damage to the European security order. Yet lilliputian European leaders are too busy squabbling over who should represent them in future peace talks to focus on how to prevent a sellout. Despite fundamental European interests being at stake in this week’s three-way US-Russia-Ukraine negotiations in Abu Dhabi, Europe is relegated to a side room, represented by a posse of officials from the UK, France, Germany, the EU and Nato.
Trump has said he is working with Moscow on a “big, beautiful deal” that is “going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe”. His seemingly Kremlin-friendly negotiator and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, says Trump has discussed with several European leaders the need for “a broader European security architecture that can help establish conditions for lasting peace”.
Strip away the rhetoric and both appear to be talking about cutting a deal with Putin behind the backs of Volodymyr Zelenskyy and other European leaders to carve up eastern Europe. Such a deal might hand Moscow permanent control of occupied Ukrainian territory – possibly more than it currently holds – and relief from western economic sanctions. It could also deny the countries of eastern Europe the right to choose their own security arrangements, by ruling out any further enlargement of Nato and possibly rolling back some of Nato’s eastern front deployments. In return, Trump’s family and business cronies would surely secure lucrative energy, commodity and perhaps real estate deals with Russia.
Such a carve-up may be only a few weeks away, since Trump has accepted the principle of a meeting with Putin, and a possible big-power threesome with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, on the sidelines of an Asia-Pacific summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November. Even if a deal is not oven-ready by then, the opportunity to shape the future of European security in the absence of either Ukrainian or other European leaders must look inviting to the US leader after his electoral drubbing. Trump will want to make advances before the new Democratic-controlled Congress takes office in January.
To force Kyiv to accept a humiliating partition, Trump has already shown he is willing to effectively blind Ukraine by withholding crucial satellite intelligence and missile interceptors. Meanwhile, Elon Musk is hobbling its drone defence by imposing crippling speed limits on his Starshield satellite network, preventing Ukrainian drones from shooting down Russia’s jet-powered kamikaze drones. Trump could also try to bludgeon European allies into acquiescing to a deal by threatening US troop withdrawals and base closures, under a Pentagon review that is nearing completion.
If this all sounds like a paranoid fantasy, remember that Trump and Musk have already used most of these tactics recently, albeit in short, deniable bursts, as an apparent warning to Zelenskyy. The Ukrainian leader has made clear he will not surrender to such coercion, but Putin’s relentless destruction of Ukraine’s energy and transport infrastructure is clearly a drive to put Kyiv in the weakest possible position before diplomatic talks proceed.
Faced with this possibly imminent betrayal, Europe is not without cards of its own, to coin a Trumpian phrase. The Europeans control hundreds of billions of dollars in frozen Russian assets and have the power to refuse any lifting of economic and financial sanctions against Moscow. Indeed, the EU could tighten the screws if they were to transfer impounded Russian central bank funds from the Belgian clearing house, Euroclear, to an EU-controlled entity, and leverage those holdings to raise a massive reparations loan for Ukraine.
As a group of sovereign-debt experts has argued, that would not only keep Ukraine in the fight by meeting Kyiv’s financing needs for at least two years – removing the need for increasingly fraught EU funding negotiations every few months – but it would ensure that Russia is held to account financially for its destruction of Ukraine, and made to contribute to the reconstruction.
Yet beggar-thy-neighbour European politics is preventing the EU from strengthening Zelenskyy’s hand here too. The Belgian prime minister, Bart de Wever, has refused to allow the impounded Russian funds to be used to support Ukraine, winning domestic popularity for supposedly standing up to Europe. As a result, the EU is likely to have to provide Kyiv with another loan to help it through next year. The risk is that elections in France and beyond could bring to power Eurosceptic nationalists who argue that their countries cannot afford to go on funding Ukraine while imposing spending cuts on their own citizens.
It is not too late for Europe in the broadest sense – including the UK, Norway, Canada and Turkey – to act to counter a great betrayal by Trump. Apart from leveraging the frozen assets, European countries can tighten sanctions on the Kremlin’s shadow fleet, choking its exports by interdicting unsafe and uninsured tankers transporting Russian oil. They could transfer more of their own stocks of Patriot missile interceptors to Ukraine, which is now by any definition Europe’s frontline of defence. And they could make much clearer by joint diplomacy towards Trump that they will reject any deal reached without their participation and assent.
The Europeans have managed to head off Trump once before: after his summit with Putin in Alaska last year, they accompanied Zelenskyy to the White House as “bodyguards”, and clearly spelled out their red lines. This time, the weakened US president is more desperate for a “deal”, and the Europeans are more divided and distracted by their own electoral politics. But there can be no greater priority for the future of European security than to prevent a sellout of Ukraine.

https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.title: Mouvement social : toujours plus précarisés, les fonctionnaires se joignent à la mobilisation du 17 novembre
https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.author: Cécile Rousseau
https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.text:
Après la maigre hausse du Smic concédée par le gouvernement en début de semaine, la mobilisation des fonctionnaires contre leur précarisation monte d’un cran. FO fonction publique se joint à la journée d’action intersyndicale du 17 novembre.
Le mécontentement des agents publics s’intensifie. Échaudée par sa rencontre avec le ministre de l’Action et des Comptes publics, David Amiel, la fédération générale des fonctionnaires de Force ouvrière, deuxième syndicat dans la fonction publique, a annoncé mardi 10 novembre se joindre à l’appel à la grève de l’intersyndicale CGT, Unsa, FSU, Solidaires, CFE-CGC, FA-FP en faveur de la revalorisation générale du point d’indice le 17 novembre.
« 35 % de perte de pouvoir d’achat en vingt-cinq ans, des carrières au Smic, des conditions de travail dégradées qui entraînent des risques psychosociaux dramatiques, ça suffit ! », a déclaré FO fonction publique dans un communiqué. Alors que les représentants syndicaux sont reçus successivement depuis le 10 novembre à Bercy, la pression s’accentue sur le gouvernement avant une réunion ce vendredi sur les salaires à Matignon.
Il faut dire que l’annonce, lundi, d’un maigre coup de pouce au Smic dès le 1er décembre, le portant à 1 502 euros net mensuels, soit une hausse d’environ 24 euros, a exacerbé la colère des 5,8 millions d’agents de la fonction publique. « En annonçant une ridicule augmentation du Smic, très loin de compenser les pertes de pouvoir d’achat, il (le gouvernement – NDLR) a donc oublié ses propres agents, ne montrant pas l’exemple au patronat », estime FO.
862 000 agents publics en dessous du Smic
Entre l’inflation et la non-revalorisation quasi systématique du point d’indice, la rémunération des fonctionnaires les plus modestes s’est largement « smicardisée » ces dernières années : en 2026, 862 000 agents publics perçoivent un salaire de base inférieur au Smic. Or, la loi oblige le gouvernement à verser une indemnité différentielle à tous les agents qui perçoivent un revenu indiciaire inférieur au salaire minimum (qui, lui, progresse au rythme de l’inflation).
Avec cette nouvelle augmentation du Smic, « on va passer largement le million d’agents concernés ! Je pense qu’on sera à 1,2 million d’agents ou plus », alerte Christian Grolier, le secrétaire général de Force ouvrière fonction publique, rappelant que l’indemnité différentielle « est une prime sur laquelle l’agent ne cotise pas. Il est payé au Smic, mais sa cotisation porte sur un salaire inférieur ».
Interrogé par l’AFP sur le nombre exact d’agents dont la rémunération de base passerait en dessous du Smic à la faveur de cette revalorisation, Bercy n’a pas répondu. Début octobre, sous la pression des manifestations, David Amiel avait proposé aux syndicats une hausse de l’indice minimum des fonctionnaires pour permettre à 400 000 agents publics de percevoir un salaire de base supérieur au Smic.
Cette piste d’une injection ciblée de points pour les plus bas salaires a été remise sur la table, mardi, de même qu’un chantier sur les grilles de rémunérations.
Mais concernant une augmentation générale de la valeur du point, « la réponse est claire : c’est non », a déploré Laure Revel, secrétaire générale de la CFDT fonction publique, qui ne participe pourtant pas à la grève du 17 novembre. Dans ce contexte de colère généralisée contre la baisse du pouvoir d’achat, la CGT a appelé de son côté à élargir cette journée de mobilisation à « l’ensemble des salariés, des retraités (et) des jeunes ».
Aux côtés de celles et ceux qui luttent !
L’urgence sociale, c’est chaque jour la priorité de l’Humanité.
- En exposant la violence patronale.
- En montrant ce que vivent celles et ceux qui travaillent et ceux qui aspirent à le faire.
- En donnant des clés de compréhension et des outils aux salarié.es pour se défendre contre les politiques ultralibérales qui dégradent leur qualité de vie.
Vous connaissez d’autres médias qui font ça ?  
Je veux en savoir plus !

https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.author: Cyprien Boganda,Marino – Stupid Economics
https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.text:
20 ans d'inégalités en France : qui s'enrichit vraiment ? | L'Observatoire des inégalités | QQEC 💸
Publié le 11 novembre 2026
Pourquoi l'inflation ne frappe-t-elle pas tout le monde de la même manière ? Comment les réformes fiscales des vingt dernières années ont-elles creusé l'écart entre les plus modestes et les ultra-riches ?
Du phénomène des travailleurs pauvres aux défaillances de notre système scolaire en matière de mixité sociale, Anne Brunner de l’Observatoire des inégalités, nous explique les causes profondes des inégalités et détaille des pistes concrètes pour y remédier.
Oui, on s’en doute : vous en avez assez
Voir ces messages d’appel au don, ça peut être pénible. Nous le savons. Et on doit bien vous avouer que nous préférerions ne pas avoir à les écrire…
Mais voilà : c’est crucial pour l’Humanité. Si ce titre existe toujours aujourd’hui, c’est grâce au financement régulier de nos lectrices et lecteurs.
- C’est grâce à votre soutien que nous pouvons exercer notre métier avec passion. Nous ne dépendons ni des intérêts d’un propriétaire milliardaire, ni de pressions politiques : personne ne nous dicte ce que nous devons dire ou taire.
- Votre engagement nous libère aussi de la course aux clics et à l’audience. Plutôt que de chercher à capter l’attention à tout prix, nous choisissons de traiter les sujets que notre rédaction juge essentiels : parce qu’ils méritent d’être lus, compris, partagés. Parce que nous estimons qu’ils vous seront utiles
À l’heure actuelle, moins d’un quart des lectrices et lecteurs qui viennent plus de 3 fois sur le site par semaine nous aident à financer notre travail, par leur abonnement ou par leurs dons. Si vous voulez protéger le journalisme indépendant, s’il vous plaît, rejoignez-les.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/bresil/le-.title: Le Brésil inflige une amende symbolique d’1,2 million à Meta pour ingérence dans la campagne de Lula
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/bresil/le-.author: Lina Sankari
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/bresil/le-.text:
Après la plainte déposée par l’équipe de Lula durant la campagne présidentielle pour ingérence, le Tribunal supérieur électoral brésilien a condamné Meta à une amende symbolique d’1,2 million d’euros, mardi 10 novembre. Une victoire pour la démocratie.
Que les géants de la Silicon Valley interfèrent dans les processus électoraux, favorisent la désinformation et minent l’égalité dans le vote n’est pas une découverte. C’est en ce sens une importante bataille qu’a emportée la démocratie brésilienne.
Meta, la société propriétaire de Facebook, Instagram et WhatsApp, accusée d’avoir favorisé les posts du candidat d’extrême droite Flavio Bolsonaro sur ceux de Lula lors de la présidentielle en octobre dernier, s’est vu infliger une amende symbolique d’1,2 million d’euros par le Tribunal supérieur électoral (TSE), mardi 10 novembre. Très symbolique même, quand on sait que déjà en 2018, le milliardaire à la tête de Meta, Mark Zuckerberg, gagnait 1,7 million de dollars… Par heure, selon le site d’information financière Business Insider.
Selon le juge rapporteur Marco Aurélio Bellizze, l’existence d’une « action délibérée visant à fausser le scrutin » n’est pas prouvée mais l’équipe de campagne du candidat du Parti des Travailleurs (PT) considère que Meta s’est adonné à une « manipulation algorithmique », se muant en « agent politique ».
Renforcer la régulation
La firme de Mark Zuckerberg plaide des « problèmes techniques » qui auraient seulement touché le Brésil… En pleine élection. Une coïncidence fâcheuse, donc.
La Cour a pour sa part considéré que Meta n’avait pas respecté les délais et manqué de transparence en fournissant au TSE des informations incomplètes, « génériques » ou même rédigées dans une autre langue, pour prouver sa bonne foi. Durant l’entre-deux tours, les soutiens de Lula se sont constitués en véritable « armée » numérique pour bloquer les influenceurs d’extrême droite.
Face à l’extrême droite, ne rien lâcher !
C’est pied à pied, argument contre argument qu’il faut combattre l’extrême droite. Et c’est ce que nous faisons chaque jour dans l’Humanité.
Face aux attaques incessantes des racistes et des porteurs de haine : soutenez-nous ! Ensemble, faisons entendre une autre voix dans ce débat public toujours plus nauséabond.
Je veux en savoir plus.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ‘Chico da Terra’: documentário sobre questão agrária na obra de Chico Buarque estreia sábado (14) em SP
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O observatório jornalístico De Olho nos Ruralistas comemora dez anos de atuação no sábado (14) com a exibição do documentário “Chico da Terra: a questão agrária na obra de Francisco Buarque de Holanda“.
O evento ocorre no Espaço Cultural Elza Soares, mantido pelo Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra (MST), localizado no bairro de Campos Elíseos, na capital paulista, das 14h às 20h, com entrada gratuita.
O curta-metragem analisa a presença do campo e das disputas agrárias na produção musical e literária do compositor. A pesquisa destaca faixas emblemáticas como “Funeral de um Lavrador”, “Cio da Terra” e “Assentamento”, além do engajamento histórico de Chico Buarque na defesa da reforma agrária e no diálogo com as pautas dos movimentos camponeses.
A programação prevê a exibição do filme às 15h, seguida por uma mesa de debate às 16h com a pesquisadora e integrante do MST Ana Chã; o professor do Instituto de Estudos Brasileiros da Universidade de São Paulo (IEB-USP) Walter Garcia; a comunicadora socioambiental Mari Sanefugi; e as jornalistas da equipe do Observatório Carolina Bataier e Vanessa Nicolav. A mediação fica a cargo do fundador e diretor do projeto, Alceu Luís Castilho.
A partir das 18h, o encerramento da celebração reúne apresentações musicais dedicadas ao cancioneiro popular. O grupo As Cantadeiras, composto por militantes do MST, interpreta clássicos da música popular brasileira e do repertório de Chico Buarque, seguido pelo músico paulistano João Suplicy, que apresenta interpretações em voz e violão.
Criado em setembro de 2016, o De Olho nos Ruralistas se consolidou como uma iniciativa especializada na cobertura e na pesquisa investigativa sobre os impactos socioambientais do agronegócio e a atuação política da bancada ruralista no país.
Serviço
Comemoração de dez anos do De Olho nos Ruralistas

- Endereço: Alameda Eduardo Prado, 474, Campos Elíseos – São Paulo (próximo à estação Marechal Deodoro do Metrô)
- Entrada: Gratuita

https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/ican/ce.title: Ce 11 novembre, être les soldats de la paix
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/ican/ce.author: Philippe Rio
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/ican/ce.text:
Ce 11 novembre, être les soldats de la paix
Le 11 novembre, 34 875 communes de France ont commémoré l’armistice de la Grande Guerre. Il y a cent huit ans, le silence des armes mettait fin à une boucherie et faisait renaître dans le pays la joie et l’espoir. Pourtant, Spinoza nous avait alertés : « La paix n’est pas l’absence de guerre, c’est une vertu, un état d’esprit, une disposition à la bienveillance, à la confiance et à la justice. »
Elle n’est donc pas un acquis. C’est un chemin, une exigence politique et un combat quotidien. Pour nous, élus locaux, cette conviction prend un sens particulier. Dans nos communes, nous mesurons chaque jour combien la justice sociale, la solidarité, l’accès aux droits, l’éducation et la dignité humaine sont les fondations d’une paix durable. Comment prétendre bâtir un monde pacifique lorsque les inégalités se creusent, que les discours de haine progressent et que les budgets militaires explosent au détriment des besoins humains ? La paix commence ici, dans nos quartiers, nos écoles et nos services publics.
Le hasard du calendrier a voulu que, le week-end dernier, le réseau français des Maires pour la paix et le Mouvement de la paix renouvellent leurs instances respectives, ouvrant un nouveau chapitre de leur histoire. Ces forces partagent une même ambition : faire vivre une culture de paix fondée sur l’éducation populaire, le multilatéralisme, le désarmement et l’élimination des armes nucléaires.
Elles portent une conviction essentielle : nos villes doivent devenir des territoires de paix, sûrs, solidaires et résilients. Cette ambition se prolongera à New York, avec Ican France, à l’occasion de l’examen du traité sur l’interdiction des armes nucléaires, duquel la France demeure absente. Comment notre pays peut-il prétendre défendre la paix tout en refusant de s’engager pleinement dans l’abolition de l’arme la plus destructrice jamais inventée ?
Une paix pensée entre puissants, dans une répartition des intérêts personnels, nationaux et économiques par des élites, ne saurait suffire. La paix ne peut se construire sans les peuples, sans les citoyens, sans celles et ceux qui, chaque jour, font vivre la fraternité sur le terrain. Ban Ki-moon, ancien secrétaire général des Nations unies, le rappelait en mai 2010 : « Construire un monde pacifique ne commence pas dans les salles de conférences à New York ou Genève. Cela commence sur le terrain, dans les quartiers, dans les communautés. » Il avait raison.
À l’heure où la guerre menace, où le repli nationaliste gagne du terrain et où l’avenir commun semble fragilisé, nous avons une responsabilité historique. Faire de nos communes des espaces de dialogue, de solidarité et de résistance à la haine. Refuser que la paix soit un slogan sans moyens, une promesse sans actes ou un privilège réservé aux plus puissants. Nous sommes les soldats de la paix. Sans armes, mais avec nos convictions, nos engagements et la force du collectif. Unissons-nous pour faire de la paix non pas une parenthèse entre deux guerres, mais un horizon commun pour l’humanité.
Être le journal de la paix, notre défi quotidien
Depuis Jaurès, la défense de la paix est dans notre ADN.
- Qui informe encore aujourd’hui sur les actions des pacifistes pour le désarmement ?
- Combien de médias rappellent que les combats de décolonisation ont encore cours, et qu’ils doivent être soutenus ?
- Combien valorisent les solidarités internationales, et s’engagent sans ambiguïté aux côtés des exilés ?
Nos valeurs n’ont pas de frontières.
Aidez-nous à soutenir le droit à l’autodétermination et l’option de la paix.
Je veux en savoir plus !

https://taz.de/Kunstschau-ueber-Freundsc.title: Kunstschau über Freun­d­schaft in Mainz: Wo der Funke überspringt
https://taz.de/Kunstschau-ueber-Freundsc.author: Lilli Braun
https://taz.de/Kunstschau-ueber-Freundsc.text:
Kunstschau über Freundschaft in Mainz: Wo der Funke überspringt
Die Mainzer Kunsthalle zeigt eine Gruppen-Ausstellung über „Freund*innenschaft“. Durch die ungewisse Zukunft des Hauses ist das Thema doppelt aktuell.
Auf den ersten Blick ist es ein starres Bild, das die Eisschwimmer*innen aus Helsinki auf der Fotografie von Tuomo Manninen abgeben. Angespannt, ungelenk – kein Wunder, immerhin stehen einige von ihnen in eiskaltem Wasser. Manche von ihnen grinsen verschüchtert und ein wenig stolz in die Kamera, andere haben ihre Arme verschränkt, eine lässt sich vom Geländer eines Holzsteges baumeln.
Schaut man sie sich genauer an, sind die elf Menschen auf dieser Fotografie ganz verschieden: manche jünger, manche älter. Manche von ihnen sind für das grau-kalte Wetter ungewöhnlich sonnengebräunt, manche blass. Auf den ersten Blick aber bilden sie eine Gruppe. Sehen sich sehr ähnlich in ihren bunten Badeanzügen und Speedo-Badehosen, in ihrer Körperhaltung, ihrem Ausdruck, im gemeinsamen Blick in die Kamera.
Schon seit 30 Jahren fotografiert der finnische Fotograf in seiner Serie „We“ („Wir“) Gruppen. Schornsteinfeger aus seiner Heimatstadt Helsinki, posierende Bodybuilder aus Kathmandu oder eine Nordic-Walking-Gruppe aus Recklinghausen. Seine Gruppen strahlen Verbundenheit aus, aber die Frage stellt sich schnell, ob sie die einzelnen Gruppenmitglieder auch spüren. Ab wann wird aus Ähnlichkeit Gemeinschaft? Und ab wann aus Gemeinschaft Freund*innenschaft?
Die Ausstellung
„Freund*innenschaft“. Kunsthalle Mainz, bis 10. Januar 2027
Manninens Fotografien bilden den Auftakt einer Ausstellung in der Mainzer Kunsthalle über „Freund*innenschaft“. Neun internationale Gegenwartsünstler*innen nähern sich dem Thema an, zusammengestellt hat die Schau Marlène Harles, Kuratorin des Hauses. Harles vermittelt Freund*innenschaft als komplexe, individuelle, aber auch universelle Beziehung, die mitunter als Gegenmittel einer Gesellschaft angesehen werden, in der sich Menschen zunehmend voneinander isolieren.
Wer hat überhaupt Zugang zu Freund*innenschaft
Nicht nur Tuomo Manninen fragt in der Schau danach, welche Räume Freund*innenschaft entstehen lassen. Roxane Mbanga erschafft sich solche Orte mit „Le Salon“ selbst: Einen Raum der Begegnung hat sie in der Kunsthalle installiert. Bunt, einladend, mit unterschiedlichen Textilien, Kissen, Spielen und Büchern. Einen Raum, der sicher ist und für alle zugänglich. Und dabei kommt der Gedanke auf, wer überhaupt Zugang zu solchen Räumen, solchen Freund*innenschaften hat.
Eindrücklich wird diese Frage auch vom Kollektiv photo.circle gestellt, das eine Auswahl aus seinem Archiv „Nepal Picture Library“ zeigt. Auf den zehn ausgestellten „Photographs of Friendship“ inszenieren sich Frauen aus dem nepalesischen Kathmandu-Tal in ähnlicher Kleidung und Schmuck oder einem gleichen Ausdruck. Sie hinterfragen das Bild der devoten, sozial-isolierten, an Tradition und Haushalt gebundenen nepalesischen Frau und zeigen sie stattdessen als eine, die ihre Freund*innenschaften zelebriert und pflegt, in gegenseitiger Solidarität.
Die Ausstellung nähert sich dem Thema mit unterschiedlichen Fragen und vielen Darstellungsformen. Wir hören Freund:Innenschaft in einem mühsam-verzerrten Zoomcall der Soundinstallation von Hanne Lippard, wo die Künstlerin ambivalente, zwischenmenschliche Situation ausbreitet, in denen stille Kompromisse ausgehandelt, Verletzungen leise vergeben werden. Wir sehen sie in den aufgehängten Kinderjacken von Eva Koťátková, verziert mit Mündern, Stacheln und Tentakeln. Oder bei Asta Grötings Elektrokabeln, zwischen denen der Funken eben nicht nur bei romantischen Beziehungen überspringt.
Erst Quartier aufwerten, dann Finanzierung kappen
Dabei steht der Wunsch nach Gemeinschaft und Solidarität schon fast sinnbildlich für ein Haus, dessen zukünftige Existenz von der Frage abhängt, wer bereit dazu ist, dafür Verantwortung zu übernehmen. Seit 2008 ist die Kunsthalle Mainz am alten Zollhafen in einem ehemaligen Maschinenhaus, das den Stadtwerken gehört und vom Büro des Architekten Günter Zamp Kelp zum Kulturbau umgeplant wurde, ein Ausstellungsort für aufstrebende und internationale Künstler*innen. Sie ist eine bedeutende Institution für Gegenwartskunst in Rheinland-Pfalz.
Die Mainzer Stadtwerke aber, die mit einem großen Betrag zur Finanzierung der Stiftung Kunsthalle Mainz beigetragen haben, kündigten vor einigen Monaten ihre Beteiligung auf. Die Kunsthalle fungierte zuvor als Leuchtturmprojekt für die Transformation des alten Hafengebiets, sie hat maßgeblich zur Aufwertung des Quartiers beigetragen. Nun, da die städtebauliche Entwicklung fast abgeschlossen ist, muss das Haus Alternativen zur bisherigen Finanzierung finden. Inzwischen konnte der Betrieb der Kunsthalle bis Ende Juli 2027 sichergestellt werden. Einen langfristigen Plan gibt es jedoch nicht. Daher hallen auch Fragen aus der Ausstellung nach: Was verbindet uns? Und was lässt die Verbindung bestehen?
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: US withdraw from U-17 World Cup in Qatar due to safety concerns
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Alexander Abnos
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
The United States men’s national team have pulled out of the Fifa U-17 World Cup, due to kick off in Qatar in just over a week. In a letter sent to players explaining the decision, the US Soccer Federation cited safety concerns for players and staff, referring them to the US state department’s travel advisory for Qatar, which encourages citizens to reconsider travel to the country “due to risk of armed conflict” and asks government employees to obtain special authorization to do so.
“Unfortunately, in light of current circumstances … we are no longer able to participate in the tournament,” US Soccer’s letter to players reads. “The wellbeing of our players and staff will always be our top priority.
“Please accept our deepest appreciation for your commitment to US Soccer and our shared disappointment about these circumstances.”
A US Soccer spokesperson said the federation would not go into details about how it reached its decision. The Guardian understands that Fifa were informed of the federation’s decision on Wednesday.
Fifa’s regulations for the U-17 World Cups stipulate that qualified nations must participate in the tournament or be fined, with withdrawal within 30 days of the tournament’s start resulting in a fine of CHF20,000 (about $24,000). Fifa has been approached for comment.
The ongoing situation in the Middle East – involving interconnected conflicts among multiple states – has already led to multiple cancellations of international sporting events. The 2027 Asian Cup, the continental soccer championship, was due to be held in Saudi Arabia in January 2027 but was postponed nearly a year due to the Houthi-Saudi conflict and the 2026 Iran war. More recently, Qatar pulled out of hosting rugby’s 2028 Nations Championship finals due to uncertainty around the conflicts.
Multiple missile strikes by the Houthis on Riyadh’s international airport killed more than a dozen people and wounded hundreds in October. Later that month, US diplomats were told to leave Saudi Arabia amid ongoing Houthi attacks.
Qatar has been acting as a mediator in talks between the US and Iran aimed at ending the nations’ conflict, which started with the US and Israel’s attacks on Iran earlier this year. A tanker off the coast of Qatar was attacked in October amid thetensions.
The U-17 World Cup is still due to begin on 19 November in Doha. The US were placed in Group J along with Montenegro, Algeria, and Chile. The US roster that was due to compete in the tournament does not contain any household names, but does feature a number of promising young players in MLS and abroad.

Iran’s parliament speaker and top negotiator says Tehran is waiting for an official US response to its seven conditions for ending war.
Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and top negotiator, has told Al Jazeera that the Strait of Hormuz will “never return” to its status prior to the US-Israel war on Iran.
In an exclusive interview published on Wednesday, Ghalibaf said Iran and Oman reached an understanding to oversee the critical waterway as part of Tehran’s seven-point proposal to end the eight-month conflict.
“There are no ‘free waters’ [international waters] there, and the 1982 [UN Convention on the Law of the Sea] does not apply to the strait … The regulations within the Strait of Hormuz are governed by the laws of the two littoral states that border it,” he said.
Seven conditions
Ghalibaf said Tehran provided a clear response to the US through a Qatari mediator that included its seven conditions for peace talks, adding that Iran is waiting for an official response.
“The ball is now in the American court,” he said.
Iran’s conditions, as outlined by the chief negotiator, include lifting the US-imposed naval blockade and sanctions, the release of Iranian frozen funds, ending fighting on all fronts, and an explicit announcement of an end to the war.
He said these demands were part of the Islamabad memorandum of understanding signed in June and their implementation was necessary before entering negotiations with the US.
“If America limits itself to what has been agreed upon without making excessive demands or engaging in behaviour that breeds distrust, then, naturally, reaching an agreement is possible,” he said.
“What stands in the way of an agreement is our lack of trust in the United States.”
Renewed conflict
Ghalibaf said US officials asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to mediate direct negotiations with Tehran during a visit to Moscow.
He warned against new US attacks against Iran, saying that US President Donald Trump will face another defeat and political pressure from the new Congress that takes office in January.
Iran is determined to move beyond a state of “no war and no peace”, he said, urging a sustainable deterrent capability, including military capabilities.
Yemen mediation
On the ongoing fighting in Yemen between the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government forces and the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for “Supporters of God”), Ghalibaf said that “no one should interfere” in it.
“If both the government in Yemen and Saudi Arabia were to ask for our help, we would certainly offer our assistance to help resolve their conflict,” he said.
Iran has previously offered to facilitate talks between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi group in October following a series of deadly attacks on the kingdom.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Fleur Hargreaves
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Saudi Arabia faces liquidity crunch even as oil exports rebound to pre-war levels
Saudi Arabia is feeling the pinch of a liquidity crisis as bank deposits slow and the economy comes under pressure from the US-Israeli war on Iran, a new report from Bank of America says.
In a note to clients, Bank of America said Saudi Arabia is grappling with “contagion” caused by liquidity tightness in the UAE and a rapid slowdown in the kingdom’s own economy, according to an article published on Bloomberg on Tuesday.
The report said Saudi banks are feeling the pain in the UAE, which is also grappling with fallout from the Iran war and tighter liquidity. Saudi banks are closely linked to their Emirati neighbours, with a high number of interbank transactions contributing to deposits at Saudi banks.
At the same time, the Saudi economy is under strain and government entities are making withdrawals from Saudi banks. But loan demand is high, which is effectively raising the cost of Saudi money.
The liquidity strain is notable for Saudi Arabia because its currency is directly pegged to the US dollar, along with Gulf states including the UAE, Qatar, Oman, and Bahrain.

Saudi Arabia faces liquidity crunch even as oil exports rebound to pre-war levels
Saudi Arabia is feeling the pinch of a liquidity crisis as bank deposits slow and the economy comes under pressure from the US-Israeli war on Iran, a new report from Bank of America says.
In a note to clients, Bank of America said Saudi Arabia is grappling with “contagion” caused by liquidity tightness in the UAE and a rapid slowdown in the kingdom’s own economy, according to an article published on Bloomberg on Tuesday.
The report said Saudi banks are feeling the pain in the UAE, which is also grappling with fallout from the Iran war and tighter liquidity. Saudi banks are closely linked to their Emirati neighbours, with a high number of interbank transactions contributing to deposits at Saudi banks.
At the same time, the Saudi economy is under strain and government entities are making withdrawals from Saudi banks. But loan demand is high, which is effectively raising the cost of Saudi money.
The liquidity strain is notable for Saudi Arabia because its currency is directly pegged to the US dollar, along with Gulf states including the UAE, Qatar, Oman, and Bahrain.

Gulf central banks can’t inject additional liquidity into their markets like the US, Europe and Russia because their currencies are set against the dollar and their interest rates track those set by the US Federal Reserve.
Oil exports rebound
Saudi Arabia has avoided the worst fallout from the US-Israeli war on Iran, but its economy is still tied to smaller Gulf states. For example, the UAE is Saudi Arabia's single largest foreign direct investor.
More recently, the kingdom’s economy has been rocked by the collapse of a ceasefire in Yemen.
Saudi Arabia has come under Houthi missile and drone attacks targeting energy infrastructure, airports and high-profile commercial buildings. The Aramco Tower, a skyscraper in Riyadh, was hit by a Houthi air attack earlier this week.
The liquidity strain comes even as Saudi Arabia’s oil exports rebound to pre-war levels.
Saudi Arabia told the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries that it pumped 10.6 million barrels per day (bpd) of oil in October, up from 8.372 million bpd in September.
The number marked Saudi Arabia's highest output since February, before the US and Israel attacked Iran.
The East-West Pipeline terminating at the Red Sea port of Yanbu allowed Saudi Arabia to bypass Iran's attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, but the pipeline has been targeted by the Houthis and militias in Iraq, according to Riyadh.
The latest strike against the pipeline occurred on Monday.

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: I went without a car for a month. How much money did I save?
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Adam Doud
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
I’m an avid ebiker, especially when the weather allows. During the summer, I drive my car close to 30% less than any other season. I have a few ebikes at home and they all go at least 20mph, so I can get around pretty quickly when I need to. There’s just something about hopping onto a bike instead of climbing into a car. There’s a certain freedom to it – probably similar to riding a motorocycle, but without the extra license, testing and insurance. Also without the speed, but you take the good with the bad.
Also, gas prices are insane these days, so any time I can spend not behind the wheel is a gift. Riding an ebike is a fun diversion from how I usually get around, but I wondered if I could actually do it for a full month and save a little money.
For one month, I rode an ebike or escooter exclusively (with a few notable exceptions we’ll discuss later) and tracked where I went and how far, and used Google Maps to track how long it would have taken to drive. I learned a few lessons along the way – a lot of big pros and cons – from safety to that extra bit of mobility.
At a glance: my car substitutes
- Engwe M20 3.0 ebike
- Segway Ninebot Max G3 Plus Scooter
Week one: Not a great start!
The biggest mistake I made was starting this experiment in October in Chicago. This meant two things: it was starting to get cold, and it was starting to get dark earlier. The error of my ways became evident when on my third day, I decided to head to my mom’s house, about 25 miles away on side streets, bike paths and even some thoroughfares (but not the highway). I got there, spent a bit of time, and started back, but I didn’t give myself enough time to get home before dark.
The bike, an Engwe M20 3.0 has headlights and enough battery power to make the long distance trek. Unfortunately – and I can’t emphasize enough that this was day three of a 30-day challenge – I got hit by a car. I’m fine. The bike was not. Yes, mistakes were made, but fortunately for everyone involved, there were no serious injuries. That bike was toast, and I have since bought some high-visibility stickers for my helmet and backpack.
Undaunted, I continued my journey – mostly during the day now. The other vehicle I’d planned to use was the Segway Ninebot Max G3 Plus, a motorized standup kick scooter that served as my primary vehicle for the rest of the month. After a few days of running around during daylight hours, I got right back up on that horse and headed out at night again because we needed dinner. From this point on, most of the rides I made were local and under seven miles – running to the store, or to a friend’s house; that kind of stuff. I only had one more long journey coming, which we will get to later.
For now, this week’s lesson is to be even more careful than you think you need to be, and by the way, look both ways and behind you when you cross a street. Who knew?
Week two: I can’t get rid of the car completely
My e-scooter journey continued into the second week with similar small trips, but I found myself looking for reasons to go out on (somewhat) unnecessary excursions. Were we going grocery shopping later that week? Sure, but we need a gallon of milk today, so headed out on the scooter because it is so much fun! The Segway scooter has three speed modes – eco, ride and sport, set to 10, 16 and 25mph respectively. (If 25mph seems fast for an e-scooter, know that there’s a reason: the side streets around me have a speed limit of 25mph, so basically if someone hits me from behind, they’re the problem, not me.)
But when the weekend rolled around, I had to hop into the car. My son wanted to spend his birthday with some friends in Rockford, which is about 60 or so miles away on Saturday. The following day, my wife and I went to Six Flags Great America which is 45 miles away. I do have a bike that can make those distances, but not back without about five hours of charging in between. They also can’t make those trips with two people.
If you came here thinking this was an instruction manual for ditching your car full time, I’m sorry to say this is not it. You still need a car for going long distances, for things such as grocery runs, and of course if you ever want to go somewhere, you know, with someone. Still, these were the only two times I found myself in the car that week, so overall, I’m calling it a win.
Week three: The long haul
Running errands on a scooter is great, but they do take longer. You’re limited to side streets, so often the route you will need to take will be longer than it would be if you just drove. And a scooter will never be as fast as a car – your speed is capped at 25mph. In terms of time, over the course of the month, I spent about 11 hours on the bike or scooter, while driving would have taken around seven hours. That’s not a huge difference all told, but it’s not nothing.
This week was also the second longest trip I had to take and it also marked my return to an ebike. The Engwe M20 is the predecessor to the one that got totaled, and its range far outperforms that of the scooter’s battery. First, I had to go by my daughter’s school to get a form, then take that form to another high school. Then, I had to run a couple of errands on the way back. It ended up being around 20 miles all told. I don’t know if I have the memory of a goldfish, or if I just don’t learn lessons, but the accident from two weeks ago never entered my mind. This was just a thing I had to do – I’d committed to riding an ebike for the month, and so I just got back on and rode.
It was also starting to get rather cold, so I added gloves and my leather coat to the mix. Sixty fahrenheit is pleasantly crisp but add in 25mph of speed with no windshield, and it gets chilly, quickly. If you’re going to try this experiment outside of the summer time, be prepared for the elements. I also got caught out in the rain this week on a trip to Target, and I had to wait it out in the store before I could head home, so pay attention to the weather forecast as well.
Week four: The home stretch
Week four brought another trip to Great America in the car, but this time I brought the scooter with me. I drove to the park, but when faced with the choice of paying $25 for a slice of not amazing pizza, or just $7 for a literal full meal at Subway, the scooter made a lot of sense. I actually did about five miles in town outside the park running to Walgreens for some OTC medicine, Subway for my lunch and McDonalds for my daughter. All the while, my car stayed in the parking lot, in a nice, close spot to the park’s front entrance, saving me gas and time looking for a new spot.
The thing I like most about the e-scooter is not just how quick it is, or how fun, but also how portable. This is the type of ride you can toss into your trunk and use it for “last mile” kinds of things. If you want to catch a ball game, but not pay insane parking fees, park a couple of miles away and scoot over to the gate. Or, if you have a series of errands to run that are all nearby, park once and ride the rest of the way!
This was also the week where the toting capacity of an e-scooter (read: non-existent) was tested: when I went to buy a toilet seat that couldn’t fit into my bag, I added some bungee cords and strapped the thing to the outside of my backpack to get it home. Every problem has a solution and sometimes that solution is more bungee cords.
Was it worth it?
Over the month I spent dodging cars – with varying amounts of success – and braving the wind, rain and pedestrians, I logged a total of 185 miles. That’s actually not bad for a scooter. I could have spent all those miles in my car, sure. It would have been less dangerous and at a more comfortable temperature. But when you factor in the ridiculous price of gas, it makes sense that a scooter looks a lot more tempting. However, there was one last surprise.
The average gas price in Illinois at the time of this writing, according to Gas Buddy, is $4.60 a gallon. My 2024 Toyota Rav4 Hybrid gets about 34 miles to the gallon which brings my total gas savings to around $25. If we go with a worst case scenario, where the max gas price around me this month was $4.94 a gallon and I’m driving my 2013 Mitsubishi Outlander Sport which gets closer to 24 miles a gallon, that total jumps to $38.
The numbers don’t lie: riding an ebike or scooter is not going to save you a ton of money. But the twist is, as I write this four days after my experiment ended, I’m still heading out on the scooter to run errands. It’s not about the money; it’s about the fun, the fresh air and the excitement that I just don’t get behind the wheel of a car. There are, frankly too many four-, five-, or even seven-seat cars out there with one occupant taking up space on the road and burning fossil fuels unnecessarily. We need to normalize adults running errands on ebikes. So, if you want to buy a bike or a scooter to save money, don’t. But if you want to buy it to have more fun and get out more, then I can’t recommend it enough.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Oil production nears pre-Iran war levels, OPEC says
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Oil production nears pre-Iran war levels, OPEC says
Saudi Arabia reports oil outputs soared to their highest levels in months despite continued shipping disruptions.
Saudi Arabia has boosted crude outputs to their highest levels since before the Iran war disrupted supplies in February, triggering a global energy and shipping crisis.
An OPEC report issued on Wednesday said the world’s biggest oil exporter pumped 10.563 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude in October, up by over two million bpd from its September output.
That is the highest level since the United States and Israel launched the war on Iran in late February, when Saudi Arabia produced 10.882 million bpd.
Rising oil production by Saudi Arabia and Russia helped increase outputs for the OPEC+ group, which includes the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and other nations including Russia.
OPEC+ pumped 41.23 million bpd in October, up by about 2.04 million bpd from September, according to its monthly report. Russia’s output increased as US President Donald Trump lifted sanctions on Russian energy and announced an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia in mid-October.
Fuel prices ease
Riyadh sharply increased its production in February ahead of US and Israeli strikes on Iran.
Saudi Arabia’s reported increase in oil production “could help ease some of the inflationary pressure facing American consumers”, Umud Shokri, an energy strategist and senior visiting fellow at George Mason University, told Al Jazeera.
“When more oil enters the global market, prices generally come under downward pressure, which can eventually translate into lower gasoline, transportation, and production costs in the United States,” he said. “However, higher Saudi production does not automatically mean lower prices at American gas stations.”
While US prices for petrol or gasoline fell below $4 a gallon for the first time in months this week, concerns over the stubbornly high cost of living drove the Democratic Party’s sweeping victories in US midterm elections last week.
Inflation has spiked since February, when it stood at 2.9 percent. Annual personal consumption expenditures (PCE) shot to a three-year high of 4.1 percent in May, when energy prices soared as the conflict closed off roughly one-fifth of global oil supplies transiting through the Strait of Hormuz.
Other producers managed to regain their supply positions, including the US.
However, the report noted a decline in imports by one of the world’s largest economies – Japan – where “crude imports fell sharply in September amid renewed disruptions to trade flows”.
The report data, while based on secondary sources, indicate that Gulf oil producers are recovering exports by using workarounds such as ship-to-ship transfers to bypass disruptions caused by the conflict.
“The UAE regained its position as the top supplier in September with a share of 49 percent, compared with 25 percent the previous month. The US was second with 28 percent, followed by Saudi Arabia with 14 percent,” the OPEC report noted.
The report indicated that Saudi Arabia’s exports have stabilised despite a secondary oil supply route – Saudi’s East-West Pipeline – coming under attack by Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen. The Houthis, who are fighting the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government in Aden, continued to target the pipeline this week.
Shokri explained that “one reason Saudi Arabia has been able to recover some of its exports is its East-West Pipeline, which allows crude oil to move across the country to the Red Sea port of Yanbu without passing through the Strait of Hormuz”.
While no longer an OPEC member, the United Arab Emirates remains a major supplier and “has a similar advantage through its pipeline to Fujairah, located outside the strait”, he said.
“The bigger picture is that Gulf countries are learning how costly dependence on a single maritime chokepoint can be,” Shokri warned. “They are looking for ways to make their exports more resilient, but Hormuz remains too important to the global energy market to be easily bypassed.”
Oil forecasts unchanged
Oil output in October was equivalent to 97 percent of the 42.72 million bpd produced by OPEC+ in February, according to Reuters.
OPEC left its forecasts for global oil demand growth unchanged after cutting them for six straight months, and made no changes to its 2027 outlook.
The producer group expects global oil demand to rise by 2.55 million bpd next year to an average of 108.3 million bpd. It forecasts growth of 180,000 bpd in 2026.
The report also forecasted that Qatar, Canada, Brazil and Argentina will drive growth in energy-related liquids production in 2027.
The report offered an optimistic outlook for the Middle East’s economic performance in the near term.
“In 2027, the region’s economy is expected to rebound and economic activity to recover, supported by a resilient non-oil sector and robust domestic demand,” it said.
