https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: Nvidia shares plunge amid reports board to discuss CEO Huang’s future
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
Nvidia shares plunge amid reports board to discuss CEO Huang’s future
Chip giants stock price falls more than 8 percent amid speculation over co-founder’s position.
Chip giant Nvidia’s stock price has tumbled amid reports that its board of directors is meeting to consider the future of CEO Jensen Huang.
Nvidia shares fell 8.6 percent in after-hours trading on Wednesday as questions swirled over Huang’s position at the top of the $4.2 trillion company.
The plunge comes after The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times reported that Nvidia’s board of directors would discuss Huang’s position over allegations that he engaged in an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia employee, in addition to an affair with a woman accused of working with Chinese intelligence services.
Nvidia, which launched an investigation into Huang on Sunday, did not immediately respond to Al Jazeera’s requests for comment.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, is one of the most visible faces of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, spearheading the development of high-end graphics processing units used to train and run frontier models.
The leather jacket-sporting tech executive’s position has also placed him at the centre of the geopolitical rivalry between the United States and China, which are locked in a battle for supremacy in AI.
As a confidant of US President Donald Trump, Huang has lobbied for the easing of restrictions on exports of high-end chips to China, putting him at odds with national security hawks in Washington who argue that Beijing must be blocked from access to cutting-edge US tech.
Seismic moment
If Nvidia’s board were to oust Huang, 63, it would mark a seismic moment for the chip giant.
Viewed as integral to Nvidia’s meteoric rise to the ranks of the world’s most valuable companies, Huang is known for a centralised leadership style that places him at the centre of the company’s day-to-day operations and strategic decisions.
“Jensen is Nvidia; without him, the company loses its central, animating spirit,” Jay Goldberg, a senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners in San Francisco, told Al Jazeera.
“The organisation is built around him and replacing him will be very painful organisationally, and impossible to do personality-wise.”
It is unclear whether Nvidia has a succession plan, and analysts see few obvious candidates to take Huang’s place.
Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said Huang has been the “hearts and lungs” of Nvidia and that investors will closely scrutinise the executive’s possible replacement.
“We believe Nvidia’s value is $300 per share with Jensen as CEO and $225 per share without Jensen as CEO,” Ives said in a note to clients, adding that the company would navigate the turmoil and “remain a core foundational piece of the AI Revolution.”
“Jensen is not replaceable by another CEO or group of interim executives, but Nvidia likely now has to move on without Jensen at the helm, which seemed like a Twilight Zone episode narrative before Sunday afternoon when the news broke,” Ives said.
International intrigue
Nvidia has been the focus of international intrigue over the past week amid reports that Huang had a relationship with a Chinese woman who US intelligence officials determined had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security.
US officials have not provided evidence for the claims about the woman, a Chinese tech executive named Alice Huang.
Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, has not publicly commented on the allegations.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has denied the claims, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.
Nvidia’s board of directors said on Sunday it had opened a probe into whether Huang had been targeted in a foreign intelligence operation, while also expressing confidence in the executive.
Huang, who admitted to being “unfaithful” to his wife and apologised to his family, pledged to cooperate fully with the inquiry and said he was committed to protecting Nvidia and US national security.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/rdc/rdc-le.title: RDC : le président Tshisekedi passe une loi pour changer la constitution et briguer sur un troisième mandat
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/rdc/rdc-le.author: La rédaction avec AFP
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/rdc/rdc-le.text:
Felix Antoine Tshisekedi Tshilombo, président de la République démocratique du Congo, a promulgué une loi dans la nuit du 10 au 11 novembre, ouvrant la voie à un changement de Constitution, dans un contexte de tensions avec l’opposition qui l’accuse de manœuvrer pour se maintenir au pouvoir et rempiler sur un troisième mandat.
Le président de la République démocratique du Congo (RDC), Félix Tshisekedi, a promulgué une loi dans la nuit du 10 au 11 novembre, ouvrant la voie à un changement de Constitution, dans un contexte de tensions avec l’opposition qui l’accuse de manœuvrer pour se maintenir au pouvoir pour un troisième mandat.
Le texte élargit les conditions d’organisation d’un référendum portant sur une révision constitutionnelle ou l’adoption d’une nouvelle Constitution. Il a été promulgué par une ordonnance lue à la télévision nationale dans la nuit de mardi à mercredi.
Félix Tshisekedi, 63 ans, est au pouvoir depuis 2019 et arrive fin 2028 au terme de son second et dernier mandat, selon la Constitution actuelle. Lors d’une rare conférence de presse en mai dernier, le président avait déclaré : « Si le peuple souhaite que j’aie un troisième mandat, j’accepterai ».
« Un coup d’État constitutionnel »
Des manifestations à l’appel de l’opposition, pour protester contre « un coup d’État constitutionnel », ont eu lieu en juin et en septembre dans la capitale, Kinshasa, et dans plusieurs autres grandes villes du pays.
Ces rassemblements ont souvent été émaillés de heurts et quasi systématiquement dispersés par la police. Les Nations unies ont déploré « au moins un mort » en juin à Kinshasa et l’opposition a dénoncé « l’assassinat » d’un opposant en septembre.
Félix Tshisekedi, le président de la RDC, avait annoncé mi-juillet l’organisation d’un « dialogue national », mais les principaux partis d’opposition ont jusqu’à présent refusé d’y participer.
Avant de partir, une dernière chose…
Contrairement à 90% des médias français aujourd’hui, l’Humanité ne dépend ni de grands groupes ni de milliardaires. Cela signifie que :
- nous vous apportons des informations impartiales, sans compromis. Mais aussi que
- nous n’avons pas les moyens financiers dont bénéficient les autres médias.
L’information indépendante et de qualité a un coût. Payez-le.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/ho.title: How Israel has engineered a system of apartheid on West Bank roads
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/ho.author: Fareed Taamallah
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/ho.text:
How Israel has engineered a system of apartheid on West Bank roads
Every afternoon at exactly 4pm, a calculated military decision transforms the exits of Ramallah and al-Bireh into an open-air gridlock of vehicles piled nose to tail, idling engines and mounting frustration.
What Israeli authorities continue to market to the world as temporary "security measures" - the iron gates, concrete barriers, earth mounds and armed checkpoints choking the occupied West Bank - has long since metastasised into a deliberate, institutionalised apparatus of spatial segregation and racial discrimination.
This architecture of control does not exist to neutralise genuine threats. It operates to clear shared arterial roads for Israeli settlers at the exact hour Palestinian civilian movement reaches its daily peak.
By subordinating the basic right of an indigenous population to travel through its own land, the system grants permanent priority to one group while punishing another for the simple act of trying to commute home after a day's work.
According to comprehensive field documentation compiled by the United Nations' humanitarian office, Ocha, and the human rights organisation B'Tselem, the landscape of the occupied West Bank is carved up by more than 900 fixed and intermittent movement obstacles.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
They comprise permanently manned military checkpoints, partial ones, remote-controlled iron gates, earth mounds, roadblocks and trenches, which restrict and dictate the daily lives of 3.4 million Palestinians.
Ocha counts 232 iron gates alone, at least 120 installed in 2025, and the Palestinian commission that monitors the wall and settlements now puts the total at 942.
Within the immediate vicinity of Ramallah and al-Bireh alone, some 160 of these closure points exist, a count exceeded only in Hebron, acting as constant choke points along the transit corridors that connect the governorate to the north, east and south of the West Bank.
To the south, Palestinian vehicular movement is funnelled through Qalandia, Jaba and the northern Jerusalem access routes, where dense local traffic intersects with bypass highways engineered to connect Israeli settlements to population centres inside the separation wall.
What was originally justified under the flimsy pretext of defence has evolved into a calculated instrument of systemic discrimination and population management
To the north, the critical arteries pass through the Ein Siniya and Atara checkpoints, the Yabrud junction and the Beit El checkpoint, known locally as the DCO after the Israeli military's District Coordination Office beside it.
The Israeli separation wall, 85 percent of which runs inside the West Bank, and its interlocking network of checkpoints have long ceased to function as anything like a border. Operating deep inside occupied territory, they actively reshape geography to annex settlement blocs, isolate Palestinian communities in fragmented enclaves and re-engineer public space.
By dictating who may travel, when, and along which permitted bypasses, the system establishes a permanent hierarchy of spatial privilege. What was originally justified under the flimsy pretext of defence has evolved into a calculated instrument of systemic discrimination and population management.
Punishing the victims
The mechanics of this structural discrimination are felt with devastating consistency each afternoon on every side of the Beit El (DCO) checkpoint. Before October 2023, this strategic crossing operated on a 24-hour basis, a fact documented by field monitors.
The army closed it outright after 7 October 2023 and reopened it to Palestinian traffic in June 2024, as Israeli settlers stoned cars at the gate and demanded that it remain closed to us. The head of the Beit El settlement council called the reopening "folly".
Crossings that were once open around the clock now close during the morning and evening rush hours. At the DCO, under arbitrary military mandates, the checkpoint is abruptly closed to Palestinian vehicular traffic in both directions at 4pm sharp, remaining shut until 9pm to clear the roadway for settlers.
This timing is neither random nor dictated by the physical capacity of the road. It coincides precisely with the period when thousands of workers, students and residents attempt to exit Ramallah and al-Bireh to return to their surrounding towns and villages. Simultaneously, this window sees increased traffic from Israeli settlers travelling along the same regional arteries.
Rather than addressing the primary source of tension on these corridors, where armed Israeli settlers have frequently intercepted, stoned and attacked Palestinian vehicles under cover of night, the occupation authorities consistently resort to collective punishment.
By shutting down the checkpoint to Palestinian drivers at 4pm, the military clears the thoroughfare, allowing settlers to travel with total freedom and speed, unencumbered by the presence of Palestinian commuters who might otherwise share the road and create perceived congestion.
The security narrative collapses under field analysis. When a vital transit artery is arbitrarily closed, the vehicular flow does not dissipate; it is forcibly redirected onto narrow secondary roads. This creates cascading bottlenecks across adjacent checkpoints, compounding the regional crisis and leaving an entire population's daily existence tethered to unpredictable military decrees.
The same decrees now operate on a larger scale. For a week from 25 September, over the Jewish holiday of Sukkot, Israel sealed the West Bank; the Atara and Ein Siniya checkpoints and the gates of Nabi Saleh and Taybeh were closed; and at Jaba, commuters spent the night in their cars.
On 27 October, every entrance to Ramallah was shut, and new checkpoints were set up on the alternative roads residents use to get around them.
The micro-physics of humiliation
The systematic suppression of Palestinian movement is executed not only through outright road closures, but through the deliberate, micro-calculated elongation of transit times at active checkpoints. Passing through a military checkpoint is rarely a straightforward verification process; it has been crafted into a tedious, multi-stage ritual designed to exhaust, delay and demoralise.
A driver approaches the stop line, comes to a complete halt and is instructed to switch off the engine. They must exit the vehicle in all weather conditions, walk towards an armed soldier positioned behind armoured glass or concrete blocks, and present their identification card and vehicle registration.
Once these are handed back, the driver is instructed to return to the vehicle, only to be ordered onto a secondary inspection zone. There, their details may undergo computer verification, photographic logging or extended background checks. Only after this repetitive sequence is completed can they restart the vehicle and drive off.
Even under ideal conditions, a single inspection lane bogged down by these contrived bureaucratic hurdles can process no more than 12 to 15 vehicles an hour. When thousands of cars are forced into single-file inspection channels, administrative friction multiplies into mile-long queues and hours of wasted time.
Beyond the immense economic toll of lost labour hours and fuel, these checkpoints frequently become sites of casual cruelty and entertainment for bored, emboldened soldiers. The systematic normalisation of petty humiliation converts basic daily travel into an exercise in psychological attrition, designed to reinforce a status of total subjugation.
This macro-structure of fragmentation and control is not merely an analytical concept; it is a deeply personal, lived reality. During my regular trips between Ramallah, where I live, and my birthplace, the village of Qira in Salfit governorate, the physical and emotional weight of these checkpoints becomes strikingly personal.
What should be a straightforward 40-minute drive through my home landscape has become an unpredictable gauntlet of military barriers, iron gates and sudden shutdowns. Each journey requires navigating a landscape of constant uncertainty, where minor procedural delays or arbitrary gate closures can turn a routine commute into an hours-long ordeal.
This manufactured hardship is shared by hundreds of thousands of Palestinians across the West Bank, serving as a constant daily reminder of an institutional directive aimed at making everyday life as exhausting and precarious as possible.
'De facto sovereignty'
In February 2023, weeks after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu returned to office at the head of a far-right coalition, his government handed Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister and himself a settler, civilian authority over the occupied West Bank, including settlement planning and the Civil Administration that rules Palestinian life.
The gates multiplied. Since October 2023, B'Tselem has counted more than 200 new checkpoints, and the Association for Civil Rights in Israel has told the High Court that some of the roadblocks were first erected by settlers, with the army taking them over afterwards.
Meanwhile, the roads are being rebuilt for the settlers. In July 2025, Smotrich announced 918 million shekels ($275m) for West Bank roads, including bypasses so that Israeli motorists can avoid Palestinian towns. "This is how you do de facto sovereignty," he said. In May 2026, the government added $270m for roads linking 20 settlements and outposts.
The settlers who use those roads have never been more violent. The 397 settler attacks Ocha logged in October were the most it has recorded in any month since it began counting in 2006.
Human Rights Watch counts 107 Palestinian communities fully or partly displaced since January 2023. B'Tselem, in its September report on the West Bank, calls a closed gate "an instrument" of dispossession and elimination.
International legal frameworks and human rights documentation unequivocally classify these measures not as legitimate defensive precautions but as severe violations of the fundamental right to freedom of movement. The International Court of Justice found the wall contrary to international law in 2004 and Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful in 2024.
What is marketed under the sanitised label of "security policy" is nothing less than an institutionalised system of apartheid, as Amnesty International and B'Tselem have both documented. It is the direct expression of an Israeli Zionist racist mentality that views Palestinians not as human beings with equal rights to their own land, but as an inconvenience to be cleared away.
While this apparatus of control generates immense daily suffering and fuels a justified, burning anger, it ultimately fails in its primary ambition. The occupation may choke our roads, steal our hours and turn simple commutes into gruelling daily battles, but it will never erase our presence or break our resolve.
We will suffer, we will rage, but we will not leave. Every Palestinian who waits through the bottlenecks returns home to their village and remains rooted on their ancestral land, turning the simple act of staying into an unyielding refutation of quiet displacement.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Hegseth entourage reprimanded by guard at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Hegseth entourage reprimanded by guard at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
Guard at memorial site can be heard yelling at group to ‘maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times’.
Hegseth scolded by security at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
A video has spread online showing a military guard scolding a group accompanying United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth during a visit to the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.
On Wednesday, Hegseth and members of his staff visited the memorial site at Arlington National Cemetery.
But as they paused to take group photos, they could be heard laughing. The video shows an Army sentinel turning to loudly reprimand them.
“All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times,” the guard yelled.
The tomb, seen as a sombre memorial to those who have died in war, marks the resting place of unidentified US soldiers from World War I and later conflicts.
A member of the 3rd Infantry Regiment – known as the “Old Guard” – watches over the site 24 hours a day.
The incident, which took place on Veterans Day, comes amid speculation over whether Hegseth will be able to maintain his cabinet-level position in the administration of US President Donald Trump.
Hegseth narrowly avoided a vote on articles of impeachment brought against him in the US House of Representatives on Tuesday, with Republican lawmakers banding together to derail the effort.
Critics have accused Hegseth of overseeing several unlawful actions while in his post, including spearheading the US-Israel war on Iran without seeking congressional authorisation first.
The war became a central topic in the November 3 midterm elections, in which Trump’s Republican Party suffered a bruising setback, losing both chambers of Congress.
Hegseth has also championed a campaign of deadly strikes targeting alleged drug-trafficking boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean. Legal scholars have called that campaign a series of extrajudicial killings.
During his time as defence secretary, Hegseth has been criticised for weakening rules meant to diminish civilian casualties in US strikes.
In addition, his tenure has been marked by right-wing culture war issues: he has sought to ban transgender service members from the armed forces and instituted testosterone testing for male soldiers.
In response to Wednesday’s interaction at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement that the sentinel had responded “correctly”.
He also underscored Hegseth’s commitment to respecting US soldiers.
“The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored – and will always honor – the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe,” Parnell said.

https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/mouveme.title: Le mandat historique des forces progressistes
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/mouveme.author: Patrick Le Hyaric
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/mouveme.text:
Par Patrick Le Hyaric
Il est des moments rares où le mouvement social cesse de n’être qu’une simple contestation pour devenir un grand élan populaire et politisé. Un élan qui ne se limite plus à réclamer, mais porte en lui des enjeux d’avenir. Des enjeux de civilisation. Nous y sommes.
C’est au cœur d’une vie quotidienne asphyxiante, marquée par la violence des guerres économiques et militaires, suspendue aux flux incertains du pétrole et de l’énergie, et au sortir d’un été caniculaire écrasant – véritable électrochoc pour les consciences –, que le mécontentement et la colère ont changé de nature.
Ce qui s’exprime désormais, c’est le rejet global d’un système dont les gouvernants et les possédants font croire qu’il est indépassable. Là est le point de bascule : entre des conditions de vie devenues insupportables et l’usure des dogmes capitalistes du vieux monde agonisant – à l’instar de cette chimérique théorie présidentielle du « ruissellement », qui prétend que les profits insolents d’aujourd’hui feraient demain le bonheur de tous –, la focale des combats s’est élargie. La vision s’est globalisée, le rassemblement s’est amplifié, et la contestation déploie sa force souveraine.
Ce souffle nouveau traverse toute l’Union européenne, porté par les révoltes d’une jeunesse en rupture. Ses protestations s’enracinent d’abord dans l’expérience brute du quotidien : le vertige du mal-logement, la morsure de l’inflation sur son niveau de vie comme sur celui des parents et des grands-parents, le délabrement de l’institution éducative, mais aussi la sélection et les contenus des programmes au service du système, les horizons professionnels obstrués et le fléau persistant des discriminations.
Le tout converge en un cri d’alarme des jeunesses s’opposant à un avenir qu’on tente de leur imposer, alors que s’aiguisent les crises anthropologique et écologique.
Au fil des mobilisations, les jeunes Européens ont forgé une certitude : ces blessures quotidiennes ne sont que les symptômes d’un même mal. Elles sont les façades d’un système global universellement bloqué, qui n’offre plus d’autre perspective que l’adaptabilité, l’employabilité, la flexibilité et la précarité de vie, et l’arrogante injonction à se résigner au moindre mal.
À chaque revendication, à chaque exigence populaire, des défilés sur les écrans de ministres et de prétendus sachants expliquent cyniquement que, si les demandes sociales sont « certes légitimes », il est rigoureusement impossible de les satisfaire.
Par cet aveu constant, ils dévoilent l’incapacité structurelle du capitalisme à répondre aux besoins fondamentaux du peuple.
Détourner les yeux des fortunes indécentes
Cette mise en scène d’une prétendue impuissance publique se joue au moment même où nos concitoyens mesurent l’ampleur vertigineuse des profits de grands groupes comme Total, des dividendes versés aux actionnaires-propriétaires et des monumentaux cadeaux fiscaux et sociaux octroyés par les pouvoirs successifs aux forces du grand capital. Il devient alors limpide pour chacun que le besoin d’accumulation du capital et des fortunes à un pôle de la société s’oppose de front, en son cœur même, au bien-être de l’immense majorité.
Face aux revendications, le pouvoir agite invariablement le spectre d’une dette publique qu’il a pourtant lui-même méthodiquement creusée. Les données objectives sont à cet égard édifiantes : selon une analyse économique parue dans les colonnes du journal La Tribune, l’assèchement des contributions des grandes firmes capitalistes et des ménages les plus aisés au budget de l’État atteint a minima le montant astronomique de 929 milliards d’euros cumulés entre 2018 et 2025.
Ce gouffre abyssal est le produit direct de choix politiques délibérés : affaissement de l’impôt sur les sociétés, mutation du CICE en allègement pérenne de cotisations patronales, liquidation progressive de la cotisation sur la valeur ajoutée des entreprises (CVAE) et démantèlement de l’impôt sur les grandes fortunes.
Dans le même temps, la décence la plus élémentaire a volé en éclats : au cours de cette même période, les dividendes distribués par ces géants économiques ont frôlé la somme vertigineuse de 2 000 milliards d’euros.
Dès lors, les appels à la « sagesse » et à la « raison » n’ont qu’un but unique : contraindre le peuple à accepter le dogme même qui obstrue l’avenir de la jeunesse et aggrave le dénuement des générations précédentes. C’est ainsi que mûrit la conscience collective : la dégradation de la vie quotidienne des travailleuses, des travailleurs, des retraités et des jeunes n’est pas une fatalité passagère, mais une crise globale intrinsèquement liée à une organisation sociale qui porte un nom : le capitalisme.
À l’opposé, les mandataires du grand capital installés au pouvoir considèrent ces aspirations populaires comme inacceptables. Ils savent pertinemment qu’elles ébranlent les fondations du modèle de société qui assoit leur domination. Pour eux, mettre fin à l’austérité, endiguer la précarité du travail ou simplement freiner la spéculation reviendrait à gripper la machine à accumuler le capital, à l’instant précis où le système exige son accélération.
Lorsque la jeunesse brandit des slogans en forme de rupture — « Quitter l’époque contemporaine » ou « la fin de leur monde » —, elle révèle l’éveil d’une conscience historique nouvelle. Les temps ne sont plus aux illusions. Ces jeunes ne croient plus aux chimères soufflées par la bourgeoisie, qu’il s’agisse du mirage d’une « croissance verte » ou de la fiction d’une « démocratie sociale » où les travailleurs demeurent pourtant exclus des décisions stratégiques de l’entreprise. Ils ne croient pas davantage à la fable d’une méritocratie dont l’ascenseur social reste désespérément bloqué au sous-sol. Autant d’historiettes qui n’ont jamais eu d’autre but que de sanctuariser les profits du grand capital.
L’heure du dépassement
Ils refusent désormais de consumer leur existence dans cette cage économique égoïste, injuste socialement, patriarcale, antiécologique et raciste ; un carcan systémique que les classes possédantes dépeignent depuis si longtemps comme naturel.
Pourtant, les mouvements en cours, quel que soit leur destin, sonnent l’heure du dépassement. Ils portent l’appel d’une alternative à inventer ensemble, car il n’existe, pour cette aube nouvelle, aucun modèle de société préétabli à copier. Il s’agit d’inventer du neuf. Tout l’enjeu d’une force de transformation démocratique, écologique et féministe, d’une force révolutionnaire, est de se mettre au diapason et au service de cette soif d’émancipation, pour permettre aux jeunes générations de prendre enfin les rênes de leur destin.
Cet enthousiasmant projet porte en lui les germes d’une évolution révolutionnaire. « Nous ne cherchons pas l’unanimité, nous cherchons le mûrissement collectif », proclame ainsi le manifeste des jeunes Italiens et Italiennes adopté le 17 octobre dernier, appelant ardemment à « construire notre propre avenir ».
Qu’y a-t-il de plus beau, de plus fort, pour un militant de l’émancipation humaine, que cette jeunesse accédant à une conscience aiguë du rôle et de la stratégie des pouvoirs en place, qui s’évertuent à caricaturer leurs demandes comme leurs actions ? Qu’y a-t-il de plus utile, de plus beau, que de hisser à la hauteur de l’enjeu historique qui s’avance vers nous ? Face à un système qui utilise la violence institutionnelle et l’autoritarisme comme agressifs boucliers. Et voici que des fractions majoritaires de la haute bourgeoisie n’hésitent plus à activer leur roue de secours, leur assurance-vie : l’extrême droite qui, jour après jour, se vante de « gagner des batailles idéologiques ». La fable des deux extrêmes ne sert en fait qu’à justifier le basculement possible vers un pré-fascisme caché derrière l’immonde projet de « priorité nationale ». Il est d’ailleurs intéressant d’observer la posture du RN/FN qui, ces derniers temps encore, prétendait canaliser la colère légitime des classes populaires contre les « élites » corrompues. Aujourd’hui, le vernis de cette prétendue vertu s’est définitivement craquelé. Et, fidèle à ses origines, le RN/FN en appelle à l’ordre, au refus de l’augmentation du SMIC et à l’accentuation de l’austérité avec son projet de « règle d’or » budgétaire.
Le cœur du mouvement conteste aussi les idées de l’extrême droite : il est vierge de tout relent nationaliste ou identitaire. Il ne se nourrit ni du rejet de l’autre, ni de la logique de concurrence, mais bien du combat contre les inégalités et pour la fraternité. Tout ce qu’exècrent les forces réactionnaires, condamnées à constater avec effroi l’alliance vivante qui se noue entre la jeunesse des quartiers populaires, celle du cœur des métropoles et celle des sous-préfectures.
Le mouvement des lycéens et des étudiants, adossé à la majorité des travailleurs et des retraités, n’est pas une simple réplique à une nouvelle « contre-réforme » ; il est le produit d’une situation existentielle devenue intenable, qui plonge la multitude dans une profonde souffrance sociale.
Ajoutons que ce séisme qui secoue la France possède une résonance profondément européenne et internationale. Les jeunesses font mouvement de concert, selon des modalités d’action similaires, que ce soit en Italie, en Allemagne, en Serbie, au Portugal ou jusqu’en Inde. De Paris à Milan, les lycéens et les étudiants appellent depuis des mois à une transcendance de leur lutte, jetant les bases d’une union populaire d’un type nouveau. Ils ont amorcé une dynamique qu’il convient désormais d’élargir.
C’est là toute la force et l’intelligence politique de la CGT et de Sophie Binet d’avoir su saisir les spécificités de ce soulèvement, en le protégeant des coups du pouvoir tout en démultipliant sa puissance d’impact.
Une convergence vers une victoire électorale ?
Nous voici donc à la croisée des chemins. C’est un tournant historique que l’ensemble des forces progressistes, par-delà leurs différences et parfois leurs divergences, devraient saisir pour faire pencher la balance du côté de la libération de l’immense majorité de la cage idéologique qu’impose un capitalisme en mutation, du côté de l’émancipation.
Qu’il serait beau et fortifiant qu’ensemble les forces progressistes, de gauche et écologistes reçoivent les représentants de la jeunesse pour imaginer les contours de la nouvelle civilisation qui se cherche.
Une convergence qui devrait ouvrir la voie à une victoire électorale, prélude indispensable à la prise de pouvoir effective des travailleuses, des travailleurs et de la jeunesse sur leur travail, sur leurs outils de production et la production même, sur leurs études et leurs formations, sur la mise à bas de toutes les discriminations et dominations. Dans un monde où la préservation du climat, la sauvegarde de la biodiversité et le choix d’une diplomatie de paix s’imposent comme des urgences vitales pour l’humanité, que pèsent encore les vaines querelles dont se repaît le système ? À quoi servent des divisions artificiellement entretenues face à un tel enjeu de civilisation pour le vivant ?
À quoi peuvent bien rimer les stériles polémiques politiciennes au moment même où se trament, sous nos yeux, de dangereuses osmoses entre un prétendu « centre », les droites et l’extrême droite ?
Les divisions entretenues, les glissements autoritaires du pouvoir et le bruit des guerres ne font qu’aplanir le chemin vers une possible victoire de l’extrême droite, à laquelle se rallierait rapidement ce qui reste des forces de droite à l’élection présidentielle. Car le plus important pour eux, c’est de sauver le système. La donne change et met entre nos mains des atouts nouveaux qu’il convient de faire fructifier.
Servir la jeunesse et les classes populaires, qui aspirent à briser la cage où on les enferme, appelle les forces progressistes, démocratiques et humanistes à assurer une mission historique : s’unir, pour sans cesse élargir une unité populaire en action, afin que le point de bascule penche non pas du côté des ténèbres de la réaction et du protofascisme, mais de celui de l’émancipation humaine, de la paix et de la vie.
Avant de partir, une dernière chose…
Contrairement à 90% des médias français aujourd’hui, l’Humanité ne dépend ni de grands groupes ni de milliardaires. Cela signifie que :
- nous vous apportons des informations impartiales, sans compromis. Mais aussi que
- nous n’avons pas les moyens financiers dont bénéficient les autres médias.
L’information indépendante et de qualité a un coût. Payez-le.

https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.title: Two skulls likely belonging to enslaved people returned to Brazil after Harvard used them in eugenics studies
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.author: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.text:
Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s greatest slave revolt but whose remains were taken to the United States and used in racist eugenics studies at Harvard University, were repatriated on Wednesday.
The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century. One was taken about 190 years ago from Salvador, the capital of the state of Bahia; the other, about 160 years ago, from Rio de Janeiro – and were welcomed back in moving, subdued ceremonies in both cities.
The skulls are believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians in the country that received more enslaved Africans than any other during the transatlantic slave trade.
Each was brought back in a padded box inside a reinforced suitcase, carried on flights by Brazilian diplomats after a four-year campaign to recover the remains from Harvard’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in the US.
Brazilian researchers from local universities will now try to learn more about who the two individuals were.
The skulls will not be displayed in museums or have their images released, and the Brazilian government has pledged that they will be buried with funeral rites as soon as the identification process is complete.
“It’s very important to restore the dignity of these people, which was taken from them in life and in death,” said Carolina Dias dos Reis, a government official who travelled to Boston to sign the agreement with Harvard.
The existence of the skulls was revealed in 2022, and Brazilian researchers sought their repatriation from Harvard, but said they faced a drawn-out process that only moved forward after the Brazilian government became involved in late 2024.
In recent months, concerns grew that Donald Trump’s sometimes hostile behaviour towards his Brazilian counterpart, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, could derail the repatriation. But everything worked out.
“We need to recover our past as a country, however difficult and violent it was, so that we can understand what we are living through in the present: the consequences and scars of structural racism,” added Reis.
Slavery was abolished in 1888, but nearly a century and a half later, Afro-Brazilians make up the majority of the population while occupying the bottom of every socioeconomic indicator, dominating the statistics on hunger, poverty, gender-based violence and victims of homicides committed by criminals or the police.
During the repatriation ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, Ivanir dos Santos, a history professor and a cleric of the Afro-Brazilian religion Candomblé, poured a glass of water on to the ground as researchers received the suitcase.
“It was a ritual act because you cannot deal with the remains of our ancestors without paying reverence to them. This is not a research object … for us, that person is still alive in memory and as our ancestor,” he said.
It is not precisely known who the skulls belonged to. The one taken to Salvador is believed to have belonged to a man who took part in the most significant urban slave revolt in Brazilian history, in 1835, when about 600 African Muslims attempted to seize control of what was then the country’s second most important city. They were ultimately defeated by police, who killed 70 rebels.
The man died at a hospital, and a US diplomat, Gideon T Snow, is believed to have sent the skull to Boston.
The Bahia Islamic Cultural Centre, one of the most active campaigners for its repatriation, has named the man Arakunrin, meaning brother in Yoruba.
Even less is known about the other person: initially, only that they were “an individual … exhumed from the ‘streets of Rio de Janeiro’” in the 1860s. Brazilian government officials, however, said on Wednesday that Harvard researchers had told them that some features – including that the skull was smaller than that of an adult man but larger than that of a child – suggested it may have belonged to a woman.
Bruno Veras, a historian who was part of the group that closely followed the repatriation, cross-referenced diaries, letters and maps of the city and believes the skull may have been taken from a cemetery for newly arrived Africans who either did not survive the long Atlantic crossing or died soon after disembarking.
The person believed to have taken it to the US was Walter Hunnewell, a student from a wealthy Boston family. He was part of an expedition led by the Harvard professor Louis Agassiz, who was in Brazil trying to document physical types to support his racist theories.
“To steal a skull and take it to another country was violent even in the context of racist research,” said Veras.
Researchers in forensic anthropology will now try to confirm the sex of the individuals and other information through measurements of the skulls – the one in Salvador is complete, while the one in Rio is missing its jaw – and microscopic analyses. If necessary, they will seek authorisation to carry out genetic or dating tests.
“This history of slavery cannot be undone,” said Irina Feisthauer Silveira, a diplomat who carried one of the skulls. “But acknowledging the mistakes of the past with transparency is a first step towards building a more equal, just and less violent future.”

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.title: US taxpayer group calls on ICC to investigate Trump, Rubio for 'aiding' Gaza genocide
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Fleur Hargreaves
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
US taxpayer group calls on ICC to investigate Trump, Rubio for 'aiding' Gaza genocide
A group of US taxpayers and international human rights lawyers have officially called on the International Criminal Court (ICC) to investigate President Donald Trump and his top diplomat Marco Rubio for "aiding and abetting genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity committed by Israel in Gaza".
They announced it at a press conference at the court's home in The Hague, in the Netherlands, on Wednesday.
The submission to the court was organised by the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (Taag), and includes sworn affidavits from doctors who worked in Gaza, firsthand eyewitness accounts, whistleblower testimony, video evidence, and extensive documentation of what they say is US military, financial, diplomatic, and political support for Israel, the group said.
Among those involved are Dr Feroze Sidhwa, a trauma surgeon who undertook two missions in Gaza, and David McIntosh, a former contractor with the scandal-plagued and now-defunct Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, both of whom have previously shared their detailed experiences with Middle East Eye.
It took nearly a year to compile the necessary proof that without the US, Israel could not have carried out what the United Nations and Holocaust scholars have described as a genocide of Palestinians in Gaza, Taag said in a press release accompanying the announcement.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Why the US, Mexico and Guatemala may lose their measles-free status
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Why the US, Mexico and Guatemala may lose their measles-free status
A independent commission is meeting to review whether countries in the Americas still meet its measles elimination criteria.
International health experts are meeting in Washington, DC, this week to determine which countries in the Americas have endemic measles transmission.
The outcome could decide whether the United States, Mexico and Guatemala retain their “measles elimination status”: a designation that the virus has not spread uncontrolled domestically for at least 12 months.
The Pan American Health Organization’s (PAHO) Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission (RVC) began its annual conference on Tuesday to assess the countries’ status. The conference will adjourn on Friday.
The review comes as a sharp resurgence of the virus has spread across the Americas, with the US experiencing its largest and deadliest measles outbreak in nearly 30 years. The US has held its elimination status since 2000, but it risks losing it this year.
The commission will review reports submitted by all 35 PAHO member states, with particular attention to countries experiencing prolonged outbreaks.
How does the process work? Al Jazeera breaks down what happens in this explainer.
Who decides whether a country has eliminated measles?
The RVC is an independent panel of international experts in epidemiology, public health and virology. The group advises PAHO, which is part of the World Health Organization, on which countries have maintained the elimination of measles and rubella.
The Americas became the first region in the world to eliminate endemic measles transmission in 2016, following decades of vaccination campaigns. For this year’s review, the commission is examining epidemiological data from 2025 and the first half of 2026.
Which countries could lose their elimination status this year?
The US, Mexico, Guatemala, Peru and Bolivia are at risk. Canada lost its status last November.
The US, which eliminated endemic measles transmission in 2000, has experienced sustained outbreaks since January 2025. Mexico has also reported prolonged transmission.
PAHO reported 57,666 confirmed measles cases across 17 countries and territories in the Americas between January and October 2026.
How does a country lose its status?
Experts at the conference evaluate whether infections result from separate introductions of the virus or whether the same strain has circulated locally.
Reported measles cases or deaths alone do not determine whether a country loses its elimination status. Some cases, for instance, come from exposure to measles during travel. A limited outbreak due to such exposure would not result in the loss of a country’s measles elimination status.
Under PAHO’s criteria, a country loses its elimination status if the same measles virus strain continues to spread uninterrupted for at least 12 months in a country or defined geographical area.
Investigators use genetic sequencing to determine whether infections are linked to the same virus strain. They also examine epidemiological data to establish how the virus has spread and whether transmission has been interrupted.
In addition, the commission considers vaccination coverage, how healthcare systems monitor measles cases, and the speed of outbreak responses in its decisions.
When will the decision be announced?
The commission’s deliberations in Washington run until Friday. It will assess the evidence and make recommendations on the status of individual countries to PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa, who will make the final determination.
The official announcement is expected early next week following the conclusion of the conference.
What happens if the US loses its status?
Experts agree that the US will likely lose its measles elimination status, marking a reversal of a major public-health achievement.
“It would be a disappointment, not a shock,” Matt Ferrari, the director of Pennsylvania State University’s Center for Infectious Disease Dynamics, told Al Jazeera. “This is moving backwards from a great public health achievement, and to see that backslide is just heart-wrenching.”
Although the loss of status would not trigger any immediate consequences, those working in the field say it would be an embarrassment.
“It’s a stain on your health programme,” Edwin Asturias, a professor of infectious disease and epidemiology at the University of Colorado, told Al Jazeera.
The long-term effects include greater pressure on public-health systems, which must devote resources to identifying infections, tracing contacts, conducting laboratory tests, isolating patients and organising vaccination campaigns.
When asked about how a country generally responds to losing its measles elimination status, Asturias pointed to Brazil, which found itself in that predicament in 2019. The country regained its measles-free designation in 2024 after launching a strategic vaccination campaign. But Asturias does not believe that the US will mount a similarly robust response.
On Tuesday, Erica Schwartz, the director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said losing elimination status would not change the agency’s approach to measles.
“Let’s say we did lose our measles elimination status. We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working with the states,” Schwartz told the news agency Reuters.
Ferrari said the announcement could nonetheless galvanise action at state and local levels by giving public-health officials and advocates shared language.
“Think globally, act locally,” Ferrari said. “We all will have the same language to talk about what’s going on. And that’s surprisingly important.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Cameroon: Who is really calling the shots?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Cameroon: Who is really calling the shots?
Biya’s absences raise questions about who holds power and what comes next in Cameroon.
Yaounde, Cameroon – A dispute over roadworks in Yaounde in March, ahead of Pope Leo XIV’s visit to Cameroon the following month, highlighted tensions between central government and municipal authorities.
The disagreement involved Housing and Urban Development Minister Celestine Ketcha Courtes and Yaounde City Mayor Luc Messi Atangana over the rehabilitation of a road along the papal visit route, according to local media reports.
The episode raised a broader question about competing centres of authority in Cameroon: Who exercises power when President Paul Biya is absent?
Biya, 93, has governed Cameroon since 1982. His prolonged absences from public view have intensified scrutiny on how decisions are made, who has access to him and how much authority is exercised by those around him.
Biya returned to Yaounde on August 20 after more than 10 weeks abroad, following a stay in Europe that began on June 7 . His return did little to dispel questions about the management of power.
The issue is not simply whether the state continues to function. It is whether the institutions and informal networks built around one president can manage power coherently when he is not visibly directing government.
Cameroon’s constitution gives the president extensive executive authority. He defines national policy, appoints the prime minister and, based on the latter’s proposal, other members of government.
He is also commander-in-chief of the armed forces. The prime minister heads the government and directs its activities within the framework of the president’s policy.
Who holds executive authority?
Under Section 10 of the constitution, the president may delegate some of his powers to the prime minister, other members of government and senior administrative officials, within the scope of their respective responsibilities.
Where the president is temporarily unable to perform his duties, he must expressly delegate some of his functions to the prime minister or, if the prime minister is also unavailable, another member of government.
An absence abroad does not, in itself, establish that the president is temporarily unable to perform his duties or automatically transfer his constitutional powers to the prime minister.
The government has not provided a detailed public account of whether a clear delegation of presidential functions is in effect during Biya’s prolonged absences.
Research by the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) found that Biya spent at least four and a half years abroad on private visits over a period of more than three decades.
The investigation, which examined records of his travels from 1982 onwards, renewed questions about how much government business depends on his direct involvement.
One figure central to that debate is Ferdinand Ngoh Ngoh, the secretary-general at the presidency.
According to the official biography published by the Prime Minister’s Office, his responsibilities include receiving the president’s instructions, monitoring the implementation of presidential decisions and coordinating administrations attached to the presidency.
On February 5, 2019, Biya signed Decree No. 2019/043, granting Ngoh Ngoh a permanent delegation of signature. The measure gave him authority to sign certain official documents on the president’s behalf.
A delegation of signature, however, is not a transfer of presidential powers. Ngoh Ngoh is not constitutionally the president’s successor, and his formal responsibilities should not be confused with the informal political influence attributed to him.
The influence of the inner circle
Other figures regularly mentioned in discussions about the presidency include First Lady Chantal Biya and the president’s son, Franck Biya. Neither holds a constitutional executive office. Claims about their influence and about rival networks around the president are difficult to establish independently.
Ryan Cummings, an Africa-focused security analyst, has argued that individuals close to the president may be playing increasingly tangible roles as questions grow about the management of power.
His assessment points to the importance of the presidential circle but does not establish who makes particular decisions or on whose authority.
Access to the president does not, in itself, establish that those around him exercise executive powers.
An uncertain succession
The succession question has become more pressing following a constitutional amendment approved on April 14 this year. The amendment reintroduced the office of vice president, with the president given the authority to appoint and dismiss its holder.
Under the revised Article 6, the vice president would assume the presidency if the office became vacant through the president’s death, resignation or permanent incapacity established by the Constitutional Council.
The vice president would complete the remainder of the presidential term.
The law also provides for circumstances in which there is no vice president or the vice president is unable to perform the duties of the office. In either case, a presidential election must be held between 20 and 120 days after the post officially becomes vacant.
The Senate president would serve as interim president until a new president is elected. If the Senate president is unable to perform the role, the responsibility passes to the Senate vice president, according to the order of precedence in the Senate.
The amendment establishes a formal succession mechanism but leaves the appointment of the vice president in Biya’s hands. As of November 10 , no appointment had been publicly announced.
The absence of a designated vice president means the new succession arrangement has yet to be tested. If the presidency became vacant before an appointment, the constitution provides for an interim presidency under the Senate president and a new presidential election. Accounts of competing factions and efforts to position potential successors should therefore be treated as assessments, not evidence of an agreed succession plan.
Military reshuffles and wider risks
Military appointments during Biya’s absence have added another dimension to the debate.
On August 4 , the Reuters news agency reported that three presidential decrees had reshuffled the senior military leadership. The changes included replacing commanders in four of Cameroon’s five joint military regions, promoting the head of the Presidential Guard from colonel to brigadier general and appointing a new commander of the Rapid Intervention Brigade.
Robert Besseling, CEO of intelligence advisory firm Pangea-Risk, interprets the changes partly through the lens of loyalty and the management of potential threats to the presidency. The decrees do not explain the reasons for the appointments, making their political significance difficult to establish independently.
The stakes extend beyond the presidential palace. Cameroon faces a separatist conflict in its English-speaking regions and attacks by armed groups linked to Boko Haram in the Far North.
Uncertainty over political authority at the centre could complicate the government’s response to these challenges, even as state institutions continue to operate.
Opposition criticism has focused on the concentration of executive authority. Social Democratic Front leader Joshua Osih criticised the constitutional amendment during the parliamentary debate in April. In remarks reported by Focus Media Afrique on April 3 , he argued that the reform weakened democratic legitimacy and reinforced the centralisation of power.
The government, meanwhile, has defended the president’s authority to make appointments. Communication Minister and government spokesman Rene Emmanuel Sadi told French broadcaster RFI in August that Biya was entitled to decide when to form a new government. The presidency did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Not all observers see an immediate breakdown in state administration. Paul Anchang, a Yaounde-based political analyst, argues that institutions continue to perform their functions. Besseling, however, offers a more critical assessment of the political situation.
The distinction between a functioning state and an accountable centre of political authority remains at the heart of Cameroon’s predicament.
Government business may continue, but the concentration of power around one individual leaves unresolved questions about who exercises authority in his absence and how it will eventually be transferred.
As Robert Besseling puts it: “The political scene suffers from distinct institutional paralysis.”

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: Tyler Perry’s The Gospel of Christmas review – Netflix unloads more slapdash festive fare
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Andrew Lawrence
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
Thanksgiving is right around the corner, which means Christmas creep is in full effect and the floodgates holding back the seasonal tide of holiday movies have opened to fully drown yuletide junkies in cheer. Among the first out of the gates is Netflix’s The Gospel of Christmas, brought to you by the maker of A Madea Christmas.
Instead of Tyler Perry in drag, reluctantly upholding the role of family linchpin, this time it’s Durrell Babbs – AKA the R&B stalwart Tank – playing Isaac, a secular musician who is forced into ministry when his pastor father charges him with resurrecting a sister congregation that’s become a blight in a New York neighborhood defined by immorality and anomie. (East New York, maybe.) The 103-minute feature is both a ploy to horn in on Hallmark’s well-established territory and a proper return to Perry’s roots in gospel musical theater – but with considerably more money behind it and greater latitude to bend the usual chestnuts on faith and family toward his Old Testament-facing sermons.
Now a billionaire studio owner, Perry has as much claim to the title of film-maker as DJ Khaled does to the title of producer. The actual production is quite secondary to the names attached – and Tank is just the start of this star parade. Fantasia Barrino Taylor plays his dutiful wife, while Chanté Moore – the ageless 90s soul siren – brings tension as the heathen ex Isaac gigged around with before settling down. The rest of the above-the-line congregation reads like the kind of lineup you might expect to see on the funeral program for an Aretha Franklin-level Black American treasure: gospel royalty CeCe Winans, super producer Fred Hammond, pulpit grand dame Shirley Caesar. It’s just viewers’ good luck that these folk arrive with plenty of onscreen experience and thus don’t have to rely on Perry’s hasty direction.
The disregard for detail announces itself from the fade-in, as a disappointing bar gig has Isaac storming out with a liquor bottle and smashing it in frustration before rushing into cross-traffic. But viewers never see the grab, the shatter or other basic coverage that Perry, as director, should have made sure was there. (So it goes, I guess, when the top dog insists on hoarding all the major credits.) Instead, Perry jumps right to the payoff: Isaac being hit by a car, flying into the air and tumbling end over end four times before his humble landing compels a come-to-Jesus turnaround.
Tank is neatly typecast here, his hooded eyes and tur-tle-necks immediately establishing Isaac as very much A Thing. But if the current season of Reasonable Doubt has proved anything, it’s that he is far better deployed as a villain than a conflicted saint. Some viewers will surely be spitting out their eggnog the first time they see Isaac leaning on the guardian angel played by John Gray – the Oprah-endorsed mega-preacher whose hallowed persona has taken a few knocks. Perry has Isaac puttering around in a sturdy Volvo wagon, a car the director famously invoked in a wider rebuke of his “highbrow negro” critics (ahem).
And yet this stage show set to screen manages to stay on track thanks to musical direction from gospel crossover king Kirk Franklin, no doubt. You can see and hear Franklin’s influence in the way the singers’ performances drive their characters’ evolution – Isaac moving from surly one-man bar show to tentative church recruit to confident gospel showman. It helps distract from Perry’s typically ham-fisted flourishes. The antagonist whose name is just “I’m the devil” spelled backwards (Beauty in Black alpha-cad Ricco Ross). The mix of Party City-grade angel costuming, kabuki stuntwork and shameless AI effects. The dead-end New York City soundstage that looks repurposed from the original production of Rent.
But if you absolutely must help Perry back to the front of Netflix’s most-watched carousel, do it for Barrino Taylor. The season three American Idol winner makes a compelling case for how much she has grown as an actor since her Broadway credits in After Midnight and The Color Purple. She is clearly in her element here as the steel magnolia – her tsunami of insecurities about her marriage, mission and mute son kept at bay by relentless optimism and unshakeable faith. And when the facade cracks and she’s forced to cry out, she doesn’t just make a joyful noise. She brings down the house.
If you can take The Gospel of Christmas for what it is – a rushed mashup of Miracle on 34th Street and The Preacher’s Wife – it should make for perfectly serviceable screen decoration. Just don’t expect to come away converted to Tyler Perry’s fruitcake approach to film-making: overstuffed, a bit nutty and growing more stale by the hour.
- Tyler Perry’s The Gospel of Christmas is available on Netflix now

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/us-ta.title: US taxpayer group calls on ICC to investigate Trump, Rubio for 'aiding' Gaza genocide
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/us-ta.author: MEE staff
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/us-ta.text:
US taxpayer group calls on ICC to investigate Trump, Rubio for 'aiding' Gaza genocide
A group of US taxpayers and international human rights lawyers have officially called on the International Criminal Court (ICC) to investigate President Donald Trump and his top diplomat Marco Rubio for "aiding and abetting genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity committed by Israel in Gaza".
They announced it at a press conference at the court's home in The Hague, in the Netherlands, on Wednesday.
The submission to the court was organised by the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (Taag), and includes sworn affidavits from doctors who worked in Gaza, firsthand eyewitness accounts, whistleblower testimony, video evidence, and extensive documentation of what they say is US military, financial, diplomatic, and political support for Israel, the group said.
Among those involved are Dr Feroze Sidhwa, a trauma surgeon who undertook two missions in Gaza, and David McIntosh, a former contractor with the scandal-plagued and now-defunct Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, both of whom have previously shared their detailed experiences with Middle East Eye.
It took nearly a year to compile the necessary proof that without the US, Israel could not have carried out what the United Nations and Holocaust scholars have described as a genocide of Palestinians in Gaza, Taag said in a press release accompanying the announcement.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Taag filed an Article 15 communication with the ICC, "providing the Office of the Prosecutor with an extensive evidence submission that achieves the legal threshold for arrest warrants to be issued for both officials", Taag co-founder Seth Donnelly said at the press conference.
"We urge the Office of the Prosecutor to act quickly on this evidence," he added. "We have tried, through extensive litigation, to have the US federal court system intervene to stop the participation of US officials in the crime of genocide. The US court system has proven incapable, again and again and again, from addressing this crime."
More than 74,500 Palestinians have been killed by Israel in Gaza over a span of three years, with Israeli air strikes and sniper fire continuing well past a year after the October 2025 ceasefire was agreed. The Lancet medical journal estimates a far higher death toll once all remains are recovered.
At least 19 children were killed by Israel in Gaza last month alone, the health ministry said.
Utilising the law
The ICC already has two outstanding warrants for the arrest of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant.
While the US has long been hostile to the ICC, the Trump administration, in particular, has made it a priority to sanction and dismantle the legal body.
Just hours after one of the ICC's founding judges won the Nobel Peace Prize last month, the US moved to cut off the court from the US-dominated international banking system.
The measures followed earlier sanctions against half of the court's 18 judges and much of its leadership, including its president and chief prosecutor.
"The ICC is fighting for its life," Reed Brody, counsel for Human Rights Watch, told MEE on Wednesday. "But Taag is doing what they should be doing."
Brody is a war crimes lawyer and organised a similar ICC submission last year to investigate former US President Joe Biden and his Secretary of State Antony Blinken.
"I would be surprised to see the court taking any kind of bold action at this point," he added, but considered it possible that the two deputy prosecutors currently in charge may want to use this moment to make a bid for the top spot by not "bending the knee to the United States".
"I think you have to do this," Brody said of Taag's efforts. "I think this is what the law and the courts are there for."
The ICC's chief prosecutor, Karim Khan, was ousted earlier this year by member states after a misconduct probe. Khan denied any wrongdoing.
'Brick by brick'
Taag was able to proceed with its court submission after a US federal judge last month blocked the Trump administration from potentially imposing civil or criminal liability on two US-based human rights groups that carry out work in "service" of ICC cases.
Taag was one of those groups, in addition to Democracy for the Arab World Now (Dawn), which was founded by the late MEE columnist Jamal Khashoggi.
Judge Jesse Furman of the Southern District of New York said the plaintiffs "demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits of their claim that the [presidential executive] Order violates their First Amendment rights to speak", and that "[t]he loss of First Amendment freedoms, for even minimal periods of time, unquestionably constitutes irreparable injury".
Furman then issued a preliminary injunction blocking any speech-based punitive measures against the two groups.
Dawn and Taag said they felt compelled to immediately go to court after Rubio wrote in an opinion piece that the US was willing to dismantle the ICC "brick by brick" earlier this year.
Four other US-based rights groups have also sued the Trump administration over its sanctions on the ICC in a separate case, insisting that Trump's power to sanction the court is "based on a pseudo national emergency that has no basis in fact". That case is ongoing.
In the early weeks of his presidency nearly two years ago, Trump signed Executive Order 14203, granting US officials the power to impose sanctions on foreigners for supporting the ICC's investigations into US and Israeli nationals for war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide.
He made it a federal offence to provide a "service" to, or receive one from, a sanctioned individual or entity.
While Washington played a role in the early development of the ICC and signed the Rome Statute in 2000 under the presidency of Bill Clinton, it never submitted the statute to the Senate for ratification, amid fears the ICC could prosecute US military personnel and officials for alleged war crimes, especially in conflicts in Afghanistan and Iraq.
But Trump himself has been blunt about needing to punish the ICC for specifically going after Israel.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
US election results could be positive for Lebanon, Hezbollah chief says
Naim Qassem says Republican losses and Israel’s election result could help Lebanon maintain sovereignty.
Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem has welcomed Republican setbacks in US midterm elections last week and a lacklustre showing for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israeli polls, calling them a boon for Lebanon.
During a speech on Wednesday honouring members of the group killed by Israel, along with their families, Qassem described the elections in the US as an “earthquake” and the Israeli elections as a “defeat”. The bloc of Netanyahu, an arch-nemesis of the group, fell short of the 61 seats it needed to stay in power after the October 27 vote.
Qassem said the results were good for Lebanon and a signal that the country should resist the Trump administration’s push to disarm the group.
“Come, let us rebuild our country together, save it from the darkness of failure, and protect it from the empty rhetoric of those who sow discord and those who rely on American tutelage,” he said in a video-link address.
“Lebanon belongs to all of us. We are partners in building it and sharing the cost of protecting its sovereignty.”
Retaining Hezbollah arsenal
Iran-backed Hezbollah is locked in a standoff with US-backed Lebanese President Joseph Aoun over whether it will relinquish its arms, in a move Washington seeks but the group says would be a surrender to Israel.
The Hezbollah leader insisted it would not hand over its weapons and cited a continued Israeli military occupation over parts of the country’s south.
“There will be no state monopoly on the resistance’s weapons, no regulation, no prohibition, and no disarmament under Israeli occupation,” Qassem said.
The secretary-general assumed the role after Israel assassinated former Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah and his successor Hashem Safieddine in 2024.
Sparking months of ongoing war, the US and Israel launched surprise attacks on Iran in February, assassinating Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Hezbollah’s retaliation by firing missiles and drones into Israel led to weeks of intense Israeli strikes on south Lebanon, in which more than 4,300 people were killed, Lebanese authorities say, and around a million were displaced, according to the United Nations.
Qassem praised Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz for causing a spike in global oil prices and suspending shipping routes, saying it would weaken American and Israeli influence in the region.
US President Donald Trump has also acknowledged the role of the Iran war and the rise in fuel prices it stoked in last week’s electoral drubbing for Republicans, as did US Vice President and likely 2028 electoral hopeful JD Vance.
“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so,” Vance said last week.
Conditions for disarmament
Qassem also warned against Lebanese authorities making commitments and deals that serve Israeli goals and urged them to focus on domestic issues.
“Why are you binding yourselves before the world to positions that serve the Israeli project?” he asked.
Israel continues to occupy large swathes of southern Lebanon and has decimated dozens of the roughly 60 villages and towns it occupies.
Although Israel and Lebanon negotiated a ceasefire with US mediation in June, Israel continues to bomb south Lebanon.
