https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Chickens are synonymous with cowardice. Is it time to stick up for our feathered friends? | Adrian Chiles
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Adrian Chiles
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Chickens don’t have it easy. On top of living largely crap, short lives, they endure the ignominy of collectively being a byword for cowardice. The campaign group People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) has written to the Oxford English Dictionary asking for this definition of “chicken” to be changed. Naturally enough, there are those who have been unafraid to holler “Woke nonsense!” as loud as cocks crowing.
For my part, I think Peta is right to stick up for chickens, but I’m not sure removing a definition – assuming definition-removal is a thing – would make any difference. Chicken, in this sense, is in common use as an adjective, a verb and a noun. It’s got deep roots that are going to take some shifting. And any such move could open up a right can of worms (sorry, worms). What about the vulture, rat, shark and sloth lobbies? Not to mention pigs, snakes, weasels, donkeys, sheep, dogs, parrots and all manner of creatures with whom we share this beleaguered planet.
Poor chickens, though. Who knows how they earned this label? They don’t seem particularly cowardly to me. And if they do seem a bit skittish at times, who can blame them, given that they’re at risk of mortal harm from man, fox and others?
If it’s any consolation to chickens, other languages don’t disrespect their courage to quite such an extent. The Spanish at least say hen rather than chicken, and the French, too, although in France to signify cowardice the poor hen needs to have been out in the rain – poule mouillée being a wet hen.
Elsewhere, Russians, Germans, Italians and Turks use hares and rabbits in this way. With other languages it gets more interesting. A Punjabi-speaking friend tells me she has heard jackals’ bravery called into question. Interesting. I’ve always thought of jackals being more on the front foot, as it were – somewhat fierce and snarly. Apparently, in Punjabi folklore, the jackal is the ultimate symbol of fear and timidity, routinely contrasted with the fearless lion or tiger. I’ll fortify myself with that thought next time I go nose to nose with a jackal. I’ll roar like a lion, so I will, and he, indeed a whole pack of them, will surely shrink away with a whimper.
In Polish the story gets even more fascinating. Here it’s tchórz, the polecat, but in this case the belief in the polecat’s cowardice is so deeply held that the word for coward is actually polecat. Again, I must say I didn’t have polecats down as particularly yellow-bellied. (Yellow-bellied!? What’s that all about? Let’s not go there.) This may be because I have in mind Michael Foot’s characterisation of Norman Tebbit as “a semi-house-trained polecat”. The Poles’ view of polecats references the animals’ defensive behaviour if frightened or cornered. At such times they release a foul smell from their anal glands. Depending on your politics, this may or may not be considered unfair on the late Lord Tebbit. The one time I met him, by the way, he was less polecat than pussy cat – until the microphone came on, at which point the polecat in him woke up and the pussy cat was absent until the interview concluded.
In a similar vein, the Welsh have put a couple of words together to make their word for coward: shit and dog, cachgi, invoking perhaps the image of a dog soiling itself in fright. Seems a bit harsh on the coward as well as the dog, to my mind, but each to their own.
I was deep in this rabbit hole (nice to use rabbit there non-pejoratively) before I thought to investigate the language closest to me after English. In Croatian, Serbian and Macedonian, the word for cuckoo – kukavica – is also the word for coward. My mum’s been calling me a kukavica all my life, in a whole variety of contexts. I’d always taken it as a term of endearment more than anything else. Now I know otherwise. I’m just a coward, plain and simple. Still, I’d rather be a cuckoo than a polecat.
Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins closely watched US Senate race in Mississippi
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Democrat Scott Colom wins closely watched US Senate race in Mississippi
The historic victory flips an eighth US Senate seat for Democrats after last week’s pivotal midterm election.
Democrat Scott Colom has won Mississippi’s closely watched United States Senate race, giving his party a historic victory in a Republican stronghold that has eluded them for decades.
Colom, a prosecutor, will become the state’s first Black senator in more than 140 years. On Wednesday, he narrowly defeated incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in one of the US midterms’ biggest upsets.
The win builds on Democrats’ success after the party delivered an electoral drubbing to the rival Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections.
The left-leaning party flipped at least eight US Senate seats that are currently held by Republicans. A US Senate race in Alaska remains undecided.
For more than a week, the Mississippi contest was too close to call as election officials worked to count more than 100,000 mail-in ballots. Thousands of other residents who could not confirm their registration at voting sites cast provisional ballots that required confirmation of their eligibility.
Colom and Hyde-Smith took markedly different approaches as remaining ballots were counted.
Hyde-Smith was not seen publicly until she returned to Washington this week for the reconvening of the Senate.
Through a statement, however, Hyde-Smith and her team had expressed confidence that she would win after “every legally cast vote is fully and accurately counted”.
Colom, by contrast, has maintained a more public profile since the November 3 midterms. After the election, Colom held a series of events where he castigated his opponent.
“Ultimately, at some point, the senator needs to speak out. Where is Cindy Hyde-Smith?” Colom told reporters on Friday in Jackson, Mississippi. “We want to hear from her. She needs to answer questions. What is her path to victory? She doesn’t have one.”
The US Senate race also was not the first time the two had crossed political paths.
Hyde-Smith, citing concerns about Colom’s position on transgender athletes, had previously blocked him from serving as a federal judge in 2023 after he was nominated by former US President Joe Biden. The position had required Senate approval.
Colom’s win upturns political expectations for Mississippi, a state that US President Donald Trump won by just over 22 points in the 2024 presidential election.
The last time a Democrat won a US Senate race in Mississippi was in 1982, when John Stennis claimed victory over Republican challenger Haley Barbour, who later became governor of the state.
Colom, who has been a proponent of raising the minimum wage, increasing protections for rural hospitals and ending the US-Israel war on Iran, will be sworn in next January.
The 120th Congress will include a record number of Black senators, with seven in total.

https://taz.de/EU-Kommission-stellt-Digi.title: EU-Kommission stellt Digitalgesetz vor: Weniger Täuschung und mehr menschlicher Service
https://taz.de/EU-Kommission-stellt-Digi.author: Svenja Bergt
https://taz.de/EU-Kommission-stellt-Digi.text:
EU-Kommission stellt Digitalgesetz vor: Weniger Täuschung und mehr menschlicher Service
Die EU-Kommission will den Verbraucherschutz im Netz reformieren. Neue Regeln soll es unter anderem für Videospiele, Händler und Influencer geben.
Ein Verbot manipulativer Designs, die Möglichkeit, suchterzeugende Funktionen auszuschalten, und besser gekennzeichnete Werbung bei Influencer:innen. Das sind drei der Punkte, mit denen die EU-Kommission das digitale Dasein von Verbraucher:innen sicherer machen will. „Diese Reform wird den Alltag für die Verbraucher einfacher, gerechter und sicherer machen“, sagte die EU-Kommissarin Henna Virkkunen zum am Mittwoch vorgestellten Digital Fairness Act.
Der Gesetzentwurf ist unter anderem das Ergebnis von diversen Umfragen, die die EU-Kommission unter Europäer:innen hatte durchführen lassen. Die zentrale Frage dabei: Welche größten Sorgen haben Sie im Digitalen? Der Entwurf adressiert nun verschiedene Punkte von mangelhaft gekennzeichneter Werbung bis hin zu süchtig machenden Mechanismen.
Eines der Probleme, die seit Jahren bekannt und trotzdem ungelöst sind: Dark Patterns. Das sind manipulative Designs etwa von Onlinehändlern und Buchungsportalen, die Nutzende zum Beispiel dazu verleiten sollen, mehr zu kaufen oder schneller einen Vertrag abzuschließen.
Klassische Beispiele sind etwa Hinweise darauf, dass nur noch eine kleine Anzahl der Ware verfügbar ist oder momentan eine große Anzahl anderer Nutzer:innen dieses Produkt ebenfalls anschaue. Im Gesetzentwurf heißt es nun: Händler dürften ihre Angebote nicht so designen, dass Verbraucher:innen manipuliert oder getäuscht werden oder ihre wirtschaftliche Entscheidung „wesentlich verzerrt“ werde.
Mehr Schutz für Minderjährige
Ein weiterer Punkt: süchtig machende Designs. Diese sind gerade bei Onlineplattformen beliebt, die die Nutzenden damit länger auf ihrer Seite halten wollen. Typische Beispiele sind Autoplay – nach dem Ende eines Videos startet direkt das nächste – und endloses Scrollen. Solche Funktionen sollen Nutzer:innen abschalten können.
Für Minderjährige sollen, neben Vorgaben aus anderen Gesetzen, die bereits rechtskräftig oder in Arbeit sind, weitere Schutzmaßnahmen Pflicht werden. Dazu gehört etwa, dass die Verwendung virtueller Währungen in Videospielen standardmäßig deaktiviert ist.
Diese virtuellen Währungen können schnell dazu führen, dass Spieler:innen hohe Summen an echtem Geld ausgeben, wenn dieses zuvor eingetauscht werden musste. Auch die umstritten „Lootboxen“ sollen bei Minderjährigen abgeschaltet sein. Das sind virtuelle Überraschungstüten, die in Videospielen teilweise gegen Geld gekauft werden können – häufig nach einem Erfolgserlebnis, sodass die Bereitschaft des:der Spielenden besonders hoch ist, zuzugreifen.
Zudem sollen Verbraucher:innen das Recht bekommen, im Kundenservice mit einem:r menschlichen Ansprechpartner:in zu kommunizieren. Das dürfte immer relevanter werden angesichts der Tendenz vieler Anbieter, mindestens die erste Supportebene mittels KI-Chat abzuwickeln.
Der Digital Fairness Act ist nicht das erste EU-Gesetz zum Verbraucherschutz im Digitalen. EU-Kommissar Michael McGrath sagte jedoch, es handele sich um die „ehrgeizigste Reform der EU-Verbraucherschutzvorschriften seit einer Generation“. Die Vorschläge der EU-Kommission gehen nun an das Europaparlament und die Mitgliedstaaten. Bis sich alle Akteure geeinigt haben, dürften mehrere Monate bis Jahre vergehen.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

For Roberto Vannacci, Giorgia Meloni’s government is too timid
Italy: right, far right and even further right
With elections due next year, Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government risks being outflanked by Roberto Vannacci’s National Future party, which is pushing hard for ‘remigration’ and ‘traditional family values’.
Roberto Vannacci’s book Il mondo al contrario (The world turned upside down) came out in 2023. It offers opinions such as ‘Women should look after the family. Working won’t bring them fulfilment.’ ‘Dear homosexuals, accept it: you’re not normal.’ ‘A foreigner who does not assimilate to the culture of the host country is not an immigrant but an invader.’ The book’s success – Vannacci claims it has sold 300,000 copies – has turned its previously unknown author into a major media presence in Italy.
Vannacci, a paratrooper and former major general who commanded several Italian and NATO special forces missions in Iraq and Afghanistan in the 2000s and 2010s, is the new standard-bearer of the Italian far right but is currently suspended from the army until July 2027. The defence ministry has imposed this punishment on him twice, in February 2024 and July 2026, on the grounds that his publications violate the ‘principle of neutrality and impartiality of the armed forces’ and damage the institution’s ‘prestige and reputation’.
Matteo Salvini, leader of the far-right Lega and Italy’s deputy prime minister, recruited him to his party shortly before the 2024 European elections. But having won a seat in the European parliament, Vannacci left the Lega in February 2026, after several months of internal tensions, and announced he was launching his own party, Futuro Nazionale (National Future), which currently stands at 7-9% in the opinion polls.
Vannacci believes the rightwing coalition government led by Giorgia Meloni (Fratelli d’Italia, far right) is too timid, especially on immigration and the defence of the traditional family. He also disagrees with them over the war in Ukraine: he opposes both military support for Kyiv and sanctions against Russia.

https://citylimits.org/keeping-taino-cul.title: Keeping Taíno Culture Alive: Bronx Exhibit Celebrates the Legacy of Bobby González
https://citylimits.org/keeping-taino-cul.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/keeping-taino-cul.text:
Share This Article
A new exhibit at the Museum of Bronx History explores the life of the Puerto Rican poet, storyteller and educator who dedicated nearly four decades to preserving Indigenous culture and challenging stereotypes about the South Bronx.
For Bobby González, preserving Indigenous history began close to home: inside his family’s bodega in the South Bronx.
Growing up near the Melrose Houses, González encountered people from different Indigenous backgrounds who visited the neighborhood store owned by his parents. Those conversations helped shape his understanding of his own Taíno heritage and inspired a lifelong commitment to educating others about Indigenous history.
Now, three years after his death, his work is being remembered through a new exhibition at the Museum of Bronx History.
“From the South Bronx Reservation: Bobby González, Taíno Indian,” which opened Oct. 8 and runs through March 2027, explores the life of the Puerto Rican poet, storyteller and educator who dedicated nearly four decades to preserving Indigenous culture and challenging stereotypes about the South Bronx.
Born in 1951, González grew up in a Puerto Rican family whose parents migrated to New York after World War II. His father worked as a short order cook before opening a bodega in the 1970s, where González and his brothers helped run the family business.
According to Stephen Payne, director of the Bronx County Historical Society, the bodega played an important role in shaping González’s identity.
Visitors included people with Cherokee, Quechua, Lenape and other Indigenous backgrounds. Their conversations encouraged González to learn more about Indigenous communities across the Americas and explore his own ancestry.
That experience later influenced the phrase “South Bronx Reservation,” which González used to describe the neighborhood’s Indigenous presence.
Payne explained that the phrase also reflected similarities between the South Bronx and some Native American reservations, including struggles with pollution and limited resources.
For González, the neighborhood was more than a place where he grew up. It became the foundation of his writing, poetry and cultural activism.
His widow, Maria Aponte González, remembered him as someone who remained deeply connected to his community.
“He was a very gentle spirit,” she said. “Never yelled, never raised his voice.”
She described her late husband as approachable, calm and someone to whom community members frequently turned for advice.
González co-founded the cultural organization Taíno del Norte, organized the annual Bronx Native American Festival and wrote several books, including “The Last Puerto Rican Indian.” He also traveled across the country, speaking at schools, colleges and museums about Indigenous history.
Some of González’s belongings, via the Bronx History Museum.
His mission was to challenge the belief that Taíno people—a native group that originally inhabited the Caribbean, including Puerto Rico—had disappeared centuries ago.
“We are Taíno, we are still here,” Payne said, recalling a phrase used by the organization González helped establish.
Payne explained that the exhibition highlights how Indigenous identity continues to shape Puerto Rican communities, particularly in the Bronx, where González became an important figure in the Taíno cultural revival movement.
The exhibition also arrives at a time when the Bronx is experiencing demographic changes. Payne said rising living costs have contributed to Puerto Rican residents leaving the borough or city, making it increasingly important for community members to share their stories now.
“It’s very important to preserve that part of the history while there still are people in the community who can speak to it,” he said.
The exhibition brings together personal belongings, writings and other materials preserved by González throughout his lifetime.
Aponte González, who co-curated the exhibition alongside documentary filmmaker Edwin Pagán, selected the objects from their home.
“Everything that you’re going to see in the exhibit is Bobby’s work,” she said.
Rather than focusing on how others described her husband, she wanted visitors to experience his legacy through the materials he created himself.
Among his contributions were poetry workshops, including a spoken word series that helped emerging poets develop their voices. He also used puppetry and storytelling to introduce children to Indigenous history and cultural traditions.
Aponte González launched the Bobby González Legacy Project in 2024, following conversations she had with her husband about preserving his work before he became seriously ill.
She described the exhibition as a project that took two years to develop, with support from Pagán and the Bronx County Historical Society.
For Payne, the exhibition also reflects a larger challenge facing historical institutions: preserving the experiences of working class communities whose personal records and belongings are often lost because of housing instability or limited financial resources.
He explained that families who have experienced eviction or frequent moves may no longer have access to photographs, documents and other materials that help tell their histories. In those cases, institutions often rely on oral histories and archival research to recover stories that might otherwise disappear.
González’s collection offered a different opportunity because he had preserved much of his own work, which his widow has made available through the Legacy Project.
Beyond celebrating his accomplishments, both Aponte González and Payne hope the exhibition encourages younger generations to learn about their cultural backgrounds.
“Young people need to make space in their heads. And be open to learn things,” Aponte González said.
For Payne, the larger message is that Indigenous history should not be understood only as something belonging to the distant past.
He hopes visitors recognize that Native American communities continue to preserve, reclaim and develop their cultural traditions today.
Through González’s writing, storytelling and activism, the exhibition offers visitors an opportunity to explore that living history through the experiences of a man who dedicated his life to sharing it.
The exhibition is on display at the Museum of Bronx History, located at 3266 Bainbridge Ave. in the Bronx, through March 2027.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.title: How Democrats Changed Everything
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.author: The Intercept Briefing
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midt.text:
The size of the Democrats’ victory Tuesday night shattered records and even the most optimistic expectations, handing the party a governing mandate with a clear demand for change.
But what do voters want that change to look like? This week on The Intercept Briefing, politics reporter Jessica Washington and managing editor Maia Hibbett break down Tuesday night’s election and hear from voters in Maine, Michigan, and Texas about what drove them to the polls in the midterms that saw a so-called “blue tsunami.”
“The rich get richer, the poor get poorer,” said one voter in Maine. In Michigan, a voter told The Intercept that politics “feels like a game that the rich play sometimes.” A Texas voter expressed anger that President Donald Trump was “spending taxpayer money to renovate the White House and turn it into this gold sanctuary.”
Frustration with wealth inequality and money in politics came up again and again in The Intercept’s conversations with voters. So did a desire for more social welfare spending, Medicare for All, freedom for Palestinians — and responses to transphobic and Islamophobic fearmongering on the campaign trail.
“When Democrats win so far across the board, you can make an argument that any faction of the Democratic Party has the mandate,” said Hibbett, “because Democrats of all stripes won Tuesday night.”
In any case, the results indicated a clear disapproval of the way the Trump administration is governing and the use of fearmongering as a tactic of distraction.
“One lesson maybe for Democrats is there’s no point in attempting to placate people when it comes to bigotry,” said Washington. “The thing that’ll motivate voters is if you can convince them that you’re going to make their lives better, not if you can convince them that you’re playing the middle on an issue of civil rights.”
For more, listen to the full conversation of The Intercept Briefing on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, or wherever you listen to podcasts.
Transcript
Bruce Bryan: We’re just hoping that people step up and tell Washington to go fuck itself.
Jessica Washington: Welcome to the Intercept Briefing. I’m Jessica Washington, politics reporter at The Intercept.
Maia Hibbett: And I’m Maia Hibbett, managing editor here.
JW: Over the past few days, Intercept reporters hit the ground in key states to speak to voters about the issues driving them to the polls. We went to Texas.
Jermiah Robinson: The food prices, for one, and the gas prices.
Darryl Moore: Gotta work two jobs just to make it.
Tiffany Williams: I never really understood, like, how important it is for the minority to vote.
Lenna Tasby: This election is important because this election is going to make or break whether we have a vote or not. There’s a reason why they’re shutting down these polling places.
Intercept reporter Akela Lacy: What are the issues that motivated you this cycle?
Charles Senter: Well, I love Trump.
Helen Dexter: Red ticket all the way. The stop of the Muslim influx.
Lenna Tasby: If you’re spending taxpayer money to renovate the White House and turn it into this gold sanctuary, that’s money that can be used for our military veterans. That’s money that can be used to help with this homeless population. The government needs to be held accountable.
MH: We heard from voters in Michigan.
Erin Horne: The election this year is very critical because Trump’s got two more years.
Zouheir Alawieh: Our democracy is in danger.
Noora Iskander: I believe in Medicare for All. People have a right to self-determination, especially in Palestine.
Wendy: There’s a lot of concern about, of course, the economy, but the data centers, our children’s education.
JW: And we spoke to voters in Maine.
Intercept reporter Noah Hurowitz: What mattered to you as a voter this election?
Tyler Echard: Cost for the most part. Everything keeps going up.
Bryan Golay: The rich get richer, the poor get poorer. At least 30 years ago, there was like a veneer of caring, and now there’s just blatant corruption and greed.
JW: So Maia, what a night.
MH: Yeah, it’s honestly embarrassing if you’re a Democrat and you did not win. They swept the House and the Senate by just about the biggest margins that the pollsters could have predicted. So luckily, the audience I’m concerned about, the pollsters, can rest easy. As of 11:00 a.m. [ET] on Wednesday morning, they had 228 seats in the House, Democrats did. They only needed 218 for a majority, so obviously that is more, and they’re expected to pick up some more seats as some more races get called. They had 54 seats in the Senate, which means that they have a big enough margin that they can’t be stopped from legislating by one lone senator, if one senator wanted to gum things up.
JW: And not at all surprising. The White House tried to spin Republican losses on Trump not being on the ballot and the quality of candidates, despite the fact that Trump repeatedly said at rallies across the country, “Pretend I’m on the ballot.”
Donald Trump: We’re going to ask you to pretend I’m on the ballot, because when I’m on the ballot, this has nothing to do with ego, I just get 49.2 percent more vote. And if we get even a good percentage of that, we’ll have the biggest victory that you’ve ever seen.
MH: He’s saying, “We’ll have the biggest victory ever” — and it was a very historic night. I think people will hear the word “historic” a lot in the coverage in the coming days because of this huge blue wave, not the kind of history Trump wanted, but also because there are some really surprising major firsts.
One of them was that last night, very early, like at 2:30 a.m. [ET], Abdul El-Sayed became the winner of the Senate race in Michigan, which means he will be the first ever Muslim U.S. senator.
Abdul El-Sayed (acceptance speech): To all the kids who watched this last month, to all the parents who struggled to explain why the president openly mocked someone for their name or how they pray, let them know tomorrow that the bad guys lost.
JW: That race was filled with Islamophobia, both in the primary and in the general election. His Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, just peddled in a million different Islamophobic tropes. Voters told our colleague, Matt Sledge, who was out in Michigan speaking with them, that they really didn’t like hearing all of this hate speech.
Zouheir Alawieh: They don’t have any programs for our economy, for our health, for our future. So that’s why they are attacking us as Muslims and as human beings.
Tea Edwards: Just, like, all of the Islamophobic hate campaigns that have been going around will probably sway a few people. The people who are actually researching what will be good for communities I think will see right through it.
MH: This was a campaign that was defined by so much panic about El-Sayed being Muslim. The race ended 25 years after 9/11, and there were all of these really kind of vitriolic Islamophobic tropes. It reminded me a lot of the campaign against [Mayor] Zohran Mamdani here in New York last year. There’s all this fear of the left and this fearmongering suggesting that there’s no way a Muslim candidate could represent American interests.
And of course, one of the big differences between El-Sayed and Mamdani is that El-Sayed is not a socialist.
JW: Say that again for the people in the back, because they are not going to believe you. El-Sayed has described himself as a capitalist who understands how capitalism works, so definitely not a socialist.
I’ve heard him described as much more of a [Sen. Elizabeth] Warren than someone in the Bernie Sanders mold.
MH: But he still faced millions of dollars in outside spending in this race, mostly because of his stance on the United States relationship to one other country.
We’ve heard in some of these deep-blue districts in the House races where socialists were elevated in the primaries, there was a lot of rhetoric on opposing Israel’s genocide in Gaza and fighting U.S. weapons flows to Israel. But it’s pretty rare to hear that from a U.S. Senate candidate, and now from a senator-elect.
JW: It also caused some really ugly drama with his former primary opponent, Haley Stevens.
MH: Do you want to try to recap that as fast as we can, or should I?
JW: I’ll get started and see if you can add in anything that I miss.
So essentially, on the Friday right before [Election Day], Haley Stevens released a statement condemning an ad that was not even created by the El-Sayed campaign, calling on him to condemn the ad, which he did disavow. She also asked him to take back his statements on Israel.
Now, things seemed fine for a second. Haley Stevens had all of these Democratic surrogates going on air saying that she promised to support him. While Haley Stevens’s staffers were at an event for El-Sayed, Haley Stevens popped up at an event supporting the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers, giving him her endorsement.
Maia, is there anything that I missed in that?
MH: Jessie, I think the only thing you missed was just how baffling and strange this episode was. So you mentioned this ad that kicked it off. It was produced by this outside group Rebellion PAC, which is the group headed by Cenk Uygur, who some listeners might know from The Young Turks. He is also famously Hasan Piker’s uncle.
Haley Stevens, as she was struggling to explain why she switched from El-Sayed to the Rogers camp, kept citing Hasan Piker and the “uncle.” It was this kind of almost incomprehensible move where Anderson Cooper, the CNN host, was pressing her at one point, saying, well, you cite his affiliation with Hasan Piker and this part of the Democratic Party you don’t like, but you knew about this before — so what changed?
It really seemed strange. So we sent Matt Sledge out in Michigan to ask some voters what they thought of it, and if they thought that this was a politically savvy move that would have any resonance. And here’s what they said.
Kathleen Britton: I’m so disappointed in Haley Stevens. I gave her serious consideration during the primary.
Jesse Craft: She fought against Mike Rogers, then said somehow he earned her vote. I don’t really understand it. I kinda think it’s career-ending for her.
Wendy: How embarrassing to use an African American church. How embarrassing for you to use our votes and then disregard them because of your own personal issues.
Intercept reporter Matt Sledge: So you don’t think it’s gonna help Mike Rogers?
Kathleen Britton: I do not.
Erin Horne: No, I think she actually helped Abdul.
[Break]
JW: Maia, before the break, you started talking about money and politics, and I want to get into how that shaped the midterms. Last week, we talked about how this election cycle became the most expensive on record. Midterms ad spending is expected to reach north of $11.6 billion. Mega-donors overwhelmingly gave to Republican candidates, including Elon Musk, who spent nearly $450 million, with large sums of that directed at boosting Ken Paxton in Texas, who, by the way, lost to James Talarico. Now, for context, the next highest donors under Musk are a Republican couple [Richard and
Elizabeth Uihlein] who spent $150 million, mostly in Wisconsin and Illinois. 
Jesse Craft: We all see where money is coming from. It’s coming from very, very wealthy billionaires. I don’t think we should be able to buy elections.
Tea Edwards: Politics, it just feels like a game that the rich play sometimes. Kind of feels hopeless when you’re just looking at all of these people and corporations giving money to each other.
MH: You hate to see Elon Musk throw away almost half a billion dollars. It only leaves him so many billions to go.
JW: Heartbreaking.
MH: But, I mean, in Texas, as you mentioned, that money really did not pan out. It didn’t seem to sway voters. It seemed like if anything from the voters who talked to our reporters in Texas, in Michigan, and in Maine, which we’ll get to later, people were really mad about outside election spending and don’t like the idea that billionaires or corporations can buy their elections.
And in Texas, a lot of that money went to propping up this anti-trans panic campaign that Paxton was running. But all that money was not enough to save Paxton from James Talarico. Paxton was a pretty bad candidate: He was mired in too many scandals to keep track of, including a 2015 grand jury indictment on felony securities fraud charges.
In 2020, eight of his top deputies reported to the FBI that he was potentially abusing his office to do favors for a donor and friend. And just earlier this year, he offered a plea deal in a child sex abuse case that seemed to anger Texans and voters.
Remember, this is the era of the Epstein files and people being very concerned about child sex abuse. It did not seem like the wisest calculation for Paxton to offer this while running for Senate.
JW: As it turns out, there is not enough money in the world to buy Ken Paxton out of being Ken Paxton and voters recognizing that. But Republicans tried this cycle to spend big on transphobia and to blanket the airwaves with these anti-trans advertisements.
Elon Musk’s Texas PAC spent $78 million on anti-transgender ads in Texas, which actually accounted for nearly half of all ad spending in support of Paxton. Republicans’ big play in Texas was transphobia — and that play failed.
While clearly it didn’t sway the election, some of those messages did appear to trickle down to voters. Our colleague, Akela Lacy, talked to voters in Dallas and the surrounding areas, and she did come across some voters who said they wanted to support Talarico or even some voters who did support Talarico but were concerned about his stance on trans rights, an issue that Republicans really fearmongered on this cycle yet again after doing it in 2024.
Akela Lacy: When you said you saw some stuff about James Talarico that made you unsure about voting for him, can you say more about that? What did you see, and what’s your impression of him?
Jermiah Robinson: I think I seen something about the LGBTQ+ community? I mean, I don’t really care about it, but I don’t know. People were saying a lot of bad stuff. I think they said something about him —
Canvasser: Encouraging sex change.
Jermiah Robinson: Yeah, on the children. I don’t really stand for that.
Maia Hibbett: The watchdog group Media Matters also put together a montage that showed just how much Republicans really leaned into this transphobic rhetoric.
Danielle Buck: He wants to trans our kids. He believes that there are six genders.
Andrew Kolvet: They wanna indoctrinate your kids. They wanna trans your kids.
Adam Sosnick: They’re gonna trans your kids. They’re gonna Talarico your kids.
Donald Trump Jr.: Trans kids back in school, trans agendas back in school, in your classrooms, with your children.
JW: Clearly, some of that rhetoric did trickle down to voters based on Akela’s conversations, and some people even believed the misinformation being spread in those ads.
But fearmongering was just clearly not persuasive enough to distract people from their lived reality, and that lived reality is that gas prices are up, rent is unaffordable, and grocery prices are up.
I think one lesson maybe for Democrats is, there’s no point in attempting to placate people when it comes to bigotry. The right can and will distort your messages, and so you can stand in your values or not, but the thing that’ll motivate voters is if you can convince them that you’re going to make their lives better, not if you can convince them that you’re playing the middle on an issue of civil rights.
MH: We saw a parallel to this in some ways in Michigan as well, where a lot of the Republican argument was based on this perception of Islamophobia and fearmongering. Ultimately, that was not enough to elevate Mike Rogers over Abdul El-Sayed. In Texas, there’s also, of course, the strong anti-immigrant sentiment that Republicans frequently run on, and I think the statewide results showed us that that narrative really fell apart this cycle.
JW: To your point, clearly, attacks on trans people, attacks on immigrants didn’t work in Texas. Democrats had an amazing night. Gina Hinojosa toppled three-term incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott. The state has not had a Democratic governor since 1990.
MH: And speaking of toppling long-term incumbents that have been hard to get out of office, our colleague Noah Hurowitz was in Maine, where Troy Jackson defeated Susan Collins last night after many Democratic attempts to get her out of office.
This issue of disillusionment with money and politics came up quite a bit when he was talking to Maine voters.
Sharon McDonnell: It’s immoral. It is immoral to have people worried about their fuel and have that much money coming into this. It’s just wrong.
Tyler Echard: The amount they spent on just mailers, not handed at the door but in the mail, is especially, it seems, on the Republican side of things, has been absolutely insane. The amount of money is more than I will probably make in my lifetime, spent in this election.
Charlie Dingman: It’s been extraordinary in Maine, the amount of spending in this race, particularly in the Senate race. I think there’s a lot of fatigue. I think people are tired of it. I have had some conversations with voters at the doors that lead me to think that the extremely negative and extremely untruthful ads may be backfiring.
JW: It seems like those ads backfired. The last voice you heard was Charlie Dingman, Maine Democratic Party chair.
Collins campaigned on her record of securing federal investments for state infrastructure, such as rural hospitals, and she really prided herself on being a moderate Republican who apparently breaks rank with President Donald Trump. But the reality of the situation is quite different.
The Congressional Quarterly Roll Call found that her votes aligned with Trump 90 percent of the time in both of the president’s first and second terms, and voters really noticed that. They understood the difference between what she said she was, a political moderate, and her voting record, which aligned with the really far-right Donald Trump. And that’s something that Noah heard from voters as well.
Sharon McDonnell: She has had this persona of moderate cross-party stuff that’s just really eroded. If you read every article about her, it’s like, “Moderate Susan Collins.” Like, wait a minute, she’s voted with Trump. She hasn’t used her power.
MH: Collins really used that line about her being a moderate and being an independent voice in Washington as a go-to for her campaign.
In past cycles, it has worked. As we alluded to a little bit earlier, the Democrats have mounted challenges against her before. In 2020, they ran a candidate named Sara Gideon, who looked somewhat likely to oust Collins. And I think this cycle, there were a lot of reasons for Democrats to be nervous about this race.
Troy Jackson, the nominee, is a former state senator, and he ran on lowering costs, really centering working-class interests. But he had jumped into the race kind of hastily. If you remember Graham Platner, Jessie, he was the former nominee for Senate in Maine for the Democratic Party, and he was really considered a rising star, but had to drop out because of a series of scandals, and Jackson had to jump in last minute and fill his place.
But ultimately, Jackson pulled it off.
Troy Jackson (acceptance speech): We did it. Working people did it.
JW: Clearly, Jackson had a disadvantage going into this race. There were people who complained and said that he wasn’t as charming as Platner, he wasn’t as polished. But in this election, the ideas and running on affordability seems to have won the day in Maine and really throughout the country.
Collins had a reputation of delivering for the state, but clearly that wasn’t enough to overcome this blue wave across the country and some frustrations with Collins as well.
But Maia, taking a step back to look at the full scope of Democratic wins, what do you make of their gains on Tuesday? Are there other races that stood out to you? What stood out to you overall?
MH: Well, there’s the spin about the spin, which is that everybody is going to be framing this election and these results in their own interests. When Democrats win so far across the board, you can make an argument that any faction of the Democratic Party has the mandate, because Democrats of all stripes won Tuesday night.
But to my view, it’s hard to see how this is a world where there isn’t a clear demand for some kind of transformational change. So I’m wondering what Democrats do with their mandate now, especially as we think ahead to 2028.
If you recall 2020 and the last time the U.S. elected a Democratic president, you might remember that the Biden campaign was the sort of centrist, moderate return to normalcy choice, but they got there after a lot of left momentum in the primary and a really serious showing of support for Bernie Sanders, who remains one of the most popular politicians in the country.
Once Biden got into office, he arguably tried to give some of that kind of left, dare we say, populist economic message some service. There was the Build Back Better plan that had a lot of social safety net spending and Covid relief. There were climate infrastructure projects. There was the elevation of Lina Khan [to Federal Trade Commission chair].
For a little while, Biden was getting called the most progressive president since FDR, and then he threw it all away supporting the genocide in Gaza and really lost the support of the left, and then lost the support of the country when he was kind of visibly melting on the debate stage and refusing to drop out of the race.
So I’m curious what Democrats have learned from the Biden years and how that will convert into the next congressional term and the next presidential election.
JW: It really feels like I’ve lived a million lives in between now and that debate that really tanked Joe Biden’s entire political career at the end there.
I will say to your point, we’re already seeing Hakeem Jeffries, who’s likely to be the House Speaker, calling for unity and saying that people don’t want to fight. But you don’t really get a blue wave like this or a political wave like this when people don’t want to fight.
Clearly, there’s anger at Republicans. There’s anger at the cost of living. There’s anger at the war. If Democrats don’t deliver, they’re likely to see a red wave come the next cycle.
But I did want to take just a little bit of a step back and talk about Black voters and what’s happened in the aftermath of the Supreme Court voting rights decision. Black voters in this election really delivered historic victories in southern states for Democrats, but Black representation in Congress thus far appears to have been slightly reduced in this election. Now, for those who remember our discussion earlier this year about the Supreme Court decision to gut the Voting Rights Act, there were a lot of deep concerns that the decision would crater Black political representation, and so far that hasn’t come to bear, but it’s worth paying attention to in cycles that are less blue, where we’ve seen really massive redistricting.
I will shout out, there was one historic victory for Black Americans: Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, won her race for governor, becoming the first Black female governor in the country.
MH: We’ve talked a lot about these historic wins, but we would be remiss to not mention a close call in Florida, where Angie Nixon narrowly lost.
Nixon is a Black woman who’s a member of the Democratic Socialists of America and had a really shocking primary upset when she defeated the establishment favorite to get the Democratic nomination. The Democrats didn’t invest very much in her Senate race in Florida. The conventional wisdom says Florida’s not flippable, but conventional wisdom also says that South Carolina’s not flippable — and they did that.
Nixon ended up coming within about 2 [percentage] points to Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent, who just won a full term after being appointed to hold the seat that used to belong to [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio. A lot of people on the left side of the Democratic Party are wondering what would have happened if Democrats had invested in a DSA candidate running statewide in Florida, which is kind of a crazy statement to make if you think of just two years ago.
JW: I mean, I listened to her [concession] speech, she is an incredible speaker, but obviously, that’s not enough to win elections. You need money, clearly, and investment from the party.
We’re going to leave it there, but there is so much more election coverage you can follow at theintercept.com.
That does it for this episode.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: One museum visit a month could improve health, new report finds
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Joe Ware
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Visiting a museum or art gallery for just one hour a month could significantly improve people's physical and mental health, according to a new report which calls for cultural engagement to become as routine as exercise and healthy eating.
The research, commissioned by the charity Art Fund in partnership with University College London professor Daisy Fancourt, recommends that people spend at least 60 minutes with art in museums and galleries every month.
However, the survey of 2,000 UK adults found that 89% fail to meet this proposed target, equivalent to an estimated 49.5 million people.
The report, “The Recommended Dose of Art: A Prescription for Health and Wellbeing”, draws together scientific evidence suggesting that regular cultural engagement can reduce stress, improve cognitive health and potentially extend life expectancy.
Previous studies have shown that regular museum and gallery visits could nearly halve the risk of developing depression over the following decade. Other studies have linked cultural participation with reduced dementia risk and lower levels of loneliness.
Viewing original artworks in galleries was also associated with a 22% greater reduction in the stress hormone cortisol compared with viewing reproductions.
Fancourt, whose book Art Cure on the scientific benefits of art came out earlier this year, says regular engagement with art should be considered a health-promoting behaviour alongside exercise, a balanced diet and spending time outdoors.
“Guidelines like eating our 5-a-day of fruit and vegetables and getting our 10,000 steps have proven effective in helping us to prioritise other health-promoting behaviours in our busy lives,” she says in a statement. “Adding regular arts engagement to this list could be a simple and joyful way of investing further in our health and wellbeing.”
But the findings also raise questions about whether Britain's struggling museums have the resources to encourage more frequent visits. Jenny Waldman, the director of Art Fund, tells The Art Newspaper that the research strengthens the case for sustained public investment in museums, including protecting free admission at national institutions and supporting local and regional collections.
“We want to see sustained, long-term public investment across the museum sector, so that all museums have the resources to care for their collections and welcome the widest possible audiences,” she says.
Waldman acknowledged that removing admission charges alone would not overcome barriers to visiting museums, including accessibility and the resources available to institutions.
She says Art Fund's research among museum directors found that 36% of museums had reduced their opening hours because of insufficient funding and staffing.
“If we want museums to play a greater role in supporting public health, we must invest in the sector and give them the means to do so,” she adds.
Waldman also points to international developments, including Greece's introduction of arts prescribing into its national healthcare system and growing recognition of cultural organisations as public health assets. She also notes efforts closer to home: “Scotland's Chief Medical Officer, Sir Gregor Smith, recently published a report recognising arts organisations as important public health assets and calling for arts and culture to be embedded more widely in Scotland's approach to public health.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Comment | John Berger at 100: why the writer and artist's legacy is as vital as ever
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: John-Paul Stonard
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
John Berger was born on 5 November 1926, making this year his centenary. Next year will be the tenth anniversary of his death. It seems a good time to look back and take stock of one of the 20th century’s most persuasive and challenging voices in art and literature, and one of only two writers on art who also wrote a Booker Prize-winning novel (the other was Anita Brookner).
The story of Berger’s 1972 Booker Prize speech, after winning for his novel G., is told by Tom Overton in his thoroughly engaging biography, John Berger: From Life, published in August this year. To a stunned and affronted audience at the prize ceremony, Berger announced he was donating half the considerable prize money to a British chapter of the Black Panthers, as a protest against the labour exploitation in British Guiana that had made the Booker McConnell fortune. It is hard to imagine an acceptance speech nowadays without acknowledgment of the reputation-laundering that is still widespread in cultural sponsorship. Berger’s bravery in making such a stand, which can hardly have been easy, is one aspect of his legacy worth remembering.
This legacy—why Berger matters—is the subject of the smattering of centenary events but is also brought into focus by their dearth. The only anniversary exhibition in Britain devoted to Berger is a small display of his drawings at Mandell’s Gallery in Norwich (until 21 November), co-curated by the artists John Christie and Martin Battye. Berger’s drawings are those of a writer intent on seeing the world around him, gathering images and experiences, but also of an artist who knows that the best way to look is to draw.
Berger’s popular legacy lies with his 1972 book Ways of Seeing, which remains, quite remarkably, a bestseller—“one of the most stimulating and influential books on art in any language”, says its publisher, Penguin. Anyone rereading the book now might pause at such a description. Berger was hardly the first to show how images are constructed by viewers, and reflect their prejudices, but he was the first to publish a book that communicated this idea so effectively, combining relentless polemic with brilliant design (thanks to Richard Hollis). It also helped that the book was based on a successful television series and contained numerous pin-up images to back up the argument that Old Master painting, through patterns of privilege and possession, relates directly to contemporary advertising.
Yet the arguments feel dated and even slack, quite unlike Berger’s later writing on art. His attacks on Seymour Slive’s interpretation of Frans Hals, and on Kenneth Clark’s book The Nude, are grounded in a personal dislike of art historians. What Gen Z art students will make of his attack on the “disingenuousness that bedevils the subject of art history”, picking apart Lawrence Gowing’s nitty argument that the figures in Gainsborough’s Mr and Mrs Andrews (around 1750) are not just enjoying nature but being philosophical about it, is anybody’s guess.
Art against the profit motive
And yet the questions Berger asks about how we value works of art, and how they exist as part of our lives and the world in which we live, are still utterly relevant. They are part of what Overton describes as the idea central to all his writing: how we live with the dead, how the past surrounds us and keeps us company. Berger spent his life tilting against a world “ordered with the logic of profit, always looking forward, never back”, Overton writes, a world therefore bent on neglecting the past and forgetting the dead.
It is an idea explored in Berger’s short story The Three Lives of Lucie Cabrol, from the novel Pig Earth, about peasant life in France at the turn of the 20th century. And it appears in the leaps of imagination and connections he draws between art from different periods in the writings collected in Portraits: John Berger on Artists: on Fayum portraits seen from a century of exile and emigration, or his description of drawing Antonello da Messina’s astonishing 1475 Christ Crucified in the National Gallery, while recalling hearing pianist Myra Hess playing in the same gallery in 1942 (before being thrown out for swearing at a security guard), or his account of Jean-François Millet, “a moralist in the only way a great artist can be, by the power of his identification with his subjects”, in his case the experience of peasants working the land.
Berger’s legacy is his remarkable ability to link art with the most important questions of our time, and so to redeem it from the clutches of the market and specialists alike.
• John-Paul Stonard is an author and art historian

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Art Collaboration Kyoto fair celebrates five years of matchmaking galleries
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Carlie Porterfield
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
This year marks the fifth edition of Art Collaboration Kyoto (ACK), the fair that pairs Japanese commercial galleries with international peers to collaborate on shared stands. The fair will take place from 7 to 9 November at the Kyoto International Conference Center. The event has become known for its distinctive exhibitor model, which has proved popular with exhibitors and fair attendees alike.
“We thought, ‘If we are going to do this, why not create a fair that galleries and artists themselves would find exciting and genuinely want to be part of?’” Miho Doi, ACK’s director of experiences, tells The Art Newspaper about the fair’s founding.
This year’s edition includes a number of high-profile Western galleries, including Hauser & Wirth, Jeffrey Deitch and Carlos Ishikawa, alongside Asian galleries such as Seoul’s Gallery Hyundai.
The collaborative format is intended to give both Japanese and international galleries an opportunity to work together and introduce their artists and programmes to new audiences. Pairing domestic and foreign galleries has been key for the success of the fair, organisers say, especially for dealers without experience in Japan.
“For an overseas gallery, participating independently in an art fair in a country it is entering for the first time is by no means easy,” Doi says. “We have heard from participating galleries that, for a variety of reasons, taking part in a Japanese fair entirely on their own would not have been realistic.”
The fair’s main section will bring together 52 galleries. Taro Nasu from Tokyo will join forces with Hauser & Wirth for a presentation focused on text in contemporary art, including works by Louise Bourgeois, Jenny Holzer, David Horvitz and Glenn Ligon, among others. Nanzuka from Tokyo will work alongside Jeffrey Deitch, while Tokyo Gallery + BTAP will team up with Gallery Hyundai for a presentation pairing post-war Japanese and Korean experimental practices, including the Korean artist Seung-taek Lee in dialogue with the Japanese artist Kishio Suga.
“Some participating galleries have even described ACK as a ‘fair built on friendship’ rather than a place for competition,” Doi says.
Another section of the fair is dedicated to presentations from 11 individual galleries with strong connections to Kyoto. Mendes Wood DM, for instance, will present works by Tomie Ohtake—who was born in Kyoto and later relocated to São Paulo, which is home to the largest Japanese community outside Japan—among other artists. Hong Kong’s Kiang Malingue will show works by Yang Chi-Chuan and Faye Wei Wei, whose sculptures and paintings respond to Kyoto’s landscapes and urban environment.
The fair also coincides with a programme of special exhibitions and projects across Kyoto. This year, the Scottish painter Andrew Cranston will present an installation at Ryosokuin Temple, a Zen Buddhist temple in Kyoto’s historic Gion district. The exhibition is organised by Modern Art and Ingleby. Elsewhere, Carlos Ishikawa will stage a presentation of work by Evelyn Taocheng Wang and Issy Wood at Korin-in Temple.
This edition of ACK takes place under a new leadership committee structure, introduced earlier this year. Rather than being led by a single fair director, ACK is now guided by a seven-member committee with expertise spanning art consulting, cultural foundations, Kyoto cultural policy, fair production, education, partnerships and collector relations. The former fair director, Yukako Yamashita, now leads the fair’s ambassador programme.
As for ACK’s next five years, Doi says the leadership committee aims to develop the fair into a platform that “connects the art scenes of Japan and the world and generates a virtuous cycle between cultural and commercial value”.
