https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: French authorities investigate claim of fraud over Picasso plates and medallions on sale
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Vincent Noce
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A criminal investigation amid a family crisis casts a dark shadow over the illustrious history of the French studio Ateliers Hugo, which produced jewellery and silverware created by major artists of the 20th century. According to a legal source, the court of Aix-en-Provence in the south of France has opened an investigation following a complaint by the Picasso family.
On 10 March, Paloma Ruiz-Picasso, representing the nine heirs of the Spanish artist, filed a complaint alleging “fraud, counterfeiting, forgery and concealment of these felonies”. The file does not name the alleged perpetrators, and their identity is not presently known. The following month the Picasso family published a formal warning in the Gazette Drouot, titled “Hugo silverware”. It urged “all art market professionals and buyers to exercise the utmost vigilance”, following the appearance of what it described as “a large number” of illegitimate silver plates and gold medallions, valued at millions of euros.
The title refers to Ateliers Hugo, a goldsmith based in Aix-en-Provence. It was founded in 1933 by François Hugo (1899-1981), the great-grandson of the famous French author Victor Hugo. In 1955 Pablo Picasso, who since 1947 had created a variety of ceramics in Vallauris on the French Riviera, commissioned François Hugo to produce plates and dishes from similar designs in fine metals, using the traditional technique of repoussé. Later, the workshop reduced them into medallions and earrings. With the help of his brother, the painter Jean Hugo, who introduced him to artistic circles, François made jewellery designed by Salvador Dalí, Max Ernst, André Derain, Jean Arp, Jean Dubuffet, Roberto Matta, Jean Lurçat and Dorothea Tanning. In 1975, his son Pierre Hugo (1947-2023) took over the company. Pierre was followed by his son Nicolas (born 1989).
Members of the Picasso family and their lawyer, Jean-Jacques Neuer, who filed the complaint, declined to comment to The Art Newspaper. But their complaint alleges that “it has been discovered that the moulds of Picasso’s works were reused for unauthorised productions of silver and gold pieces, followed by duplicates, some of them bearing three times the same number, and unnumbered specimens”.
According to a source close to the investigation, the Picasso Administration, which represents the family, says it has discovered at least 17 complete or almost complete suspicious collections, amounting to hundreds of pieces. The first red flag was raised by the Museum of Old and New Art (Mona), a private Australian museum in Tasmania. According to this source, in May 2023 the museum informed the Picasso Administration of its doubts over plates it had bought at Sotheby’s in London. An auction catalogue of 13 October 2021 describes a “complete set of 24 silver plates” bearing the signature of the artist, completed with an additional “unnumbered proof of Visage aux mains”. The pieces were “accompanied by a certificate of authenticity issued by Pierre Hugo”. The lot was sold for £1.4m. Sotheby’s declined to comment for this story.
According to the legal files, the seller was the British dealer Mark Maurice, from a now dissolved gallery named Masterpiece. The source close to the investigation says the dealer allegedly produced documents showing that he had commissioned a set of plates and a set of medallions from the Ateliers Hugo between 2017 and 2020. Mark Maurice indicated he was “unable to respond” to The Art Newspaper’s inquiries “due to strict non-disclosure agreements in place”.
In summer 2023 the ceramics museum in Vallauris, Musée Magnelli, exhibited another collection of 24 silver plates as well as gold medallions attributed to Picasso.
According to the legal files, the Picasso Administration protested, having found that they bore no number, mark or punch, as legally required. Nicolas Hugo acknowledges these facts, but tells The Art Newspaper that the works exhibited at Musée Magnelli were so-called “author’s copies, made for the exhibition, duly indicating in the catalogue that they were not for sale”. He adds that he “recovered them and had them melted after the show”. Representatives for the museum did not respond to a request for comment.
In June 2023, as reported in the legal files, the French branch of the auction house Bonhams made a request to the Picasso Administration for the right to reproduce silverware for a catalogue. The auction house was planning a sale of 95 lots from the Ateliers Hugo collection, including works by Ernst, Derain and Cocteau, valued between €400 and €50,000 each. The most valuable were 59 pieces, “made by” or “after” Picasso.
Works withdrawn from Bonhams sale
On 26 September 2023 Bonhams was informed by the Picasso Administration that these pieces were considered to be “unauthorised” editions. The auction house then decided to “delay the whole sale”, just two days before it was due to take place. Nicolas Hugo acknowledges he “did initiate, in the wake of good results obtained at Bonhams UK, this sale of pieces”, produced, he says, by his “father and grandfather”. But, he adds, “When we were informed by dealers of the presence of possible duplicates, I agreed to withdraw the sale and collaborated with the Picasso Administration to identify them.”
Bonhams declined to comment, but according to the source close to the investigation, the lots attributed to Picasso were sequestered when a British financial company, Suros Capital, tried to recover them as collateral for a €256,000 loan. A spokesperson for Suros confirmed the operation to The Art Newspaper, adding that “it was secured against not only the Picasso pieces, but a range of assets which are progressively realised, so the company expects to recover the loan in full”.
In November 2023, according to the source close to the investigation, a representative for Bonhams France informed the Picasso Administration that a Spanish collector contacted the auction house to sell 24 silver plates, estimated at £900,000. Again, the auction house refused on the basis of Picasso Administration’s doubts about the objects’ authenticity. In the legal files, the Picasso Administration claims the same collector had sold another set of 24 silver plates and one of 24 gold medallions in private sales through Bonhams in London in 2022. Neither the British auction house nor the Spanish collector made any comment.
The rights to reproduce the items disappeared with [my father and grandfather], so I have never minted any of Picasso’s creations Nicolas Hugo, Ateliers Hugo
Nicolas Hugo, who says he has not been interviewed by the investigators, claims he has no knowledge of the proceedings and “is unaware of the content of the complaint” issued by the Picasso Administration. But, he says: “The criminal investigation can only deal with facts related to the time of my father and grandfather, therefore falling under the statute of limitations and concerning persons now deceased.” He adds that “the rights to reproduce the items disappeared with them, so I have never minted any of Picasso’s creations”, and he does not have the legal status of a goldsmith. However, he says: “I have signed some certificates of authenticity, but only to confirm my father’s own signature.”
In interviews with The Art Newspaper, Nicolas Hugo describes himself as a “self-taught art dealer”. When he was around 20 years old, he started to work as an assistant in galleries in Paris, before moving to London. He is now an agent for several artists and a curator. In 2022, the French magazine Les Hardis described him as a “mix of British and Saint-Germain-des-Prés charm”. “My father became very ill in 2018,” he told the magazine. “I had an epiphany. I decided to take over the workshop. I immersed myself completely,” and started to train in manufacturing jewels.
“From 2019,” he tells The Art Newspaper, “I became involved in the history of his workshop and helped my father to showcase this heritage, for memorial and commercial reasons. I set up exhibitions in places like Barcelona or Vallauris and initiated this sale of the fonds d’atelier at Bonhams Paris. I have not taken over my father’s company and was not his partner.”
Ateliers Hugo in limbo
Nicolas Hugo says: “There have been some duplicates on the market, dating from my father’s period, but I have no idea who had made them in the workshop.” He says he has “no idea who put a collection on sale at Sotheby’s in 2021” and knows “nothing of the three sets proposed by this Spanish collector to Bonhams in 2022 and 2023”.
The criminal investigation is still at the preliminary phase. It comes at a time when the company is already in limbo. Pierre Hugo died in October 2023 and his five children have turned down his inheritance. Nicolas Hugo’s brothers and sisters declined to comment to The Art Newspaper due to the ongoing investigation.
However, sources close to the case say that Pierre Hugo’s heirs’ inheritance came with a €2.5m tax debt. According to these sources, three of the Hugo siblings said in police interviews they were “not at all” aware of the conduct of the workshop by their brother Nicolas, who had succeeded their ailing father in 2019. The sources said the three Hugo siblings were on alert after learning that Bonhams Paris declined to sell the collection from the Ateliers Hugo in September 2023. According to the same sources, when Pierre Hugo died a month later, the three siblings went to the workshop and took 21 moulds of plates that they decided to hand over to the Picasso Administration. Three moulds from the set were missing and they did not find those for the medallions.
According to these sources, the three Hugo siblings explained to the investigators that, “knowing that the rights of reproduction were extinct, they wanted to be sure this would be respected”. The siblings also asserted that they “did not want in any way to be implicated in these operations and made it clear to the Picasso Administration”, according to the sources.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: ICA Miami selects architect to renovate recently acquired building
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Constanza Ontiveros Valdés
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami (ICA Miami) has appointed the global architecture firm Gensler to renovate a 30,000-sq.-ft building the museum acquired in 2024, doubling its exhibition and public-programming space.
Steps away from its current venue in Miami’s Design District, the new wing is scheduled to open in late 2027—as the museum marks its tenth anniversary at its current location. Focused on expanding the free museum’s community outreach, the project will transform the ICA into a multi-site complex and house the first permanent display of its collection.
The museum’s new building formerly housed the De la Cruz Collection, a private museum that closed after the 2024 death of its co-founder Rosa de la Cruz. Since its $25m acquisition later that year, the site has mainly hosted the ICA’s educational programmes. It will close once construction begins. The renovation is part of a $40m capital campaign, supported entirely by private funds.
The new design will adapt the existing structure. “The building was developed to house a contemporary art collection,” Alex Gartenfeld, the ICA’s director and chief curator, tells The Art Newspaper. “But with the spaces we are constructing, we intend to enhance the museum’s story-driven narrative approach to the collection and exhibitions.”
Eight new galleries will occupy the building’s first and second floors. Among them will be the museum’s first dedicated spaces for its growing permanent collection of more than 2,000 works.
“The programme between the two buildings is blended, but we will now have two full floors dedicated to our permanent collection,” Gartenfeld says. “Around every six months, we will refresh the collection display to reflect the collection’s emphasis and recent acquisitions.”
The entire third floor will be dedicated to public programming, including talks, symposia, lectures and performances. “Beyond adding galleries, this renovation will strengthen the ICA’s ability to support artists, expand learning and create a platform for exchange and belonging in one of the world’s most dynamic cultural cities,” says Bevin Savage Yamazaki, Gensler’s global culture and museums leader.
A reimagined façade with transparent components is key to the design. Gartenfeld says the façade aims to provide a connection between street-level traffic and the museum itself.
The renovations focus on visitor experience and accessibility as well. The lobby will be redesigned. And reconfigured outdoor areas will include social spaces, a sculpture deck and an expanded café. “We are aiming to create a more collective experience,” Gartenfeld says.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Ex-husband of Brent Sikkema sentenced to life in prison over murder-for-hire killing
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gabriella Angeleti
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The former husband of the late New York art dealer Brent Sikkema, Daniel Sikkema, aged 56, has been sentenced to life imprisonment for organising Sikkema’s murder in 2024. A federal court in Manhattan handed down the sentence on Wednesday (4 November).
In May 2026, after a two-week trial, Daniel Sikkema was convicted on charges of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit murder in a foreign country. In addition to life imprisonment, he was sentenced to five years of supervised release.
Brent Sikkema, who was aged 75 at the time of his murder, was found stabbed to death at his home in the Jardim Botânico neighbourhood of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on 15 January 2024. According to prosecutors, Daniel Sikkema began planning the murder in 2023 in the midst of his divorce from the dealer, with whom he had been married for around 15 years and shared a son.
As the couple’s divorce proceedings became more acrimonious, Daniel Sikkema, who holds dual US and Cuban citizenship, recruited the Cuban national, Alejandro Triana Prevez, as the hitman. On the night of the murder, Prevez entered the late Sikkema’s residence and stabbed him 18 times. Prevez subsequently received $5,000 from Daniel Sikkema and was promised further payments.
Prosecutors said Daniel Sikkema made 11 payments to Prevez and Prevez’s partner in Cuba, using the identities of unwitting friends, employees and family members to conceal the transactions. Prevez was arrested by Brazilian authorities four days after the murder at a gas station on the side of the highway in the state of Minas Gerais, around 600 miles from Rio de Janeiro. He had stolen cash and jewellery in his possession. His case is being handled separately by a Brazilian court.
Brent Sikkema was born in 1948 in Morrison, Illinois, and studied at the San Francisco Art Institute before beginning his career. In the early 1990s, he founded Wooster Gardens in SoHo, moving the gallery to Chelsea in 1999. The business became Sikkema Jenkins & Co in 2003 following the involvement of Michael Jenkins and Meg Malloy.
The gallery is now known as Sikkema Malloy Jenkins and continues to operate in Chelsea. It has championed the work of artists including Kara Walker, Vik Muniz, Sheila Hicks, Jeffrey Gibson and Arturo Herrera. A representative for Sikkema Malloy Jenkins told The Art Newspaper that the gallery will not be providing any statement regarding the conviction or sentencing.

https://hellgatenyc.com/looking-back-at-.title: Looking Back at New York's Glamorous, Silent Film Past
https://hellgatenyc.com/looking-back-at-.author: Kelly Faircloth
https://hellgatenyc.com/looking-back-at-.text:
To walk into "Goddesses in the Machine: Fashion in American Silent Film," the new exhibition at the Bard Graduate Center, is to feel a little bit like a kid in a candy shop—or rather a theater kid turned loose on the Paramount backlot, circa 1922. Everywhere you look, there's another lighter-than-air silk gown, or pair of beautiful metallic pumps, or bedazzled brassiere.
If you have a mental picture of silent film, there's a good chance it involves tinny piano music and overdramatic facial expressions—the era as retold by "Sunset Boulevard." This exhibition, which aims to tell the story of style and costume in early film, will overturn that impression, conveying just how vibrant, thrilling, and downright sexy these movies and their stars must've seemed to contemporary audiences. One of the displays quotes a costume designer who wrote that in the silent era he "wallowed in rhinestones and feathers and furs and loved every minute of it." That opulence and enthusiasm come through loud and clear in the exhibition.
What's more, the exhibit offers a rare window into a fascinating chapter in the history of the American movie business: when its beating heart was not on the West Coast, but in New York City.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: What's Behind Trump’s Obsession With Butts?
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jeet Heer
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
One of the mysteries of the 2026 midterms will always be why Donald Trump thought he could charm voters by repeatedly and lasciviously celebrating the human buttocks.
On October 12, Trump astonished a rally in Ohio with his lurid leering at Senator Jon Husted. “I started examining his body because I didn’t know he was a great athlete,” Trump said, alluding to Husted’s history as a college football player. “And I looked—I watched up, and down, I looked at his ass, and I looked at the whole…” Tributes to Husted’s rear would remain a staple until the end of the campaign.
But Trump wasn’t content to ogle just Husted. Speaking in Michigan on October 25, Trump made similar comments about both the singer Nicki Minaj (credited with “one hell of a beautiful ass”) and senatorial candidate Mike Rogers. Trump added, “I’d say that about your ass too, Mike, if it gets you a guaranteed victory.”
The degree to which Trump talks about other people’s bums really is bizarre and arguably without precedent in American political history. Abraham Lincoln did enjoy making scatological jokes about bodily functions, but that was in keeping with his persona as a son of the soil born in a log cabin—and he was not known to constantly praise, say, Charles Sumner’s behind on the campaign trail. In 2020, then–vice presidential candidate Sarah Palin appeared on The Masked Singer to perform “Baby Got Back,” Sir Mix-a-Lot’s classic rap tribute to the posterior. This was unusual but a one-off event—and by that point, Palin had long transitioned from a serious political figure to, well, the kind of D-list celebrity who sings about butts on television.
By contrast, Trump’s butt commentary is relentless, and coming from the incumbent president of the United States. And because of the cult-like hold that Trump has over the Republican Party, ass-talk started to proliferate. On October 29, during an appearance on Fox News, vice president JD Vance was asked a serious question from a voter about how the affordability crisis was harming young people. Inexplicably, Vance responded, “I want to point out that I’ve only gotten one question about Jon Husted’s ass.” A few days later, Florida senatorial candidate Ashley Moody told a rally, “Maybe I should be upset [Trump] didn’t talk about my asset.”
All of this loopy bum talk didn’t help the Republicans, despite Trump’s absurd claim that his praise of Husted’s rear caused the senator’s poll numbers to vault 14 points. Husted and Rogers went down to defeat, while Moody won an unexpectedly narrow race, helped by the fact the Democratic Party didn’t sufficiently fund her rival Angie Nixon.
After the Republicans were soundly trounced in the worst midterm defeat in half a century, Republican operative Todd Gillman told Politico, “Honestly, we need to move as far away from Trump as we can. I think Republicans might be screwed all the way until ’30. Talking about Nicki Minaj’s fat ass. All that stuff is just wearing people out.”
Even if it is politically ineffective, Trump’s ass-talk is a political fact, one that demands an explanation. On November 1, The New York Times published a lengthy analysis of Trump’s increasing verbal incoherence, including “his baffling fixation with admiring men’s posteriors.” “He is cruder than he used to be,” the paper reports, “using nearly 15 swear words per 10,000 words compared with 14 two years ago and six a decade ago, a change consistent with age-related disinhibition.”
It makes sense that, at the age of 80, Trump is less willing or perhaps less able to censor himself. But while this cognitive explanation offers a necessary context for Trump’s rough language, it doesn’t explain the specific content of the speech. Why does he have an anal focus, rather than, say, a genital or oral one?
Further, the fact that Trump’s ass talk was echoed by respectable Republicans such as Vance and Moody means it has a social meaning that goes beyond the peculiarities of Trump’s admittedly twisted personality. Trump is a freak but not an isolated case. He’s a weirdo with an immense mass following, so his quirks have a wider social resonance.
Saturday Night Live, less restricted by the rules of propriety than The New York Times, offered an unvarnished sexual explanation in a recent skit that shows the president suffering from “gay dementia.”
This joke is, as often with SNL, both too glib and borderline offensive. The truth is that Trump’s ass-talk is only occasionally sexual but more frequently involves excretion; it targets women as well as men, and is as much about asserting domination and humiliation as about expressing desire. In other words, Trump’s fixation is scatological and anal, rather than narrowly erotic.
Consider Trump’s description of Norway as a “shithouse country” (a term of abuse Trump has used against other nations in the past). Similarly, Trump has obsessed in speeches about the dangers of low-flow toilets, lamenting in 2019 the need to flush “10 times.”
Writing in Rolling Stone, Jack Crosbie argued that Trump’s ass talk is “ripe for armchair psychoanalysis: Trump is self-conscious about his own aging body, Trump values the superficial and material above all other things, Trump sees validation from the strong and tall and beautiful as evidence that what he is doing is good and just.”
This is all very suggestive, but it’s useful to move beyond such amateur speculation and consult the work of a true expert. In thinking about Trump’s anal fixation, few works are more illuminating than Normal O. Brown’s towering study Life Against Death: The Psychoanalytical Meaning of History. Brown was a distinguished classicist, and the virtue of his book lies in its provocative application of Sigmund Freud’s psychoanalytical theories to social and political analysis. As such, it rivals other mid-20th-century works of daring, psychologically informed social theory by figures such as Herbert Marcuse and Wilhelm Reich.
Surprisingly, Brown’s book has a Trump connection. It was originally published to obscurity by an academic press but found fame when it was championed by Norman Podhoretz, a New York literary critic and editor at Commentary. Podhoretz would later become one of the founding fathers of neoconservatism and, late in life, one of the most prominent pro-Trump intellectuals. In a 1999 essay in Harper’s, Christopher Hitchens noted that Podhoretz and other neoconservatives have an “obsessive” and prurient focus on anal sex.
In a brilliant and celebrated chapter on “the excremental vision” of Jonathan Swift, Brown notes,
according to Freudian theory the human infant passes through a stage—the anal stage—as a result of which the libido, the life energy of the body, gets concentrated in the anal zone. The infantile stage of anal eroticism takes the essential form of attaching symbolic meaning to the anal product. As a result of these symbolic equations, the anal product acquires for the child significance of being his own child or creation, which he may use either to obtain narcissistic pleasure in play, or to obtain love from another (feces as gift), or to assert independence from another (feces as property), or to commit aggression against another (feces as weapon).
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
The anal stage is universal, but as the infant matures, these impulses are sublimated into more socially acceptable behavior. If Trump is in fact suffering cognitive decline, it could be that sublimation is no longer possible. It’s broadly true that for Trump, subtext and text are often one: He doesn’t sublimate desire but gives it free vent, often in erratic and socially aggressive ways.
In the writings of Swift, one sees anal aggression brilliantly sublimated into a harsh and compelling satirical vision of humanity. Brown demonstrates that this is both Swift’s practice as a writer and his thematic concern. Trump, lacking Swift’s genius, turns anal aggression into mere verbal abusiveness: In the vernacular, Trump is a man who loves to shit talk.
Elsewhere in his study, Brown links the anal stage to hoarding, particularly of gold. Very slightly sublimated, hoarding gold turns into a love of the gold standard. This cluster of compulsions (narcissism, abusive language, hoarding, the fetishization of gold) can easily serve as a quite acute account of Trump’s psychology. Even if one doesn’t accept the scientific validity of Freudian categories, there is no denying that it offers a fresh and original way to think about commonly linked character traits.
While Brown was fully aware of the sadism of the anal stage, he also entertained the utopian hope that humans might be able to deprogram themselves of their social conditioning and achieve a return to the childhood ecstasy in the polymorphous perverse. The case of Trump suggests that this program might be dangerous if applied unilaterally. If one individual reverts to the anal stage while the rest of society remains committed to sublimation, you have a recipe for tyranny: the alpha male baboon who smears his shit over everyone in order to assert dominance. In other words, Trump’s impulse to constantly talk ass is symptomatic of the fact that he is an asshole.

https://hellgatenyc.com/carl-heastie-spo.title: NY Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie Goes to a Celtics Game…
https://hellgatenyc.com/carl-heastie-spo.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/carl-heastie-spo.text:
Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie, one of the most powerful people in New York, is a man of sundry interests. He loves cars, he loves bail reform, he loves his dog, he LOVES Prince. And he really loves sports. Specifically, the strange combination of the Dallas Cowboys, the Boston Celtics, and the New York Yankees. 
As New York Focus reported this week, you can find evidence of Heastie's sports mania in the campaign finance filings of the Democratic Assembly Campaign Committee, which, since Heastie became speaker, has spent upwards of $1 million on sports-related expenses including luxury box tickets, meet-and-greets, and lavish concessions. And Heastie's social media is full of honestly envy-inducing sports experiences. 
The DACC is supposed to be a fundraising mechanism for Assembly Democrats, and Heastie has claimed that the sporting events were fundraisers. "That story is beyond pointless," Heastie's spokesperson Mike Whyland wrote in an email to Hell Gate. "Those sporting events raised more than $10 million and after Tuesday it looks like it was money well spent." Heastie responded to the New York Focus story on Instagram, writing in part, "For years this newspaper has been trying to insinuate illegal and unethical things…It’s called fundraising stupid." But it's not always clear how the luxury tickets benefited any New York assemblymembers' campaigns—especially when some took place at Boston's TD Garden. In its filings, the committee characterized much of its sports spending as "office expenses."

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Inside France’s Biggest Uprising Since 1968
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Marlon Ettinger
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
Inside France’s Biggest Uprising Since 1968
Despite harsh reprisal from the government, students show no sign of stopping.
In the middle of September, blockades set up by high-school students protesting the abysmal educational and sanitary conditions in their schools swept France. Galvanized by a wave of actions in the Paris suburbs, the movement quickly spread across the country. At its peak in the beginning of October, more than 1,000 schools were blockaded, and the government was scrambling.
The national police responded with a spasm of extreme repression, arresting around 7,000 minors—a third of whom were detained on the nebulous charge of participating in an “unauthorized assembly.” Law enforcement deployed shocking violence; social-media feeds and TV screens overflowed with videos of students as young as 14 being strangled, beaten, and tear-gassed. By the middle of October, the police had fired 145 crowd-control grenades at children and injured 215 middle- and high-schoolers. Two teenagers were partially blinded, seemingly after being hit by crowd-control weapons. A 15-year-old had his hand torn off by a grenade, and another grenade broke a 14-year-old’s jaw and shattered his teeth.
There were also widespread reports of children being mistreated in police custody. One 16-year-old arrested in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis told the online news journal Mediapart that police officers dragged him by the hair into a police car and pulled his arm so hard he thought it would break. Like many others, he was detained for 48 hours and served a single meal each day. In another case, a lawyer told a reporter from the independent newsroom Off Investigation about a severely diabetic teenager who was arrested and held without being medically evaluated properly. The teenager suffered a hypoglycemic attack, then slipped into a diabetic coma that required hospitalization.
“The goal of this strategy was to scare the students and their parents into stopping the uprising as soon as possible,” one police commissioner told the weekly paper Le Canard enchaîné.
Instead, this harsh repression prompted popular anger, which drew more segments of French society into the movement. One poll at the end of the first week of October found that over 80 percent of the country believed the police violence against the high-schoolers was unjustified. In the second and third weeks of October, hundreds of thousands of people across the country joined large demonstrations against the high cost of living and soaring fuel prices.
On October 17, over 100,000 people marched in Paris alone. The demonstration had been planned for weeks. In Paris, the police were well aware of the expected turnout, as well as the fact that there was a threat of large-scale looting from some groups. During the day, marches full of righteous anger bloomed as half a million people protested across the country. Most places where the riot police didn’t intervene stayed calm; in others, the police used tear gas early and indiscriminately, diverting the orderly processions into cramped side streets and sowing chaos.
The Interior Ministry later admitted that it had lost control of the streets at night, a situation likely exacerbated by the heavy-handed response during the day. The ministry has not yet explained why it deployed only 42 riot-police units and left 14 units inactive. In the Southern Marseille region, where hundreds of businesses were looted, only three units were deployed, while seven were left inactive. And in Le Touquet and Amiens, special riot police were mobilized to protect the artisanal-chocolate shops owned by the family of President Emmanuel Macron’s wife.
After fiery images from the night’s riots spread across the world, the international far right, including the president of the United States, joined France’s home-grown racists in Islamophobic attacks blaming French Arabs and Africans. Those with no answers for popular demands also blamed immigrants and outside agitators for the October 24 riots following housing protests in Barcelona, Spain, and high-school demonstrations in Belgium, both partially inspired by the French blockades.
President Macron told citizens not to march at all, as the Senate accelerated legislation introducing harsh penalties for protesters who are merely present near acts of violence and looting, and the government has drafted plans to cut off access to social media at the discretion of Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. The government has also blamed the left, including Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the presidential candidate of the left-wing party La France Insoumise, whom Lecornu reportedly explored prosecuting for “inciting rebellion.” Similar charges were being considered for the LFI mayor of Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko.
On October 24, when protesters defied the government’s warning and came out in nearly the same numbers as they had the week before, I talked with Ozana, a 20-year-old who was marching in the rain with a friend and was angry about the government’s response. “We’re in France—we have the right to make demands, we have the right to protest!” she said. On October 26, the Education Ministry announced that some of the high-schoolers’ demands would be met. Student unions and organizations responded with calls to increase the pressure on the government and to continue the protests during the coming weeks.
“We got crumbs compared to what we are asking for,” one student organization’s representative, Clément Vieillot, told BFMTV, a major news channel.
Ozana vowed to me that they would continue to come out to protest for as long as they needed to. “Even in the rain?” I asked.
“Even in the snow!” she replied.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Democrats Crushed Trump. Here’s What They Should Do Next.
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Katrina vanden Heuvel, John Nichols, The Nation
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Democrats Crushed Trump. Here’s What They Should Do Next.
Seeking facile compromises with Trump is a fool’s mission—and voters who are hungry for change will not accept half-measures.
Donald Trump made one thing crystal clear to Americans who have been suffering because of his failed economic policies, disastrous wars of whim, and rampant corruption: that the 2026 midterms should be seen as a referendum on his presidency. Time and time again, on campaign swings to try and boost hapless Republicans from Ohio to Texas, the president told voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.”
The voters listened—and on November 3, they delivered an epic rebuke to Trump and his scandal-plagued party.
Democrats did not just win the House, where they are projected to win as many as 258 seats as this issue goes to press—a majority similar to the one a newly elected Barack Obama enjoyed when he and then–House Speaker Nancy Pelosi enacted the Affordable Care Act. They flipped at least seven seats in the Senate as well, taking control of a chamber that, during the first two years of Trump’s second term, had rubber-stamped such noxious cabinet picks as Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. And they made these gains not just in reliably blue territory, but with dramatic victories in state after state where Trump had prevailed just two years ago—including Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, South Carolina, and Texas—and in at least one state (Kansas) where they hadn’t won a Senate seat since the 1932 election that saw Franklin Roosevelt defeat Herbert Hoover.
Coupled with statehouse wins that put Democrats in charge in all seven of the swing states that backed Trump in 2024, and the victories of a multiracial, multiethnic slate of Democratic governors in states where the party has not prevailed in decades—including Texas and Georgia—this is truly a national mandate. It gives congressional Democrats the authority at the federal and state levels to check and balance a historically unpopular president—the Pew Research Center put Trump’s approval rating at a record-low 30 percent just before the election—and to develop a robust alternative to Trumpism, that toxic blend of authoritarianism, bigotry, corruption, unnecessary wars, tax cuts for the rich, surrender to AI oligarchs, and a cruel neglect of human needs.
The winners tell the story. From coast to coast, voters backed Democrats who called for more than just status-quo politics with a little blue coloring. Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who overcame Trump’s vicious attacks on his Muslim faith, won with a motto of “Money out of politics, money in your pocket, and Medicare for All”—as well as an outspoken opposition to the genocide in Gaza and AIPAC’s influence on American politics. James Talarico beat Trump’s “Talafreako” labeling and a $158 million attack campaign by Elon Musk to become the first Democrat to win a Texas Senate seat since 1988. In his victory speech, Talarico called for “a new kind of politics: a politics rooted in a deep love—for our state, for our country, and most importantly, for all of our neighbors,” one that “requires that we stand between the bullies and the bullied.” The senator-elect wasn’t alone; Lone Star voters, long known for dashing Democrats’ hopes, went straight-ticket blue, handing Democrats every statewide position on the ballot and electing Texas’s first-ever Latina governor, the anti-corruption campaigner Gina Hinojosa.
In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the nation’s first Black woman to win a governorship. In Ohio, Amy Acton triumphed over the hateful politics of the Republican right. In New Mexico, Deb Haaland became the country’s first Native American woman governor, while Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan will go to the US Senate as a proud member of the White Earth Nation in northwestern Minnesota, as well as a former head of the Children’s Defense Fund–Minnesota and—along with El-Sayed and Troy Jackson in Maine—a close ally of Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders.
Many newcomers to the House are unapologetic progressives who ran with support from Sanders and the surging Democratic Socialists of America, including New Yorkers Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, Melat Kiros in Colorado, Donavan McKinney in Michigan, and Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania. And a proud economic populist, Ohio’s Sherrod Brown, will return to the Senate as an unabashed advocate for breaking up monopolies, regulating banks, strengthening unions, taking on Big Tech, regulating data centers, and going after Trump’s corruption.
The scope and character of this rebuke to Trump is vitally important: It gives the new Congress a mandate to check and balance “the most dangerous president in the history of the United States,” as Sanders referred to him during the midterm campaign.
Trump is indeed dangerous, and he will remain so in the last two years of his presidency. He retains the much-abused powers of his office—including the ability to unilaterally launch wars abroad—and he will no doubt redouble his efforts to bypass Congress, ignore the courts, target enemies, and obstruct meaningful progress.
But he will do so now as a more diminished and discredited figure than ever before. Voters everywhere appeared repelled by Trump: His corruption and self-dealing finally became an albatross around his neck, with Democrats moving the issue to the top of the political agenda. “While the crook president and his crook family rake in billions from around the world, you pay more for everything,” Senator Jon Ossoff told Georgia voters as part of a scorched-earth campaign that saw the Democrat—a potential 2028 presidential contender—finish with 59 percent of the vote.
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, a key campaigner along with Sanders for progressives across the country, drew thunderous applause on election eve when she argued against “playing nice with people who are committed to the destruction of our democracy” and declared: “There must be accountability for crimes that have been committed and wrongs that have been done against the country and the people of the United States of America.”
To do that, Democrats need smart accountability strategies—such as those of Representative Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the presumptive chair of the House Appropriations Committee—that follow the money and connect the costs of the self-dealing by Trump and his cronies to oligarchical wealth, the affordability crisis, and lousy healthcare. Accountability and affordability can go hand in hand, but it will happen only if Democrats make a true break with the rotten status quo. A failure to reject Trump’s foreign policy—particularly when it comes to the war with Iran and his near-total support of Israel, two issues that Vice President JD Vance quickly identified as liabilities for the GOP—will send exactly the wrong message to voters. And pulling punches on economic issues will only raise questions about whether Democrats are sufficiently distinct from Republicans.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Democrats need to recognize that seeking facile compromises with Trump, who vows that he’ll be “Mr. Veto” on the issues that matter, is a fool’s mission—and voters who are hungry for change will not accept half-measures.
Unfortunately, some Democrats still don’t get it. Before the election, Hawaii Senator Brian Schatz suggested that Democrats should avoid “aspirational” agendas. “I do not think it is time to propose things that the president of the United States is guaranteed to veto,” Schatz said.
That’s the wrong take.
Congressional Progressive Caucus chair Greg Casar of Texas has wisely warned, “We cannot be the party of nervous lawyers who just tinker around the edges.” Casar was spot-on when he said that Democrats “have to show we’re more than anti-Trump. That starts with cracking down on corporate greed to bring down the cost of health care, housing, child care, groceries, and gas…. If Donald Trump chooses to veto our popular, pro-affordability policies, the fight is far from over. We’ll run on them in 2028 and pass them in 2029.”
Democrats must counter Trump’s self-enriching schemes, crude abuses of power, and ugly theatrics with big ideas and clarity about how to implement them. Where to begin?
take on big money
The 2026 midterms saw record election spending—roughly $12 billion, according to OpenSecrets. Close to a half-billion dollars came from Musk alone. Republicans had an overwhelming money advantage. Democrats beat the money this time, but the party needs a comprehensive legal, legislative, and state-based strategy to address the crisis.
regulate ai
Democrats should follow the lead of Peggy Flanagan, who proposed an independent federal body to provide AI regulation and oversight. They should also encourage states to lead as “laboratories of democracy”: Polls show that 80 percent of Americans favor laws that choose humanity over machinery.
let abdul el-sayed lead on medicare for all
When Barack Obama campaigned in Michigan, he said that El-Sayed would “finish the job we started with the Affordable Care Act and guarantee quality, affordable healthcare to every single American.” Yes! El-Sayed proposes to “finish the job” by “[expanding] Medicare to cover all necessary healthcare, including vision, dental, and hearing, and extend it to every single American from cradle to grave without premiums, copays, or deductibles.” El-Sayed is the right leader to join Sanders, who is expected to head the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, in fighting for an agenda that—as the midterm results make clear—is seen by the electorate as radical common sense. It is high time to ignore the establishment’s hand-wringing over the populist energy that was key to winning the midterms, to reject Trump’s corruption and his billionaire allies and declare, as Troy Jackson did at the finish of his campaign: “We’re not from the left, we’re not from the right, we’re from the bottom, and we’re rising!”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Budapest exhibition explores Van Gogh and Gauguin's artistic excursion to Montpellier
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Martin Bailey
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
After Paul Gauguin arrived in Arles in October 1888 to stay with his friend Van Gogh, the two artists would go out to paint together and then socialise and discuss art in the evenings over a glass of wine. Their very different personalities, however, soon led to tensions. Living together in the confines of the Yellow House and sharing a small room as a studio, they began to row. As winter approached, and the weather made it impossible to work outside, the situation only worsened.
In mid-December, in an attempt to clear the air, Gauguin suggested that they should make a trip to Montpellier, 70 km west of Arles. Their goal was to visit the Musée Fabre, renowned for its fine collection of paintings.
The artistic result of this trip forms a central part of a major exhibition on Gauguin which opened this week at Budapest’s Museum of Fine Arts. Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin: The Circles of Post-Impressionists and Symbolists (until 28 February 2027) provides a wide-ranging exploration of the art of Gauguin and his associates. The show’s title comes from a key painting by the artist inspired by the Montpellier visit, Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin (late 1889).
Van Gogh and Gauguin travelled from Arles to Montpellier by train, which took around four hours. Although it has long been assumed that they made a day trip on either 16 or 17 December 1888, it is arguably more likely that they spent the night there and stayed for both days. The Musée Fabre had over 800 paintings on display, so they would surely have wanted time to savour the works. Many of the finest pictures were French, given by Alfred Bruyas, a local collector and patron of Gustave Courbet.
For Gauguin, the highlight of the museum was Courbet’s Bonjour Monsieur Courbet (1854). This landscape composition includes the figure of Courbet himself, laden with his equipment and holding a walking pole. He is greeting Bruyas, who is accompanied by a bowing servant.
Gauguin, who was impressed with the Courbet, painted a work in response, a year later, in the Brittany fishing village of Le Pouldu. The main figure in this work is Gauguin himself, facing a Breton woman on the other side of a gate.
Superficially, the Gauguin painting bears little resemblance to the Courbet. Stylistically, Courbet’s smoothly painted picture contrasts with Gauguin’s rough brushwork. The compositions appear to have little in common, other than showing an artist encountering other people—and being greeted with a “good day” (and, incidentally, both scenes also include a dog).
The moods seem very different. Courbet appears thrilled to greet his patron and friend. Gauguin’s encounter with the Breton woman, however, is fleeting, as they happen to pass each other at a gate. The Budapest exhibition’s lead curator, Judit Geskó, sees the Gauguin picture as representing “the artist as a solitary wanderer”.
But despite the differences, Gauguin’s decision to entitle his work as he did shows that he was directly acknowledging the source of his inspiration, the Courbet. Gauguin’s title is actually inscribed on the painting, in the lower-left corner.
Gauguin made two versions of his composition: the one on loan to Budapest from the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles and the other (which was unavailable for borrowing) at the National Gallery in Prague. The Hammer picture, which was the original, was created to display on the dining room door in the small inn where he was staying in Le Pouldu.
As for Van Gogh, the Dutchman was particularly struck in the Musée Fabre by the portraits by Courbet. These included a self-portrait, The Man with the Pipe (around 1849), which may well have inspired Van Gogh one month later to paint his Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear and Pipe (January 1889).
Bruyas was depicted by a range of artists and these portraits were also much admired by Van Gogh in the Montpellier museum. Vincent described Bruyas’ appearance to his brother Theo as “a gentleman with a beard, red hair, who looks damnably like you or me”.
Electric discussions
Both Gauguin and Van Gogh were great admirers of Courbet, who was very well represented in the Musée Fabre. Although they agreed about Courbet, their tastes for other artists were often rather different. Vincent wrote to Theo that their artistic discussions in Montpellier had been “excessively electric”. He explained: “We sometimes emerge from it with tired minds, like an electric battery after it’s run down.”
Despite these animated discussions, the inspirational visit seemed a success. Vincent reported back to Theo the day after their return that in the museum they had been “right in the midst of magic”. He added: “Gauguin said to me this morning, when I asked him how he felt: ‘that he could feel his old self coming back’, which gave me great pleasure.”
Sadly, the reconciliation did not last long: just four days later Van Gogh severely mutilated his ear. Although the trigger was probably news he had just received that Theo had become engaged (which Vincent feared would threaten his brother’s support), tensions with Gauguin were also a contributing factor.
Van Gogh in the Gauguin show
Budapest’s Gauguin exhibition is ambitious, with 80 works by the French master and 70 by other artists. Although financial valuations for exhibitions are rarely revealed, The Art Newspaper can report that its total insurance value is €1.5bn.
The show includes three works by Van Gogh: the landscape painting Field with Irises near Arles (May 1888, Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam) and two rarely-displayed drawings from the collection of the Budapest museum, The Parsonage Garden at Nuenen in Winter (March 1884) and Haystacks (July 1888).
The Budapest exhibition has two Gauguin paintings dating from his stay with Van Gogh in Arles: the landscape Les Alyscamps (October 1888, Musée d’Orsay, Paris) and the portrait Madame Roulin (November-December 1888, Saint Louis Art Museum). Both of these subjects were also tackled by Van Gogh.
Among the other Gauguin highlights in the show is Sunflowers on an Armchair (1901, Bührle Collection, on loan to the Kunsthaus Zurich). This is one of four still-life paintings inspired by Van Gogh’s favourite motif—sunflowers. Gauguin painted these in the Marquesas Islands (north of Tahiti), with flowers grown from seeds he was sent by a friend from Paris.
The museum estimates that the Gauguin exhibition could see up to 350,000 visitors, a huge number for a medium-sized European capital. However, even this won’t match Geskó's Van Gogh show in 2006, which attracted 486,000 people to the museum to see the Dutch painter's works.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/public-optio.title: Enough With the “Public Option” Already
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/public-optio.author: John Canham-Clyne
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/public-optio.text:
Enough With the “Public Option” Already
The public option sounds like a step toward universal health care, but it’s really a delay tactic. The latest versions would force public plans to mimic private insurers, while the fight over the arcane details buys the industry another decade or two.
The difference between a vampire and a bad health care policy idea is that vampires jump out of their coffins and drink blood at sunset. Undead health care proposals emerge from think tank closets and suck the life out of useful ideas when the sun rises on a national health care debate. As public fury at exploding costs and deadly corporate claims denials boils over into historic Democratic election gains, can someone please find a wooden stake for the public option?
Improved and expanded Medicare for All would give everyone full coverage at much lower cost than the combined private premiums, taxes, and out-of-pocket payments that are eating up family income today. But it violates a cardinal rule of federal politics: never do anything that causes corporations or the ultrawealthy any pain.
Instead, corporate Democrats wanting to be seen “doing something” about the imploding US health care system have long peddled a vague public option notion because it sounds like the marriage of a big noncorporate vision (it’s public!) with competition and freedom of choice (it’s an option!). Liberal nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) and pundits revived its rotting corpse in response to pro–Medicare for All candidates’ primary victories and Tuesday night’s stunning results.
It’s a perfect nonsolution to our three-headed crisis of health care cost, access, and quality. Nobody knows what a “public option” is because there’s no common definition and nothing like it has ever been seen in the wild, so it can be anything weaselly politicians want it to be. It needs to be put out of our misery.
The “Right” Path
There’s danger in chasing the content of various “public options.” The concept is designed as a distraction. Wasting years on policy rabbit holes is the point. But killing it requires some analysis, so it’s worth pointing out that every one of its shape-shifting forms withers under cursory scrutiny.
Rising Democratic Senate star Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) says she “wouldn’t say no forever” to a White House run if “there’s not anyone else who’s on the right path.” Slotkin’s favored path leads to one of the sillier public option proposals. In January, Slotkin, Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), and Rep. Jan Schakowsky (D-IL) introduced the Affordable Consumer Health Options and Insurance Competition Enhancement (CHOICE) Act, or the Affordable CHOICE Act (“ACA” — get it?). The CHOICE Act would get the federal government into the business of selling crummy insurance to almost nobody by allowing the feds to market their own versions of “bronze,” “silver,” and “gold” plans on the Obamacare exchanges.
Even at record enrollment, the Affordable Care Act exchanges covered less than 7 percent of Americans. Nearly everyone with insurance has Medicare, Medicaid, or private insurance through a job. Three-quarters of US working-age adults are eligible for job-based coverage, nearly all of which is considered legally “affordable” by ACA rules. That means almost all workers are barred from receiving ACA premium subsidies. Presumably they could buy a Slotkinized plan by paying the full premium cost if they really wanted one. Nice option.
Subsidized or not, Slotkinized plans would cover only between 58 and 82 percent of the actual cost of health care after premiums, depending on the “metal” label attached to the plan.
CHOICE Act public option plans would have to play the same failed “cost control” game as private insurers, building their own private provider networks and trading privileged access to their patients for discounts off market price from providers who join those networks. So, Senator Slotkin’s options will come loaded with the copays, coinsurance, and deductibles that private insurance corporations use to coerce patients into accepting in-network doctors and hospitals. It’s a mockery of “affordability” for patients and would offer neither better nor worse provider payments than UnitedHealth, Aetna, or Cigna.
The contrast between Senator Slotkin and the winner of Michigan’s other Senate seat couldn’t be clearer. At his victory celebration, Abdul El-Sayed turned his three-line slogan into a roaring call and response, with Medicare for All as the closer: “Money out of . . . POLITICS! Money in your . . . POCKET! Medicare for . . . ALL!” Corporate Democrats are still trying to paint Medicare for All as too radical and urge progressive winners toward “moderation,” torturing voting data into arguments about electability. The facts: In 2024, Elissa Slotkin defeated Mike Rogers by a 0.3 percent margin. With unlimited American Israel Public Affairs Committee and corporate cash arrayed against him and in the face of nakedly racist opposition, El-Sayed beat Rogers by a full 7 percent.
Wait, Not That Public Option
Criticize one slippery idea and the optionites will just say, “Hey, I didn’t mean that public option.” In two recent posts, economist Paul Krugman hyped a Medicare “buy-in” version to “allow individuals, and possibly more important, employers, to sign up for Medicare benefits, paying actuarially fair premiums to Medicare reflecting the health status of their workers” (emphasis added). Krugman insists that “many people and many employers would surely take it.”
Surely many who need it the most wouldn’t. The US health care system is so broken in part because we’ve asked six million separate employers who don’t know and shouldn’t be expected to know much about health care to buy it for most of us. But even they know that premiums reflecting the health status of workers would immediately price employers who most need an affordable option — those with high-cost employees — out of any “buy-in.”
The Krugmanite option violates a core Medicare precept. Of course, individual Medicare premiums shouldn’t exist at all. Paying taxes should buy your health care. Even so, except for a few high-income people, everyone pays the same Medicare premiums right now. “Actuarially fair premiums” tailored to health risks contradict the basic notions of solidarity at the heart of public benefits and the very idea of insurance, which is supposed to pool risk across groups of people, not segregate it.
Offering existing original Medicare as a standalone option for employers and nondisabled individuals younger than sixty-five to “buy” is an idea only a Nobel-winning trade economist dabbling in health care could love. Original Medicare’s cost-sharing has already driven most eligible people into Medicare Advantage plans run by the very companies that Krugman dismissed as “parasites.”
So, to fully cover their workers, employers would have to — you guessed it — buy supplemental insurance from the private insurance industry. Never underestimate the power of Nancy Pelosi’s Iron Law of Democratic Health Policy: Congress shall make no law respecting expansion of health care access that does not subsidize the private health insurance industry, and all gestures to the contrary shall be performance art.
False Equivalence
Some people may actually take these ideas seriously, but the essence of public optionism is a bully’s taunt.
Virtually every economic analysis of the issue has concluded that a single-payer system would generate large savings to fund both expanding coverage to everyone and dramatically improving existing coverage. Two key sources of those savings are huge, useless administrative costs: the insurance industry’s skim, and the massive bureaucracies that providers have to build just to get paid by thousands of private insurance plans whose terms and members constantly change.
Original Medicare is far more efficient than private insurance, spending 97 to 98 percent of revenue on actual health care, while private plans capture more than 10 percent of our premiums as overhead and profit.
If public insurance is so darned efficient, the argument goes, a public option should outcompete private insurance. That would have the dual benefit of giving people cheaper, better coverage, and proving to a socialism-averse public that something like Medicare for All could work. So prove it, lefties!
The problem, of course, is that operating in existing markets under rules that will force public options to behave like private insurers strips these plans of the permanence and power that make Medicare and truly “public” insurance relatively efficient.
Medicare controls prices because it permanently covers everyone in the largest group of people who use a lot of health care. When you turn sixty-five and enroll, you’re in for life. If hospitals want to treat the group of people most likely to need their services, they have to take Medicare prices.
The CHOICE Act makes a head fake in that direction. The bill instructs the Health and Human Services secretary to create a provider network and set hospital and physician prices “through a negotiated agreement with health care providers,” without naming which providers or how they’ll negotiate. In the absence of successful negotiations, CHOICE Act plans can just pay any claim at existing Medicare prices. That may sound like a little public muscle flexing to hold prices down, but the CHOICE Act also allows hospitals and doctors to opt out of the public options’ networks, turning Medicare prices into a backstop that applies only to out-of-network claims.
Having a guaranteed right to impose low prices on out-of-network care would give public option plans a little pricing leverage. But in the end, the Slotkinized plans would likely wind up creating networks and setting prices in a manner similar to private plans, whose tussles with hospitals are based entirely on market power. Having surrendered the power that allows Medicare to set its own prices and competing as start-ups with private insurance to entice “covered lives” to enroll, the public options would soon find themselves face-to-face with massively powerful regional health systems affiliated with Ivy League schools or the Catholic Church. Have fun.
To persuade the necessary “covered lives” to enroll, CHOICE Act plans will have to ape private plans by constantly marketing themselves and enrolling and disenrolling clients. Alongside the headache of managing networks, that work requires skimming billions in premium dollars off the top, just like private insurers.
Slotkin, Krugman, and their optional pals have also managed the remarkable feat of finding an idea that would add a little more bureaucracy to the already bloated administrative expenses that choke US hospitals. The CHOICE Act doesn’t create an option. It envisions hundreds of local public option plans with premiums set geographically — ACA plans are offered on a county-by-county basis. Viewed from a hospital’s business office, that means at least three separate local plans, one per “metal,” with each becoming just another payer with its own unique prices, networks, utilization review, and patient cost-sharing to follow, track, bill, and sue when payments don’t show up.
Finally, should policymakers and regulators fool themselves into thinking that these options will be efficient because, you know, they’re “public” and offer below-market premiums, the plans face a potential flood of high-risk sign-ups (the “adverse selection” problem). As Jim Kahn and Hank Abrons point out in Health Justice Monitor, even the more-expansive-than-Krugman version offered by The American Prospect is particularly vulnerable on this question. Being stuck with disproportionately high-cost patients wouldn’t be good for plans trying to prove the efficiency of public insurance, but it would be great for politicians seeking to prove that the government really can’t do health care.
We could go on forever about the details, but the content doesn’t really matter. These ideas are little more than lumps of lead over which political alchemists like Slotkin and Krugman chant their two magic words to dazzle us into believing they’re creating gold. Public options aren’t incremental reforms toward universal coverage. They’re increments of nothing that enable the status quo.
This fantasy nonidea endures because fighting for it achieves a critical bipartisan goal: buying time for corporate control of the rest of the health care system. A legislative timeline would likely look like this: two years until the Democrats have a shot at the White House, followed by a year or two of GOP panic about “communism.” Throw in two to three years to write the regulationss, then five or ten years to roll out the plans and watch them fail. Presto! A decade or two of corporate looting passes, with trillions of dollars squandered and another million or two preventable deaths.
There are plenty of meaningful steps on the way to a publicly financed universal health care system that ensures everyone gets the care they need without facing personal bankruptcy or fighting off bloodthirsty private bureaucrats. Politicians who want to improve access or cost control could jump on a few of these sample bandwagons. Don’t expect a rush, though. Most of these ideas take a bite out of the industry’s hide, and letting poor people who make an extra penny keep their health care will give alleged conservatives apoplexy. But here they are:
- Set fair hospital prices by regulation for all payers, to stop the gouging of employers and patients and end the episodic waves of terror that engulf communities when big insurance companies and hospitals threaten patients with loss of access during local rate negotiations.
- Lower the age at which everyone becomes eligible for Medicare to fifty or fifty-five.
- Eliminate the extreme cost-sharing in the original Medicare program.
- Abolish the Medicare Advantage privatization scheme that lets private insurance companies overcharge the federal government tens of billions of dollars a year, and use the savings to fund said elimination of original Medicare cost-sharing.
- Buck Washington, DC’s current antitrust fad by lifting restrictions on employers who want to join together to bargain for health care and administer benefits. Look, employer control of health care makes no sense. But if corporate politicians fantasize that it’s a route to better benefits and lower costs, let bosses gather the power to control prices and administrative costs, as long as they do it themselves without the insurance industry, and as long as they’re willing to pay the price of offering uniform plans across their cartel — no more tiny tweaks to networks or boutique cost-sharing provisions for each employer.
- Dramatically expand the time people can stay on Medicaid. Medicaid’s constant means-testing makes it an unreliable source of coverage. California applied for a waiver to keep kids enrolled through the first five years of their lives instead of making their parents reapply every year. Do more of that and for longer.
The worst thing about public optionism is enduring smug lectures that Medicare for All is a political fantasy that could never happen from people promoting a vague, unworkable idea now enjoying its twenty-third year of politically viable nonexistence. Yet The American Prospect casually assumes that a series of essential Medicare for All elements against which the industry will fight like rabid dogs can easily be grafted onto a public option.
Health care is a public good. Pretending that having government act like a health insurance corporation will do anything useful is absurd. Let’s kill this putrefying political monster right now.
