The Bases of US Empire Are Crumbling
In recent decades, the basis of US hegemony has shifted from domestic industrial strength to its ability to enforce the rules that organize global production, finance, and money. Today this imperial role is now increasingly under strain.
Imperialism is again at the forefront of world politics. Large-scale war has become a permanent feature of the present era, from Ukraine to Gaza. Donald Trump’s second term has added a tariff war, threats to annex Greenland, the abduction of Venezuela’s president, and, together with Israel, an unprovoked war on Iran. This is not the whim of one man, for the confrontation with China began under Trump’s first term and deepened under Joe Biden.
At the same time, politics across the mature capitalist countries is in deep turmoil. In the United States, the Left has become a force in mass politics, with a democratic socialist as mayor of New York and widespread opposition to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Israel’s genocide in Palestine, and the war on Iran. In France, governments have fallen one after the other, and social unrest is spreading. But the far right is also rising powerfully, from France’s Rassemblement National and Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland to Reform UK and Austria’s Freiheitliche Partei Österreichs, alongside the Trump White House.
Left and Right draw on the same realities of stagnant wages, industrial decline, and degraded public services. If the Left is to offer a credible political program to the working class and the poor, it must grasp what links resurgent imperialism to the decay of capitalist accumulation in the historic core of the world economy. With millions of people now looking for answers, this means offering a politics of class rupture.
The US Paradox
The starting point is the paradox at the heart of US capitalism, which is also the central paradox of contemporary imperialism. In 1945, the United States produced about half of world manufacturing output; today it produces roughly one-sixth. Productivity growth has been feeble since the great financial crisis of 2007–9, investment has remained weak, and real wages have stagnated for over a generation. Yet the dollar’s share of official reserves has slipped only slightly below 60 percent. US productive preeminence has declined, but the monetary hierarchy has hardened.
The United States alone settles its international obligations in its own liabilities. Everyone else must acquire dollars, manage dollar exposures, and adjust to the policy of the Federal Reserve. Foreign investors hold around $9 trillion of US Treasury bonds, about a third of the marketable stock, and central banks across the world are stuffed with US public paper.
The material basis of US hegemony has thus shifted from domestic industrial strength to the capacity to set and enforce the rules that organize global production, finance, and money. This is also where its imperial power truly lies.
US corporations have flourished within this structure. Among the largest globally active enterprises, US corporations take around 44 percent of profits and hold 34 percent of intellectual property, compared to 11 and 14 percent for their Chinese counterparts. US multinationals led the globalization of production from the 1980s onward, exporting productive capital and building the global chains that shifted industrial capacity abroad, while relying on the dollar to run them.
This was a triumph for private US capital, but it hollowed out industry within the United States and created the social wreckage that became Trump’s political raw material. Global monetary, financial, and corporate dominance has gone together with domestic deterioration.
This is why neither of the two main US parties has been able to reverse industrial decline. Trump’s 2018 tariffs brought little reshoring, since many corporations simply moved their supply chains to Vietnam and Mexico. Biden kept the tariffs and added the subsidies of the Inflation Reduction Act and the CHIPS Act but left US capital’s global strategy untouched.
Trump now wants to restore domestic industry while at the same time defending the privileges of multinationals. One of his first acts on returning to office was to withdraw from the Base Erosion and Profit Shifting framework of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which more than 130 countries had signed, including the Biden-era United States. It would have allowed states to tax a share of the profits generated by multinationals within their borders and to impose a minimum tax of 15 percent, curbing the transfer of profits to tax havens through intellectual property held offshore.
But Trump’s aims cannot be reconciled. To see why, we must look at how production and finance are organized around the world today.
Lenin, the Dollar, and the F-35
Vladimir Lenin insisted in 1916 that imperialism must be grasped through the dominant mechanisms of accumulation of its time. Drawing primarily on Rudolf Hilferding, he identified these as the fusion of banking and industrial capital into finance capital, the export of capital, and the territorial division of the world among rival powers. His method remains indispensable, but the concrete forms of imperialism have changed profoundly.
Applied to contemporary capitalism, Lenin’s method reveals two structural foundations of imperialism: first, the pairing of globalized productive capital with internationalized financial capital; second, the dollar as world money, which turns that pairing into a hierarchy enforced ultimately by US military power. World money is a crucial element of imperialism today but a consideration that classical Marxist theory never developed.
Contemporary production is organized through global chains coordinated by multinationals — mostly US, European, and Japanese — that control design, intellectual property, logistics, and access to markets. Finance has become global alongside production, but the two have not fused as in Hilferding’s time. They form a pairing in which neither side simply commands the other. Productive capital generates value and surplus value; financial capital supplies the credit, liquidity, and means of payment without which global production could not run. US capital has led on both sides of the pairing: its multinationals built the chains, and its banks and asset managers globalized finance.
The pairing of capitals operates in a world market that has no world state, no world central bank, and no world court of justice. What holds it together is world money, which must serve across separate jurisdictions as unit of account, means of payment, and reserve of value, especially in a crisis. Only the dollar performs these functions.
A manufacturing supplier in Vietnam or Mexico ships components today and waits sixty or ninety days to be paid, but wages and inputs must be paid now. The gap has to be financed, and because the lead firm in the chain invoices in dollars, it is financed in dollars at rates priced off dollar benchmarks. This is not an economic choice but the price of admission to the chain. Between 1999 and 2019, about three-quarters of exports in the Asia-Pacific and virtually all exports in the Americas were invoiced in dollars. Through these chains, the monetary policy of the Federal Reserve reaches directly into workshops on the other side of the world.
The state that issues the necessary dollars is not just another power pursuing its interests abroad. It is the authority that ultimately guarantees settlement, liquidity, and enforceability for globally mobile capital, deciding whose liabilities count as money and whose balance sheets must adjust. Production remains the foundation, but the hegemon’s command over world money is the hinge of imperial power, the point at which the pairing of capitals is disciplined across the world.
The hierarchy becomes fully visible in a crisis. In 2008 and again in 2020, the Fed opened dollar swap lines to a select circle of fourteen central banks. Those inside stabilized their financial systems in days. Those outside, including India, Indonesia, and South Africa, faced currency depreciation, loss of reserves, and austerity. Sanctions and exclusion from payment systems complete the apparatus of coercion, as the freezing of approximately $300 billion of Russian central bank assets in 2022 showed. The fourteen account for roughly 55 percent of US imports and 60 percent of US exports. They also host more than 90 percent of US military personnel stationed abroad. The map of monetary privilege and the map of US military power largely coincide.
The dollar and the F-35 are two moments of a single structure of domination, and US air and naval power guards the choke points through which world trade moves. This is imperialism running through the balance sheets of firms, banks, and states, backed by military power. It does not need to plant a flag over a territory or to establish an expensive colonial administration.
Financialization Mark II
Crucially, the financial side of the pairing has itself been transformed since the great financial crisis of 2007–9. Before the crash there was Financialization Mark I, centered on globally active commercial banks, which turned workers’ homes into a prime terrain of extraction through mortgages and consumer debt. At its peak, bank profits in the United States approached 40 percent of all corporate profits. The crash ended that regime.
It was replaced by Financialization Mark II, resting on shadow banks — above all, asset managers such as BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street. Research that I and colleagues have recently done on 426 major asset managers shows that the equity they manage rose from $13 trillion in 2013 to $46 trillion by mid-2025. That is roughly 40 percent of the equity of all billion-dollar listed companies in the world. In every region outside North America, US asset managers are the largest group of foreign investors. They represent imperial power exercised through balance sheets rather than territory.
Unlike commercial banks that draw their profits mostly from the spread between the lending and the borrowing rates of interest, asset managers depend on the gap between the rate of profit and the rate of interest — what Hilferding called founder’s profit. Such profits are realized primarily through rising asset prices. Stock market inflation has thus become a leading channel of financial accumulation.
The entire edifice of Mark II rests on the state. US gross public debt rose from just over 60 percent of GDP in 2007 to more than 120 percent by 2025. At the same time, the Federal Reserve absorbed public debt securities on a historic scale, created vast amounts of new dollars on its balance sheet, and became dealer of last resort for the shadow banks and others in the money markets. Whatever the neoliberal rhetoric of free markets might say, contemporary capitalism survives through state hyperinterventionism, but on behalf of finance, not to rebuild production.
Investment and productivity outside a narrow set of sectors have consequently stayed weak. The vast AI boom does not alter this picture; it confirms it. Spending on data centers and chips is concentrated in a handful of giant corporations, financed from their enormous cash holdings and increasingly by vast debt, while asset managers pour capital into the same few stocks. The promised productivity gains remain largely a matter of expectation, already priced into shares long before they appear in production. This is still primarily accumulation through asset price inflation, not yet a true transformation of production.
The historic core of the world economy thus continues to drift in an interregnum. The old order has lost its dynamism, but no new one has emerged.
Subordinate Financialization
Still, the reach of the Fed extends far beyond the borders of the United States, since the dollars it creates are world money. The dollar dependence created by global production chains accumulates into national pressures: dollar debts that must be serviced, profits that must be repatriated, technology payments that must flow abroad. The burden falls heaviest on the Global South, and the result is subordinate financialization. This is not an immature version of the financialization of the United States or Britain but a distinct form produced by subordination in both production and finance.
A peripheral central bank cannot expand its balance sheet at will or ignore the exchange rate when it forms monetary policy, since it operates in the highly precarious environment of loanable capital flowing in and out of the country. Much of that capital is managed by the same US asset managers that dominate Mark II.
In October 2025, the average policy interest rate in Brazil, India, Indonesia, Mexico, and South Africa stood 4 percentage points above the Fed’s. This is a liquidity tribute, levied by the monetary hierarchy itself. High rates choke domestic investment, attract speculative inflows, push up the exchange rate, and undermine domestic manufacturing. Peripheral states are forced to stockpile dollars as self-insurance and park them in US Treasuries, while their own governments and firms borrow at far higher rates. Resources that could build factories, railways, and hospitals are, in effect, lent to Washington.
Tribute on this scale needs local beneficiaries. Large firms in peripheral countries borrow cheaply in dollars and invest in domestic financial assets at high yields; banks profit from the public debt issued to absorb the inflows; and sections of the middle class enjoy cheap imports. In a peripheral country, the exchange rate is a class weapon as much as an economic variable. And the United States does not need a viceroy to collect the tribute, for it flows through the ordinary workings of the world market.
Empire Without Hegemony
China presents the opposite picture to the United States. It accounts for close to 30 percent of world manufacturing value added and around 15 percent of world merchandise exports. State-owned enterprises dominate its strategic sectors, and it has built institutions that partly bypass the US-led order, such as the Belt and Road Initiative and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank.
Yet China is not attempting to construct a separate imperial bloc or to acquire territory. It seeks a determining voice in the rules that govern trade, technology, and investment, and, in the longer term, new arrangements for world money.
That is where it is at its weakest. The renminbi accounts for less than 3 percent of global reserves and international payments, and less than 5 percent of world trade is invoiced in it, against roughly half in dollars. Chinese public debt does not serve as global collateral, the People’s Bank of China offers no liquidity backstop to the world market, and China’s own payment system processes little more than 12 percent of the dollar volume handled by the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication.
The barrier is structural, not a matter of will. World money requires deep markets in safe public liabilities, legal protection for foreign creditors, and an open capital account. The capital controls and public command over finance that protected China’s industrialization are precisely what prevent the renminbi from becoming world money. China is a productive superpower obliged to settle its obligations in a currency it does not issue and to hold its reserves in its rival’s debt.
Nor is Chinese domestic accumulation free of contradictions. Since 2007–9, growth and profitability have fallen to a “new normal.” China still invests roughly double the US share of GDP, but the returns on that investment have declined sharply. The rational course would be to lower investment and systematically raise the incomes and consumption of Chinese workers, but the economic, social, and political risks of doing so are enormous.
The result is an impasse. The hegemon cannot recover its productive foundations, and the challenger cannot issue world money. Neither can impose a resolution, and neither will accept permanent subordination. There is no orderly path of succession within a monetary hierarchy that is singular, coercive, and increasingly contested, and therein lies the danger for the world.
The United States has stopped acting as the hegemon, that is, as the power that presents its own interests as the general interest. It acts instead as the biggest and most aggressive contestant in an increasingly open field, treating even its allies as subordinates. When Washington demanded sanctions on Russian energy after 2022, Germany accepted them at severe cost to its own industrial base. Yet US military predominance is no longer uncontested, and the war on Iran has shown that even weaker opponents cannot simply be made to submit. The situation echoes the rivalries before 1914. World war is not inevitable, but proxy wars, reserve seizures, payment exclusion, and technology embargoes have become an embedded feature of world politics.
Should the Left, then, cheer for de-dollarization and the BRICS? Weakening the monopoly of the dollar would loosen a crucial mechanism of domination. But the putative challengers are neither a socialist bloc nor a new anti-colonial movement. They are states competing in the world market and seeking ways around the dollar, not a fairer world money. Multipolarity is not a class category. The Left should oppose sanctions, the liquidity tribute, and the forced accumulation of reserves without enlisting in anyone’s camp.
The Politics of Class Rupture
One of the most encouraging political developments in this gloomy conjuncture is the US left seriously debating how to win and use governing power. Max Elbaum has rightly argued here that it cannot limit its positive platform to domestic issues while saying only what it opposes in foreign policy.
The analysis above shows why. The domestic and the imperial are two sides of the same structure, and a left government would confront that structure from day one. Success is not possible without overturning the prevailing capitalist mechanisms of social, economic, and political power. This is precisely the politics of class rupture that the Left should be offering to the millions seeking change.
I saw what this means at close quarters in Greece in 2015. Syriza’s election win had little significance in itself — it was at best only the beginning. A left-wing government that truly sought to save Greece from the disaster of the bailouts had to break the established mechanisms of power. That could only be done by using the machinery of the state in conjunction with the mass movement. To deliver results, a left-wing government would be obliged to transform the state.
The challenge crystallized on one issue — as it typically does in times of a radical upheaval. That was, to stay in the European Monetary Union (EMU), or to exit? Breaking with the euro would have required capital controls, public command over the banks and money, and a far-reaching reorganization of the economy that could have shifted power toward workers and the poor. Inevitably, there would have been a profound rupture with the entrenched class and imperial interests stifling Greece, both of which threw their weight behind the policy of remaining with the EMU. The mere thought was enough to send shivers down the spine of the timid Syriza leadership. Abject surrender followed.
There is a lesson here for the US left — and beyond it — despite the vast difference between the preeminent imperial power and a small European power. If it seeks to offer a politics of rupture that tilts the balance decisively in favor of workers and the poor, it must use and transform the machinery of the state while drawing on the strength of the mass movement. It should also be clear that there will be fierce and violent opposition on all levels. Success will not come without decisively overturning the domestic and the imperial configuration of class power in the United States. Of that there can be no doubt. It is almost redundant to say that the task is of world-historic importance.
Popular Sovereignty Against Empire
There is, however, plenty of historical experience on which the US left can draw as it seeks a class politics that could bring success. The first step involves developing a program of reversing domestic US productive decline, with the working class in the lead, as has already been argued for other developed capitalist countries.
That means public investment on a scale not seen in generations, public banks directing credit to production, and a central bank brought within a democratic economic plan instead of serving as dealer of last resort for BlackRock. It also means restoring capital controls as a normal instrument of policy and extending public ownership in energy, infrastructure, and housing, where social need and private profit sharply diverge. And it further means democratic, worker-based control of corporations, since a bureaucratic state corporation run on the priorities of capital changes nothing essential.
Such a program would reverse the global accumulation strategy of US capital, subordinating multinational and financial capital to democratically determined priorities. In short, it would aim to deglobalize and definancialize the US economy. This is neither isolationism nor autarky. The aim is an open economy that continues to trade, invest, and cooperate across borders but on terms set democratically rather than by multinationals and footloose financial capital. Openness should serve the reconstruction of production at home and genuine cooperation abroad, not the global strategy of US capital.
A program of this kind ultimately rests on the issue of sovereignty. The problem is that this term has been appropriated by the Right, which uses it to assert the unrestrained power of the US state abroad while defending the interests of capital at home. But for the Left, sovereignty has a different and older content, that of popular sovereignty. If democracy is to have real meaning, workers and the poor ought to have both voice and power at the workplace, the neighborhood, the town, the city, and the country. Popular sovereignty does not mean only electing a government that spends more on social care, housing, and infrastructure while taxing the rich, necessary as that is. It requires building the organized power of working people — channeling the renewed strike militancy of the United Auto Workers and the drives to organize the nonunion factories of the South — alongside the communities and movements that have resisted ICE, the genocide in Palestine, and the war on Iran.
Since, moreover, there is no democratic space beyond the borders of the nation-state, a program of class rupture would also rest on national sovereignty. This is an even thornier issue for the Left to grasp. In a subordinate country, such as Greece in 2015, national sovereignty means breaking out of imperialist domination. But the United States sits at the top of the imperialist hierarchy, and the sovereignty of the US state is a lever through which other nations are subordinated.
For the United States, therefore, national sovereignty raises directly the question of what the nation is and which class constitutes it. For the Right, the nation is the imperial state and the capital it serves. For the Left, national sovereignty is anti-imperialist at its core and means fighting against the oppression of others. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels put it plainly, after stating that workers have no country: the proletariat must “rise to be the leading class of the nation, must constitute itself the nation,” and is in that sense “itself national, though not in the bourgeois sense of the word.”
This is the opposite of nationalism, which asks workers to line up behind their own ruling class. The task is then clear. The US working class can constitute itself as the nation only by taking command of the instruments of imperial power — the Fed, the sanctions machinery of the Treasury, the military budget — and ending their use to subordinate other nations. US workers gain nothing durable from the dollar order. The more Washington pursues imperial primacy, the more it hollows out the domestic economy.
Antiwar politics and anti-capitalist politics are one struggle. Opposition to war that leaves domestic property relations untouched is incomplete, and transformation at home that ignores the imperial order will be crushed by it. The system that extracts value from the periphery is the same system that hollows out the core. That is what gives working-class internationalism a material content, instead of leaving it a liberal slogan compatible with the free movement of capital. It is the ground on which a genuinely internationalist socialist politics can be built.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/volkswagen-e.title: The Volkswagen Crisis Exposes Germany’s Industrial Decline
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/volkswagen-e.author: Alexander Görlach
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/volkswagen-e.text:
The Volkswagen Crisis Exposes Germany’s Industrial Decline
A proud symbol of German industry, Volkswagen enjoys far-reaching government support. Yet as it leans on the Chinese market, it’s far from clear that the firm is going to save jobs at its German sites.
On October 9, European Union Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič announced an agreement on hybrid vehicles, following two days of talks with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao in Beijing. According to Šefčovič, over the next four years or so, Chinese exports of full and plug-in hybrids to the EU are expected to fall below half of previous forecasts. The specific quotas, minimum prices, or monitoring mechanisms were not disclosed. The agreement is provisional, with further talks scheduled for 2027.
Shortly before Šefčovič’s trip, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron had been putting pressure on the European Commission. In early October, in a letter to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and a joint paper, they called for the commission to be given more powers to act against market distortions by non-EU countries. A new instrument would allow companies, or even entire countries, to be excluded from the EU’s single market in serious cases. The paper names plug-in hybrid vehicles as one of such a potential case. Neither document mentions China by name, but the initiative is mainly aimed at Beijing.
For Germany’s Merz, a lot is at stake politically. According to recent polling, his Christian Democrats (CDU, plus their Bavarian ally, the Christian Social Union) now enjoy just 19 percent support, 11 points behind the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). The looming loss of tens of thousands of jobs at German automakers, led by Volkswagen (VW), and possible plant closures would further weaken his position.
Merz himself has cast the issue in fundamental terms. “Germany must remain an industrial country!” he told a CDU rally in Langenhagen near Hanover in early September, shortly after Volkswagen’s supervisory board approved its restructuring plan. “We are currently losing industrial jobs on a large scale.” No German state, he added, “is shaped as strongly by one large industrial company as Lower Saxony.” Olaf Lies, the Social Democratic premier of Lower Saxony, which holds 20 percent of the voting rights in Volkswagen, promised that “the Volkswagen sign should stay on the plants” in Emden, Hanover, and Zwickau.
Rising in the polls, the AfD presents the crisis in the auto industry as proof of the government’s failure. Its coleader, Tino Chrupalla, called the possible end of “traditional German car plants” “the result of a failed economic and energy policy” and blamed it on a “one-sided and premature fixation on electromobility.” His conclusion: “Zwickau must remain a car city beyond 2031!” In France, meanwhile, some four hundred thousand people work in vehicle and parts manufacturing.
Beyond its specific subject matter, the joint initiative by Merz and Macron is also meant to demonstrate that the Franco-German partnership within the EU is working again, after having frequently stalled in recent times. What’s less clear is whether this show is going to have its intended effects.
Protectionism
As early as October 2024, the EU had imposed countervailing duties of up to 35.3 percent on electric cars built in China, in addition to the regular 10 percent import duty. Hybrid vehicles were not subject to these duties. Since January, manufacturers have been able to avoid the duties if they commit not to sell an electric car in the EU at a price below a specified minimum. Yet none of this has slowed the influx: according to the industry group Chinese Passenger Car Association, China exported 490,000 plug-in hybrids to the EU in the first eight months of this year, 179 percent more than in the same period last year, and 630,000 fully electric cars, an increase of 49 percent.
Not all of these carry Chinese brands; exports from China also include models built there by Western manufacturers. For comparison, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), around 1.64 million fully electric cars and 758,000 plug-in hybrids were newly registered in the EU between January and August, accounting for 21.7 and 10 percent of the market, respectively. Chinese brands accounted for about a quarter of plug-in hybrid registrations in the EU in the first half of the year, and a reported 14.2 percent of fully electric car sales in Western Europe’s eighteen largest markets up to May. In August, Chinese-owned carmakers, including Geely’s Volvo, sold 10.8 percent of all new cars in the EU, up from 6.6 percent a year earlier.
Merz and Macron’s renewed effort was a response to the weak outcome of previous measures. For example, the countervailing duty on BYD, China’s largest electric vehicle manufacturer, stands at 17 percent, or 27 percent including the regular import duty. However, even such high tariffs do not offset the cost advantage of Chinese production. At the same time, Chinese manufacturers are increasingly pushing into Europe as a price war rages in their home market and domestic sales decline. And Chinese hybrids, which are seeing the strongest export growth, were subject only to the regular import duty until the understanding reached by EU leaders last month.
On October 12, Emmanuel Macron opened the Paris Auto Show by calling for even stronger protection of the European market. On the same day, Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume, at a joint appearance with French Industry Minister Sébastien Martin on the sidelines of the show, spoke out in favor of closer cooperation between the two countries: “Now is the moment when France and Germany, as Europe’s largest automotive nations, must work together.” He added, “I’m not talking about protectionism. Rather, I’m talking about an industrial policy driven by European interests.” Regarding Šefčovič’s negotiations, he said, “We welcome the progress made in the talks with China.”
The CEO can use all the relief he can get, as Volkswagen is in crisis in Germany: On September 3, the supervisory board approved the “Future Plan 2030.” It stipulates that a further fifty thousand jobs worldwide are to be cut, with Blume estimating that about half of those will be in Germany. This adds on to a decision already made in December 2024 to cut more than thirty-five thousand VW jobs in Germany by 2030. The company says it can no longer guarantee that it can competitively use its capacity at plants in Emden, Hanover, and Zwickau, and at Audi’s Neckarsulm facility. However, no decisions on closures have been made yet. Alternatives are being explored, including the production of Chinese VW models in Germany. Among other reasons, the company cites an overcapacity of approximately five hundred thousand vehicles in Europe and competition from China.
That competition isn’t just about subsidies. In 2024, the European Commission concluded that China’s electric car industry benefits from unfair state subsidies that threaten to harm European manufacturers; this finding is the legal basis for the countervailing duties. But in reality, China’s strength does not rest on subsidies alone. Chinese manufacturers have also advanced technologically. Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Ltd. (CATL) and BYD are among the world’s largest battery producers. According to consultancy McKinsey & Company, Chinese electric car makers launch new models in about twenty-four months, compared with up to forty-five months for established mass-market manufacturers. Volkswagen itself has taken a stake in XPeng to jointly develop models for the Chinese market, thereby acquiring expertise in China. Added to this is the model strategy. Chinese manufacturers are bringing affordable, compact cars to Europe; BYD’s Dolphin Surf, for example, starts at €23,490 in Germany. Volkswagen and other German manufacturers, on the other hand, have relied on high-margin SUVs and premium models for years.
Combustion-Engine Ban
As one of the first Western automakers in the People’s Republic, Volkswagen has a long history of dependence on China. In October 1984, the company signed a joint venture agreement with the state-owned conglomerate Shanghai Automotive Industry Corporation (SAIC). Mass production began in 1985: in its first year, the joint venture sold 1,684 vehicles; by 1993, that number had risen to around 100,000. In 2019, Volkswagen delivered 4.23 million vehicles there, accounting for nearly 40 percent of its global sales. In January of that same year, then CEO Herbert Diess said, “The future of Volkswagen will be decided on the Chinese market.”
While Volkswagen saw its future in China, the outlook for the internal combustion engine in Europe was in flux. In fall 2022, the European Parliament and member states agreed that, starting in 2035, only zero-emission new cars would be permitted for registration. In March 2023, German Federal Minister of Transport Volker Wissing called into question Germany’s previously given approval; the law was finally passed at the end of the month only after a commitment to electrofuels was secured.
Manufacturers, too, made commitments and in some cases backtracked on them: Volkswagen announced in 2021 that it would phase out internal combustion engines in Europe between 2033 and 2035. Mercedes-Benz had declared in 2021 that it would sell only electric cars wherever possible by the end of the decade but abandoned this goal in 2024. At the end of 2025, the European Commission proposed scaling back the 2035 target to a 90 percent reduction in CO2 emissions.
China, on the other hand, has pursued a consistent policy for years: from 2010 through the end of 2022, the government paid manufacturers subsidies for every electric or plug-in hybrid vehicle sold in the country, and the “Made in China 2025” strategy designated electric mobility as a key industry. This support may have distorted market competition, but it gave the country’s manufacturers planning certainty. Europe, by contrast, has put its car industry at a disadvantage with its political flip-flopping.
Now Volkswagen is also coming under pressure in China: in the third quarter of 2026, the company delivered 405,800 vehicles there, 38.5 percent less than a year earlier. Globally, the decline was 14.3 percent. Volkswagen is thus facing three simultaneous developments: sales in China are falling; the company is increasingly sourcing technology from Chinese partners; and in Europe, the EU is protecting the market from Chinese imports, including vehicles from Volkswagen’s own Chinese plants, with tariffs, minimum prices, and volume agreements.
The pressure on Berlin’s political leaders to stand by its carmakers is considerable, and the government has responded. Since May, buyers of electric cars have been able to claim a state bonus of up to €6,000; plug-in hybrids also qualify. The program is funded with €3 billion until 2029. Yet because eligibility does not depend on where a car is made, Chinese models also benefit. Merz has also campaigned against the EU’s planned ban on new combustion-engine cars from 2035, which matters greatly to German manufacturers. “We will no longer hold on to this stubborn and wrong ban on combustion engines in the European Union,” he told a CDU party conference in late November 2025.
Last month, Berlin and Paris agreed on a joint position: a 90 percent cut in new cars’ CO2 emissions by 2035, without requiring the remaining 10 percent to be offset. Two committees of the European Parliament have since backed a 95 percent compromise, with additional allowances for European green steel; the plenary is due to vote in December. The political pressure is also coming from German states. In July, Lower Saxony’s Social Democratic premier, Olaf Lies, wrote to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Merz, and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil calling for tariffs on hybrids from China.
Yet it’s also clear that support for the car industry is not the same as support for German jobs. By the end of June 2027, Volkswagen plans to present a strategy for its European production, which will also determine the future of its plants in Emden, Zwickau, Hanover, and Neckarsulm. The German government faces the question of whether the interests of a corporation that manufactures in China and exports from there to Europe still align with those of its German sites and their workers.

https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorks-hou.title: New York’s House delegation will include 20 Democrats and six Republicans
https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorks-hou.author: Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorks-hou.text:
Twenty Democrats and six Republicans will be heading to Washington in January as New York’s delegation in the U.S. House of Representatives, according to the Associated Press.
Most of those seats were decided quickly on Election Day, as Democrats largely trounced Republicans around the state and the nation. But it took much of the week for the Associated Press to declare winners in a handful of tight races.
Democrats flipped just one seat, the 17th congressional district in the Hudson Valley, where Democrat Cait Conley defeated Rep. Mike Lawler. Lawler conceded the race on election night, but results were slow to report because of widespread ballot-scanning machine failures in Westchester County on Tuesday.
New York City’s congressional delegation will continue to include just one Republican. Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, who represents Staten Island and parts of Brooklyn, successfully fended off a Democratic challenge from Mike DeCillis, a former police officer and special education teacher.
One of the closest races was in the North Country, where Republican Andrew Constantino, the CEO of the custom printing company Sticker Mule, edged out Democrat Blake Gendebien, a dairy farmer. The seat was previously held by U.S. Rep. Elise Stefanik, who announced last year she was leaving public office after abandoning a bid for governor.
Long Island’s four congressional seats will continue to be held by two Democrats and two Republicans. Rep Tom Suozzi and Rep. Laura Gillen, both were re-elected as Democrats, while Republican incumbents, Rep. Nicholas Lalota and Rep. Andrew Garbarino, also won re-election.
After Tuesday's blue wave election, Democrats are projected to control the House by a margin of 254 to 162 seats, the Associated Press reported. The winning candidates will be sworn into the Congress on January 3.
New York’s election results will be official after the vote tallies are certified by county authorities and the New York State Board of Elections.

https://gothamist.com/news/jazz-age-fash.title: Jazz Age fashions return to Governor’s Island for the Lawn Party's fall edition
https://gothamist.com/news/jazz-age-fash.author: Stephanie Keith
https://gothamist.com/news/jazz-age-fash.text:
On a brisk autumn day, ferries to Governor’s Island filled with feathers, silk crepe, chiffon and wool tweed of passengers headed to the Jazz Age Lawn Party, a Roaring ‘20s-inspired event celebrating its 21st anniversary with a special autumn edition.
Participants spread their blankets on the ground under a canopy of graceful sycamores whose leaves were a bright yellow and orange. A large dance floor had been laid out where host and founder Michael Arenella played jazz with his Dreamland Orchestra.
The event showcases the flapper dresses, pearls and linen suits of the day and allows participants to relive “one of the most colorful and formative epochs in American history," organizers say. The 18th Amendment, establishing the prohibition of alcohol, took effect in 1920. The 19th Amendment granting American women the right to vote was ratified later that year.
The gathering, which started in 2005, is typically held over a weekend in June.

https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-jogg.title: Brooklyn jogger killed in stabbing saves 4 lives through organ donations
https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-jogg.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-jogg.text:
Katie Suarez, the 28-year-old woman who was fatally stabbed while jogging in Brooklyn, has saved four lives through organ donation, according to the nonprofit LiveOnNY.
Suarez donated her heart, liver, pancreas and both kidneys, LiveOnNY, which oversees and coordinates organ donation in the greater New York area, confirmed on Sunday. The organs were successfully transplanted into four recipients between the ages of 12 and 75, three of whom were in New York and one in Florida. Suarez also donated her corneas.
“This is an unimaginable loss for any parent and family,” said Leonard Achan, president and CEO of LiveOnNY. “That Katie thought of others in being a registered donor is a powerful testament to her generosity and will ensure that she will live on through these gifts of life.”
Suarez was stabbed in the neck as she was running on the Shore Parkway Greenway on Oct. 30 and later died from her injuries. On Saturday, just over a week after the attack, NYPD officials said they arrested Department of Education employee Sayed Mohassib, 27, and charged him with murder, criminal possession of a weapon and tampering with physical evidence.
Mohassib pleaded not guilty at his arraignment Saturday and was ordered held without bail, according to court records.
Mohassib's attorney could not be reached for comment Sunday.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: E-Bike Battery Fires Hit Record in NYC, But Solutions Remain Elusive
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Greg B. Smith
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
It’s a record. Already in 2026, New York City has suffered 406 lithium-ion battery fires, sparked by the electric cells that power an ever-growing fleet of e-bikes and electric scooters.
Since 2019, when the Fire Department first started keeping these stats, such blazes have resulted in 46 deaths and 628 injuries.
All this occurred despite an aggressive effort to end this grim but persistent trend. Laws were passed. Policies changed. The FDNY warned people again and again not to charge off-label batteries without safety certification.
And yet last month, four tenants of a Bronx public housing development perished in a fast-moving fire triggered by a battery charging inside their apartment.
Then last week, six people died in a Sunset Park blaze. A cause has not been officially released, but FDNY officials noted two charred lithium-ion battery-powered devices were removed from the scene. Not counting the victims of the most recent Brooklyn fire, that’s nine battery-fire deaths already this year.
And once again, elected officials are calling for reforms.
Last week, the City Council announced it will hold an emergency hearing on this issue on Nov. 20. And on Friday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani told reporters his administration is focusing on finding a solution, “whether it’s exploring additional legislation or it’s exploring additional policy that we can make at the administrative angle.”
Dwindling Enforcement
The solutions may not be so simple.
Workers who rely on e-bikes continue to buy and charge unsafe, off-label batteries, which are less expensive. Retailers and on-line outlets continue to sell them.
At times, the city bureaucracy has struggled to respond, even when they’re clearly warned of potential danger. In February 2023, journalist Fazil Khan perished in a raging fire in Harlem that erupted in an apartment below him where tenants were charging multiple batteries. Callers to 311 had warned the city weeks earlier, but there was no response.
That same year, the City Council took the first major step to confronting this issue, passing a law banning the sale of lithium-ion batteries that were not safety certified. This was a crucial step: Fire officials say batteries that are certified by the Underwriters Laboratory (UL) or aren’t charged via their manufacturer’s approved charger are vulnerable to bursting into flame. The resulting chemical fire is difficult to extinguish — and spreads quickly.
Since then, however, enforcement of the ban has wavered, according to Department of Consumer & Worker Protection (DCWP) records obtained by The City Reporter.
The law went into effect Sept. 1, 2023, while Eric Adams was mayor, and in the first four months his DCWP launched a wave of inspections citywide, issuing summons to 105 retailers at a rate of more than 26 per month.
In 2024 the agency issued summons to 108 businesses over 12 months, which dropped the rate to nine per month. Then in 2025, the last year of the Adams administration, enforcement fell even further, with summons issued to just 46 sellers all year for a rate of less than four per month.
In 2026, the first year of the Mamdani administration, enforcement got off to a slow start. By the beginning of August, DCWP had issued summons to just 26 sellers, but in August and September the city launched a sweep, bringing the total to 68 retailers hit with summons by last week. That was still a rate of just under seven per month.
And records show some of these retailers broke the law again and again, with some being hit with multiple summons for selling unsafe batteries since the law went into effect.
DCWP spokesperson Stephany Vasquez Sanchez said the agency “focuses on bringing businesses that remained in violation of (the law) into compliance,” and the agency’s tactics of shutting down repeat offenders “have improved compliance.”
“We’ve found that the majority of businesses stay in compliance once they learned to sell safe and certified devices,” she said. “We will continue our work to ensure compliance in this industry, especially to hold recidivist businesses accountable with our full authority.”
Another effort to get the delivery drivers who rely on e-bikes to stop using non-certified batteries kicked off in June 2025 under a law sponsored by then-Councilmember Keith Powers. The law created an exchange program for eligible drivers to turn in their unsafe batteries for those that were UL listed.
But the exchange program expired in 2025.
Last week after the Sunset Park catastrophe, Powers, now a state assemblymember, took to social media to call on the Mamdani administration to “resume that program and save lives.”
What Can Washington Do?
Another elected official who’s tried to staunch the sale of unsafe batteries is Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-The Bronx), whose district includes the Patterson Houses where a battery fire last month killed four tenants, including an 11-year-old boy, two teenage boys and a 33-year-old woman.
In 2024, and then again in 2025, Torres sponsored a bill that would require the Consumer Product Safety Commission to establish a safety standard for rechargeable lithium-ion batteries used in micromobility devices such as electric scooters and bikes. Nationally retailers would be barred from selling batteries that don’t meet those standards. In both years, an overwhelming and bipartisan House majority voted for it.
The bill, nevertheless, has been unable to get to the floor of the Senate, where Torres said it would also be overwhelmingly supported. The obstacle, he says, is Sen. Rand Paul (R-Kentucky), who’s employed a tactic that allows a single senator to block a bill from getting to the floor, without explanation.
Torres is marginally optimistic that the Democratic wave gave control of Congress to his party “would improve the prospects” of the bill seeing the light of day.
But, Torres added, “a Republican minority in the Senate could remain an obstacle.”
“I see it as a matter of life and death,” the congressman said. “Poorly manufactured lithium ion batteries are literally ticking time-bombs and it’s communities like the Bronx that are hardest hit.”
Finally the deadly fire in the Patterson Houses in The Bronx last month cast a spotlight on another attempt to prevent more of these fires from costing lives.
In 2023, the same year the council passed the law barring the sale of uncertified batteries, the New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) was considering prohibiting the charging of e-bike batteries, certified or not, on all public housing property. That September they dropped that plan and instead adopted a compromise: households could charge one battery per unit, as long as it was safety-certified and the charging could not block any exit from the apartment.
Since then, that compromise solution has been followed by no fewer than 53 e-bike battery fires in NYCHA apartments. In the Patterson Houses blaze, the residents were charging the battery in the kitchen, in a place that blocked the family from escaping.

https://gothamist.com/news/gov-hochul-wo.title: Gov. Hochul won with a mandate from voters. But what was the message?
https://gothamist.com/news/gov-hochul-wo.author: Jon Campbell
https://gothamist.com/news/gov-hochul-wo.text:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul scored the type of political victory on Election Day that typically comes with a mandate — but what message voters were trying to send depends on who you ask.
The Democratic governor topped her Republican opponent Bruce Blakeman by about 20 percentage points, or 1.2 million votes, tripling her margin of victory from the last time she ran in 2022. She increased her vote share in every single one of New York’s 62 counties, in red and blue areas alike, and won eight counties she lost four years ago — including Nassau, where Blakeman is county executive.
But what, exactly, does that result tell us about what voters are expecting from Hochul in her second full term? Everyone seems to have a different answer.
Christina Greer, a Fordham University political science professor, said the blue wave that swept the nation on Election Day — which saw Democrats win key races in traditionally Republican states — makes a New York-specific mandate difficult to define.
“I'm not sure if the governor has a mandate, and I think this goes for not just Kathy Hochul, but a lot of the Democrats who were successful on Tuesday,” she said. “I think we need to be careful as to: Is it a vote for Kathy Hochul, or is it a vote against Donald Trump?”
Hochul ran a campaign revolving around the cost of living.
She ran advertisements that touted the state’s free school meal program, her moratorium on data center construction and a round of energy rebate checks, which resulted in millions of payments of up to $200 landing in voters’ mailboxes shortly before Election Day.
Hochul’s campaign also focused on tying Blakeman to Trump, his friend and ally who headlined a rally in Syracuse just before voters started casting their ballots. Her ads frequently included a clip of Blakeman saying he would “never be disloyal” to the Republican president.
More than 60% of voters in New York view the president unfavorably, according to recent public opinion polls. Many voters blamed Trump for raising the price of gas through the war in Iran.
“ The Democrat message last night was basically, ’We’re not him,’” said Republican political consultant Mike Dawidziak. “And that message worked last night, but it’s not gonna work in two years.”
In 2018, the last midterm election with Trump in office, then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo, a Democrat, defeated Republican Marc Molinaro by 23 percentage points.
A Marist University poll last month showed Trump was clearly on voters’ minds when they headed to the polls this time, too.
Among likely voters in New York, 47% said their vote in their local congressional race was mostly a vote against Trump, while 18% said it was mostly a vote for Trump. About a third of voters said Trump wasn’t much of a factor at all.
In that same poll, 41% of likely voters said they had a favorable impression of Hochul, compared to 51% unfavorable. (A Siena University poll the same week was more favorable to Hochul, with 51% saying they had a favorable view of her.)
Hochul said she believes her huge margin of victory says more about her than it does the Republican president.
At an annual post-election conference in Puerto Rico on Friday, the governor said the takeaway from her huge margin of victory is simple: New York voters support her policies and want her to continue on.
“They want me to keep fighting to deliver affordability for New Yorkers,” she said. “They want me to keep building more housing. They want me to focus on energy resiliency and focus on the threat of climate change. And the other major one is childcare.”
Hochul, a centrist, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist whose 2025 victory marked a win for the left wing of the Democratic Party, have jointly implemented a major expansion of childcare in New York City and state that will persist into 2027.
Hochul endorsed Mamdani after he won the mayoral primary last year, and Mamdani, in turn, hit the campaign trail for Hochul, urging his supporters — many of whom are younger than Hochul’s base — to hit the polls.
Grace Mausser, cochair of the NYC Democratic Socialists of America, said Mamdani’s support of Hochul clearly paid off for the governor. She pointed to increased voter turnout in parts of Brooklyn and Queens that heavily supported the mayor in 2025.
She said Hochul would be wise to remember that when lawmakers return to the state Capitol in January. The governor will face renewed pressure from the left to raise income taxes on the wealthy — a move the governor has resisted.
“Taxing the rich isn’t just a DSA position, it’s a centrist position, too,” Mausser said, pointing to polls that have shown broad support for the issue.
Liz Benjamin, managing director of New York public affairs for the consulting firm Marathon Strategies, wrote an op-ed making the case that Hochul’s victory is a mandate to continue her brand of moderate politics and governing, rather than tack left.
She said Hochul’s margin shows that her win wasn’t a matter of progressive voters “holding their nose and voting for her.”
“I just don't think that that's in fact the case,” Benjamin said in an interview. “I think that this is because she actually made a viable argument to people and had a record of accomplishment and grew into the role.”
Bryan Lesswing, a former senior adviser to Hochul who now is a senior vice president at consulting firm SKDK, said the governor’s campaign excelled in appealing to voters with varying viewpoints.
“Her performance really shows, I think, a playbook for Democrats on the big tent politics that we're all talking about here that we need to shift toward, especially in the wake of [Trump’s win in] 2024,” he said.
Includes reporting by Walter Wuthmann

https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-says-.title: Mamdani says more help is coming to homeless New Yorkers living outside this winter
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-says-.author: Karen Yi
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-says-.text:
The Mamdani administration will deploy more nurses and add warming buses and beds across the city this winter, to better protect New Yorkers sleeping on the street from extreme cold.
The city announced the sweeping changes to its Code Blue policy Monday, as well as $25 million in new funding for it. Code Blue is triggered when temperatures drop below 32 degrees Fahrenheit. The new measures include deploying another 300 canvassers to reach out to homeless residents, 800 more beds to keep New Yorkers warm and hiring additional nurses who can provide care on site.
Last winter, more than two dozen people died outdoors or in their homes during a brutal stretch of freezing temperatures.
“We have spent the past year preparing for any challenge winter throws our way. We have trained our workers, readied our equipment and strengthened our protocols because keeping New Yorkers safe can’t begin when the first storm hits,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement.
“This winter, we’re doing things differently — we’re expanding Code Blue to reach more New Yorkers in need, equipping New York’s Strongest to clear snow and ice faster and leaving no stone unturned when it comes to protecting our neighbors from the cold. No New Yorker should face the dangers of winter alone, and no part of our city should be left behind.”
This winter, street canvassers will reach out to every homeless person they meet, rather than focusing on a list of at-risk individuals. More than 50 mobile vans run by the city’s public hospital system will provide medical care and transportation to warming facilities.
The Department of Homeless Services will also open four additional warming centers and deploy 20 warming buses.
City officials also announced improvements to its snow clearing efforts, putting a priority on keeping sidewalks clear for older adults and New Yorkers with disabilities. The city’s sanitation department will include more snow clearing routes on Staten Island and upgrade snow plows to more effectively clear roads. It also purchased the agency’s first snow blowers to clear bus stops and crosswalks faster.
New Yorkers can sign up for emergency alerts about extreme weather and emergency resources by texting NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 or download the app. Those interested can also sign up to be a snow shoveler earning $30 an hour.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/09/w.title: Winter Is Coming: Will Mamdani Do A Better Job For Bus Riders And Citi Bikers This Year?
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/09/w.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/09/w.text:
Mayor Mamdani (seen not holding a shovel at all but merely represented as such by our graphics team) vowed a better winter for New Yorkers trying to get around. The Streetsblog Photoshop Desk
It’s a winter wonder-land.
Mayor Mamdani is overhauling the city’s emergency response to better address the needs of homeless New Yorkers and others after last year’s extreme weather killed 18 people — but the portion of the plan related to transportation is light on details, and would rely on cooperation from the private companies that operate and maintain the Citi Bike docks and bus shelters on which thousands of New Yorkers rely.
On Monday, Hizzoner announced a number of improvements to, and investments in, the city’s winter weather protocols — a reaction to the harrowing winter that tested his fledgling team’s emergency response just weeks into his mayoralty. This includes a $25-million investment into the city’s “code blue” response to get vulnerable New Yorkers inside on the worst nights. The city will deploy 300 more outreach workers, use mobile warming vans, open city hospitals as warming centers and open more beds to homeless New Yorkers who need a place to stay.
But pedestrians, cyclists and bus riders who bore the brunt of the mobility dysfunction last winter will still have a blizzard of questions about this winter’s plan.
For instance, the mayor’s announcement said that the city had “established new protocols with JCDecaux and Citi Bike to clear bus stops, bike-share infrastructure and other priority transit areas faster” — but when Streetsblog inquired further about what exactly these new protocols entailed, a City Hall spokesperson said that conversations are ongoing, but include clearer expectations for the companies.
Lyft, which operates Citi Bike, has already committed to do better this winter, its spokesperson said.
“Lyft and the city share a commitment to keeping Citi Bike running throughout the winter,” said spokesperson CJ Macklin. “We’re working with the mayor’s office and DOT on updated protocols to prepare for winter weather and keep bikes and stations available for the New Yorkers who rely on them year-round.”
Last year, Citi Bike docks remained snowed in for weeks, bus riders traversed snowbanks and waited in the middle of the street for their ride, and pedestrians shuffled single file through narrow paths in the accumulated ice and slush. But the clarity of the expectations isn’t really the problem.
The city subcontracts with the advertising firm JCDecaux to operate bus shelters at 3,400 stops, meaning that the company, not the city, is responsible for clearing those bus stops after a storm. But private property owners are still responsible for the more than 10,000 bus stops not maintained by JCDecaux.
For Citi Bike the situation is similar. Lyft, the company that operates Citi Bike and owns the bikes and the docks, is clearly responsible for clearing them out in the event of snow. The company’s contract with the city has strict Service Level Agreements that are meant to keep the system operable for paid members. Lyft must remove snow within 12 hours of the end of the storm and must maintain parallel paths for pedestrians perpendicular to and parallel to the stations. The penalty is $50 per station, per 12-hour period.
But, these agreements are largely suspended during winter weather whenever alternate-side parking regulations are also suspended, making it impossible for the city to even fine Lyft for failing to clear out the docks, according to Lyft’s contract with the city that Streetsblog obtained through a records request.
It is unclear if any of these systems are actually changing, and City Hall would not say.
On the plus side, the city has purchased 120 snow blowers to help public workers clear areas that can’t be reached by typical plows. The Mamdani administration has added an unspecified number of small snow plows for the city’s protected bike infrastructure, a brigade that now numbers 47.
Last year, major protected bike lanes remained unplowed days after major snowfall forcing commuting cyclists and delivery workers into traffic.
And last year’s twin storms — which also came during prolonged stretches of cold weather that prevented melting — revealed existing flaws in the city’s approach to clearing crosswalks and sidewalks. The Mamdani administration says it is addressing those flaws by formally incorporating bus stops and crosswalks into official snow removal routes. In practice, property owners will remain responsible for clearing the sidewalks, but the Sanitation Department will now use an internal dashboard to identify areas for the city to step in.
“The Department of Sanitation will now be monitoring unsheltered bus stops and crosswalks in high-volume corridors and other pedestrian infrastructure via an internal dashboard and will dispatch Emergency Snow Shovelers as needed to ensure the safety of all New Yorkers,” said agency spokesperson Vincent Gragnani.
This winter is expected to be very different than last year. Meteorologists don’t expect long cold stretches that keep snowfall and ice on the street. Instead a strong El Niño will cause warmer weather. This will bring heavier, wetter snow, which, followed by short cold snaps, can create slippery ice, emergency management officials said at Monday’s press conference.
Last year, the city implemented its so-called “winter plan” for 50 consecutive days. DSNY workers laid one billion pounds of salt, cleared 135,000 crosswalks and plowed 6,300 miles of streets. On typical years the plan is only in place for around 10 days per winter, officials said. Officials promised that all New Yorkers’ transportation needs would be taken care of this winter.

The Julia Stoschek Foundation will reopen in its Düsseldorf space in April 2027, just in time for the organization’s 20th anniversary. “Selfish in Bed”—a group exhibition curated by Krist Gruijthuijsen comprising 52 works from 43 artists in the foundation’s archive—will inaugurate the newly renovated galleries.
“Selfish in Bed” takes its title from a Sarah Lucas self-portrait, Selfish in Bed II, 2000, which depicts the artist (standing in front of a gnome statue) wearing a t-shirt that reads “Selfish in Bed.” The exhibition will include work by Bill Viola, Wolfgang Tillmans, Tracey Emin, Simon Fujiwara and Rosemarie Trockel that span from the late 1960s to the present day. According to a press release for the exhibition, “Selfish in Bed,” will “use the confined and seemingly safe space of the bed as its narrative framework,” across the Foundation’s two levels.
A publication celebrating the Foundation’s 20th anniversary will accompany the exhibition, including contributions from Erika Balsom, Benjamin Buchloh, Rachel Cusk, Dana Dawud, Dean Kissick, Udo Kittelmann, Chris Kraus, Lil Internet, Meg Onli, Mindy Seu, Jeppe Ugelvig, McKenzie Wark.
“I am a very emotional collector,” Stoschek said in the press release, “An artwork has to get under my skin. I need images that stay with me. Over the past 20 years, I’ve built a collection of time-based art from the 1960s to the present, driven by the energy of the works and the artists who create them. From the very beginning, I wanted to share that experience with the public. Seeing the collection continue to grow and welcoming new audiences two decades on brings me enormous joy.”

Hundreds gathered around Anish Kapoor’s iconic Cloud Gate, knows as the “Bean,” in Chicago’s Millennium Park on Sunday in an attempt to shift the sculpture seven inches to the left. Despite the crowd’s best efforts, the silver 110-ton stainless steel sculpture could not be moved.
ARTnews reports that the stunt was based on a viral online joke, which holds that a man is trapped inside the 66-foot-long, 33-foot-high, kidney bean–shaped sculpture. An unknown party created a Partiful event invitation announcing that “new findings suggest that there might be [a] latch door under the right side of the bean. If we move the bean about 7 inches to the left we might be able to access that door and give the man inside the bean resources.”
Alderman Brendan Reilly, who represents the ward that includes Millennium Park, told Book Club Chicago that his office received multiple calls about the rumor last summer. “I am happy to confirm that a man has not been trapped inside ‘Cloud Gate’ (a.k.a ‘the Bean’) for the past 21 years,” he wrote in a statement.
On July 31, 2025, a group dressed in black gathered near the Bean with signs calling for the release of “the man in the Bean.” A video of that event went viral on Instagram and TikTok, resulting in the flood of calls to the alderman’s office.
The Instagram account @thingstodoinchicago posted a video of Sunday’s mob, capturing the group surrounding one end of the sculpture and appearing to give a concerted push. “What started as a viral internet joke turned into a real-life gathering,” the post reads, “proving once again that Chicago has a sense of humor like no other.”

Billionaire Les Wexner’s name will remain on Ohio State University’s Wexner Center for the Arts, even though the school received hundreds of requests to remove it owing to his ties to Jeffrey Epstein, the Columbus Dispatch reports. More than five hundred requests sought to remove the name from the campus’s arts center, medical center, and football complex in Columbus. The decision to keep it was made by OSU interim provost Trevor Brown, who on November 6 rejected an advisory committee’s recommendation that the school look into the mogul’s relationship with the late pedophile and that it review allegations of sexual misconduct by Wexner and abusive employment practices at his businesses.
Wexner, the founder of clothing brand The Limited, a cofounder of Bath & Body Works, and a former principal of lingerie retailer Victoria’s Secret, is OSU’s biggest donor, having gifted the school more than $200 million to date, according to the New York Times. He was mentioned more than one thousand times in the Epstein files released by the US Department of Justice earlier this year.
Brown, in a letter to the advisory committee, noted that Wexner had not been charged with or convicted of any crime, further stating that the committee had never been meant to serve as an investigative organ. Though he affirmed that the university would revisit the matter if new evidence became available, this was cold comfort to the members of Wex Workers United, the arts center’s union, which had campaigned to have the name removed.
“Workers will bear the brunt of this decision, fielding angry and hostile comments from the public and having the work we do questioned for its association with the Wexner name,” a representative of WWU told Hyperallergic.
The release of the Epstein files has reverberated throughout the worlds of art and education, with School of Visual Arts chair David A. Ross and L’Institut du Monde Arabe president Jack Lang among those who vacated their roles after being named in them.

https://hyperallergic.com/brokies-this-m.title: Brokies, This Met Gala Is for You
https://hyperallergic.com/brokies-this-m.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/brokies-this-m.text:
Brokies, This Met Gala Is for You
T-shirts revolutionize the Costume Institute’s programming, the sociability of MoMA’s Brancusi exhibit, and the curators of the 2028 Whitney Biennial announced.
A saturated blue sky and cascades of complementary golden-yellow foliage laid the foundation for a vibrant, picturesque Diwali weekend in the suburbs. It wasn’t the most festive Diwali for me — instead of lighting diyas and playing with sparklers, I spent a majority of the weekend hand-feeding a friendly yard squirrel while wearing some bullshit pajamas extracted from the depths of my childhood closet.
Think I’m slumming it? Well, think again! Because those dilapidated pajamas are almost certainly what inspired the theme for next year’s Met Gala and related Costume Institute exhibit: extraOrdinary: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday, a program “devoted to the undersung beauty and allure of quotidian garments.” (That’s code for jeans.)
(And t-shirts. And raincoats. Maybe pajamas, but also maybe not.)
It’s an exasperated, last-minute pivot after controversial British fashion designer John Galliano, who was central to the Costume Institute’s original program for 2027, withdrew from participating entirely this August in response to the public backlash toward his racist behavior in the past. Between “elevating” daily wear into runway fashion and exploring how “humble, even ‘disposable’ materials” like paper and aluminum can become wearable, this enormous exercise in putting a positive spin on gentrifying economic recession is at odds with NYC residents who are buckling from profound unaffordability as the city speedruns its transformation into a private equity playground.
I guess I can’t really say which is worse — the current standard of celebrities in bespoke, extravagant garments from elite fashion houses hanging off their GLP-1 frames, or the notion that a Met Gala dress code calling for aluminum foil pants, a shrunken tee, and maybe a jacket made from hole-punched plastic circles is what’ll push people to consider everyday wear in a different light.
However, before we get too pressed, we have to acknowledge that this is a big moment for the Bad Bunny x Zara collection! On the plus side, it might make it easier for some ~lowly civs~ to sneak in and eat all the cheese cubes. Dress for the job you want, right?
Speaking of jobs — Whitney Museum curator Meg Onli returns as a co-curator for the 2028 Whitney Biennial, sharing the stage with director and dancer Zack Winokur, who co-founded the interdisciplinary American Modern Opera Company in 2017. I found the 2026 Biennial to be a textbook case of the whole being less than the sum of its parts. Let’s see how Winokur’s hand in artistic performance direction manifests in this curatorial behemoth; I’m sure he’s used to working with a lot of moving parts.
Back to the here and now, I’m long overdue for multiple museum visits at the peak of the season. The days keep slipping through my fingers before I’ve had a chance to visit the Krasner Pollock show at The Met or the Architects of Liberation at the MoMA. Mayor Mamdani actually paid a visit to the MoMA show before I did, and he’s significantly busier than I am, so there’s really no excuse!
In another nudge for me to make the journey uptown, MoMA recently opened its Brancusi exhibition. With a replica of Brancusi’s studio and a selection of rare media documenting his work environment and the social atmosphere he cultivated between his sculptures and his guests alike, the exhibition spotlights the artist’s labor-intensive process as an art form in itself.
Critic Aruna D’Souza noted that the “sculptures seem to be maintaining COVID-era social distancing protocols,” and chalked that awkward dynamic up to the MoMA’s renovated gallery layout, recalling the previously approachable setup’s capacity to “allow for art objects to talk to each other.”
On Sunday, I bore witness to a conversation that made me think about Brancusi’s glinting buffed bronzes and smooth marbles. The chatter between a yellowing tree branch, an overturned recycling bin, and the white picket fence behind them might have been too maximalist compared to the Romanian sculptor’s sleek, pared-down modernism. Nevertheless, I pulled over to eavesdrop.

The organizers of the Liverpool Biennial have revealed the theme and artists for the event’s fourteenth iteration, cocurated by Aimee Harrison and Lucía Sanromán and slated to run June 5–September 12, 2027. Titled “The Age of Magical Thinking,” the exhibition takes as its starting point psychologist Jean Piaget’s theory of cognitive development, which is based on the idea that an individual’s imagination is especially fertile during a specific period of childhood. To that end, the biennial will center the experience of childhood as it pertains to past, present and future.
“I think of childhood and youth as a period of constant transition, of change and possibility, but also a time that demands and requires the urgency to question the present,” said Sanromán in a statement. “Artists in the exhibition give us insights into the imagination of childhood, spurring us to boldly ask for a better future. The exhibition responds to the loud demands by young people throughout the world to be taken seriously in how political decisions are made, and for whom.”
Among the twenty-five participating artists are British Argentine artist Amalia Pica, who explores communication through installations, sculptures, and collages; the Kosovo-born Petrit Halilaj who investigates topics including cultural identity, nationhood, and heritage; and Dutch photographer Rineke Dijkstra, known for her starkly intimate portraits of adolescents.
The biennial will take place across multiple venues, including Bluecoat, Exhibition Research Lab at Liverpool John Moores University, FACT Liverpool, Open Eye Gallery, Victoria Gallery &
Museum, and Walker Art Gallery, with more to be announced.

https://hyperallergic.com/gochman-collec.title: Gochman Collection Builds a Home for Native Art in Westchester
https://hyperallergic.com/gochman-collec.author: Petala Ironcloud
https://hyperallergic.com/gochman-collec.text:
Gochman Collection Builds a Home for Native Art in Westchester
The private collection opened its Branchline location in Katonah as a way to bring Native art into public view, though questions linger about its engagement with the local Lenape community.
KATONAH, NY — In 1680, English colonists bought the land that would become Bedford, New York, from a Munsee Lenape sachem named Katonah, meaning “great hill.” Today, his name belongs to a Westchester village that is now home to Branchline, the Gochman Family Collection’s (GFC) new gallery and studio space, which opened to the public on November 6 with Line Break, an exhibition of works drawn primarily from its holdings of contemporary Native American art.
Since its founding in 2021, GFC has collected over 800 works with support from Native and non-Native gallerists, artists, and curators alike, including Creative Director and Curator Rachel Martin (Tlingít), curator and Hyperallergic contributor Shándíín Brown (Diné), and Director Laura Phipps, who also serves as Branchline’s director. Designed by Elizabeth Roberts Architects, the new space occupies two historic storefronts steps from Katonah’s Metro-North station, with free-admission galleries, skylit artist studios, a community ceramics studio, and apartments for invited artists.
Branchline makes a public home for what has essentially been a lending operation: According to GFC, more than 260 of its works have appeared in over 100 exhibitions at institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, and The Broad, and it charges no loan fees. That model speaks to a known problem with private collecting, explained Joseph Pierce (Cherokee), professor and founding director of the Native American and Indigenous Studies Initiative at Stony Brook University. “Just because you collect something doesn’t mean you’re going to show it,” Pierce told Hyperallergic. “The risk is that it doesn’t circulate.”

The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts has named Franklin Sirmans as chair of the board. Three other board members have also been named: Cheryl Finley, Candice Hopkins, and Suzi Kwon Cohen.
Since 2015, Sirmans has been the Sandra and Tony Tamer Director of the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). During his tenure, he has overseen the acquisition of over a thousand works of art, both by donation and purchase. Prior to joining PAMM, Sirmans was the department head and curator of contemporary art at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA). He was also the Artistic Director of the 2014 Prospect New Orleans biennial. At LACMA, he oversaw major retrospectives by Glenn Ligon and Blinky Palermo and curated “Noah Purifoy: Junk Dada” and “Fútbol: The Beautiful Game.” Sirmans is the former U.S. editor of Flash Art and editor in chief of ArtAsiaPacific.
The Foundation’s board is composed of 18 individuals across the arts. Sirmans succeeds Deborah Willis, while Naomi Beckwith and Cary Davis will also leave the board. “Our new board members bring valuable expertise and fresh perspectives that will deepen the Foundation’s commitment to artists and the visual arts field,” said Joel Wachs, President of the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, in a press release. “Together with Franklin Sirmans’ leadership, their knowledge, insight, and experience will help us advance our mission and meet the evolving needs of artists and the organizations that support them.”
