https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ‘Nada voltará a ser como era antes da guerra do Irã’, diz professora da Universidade de Teerã
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Mauro Ramos
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
“Nada voltará a ser como era antes da guerra. A justificativa para a presença militar dos Estados Unidos na região [do Golfo Pérsico] era dissuadir a ‘ameaça’ iraniana, mas, na prática, ela se tornou um alvo de retaliação”, diz a professora assistente da Faculdade de Estudos Mundiais da Universidade de Teerã, Setareh Sadeqi, em entrevista ao Brasil de Fato.
Sadeqi participou do lançamento da campanha “Tirem as Mãos da Ásia“, lançada em julho de 2026 em Colombo, no Sri Lanka, reunindo 80 delegados de 46 organizações de 17 países para conectar as lutas contra as bases estadunidenses, as sanções e as guerras na região.
Em outubro, ela também participou do Fórum Acadêmico do Sul Global, em Xangai, na China, onde foi panelista do debate sobre paz e responsabilidade política na Ásia. O Fórum, em sua quarta edição, reuniu representantes de partidos, movimentos populares e centros de pesquisa do Sul Global. Ela classifica como “guerra existencial” o conflito imposto pelos regimes israelense e estadunidense contra seu país.
Na entrevista, Sadeqi descreve as sanções como “terrorismo econômico”, afirma que o pretexto da presença militar dos EUA na região caiu e defende que países pequenos sob cerco, como o Iêmen, estão exercendo sua autonomia. Ela também fala da aproximação entre povos da Ásia Oriental e Ocidental contra a militarização. A conversa aconteceu durante o Fórum.
Confira a entrevista na íntegra:
Brasil de Fato: Os Estados Unidos afirmam que venceram a agressão contra o Irã desde o início, mas tudo indica que o Irã passou a controlar o Estreito de Ormuz. Poderia nos atualizar sobre a situação?
Setareh Sadeqi: Tudo o que acontece no Golfo Pérsico e em relação ao Irã é parte de uma disputa maior entre a ordem liberal imperial e o Sul Global. É assim que eu interpreto. Nesse sentido, o Irã não vive uma guerra apenas militar. Houve conversas sobre um memorando de entendimento e o fim da guerra, mas, na prática, são outras formas de guerra que se impõem ao Irã, incluindo o que eu chamo de terrorismo econômico: as sanções e as medidas coercitivas unilaterais contra o país. O chefe do Tesouro dos Estados Unidos se gabou de que essas sanções paralisariam a economia e dobrariam o establishment político, assim como pressionariam os iranianos na esperança de que se revoltassem contra o sistema. O que observamos é que, no fim, os iranianos não capitulam sob pressão. Eles tentam fazer o que for para proteger a soberania. Os acontecimentos recentes mostram que, mesmo com as tentativas de retirar a agência e o poder das autoridades iranianas no controle do Estreito de Ormuz, esses confrontos continuam, e o Irã tenta reagir e deixar claro que continuará exercendo influência sobre suas águas territoriais e o estreito.
Alguns analistas afirmam que, depois da resposta do Irã aos ataques do governo Trump, a situação na região mudou, talvez para sempre, porque Trump teve a proeza de fazer desaparecer muitas das bases militares dos EUA na região. Qual é a sua leitura sobre essa presença militar dos Estados Unidos?
Nada voltará a ser como era antes da guerra. A justificativa para a presença militar dos EUA na região era dissuadir a “ameaça iraniana”. Mas, na prática, ela se tornou um alvo, o alvo principal, de mais retaliação. E criou insegurança para os Estados Unidos e para os países da região que abrigam bases militares. Como essa justificativa desapareceu, os EUA não podem mais justificar a presença militar dizendo que estão lá para dissuadir a ameaça iraniana porque, na prática, estão importando o conflito para a região, para os Estados do Golfo Pérsico. Como essa justificativa está sendo profundamente questionada, é muito difícil para os EUA manterem a presença militar como antes. Isso não significa que agora os EUA vão retirar as bases. Mas vai se tornar muito mais difícil justificar a presença na região.
Poderia também nos atualizar sobre a situação do Iêmen? Porque isso também é inédito. O Norte Global gosta de chamar os iemenitas de “grupos apoiados pelo Irã” (proxies, em inglês), quando, na verdade, eles são aliados do Irã nas mesmas causas. Poderia nos atualizar sobre o que essa nova fase da resistência significa para eles e para a região?
Primeiro, a hipocrisia das potências hegemônicas e da mídia associada ao Norte Global. Quando se trata dos persas, das monarquias do Golfo Pérsico, eles as chamam de aliadas dos EUA. Mas, quando se trata das forças de resistência, as chamam de proxies do Irã. Na prática, vemos o Iêmen exercendo a própria autonomia. Recentemente, o governo iraniano ofereceu mediar entre a Arábia Saudita e o Iêmen, e o Iêmen rejeitou. Isso significa que eles agem por conta própria, têm autonomia e decidem o que é melhor para a nação, para o país. Também por causa do cerco: até comida era muito difícil de chegar ao Iêmen. Mas a guerra contra o Irã e contra o Iêmen questionou totalmente a suposição de que esses pequenos Estados não podem se defender, não têm autonomia e precisam de uma potência externa para controlá-los e moldar a geopolítica da região. Na realidade, vimos que tanto o Irã, sob sanções paralisantes há décadas, quanto o Iêmen, sob cerco e pressão, conseguiram resistir.
Os mísseis patriots e THAAD dos Estados Unidos, que estavam estacionados na República da Coreia, foram realocados para disponibilizá-los para atacar o Irã. E houve resistência entre a população coreana.
Isso é um exemplo da vontade dos povos dos nossos diferentes países. Em alguns casos, ela difere da vontade dos chamados governos representantes. Na Coreia do Sul, havia uma posição de maior envolvimento militar dos EUA, por exemplo, o envio de tropas para o Estreito de Ormuz, e até dentro da região, nas monarquias do Golfo Pérsico. Está cada vez mais claro que esses regimes não representam a vontade das nações, mesmo depois de absorverem os ataques de retaliação do Irã. Existe um desejo forte entre os povos de se unirem e dizer não à militarização da Ásia. E a plataforma [do Fórum Acadêmico do Sul Global] está cumprindo um papel nesse sentido. Para mim, foi muito inspirador ver pessoas do Japão, da Coreia do Sul, da China. Existe uma resistência. Se você sente que sua resistência está isolada, pode perder o ânimo de continuar. Mas, quando vê que pessoas ao redor do mundo entendem isso e querem rejeitar, é fortalecedor e inspirador. Por isso acho muito importante fazer parte dessas plataformas e campanhas.

https://taz.de/Wirtschaftsexperten-zu-Ha.title: Wirtschaftsexperten zu Haushalt für 2027: Militär mit Steuern finanzieren
https://taz.de/Wirtschaftsexperten-zu-Ha.author: Hannes Koch
https://taz.de/Wirtschaftsexperten-zu-Ha.text:
Wirtschaftsexperten zu Haushalt für 2027: Militär mit Steuern finanzieren
Die Wirtschaftsweisen raten, die hohe Verschuldung für Verteidigungsausgaben zu verringern. Dafür müsste im Bundeshaushalt aber hart gespart werden.
Mit der gegenwärtig hohen Staatsverschuldung gehe es nicht ewig so weiter, mahnen die Wirtschaftweisen. Sie raten der Regierung, die Kreditaufnahme für die Verteidigung bald zu begrenzen, dafür unter anderem bei der Rente zu sparen und zur Not auch Steuern zu erhöhen.
Im Bundeshaushalt sieht der Sachverständigenrat für Wirtschaft einen „Handlungsbedarf von historischem Ausmaß“. Die zwei Professorinnen und drei Professoren präsentierten am Mittwoch ihr neues Gutachten. Union und SPD im Bundestag verhandelten währenddessen den Bundeshaushalt für 2027, der zu knapp einem Drittel durch neue Schulden finanziert wird.
Vor allem die hohen, kreditfinanzierten Militärausgaben betrachten die ÖkonomInnen als langfristiges Problem. 2027 sollen diese etwa 150 Milliarden Euro betragen, zwei Drittel durch zusätzliche Schulden. Die Koalition aus Union und SPD hat dafür 2025 die sogenannte Bereichsausnahme als Umgehung der Schuldenbremse im Grundgesetz eingeführt: Verteidigungskosten, die 1 Prozent der Wirtschaftsleistung übersteigen, dürfen mit Kreeinditen gedeckt werden.
Damit die Zinsen dieser Schulden den Bundeshaushalt in zehn Jahren nicht sprengen, schlagen die Wirtschaftsweisen nun vor: Die Koalition solle noch in dieser Wahlperiode beschließen, dass ab 2031 jedes Jahr ein zusätzliches Viertelprozent der übersteigenden Militärausgaben aus dem normalen Haushalt, das heißt mit Steuereinnahmen zu finanzieren sei. „Die schrittweise Rückführung der Kreditfinanzierung sollte grundgesetzlich verankert werden“, sagte Monika Schnitzer, die Vorsitzende der Sachverständigen.
Steuererhöhungen fürs Militär?
Die Folge: Im Bundeshaushalt entstünde eine zunehmende Finanzierungslücke in der Größenordnung von künftig 100 bis 200 Milliarden Euro pro Jahr, die spätere Regierungskoalitionen irgendwie schließen müssten. Auch dafür unterbreiten die Wirtschaftsweisen Vorschläge. Beispielsweise ließen sich „Finanzhilfen“ und „umweltschädliche Steuervergünstigungen“ kürzen. Infrage käme etwa die Abschaffung der Steuervorteile für Diesel-Treibstoff und Flugbenzin. Solche Posten brächten jährliche Einsparungen von insgesamt 17 Milliarden Euro oder mehr.
Weiterhin plädieren die ExpertInnen für Einsparungen in der Rentenversicherung. Sie sprechen sich gegen die teure Mütterrente III aus, die die CSU gern haben möchte. Und sie erklären, dass die sogenannte Haltelinie beim Rentenniveau zu teuer werde. Gibt man sie auf, erhalten RentnerInnen auf die Dauer weniger Alterssicherung im Vergleich zu den Arbeitslöhnen. Schließlich ziehen die ÖkonomInnen auch Steuererhöhungen in Erwägung. Konkret nennen sie etwa den „Abbau von Steuerprivilegien bei Immobilienveräußerungen“. Auch höhere Grenzsteuersätze in der Einkommensteuer stehen auf der Liste.
Schnitzer betonte, die Ausgabenkürzungen seien „fair zwischen Generationen und Gruppen zu verteilen“. Leider reichten sie trotzdem nicht, um die verbleibenden großen Lücken in künftigen Haushalten zu schließen, räumen die Sachverständigen ein – unter der Voraussetzung, die Bundeswehr bekomme weiter so viel Geld wie momentan. Nahe liegt deshalb diese Schlussfolgerung: Mit der gegenwärtigen Schuldenbremse im Grundgesetz wäre der Geldbedarf nicht in Einklang zu bringen. Sie müsste gelockert werden. Darüber kann sich die aktuelle Koalition aber nicht einigen.
Die Wirtschaftslage in der nächsten Zeit beschreibt der Sachverständigenrat so: Dieses Jahr wachse die deutsche Wirtschaft um 1,3 Prozent, 2027 wohl um 1 Prozent. Die Arbeitslosigkeit gehe leicht auf 6,3 Prozent zurück, dagegen steige die Inflation von 2,8 Prozent in diesem auf 3,3 Prozent im kommenden Jahr.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ‘Taxa de juros deve ser encarada como causa e não consequência’, afirma economista sobre ajuste fiscal
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Gabriela Carvalho
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O governo Lula, junto ao Congresso Nacional, vai formular um Projeto de Lei Complementar (PLP) para um ajuste fiscal de 0,5% do Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) em 2027. O acordo foi costurado em reunião entre o presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União Brasil-AP), e o ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan.
Ao Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, a economista Leda Paulani, professora na Universidade de São Paulo (USP), afirma que os donos da riqueza financeira acabam tendo armas poderosas de pressão. Tanto é que o mercado teve forte oscilação após os dois turnos das eleições deste ano, indicando preferência ao candidato Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), que já anunciava um corte de gastos drástico, o chamado “tesouraço”.
Paulani aponta que as informações dão conta de que a desvinculação dos gastos em saúde e educação não está prevista. “O que foi anunciado é um micro-ajuste. O que se faz é uma redução da base de cálculo das receitas”, explica. “Eu acho que é uma medida bem marginal, considerando aquilo que o mercado espera.”
A economista também avalia como positiva a previsão de cortes maiores nos benefícios tributários, algo que o governo Lula já vinha tentando há algum tempo. “A questão da desoneração da folha de salários, o governo vem tentando há muito tempo reduzir isso porque não traz nenhum benefício ao país. Ao contrário, só reduz, de fato, a renda disponível do governo e a base de cálculo desses benefícios sociais, sobretudo a Previdência, que fica molestada com isso”, aponta. Paulani lembra que o ex-ministro Fernando Haddad tentou passar projeto de desoneração no Congresso e acabou derrotado, porque existe uma resistência.
Para a professora, será necessário alguma “costura política para impedir que o mercado atire muita pedra”. Leda Paulani critica a taxa de juros, que acaba pressionando a relação dívida-PIB. “O PIB cresce 2,5%, 3% ao ano e a dívida cresce na base da taxa de juros de quase 15%. Os juros estão num patamar que não tem justificativa. Eles são absolutamente irracionais do ponto de vista macroeconômico”, pondera. “O único resultado possível é agravar as contas públicas que o mercado diz defender tanto. A taxa de juros é causa e não consequência”, resume.
Assim como outros economistas nas últimas semanas, Paulani alerta para o que chama de “equívoco teórico” na afirmação de que a única forma de controlar preços é a alta de juros e afirma que a alta da inflação é global porque ela é impactada por diversos acontecimentos.
“Você tem pressões de custo porque pode ter desastres climáticos que prejudicam a produção agrícola, você pode ter guerra que prejudica o preço do petróleo, você pode ter estrangulamentos de cadeias produtivas por conta de fatores associados ao controle da pandemia, como tivemos, e tudo isso vai rebater nos preços”, argumenta.
Para ouvir e assistir
O jornal Conexão BdF vai ao ar em duas edições, de segunda a sexta-feira: a primeira às 12h e a segunda às 17h, na Rádio Brasil de Fato, 98.9 FM, na Grande São Paulo, com transmissão simultânea também pelo YouTube do Brasil de Fato.

https://taz.de/Sparpolitik-an-Hamburgs-S.title: Sparpolitik an Hamburgs Schulen: Rot-Grün hat keinen Bock mehr auf Debatte
https://taz.de/Sparpolitik-an-Hamburgs-S.author: Kaija Kutter
https://taz.de/Sparpolitik-an-Hamburgs-S.text:
Sparpolitik an Hamburgs Schulen : Rot-Grün hat keinen Bock mehr auf Debatte
Hamburgs Ganztagsschulen werden kaputtgespart, obwohl sie das günstigste Modell für Nachmittagsbetreuung sind. Der Senat will das nicht zugeben.
H uch, da will uns jemand verschaukeln, könnte man am Ende der Lektüre des 90-seitigen Protokolls der Anhörung des Hamburger Schulausschusses zu den Kürzungen bei den Ganztagsschulen denken. Nicht nur Lehrer und Eltern, auch Kinder hatten bei dieser Sitzung am 7. Oktober im Festsaal des Rathauses mit viel Herzblut erklärt, warum ihnen die heutige Form der Ganztagsgrundschulen (GTS) so wichtig ist.
Denn ab dem nächsten Schuljahr sollen die 85 Schulen nachmittags nur noch mit Erziehern arbeiten und die dort bisher tätigen 220 Lehrkräfte abgezogen werden. Die Begründung ist rein finanziell, gut 16 Millionen Euro soll dies sparen. Doch damit gerät ein über Jahre fein austariertes Schulsystem aus den Fugen. Lehrkräfte müssen gehen, Schulkonzepte müssen neu entwickelt werden. Und die Rhythmisierung des Ganztags, der Wechsel von Unterricht und anderen Angeboten für die Kinder, steht ernsthaft infrage.
Ein überraschendes Argument hatten die für die GTS streitenden Schulleitungen in petto. Hamburg bietet seit 2012 flächendeckend Nachmittagsbetreuung an jeder Grundschule an. An den übrigen 128 Schulen heißt dies „Ganztätige Bildung und Betreuung“ (GBS) und wird ab 13 Uhr von Kita-Trägern übernommen. Weil diese auch noch Kosten für Aufgaben haben, die an den GTS die Schulleitungen übernehmen, sind Letztere schon heute – also vor den Sparmaßnahmen – das günstigere Model.
Schulsenatorin Ksenija Bekeris (SPD) wurde im nun im Schulausschuss vom Linken-Abgeordneten David Stoop gefragt, wie das Verhältnis der Kosten von GTS zu GBS heute ist. Er bat explizit auch darum, die Overheadkosten mit aufzuführen. Bekeris antwortete, das gebe sie zu Protokoll. Sprich: Die Antwort ist vier, fünf Wochen später in der Parlamentsdatenbank nachzulesen.
Allerdings liefert ihre Behörde nur eine Tabelle mit reinen Kosten des „am Kind tätigen pädagogischen Personals“. Und, was Wunder, hier ist die GBS günstiger mit derzeit 1.935 Euro pro Kind im Jahr gegenüber den 2.547 Euro der GTS, die am Nachmittag zu 20 Prozent Lehrkräfte beschäftigen.
Gefragt, warum in der Tabelle nicht wie gefordert die Overheadkosten genannt wurden, erklärt Bekeris’ Sprecher Peter Albrecht, diese ließen sich auf Seiten der Schulbehörde nur schwer zuordnen. Darum ließen sich mit den genannten Zahlen „die Kosten für GTS und GBS am besten vergleichen“.
Beide Modelle haben ihre Stärken
Das kann man auch anders sehen. Ein Blick in den aktuellen Landesrahmenvertrag zur GBS zeigt, dass die Entgelte für die Betreuungszeit von 13 bis 16 Uhr für Schulen je nach sozialer Lage zwischen 3.514 Euro und 3.136 Euro im Jahr liegen. Also deutlich höher. Da nicht wahrscheinlich ist, dass der Verwaltungsaufwand der Schulbehörde pro GTS-Kind in dieser Spanne liegt, muss die GTS heute schon günstiger zu sein. Muss man sie dann noch kaputtsparen?
Beide Modelle haben ihre Stärken, und auch die GBS ist keineswegs zu teuer oder üppig finanziert, denn pro Tag und Kind sind es gerade mal 16 bis 18 Euro. Hamburg hat vor 15 Jahren einen günstigen Weg gewählt, um die flächendeckende Schulkindbetreuung und damit die Berufstätigkeit der Steuern zahlenden Eltern zu sichern.
Es wäre angebracht, diese Sparmaßnahme auszusetzen, statt eine derart gewachsene Schulkultur zu zerschlagen. Rot-Grün plant übrigens nach Berechnung von engagierten Lehrkräften über 1.000 Lehrerstellen ein. Auch gegen die Verschlechterung der Stundenversorgung an Gymnasien und Stadtteilschulen regt sich Widerstand.
Darum beantragte die CDU-Politikerin Birgit Stöver für Montag eine Sondersitzung zu den Auswirkungen dieser Kürzungen. Nur will Hamburgs SPD nicht mehr diskutieren. Die Sitzung werde stattfinden, wurde Stöver mitgeteilt. Aber Rot-Grün werde verhindern, dass das Thema dort debattiert wird.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on Maga after the midterms: doubling down on Trumpism | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Shortly after polls closed last Tuesday, with the scale of the Republican trouncing in the midterms still becoming apparent, Donald Trump briefly adopted an oddly conciliatory tone. He declared that he was “absolutely” willing to accept the results, would look forward to working with Democrats and that deportation policies might have been “too tough”.
It was never going to last. He soon cast doubt on the elections’ legitimacy. On Friday, he replaced his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with her deputy, Stephen Miller – a white nationalist, or “stone-cold racist”, in the words of Hakeem Jeffries, likely to be the next House speaker. Ms Wiles executed the president’s decisions faithfully, but was seen as a somewhat calming if not restraining influence, which may help explain her departure.
Every high-profile woman in the administration has now quit or been ousted, and its machismo has increased. Mr Miller is an ideological extremist and attack dog who has spearheaded the expansion of executive power as well as the draconian immigration excesses that alienated many (particularly Latino) voters. He reportedly wants to wind down the war on Iran, but played a leading role in strikes against alleged drugs boats in the Caribbean – extrajudicial killings.
Happily for Mr Trump, the reshuffle has turned discussion away from lame ducks and the Republican succession. He does not need the mixed martial arts supremo Dana White as his press secretary; he has enough brawlers. On Tuesday, House Republicans picked another aggressive hardliner, Jim Jordan, as minority leader. He has pledged to fight investigations by the new Democratic majority. On the same day, they blocked the attempted impeachment of Pete Hegseth, the self-styled “secretary of war” (with some Democrats also missing the vote). The outgoing Republican congressman Thomas Massie was pressing the case against him over the Iran war and attacks on drugs boats. Mr Hegseth is manifestly unfit for office. He has shared highly sensitive information on a messaging app and wanted to live stream a military execution. But a case against him might embarrass Mr Trump.
Some still hope that Republicans will have little choice but to hold Mr Trump accountable for last week’s defeat. JD Vance sought to distance himself by criticising the Iran war, and Ron DeSantis declared that there was “no question” that the results were a rebuke of Mr Trump. But GOP politicians either want more Trumpism, or are extremely wary of taking him on, after he torched previous critics. Trump voters are split between the Maga base, which wants to double down (and who turned out last Tuesday) and the rest who want to moderate (and stayed home) – with divisions on everything from datacentres to deportations. The Republicans can’t win in 2028 with Maga votes alone. Yet the GOP regained power in 2016 by becoming more extreme.
The Democrats now have their own challenge. They must use their new congressional power to ensure accountability – including pinning corruption in Mr Trump’s circle to the cost of living crisis – while also trying to deliver for voters who need real improvements in their lives. Republicans will seek to tie them up in fruitless congressional battles.
The Trumpist message is so clear that the outgoing speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, even said it out loud: “The voters made the wrong choice.” The Republicans are promising the electorate more of what they didn’t want. The people have spoken, but the president – and his party – won’t listen.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Festival Rec n’ Play leva maratona de atividades e shows ao Bairro do Recife até o próximo sábado (14)
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A partir desta quarta-feira (14), o bairro do Recife é ocupado pelas centenas de atividades do festival de tecnologia Rec n’ Play, realizado pelo Porto Digital e pelo Sebrae. São realizadas atividades como palestras, bate-papos e oficinas e ações em eixos como tecnologia, negócios, cidade, sustentabilidade, sociedade, criatividade e cultura. A programação também conta com shows de grandes figuras da música pernambucana, como Otto, Lenine, Cordel do Fogo Encantado, Devotos e Ave Sangria.
O festival, considerado o maior gratuito de tecnologia, empreendedorismo e economia criativa segue até o próximo sábado (14). Nesta oitava edição, ele vem com o tema “O Futuro Nasce Aqui”. Entre destaques da programação, estão a presença de nomes como o jornalista Caco Barcellos, a podcaster Déia Freitas e o escritor Fabrício Carpinejar. A lista completa das atividades está disponível no site recnplay.pe, assim como as inscrições.
A programação musical é dividida entre três palcos: Jornada dos MC’s (Rua do Bom Jesus), Sesc (Rua da Moeda) e Recife Cidade da Música (Praça do Arsenal). Além dos shows, que começam a partir das 19h, a programação também conta com batalhas de rap e cyphers. Nesta quarta-feira (11), Otto sobe ao palco na Praça do Arsenal, em uma noite que ainda contará com shows de Devotos e Bione. Na quinta-feira (12), é a vez do Cordel do Fogo Encantado, ao lado de Murilo Gun e a big-band Gunzito e Dani Carmesim.
Sexta-feira (13), o principal destaque é Lenine, que divide a noite com Eddie e Bela Maria. No sábado de encerramento (14), De Cara com o Samba encerra o festival, que ainda conta Karynna Spinelli, Galo da Madrugada e programação infantil às 16h com o Mundo Bita.
Já entre as atividades, destaque para a presença do deputado federal eleito Renato Freitas (PT), do Paraná, que participará de uma mesa com outras figuras da política pernambucana, como o também deputado federal eleito Jones Manoel (Psol), e os deputados estaduais Dani Portela (PT) e João Paulo. Eles participam da mesa “Vozes do Agora, Futuros Possíveis”, realizada na sexta-feira (13), às 15 horas, no Cais do Sertão.

https://taz.de/Weltklimakonferenz-in-Ant.title: Weltklimakonferenz in Antalya: Kein Kuchen für Merz
https://taz.de/Weltklimakonferenz-in-Ant.author: Nanja Boenisch
https://taz.de/Weltklimakonferenz-in-Ant.text:
Weltklimakonferenz in Antalya: Kein Kuchen für Merz
Der Kanzler kassiert weiter Kritik, weil er der Klimakonferenz fernbleibt. Und auch eine neue Studie zeigt, dass Deutschland beim Klimaschutz schwächelt.
Das Stück Torte, das vor Luisa Neubauer auf dem Tisch steht, das hätte Friedrich Merz bekommen sollen. „Schade, Schokolade“, sagt die Klimaaktivistin – denn Merz ist nicht da, um sich sein Stück abzuholen.
Mit Neubauer sitzen noch zehn weitere Klimaaktivist:innen auf dem Kongressgelände im türkischen Antalya, wo sich Staaten und Verbände seit Montag zum 31. Mal zur Weltklimakonferenz (COP31) treffen. Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (CDU) hatte einige Tage vorher vermeldet, dass er nicht nach Antalya reisen würde: Er müsse in Berlin die Kabinettsitzung leiten – und wolle am Mittwoch, seinem 71. Geburtstag, mit Frau und Tochter „schön zum Italiener“ gehen.
Aus Protest wünschen die Klimaaktivist:innen Merz deshalb aus der Ferne „Happy Birthday ohne Happy Future“. Sie würden auch gern irgendwann ihre 71. Geburtstage feiern können, „in stabilen planetaren Bedingungen“, sagt Neubauer. Der Kanzler habe die ganze Weltgemeinschaft enttäuscht mit seiner Entscheidung, nicht bei der UN-Klimakonferenz aufzutauchen.
Weltklimakonferenz in Antalya
Vom 9. November an treffen sich Regierungen aus aller Welt, um über Klimakrise sowie Klimaschutz zu verhandeln – und darüber, wer zahlt. Die taz berichtet von vor Ort.
Schon am Dienstagabend hatte Merz dafür das Fossil des Tages kassiert – einen Schmähpreis des Climate Action Network. Den erhielten auch die Regierungschef:innen aus Frankreich, den Niederlanden, Italien, Dänemark, Schweden, Irland, Kanada und Japan. Sie alle lassen die Weltklimakonferenz sausen.
Deutschland rutscht im Ländervergleich ab
Dass Deutschland im Moment nicht zu den Staaten gehört, die sich einer ehrgeizigen Klimapolitik rühmen können, zeigt auch eine neue Untersuchung der Umweltorganisationen Germanwatch und NewClimate Institute. Im jährlich erscheinenden Klimaschutz-Index rutschte die Bundesrepublik das dritte Jahr in Folge ab und belegt jetzt Platz 25. Die Organisationen bewerten die Klimapolitik der Bundesregierung als „mäßig“, auf nationaler Ebene sogar als „schwach“.
Das Absacken sei „vor allem das Ergebnis der Politik von Wirtschaftsministerin Katherina Reiche“, sagt Jan Burck, Klimaexperte bei Germanwatch. Reiche behindere den Ausbau der Erneuerbaren und wollte stattdessen mehr Erdgas nutzen.
Empfohlener externer Inhalt
Wir würden Ihnen hier gerne einen externen Inhalt zeigen. Sie entscheiden, ob Sie dieses Element auch sehen wollen:
Ich bin damit einverstanden, dass mir externe Inhalte angezeigt werden. Damit können personenbezogene Daten an Drittplattformen übermittelt werden. Mehr dazu in unserer Datenschutzerklärung
Platz 1 bis 3 im Länderranking bleiben wie in den vergangenen Jahren unbesetzt, weil laut den Index-Autor:innen keiner der untersuchten Staaten genug tue, um die im Pariser Klimaabkommen festgeschriebenen Ziele zu erreichen. Quasi-Spitzenreiter ab Platz 4 sind dann Dänemark, Litauen und Luxemburg. Der größte Aufsteiger ist Ungarn. Die neue Regierung unter Péter Magyar habe klimaschädliche Gesetze des Ex-Ministerpräsidenten Viktor Orbán gekippt und neue Klimaziele ausgerufen. Portugal, Spanien und Marokko böten wiederum stabile Rahmenbedingungen für Klimaschutz, die auch Regierungswechsel überdauerten.
Insgesamt gebe es trotz des politischen Drucks, dem Klimapolitik in vielen Teilen der Welt ausgesetzt ist, Chancen auf mehr Klimaschutz. Erneuerbare, E-Autos und weniger Abholzung böten Möglichkeiten für schnellen Wandel. Selbst Öl- und Gasstaaten wie Saudi-Arabien und Usbekistan hätten erneuerbare Energien ausgebaut. „Regierungen müssen jetzt handeln, um daraus nachhaltige Emissionsminderungen zu machen“, forderte Niklas Höhne vom NewClimate Institute.
There is no planet B
Die Klimakatastrophe braucht unsere volle mediale Aufmerksamkeit. Dafür bündelt die taz seit Jahren ihre Kräfte und begleitet Konflikte und Fortschritte auf allen Kanälen. Und das schon lange: Die taz hat über radikale Klimaveränderungen berichtet, als andere Medien noch treu von unendlichem Wachstum sprachen. Und sie macht weiter, wenn andere ihre Berichterstattung zurückfahren. Unsere Artikel sind und bleiben frei zugänglich – ohne Paywall, dank über 52.000 freiwilliger Unterstützer*innen. Wir sind der Überzeugung, dass es kritische Informationen im Netz geben muss, die nicht kostenpflichtig sind. Gerade zum Thema Klimaschutz. Nur wenn unser Journalismus so viel wie möglich gelesen wird, kann er gesellschaftliche Veränderungen bewirken. Aber das geht nur, wenn sich unsere Leser*innen an dieser Idee beteiligen und den taz-Journalismus mittragen. Sind Sie schon dabei? Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Falta de estrutura compromete acolhimento de crianças e adolescentes do Distrito Federal
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Kennedy Cruz
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O Sindicato dos Servidores da Assistência Social e Cultural do Governo do Distrito Federal (Sindsasc) denuncia a falta de vagas e de estrutura na rede pública de acolhimento de crianças e adolescentes do Distrito Federal. Segundo o sindicato, seis adolescentes permaneciam na Central de Acolhimento de Crianças e Adolescentes (Centrac), unidade da Secretaria de Desenvolvimento Social (Sedes-DF), em uma situação de permanência prolongada que compromete as condições de atendimento e proteção.
Destinada a funcionar como porta de entrada do sistema, com atendimento emergencial, avaliação inicial e encaminhamento para unidades adequadas, a Centrac passou a manter adolescentes por períodos prolongados diante da ausência de vagas na rede conveniada. A denúncia aponta ainda dificuldades no fornecimento de itens básicos de higiene pessoal e falta de condições físicas para receber os jovens.
O cenário foi detalhado por Edglay Avelino, servidor ocupante do cargo de Auxiliar da carreira de Desenvolvimento e Assistência Social do Distrito Federal, que atua na unidade. Segundo ele, parte dos adolescentes está no local há mais de 15 dias e a chegada de novos casos continua. “Estamos vivendo uma situação de estrangulamento, tendo seis adolescentes em uma unidade que não foi concebida para isso. Ela não foi pensada para ter um espaço de acolhimento. Tem meninos que estão dormindo em colchonetes no chão. Às vezes não tem nem mesmo itens básicos de higiene para esses adolescentes”, relata.
A falta de vagas na rede conveniada impede que a central cumpra sua função de encaminhar crianças e adolescentes para espaços de acolhimento compatíveis com suas necessidades. “Nós não temos mais espaços destinados ao acolhimento. A criança ou o adolescente que chega tem que permanecer no máximo 24 horas, porque a gente já tem que encontrar um espaço para colocar. Só que hoje nós não temos mais vagas”, afirma o servidor.
A falta de vagas e de estrutura compromete diretamente os direitos de crianças e adolescentes que dependem da proteção do Estado. “Estamos falando de crianças e jovens em situação de vulnerabilidade, que deveriam ter asseguradas condições dignas de proteção e atendimento”, destaca o Sindsasc na denúncia.
Falta de atendimento especializado
Segundo o Sindsasc, a situação foi agravada pelo fechamento do Serviço de Acolhimento Institucional para Crianças e Adolescentes (Saica II), no Recanto das Emas, região administrativa do DF, que levou o Saica I a receber parte da demanda.
Outro ponto levantado pelo sindicato é o perfil dos adolescentes encaminhados à Centrac. Segundo a denúncia, grande parte apresenta demandas relacionadas à saúde mental, o que torna ainda mais delicada a permanência prolongada na unidade. “Esses adolescentes precisam de encaminhamentos para serviços e unidades compatíveis com suas necessidades, já que a Centrac não possui finalidade nem estrutura para esse tipo de acolhimento continuado”, alerta o Sindsasc.
Edglay Avelino afirma que as mudanças na política de acolhimento não foram acompanhadas pela estruturação de alternativas na rede. Quando entrou na unidade, então chamada Centro de Recepção e Triagem (CRT), o espaço contava com pediatras, enfermeiros e dentistas, além de setores organizados por faixa etária. Ao longo dos anos, o serviço passou por diferentes mudanças de nome e funcionamento. “A Centrac tem aproximadamente um ano e meio desde que foi criada, e a concepção dela, originalmente e de fato, é para que não fique adolescente”, explica Avelino
Sem atendimento especializado, os trabalhadores precisam lidar com episódios de crises e autoagressão. Em um dos casos relatados pelo servidor, um adolescente precisou ser levado ao hospital depois de se machucar durante uma crise. No plantão seguinte, voltou a apresentar o mesmo quadro, e os trabalhadores tiveram que acionar o Corpo de Bombeiros.
A permanência prolongada na Centrac também cria obstáculos para o acesso à educação e a benefícios. Edglay relata dificuldades para matricular os adolescentes na escola e para que jovens com direito a benefícios consigam sacar os valores, já que não têm uma pessoa de referência para acompanhá-los. “A matrícula no colégio, por exemplo, a gente não pode fazer porque eles estão lá transitoriamente”, explica.
Trabalhadores também são afetados
Além das condições enfrentadas pelos adolescentes, a denúncia do Sindsasc aponta dificuldades para os servidores que atuam na linha de frente do atendimento. A permanência prolongada aumenta os conflitos entre os jovens e expõe os trabalhadores a situações para as quais, segundo o relato, não há estrutura suficiente.
Os servidores também são responsáveis por administrar medicamentos controlados, seguindo prescrições e horários específicos. Edglay afirma que a organização dos plantões de 24 horas exige atenção redobrada na passagem das informações entre as equipes. “Imagine se, numa troca de plantão, a gente esquece de dar o medicamento ou alguém já deu, mas, na correria, não passou a informação para a equipe seguinte. O próximo plantão pode repetir a dose se o adolescente disser que não tomou. Aí a gente tem uma questão muito mais séria”, relata.
O servidor também afirma que já sofreu agressões durante o atendimento. Em uma das situações, ficou com hematomas nas pernas após receber chutes de um adolescente durante uma intervenção. “Quando há muitos adolescentes na unidade, eles acabam entrando em conflito entre si, o que deixa o ambiente muito tenso. Às vezes, você não consegue nem trabalhar, dada a questão psicológica. O índice de adoecimento dos servidores é muito grande. Vários trabalhadores já foram agredidos”, destaca.
O Sindsasc cobra que o Governo do Distrito Federal (GDF) apresente providências para aumentar a capacidade de acolhimento, garantir o encaminhamento adequado dos adolescentes e assegurar condições dignas de atendimento. “Crianças e adolescentes não podem ficar sem proteção adequada pela falta de planejamento, estrutura e vagas na rede pública de acolhimento”, conclui o sindicato na denúncia.
Outro lado
Procurada pelo Brasil de Fato DF, a Secretaria de Desenvolvimento Social informou que está elaborando um plano de ação emergencial para a desinstitucionalização de crianças e adolescentes, com estratégias de reintegração familiar e comunitária, sempre que possível, considerando o melhor interesse dos jovens.
A pasta afirmou que, em outubro, formalizou dois termos aditivos para aumentar em 30 vagas a capacidade de acolhimento da rede, que atualmente conta com 455 vagas. Também informou que elaborou um edital de chamamento público para ampliar a oferta de serviços, cuja publicação deve ocorrer em breve.
Sobre as condições da Centrac, a secretaria declarou que o atendimento foi normalizado, com a reposição dos itens básicos de higiene pessoal. A Sedes acrescentou que mantém articulação com o Ministério Público do Distrito Federal e Territórios (MPDFT), o Tribunal de Justiça do Distrito Federal e dos Territórios (TJDFT) e os conselhos tutelares para construir estratégias de acolhimento.

Cop31: Turkey signs $5.1bn loan deals to boost green transition
Turkey signed 10 loan agreements worth $5.1bn with multilateral development banks on Thursday to accelerate its green transition.
Speaking at the signing ceremony on the sidelines of the UN climate conference Cop31 in Antalya, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said no country could finance the green transition alone.
"No country's budget can meet the investment needs of this transformation on its own," he said. "That is why support from multilateral development banks is critically important to us."
The agreements were signed between the ministry and the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), the World Bank and the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB).
Simsek said Ankara had done its homework by thoroughly preparing projects and securing the financing needed to implement them.

Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
The projects, he said, would create jobs and strengthen the Turkish economy. He added that Turkey had secured approximately $50bn in external financing from its development partners since 2023.
Turkey signed its first loan agreement with the ADB in November 2025, Simsek said.
With the latest deals, the bank's financing for Turkey would reach $3.1bn within a year, helping accelerate climate investment and improve access to finance for small and medium-sized enterprises.
ADB President Masato Kanda said the new agreements would support the construction of disaster-resilient hospitals, strengthen healthcare services and help train the next generation of doctors.
They would also expand long-term financing for small businesses, focusing on less-developed and earthquake-affected provinces and female entrepreneurs.
"Longer repayment periods will enable businesses to invest, rebuild, create jobs, and grow. Today's focus at COP31 is resilient cities, and the agreements signed support that goal," he said.
AIIB President Zou Jiayi said the bank would provide $1.6bn for the Turkey Climate Action Acceleration Program and its additional financing to support implementation of the country’s climate regulations.
The bank would also provide $300m through Turk Eximbank.
"This loan supports Turkey's green transition and helps its businesses withstand economic shocks," she said.
$15bn China agreement
Ajay Banga, president of World Bank Group, said three agreements totalling $1.5bn had been signed that day to support cities, agriculture and industry.
That figure excludes the additional private-sector investment the bank hopes to mobilise.
Separately, Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar announced that Ankara had signed a preliminary deal worth $15bn with China's National Energy Administration to invest in renewable energy in Turkey, also on the sidelines of Cop31.
“With this agreement, which envisions a massive investment of approximately $15 billion in our country, we aim to implement a total of 7,000 megawatts of solar and wind power capacity, new energy storage systems, and 4,000 megawatts of electricity transmission infrastructure,” Bayraktar said.
He added that the memorandum of understanding will also facilitate technology transfer, enabling the production of wind turbine equipment within Turkey and giving a powerful boost to the development of its domestic industry.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.title: Ukraine hit by ‘significant’ Starshield disruptions as US envoys meet Putin, Zelenskyy says - Europe live
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.author: Jakub Krupa
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text:
Ukraine faces 'systemic speed restrictions' on Starshield again that 'help Russians kill more Ukrainians', Zelenskyy says
Oh-oh.
Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy has just taken to X to say that the Ukrainian army is once again experiencing “significant disruptions to Starshield’s operations over the territory of Ukraine.”
He said the problem has been going on “for several days now,” affecting operations “along the entire frontline and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.”
“Specifically, systematic speed restrictions are being imposed on Starshield, limiting it to 161 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour). The Ukrainian military have already investigated the circumstances, and these are not random errors but systematic speed restrictions.”
Spelling out the real life consequences, Zelenskyy said the disruption complicates intercepting Russian jet-powered drones, with “strikes that got through because our interception systems cannot reach sufficient speeds and are unable to intercept in time.”
“Unfortunately, this is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine. We are trying to establish all the circumstances with the American side.”
Supporting Ukraine 'a collective European responsibility', Merz says
Germany’s Friedrich Merz has said that further support for Ukraine should be seen as “a collective European responsibility,” with the immediate need to “close the funding gap for 2027.”
Ukraine “faces a very, very difficult winter, and it is essential that we Europeans stand together,” he added.
Merz also said he was hearing “some positive signals” about the talks in Abu Dhabi, but cautioned “there is a long way to go.”
He urged Russia’s Putin “to finally agree to joint discussions,” and stressed that “the Europeans must be at the table” during any potential talks.
But he added that the focus should not be on who the EU appoints to represent it at the talks, but on getting Putin to take part in the discussions.
“I note with some satisfaction that there is evidently a growing willingness on the Russian side to recognise that one cannot talk about Europe without involving Europe. And that, for a start, is good news. Whether it will stay that way remains to be seen,” he said.
von der Leyen 'very much welcomes' Abu Dhabi talks, confirms work on new sanctions package
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen had only a few words to say on her arrival for the EPC talks in Dublin.
She said she “very much welcomed” the peace talks in Abu Dhabi, and that she was happy “the Europeans were represented to safeguard our interests,” and also acknowledging that Ukraine’s Zelenskyy “asked for it” to happen.
She added:
“We are preparing the 22nd sanctions package, and we are, as the commission, preparing a proposal how to cover the financial needs of Ukraine in 2027. We will come with the sanctions package and the proposal for the financial needs before the next European Council.”
EU's Kallas warns there is no 'good will' from Russia as attacks on Ukraine continue
EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has warned that “we do not see any goodwill from the Russian side” in Ukraine talks, calling for any attacks to stop first before formal peace talks can be held.
“There should be [the] right sequenc[e] first to have a ceasefire, so that the bombing of the civilians really [needs to] stop and then sit down and talk over the peace agreement. Then, only then, we can talk about peace, or security architecture of Europe.”
Kallas said there was also the issue of trust given Russia “is not keeping” to previous agreements, including the Budapest memorandum.
“The focus should be on how we make sure that Russia actually keeps to their obligations,” she said.
Kallas also repeatedly hinted she should be a part of the EU’s delegation on Ukraine, pointing to the fact that the EU leaders “had those discussions” in 2024 when appointing the current holders to the three top jobs in the bloc.
“The leaders, of course, may choose differently and go into these discussions again, which is always difficult, or we [could] just stick to the agreements that we made in 2024.”
Luxembourg's PM Frieden backs EU's Costa to represent Europe in Ukraine talks
Luxembourg’s PM Luc Frieden looks to be absolutely chuffed to be representing all three Benelux countries at today’s summit, as his Belgian and Dutch colleagues are too busy to attend as they face domestic crises.
“I have the privilege of representing 30 millions citizens today,” he said on arrival to Dublin, with a massive smile on his face.
“On the agenda, we have democracy … we have Ukraine, and on all those issues, the Benelux partners are totally aligned. We met in Maastricht just two days ago, and I could feel we were totally aligned,” he said.
Rob Jetten’sminority government in the Netherlands could fall later today over a tax deal with the opposition, prompting a furious reaction from the right-wing VVD party which accused its partners of breaking the coalition agreement. If the government falls, it would probably lead to a snap election early next year.
Responding to a question from a Dutch reporter, Frieden wished the Netherlands “good luck” with the negotiations.
Meanwhile, over in Belgium, Bart De Wever continues holding frantic negotiations on the next year’s budget, which already saw him close to resigning from the post. He is also running against the clock, with another deadline set by King Philippe expiring next week.
On substantive issues, Frieden said “it’s important that we speak with a common message,” stressing “the message is more important than the person.”
“The message is clear: we stand with Ukraine, we stand with the principles of the UN charter,” he said.
But he added that he felt there was “a natural person to represent the EU” in the European Council president and former Portuguese PM, António Costa.
Heightened security measures in Dublin with 'largest deployment in history'
Ireland’s Martin was also asked about any potential bomb threats or any other potential disruptions to the summit.
He said that the Irish police “are best placed to make judgment calls in respect of this,” and “have established protocols” in place to deal with any issue.
Irish public broadcaster RTÉ reported that some 5,000 police officers will be on the streets of Dublin, “the largest deployment … in the history of the force in an operation that has been described as unique and complex.”
EU needs a 'clear, coherent' leadership voice in Ukraine talks, Ireland's Martin says
Meanwhile, over in Dublin, Ireland’s Micheál Martin has stressed the need to have a “clear, coherent” European voice in the Ukraine talks, as he answered reporters’ questions ahead of today’s meeting of the European Political Community in Dublin.
He said that the issue of Europe’s representation in any talks on Ukraine will be discussed “in the margins” today, with a more formal discussion at the EU informal summit tomorrow.
He said there were “some obvious candidates” as to who could represent the EU, but declined to speculate on names, other than stressing “there is clearly a need for a coherent voice agreed by the EU27.”
Curiously, he said the EU voice around the table “is not necessarily one person,” but “a clear, coherent leadership” voice from the EU.
“Obviously, Europe will want a voice at that table, particularly in so far as issued impact on Europe, because of the economic inputs, the security inputs, and in terms of Ukraine’s membership of the EU.”
He also defended the EU’s involvement so far, saying the coalition of the willing “has been particularly impactful” in “persuading the US on quite a number of issues.”
Martin also said Europe continues to be “genuinely shocked at the level of death and destruction” coming from Russia’s actions in Ukraine and “the imperialist agenda of Vladimir Putin.”
On the Abu Dhabi talks, Martin welcomed the potential prisoners swap as a “significant measure in and of itself,” welcoming the work of Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on these issues ahead of their arrival to Dublin later tonight.
“I think the objective of tonight’s meeting is to debrief president Zelenskyy on the engagement by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner with president Putin, and it’s a moving situation.
Our view up to now has been that Russia hasn’t shown any genuine interest in a peaceful resolution of this conflict. It remains to be seen whether that has changed or not.”
More broadly, Martin said the EPC was a useful format as it “broadens” conversations held among the EU 27 to “many other countries,” including Canada, and “we can develop common solutions to those particular problems, be it affordable energy, security and protection, technological attacks … [or] economic security.”

We apologise to our customers for any inconvenience caused, and will keep them updated with the latest information.”
The disruption is having a knock on effect on French and international trains: Eurostar services to and from London are delayed as a result, with passengers warned about delays and potential further disruption.
“Due to a request for police assistance at Calais-Fréthun, your train is delayed. We’re waiting for more information and we’ll confirm your estimated delay as soon as possible. Thanks for your patience.”
Ukraine faces 'systemic speed restrictions' on Starshield again that 'help Russians kill more Ukrainians', Zelenskyy says
Oh-oh.
Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy has just taken to X to say that the Ukrainian army is once again experiencing “significant disruptions to Starshield’s operations over the territory of Ukraine.”
He said the problem has been going on “for several days now,” affecting operations “along the entire frontline and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.”
“Specifically, systematic speed restrictions are being imposed on Starshield, limiting it to 161 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour). The Ukrainian military have already investigated the circumstances, and these are not random errors but systematic speed restrictions.”
Spelling out the real life consequences, Zelenskyy said the disruption complicates intercepting Russian jet-powered drones, with “strikes that got through because our interception systems cannot reach sufficient speeds and are unable to intercept in time.”
“Unfortunately, this is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine. We are trying to establish all the circumstances with the American side.”
EU to approve new sanctions on Russia on Monday, France's Europe minister says
Meanwhile, the EU is planning to approve new sanctions on Russia on Monday, France’s Europe minister Benjamin Haddad said.
“On Monday, we will take new sanctions against Russia, on 150 additional entities, 50 banks and it’s France which proposed the bulk of the entities to add,” Haddad told LCI television, as reported by Reuters.
“We will continue to put economic pressure on Russia and of course support Ukraine,” he added.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are in Moscow this morning, where they are expected to meet Russia’s president Vladimir Putin to advance some of the issues discussed at trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi over the last two days.
The meeting is expected to get under way around 9am GMT, with Russia’s deputy foreign minister Sergei Rybakov trying to manage everyone’s expectations by saying it was too early to say that necessary trust had been restored between Russia and Ukraine.
The US envoys are then expected to fly to Dublin to meetVolodymyr Zelenskyy on the margins of the European Political Community summit, which is being attended by more than 40 leaders from Ukraine’s allied countries.
The EPC – set up on the initiative of France’s Emmanuel Macron – offers a rare chance to discuss key European issues with non-EU allies, including Britain’s Andy Burnham and Canada’s Mark Carney.
For Burnham, it’s also an opportunity to dot the i’s and cross the t’s ahead of next week’s EU-UK summit, which is a key part of his proposed reset in relationship with the bloc. Let’s see what we are going to hear on this today.
For Dublin, the meeting comes with a massive security operation, particularly after some past concerns about drones, particularly around Zelenskyy’s visit to Ireland last December.
I will keep an eye on both of these events and bring you all the latest here.

https://taz.de/Afrikamera-Filmfestival-i.author: Katharina Böhm​

Afrikamera-Filmfestival in Berlin: Stille und Zusammenhalt
Unter dem Motto „Reflect“ widmet sich das diesjährige Afrikamera-Festival unter anderem den (Spät-)folgen von Kolonialismus und Apartheid.
Als der Völkermord an den Tutsi ihre Heimat entzwei reißt, ist Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo sieben Jahre alt. Von den sogenannten Gacaca-Volksgerichten, die anschließend in Ruanda abgehalten werden, erfährt sie erst als Erwachsene, durch die Arbeit an ihrem Spielfilm „Ben’Imana“. Er folgt Vénéranda, einer Frau, die bei jenen Volksgerichten und in Gesprächsgruppen um Gerechtigkeit und Versöhnung ringt. Dabei sitzen Mütter von Tätern neben Frauen, die auch 20 Jahre später kaum Worte finden für das, was ihnen und ihren Familien angetan wurde.
Die ruandische Kultur sei von Stille geprägt, sagt Dusabejambo. Eine Mutter habe ihr einmal erklärt, man sage seinem Kind nicht: Ich liebe dich. Weil es Dinge gebe, die „so kraftvoll sind, dass man sie nicht durch Worte verwässern sollte“. Wie aber lässt sich dann von Grausamkeiten, Trauma, Verlust sprechen? Mit ihrem Debüt findet die Regisseurin einen überzeugenden Weg, filmisch vom Unsagbaren zu erzählen. Das gelingt nicht zuletzt dank Dusabejambos Mut, Geschichte so nuanciert wie möglich zu behandeln; frei von jenem Pathos und der naiven Betroffenheit, von denen „afrikanische“ Filme ortsfremder Regisseur:innen zu oft durchtränkt sind. „Ben’Imana“ ist das Werk einer ruandischen Frau aus der ersten Generation nach 1994.
Berührender Austausch im Kinosaal
Im Mai beim Filmfest in Cannes als bestes Debüt geehrt, eröffnete es im ausverkauften City Kino Wedding gerade die 19. Ausgabe von Afrikamera. Seit 2007 tritt das Festival an, um die Berliner:innen mit zeitgenössischem Kino aus dem gesamten Kontinent bekannt zu machen. Wobei am Eröffnungsabend auch junge Menschen aus Ruanda im Kino sitzen, die in Dusabejambos Film Nuancen erkennen, sprachliche etwa, die anderen hier naturgemäß entgehen. Der Austausch, der nach „Ben’Imana“ im Saal entsteht, gerät kaum weniger berührend als der Film selbst.
Nicht nur die vielen Publikumsfragen nach diesem ersten der bis Sonntag stattfindenden Screenings lassen vermuten, dass sich das ambitionierte Programm von Festivalleiter Alex Moussa Sawadogo auch für deutsche beziehungsweise Berliner Besucher:innen als anschlussfähig erweist. Die sehenswerte Dokumentation „Mother City“ solidarisiert sich mit der „Reclaim the City“-Bewegung aus Kapstadt, die rund 30 Jahre nach Ende der Apartheid versucht, bezahlbaren Wohnraum für diejenigen zu erstreiten, denen das Stadtzentrum höchstens zum Arbeiten offen steht. Während öffentliche Flächen in der Innenstadt unter Wert an Privatinvestoren verkauft wurden, die sie in Golfklubs umwandeln, lebt ein Großteil der Schwarzen Bevölkerung noch heute auf engem Raum an den Rändern oder außerhalb. Schmerzhaft führt „Mother City“ vor, wer seine Rechte fortlaufend erkämpfen muss, und zu welchem Preis. Er zeigt aber auch, wie gelungenes Organizing funktioniert, was Kapstadt und andere Orte dabei etwa von Barcelona lernen können.
Mit „And She Didn’t Die“ zeichnet Kethiwe Ngcobo den Lebensweg ihrer Mutter Lauretta nach, einer Geschichtenerzählerin aus dem ländlichen Südafrika, die während der Apartheid mit ihren Kindern nach London flieht. Ihr Mann, Mitglied des Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), wurde bereits inhaftiert. Im Exil lebt Lauretta Ngcobo in einer „weißen Welt“, wie sie ernüchtert feststellt, findet darin aber auch zum Feminismus und einer eigenen Stimme als Schriftstellerin. Sie wird als eine der ersten Autorinnen des Kontinents bekannt. Die Regisseurin Ngcobo stellt den Dokumentarfilm über ihre Mutter im Kino Arsenal vor, einer weiteren Spielstätte neben City Kino Wedding, fsk und Sputnik.
Von weiblicher Emanzipation und dem Verlust des eigenen Bodens handelt auch „One Woman One Bra“ von Vincho Nchogu. Im Mittelpunkt von Kenias Beitrag für die kommenden Oscars steht Star, die als Waise in einem kenianischen Dorf aufgewachsen ist. Zum ersten Mal können dessen Bewohner:innen ihren Landbesitz anhand familiärer Herkunft bestätigen. Bloß wie, wenn man wie Star weder weiß, wer die eigenen Eltern sind, noch verheiratet ist oder Geld besitzt, um das Land zu kaufen? Aus Not lässt die Frau sich auf die fragwürdige Kampagne einer NGO ein, die „One Woman One Bra“ seinen ironischen Titel beschert. Als Inspiration für den Film diente Nchogu übrigens die US-Kampagne KONY2012, mittels der die kalifornische Organisation „Invisible Children“ den ugandischen Rebellenführer Joseph Kony als mutmaßlichen Kriegsverbrecher outete.
Davon, dass Emanzipation kein strikt weibliches Thema ist, zeugt „Congo Boy“, mit dem Musiker Rafiki Fariala die eigene Lebensgeschichte verfilmt. Energiegeladen und zugleich zart erzählt er vom Alltag eines 17-jährigen Jungen in Bangui, in dem sich Not ebenso findet wie Zusammenhalt.

Mississippi geht an die Demokraten
Erstmals seit 145 Jahren zieht ein Schwarzer Senator aus Mississippi in den US-Senat ein. Colom konnte viele Nichtwähler mobilisieren.
Washington. Der US-Demokrat Scott Colom hat die Senatswahl im südlichen Bundesstaat Mississippi für sich entschieden. Nach übereinstimmenden Angaben der Sender CNN, CBS und NBC gelang es ihm, sich bei der Kongresswahl am Dienstag vergangener Woche gegen die republikanische Amtsinhaberin Cindy Hyde-Smith durchzusetzen. Colom ist damit der erste schwarze Senator aus Mississippi seit den 1880er Jahren.
Nach CNN-Angaben kam Colom nach Auszählung von 99 Prozent der Stimmen auf 49,2 Prozent; Hyde-Smith erreichte 48,7 Prozent. In einer feierlichen Siegesrede am Mittwochabend (Ortszeit) in Jackson würdigte Colom Mississippis lange Tradition des schwarzen Aktivismus. »Unsere Gebete haben den Lauf der Geschichte verändert«, rief Colom seinen Anhängern zu. »Gott wollte nicht, dass wir einen leichten Sieg erringen. Er wollte, dass wir es auf die Mississippi-Art machen.«
Hyde-Smith erkannte die Niederlage an. »Auch wenn das nicht das Ergebnis ist, für das wir gearbeitet oder das wir uns erhofft haben, erkenne ich die Entscheidung der Wähler von Mississippi an«, sagte die 67-Jährige. »Ich möchte Scott Colom gratulieren und ihm alles Gute wünschen, denn er hat jetzt eine enorme Verantwortung, unseren großartigen Staat zu vertreten.«
»Scott Colom ist der einzige, der das hätte schaffen können. Ich wusste es von dem Moment an, als ich ihn zum ersten Mal getroffen habe«, erklärte der bisherige Minderheitsführer Chuck Schumer von den Demokraten im Onlinedienst X. »Blue Mississippi ist da«, fügte er hinzu.
Coloms Sieg im tiefen Süden ist eine schmerzhafte Ohrfeige für den republikanischen Präsidenten Donald Trump. Mit seinem Sieg kommen die Demokraten im US-Senat auf 55 der 100 Sitze; 44 entfallen bislang auf die Republikaner. Das Ergebnis im Bundesstaat Alaska steht noch aus; dort wird nach wie vor ausgezählt. Insgesamt gelang es den Demokraten bei den Midterms nach jetzigem Stand, den Republikanern acht Senatssitze abzunehmen. AFP/nd

Yair Netanyahu to release book on 'deep state' war against his father
Yair Netanyahu, the activist son of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is set to release a book through a major publisher detailing a plot against his father by the "deep state" in Israel.
Two-Front War: Inside Israel's Fight for Survival – Against Foreign Enemies and Domestic Saboteurs is set to be distributed by Simon & Schuster and, according to the publisher's website, will detail a "project to destabilise the West and erode the foundations of free civilization".
"[Yair Netanyahu] has always been a proud Jew and a devoted Zionist," says the publicity blurb. "But when the institutions that govern Israel – its prosecutors, judges, intelligence bureaucracy, military command, media networks, and foreign-funded NGOs – turned their attention toward removing his father from power, he found himself inside a Kafkaesque system that few citizens ever see."
The book will be a "report from within the Matrix", a reference to a term popularised by misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and used by conspiracy theorists generally to describe a system of illusions that dominates mainstream society.
Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc won 53 seats in the 27 October parliamentary elections, falling short of the 61 needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, though it remains the largest grouping in parliament.

The opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot won 48, while Arab-led parties secured a record 19 seats, giving them a potentially decisive role in coalition talks.
Yair has long been a proponent of far-right conspiracy theories on X, and since the elections he has alleged that a range of forces – including money from Arab states – were involved in rigging the vote against his father.
In a post on X on Tuesday, he reiterated his claim that it was "an election stolen by enemy states that bribed Arab voters".
He has also alleged similar machinations were behind a long-running corruption trial against Netanyahu. The prime minister has been on trial since 2020 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three corruption cases.
He has failed to attend many of his court appearances, usually citing events relating to his premiership as justification.
According to Haaretz, the company behind Yair's new book is RatPac Press, founded by Australian James Packer – a friend of the Netanyahu family and witness in his corruption trial – and American film director Brett Ratner, who moved to Israel following sexual assault accusations.
The indictment against Netanyahu says the prime minister received expensive cigars and champagne from Packer over the course of several years. Packer also owned a luxury apartment in Tel Aviv which was occasionally used by Yair Netanyahu.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Cop31 live: ‘No one is coming to rescue us,’ Greta Thunberg tells climate summit
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Ajit Niranjan
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Greta Thunberg says the planet is 'being killed, and we know by who'
Oliver Milman
Greta Thunberg has said that the planet is “not dying, it is being killed and we know by who” in a stark intervention at the Cop31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey.
“It is being killed by the very same people thought to come to our rescue,” Thunberg, the Swedish climate activist, said. “No one is coming to our rescue.
“When our human rights are being threatened by states and other institutions, it’s our duty to stand up and be the adult in the room and fight for everyone’s human rights.”
Thunberg spoke at a packed press gathering in the Cop31 venue alongside other activists from Nepal, Australia, Palestine and Canada. All of them lambasted governments’ inaction on the climate crisis and called for the end of Turkish energy shipments to Israel, which Thunberg said was “directly feeling the genocide in Palestine.”
“We are heading towards a future of more genocides and more ecocides and the complete compromise of our basic rights and where basic necessities become luxuries,” Thunberg said. “It’s more clear than ever in spaces like these that the situation could not be any less under control, the planet is not dying, it is being killed.”
Thunberg has not attended a Cop since 2021, where in Glasgow she famously said that the talks amounted to “blah, blah, blah”. In this time she has shifted her focus somewhat away from the climate crisis to include causes such as the plight of the Palestinian people.
Her arrival in Turkey has caused much excitement among delegates at Cop, with a throng of people clamouring to speak to her after she finished the press conference.
We’ve been hearing from world leaders for the best part of two days now. But one country we’ve not heard from is Israel – one of Turkey’s closest neighbours. And there is a very good reason for that. They have not been invited.
“As the host country for the leaders’ summit, we did not send an invitation to Israel,” Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop31 president, told local media, according to The National.
“Of course, we will discuss the climate and climate justice here. We say that there can be no climate justice where peace does not prevail.”
Chinese outlet The Chosun Daily, again citing local media, quoted Kurum as saying: “We will not remain silent about the mass killings in Gaza … Our political stance is clear, and we will maintain this attitude during the conference.”
But while Israel is notable for its absence, in the Cop31 exhibition space a corner has been set aside for the Palestinian delegation. Featuring black cloth hung haphazardly from the ceiling, in a manner reminiscent of refugee tents, the “Gaza tent” seemed to replicate Gaza itself, Chosun Daily noted.
However, none of Gaza’s population was there, only Palestinians from the West Bank. Survivors in Gaza are banned by Israel from international travel.
There was a frenzy of attention upon Greta Thunberg when she appeared this morning in Antalya. I had my toe trodden upon several times in the scrum that formed around someone who spearheaded a surge of global climate activism that has somewhat faded from view amid various other crises in recent years.
The climate crisis hasn’t gone anywhere though, even if political and media attention has, and the activists who stood alongside Thunberg outlined the mounting toll of our overheating planet.
Sagar Dhakal, a Nepalese MP, spoke about how he helped dig people out of the debris of a deadly landslide, caused by a melting glacier along the Nepal-Tibet border, earlier this year. “I don’t think there are words in the dictionary to describe it,” Dhakal said.
“Vulnerable countries need support from the developed world, we need to work together,” she said. “If we all work together we can prevent the next disaster.”
Rikki Dank, an Indigenous Australian who is taking the Australian government to the UN human rights committee over its fossil fuel exports, said that “we need to start demanding better of our governments, not just for ourselves but for our communities.”
Dank took aim at Anthony Albanese, Australia’s prime minister who appeared here yesterday to claim that the co-host was playing its part and was a leader in climate action.
“Our prime minister needs to stop speaking and start listening when we say no to fracking of our country, to stop speaking and start listening when we say no to poisoning of our water and our sacred sites”, she said. “He needs to stop speaking and start listening when the Australian people say no new coal, oil and gas.”
Mohammed Usrof, founder of the Palestinian Institute for Climate Strategy, said that the fossil fuel economy is underpinning what he called a genocide committed by Israel that has killed 20 members of his own family.
“This militarized fossil economy continues to profiteer off genocide but also the complete devastation of our land,” he said. “There’s an intentional act of ecocide and environmental devastation.”
Usrof said that Israel should be removed from the UN framework on climate change, as well as the UN itself, and called on countries including Turkey to stop providing the fuel that is supplying Israel’s military.
Celine Isimbi, born to refugees from Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo and now living in Canada, criticised Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, for not showing up at the talks but said that even leaders at Cop31 are failing their people.
“Showing up means nothing when families are under rubble, when families have to be rescued from flash flooding,” she said. “Whether they show up or don’t show up, what changes for us on the ground is nothing because they aren’t putting their money where their mouths are, they aren’t meeting our material demands.”
That brings us to the end of the leaders’ speeches. Some themes seemed to repeat. Time and again over the last two days, leaders from poor, low-emitting countries urged rich polluters to stump up more cash. Small island states pleaded for emissions cuts that would limit how much global heating overshoots the 1.5C target. Rich countries (those that showed, at least) were enthusiastic about electrification. Only a few of them, though, were also willing to call out fossil fuels.
Now the heads of state have come and gone, more of the attention at Cop31 will go to the negotiations happening behind closed doors.
Ruslan Edelgeriyev, special representative of the president of the Russian Federation on climate issues, said the future is in “natural gas and viable new technologies”.
He added that “while politicians argue, actual problems” are being solved by clean energy businesses in Russia, and that “states should preserve the sovereign right” to choose their “optimal energy balance”.
Hello, it’s Ajit Niranjan here again, taking back the blog from my colleague Matthew Pearce.
We’ve just heard from Kang Kum-Sil, South Korea’s climate ambassador, who has spoken about some of what her country – a major coal consumer – is doing to electrify. She’s also echoing what many leaders have said about geopolitical crises. “Cop31 must demonstrate that multilateral cooperation remains an effective means of addressing climate change.”
Every day during Cop31 we are hearing from people affected by the climate crisis. Earlier this week, we published a powerful testimony from Darcy Ruddy, the owner-operator of an excavation company in western Canada.
Just before a wildfire swept through parts of his home town, Jasper, he was finishing work at a nearby luxury heliskiing lodge. Climate change made the higher temperatures the week before the fire and the day it ignited more likely. This is his story:
I’d landed this big job at a heliskiing lodge in Valemount. I finished 95% and was excited because I was going on this mountain biking trip in the Chilcotins [mountain range]. I was like: “I’m just going to leave the machines here. I’ll go home tonight, grab my camper van, and I’ll move them when I get back.” Had I not done that, I would have lost everything.
As I was driving back into town, there was this intense warm air. It was nice out, but it was stormy. I made a joke that morning: “Big lightning come to town tonight? About time Jasper burns.” Didn’t expect it to happen but, as I drove into town, I looked at my gas gauge and I was like: “I better go fill this thing up.”
At home, I pulled my van into the back. I was looking at the sky and enjoying a leftover gin and tonic. I was like: “Something doesn’t feel right.” My buddy Alex messaged me: “There was a lightning strike out here. I see open flame.” I turned on my radio and my buddy, who works for parks, was evacuating a campground. I could hear the intensity in his voice. Holy fuck, this is it.
I called my dad. He was out for dinner with a friend. I was like: “Dad, pay for dinner, get the hell out of there. We got to start packing.”
Nthomeng Majara, deputy prime minister of Lesotho, reminded world leaders that small countries like hers suffer the worst impacts of climate change, “despite contributing negligibly to greenhouse gas emissions”.
She said that people of Lesotho are facing adverse effects of changing rainfall patterns, recurrent droughts, floods, land degradation and other climate risks, which affected food production and security.
“Countries that have contributed least to the problem should not bear a disproportionate burden of its consequences, she said. “Global climate action must be guided by equity and respective capabilities.
She called for climate finance to be scaled up and made more accessible, for financing arrangements to not exacerbate debt, and for adaptation to be made a global priority.
Fatafehi Fakafanua, prime minister of Tonga, said the developed world must “finally meet its moral and legal duties” to reduce emissions and help smaller economies reduce theirs.
“At forums like this, we’ve been told that we ask too much – that our red lines are unreasonable,” he said. “We all have a part to play. For when these meetings end, each of us, must live with our conscience. What we know to do, we cannot leave it undone.
“Antalya must be the turning point where the developed world finally meets its moral and legal duties.”
Matthew Wale, prime minister of Solomon Islands, said his country is in “perpetual climate disaster recovery mode” because of climate breakdown.
“As I speak, my people face a protracted El Niño, while recovering from a category 5 cyclone. We remain in a perpetual climate disaster recovery mode.
“There must be some moral thinking on this. The Cop31 climate action agenda targets must result in tangible outcomes.”
He called on leaders to start publishing “pledge disbursement timelines” to spotlight whether climate finance is making its way to small economies, and independent tracking on delivery.
The prime minister of Lebanon, Nawaf Salam, said climate rehabilitation must be woven into rehabilitating the country from Israel’s war on Lebanon.
“The environmental scars of war will affect ecosystems, livelihoods of communities for years to come,” he said. “Recovery therefore must go beyond rebuilding homes and rebuilding homes and roads. It must restore agricultural roads, rehabilitate ecosystems and revive livelihoods.”
“Lebabnon insists that environmental restoration and climate resistance be integral to the reconstruction, alongside stability, the restoration of our sovereignty, and respect for international law.”
“Showing up is not enough”. That’s the message that civil society organisations have for Andy Burnham. The UK prime minister spoke at Cop31 earlier, underlining that Britain was “ready to play its full part” in tackling the climate crisis.
While broadly welcoming his making the effort to actually go to the summit, green groups have been sceptical about his intervention. Beth John, Oxfam GB’s climate justice adviser, said Burnham’s appearance “sends a positive signal”.
But, she added: “Showing up is not enough: a crisis of this scale needs substantive action, not just signals. The real test of climate leadership is delivery, not declarations.”
Burnham indicated his support for Turkey’s called for increased electrification, which has been a major target of Cop31. But without nuance, that target risks embedding global inequalities, pointed out Leon Sealey-Huggins, senior climate justice campaigner at War On Want.
“The Cop’s 35% electrification target is based on extending current global energy inequalities,” Sealey-Huggins said. “According to various scenarios used in the IEA’s analyses that inform its targets, the US is projected to consume five times more energy per capita than in South Asia, and 17 times Africa’s per capita energy consumption.
“Worse, the electrification pledge can only be realised if climate finance is provided to those countries that need it, including those 730 million people who still lack access to electricity.”
Mohammed Mustafa, prime minister of Palestine, received a standing ovation to his speech. He said despite the Israel’s destruction of Gaza, Palestine remains committed to reaching its climate targets. He went on to implore world leaders to do more to help the people of his country.
“Our message from Palestine is clear: no people should be deprived of the right declined of the right [to climate justice] because of occupation,” he said. “We still need your support.”
