https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: Victorian Psycho review – Maika Monroe has a blast in unsteady horror romp
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Benjamin Lee
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
It’s not that hard to figure out why a lower-class woman toiling away in Victorian England would be so easily driven to violently murder everyone around her. If it’s not the brittle entitlement of those who employ you, it’s the unending misogyny of the system you’re forced to be a subservient part of, all the while being underpaid and undervalued and at the mercy of sexual violence, a multitude of diseases and an average lifespan of just 42.
As Winifred Notty (Maika Monroe) fills the frame in Victorian Psycho, heading to a new job as governess for a rich family, it’s easy to be on her side. Even as her murderous impulses start to rear their head, they’re made somewhat understandable, although Winifred isn’t just a woman reacting to the various injustices of the time – she’s one responding to a demon within her, a darkness she has chosen to embrace rather than resist. Darkness is her friend, a protection against harm, and a way to possess some sort of control in a world that has denied her any of it.
The film, based on the recent book by Virginia Feito, is less interested in taking Winifred and her psychological unravelling all that seriously, and more in what gonzo fun might be had in watching what happens when she takes an axe to the world around her. Feito, who also acts as screenwriter, and director Zachary Wigon, who last made dom/sub chamberpiece Sanctuary, wisely avoid turning her into a simplified Victorian girlboss fighting back against the patriarchy, and instead there’s something stranger and possibly supernatural in her urge to kill. We spend the film alongside her, and Wigon employs some marvelously unsettling sound design to denote that there is also a truly monstrous presence under the surface. But his greatest special effect is Monroe herself.
The actor has become known as a bit of a scream queen (an all too easily crowned title these days) ever since she broke out in It Follows, but despite roles in hits such as Longlegs and Watcher, she’s never really been afforded that much to do beyond looking petrified. Maybe that’s why it feels like she has so much more to give and prove here, really tearing into a character that requires her to do the petrifying. It’s not just the malevolent soundscape that makes it seem like there is an evil within her but Monroe’s unearthly contortions, an all-in, all-body performance that avoids slipping into histrionic silliness.
The film around her isn’t quite as steady, with the comedic elements pushing some scenes closer to the over-egged buffoonery of Downton Abbey spoof Fackham Hall (it also shares a star in Thomasin McKenzie, here playing a gullible co-worker). Ruth Wilson and Jason Isaacs play the vile heads of household with Hamnet’s Jacobi Jupe and Wednesday’s Evie Templeton as their increasingly disturbed offspring. As absurd as the upper classes were then and still are now, the extremes become a little too extreme here, and like Winifred herself, Feito and Wigon are often incapable of showing some necessary restraint (as a comedy it’s resoundingly unfunny). The direction, while often effectively off-kilter, can also be a little excessive (did we really need an immersive CG shot of a key going into a door?), so while the story does involve the character spiralling into chaos, the film itself could often do with spiralling a little less.
For all of its many flourishes, the plot is essentially a classic domestic thriller narrative, close to The Hand That Rocks the Cradle, the remake of which actually starred Monroe in the Rebecca De Mornay role (she fares far better here). There’s even a rather predictable reveal that, yes, there is also an ulterior motive aside from just madness, so while there’s great glee in pushing past boundaries (cannibalism, incest, infanticide), the structure is not one that ever truly surprises. There are a few too many touches, like some zany chapter titles, that fall into the self-congratulatory “aren’t we being wicked?” category, yet it’s just not as wicked as the makers seem to think it is or as wicked as Monroe deserves. It’s a film of great bloodshed, of cutting, slitting and stabbing, yet it never quite gets under our skin.
- Victorian Psycho is out in US cinemas on 13 November, in Australia on 4 February, and in the UK at a date to be announced

https://www.humanite.fr/societe/bfmtv/re.title: Refus d’obtempérer : habitué de CNews et BFMTV, le policier Axel Ronde interpellé après avoir failli renverser un collègue
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/bfmtv/re.author: La rédaction
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/bfmtv/re.text:
Le président du syndicat de police CFTC Axel Ronde a été interpellé mercredi 11 novembre, annonce Franceinfo, dans le cadre d’une enquête pour refus d’obtempérer. Le policier habitué des plateaux de BFMTV et CNews a tenté de fuir après avoir été repéré en train de slalomer dans les rues de Paris, sirène et gyrophare allumé, avec sa voiture personnelle.
Président du syndicat de police CFTC, Axel Ronde possède son rond de serviette sur les plateaux de CNews et de BFMTV. De sa demande de « carte blanche pour ramener l’ordre » à la comparaison du mouvement social en cours à des « appels au meurtre » et « à une insurrection armée », le syndicaliste s’est avéré être un client parfait pour les chaînes d’infos en continu.
Sa présence médiatique risque cependant d’être plus rare : Axel Ronde a été interpellé. Le policier est visé par une enquête pour un refus d’obtempérer au soir d’une manifestation à Paris, le 31 octobre dernier, a annoncé Franceinfo, le 11 novembre. Les investigations ont été ouvertes par le parquet de Créteil et confiées à l’IGPN.
Pour rappel, le Canard enchaîné révélait la veille qu’Axel Ronde a été « coursé par ses collègues à travers Paris » après avoir manqué de peu d’en écraser un. Le syndicaliste très droitier circulait alors dans le 12e arrondissement de la capitale, vers 20 heures. La sirène de sa voiture était enclenchée, le gyrophare allumé et le pare-soleil siglé « Police ».
Après avoir grillé un feu rouge, Axel Ronde a slalomé dans la circulation et même éraflé un véhicule, sans s’arrêter. Un policier hors service témoin de la scène a alors décidé d’interroger le conducteur, au volant d’une Seat rouge près du bois de Vincennes.
En tort, il prend la fuite
Ce dernier lui demande alors s’il est bien policier et les raisons de ces manœuvres dangereuses. À l’arrêt, gyrophare rapidement coupé, Axel Ronde confirme être policier et prétexte devoir se rendre en urgence sur un dispositif situé non loin de là – la manifestation du jour est alors en cours de dispersion. Son interlocuteur vérifie ensuite par téléphone son identité et demande si la Seat est autorisée à rouler dans ces conditions.
La réponse de la centrale est claire : la Seat n’est pas liée n’est qu’un véhicule personnel. En tort, le syndicaliste prend la fuite, manquant de renverser son collègue. Ce dernier a confirmé auprès de sa hiérarchie avoir même vu le fuyard jeter son gyrophare par la fenêtre. Axel Ronde a finalement été interpellé, pistolet automatique et matraque télescopique attachés à la ceinture, après une course-poursuite dans les rues de Paris.
Arrêté, le président de la CFTC Police – moins de 1 % des suffrages lors des dernières élections professionnelles en 2022 – a finalement été relâché le soir même. Deux heures après l’intervention, Axel Ronde était visible… sur le plateau de BFMTV pour évoquer la journée de manifestations.
Contacté par Franceinfo, Axel Ronde a affirmé que le récit de son collègue, relayé par la presse, « n’est pas du tout ce qu’il s’est passé ce soir-là ». Le représentant syndical a ajouté qu’il s’expliquera devant la justice.
Face à l’extrême droite, ne rien lâcher !
C’est pied à pied, argument contre argument qu’il faut combattre l’extrême droite. Et c’est ce que nous faisons chaque jour dans l’Humanité.
Face aux attaques incessantes des racistes et des porteurs de haine : soutenez-nous ! Ensemble, faisons entendre une autre voix dans ce débat public toujours plus nauséabond.
Je veux en savoir plus.

Haushaltsstreit der Koalition: Nein, nein, nein
Abermals haben sich Union und SPD nicht einigen können. Stromsteuersenkung, Plastiksteuer, Zuckersteuer: Wie geht es weiter?
afp | Die Haushälter von Union und SPD haben sich nicht auf eine Gegenfinanzierung für eine Senkung der Stromsteuer einigen können. Die von der Union gewünschte Steuersenkung sei aber nicht abgesagt, sondern solle zu einem späteren Zeitpunkt umgesetzt werden – etwa zu Jahresbeginn 2028, sagte Unionsfraktionschef Thorsten Frei (CDU) am späten Mittwochabend in Berlin. Die von der Union kritisierte Plastiksteuer werde nicht kommen, und die Einführung der Zuckersteuer werde auf 2028 verschoben, sagte er.
„Ich kann für unsere Fraktion nur sagen, dass die Senkung der Stromsteuer oberste Priorität hat“, sagte Frei weiter. „Wir werden in diesem Sinne auch versuchen, das gemeinsame Ziel so bald wie möglich auch in die Umsetzung zu bringen.“
Auch auf eine Gegenfinanzierung für einen vollständigen Ausgleich der kalten Progression konnten Union und SPD sich nicht einigen. Entlastungen bei der Stromsteuer und der kalten Progression seien zwar „wünschenswert“, sagte SPD-Fraktionschef Matthias Miersch. „Aber man muss es solide gegenfinanzieren – und deswegen werden wir jetzt in den nächsten Tagen auch gucken müssen, gibt es diese Gegenfinanzierung, die bis jetzt nicht vorliegt.“

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Sem informações, familiares e líderes Mẽbêngôkre exigem suspensão da exibição de documentário sobre Raoni na COP31
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Alegando que não tiveram acesso às informações sobre o documentário, familiares e líderes Mẽbêngôkre (Kayapó) exigem a suspensão da exibição do filme “Raoni”, dirigido pelo cineasta francês Alexandre Bouchet, prevista para sexta-feira (13), durante a 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP31), na Turquia.
O Instituto Raoni encaminhou uma notificação nesta quarta-feira (11), exigindo a suspensão imediata do filme, que mostra a trajetória do importante líder indígena de 94 anos, e de sua divulgação. A Presidência da Fundação Nacional dos Povos Indígenas (Funai) também solicitou providências à Procuradoria da instituição.
O impasse, segundo o g1, acontece desde 19 de outubro, quando a produtora Yemaya Productions havia sido notificada extrajudicialmente. No dia 30, a produtora alegou sigilo empresarial para não fornecer informações solicitadas sobre acordos comerciais. Em carta assinada em 7 de novembro, familiares e lideranças reafirmaram que não autorizam o lançamento, a divulgação ou a exibição pública do documentário.
“A história do Cacique Raoni representa a memória, a resistência e a luta coletiva de seu povo. Sua trajetória precisa ser respeitada!”, escreve a Mídia Indígena, em apoio ao Instituto Raoni.
No documento enviado, o instituto afirma estar disposto a dialogar com a produtora, desde que sejam apresentadas informações completas sobre o filme e sua distribuição.
Raoni foi diagnosticado com câncer no sistema digestório em setembro deste ano e está recebendo cuidados paliativos em Peixoto de Azevedo (MT).
O líder indígena é uma das vozes mais influentes do Brasil na defesa dos indígenas e do meio ambiente. Ele iniciou seu ativismo em 1954, aprendeu português e foi uma voz importante para o reconhecimento dos direitos dos povos indígenas na Constituição de 1988.

Iran updates military target list to include no geographical restrictions on retaliatory strikes
12 November 2026 06:38 GMT
Iran’s armed forces have updated their list of possible targets in the case of a renewed war, including having no geographical restrictions on retaliatory strikes.
"The armed forces’ target list has been updated and is ready to be communicated to army and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commanders," senior military commander Kioumars Heydari, who serves as the deputy chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces, said.
He indicated that the updated list reflected previous Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei’s instructions for an "immediate, effective response without geographical limitations" to any threat, warning that Iran's response to any future conflict would be "truly crippling" for the enemy.

https://taz.de/Guten-Morgen-Kreuzberg/!6.title: Guten Morgen Kreuzberg: Fragen, die ich mir um 7 Uhr morgens stelle
https://taz.de/Guten-Morgen-Kreuzberg/!6.author: Luciana Ferrando
https://taz.de/Guten-Morgen-Kreuzberg/!6.text:
Guten Morgen Kreuzberg: Fragen, die ich mir um 7 Uhr morgens stelle
Auf dem Arbeitsweg trifft unsere Autorin neben Frühaufstehern auch gutgelaunte Enten und Eichhörnchen. Außerhalb der Hasenheide setzt der Trubel ein.
A uf einmal lachen alle Enten am Ufer des Teichs im Berliner Hasenheidepark los. Die Schwäne ziehen in Dreiecksformation durch den Nebel, der um sieben Uhr morgens noch über der Wasseroberfläche schwebt. Werden sie gerade ausgelacht?
Ein Mann schiebt sein Fahrrad über den Holzsteg und schaut zwischen den Ästen hindurch. Vielleicht wartet auch er, wie ich, darauf, dass die Vögel und die Eichhörnchen kommen. Oder zählt er die Blätter, die sich bereits gelb gefärbt haben?
Ein anderer Mann, mit Baskenmütze und Schnurrbart, blickt auf eine Wiese neben einem Mülleimer. Seine Hände hat er hinter dem Rücken ineinandergelegt. Als ich näher an ihm vorbeilaufe, erkenne ich, dass er etwas zwischen den Kleeblättern sucht. Vielleicht ein vierblättriges? Und wenn ja, wofür braucht er heute Glück?
„Süße Hasen wählen links“
Dann nehme ich den Weg, der zum Café Blume führt. Und wie immer, wenn ich an der Gruppe abgestorbener Baumstämme vorbeikomme, frage ich mich, ob noch jemand anderes sie mit schlafenden Dinosauriern verwechselt.
An der Ampel gegenüber dem Columbiabad hängt ein handgemaltes Schild: ein Hase, darunter der Spruch „Süße Hasen wählen links“. Hat dieselbe Person im Sommer auch die handgezeichnete Erklärung zu den Junikäfern auf dem Tempelhofer Feld aufgehängt?
Sobald ich das Tempelhofer Feld erreiche, scheinen alle Radfahrer*innen in Eile und gestresst zu sein. Sind sie auf dem Weg zur Arbeit? Schauen sie mich böse an, weil ich zu laut atme?
Am Eingang des Jobcenters in der Mainzer Straße endet fast meine Laufstrecke. Wie immer stehen dort Grüppchen vor der Tür, rauchen und plaudern. Sind das Mitarbeiter*innen? Und gehört Rauchen etwa zu den Einstellungsvoraussetzungen?
Zum Schluss, während ich bei mir die Treppe hochgehe, frage ich mich, ob heute ein besonderer Tag ist. Oder verpasse ich jeden Morgen, während ich noch schlafe, schon so viel?

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.title: Larissa Bombardi: ‘O debate das terras raras deve priorizar a soberania do povos indígenas’
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.author: Conversa Bem Viver
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.text:
Instituída no mês de setembro deste ano, a Política Nacional de Minerais Críticos e Estratégicos (PNMCE) tem entre seus objetivos alinhar o aproveitamento dos recursos minerais à soberania nacional, ao desenvolvimento industrial e à transição energética.
Para a professora Larissa Bombardi, integrante do laboratório de agroecologia da Universidade Livre de Bruxelas e pós-doutora em Geografia Humana, a política para terras raras deve priorizar a soberania, a segurança dos povos indígenas e também o meio ambiente.
“Como é que a gente administra essa balança? Colocando a saúde humana, a saúde ambiental e, obviamente, os direitos dos povos originários e dos camponeses acima do lucro. Nesse sentido, o que a gente vai priorizar? Os territórios indígenas ou a exploração das terras raras que se encontram no subsolo?”, afirmou a professora ao programa Conversa Bem Viver, da Rádio Brasil de Fato.
A acadêmica alerta também para os riscos do desenvolvimento tecnológico desenfreado. “A gente tem que pensar qual é o limite do avanço tecnológico que a gente quer. Olha os riscos todos que a gente está sujeito em função desse descontrole! Temos inteligência artificial nas guerras, os ataques que a gente viu nas geladeiras dos supermercados na Europa, também os ataques aos bancos de sangue dos hospitais, isso vai na contramão da soberania dos povos, do direito das pessoas, da construção de uma sociedade que seja igualitária”, diz a geógrafa.
Ela explica que o sistema capitalista apresenta tecnologias de modo a criar uma falsa impressão de que são etéreas, não utilizam materiais naturais. O que acontece de fato é que as IAs [tecnologias de inteligência artificial] necessitam de cada vez mais exploração da natureza, seja para implementar data centers ou extrair elementos para sua infraestrutura.
“A informação é matéria, ela não está no ar. Ela não está nas nuvens. Está precisamente em lugares físicos, com estruturas que dependem tanto de água massivamente, para o todo processo de resfriamento quanto de minerais, sobretudo das chamadas terras raras, cada vez mais e mais.”
Na avaliação de Larissa Bombardi, vivemos, enquanto humanidade, um momento comparável ao das grandes navegações entre os séculos XV e XVII. “A gente está vivendo um outro ponto de inflexão da humanidade, como foram as grandes navegações. Eu penso que a gente está num outro momento mundo e a gente tem que resgatar o que é que nos faz pensar do que a gente quer como futuro”.
Conversa Bem Viver

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Steve Rose
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
‘It was pretty cool, when they were building it. It looked like a very large Ikea,” says John Wernvik, of EcoDataCenter. He is giving me a tour of their facility in Falun, Sweden, which could lay claim to being the world’s greenest datacentre – although to many, that is a contradiction in terms.
One difference is immediately visible: this datacentre is made out of wood. Huge panels of cross-laminated timber arrived at the site pre-cut, and were assembled by crane according to instructions, like flatpack furniture. Aesthetically, this section of the datacentre is more like an Ikea before the fit-out, a cavernous, echoey, immaculately clean hangar. The wood is not EcoDataCenter’s only claim to sustainability; it is more than just cosmetic, says Wernvik, the company’s chief external relations and sustainability officer. “Compared with a traditional datacentre built with steel and concrete, we lower the embodied carbon of the full structure by three times.” With a complex the size of a football pitch, that is a lot of wood, but, says Wernvik, “the amount of timber one of our datacentres uses takes the Swedish forest about 10 to 15 minutes to grow back”.
Datacentres have become a dirty word and a political issue in much of the world – especially the US, where opposition to them was said to be a factor in the recent midterm elections – but here in Sweden, not so much.
There is a familiar litany of reasons why datacentres are bad: they are being built without the consent or knowledge of local people; they consume vast amounts of land, electricity and water, with knock-on effects for communities and the environment; they provide no jobs and enrich rapacious tech companies.
What’s remarkable is how little any of those arguments apply in Sweden, especially here in Falun, a former copper-mining town a few hours north of Stockholm. If your abiding image of a datacentre is something like xAI’s Colossus facility in Tennessee, built at lightning speed with little public notice, partly powered by banks of unpermitted, methane gas-burning temporary generators, releasing huge amounts of CO2 and harmful pollutants into the atmosphere and the community, then EcoDataCenter is practically the polar opposite. “I’m biased, but we believe that we build datacentres in a somewhat different way,” says Wernvik.
For starters, the company’s electricity supply is 100% renewable: 75% from hydroelectric power and 25% from wind. Sweden’s power mix as a whole is virtually carbon-free – just 1% of it comes from fossil fuels (in the EU as a whole, the figure is 29%, in the US it is 55%). In rural areas like Falun, there is sometimes too much electricity being generated by nearby hydroelectric, solar and wind, so power-hungry datacentres are actually helpful in balancing the grid.
Conditions for datacentres are pretty good in Sweden as a whole. The cold northern climate means less cooling is required; the energy is not only green, it is cheap and reliable; there is plenty of water and space; and the country is relatively politically stable and well-regulated – as Wernvik puts it, “it’s very hard to develop something in Sweden where there’s not a consensus”.
Energy is still a concern at EcoDataCenter, considering this place has a capacity of 80MW (the equivalent of about 60,000 homes). There are two key measures of datacentre performance. One is carbon usage effectiveness (CUE): the carbon emissions for each kWh of energy consumed. The average for US datacentres is 414gCO2/kWh, the European Union’s is 263gCO2/kWh, EcoDataCenter’s is 1.17gCO2/kWh. Another key measure is power usage effectiveness (PUE); how efficiently the datacentre uses the power going into it. The EU average is 1.36 (where a score of 1 would be 100% efficiency), EcoDataCenter’s is 1.15. The company is bringing down both its CUE and PUE year by year, according to EcoDataCenter’s sustainability report.
The primary use for energy is powering the graphics processing units – the expensive chips that do the computing, mostly made by the US company Nvidia. (Wernvik reminds me that although 70% of their computing power goes towards AI, almost everything online is run through datacentres somewhere, from banking transactions to streaming TV.) The supply must be constant – even a small drop in current for a few milliseconds could be consequential – so there are numerous backup generators on site, but even these are fuelled by hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), a biofuel made from waste vegetable oil and animal fat, so also fossil fuel-free.
The other main energy use is cooling; removing the vast amounts of heat the chips generate. This is where controversies have arisen in the US over extracting from the local water supply, but it is less of an issue here, says Wernvik. The Swedish climate means less cooling is required, and there is plenty of water around (they get most of theirs from a nearby lake that was once used for drinking water). On a dreary, rainy day, no water is needed: the air is cold enough already (15C – anything below 20C will do). They simply have to pipe it around the building. On days when it is hot, or there is surplus electricity to use, there are electrically powered chillers on the roofs that cool air using a mist of water before it is circulated around the buildings.
The future, however, lies in liquid cooling – where the heat from the chips is transferred directly to liquid, rather than through the air. The latest generation of chips require this, Wernvik explains, as we walk through a spotlessly clean room containing several fridge-sized racks of chips, arranged in two parallel rows. They take up about the same amount of space as a bus. The noise is deafening (but inaudible outside), the chips themselves are barely visible behind a spaghetti of cables and cooling tubes connected to the backs of the server racks. It is a closed-loop system, so it does not use any external water, he says. “Each rack here is basically 25 saunas that we need to cool away and keep at about 27 degrees for it to not burn up inside,” says Wernvik. “That’s the whole engineering challenge we’re trying to solve.”
These particular Blackwell chips are powering DeepL, the German-based AI translation platform. Some of EcoDataCenter’s clients are confidential; declared ones include US cloud computing company CoreWeave, French AI firm Mistral, and research institutes including the universities of Hull and York. Supporting sovereign European tech is one of their key aims, Wernvik says.
The final part of the energy equation is excess heat, which EcoDataCenter reuses as much as possible. Much of it is used to dry wood pellets – a byproduct of the timber industry. The pellets go into incinerators in populated areas to provide heating. There is one right next door, which is no coincidence. (Admittedly, burning them emits CO2, but given the circular nature of the timber industry, they are arguably carbon-neutral.)
The rest of the heat (such as from the liquid cooling) goes directly into the local district heating system in Falun. Since the 1950s, Sweden has been building district heating networks across the country, where water is heated at large, centralised boilers, rather than in individual homes, then piped around towns and cities in underground pipes, typically at 60C to 80C. Homes and businesses extract the heat via a heat exchanger on their property. Already, district heating systems make use of excess heat from wastewater, sewage and supermarket refrigerators; datacentres are now another source to add to the mix.
There’s another aspect of EcoDataCenter’s operation that stands out. While datacentres are being imposed on many communities from the outside, in Falun it was practically the opposite. The project was initiated by local government, says Wernvik, “so the idea from the beginning was very much based on, how do we integrate a datacentre in the local community in order for it to fit the municipality?” This was in 2010, long before the AI revolution. The municipality (like a local council) decided the project would be better handled by a private company, which led to the formation of EcoDataCenter in 2014. The first part of the Falun site was up and running in 2019. The final phases are still under construction.
Local benefits were built in from the outset: 90% of its suppliers are sourced locally and 60% of its capital expenditure is spent locally, Wernvik says. It invests in local education and training, including sponsoring local sports teams and youth activities.
Local integration is even more evident at EcoDataCenter’s second site, in the industrial city of Borlänge, about a 20-minute drive away. This facility, the first phase of which will open in 2027, has a capacity of 240MW – three times larger than Falun. And the site is enormous: 200 sq km. In Borlänge, by contrast, they are building on a brownfield site. Poetically, perhaps, it used to be a paper mill, which closed in 2021. A datacentre is a good replacement: it can plug into the existing industrial infrastructure in much the same way – the power grid, the nearby water supply, the district heating. It will also employ 200 to 300 people, roughly the same number that worked at the paper mill before it closed, says Wernvik. “The discussion that datacentres don’t generate that amount of jobs, that needs to be put in context. There are a lot of different datacentres.”
In Stockholm, the datacentre strategy is different, but no less joined up. Sweden’s capital has become something of a European tech centre in its own right, and demand for datacentres is high. Stockholm Data Parks – a joint initiative by the city council and the city’s energy, power grid and fibre optic companies – was founded in 2014 as “a one-stop shop in order to make it easier to attract datacentre operators,” explains Michael Gullberg, product manager at energy company Stockholm Exergi. They free up suitable land, and again, the emphasis is on sustainability, including clean power (the city hopes to be net zero by 2035) and recycling waste heat. Stockholm claims to have the world’s largest district heating system, with more than 3,000 km of pipes, serving close to 90% of the capital. There are about 50 small-scale datacentres in the region (typically less than 20MW), and about 20 are connected to the district heating. They contribute about 1.5% of the city’s annual heat demand, which might not sound much, “but 110 gigawatt-hours of recovered heat is still a decent amount, because the system is so vast,” says Gullberg.
I visit one such facility in Kista, a suburb north of the city centre that has become Stockholm’s tech hub. It is an unobtrusive shed on an industrial estate, with a capacity of 12MW. Crucially, it is right next door to a district heating plant, so the datacentre basically pipes its heated water over the fence. It’s a win-win, says Sandra Karlsson, senior public affairs manager: “When they need to do district heating, they don’t need to boil the water from six degrees, they get it at 30 degrees from us, so they save a lot of energy.” In return, it takes in cold water from the district heating plant, which it uses for cooling.
This datacentre is run by atNorth, a company that began in Iceland, and now has 13 datacentres running or under construction across Sweden, Iceland, Norway, Denmark and Finland. Conditions are similar to Sweden in all these countries, says atNorth’s CEO, Eyjólfur Magnús Kristinsson: renewable power, reliable grids, district heating, “as well as the crappy weather that we have. We barely can live there as human beings, but datacentres love it.” As with EcoDataCenter, it claims to put sustainability and community engagement to the fore, investing and employing locally, using resources efficiently.
In terms of heat recovery, it’s a bit of a catch-22, Kristinsson points out: larger datacentres must be built in more remote areas, where there is less need for district heating, and vice versa. So they have been thinking of other ways. At its “mega site” in Varde, Denmark, with an initial capacity of 250MW, as well as district heating the plan is to channel excess heat into a 20 ha complex of greenhouses. “That means that Denmark can be self-sufficient with tomatoes during the six months of winter,” says Kristinsson. In turn, that means fewer imported vegetables: “that also saves a lot of carbon footprint, creates local jobs, and increases energy efficiency.” In Rjukan, Norway, Green Mountain’s datacentre channels excess heat to the fish farm next door.
Could other countries replicate this model? Yes and no. For one thing, the AI “hyperscalers” – such as Google, Meta, Amazon Web Services and Microsoft – dwarf Europe in terms of demand. Currently Europe’s datacentre capacity is estimated to be between 15% and 25% of that of the US. In addition, the renewable energy infrastructure in countries like Sweden has taken decades to establish; it is difficult to see the US catching up quickly. Added to which, European countries are relatively strict, both in terms of building and environmental regulations, and in areas like data privacy and protection. Elon Musk would never get away with trucking in some gas generators without permission in Sweden. To many critics, tighter regulation is exactly what the US datacentre landscape is crying out for. In July 2025, the Trump administration announced its AI Action Plan, which dismantled environmental and planning protections and rejected “radical climate dogma” in order to win the AI race.
Having said that, the US is building big in Nordic countries, to service their European users. In Sweden, Meta is building a 723MW facility in Lulea, Canadian-American firm Brookfield is planning a 750MW datacentre in Strängnäs, and Google broke ground on a 150MW plant in Horndal this June. These companies profess to be adopting the Nordic model, including building their own renewable energy supplies, although last month, the Guardian reported that Google had illegally felled 250,000 trees in Muhos, in northern Finland, to clear a site for its datacentre, leaving a barren 330 ha landscape. Google’s Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, has apologised for the forest clearings but claimed the company had acted “on the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time” and planned to plant trees across 130 hectares there. Contractors building Microsoft’s datacentre in Gävle, Sweden, have been accused of housing their mostly foreign workers in poor conditions and subjecting them to long hours. Microsoft said of its contractors and suppliers, it “set clear requirements on health and safety, working conditions, and the freedom of association and right to collective bargaining” and had “robust processes in place” to ensure contractors’ compliance with Microsoft’s human rights and fair labour policies. The community engagement has not gone so smoothly for Google in Sweden, either. In 2021, a local metal band, also named Horndal, released an album railing against Google’s imminent arrival, called Lake Drinker (sample lyrics: “The digital devil shivers of thirst … First you took our trees / Now you drink our lake”).
Both atNorth and EcoDataCenter avoid importing cheap foreign labour, they say, but Kristinsson acknowledges that opposition to datacentres in the region has been growing, largely fuelled by the backlash in the US: “It’s probably not as strong [here], but Nordics are early adopters of everything that is new. We adopt, also, the same TikTok propaganda that is showing now in the US.”
Wernvik is more measured: “The American companies and the hyperscalers are definitely needed in the ecosystem as well because they possess unique competitiveness and capabilities.”
Could Sweden become a victim of its own success? The prospect of more and more of these gigantic facilities eating up the landscape is pretty dystopian even in a large country like Sweden. Wernvik is not too worried, though: “Our core components into what we sell are land and power. It’s a very linear business in that way. It’s very hard to have exponential growth because we work with physical constraints.” Exactly how many datacentres the world needs is largely a question of demand: how much more AI we require, and how much the benefits offset the harms. That’s really a separate conversation, but at the very least, Sweden’s joined-up, long-term approach to tech, energy and communities shows that there are better and worse ways to build our digital future.

https://www.humanite.fr/medias/journalis.title: Les syndicats de journalistes portent plainte contre les violences policières en manifestation
https://www.humanite.fr/medias/journalis.author: Caroline Constant
https://www.humanite.fr/medias/journalis.text:
Quatre syndicats de journalistes portent plainte contre X pour soutenir leurs pairs molestés, parfois lourdement, par les forces de police ces dernières semaines lors des manifestations, au mépris de la loi.
Sept journalistes ont porté plainte, le 10 novembre dernier, après avoir subi des violences policières lors de manifestations ces dernières semaines. L’intersyndicale SNJ-CGT, SNJ, CFDT-Journalistes et SGJ-FO les soutient, et porte plainte contre X à leurs côtés. Les syndicats, qui doivent rencontrer ce jeudi matin 12 novembre le ministre de l’Intérieur Laurent Nunez, rappellent dans un communiqué commun que « la liberté de la presse est un droit fondamental et l’une des conditions essentielles de toute société démocratique. L’empêcher entrave le droit de chacun d’être informé. »
Contraire au Schéma du maintien de l’ordre
L’intersyndicale estime que « les journalistes doivent pouvoir couvrir les manifestations, y compris les opérations de maintien de l’ordre, librement, sans subir de pressions, de menaces ou de violences de la part de ceux-là mêmes qui sont chargés d’assurer la sécurité publique ». Ils tiennent pour « particulièrement grave que des agents investis de l’autorité publique puissent être mis en cause pour des comportements portant atteinte à l’exercice d’une liberté fondamentale ».
Pour eux, ces attaques délibérées contre la presse par la police sont une « négation du Schéma national de maintien de l’ordre (SNMO) qui en 2021 a affirmé le rôle protecteur des forces de l’ordre vis à des journalistes, sur les manifestations ». Les syndicats appellent de leurs vœux des « investigations effectives, indépendantes et approfondies » pour identifier les auteurs de ces violences et « le cas échéant, d’engager leur responsabilité pénale ».
Ils appellent les journalistes victimes de ce genre de violences à les contacter dans le cadre d’une démarche commune.
Oui, on s’en doute : vous en avez assez
Voir ces messages d’appel au don, ça peut être pénible. Nous le savons. Et on doit bien vous avouer que nous préférerions ne pas avoir à les écrire…
Mais voilà : c’est crucial pour l’Humanité. Si ce titre existe toujours aujourd’hui, c’est grâce au financement régulier de nos lectrices et lecteurs.
- C’est grâce à votre soutien que nous pouvons exercer notre métier avec passion. Nous ne dépendons ni des intérêts d’un propriétaire milliardaire, ni de pressions politiques : personne ne nous dicte ce que nous devons dire ou taire.
- Votre engagement nous libère aussi de la course aux clics et à l’audience. Plutôt que de chercher à capter l’attention à tout prix, nous choisissons de traiter les sujets que notre rédaction juge essentiels : parce qu’ils méritent d’être lus, compris, partagés. Parce que nous estimons qu’ils vous seront utiles

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: World heading for ‘irrevocable overshoot’ of global temperature thresholds, analysis warns
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Oliver Milman in Antalya, Turkey
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
The world is heading for an “irrecoverable overshoot” of global temperature thresholds that will plunge billions of people into disastrous climate impacts because governments have stalled for so long to cut planet-heating emissions, analysis has found.
Under current policies, the planet will heat up by 2.7C on average by the end of the century compared with preindustrial times, the report by Climate Action Tracker (CAT) found. This is up slightly from a prediction of 2.6C in the group’s analysis conducted last year.
This level of warming smashes the 1.5C threshold that was agreed by countries a decade ago but is set to be breached in just a few years. Scientists have warned that beyond this point already harmful storms, droughts, heatwaves, flooding and other impacts will become intolerable for parts of the world and potentially trigger runaway climate change that won’t be contained.
Countries, minus the US, are gathered in the Turkish city of Antalya for UN climate talks that have centred on the looming “overshoot” of the temperature target. This reality should compel governments to act quickly to phase out use of the fossil fuels that are causing the climate crisis, the UN secretarygeneral, António Guterres, said on Tuesday.
If countries did act decisively to slash emissions then the future temperature projections would become less daunting, the CAT report states. However, in even the most optimistic scenario – where all pledges, targets and other long-term promises made by countries were fulfilled – the world would still heat up by 1.9C by the end of the century.
Such targets have been routinely flouted by the countries that have made them, however. This means leaders face a crunch moment, experts say.
“The stark choice for governments is to either continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to – or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever,” says Bill Hare, chief executive of CAT partner organisation Climate Analytics.
Hare said exceeding 1.5C warming “cannot be an excuse to open the door to defeatism” and that every small increment of temperature rise will be significant. The CAT analysis is similar to one recently put out by the UN, which uses previous CAT data to inform its own projections.
While the world is failing to cut emissions in line with the science and countries’ own promises, carbon pollution is set to dip slightly this year and CAT pointed to some causes for optimism. Clean energy investment is now double that of fossil fuels, electric car use is soaring and the deforestation of the Amazon in Brazil has fallen sharply.
But much more will need to be done to avert disastrous climate impacts. Greta Thunberg, the Swedish climate advocate, arrived in Antalya on Tuesday and warned that “everything and everyone we love is at stake” because of the failure to confront the climate crisis.
“Governments collectively are simply not moving fast enough to adopt the policies that would enable us to escape from the emerging overshoot trap,” said Sarah Heck, lead author of the CAT report. Some countries, such as the US, Canada and New Zealand, are even slowing down their climate action to a “staggering level”, she added.

https://citylimits.org/opinion-dcs-newes.title: Opinion: DC’s Newest Bosses Are From New York. They Must Deliver the IBX.
https://citylimits.org/opinion-dcs-newes.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/opinion-dcs-newes.text:
Share This Article
“New York’s civic and business leaders remain pessimistic about relying on the federal government’s support to bring the IBX to life; this is exactly the moment we need commitment from this Congress.”
We learned Tuesday evening that the Democrats will take control of the U.S. House and Senate. And it appears leaders of both chambers will be not only New Yorkers but Brooklynites—at no other time in U.S. history have both chambers been led by New Yorkers.
As a rent-stabilized Queens resident and member of Queens Community Board 5, I am calling on this new federal government to make an unwavering and comprehensive commitment to the construction of the Interborough Express (IBX). Strong federal support is the last remaining key to building the IBX. Our city cannot miss this opportunity.
The IBX is perhaps the most significant American public transit project in generations, establishing a new, non-Manhattan-oriented spine connecting the Brooklyn Army Terminal in Bay Ridge to Jackson Heights, Queens. This corridor would serve 160,000-plus weekday riders and connect nearly 1 million residents across some of the most transit-starved neighborhoods in New York City. Notably, my neighborhood may stand to benefit the most: bringing our district three to four new rail stations with connections to 16 more subway lines, up from our current one, the M train.
This new Congress comes at the heels of the draft environmental impact statement’s (DEIS) publication, a make-or-break moment for the IBX. Simultaneously, New York’s civic and business leaders remain pessimistic about relying on the federal government’s support to bring the IBX to life; this is exactly the moment we need commitment from this Congress.
New York now has the leverage to steward a century-long vision through the next two years of solvable engineering challenges, financial hurdles, and bureaucratic speed bumps with executive dedication and robust public collaboration. During this crucial phase, this Congress can show both New Yorkers and Americans what a serious government can do: deliver modern marvels that materially improve all of our lives, something generations past regularly enjoyed.
This leadership must take several forms.
First, it must courageously fund the IBX. New Yorkers cannot afford delays due to MTA funding deficits, and the federal government must readily fill in gaps should they arrive. Simply put, we must secure bigger checks from this government. We deserve the investment.
Although we are working toward 50 percent federal support for the IBX through the Federal Transit Administration’s New Starts program, these grants can cover up to 60 percent. An extra 10 percent, roughly $550 million, offers capital flexibility the MTA can direct quicker as the project progresses.
Similarly, mechanisms like the Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act’s low-interest loans, greater congestion mitigation and air quality (CMAQ) grants, and expanded formula funding flexibility already have and must continue supporting nimble and adaptive budgets. Completing the IBX shouldn’t require innovative public financing—we have all the tools. We just need a Congress committed to them.
This political leadership must also embody bureaucratic excellence for the IBX. This can look like easing red-tape and ensuring smooth, synchronized partnership between federal and MTA leaders. It is already taking shape in notable ways. Federal funding is right now supporting design and engineering prerequisites for IBX transfers.
Given the highly competitive pool of New Start grant monies, however, this federal government must also classify the IBX under federal dashboard streamlining initiatives to prioritize its review, ensuring that federal agencies respond quickly to environmental impact assessments. Further, this federal government can issue swift Federal Railroad Administration regulatory waivers, protecting the IBX from freight regulatory disputes.
Ultimately, I am calling on this federal government to be nonstop cheerleaders for the IBX. It is through the constant drumming of support that the IBX can fulfill and expand its promise; Gov. Kathy Hochul, Mayor Zohran Mamdani, community boards, and countless New Yorkers are already exemplifying this.
Likewise, U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer and Congressman Hakeem Jeffries must routinely visit station sites, organize public forums, and champion the IBX throughout the media. Setting this tone has real economic value, too. The sooner the IBX is operational, the sooner both its broad economic multipliers compound and increase while its overall per-rider costs decrease.
Delivering the IBX is not only an easy political homerun for their constituencies, but with their new leadership roles, the Democrats can take significant ownership of the IBX’s success.
Take this opportunity, Sen.Schumer and Congressman Jeffries. Remind the people what America is capable of. Imagine! Congress’s two Brooklyn leaders delivering our city the promise of the IBX. Show us that the mandate you received Tuesday night can work, that neighborly politics can deliver. Show us that the government can make our lives better. We deserve it.
I cannot wait to share IBX rides with my neighbors. I cannot wait for the IBX to connect me to new neighbors. I cannot wait to look into the future knowing the IBX will be there. What I’m asking of our Congress here is to step up. We need your help. We are so so close.
Gentry Fitch is a rent-stabilized tenant of Ridgewood, Queens and member of Queens Community Board 5. The views represented here are solely his own and do not reflect the views of QCB5.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/05/midt.title: Blue Tsunami’s Clearest Takeaway: People Hate Data Centers
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/05/midt.author: Sanya Mansoor
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/05/midt.text:
America’s data center buildout suffered a resounding defeat in the midterms at all levels of government. Candidates and ballot measures in favor of restricting or altogether stopping the development of the facilities powering the artificial intelligence boom won overwhelmingly on election night.
Newly elected Democratic governors in Georgia, Ohio, and Texas have promised moratoriums on new data center construction and all took tougher stances on regulation than their incumbent Republican opponents. The trend carried over in various congressional races, in which candidates who were critical of their competitors’ record of promoting data center development came out on top, even flipping key districts in Ohio and South Carolina.
Many local communities, mostly in Ohio and Illinois, voted directly on their AI concerns and passed a flurry of ballot initiatives restricting data center development — close to 40 proposals, according to a tracker by research firm Redbud Consulting.
“What’s good for the AI industry is clearly not good for average voters,” said Shobita Parthasarathy, a public policy professor at the University of Michigan. “I wish that data center operators and the AI industry really take this as a sign that they’re done a very poor job of considering public concern and taking it seriously.”
Parthasarathy pointed out that many Americans are now deciding how they feel about these energy-guzzling facilities based on their experience of living near one and “real knowledge” about their deficiencies. Those concerns range from negative impacts on energy bills, to the environmental and health issues, but also include anger toward the outsized power that the tech oligarchy wields.
Americans’ vote in the midterms has given them a tangible way to fight back, Parthasarathy said: Blocking the brick-and-mortar, water-sucking, heat-spewing buildings that power tech billionaires’ rapid wealth accumulation.
Tech Money ≠ Change Minds
A long track record of polls have recorded Americans’ anger about data centers. About three-quarters of voters polled by NBC News on Election Day said they opposed building these facilities in their communities. Those sentiments are consistent with a Heatmap survey from August that found a similar proportion of Americans would strongly oppose a new data center near where they live.
More than half the voters polled by NBC this week said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision, though they were almost equally divided when it came to deciding which party would be better at addressing their AI concerns.
The AI industry tried to make a dent in the midterms, but much of their money was focused on a congressional primary in New York, where the cash helped defeat AI critic Alex Bores.
In the general election, an Intercept analysis found, AI super PACs dramatically scaled back their spending on congressional races compared to primaries amid growing anger toward data centers; only 5 percent of their direct expenditures went toward contested general election races. Industry observers told The Intercept that this suggested developers and tech CEOs have taken note of the electorate souring on AI and data centers.
That’s not to say that tech magnates, more broadly, have been stingy with their money. Elon Musk spent nearly $450 million ahead of the midterms, including more than $200 million in Texas, where his companies are headquartered.
“If Elon Musk wants to continue to burn half a billion dollars to get no results, there are probably other ways he can do that,” said Mitch Jones, deputy director of Food & Water Action, which has advocated for regulations on data centers on the federal, state, and local level. “It shows when an issue is deeply and broadly felt by American people, no amount of money can change their minds.”
Musk’s money wasn’t enough for the races in Texas to go his way. Surprise upsets in the state’s Senate and gubernatorial races resulted in victories for, respectively, Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa.
Talarico promised to end tax breaks for data center developers and minimum federal requirements to protect the grid, environment, jobs, and transparency. Hinojosa called for a moratorium on all data center approvals “until laws can be passed by the Legislature to protect Texans.” Outgoing Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott had already temporarily halted environmental permitting and grid connections until about the end of the year, but Hinojosa’s proposal would last longer and be more expansive.
Promises to Rein In AI
Congress’s new incoming class includes many Democrats who have promised to rein in the harms of AI. Ohio’s Democratic Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown flipped a district after portraying his opponent in ads as cheerleading the data center industry.
In typically red South Carolina, Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews defeated her opponent, Sen. Darline Graham, after accusing her of being bought by developers. Pro-AI super PAC Building the Future spent $2.5 million to support Graham, according to Politico.
In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom, who called for a temporary ban on data centers, was narrowly ahead of his incumbent opponent on Wednesday evening in a state that has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in more than four decades.
Just because Trump is expected to veto Democrats’ proposals to regulate AI, that doesn’t mean they shouldn’t push for them, said Jones, of Food & Water Action. He’s hoping Congress will approve a ban on “artificial superintelligence,” as well as a federal moratorium on new data centers.
“They should show the American public they are standing with us and taking actions to force Trump to veto those bills,” Jones said.
Although moratoriums typically target new construction and not existing data centers, Jones says they are still necessary to prevent an even more expansive buildout.
“We don’t need any more,” he said, citing a Forbes estimate that the total cost of the projected buildout ranges from $2.8 trillion by 2030 to $10.30 trillion by 2032 in the U.S.
With Trump still in charge, states led by Democratic governors may be where more forceful regulation on data centers occurs.
In Georgia, Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms promised a temporary statewide pause on data centers. Ohio’s new incoming Democratic Gov.-elect Amy Acton proposed an “immediate moratorium upon taking office on any new construction.” And in Kansas, Democrat Cindy Holscher, who declared victory in the gubernatorial race, has advocated for halting new development.
Ballot Measures
Local communities are getting creative, too. Jones said that some towns and cities have turned to ballot measures to bypass “elected officials who are not keeping pace with their voters.”
About half of the roughly 40 ballot measures in the midterms were in Ohio. Most succeeded by a wide margin, and as of Thursday morning, all but one vote were in favor of restrictions, according to Redbud Consulting’s tracker.
Nick Owens, who helped draft 10 local ballot measures in Ohio that restrict data center development after an unsuccessful attempt at a statewide petition, said this gave voters quicker and easier access to the ballot to curtail the “humongous growth of hyperscale data centers.”
“Communities know how best they want to govern themselves,” said Owens, who was a Trump delegate at the 2024 Republican National Convention and is currently co-founder of grassroots group Conserve Ohio. The results “just validated everything I’ve been seeing on the ground, talking to people, and in nationwide polling,” he added.
Owens is looking ahead, once again, toward pushing for a statewide moratorium, as well as curtailing the secretive use of non-disclosure agreements by tech companies and developers.
Parthasarathy, the public policy professor, said more communities may explore ballot measures as a response to developers’ lack of transparency and drive to build more.
“I don’t think their thirst for data centers is going to go away,” she said. “They might move into localities where there is less organized pushback.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://citylimits.org/it-reflects-every.title: ‘It Reflects Everyone’: The Country’s Tallest Mural Spans the Length of This NYCHA Building
https://citylimits.org/it-reflects-every.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/it-reflects-every.text:
Share This Article
Towering at 307 feet, Dominican artist Angurria completed the piece in just 22 days, spending up to nine hours a day on a scaffold lift. “I grew up in Los Alcarrizos painting the people of my neighborhood,” he told City Limits. “In the South Bronx I found the same pride, the same strength, the same families.”
When Nestor Omar García, a Dominican artist widely known as “Angurria,” began painting a gargantuan mural—covering all 29 stories of a public housing development in the South Bronx—one of the first faces to come to life on the empty canvas was a young child, wearing headphones and perched atop a woman’s shoulders.
Tanya Pedler, president of the New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) development’s resident association, who has a 7-year-old son who is autistic, told City Limits it’s her favorite part of the piece.
“We have a lot of children in this neighborhood that suffer from sensory processing disorders,” she said, “and I wanted to make sure our special needs community was represented.”
Towering at 307 feet tall, the mural, titled “Un MAR de Gente / From Every Shore,” is the largest in the country, according to organizers—and Angurria completed it in just 22 days. 
He used a scaffold elevator—often spending eight to nine hours on the lift each day—and help from two assistants to paint the southwest facing side of Morrisania Air Rights, a public housing development built in 1980 using air rights over Metro-North rail tracks in the South Bronx.
The complex is home to some 1,950 residents, who played a role in deciding what the record-breaking mural should include. “I hope that it reflects everyone who not only lives in the Bronx, but all these children who are here today,” Angurria said at the .
One of the only challenges, Angurria said, was the wind. “When it’s windy, the lift moves maybe two or three meters,” he said. “That was very difficult, but only for us. Everyone was so kind here.”
“This was an incredible experience for me,” Angurria told City Limits. “I grew up in Los Alcarrizos painting the people of my neighborhood, and in the South Bronx I found the same pride, the same strength, the same families.”
ArtBridge, a New York City-based nonprofit that transforms urban infrastructure like construction scaffolding into canvases for public art, commissioned Angurria to complete the mural.
They worked with another nonprofit group called Public Housing Community Fund (PHCF), created by the NYCHA in 2016 to facilitate design, construction and resident input for public projects that are funded by private donors. The M·A·C VIVA GLAM Fund awarded ArtBridge a $165,000 grant to support the mural.
Pedler said she reached out to the PHCF about a year ago, saying, “we needed to have a mural here, because the walls were a little hideous.”
“They connected us to ArtBridge, and this whole process was quite quick,” Pedler told City Limits. “We started talking about this last winter, and it’s completed before the year is out.”
A Jamaican immigrant who was raised in Queens after her family immigrated in 1989, Pedler also spent time in the city’s foster care system. She described how her past experiences with instability now inspire her to seek improvements for her neighbors, or help others who are struggling—with being a teenage mom, for instance, or transitioning to their first home in public housing, like she once did.
She’d previously collaborated with PHCF on other improvements at Morrisania Air Rights, like when she called on the city in 2022 to renovate the development’s playground, which several residents said was too dangerous for children to use because of unmanageable drug and criminal activity.
Former Mayor Eric Adams visited the playground in 2022, and it’s since received about $1 million in investments, largely through federal funding secured by Congressman Ritchie Torres in 2024. About $750,000 of that is being used to install a sensory playground and garden at the public housing development.
“This is a welcome sign that no matter who you are, or where you’re from, or what language you speak, or what God you worship, you are welcome right here in the Boogie Down Bronx,” Torres said at a ribbon cutting for the mural on Oct. 27.
After ArtBridge commissioned the mural, Pedler said she went to events in the borough, hung up flyers and shared information on social media about ways residents could influence details in the design, including identities that were important to them. The nonprofits, along with Angurria, then held workshops with residents to gather insight on themes and imagery they’d like to see in the art.
“The residents came out, young and old,” Pedler said. “They wanted to make sure that their voices were heard, and I’m grateful for them because we wouldn’t have this beautiful masterpiece if it wasn’t for them.”
Pedler also noted a particular request from 13-year-old resident Hawa Batchilly, who asked for more representation of Black and brown Muslim girls in their community. Of the finished mural, Batchilly said “it shows me that Muslim girls are all allowed to be here.”
“Children deserve beauty, representation, and a chance to believe that something extraordinary can happen where they live,” Pedler said.
Pedler’s message for other public housing residents, and especially other tenant association leaders, is “to dream and dream big.”
“Our residents look up and see stories that reflect our mothers, grandmothers, and children,” Pedler said. “Whether your roots are American, Jamaican, Honduran, Mexican, Dominican, Panamanian, African or whatsoever else, you belong in this story.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: New museum dedicated to Italian Modernist Mario Sironi must not become ‘endorsement of fascism’, art historians warn
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: James Imam
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Plans by Giorgia Meloni’s government to open a new museum in Rome dedicated to Mario Sironi, the Modernist painter who was a supporter of Benito Mussolini, risk sanitising Italy's fascist past, two leading historians have warned.
The state-run museum is expected to open next year within the Associazione Nazionale fra Mutilati ed Invalidi di Guerra (National Association of War Disabled and Wounded Veterans), a monumental fascist era building inaugurated in 1928. The building is home to two major frescoes by Sironi painted ten years later. One depicts Mussolini on horseback.
The museum will display 30 works recently acquired by Italy's culture ministry from the Mario Sironi Archive in Rome, including paintings, drawings and preparatory sketches. A further 90 works will be loaned by the archive.
Unveiling the plans on Tuesday, Alessandro Giuli, the culture minister, said the project was “the defining achievement of my term in office, and the one of which I am most proud”.
Meloni's Brothers of Italy has political roots in the postwar Italian neo-fascist movement. Press materials for the museum do not mention fascism or Mussolini.
Sironi joined the fascist movement in 1919, contributing more than 1,700 political cartoons and illustrations to Il Popolo d’Italia, Mussolini’s newspaper. The museum will feature works spanning more than four decades from the 1910s to the 1950s, covering distinct phases from Sironi's artistic development including Futurism, metaphysical-influenced works and monumental commissions awarded under the fascist regime.
Members of Italy’s cultural sector have emphasised the need for the institution to address Seroni’s politics.
Tomaso Montanari, an art historian and rector of the Università per Stranieri di Siena (University for Foreigners of Siena), said that he did not oppose the museum but insisted it must explicitly distance itself from fascism.
“Since Italy is a republic founded on anti-fascism, the museum's educational material must make clear that there is no endorsement of fascism," Montanari told The Art Newspaper.
Montanari, who sits on the culture ministry's scientific committee, said that the initial project for the museum focussed “overwhelmingly” on Sironi's fascist period work. He added that the ministry "partially" heeded his argument for works from other periods to be included.
The art historian and curator Fabio Benzi, who is on the Sironi museum's scientific committee, told the French-language publication Le Journal Des Arts: "The danger is of legitimising a certain authoritarian aesthetic under the guise of cultural rediscovery".
The culture ministry has been contacted for comment.
Last year, the ministry announced it had acquired the former Rome home of Giacomo Balla, the futurist painter who initially supported fascism, which operates as a museum.
On Thursday [5 November], key members of Meloni's government presented a new exhibition celebrating the 90th anniversary of the EUR district in Rome, the city's grandest example of fascist-era planning.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Sydney Powerhouse scandal, heritage destruction in Lebanon, Dan Flavin—podcast
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Ben Luke, Alexander Morrison, David Clack
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
This weekend, Powerhouse Parramatta, a vast new arts and technology museum, opens in Sydney, Australia. But its unveiling is shrouded in allegations of misconduct relating to the chief executive who had led the project, Lisa Havilah, who stepped down in August. Ben Luke speaks to The Art Newspaper’s Australian reporter, Elizabeth Fortescue, about the building and the scandal.
In southern Lebanon, despite a supposed ceasefire in the war between Hezbollah and Israel, heritage continues to be damaged by Israeli military activity. Ben talks to Sarvy Geranpayeh, who has been talking to politicians, heritage professionals and artists about the destruction.
And this episode’s Work of the Week is greens crossing greens (to Piet Mondrian who lacked green) (1966) by Dan Flavin. A landmark work for the US artist, first shown at the Van Abbemuseum in Eindhoven, it is one of the highlights of the exhibition Dan Flavin: Some Light at the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, Spain, which opens next week. Ben discusses the work with Lauren Hinkson, curator for collections at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York, who is organising the Bilbao show.
- Powerhouse Parramatta opens on 7 November.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Organizing Brought Us to This Moment
Voters across the country have given the keys to Democrats. But can the party get in gear?
Victory has a hundred parents, as President Kennedy would doubtless have put it if he’d lived to our more enlightened times, but defeat is an orphan.
Tuesday’s stunning electoral tsunami was big enough, and blue enough, to allow everyone from Chuck Schumer (who recruited Janice Mills to stop Graham Platner in Maine, and also backed Haley Stevens to block Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan) to Our Revolution (the Bernie Sanders–aligned group that pushed Maine Democrats to pick Troy Jackson, rather than a more anodyne centrist, as their candidate after Platner withdrew) to claim a share of the credit. This wave was also wet enough to water whatever pet theory you had ready, whether that was The New York Times’ incessant evangelizing for “moderate Democrats” or journalist David Sirota’s claim that “Bernie Sanders’ form of anti-oligarch populism is now the real center” of the Democratic Party. In the blinding light of this new electoral dawn, even Mamdani strategist Morris Katz’s rash prediction that “the Rahm Emanuel Democrat hardly exists anymore” had a kind of crazy plausibility—though this old leftist is keeping my hammer, stake, and garlic ready to hand.
Still, while we’re handing out trophies, here are my four nominees for PVP (Particularly Valuable Player) in Tuesday’s election victories:
- Howard Dean: As chair of the Democratic National Committee from 2005 to 2009, the Vermonter pressed hard for a 50-state strategy. Even though Dean’s spadework prepared the ground for Barack Obama’s presidency, his argument that no state should be abandoned as “unwinnable” by the national party was roundly dismissed by his successors and the party hierarchy. Even Wikipedia complains that Dean’s approach “requires a campaign to spend resources in a rival’s strongest states, when those resources could be concentrated in swing states.” With not only Texas and South Carolina but Kansas and Iowa and even Mississippi now very much in play, Dean is looking much more like a prophet than a crank.
- Stacey Abrams: Like Moses, Abrams herself might not have made it into the promised land (or the governor’s mansion in Atlanta), but does anyone believe that Jon Ossoff or Raphael Warnock would be in the Senate without her leadership organizing the fight against voter suppression? Or that Keisha Lance Bottoms would not only have won but won so convincingly, if Abrams hadn’t made straight the way in 2018 and 2022?
- The Texas Organizing Project: While the dream of a Democratic revival in the state that once produced crusading progressives like Maury Maverick, Lyndon Johnson, and Barbara Jordan has been gestating since 1994 (the last time Democrats won a statewide election), it wasn’t until 2009 that two women, Ginny Goldman and Michelle Tremillo, started to do something about it. Focusing their work on Black and Latino Texans, and running toward, rather than away from, fights on climate justice, immigrant rights, healthcare, and education, the TOP’s Movement Voter Project ran trainings and did the hard fieldwork in races all the way down the ballot, from Gina Hinajosa and James Talarico down to the Texas agriculture commissioner and numerous contests for the state legislature.
- Iowa Citizens for Community Improvement: It’s been 10 years since Hugh Espy, a CCI organizer, sat me down in his Des Moines office and explained why, for most of Iowa’s working class, Republican and Democratic politicians were “two sides of the same coin: They do the bidding of corporate power. They don’t want to take on Big Ag, the Farm Bureau, Monsanto.” Things got so bad in the state that, as Art Cullen, legendary editor of the Storm Lake Times-Pilot put it just last year, “Nowadays, people who do not believe in banning books or Black history call themselves ‘Concerned Citizens of Sac County’ and not ‘Sac County Democrats.’” Yet all that time Espy and his comrades kept on doing the work of seeding democracy—at picket lines, Farm Aid forums, country fairs, and public hearings. Something big happened in Iowa on Tuesday. But as in Texas, the ground had to be cultivated for a long time before bearing fruit.
The Nation’s late and much-lamented strikes correspondent, Jane McAlevey, always insisted there are “no shortcuts” in politics, and whatever else it does or doesn’t prove, Tuesday’s unexpected redrawing of the electoral map ought to remind us that with sufficient organizing no cause need be regarded as hopeless. I donated money to three candidates this cycle: Brad Lander (because I live in his district, and know him to be a mensch), Dan Sullivan (the Alaska “spoiler” who made the Times clutch its pearls—because why should the other side have all the fun?), and Scott Colom, who at the time seemed like the unlikeliest of the three (despite some of the best ads in this or any political season). If bare-knuckled, profane economic populism can win statewide in Mississippi, it can win anywhere.
But will it be given the chance? Will Chuck Schumer, the “senator from Wall Street,” who is almost certain to run unopposed for majority leader, really pursue economic policies that will make a difference to working families? Will Hakeem Jeffries start harmonizing with the Squad just because it is in the nation’s interest? The politics of dislodging either are not encouraging—at least in the short term. Rather than recruiting sacrificial candidates to oppose them, congressional progressives might consider adopting a “short leash” approach to the Democratic leadership—and a short list of legislative demands to test their good faith.
As Corbin Trent, one of the cofounders of Justice Democrats (a group that also deserves considerable credit for never buying the Trump “vibe shift” fairly tale) put it on NBC, “We’ve been given the keys by the American people, and it’s time to drive the car to a better place.”
What does that look like—especially when Donald Trump still has two more years left in office? As my colleague Robert Borosage notes, “Americans want their leaders to focus attention and resources at home.” This means bold action to end the war with Iran—starting now, not (as the infinitely patient Schumer proposes) waiting until next year. It means ending military aid to Israel, and making clear to whoever forms that country’s next government that America will no longer be complicit in genocide or the slow strangulation of Palestinian hopes for justice and self-determination.
But in an election where voters told pollsters their top three concerns were the economy, the future of democracy, and healthcare, it is domestic matters that will rightly preoccupy Democrats. Clawing back GOP handouts to the Epstein class (and redistributing them downward), restoring the Affordable Care Act subsidies eliminated by Trump, and banning stock trading by sitting government officials and members of Congress would all signal the kind of change in direction Americans just voted for. Vetoing any of these measures would also be an albatross Democrats could hang around the necks of Republicans for the next two years and beyond.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
As would my own favorite policy proposal: a phased transition to Medicare for All. From El-Sayed in Michigan to Annie Andrews in South Carolina, fixing our broken healthcare system is an issue that cuts across both state and party lines, with 65 percent of Americans saying they would be in favor. The details of getting there may be “gnarly,” but bold action by the next Congress on healthcare cost and access—making Trump and his GOP loyalists the defenders of the status quo—would be smart politics now, and potentially transformative later.
Speaking of smart politics, what about accountability? No matter how richly he may deserve it, anyone with a functioning memory should be wary of devoting too much time and energy pursuing yet another futile impeachment of Donald Trump. But that needn’t deter Congress from using its oversight powers to illuminate the depths of Trump and his family’s corruption and profiteering from office—or from investigating the tech oligarchy’s cozy relationship with the Trump White House. A full reckoning with Elon Musk (anyone else for nationalizing Starlink?), or Jeff Bezos, or Mark Zuckerberg, may have to wait until there’s a (social) Democrat in the White House. But can we at least stop the fawning?
Because that breeze we’ve all felt since Tuesday night is the Overton window blowing wider open than it has been in decades. Let’s not waste the moment.
