https://jacobin.com/2026/11/portland-dem.title: Portland’s Socialists Have Built a Political Machine
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/portland-dem.author: Roman Broszkowski
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/portland-dem.text:
Portland’s Socialists Have Built a Political Machine
While New York City gets much of the media attention, the Democratic Socialists of America chapter in Portland, Oregon, has quietly built a local political powerhouse over the last few years.
Over the last two years, the Portland, Oregon, chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) has developed a reputation for punching far above its city’s weight.
The chapter sits just behind the New York, Los Angeles, and Washington, DC, chapters in terms of size, and roughly one in two hundred Portlanders is a member (compared to about one in 530 New Yorkers). Today one-third of Portland’s city council actively participates in the group’s Socialists in Office Committee (SIOC); this election cycle, the chapter ran candidates for state and county office. Yet for most of the chapter’s history, elections weren’t a focus, and candidates for office were often kept at arm’s length.
“For a significant period where I was involved, a number of people just believed that candidates couldn’t do anything for you,” said Dave Coburn, the chapter’s former Electoral Working Group cochair. “People really only wanted to do things via ballot measure.”
That would start to change with the fallout of Portland’s long-lasting George Floyd protests. The protests supercharged existing frustrations with the city’s political status quo — and created an opening for outsiders to achieve significant electoral victories.
Electoral Reforms Open the Gates
Few American cities experienced 2020 like Portland. For almost a year, the city’s downtown saw sustained demonstrations and an intense response from local and federal law enforcement. The protests and ensuing criticism of the aggressive actions taken by local police hobbled the tenure of moderate Democratic Mayor Ted Wheeler and energized popular calls to reform the city’s commission, its governing body at the time.
In 2022, voters approved Measure 26-228, changing Portland’s legislative structure from four at-large commissioners to a twelve-member city council drawn from four multimember districts elected with ranked-choice voting. Combined with a small donor public financing scheme enacted in 2016, this system significantly lowered the bar for political participation in the 2024 election.
In many ways, the new electoral format catered well to DSA’s strengths. Smaller-district and multimember elections benefited candidates who could mobilize large field operations while also being able to hold a clear lane within a crowded field — unlike in previous elections, candidates would only need 25 percent +1 to win. Similarly, ranked-choice voting allowed candidates to pick up votes from coalition allies, benefiting those with platforms that spoke to a wide range of voters, while the matching funds program helped campaigns critical of the city’s traditional donor class to compete.
These reforms came right as Portland DSA was trying to revitalize itself. The pandemic had seen a sharp downturn in the chapter’s membership, and organizers began looking for opportunities to rebuild their capacity.
One came as part of a push to establish universal pre-K that the chapter had initiated in mid-2019 with the goal of getting a measure on the November 2020 ballot. A month after the Universal Pre-School Now! (UP Now!) coalition submitted the proposed language for the measure, pandemic restrictions were enacted in Oregon, hampering signature collection. Simultaneously, UP Now! faced competition from a more moderate universal pre-K project at the county level called Pre-School 4 All (P4A).
That summer, the chapter threw itself into building support for the campaign and managed to collect more than 32,000 signatures. Its success facilitated a merger with an updated P4A in order to avoid both proposals appearing on the ballot and potentially failing due to voter confusion. The unified measure passed overwhelmingly and marked one of Portland DSA’s first real electoral wins. Both of the chapter’s future 2024 city council candidates, Mitch Green and Tiffany Koyama Lane, were involved in the effort.
“It was an interesting test of our organizing ability,” said Green. “We were able to pass that, and that built the foundations for our city council races.”
The chapter also saw large success during the 2021 Nabisco strike and the 2023 Portland teachers’ strike, when its members organized fundraisers, held rallies supporting strikers, and walked picket lines. Both periods brought in new members and reactivated existing ones. The work also surprisingly helped convince the chapter to take another look at running candidates, according to Coburn.
“Having some elected officials weigh in on the side of the strikers proved to be more impactful to the strikers than many of us thought it would be and also ended up sometimes being more impactful on negotiations than many of us thought it would be,” he said.
Entering City Council
By the time candidates began announcing their campaigns in 2024 under the new system, Portland DSA was well positioned to run. It had proven it could manage a strong ground game, had built a name for itself among the city’s progressive ecosystem, and, importantly, felt that it could recruit strong candidates.
Still, worried about potentially overextending itself, the chapter only endorsed two candidates, Green and Koyama Lane. However, when the dust settled, not only had both won, but so had two more DSA-aligned candidates who hadn’t received the chapter’s endorsement.
“I think we were concerned about endorsing other folks who were progressive but were not close with DSA,” said Carolyn Roderique, the current cochair of Portland DSA. “But the election showed that we had so much more of a lane than we expected.”
Within a single cycle, DSA had gone from no representation in city politics to holding a third of the council. Two additional progressives were also elected, forming a larger progressive bloc nicknamed “Peacock.”
“It’s short for progressive caucus (P-Cauc),” explained Green. “And then, also, peacocks are an ostentatious bird.”
Following the election, Portland DSA created a Socialists in Office Committee in order to coordinate with councilors and facilitate an ongoing dialogue.
“There have been a ton of benefits [to having the SIOC],” said Koyama Lane, who was up for reelection this year. “Just having that time where we can share what’s upcoming, give a heads-up . . . and then also for them to bring back questions to us too.”
The SIOC has also helped the chapter’s candidates cement their status as a bloc, which has helped amplify their power within city council and during elections. In addition to Koyama Lane, Green, and Angelita Morillo — one of the DSA-aligned candidates who did not receive the chapter’s endorsement in 2024 — also faced reelection this year. All three won.
“[Being part of the SIOC] made it so like me, Angelita, and Mitch — people [could] just donate to all three of us at the same time through DSA,” said Koyama Lane.
Increasing Political Success
As members of the city’s legislative branch, DSA’s city councilors have focused on oversight and accountability.
“We’ve got councilors grilling the city administrator on why [they] didn’t disclose a bunch of housing money and why [they are] spending that on sweeps instead of rental assistance and that sort of thing,” said Green. “We’ve been fighting very publicly and racking up wins.”
Those victories — including banning AI price-fixing and fining the landlord behind the South Portland US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility — appear to be feeding Portland DSA’s popularity.
According to reporting by The Oregonian, recent polling has found that the DSA has a 61 percent approval rating among Oregon Democrats, with 44 percent of Portland voters saying that the group’s endorsement would make them more likely to support a candidate.
For Portland DSA members, these numbers reinforce the validity of the lessons they say they’ve taken from their recent victories. These have included using elections as opportunities to build capacity, consistently reactivating members through regular engagement, and publicly identifying opponents.
“I think one of the things that has been exposed through all of the successes that the DSA has had is actually bringing out the bad guys,” said Colleen Carroll, a chapter member working on the campaign of Nathan Ong Norris, who ran this year as a Portland DSA–endorsed candidate for Multnomah County commissioner. “Naming the villains who are harming our communities and keeping us from having the things we want, I think, has been a huge part of the project.”

https://gothamist.com/news/1-dead-after-.title: 1 dead after early morning fire rips through Hamilton Heights apartment building, FDNY says
https://gothamist.com/news/1-dead-after-.author: Walter Wuthmann
https://gothamist.com/news/1-dead-after-.text:
One person died and at least five others were injured after a fire tore through a six-story Hamilton Heights apartment complex Monday morning.
An FDNY spokesperson said the fire started in a heavily cluttered 3rd-floor unit at the Riverside Drive building around 1:30 a.m.
First responders transported one person with life-threatening injuries to a nearby hospital, and two others were treated for minor injuries. FDNY officials said two firefighters were also injured in the blaze.
One person, who has not yet been identified, was pronounced dead on scene.
Firefighters got the flames under control Monday morning. Investigators are still determining exactly what caused the fire.
Eighty-seven people have died as a result of fires this year, according to FDNY data. That’s up from 45 by this time last year.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: New York’s Pension Funds Soared in the AI Boom — and Could Crash With the AI Bubble
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Greg David
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The city’s five pension funds — which cover city employees and currently provide benefits to some 160,000 retirees — climbed by about 23% in their last two fiscal years, as tech stocks and artificial intelligence-related investments skyrocketed. As a result, the city anticipated that its pension fund contributions could decline by about $8 billion over the next five years — while still meeting its obligations to retired city workers.
It’s a similar story for the state’s pension funds, which grew by about 17% over its last two fiscal years. They cover all state and municipal workers outside of New York City and currently make payments to more than 500,000 retirees.
But with the sharp drop in tech stocks last week and growing fears that the unprecedented surge in AI investments will not pay off, both the city and state now face the possibility of sharp declines in pension fund values. 
And that would require them to boost the amount they direct to pension funds each year to meet their commitments.
That, in turn, could crowd out other budget priorities — like expanded childcare or new investments in housing.
“AI is touching us everywhere in the pension funds,” City Comptroller Mark Levine told The City Reporter. “It is a massive component of the S&P 500 and Nasdaq. Our private equity investments are heavily in AI-related companies. We have gone big into private credit. And who is it being lent out to? AI.”
Markets plunged last week after the midterm elections, in part because winning Democratic candidates have pledged to slow the construction of data centers, without which the largest AI companies won’t be able to achieve the kind of growth they have promised investors.
The benchmark S&P 500 fell almost 3% for the week. The Nasdaq composite index declined 10% from its previous peak on Thursday, a drop called a correction, before slightly recovering on Friday to end the week down 6%. The Wall Street Journal reported that Anthropic, which is expected to launch its initial public offering before Thanksgiving, has been told by potential investors that it would have to reduce its expected valuation by at least 25%.
The city’s pension funds control $326 billion and the state’s funds are now at $310 billion, making them the third- and fourth-largest public pension funds in the country. The investment strategies for both are similar.
About a third of the assets are invested in U.S. stocks, with most of that in index funds that simply track key measures of the market.
International stocks — which have soared in the last year, primarily because of huge gains among South Korean companies providing chips for AI — bring the total equity investments up to 40%. Those gains are now endangered as well by an AI bubble bursting.
The index strategy, while regarded as the most prudent form of investing for individuals and pension funds, means the city has huge stakes in AI-centered companies, including chipmakers like Nvidia, Elon Musk’s SpaceX and older tech companies pushing aggressively into AI, like Meta (Facebook), Alphabet (Google) and Microsoft.
Bonds account for about a quarter of all funds, and AI companies have been issuing billions in corporate bonds this year. AI is also a growing part of stakes in real estate, private equity, pools of capital that are used to buy, fix up and sell companies, and private credit, a relatively new area in which firms lend money instead of a bank. So the city and state pensions funds’ investments outside of stocks also bring wide exposure to an AI bubble.
The city’s pension funds will not immediately buy shares in Anthropic if it goes public this month, the comptroller’s office says. But it will own Anthropic shares once the company is added to the Russell 3000 index, which tracks the 3,000 largest publicly held companies in the country and is expected to add Anthropic almost immediately. It will own more shares if, as expected, Anthropic is added to the S&P 500 about a year after its initial public offering.
“We don’t want to be overconcentrated in AI,” Levine said. He recently decided not to invest in a private-equity deal involving an AI company even though the proposal met the fund’s investment standards.
State Comptroller Tom DiNapoli, who decisively won his fourth term last week and is the sole trustee and makes all investment decisions for the state pension funds, was not available to comment last week.
Levine’s office is beginning a major reevaluation of the pension funds’ investments, something the office conducts every three to five years. Exposure to AI will be one of the top priorities, Levine notes, with the results expected within five months.
In the meantime, there is a role for AI in the city comptroller’s office.
“AI will help us by giving us new tools to assess risk,” he said.

https://gothamist.com/news/will-voters-b.title: Will voters' ‘blue tsunami’ mean a reset on healthcare for NY?
https://gothamist.com/news/will-voters-b.author: Caroline Lewis
https://gothamist.com/news/will-voters-b.text:
With Democrats poised to take control of the House and Senate in January, some New Yorkers have big expectations for a healthcare policy reset — even reversing the funding cuts to Medicaid and other safety net programs that President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans pushed through.
“Tuesday's election results were a lifeline to those in the healthcare community,” said Kenneth Raske, president of the Greater New York Hospital Association. “We will move from a position of despair to a position of hope for the future.”
Policy experts expect Democrats to advance new healthcare affordability legislation, and to try to at least partially undo healthcare spending cuts that would strip insurance from millions of people nationwide. But the experts also caution that the new Democratic majorities in Congress will still face roadblocks with Trump in office.
The stakes are high for healthcare consumers and providers in New York.
Cuts included in last year’s H.R. 1 domestic policy bill have already resulted in hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers losing coverage they held through the low-cost public insurance program known as the Essential Plan.
Many consumers are now staring down high costs for private plans on the Affordable Care Act marketplace, which increased after Republicans allowed enhanced federal insurance subsidies to expire last year.
Starting in January, many of the more than 6 million New Yorkers statewide who are insured through Medicaid will also face new requirements to maintain their health insurance. New York hospitals and clinics have raised concerns that more uninsured patients will result in revenue losses that could affect their services.
“It’s certainly possible for Democrats in both the House and the Senate to pass legislation that would roll back most or all the healthcare cuts in H.R. 1 and restore the enhanced premium tax credits,” said Matthew Fiedler, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a nonpartisan policy think tank.
But, he said, it would be far more challenging for that legislation to become law without a change of administration. “It requires a signature from President Trump and I think it's very likely that he would veto that type of legislation,” Fiedler said.
Despite last week’s "blue tsunami," Democrats still won’t have the supermajorities needed in both houses to override presidential vetoes — and Fiedler noted that some of the more moderate Republicans who might have been persuaded to vote with Democrats on healthcare legislation just got voted out of office.
Larry Levitt, the executive vice president for healthcare policy at the nonprofit KFF, echoed Fiedler’s sentiments. But he added that Trump can also be unpredictable and Democrats might be able to play some “3-D chess” to get healthcare concessions.
For instance, he said, Democrats in Congress could try to get a signature on legislation restoring more robust federal subsidies for ACA health plans by offering to include a measure Trump wants, such as an expansion of health savings accounts.
Or, he said, Democrats could try to use their power to hold up “ must-pass” legislation such as government funding bills to get what they want.
A brewing rift over Medicare for All
Policy experts and healthcare reform advocates said the Democrats’ gains not only set the stage for a potential reversal of healthcare cuts but also for Democrats to lay out a proactive vision for the future. That could include a renewed push for Medicare for All, a form of universal, federal health coverage.
“Everything’s on the table,” said Elisabeth Benjamin, vice president of health initiatives at the Community Service Society of New York, a nonprofit that advocates for access to affordable healthcare.
Though denounced by some critics as a far-left idea, Medicare for All is supported by a growing share of the electorate. Two-thirds of U.S. adults said they either strongly or somewhat favored having a national health plan in an October poll conducted by KFF. About 85% of Democrats polled supported such a plan, compared with about a third of Republicans.
But it’s also a point on which Democrats in Congress — including the New York delegation — are divided.
The current version of the Medicare for All legislation in Congress is sponsored by New York Democrats including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rep. Ritchie Torres.
But it has not been sponsored by Rep. Hakeem Jeffries or Sen. Chuck Schumer, who could be House speaker and Senate majority leader next year, respectively. The two New Yorkers are the current minority leaders in their chambers.
Schumer and Jeffries did not respond to requests for interviews on their healthcare priorities. But Jeffries told NBC in August he had reversed his previous stance in support of Medicare for All and now opposes it.
“I do support the notion we have to find a path forward to fix our broken health care system and make healthcare affordable for every single American,” Jeffries said.
Grace Mausser, cochair of the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, said she was optimistic about the the midterm elections creating new momentum for progressive initiatives, including Medicare for All, even if many of the Democrats elected are more moderate.
She said she was hopeful there could be incremental advancements with Trump still in office in preparation for the possibility of having a Democrat in the White House in 2029.
“ We would love to see Medicare For All go through committee markup,” Mausser said, keeping her expectations in check.
Democrats could also try to pass more incremental reforms such as lowering the age for Medicare eligibility from 65 to 55, Benjamin said.
Even if getting Trump’s signature on some of these proposals is unlikely, the next two years will be the time to lay the groundwork for future change, said Fiedler of the Brookings Institution.
He noted that a version of the Medicaid work requirements Republicans included in H.R. 1 were initially laid out in legislation that passed the House during the Biden administration.
“Just because something doesn't become law doesn't mean that important health policy work isn't happening over the next couple of years,” Fiedler said.

https://gothamist.com/news/digital-skill.title: Digital skills are an increasing requirement in NYC jobs beyond tech, report finds
https://gothamist.com/news/digital-skill.author: Walter Wuthmann
https://gothamist.com/news/digital-skill.text:
A new report finds that nearly half of all job postings in New York City now seek digital skills, including home health care, construction and retail jobs.
Forty-four percent of job postings in the city now seek applicants proficient with things like productivity software and AI, compared to 35% a decade ago, according to a study released earlier this month by the Center for an Urban Future, an independent think tank.
“ These are jobs that have long provided a foothold in the economy, and they're becoming harder to access,” said Eli Dvorkin, the center’s editorial and policy director. “The danger is that there is a new barrier to opportunity for New Yorkers who are already struggling, in many cases, to get ahead.”
Researchers analyzed hundreds of thousands of public job postings between 2015 and 2025. The report found that the share of job listings asking for digital skills increased in nearly every sector the study tracked.
For home health care services, where over half of workers have a high school diploma as their highest level of education, the report found nearly a quarter of job listings now ask applicants for digital proficiency.
“For years as a city, we've thought about the digital divide largely in terms of who has a computer or an internet connection,” Dvorkin said. “Those things still matter, but the new digital divide is about who has the skills to succeed in an increasingly digital economy.”
Data shows the top five in-demand digital skills were Microsoft Office, Data Analysis, Python coding language, Microsoft Outlook and familiarity with AI software.
The report also found roles that required electronic proficiency correlated with higher wages. Full-time job postings asking for at least one digital skill had a median salary of $110,000, compared to $87,900 for those that did not seek digital skills, according to the report.
The report authors argue the city needs to put more resources toward workforce development programs, educational institutions and libraries to better train potential applicants.
“ If Mayor Mamdani is to succeed in making New York more affordable, it's not going to be enough to only focus on lowering the cost of living. Policymakers are also going to need to help more New Yorkers qualify for better-paying jobs and building digital skills across our economy,” Dvorkin said.
A City Hall spokesperson said they’re bolstering their workforce development efforts through programs like CUNY Tech Futures, which teaches students AI and data skills.
“The City is committed to supporting its homegrown talent with hands-on fluency with the technologies they’ll be using on the job,” Matthew Beller, spokesperson for the NYC Office of Talent and Workforce Development, said.
The city's Economic Development Corporation did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
This story has been updated with comment from Matthew Beller, spokesperson for the NYC Office of Talent and Workforce Development.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/conservative.title: Reactionary Feminists Offer Bad Solutions to Real Problems
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/conservative.author: Kaja Kröger
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/conservative.text:
Reactionary Feminists Offer Bad Solutions to Real Problems
Reactionary feminist writers Mary Harrington and Louise Perry dress up arguments for marriage and sexual restraint in Marxist rhetoric. But they also point to the limits of liberal feminism — limits that the Left needs to grapple with.
To more and more people, the promises of sex-positive liberal feminism feel empty. The sexual ideas that have dominated feminism in the last two decades — including that sexual liberation always serves women’s interests, that consent is the only relevant sexual ethic, and that consuming porn and buying sex are benign practices like any other — are beginning to ring hollow.
In this context, an emergent theoretical strand with the pointed, self-chosen name “reactionary feminism” has drawn considerable attention. It calls into question the liberal assertion that every form of sexual morality is anti-feminist — a view the Left has absorbed in recent decades. Although they work to maintain an appearance of ideological ambivalence, reactionary feminists are aligned with the post-liberal right, and they are finding success in attracting to that project women who are disenchanted with feminism’s wholesale embrace of sexual openness for its own sake. Their prescriptions are often at odds with what many feminists would consider emancipatory, but they are identifying real flaws in liberal feminism, and the Left should take notice.
At the forefront of this new conservative feminism are British authors Mary Harrington and Louise Perry. Both have written popular books on how postwar sexual liberation in the West has failed women.
In her 2022 book The Case Against the Sexual Revolution, Perry argues that shifting cultural norms around casual sex have led to a hookup culture that frustrates many women — even if they endorse these norms politically. In Perry’s telling, this is no wonder: as rigid sexual morality has receded, a liberal feminist paradigm has taken its place, one that de-exceptionalizes sex and portrays it as inconsequential. With contraception and a sexual culture in which casual sex doesn’t require emotional commitments, why would we need to have special guardrails around sex? For straight women on the dating market, this often manifests as feeling simultaneously sexually pursued and emotionally neglected.
Many liberal women are responding to this dilemma with heteropessimism, or a bleak outlook on male-female pairings altogether. While reactionary feminism indulges its own form of gender fatalism (I return to this below), Perry is suggesting that these disappointed women look elsewhere: the problem is not heterosexuality but a culture of sexual casualness pursued erroneously in the name of progress.
By making implicit liberal assumptions about casual sex and social progress explicit, Perry taps into intuitions most people share: for instance, that the expectation of emotional commitment after having sex is not too much to ask, or that sex can be a site of exceptional vulnerability and risk. Her willingness to say these things aloud has earned her an audience eager to hear something more nuanced than slogans about sexual autonomy.
Frustration With Liberal Sexual Culture
In academic feminism, sex is often presented as a banal activity, like going on a walk together. What happens in the course of sex is equivalent to deciding to go down this path or climb up this hill — with both people able to say at any time that they would like to turn around and go back home.
This neutralized view of sex might appear emancipatory, promising as it does to overturn the sexual scripts and social stigmas that hold up the status quo. But unfortunately, it doesn’t align with actual experience. The vulnerability and boundary crossing involved in sex can have far-reaching consequences if someone takes advantage of them. For most people, the stakes of sex going well or poorly are thus much higher than those of going on a walk, even when people consider it casual.
The broad Left’s consensus on this view of sex poses a dilemma for many women. If I’m expecting emotional engagement from a man after a hookup, does that secretly make me “trad” and a conservative? If monogamy fosters moralism and possessiveness in sexuality, does that not make nonmonogamy far more feminist? The success of Perry’s book, which came out when #MeToo was still relatively fresh, and there was cultural space to consider the potential downsides of sexual liberalism, suggested that many women had been privately entertaining these questions for years. Perry shined a light on the gap between political endorsement of goals like sexual freedom and conflicted attitudes about what that actually looks like in real life.
There is no doubt that being “sexually liberated” — expressed, for instance, by engaging in nonmonogamy and kink or BDSM — has accrued social status and moral value among progressive feminists. Countless self-help books and articles about ethical nonmonogamy have come out in recent years. It seems simply cool to be chill enough to have an open relationship and not to really want someone to commit only to you. The alternative of wanting a committed romantic partner is, by contrast, conservative and uncool. Last year, writer Chanté Joseph went viral with a Vogue article that aptly captured this dynamic and asked, “Is having a boyfriend embarrassing now?” One of the women Joseph quotes says that having a boyfriend feels “Republican.” A hard blow for romantics.
At the same time, it has also become cool to enjoy more physically violent sex. We can see this most evidently in the mainstreaming of “kinky sex” in popular culture since Fifty Shades of Grey. Data backs this up. If you’re a woman under twenty-four, the chance that your partner choked you during your last sexual encounter is about one in three, according to a representative survey by Indiana University researcher Debby Herbenick. Among millennial women (age twenty-five to thirty-nine), the figure was only 11 percent, and for women above the age of forty, it was 3 percent. This is an immense shift in sexual behavior across a single generation.
In interviews with psychologist Nicola Gavey, young women who experienced such “rough sex” said they felt pressured by current sexual norms to make themselves want it in order not to seem boring or prudish. The reality of these parallel cultural developments is what makes Perry’s critique of liberal sexual culture more complicated than closed-minded conservative moralism.
Marxist Rhetoric
Reactionary feminists are not hesitant to offer women well-established conservative solutions for sexual liberalism’s discontents: refrain from casual sex, don’t get drunk with strange men around, get married. But they wrap these solutions in new leftist rhetoric.
For many liberal and leftist feminists, marriage is a historically sexist institution aimed at controlling women and property. For Mary Harrington, by contrast, marriage enables “radical solidarity between the sexes.” It acts “as the smallest possible unit of resistance to overwhelming economic, cultural and political pressure to be lone atoms in a market,” as she writes in her 2023 book Feminism Against Progress. Rather than striving to be a girlboss or buying yourself flowers, Harrington proposes an attractive vision of monogamous marriage as radical solidarity. Who wants to be a lone atom in the market?
In her book, Harrington argues that the belief in progress has led feminism astray: toward individual freedom, away from solidarity and care for others. For Harrington, this has to do with extending the concepts of freedom and trade from the economy to human relationships. But this “logic of individual profit” goes against our human nature as social animals. Harrington therefore wants to defend the relational interests of humans against “the market’s power to liquefy, to commodify and to alienate.”
The concepts of commodification and alienation are laden with the Marxist critique that capitalism is not the right way to organize work and production. From a Marxist perspective, commodification and alienation are wrong because they thwart what is most distinctive about being human: free conscious activity (you could call that human nature).
In the reactionary feminist view, things are not as clear. The cases of commodification they focus on are surrogacy, prostitution, and paying another woman to take care of one’s children.
Reactionary feminists are quick to use leftist rhetoric in their critiques, but they remain vague about why surrogacy and prostitution are wrong. Is it because no one should divert women’s bodies from their “proper” use — reproductive sex within heterosexual marriage? Or is it because of the exceptional nature of exploitation involved in renting a woman’s womb or circumventing the mutuality of sexual attraction with money? We can find indications for both lines of argument in Harrington and Perry.
Struggle of Interests
For Perry, it is no wonder that men and women have had very different experiences in this liberated sexual culture. She argues that men and women have fundamentally opposing interests in the “sexual marketplace,” as she calls it, a contention that revolves around divergent proclivities and vulnerabilities rooted in biological reality. Women may be choosier about mates, for example, because women are uniquely vulnerable to becoming pregnant and bearing children after a sexual encounter, whereas men’s reproductive imperatives may motivate them toward sexual novelty and variety. For Perry, drawing on a concept that the Marxist radical feminist Shulamith Firestone first introduced, women thus constitute a “sex class,” which is locked in conflict with an opposing class, even while heterosexual men and women are oriented toward each other.
If women and men simply have different interests by nature, then the possible political solutions seem reassuringly simple. One can become a revolutionary to overthrow nature (Firestone wanted to outsource pregnancy to artificial wombs) or become fatalistic about sexual relationships between men and women. While reactionary feminists tend to push back against heteropessimism, they are guilty of a version of it themselves. To them, women and men can never fully overcome their fundamental struggle of interests. We must all instead make peace with them and tame them through institutions like marriage, which they argue contains the excesses of an unchecked sexual marketplace.
The problem with proclaiming an eternal struggle of interests between women and men is that it obscures the forces of socialization on gender relations and sexual violence. It takes women’s submission and men’s aggression to be natural facts.
For Perry in particular, each notable difference in men and women’s behavior ultimately comes down to how women and men are simply wired differently and always have been. Although she is a critical thinker in other regards, Perry is captivated by evolutionary psychology and very keen to incorporate every “just-so” story that emanates from the field. Feminists have often disputed and criticized this science for naturalizing what is inherently social: gender roles.
In the status quo, then, Perry might be right that women and men have different interests in the “sexual marketplace.” But when we take gender roles into account — and resist being satisfied by speculative stories that neatly explain how each gender stereotype has a deep root in our prehistory — we can begin to see that it needn’t be this way forever.
Conservative Materialism
With their Marxist rhetoric, reactionary feminists pick up, in a new and more explicit way, a well-established materialist thread in conservative argument: washing machines did more for the advancement of women than equal rights ever could. Conservative crusader Phyllis Schlafly declared as much in the 1970s. If we step back from the obvious political function of Schlafly’s assertion — cementing the view that homemaking is women’s true nature — we can see a materialist argument. Schlafly claims that what changed women’s lives and work most profoundly was not equal rights but electricity, mass food production, and household appliances.
Harrington argues in a similar albeit more sophisticated vein that “the story of feminism is one of economic transitions — and particularly of the Industrial Revolution.” What enabled feminism’s fight for women’s equal rights was that women went from being producers in the agrarian household to wage workers and consumers.
Harrington holds that as capitalism made work “more centralised, more mechanised and less agrarian, the resulting split between ‘work’ and ‘home’ drove women increasingly into a domestic-only role.” In the reactionary feminist view, then, the core of feminist politics is less a question of moral progress than of material conditions.
This sounds eerily similar to a Marxist feminist perspective. And it also seems at odds with propagating women’s and men’s eternal struggle of interests. But Harrington and Perry see the biologistic opposition of interests as part of the material conditions of women’s lives. In doing so, they muddle the concerns of those radical feminists who are hyperfocused on women’s biology, with those of Marxist feminists, who look at economic and structural reasons for women’s situation.
Reactionary feminists use ideological ambivalence as a strategy in their political project. As Harrington told The Atlantic about her book: “There are a great many conservatives who haven’t noticed quite how much Marxism I’ve smuggled in.” But she is also candid about the mission of reactionary feminists to build conservative and, if need be, “illiberal” institutions.
Why the Left Should Care
Reactionary feminists aim to convince us that, given the persistence of sexual violence and disrespect of women in liberal sexual culture, monogamous marriage is our best choice. They assert gendered behavior and preferences to be natural facts that we can only passively defer to — women and men will allegedly always have antagonistic interests due to their supposedly ingrained and static biological imperatives. Although they use Marxist rhetoric, their concept of women’s interests lacks a clear class analysis. While they acknowledge that not all women have the same interests, they never address class antagonism in capitalism but rather talk solely of the cultural expressions of “liberalism” and “market society.”
That said, the Left needs to take seriously the offer reactionary feminists make to women dissatisfied with liberal feminism: a clear-cut judgment that what flies under the banner of sexual freedom is not always good for women. The rapidly rising number of women who are choked during sex, often enough against their will, is just one telling example of a sexual culture in which women still experience a lot of harm. This harm persists even though rigid sexual moralism has considerably lessened or fallen away.
Adherents of sex-positive feminism have little to say about this — for fear of moralism — and understandably so. But that fear has created a void in which it is difficult to talk about what sex should and should not look like. A substantive feminist vision of sexuality and of what the good life for a woman is could fill this void. Instead, conservative women have mostly filled it with their gender fatalism.
Many on the Left mistakenly think of all feminist cultural critiques as moralism that distracts from the real concern: economic interests. As the Russian revolutionary Alexandra Kollontai argued more than a century ago, even under socialism, people still need morality to guide gender relations and sexuality. Sexual violence does not disappear through economic reorganization.
Thus women also have a material interest in something that is difficult to grasp in purely economic terms: comradely men. But the feminist left rarely taps into this moral critique. There seems to be a larger focus on poses of political radicalism (like abolishing the family) that can be hard to relate to for the majority of people.
Reactionary feminists are right that it does women no favors when enjoying “rough sex” becomes a marker of being liberated. They are right that the sexual revolution’s promise of freedom has left many women feeling unsatisfied and vulnerable. But they are wrong in proclaiming women’s perpetual vulnerability for biological reasons.
What they ignore is that women’s vulnerability is socially made and culturally scaffolded, and that there can be a society in which biological sex does not make women vulnerable. However, such a world requires not only a widely shared vision of gender equality but also the willingness to proclaim some sex practices as bad for those involved. Even if it’s a hard pill to swallow for those for whom feminist politics means radicalizing liberalism, such a world will require some degree of sexual morality.

https://gothamist.com/news/man-denied-st.title: Man denied stabbing Brooklyn jogger but described being covered in blood, complaint says
https://gothamist.com/news/man-denied-st.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/man-denied-st.text:
The man accused of fatally stabbing a Brooklyn jogger last month told police he came to the bike path with a knife because “people were going to come to kill his family,” according to a criminal complaint.
Sayed Mohassib, a 27-year-old Department of Education employee with documented mental health issues, was arrested and charged with murder Saturday in connection with the killing of 28-year-old Katie Suarez.
Suarez was stabbed in the neck as she was running on the path on Shore Parkway near Bay 17th Street on Oct. 30, and died at a local hospital days later, officials have said.
The criminal complaint states Mohassib told investigators that he went along the bike path to the Verrazzano Bridge, then came back, sat on a bench, and “became covered in blood” on his jacket, pants and clothes. But he denied stabbing anyone and did not mention crossing paths with Suarez, the complaint states.
NYPD detectives previously said they believed it was a random attack.
The complaint also states that surveillance video captured him running away from the scene, returning to his apartment, and then emerging in his underwear about 15 minutes later to throw things into the garbage chute.
Despite denying stabbing anyone, Mohassib told police that he got rid of his bloody clothing and the knife, and tried to clean blood off his hands and off the walls of his apartment, the complaint states. Detectives who visited his apartment observed a reddish stain on the wall that later tested positive as blood, according to the complaint. Mohassib also identified himself in the surveillance video, the complaint states.
Besides the murder charge, Mohassib is also accused of tampering with physical evidence and criminal weapons possession, according to the documents. A Brooklyn judge ordered him held without bail as the case proceeds, and his attorney did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Local lawmakers on Saturday demanded a full investigation into Mohassib’s hiring by the city’s Department of Education. They said he’d previously been discharged by the U.S. Marine Corps for psychiatric issues and had a brief stint at the NYPD before being hired by the city schools in 2024. City payroll records show he was working as a "substitute school aide.”
Mohassib is due back in court on Tuesday.

https://gothamist.com/news/nj-gov-sherri.title: NJ Gov. Sherrill announces her new lieutenant governor pick
https://gothamist.com/news/nj-gov-sherri.author: Mike Hayes, Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/nj-gov-sherri.text:
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced Monday she has selected Shirley Emehelu, a former prosecutor currently serving as New Jersey’s acting secretary of state, as her new lieutenant governor.
The appointment marks a historical milestone and follows big electoral gains for Democrats in last week’s midterm elections. For the first time in New Jersey, the two highest executive offices in state government are now held by women. Democrats will also send a record number of women to Congress, including Rebecca Bennett, a first-time candidate who ousted a well-known New Jersey Republican in the House of Representatives.
The governor said Emehelu’s leadership of the state’s midterm election amid “attacks” by the Trump administration was a reason she selected her for the role.
“That was pretty impressive,” the governor said. “She worked around the clock.”
Sherrill said selecting a woman for the roll was not a priority for her.
“I did not go into the process thinking we had to have a certain gender in the role,” she said, adding that Emehelu, a Nigerian-American, is the first immigrant to hold the lieutenant governor position.
Emehelu said it was a “profound honor” to make history with Sherrill. She was sworn in as her family and Sherrill looked on.
Her appointment follows the September resignation of former Lieutenant Governor Dale Caldwell.
Sherrill had demanded Caldwell, her running mate in last year’s election, step down after an internal investigation determined he had sexually harassed female staff in his office and committed ethics violations.
Caldwell has challenged the investigation’s findings. He has not been charged with any crime.
The investigation into his behavior dovetailed with a voter registration scandal that rocked New Jersey ahead of this year’s mid-term elections.
State law requires that the Lieutenant Governor hold a cabinet office as well. Caldwell served as secretary of state, making him New Jersey’s top elections official.
Emehelu, who originally joined the Sherrill administration as the acting state comptroller, was tapped to become acting secretary of state on the day he resigned.
Caldwell, a Black pastor who had served as the president of Centenary University, boosted Sherrill’s standing with the Black community during her campaign. On the day he resigned, Sherrill commended Caldwell for his commitment to advancing policies aimed at improving the lives of Black New Jerseyans. Influential Black politicians and community leaders around the state publicly urged Sherrill to continue that commitment after Caldwell’s departure.
Democrats secured an 11-1 advantage in the state’s congressional delegation. The party flipped two Republican seats in New Jersey.
In North Jersey, Bennett defeated Rep. Tom Kean in the state’s 7th Congressional District. In South Jersey, Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock denied Rep. Jeff Van Drew a fifth term in congress. Sherrill and other prominent Democrats in the state hit the campaign trail for both candidates.
This story has been updated with comment from Gov. Mikie Sherrill and Lt. Gov. Shirley Emehelu.

https://hyperallergic.com/art-problems-s.title: Art Problems: Should I Get an MFA?
https://hyperallergic.com/art-problems-s.author: Paddy Johnson
https://hyperallergic.com/art-problems-s.text:
Art Problems: Should I Get an MFA?
Paddy Johnson breaks down the factors to consider when applying for your master’s, from loans and salaries to professional development.
I’m a 33-year-old painter living in New York City who makes a living as an art handler. I have about $30K in loans, plus credit card debt. I’m thinking about applying to Yale, Columbia, and Hunter to do my MFA. I want to have the option to teach, make better art, and expand my community. However, I could be spending more than $200K if I go to the Ivy League. Do I need an MFA? —Dazed and Degreeless
If aliens with basic math skills came down from space and were informed of this scenario, they’d say you were nuts for even considering getting an MFA. And yet, in this industry, we spend a lot of time waxing poetic about how important art is to the culture and how capitalism shouldn’t decide its value. So, of course we need art schools, whatever they cost.
But let me ask you this: Do you want to spend the rest of your life in crippling debt? If it’s a price you’re willing to pay, then sure — that MFA is a great idea. If not, maybe it’s time to let go of the hope that the education you get is going to pay off financially.

https://hyperallergic.com/free-lyric-tel.title: “Free Lyric” Tells the Story of a Young Black Female Rapper Cancelled for Her “Provocative” Lyrics
https://hyperallergic.com/free-lyric-tel.author: Field of Vision
https://hyperallergic.com/free-lyric-tel.text:
“Free Lyric” Tells the Story of a Young Black Female Rapper Cancelled for Her “Provocative” Lyrics
Watch the new documentary by BAFTA award-winning filmmaker Cherish ‘Chez’ Oteka on Field of Vision.
Free Lyric revisits one of rap culture’s first-ever viral moments: the public shaming of a 17-year-old Black female rapper. Created by BAFTA award-winning filmmaker Cherish ‘Chez’ Oteka, the documentary is now available to watch for free on Field of Vision.
In 2011, O.G. Niki released a freestyle detailing her experience of sleeping with six men on one occasion, a sexual confession that shocked the internet. With the rise of social media as the backdrop, Free Lyric follows the journey of Niki and her unique experience of being an early victim of modern-day cancel culture.
Told as an unfolding narrative during the digital era of the early 2010s, this 31-minute short documentary reconstructs the investigations of internet sleuths and online trolls who worked to expose the identity of the girl behind the controversy. Archival footage and social media clips recreate the overwhelming noise of going viral overnight, while dramatized scenes and present-day interviews deliberately challenge the audience’s certainty in what is and isn’t true.
Public understanding of consent and coercion has evolved since the freestyle initially went viral. As Niki prepares a musical comeback for the first time in 15 years, Free Lyric revisits the events that made her infamous with a different understanding of the sexual encounter that once defined her online.
Field of Vision is honored to collaborate on the film’s release with me too. International, who have created a viewer guide to assist audiences in processing the various themes explored in the film. me too. International is a convener, thought leader, and organizer in the global movement to end sexual and gender-based violence.
Watch now on fieldofvision.org.

https://hyperallergic.com/contemporary-b.title: Contemporary Beadworker Ken Williams Jr Awarded Rakow Commission by Corning Museum of Glass
https://hyperallergic.com/contemporary-b.author: Corning Museum of Glass
https://hyperallergic.com/contemporary-b.text:
Contemporary Beadworker Ken Williams Jr Awarded Rakow Commission by Corning Museum of Glass
Marking the prize’s 40th year, "I Am the Hungry Cat" is the first Rakow Commission awarded for beadwork.
The Corning Museum of Glass selected Northern Arapaho and Cattaraugus Seneca artist Ken Williams Jr as the recipient of the 2026 Rakow Commission. Williams began learning beadwork at an early age on the Cattaraugus Seneca Indian Territory and later refined his technique alongside master beadworkers from his mother’s Northern Arapaho family.
Widely celebrated for his pictorial beadwork, Williams used the Commission as an opportunity to move beyond functional and wearable forms, creating a standalone wall panel. Utilizing 68 different colors from a range of historic to contemporary made beads, the framed composition features a graphic depiction of the artist’s cat, Valentino, complete with thought bubbles depicting his favorite foods as part of his “Yum Series.” In centering imagery of his cat and favorite foods detailed in bold colors and expressive lines, Williams is actually presenting a self-portrait through the work.
“Beadwork is something I grew up with. It is both familiar and comforting, carrying generations of knowledge passed down through my heritage. To have this traditional art form recognized through the Rakow Commission is deeply meaningful. I’ve always used glass beads to tell stories, but experimenting with a new vehicle and format gave me the freedom to try something fresh and personal. Glass beads allow me to honor my ancestors while pushing my practice toward the future, and I’m thrilled to be able to bring that spirit to CMoG.”
— Ken Williams Jr
Now on view in the Museum’s Contemporary Art + Design Gallery, I Am the Hungry Cat, draws inspiration from Pop Art and a vibrant color palette and bridges ancestral artistic traditions with a playful contemporary sensibility, expanding the possibilities of glass as a medium for narrative art.
The Rakow Commission is one of the most prestigious annual awards for artists working in glass and supports the creation of a new work by encouraging artists to venture into technical or conceptual projects that they would have been unable to explore due to financial limitations. The annual program was endowed by the late Dr. and Mrs. Leonard S. Rakow, who were Fellows, benefactors, and dear friends of the Museum.
In its 40th year, the annual award was first presented in 1986, and recipients ranged from emerging to established artists including Te Rongo Kirkwood, Charisse Pearlina Weston, Leo Tecosky, Preston Singletary, Silvia Levenson, Klaus Moje, and Lino Tagliapietra.
Learn more at info.cmog.org/rakow-commission.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Marcha da Maconha vai às ruas de Porto Alegre neste domingo (15) contra racismo na política de drogas
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Marcelo Ferreira
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A Marcha da Maconha de Porto Alegre volta às ruas neste domingo (15) com o tema “Pito do Pango: a lei é racista!”. A concentração começa às 14h, nos Arcos da Redenção, no parque Farroupilha. A mobilização propõe discutir as origens racistas da proibição da planta no Brasil e denunciar os impactos da política de drogas sobre a população negra, pobre e periférica.
Além da legalização, o coletivo organizador reivindica desencarceramento, reparação histórica e social e políticas orientadas pelos direitos humanos e pelo cuidado. A programação da concentração terá atividades culturais, incluindo oficina de serigrafia e capoeira, e a manifestação contará com uma equipe de redução de danos durante a concentração e o percurso.
O tema recupera uma expressão utilizada historicamente para designar a maconha e remete a uma norma aprovada pela Câmara Municipal do Rio de Janeiro em 4 de outubro de 1830. Em plena escravidão, a medida proibia a venda e o uso do “pito do pango”, estabelecendo multa para vendedores e prisão para quem consumisse a substância. Para a organização, revisitar esse episódio ajuda a compreender as raízes racistas da criminalização da maconha.
Para o coletivo, a proibição da maconha naquele período não pode ser dissociada do racismo e da perseguição às manifestações culturais de origem africana. Ao longo da história brasileira, práticas como a capoeira, o samba e outras expressões culturais negras também foram alvo de repressão, estigmatização e criminalização.
“A guerra às drogas tem raça, classe e território. Seus efeitos recaem desproporcionalmente sobre a população negra, pobre e periférica, historicamente submetida à violência policial, ao encarceramento em massa e à violação de direitos fundamentais”, afirma Raquel Meyer, integrante do coletivo da Marcha da Maconha de Porto Alegre.
Para o movimento, o racismo está relacionado às próprias origens da criminalização da maconha no Brasil. Quase dois séculos depois da proibição do “pito do pango”, a organização aponta a permanência de estruturas que utilizam a política de drogas para legitimar desigualdades e violações de direitos.
Legalização com reparação e participação popular
Entre as reivindicações estão o direito ao autocultivo, ao cultivo associativo e comunitário e a participação de pequenos produtores e da agricultura familiar em uma futura regulamentação. O coletivo também defende a valorização dos saberes tradicionais e modelos sustentáveis de produção e distribuição, contrapondo-se à concentração do setor em grandes empresas.
“Não basta transformar a maconha em um produto legalizado enquanto as populações historicamente perseguidas pela proibição permanecem excluídas dos direitos, das oportunidades e dos benefícios de uma eventual regulamentação”, afirma Andressa Fenix33, também integrante do coletivo.
A organização considera insuficientes mudanças legais que não enfrentem os mecanismos de criminalização e repressão. Em junho de 2024, o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) afastou as consequências penais do porte de maconha para consumo pessoal. A decisão, porém, não legalizou a substância nem o comércio. O tribunal estabeleceu a presunção de uso pessoal para até 40 gramas ou seis plantas fêmeas, admitindo que outros elementos do caso possam afastar esse enquadramento.
O debate sobre os limites dessa mudança já estava presente na Marcha da Maconha de Porto Alegre em 2024. Naquele ano, o manifesto da marcha cobrava agilidade na revisão de prisões relacionadas à maconha, acompanhada de responsabilidade e reparação por parte do Estado.
Cultura e cuidado durante a mobilização
A carta de princípios do coletivo articula a luta antiproibicionista às pautas antirracista, antimanicomial, feminista e socioambiental. O documento defende políticas de drogas construídas com participação popular e protagonismo das pessoas e comunidades diretamente atingidas pela repressão.
Na área do cuidado, a organização reivindica o fortalecimento do Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS) e do Sistema Único de Assistência Social (Suas). A proposta é ampliar o acesso à saúde e à proteção social, respeitando a autonomia das pessoas que usam drogas e considerando condições de vida como moradia, alimentação, trabalho e educação.
A manifestação deste domingo, segundo a organização, vai contar com uma equipe de pessoas capacitadas para desenvolver ações de acolhimento, orientação e cuidado. Está prevista a distribuição gratuita de água e insumos de redução de danos, além de apoio em situações de mal-estar, violência e assédio.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Violência política no 2º turno dispara em relação a 2022 com 93% dos casos provocados pela extrema direita
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Luis Indriunas
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Um caso de violência política relacionado às eleições aconteceu a cada duas horas entre os dias 5 e 31 de outubro de 2026, período do segundo turno, de acordo com a quarta edição da pesquisa Violência Política e Eleitoral no Brasil, divulgada nesta quarta-feira (11). Foram 379 episódios ao longo de 27 dias, em 198 municípios, 27 unidades da Federação e no exterior. A extrema direita foi protagonista de 93% desses casos.
No segundo turno de 2022, que teve dois dias a mais, a média foi de um caso a cada 12 horas, índice seis vezes menor. Em 2026, dezoito pessoas morreram por ódio político. Outras dezoito tiveram suas vidas ameaçadas.
Em Campo Novo do Parecis (MT), um homem parou em frente a um bar, perguntou quem era petista e abriu fogo. O investigador da Polícia Civil Emilson Ormond Souza, de 56 anos, morreu. Em Mangueirinha (PR), um motorista embriagado furou um bloqueio policial e atropelou quatro pessoas que comemoravam a vitória de Lula. O militante Eliseu Pedrozo dos Santos morreu no dia seguinte.
A chamada violência difusa — na qual o alvo não é o candidato, mas o eleitor — teve 242 registros, dos quais 225, ou 93%, foram protagonizados pela extrema direita.
O ano de 2026 também foi marcado por uma onda de retaliações após eleições, com demissões, ameaças e listas de boicote contra eleitores do presidente reeleito Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
“O recrudescimento da violência política em 2026 exige respostas firmes das instituições brasileiras, enfrentando a impunidade e garantindo a integridade do processo democrático. As divergências ideológicas ou partidárias não buscam mais somente calar representantes políticos e candidaturas, atingem em grande proporção cidadãos comuns no exercício da cidadania!”, destaca a coordenadora de Incidência Política da Terra de Direitos, Gisele Barbieri.
O segundo turno também foi mais violento em comparação ao primeiro turno. Entre 16 de agosto e 4 de outubro, a pesquisa registrou 134 episódios contra pessoas candidatas ou eleitas, com média de um caso a cada nove horas.
A eleição não acabou
Segundo o levantamento, a violência chegou ao auge entre o anúncio da vitória de Lula, no início da noite de 25 de outubro, e a madrugada do dia seguinte, com 54 episódios em 43 municípios de 16 estados. A maioria contra pessoas que comemoravam a reeleição. Em 13 ocorrências, os autores identificados eram agentes do Estado, entre policiais militares, guardas municipais e um policial penal.
“É uma violência que não se encerra com o resultado das eleições e escala de discussões políticas para ataques graves, como espancamentos e assassinatos em espaços públicos, locais de trabalho ou eventos de campanha. A democracia exige segurança tanto para quem disputa o voto quanto para quem vai às urnas”, complementa Barbieri.
Na semana após a votação (26 e 31 de outubro), foram registrados 101 episódios, dos quais 78 envolveram demissões, ameaças de demissão, incitação ao boicote ou listas de pessoas identificadas como eleitoras de Lula.
No Paraná, a deputada estadual eleita mais votada, Jessica Ramos Moreno, conhecida como Jessicão (PL), publicou nas redes sociais uma convocação para que empregadores demitissem funcionários petistas. “Você tem uma empregada que é petista? DEMITA!”, escreveu. O Ministério Público do Trabalho abriu investigação e recomendou a retirada das publicações. O vereador de Curitiba Guilherme Klitter (Novo) foi outro político que incentivou demissões. 
Em Fortaleza, uma fábrica de jeans demitiu ao menos 22 trabalhadores na manhã seguinte à eleição, após ameaças relacionadas ao posicionamento político dos funcionários. A Justiça do Trabalho determinou a reintegração de todos em 48 horas.
“Quando votar ou manifestar uma preferência política pode custar o emprego ou colocar a própria vida em risco é a democracia que está em risco”, destaca a coordenadora da Justiça Global, Glaucia Marinho.
Os números oficiais também indicam a dimensão do problema. Até 29 de outubro, o Ministério Público do Trabalho havia recebido 3.754 denúncias de assédio eleitoral em 2026, superando as 3.373 registradas durante toda a eleição de 2022. Desse total, 1.459 denúncias chegaram nos três dias e meio seguintes à votação.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: O que os discursos de ódio nas faculdades de medicina revelam sobre o Brasil?
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Rede Nacional de Médicas e Médicos Populares
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Após o resultado das últimas eleições, que deram vitória ao presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), crimes de ódio foram disseminados em grupos de WhatsApp partindo de estudantes de medicina contra outros estudantes que se posicionaram favoráveis ao candidato da esquerda.
Os casos ocorreram em faculdades particulares do Paraná, com mais evidência, na Fundação Assis Gurgacz (FAG) e na Unicesumar. As mensagens envolviam conteúdos de apologia ao nazismo, trazendo imagens e referências ao regime fascista que defendia o racismo científico; falas de ódio aos alunos bolsistas (Prouni e FIES), a pessoas nordestinas e a pessoas pobres. Incitação, inclusive, à violência de gênero, ao estupro e à miséria, bem como ataques ao Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS).
O acontecimento é chocante, ainda mais vindo de futuros médicos, pessoas que se propõem à prática do cuidado.
Porém, infelizmente não é uma surpresa. Fatos como esse se repetem sistematicamente nas faculdades de medicina pelo Brasil e têm origem no cerne colonial, em que são reproduzidas as opressões estruturais da nossa sociedade. Muitas vezes, as expressões do ódio são trazidas em letras de músicas de trotes, competições ou festas, manifestações em redes sociais.
Também se manifestam em perseguições a coletivos e a indivíduos nos espaços da universidade, abuso moral exercido por professores, retaliações, incitando o ódio a alunos cotistas ou bolsistas, em sua maioria negros, indígenas e pobres, ligados ou não a movimentos sociais.
Podemos citar experiências vividas de uma década atrás, período que precedeu o golpe contra a ex-presidenta Dilma Rousseff, em 2016. Vivíamos um momento de contradições dentro do governo PT, mas era nítido o crescimento das políticas públicas, como as cotas nas universidades, Prouni e FIES, Mais Médicos, além de tantas outras políticas, bem como a ampliação da mobilização popular. Como resposta, o fascismo passou a ser alimentado de forma escalonada, numa tentativa da extrema direita de frear os avanços e mobilizações sociais em todo o país, alimentando a polarização.
Em diversas faculdades de medicina públicas e privadas, talvez com mais intensidade nas regiões Sul e Sudeste, estudantes presenciaram violências. Os principais alvos eram estudantes negros, seja oriundos da política de cotas ou estrangeiros vindos de países africanos, estudantes LGBTQIA+, estudantes feministas, estudantes posicionados à esquerda.
E as violências estavam presentes desde espaços de convivência (festas e competições de atlética, bateria) até dentro da própria universidade, como nas salas de aula, corredores, colegiados e hospitais.
As violências eram exercidas por professores e estudantes, com discursos de ódio e perseguições, sem estruturas de denúncia e apoio fortes suficientes para reforçar o posicionamento e o combate a essas violências. A apologia ao fascismo e ao nazismo também apareceu nessa época, como em um episódio em que um estudante escreveu na parede de um centro acadêmico que “Hitler era um cara legal”.
Em comunicado público, a Unicesumar relata haver investigação em sindicância interna e já ter aplicado advertências, suspensões e até expulsões para alunos envolvidos com a situação criminosa. Já pela FAG, por enquanto não há mais informações, além de a faculdade ter dito estar apurando os fatos.
O Centro Acadêmico Miguel Nicolelis, a Bateria Rinocerada, a International Federation of Medical Students’ Association of Brazil (IFMSA Brazil Unicesumar), o Humanizart, a Associação Atlética de Medicina Unicesumar e a Equipe de Cheerleading de Medicina Unicesumar lançaram uma nota de repúdio conjunta. O Conselho Regional de Medicina do Paraná (CRM-PR) também emitiu uma nota própria e prometeu acompanhar os casos. A Associação dos Estudantes de Medicina do Paraná (Aemed-PR) disse ter encaminhado o caso para investigação.
Esse tipo de comportamento deve ser punido e rechaçado com firmeza e jamais deve ser tolerado ou banalizado. Também é essencial dar apoio às vítimas com canais de denúncia efetivos, acolhimento e acompanhamento, promovendo a permanência estudantil. É importante que o CRM não se omita e realmente acompanhe a apuração e o andamento dos casos, visto que é conhecida a omissão do Conselho em inúmeras situações passadas envolvendo crimes de ódio.
Além disso, precisamos sempre lembrar a quem interessa a formação do médico. As diretrizes curriculares nacionais mais recentes do curso de Medicina têm promovido mudanças no perfil do profissional de que a sociedade brasileira necessita: o pensamento crítico e um cuidado que considere o papel das desigualdades sociais no adoecimento da população são indispensáveis para o exercício da medicina com excelência.
Durante a graduação, o aprendizado ocorre majoritariamente com usuários do SUS. Cerca de 76% da população brasileira depende exclusivamente do sistema e, nesse grupo, 67% são pessoas negras. O que evidencia também a necessidade de que cada vez mais estarmos propondo educação crítica e antirracista.
Prestar um cuidado de qualidade exige compreender o contexto das pessoas de quem se cuida e adotar uma postura empática em relação à população assistida. Por isso, quando futuros profissionais de saúde se colocam acima de outras pessoas exclusivamente em razão de sua condição socioeconômica, evidencia-se o quanto ainda estamos distantes do perfil profissional preconizado pelas diretrizes.
*Coletivo que reúne estudantes e profissionais comprometidos com a defesa do SUS, da saúde popular e alinhados com os movimentos sociais. Para conhecer mais a Rede, entre em contato pelo instagram: @medicospopulares.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: DF executou menos de 6% dos recursos da Aldir Blanc e fica de fora de novos repasses
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Ana Gonçalves
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O Distrito Federal é a única unidade da federação que não cumpriu o percentual mínimo de execução financeira exigido pelo Ministério da Cultura (MinC) para receber novos recursos da Política Nacional Aldir Blanc de Fomento à Cultura (Pnab). O resultado provocou preocupação entre artistas, produtores e representantes da sociedade civil.
Na avaliação divulgada em outubro, o governo distrital havia executado apenas 5,78% dos R$ 15,79 milhões considerados na aferição, enquanto o mínimo exigido era de 60%. Para quem depende de editais e políticas públicas de fomento, a baixa execução significa mais do que um problema administrativo: representa projetos parados, pagamentos pendentes e incerteza sobre a continuidade do trabalho.
A produtora cultural Ava Scher afirma que o resultado foi uma “surpresa dentro do esperado”. Segundo ela, as dificuldades de transformar recursos disponíveis em políticas públicas efetivas já eram percebidas pelo setor.
“Ver o DF como a única unidade da federação não habilitada causa um impacto emocional forte. Mas, para quem acompanha a gestão cultural local, a notícia confirmou um padrão: o DF sempre teve dificuldade de transformar recursos em políticas públicas efetivas, seja por gargalos burocráticos, seja por descontinuidade administrativa”, avalia.
Editais parados afetam trabalhadores
Ava aponta que a baixa execução tem consequências concretas para quem trabalha com cultura. Ela cita o Edital nº 06/2026 do Fundo de Apoio à Cultura (FAC), que previa R$ 36 milhões para diferentes linguagens artísticas e foi suspenso. A justificativa apresentada pelo GDF foi a falta de recursos para contratar pareceristas.
“O efeito mais imediato é a paralisia e a incerteza. Quando o ente não consegue executar, os editais não saem, os pagamentos atrasam e os projetos que já foram aprovados ficam suspensos. O produtor cultural planeja seu ano com base nesses recursos e, quando eles não chegam, não consegue pagar equipe, alugar espaço ou produzir”, afirma.
O impacto, explica, alcança profissionais que não aparecem necessariamente nos palcos, mas fazem parte da cadeia produtiva, como técnicos de som, iluminadores, produtores, designers e trabalhadores do transporte e da alimentação.
“Quando o recurso público não circula, o efeito dominó atinge toda a base da pirâmide, não apenas o artista no palco. E o mais grave: os trabalhadores da cultura não têm carteira assinada, não têm FGTS, não têm estabilidade. Um atraso de meses significa, para muitos, a diferença entre continuar produzindo e abandonar o setor”, diz.
Para a produtora, a dificuldade de execução também expõe um problema estrutural da administração pública: a falta de equipes técnicas para conduzir os processos. Ela defende a contratação de servidores e a regularidade no funcionamento dos mecanismos de financiamento.
“Sem gente qualificada para analisar projetos, fiscalizar contratos e executar editais, nenhum recurso anda. Não é falta de dinheiro; é falta de capacidade estatal para gastar o dinheiro”, afirma.
Fórum cobra diálogo e pagamento dos contemplados
Integrante do Fórum de Cultura do Distrito Federal, Neide Nobre também critica a condução da política cultural. Para ela, a promessa da Secretaria de alcançar o percentual mínimo de execução nas próximas semanas não elimina os prejuízos provocados pela demora.
“A Secretaria afirmar que pretende alcançar o percentual mínimo agora é uma tentativa de reparação de danos, mas esses danos já estão aí”, afirma.
Neide cobra maior participação da comunidade cultural nas decisões sobre a aplicação dos recursos. Segundo ela, foram realizadas consultas públicas nos dois ciclos da Pnab, mas ainda não houve devolutiva sobre as contribuições apresentadas.
“Quando a gestão escuta a população, quando atende às demandas da comunidade, porque é ela que sabe quais são suas necessidades, com certeza o gestor erra menos. Foi feita uma consulta pública, foi feita também no segundo ciclo, só que até hoje a gente não tem a devolutiva em relação à parte quantitativa e qualitativa das indicações para utilização do recurso”, relata.
A representante também questiona a continuidade da atuação da organização responsável pela operacionalização dos recursos da política no DF. De acordo com Neide, problemas já haviam sido identificados no primeiro ciclo, e o setor esperava a abertura de um novo chamamento para selecionar outra organização.
O Fórum acompanha a situação e articula medidas junto aos órgãos de fiscalização. Para Neide, a publicação de editais e a conclusão das avaliações não são suficientes se os recursos não chegam aos trabalhadores contemplados.
“Não basta lançar ou terminar a avaliação dos editais que foram lançados no segundo ciclo. É preciso fazer o recurso chegar até a conta das pessoas que buscaram acessar e foram aprovadas, habilitadas para esse recurso”, cobra.
Fomento é direito, afirma maestro
O maestro e pianista Reino Quintas considera que a baixa execução da Pnab agrava as dificuldades enfrentadas pelo setor cultural no Distrito Federal. Para ele, a política federal deveria representar uma oportunidade de fortalecer a produção artística local, especialmente diante dos problemas que também atingem os mecanismos distritais de financiamento.
“A baixa execução da Pnab é uma tragédia. A Pnab viria como um socorro, e agora também é penalizada. A gente tem uma produção cultural de altíssima qualidade, com as periferias crescendo, explodindo de fazer cultura, e o Estado jogando contra essa comunidade”, afirma.
Reino defende que o financiamento público seja tratado como parte da garantia do direito à cultura, e não como uma ação pontual de governo.
“O fomento é um direito constitucional, previsto nos artigos 215 e 216, e tem relação direta com a sensação de pertencimento, de cidadania. É fundamental”, argumenta.
Secretaria promete atingir 60% até dezembro
Em nota, a Secretaria de Cultura e Economia Criativa do Distrito Federal (Secec-DF) afirma que mantém quatro processos seletivos em andamento, que somam R$ 28,84 milhões. O maior deles é o Edital nº 15/2026, destinado a produções audiovisuais e culturais, com R$ 23,05 milhões. Segundo a pasta, o processo está na fase de recursos após a análise de mérito, e os pagamentos aos selecionados estão previstos para a primeira semana de dezembro.
Os demais processos são voltados a Pontos e Pontões de Cultura e somam R$ 5,79 milhões. A Secretaria afirma que a conclusão do edital de maior valor permitirá ao DF ultrapassar o percentual mínimo de 60% de execução nas modalidades estadual e municipal.
A pasta também argumenta que, devido às particularidades político-administrativas do Distrito Federal, os recursos recebidos nas duas modalidades são executados de forma integrada, por meio de editais unificados. Em ofício encaminhado ao Ministério da Cultura em 29 de outubro, a Secec solicitou a prorrogação do prazo de aferição ou tratamento excepcional para o DF.
No documento, a Secretaria informa que os recursos estaduais foram recebidos em 8 de outubro de 2025 e os municipais em 26 de dezembro do mesmo ano. A pasta sustenta que a diferença entre as datas e os procedimentos necessários à operacionalização da política reduziram o prazo disponível para a execução.
