https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/fr.title: Frida Kahlo’s Image Has Become a Global Brand. A Viral AI-Generated Ad Makes Things Worse.
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/fr.author: Alex Greenberger
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/fr.text:
In our Frida Kahlo–obsessed moment, it’s may be difficult for some to remember that the Mexican artist almost died before she could change art history. In 1925, when she was just 18 years old, she was riding a bus that collided with a trolley, an accident that severely injured her pelvis, abdomen, and uterus. During the painful recovery, she took up painting. “I am not sick,” she said. “I am broken. But, I am happy to be alive as long as I can paint.”
A little over a century after the accident, the fashion brand Les Énervés, which has its roots in Paris and Bali, released an ad campaign that seemed determined to posthumously break Kahlo all over again, this time using AI.
In the bizarre ad, which was first posted to Instagram in October and started going viral on X this month, a bubblegum-chewing Kahlo recklessly drives a bus through Paris. Her passengers include the Mona Lisa and Vincent van Gogh, his severed ear replaced with a steel prosthetic. It’s worth noting that the Kahlo depicted here downs multiple drinks before getting behind the wheel; the real artist struggled with alcohol and drug addiction.
“It’s Frida, bitch,” she says, just before the soundtrack switches from an Édith Piaf song to Britney Spears’s “Gimme More.”
According to a release by Les Énervés, the ad was directed by the brand’s founder, Wakim Krari, and was produced using what is described as “AI, and a lot of patience.” The brand’s website adds that AI has been used to recreate Kahlo’s bus, this time as a Renault TN, which might have been seen in Paris when Kahlo staged an exhibition there in 1939.
Les Énervés has attempted to frame the ad as some sort of statement of reclamation. “A hundred years later, she is the one driving,” Les Énervés notes. “Vincent and Mona Lisa are in the back. Nothing is going to hit her this time.”
Not everyone has the same interpretation. One X post with 46,000 likes says the ad is “disrespecting the dead.” I concur.
Worse, it’s far from the first generated AI-generated Kahlo project to disrespect her memory. Another AI-generated video, also making the rounds on TikTok and X, finds Kahlo recast as a Spice Girl, singing “Wannabe” alongside the Mona Lisa, Vermeer’s model from Girl with a Pearl Earring, and the woman from Jan van Eyck’s Arnolfini Wedding. There are also quite a few Kahlo chatbots online, including one that implores viewers with this prompt: “Ask me about my struggles with physical pain, my relationship with Diego Rivera, or my feminist beliefs.”
It’s one thing to feed the Mona Lisa into AI, and quite another to use AI to mess with Kahlo, who carefully fashioned her own self-image in ways that resisted the social norms expected to guide a 20th-century Mexican woman. In her painted self-portraits, she consciously sported a darkened unibrow and facial hair men’s clothing, flouting gender expectations. She was famous, too, for wearing Tehuana skirts, positioning Indigenous Zapotec culture as central to Mexican identity. (Her unibrow also figures in the Les Énervés ad, here because Kahlo draws it onto the Mona Lisa, who has little to no eyebrows. “The woman who has too much of it gives some to the woman who has none,” the brand informs viewers.)
The nuances of her fashion are increasingly sandblasted by brands ranging from Barbie dolls to tequila bottles. Mari Carmen Ramírez, the curator of a show called “Frida: The Making of an Icon” that is now on view at Tate Modern in London, has said that Kahlo’s image has become “subsumed” by artists and activists, seemingly both for the better and the worse.
To me, all this AI-generated Kahlo content is subsuming the artist by another means. The reason to be concerned about all this, though, is only partly to do with the commercialization of Kahlo—it’s more about AI and the ways it can be used to distort, and perhaps even disregard, art history.
It might seem cute, for example, to place Kahlo at the center stage of art history, in such a way that sidelines her husband, the artist Diego Rivera, who features in the Énervés ad as trying to keep up with Kahlo while she walks down a rain-slicked street.But their 25-year relationship was more complicated than that: Kahlo was both deeply in love with and frequently frustrated by Rivera, who betrayed her by having an affair with her younger sister. The gesture here is a simple-minded one, easily made given that Kahlo is alive to comment. (She died at 47 in 1954, when she was nowhere near as famous as she is today.)
One is tempted to invoke Britney Spears, just as Les Énervés has done, and say to this brand: Leave Frida alone. Perhaps Les Énervés will do just that, but the brand has seemingly already found its next target. “The next chapter is coming soon, with a new muse and new things hidden in the frame,” the brand promises on its website. It reads like a threat.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/10/l.title: Lower Manhattanites Call for Parking Placard Purge
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/10/l.author: Kevin Duggan
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/10/l.text:
New York City’s government-parking placard system needs to be torn down and rebuilt from first principles, starting in the illegal parking epicenter of Lower Manhattan, the Community Board 1 transportation committee charged last week.
“What exists today is not a rules-based permit program that is occasionally abused, but a culture of illegal parking in which a placard, vest, or badge on the dashboard signals that the law does not apply,” the committee wrote in a 10-page resolution [PDF] passed last Wednesday. “Such a system cannot be repaired — it must be replaced.”
Parking placards effectively give drivers carte blanche to dump their vehicles wherever they want — particularly in areas with a lot of municipal buildings, like the Financial District, which sits entirely within the area represented by Manhattan CB1.
“There are a lot of people with placards, and there are a lot of people who won’t enforce against placards as a courtesy,” said CB1 Transportation Co-Chair Betty Kay. “It ends up incredibly non-functional and pedestrians feel very unsafe.”
The CB1 committee endorsed a slate of prior efforts to rein in the seemingly immovable problem of placard parking. The full board will vote on the resolution on Nov. 24.
The list of measures backed by the resolution included state legislation authorizing automated camera parking enforcement and a City Council bill allowing citizen reporting of illegal parking. The city to should also follow the 11 recommendations laid out in a bombshell 2024 Department of Investigation report, the resolution said, such as eliminating NYPD’s so-called self-enforcement zones around precinct station houses, and replacing physical placards with a single digital system that ties each permit to a license plate.
Placard corruption complicates attempts by Mayor Mamdani to remake the streets to be the “envy of the world,” with bike lanes and bus lanes across the city routinely spoiled by unchecked illegal parking. 
“If we can’t take on that issue, we’re just not going to be able to do anything with our open space,” Jess Coleman, Kay’s co-chair, told Streetsblog. “The scale of the problem is just enormous.”
The civic push comes as Department of Transportation leaders have been looking into automating enforcement of parking in FiDi, after a complete abdication by the Police Department to rein in the illegal driving habits. 
The board members hope the new mayor will finally take on the placard class. 
“It just keeps getting worse and worse, and originally with the new mayor — who looked like he would make some new movement — there was some hope, but we haven’t seen any,” said Kay.
There are upwards of 100,000 official placards in circulation, issued by three agencies: NYPD, the Department of Transportation and the Department of Education. The permits technically only allow holders to park in No Parking areas, loading zones, metered spots without having to pay and zones signed for agency parking, according to city rules.
There is no publicly available database of who has these parking perks, and the NYPD recently rejected a Streetsblog request under Freedom Information Law to release its list of roughly 35,000 placards.
Streetsblog has documented how drivers with the permits have a disproportionately unsafe record on the road, including NYPD officers, city marshals and non-profits workers. 
“Leadership at the agencies and the elected officials are out of excuses and need to take action to finally clean this corruption off of our streets,” the anonymous yeomen behind the social media watchdog @placardabuse said in response to an emailed request for comment. “Deliberate failure and open fraud can no longer be an option in New York City.”
The placard abuse issue has flared up in FiDi repeatedly over the years. Illegal parking exacerbates the lack of space on the narrow and windy street grid that dates back to the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam.
Business leaders and politicos have urged Mamdani to make good on his campaign promise to reclaim space from cars in Manhattan’s oldest neighborhood. 
The mayor in the spring said he would tackle the city’s curb management with a dedicated office at DOT. The agency has since hired Laura MacNeil, who previously led a similar division at the U.S. Department of Transportation to head the New York City curb office, along with more than 30 employees and additional hiring “underway,” according to an agency rep. 
“Creating streets that are the envy of the world starts at the curb, because the curb lane is critical to a street’s success — if it isn’t working, the whole street isn’t working,” said DOT Commissioner Mike Flynn in a statement. “New York City’s curb regulations have not evolved quickly enough since 1950, when overnight street parking was legalized. The result is a curb that too often feels chaotic and unsafe, and our Office of Curb Management will lead the charge on modernizing how we use curb space.”
The agency did not respond to a separate request for comment about the CB1 placard resolution, and neither did City Hall, NYPD or DOE.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/10/s.title: ‘Sociopaths’ Illegally Blow Safety Redesign Outside Greenpoint School
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/10/s.author: Sam Brule
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/10/s.text:
A crossing guard and a stone are all that prevents drivers from blowing off the city's new traffic diverter in front of a school on Driggs Avenue. Photos: Sam Brule (main), Noel Hidalgo (inset)
The newly redesigned low-traffic intersection in front of a Greenpoint school is mostly successful — except for some “sociopaths,” that is.
That’s how one local activist referred to the drivers who still plow through the city Department of Transportation’s traffic diverter that, at least on paper and in plastic, prevents drivers from using Driggs Avenue as a neighborhood cut-through. The diverter is an increasingly common tool for reducing car traffic in residential communities, especially near schools like PS 110.
But neighbors are still noticing broken plastic most mornings, the result of some drivers who simply won’t play by the new rules.
“You can’t prevent someone who’s just that much of a sociopath,” said Carrie Hill, a school parent and advocate.
Despite the few drivers who cut through, Hill said the redesign, which was installed last month, was mostly successful.
“It’s slowing traffic down,” she’s aid. “I’m hoping that after a couple times of someone making this error and being like, ‘Oh, this isn’t a cut-through anymore,’ they will just use the suggested route.”
For now, though, some of Hill’s “sociopaths” have been driving over (and around) the flexible bollards to save time. Streetsblog checked out the scene on Monday and, as if on cue, a westbound Tesla driver drove onto the sidewalk to continue straight on Driggs, now an illegal move.
This reporter was so shocked by the driver’s high-speed move that he didn’t have time to get an in-focus photo of the offender. Not one minute later, a class of young children from P.S. 110 took that same path after an outing at the nearby McGolrick Park.
One local said the diverter makes the roadway a bit “more chaotic” for now, but thinks it’s just a matter of time before drivers become accustomed to the changes (just as they did on the 39th Avenue bike boulevard in Queens).
“Right now it looks like, at the very least, people have not gotten used to it,” said Liam McCormick of Little Dokebi.
The DOT says the diverter will reduce cut-through traffic in the neighborhood, which then makes streets safer.
“The traffic diverter at Driggs Avenue and Monitor Street puts the safety of students, pedestrians, and cyclists first by limiting cut through traffic while maintaining necessary local access,” a DOT spokesperson said.
But the agency offered no comment about the psychology of drivers who are abusing the new road design, but said it will add planters and granite blocks to further encourage drivers to obey the new traffic pattern.
The diverter and other improvements nearby were a long time coming. In 2021, beloved PS 110 teacher Matthew Jensen was killed by a hit-and-run driver on McGuinness Boulevard, just blocks from the school. Days after, then-Mayor Bill de Blasio promised extensive safety improvements, which were initially blocked by his successor, but reinstated by Mayor Mamdani.
In 2023, tragedy in the form of a driver struck and killed cyclist Teddy Orzechowski, 73, at Monitor and Driggs right outside the school.
Since 2024, there have been 36 reported crashes on just the eight blocks of Driggs Avenue between Meeker and McGuinness, according to city stats, injuring 11 people.
The killings emboldened activists and city officials to take on the entrenched car culture as well as the Adams administration, which took bribes from a local business owner to stall the safety improvements, according to law enforcement authorities.
“This neighborhood has been a victim of Robert Moses since the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway was put in,” said Noel Hidalgo, a resident of the neighborhood who has been tracking reckless drivers at the diverter. “These are neighborhood streets and they should be for neighborhood vehicles.
Hidalgo said the changes are largely working. “This weekend was one of the most peaceful in the neighborhood,” he said.
One thing everyone could agree on, was that the intersection was a good first step to a true low-traffic neighborhood. The other steps? The DOT closed slip lanes from high-speed Meeker Avenue onto Engert Avenue and from McGuinness Boulevard onto Newton Street.
Some drivers still complain that they need to find different routes, but none of the changes are permanent. Besides, drivers can access every location that they previously could access, just from another direction.
“People get way too wrapped up in like, ‘What if it’s going to be terrible?'” Hill said. “Try it. If it works, it works. If it doesn’t, it doesn’t. And we try something else.”
The only thing that’s permanent, after all, is road violence, but that, too, could change.
Sam Brule is a senior at The New School. He’s previously worked at the New School Free Press, the Sopris Sun in Colorado, and most recently amNY. When he’s not writing, he works as a bike messenger.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/11/c.title: Cycle of Rage: DOT Issues Placards But Claims It Can’t Revoke Them For Reckless Driving
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/11/c.author: Gersh Kuntzman
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/11/c.text:
Pretty please, don’t drive like a sociopath.
The Department of Transportation just told me that it will not revoke city-issued parking placards issued to 17 non-profit organizations whose employees who have repeatedly driven recklessly in cars bearing said placards.
In response to a bombshell report in these pages that revealed that 24 cars owned by the 17 non-profits had more than 16 speed-camera infractions in the last 12 months, DOT offered the ultimate bureaucratic shrug: There’s nothing we can do.
The same shrug applies to the hundreds if not thousands of cars with city-issued placards that are also being driven recklessly. 
The agency lofted that preposterous punt on the grounds that section 19-166.1 of the New York City administrative code states that a parking placard “shall be revoked” in three situations:
- A car has three or more violations of rules regarding misusing parking placards.
- An organization violates the rule against making fake placards.
- The car has unpaid parking or traffic violations of more than $350.
I’m not a lawyer, but it’s clear the section doesn’t say that those are the only situations where a placard can be revoked. It seems plain to me — again, not a lawyer — that placards that get issued by the city can simply not be issued if the city so chooses.
I’m not the only non-lawyer who believes this. One activist who studies super speeders says the agency has broader powers to rein in the drivers that it knows are the most dangerous.
Jehiah Czebotar — again, not a lawyer — pointed out section 4-08(3)(ii) of the same code restates the three situations above, but adds a section that broadens the DOT’s power to revoke permits:
- (v) Revocation of an agency-authorized permit. The Commissioner or their designee may, at their discretion, revoke or suspend agency-authorized permits … 
  - (A) … where the Commissioner finds that the continued use of an agency-authorized permit is a danger to public safety.
Czebotar — have I mentioned that he’s not a lawyer — is convinced that DOT Commissioner Mike Flynn could act right now to revoke the placards of organizations whose drivers have proven reckless.
“DOT’s own data shows drivers that excessively speed and run red lights present a pronounced safety risk,” he said, citing this DOT study. “Recognizing that risk, [Flynn] must exercise his discretion and immediately revoke all agency-issued placards … ensuring that city-issued placards are not supporting dangerous behavior on our streets.”
            
    
To dot a few I’d, I called an actual lawyer, who backed up the legal reading by non-lawyer Czebotar.
“The administrative code doesn’t expressly say that those three situations are the only situations where a placard can be revoked,” said Michael Linhorst of Cornell Law School (and, full disclosure, Streetsblog’s lawyer in multiple battles with DOT and the NYPD). “DOT seems to be interpreting it as an exclusive list — that they can’t revoke for any reason other than the three in the list. … The [section section 4-08(3)(ii)] would give DOT a good argument that the three situations on the list are only examples, and that they can revoke for other reasons, too.”
Nonetheless, a DOT spokesperson said the agency would need specific authorization in the city administrative code to revoke placard privileges based on traffic violations themselves.
“Drivers who don’t follow the law, especially those that have been granted the privilege of using a parking placard, are selfishly putting the lives of New Yorkers at risk,” said Will Livingston, a DOT spokesperson. “DOT currently uses all methods within our authority to discourage placard recipients from driving dangerously and to discipline placard recipients who violate the law.”
The amount of undigested victuals stuck in my craw was so voluminous that I called another veteran lawyer, who, indeed, piled on.
“I would agree with your analysis,” said lawyer Daniel Flanzig, whose clients include injured cyclists and pedestrians. “It does look like the department has the right to revoke permits. … The three listed grounds (repeat permit misuse, fraud, more than $350 in unpaid tickets) are examples, not a complete list. The code sets a minimum, not a limit.
“The DOT has more room than its statement suggests, and if it wants to remove any doubt, it can write a dangerous-driving ground into its own rule,” Flanzig added. “Saying it needs ‘additional authorization through the city administrative code’ understates the authority it already has. I would also think that as a matter of public policy, that we would not want to reward scofflaws.”
Let’s get off the DOT’s back for a second because the larger villain here is the state legislature. As Streetsblog readers well know, the state legislature bars the Department of Motor Vehicles from adding points to the licenses of drivers who acquire camera-issued speeding and red-light tickets (even though just three of the same tickets written by cops would cause a license to be suspended). As far as the state legislature is concerned, as long as the $50 tickets are paid, they more or less disappear (though starting next year, the city can require the drivers with 16 or more speed-camera tickets in 12 months to install speed-limiting devices in their cars).
Because automated enforcement tickets don’t count on a driver’s license, drivers are able to accrue scores of them, hundreds even, like Staten Island cop James Giovansanti, without any punishment at all beyond the $50.
Richard Robbins, a street safety advocate, who wrote the non-profit investigation for Streetsblog last month, said he was disappointed that DOT is hiding behind the administrative code to “protect” reckless drivers.
“It is crazy that state law protects extreme recidivist speeders by specifically preventing speed- and red-light camera violations from being used for insurance purposes, when DOT’s great analysis finds that drivers of these vehicles are far more likely to seriously injure or kill on our streets,” Robbins said.
For now, Robbins called on the non-profit organizations to crack down on their own reckless drivers — a request that reveals yet another flaw of the city placard program: When Streetsblog asked DOT if it would address the non-profit organizations’ recklessness, the agency merely said that the organizations have a responsibility — DOT’s word — to document and discipline their drivers who commit traffic violations.
How is that documented? Is it ever documented? Has any driver for a non-profit ever been disciplined for driving recklessly with a city placard? The DOT refused to answer those questions.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/11/w.title: Wednesday’s Headlines: The Phantom Menin Edition
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/11/w.author: Gersh Kuntzman
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/11/w.text:
We’re all still waiting for the Council to vote on the so-called “Delivery Protection Act,” which could dramatically alter Amazon’s business model here in the city. Streetsblog’s Sophia Lebowitz has covered the bill nine ways to Sunday, but the long and short of it is that proposal has the support of a majority of the Council and would likely pass if Council Speaker Julie Menin would let it come to a vote.
Not much happened yesterday except dueling social media posts by Mayor Mandani (on the pro side) and Council Member Vickie Paladino, who never met a street safety improvement she could love.
First, the mayor put out another of his glitzy videos, pointing out that the bill, Intro 518, would simply require Amazon to actually hire the workers wearing their branded vests, delivering their branded packages and driving around in their branded vehicles.
“Companies like amazon have built business models around denying workers their fundamental rights,” the mayor says on the video.
The mayor’s video prompted the Queens Republican to call supporters of the bill “lunatics” and claim that same-day deliveries is some kind of birthright for New York consumers, no matter how exploitive the business model that makes such deliveries possible.
“People need to see socialists actively breaking the things that work,” Paladino said of Amazon’s delivery model — which simply does not “work” for street safety, air quality, or congestion.
But to listen to the Council member, if her constituents can’t get their hemorrhoid cream delivered in six hours, the world is coming to an end.
Meanwhile, the National Urban League took a more measured tone in an amNY op-ed.
What will happen next? It’s all up to the Speaker, who is, as Streetsblog has reported many times, is still deliberating — a phantom Menin, if you will.
In other news:
- We haven’t written much on Streetsblog NYC about Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s revanchist crusade against bike lanes in Toronto, but Momentum Magazine brings you up to speed with a pitch-perfect petition by pro-bike forces to require the removal of car lanes on the streets in question.
- NY1 is already trashing a still-unfinished street safety improvement in Queens — and the reporter in question boasts of her suburban-eye view of things. 
- Xenophobia alert: Council Member Joann Ariola (R-Queens) would rather have no parking rather than metered parking on Shore Front Drive in the Rockaways. (The Wave)
- A hit-and-run driver injured a scooter rider in Williamsburg. (Williamsburg 365)
- Do you live or work in Tribeca? Fill in the local survey (hint: and demand more public space and fewer cars).
- Road rage on the Rock. (ABC7)
- Welcome to the Wednesday Night Skate. (NY Times)
- A pedestrian was badly injured by a driver at a notorious Chinatown intersection. Of course, if amNY had run the plates on the car, the paper would have found that its driver(s) have 15 speed-camera and three red-light tickets, which most news outlets would consider relevant information after a crash.
- The MTA’s EAGLE team will fly high again … after some retraining, the agency says. (amNY)
- Clarence Eckerson Jr. shares his joy at the reception of his feature-length documentary, “Close Encounters of the 34th Avenue Kind.” ()
- On a personal note, no one needs this Wikipedia “NYC journalism edit-a-thon” on Dec. 3 more then I do: no one has updated my Wikipedia page for years — and whoever is doing it is a relentless troll and possible anti-Semite. Help, please!

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: ‘Maga is dead, Maga is effeminate’: why has the manosphere rejected Trump?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Sam Wolfson
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Earlier this week, Donald Trump announced that the UFC president, Dana White, was to become his press secretary. The US president hoped the creator of Power Slap, a face-slapping league which one of the world’s leading neurologists called “a sport inconsistent with the intelligence of humans”, might be the right man to deliver his daily rebuttals to the media.
Trump later backtracked on the appointment, saying he was “only kidding”, yet it is easy to understand why he might be pining for White’s muscles, trash talk and thirst for athletic violence. White is representative of the way Trump transcended politics in 2024 to become a celebrated figure in the manosphere, the loosely defined cluster of male content creators who have a direct line to America’s bored and aggrieved young men. On the night of the 2024 election, White stood at the victory podium reading out “thank yous” to the formerly heterodox podcast bros who came out for Trump: “the Nelk Boys, Adin Ross, Theo Von, Bussin’ With The Boys, and last but not least, the mighty and powerful Joe Rogan”. Trump ended up winning 63% of young white men that night, unheard of for a Republican politician.
Two years later, it’s a different story. Republicans lost young white men badly in the 2026 midterms: only 43% voted for a Republican US House candidate. So what went wrong? Did the manosphere lose its ability to persuade young voters, or did its most influential figures simply lose faith in Trump?
Analysts may debate the precise contours of the manosphere, but its 2024 incarnation emerged from the alignment of three existing groups: the hard-right Maga media universe of Tucker Carlson, Shawn Ryan and Dan Bongino; the mainstream “brocast” comedy world dominated by figures like Rogan, Theo Von, the Nelk Boys, Tim Dillon and Andrew Schulz; and a darker, overtly misogynistic online underworld led by Andrew Tate, Sneako and Nick Fuentes. Together, these factions allied to stoke male grievance with gay jokes, casual racism and rape apologia. They also normalised or openly championed Maga politics with their platforms, even if some like Fuentes also criticised Trump for not being far-right enough.
After Trump was elected, the manosphere relished in its own soaring cultural influence. Tony Hinchcliffe, who said that Puerto Rico was a “floating island of garbage” during a 2024 Trump rally, landed a huge Netflix deal for his Kill Tony comedy show. Rogan and Von had the two most popular podcasts in the US (out of Rogan’s last 50 guests, 49 have been men). The Nelk Boys, who prior to their support of Trump were best known for YouTube videos like Farting in a Black barbershop prank!, scored an interview with the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, almost two years into his genocide in Gaza.
Fuentes didn’t vote for Trump, because he said Trump was “owned by the Jews”. Nevertheless he celebrated Trump’s win by tweeting “your body my choice”, a grotesque inversion of the pro-choice slogan that signaled an expectation of systemic subjugation of women. Since then, chapters of young Republican groups at US college campuses have been taken over by Fuentes-affiliated “Groypers” who preach a more virulent antisemitic, pro-misogyny, ethnonationalism than even Maga. And Fuentes’s channels have brought in progressively bigger donations, according to the Washington Post.
But as Trump’s popularity waned, especially as the public mood shifted on Israel’s war on Gaza, and after the US-Israel war in Iran began, so did the manosphere’s infatuation with him. Voices such as Carlson and Fuentes were openly critical of the president. Von said in April that Trump’s policies around Iran were “fucking baffling” and suggested he had been compromised by the “dark government” in Israel.
Mariel Barnes, assistant professor at the La Follette School of Public Affairs who researches manosphere spaces, says that some podcasters were opposed to the Iran War for one unexpected reason. “They immediately began talking about conscription, which has no basis in fact,” Barnes said. “The US is not going to implement the draft to fight a war with Iran, but the manosphere has always seen the draft as deeply inequitable because it doesn’t draft women. And they hate that.”
As the midterms approached and Trump’s unpopularity deepened, some podcasters stopped talking about him much at all: analysis by Media Matters for America of nine manosphere podcasts that hosted Trump or JD Vance in 2024, including Rogan’s and Von’s, found that mentions of Trump dropped off from an average of 35 per podcast episode at the start of 2026, to just five mentions in the weeks leading up to the midterms (and most of the mentions came from the Patrick Bet-David podcast, which is more hardcore Maga than shows like Rogan’s). On the comedy side of things, these voices abandoned politics and went back to talking about pop culture and sports.
But Seth Simons, who analyses comedy’s rightwing bent on his Substack, Humorism, says some things remain unchanged.
“It’s true that a lot of these guys have stopped talking about Trump, but they haven’t abandoned the politics that led them to Trump in the first place,” Simons said via email. “Just the other week Andrew Schulz praised Nayib Bukele, the Salvadorian dictator, for his mass incarceration policies. In his Patreon-only episode reacting to the midterms this week, Tim Dillon wished that Trump had pursued a “smart” immigration policy, basically skipping the ICE theatrics and simply deporting “the 10 million people that came in under Biden”.
What has changed is that “these guys have correctly detected that Trump isn’t cool any more”, Simons continued. “They’ll happily rally behind a GOP candidate free of Trump’s baggage.”
Trump is not their masculine candidate any more, either. Despite attempts to feminise Democrats in the midterms, calling them “low-T” (as in testosterone) or “trans”, it seems the manosphere no longer sees Trump as butch now that his candidates lost. The day after the midterms, Carlson told his listeners: “a lot of men who voted for Trump two years ago imagined that this was a masculine, vigorous leader. But then … here’s a guy who’s vain and venal and indecisive … he seems more like a bitchy old woman than an alpha male.” In the darker corners of the manosphere, the repulsion was even more evident. The far-right Christian podcast NXR, for example, announced: “Maga is dead, Maga is gay … Maga is effeminate, Maga is for losers.”
Trump, perhaps insecure, had tried to tap Dana White for press secretary, hoping for an injection of testosterone to boost his flagging popularity. When that didn’t work, Stephen Miller, newly appointed White House Chief of Staff, told aides that he was going to make getting young men back to Maga the focus of his tenure, according to Axios.
The more explicitly political manosphere podcasters such as Bet-David, Gerry Callahan and Steven Crowder are already thinking about their post-Trump careers. In the days after the midterms they praised one man who had managed electoral success while staying true to the anti-woke cause: Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis.
The manosphere lives on
Will anyone care about the manosphere by the 2028 election? Because not only have podcasters soured on Trump, there is also a suggestion that audiences are souring on them. Since 2024 Rogan’s favorable rating among young men dropped by 11 points, Carlson’s by 12 points and Tate’s by 30 points, according to research by the Sam project.
John Della Vope, the director of the youth-polling firm SocialSphere, told Puck the research suggested that because the brocasters had “endorsed and basically kind of carried water for Trump and said, ‘trust us’”, they were now tied to his agenda. But exit polling suggests young men are unhappy with Trump’s handling of the economy, healthcare and the war. And so, Vope posits, as they grew disillusioned with Trump they felt betrayed by the people who vouched for him, “and a year later each of those figures has a little bit less influence among younger people”.
Likewise, a July New York Times analysis of listenership to Maga media creators via YouTube, Rumble, X and podcasts found that all saw significant audience drop-off across platforms since 2024. (The Times’ Maga media cohort included manosphere voices like Fuentes and Crowder as well as more traditional rightwing hosts such as Megyn Kelly and Ben Shapiro.)
However, Barnes says it’s a misunderstanding to say the manosphere is losing influence, especially as the economy remains precarious for young people. “The manosphere existed before Trump got elected, it has existed independently of Donald Trump and while Maga were very successful in appealing to those kind of disaffected men, it will go on without Trump,” she said. “Manosphere participants want to know, ‘what’s going to make this better for men?’ and also ‘what is going to hurt women?’ Those are ideas that can ignite at any time.”
Perhaps the most telling analysis came from David Sacks, a venture capitalist and Trump’s former AI czar, on the All-In podcast. During his mea culpa on predicting the midterm election result completely wrong, Sacks said: “The Republicans are dependent on the podcast circuit, and we lost all the podcast bros … frankly we should have done a better job giving them all front row seats. I think our side has to pay a lot of attention to them because without them, we don’t have any media.” If he’s to be believed, Maga needs the manosphere a lot more than the manosphere needs Maga.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Pro-Palestine philanthropist faces US extradition hearing in Spain
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Pro-Palestine philanthropist faces US extradition hearing in Spain
James ‘Fergie’ Chambers denies wrongdoing, while his wife urges PM Pedro Sanchez to grant him political asylum.
Madrid, Spain – The wife of a pro-Palestine philanthropist who faces extradition to the United States has urged the Spanish prime minister to grant asylum, to save him from being sent to his own country.
James “Fergie” Chambers is the first US citizen to face extradition to their own country. He is accused of supporting Hamas, an allegation apparently linked to a money laundering charge and donations that he made to support Palestinians in Gaza.
“I am pleading with [Spanish Prime Minister Pedro] Sanchez to use his powers to ensure Fergie’s political asylum claim is expedited for urgent consideration by the panel of ministers. This is within his gift. If he chooses not to act, he risks enabling [US President Donald] Trump to establish a precedent in Spain and across Europe which criminalises solidarity with the Palestinian people,” Stella Schnabel told Al Jazeera.
Spain’s National Court will hear evidence from the US authorities on Thursday and a final decision will be made later.
Chambers, a left-wing activist with a reported $250m net worth, is also facing charges of riot and conspiracy to riot relating to a protest at an Israeli arms company in 2023 in the US, for which he could face up to 30 years of imprisonment.
The self-proclaimed anti-imperialist denies any wrongdoing.
Chambers was arrested in July in Ibiza as he and his partner, Schnabel, an actress, searched for a school for their son, after Interpol issued a Red Notice for his detention. Since his arrest, he has claimed asylum, alleging he is the victim of political persecution.
Chambers cannot be extradited until the asylum claim is resolved, and if it is successful, he cannot be extradited.
The US government’s case centres on Chambers’s alleged laundering of $7.5m, which he is said to have wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, allegedly using the cash to support Hamas.
Schnabel said in an earlier interview with Al Jazeera that the money was to support Club Africain, a Tunisian football club, to pay off its debts and overdue salaries, to reconstruct a training centre and build pitches for youth sides.
‘There is no evidence’
Lawyers for Chambers said mistranslations between the US criminal charge in English and the version presented to Spanish authorities in Spanish make the allegations seem more serious.
Under Spanish law, all extradition requests must be translated into Spanish.
The alleged mistranslations, which relate to protests in 2003 in the United States that targeted the US-based facilities of Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest weapons manufacturer, changed “direct action” to “direct violence”.
Lawyers also said there is no reference to violence in the original US criminal complaint, but the translated version submitted to Spanish authorities mentions “three fires” even though no fires are mentioned in the original text.
US authorities also changed the description of protesters’ “activation” of smoke canisters to “detonation”, which, defence lawyers say, is usually used to describe an explosive device, not the release of smoke canisters.
The most serious mistranslation, say defence lawyers, involved a conversation between third parties that in the original criminal complaint described Chambers as being part of a “global terrorism game”.
However, in the translated version submitted to Spanish authorities, this phrase is changed to “global terrorism activities”. Chambers has not been charged with any “terrorism” offences.
“It’s important to highlight that the US administration has not charged Fergie with material support for or financing terrorism or any terror-related offences, nor presented a shred of evidence that even a single cent has been used for violent or terrorist acts,” Aitor Martinez, one of the defence lawyers, told Al Jazeera.
“The reason not to charge him with those offences is clear: there is no evidence.”
If the court backs the US extradition request, defence lawyers for Chambers will appeal, dragging the case on longer.
However, the Spanish government’s Council of Ministers may have the last word on the case and could refuse to send him to the US if they believe the case is politically motivated.
The situation is complicated by the fact that Spain is holding an early election on November 29, which, according to the polls, the conservative People’s Party is likely to win, potentially requiring the support of the far-right Vox party.
Both right-wing parties may be more inclined to support extraditing Chambers than Spain’s Socialist prime minister Sanchez, an outspoken critic of Trump’s support for Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza.
Chambers, 46, is heir to the Cox family, owners of the Atlanta-based Cox Communications. As part of a deal in which his family cut ties with him at the time, he sold stock back to his family worth about $250m in 2003.
Since then, he has funded about 100 projects in 20 countries, Schnabel said.
The US Department of Justice declined to comment when contacted by Al Jazeera.
Two of the three charges in the US complaint – riot and conspiracy to riot – are related to allegations that he funded the legal fees of activists arrested in the 2003 protests against Elbit.
Chambers has commented publicly on Israel and Gaza.
In the wake of the 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be punished for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”
On the day of the court hearing, demonstrations will be held in support of Chambers outside Spanish embassies in London, Brussels. Amsterdam and Tunisia, where Chambers lived for some time.

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: Home sales in the US are at their lowest level since 2016
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
Home sales in the US are at their lowest level since 2016
Home sales dropped 5.5 percent in October, the lowest level since August 2010.
Sales of previously owned homes in the US have hit the lowest level since 2010 as mortgage rates hover above 7 percent.
The National Association of Realtors (NAR) said on Thursday that home sales dropped 5.5 percent in October to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million units. That was the lowest level since August 2010.
“Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023. As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010,” said NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun.
He said, “It is just a tough market for buyers and sellers.”
“Sales decreased by 8.8 percent year-over-year,” the NAR report found. “Month-over-month sales declined in the Midwest, South and West and held steady in the Northeast. Year-over-year sales declined in all four regions.”
The home sales used in the report are counted at the closing of a contract and are a look at previously occupied ones. October’s sales likely reflected contracts signed in August and September.
“Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” said the report.
First-time buyers accounted for just 29 percent of home purchases last month, down from 31 percent in September and 32 percent in October last year, NAR said. First-time buyers have historically made up closer to 40 percent of home sales.
The US housing market has been in a slump since 2022, when mortgage rates increased from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied US homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. Yun expects home sales this year will likely end up lower than in 2025.
The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was 7.33 percent in October, according to the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation, more commonly known as Freddie Mac, up from 6.86 percent in September and 6.25 percent one year ago.
The rate, however, averaged 7.18 percent last week, down from 7.24 percent in the previous week.
Rates on home loans are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans.
Until the past few weeks, mortgage rates had been on the rise since late February, when the US war with Iran began, pushing up the price of oil and driving inflation higher. The run-up in rates also reflected heightened bond market volatility, which led to rising yields on US Treasuries.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on venture capitalism: investor profits are no industrial strategy | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Britain keeps selling its most valuable companies. The Financial Times calculates that 300 went to foreign buyers, mostly American, over the past decade. What if innovation were scaled up to serve social needs here rather than US investors’ profits? That is the provocation issued by the thinktank Common Wealth in a paper titled We Aren’t the Champions, which takes aim at the UK’s venture capital (VC) industry.
The authors say that as long as the UK is subordinated to US cash, getting startups to a heavyweight size will be a sisyphean task. Britain’s tech pioneers are often sold before they become giants. DeepMind, founded in London in 2010, went to Google just four years later. Britain’s venture capitalists might argue that they are in it for themselves, not for building up British tech.
The conventional wisdom is that if startups are struggling to grow, the problem must be that they lack capital. That is why Rachel Reeves, as chancellor, wanted pension funds to invest in UK assets. But the paper says that this risks making things worse. Putting cash into startups risks inflating eventual sale prices without securing British ownership or control.
The London School of Economics’ Nils Peters and David Kampmann expose a circular logic. The UK lacks tech giants that can acquire successful startups, but selling those startups overseas helps perpetuate that problem. The authors say US and European incumbents won big from the exit of the 38 biggest UK VC-backed tech firms between 2010 and 2023, including businesses at the forefront of AI, fintech and biotechnology.
Selling British technology companies abroad can enrich investors while thwarting ambitions to build domestic champions. The social costs also matter. A system geared towards maximising capital gains favours businesses that promise lucrative exits. The paper argues that this has encouraged surveillance technologies, from wearables to AI chatbots, and exploitative gig platforms, concentrating wealth among a few rather than delivering social benefits.
Gordon Brown is right: Britain should retain ownership of its innovations. But there is a difference between financial returns and industrial development – and improving the former doesn’t necessarily deliver the latter. Although industrial policy has returned rhetorically in the west, this has not translated into meaningful policy. The Common Wealth paper suggests that is a mistake and argues for democratic control over innovation, with investment directed towards social purposes.
The paper’s preferred capitalism is one that is historically associated with the global south: curbing extractive intermediaries, limiting foreign capital and building domestic capacity. India’s publicly funded space programme and Ethiopia’s state-owned airline show how sustained public investment can support homegrown capabilities rather than hastily readying businesses for sale.
Most daringly, Brazil linked universal healthcare for 215 million people to industrial policy, using public purchasing, laboratories and technology transfer. The payoff came during the pandemic: by August 2021, almost three-quarters of Covid vaccine doses administered had been produced at home. Brazil shows that a state can finance, research and produce a universal healthcare system that creates employment and productive capacity. It is surely a powerful idea that providing for people could be a way of sustaining output. Making the fulfilment of social needs a motor of economic development would give Labour a purpose beyond managing scarcity.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: What to know about the Logan Circle shooting in Washington, DC
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
What to know about the Logan Circle shooting in Washington, DC
Trump has showcased the capital city as an example of his tough-on-crime approach.
Police say a gunman is dead after he allegedly shot five people, killing one, in a busy thoroughfare in the centre of Washington, DC, on Thursday morning.
Mass shootings are not uncommon in the United States, but this one drew a swift and massive response from local police as well as federal security forces. Law and order in the capital city has been at the centre of a national debate about the administration of US President Donald Trump.
What happened in the shooting?
About 8am local time (13:00 GMT), during a busy rush hour commute, a gunman entered a gym in Logan Circle, a trendy neighbourhood near foreign embassies and fashionable restaurants, about 1.6km (one mile) north of the White House.
“Within seconds, there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out,” said James Spellman, who witnessed the attack and said there were about 50 people in the gym. “One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck.”
Spellman said he and other gym members ran out of the gym and he heard more gunfire in the area of 15th Street. He said he heard about two shots fired in the gym and about five or six fired outside.
Law enforcement arrived within minutes, cordoning off the area and working to apprehend the suspect. They included personnel from the Metropolitan Police Department, the city’s law enforcement agency, as well as heavily armed officers from federal agencies including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Secret Service.
Authorities sent out alerts to people in the area warning them to shelter inside because of an “active shooter” situation. Schools near the scene were placed on lockdown. “Go inside the nearest building, stay away from windows, and remain indoors until further notice,” police instructed the public.
Washington, DC’s interim police chief, Jeffery Carroll, said the suspect was a white male wearing a grey shirt.
The suspect, police said, opened fire inside the gym, then exited the building and entered another adjacent building, where he barricaded himself inside a room on the seventh floor. Officers then began trying to negotiate with the suspect, with specialised negotiators talking to him over the phone, as snipers kept watch from nearby rooftops. At one point, he shot at police through the barricaded door.
About an hour after they began speaking to him, police say they heard gunfire over the phone, and they decided to breach the room where the suspect had been holed up. They found him with a self-inflicted gunshot wound, and he was pronounced dead at the scene.
What do we know about the suspect and the victims?
Washington, DC Council member Brooke Pinto said the suspect, identified as a physician named Matt Lambert, initially shot a person in the gym with whom he was involved in a court case over a dispute over the condominium where he lived.
Police Chief Carroll, speaking to reporters shortly after the suspect was found dead, said the shooting appeared to have stemmed from a “conflict between him and the homeowners association of the building”.
Some unconfirmed reports cited a social media account as possibly belonging to the suspect, which appeared to frequently feature posts about bad living conditions in a condominium in the area where the attack occurred.
Little has been released about the victims of the shooting. Authorities said one person had died, and another was in critical condition in the hospital.
What are the larger political implications of this mass shooting?
An assault in the same Logan Circle area back in August 2025 was cited by President Trump as a reason for deploying troops to the capital, launching a national push that saw controversial deployments to several Democratic-controlled cities.
A former Department of Government Efficiency official said he was assaulted in the early hours in the same area by a group of teenagers attempting to carjack him and a woman he was with. Trump declared a crime emergency and said his administration was taking control of the federal district’s local police force.
Although Washington, DC, has a mayor and city council, it is not treated on equal footing with other states in the country, and Congress as well as the president have some authority over things like its budget and law enforcement activities.
Trump deployed thousands of National Guard troops to the capital, who continue more than a year later to patrol the city in groups, including in the Logan Circle area.
The troops are a regular presence inside metro stations and locations across downtown, but local officials have pointed out they have largely stayed away from areas of the city that experience higher crime, and their impact has not been as large as President Trump has claimed.
The troops themselves have also drawn attacks.
In November last year, a National Guard member was killed by a gunman while on duty near 17th and I Streets NW. A second National Guard member was wounded. And in October, another National Guard member was shot during a gunfight in southeast Washington, DC.
The presence of the soldiers has at times caused friction with local officials, including Washington, DC Mayor Muriel Bowser.
Speaking at a news conference alongside the police chief after the shooting on Thursday, Bowser praised local police for their quick response to the incident and dismissed the suggestion that law enforcement had treated it with unusual importance.
“I praise [DC police] for bringing down crime in this city, and I praise our prosecutors,” Bowser said. “It’s not typical to have an active shooter that guns down people in the city, so all our law enforcement responded.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Police identify suspect and victim in Washington DC gym shooting that also injured four
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Anna Betts and Joseph Gedeon in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Four people were injured and one person died after a shooting in Northwest Washington DC on Thursday morning, local police said.
In a Thursday afternoon press conference, law enforcement identified the suspect as 55-year-old Matt Wade Lambert, who died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.
Law enforcement identified the victim as 46-year-old James Stuart, the building manager for the Vida Fitness gym in Lambert’s building, where he allegedly fired his handgun. After leaving the gym, Lambert continued firing from his apartment patio, law enforcement said.
Two men and two women were injured in the shooting and were transported to the hospital, law enforcement said. Among those who were transported, one is “determined to be in critical condition” and the others have non-life-threatening injuries.
Earlier Thursday, the police said that the shooter had a “conflict between him and the homeowners association of that building”. Court records show that Lambert had been involved in a civil dispute with the association since March 2025, alleging that his unit had mold, moisture issues and water damage after repairs to the building’s facade. The association denied allegations of negligence in court filings, and the litigation remained ongoing.
Joel Braithwaite, the attorney representing the suspected shooter in the matter, said in a news conference that he heard about the shooting after being contacted by CNN, and initially thought his client was the victim. He added that the last time he spoke to Lambert on Tuesday, he sounded fine and was looking forward to starting a new job this coming Monday.
He had never heard his client mention owning a gun, he said.
“I can’t tell you how surprised I am because the person I knew as a client is someone who is in the business of healing people,” Braithwaite told reporters.
He added that his client had spent at least $300,000 on litigation so far, and was likely going to spend more as proceedings continued. And while the exposure to mold, and the ongoing dispute with the homeowners association were stressful, they shouldn’t have led to violence.
“I don’t know how all of those things coalesce, but unfortunately this is a choice I hope my clients or anyone in litigation would never make,” Braithwaite continued. “Litigation is supposed to prevent these results by having people litigate in court and not have that spill out into the streets.”
Jeffery Carroll, the interim chief of police for the Metropolitan police department (MPD), told reporters earlier Thursday that the department received a report of a shooting just before 8am ET at the 1500 block of 15th Street inside of a gym. He said officers were dispatched to the area and were on the scene within 30 seconds.
“When officers got on the scene, they began canvassing, attempting to locate the suspect in this case,” Carroll said. “While they were on the scene, they were able to begin to clear the building where the shootings occurred.”
While clearing an apartment building on the block, Carroll noted that “gunshots rang out on the seventh floor”. The emergency response team “responded to the scene as well as additional resources from many federal partners”. Lambert was found to have three firearms, he said.
Lambert also broke a gas line in the apartment and started a fire, law enforcement said.
Carroll said emergency response team negotiators contacted Lambert and spoke with him for at least an hour before hearing another gunshot ring out. “As a response to that, officers forced entry into the apartment,” Carroll said, finding Lambert suffering from a gunshot wound.
Brooke Pinto, a DC council member, later confirmed that the suspect had “shot himself” and was “now dead”.
Muriel Bowser, the mayor of Washington DC, called the shooting a “senseless act of gun violence” at the news conference and confirmed that the White House had been briefed.
Janeese Lewis George, the city’s mayor-elect, called the shooting “horrifying” and offered her “sincere condolences to all the victims, their families, and DC residents living through this fear”.
VIDA Fitness DC confirmed in a statement on social media that its Logan Circle location was “temporarily closed” following the shooting and that it will remain closed until further notice.
In a joint statement emailed to the branch’s members, Vida Fitness’s owner David von Storch and its president, Aaron Moore, said they were “devastated by the tragic loss of life” and that while there is no active threat to the gym at this time, it’s unclear when gym members will be able to retrieve the items they left behind while evacuating.
“We know that today’s events have been frightening and deeply unsettling, particularly for those who were present … Our hearts are with everyone affected by this tragedy,” the pair wrote.
A witness to the shooting, 23-year-old Anthony Mirones, said he had gone to VIDA Fitness in the morning and was on the treadmill when he heard the first loud “bang” at about 8am and saw a man lying dead on the floor with blood nearby.
“Everyone’s confused. I’m confused,” Mirones said. “Did the painting fall?”
He went toward the noise and saw someone on the ground. A person standing closer to the body looked back and told him the man was dead.
“So I come a little closer and I see a body on floor, some blood,” Mirones said. “I’m thinking about the loud bangs. I’m like, ‘Gunshot.’”
Outside, at the entrance, police officers rushed in. “One police officer unholsters his gun, and then another police officer is asking for a description of the assailant,” Mirones said. “While [another witness] is describing the assailant, we hear five or so gunshots, and then we just all scatter and run.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Family Dollar to pay $63m to settle overcharging allegations
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Michael Hudson
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Discount store giant Family Dollar will pay $63m to settle claims by state and federal authorities that it frequently overcharged its customers for milk, diapers, batteries, toilet paper and other household goods.
The enforcement action announced Thursday by the Federal Trade Commission and 17 states followed a Guardian investigation that revealed Family Dollar and its larger rival, Dollar General, frequently charge more at checkout than the prices listed on their shelves. Family Dollar failed at least 2,100 price inspections in 20 states from 2022 to late 2025, the Guardian found.
In a lawsuit publicly released for the first time as part of Thursday’s settlement, the FTC and the states allege that “Family Dollar knows that it harms consumers by persistently charging prices at the register that are higher than those it advertises”.
Despite widespread consumer complaints and increasing government scrutiny, the suit says, the dollar-store chain has failed to put in place adequate safeguards to prevent continued overcharging.
“Even now,” the suit asserts, “Family Dollar continues to overcharge customers.”
The suit says that it was not until the fall of 2025 – after the company learned of the coming publication of the Guardian’s investigation – that “employees at Family Dollar’s corporate offices devoted more attention and resources to addressing state pricing inspections”.
Family Dollar, which says it offers “affordable products and trusted values to families across America”, has roughly 7,000 stores.
The company did not deny or admit to the state and federal authorities’ allegations. It previously told the Guardian that “we take customer trust seriously and are committed to ensuring pricing accuracy across our stores … We continue to be focused on providing a consistent and transparent shopping experience.”
The Guardian has sent questions to Family Dollar about the settlement and lawsuit.
The FTC made undercover visits to Family Dollar and Dollar General stores after the December 2025 publication of the Guardian’s story about the two chains. In January, the agency said, an FTC investigator was overcharged on 15 of the 50 items she purchased at a Family Dollar in Euclid, Ohio.
The agency also sifted through large numbers of customer complaints to the company itself as well as to the FTC, state regulators and consumer groups.
The lawsuits says that customers from at least seven states reported in January 2025 that Family Dollar refused to honor a “2 for $20” offer for diapers advertised on shelf tags, its weekly flyer and its mobile app. A consumer in Michigan, for example, said they took a photo of the discount price displayed on the shelf for diapers but that the manager “told me that the price was wrong and he would not sell to me at that price”.
A customer in South Dakota, meanwhile, complained they had been charged $25.50 for three packs of Dr Pepper that were listed as “3 for $12”. When they complained, the consumer said, an employee “freaked out on me” and screamed “in front of 20 people” – saying the higher price was correct and the customer was no longer welcome at the store.
Under the settlement, Family Dollar will be required to set up a $40m consumer redress fund, provide $20m in discounts to customers and pay more than $3m to state authorities. It also must create a program to ensure that it regularly monitors and verifies prices, trains employees to identify pricing problems and promptly corrects overcharges.
The settlement comes at a time of growing attention on overcharges at dollar store and convenience store chains. The Family Dollar lawsuit says the consequences of overcharges “fall most heavily on shoppers living on razor-thin margins – families who carefully budget every dollar and rely on accurate, transparent pricing simply to meet their day-to-day needs”.
In October, the FTC and 20 states sued Dollar General, the largest dollar-store chain, accusing it of a “staggering” level of “pricing misconduct”.
In response, Dollar General said it would “defend this litigation vigorously”. It added that, in the retail market, “occasional price discrepancies can occur. When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered and expected to make things right for the customer.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Donald Trump Jr exits as paid adviser for prediction market Kalshi
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Donald Trump Jr is no longer a paid adviser for Kalshi, the prediction market company said Thursday.
Kalshi described it as a mutual business decision between the two parties that followed a decision by Trump Jr’s investment firm, 1789 Capital, to increase its investment in Kalshi’s biggest competitor Polymarket.
But the announcement comes a week after Democrats were able to take control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections.
Democrats have said they planned to investigate the Trump family’s investments, including their business relationships with both prediction markets.
“We have mutually agreed to end Don’s advisory role after his firm’s significant investment in a competitor this past summer,” said Dani Lever, a spokesperson for Kalshi. “We are grateful for his contributions in helping us market Kalshi to more customers.”
The president’s eldest son became a paid “strategic adviser” for Kalshi shortly after President Trump was sworn into office for his second term in January 2025 and has been an investor in Polymarket since August 2025. Both companies have seen their popularity and use jump significantly in the past two years.
At the same time, both companies have received favorable treatment from the White House. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has backed the industry’s efforts to expand their products nationwide, including allowing their customers to trade sports-related contracts.
Both companies have adamantly denied that the financial relationship between Polymarket, Kalshi and the Trumps played any role in how the industry has been regulated under this administration.
1789 Capital increased its investment in Polymarket this past August, as part of Polymarket’s latest fundraising round. It was this investment that started the conversation about ending Trump Jr’s advisory role with Kalshi.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after alleged affairs
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Dan Milmo and Dara Kerr
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Jensen Huang has resigned as chief executive of Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two company employees.
He will be replaced on an interim basis by Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, until a full-time successor is named.
Shares in the chipmaker plunged by 13% when Wall Street opened, after Huang’s departure was announced. After a partial rebound, they closed down 4.3% on Thursday, wiping more than $180bn (£135bn) off Nvidia’s value on the day and around $490bn for the week – valuing the company at $4tn.
The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to Huang’s “profound” contributions to the company he co-founded.
“Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” the statement said.
It added that Huang had resigned as chief executive, president and Nvidia board member “effective immediately”.
Donald Trump, who had defended Huang at first as the scandal threatened to overwhelm the Nvidia co-founder, quickly moved on to potential successors on Thursday, posting on social media that he should be replaced by Tim Cook, Apple’s former chief executive and current executive chair.
“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump wrote, adding: “A Legend replaces a Legend!”
The chipmaker’s board earlier this week appointed the leading law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship with Alice Huang, an Nvidia customer and Chinese citizen who is no relation to the Nvidia boss. Nvidia had previously denied anything unusual about the relationship, but that changed on Sunday when Jensen Huang admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife, Lori, without referring to Alice Huang directly.
The law firm had directed Jensen Huang to continue to lead Nvidia as the investigation continued.
However, late on Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang had a separate extramarital affair with a company employee named Kimberly Powell. She was Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare and was reportedly captured on video being affectionate with Huang at a hotel during a company conference in March.
The report added to the pressure on Huang, as the board called a meeting late on Wednesday to discuss the chief executive’s future.
Powell has been approached for comment.
After Huang’s resignation was announced on Thursday, Reuters reported a third alleged affair. The newly uncovered liaison was another Nvidia employee, according to two people familiar with the matter who spoke to the news outlet. Reuters did not reveal her name.
Nvidia’s board said it would consider internal and external candidates for the chief executive’s role, with Cook featuring among potential runners and riders before Trump’s intervention. Cook stepped down as chief executive at Apple in September but still has a senior executive role at the company. Rene Haas, the chief executive of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker, has also been mooted, along with Lisa Su, the chief executive of the chipmaker AMD.
Huang ran Nvidia tightly and managed about 60 direct reports. Internal candidates include Kress and Ian Buck, who manages the company’s AI hardware and software products. Huang’s two children, Madison and Spencer, also work at Nvidia but are in their mid-30s and relatively inexperienced. The chipmaker also announced the appointment of Harvey Jones, a tech investor and entrepreneur, as its first-ever chair.
Dan Ives, a senior US tech analyst, said the board had done what “it needed to do, which is rip off the Band-Aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter without him” and that the company remained ahead of its competitors.
However, Neil Wilson, an analyst at the investment platform Saxo UK, said Nvidia would need a “great CEO” to replace Huang.
“His technical knowledge and understanding of every last bit of product is basically unique and impossible to replicate,” Wilson said, adding nonetheless that Nvidia was well placed in terms of upcoming products and orders.
Huang’s exit from the company he co-founded in 1993 removes a senior figure in Silicon Valley at a time when the AI arms race between the US and China is at an apex. He owns more than 870m shares, or about 3.6% of the company, and was worth $145bn on Thursday morning, according to Bloomberg, making him the world’s 13th richest person.
Unlike many of his contemporaries at other leading tech companies, Huang has dozens of direct reports, an unusual management structure that emphasises his control over the company.
The entire AI ecosphere relies on Nvidia, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. It is also one of the most valuable companies on Earth, with a market cap that hit $5tn at one point last year.
Huang has denied any knowledge that Alice Huang allegedly worked for the Chinese government. The pair were seen together around the world, dining in restaurants and attending meetings, over the past few years. Alice Huang is a businesswoman and head of the Singapore-based datacentre firm Megaspeed, who US intelligence services suspect of being a Chinese asset according to multiple reports.
On the same day that Jensen Huang admitted having an affair, Nvidia’s board of directors announced the company was launching an investigation regarding reports that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang has agreed to testify before US Congress.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Microsoft outage hits tens of thousands of users
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Microsoft outage hits tens of thousands of users
Microsoft says servers unexpectedly went offline, disrupting Outlook email, Teams, Copilot and other services.
Thousands of Microsoft users reported trouble accessing their email and connecting to work apps after a widespread outage hit Outlook and other services on Thursday.
Reports of problems with Outlook, the company’s email client, climbed to about 130,000 on the outage tracking site Downdetector shortly after 1pm Eastern Time (18:00 GMT), with some users saying emails weren’t being sent or received, while others couldn’t open their inboxes.
By just before 3pm (20:00 GMT), that figure had fallen to about 77,000.
Users also reported having trouble accessing Microsoft’s workplace messaging app Teams and its AI assistant Copilot, along with other Microsoft 365 services. The company said the issues could impact users in any region.
Microsoft said on X that servers were unavailable and failing automatic health checks, putting pressure on those still operating. It said it was testing a configuration change to redistribute traffic that was elevated on parts of its infrastructure and restarting affected services to bring them back online.
“We’re working to safely return them to service,” the company said.
Microsoft did not state when it expected services to be fully restored.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120383.title: Modell Kuba | Allein auf der Autobahn in Kuba
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120383.author: Andreas Knobloch
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120383.text:
- Kultur
- Modell Kuba
Allein auf der Autobahn in Kuba
Manchmal kommt es einem so vor, als sei das Leben auf der Karibikinsel wie ein Theaterstück. Es gibt eins von der Regierung und eins von der Bevölkerung.
Der Besuch eines Freundes aus Deutschland ist ein willkommener Anlass, mal ein paar Tage aus Havanna herauszukommen. Mache ich viel zu selten. Ein anderer Freund mit Auto, der immer für ein Abenteuer zu haben ist, lässt sich schnell überreden, sodass wir sogar relativ bequem reisen. Benzin gibt es in diesen Tagen wieder ohne größere Probleme – für 2,20 bis 2,50 US-Dollar pro Liter an der Tankstelle, aber immerhin. Auf der Straße wird der Liter Benzin zwischen 2.000 und 2.300 CUP gehandelt, was mehr oder weniger derselbe Preis ist.
Die Carretera Nacional, die Autobahn, ist kaum befahren. Bis auf ein gelegentliches Taxi oder einen Lkw hatten wir die Straße für uns. Kilometerlang geht es schnurgerade durch eine mit Marabú überwucherte Landschaft. Landwirtschaftlich bebaute Fläche ist kaum zu sehen. Auf halber Strecke ein privater Raststopp. Wir sind gefühlt die ersten Gäste heute – und werden entsprechend freudig begrüßt. Die Inhaberin erzählt, dass hier früher um die Mittagszeit im Schnitt drei, vier Reisebusse gleichzeitig gestanden hätten und das Geschäft mit kubanischem Essen und Mojito gebrummt habe. Früher, damit sind die guten alten Obama-Jahre gemeint, als viele noch mal nach Kuba kommen wollten, bevor die ersten Filialen von McDonald’s auf der Insel öffnen. Auf den ersten McDonald’s warten sie hier noch immer; Touristen aber kommen keine mehr.
Seit Jahrzehnten von den USA boykottiert, kämpft das sozialistische Kuba ums Überleben. Andreas Knobloch berichtet aus Havanna, wie sich das anfühlt. Alle Texte sind hier abrufbar.
Die Speisekarte ist reichhaltig. Es gibt Fisch, Languste, Huhn, Schwein, dazu Reis mit Bohnen und hinterher einen hausgemachten Flan und Kaffee. Nach und nach füllen sich die Tische um uns herum dann doch. Ein Auto breiter als das andere rollt auf den Parkplatz vor dem Lokal: SUVs, breite Reifen, aufgedockt. Die neue Mittelschicht Kubas trägt Sonnenbrille, Glitzer-Shirts und hat das neueste iPhone in der Hand.
Je näher wir Santa Clara kommen, desto akkurater sind die Hecken auf dem Mittelstreifen geschnitten. Erstaunlich, welche Dinge dann doch funktionieren. In der Casa in Santa Clara, in der wir absteigen, eine ähnliche Geschichte. Die Besitzer leben in Italien; der Verwalter erzählt, dass im Oktober ganze drei Gäste dagewesen seien; in diesem Monat sind wir die ersten. Der Strom wurde gerade abgestellt, eine Autobatterie in einer Plastikkiste in der Küche sorgt für Beleuchtung und warmes Wasser.
Zum zentralen Platz mit dem Hotel »Santa Clara Libre« sind es keine 300 Meter. Am späten Freitagnachmittag brummt hier das Leben. Bars und Cafés sind gut gefüllt, aus einem Lautsprecher scheppert Reggaeton, in der Mitte des Platzes fahren Kinder unter den Augen ihrer Eltern auf elektrischen Spielzeugautos und -mopeds im Kreis. Ein findiger Geschäftsmann hat dort einen ganzen Fuhrpark aufgebaut. Einen »nahezu vollständigen Zusammenbruch des Staates«, von dem das US-Magazin »The Atlantic« Ende Oktober schrieb, stellt man sich anders vor.
Was auffällt: Fast alle elektrischen Dreiräder haben ein Solarpanel auf dem Dach verschraubt, das direkt den Motor speist. Bei nur zwei bis drei Stunden Strom am Tag natürlich sinnvoll. In Havanna fahren die Dreiräder meist noch ohne Panel. Aber auch dort werden die Stromabschaltungen immer länger.
Ein paar Straßenecken weiter liegt das »El Mejunje«, Santa Claras berühmtes Kulturzentrum. Auch hier reges Treiben. Ein paar Leute spielen lautstark Domino, junge Leute kommen und gehen. Da es keinen Strom gibt, wird der Kaffee auf einer kleinen Feuerstelle in der Cafeteria zubereitet. Für den Abend ist eine Theatervorstellung angekündigt. In Kuba sei das Leben selbst ein einziges Theaterstück, sagt einer meiner Begleiter. Die Regierung führt jeden Tag etwas auf und die Bevölkerung selbst auch. Wir beschließen, uns das Stück am Abend anzuschauen. Der Titel ist vielversprechend: »Mejor Vida« – besseres Leben.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.
