https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: ‘My reward for waiting in the cold was this painting-like view of the ghat’: Priya Ojha’s best phone picture
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Grace Holliday
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
When Priya Ojha first arrived at Yamuna Ghat in New Delhi, late in December 2021, she was disappointed. She had left her home at 5am especially to capture shots of one of the most sacred rivers in India, but had arrived in dense fog and almost complete silence.
“Visibility was so low that all I could do was wait in the cold,” Ojha recalls. “Around 8am, I heard a voice call out, ‘Dhoop aa gayi’ – the sunrays have come out. They were right. This place that had looked like a graveyard slowly became more lively as local priests started their daily routines and boat riders took out their craft for business.”
Ojha recalls that a young boy appeared at her side and said, “Help me make my first ride and I will show you the ghat.” She agreed: “And that’s how I came across this scene.
“The two boats layered between the foreground and the background give a sense of depth, which makes the photo feel more lively,” she adds. “I liked that I captured not just this majestic place and the hundreds of swirling seagulls, but people just like me who had come to experience its beauty, too.”
When she reflects on the photograph now, Ojha is reminded of her patience that morning. “My reward was this painting-like picture of the ghat,” she says. “Just what I had set out for.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: The Strange, Empathetic Allure of Andy Beshear
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Grace Byron
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The Strange, Empathetic Allure of Andy Beshear
The potential Democratic hopeful for president is not a socialist. But he has a folksy demeanor and moral compass.
Ever since I moved to New York, I’ve become accustomed to watching people’s eyes glaze over when I tell them I went to Indiana University. Many of these East Coast dilettantes who went to Yale or NYU, even some of my friends, cannot point to Indiana on a map. I’ve learned that New Yorkers all have a very different idea of what constitutes the Midwest. My home state borders Kentucky to the south and has plenty of cultural similarities with the Commonwealth. Fried chicken, gravy, and corn are staples throughout Indiana, but especially when you drive south through the hills. I grew up in Mike Pence’s Indiana; I was very aware of what it meant to live in a “red state.” Of course, I had a complicated upbringing, but I tell people they can’t talk shit about the Midwest unless they’ve lived there; These states are diverse. Many kinds of people call the region home.
For Governor Andy Beshear, this is familiar territory. He’s won big in Kentucky, a Republican-majority state, multiple times, rising through the ranks to become a potential Democratic presidential nominee for 2028. He’s yet to announce—and he’s not the only in the area running on an anti-Trump agenda—JB Pritzker seems potentially poised to run too. It’s a crowded race, and there’s a divide between the far and center left. Who will pull the party further? Alexandria O’Casio Cortez seems to be entertaining a run, and it seems Kamala Harris may try her luck again, despite the previous failure of her last-minute entry during the war on Gaza. Gavin Newsom remains a front-runner too. Early as it is, Andy Beshear, a lesser-known candidate who has only recently entered the spotlight, has released his memoir-cum-platform, too, called Go and Do Likewise.
Beshear lies somewhere in the middle among his fellow Democratic hopefuls. He may admire Zohran Mamdani, but he’s not a socialist. He may believe in liberal ideals like accessible healthcare for all and minority rights, but he has some critiques for mainstream MSNBC-loving liberals whose rhetoric abandons the working class. “Not thinking about health care as essential to rural America is not understanding how the economy works,” Beshear told The New Republic last year, before emphasizing affordability as the defining issue that concerned his rural constituents. He believes in protections against climate change, but thinks it is just as important to create new jobs in rural Kentucky and protect farmers from tariffs. He wants a ceasefire in Gaza, but believes Israel is a “critical ally” to the United States and has yet to use the term “genocide” to describe what’s going in Palestine. The author of a profile on Beshear put it this way while reflecting on his Christian faith for Vogue: “But as devout as Beshear is, I note an equally fervent faith in the power of pragmatism.” While some more provocative ideologues like Jennifer Welch and Hasan Piker have become spokespeople for the left, the path seems clear for a more stringent liberal like Beshear. He emphasizes social rights while still appealing to some mainstream Democrats. His local wins have already shown how Democrats can win votes “anywhere.” His upset victory has been heralded as a way forward for the left to win red states and seats—even if he barely won. Sometimes squeaking by is the only option.
Sometime last year, Beshear started receiving the profile treatment in the mold of a Kennedy. It was the black-and-white photos in Vogue that first caught my attention. He seemed like he was trying to seem like a Real American Man, relatable and folksy, with a clear, calm, empathetic, rational plan for the country. In an interview with Tyler Foggatt for The New Yorker’s Political Scene podcast, he spoke about red-state electability and the economy. Now, as Beshear returns for a new press cycle, he’s going after Trump: “He doesn’t give a damn about the Constitution,” he told MS NOW.
While Beshear wants the Democrats to be more than the party of #resistance, his memoir spends a fair amount of time differentiating his faith and politics from the current president’s crass, hawkish version of Christianity. He even nicknames his political foe Matt Bevin “Trump Lite.” According to Beshear, Bevin practices “Us” and “Them” politics and would rather die than admit he’s wrong. In short, he’s a bully—like Trump himself. In Go and Do Likewise, this tactic stands out. Trump is front and center by page two, scrunched between Bible verses and the Parable of the Good Samaritan. Later, Beshear points out that “Trump throws Gatsby parties with his billionaire friends, while Jesus hung out with the exact opposite.” He implies that “Now go and do likewise,” the command at the end of Jesus’s story, “means treating all people as people of God—not dividing the country by party, race, ethnicity, or even sexual orientation.” Empathy, he argues, is “neither liberal nor conservative.” They “certainly aren’t woke—a word that has become a pejorative to some people.” Moving beyond the lingo while still embracing its zeitgeist, he extolls us to “Make America Kind Again.”
For Beshear, the truth is that community is all around us. We don’t have to like our neighbor to care about them. Go and Do Likewise is full of Good Samaritans who don’t ask about pronouns in the face of a flood; they just get to helping their neighbors. It’s a value he sees everywhere he travels in Kentucky. “This is what our faith should teach us—that our own comfort does not have to come at another’s expense,” he writes.
This was not the version of faith that I grew up with; I am more familiar with JD Vance’s vision of the world—preaching one thing and practicing another all with a stern grip on right and wrong. Beshear notes that many Republicans cast faith in “militaristic terms,” rather than as the work of a beloved community. His brand of Christianity is not to make a Christian nation but to inspire through his faith. “God-talk is easy,” he says. “Living it out consistently is tough.”
As the former attorney general of Kentucky, Beshear fought for the rights of the many rather than the few. Even when it wasn’t politically expedient. He wanted everyone to be able to get healthcare and vaccines—including those with preexisting conditions and in rural, underserved areas. Beshear slowly unspools these victories over the course of the book: his achievements as a lawyer, his father’s own legal wins and political aspirations. As attorney general, Beshear took on opioid companies, winning settlements for those who had become addicted to pain pills. When talking about such cases, he likes to be clear. He doesn’t like to use the phrase “substance abuse disorder” but “addiction.” For Beshear, it’s important to use the language of his constituents. He wants to be the kind of candidate you can envision yourself having a beer with and shooting the shit. He’s certainly easier to imagine having a gab session with than Newsom or Harris.
“Candidates don’t sound like normal human beings when they use terms like ‘food insecurity’ when they should say people are hungry,” he writes. “I talked to people, not down to them.” He prefers to say why he is doing something rather than merely use empty rhetoric. Of course, that’s much easier on a state level than a national one, even if Beshear has already faced intense criticism from Republicans for his pro-choice and pro-trans stances. He even took a picture with the infamous drag group Ladies of Perpetual Indulgence at a Pride event. Unlike Newsom, who has consistently folded on trans issues, Beshear has defended trans women in sports, calling the restrictions just plain mean. This folksy, simple down-home talk of right and wrong and acceptance strikes me as a similar recipe to Dolly Parton’s anti-politics politics. She wanted everyone to get along and have a chance at a happy life. The Golden Rule was more important than partisan divides.
Beshear includes plenty of stories about other people in his book, including a Democratic senator from Louisville whose trans son took his own life. “The response? No compassion. No empathy,” he writes in anger. He vetoed the bill that sought to keep trans people out of sports, something he continually gets flak for to this day even as he’s instead sought to move the conversation to things like jobs and affordability. “Don’t tell me the Democratic Party should stop fighting for the rights of all people. Just explain your authentic why, and then get back to focusing on the issues that touch all our lives on a daily basis.” I can’t imagine a Democrat in Indiana saying something like during my teen years: “The moment we fail to see our shared humanity is the moment we let people fall through the cracks.”
It does seem, by and large, that Beshear is walking the walk as much as any politician can in his position. He helps everyone after tornados and floods, not just those who voted for him or adhered to strict Covid protocols. He is comfortable partnering with YouTube maverick and provocateur Mr. Beast for disaster relief fundraising as he is giving a speech at the Martin & Coretta King Unity Breakfast. From healthcare to racial justice, the back half of God and Do Likewise is a chapter-by-chapter breakdown of his more tightly held political beliefs. The “dream is nonpartisan,” he says, and admits that Democrats too make mistakes. Some critics have pointed out he’s a bit cautious when it comes to taking on Republicans like Mitch McConnell. He may be less compromising than someone like Gavin Newsom, but that doesn’t mean he can’t be timid about challenging the Republican establishment. It’s a classic paradox. Everyone has to pick their battles.
The personal stories that Beshear shares—from a friend who died in a mass shooting to a woman who got an abortion after her father sexually abused and raped her—inform his public ideology. He uses these parables to explain his positions. It is difficult to believe any politician fully, but there do seem to be a lot of genuinely held beliefs in Go and Do Likewise. There are a lot of natural disasters stateside, but foreign policy is largely absent—unlike in many other political hopeful’s books. Often, these publications are vanity projects—business cards for those trying to get in the game and do the press circuit. It’s a policy book sprinkled with faith rather than the other way around. JD Vance’s book, on the other hand, Communion, is a book instrumentalizes faith as a back door into his cruel beliefs about immigration and minorities.
Whether or not the kind of empathy Beshear champions takes root, it’s clear that the Democrats need a new strategy. They’re struggling to decide what that means. There are signs the midterms could be a win for liberals, but that hardly guarantees a certain victory. A politics of empathy, that grounds those often betrayed by the establishment—the poor and the downtrodden, people of color and queer people—would be a decisive refutation of mean-spirited MAGA politics. I’m not sure America is ready to become kind again. For many, I worry it is too late. I want to believe that we can still find connection, but in the isolation, misinformation, and division, many seem afraid to befriend anyone who doesn’t look like them. As the public sphere shrinks, we become more terrified than ever to engage with the other. For some, like Andy Beshear, the face of the other inspires compassion. For others, it merely inspires fear.

Texas Chose the Willie Nelson Slate
The country singer was an enthusiastic supporter of the Democrats who won every major statewide race in Texas.
There are many factors behind Tuesday’s great-big, Texas-size victories for Senator-elect James Talarico and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa—and for the rest of the long-beleaguered Texas Democratic Party, which swept the GOP out of power in races up and down the ballot.
Donald Trump won the Lone Star State in 2024 by more than 1.5 million votes and carried 242 of the state’s 254 counties. But by 2026, Texas, like every other corner of the United States, had soured on the president. And this year’s Republican slate was uninspired, not just because of the many scandals associated with Trump-imposed Senate nominee Ken Paxton, but also because once-popular GOP stalwarts, such as Governor Greg Abbott, had messy records on everything from public education to immigration policy to data centers. Clearly, this was fertile territory for a Democratic rout.
But Talarico and Hinojosa also had the advantage of having been vetted by the man who invariably ranks at or near the top of lists of influential, and beloved, Texans.
That would be Willie Nelson.
The 93-year-old country singer has released more than 100 studio albums, won a dozen Grammys (having been nominated 59 times in seven different genres) and continues an endless tour that still fills arenas on his own and with a crowd of outlaw country players, folkies, rockers and rappers. It’s fair to say he has achieved “national treasure” status, as the songwriter who gave us “On the Road Again,” “Always On My Mind,” “Blue Eyes Crying in the Rain” and “Whiskey River.”
Nelson is a savvy longtime observer of the politics of his state and nation. And he speaks up.
Last month, the singer shared a video in which he announced, “I’ve gotten to know James Talarico. He’s a good man who will be a good senator for the state of Texas. Please vote and vote for James Talarico.” The two had indeed gotten to know one another; Talarico joined Nelson at his Austin show celebrating the nation’s 250th birthday, posting a photo of the pair and the message: “Happy Fourth of July from Willie and me!”
On the same day, Hinojosa shared a photo of her with the singer-songwriter and wrote: “Texas in our souls Willie Nelson.”
Nelson formally endorsed Hinojosa on October 3, along with a widely circulated message that urged viewers to visit her campaign website. Hinojosa responded, “We’re one month out from Election Day. Listen to Willie. Vote for change this year.”
As with the Talarico endorsement, Nelson’s Hinojosa backing was covered all over Texas media—along with endorsements of Democrats by other musicians with Texas ties, such as Don Henley of the Eagles and the members of the Chicks.
Nelson also went down ballot, endorsing Texan Vikki Goodwin for the powerful post of lieutenant governor—telling voters, “We need her!”
Nelson is not new to progressive politics. He was an active supporter of former US Representative Dennis Kucinich’s anti-war presidential bid in 2004, and has backed a number of Texas Democrats along the way—in particular Beto O’Rourke, who mounted serious bids for the US Senate in 2018 and governor in 2022. O’Rourke lost to Republican Ted Cruz in the Senate race and, this fall, Cruz snarkily announced, “Willie’s music is great, but historically, this has been the beginning of the end for Democrat campaigns in Texas.”
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Cruz got it wrong.
Democrats swept statewide contests on Tuesday, producing an epic political shift.
Goodwin beat longtime Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick on Tuesday, and will become the first Democratic lieutenant governor of the state in almost three decades.
Hinojosa will be the first Democratic governor since Ann Richards was defeated in 1994.
And Talarico became the first Democrat to win an election for a Texas US Senate seat since 1998—with 55 percent support and a margin of almost 1.2 million votes over Paxton.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Monica Dolan looks back: ‘I was repulsed by Rose West, yet I had to work out what made her tick’
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Harriet Gibsone
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Born in Middlesbrough, North Yorkshire, in 1969, Monica Dolan is a TV, film and stage actor. She trained at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama and won a Bafta for her portrayal of Rosemary West in ITV’s Appropriate Adult in 2011. She won the Laurence Olivier award for best supporting actress for her role in the West End production of All About Eve in 2019. Her other television credits include Mr Bates vs the Post Office, W1A, Sherwood, Alan Partridge: Alpha Papa, and Smoggie Queens. She stars in Onwards and Sideways, in UK cinemas from 6 November, ahead of its release on BBC iPlayer later this year.
That’s me staging a puppet show with a Waldorf Muppet, my head poking through the very 1970s-looking hatch in our house in Woking, Surrey. There’s a somewhat neglected Sindy on the side. I think she was an ice-skating one – I wasn’t massively keen on dolls, but I liked that you could move her legs around quite acrobatically, and if you bent her knee too far the plastic would snap and a wire would poke through.
I was teased for having chubby cheeks a lot at this age, and it was right before the dentist sent me to get the gap in my teeth closed in hospital. I could have been Madonna if I’d kept it. Or maybe I’d have never got a job as an actor.
I wasn’t one of those extrovert performer types as a child, but I remember recognising how useful having a sense of humour was in terms of connecting to my family, especially as I was the youngest of four. Once, after my dad had sent me to my room for being naughty, I decided I would come downstairs in my red dressing gown. As I strode through the door I did a few karate chops and delivered some lines from Hong Kong Phooey, the cartoon I liked to watch after school. The whole family laughed. Dad might have even laughed a little bit, too. It certainly made it harder for him to carry on being mean.
My teen years were complicated. People at school were forming groups, and I was never that sort of person – I was more of a satellite when it came to friendship circles. I wasn’t into boys in the way that the other girls were. I’d get massive crushes on some poor person but always from afar. But I was quite a joker as well – someone who was outspoken in class. It didn’t always go down well, and I am sensitive, so it wasn’t easy being told to stop talking.
My parents met at University College Dublin while studying sciences. There was a certain expectation that I might follow in their footsteps, because science was so important to them – basically, Mum thought if you didn’t study science you weren’t very bright. When I was choosing O-levels, they had filled in a form and underlined my options for me: physics, chemistry and biology. When I saw it, I absolutely blew my top. They came to my room to talk to me and genuinely couldn’t see why they’d done anything wrong. I said to Dad, “This is a life decision. It is like getting married. It should be mine to choose.” Eventually he said he’d Tipp-Ex it out. I did end up doing those subjects, but I wanted it to be my choice, not theirs.
In contrast to my school days, university was a place I flourished. I had finally found my people. I was in my final year when I met an agent. I asked her, “What should I do if I get a job before I leave drama school?” She said, “Well, that’s not going to happen to you.” Anyway, it did. I’d met the head of Northcott theatre, in Exeter, who offered me a season there. We did a variety of plays, everything from Outside Edge to To Kill a Mockingbird and The Merchant of Venice. My parents came to see me in all of them; they were so supportive. Even Mum, who found a lot of cultural things a real chore.
After that I had quite a long period of unemployment. I sat around and got impatient. Then I went back to Guildhall to be part of someone’s final‑year production. My agent wasn’t very pleased – he thought it was a bad look for a new actor to go back to university to work free of charge. I said, “Well, you’ve not got me anything. And I want to do something.” I was right because, to return the favour, the Guildhall told me about a director who was looking for people for their production of Jane Eyre. They said they’d make sure I got an audition. I got the part. That was the start of everything.
When I worked with Mike Leigh on Topsy-Turvy, he would get cross if you referred to your character as “I”. “Always call the character she or he,” he’d say. “They’re not you!” It was releasing, because acting can become very involved. But it wasn’t until I played Rose West that I understood how much that distance matters. I was repulsed by her, yet I had to work out what made her tick and what her priorities were. So I got the transcript of the case from her solicitor and treated it like a play, focusing on the technicalities. That let me stay objective and at a distance.
Even so, after that performance I was a bit of a husk. A bit rubbed out as a person. When that happens it’s important to remember basic things that you like, to keep you connected to who you truly are. For me that was getting a dog. Having a dog is earthing, as they live in the moment and you have to go out for a walk every day, to spend time with this being who isn’t bothered about what’s going to happen next. As I’ve got older I’ve realised you shouldn’t work all the time, either. Dad helped me with that. I told him I was unemployed and he said, very firmly, “No, you’re resting.”
I’ve played a lot of characters who are real people. It is probably awful to admit, but I’ve never thought in terms of disappointing them. But I can’t pretend that I don’t get very nervous, particularly when I played Jo Hamilton [the subpostmaster in Mr Bates vs the Post Office]. When we did the first screening, the subpostmasters were there, people who felt so broken by what they’d been through. I thought, “What if they just think, that’s not me; that’s not my story at all?” There were real‑life consequences, and I felt a lot of pressure.
The stakes are lower with comedy but it is still demanding. There’s nowhere to hide if the timing’s not right, and it can be humiliating. One day shooting W1A, I was on take 11 of a scene and [writer and director] John Morton was clearly thinking, “This still isn’t right” while I kept thinking, “What am I doing wrong?” I got there in the end.
One thing that’s remained a constant is how much I care. The girl in the photo wanted to have an effect on people, to make people laugh. If you look closely at her, there’s a little bit of hope – something eager to be liked. I still feel that now. A need to entertain. To be seen. That seven-year-old is trying to make a difference and so am I.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/oil-currency.author: Matías Vernengo
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/oil-currency.text:
The Dollar’s Power Never Came From Oil
The emergence of the dollar as the world’s currency was the result of the rise of the US as the preeminent global power. But the slow erosion of US economic and political power will not automatically spell the end of the dollar system.
The war in Iran and the disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have renewed an old debate about the foundations of American global power. Oil has been central to the geopolitical order dominated by the United States since World War II. The dollar is the principal international currency, oil is overwhelmingly priced in dollars, and American military power has been essential to controlling access to petroleum, particularly in the Middle East. The question raised by some analysts is whether the erosion of this arrangement, accelerated by the transition to cleaner sources of energy, signals the end of American hegemony and of the privileged position of the dollar.
There are good reasons to take this possibility seriously. China has become the leading producer of solar panels, batteries, electric vehicles, and many of the technologies essential to the transition away from fossil fuels. The transition to new energy technologies could therefore profoundly reshape the distribution of global economic power at a time when American military superiority is being questioned.
But there is a problem with moving directly from the decline of petroleum to the decline of the dollar. International monetary hegemony does not depend primarily on which commodities are traded, and only secondarily on which country possesses technological superiority in the industries of the future. It rests on a broader structure of fiscal, financial, productive, and military power that has historically developed over centuries. Understanding that distinction requires looking beyond oil to the historical relationship between money and empire.
The Hydrocarbon Dollar Thesis
An influential interpretation of international economic power emphasizes the relationship between energy technologies and geopolitical hegemony. Britain’s rise coincided with the coal-powered Industrial Revolution, while American dominance was associated with the age of petroleum, particularly as oil became essential to modern warfare and transportation. In this interpretation, China’s predominance in renewable energy technologies raises the possibility of another hegemonic transition. Daniel Bessner has suggested that China’s predominance in renewable energy technologies may herald that transition.
Helen Thompson, in her book Disorder: Hard Times in the 21st Century, provides a sophisticated historical version of this argument. She shows how successive energy regimes shaped imperial rivalry, international finance, and the geopolitical conflicts of the twentieth century. For her, oil altered the material foundations of military and geopolitical power, creating a structural disadvantage for Britain and an advantage for the United States. Britain had become the leading industrial and naval power during the age of coal, a resource it possessed in abundance. The transition to oil, initially for naval propulsion and subsequently for motorized transportation and aviation, changed the strategic equation.
In 1911, Winston Churchill, as First Lord of the Admiralty, decided that oil should replace coal in the Royal Navy. Oil-powered ships offered military advantages, but the change created a serious strategic vulnerability. The energy transition forced Britain to import a resource it previously did not need. In addition, the United States possessed an enormous advantage in oil production. Its rapidly expanding oil industry gave it the capacity to supply both its own economy and the Allied war effort. Thompson notes that approximately 80 percent of the oil used by the Allies in World War I came from the United States.
During the interwar period, British governments tried to establish secure supplies through their Middle Eastern concessions. Nevertheless, their reliance on western hemisphere oil persisted. During World War II, Britain again needed oil supplied by American companies, paid for in dollars. Thompson’s point is not simply that oil was a superior energy technology. It is that the geographical distribution of petroleum reserves fundamentally altered the capacity of competing states to sustain modern warfare. More importantly, Thompson’s contrast between Britain’s ascent during the age of coal and America’s ascent during the age of oil suggests that, in the next renewable energy age, based on minerals, batteries, and electrification, China might become the key player.
There is much to this argument. Countries that depend heavily on imported oil are vulnerable to changes in international oil prices and the availability of foreign exchange. The expansion of renewable energy can reduce these vulnerabilities. It may also weaken the strategic importance of oil-producing regions and the influence of countries that dominate them. But reducing the external dependence associated with energy imports is not the same thing as escaping the international monetary hierarchy.
The ascent of the United States implied that the infrastructure of international trade and finance was organized around the dollar — most clearly after the Bretton Woods Agreement in 1944. Many internationally traded commodities, including oil, were priced in dollars. By the 1970s, after the collapse of the Bretton Woods system and the two oil shocks, oil-exporting countries earned large dollar surpluses and recycled their revenues through American banks and Treasury bonds. The petrodollar system thus helped sustain the international demand for the dollar. A conventional fear is that international investors might lose confidence in the dollar and shift their holdings into other assets. If the international demand for dollars is partly sustained by the hydrocarbon economy, then a transition to renewables could reduce that demand and thereby weaken dollar hegemony. In that sense, petrodollars might become eventually battery-renminbis.
However, pricing oil in another currency would not necessarily undermine the international role of the dollar. Foreign exchange markets make it possible to acquire currencies for particular transactions without fundamentally changing the denomination of international debts, the composition of reserves, or the structure of international credit. The critical question is therefore not simply what currency is used to purchase oil, even if that matters. It is why the rest of the world continues to need dollars, and why the United States does not face a comparable need for foreign currencies.
Money and the Fiscal-Military State
Another explanation, developed recently by Ho-fung Hung in Greenback Empire, places geopolitical and military power at the center of international monetary relations. The postwar international monetary order was intrinsically connected to the overwhelming predominance of the United States following World War II. First its wartime allies, and subsequently even its former enemies, Germany and Japan, became dependent on American military protection.The United States also exercised considerable control over access to strategic commodities, particularly petroleum, and maintained close security relationships with major oil-producing countries, even as they sought greater autonomy through the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC). Even geopolitical adversaries remained, to varying degrees, dependent on the dollar-centered international financial system. The widespread use of dollars and accumulation of American financial assets cannot be separated from these political and strategic relationships. The resulting system is self-reinforcing. American military superiority supports the international role of the dollar, while dollar hegemony allows the United States to sustain military expenditure and international commitments on a scale that would be considerably more difficult for other countries.
Nevertheless, a fuller explanation requires placing these relationships in a longer historical perspective. The fiscal-military state was central to the development of modern capitalism and the rise of successive hegemonic powers. Public debt, central banking, and military expenditure did not merely support economic development after the fact. They were essential institutions in the creation of modern capitalist economies.
The Bank of England, founded in 1694, was established principally to finance the British state during its wars against France. Public debt became the foundation of an expanding financial market. The central bank helped transform government obligations into liquid financial assets, supporting both private finance and state expenditure. The development of the British fiscal-military state, to use John Brewer’s apt concept, allowed the government to finance its navy, sustain prolonged wars, protect commercial routes, and promote the international expansion of British capitalism. This process helped establish the foundations of sterling’s international predominance. It was not simply that British industrial and naval power made sterling an international currency. The institutions associated with public finance and monetary development helped create that industrial and naval power in the first place.
The same relationship would later emerge in the United States. Government expenditure, public credit, and the creation of financial institutions supported national economic integration and industrial development. Alexander Hamilton understood the significance of public debt and banking institutions for the construction of a national economy. The federal fiscal and monetary apparatus developed further during the Civil War, while the creation of the Federal Reserve in 1913 helped establish the financial infrastructure required for the dollar’s international expansion.
The relationship between fiscal-military and monetary power is circular. The fiscal capacity anchored in taxation, public debt, and central banking makes possible government expenditure on military procurement and research that promotes technological development and military power. These capabilities, together with geopolitical alliances and financial institutions, help sustain the international use of the hegemonic currency as the unit of account in trade and debt contracts, and as the main reserve asset. Monetary predominance then reinforces the original advantage. The hegemonic state can borrow and settle its external obligations in its own currency without having to accumulate foreign exchange as other countries do. It also acquires leverage over the external financial constraints faced by other states through its control over international liquidity and financial infrastructure. Rather than deriving simply from commodity pricing, market confidence, or network effects, monetary hegemony is thus both a product of fiscal-military power and a central means of reproducing it.
How Britain Actually Lost Monetary Hegemony
The transition from British to American hegemony provides a particularly revealing historical example of how currency competition works. It is tempting to associate Britain’s decline with the transition from coal to petroleum, just as it is tempting to interpret America’s current difficulties as a consequence of its attachment to fossil fuels. Energy certainly mattered. Coal was fundamental to British industrialization and naval power, while petroleum became increasingly important for modern transportation and warfare. But the crucial transformation in the international monetary hierarchy occurred through a different mechanism.
During the nineteenth century, Britain was the world’s principal financial center. London supplied international credit, financed trade, and exported capital on an enormous scale. Sterling became the leading currency of international transactions. As Jay Sexton shows in Debtor Diplomacy, the United States, despite its growing productive capacity, remained dependent on British finance. American railroads, infrastructure, and industrial expansion benefited from access to London’s capital markets, which British financial diplomacy helped facilitate. By the beginning of the twentieth century, however, the United States had become the world’s largest industrial economy. Its productive predominance was not yet matched by equivalent international monetary power.
World War I transformed this relationship. Britain entered the war as the leading international creditor but became increasingly dependent on American productive resources and finance. Maintaining its military commitments required massive purchases from the United States, financed through the liquidation of foreign assets and increasingly through American credit. By 1917, Britain could no longer sustain its war effort without substantial American financial assistance. The United States, which had previously depended on British finance, emerged from the war as the principal international creditor. John Maynard Keynes, who worked at the British Treasury dealing with the interallied web of debts, observed that “[i]n another year’s time we shall have forfeited the claim we had staked out in the New World and in exchange this country will be mortgaged to America.”
The transformation of monetary power followed. The creation of the Federal Reserve supported the development of dollar-denominated trade finance. As suggested in Charles Kindleberger’s classic account of the interwar period, The World in Depression, 1929–1939, the economic collapse and the geopolitical turbulence that led to two world wars were intrinsically connected to the global crisis of British hegemony and the absence of a clear hegemonic power. World War II and the establishment of the Bretton Woods system institutionalized American monetary predominance. Sterling continued to play an important international role, particularly within the sterling area, but Britain had become subordinate to the United States.
As David James Gill shows in The Long Shadow of Default, American financial assistance through Lend-Lease, the 1946 Anglo-American Loan, and Marshall Plan aid had cushioned Britain’s decline. At Suez, Washington demonstrated that it could also use its financial predominance to impose constraints. The Suez Crisis of 1956 dramatically demonstrated the limits of American support. When Britain and France, together with Israel, intervened militarily against Egypt following the nationalization of the Suez Canal, the Eisenhower administration opposed their operation. Britain faced a financial crisis as sterling came under speculative pressure and its dollar reserves declined. The United States had the capacity to provide the financial assistance Britain required, but withheld support until the British government agreed to withdraw.
The significance of Suez was not simply that Egypt could disrupt an important petroleum route, as Iran is doing now in the Strait of Hormuz. It was that Britain could no longer conduct an independent imperial military operation when the United States opposed it, because Washington could impose an external financial constraint that London could not escape. Suez did not create Britain’s monetary subordination. It made visible the hierarchy that had emerged through the two world wars. An equivalent moment for the United States would require another power capable of imposing a comparable external constraint on Washington. Disrupting international petroleum supplies is not by itself sufficient, in particular because the United States is not dependent on imports of energy commodities.
The Global Fiat Dollar Standard and the Rise of China
The history of international monetary standards reinforces the argument. The transition from Dutch to British hegemony coincided with the gradual displacement of silver by gold as the principal international monetary standard. The transition from British to American hegemony eventually produced a more radical transformation, namely, the demonetization of gold itself.
The gold standard collapsed during the interwar crisis of the 1930s, although gold remained central to the international monetary arrangements established at Bretton Woods. Under that system, foreign monetary authorities could convert dollars into gold at a fixed price. When President Richard Nixon suspended dollar convertibility in August 1971, many observers expected American monetary predominance to decline. The United States could no longer guarantee the metallic backing of its international liabilities. Yet the dollar did not lose its position as the principal international currency. On the contrary, the eventual consolidation of the global fiat flexible dollar standard eliminated the requirement that the United States settle foreign official dollar claims in gold. The international monetary system remained organized around American liabilities but without the same metallic constraint.
The aggressive reassertion of American monetary power in the early 1980s was central to the restoration of American hegemony, as Maria da Conceição Tavares argued at the time. Susan Strange similarly challenged the conventional view that American structural power was declining. The Volcker shock demonstrated the international consequences of American monetary power. The sharp increase in American interest rates helped produce the debt crisis of the developing world, forcing countries throughout Latin America and elsewhere into painful external adjustment. The aggressive reassertion of American monetary power in the early 1980s was central to the restoration of American hegemony.
This history presents a serious problem for interpretations centered on the material backing of money or the pricing of particular commodities. The disappearance of gold convertibility did not end dollar predominance. The petrodollar arrangements of the 1970s reinforced an already existing monetary hierarchy. They did not create it. Together with the expansion of offshore dollar markets and private international banking, they helped consolidate what Peter Gowan called the Dollar-Wall Street Regime. Neither the deindustrialization of the United States nor the rise of Japan, the Asian Tigers, and China necessarily implies the end of American hegemony or of the international position of the dollar. The Dollar-Wall Street Regime survives even if the United States has been challenged in the productive arena.
The distinction between productive and monetary predominance is essential for understanding the current international order. China has become a leading industrial power and an increasingly important source of advanced technology. In renewable energy, China clearly challenges the productive predominance long enjoyed by the United States. But China does not possess an equivalent position in international finance. The dollar remains the principal currency of international credit, foreign exchange trading, and official reserves. China itself continues to hold substantial dollar reserves, and much of its international lending and trade remains connected to the dollar system. The United States does not face a symmetrical dependence on the renminbi.
This asymmetry is the foundation of American monetary privilege. The United States can finance international commitments and external liabilities in its own currency. Most other countries, including China, must continue to consider their access to the principal international currency. More importantly, the dollar’s position allows Washington to influence the external financial constraints faced by other countries. American sanctions can restrict access to international payment systems and financial markets. Conversely, the Federal Reserve can provide emergency dollar liquidity to selected foreign central banks, alleviating pressures that might otherwise produce financial crises. This ability to impose or relax external constraints is not simply an incidental benefit of the dollar’s international role. It is one of the central mechanisms through which monetary hierarchy sustains geopolitical power.
China’s growing technological capabilities could certainly alter this balance over time. Dependence on Chinese strategic minerals, equipment, and manufacturing capacity already creates vulnerabilities for the United States. But dependence on particular imported commodities or technologies is different from financial dependence on another state’s currency. For a transformation comparable to the British-American transition, the United States would have to become dependent on Chinese-controlled resources or finance under conditions in which China could determine the terms of access. The emergence of substantial international borrowing, credit, and settlement in renminbi could form part of such a transformation, but nothing of the sort is in the cards in the near future.
The Resilience of the Dollar
None of this means that American monetary hegemony is permanent. China’s advances in batteries, electric vehicles, and renewable energy could erode American productive predominance, at least in some sectors. The increasing use of financial sanctions and other coercive measures may also encourage countries to develop alternatives to the dollar. But greater currency competition is not the same as a reversal of the underlying international financial hierarchy.
Britain’s loss of monetary hegemony was ultimately tied not only to its dependence on American production but also to its reliance on dollar financing during the two world wars. Suez demonstrated that Washington could use that dependence to constrain British policy. The United States, by contrast, does not need to borrow in renminbi to sustain its international commitments, and China cannot yet impose a comparable external financial constraint on Washington. China’s challenge to American productive predominance is real, but no significant decline in the dollar’s international market share has occurred. Even if such a decline were to take place, it would not by itself establish a new monetary hegemon.
Indeed, as America’s productive lead and the legitimacy of its international leadership erode, its reliance on sanctions, financial exclusion, and military pressure may increase. The problem may therefore be less the imminent disappearance of American monetary hegemony than its increasingly coercive character. The transition away from fossil fuels is essential for addressing climate change and could substantially reduce the external vulnerabilities of oil-importing countries. But it will not automatically create an alternative international monetary order. To paraphrase John Connally’s famous dictum, the dollar remains America’s currency and the rest of the world’s problem.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: London’s National Gallery publishes recommendations of its citizens’  assembly
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The National Gallery in London says in a new report that a new public body founded to advise the UK national museum on its future policy and direction has given it “a mandate to be brave”.
The new initiative, titled NG Citizens, was announced in July last year. The museum aims to transform its governance model by launching a citizens’ assembly made up of members of public from across the UK.
The accompanying report outlines the recommendations and shared vision developed by 55 participants who took part in five sessions between November 2025 and March 2026.
The new assembly recommended that the museum should “embrace and grow commercial opportunities” and also use technology to support personalised itineraries, especially for “under-represented” groups, among other objectives.
Other key recommendations for the museum include being more informative about its wider history, representation and context behind the art. The collection also urgently needs to be a true reflection of the UK, said the assembly members.
The overarching question put to the assembly members was: “What do you want from the UK’s National Gallery? How can it bring people and paintings together in authentic and meaningful ways, now and in the future?” A series of eight principles, defined as the “core values that guide how the gallery can move towards the vision”, were discussed at the sessions.
Core challenges on the agenda included: “How can the National Gallery balance its role as a free public gallery whilst being commercially minded? What is the social value of art? How can art galleries explain and support this? Can art ever be open to everyone?” Other issues discussed include “how to bring in new, diverse and loyal audiences.”
Over the next four years, a series of smaller panels, made up of assembly members, will work directly with the gallery to oversee the implementation of these ideas. “NG Citizens will now continue into its second phase: the Citizens’ Panel. The panel will consist of three separate cohorts between 2026 and 2030,” says the report.
Some issues were not up for discussion at the sessions says the report, such as ideas that would result in significant changes to existing buildings; ideas that involve buying or selling paintings; and ideas that might compromise the gallery’s role as an arm’s length body of the UK government.
The report concludes: “The National Gallery was the first of its kind to do this on this scale, in the world. We can accept it was never going to be perfect; it would present challenges, but we hope observers can learn from our experience… To have a group of people that we can work with over future years, who will maintain a critical and supportive perspective, presents opportunities far beyond the usual focus group approach.”
Maurice Davies, a UK culture consultant at Cultural Associates Oxford, says the report is “quite remarkable” but questions whether the National Gallery will be “bold and brave enough” to take forward the assembly’s recommendations.
He tells The Art Newspaper: “The panel have concluded that the gallery needs to be far more than it currently is; a collection of European paintings based in the centre of London. They say the collection ‘urgently’ needs to be far more diverse and to represent the diversity of the UK so it needs to change its collecting policy significantly.
And they say the gallery should share ‘paintings and resources’ throughout the UK which suggests the gallery might want to reconsider its current hugely expensive project to extend its building in central London in favour of using resources to work with museums and galleries in a wide range of locations.”
Last September, the National Gallery received pledges of £150m each (from Michael Moritz’s Crankstart foundation and the Julia Rausing Trust) for its planned major new extension scheduled for completion in the early 2030s.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Lost Rubens sketches return to German castle after 80 years
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Catherine Hickley
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Five oil sketches by Peter Paul Rubens will be shown together at the Ducal Museum in Gotha, Germany, for the first time since they were lost more than 80 years ago.
The five works depicting saints were part of a group of 22 sketches that Rubens painted on wood in 1620 and 1621 as preparation for the ceiling paintings of the Jesuit church in Antwerp, which was the biggest commission he had received by that time. The sketches are particularly important because the ceiling paintings, which were famous in the 17th century, are no longer in existence. The church was hit by a lightning bolt in 1718 and burned down.
The sketches were among the most valuable works in the collections at Schloss Friedenstein in Gotha, where they had been since at least the early 19th century; one had been there for three centuries. But by the end of the Second World War, all five had disappeared.
Three were taken by representatives of the ducal family—which had not been their owners since 1918. They returned to the castle as American and Soviet forces closed in on Gotha and, according to experts, removed truckloads of art in the last weeks of the war. Three sketches were transported to the city of Coburg for protection and from there, they were illicitly sold and ended up on the US art market. The two remaining studies were looted by the Red Army and were restituted to Gotha in 1959.
For many decades the three sold by the ducal family remained lost. Then in 2024, one of them, St. Gregory of Nazianzus, was returned by a museum in Buffalo, New York, with help from Christie’s. Now a fourth, The Prophet Elijah in the Golden Chariot, which ended up in a private US collection, has been recovered in a private settlement mediated by the Paris auction house Cabinet Turquin. The recovery was funded by the Ernst von Siemens Art Foundation, which frequently acquires art for German museums.
Martin Hoernes, the secretary general of the Ernst von Siemens Art Foundation, said a “figure in the low millions” had been agreed, below the market price. “No one wanted to criminalise the current owners,” he said, describing their acquisition of the sketch as a “good-faith purchase”.
The fifth sketch, showing St. Augustine, belongs to the Foundation E. G. Bührle Collection, which is on display in the Kunsthaus Zurich. The Bührle Foundation has agreed to loan it to Gotha’s Ducal Museum so that it can be shown alongside the other four for an exhibition, which opens today (9 November) and marks the 450th anniversary of Rubens’ birth next year.
“It is nothing short of a miracle that Peter Paul Rubens’ five oil studies can now be seen together at the Ducal Museum,” Tobias Pfeifer-Helke, the director of the Friedenstein Foundation Gotha, said in a statement. “They are not only five unique masterpieces by the Flemish painter and the jewels of the Gotha art collection, but also bear witness to European and international history.”

https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-calls.title: Mamdani calls for investigation on how a man charged for jogger's murder was hired by DOE
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-calls.author: Carol Chen, Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-calls.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani has ordered a probe into how the man charged with killing Brooklyn jogger Katie Suarez got a job in the city's public school system despite a documented history of psychiatric issues.
"I have directed my team to conduct a full review into this matter," Mamdani said at a press conference on Monday. The city’s department of education has suspended Sayed Mohassib, 27, the mayor said, and the city is offering counseling to students and families at P.S. 200 in Bath Beach, where Mohassib worked as a paraprofessional.
Mohassib was arrested on Saturday and charged with murder, tampering with physical evidence and criminal possession of a weapon.
Suarez, a 28-year-old TD Bank employee, was stabbed in the neck on Oct. 30 while running on the Shore Parkway Greenway. She died several days later. According to news reports, Mohassib returned to work in the days after the alleged murder.
The case has drawn attention from elected officials and community members, who voiced concerns about how the city screens public school employees.
“I think to myself, ‘Just imagine what could have happened there with the children,’” said Cristina Romero, 47, who has two children at the school. “Why was that person there? Why wasn’t that person evaluated? Why were our children put in danger?”
City payroll records show Mohassib was employed by the DOE starting in April 2019. The department paid him as an hourly support staff through the 2023 fiscal year, then listed him as a paraprofessional in fiscal years 2024 and 2025. The DOE has not confirmed the specific responsibilities of his job at P.S. 200.
But during that same period, questions were raised about Mohassib’s mental fitness, according to a statement from the local elected officials and an NYPD spokesman.
In the fall of 2022, Mohassib was placed on military leave after a brief assignment with the NYPD, the police spokesman said. But, according to elected officials, Mohassib was discharged from the Marines for psychiatric reasons soon after. The Marines did not respond to Gothamist’s request for comment.
On Jan. 11, 2023, Mohassib asked to be reinstated to the NYPD. But several supervisors noted that he “appeared disheveled” and was behaving in a concerning way, the police spokesman said. The NYPD denied his request and he was taken to Bellevue Hospital.
“If the NYPD deemed him unfit, why would he then be deemed fit to serve in a classroom of children?” said City Councilmember Kayla Santosuosso, whose district includes the school where Mohassib worked, adding that the DOE needs to “take a hard look at how he was able to pass through DOE screening.”
DOE applicants are subject to criminal records searches, but there is no assessment of their psychiatric history and issues that come up during their employment might be missed, said Jennifer Weber, an education policy fellow at the Manhattan Institute.
"Once you're kind of in the system, they're not necessarily reevaluating your role in the system or reevaluating your records in the system," she said.
Jay Brown, president of Community Education Council 21, which borders the district that includes P.S. 200, said the case represented a systemic failure.
"We don't demonize people who are navigating mental illness," Brown said. "But in this case, there were warning signs."
State Sen. Andrew Gounardes, one of the elected officials who issued the joint statement, said that he wants Mamdani's review to determine how the DOE can work with other city agencies that have “orange flags or red flags about applicants."
Nicole Brownstein, a spokesperson for the DOE, said student safety is “our very top priority.”
“We are supporting the NYPD in their investigation however is needed,” Brownstein said.
The mayor's office has not said who will lead the review or when it will finish.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Veering From Campaign Pledge, Mamdani Brings Back NYC Property Lien Sale for 2027
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Samantha Maldonado
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani campaigned on a promise to end New York City’s practice of selling property owners’ municipal debts to investors, but his administration says it is bringing back what is known as the lien sale, one more time.
The city will hold a lien sale in mid-2027 before its authorization to do so expires under a local law the following year, City Hall confirmed. Administration officials said they want to collect overdue taxes while also contacting delinquent owners early so they have a chance to pay what they owe and avoid potential foreclosure.
“A consistent and standardized property tax enforcement system is critical for our city’s revenue and to be able to enforce the property tax in a fair way,” Cea Weaver, director of the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants and one of Mamdani’s closest housing advisors, said in an interview. “Continuing to push off the lien sale would just mean that homeowners who really need help are digging themselves even further into a hole that we would then have to dig them out of.”
As a mayoral candidate, Mamdani vowed to “stop the tax lien sale on Day One,” if elected. He suspended the sale in March to complete a six-month review of the program. Officials said they concluded a lien sale with more outreach to homeowners would be more appropriate than ending it right away. Property taxes are the city’s largest source of revenue.
The city Department of Finance puts liens, or legal claims, on properties for unpaid property taxes and water bills. When the debt gets to a certain amount depending on the type of property — typically $5,000 for taxes three years overdue — the city can sell the liens at a discount to privately managed trusts, some of which issue bonds to investors. The trusts attempt to collect the debt and have the power to initiate foreclosure.
The city will issue a 90-day notice list of tax-delinquent property owners who may be eligible for the 2027 lien sale in late February or early March, according to DOF Commissioner Richard Lee. Outreach by the Mayor’s Public Engagement Unit and nonprofit organizations will begin before the list goes out to give owners a heads-up and allow them to start a payment plan or take other action to avoid the sale, City Hall said.
Some elected officials and community advocates have for years pushed to end the lien sale and find a different way for the city to do tax enforcement, arguing the practice disproportionately affects homeowners of color and tenants. City laws enacted earlier this year end the current lien sale process by 2029 and stipulate the city may transfer debts to an entity known as a land bank, which an official group is in the process of setting up.
“The important thing is that we have a tax system in which individuals are compliant,” Lee said in an interview. “We want to provide all the resources that we can in order to achieve that.”
Disproportionate Impacts on Homeowners of Color
Then-Mayor Rudy Giuliani created the lien sale in 1996 to address property abandonment and collect unpaid taxes. Since then, the lien sale has been a source of revenue for the city, with about $80 million raised on average each year.
But the sale has had harmful effects for some property owners, who often must pay more fees and interest on top of what they already owe — which sends them further into debt and can result in foreclosure, with owners losing their homes.
Elected officials and community advocates have long criticized the tax lien sale for targeting homes in majority-Black and -Hispanic neighborhoods, where most liens were sold in the two most recent lien sales. Critics also argue the lien sale strips the city of control over its debt, and thus the opportunity to steer the future of distressed properties.
In policy materials, Mamdani’s campaign echoed those criticisms, slamming the lien sale for “racism” and pointing to the negative effects on working-class homeowners and homeowners of color. The campaign also promised a Mamdani administration would work with the City Council to “permanently abolish the system,” calling it “a relic of the Giuliani era that has been a blight on our city for decades.”
Jakob Kendall Schneider, senior program manager of research and policy with the East New York Community Land Trust and a member of the Abolish the Tax Lien Coalition, said the group was reviewing the specifics of the 2027 sale, but emphasized holding the sale at all falls short of the group’s demand.
“Our goal is to abolish trust-based lien sales. That has not changed,” he said.
Referring to Mamdani’s campaign pledge, Schneider said, “It’s past Day One and there’s going to be a lien sale.”
The city’s last lien sale was in 2025 during the administration of Mayor Eric Adams. More than 4,500 liens were sold for $220 million, with hundreds of millions of dollars more collected from homeowners’ debt payments during the notice period, according to the city’s Independent Budget Office. Last year, 85% of eligible property owners avoided inclusion in the sale.
Adams also came out against the sale and as a candidate vowed to end it “for good.” The 2025 lien sale included exemptions and off-ramps for certain homeowners to offer greater protection.
‘Very High Bar for Lien Sale’
City officials said outreach for the forthcoming sale will include an increase in text and email notifications, getting in touch with homeowners in advance of the 90-day list, and engaging more with those who remain on the list within 10 days of the sale.
The process will feature new measures making it harder for some owners to become eligible for the sale in the first place and have their homes foreclosed on later.
To be eligible, two-and three-family homes must have $5,000 of water and sewer debt overdue by at least a year — an increase from $3,000 in the past. And a property can be foreclosed on only a year after the lien sale and if the value of the lien reaches $70,000 or 15% of the property value, whichever is less, as per the recent law.
“There is a very, very, very high bar to reach for the lien sale at this point to lead to a loss of equity in your home,” said Weaver, who is a member of the land bank group. “So given that very high bar that is in place and the significant outreach mechanisms that we have in place and that our administration is known for, we are clear that we think it’s appropriate to proceed with a lien sale.”
City Councilmember Sandy Nurse (D-Brooklyn) said the changes align with the reforms the City Council passed to eliminate the lien sale’s predatory elements and keep people in their homes.
“This builds in more of a human touch, it builds in more guardrails, it builds more offerings for people to not have a lien placed on their property and the lien not to be sold to these service providers,” she said. “I think with the reality of our financial situation and with the legislation that we passed and with the land bank coming online, we’re in a place where there are a lot of protections, and ultimately, we do need to collect municipal debt.”
It’s not the first time Mamdani’s actions as mayor have veered from his campaign promises, particularly when it comes to housing and staring down a challenging city budget forecast.
While campaigning, Mamdani said he’d implement an expanded version of a costly city-funded housing voucher program called CityFHEPS, based on laws the City Council had passed. But faced with a multibillion-dollar budget gap once in office, he didn’t follow through, and instead agreed to a more limited program that would operate in addition to CityFHEPS. His administration is currently rolling out that program, which will benefit about 5,600 New Yorkers living in shelters or facing eviction from rent-stabilized apartments.

https://gothamist.com/news/ny-students-w.title: NY students will still have to take Regents exams, even as graduation rules change
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-students-w.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-students-w.text:
Students across the state will no longer need to pass Regents exams to graduate, but most students will still need to take them.
State education officials on Monday said high school students will still need to take assessments in four subjects to meet federal testing requirements.
The New York Board of Regents nixed passing the exams — which assess students' knowledge of English, math, social studies and science — as a graduation requirement earlier this year, creating uncertainty about how the changes would play out.
Passing the exams will no longer be required to graduate starting in the 2027-2028 school year. State officials have said the tests can be obstacles to graduation for students with disabilities, different learning styles or limited English proficiency.
But during a Board of Regents meeting on Monday, education officials said students would still need to take Regents exams or approved alternatives in each of the four subjects to satisfy statewide testing requirements under federal law.
The state will continue administering the Regents exams as it works on a new assessment system it aims to introduce in spring 2030.
Education advocates have raised concerns about the changes. In a June 2024 statement, EdTrust-New York warned that eliminating Regents exams as a graduation requirement could lead to inconsistent academic standards across school districts and make it harder to determine whether students are prepared for college and careers.
The group also raised concerns that the changes could worsen educational inequities, particularly for students of color and those from low-income backgrounds.
The New York State Education Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-fire-deat.title: NYC fire deaths nearly double in 2026 as deadly Brooklyn blaze’s victims are identified
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-fire-deat.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-fire-deat.text:
Fire deaths in New York City have nearly doubled this year, the FDNY says, as police identified three of the six people killed in a house fire on 58th Street in Sunset Park, Brooklyn, last week.
Eighty-seven people have died in fires in the city so far in 2026, compared with 45 during the same period last year, according to the FDNY. The count includes two people who died this year from injuries sustained in fires in 2023 and 2025.
Police identified three of the people killed in Thursday’s fire as Lin Cheng Zong, 47; Weixiu Zeng, 52; and Li Sun Zhu, 21, all of whom lived in the house. The other three victims were badly burned and will require additional steps to be positively identified, police said.
Before the fire, city building inspectors had tried four times to get inside the two-story home, most recently less than three months before the blaze.
Inspectors went to the house on Sept. 9 and Oct. 22, 2025, and on Feb. 13 and Aug. 10, 2026, in response to 311 complaints made in the summer of 2025. No one let them in, the Department of Buildings said in a statement last week.
One complaint, in August 2025, reported illegal apartment conversions in the basement and on the first and second floors, city records show.
Inspectors left a notice on the door each time, then closed out the complaints under the agency’s standard procedures, the department said. It added that inspectors have no legal authority to force their way into a building.
Records kept by the city and the state attorney general list Wei Wang as the property’s owner. Wang, a doctor at Total Care Medical Center, a low-cost clinic serving the neighborhood’s Chinese community about 100 feet from the house, declined to answer Gothamist’s questions on Thursday.
“My lawyer said not to talk,” Wang said last week.
He declined to give his lawyer’s name. Messages left Monday were not returned.
Fire marshals are still investigating the cause, the FDNY said. Officials said Thursday that a lithium-ion battery was found at the scene, but that it was too early to tell whether it started the fire, which also injured nine people, including five first responders.
Fires caused by lithium-ion batteries have also increased across the city, according to FDNY data: 276 between Jan. 1 and Sept. 7 this year, up 42% from 195 during the same period in 2025.
The Sunset Park fire came less than a week after four members of a Bronx family, including 11-year-old Zion Maine, died when a lithium-ion battery caught fire.

https://gothamist.com/news/t-mobile-slow.title: T-Mobile slowed Internet to a crawl for NY low-income users, AG says
https://gothamist.com/news/t-mobile-slow.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/t-mobile-slow.text:
T-Mobile has agreed to improve the home internet service it provides to low-income New Yorkers after the New York Attorney General’s office found it drastically capped speeds for participants in a state-mandated affordable service program, and made the plans difficult to find.
The Affordable Broadband Act mandates home internet providers offer high-speed broadband plans at reduced costs to qualifying households. The service can cost no more than $15 per month for download speeds of 25 Mbps, or $20 per month for speeds of at least 200 Mbps. It’s open to households that receive government benefits including Medicaid, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits and Home Energy Assistance Program benefits.
Just 15 households statewide were enrolled in T-Mobile’s Affordable Broadband Act plans, a spokesperson for Attorney General Letitia James said. Her office said the company coded its website so that information about the plans wouldn't appear in search engine results, despite the law's requirement that internet service providers make an effort to promote their affordable broadband plans.
James said customers in the program saw their speeds reduced more than 97%, to just 650 kilobits per second, after using 50 gigabytes of data in a month — a limit her office estimated a typical user would hit after four days of service.
“Reliable and affordable internet service is a basic need for all New Yorkers, but T-Mobile flouted the law designed to help vulnerable New Yorkers access it,” James said. “My office is committed to seeing the Affordable Broadband Act realize its goal of ensuring that New Yorkers in need are not denied access to affordable home internet. I encourage all eligible New Yorkers to enroll in a low-cost home internet plan through the ABA.”
James’ office said T-Mobile has agreed to remove the data caps for Affordable Broadband Act plan subscribers, and deliver the download speeds in compliance with the law. The company also agreed to expand its ABA offerings to more areas in the state, and make it easier for eligible New Yorkers to find and sign up for the plans, according to the attorney general’s office.
A spokesperson for T-Mobile said the agreement provides more clarity around the company’s offering and makes the plan available to more customers.

https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-curbs-sp.title: NYPD curbs spitting and idling tickets amid complaints about quality-of-life crackdown
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-curbs-sp.author: Ben Feuerherd
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-curbs-sp.text:
The NYPD is telling officers to stop giving out tickets for spitting, except in the transit system, and vehicle idling, except in response to specific complaints, according to internal NYPD guidance issued Friday that was reviewed by Gothamist.
The directive also cautioned officers not to issue summonses for jaywalking, which has not been a criminal offense since 2024.
It follows criticism by some New Yorkers over an increase in so-called quality of life enforcement by the NYPD. In October, a video circulated on social media that showed an NYPD officer forcefully arresting someone they had stopped for spitting in Brownsville, Brooklyn. Days later, City Councilmember Chris Banks announced that he would introduce a bill striking spitting from the city’s litter ordinance.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani has faced criticism over his handling of policing issues on a number of fronts. After his election, Mamdani retained NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch who began the quality of life crackdown under Mayor Eric Adams. As a candidate for mayor, Mamdani said he would take a community-based approach to public safety and ask police officers to focus on solving serious crimes.
Residents who spoke to Gothamist for a number of stories about the low-level enforcement had mixed opinions about such summonses, with some supportive of the enforcement, and others critical.
An NYPD spokesperson characterized the guidance issued Friday as a routine reminder to officers about enforcement rules and expectations. The spokesperson said it was not done in response to Gothamist reporting.
Last week, NYPD spokesperson Bradley Weekes said officers are writing quality of life summonses because of an increased number of 311 complaints from residents. “People are asking the NYPD for help, and we are responding to what the community is asking us to do,” Weekes said in a statement.
City Hall declined to comment about the guidance issued Friday.
549 Summonses
In the last fiscal year, which ended at the end of June, NYPD officers wrote 549 civil summonses for spitting violations, according to Marisa Senigo, a spokesperson for the city’s hearing and trials office. NYPD officers wrote 222 civil tickets for engine idling in the same time period, she added.
After the video of the arrest in Brownsville, Councilmember Chris Banks told Gothamist in October that he was unhappy about how the arrest happened.
“We all want clean and safe and orderly neighborhoods, but we want to make sure that it's not at the expense of people's dignity,” Banks told Gothamist at the time. “And it can't be an excuse for the unnecessary or disproportionate confrontations that we're seeing.”
“We’ve seen how interactions between young Black and brown men particularly have become a death sentence for them or has got them involved in the criminal justice system,” Banks added.
Jaywalking has not been a criminal offense since 2024, when the City Council passed a bill that legalized the practice and then-Mayor Eric Adams did not veto the legislation.
The NYPD has not issued summonses for that offense since the law change, but has continued to enforce a similar violation called “pedestrian in the roadway.”
So far this year, NYPD officers have written dozens of criminal tickets for that offense, with most of the violations written by officers in a single precinct on Staten Island, according to a data analysis by the Data Collaborative for Justice at John Jay College.
Tickets tossed
Critics of the department’s quality-of-life enforcement have argued the process is a waste of police resources, and New Yorkers’ time.
In the last fiscal year, NYPD officers wrote more than 98,000 civil tickets for infractions like open containers and public urination. But nearly half of those summons were dismissed by hearing officers because they were defectively written or did not properly identify who received it.
“These summonses still force New Yorkers to spend time navigating the legal system and appearing at hearings, often over cases that should never have proceeded,” Amanda Jack, the policy director of criminal law reform at the Legal Aid Society told Gothamist at the time. “A dismissal rate this staggering only underscores how little justification there is for subjecting so many New Yorkers to this process at all.”
Weekes, the NYPD spokesperson, said at the time that the civil tickets were dismissed “based on technicalities” and that officers were identifying unlawful behavior and taking the correct action.
Criminal tickets issued by officers are dismissed at a similar rate, according to another analysis by the Data Collaborative for Justice.
In 2024, judges who presided over criminal summons cases threw out more than 65% of the cases because the tickets were not written properly or they did not correctly state what law had been broken.
Just 9% of criminal summonses issued that year ended in a conviction, the research concluded. The authors determined the process itself was the punishment for the New Yorkers given the tickets because they were forced to spend time fighting it in court and navigating the legal system.
If the recipient of a criminal summons does not pay the fine or fight to dismiss the ticket, a warrant for their arrest will be issued. In response to the quality-of-life enforcement, the Brooklyn district attorney’s office held an event last month to clear residents’ outstanding warrants that were triggered by unpaid criminal summonses.
In an interview with Gothamist at the time, District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said people with outstanding warrants for small infractions may be less likely to help law enforcement.

https://gothamist.com/news/man-charged-w.title: Man charged with murder after woman found stabbed to death in Queens, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/man-charged-w.author: Phil Corso
