https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: 12 12 12 review – Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan’s super fun heist hunt
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Lucy Mangan
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
A contortionist crawls out of a safety deposit box in the wall of an underground Swiss bank vault, legs wrapped around his waist, feet resting on his lumbar spine, landing on hands and displaced knees on the tiled floor. You know what? SOLD. You have just earned my undivided attention for the next hour of whatever you want to present to me.
Under such highly promising circumstances does the new heist thriller 12 12 12 begin. It stars Anthony Mackie of the Marvel Cinematic Universe and Jamie Dornan (building a nice career since 2013’s The Fall, if we gloss over the 50 Shades movies and the one where he played a romantic hero who believed he was a bee) as its antagonists locked in an international cat-and-mouse game over eight episodes. One can only imagine the anguish when no one could make it stretch to 12.
The 12s, it rapidly and disappointingly becomes clear, are the point. The high – heist – concept is explained to us at the top of each of the eight (like an octet of knives to the producers’ hearts!) episodes. A big heist – and our bendy guy is limbering up to gather $800m in Swiss notes, a literal ton of money – takes 12 months to plan, 12 hours to execute and if the perpetrators are not caught within 12 days, they tend not to get caught at all.
But wait! you say. A grand theft could take any amount of time to plan. And to execute. And what do you mean there’s a 12-day cut-off point for capture? That seems … unlikely. To which one can only reply: did you not just see the contortionist crawl out of a safety deposit box in the wall of an underground Swiss bank vault, legs wrapped round his waist, feet resting on his lumbar spine, and landing on hands and displaced knees on the tiled floor? You did? Right, then. Tcch.
Each episode plays out over the three timelines, so we gradually see how the audacious robbery was put together, how it went down and how, in the here and now, those 12 days to escape are panning out. The short answers are: very well, thank you; could have been better, and are you really still pretending that’s a thing?
The longer answers? Well, the heist around which the series revolves was masterminded by Pauly Galvin (Dornan), son of a New York ne’er do well, brother of Bobby (Jack Kesy) and fiance of a joyfully pregnant Severine (Agathe Rousselle), with whom he had started a new and crime-free life in Marseille. Just when you think you’re out, of course, is when they pull you back in and Bobby duly reveals that his gambling debts have placed his own, Pauly’s, Severine’s and the foetal Galvin’s life in danger and that the baddies to whom he is in hock require Pauly’s legendary robbery-planning services. This is why you should never become a recidivist if you have siblings. Your life is not your own.
So Pauly reluctantly Hannibal Smiths it and gradually a plan and a team come together. It includes Severine’s father Serge (José Garcia) because Pauly needs a tunnel and Serge is – to give you the script’s full description – “a tunneller”.
The 12-hour timeline is the most fun one. The contortionist, an unaccounted for mercury tilt switch in the floor of the vault, a big underground drill, a diverted subway train for the literal ton of cash, an Alpine retreat and jet-skis aplenty – none of the suavity of Thomas Crown’s affairs perhaps, but just as much satisfaction.
Dominating the 12-hour “Takedown” timeline is Mackie as grieving, embittered, self-loathing FBI agent Jack Strickland, so called because he is stricken by his part in the death of a fellow agent when they attempted to foil the Galvin brothers’ last robbery together, in Newark. Now he is in Zurich following up a tip-off that they might be about to strike again, and even the Swiss consider him to be no fun at parties.
Unlike the complacent native force, Strickland has US street smarts and is soon seeing clues they have all missed and is closing in on his prey. This starts immediately, which makes even more of a mockery of the supposed premise, which surely must at least be that – like the “golden hour” after a murder – you have so long to gather leads before the trail goes cold. Not 12 days/one hour to put handcuffs on your guy. But again, we remind ourselves of the contortionist and adjust our suspension of disbelief accordingly.
12 12 12 is fantastically slick, and fantastically well-shot and structured, but once the novelty of the triple timelines wears off there is the inescapable feeling that that is where all the inspiration went. Everything else – the troubled cop, the bad guy trying to go straight, the troublesome brother, the endangered new family, the gang fracturing under pressure – has been done many times before. It’s great fun. But is it 12/12 fun? No. It is three out of five.

https://taz.de/Reform-der-internationale.title: Reform der internationalen Rechtshilfe: Gegen Nacht-und-Nebel-Auslieferungen
https://taz.de/Reform-der-internationale.author: Christian Rath
https://taz.de/Reform-der-internationale.text:
Reform der internationalen Rechtshilfe: Gegen Nacht-und-Nebel-Auslieferungen
Der Bundestag will erstmals Rechtsmittel gegen Auslieferungsentscheidungen zulassen. Allerdings sollen gleiche Richter:innen erneut entscheiden.
Der Rechtsschutz gegen Auslieferungen soll verbessert werden. Das wird der Bundestag voraussichtlich am heutigen Donnerstagabend beschließen. Nacht-und-Nebel-Auslieferungen wie bei Maja T. sollen damit verhindert werden. Linke und Grüne begrüßen das, haben aber weitergehende Vorschläge.
Geplant ist eine Novellierung des Gesetzes zur internationalen Rechtshilfe (IRG), die insgesamt die Rechtsstellung der Betroffenen stärkt. Unter anderem erhält die auszuliefernde Person erstmals einen Anspruch auf Anhörung vor dem Oberlandesgericht, das über die Zulässigkeit der Auslieferung entscheidet. Im Rechtsausschuss stimmte Anfang November neben der Koalition auch die Linke dem Gesetzentwurf zu, die Grünen enthielten sich, nur die AfD stimmte dagegen.
Die IRG-Novelle war ohnehin geplant, stand aber unter dem Eindruck der rechtswidrigen Auslieferung der nonbinären Antifaschist:in Maja T. im Juni 2024 nach Ungarn. Die Auslieferung wurde bereits vollzogen, während das Bundesverfassungsgericht noch über einen Eilantrag beriet. Als Karlsruhe die Auslieferung per Eilbeschluss zu stoppen versuchte, war Maja T. bereits in Ungarn. Im Februar 2025 stellte das Bundesverfassungsgericht dann nachträglich fest, dass die Auslieferung verfassungswidrig war, weil zuvor die Lage von nicht binären Personen im ungarischen Strafvollzug zu wenig geprüft wurde.
Mit dem Gesetzentwurf der Bundesregierung soll nun der Rechtsschutz gegen Auslieferungen deutlich verbessert werden. Gegen die grundlegende Entscheidung des Oberlandesgerichts (OLG), dass eine Auslieferung zulässig ist, ist nun erstmals ein Rechtsmittel möglich. Das hatte die Anwaltschaft schon lange gefordert. Bisher konnte nur noch das Bundesverfassungsgericht angerufen werden.
Eine Woche Zeit
Nach der OLG-Entscheidung soll künftig eine Woche Zeit sein, um Rechtsmittel einzulegen. In dieser Zeit ist keine Auslieferung möglich. Bei Auslieferungen in Nicht-EU-Staaten soll künftig noch eine weitere Woche Zeit sein, um das Rechtsmittel zu begründen. Die Koalition reagierte damit auf Kritik von Sachverständigen. Bis zur Entscheidung ist dann die Auslieferung blockiert. Grüne und Linke fordern generell sogar zwei Wochen Begründungsfrist.
Allerdings wird über das Rechtsmittel das OLG in gleicher Besetzung mit drei Richter:innen entscheiden, wie schon zunächst über die Zulässigkeit der Auslieferung. Die Grünen hatten wenigstens eine Besetzung mit fünf Richter:innen gefordert. Die Linken forderten eine Entscheidung durch einen „übergeordneten Spruchkörper“. Das wäre dann der Bundesgerichtshof in Karlsruhe.
In der Anhörung zum Gesetzentwurf Anfang Oktober kritisierte Anna Oehmichen vom Deutschen Anwaltverein, dass nur ein „Rechtsmittel light“ eingeführt werde. Es sei kaum zu erwarten, dass die gleichen Richter:innen als Rechtsmittelinstanz anders entscheiden werden als zuvor. Holger Matt von der Bundesrechtsanwaltskammer ging davon aus, dass auch künftig die meisten strittigen Auslieferungsverfahren beim Bundesverfassungsgericht landen werden.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: From ocean legend to undersea reef: Why has the SS United States been sunk?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
From ocean legend to undersea reef: Why has the SS United States been sunk?
The ship had been inactive for years despite various owners attempting to save and restore it.
The historic SS United States ocean liner has taken its final trip, this time to the bottom of the ocean, as it becomes part of an artificial underwater reef.
The nearly 1,000-foot (302m)-long vessel, the fastest ocean liner in the world, was sunk on Wednesday after its hull was hollowed out to ensure it remains on the ocean floor, in a process also known as scuttling.
Over five hours, the ship gradually filled with water and, in its final moments, tilted to its side and sank to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico off the coast of Destin, Florida.
The vessel will now feature as part of the world’s largest artificial reef, which is expected to become a popular diving destination.
Here’s what we know about the vessel:
What was the SS United States?
Built between 1950 and 1951, the ship was larger than the Titanic, which was 882 feet nine inches (269.1 meters) long. The SS United States was known for its speed, strength and luxury.
Officially launched in 1952, the vessel made history by setting a transatlantic speed record during its first trip, crossing the Atlantic in three days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes at an average speed of 35.59 knots (almost 66km/h). The ocean liner’s record has yet to be broken by another passenger liner.
During 17 years of operation, the SS US carried thousands of passengers, including former Presidents John F Kennedy, Bill Clinton, Harry Truman and Dwight Eisenhower.
Hollywood stars Marilyn Monroe, Elizabeth Taylor and Marlon Brando also graced the ship, as did surrealist painter Salvador Dali and jazz musician Duke Ellington.
With the advent of air travel, the ship’s career came to an end in 1969.
Why was it sunk?
The ship had been inactive for years and remained docked in Philadelphia as various owners attempted to save and restore it.
However, the costs of maintaining the vessel mounted. In 2021, Philadelphia port authorities raised the daily dockage fee to $1,700, which the nonprofit SS United States Conservatory could no longer afford.
In 2024, Florida’s Okaloosa County bought the ship for $1m, with plans to transform it into the world’s largest artificial reef.
According to the county’s website, the ship underwent a yearlong process to ensure it would be environmentally safe to sink as an artificial reef, and the county said it followed all standards set by regulatory agencies.
“Artificial reefs prepared in this way are a benefit to the marine ecosystem, not the other way around. They create habitat that did not previously exist and foster the development of a diverse environment that can thrive for the overall health of the environment that benefits marine life, our fishing industry and tourism as a whole,” a statement from the county says.
The forming of the world’s largest artificial reef is expected to attract wreck divers to the site, creating more tourism opportunities for Florida.
Why are ships sunk to become reefs?
There are an estimated three million shipwrecks lying on sea and ocean floors around the world, according to a 2007 report from the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation.
Many are reclaimed naturally by marine life and are used by coral, eels and snappers as homes.
While some ships are sunk through disaster, others are deliberately sunk to begin reef deployment and attract fish.
Preparation for the sinking of ships is extensive, as harmful substances including paint, wiring and fuel must be removed before they can safely become part of marine life.
Eventually, a sunken ship’s facade will be unrecognisable, with marine life such as fish, barnacles, and crustaceans all inhabiting or using the vessel.
What else has been sunk to make reefs?
Besides other decommissioned ships which have been deliberately sunk, oil rigs, radio towers and train boxcars have also been used to make artificial reefs on which fish and other marine life can thrive.
More than 600 oil rigs and gas platforms previously installed on the US outer continental shelf were used as part of a 1984 US programme called “Rigs to Reefs” in the Gulf of Mexico.
Other materials have also been used to make artificial reefs, including log huts, household goods such as fridges and shopping trolleys, and even retired New York City subway cars.
Last year, one of the world’s largest artificial reefs was installed around the base of a single wind turbine off the Sussex coast in England. It is made up of 75,000 specifically designed, low-carbon, concrete reef cubes, each with a central chamber and an outer honeycomb texture to encourage marine life to use them.
The cubes were also designed to help the wind farm withstand erosion by acting as a barrier against sea currents and wave energy, slowing sediment that could scour the base.
In Australia, the Queensland Government established its eighth artificial reef in Moreton Bay Marine Park in 2018, using concrete blocks.
Under the official government programme, the first of these reefs expanded the existing Harry Atkison artificial reef, established in 1975 using old car tyres, in 2008 by deploying granite boulders to create new habitats for small fish.
In 2011, the East Coochie Artificial Reef was established using “reef balls” made of hollow concrete; the Wild Banks Artificial Reef was formed by deploying “fish caves”, which are structures made from steel designed to attract more fish species.
In 2011, the South Stradbroke Artificial Reef was also established, and 20 “fish boxes” – cubes with a cross brace made from reinforced concrete – were deployed.
In 2015, the North Moreton Artificial Reef was established in Australia, also using fish boxes. The same year, the Turner Artificial Reef was established, and concrete clusters were deployed.
In 2010, the West Peel Artificial Reef was formed using reef balls.
In 2000, the Mexican government sank two World War II-era decommissioned minesweepers – small warships – and established an artificial reef in the Caribbean marine area.

Empfohlener externer Inhalt

Ich bin damit einverstanden, dass mir externe Inhalte angezeigt werden. Damit können personenbezogene Daten an Drittplattformen übermittelt werden. Mehr dazu in unserer Datenschutzerklärung
Weltweit ist Politik gegen die Erderhitzung unter Druck geraten. Ist die UN-Klimakonferenz ein verstaubtes Relikt oder kann sie noch etwas in Gang setzen?
Friedrich Merz feiert lieber seinen Geburtstag beim Italiener, als zur UN-Klimakonferenz ins türkische Antalya zu fahren. Das passt zur Klimapolitik seiner Regierung: Statt den Kampf gegen die Erderhitzung voranzutreiben, setzt sich der Bundeskanzler für eine Verschiebung des Verbrenner-Aus ein und lässt seine Wirtschaftsministerin Katherina Reiche (CDU) die Energiewende ausbremsen.
Elf Jahre nach der legendären Klimakonferenz in Paris scheint die engagierte Politik gegen die Erderhitzung ihre beste Zeit hinter sich zu haben. Die Rechten haben Klimapolitik zu einem Kulturkampfthema gemacht, nicht nur in Deutschland. US-Präsident Donald Trump hat ein immenses Rollback in der Klimapolitik eingeleitet, das weltweite Auswirkungen hat. Währenddessen werden die dramatischen Auswirkungen der Klimakrise immer sicht- und spürbarer.
Kann die Weltklimakonferenz dagegen noch etwas unternehmen? Wird Deutschland wie geplant 2045 klimaneutral sein? Und wo ist die Klimabewegung in diesen Zeiten geblieben, in denen sie so dringend gebraucht wird?
Weltklimakonferenz in Antalya
Vom 9. November an treffen sich Regierungen aus aller Welt, um über Klimakrise sowie Klimaschutz zu verhandeln – und darüber, wer zahlt. Die taz berichtet von vor Ort.
Über diese Fragen spricht taz-Parlamentsredakteurin Anja Krüger mit taz-Klima-Redakteur Jonas Waack, taz-Klimahub-Redakteurin Tabea Kirchner und dem taz-Klima-Autor Nick Reimer.
„Bundestalk“ – Der politische Podcast der taz erscheint jede Woche auf taz.de, Apple Podcast, Spotify und überall, wo es Podcasts gibt.
There is no planet B
Die Klimakatastrophe braucht unsere volle mediale Aufmerksamkeit. Dafür bündelt die taz seit Jahren ihre Kräfte und begleitet Konflikte und Fortschritte auf allen Kanälen. Und das schon lange: Die taz hat über radikale Klimaveränderungen berichtet, als andere Medien noch treu von unendlichem Wachstum sprachen. Und sie macht weiter, wenn andere ihre Berichterstattung zurückfahren. Unsere Artikel sind und bleiben frei zugänglich – ohne Paywall, dank über 52.000 freiwilliger Unterstützer*innen. Wir sind der Überzeugung, dass es kritische Informationen im Netz geben muss, die nicht kostenpflichtig sind. Gerade zum Thema Klimaschutz. Nur wenn unser Journalismus so viel wie möglich gelesen wird, kann er gesellschaftliche Veränderungen bewirken. Aber das geht nur, wenn sich unsere Leser*innen an dieser Idee beteiligen und den taz-Journalismus mittragen. Sind Sie schon dabei? Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘I spend less, that’s all that matters’: life in the world’s most electrified countries
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Miranda Bryant, Ignatius Ssuuna and Xiaoying You
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
The race to electrification has emerged as a key theme of this year’s UN climate summit: increasing the use of electricity – particularly from clean sources – has the potential to improve daily life for people around the world.
The summit’s co-hosts are now trying to get countries to promise to increase their electricity use to 35% of all energy used by 2035. The global figure currently stands at 23%, but some countries are already striding ahead. As 100,000 delegates, negotiators and world leaders thrash out the details in Antalya, Turkey, the Guardian spoke to three people in Norway, Rwanda and China to find out what life looks like in more highly electrified countries.
An office worker in Oslo, Norway
Norway is a world leader in the race to 100% electrification. In September, a record 98.81% of new cars sold were electric, and hydropower produces 90% of all electricity. But with rapidly rising energy demands, including from new datacentres, authorities warn that the country could soon face a power deficit and higher energy prices.
Unni Berge, 47, lives in Oslo with her husband and two teenage sons and works as the head of communications at the Norwegian EV Association. She describes how electricity features in a typical day:
“I use electricity in my three-bedroom flat and I have district heating [where heat is transported around a local network from a centralised source rather than individual boilers to heat homes and buildings]. For electricity we are connected to the Norwegian central grid, which is mainly hydropower.
“I live in a rather energy-efficient flat, so our electricity bills are comparatively low. In October, we spent 730 Norwegian kroner [£57] on electricity for our apartment, and in September it was 500 kroner.
“I go to work by bus. Almost all the buses in Oslo are fully electric. I also have an electric car, but driving in the middle of Oslo for work is not an option because we have a lot of restrictions on cars in the city centre. In my street, the bus comes every fifth minute, so I don’t have to plan. I go outside and a bus comes.
“I mostly use my electric car on weekends. A lot of the trips are driving to sports activities with my two children, who are 18 and 15. I also train a handball team, so I use it to go to a lot of handball matches and tournaments.
“We charge our car with a charging box in our garage where, like most apartment garages in Oslo, we have built a collective charging system. If everyone put their charging on at the same time it would go slow, but in practice that doesn’t happen.
“I have a large battery on my EV so I charge it once every two to three weeks. Of course we pay for the electricity and a system fee, but it’s much cheaper than petrol and diesel.
“In my office, we have district heating, which is quite common in Oslo in larger buildings, then we use electricity for light and computers. Lunch is made in my office in the internal canteen with electricity. At work I use Microsoft Copilot, which is a really helpful tool, but of course there are big questions there – energy demands will get too high if everyone is using AI more.
“I come home and use electricity to make dinner, watch television and go to the cinema. Growing up in a small village on the western coast of Norway, we also used wood for heating as well as electricity. But it is fair to say that electricity is common part of Norwegian life and has been for a long time.
“What has changed is that our transport sector is also now run on a rising amount of electricity: passenger cars, buses and also ferries. That happened quite fast. Heavy goods vehicles are also increasingly electric, so of course that changes the system and society.
“Perhaps because of the war in Ukraine and more extreme weather conditions, people are becoming aware that they are quite dependent on electricity, so in recent years there has been debate on how to prepare for a crisis. In previous power cuts, some people have used their electric cars as a battery to power electric equipment.
“There is also a big debate about electricity prices. In Norway we have nearly 100% renewable electricity, but even so we are connected to the European grid. So the gas prices still influence our electricity prices. And when we have dry winters, electricity prices rise because if we have less snow, the hydropower gets less water. Rising numbers of datacentres is also something consumers are starting to wonder about – what this development is going to look like and how much energy it is using.”
As told to Miranda Bryant
An e-motorbike taxi driver in Kigali, Rwanda
Six years ago, the Rwandan government embarked on an enthusiastic promotion of e-mobility by removing a number of taxes on e-bikes and vehicles and offering incentives for businesses operating charging stations.
The government has also banned registration of new fossil fuel-powered motorcycles in Kigali, the capital and Rwanda’s largest city, and is prioritising EVs in its vehicle acquisition.
Claver Habagusenga is an e-motorbike taxi driver living in Kigali. He shares a typical day:
“My day begins at 5am and ends late in the evening. My first job is a general clean of my bike, checking tyre pressure, seeing if the brakes are in order, verifying battery health. I have come to learn that riding on Rwandan roads requires strict discipline, as traffic regulations are strictly enforced and a breach attracts heavy fines.
“In the last five years, I have learned to prepare my breakfast using an induction cooker. In the past, I used to use a charcoal stove, which would delay my food and my work. Besides, a charcoal stove would affect my entire family with heavy smoke, and also cost me heavily in fuel each day.
“After my breakfast, the hustle begins in earnest. First, I rush to the nearest swap stations in case my battery is down. I have a varied working schedule daily. Some of my passengers are permanent clients. Two months ago, I was contracted by three families in Kigali to safely transport their three nursery kids to and from school each day.
“Three years ago, I owned a petrol motorbike and I would wake up every Saturday to visit petrol stations to have my bike oil changed, air filter cleaned and other maintenance, at a cost of around US$1.15 [85p]. I love riding an electric motorbike because it’s automatic and isn’t noisy. I always advise my colleagues with fuel bikes to switch to electric ones.
“I feel privileged to work and live in a country that has the commitment of protecting the environment and feel honoured to share my ideas and experience with colleagues.
“Lunchtime is rush hour, especially in the capital. There is one major problem that many electric motorbike riders are guilty of: many have just acquired bikes and are lacking skills, yet are always in a rush.
“Sometimes I skip lunch, but when time allows I’ll be in any restaurant. It’s the time to talk about the unpredictability of our business, the cost of living rising daily, let alone high inflation making the majority of us suffer.
“My daily work has become busier because I have more passengers, since an EV motorbike is cheaper for them compared to a fuel bike.
“Each kilometre I make today costs a fraction of what a petrol-powered motorcycle rider spends on fuel, cutting daily energy expenses significantly, and carbon emissions.
“My electric motorbike costs $2.03 for an annual road licence, while a fuel motorbike is charged $6.77. It means I can offer good prices to my clients, and also clients love to use our bikes since they are trackable.
“I visit battery swap stations three times a day and I am charged $1.69 per battery swap. I always remember that when I had a petrol bike, I could use 3 litres of fuel a day and make a profit of $6.09, but today I earn $11.50 a day with an electric bike.
“On Sunday, it is time for rest with my family. For me, what matters is that we have cleaner motorbikes that also cost less to own, and operate better than the fuel one I once depended on.
“I spend less today. That is all that matters to me and my family.”
As told to Ignatius Ssuuna
A journalist in Shanghai, China
From rows of scooters plugged into charging pods outside supermarkets to armies of buses shuttling back and forth on high streets, electric vehicles have taken over China’s roads with astonishing speed.
Phate Zhang, the founder of the Shanghai-based news outlet CnEVPost, describes his typical day:
“I usually wake up at 6.30am to get ready for my day. After breakfast, school runs are looming large.
“My family own three electric scooters, Vespa-like two-wheelers perfect for running errands. I ride one to take my six-year-old daughter to her school, which is two blocks away. My father, who lives with us, rides another to ferry my nine-year-old son to his school, which is about 4km away. My wife rides the third to the nearest subway station to catch the train to work.
“When I get home, I start work. My job mostly involves writing news reports about Chinese EV companies for my own website, which I founded in 2020. That was also when I bought my EV to replace my old diesel car because I realised it would be much cheaper to power my car with electricity. Plus, I could get a number plate in Shanghai – which would cost about 90,000 yuan [£10,000] for a fossil-fuelled car – for free thanks to a government policy to promote EVs. I spend an average of 200 yuan [£22] charging my car each month. If I had gone for another diesel car, the bill would be about 400 yuan more.
“My father takes care of the school runs in the afternoon for both of my children to allow me to focus on work. Once that is done, he always makes sure that his scooter is charged up for the next day by plugging it into a charging pod in the communal bike garage under our apartment building. It normally costs 0.6 yuan [7 pence] to charge one scooter fully, which would be enough to cover 20km.
“At the weekend, my wife and I usually drive our daughter to her swimming lesson at noon, and then take her and her brother out for a relaxing afternoon in a shopping mall or park. It is so common for families in Shanghai to own an EV nowadays, and there are usually plenty of charging pillars in the parking lots in commercial districts. Just scan a QR code, and your charging starts.
“A couple of times a year, I drive my whole family back to our rural home town in central China. A one-way journey covers about 800km and takes 12 hours or so, including several stops at service areas for charging and rest. When I went home with my EV for the first time in 2020, there weren’t any charging pillars in my village, but now there are at least three within 3km of our house. In October, I also saw many electric trucks on the main road near my village – a promising sign that more types of vehicles are switching away from fossil fuel in China.”
As told to Xiaoying You

https://taz.de/Berechnungen-von-Climate-.author: Nanja Boenisch
https://taz.de/Berechnungen-von-Climate-.text:
Berechnungen von Climate Action Tracker: Dem Planeten drohen 2,7 Grad
Eigentlich sollte sich die Erde um höchstens 1,5 Grad Celsius aufheizen. Mit der aktuellen Klimapolitik wird das nichts, zeigen neue Berechnungen.
António Guterres nennt es eine „brutale Wahrheit“: Die Klimakrise laufe den Menschen davon, sagte der UN-Generalsekretär am Mittwoch bei der Weltklimakonferenz (COP31), die seit Montag im türkischen Antalya läuft.
Wie sehr sich Staaten weltweit anstrengen müssen, um die Klimakrise wieder einzuholen, machen auch neue Berechnungen des Wissenschaftsportals Climate Action Tracker (CAT) deutlich: Mit der jetzigen Klimapolitik steuere die internationale Gemeinschaft auf 2,7 Grad Celsius Erderwärmung bis 2100 zu, verglichen mit der vorindustriellen Zeit.
Erst kurz vor der COP31 hatte auch Unep, das Umweltprogramm der Vereinten Nationen, bekanntgegeben, dass sich die Erde bis 2100 um 2,8 Grad zu erwärmen droht. Die 1,5-Grad-Grenze des Pariser Klimaabkommens wird demnach mit Sicherheit zumindest zeitweise überschritten – mit unumkehrbaren Folgen für Ökosysteme und die globale Ernährungssicherheit.
Fortschritte bei Erneuerbaren, E-Autos und Abholzung
Die Wissenschaftler:innen vom Climate Action Tracker rechnen selbst dann noch mit einem Anstieg der Erderwärmung auf 1,9 Grad in den nächsten 73 Jahren, wenn alle Staaten ihre Versprechen zur Emissionsminderung halten. Zwar gehe der Erneuerbarenausbau voran, die Abholzung des Amazonasregenwalds zurück und Elektromobilität setze sich durch. „Doch trotz dieser positiven Entwicklungen steigen die globalen Treibhausgasemissionen“, heißt es in einer Mitteilung des CAT.
Dennoch: Es stehe in der Macht der Menschen, wie lang und stark die kritische 1,5-Grad-Grenze überschritten wird. Um das Überschreiten so kurz wie möglich zu halten, brauche es einen schnellen Ausstieg aus fossilen Energien sowie den Ausbau Erneuerbarer und mehr Elektrifizierung. Wälder dürften nicht abgeholzt werden, Methanemissionen müssten schnell sinken und Technologien zur CO2-Abscheidung eingeführt werden.
Climate Action Tracker
Darüber, wie der Ausstoß des klimaschädlichen Gases Methan gesenkt werden kann, berieten am Donnerstag in Antalya auch die Regierungschef:innen – bisher jedoch ohne ehrgeizige Ergebnisse. Australien schloss sich einer Erklärung zur drastischen Reduktion der Methanemissionen in der fossilen Industrie an, initiiert von Großbritannien. Was daraus folgt, bleibt abzuwarten.
There is no planet B
Die Klimakatastrophe braucht unsere volle mediale Aufmerksamkeit. Dafür bündelt die taz seit Jahren ihre Kräfte und begleitet Konflikte und Fortschritte auf allen Kanälen. Und das schon lange: Die taz hat über radikale Klimaveränderungen berichtet, als andere Medien noch treu von unendlichem Wachstum sprachen. Und sie macht weiter, wenn andere ihre Berichterstattung zurückfahren. Unsere Artikel sind und bleiben frei zugänglich – ohne Paywall, dank über 52.000 freiwilliger Unterstützer*innen. Wir sind der Überzeugung, dass es kritische Informationen im Netz geben muss, die nicht kostenpflichtig sind. Gerade zum Thema Klimaschutz. Nur wenn unser Journalismus so viel wie möglich gelesen wird, kann er gesellschaftliche Veränderungen bewirken. Aber das geht nur, wenn sich unsere Leser*innen an dieser Idee beteiligen und den taz-Journalismus mittragen. Sind Sie schon dabei? Jetzt unterstützen

US Senator Chris Van Hollen seeks to lead Democrats: Who is he?
Van Hollen is the son of former US diplomats known for his antiwar position and for championing progressive causes.
United States Senator Chris Van Hollen has declared that he is running for Senate majority leader as Democrats prepare to take charge of the US Congress in January, following a Democratic landslide in this month’s midterm elections.
Van Hollen said in a post on X late on Thursday that Americans had “called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption”.
“To deliver, we need new leadership,” he wrote, adding that “this isn’t about any one person – it’s about answering that call.
“That’s why I’m running,” he said.
Who is Chris Van Hollen?
He is a Democratic senator from Maryland who has been in Congress since 2003, rising to prominence for his opposition during the second term of US President Donald Trump.
Van Hollen was born in 1959 in Karachi, Pakistan. His father was a Foreign Service officer who later served as the US deputy assistant secretary of state for Near Eastern and South Asian affairs.
His mother worked at the CIA and the US Department of State.
Why is he running for Senate majority leader?
Van Hollen has had mounting calls to enter the race for Senate majority leader amid growing opposition to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s continued tenure, over criticism of his handling of the Democratic caucus during the Trump presidency.
US Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed from Michigan has said he will not support Schumer as the majority leader in the Senate and welcomed Van Hollen’s decision to run.
In a post on X, El-Sayed said: “I called on Sen. Chris Van Hollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience.
“We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority,” El-Sayed said.
What is Van Hollen known for?
El Salvador visit
In April 2025, Van Hollen drew attention when he travelled to El Salvador to meet a Maryland resident mistakenly deported by the Trump administration, in a case which ultimately saw Kilmar Abrego Garcia returned to the US.
West Bank vote
In September, Van Hollen forced a vote on a resolution that would have required the Trump administration to report on the killing of nine Americans in the occupied West Bank and on Israel’s treatment of Palestinian children in military detention. The resolution failed 47-53, with senators voting largely along party lines.
Rafah crossing visit
In August 2025, Van Hollen accompanied US Senator Jeff Merkley to the Rafah crossing at Egypt’s border with Gaza as Israel continued to prevent humanitarian aid delivery to Palestinians in the enclave.
Criticism of Israel
Van Hollen has repeatedly challenged Washington’s relationship with Israel and has called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a “chronic liar“. He told Al Jazeera earlier this year that the US-Israel war on Iran “is making America and our allies less safe”.
Van Hollen has been one of the foremost advocates for ending Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and violations in the occupied West Bank.
He has consistently pushed for strict accountability for Israeli actions and for restricting US military assistance to Israel.

https://taz.de/Ohrenstaebchen-Unfall/!62.author: Olga Hohmann
https://taz.de/Ohrenstaebchen-Unfall/!62.text:
Ohrenstäbchen-Unfall: Mein Q-tip, mein Ohrenschmalz, mein Blut
Ich mache, was ich am liebsten tue – dann steckt das Ohrenstäbchen fest. Plopp. Komisch, dass in der HNO-Praxis so wenig Überraschung herrscht.
N eulich packt es mich ganz unvermittelt. Ich gehe so schnell ich kann ins Badezimmer und nehme ein Ohrenstäbchen, ein „echtes“ Q-tip, aus dem Badezimmerschrank. Ich stecke es mir ins linke Ohr. Ich drehe leicht an dem Werkzeug, erst nach links und dann nach rechts. Ich wiederhole dasselbe im rechten Ohr. Mein Gesicht im Badezimmerspiegel: voller Schmerz und Genuss. Ich weiß: Ich tue gerade, was ich am allerliebsten tue, von allen Dingen, die man tun kann, auf der ganzen Welt.
Dann passiert es. Ich werde übermütig und drehe das Stäbchen noch einmal im Kreis – es macht plopp. Dann ist es still. Der Schmerz setzt erst im Nachhinein ein. Ich stehe, überrascht und entgeistert, vor dem Spiegel, ich bin ziemlich bleich geworden. Ich ziehe, ganz vorsichtig, an dem Stäbchen. Es steckt fest.
Ich versuche, mir etwas anzuziehen, womit ich das Haus verlassen kann. Ich trage nur ein T-Shirt und eine Boxershorts, in denen ich auch geschlafen habe. Keine Unterwäsche darunter. Ich ziehe mir ein großes weißes Männerhemd über und schlüpfe in Schuhe ohne Schnürsenkel. Es fängt an, leicht aus meinem Ohr zu bluten.
Ich laufe vorsichtig die fünf Etagen herunter und nehme die U8 zur nächsten HNO-Praxis. Die Frau im Wartezimmer winkt mich nach vorne. Die anderen Patient:innen sehen aber ebenfalls überraschend wenig überrascht aus, als sie mich sehen.
Dann werde ich aufgerufen. Der Arzt schmunzelt und sagt: „Husten Sie mal.“ Mit einem weiteren Plopp zieht er das Stäbchen, während ich ein Husten simuliere, aus meinem Ohr und hält es mit der Pinzette hoch. Es ist sehr gelb und ganz leicht blutig.
Der Arzt sagt, mein Trommelfell sei nicht perforiert. Er ermahnt mich, keine Q-tips mehr zu benutzen. Er steckt das Stäbchen in eine kleine durchsichtige Plastiktüte. Ich frage, ob ich es haben kann. Er sagt Nein. Ich frage ihn, ob es nicht mein Eigentum sei – mein Q-tip, mein Ohrenschmalz, mein Blut? Er sagt Nein. Er steckt den transparenten Beutel in eine Schublade.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: Darth Vader’s lightsaber, used in Star Wars movies The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi, sells for nearly $5m
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Emma Joyce and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
Auctioneers estimated it would sell for over $1m, but on Thursday a Star Wars lightsaber used by Darth Vader in the famous “I am your father” scene from The Empire Strikes Back ended up selling for nearly $5m.
Darth Vader’s saber was one of 27 lightsaber props up for sale by Heritage Auctions in the US, including ones used by Ewan McGregor’s Obi-Wan Kenobi and Hayden Christensen’s Anakin Skywalker in Revenge of the Sith.
The movie prop, which was used in the 1980 film as well as 1983’s Return of the Jedi, sold for $4.875m at an event titled “the Ultimate Star Wars auction”.
The sale marked a world auction record for any Star Wars prop used on screen, Heritage Auctions said, and surpassed the auctioneer’s previous sale of Luke Skywalker’s lightsaber and severed hand from The Empire Strikes Back, which sold for $3.75m in July.
Items up for sale spanned the far reaches of the universe created by George Lucas, including an blaster used by Boba Fett and a Yoda puppet hand used during the character’s original appearance in The Empire Strikes Back.
Brian Chanes, the senior director of Hollywood and entertainment at Heritage Auctions, said the Darth Vader saber was “like the Holy Grail” to a Star Wars collector.
“It’s the one on the set,” he said. “It’s from the most iconic sequence of the entire franchise.”
Associated Press contributed to this report.

https://taz.de/Kehrtwende-bei-Steuerpoli.title: Kehrtwende bei Steuerpolitik: Schwarz-Rot schwimmt gegen den Strom

Kehrtwende bei Steuerpolitik: Schwarz-Rot schwimmt gegen den Strom
Haushaltspolitiker der Regierungskoalition sehen keinen Spielraum für die Senkung der Stromsteuer. Wirtschaftsvertreter empört der Zickzackkurs.
Die Regierungsfraktionen von Union und SPD vollziehen bei wichtigen Steuervorhaben eine Kehrtwende: Die Stromsteuer soll nach dem Willen der schwarz-roten Haushaltspolitiker:innen doch nicht für alle gesenkt werden, die Einführung der Zuckersteuer wird verschoben und die geplante Plastiksteuer wird ganz kassiert. Wirtschaftsverbände kritisieren die ausbleibende Entlastung harsch.
Das Senken der Stromsteuer für alle auf das europäische Mindestmaß war ursprünglich im Koalitionsvertrag von Union und SPD vorgesehen. Die schwarz-rote Regierung hat dann aber nur die Stromsteuer für Großverbraucher herabgesetzt, also nicht für Privathaushalte und kleinere Unternehmen. Mehr als 80 Prozent aller Firmen profitieren nicht.
Das Reduzieren der Steuer auch für sie würde zu niedrigeren Einnahmen des Staates von rund 5,4 Milliarden Euro führen. Pro Kilowattstunde Strom würde der Preis um rund 2 Cent fallen. Für einen Single-Haushalt mit durchschnittlichem Verbrauch läge die Ersparnis nach Angaben des Vergleichsportals Verivox bei rund 35 Euro im Jahr, für einen Drei-Personen-Haushalt wären es 95 Euro gewesen.
Am Mittwochabend hatten Koalitionsvertreter:innen erklärt, keine Gegenfinanzierung für die Senkung gefunden zu haben. Dabei hatte Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (CDU) nach den verlorenen Landtagswahlen im Oktober angekündigt, sie für alle zu senken. Das sei ein wichtiges Signal, um verlorenes Vertrauen zurückzugewinnen, hatte er erklärt. Medienberichten zufolge will Merz bei den Koalitionsgesprächen am kommenden Dienstag die Senkung doch noch durchsetzen. Mehrere CDU-Ministerpräsidenten fordern ebenfalls eine niedrigere Stromsteuer.
Wirtschaftsvertreter empört das Hin und Her. „Der Zickzackkurs aus immer neuen Versprechen und Rückziehern erschüttert das Vertrauen in die Bundesregierung“, sagte der Präsident der Deutschen Industrie- und Handelskammer (DIHK), Peter Adrian. Die Absage von Mittwoch sei eine herbe Enttäuschung für die Unternehmen in Deutschland.
Zuckersteuer wird verschoben
Adrian kritisiert, dass die Unternehmen bei den Stromkosten statt ent- weiter belastet werden, weil der staatliche Zuschuss zu den Netzentgelten gekürzt werden soll. Niedrigere Stromkosten würden nicht nur die Betriebe entlasten. „Sie stärken zugleich Investitionen in klimafreundliche Technologien, von der Wärmepumpe über die E-Mobilität bis zur Elektrifizierung industrieller Prozesse, und machen uns damit unabhängiger von fossilen Energieimporten“, sagte er.
Wolfgang Weber, Geschäftsführer vom Verband der Elektro- und Digitalindustrie
Auch der Verband der Elektro- und Digitalindustrie ist enttäuscht. „Die Stromsteuer droht zum Symbol einer Reformpolitik der Koalition zu werden, die zu viel verspricht und zu wenig liefert“, sagte Geschäftsführer Wolfgang Weber.
Wer wiederholt Zusagen mache und sie dann zurücknehme, verspiele Vertrauen, sagte auch die Chefin des Verbraucherzentrale Bundesverbands (vzbv), Ramona Popp. „Das erneute Aus der Stromsteuersenkung ist Verbraucherinnen und Verbrauchern nicht mehr zu vermitteln.“ Sie kritisierte, dass gleichzeitig die Einführung einer Zuckersteuer erneut zur „Zitterpartie“ werde.
Denn die Regierungsfraktionen wollen die Einführung der Steuer für mit Zucker gesüßte Getränke verschieben. Sie sollte ursprünglich Mitte 2027 in Kraft treten. Das soll nun erst Anfang 2028 geschehen. Die Industrie solle damit größere Spielräume erhalten, um sich auf die neuen Regeln einzustellen, hieß es. Hersteller haben so länger Zeit, um die Produktion auf einen niedrigeren Zuckergehalt umzustellen. Anders als ursprünglich vorgesehen, soll es je nach Zuckergehalt nicht zwei, sondern drei Steuerstufen geben.
Gestrichen ist die ursprünglich von Union und SPD vereinbarte Einführung einer Plastiksteuer. Damit sollte die Flut an Plastikabfällen eingedämmt werden. Die Koalition habe keine unbürokratische Regelung dafür gefunden, erklärte Unionsfraktionschef Thorsten Frei. Die Plastiksteuer hätte dem Staat 2027 rund 800 Millionen, ab 2028 knapp 1,5 Milliarden Euro bringen sollen.

https://taz.de/Einkommensgrenze-bei-Unte.author: Celine Hog
https://taz.de/Einkommensgrenze-bei-Unte.text:
Einkommensgrenze bei Unterhaltsvorschuss: Ab 4.500 Euro gibt's nix mehr
Wenn ein Elternteil den Unterhalt nicht zahlt, bekamen Alleinerziehende bislang Unterstützung vom Staat. Für manche könnte sich das bald ändern.
Nach heftiger Kritik an der im Juli 2026 vorgestellten Änderung des Unterhaltszuschusses hat Bundesfamilienministerin Karin Prien (CDU) in einer Befragung der Bundesregierung am Mittwoch im Bundestag einen neuen Referentenentwurf vorgestellt.
Anders als im vorherigen Vorschlag sollen Unterhaltsvorschüsse für Jugendliche ab 16 Jahren weiterhin beibehalten werden, dagegen sehen sich Alleinerziehende ab 2029 womöglich mit einer Einkommensgrenze von versteuerten 40.000 Euro jährlich konfrontiert – darüber entfällt der Vorschuss. Und das nicht etwa stufenweise, sondern komplett. Laut Prien entspreche das einem Bruttoeinkommen von etwa 4.500 Euro monatlich. Pro weiterem Kind hebt sich die Grenze um je 10.000 Euro im Jahr.
Bislang leistet der Staat den Vorschuss an Alleinerziehende, wenn der andere Elternteil nicht oder nur unzureichend bezahlt. 6 Prozent der Alleinerziehenden würden durch die Regelung künftig den Vorschuss verlieren.
Mehr Druck auf Unterhaltspflichtige
Neben der Einführung einer Einkommensgrenze gibt es noch einen weiteren zentralen Punkt im Referentenentwurf: Die Bundesregierung will das zahlungsunwillige Elternteil stärker in die Verantwortung nehmen. Bei einer Verweigerung der Vermögensauskunft oder der Abwesenheit bei Einberufungen von Behörden soll sich das Bußgeld von aktuell 1.000 auf künftig 2.000 Euro verdoppeln. Bei wiederholten Verstößen kann sogar ein Fahrverbot von bis zu drei Monaten ausgesprochen werden. Der Entwurf wird im nächsten Schritt im Kabinett beraten.
Durch die Änderung erwartet die Bundesregierung eine finanzielle Entlastung von Bund, Ländern und Kommunen. Ab nächstem Jahr sollen so 16 Millionen Euro gespart werden. Nach dem Inkrafttreten der Einkommensgrenze sollen diese Einsparungen 2029 dann auf insgesamt 250 Millionen Euro steigen.
Fernab von der Lebensrealität von Alleinerziehenden
Die Bundesministerin bezeichnet den Entwurf als guten Kompromiss. Die Vorstandsvorsitzende des Vereins Fair für Kinder ist zwar froh, dass die Streichung des Unterhaltsvorschusses ab 16 Jahren vom Tisch ist und lobt auch den Druck auf Unterhaltspflichtige, kritisiert den neuen Entwurf trotzdem: „Wer Alleinerziehende mit Einkommensgrenzen bestraft, setzt Fehlanreize statt Anreize zur Erwerbsarbeit. Mit ihrem Vorschlag untergräbt Familienministerin Prien finanzielle Unabhängigkeit, statt sie zu fördern. Alleinerziehende werden bereits steuerlich benachteiligt. Jetzt sollen sie auch noch für den ausbleibenden Unterhalt des anderen Elternteils geradestehen“, meint Delia Keller.
Das sei für die Mütter, die den Großteil der Alleinerziehenden ausmachen, eine weitere finanzielle Belastung zusätzlich zur Sorgearbeit und verdeutliche, wie wenig die CDU von der Lebensrealität Alleinerziehender wisse.
Auch die Opposition blickt kritisch auf den Entwurf. Die Grünen betonten ebenfalls die sinkenden Arbeitsanreize für Alleinerziehende, die durch die Änderung entstehen würden. Die Linke hat einen Antrag eingebracht mit der Forderung, das Kindergeld beim Unterhaltsvorschuss nur zur Hälfte anzurechnen, wie es bereits bei Kindern gehandhabt wird, die Unterhalt von Unterhaltspflichtigen erhalten.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Iran says it targeted US radar site in Bahrain
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Iran says it targeted US radar site in Bahrain
IRGC claims Bahrain radar strike is a response to attacks on Iranian telecom tower in southern Hormozgan province.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has targeted a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in retaliation for what it described as an air attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran.
The claim came hours after Iran’s state news agency IRNA, citing official sources, reported that the port city of Sirik in Hormozgan province was hit by “enemy fire” on Thursday.
In a statement carried by the semi-official Tasnim news agency, the IRGC called the strike a “serious warning” to the “aggressor enemy” to stop what it said was a series of aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz.
“Should these violations and acts of aggression recur, the IRGC Aerospace Force stands in full readiness to engage without limits,” the statement said.
The IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency said the IRGC’s Aerospace Force had “targeted and destroyed” the radar installation.
There was no immediate comment from Washington or Manama.
Bahrain hosts the headquarters of the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet.
The Fifth Fleet headquarters, at the Naval Support Activity base in the capital, Manama, is the main command centre for US naval operations in the Middle East.
It was hit in the opening hours of the war on February 28, and satellite images analysed by Al Jazeera showed direct hits on several radar domes and damage to buildings across the base.
The US has reportedly reduced its troop numbers at bases in the region and ordered some diplomatic staff to leave, according to news outlets, as Trump weighs new strikes on Iran,
US Central Command said it “regularly” moves personnel and assets to “optimise mission readiness”.
First Bahrain attack since September
According to the Reuters news agency, it is the first time since early September that Iran has claimed an attack on US military assets in a Gulf country.
The claim comes as Israel’s security cabinet has ordered the military to step up preparations for a possible attack on Iran, according to Israeli media, including the public broadcaster KAN.
Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei has warned that if the US launches another war, every military base involved, anywhere from West Asia to Europe, would be a legitimate target for Iranian strikes.
A Pentagon inspector general’s report released in September found that Iranian attacks damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings at US installations in eight countries, including Bahrain, in the first four months of the war.
Analysts say several US bases in the region have been almost rendered unusable.
US President Donald Trump has said he is prepared to return to war if the diplomatic track offered by Qatar fails to deliver a deal.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, however, has said economic pressure on Iran is working well enough that resuming large-scale military operations is unnecessary.
In an exclusive interview with Al Jazeera on Wednesday, Iran’s parliament speaker and lead negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Strait of Hormuz would never go back to how it was before the war, and that “the ball is now in the American court“.
Meanwhile, US Central Command says its forces are still strictly enforcing the naval blockade on Iranian ports.
The war began on February 28 with US and Israeli attacks on Iran.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Three dead in Los Angeles after driver crashes into pedestrians, officials say
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
At least three people are dead and three critically injured, after a car struck pedestrians on a Los Angeles corner during Tuesday rush hour, authorities said.
The fatal crash took place near a North Hollywood metro station.
The driver, whose identity remains unknown, is hospitalized in critical condition, according to Los Angeles police. The three injured people were also taken to area hospitals for treatment, according to an online statement posted by the the LA fire department. The fire and police departments did not offer additional details on the deadly crash.
A local CBS News affiliate station reported that the car crashed into a food stand near a bus stop along a major thoroughfare, Lankershim Boulevard, that runs through the busy NoHo commercial and arts district in the city’s San Fernando Valley.
The LA mayor, Karen Bass, said the victims included street vendors and pedestrians.
“I’m heartbroken for the families of everyone impacted,” she said in a post on X.
Authorities will be checking the video in the area in what will be a “prolonged but very deliberate investigation,” said LA police chief Jim McDonnell.
Aerial news video footage of the scene showed a white-colored, partially crumpled small SUV that appeared to have run up onto the sidewalk and into the side of a mass-transit shelter structure.
An investigation is under way.
With Reuters

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Coyote officials thought they had killed after child attack seen alive in LA neighborhood
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo in Los Angeles
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A coyote that California wildlife officials believed they had euthanized after it bit a toddler and menaced residential pets in a trendy Los Angeles neighborhood was seen alive recently, neighborhood residents said.
Wiley, the name some Atwater Village residents gave to the coyote, had vexed the area with its increasingly aggressive and brazen behavior. The wild animal, which scampered through people’s backyards, was reportedly being fed by an unidentified man. Wiley’s presence drew local uproar after he bit a 16-month-old child.
The attack prompted California department of fish and wildlife officers to shoot Wiley in October, an intervention that appeared to cap the neighborhood saga.
That is until residents observed a limping Wiley back in Atwater Village in recent weeks.
When asked what went awry, the California department of fish and wildlife said in a statement provided to KTLA that officials shot Wiley on 16 October. The department’s officers could not locate the coyote’s body and concluded it had died.
The department returned to Atwater Village, where they shot Wiley for a second time, confirming on Tuesday that the coyote had been killed.
The twist in Wiley’s tale brought cold comfort to some residents, who feel that the coyote’s death could have been prevented.
“I don’t think he should have been euthanized because coyotes are predators, and they’re going to do what they’re going to do,” one neighbor, Ana Fishman, told KTLA. “And that’s not his fault. He should have been relocated. I think the fact that coyotes apparently, in the state of California, can’t be relocated is wrong.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US Coast Guard suspends search for woman swept out to sea in California
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Anna Betts
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The US Coast Guard announced that it has suspended its search for a 24-year-old woman who is believed to have been swept out to sea in California.
The woman, identified as 24-year-old Senah Park, was last seen near Panther state beach in Santa Cruz county at about 8.30pm local time on Sunday, authorities said earlier this week.
In a statement, the Santa Cruz county sheriff’s office said deputies responded to the beach at about 8pm on Sunday night, after receiving a report “of a woman who was believed to have been swept into the ocean”.
According to the sheriff’s office, a group of friends were on the beach when an “incoming tide knocked several of them over”. During that incident, Park “is believed to have been swept out to sea”, they said.
The San Mateo-Santa Cruz unit of California Fire CZU said firefighters were dispatched to the beach at about 8.30pm on Sunday. The unit said: “Four people had gone through the keyhole on the beach and when the tide rose, they became trapped.”
“Three people were able to escape the rising tide,” they said, adding: “One person, described as a woman in her twenties, was not able to escape and was believed to have been swept out to sea.”
Authorities said that an “extensive search” began on Sunday night, involving drones, ground crews, helicopters, and search and rescue teams.
In an update issued on Tuesday, the sheriff’s office said that its “fixed wing Air Unit and Drone Team have been searching the coastline and surrounding waters” for Park.
“While there are no significant updates to share at this time, our thoughts are with Senah’s family and friends during this incredibly difficult time,” the sheriff’s office statement on Tuesday said.
In a separate statement on Tuesday, the US Coast Guard said watchstanders at its San Francisco command center received a notification on Sunday night from Santa Cruz fire department personnel “of a confirmed person in the water near Panther State Beach”.
The Coast Guard said that watchstanders issued an urgent marine information broadcast and coordinated the launch of a 47ft motor lifeboat crew and MH-65 Dolphin helicopter aircrew for the search.
The agency said that it also coordinated “eight hours of search efforts across 95 square miles” and deployed assets including helicopter aircrews, boat crews, drones and more.
But, in the statement on Tuesday, the Coast Guard said that it had “suspended its search” on Monday afternoon.
“Suspending a search is a difficult decision,” Lt Max Holloway, San Francisco sector search and rescue mission coordinator, said in a statement on Tuesday. “Given the extensive search effort of the surrounding area and environmental conditions, we have suspended active search efforts pending further developments.
“We worked closely with our partner agencies and exhausted all available resources in our attempt to locate Ms Park,” he added. “Our deepest condolences are with her family and loved ones.”
The announcement comes as the National Weather Service’s San Francisco Bay Area and Monterey office warned on Tuesday that high surf is expected this coming weekend, with “dangerously large breaking waves” of between 20 and 30ft expected.
“It is highly advisable to stay away from beaches and off of jetties, piers, and rocks,” the NWS office said. “Remain out of the water. Never turn your back to the ocean!”
It also comes as in recent weeks parts of California have experienced historic high tides and record-breaking water levels, as the impacts of an exceptionally strong and still-strengthening El Niño continue to unfold.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/jd-v.title: Republicans Are Desperate to Pretend They Never Supported the War With Iran
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/jd-v.author: Alain Stephens
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/jd-v.text:
Alain Stephens is an investigative reporter covering gun violence, arms trafficking, and federal law enforcement.
To say that Americans were pissed off is an understatement.
On Tuesday, Democrats didn’t just seize control of both houses of Congress. They redrew the American political map, capturing offices that had remained reliably Republican for generations, from the Deep South to Kansas and Texas. The Lone Star State alone, with its 40 Electoral College votes, now raises the possibility of a seismic shift in the calculus of future presidential elections.
The sheer scale of the historic Democratic surge delivered an unmistakable rebuke to America’s supposedly populist president. The message was clear and simple: We do not like you.
Much of Americans’ rapid disillusionment with the Trump administration can be traced to a single word — Iran — and the cascading economic hardships Americans have endured as the war has dragged on.
For the GOP, the threat is existential. The war has gone from a Republican loyalty test to a political albatross for many of its former supporters, one that many Republicans are now jettisoning themselves away from to salvage their own political futures.
By Wednesday, it had become the chief explanation for the party’s sweeping electoral defeat, with Vice President JD Vance declaring unequivocally on X that “the reason we lost is the war.”
“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” he wrote. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” Coming from Trump’s own vice president, it was a striking about-face.
The tirade also raised an awkward question ahead of the 2028 presidential race: How does a potential successor to the MAGA mantle campaign against a war waged by his own administration?
Trump, however, has not gone nearly as far as his VP. Although the president acknowledged the war hurt Republicans, he still defended it on its merits. Speaking with reporters Wednesday after expounding at length about his White House ballroom, Trump said, “The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it.”
Where Did All the Warmongers Go?
But on the campaign trail, Republicans were not completely oblivious to Americans’ collective frustration with the Iran war.
In September, ABC News identified 17 Republican lawmakers and candidates who had called for ending the war through public statements or votes. Much of the pressure came in competitive midterms races, as the conflict’s effects on oil, diesel, and fertilizer prices reached American households.
In Iowa, Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson called for a “successful and immediate end” to the war in September, warning that voters were paying the price at gas pumps and grocery stores. Yet she voted six times against House measures directing Trump to halt the attacks. During an October 25 ABC interview, Hinson said she would not rule out a post-election U.S. offensive and said she trusted Trump and the military to choose the right timetable. Despite the president praising her weight loss at a recent rally, tepidly breaking with Trump wasn’t enough to get Hinson over the line, and she lost to Democrat Josh Turek by 4.5 percentage points.
Michigan also had its share of Iran backtrackers. Republican Senate hopeful Mike Rogers described Iran as an “imminent threat” when the bombing began on February 28. In May, he called the conflict a potential “win-win-win.” But with the midterms fast approaching, Rogers released a campaign ad declaring “the war with Iran needs to end” quickly and warned Michigan families could no longer afford the economic fallout.
Rep. John James, the Republican candidate for Michigan governor, likewise praised Trump’s use of force early in the war, saying the president “had the balls” to “assure the survival and success of liberty.” He voted against six House war-powers resolutions, including as recently as September. Days after that vote, he said the war needed to wrap up “quickly.” He went on to declare in an interview, “the position has always been, I hate war.”
Both Rogers and James lost their races.
Even Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a possible contender in the Republican Party’s next presidential contest who could reportedly be up for Pete Hegseth’s job, warned Monday that the war was a “big, big drag” on his party. Trump, DeSantis pointed out, campaigned against another Middle Eastern war. Now voters are dealing with higher fuel costs, and Republicans who refuse to acknowledge the connection are “gaslighting” them. But back in spring, DeSantis defended the strikes on Iranian leadership, describing its government as “a fanatical, apocalyptic, militant Islamist regime.”
The polling helps explain the Republican panic. An Associated Press poll found roughly 6 in 10 voters believed the U.S. made a “wrong decision” in attacking Iran. And it’s not as though Republicans weren’t warned. A handful within their own ranks, including Thomas Massie and Rand Paul, opposed the war from its earliest days and backed efforts to rein it in. But those criticisms seemed to fall on deaf ears.
A Hasty Retreat
With plenty of blame to go around, the criticism has gone beyond candidates and into the conservative media ecosystem.
During the network’s primetime Election Night coverage, Fox News host Sean Hannity told his colleague Bret Baier that the results would have been different without the Iran war. Conservative commentator Matt Walsh called the war a betrayal of America First principles, demanded new Republican leadership, and labeled the conflict a “catastrophically stupid decision.”
Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene called Trump breaking his promise not to start another foreign war his “biggest betrayal” and said “Americans are fed up with it.”
Other commentators placed the responsibility squarely on Trump himself for sucking his own party into a political quagmire. In The Federalist, senior editor John Daniel Davidson blamed the party’s collapse on Trump’s undermining of a GOP coalition built upon rejecting the interventionist politics of the George W. Bush era.
Some prominent Republican operatives are sure to be thrown under the bus by their own party in the retreat. The first to get the boot may be none other than Hegseth, America’s chief “warfighter,” who has been one of the war’s most enthusiastic, and public, cheerleaders. The defense secretary responded to the criticisms in a nearly six-minute-long video posted online on Thursday, in which he seemed to make the case for keeping his job, touting his elimination of the “Marxist ideology” of diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives and tarring transgender troops as having a “mental illness.”
“Regardless of how people care about the war, which I believe is a courageous and historic effort that will ensure Iran never gets a nuclear weapon, we need to continue, as President Trump did in his first term, to rebuild our military,” he said. “This is not about me, but of course, the other side, in case you noticed, they’re obsessed.”
Already facing growing Republican dissatisfaction and a ballooning roster of disgruntled and ousted senior military officials, Hegseth now faces the prospect of investigations by a Democratic-controlled Congress and an impeachment effort led by Massie. And while Trump has so far publicly defended his defense secretary, he has also reportedly consulted allies about whether to hit the ejector seat on Pete.
But while Republicans and Democrats read polls and calculate the political currency of war and economic hardship, the human cost cannot be measured in votes. At least 3,636 people had been killed in Iran as of early April, including 1,701 civilians and 254 children, according to human rights monitors. More fighting has followed and likely driven that number far higher.
At least 23 American service members have died in operations connected to the war, with almost 900 wounded by enemy fire. But these are estimates, and the Trump administration has worked to actively obfuscate the true casualty rates of the war. These are not electoral statistics. They are lives lost, families shattered, and consequences that will endure long after administrations swap office spaces.
For Republicans now scrambling to distance themselves from a deeply unpopular war, the political consequences may be harder to escape than their own voting records. Tuesday’s results show voters are increasingly willing to hold politicians accountable for needless wars, and the suffering inherited from them.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-republi.title: New York Republicans Are Ripping Each Other to Shreds
https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-republi.author: Holly Pretsky
https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-republi.text:
New York City's Republican of the Moment Curtis Sliwa is DEFINITELY NOT demoralized by the absolute shellacking his party got on Tuesday.
"I view this complete tsunami, this blue tsunami, especially when it relates to the 62 counties of New York, as Liberation Day for Republicans who no longer feel that if they're not MAGA, they don't exist," Sliwa told Hell Gate. "You know, 'We're RINOs.' Well, guess what? I'm a proud RINO." (In case you've never seen Fox News, that's a Trumpworld pejorative that stands for "Republican In Name Only.")
The losses went far beyond GOP candidate Bruce Blakeman's double-digit defeat by Governor Kathy Hochul. Republicans lost at least six state Senate seats, at least seven Assembly seats, a major congressional seat in the Hudson Valley, all three statewide races by double-digit margins, and they barely hung onto a seat in the deep red North Country with a pretty embarrassing candidate.
Still, Sliwa's feeling…optimistic.
"This is a perfect opportunity for Republicans to organize and mobilize. The people united will never be defeated," he said. "That's a phrase that is very left-wing, very progressive. But this is what Republicans, if they want to save their party, must begin to do: Stop complaining, stop moaning and groaning. Your whole campaign was to basically call Zohran [Mamdani], you know, attaching him to Hochul, a communist, a socialist, a jihadist, and an Islamist. I don't even think they understand what a communist is. I don't think they understand what an Islamist is. But then again, they just attached it all together, and when all was said and done, Zohran helped Hochul, and Trump helped destroy Team Blakeman and other Republicans who were running under that MAGA mantra."

https://citylimits.org/new-jerseyans-acc.title: New Jerseyans Accused of Stealing NYC Rental Assistance Money, And What Else Happened This Week In Housing
https://citylimits.org/new-jerseyans-acc.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/new-jerseyans-acc.text:
Share This Article
Three New Jersey residents were arrested Wednesday night on charges that they stole over $1 million from New York City’s One Shot Deal program by using fraudulent identities, according to the Department of Investigation.
The city’s Department of Investigation alleges that scammers stole over $1 million from a pool of city money designated to help people facing eviction and homelessness.
The scammers used fake identities and front companies posing as landlords to swindle the city’s New York City’s Human Resources Administration (HRA), the complaint claims.
Tenants behind on rent due to hardship like the loss of a job can apply to New York’s “One Shot Deal” program, which will pay up to six months of back rent and help stave off eviction or homelessness. Allegedly, the defendants used false identities to submit 170 applications to HRA, with the agency approving 94 of them.
The agency rejected most rental assistance applications so far this year, according to Gothamist, often sending them back for resubmission.
In a statement, the Department of Social Services, which oversees HRA, said that its “integrity review process identified these suspicious applications and referred the matter to the Department of Investigation two years ago, exactly as our oversight systems are designed to do.”
The defendants—Erica Williams, Kareem Canty, and Tajizhanae Whitaker—were arrested Wednesday night in New Jersey and charged with conspiracy, wire fraud, and aggravated identity theft. The city’s Department of Investigation investigated alongside the United States Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York, which is prosecuting the case.
“These defendants allegedly manipulated sensitive personal information as well as the City’s One Shot Deal application process to fraudulently divert emergency rental assistance payments,” said DOI Commissioner Nadia Shihata in a statement.
With One Shot Deals, HRA pays landlords directly on behalf of eligible renters. The city issued 54,343 one shot deals in the last fiscal year that ended in July. The year before, the city spent $555 million on the deals, with an average of $9,700 each, according to the New York Housing Conference.
The funds were “intended to keep the most vulnerable New Yorkers in their homes,” said Shihata.
In one instance, investigators allege that Williams submitted a One Shot Deal application from her home IP address in New Jersey. The application listed an address in Rego Park, Queens and included copies of a birth certificate and passport, “belonging to a certain individual that was purportedly Applicant-2 but in fact belonged to someone else,” the charging documents read.
The applicant, who prosecutors allege was Williams, listed the property manager as ALC Development LLC. But the LLC does not own or operate any housing in New York City, according to investigators, and was controlled by Williams. In June 2022, HRA sent seven checks totaling $14,000 to ALC Development LLC’s bank account.
Williams, Canty, and Whitaker allegedly submitted 170 applications from New Jersey computers, using falsified identities and naming three LLCs registered in New Jersey and controlled by Williams as the property managers, the complaint says. Williams then used the LLCs to transfer funds to the personal bank accounts of Canty and Whitaker, the alleged co-conspirators.
Attempts to reach the defendants were unsuccessful.
Here’s what else happened in housing this week—
ICYMI, from City Limits:
- The tallest mural in the U.S. debuted recently in the South Bronx, spanning all 29 stories of a building at NYCHA’s Morrisania Air Rights development.
- Nine homeless New Yorkers who died of hypothermia during last winter’s brutally cold weather were laid to rest this week in Manhattan, after advocates stepped in to claim their remains, which were initially headed for burial at the city’s potter’s field on Hart Island.
- City Hall released a long awaited plan to increase the number of public restrooms across the city, but homeless advocates—who’ve pushed the issue for years as part of a “Free to Pee” campaign—say it lacks detail and funding commitments.
ICYMI, from other local newsrooms:
- The Mamdani administration intervened to try and halt an eviction in Brooklyn which advocates say is a case of deed theft, according to The City Reporter.
- City Hall scored a court victory this week in one of the legal challenges to the mayor’s pied-à-terre tax on pricey second homes, Gothamist reports.
