https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/pent.title: Pentagon Officials Float Names of Hegseth’s Replacement
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/pent.author: Nick Turse
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/pent.text:
Replacements for embattled War Secretary Pete Hegseth are increasingly being discussed at the Pentagon, according to current and former defense officials. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is at the top of many lists. Mike Waltz, the disgraced former national security adviser at the center of the 2025 Signalgate messaging scandal and currently U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, has also been mentioned.
Those and other names have emerged as Hegseth is facing down a bipartisan impeachment effort as early as next week and is in a mad scramble to hold onto his job.
Officials acknowledged that both DeSantis and Waltz were dismal choices, but all who spoke with The Intercept said even the most problematic picks would be preferable to Hegseth, who has been excoriated at the Pentagon and beyond for Signal-gate, his purge of top military leaders, his inability to defeat Yemen’s Houthis in 2025 or win the Iran war in 2026, his campaign of extrajudicial killings in attacks on so-called drug boats, his efforts to weaken transparency and scuttle accountability, and his obsession with troops’ testosterone levels, among other distractions.
In the wake of an election rout that handed Democrats firm control of the House and the Senate, Hegseth is in the crosshairs of lawmakers whom he has treated with contempt for two years. “Dead man walking,” said one official in an exposé published by The Intercept Thursday. Hours after publication of that report, Hegseth launched a desperate bid to stave off his ouster, employing his Fox News-host-honed skills at fanning culture war flames to air his grievances and whip up the support of his boss and the MAGA faithful.
In a video posted on X, the self-styled secretary of war pulled out the stops: “He literally took a bullet for this nation,” Hegseth said amid obsequious flattery of Trump. “He shook his fist and said ‘fight, fight, fight,’ and so will we.”
The chief of what he recently called “the most powerful, most lethal and most prepared military on the planet,” Hegseth cast himself as a besieged victim and tied himself to Trump in a naked attempt to save his job. “A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice,” Hegseth carped in a video filmed outside the Pentagon.
Hegseth was referring to outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who said Wednesday that he plans to reintroduce articles of impeachment for high crimes and misdemeanors when the House is back in session next week. Numerous Democrats have indicated a desire to join Massie’s effort to oust Hegseth since their midterm election landslide, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is poised to be the next speaker.
Hegseth’s missive to Trump hit many hot-button issues that Americans seemingly repudiated in Tuesday’s electoral landslide. He boasted about driving “the weird and the woke” out of the military and took aim at his and Trump’s enemies. “Why do the Democrats and the deep state radicals really hate us? Because we tore down their sacred cows one by one and without apology,” said Hegseth, who rattled off a list of things he has torn down, such as diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives; military efforts to combat climate change; the rechristening of military bases named for Confederate leaders; and the rights of trans service members.
Hegseth’s video rant was part of a doomsday plan coordinated by chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell, first reported by CNN and corroborated by a defense official who spoke with The Intercept. It was accompanied by a coordinated campaign of social media posts by Pentagon underlings trying to tie Hegseth’s fortunes to the president, consisting of photos of the war secretary posturing accompanied by the text, “STAND. FIGHT. DEFEND THE REPUBLIC.”
While it was a brazen attempt to cast any future effort by Trump to cut him loose as an enormous defeat for the president, officials said Parnell’s Hail Mary could succeed. “It’s sad. But it may work because Trump is so easy to manipulate,” said one defense official. “Hegseth knows he is dealing with a president with the mind of a three-year-old.”
During the Pentagon’s Thursday afternoon social media blitz, one of those Hegseth underlings messaged this reporter a clip from the 2013 film “The Wolf of Wall Street,” in which Leonardo DiCaprio’s stockbroker character pivots mid-way through announcing his resignation and a deal with the Securities and Exchange Commission, declaring: “I’m not fucking leaving! … They’re gonna need a fuckin’ wrecking ball to take me outta here!”
The House has only impeached two Cabinet secretaries: William Belknap, the secretary of war, in 1876; and Alejandro Mayorkas, the secretary of homeland security, in 2024. In neither case did the Senate vote to convict. Should Massie’s lame-duck impeachment measure succeed in the House, it would likely languish in the Senate where Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., would have little incentive to bring it to a vote, said a congressional staffer for a member on the Armed Services Committee. Still, some pundits predict Hegseth may not survive the weekend, much less the month or the year.
If and when Hegseth is ousted, there will be no shortage of people jockeying to take his place. In addition to DeSantis and Waltz, other names bandied about at the Pentagon or on Capitol Hill include Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst, a retired military officer who chose not to run for reelection this year, as well as failed Republican Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers, who was defeated by Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. Some of those names were mentioned in a Thursday post on X by James Stavridis, a retired four-star Navy admiral, former supreme Allied Commander of NATO, and partner and vice chair of Carlyle, a global investment firm with deep Pentagon ties. Stavridis also named Mike Pompeo, Trump’s former secretary of state.
While DeSantis and Trump had been bitter rivals during the 2024 Republican presidential primary campaign, the outgoing Florida governor and assumed 2028 GOP presidential hopeful has since vocally supported Trump’s crackpot initiatives. To advance Trump’s anti-immigrant agenda, DeSantis hastily constructed (and then quickly shuttered) “Alligator Alcatraz,” a detention hellhole that the Department of Homeland Security’s watchdog found did not comply with a slew of federal and state standards. The Florida governor was also the first official to use Trump’s renamed “Gulf of America” for the Gulf of Mexico, in an official document.
Amid the rubble of a devastated Republican Party, DeSantis — a longtime culture warrior who rode what he called what he called “woke gender ideology” to national prominence — quickly pivoted. “The ground shifts and the emphasis, then, is on different things,” he said on Wednesday. “Four years ago, we were in that peak woke era. … Now, the issues are different and Republicans, it seemed like, in some of the ads I was seeing, with how much money they were spending, they really were fighting yesterday’s battle.”
DeSantis also has a troubling military background. As a lieutenant in the Judge Advocate General’s Corps — a role akin to that of a first-year associate at a law firm — he served at the notorious American prison at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba. He also served in the failed forever war in Iraq, as a senior legal adviser to the commander of SEAL Team One in Fallujah.
Asked about DeSantis’s standing within the Pentagon, an official said: “Anything is better than Hegseth.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/demo.title: Is There a Left Candidate for President?
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/demo.author: Akela Lacy
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/06/demo.text:
The race for 2028 is already starting, and progressives are all asking one question: Who will take up the left’s mantle in the next presidential election?
An obvious first choice for many self-described leftists, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., has said she is seriously considering a run. Ocasio-Cortez laid the groundwork for a potential presidential bid rooted in economic populism and “fighting oligarchy” while campaigning alongside Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., for midterm candidates around the country this cycle.
Democratic strategists, however, have pointed out it would be far easier for Ocasio-Cortez to run for Democratic New York Sen. Chuck Schumer’s seat in 2028; and it’s even possible the 75-year-old presumptive majority leader will retire.
There isn’t a clear pick for another Democratic candidate with star power who could mount a truly progressive campaign — presenting the left with the threat of losing the momentum that fueled a democratic socialist wave during the primaries and animated campaigns across the ideological spectrum on Tuesday.
That, said her former spokesperson Lauren Hitt, is not Ocasio-Cortez’s problem.
“I think the wrong reason to run would be because nobody else is running in the progressive lane,” said Hitt, who now advises progressive and moderate candidates. “She has made a lot of good investments in the midterms and in helping build up the progressive bench, but it was not her job to make sure we had another person to run.”
(Representatives for Ocasio-Cortez did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)
So if Ocasio-Cortez doesn’t run from the left, who will?
The Field So Far
Candidates exploring potential presidential bids include a few newer faces alongside a very similar cast of moderates who campaigned for the Democratic nomination in the 2016 and 2020 primaries.
Names like New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, and even the party’s former nominee Kamala Harris are making the rounds; Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., has also laid the groundwork for a run. The recently reelected Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has long been viewed as a potential contender, as has Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, though he said last month he’s not planning on a run.
None of them are people you would necessarily liken to someone like Ocasio-Cortez or the grandfather of the movement behind her, Sanders himself.
Rep. Ro Khanna of California is so far the most “progressive” person openly considering a run. Khanna served as national co-chair of Sanders’s 2020 presidential campaign, and he’s long been a voice for an anti-interventionist foreign policy. He drew the ire of tech billionaires for supporting a wealth tax in California.
Yet there’s a palpable skepticism around Khanna among leftists, even if they can’t quite put their finger on why. Some weren’t impressed when he defended his support for funding Israel’s Iron Dome missile defense system after publicizing an arrest in the West Bank earlier this year. (Khanna later came out against funding the Iron Dome). And as a multimillionaire, he’s also drawn criticism from the right and the left for his personal wealth.
Like Ocasio-Cortez, Khanna has said he will back Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., for House Speaker despite pledges from other candidates to withhold their support for either Jeffries or Schumer, both moderates, for leadership positions next session.
Leveraging Economic Populism
It’s still incredibly early, but there’s one unifying theme emerging from Tuesday’s results for whichever candidate decides to try to court the progressive vote.
“All I know is that the populist lane is wide open for someone to seize it,” said Ravi Mangla, the spokesperson for the Working Families Party.
Victories over the past two years, from Zohran Mamdani’s election as mayor of New York City to the clutch of democratic socialists and progressives heading to Congress in January, show that Democrats can marshal discontent with Donald Trump and the far right to elect candidates running on progressive policies.
”Voters were very clear: People are very, very angry,” said Greg Krieg, a progressive Democratic strategist who works with Slingshot Strategies and is the spokesperson for the pro-Palestine super PAC American Priorities. “There is a focus on economic populism that transcends the ideological splits in the party.”
With the rising cost of living, and candidates tapping into that populism, the question for progressives is how to best wield the blue version of economic populism against the right-wing version that powered Trump’s rise.
“Right-wing populism didn’t really defeat left-wing populism, it just ran against a kind of corporate slop for many years,” Krieg said.
This era’s new “kitchen table” issues are a constellation of economic woes that voters are increasingly connecting to the forces concentrating wealth and political power in the hands of the few. Democrats should respond to that by fighting, visibly, against the things that take money out of people’s pockets, corruption and price-gouging among them, Krieg said.
“I think that the American people, if they are presented a choice of right-wing populism and left-wing populism, will opt for the left-wing populism,” Krieg said. “And I think that’s quadruply true now that we’ve done the right-wing populism experiment and it’s been such a fiasco — so let’s give them that option.”
The factors influencing how Democrats approach 2028 are taking shape now. They include the debate over who will lead the party in the House and Senate, though any effort to stop Schumer or Jeffries from leading roles would face long odds. And how Democrats fare in the next presidential race will depend in large part on what they do with their control of Congress during the last two years of Trump’s final term in office.
DSA Endorsement?
Then there is the group that helped power the rise of Ocasio-Cortez, Mamdani, the next mayors of Washington and Los Angeles, and the largest incoming bloc of socialist members of Congress in history: the Democratic Socialists of America.
Any candidate that gets buy-in from DSA will have to support policies like Medicare for All, taxing the rich, a Green New Deal, and an embargo on U.S. arms to Israel. DSA, which endorsed both Sanders’s 2016 and 2020 primary bids, is running a presidential exploratory committee that will eventually vote to endorse a candidate after collecting input from its members.
DSA passed a resolution to explore a 2028 endorsement at its national convention last year. And there isn’t necessarily a consensus among its members — more than 125,000 people across 130 chapters in 43 states — on whether or not they want to see Ocasio-Cortez run, said Ella Teevan, who chairs the group’s presidential exploratory group and sits on its National Political Committee.
“The Bernie case feels just a little bit different because I think the membership was a little bit more united around Bernie, although by no means unanimously,” Teevan said. “If and when we do consider an AOC endorsement, hers will be a little bit more contentious. But like I said, that’s the beauty of DSA.”
Though Ocasio-Cortez is no shoo-in, DSA members haven’t coalesced around any other candidate — and it’s not clear they will.
“I know that there are other quote-unquote progressives who might be considering a presidential run in 2028, but I think it’s really clear for us that they need to support DSA’s core demands that most people in the United States support,” Teevan said.
“If a candidate were to come along who supported those policies, I think a considerable portion of membership would think about whether we should endorse them,” she said. “But yeah, I don’t think that there’s a natural other person with name recognition in the field that, at least, I can think of right now.”
And there may yet be candidates who enter the race who aren’t yet on the radar, said Hitt, Ocasio-Cortez’s former spokesperson: “It’s totally possible there’s a progressive champion who could fill that lane that we aren’t even thinking of yet.”

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: From the streets of Lagos to the Chanel catwalk: how a creative’s thrift-shop style took her to Paris
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Valentine Benjamin in Lagos
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
Before Paris, there was Lagos, with its busy markets, roadside stalls and maze of disorderly streets. And then there was Rachel Ojuromi, sashaying through it all and turning the everyday into an unlikely catwalk.
For the past six months, Ojuromi has taken social media by storm, transforming the vibrant streets of Lagos into her personal runway, showcasing designs made from secondhand, thrifted clothes and scraps mostly sourced from local open-air hubs such as Yaba market.
Her childhood friend, neighbour and stylist, Debby Fasingha, puts her looks together. Filmed in Gbagada, Yaba and other parts of Lagos without disrupting traffic, the videos often draw amused stares, smiles and cheers from pedestrians, traders and drivers as she struts past.
In one video, Ojuromi turns a busy Lagos road into a runway, walking confidently through traffic with a tray of bananas balanced on her head. In another, she sits drinking tea with a teenage boy at a table outside a street-side shop, with a kettle in front of them.
The shot was inspired by a Japanese advertising campaign; she had imagined the scene but needed someone to play the tea drinker. When a passerby, curious about the filming, was told that they needed an extra, she went off and brought back her son to appear in the shot.
For Ojuromi, better known on Instagram as Give Rachel a Shot, that unexpected moment sums up the joy of shooting fashion photos in Lagos.
“There is something meaningful about knowing that a particular image or video exists because of a moment that happened at a specific time and place,” she says. “Even if somebody tries to recreate it, it will never be the same.”
That instinct for finding beauty in the everyday has helped take the 22-year-old Nigerian from filming in Lagos markets to a Chanel fashion show.
Ojuromi’s love of creativity started long before she embraced it as her digital identity. Growing up, she was surrounded by clothes because her mother sold them in local markets, but she first aspired to a career in medicine. Inspired by Gifted Hands, the autobiography of Ben Carson, an African-American doctor from Detroit, she dreamed of becoming a neurosurgeon who breaks down barriers.
But after complications with her college application, she took a year off and began exploring film-making. She eventually decided that surgery was not for her.
“I wanted to contribute something meaningful and push boundaries,” she says. “I discovered that I could pursue that ambition through creativity rather than medicine.”
The Lagos videos began with experiments in creative direction and street photography. Working with Fasingha, Ojuromi started reinterpreting global fashion collections using secondhand clothes and wardrobe finds before taking the creations to the streets.
“One of my mantras is to live within the reality of your situation,” she says. “I am not going to spend money on something I cannot afford simply because I want to create a particular look.
“We are more interested in the conversations happening around those clothes. We ask ourselves what the designer is trying to communicate through the collection. What is the central message? What is the cultural reference?”
For six months, beginning in March this year, she and her team committed themselves to publishing a new fashion video every day.
Then Chanel came calling.
Ojuromi and Fasingha had created looks inspired by the fashion house’s Métiers d’Art 2026 collection. After Chanel’s casting director, Anita Bitton, gave them the go-ahead to publish their versions, their clip caught the attention of several influential figures in fashion, including Chanel’s creative director, Matthieu Blazy.
The conversations that followed eventually took Ojuromi from Lagos to Paris, where she walked for the Chanel spring/summer 2027 show at the Grand Palais last month.
But her ambitions extend well beyond modelling. She is also a film-maker, creative director and founder and editor of the Process Africa, a platform promoting young African creatives.
Launched in 2023 following an event organised by her young artist friend Temidayo Aríṣe, it aims to address the barriers faced by young artists, designers, photographers and other creatives in Africa, particularly those who struggle to access the opportunities needed to establish themselves.
“I remember looking around [at the event] and thinking that somebody needed to tell the stories of these people,” she says.
Her aim is also based on the idea that African creativity should not have to justify itself through its geographical identity.
“I don’t want people to constantly feel the need to introduce their work as African fashion or African art, as though it belongs to a separate category,” she says. “It is fashion. It is art. It is music. It is creativity.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Chad Harbach’s Novel of Millennial Intellectuals
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Kevin Lozano
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
A Dangerous Feeling
Chad Harbach’s novel of millennial intellectuals
Chad Harbach’s Novel of Millennial Intellectuals
In The Brightness, Harbach examines life before 2016.
In season six of Sex and the City, Carrie’s budding relationship with her new boyfriend, a novelist named Jack Berger, falls apart after they argue about an article of clothing that features prominently in his latest book. Carrie can’t get over the scrunchie. No New York woman, Carrie insists—especially the protagonist of his novel—would be caught dead wearing one. Berger dismisses her, but the argument still gnaws at him: He is keen to prove Carrie wrong, and he thinks he does when he spots a scrunchie-wearing woman at a “hip downtown restaurant,” but she ends up being a tourist. The fashion choices of early 2000s tourists aside, the entire fracas highlights a greater issue in their relationship: Why did he think he knew better in the first place?
Books in review
The Brightness: A Novel
Buy this book
The matter of the scrunchie is more than just a relationship mishap; one can’t help but wonder if Berger is all that competent in his chosen field. If he got the scrunchie wrong, how much else did he miss? Put another way, what is the proper barometer for judging realism in fiction: Is it meant to hold up a mirror to our world so that we might see it more clearly? Or more pointedly: What does Berger’s insistence say about his ability to understand and make claims on what women are like? Most readers might agree with Carrie here—that the scrunchie is not just a scrunchie, but a sign that Berger is a man (and a writer) whose sense of the world is not to be trusted.
In Chad Harbach’s new novel, The Brightness, we are transported back to 2015 and 2016, when the great signifying detail in the dress of urban millennial men is described as follows: “The trend in menswear” in this period “was toward an insinuation of gayness, in the form of slim striped tank tops and tight-fitting shorts.” We could debate what Harbach means by “insinuation,” but the point is clear enough: Truly fashionable dudes can see around the corner and have stocked up on big pants and flowing fabrics. And his idea of heterosexual male attractiveness flatters that of the putative novel reader: the kind of guy who wears “moss green jacket[s]” and “cognac boots” and writes book reviews for New York’s little magazines.
It’s the women of The Brightness—a mixed cohort of feminist students at Westish College, early-career editors and writers, and in one case the owner of a small brewery in Red Hook—whose modes of dress Harbach spends many pages describing. More than once, a student’s red lipstick is made to indicate her determination to court notoriety. The game of attention-seeking moves beyond makeup, Harbach tells us, because women, more than men, must think about how they look and what it says about them—whether it’s owning things like “wide-legged golden jumpsuits” or a vintage “kimono-like mini-wrap,” or knowing that “a certain shade of yellow, a rich pastured egg-yolk hue, [is] destined to rule New York that season.”
If Carrie compelled us to consider the scrunchie, what do we think Harbach is trying to do here? What does all this grousing about clothing say about that fateful year before the American lexicon expanded to include phrases like “shithole country” and “pussy hat”? Is he saying that we shouldn’t take for granted how easy we once had it? Does he mean to mourn these years? Or is his verdict on 2015 and 2016 much uglier—as ugly as a wide-legged golden jumpsuit?
Like many a campus novel before it, The Brightness begins with a prank. It’s the start of the school year at Westish, and before classes have commenced, frat row is crowded with revelers. Three students—Irma, Pammy, and Dahlia—have been talking all summer about making a statement at their little Midwestern school’s annual bacchanal, known as “the Parties.”
The three call themselves the “Witches of Westish.” And what they mean to expose is something rotten at the heart of the campus experience: what in the 2010s was often called “rape culture,” the latest moniker for a source of conflict and pain that every generation of college students has faced in one way or another, including today. (It should be no surprise that there remains little accountability on the matter within higher education, as the ongoing case of the Cornell 7 has recently made clear.)
To address the violence and assaults on their campus, the Witches of Westish set out to do a performance piece. Targeting a trio of incapacitated jocks at the Parties, they plan to stamp temporary tattoos on their foreheads that read “Rape Victim.” The next day, the jocks would wake up, look in the mirror, and discover the message imprinted on them, in ink that is very hard to wash off. They would be walking advertisements for the project’s goal: To make visible the sexual violence that pervades college life.
The Witches only manage to tattoo two of the jocks, because Irma is excused from her duties. She has too much to lose: A child of working-class rural Wisconsin, Irma is a scholarship kid, and the coven doesn’t want to risk screwing up her life. Her job instead is a more literary one: She is responsible for writing the Witches’ “manifesto,” which the college newspaper publishes soon after the men are tattooed. In a few weeks’ time, the prank makes the national news, and the Witches are famous, Dahlia most of all. After being suspended, she becomes, in short order, a martyr, then a blogger and podcaster for an online feminist magazine (à la Jezebel) called The Brightness. The other two Witches are noticed as well: At a wedding later in the novel, Irma is even offered the chance to write for The New Yorker.
That this might all sound a bit confusing is natural—Irma, our guide for most of the novel, spends her last year of college utterly bewildered—by her future, by all the attention, by desire. Yet the fact that this opening set piece might be more than a little ridiculous is perhaps the point. In many ways, The Brightness bears a striking resemblance to Tom Wolfe’s 2004 novel I Am Charlotte Simmons—a bleak right-wing satire of campus politics in which Wolfe targeted what he felt to be the crass sexual mores and hollow politics of university students. But Harbach’s handling of the Witches’ scheme is more curious: He can’t quite seem to decide whether his subjects are half-baked pseudo-intellectuals or are perhaps worth taking seriously.
What is stranger still is that the prank is only one of the novel’s many tangled plot lines, all which converge at a New England wedding to celebrate the nuptials of Owen Dunne, a young gay novelist who first appeared as one of the heroes in Harbach’s debut novel, 2011’s The Art of Fielding, and who has also written a critically acclaimed novel by the name of The Art of Fielding.
The veil between the two novels is lifted by Pella, another of the heroes of The Art of Fielding. In that book, Pella was 23, about to divorce her much older husband, and she landed at Westish looking for safe haven with her estranged father, the college’s president. By the novel’s end, her father has died after a heart attack (brought on, it is implied, by his invigorating affair with Owen), and Pella has shacked up with the captain of the baseball team, Mike Schwartz, and decided to get her life back on track by enrolling at Westish.
Four years have passed when we meet her again in The Brightness. Pella is now a recent graduate and engaged to Mike. She is also, we learn, best friends with Irma and was the first (but uncredited) editor of Owen’s now-successful novel. And despite publicly professing happiness for her friends, she feels somewhat used by them, or at least underappreciated, and her attraction to Mike has waned. The novel’s second (and, arguably, primary) plot involves Pella’s post-college life and her fumbling attempts at cultivating an identity away from the people she has helped nurture. And it should be no surprise that her bildungsroman is pockmarked by many indignities; more than any other character in this novel, Pella is a tragic figure.
The metafictional sleight of hand at the center of The Brightness lacks a certain elegance; it is hard to justify, I think, the need for an Art of Fielding Extended Universe. Still, it is worth pausing here to examine the binary that Harbach’s two books represent. The Art of Fielding is about male friendship and presents a vision of a nontoxic version of it, in which throwing a baseball and quoting Marcus Aurelius might allow men to find the best in each other. The Brightness, on the other hand, is about the mysteries of female friendship, which, in Harbach’s telling, is passionate, without logic, and guided by petty jealousies. Irma and Pella, the novel’s main dyad, spend most of the book apart, their friendship strained by the tattoo prank and what it says about their divergent ambitions: Irma is hungry for accolades and attention, while Pella is more than willing to follow a traditional path after having such a late start to her adulthood.
The two novels differ in another crucial way. The Art of Fielding was confined to what took place either on the baseball diamond or on the campus itself; it made no attempt to supply its readers with an argument about the state of the world at the time. Certainly, a lot was happening in 2012 that was on the minds of college-age kids: America had yet to recover from the 2008 financial crisis, though the anger and sense of precarity that suffused the elder members of the millennial generation are completely absent from that novel’s idyll. In part, that separation from the world was to the novel’s benefit: It allowed The Art of Fielding to be charming and spritely precisely because of its light touch and its pleasing accounts of baseball; indeed, Harbach marked himself as one of the most talented describers of the act of fielding itself—the fluid beauty of a shortstop at work. The world, by contrast, weighs down The Brightness. Leaving aside all the acrobatic leaps required to make the novel fit within the fictional world of its predecessor, The Brightness is crammed with references to recent history: There are mentions of Trump and Bernie, Lana Del Rey and blogging, and, of course, all of those clothes and Harbach’s many thoughts on how people looked and acted in the 2010s.
The accumulation of proper nouns and era-specific details invites us to judge Harbach’s rendering of the 2010s against our own experience.

Granted, my own sense of things is very much defined by the fact that I was a college student during the years Harbach is writing about. I am therefore either the ideal or the worst possible reader of this novel. I find that it is at once clotted by nostalgia—for craft beer and little magazines—and totally dismissive (lest we forget how Harbach feels about skinny jeans or red lipstick) of the years it has chosen to ruminate on. Rather than coolly distant or artfully ambiguous, the tone of The Brightness often comes across as diffident. The treatment of its two central characters, Irma and Pella, exemplifies this ambivalence. Harbach is especially unsure of his feelings toward these women: They are brilliant and beautiful and beacons of a possible future, but they also get dragged through the mud, humiliated over and over again. Their fitful struggles to “find themselves” might serve as fuel for the plot’s engine, but Harbach’s judgments of this generation of women and their struggles can verge on cruel or seem pointless.
We spend hundreds of pages with Irma and Pella, line after line devoted to what’s going on inside their heads, and yet their psychological complexities often boil down to the question of whether to commit one’s life to making art or to making a family. Irma chooses the former, Pella the latter, but both paths leave them insecure at the novel’s end. At one point, after much agita, Irma concludes: “You could be an intellectual and yourself, but not without an irksome sense of narrowness, penury, and incompletion. You couldn’t enjoy, relax, have fun, take pleasure, cut loose, party, whatever you wanted to call it.” Ultimately, this same binary casts its shadow on Pella’s story. She knows some clock is ticking (“When the powers that be get bored and move on, that’s when things get really bad. Then you have to figure out how to be something other than the thing you’ve spent your whole life trying to be,” she says at one point), and she upends her life trying to outrun what she feels to be the forces of some shabby fate.
These tortured lines of thought are meant to signal that both women are working through something, that once they can reconcile the contradictions of mind and body, they may finally be able to enter the world. Or, alternatively, these contradictions can’t be reconciled—that to achieve the thing one wants also requires denying other lives that could be lived, other ways of being. But are either of these points all that terribly revealing? And who is Irma, really? What we know of her is that she wants to do well, and she wants to be liked; she wants to have the right opinions and, ideally, to elicit the respect of the public at large. She is quirky and culturally literate—she even named her cat Anderson Cooper!—but all we learn about Irma is that her hardships across these pages have left her with a dangerous feeling: the desire to write a novel.
Pella’s fate is even worse. By the end of The Brightness, she has left Mike for Nick, a freelance writer by night and accountant by day whom she meets at Owen’s wedding. This is no act of liberation either: “The Most Fucked Man in America,” Pella learns, isn’t exactly a catch. Despite it all, she rushes headlong into the relationship, in part because she is drawn to Nick’s mother, a reclusive and retired feminist artist named Sylvie. It is Sylvie who imparts the novel’s great lesson: You can make art, or you can make babies, but if you do both, one will negatively influence the other, no matter what. A stark lesson indeed—especially since the product of Sylvie’s own toils is that worst of all things, a book critic. Nick is also, unbeknownst to him, a father to be: Pella learns that she is pregnant in the novel’s final pages and decides that a family—with or without Nick—is what she wants. So after hundreds of pages, we are left with a choice as old as the novel itself: book or baby?
That these are the two paths on offer might leave some readers feeling a bit insulted, but Harbach, for just a moment, indulges in the idea that our heroes can have it both ways. There are half-joking hints that the two, together, can fashion a world in which they could raise the future child and future novel without the assistance of men: “I could help with your book, you could help with my baby,” Pella says to Irma. She thinks to herself, flying high on this dose of utopia, that “friendship could be a looser, freer realm within which to try the tender experiment of living and of nurturing life—away from the structures and strictures, the painful overemphasis, attached to romantic love.” Just as quickly, Irma casts some doubt: “A world without men,” she says with a dash of irony. And Pella laughs: “Maybe not entirely.”
We are told, though, that “this new life continued to unfurl in Pella’s mind” and that maybe, just maybe, she and Irma might find a loophole, one less preordained than the novel might imply. Yet if this is where we end up, why have us marooned in the 2010s at all? It could be that stalking such optimism is the sense that in just a few weeks, and for years to come as well, the world will change, and whatever future these women imagine for themselves and their progeny will be all but foreclosed. That like the clothes, the hopeful sentiments of 2015 and early 2016 were passing ones, and that the choices before us today are not as simple as book or baby.

Russia’s Last Independent Newspaper Is Going Dark
The closing of “Novaya Gazeta” marks the end of what little press freedom remained in Putin’s Russia.
Novaya Gazeta—one of Russia’s last bastions of independent journalism—will publish a final issue and shut down next week.
The paper has faced mounting institutional pressures: It was evicted from its office space and labeled a foreign agent by the Kremlin, and banks have refused Novaya their services. Its reader-supported funding platform was also shut down.
The fact that the publication survived for this long is a testament to its reporters’ extraordinary bravery. Since its founding in 1993, Novaya has earned international acclaim for reporting in areas including human rights violations during the second Chechen War, the persecution of Chechnya’s LGBT community, and abuse inside Russian prisons. Over its years of courageous muckraking, six Novaya journalists were killed, including the crusading reporter Anna Politkovskaya.
After Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and the free-speech crackdown that followed, much of the paper’s staff fled to Latvia, where they launched Novaya Gazeta Europe. This outlet is expected to continue operations—but its website is blocked in Russia.
However, while the original paper will soon cease publication, readers and historians can still access its work. Kronika, a project from PEN America and Bard College dedicated to preserving journalism at risk of suppression, is digitizing the newspaper’s entire archive. In doing so, the project is keeping Novaya’s ideals and principles alive.
Novaya cofounder and former editor in chief Dmitrii Muratov told Columbia Journalism Review that, if not for the archive, decades of Russia’s historical memory could vanish. And if such a public record were lost, he said, “we would not know how dictatorships take shape.”
To mark the legacy of this singular newspaper, The Nation is republishing the piece below, which I originally wrote when Muratov and the Filipino American journalist Maria Ressa were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021.
In the Nobel lecture he delivered later that year, Muratov saluted his colleagues, who risked their lives to hold those in power to account and promote the public interest.
“We are the prerequisite for progress,” he said. “We are the antidote against tyranny.”
The following was originally published in The Nation, October 8, 2021.
A Courageous Voice for Press Freedom and Independence in Russia
As the Nobel Prize committee recognized with today’s award to Dmitrii Muratov, independent journalism and media freedom in Russia confront growing threats.
katrina vanden heuvel
I and my late husband, Stephen Cohen, first met Dmitrii Muratov in 1993. He and a few other colleagues had gathered in the basement cafeteria of Moscow News—then a bold newspaper of the glasnost era—to plan the launch of Novaya Gazeta. Survival was on their minds at that time; they were beginning the paper with two computers, one printer, two rooms—and no money for salaries. A few months later, an initial boost of support came from President Mikhail Gorbachev, who contributed part of his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize money to buy the newspaper its first computers.
Nearly 30 years later, the newspaper has another Nobel in its history. On October 8, Muratov was jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize with Filipina journalist Maria Ressa “for their efforts to safeguard freedom of expression, which is a precondition for democracy and lasting peace.”
I knew in 1993 that “Dima” was a bold and creative editor. What I did not foresee was that he would become such a vital defender and advocate of press freedom in Russia. The newspaper, which continues to publish against great odds, has paid a heavy price for its crusading investigations into Putin’s and other high-level officials’ corruption, human rights violations, the persecution of the LGBT community in Chechnya, right-wing nationalist extremism, and abuses of power. The paper has also spent decades carefully tracing Stalin’s crimes in newly opened archives.
Six of its courageous reporters—among them Anna Politkovskaya, who was killed exactly 15 years ago—have been murdered for their unflinching investigations. (Fewer than half the killings have been solved.) “When Anya was killed, I called an emergency editorial meeting and wanted to close down the paper,” Muratov told me once. “I told my staff no story is worth dying for. But they wouldn’t let me do it.… I knew we had to go on.”
Muratov is not afraid to publish dissenting, oppositionist views on Crimea, Donbas, Syria, and growing poverty and the abuse of civil liberties in Russia. He handles at least 10 lawsuits a month—filed by official organs. It is remarkable that amid the escalating crackdown on press freedom, he has managed to preserve a sense of humor and visibly enjoy mentoring a new generation of investigative journalists—and readers. Elena Milashina, who started at Novaya in her late 20s, is one of those journalists; since the publication of her article in March documenting the murders of LGBT people and reporting on the cold-blooded murders instigated by Chechnya’s leader Ramzan Kadyrov, she has faced physical threats and death threats.
Indeed, most of the journalists working at the paper are like Milashina: the same age as, or a few years older than, the publication itself. Younger generations may not read the print edition, but Novaya’s print circulation as of October 2021 is 90,000, social-media traffic is 30 million a month, and its website receives 8 million to 11 million monthly page views.

The paper’s founding independence was boosted by the fact that, until 2006, Novaya journalists owned 100 percent of its stock. In 2006, to secure a capital infusion, Muratov persuaded his staff to sell 49 percent of their stock to Gorbachev (10 percent) and a partner, mini-oligarch Aleksandr Lebedev (39 percent). Lebedev invested nearly $4 million to raise staff salaries, upgrade the paper’s offices, and turn Novaya into a paper with national reach. (In 2015, Lebedev stopped funding Novaya, revealing in a Guardian interview that he had ceased because of the expense and also the strain.)
Fifteen years after Politkovskaya’s murder, nearly 30 years after Novaya was founded, independent journalism and media freedom in Russia confront growing threats. An array of media regulations and laws, the labeling of independent media outlets as “foreign agents,” and increasingly restrictive regulation of the Internet are all deeply troubling. Some Russian media analysts and journalists believe that many of these new restrictions are fueled by the West’s anti-Russian sanctions, increasing political tensions, and a deepening and dangerous cold war. In such times, the already narrow space for diversity of views and freedom of speech shrinks. Many analysts also see the culture of impunity—the ongoing failure to hold accountable those who threaten, attack, or kill journalists—as posing a grave threat to media freedom and democracy itself.
How Dmitrii Muratov has navigated for decades the dangerous waters of Russian politics—he has friends across all levels of Russian society, including top politicians—often irritates members of Russia’s more hard-core opposition and some Western observers, who think he has sold out to the Kremlin. As I ventured onto Twitter this morning to post a congratulatory note, a cat lover named Svetlana posted: “With tremendous respect to Dmitry—in Russia there is a saying, ‘If he’s still alive, he’s working for them.’ I admire his courage. And so did Peskov [Putin’s press secretary]. Where does it leave us? Thank you.”
Muratov has used his influence and connections not for his personal ambitions, nor to enrich himself, but to keep alive one of the last havens of investigative journalism inside Russia. The Nobel Prize will likely give Novaya and Muratov domestic protection, but may well also earn Muratov more enemies among the Putin elite, who will allege that he has betrayed the country for awards and foreign funds. What matters, as Muratov said on learning of Oslo’s call, are “Igor Domnikov, Yuri Shchekochikhin, Anna Politkovskaya, Stas Markelov, Nastya Baburova—these are the people who won the Nobel Prize today.”
Today’s prize will be wind at the back for all Russian investigative journalists.

An Effective AI Pushback Has to Go Beyond the Local
The midterms made clear that Americans are angry about the headlong rush into artificial intelligence. We are blocked from needed federal action for now, but states and localities have options that can move us toward eventual national regulation.
Last week’s election returns embodied a broad, national, and bipartisan reaction against data centers. In forty-six of the forty-seven local referenda held across some thirteen states, voters rejected new data center construction. Public opposition reflects local concerns about water usage, grid sustainability, and noise pollution. This opposition is also bubbling up at a moment when most of the public distrusts artificial intelligence (AI) in general, when two-thirds of Americans hold negative views of AI firms and their close ties to the Trump administration, and when fears about AI rank high among Americans’ leading worries.
This confluence of AI-adjacent fears is no accident. Each anxious spark leaps from a different facet of a single Silicon Valley strategy for hyperscaling AI. If this strategy works, it would induce a dramatic decline in labor’s income share of income. If it fails, it would saddle the state with crushing mountains of debt.
Voters, to be sure, likely perceive this dilemma only weakly. Yet their vivid fears create a chance for the Left to articulate a comprehensive diagnosis of hyperscale AI’s manifold problems — one that not only affirms the public’s fears but also articulates a coherent response. And just as the Silicon Valley strategy runs on a logic of scale, so too an effectual pushback must escalate beyond the local.
Heads, AI Wins. Tails, You Lose.
Generative AI is being developed by a small handful of firms. They are taking on massive amounts of debt to build computing power on which costly new tools can be offered at scale. Given the size of these investments, the firms are commercially viable only if they sell their wares at scale. This means either tapping hidden wellsprings of productivity growth (unlikely) or being used as a low-marginal-cost substitute for white-collar labor (more likely).
The ensuing debt-fueled displacement of white-collar labor, if successful, will induce a massive shift of income from labor to capital, as even the AI firms concede. The ruination of ecosystems and acceleration of the climate crisis are mere side effects. There is strong historical evidence of technology’s corrosive effect on the labor share: recent data from Europe suggests that AI, no less than other recent tech leaps, causes losses to labor and corresponding gains to capital. Worse, because most democracies tax capital at lower rates than labor, that shift will constrict the state, diminishing its fiscal capacity to cushion job losses and declining wages. In effect, hyperscale AI creates a distributional crisis and robs the state of tools to address it.
Of course, this strategy might not work. AI might not be transformative as its boosters claim. Markets may lose their nerve before profits can be reaped. But if the AI strategy isn’t successful, the leading firms now dominant in public equity markets (and hence our pensions and 401[k]s), will almost certainly demand a “rescue” akin to the 2008–9 federal financial-crisis interventions.
As of August, hyperscale AI firms had accrued more than $500 million in debt from private equity, banks, and institutional investors such as Blackrock and Pimco. If that debt sours, the repercussions of the crisis, as in 2008–9, would likely force the government’s hand. If that happens, a massive transfer of risk to public balance sheets will follow. This is capitalism as a “heads I win, tails you lose” proposition.
Whether or not it founders, hyperscale AI capitalism will cleave open immense lost opportunities for society at large. On one estimate, US AI investments will add up to some $10.3 trillion between 2025 and 2032, or an average of 3.63 percent of US gross domestic product per year. This is $10 trillion that will not and cannot be spend on maternal care, pre-K education, cancer treatment, environmental mitigation, or any other social programs and planetary reparative work we desperately need. It is, by any measure, a staggering divergence of investment away from areas of urgent moral priority.
No wonder, then, that the American public has such profound anxieties. The data center build-outs are simply the most apparent of the many economic, political, fiscal, and environmental crises that hyperscale AI is inducing.
Building Toward a National Response
What then might be an effectual response? Except in Harwood, North Dakota, voters have pushed back at a local level by denying construction permission, or in Perry, Ohio, demanding that firms post a bond as insurance against the risk of fiscal implosion. Localities’ responses are circumscribed, though, by their limited powers and their small geographic reach. Cities and counties can do little about the labor market effects or fiscal risk. Many environmental costs associated with new demands on the electric grid are out of their reach. Some cities such as Austin and San Antonio own and operate their own electrical utilities, giving them a lever that doesn’t exist elsewhere in the country. But these are exceptions. Solely local responses are usually tightly constrained.
Since the effects of hyperscale AI capitalism emerge at the national level, it would ideally be the federal government that drives a comprehensive response. Pessimism about the prospect of federal action is wise for now. After Tuesday’s election, Trump reiterated his belief that data centers are “gold . . . only foolish leadership will say NO.” His December 2025 executive order, barring states from regulating AI, remains in force, although the legal theories upon which it rests are flawed. Even if a Democratic-controlled House and Senate can overcome his veto, any resulting AI legislation will likely be weak thanks to the need to assemble supermajorities to ensure bills’ passage.
The difficulty of federal action, however, does not mean that progressives should give up addressing hyperscale AI capitalism. They still have ways to use both their control at the state level and at the regional level to highlight its costsand offer the beginnings of a commensurate response — indeed, one that might be fully nationalized in two years.
In January, Democrats will have “trifectas” in twenty-two states and hold the governor’s office in seven more (Kansas and Alaska are still not called as I write). This is a first platform for action. To date, states’ responses have been reactive and purely negative: New York’s and Oregon’s governors paused data center construction, while laws imposing moratoria have been introduced but not passed in sixteen states. Advocates of successful local ballot initiatives have indicated that they plan to turn to bans in their states.
Yet a pause is not a policy. It does nothing to communicate the complex and interconnected harms of hyperscale AI capitalism. So it leaves the field open for AI’s advocates to advance their tall tales of illimitable gain. Nor does it prevent the building of data centers elsewhere in the nation and so does nothing to rein in its fiscal and labor costs.
An alternate approach would be for states to force tech firms to not just account for the local effects of data centers but also recognize and take responsibility for all the social costs of their hyperscale strategy. It would seek to channel economic development into less costly, more decent forms. Bans, however, are a badly formed tool to this subtle end.
As a start, states could recognize their own complicity in hyperscale AI. In forty states, data centers benefit from exemptions from the sales and use taxes that would ordinarily accrue on building materials, machinery, and equipment. The nominal justification for such exemptions is the jobs new builds purportedly bring. But a data center at best tends to create only two or three hundred jobs, with no long-term effect on wages. Where a landlord like Equinix, Data Realty, or CyrusOne rents computing power to remote clients, even that meager gain goes unrealized.
States’ and localities’ ensuing revenue loss is hard to measure, because only some of the states with these tax exemptions report their fiscal effect. Texas, however, lost some $1 billion in FY2025; in 2024, Illinois lost $370 million; and Arizona lost $19 million. A simple first step is terminating all these tax exemptions on the ground that the local benefits from data centers have been illusory, following Maine’s example. That might also prompt states to reconsider more generally their blind pursuit of corporate investments through tax relief.
Having withdrawn their reckless subsidies, states should follow Perry, Ohio’s lead by forcing tech firms to bear the social costs of their speculative investments. New construction, for example, might be conditioned on bonds tied to the environmental and state-level labor market effects of their business models. Firms would first be required to report not only on expected environmental harms (including from increased energy demand) but also address whether a data center’s expected uses will displace human labor or otherwise have wage-suppressive effects (as a leading study has already found). It would then have to post bonds sufficient to pay for state investments to buffer those effects.
The law might impel an AI-funded guarantee fund to sustain state unemployment payouts and retraining costs generated by AI. States could also require that data center investments be backed by sufficient nondebt financing to mitigate any risk of catastrophic fiscal events. And even if data centers are not fully banned, states might simply target specific uses as verboten — say, the large-scale automation of American jobs. Firms that flout this would see their centers shut down.
At the same time, states need not act alone. An underappreciated part of the American constitutional order is groups of states’ latent authority to enter into binding “compacts.” These are treaty-like agreements, often created without Congress’s approval, to coordinate regulation between a pool of states. Existing compacts address drivers’ licenses, insurance coverage, and medical practice. They allow states to set uniform standards and realize regulation at scale, even if the national government is AWOL.
Imagine Texas, Virginia, California, Pennsylvania, and New York forging an interstate compact on AI and data centers. No firm would be permitted to operate data centers in any state unless they agreed to meet certain environmental standards and avoid use cases that threatened serious job loss. The compacting states could require a common set of disclosures — not only about the data centers themselves but also about the fiscal and labor market risks associated with AI more generally, and perhaps about other AI-related harms.
Unlike simple bans, this arrangement is more likely to be politically self-sustaining. Firms would, in effect, have to document on an ongoing basis the knot of harms that flow from hyperscale AI — hence supplying the grounds for their own regulation. And they could not simply blame states for quashing economic growth. A race to the bottom as firms tried to pit states against each other would be more difficult.
It is true that hyperscale AI capitalists are likely to flee from compacting states. But notice that the creation of a robust compact would limit their flight options, at least within the United States. To see this, consider the political costs to a red state governor who welcomes fleeing data centers that decline to comply with environmental and labor market protections. Recall that some 89 percent of Americans oppose data center siting near them. Isn’t it likely that the governor will meet the same fate as other erstwhile champions of AI, such as outgoing Texas Governor Greg Abbott? Compacting to clarify AI’s harms makes it politically more difficult for noncompacting states to embrace the industry.
No doubt, these solutions are incomplete. But they offer a pathway for dealing with not just the local but also the national harms of hyperscale AI in a politically durable way. They not only signal clearly that voters’ concerns have been heard but also help build virtuous circles of disclosure, action, and revenue so the perils of hyperscale AI can be enduringly addressed — a groundwork that offers a foundation for national action when the time is right.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: James K. Galbraith
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Notes From the Blue Star State
Texas is predominantly and pragmatically populist. If the national Democratic Party wishes to conquer the Electoral College for a generation, it will follow the lead of the voters.
From the standpoint of The New York Times, Gina Hinojosa is the “first Hispanic” governor-elect of Texas, while James Talarico is a moderate from a “deeply conservative” state—and therefore likely to join the incumbent Senate leadership against challenges from what the Times calls the “far left.”
That’s not the way it looks from here. Hinojosa—a labor lawyer!—self-identifies as a “populist” in the grand farmer-labor tradition of the late 19th century (you can read about it in a book by Tom Frank). She rejects the “culture wars” of the “liberal-progressives” in the Democratic Party. Her issues are about the power of money and the price of power. Talarico, too, focused on billionaires, oligarchs, elections bought by AIPAC, and a message of basic human decency, motivated by faith.
According to the Times, the election was primarily a repudiation of Donald Trump. But in Texas, the campaign turned on Elon Musk, data centers, public schools, and the dark atmosphere of repression that had settled over this state as the local ruling class grew old. It was about the price of gas, the price of food, the soaring rents, and about whether abundant electricity would continue to underpin life in Texas. Ultimately, it was about who was in charge.
Foreign policy influenced the outcome only through Trump’s war on Iran. Oil was $65 a barrel in February and about $100 on Election Day. Texas produces oil, and those prices brought good money to the Permian Basin. But most of that flowed to refiners and to private equity—not to the urban commuters who vote here. The gas price measured Trump’s fealty to Netanyahu and, behind that, the catastrophe visited on Palestinians in Gaza. No other foreign issue mattered much. A colleague, taking the broad view, wrote that voters were offended by how Trump treated Zelensky. There weren’t 10 votes in Texas that turned on Ukraine.
The Democratic majorities that will ride to Washington in January will be fractious. The party is still dominated by Big Money, and those who campaigned against the Republican oligarchy will shortly have to confront its Democratic twin. The campaign-industrial complex that spent $1.5 billion on Kamala Harris two years ago is still in control. It is trying to keep the focus on Trump, to spin the victories in identity terms—a Black here, a Hispanic there, and many women, of course—and to keep the narrative away from the power of money and that despised label, “populism.”
Texas populism is not “democratic socialism.” The DSA is a rebellious force in solidly Democratic states; there, it can appeal to a narrow and concentrated base. Texas is not New York City or Los Angeles or Seattle, and after 30 years of Republican hegemony, there was no Democratic establishment to overcome. Texas populism is a form of Christian community socialism—dare I use that word?—which has always enjoyed latent appeal around here. That is why Talarico and Hinojosa (and Goodwin, Johnson, Eckhardt, and every other down-ballot Democrat) won votes previously cast for Trump. Given that Texas is a resource state, Texas populism also understands the realities of the energy system as coastal city dwellers often do not.
“Affordability” was the watchword of 2026. The next phase, within the Democratic Party, will separate those for whom it is just a question of talking points from those who feel the need to deliver. Higher wages. Lower prices. Stable rents. Good public schools. Healthcare that doesn’t break the bank. Electricity that becomes, once again, cheap and abundant. Housing that is decent and, well, affordable. Roads, bridges, rails, and water systems that are built to last.
To deliver affordability means stepping on toes and breaking taboos. Not least, the economists’ cartel with its aversion to rent and price controls. Not least, the health insurance industry and the pharmaceutical companies. Not least, the private-equity energy mafia. Not least, the budget and resource drain that is our distended, obsolete military. And not least, the shibboleth that interest rates are the sole domain of the Federal Reserve, to be raised—crushing housing while enriching the banks—on the empty pretext of “fighting inflation.” A comprehensive national affordability plan remains to be written. When it is, the Democratic donor class will be shocked.
Then there is the question of what to do about Trump. Those who tried to destroy him legally in the Biden interregnum will be back. To take up that cudgel again would be stupid. As a political force, Trump is already destroyed. His administration is breaking apart. He is also an old man in the last phase of his power. The Texas message, I believe, is to let him fade away, bring the cycle of personal political vengeance to an end—and focus on the problems of the people.
To those like Talarico, heading to Washington for the first time, the overseas trifecta—Russia, China, and Iran/Israel—will loom large. The foreign policy establishment is waiting. It will urge hectoring China, financing Ukraine, and sending bombs to Israel, come what may. The new group will have to figure out for itself that China is immune to American pressure. That Russia cannot be defeated—not on the battlefield, as US military intelligence has always known, and also not by sanctions. And that Iran, having won the war, will dictate terms in the Middle East—including on key matters to the Israelis. These facts are locked down, and the Obama-Biden foreign policy era is now over. The peace to come—which must come—will have to respect the realities of the world as it is.
At the national level, the wedge of Texas populism will be thin. It may be absorbed by the national leadership. It may be overshadowed by the all-or-nothing politics of the sectarian left. Or by a wave of scorched-earth revanchism from the Obama-Biden crowd. In the smog of elite Washington, it may have trouble discovering the realities of the larger world, and even more difficulty making its discoveries heard. The consultants and donors and experts will be on the newcomers—on Talarico, also on El-Sayed and any others inclined to think for themselves—like flies on honey.
Nevertheless, Texas has flipped. The state is no longer “deeply conservative.” It is predominantly and pragmatically populist. And Texas is still a very big state. If the national Democratic Party wishes to conquer the Electoral College for a generation, it will follow the lead of the voters here, of the new state government here, and of the new Texans in Washington.
I doubt that this is possible. But then, who expected Tuesday’s election result?
