https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: The Big Review: Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous ★★★★½
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Linda Yablonsky
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Total star rating: ★★★★½
The works: ★★★★★
The show: ★★★★
He was Jack the Dripper. She was The Wife. That is how it went for artist couples in gender-coded mid-century America (and elsewhere). Yet, Lee Krasner (1908-84) played more than a supporting role in her decade-long marriage to Jackson Pollock (1912-56). When his work eclipsed hers, she remained as committed to her own painting as she was to every aspect of his life—except his infidelity and the alcoholism that in 1956 drove him to his death. Even then, she put her devotion to consequential use in securing his legacy. Now the time has come to fully appreciate hers.
Signature Pollocks ricochet off shape-shifting Krasners, and vice-versa
That is the organising principle behind Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous, the gorgeous and largely convincing blockbuster at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. While other US museums have previously surveyed the artists separately and in tandem, for the Met curators David Breslin and Brinda Kumar, none gave Krasner, a first-generation Abstract Expressionist, a fair shake.
Their exhibition strives to give a primacy to Krasner’s work that parallels Pollock’s. Note whose name comes first in the show’s title. Its subtitle likewise derives from a Krasner at the she-who-laughs-last finale. What’s more, a dramatically lit, black box of a gallery starts it off with a bracing presentation of six vertical abstractions that Krasner made in the 1950s by collaging cuttings from her unsold paintings with pieces of canvas and bits of Pollock’s drawings punctuated by slashes of pink and orange.
Nonetheless, the eye keeps moving to a window-like opening that functions as a proscenium for the theatre of Pollock’s Convergence: No. 10 (1952), an immense and riveting painting of black paint skeins shot with explosions of colour. Mounted on an angled, freestanding wall in another room, the sight offers viewers a taste of what is in store: signature Pollocks ricocheting off shape-shifting Krasners, and vice-versa.
If only the curators did not show Krasner still riding his coattails. Pollock’s name remains the bigger draw. Ultimately, he still comes off as the bigger trailblazer, and she, his foremost champion, more willing to risk failure to experiment and invent. As Breslin speculated during the press preview: “I don’t think we would have a Jackson Pollock if it weren’t for what Krasner did to support his work.”
There is no way to test that theory, but if Krasner and Pollock proves anything, it is that the artists’ relationship was so codependent that the reverse may be just as true. Yet, today her influence and market value pale before his. Krasner’s auction record, set at Sotheby’s in 2019, is $11.7m for The Eye is the First Circle (1960), one of her larger canvases in the show. That is not chump change, but this year Christie’s sold Pollock’s Number 7A (1948) for $181.2m, an eye-watering price but still short of the reported $200m that financier Ken Griffin paid David Geffen, in 2016, for Number 17A (also 1948).
She was better-known
Krasner and Pollock met in 1942, when she was better-known to the Abstract Expressionist crowd in New York and Pollock the only unfamiliar name in a show of American and European Modernists (partially recreated at the Met) that the painter John Graham organised and included works by both. By linking their small, vibrant abstractions with works by Pablo Picasso, Joan Miró, Henri Matisse, Amadeo Modigliani, Giorgio de Chirico and Willem de Kooning, the show virtually jumpstarted their careers. It also made them a couple.
Krasner introduced herself in a spontaneous visit to Pollock’s studio and was so dazzled that she hit a creative block. That did not stop them from dating. He was a Midwestern former student of Thomas Hart Benton in thrall to Picasso and Mexican muralists. She was inspired by Arshile Gorky’s abstractions and Matisse’s cut-outs. Soon he was importing a Matissean palette to his painting and showing at Peggy Guggenheim’s Art of this Century gallery. Sales were not brisk. Pollock’s drinking was more prodigious. Krasner insisted they marry and move to Springs, in East Hampton—to protect him from himself—and persuaded Guggenheim to cover the downpayment.
Relocating did the trick for three unusually sober years—long enough for Pollock to produce his breakthrough drip paintings and achieve lasting fame, before settling, intermittently, into new bouts of alcoholism and depression; a creative paralysis set in. Krasner’s career took off, with a confident 1955 solo show at New York’s Stable Gallery.
Breslin and Kumar take care not to place the artists’ works close together, so Krasner’s modestly-scaled paintings can hook the eye without being overwhelmed by Pollock’s volatile monumentalism. Until she was widowed and took over Pollock’s now-famous barn, Krasner worked in their kitchen and he in an upstairs bedroom. Two contiguous galleries, both painted black, approximate the size of the artists’ studios and distill the show’s thesis with luminous economy, leading viewers from the lyrical, early choreography of his pours, drips and stains to her smaller but exquisite Little Images—mosaic-like geometries painted with a palette knife.
From these sepulchral chambers the show opens to a large, high-ceilinged gallery flooded with daylight from newly revealed windows on Central Park. Here, Convergence hangs, backed with the Met’s prize Pollock, Autumn Rhythm: Number 30 (1950). The operatic shift in tone and scale drives home the outsize renown Pollock achieved after a 1949 feature in Life magazine posed the question, “Jackson Pollock: Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?”
In the same gallery, tellingly, the eight collage paintings Krasner showed at Stable Gallery turn from the Pollocks to face each other like the stones of Stonehenge and look just as ritualistic, if more elated. After that, it’s back to black for a segment titled Re:Echo (after a Krasner), where Pollock’s arabesque, later works hang near her Robert Motherwell-like abstractions of the same period.
The rest of the show is all Krasner, but she outlived Pollock by 28 years. The swirling, abstracted floral landscapes became monumental, but appear in a few too many galleries, homogenizing their visual impact. The point—that no full understanding of one artist can come without the other—has already been made, capped by the one side-by-side juxtaposition: The Deep (1953), a chilling canvas where Pollock nearly obliterated a dark biomorph in clouds of white, and Birth (1956), an image of interlocking pink and black forms that Krasner painted the year he died. That pairing said it all.
Will this show correct a historic imbalance? Probably not market-wise, but a reputational correction seems both necessary and likely.
- Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous, Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, until 31 January 2027
- Curators: David Breslin and Brinda Kumar
- Tickets: $30 (concessions available)
What the other critics said
The New York Times’s Holland Cotter describes the exhibition as an “exercise of art-historical reset”, and calls its installation of Pollocks “an entrancing sight”, while exulting in the “distinctive impression of personal joy” in Krasner’s post-Pollock work. In The Wall Street Journal, Karen Wilkin applauds the curators for encouraging “concentration on their work, rather than the mythology attached to both painters”, and on her Instagram, Jasper Johns’s biographer Deborah Solomon raves: “It’s like holding two opposed thoughts in your brain at the same time and wondering if your head will explode from the exhilaration of it all.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Getty to help conserve art-filled 17th-century church in Peruvian Andes
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Graciela Ibáñez
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
An art-filled 17th-century church in the Andes mountains will soon begin five years of conservation work. The project will strengthen the building and preserve its collection of 330 historical objects—including eight paintings by the artist Bernardo Bitti (1548-1610), an Italian Jesuit priest who introduced Mannerism to the Viceroyalty of Peru in the 16th century.
Getty will work with the Peruvian Ministry of Culture to conserve the Church of Santo Tomás de Aquino, also known as the Church of Rondocan—named for the town in the Cusco region where it was built. The project will include seismic stabilisation using local materials; located 3,400m above sea level, the 340-sq.-m church is in an area prone to earthquakes.
“We provide all the advanced conservation techniques available, and we handle the structural design of the project,” Claudia Cancino, a principal project specialist at the Getty Conservation Institute (GCI), tells The Art Newspaper. The Peruvian government will finance the work, which will cost $5m and start in 2027. Like other churches in the Andean highlands, Rondocan has adobe walls (1.2m thick), buttresses and a wooden truss roof.
“The project is not only about the temple and its walls. It’s about the cultural and spiritual heritage of the church,” says César Ccorimanya Mayta, the parish priest at Rondocan for the past 17 years.
Involving the community as caretakers of the temple is part of the conservation process. Cancino and her team completed a similar project at the Church of Santiago Apóstol in the nearby town of Kuñotambo in 2019. As part of that initiative, they showed locals how best to take care of the building—including deceptively simple tasks, like cleaning the floors.
“You have to understand how to sweep the church and with what, because if you stir up too much dust it sticks to the murals,” Cancino says. “All this training was done with the community of Kuñotambo. We even have a manual in Quechua,” the local Indigenous language.
Through the work in Kuñotambo, the GCI became familiar with the Church of Rondocan. “The community asked for our support so that they could request the Archdiocese of Cusco and the Ministry of Culture to work on their church,” Cancino says.
“This church is much more than a historic building. It is part of the community’s memory, identity and everyday life,” Fernando López Sánchez, Peru’s vice minister of cultural heritage, said in a statement.
As part of the conservation project, a Bitti painting will travel to Los Angeles for scientific analysis and conservation on the Getty campus.
Bitti arrived in Peru in 1575, creating paintings for churches in Lima and Cusco. When the Jesuits were expelled from the Americas by the Spanish Crown in 1767, their works were sold. It is believed that the parish priest at Rondocan at that time bought Bitti’s paintings in Cusco and had them transferred to the church. The discovery, less than two decades ago, of the only complete series of eight Bitti canvases has sparked renewed interest in the study of his work.
In addition to the paintings, the church’s collection includes sculptures from the viceroyalty era, manuscripts and silver liturgical objects. “The art collection in this small town in the middle of nowhere is breathtaking,” Cancino says.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Art Gallery of Ontario sets opening date for $73m new wing
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Larry Humber
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Art Gallery of Ontario (AGO) in Toronto has announced that its new five-storey, C$100m ($73.4m), Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery, which will display around 400 modern and contemporary works, will open to the public on 25 September 2027. The expansion project was first made public in April 2022.
“The Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery is more than an expansion project—it is Toronto and Canada announcing its global position,” Stephan Jost, the AGO’s outgoing director and chief executive, said in a statement. “When this gallery opens in September 2027, the world will be made aware of the strength of the AGO collection and the degree to which it has evolved to be truly global.”
The new building is the result of a collaboration between three architecture firms: the Toronto-headquartered firm Diamond Schmitt (known for its revamp of Emily Carr University of Art + Design in Vancouver and the forthcoming New Brunswick Museum in Saint John); the New York-based firm Selldorf Architects (of the recent renovations of the National Gallery in London and the Frick Collection in Manhattan); and Two Row Architect, headquartered in Ohsweken, Ontario (known for the Perry Centre for Native American Art at the Shelburne Museum in Vermont).
“It’s not a small project,” Jost said at the time of the launch in 2022. The 40,000-sq.-ft expansion, which overlooks downtown Toronto’s Grange Park, increases the AGO’s display space by around 30%, including 5,000 sq. ft of gallery spaces with 23ft-tall ceilings.
The gallery is certainly in need of additional space for its collection of modern and contemporary work, which has grown by around 18,000 pieces in the past decade. In 2024 it received a gift of 37 works from the estate of the telecoms executive Philip B. Lind, including pieces by Laurie Simmons, Stan Douglas, Jeff Wall, Ai Weiwei, William Kentridge, Rodney Graham, Philip Guston and others. Last year, the gallery acquired more than 200 photographs by Peter Hujar and received more than 450 works from the late collectors Carol and Morton Rapp—among them works by Robert Rauschenberg, Claes Oldenburg, Kara Walker, Rachel Whiteread, Jasper Johns, Roy Lichtenstein, Lee Bontecoue, David Hockney and others. (The gallery also found itself at the centre of a culture war debate after opting not to acquire a work by the US photo-based artist and activist Nan Goldin.)
The AGO also boasts the largest public collection of Henry Moore’s work outside the UK—so much so that two years ago, to mark the 50th anniversary of the gallery’s Henry Moore Sculpture Centre, the city of Toronto declared 13 November to be Henry Moore Day.
The project of building a new wing was sparked by a lead gift of C$35m ($25.7m) from Dani Reiss, an art collector, chairman and chief executive of Canada Goose and member of the Order of Canada. The Reiss Gallery project is now fully funded, thanks to contributions from a community of supporters and the governments of Ontario and Canada.
Speaking on behalf of the federal government, Gregor Robertson, the minister of housing and infrastructure, said: “The federal government is proud to support this sustainable, state-of-the-art gallery that will host some of the world’s best modern and contemporary art for generations to come.”

https://gothamist.com/news/manhattans-ca.title: Manhattan's Canal Street is getting a face-lift, but it'll take a while
https://gothamist.com/news/manhattans-ca.author: Willow Higgins
https://gothamist.com/news/manhattans-ca.text:
There’s a long road ahead for Canal Street in Manhattan.
The downtown thoroughfare, known for its mercilessly crammed sidewalks and vendors hawking designer-ish handbags, watches and other goods, is getting a much-anticipated face-lift, but it isn’t going to happen quickly.
The Department of Transportation told a local community board committee meeting that much of the construction it planned for the west side of Canal Street will be delayed until 2027.
“Anything involving concrete work is going to be pushed to the next year,” said Lauren Rennée, a deputy commissioner for the Department of Transportation.
“We would have loved to do more,” she added.
The Department of Transportation has split the Reimagining Canal Street project into two phases. The first phase, which was scheduled for this fall, entails improving west Canal Street, where, according to the transportation department, vehicle traffic is the biggest concern.
The second phase targets east Canal Street, where concerns about walkability are paramount. Specific plans for improvements to the eastern side of the street have yet to be announced, but that work is scheduled for 2027.
East Canal, where most of the vendors are stationed, is where collisions happen the most. According to data from the department, 190 people were injured on East Canal St. between 2020 and 2024, and two were killed in a car crash. New Yorkers have been anticipating wider sidewalks for decades.
The west side improvements include adding new crosswalks, two-lane bike lanes, pedestrian areas lined with planters and concrete blocks, and painted curb extensions from the West Side Highway to Broadway.
The only undertaking that has been executed this fall is painted curb extensions — essentially extending the pedestrian area into the shoulder — at five different sites near west Canal, Rennée told the community board meeting.
Signs about the construction project are plastered across the area, but there is little sign of any major work.
The transportation department contends that the project is still on schedule, and that more work will be done in the coming weeks, including the installation of planters. Any remaining work, Renée said, will be picked up next year.
The project is an important step in making sure New Yorkers have safe streets, said Mona Bruno, a spokesperson for the transportation department, in a statement.
“We began installing Canal Street West this fall as promised and substantial progress has been made as we work around the clock to deliver these upgrades to enhance safety," Bruno said in a statement.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Union Hits Local News Giant With Federal Labor Complaint After Reporter Is Fired
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Claudia Irizarry Aponte
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The union representing editorial staff at the city’s biggest local newspaper chain says in a federal complaint that a reporter was fired in retaliation for union organizing, as the two sides head into their first bargaining session this week.
Renee DeLorenzo, who most recently covered business features and cultural issues at local news site QNS, was dismissed from her job on Oct. 29, the same day that Schneps Media acquired a competing Queens paper.
Schneps Union, which represents editorial staff at amNewYork and other neighborhood papers across the five boroughs and Long Island, filed a complaint with the National Labor Relations Board accusing Schneps Media of failing to inform the union of its decision to dismiss DeLorenzo and refusing the union’s attempts to discuss the matter further.
In a complaint submitted last week, Schneps Union suggested DeLorenzo’s firing was linked to her union activism: “Renee was an outspoken proponent of the Union during the unit’s recent organizing campaign, a fact the Employer knew.”
At her firing, DeLorenzo was told that she was being laid off as a result of the company’s acquisition of the Queens Chronicle, a competitor. But she told The City Reporter that as she became more involved in the union, appearing in two Instagram videos promoting their campaign, management retaliated, first reassigning her from a beat covering politics, and then firing her last month.
Schneps Media CEO Josh Schneps told The City Reporter “it would be inappropriate to comment on an issue now currently under review by the NLRB.”
Approximately 30 Schneps Media reporters voted to join Local 1096 of the NewsGuild of New York in July. Since then, they’ve accused Schneps of stonewalling negotiations for better wages, benefits and working conditions. The two sides are scheduled to meet for their first bargaining session on Thursday. Starting salaries for reporters range between $40,000 and $50,000 a year.
DeLorenzo said she was “in shock” and started “panicking” when she learned of her dismissal.
MORE: Follow The City Reporter’s Award-Winning Labor Coverage
Union leaders said they were blindsided by Schneps’ announcement last month that it had purchased a competitor, the Queens Chronicle, the same day the company laid off DeLorenzo, who had been working at QNS for about a year.
Schneps Media is owned by Victoria and Josh Schneps, a mother-son duo who jointly operate dozens of hyperlocal newspapers in New York City and Long Island. The company boasts 2 million weekly readers across its brands and formidable advertising prowess among its network of community papers.
The company has faced criticism for cozying up to the centers of political power in New York: for years it distributed a free, semi-regular paper, boosting then-Brooklyn Borough President Eric Adams to about 140,000 households in the borough. Postage for that paper, One Brooklyn, was paid for by taxpayers while Schneps collected advertising revenue.
Victoria Schneps founded the company in 1985 with the Queens Courier from her Bayside home “with four children, a dream and a prayer and $250,” she told the New York Times in 2017. She slowly pieced together a media empire including the Gay City News, Brooklyn Paper, the Bronx Times, the Long Island Press and others. In 2019, Schneps acquired and merged two free citywide papers, amNewYork and Metro New York, in a major coup for the company that led to layoffs at those papers.
The company fiercely resisted its staff’s union effort, first rejecting its request for voluntary recognition, forcing an election overseen by the NLRB, and then trying to toss six of its members out of the union by challenging their eligibility. Schneps hired Bond, Schoeneck & King, a notorious union-busting law firm.
Since launching its organizing push, Schneps Union has mounted escalating actions to move the company to bargain on a first contract. Last month, its members rallied outside a company gala celebrating Queens business leaders; the union also took credit for the company’s last-minute cancellation of a September gala celebrating labor leaders where the union also planned to protest.
MORE: Welcome to Hotel RAV4: The Brutal Commute of New Yorkers Priced Out to the Poconos
The union sometimes poked fun at management. In late July the union published a video on its Instagram page, starring DeLorenzo, where a cartoonish voice narrates portions of an email that Victoria Schneps sent to staff in the lead-up to the union election that month.
“Vote NO to the union. Give us a chance to address your concerns without a third party,” wrote Schneps.
DeLorenzo was hired a year ago as a general assignment reporter at QNS, an online publication covering Queens, where she worked on politics, elections and other stories. But this summer — around the same time she appeared in two pro-union Instagram videos — she was asked to cover arts and culture instead.
On Oct. 29, she was preparing to work on stories about street safety and the New York City Marathon when she received a message asking to meet immediately with her boss and the company’s HR director. Anticipating her firing, DeLorenzo said she twice and without success requested that a union representative be present for the meeting. She said she rejected an offer of two weeks’ severance because she would not sign a separation agreement she believed “would have signed away my right to speak about what happened.”

https://gothamist.com/news/emerald.title: Rent-stabilized buildings hit auction block, despite Mamdani’s efforts to intervene
https://gothamist.com/news/emerald.author: David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/emerald.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s effort to steer the sale of crumbling apartment buildings to tenant-approved owners has suffered another setback. Dozens of deteriorating properties in East Harlem that City Hall tried to deliver into the hands of an affordable housing developer are instead heading to the auction block in Manhattan starting Tuesday afternoon.
Mamdani administration officials had supported a bid by the firm Spatial Equity to purchase the 38-building portfolio before its lenders auctioned it off. The properties were previously owned by bankrupt real estate investment firm Emerald Equities Group and contain a combined 850 mostly rent-stabilized apartments.
But tenants and attorneys involved in the potential deal say negotiations fell through, and the banks and other financial institutions that control roughly $250 million in mortgage loans will proceed with foreclosure sales for each individual building over the course of three auction days.
Cara Polte, a resident of one of the buildings on East 103rd Street and the co-founder of the East Harlem Tenant Union, said tenants will continue advocating for a new buyer committed to resolving thousands of housing code violations that have plagued the buildings for decades,
“We’re definitely not stopping,” Polte said. “But this obscures the pathway a little.”
Mayor's Office to Protect Tenants Director Cea Weaver said the foreclosure sale isn't the end of the city's effort to force owners to improve conditions in the building.
"The Mayor's Office is proud to support the tenants of the East Harlem Tenants Union as they organize for better living conditions and more control over the future of their homes," Weaver said in a written statement.
The stalled negotiations mark a new obstacle to the Mamdani administration's efforts to influence transactions involving financially distressed and derelict buildings – a priority he described on his first day in office.
Hours after his inauguration, Mamdani announced that he had directed city lawyers to attempt to block an unrelated bankruptcy sale of nearly 5,000 rent-stabilized apartments. That unprecedented intervention ultimately failed to stop the transaction, but it did help compel the new buyer to commit to resolving hundreds of outstanding violations in the buildings.
Mamdani has also championed other policies meant to help nonprofits and some private developers acquire buildings, including a measure known as the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act that would give some groups a head start on buying financially distressed properties before they hit the open market. His predecessor, Mayor Eric Adams, vetoed a previous version of the legislation before the City Council approved a revised measure last month.
Polte said the auction complicates the tenants’ goal of turning her building and four others along East 103rd Street into a “community land trust” – a form of nonprofit ownership that gives tenant groups power over housing decisions or allows residents to purchase their units at permanently affordable rates.
“I don't think anyone has a clear vision about what comes next because the lender was not willing to play ball with negotiations,” Polte said.
Spatial Equity had attempted to purchase the buildings but had its initial $68 million bid – roughly a quarter of the debt – for the portfolio rejected, City Limits reported in July.
Polte said the lenders also rejected a $110 million offer from Spatial Equity last month and have not communicated about the amount they would accept.
“It’s been difficult to try to negotiate or even hear what would get them to say yes,” she said.
The mortgage loans are controlled by a trust managed by a variety of banks, as well as the lender Sabal Investment Holdings. The loans were partially insured by Freddie Mac.
Sabal executives did not respond to requests for comment on Monday.
Spatial Equity principal Teg Sethi declined to comment on the failed purchase.
Roughly 1,600 buildings with rent-stabilized apartments are facing financial distress, meaning their expenses outpace revenue from rent, according to data published by the city’s Rent Guidelines Board earlier this year. Landlord groups say sharp restrictions on rental increases, exacerbated by the board’s recent two-year rent freeze, have made ownership untenable and have warned of a dramatic rise in foreclosures.
Tenant advocates counter that many property owners facing financial problems, like Emerald Equities, took on too much debt with a plan to pay it back by raising rents before new laws limited their ability to do so.
The East Harlem efforts hint at the complexity of housing deals that involve those rent-regulated buildings now at risk of foreclosure.
“These things are very complicated,” said David Lebenstein, an executive managing director specializing in nonprofit purchases at Cushman & Wakefield. “Every deal has to be analyzed given the cash flow, the rent rolls and the occupancy levels.”
Lebenstein said lenders of rent-stabilized apartment buildings are often willing to wipe away debt if it means salvaging some value.
“They recognize they’re underwater,” he said. “If they’re owed $100 million and they get $70 million, that’s a victory.”
That does not appear to be the case with the former Emerald portfolio.
The upcoming foreclosure auction is the latest twist in the tangled history of the East Harlem apartment buildings.
Emerald Equities acquired the 38 buildings for $350 million in 2016 and began raising rents on the stabilized apartments to increase the company’s revenue and pay off its debts – a strategy allowed by state law at the time and common in gentrifying sections of the city.
Emerald took out another $180 million loan on the buildings in December 2018, just six months before state lawmakers passed a package of tenant protection measures that outlawed many of the tactics Emerald used to increase rents.
Lenders foreclosed on the properties in 2024, and Emerald filed for bankruptcy a year later. An investigation by the New York Attorney General’s Office and the state’s Division of Homes and Community Renewal found the company had also illegally lifted 21 apartments out of the rent stabilization system.
A previous owner, British investment firm Dawnay Day Group, had pursued a similar strategy for deregulating apartments and raising rents nearly a decade earlier before it too declared bankruptcy in 2009.
The procession of owners has left the buildings in disrepair. A retaining wall collapsed in the rear of buildings on East 103rd St. earlier this year, days before Mamdani and Cea Weaver, the head of his tenant protection office, visited to meet with tenants in March.
When Gothamist toured the buildings in April, a single boiler serviced three of the properties and one first-floor tenant covered a gaping hole in his kitchen with rotting plywood.
Attorney Matthew Latterner said conditions have only worsened for renters. He said he and tenants “appreciate that the Mamdani administration is intervening,” even if the efforts have so far failed to influence the lenders.
He said he would immediately sue whoever takes over the buildings following the foreclosure sales to demand they improve conditions at buildings that totaled more than 2,300 housing code violations in April.
“Our number one priority has been to fight for these tenants and we’re going to keep doing that no matter who the owner of the buildings are,” Latterner said. “Whoever the new owners are, we’re prepared to sue the living bejeezus out of them on day one to make sure tenants get the repairs they need and keep their families safe.”

https://gothamist.com/news/study-links-a.title: Study links ADHD to NYC’s deadly subway surfing trend
https://gothamist.com/news/study-links-a.author: Ramsey Khalifeh, Stephen Nessen
https://gothamist.com/news/study-links-a.text:
People killed “surfing” on top of New York City subway trains tend to be teen boys diagnosed with ADHD, according to a new study published this week.
The trend of young people subway surfing has persisted in recent years, despite at least 12 people being killed riding on the outside of trains since the start of 2024.
The study, which was conducted by researchers from NYU-Langone and the city hospital system, analyzed records of 43 patients under the age of 21 who were taken to Bellevue Hospital between 2018 and 2025 with some form of subway-related trauma.
The research, which was published in the Journal of Adolescent Health, is the first of its kind that looks into subway surfing in the United States. The study identified 10 patients who were injured from subway surfing. All of those surfers were male teenagers who had “markedly higher rates of ADHD” compared to the rest of the group.
“The most striking finding in our series is the overrepresentation of ADHD; 60% of surfers carried the diagnosis versus 6.1% of nonsurfers,” the study said. “This association has not been previously described in the train surfing literature and is among the most notable findings of our study.”
Researchers behind the study acknowledged the sample size is too small to make a sweeping generalization of all young people in New York City who ride on top of trains. The analysis doesn’t include two young girls, 12-year-old Zemfira Mukhtarov and 13-year-old Ebba Morina, who died while riding on top of a J train in Williamsburg in Oct. 2025.
Eveline Teresa Hidalgo, senior author of the study and pediatric neurosurgeon at NYU and Bellevue, said the subway surfers diagnosed with ADHD had also been treated for the disorder.
“We don't know what this means exactly, and it's not that ADHD causes them to subway surf, but it means that it's something that we need to investigate further,” said Hidalgo. ”It could be associated with some attention-seeking behavior. It could be associated with the thrill-seeking behavior, and it's a typical teenage behavior.”
Hidalgo said the study shows how subway surfing can cause life-altering injuries among people who don’t die after falling from trains. Some patients they studied at Bellevue suffered injuries to their brains and spine, and some had their limbs amputated.
Both the MTA and NYPD have attempted to prevent subway surfing in recent years.
The transit agency has teamed up with city officials to lobby social media giants like Meta and TikTok to ban or censor videos of teens subway surfing in New York City. The MTA has also piloted installing barriers between subway cars on the 7 line — where subway surfing is prevalent as the line is mostly elevated — to prevent people climbing on top of cars. The NYPD has also deployed drones to monitor elevated train tracks to spot and catch surfers.
NYPD data shows 185 people have been arrested for subway surfing so far this year, a 12% increase compared to the same period last year.
The study compared New York City’s subway surfing wave to a similar trend in Berlin in the 1990s. After 18 people died subway surfing over a six-year period in the German capital, the city’s S-Bahn transit system slowly decommissioned a fleet of train cars after finding they were easier for riders to climb.

https://gothamist.com/news/central-park-.title: Central Park rape suspect taken into custody at Miami Burger King, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/central-park-.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/central-park-.text:
A man accused of raping a woman in Central Park last month was taken into custody Tuesday while working at a Burger King in Miami, police said, adding that he will also be charged in two earlier rapes in the park.
In a social media post, police identified the man as Dereck Rivera-Deleon and said the earlier attacks happened in 2021 and 2023.
The department did not say how investigators linked him to those attacks or release any details about either. Several days after the attack on Oct. 24, the NYPD released images of a man in his 30s wearing a black hoodie.
The most recent attack happened near East 66th Street and Fifth Avenue around 8:30 p.m., police said at the time. The victim, a 39-year-old woman, was taken to a hospital, and the man fled, according to police.
NYPD detectives assigned to a U.S. Marshals regional fugitive task force took Rivera-Deleon into custody with help from the U.S. Marshals Service, officials said on X.
Police did not say what charges he faces in the October attack or when he will be brought back to New York.
It was not immediately clear whether Rivera-Deleon has a lawyer.

https://gothamist.com/news/man-indicted-.title: Man indicted in stabbing murder of Brooklyn runner Katie Suarez
https://gothamist.com/news/man-indicted-.author: Ben Feuerherd
https://gothamist.com/news/man-indicted-.text:
A Brooklyn grand jury Tuesday voted to indict Sayed Mohassib, 27, on second degree murder charges in the killing of jogger Katie Suarez last month, the Brooklyn district attorney’s office said in a statement.
Mohassib was arrested Saturday and charged with killing Suarez along a bike and running path in Bath Beach on Oct. 30.
“Katie Suarez was a young woman with her whole life ahead of her, brutally taken from her loved ones in a senseless act of violence,” District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said in a statement. “Today’s indictment marks an important step toward securing justice and I commend the NYPD for its swift and thorough investigation.”
Mohassib, who worked for the city Department of Education, denied killing Suarez but told investigators that he was sitting on a bench along the path and became “covered in blood,” according to the criminal complaint against him after his arrest.
Police say there is surveillance footage of Mohassib running away from the scene of the stabbing, entering his apartment building and then walking out about 15 minutes later to throw items in the garbage, the complaint said.
He later told police that he got rid of his clothing and the knife and tried to wipe his hands and the wall of his apartment clean of blood, according to the complaint. Detectives investigating the case saw a reddish stain on a wall in his apartment that was later identified as blood, the complaint states.
Mohassib's attorney could not immediately be reached for comment Tuesday.
Prior to his employment with the Department of Education, Mohassib served briefly as an NYPD officer and in the U.S. Marine Corps, but was thrown out due to psychiatric issues.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani has said the city will investigate how he was allowed to work in the education department despite that history.
Prior to Mohassib’s arrest, NYPD Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny told reporters that Suarez’s killing was believed to be a random attack.
Suarez, who worked at a nearby bank, was doing her usual routine of going on a late afternoon run along the path, which runs along the waterfront in Southern Brooklyn.
Her mother and father were waiting nearby to drive home with her when she finished her run. When she didn’t arrive on time, Suarez’s father walked the path, looking for her. He ended up discovering her lifeless body near the path where she collapsed after being stabbed.
Mohassib was ordered held without bail after his arraignment on the charges from the criminal complaint. He will be arraigned on the indictment in the coming days, but the hearing has not yet been scheduled.

https://gothamist.com/food/its-cold-in-n.title: It's cold in New York. Soup season in the city has begun.
https://gothamist.com/food/its-cold-in-n.author: Robert Sietsema
https://gothamist.com/food/its-cold-in-n.text:
Sure, soup can be eaten all year round. But what can be better for a light lunch in early November than a bowl of Manhattan clam chowder with a handful of oyster crackers? As the days get colder, we search for heartier soups, or a bowl to warm ourselves with soups as a prelude to a main course. Soups are also an easy way to eat vegetarian, and even save some calories.
So, welcome to soup season! Here are 10 of the most diverse, exciting bowls in the city we could find, including some that will be familiar, and others that will make you slurp with surprise. This is an international group, and they are arranged in no particular order.
White and red clam chowder
The perpetual battle rages on between chowder lovers: red or white? The white c was carried by Bretons to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and thence to New England. The red originated here in New York, presumably among those of Italian descent. The white is creamy and soothing, with a jolt of flavor from the shellfish; while the red is more aggressive, and loaded with vegetables. Why not get a bowl of both for slightly over $12 each at Grand Central Oyster Bar, in one of the city’s most dramatic restaurant settings? Grand Central Terminal, 89 East 42nd St.
Pickle soup
Poland is a soup-intensive country, and scanning the menu of any Polish restaurant you’ll find red borscht and white borscht, tomato, tripe, chicken noodle and split pea, but also some with unexpected ingredients like sauerkraut, sorrel, duck blood and cucumber pickles. The latter is a frequent offering at Retro as a daily soup ($8.50). It’s more mellow than you might expect with pickle juice as its base. Sour cream does the trick to neutralize, along with potatoes and fistfuls of dill. 853 Manhattan Ave., Greenpoint
Sancocho
Every culture has its “everything but the kitchen sink” soup, with an infinitely expandable roster of ingredients. Sancocho is a fine example, a soup found in every Dominican restaurant in town, including Don Emilio Diner in Castle Hill, where on the day we tried it, the soup ($8) contained pork ribs, chicken, plantain, and yuca in a broth of disintegrated pumpkin, propelled by the pungent flavors of oregano and garlic. 1315 Castle Hill Ave., Bronx
Assam laksa
Want a soup that bombards you with strong flavors, leaving you reeling from the taste? Such a soup is the Malaysian assam laksa found at the venerable Taste Good. Just look at its partial catalog of ingredients: fermented shrimp paste, funky and fishy mackerel, sweet pineapple, fresh lemongrass, chiles and mint. Fortunately, the bulbous rice noodles are as bland as can be. 82-18 45th Ave., Elmhurst
Matzoh ball soup
After that bowl of assam laksa, what stands at the opposite end of the pungent-bland spectrum? Matzoh ball soup, that’s what! At newly reopened Carnegie Deli, the broth is unimpeachable in its soothing plainness, the matzoh balls more bouncy than usual, with plenty of fortifying veggies minced into the broth. The totality ($16, with noodles added) is wonderful in its savory subtlety. 834 7th Ave., Midtown
Luosifen
Stall #19 at the new 99 Ranch Market basement food court, known as Luo Xiao Du, specializes in luosifen soup in a half-dozen varieties. The pottage hails from Guanxi, an autonomous coastal region between Hong Kong and Hanoi, and employs a broth famously made from snails. This version ($11) has a few snails dropped in for visual effect, along with bamboo shoots, a boiled egg, chili oil, peanuts, and a half dozen other things, for a very rich and fortifying bowl, but one that will leave you fanning your mouth. 37-11 Main Street, Flushing
French onion soup
French onion soup as we know it was supposedly invented in the Les Halles Market in Paris to feed workers using ingredients common in the market: onions, butter, cheese and stale bread. Today, it is found in nearly every French bistro, including Bar Six in the Village, where a powerful caramelized onion broth buoys up a raft of gruyere, and conceals a thick slice of bread in its depths ($15). Your only challenge is how, exactly, to eat it, since the cheese clings mightily to the spoon. 502 6th Ave., Greenwich Village
Cow foot soup
Soups made from the long-boiled feet of cows are common throughout the Caribbean, and evidence of the “everything but the squeal” approach that makes those cuisines more eco-friendly through their use of the entire animal. The swatches of trotter at the Trinidadian Bake & Things in the soup ($8) are pleasantly rubbery and gelatinous, and potatoes are mixed into the mellow yellow broth. Every bite is a sunny delight with lots of chewing involved, and the collagen and gelatin are bound to help your skin. 1489 Flatbush Ave., Flatbush
Lagman
Lagman is the signature soup of Uyghur cuisine, a soup indispensable to the menus of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, as well as the Xinjiang autonomous region of northwestern China. At its heart are irregular handmade wheat noodles in a rich beef broth flavored with dill and cilantro. In the version found at Shashlik Uz N1 in Ditmas Park, the soup ($11.99) also contains colorful bell peppers, fennel, celery, onions, green beans, and giant wads of fresh dill, tasting of the stockyard and the meadows. 115 Ditmas Ave., Kensington
Scandinavian fish and shellfish bisque
Located on the ground floor of the Scandinavia House, Bjork Café & Bistro offers a full range of Scandinavian specialties, from Swedish meatballs to preserved fish platters to the open face sandwiches known as smorrebrod. Several soups are offered, including a fish and shellfish bisque ($19) featuring cod, gray shrimp and mussels bobbing in a yellow broth of surpassing mellowness, with shredded leeks and carrots waving like seaweed in tidal pools along the shoreline. 58 Park Ave., Murray Hill

https://gothamist.com/news/ice-subpoena-.title: ICE subpoena puts a spotlight on the last emergency migrant shelter in NYC
https://gothamist.com/news/ice-subpoena-.author: Arya Sundaram
https://gothamist.com/news/ice-subpoena-.text:
The Mamdani administration is “evaluating next steps” after a federal judge ruled City Hall must comply with a federal subpoena seeking information about certain residents of a South Bronx shelter for migrant men, according to spokesperson for the mayor.
Ivonne Rodriguez, spokesperson for Mayor Zohran Mamdani, had no further comment after U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan in Manhattan ruled the city must provide to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement the names and birthdates of any shelter residents who had “serious criminal histories.” That includes residents charged with any of eight crimes: murder, manslaughter, rape, robbery, assault, grand larceny, burglary or assault of a law enforcement officer.
An ICE official previously stated in a sworn affidavit that the agency is aware of 20 immigrant residents of the shelter who have entered the country illegally and 12 who had been charged with a “serious” criminal offense.
City attorneys have fought the subpoena, arguing the request would require the city to conduct an unduly broad and burdensome investigation to produce the information.
The Department of Homeland Security declined to comment on the matter, citing ongoing litigation.
The legal action focuses on the last emergency shelter for migrants in the city. During the peak of the “migrant crisis,” as former Mayor Eric Adams termed it, the city maintained more than 260 shelters, including in sprawling tent cities and hotels across the five boroughs and in upstate communities, to house an influx of more than 240,000 migrants and asylum seekers.
Over 1,400 single adult migrant men resided at the Bronx shelter as of the end of June, according to City Hall data provided to City Council. The Bronx shelter's population has slowly shrunk over the course of this year, down from 1,670 residents in February, according to the data. The shelter was originally designed to hold up to 2,200 residents.
As of the end of June, shelters across the city were housing 27,120 migrants and asylum seekers, the vast majority of whom are families with children, according to the City Council data. That’s down from a peak of nearly 68,000 in January 2024, according to city comptroller data.
The ruling comes amid a drop-off of in visits by federal immigration officers to city shelters, seeking access to and information about immigrant residents. Federal immigration officers visited city shelters six times in the second half of last year and four times in the first half of this year, according to quarterly city reports.
That follows a surge in such visits in the first six months of President Donald Trump’s second term, a trend first reported by Gothamist. The Gothamist analysis of those visits found that federal immigration officers were able to enter private areas of city shelters or obtain resident information without presenting judicial warrants at least five times earlier this year, raising questions about whether both federal officers and local shelter employees were following the law.
The Bronx shelter opened in February 2025. Soon after taking office Jan. 1, 2026, Mamdani announced plans to close the shelter by the end of the year.
While thousands of other migrants and asylum-seekers continue to reside in the city’s shelter system, the Bronx shelter is unique in that it’s the only shelter specifically designated for migrants and operating outside of the normal Department of Homeless Services system. That allows the city to operate outside the framework of laws governing city shelters, including restrictions on size. City law currently prohibits most shelters larger than 200 people.
The shelter is currently run by the mayor’s office of Housing Recovery Operations. It is the last official Humanitarian Emergency Response and Relief Center, generally large-scale migrant shelters first announced by former Mayor Eric Adams’ administration in September 2022.
The Bronx shelter has been plagued by concerns of bed bugs and poor food, as reported by local news outlets the City Reporter and Documented. Before opening, the shelter also garnered the ire of local residents and officials, who saw the placement of the shelter in their borough as further representation that the Bronx was unfairly shouldering the city’s undesirables.
Bronx Borough President Vanessa Gibson, who originally opposed the shelter, has also spoken out against the judge’s ruling requiring City Hall to hand over to ICE information about some of the shelter’s residents. In a social media post over the weekend, she wrote “HELL NO!”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/spain-housin.title: On Strike for a Different Spain
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/spain-housin.author: Mario Arguiriano, Chris Mills Rodrigo
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/spain-housin.text:
On Strike for a Different Spain
Spain will see a general strike on Wednesday, following mass protests around housing. A member of Marxist group Coordinadora Juvenil Socialista discusses how these protests have cohered a militant class-based movement for more sweeping change.
- Interview by
- Chris Mills Rodrigo
Spain’s streets and town squares have been flooded with protesters this fall, since the brutal eviction and subsequent death of eighty-seven-year-old María del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen. This September, she was removed from her Madrid apartment of some seventy years, after an investment fund quintupled her rent.
The marches and encampments, first called by Madrid’s tenants’ union, have primarily focused on Spain’s housing crisis. The situation has intensified over the last decade as rents have nearly doubled while wages have remained largely stagnant. The protests have already triggered a general strike this Wednesday, November 11, and snap elections called by Pedro Sánchez’s center-left Partido Socialista (PSOE) for November 29.
The promise of a strike and elections did not quell the protests. The encampment in Puerta del Sol in Madrid that kicked off this cycle remained active until police tore it down last week. Spin-off strikes focused on disinvestment in public education have closed down major motorways.
Comparisons to the Indignados protests (also known as 15-M) of 2011 come easily. Both kicked off with encampments in the center of Madrid and centered on housing affordability. And yet things are markedly different this time around. While 15-M aimed to include everyone regardless of class position and was organizationally anarchic, today’s protesters are speaking much more openly of class struggle and organizing themselves into people’s assemblies.
The prominent presence of the Coordinadora Juvenil Socialista (CJS, Socialist Youth Coordination) in the current protest movement is both emblematic of those changes and critical to understanding them. CJS is a Marxist revolutionary organization and part of the broader Movimiento Socialista (MS), a communist current that originated in the Basque Country in a 2018 split from the local left-nationalist front. Since its national inception in 2024, CJS has grown to over a thousand members all across Spain. It has been the most visible organization in the recent protests apart from the tenants’ unions and represents a militant left-wing flank not satisfied with letting this moment of upheaval be tranquilized by elections or tepid strikes.
Ahead of November 11, CJS has organized over a hundred youth strike committees aimed at ensuring the demonstration will be a class-based action that challenges rent-seeking, the current government, and capitalism itself. In an interview for Jacobin, Chris Mills Rodrigo spoke with a member of CJS, Mario Arguiriano, about the organization’s role in the recent protests and how it hopes to direct the anger and energy of the Spanish public into structural change. This interview was translated from Spanish by the author and lightly edited for length and clarity.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo Let’s start with the immediate context of what’s happening in Spain. Who was Maricarmen?
- Mario Arguiriano Maricarmen was a sick eighty-seven-year-old woman who had rented an apartment in the center of Madrid for seventy years. Not very long ago, the apartment was bought by a Spanish company called Urbagestión that basically wanted to kick her out to make money. It tried to raise her rent by 500 percent, which she could not afford living on a modest pension, and a judge ordered an eviction. Maricarmen’s eviction was a brutal one in which over two hundred police participated. There was a lot of violence toward the people there defending her. It makes sense that Maricarmen has become a symbol of a fight that confronts the public’s needs with the needs of the housing market and the minority of parasites that live off of speculation and extracting ever more of workers’ salaries.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo Why did her eviction provoke such a visceral response?
- Mario Arguiriano I believe that there exists and has been forming for years among the working class, especially among the youth of the working class, a wide dissatisfaction — with housing conditions, salaries, rising military spending, the genocide in Palestine, the authoritarianism of capitalist states, and also a dissatisfaction with [Pedro Sánchez’s] so-called progressive government. That dissatisfaction has taken on various forms when it comes to protests. Last year, there were massive solidarity protests with Palestine in Spain. We could call Maricarmen’s eviction the spark that lit the prairie of dissatisfaction. After that, it was a good decision to steer the protests toward a more permanent form in the shape of encampments, which have allowed for the accumulation of strength and energy in the context of the fight for housing, which also goes further than housing to a more general indictment of the system.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo Housing has been a major focus of the protests and their coverage. But it sounds like your analysis is broader. How do you all understand the current conjuncture for the Spanish working class?
- Mario Arguiriano For us, the housing problem is an expression of both the functioning of capitalism and the crisis of capitalism in decline. We have low interest rates, which creates the conditions for overaccumulation of capital, causing idle capital to tend toward speculation on things like housing. The current “progressive” government in Spain is very comfortable targeting vulture funds, but if you look at the data, vulture funds represent a small portion of the housing market. What we have instead is a bourgeoisie and also a petty bourgeoisie, so to speak, that has found housing to be a comparatively lucrative investment and a way to suck the blood of those who need it. The housing market under capitalism generally has an inflationary tendency because it’s based on a logic of rent extraction in which the best way to make the most profit is to have prices rise constantly. And, without grand historical struggles, that’s the way the market normally functions. Today the market around housing is stimulated by governments exactly because it offers opportunities for business to a portion of capital that would otherwise be idle. These days in Spain — although this happens practically everywhere — basically any rich person you can think of owns fifty, one hundred, two hundred homes. [Diego] “Cholo” Simeone, the coach of Atlético Madrid, for example, owns more than 180 apartments. Amancio Ortega, the richest man in Spain, has a ridiculous number of apartments. It’s a general practice that can’t be reduced to vulture funds. On the other hand, I’d say that the housing problem is also the problem of salaries. Salaries in Spain have been stagnant for decades, and, in fact, low salaries have been a structural element of Spain’s capitalist model forever. One of the primary elements that Spain offers international capital, at least since [Francisco] Franco’s time, is a structurally precarious labor market with low wages. We have had unending housing price increases like other European countries — especially in the last eight years with the progressive government. Even after it approved housing laws that it promised were historic, nothing has changed. The problem of housing is also a problem of the authoritarian character of capitalist states. Without going too deep into it, the housing movement in Spain is one of the primary victims of the repressive laws that were passed by the last right-wing government and maintained by the progressive one. The Ley Mordaza (Gag Law) has permitted an increase in police power and fines. The housing movement has had to pay millions and millions of euros in fines over the last ten years based on this law that the PSOE and Podemos governments have maintained. So, as you see, if you start pulling on the thread of housing, you end up coming to more structural questions. In fact, in the final instance, the problem of housing is the problem of capitalism and the capitalist form of the state. A government of workers could resolve the problem of housing quickly via measures like nationalizing land or other proposals we’ve made like expropriating speculators, prohibition of speculation on housing, and planning and distribution of housing geared toward social needs. That would solve the problem of housing and has happened in other countries starting with worse conditions. But those solutions aren’t accessible, aren’t feasible, at least not fully, under the capitalist form of the state. It’s important to fight for short-term improvements without selling smoke to the public and without pretending that the resolution to these problems is simple, because while in the short term that can generate excitement, in the medium term it can generate demobilization, disengagement, and disenchantment.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo I’d like to hear a little more about what infrastructure CJS developed before the protests and how you put it into action.
- Mario Arguiriano CJS has had a brief existence, yet from the start we have insisted that our goal is to generate a mass communist organization, based on militancy and discipline. We’re radically opposed to forms of political parties opposed to what the working class needs, like the parties that keep popping up in Spain, formed of four famous people with wide media presence but lacking militant bases. So, from early on we have made clear that our objective, and the only route the working class has to reach revolutionary objectives and build strategic strength, is permanent, disciplined, and constant work out of the spotlight, out of the daily trends. This type of organization can later act appropriately in moments of rupture. I think we’ve had a strategy of patience and slow accumulation of strength aimed at building a revolutionary project. We believe that recent events have shown that our model works — that an organization with clear strategic objectives, strong messaging, and a hardworking and disciplined membership that remains tactically flexible can make good use of big protest moments to share its message, reinforce itself organizationally, and reinforce the movement in general. We have presence in the majority of cities in Spain and are looking to reinforce our reserves in those cities and others where we don’t have a presence, in villages, and ultimately in all environments and spaces.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo What’s your relationship with the tenants’ unions that have also played a big role in these protests?
- Mario Arguiriano The tenants’ unions were the ones who organized against Maricarmen’s eviction, who initiated the protests, and even led on the creation of the encampments. We have never hidden that we have strategic differences with the tenants’ unions, which are a project more oriented toward reform than revolution. We have insisted to them that reform is important and we don’t reject it, but it’s important to orient them toward a revolutionary, emancipatory, or socialist project. However, it’s clear that despite these differences, there’s space for joint work and unity of action in terms of protest and mobilization for worker interests. We’ve seen that these past days, and not just with tenants but also with many other actors. We have differences and strategic debates, but we can and should work toward basic common objectives without obscuring those differences, maintaining debate, and with liberty for everyone to espouse their own analysis and lift up their own projects.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo I’ve seen a lot of comparisons to 15-M. In what ways is that comparison accurate, and how is this movement distinct?
- Mario Arguiriano During the first few days of the encampments, the comparisons with 15-M were everywhere, but over time they started to disappear. Even the mass media, which is normally a medium of organized idiocy, has realized that this is something different, or at least that there are important differences. I believe that the key social and historical difference is that in the last fifteen years we’ve seen a change in the composition of classes, or a change in class relations, that has essentially been a process of proletarianization of a sector of the middle class, especially in the sector that remains prominent in the protests: young people, normally with college degrees, that are part of, in their working conditions and in their relationships with capital, the working class. In 2011, although we experienced a difficult crisis, the generation that led 15-M still lived accustomed to a period of expansion of the middle class and expansion of certain expectations. The best way to illustrate it is to say that during 15-M people protested not being able to buy a house, and today people protest not being able to rent a room. It’s normal that that difference generates a different political consciousness. So in the current protests we see a much more positive opinion toward organization, working-class consciousness, the concept of the working class, and socialism. We’ve seen the normalization of red flags, chants like “Socialism or Barbarism,” and radical critiques of capitalism. This would have been unthinkable during 15-M. Communism was frowned upon, and there was broad skepticism toward the concept of organization. There was also a much more interclass and less politically developed consciousness, without wanting to exaggerate the consciousness of the current encampments and protests — which remain a pluralistic space where many sectors, different organizations, and different levels of consciousness coexist. There are notable differences [with respect to 15-M] that even the smartest bourgeois thinkers are acknowledging.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo One impact of the protests is that there will now be general elections in November. How is CJS approaching those?
- Mario Arguiriano We will not participate in the elections, and we maintain a critical perspective on existing parties. We insist on the need to keep constructing a party of workers, and that none of the existing parties represent the interest of workers or are at the level needed to confront a capitalism that is increasingly catastrophic, linked to wars, genocides, and ecological crisis.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo Before the elections, there will be a general strike. How are you preparing for that day, and what are your objectives?
- Mario Arguiriano The general strike that has been called, which we will support with all our resources, is one where there will be two models of strike in dispute. One is the government’s strike, which is the model being pushed by the major unions — the Comisiones Obreras (CCOO) and the Unión General de Trabajadores (UGT) — which work like transmission cables for the state and the government. That is a strike against the political opposition and is part of a political campaign. We believe that that model is an embarrassment, an insult to the concept of a general strike. Instead what should be created, by all organizations with a focus on class, is a class-based strike against the whole capitalist government. Strikes are spaces for working-class struggle against capital and capitalist states. That’s a general strike. Any model that supports one or another capitalist government is a farce and an insult to the Spanish working class. We want to insist on that in all kinds of spaces. Right now, you have to put in a lot of effort to impose a baseline of rationality in Spanish public debate, because we’re living through a process of the dumbing down of the public via crude lies. Maricarmen was evicted with a PSOE law, under a PSOE government, by police under the PSOE, and it’s talked about like the [conservative] opposition killed her. This is not true. Any party in charge of the capitalist state will enact evictions because all of them reinforce the model of housing as a market, and we’re not going to let any of them off the hook. A few years ago, Podemos, which now presents itself as a left-wing party, argued that the current housing law was a panacea, that it had practically saved the working-class public of Spain with it. It’s delirious that it now wants us to forget that. This strike by itself will not impose major demands. This strike should serve to build class power with the aim of an independent project and to stimulate fights for housing, improved salaries, and against the authoritarianism of capitalist states. Within the strike, CJS will push the need to construct an alternative political structure for workers — not just strong unions but a party for workers. To achieve that, we will participate in broad committees and promote strike youth committees open to whomever.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo What’s the role of unions in the Spanish working-class struggle? I understand that the major unions are quite linked to the government, but is there a future where unions can be part of the fight that you’re starting?
- Mario Arguiriano Of course, there are numerous unions in Spain that have a focus on class and are engaged in righteous struggles for workers’ rights. And even in the membership of major unions like the CCOO, there are people who fight daily for workers. We criticize the leadership of unions, which doesn’t represent the needs of workers. Unions are very important in working-class struggle; they should be organs for that and not for collaboration between classes. The leader of CCOO, Unai Sordo, wrote an article about the strike that is essentially apologia for the PSOE’s economic policy. How is it that you are going to go on a strike defending the government and its economic policies? We can’t accept this; it’s essentially an insult. That’s how we approach the question of unions. We don’t denounce or disregard union work. In fact, we will work with class-focused unions to try to drive mobilizations separate from the mobilizations that will be apologia for the government, or that might even include government ministers. The idea that there could be ministers protesting against their own government could make anyone go nuts.
- Chris Mills Rodrigo When the protests and the encampments end, what’s the plan to keep the critiques that have been levied going?
- Mario Arguiriano In Movimiento Socialista, we plan to work around two axes. The first is to strengthen the working-class movement, collaborating with other actors like labor unions and tenants’ unions toward shared objectives. For example, it’s very important for us to create a wide front for political rights capable of confronting the state, its authoritarianism, militarism, and new repressive laws. Our other axis of work, complementary with the first, is to keep working to build a mass revolutionary party, not only in Spain but across Europe and, ultimately, around the world. That requires diversified work: exposition of strategies, development of different tactics, and the production of a revolutionary political program in favor of a different form of state, a different mode of production, and a different way to live that the working class can coalesce around. We believe that is absolutely urgent. We have to fight at all levels, which includes the political. We have to counter-propose a workers’ program, a socialist program, against the program of capital.
