https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Can Netanyahu launch a strike on Iran before he leaves?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Can Netanyahu launch a strike on Iran before he leaves?
PM’s caretaker government can legally go to war, though it would likely inflame domestic divisions.
Despite losing its majority in last month’s parliamentary elections, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is still in power in a caretaker capacity.
That will continue until a new governing majority is formed – a process that could take months as Israel’s opposition struggles to form a coalition.
And while he may be politically weakened, Netanyahu is reported to be weighing new military action against Iran, despite a lack of enthusiasm from the United States, his own military establishment, and the politicians vying to replace him.
But does Netanyahu’s caretaker government actually have the authority to send Israel back to war, and how would such a move be received at home?
What military options does Israel’s caretaker government have?
Officially, Israel’s caretaker government has the same authority as a regular government. Article 30 of the country’s Basic Law states that an interim government continues to carry out the same duties until a new one takes its place.
However, Israel’s Supreme Court has previously ruled that an outgoing government must avoid irreversible policy moves unless they are urgent – a principle known as the “duty of restraint”.
In practice, Netanyahu can still initiate military action with the approval of his caretaker government, which he could present as “urgent and in the national interest”, Neve Gordon, a professor of international law at Queen Mary University, London, and the author of “Israel’s Occupation”, told Al Jazeera.
Or Asher, a researcher at the Tel Aviv-based Tachlith Institute, told the Reuters news agency that security issues generally are “the clearest exception” to a caretaker government’s duty of restraint.
“The Supreme Court has historically avoided intervening in decisions to go to war, and parliamentary oversight is at its thinnest in the weeks after the new Knesset [parliament] convenes and before its committees are formed,” said Asher.
“A caretaker prime minister can legally take Israel to war, including against Iran,” he added.
Ehab Jabareen, an analyst and Palestinian citizen of Israel, told Al Jazeera the government’s caretaker status raises the “political burden of proof”.
“Netanyahu would be asking the country to accept the consequences of a decision that could outlast his government,” he said.
Is Netanyahu pushing for a return to war with Iran?
On Wednesday, Israeli media reported that the security cabinet chaired by Netanyahu had ordered the military to step up preparations for an attack on Iran.
“The directives issued by the security cabinet to the Israeli military could lead it to carry out activities that could trigger a war,” public broadcaster KAN reported.
That followed reports that Netanyahu has been repeatedly calling US President Donald Trump to press for a new military campaign against Iran, conversations that on at least one occasion became heated, according to Israel’s Ynet News site.
On Thursday, a US military official was quoted by KAN as saying that Washington had told Israel to get ready for a potential new round of confrontation. But the US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) later dismissed the reports, telling Al Jazeera they were “mere speculation”.
According to Israel’s Channel 13, the Israeli military establishment sees no urgent need to attack Iran. It said that assessment had been presented to Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming the next government, during a briefing on Wednesday.
What has Israel’s opposition said?
The opposition has demanded that Netanyahu avoid any military action unless it is critical.
Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Lieberman, a member of the opposition bloc, said the prime minister’s caretaker government must not “make decisions that could drag Israel into war without parliamentary oversight and without the full agreement of all security officials”.
Eisenkot echoed this sentiment in a letter to Netanyahu on Wednesday, saying that deploying Israeli forces “without a direct and immediate threat that cannot wait could have devastating consequences for Israeli democracy and public trust in the institutions of government”.
The Israeli premier responded by insisting the government makes all decisions based only on “security considerations”.
How would Israeli parties and the public react to renewed war?
There would be serious divisions.
“Obviously, those who voted for Netanyahu and parties from his coalition would be in favour, while most of those who supported the so-called change bloc would be upset at Netanyahu’s use of the war to try to remain in power and block their electoral success,” said Gordon.
But ultimately, he said, most people who voted against Netanyahu’s bloc would “rally around the flag” if he resumes hostilities.
Jabareen agreed that Israelis would likely rally if a new war breaks out and missiles are incoming. But he said that “tells you very little about whether they think Netanyahu was right to start another round [of conflict]”.
“And the harder test comes when reservists are called up again, families are back in shelters and the government has to explain what the campaign can achieve that the previous one didn’t,” he added.
Jabareen said the debate in Israel over any new confrontation on Iran would likely centre on “why now?”
“If the case for urgency is weak, especially if Washington is opposed and senior Israeli commanders have reservations, the decision could be seen as an attempt to change the political agenda while Eisenkot is trying to form a government,” he said.
Beyond domestic considerations, an obstacle to Netanyahu restarting attacks may be the position of Israel’s main ally, the US, which has said it is doubling down on its economic pressure campaign against Iran rather than pursuing more large-scale military action.
“Netanyahu’s problem … is not the Israeli public, but what seems to be a loss of appetite in the US,” said Gordon.
Anders Persson, a political scientist specialising in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, said it would be easier for Netanyahu to pull off a new military campaign if it is undertaken jointly with the US.
But “the more openly Netanyahu provokes Iran, and the less support he receives from Trump, the harder it will be for him to get away with it – and for the Israeli public to accept it”, Persson told Al Jazeera.
Has an Israeli caretaker government previously launched military action?
Yes. And in one case, the government was led by Netanyahu himself.
In May 2021, weeks after his party lost seats in legislative elections and while negotiations for a new government were under way, the prime minister launched an 11-day war in Gaza that killed at least 260 people in the Palestinian enclave. Thirteen people also died in Israel.
While that conflict temporarily stalled efforts to replace Netanyahu, a new government, led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, was formed the following month, ending a 12-year run as prime minister.
Former Israeli prime ministers Ehud Olmert and Yair Lapid also ordered military action in Gaza while serving in a caretaker capacity. The 2008 war directed by Olmert was by far the most deadly, killing about 1,400 Palestinians.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/greta.title: Greta Thunberg at COP: Turkish energy shipments 'directly fuelling the genocide of Palestine'
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/greta.author: Katherine Hearst
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/greta.text:
Greta Thunberg at COP: Turkish energy shipments 'directly fuelling the genocide of Palestine'
Activist Greta Thunberg has called for an end to Turkish fuel shipments to Israel at the Cop 31 climate conference in Turkey’s Antalya, as a new report has revealed that 77 crude oil shipments left Turkish ports for Israel in violation of Ankara’s energy embargo.
Thunberg, who addressed a packed press conference on Thursday alongside activists from Nepal, Australia, Palestine and Canada, called on Ankara to “stop the transfer of oil and energy from its territory to Israel”, which she said is “directly fuelling the genocide of Palestine”.
Her comments came shortly after Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan declared in his opening address to the conference that Gaza has suffered "not only a genocide but also an ecocide", and called for the immediate entry of aid into the war-torn enclave.
Minister of environment and COP31 president, Murat Kurum, told Turkish media earlier this week that Turkey did not invite Israel’s leaders to participate at the summit due to the mass killings of Palestinians in Gaza.
The campaign group Energy Embargo for Palestine (EFFP) told Middle East Eye that while they welcomed these statements and actions, an "uncomfortable contradiction still follows Türkiye throughout COP".
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
"How can a government present itself as a climate leader while its territory remains an essential element of supply chains providing oil to Israel during its genocidal assault on Palestinians?" a spokesperson for the group said.
Turkey - which is jointly hosting this year's climate conference with Australia - is coming under increasing scrutiny for continued shipments of Azerbaijani crude, which is pumped through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan (BTC) pipeline from Azerbaijan and shipped out from the Turkish port of Ceyhan.
An updated report jointly authored by EFFP, the Palestinian Youth Movement and the Progressive International revealed last week that 77 crude oil shipments - totalling nearly 6,463 kilotonnes - left the Turkish port of Ceyhan for Israel between May 2024 and June 2026.
Ankara declared a trade embargo against Israel in May 2024.
Covert shipments
The latest findings build on a previous investigation published in January by the same groups that found that 57 shipments of Azerbaijani crude oil had sailed from Turkish to Israeli ports between May 2024 and December 2025.
According to the report, the fuel transfers were conducted covertly, with vessels listing false end destinations and disabling their tracking systems to avoid detection.
The researchers pieced together the journeys, confirming that the boats docked in Israel through satellite imagery and shipping data.
They identified that oil pumped through the BTC pipeline accounts for over 40 percent of Israel’s total oil imports over the course of its genocide in Gaza, and that the oil is refined and used to fuel Israel’s fighter jets, tanks and military vehicles.
Turkey has maintained that it does not control where the oil pumped through the BTC is sold. The pipeline is managed by Turkish state-owned energy company Botas but owned by the Azerbaijani state-owned company Socar.
In November 2024, the Turkish minister of energy said that exporters using Ceyhan "respected its decision to end trade with Israel" and that oil was not being loaded onto ships which listed Israel as a destination.
But data from vessel-tracking firm Kpler, cited by Reuters, showed that exports of Azerbaijani crude to Israel surged by 31 percent in 2025, the highest level since 2022.
Following the initial report, EEFP said that Turkish government ministries reviewed their data and stated that they would launch legal action against shipping agents accused of listing false destinations for shipments bound for Israeli ports.
However, the updated data shows at least 20 shipments, totalling an estimated 2,411 kilotonnes, leaving Turkey for Israel between 2 December 2025 and 30 June 2026, suggesting that shipments continued after this pledge.
Turkish diplomatic sources told MEE in response to a request for comment that the BTC pipeline is governed by international agreements and that the project is a partnership of 10 firms, with the Turkish Petroleum Corporation (TPAO) holding a 6.53 percent share.
They emphasised that “there is no sale of oil belonging to TPAO to Israel”, adding that “other companies utilizing the BTC pipeline respect Türkiye’s decision to cease trade with Israel, and no shipments are being made to Israel as the designated delivery point”.
Greek shipping companies
According to the data, the majority of the shipments were managed by Greek shipping operators Kyklades Maritime Corporation and Thenamaris Ships Management.
MEE previously reported, citing No Harbour for Genocide, that from 2 May 2024 to 1 December 2025, the two Greek firms accounted for 91.23 percent of oil shipments from Turkey to Israel.
Kyklades ran all but one of the 20 shipments which were conducted between December 2025 and June 2026.
These journeys appeared to follow the same pattern as previous shipments, with vessels listing destinations in Egypt and Italy but, according to port records, not docking there during the stated timeframes.
In the majority of cases, the ships disabled their signals while heading south from Turkey and turned them back on again several days later, often with a lighter weight - suggesting that they offloaded cargo between the two recorded stops.
MEE contacted Kyklades and Thenamaris for comment but did not receive a response by the time of publication.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Ukraine claims record 3,000 Russian casualties in one day as war drags on
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Ukraine claims record 3,000 Russian casualties in one day as war drags on
Meanwhile, Russia appears to suggest it has control of half of unoccupied Donbas.
As Ukraine, Russia and the United States engaged in their first peace talks since February this week, the front lines continued to deteriorate for Moscow as its casualties rose to a possible new record without any significant territorial gains.
Ukraine’s military said it had caused more than 26,000 Russian casualties – meaning those killed and seriously wounded – in the first 10 days of November, suggesting this month’s figure could mark a new record topping October’s 54,400.
On November 9, Ukraine also claimed a new daily record of 2,980 Russian soldiers killed or wounded. That marked the fourth reported daily record this year.
Al Jazeera cannot independently verify casualty claims by either side.
This cluster of new casualty records in the autumn, accompanied by a lack of any significant territorial gains by Russia, suggested that Moscow was not coming any closer to its goal of seizing the last remaining quarter of Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region this year.
A group of pro-Ukrainian hackers from Belarus said they had accessed records of the Russian state statistical service, Rosstat, and discovered an official tally of 450,000 Russian fatalities for the entire full-scale invasion, since 2022.
Independent assessments indicate that Russia has seized a net 117sq km (45sq miles) this year, a poor showing for its pains.
Yet, Russia was as defiant as ever at peace talks in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11.
Presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky, who headed the Russian delegation, told Vesti television after the talks concluded that he would be satisfied “only when we win and sign a peace agreement on our terms”.
Russia has demanded territory Ukraine is not willing to surrender, and said NATO needs to pull out of all the former Soviet bloc countries which joined it since 1997.
Medinsky called for “a new, comprehensive, and just security system in Europe,” because the one put in place after World War II “is functioning very poorly, and, in fact, the entire system is sick. In Ukraine, a festering wound has simply burst.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saw it differently.
“When the Russians now talk about a security architecture for themselves … What they really want is to freely interfere in the affairs of other countries, and to use force whenever they want, and to make sure that no one can support liberty inside Russia,” he told the Danish parliament, the Folketing, on the day the talks concluded.
Although US negotiators agreed to table the subject of a European security architecture at Abu Dhabi, the three European powers present – Germany, France and the United Kingdom – did not, and they were excluded from the proceedings.
“We did not communicate with them. We don’t really understand what their status is here,” Medinsky said.
Europe agrees with Ukraine that such a discussion puts the cart before the horse.
“The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is a complex and potentially dangerous one,” Zelenskyy said on the eve of the talks. “First, we must discuss how to end Russia’s war against Ukraine. Second, what the security infrastructure will be for Ukraine.”
Ukraine has asked for an ironclad guarantee of military intervention if it is attacked again, as offered in NATO’s Article 5.
Instead, Zelenskyy said, the Trump administration offered “something similar to NATO”.
Russian President Vladimir Putin received the US negotiating team in Saint Petersburg after talks in Abu Dhabi, and repeated the Russian position that the presence of European peacekeepers in a post-war Ukraine would also be “absolutely unacceptable”.
Zelenskyy attributed Russia’s absolutism to its inaccurate understanding of realities on the ground.
“Putin lives in a different reality,” he told journalists in Copenhagen on November 11. “When I received the second report from our negotiating group after the meetings in Abu Dhabi, they told me that the Russians believe and claim that they have already occupied half of the [part of the] Donbas region which is actually under our control. These were military officers, Russian intelligence.”
Russia’s defence ministry has claimed to have seized 3,600sq km (1,400sq miles) of Ukraine this year, and Putin has repeated the claim.
Still, Abu Dhabi did produce some results.
Russia and Ukraine said there would be a new POW exchange of at least 1,000 or possibly 1,500 prisoners on each side. And Zelenskyy said de-escalation steps were discussed.
‘Ukraine faced constant alarms’
In the run-up to Abu Dhabi, Russia pounded Ukraine’s cities.
“For 10 days and nights, Ukraine faced constant alarms,” said its General Staff. During that period, Russia launched 3,519 drones, and Ukraine managed to intercept 3,068 of them, they said, including 83 percent of the jet-powered drones, which now comprise roughly half of the swarm.
On the night of November 7, Russia unleashed 36 ballistic missiles into Ukraine, including some reportedly manufactured by North Korea, striking energy infrastructure.
Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi has asked European allies to provide generators and battery packs for homes, as well as mobile shelters and buses to keep urban transport moving during blackouts.
On November 12, Ukraine reported it was experiencing renewed restrictions on its use of the Starlink satellite service, which it needs to coordinate interceptors to incoming Russian drones.
“This directly impacts our ability to intercept Russian kamikaze drones,” said Zelenskyy. “Due to the speed limitations, we simply cannot intercept them in time.”
This came as Ukraine continued its own strikes inside Russia, targeting ballistic missile launchers and factories as a forward defence.
On November 7, a fire burned almost a hectare of storage space next to an Almaz factory in Rostov, which makes communications equipment. It was unclear whether Ukraine caused it. On the same day, Ukraine fired Neptune missiles into the Proton-Electrotex conglomerate which makes parts for Kormoran cruise and Iskander ballistic missiles, and destroyed two ballistic missile launchers.
On November 9, Ukraine struck the Morozov plant near St Petersburg, which makes solid rocket fuel for ballistic missiles, and the Redkino plant in Tver, which makes chemical products used in missiles.
On November 10, Ukraine struck the 123rd Aircraft Repair Plant in Novgorod, which services Russia’s increasingly rare A-50 early warning and targeting aircraft.
On November 11, Ukraine struck the Naro-Forminsk cruiser, which launches Kalibr and Onyx cruise missiles.
“We are acting asymmetrically,” Ukrainian defence minister Yevhenii Khmara told his Dutch counterpart. Ukraine had struck a total of 12 ballistic missile launch sites inside Russia, he said without specifying the timeframe, and said the strikes on factories were reducing Russian production capacity.
Zelenskyy renewed his call for German Taurus missiles with which to strike Russian launchers.
Ukraine also struck a series of refineries during the past week, including the Afipsky, Saratov, Kirishi, Ust-Luga and Omsk refineries. Russian military reporters said three Russian helicopters had been downed by friendly fire during attempts to defend the Ust-Luga refinery.
Since the end of October, its General Staff said, Ukraine had struck Russia’s five biggest refineries.
Sources told Reuters that Ukraine has destroyed at least 30 percent of Russia’s refining capacity.
The purpose of refinery strikes is to diminish Russian export revenue for petroleum products and to disrupt its economy. Those goals appeared to be working last week, as Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service reported Moscow projecting a $63bn-$67bn deficit for 2026, double its intended figure, and Russian media reported staff layoffs at the parliament, or Duma, and the Russian Federation Council.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Russia is ‘setting traps’ in Ukraine talks, EU foreign policy chief warns
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Jennifer Rankin in Dublin
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
The EU’s foreign policy chief has warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression.
“We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. “Nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”
In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revived its hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security – demands that were rejected in 2021 because they were seen as an infringement of the sovereignty of central and eastern European countries. The latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US were held this week in Abu Dhabi.
Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on Thursday night that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include the Europeans. However, Russia quickly contradicted that assurance.
European leaders have long said they will support Ukraine in any peace talks, but want to see a ceasefire before negotiations. They also stress the continent has an extensive web of security agreements that Russia has violated.
Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, said: “Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that; it already exists.” He added that it was a “given” that his country would be part of any European delegation.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said it was “self-explanatory that Europe is included in the peace talks to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine”.
The Kremlin said on Friday: “Once we understand [Europe’s] real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format.” Russia’s lead negotiator in Abu Dhabi, Vladimir Medinsky, said it was “unclear what there is to discuss” with Europe.
The US call to involve Europe in talks has turned the spotlight on who would represent it.
Despite more than two years of on-off talks, the EU has not settled on a choice. But there is a growing view that Europe should not be represented by a single person, but by different interlocutors from the wider continent.
Paris and Berlin support a continued role for their own envoys in the E3 format of Britain, France and Germany, alongside EU representatives. Smaller member states put the emphasis more firmly on the EU representatives: the European Council’s president, António Costa, and Kallas, the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy.
Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said the discussion on who should represent Europe was “slightly overstated” as it had differing interests.
Some of the issues in peace talks were “pure EU interests”, he said, citing financing Kyiv and Ukraine’s future membership in the bloc. He also supported other formats, such as the “pretty uncomplicated” E3 and the “very legitimate” E5, which includes Italy and Poland, as well as a role for EU representatives. He said: “I am quite flexible on that. I think what we actually say is more important than the exact configuration of the people in the room.”
Several at the summit, including Kallas, also pointed to the importance of including the UK, a founder member of the coalition of the willing, a broad group of countries committed to future peacekeeping in Ukraine.
Ireland’s taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said the UK and Norway each had a significant role and “that all has to be taken into consideration because it’s a European, continent-wide issue”.
The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was for the EU to decide who would represent the bloc. He said there was a strong view among European leaders that it was for Europe – in the wider sense – “to decide its own arrangements” on security.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Democrats won big in the US midterms. Now, organizers want them to deliver
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Fabiola Cineas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The bright blue map that emerged on election night in the US was unthinkable two years ago. When Donald Trump won the 2024 presidential election, many Democratic voters curled up in bed and doomscrolled, fatigued and fearful about the direction of the country. Any desire to fight back was dampened by the enormity of the loss.
But the mood gradually shifted over the following two years, culminating in a generational shift on election day: Democrats flipped five governors’ seats and took control of the House and Senate by wide margins. Voters were angry about the rising cost of living, the war in Iran, masked immigration agents in their neighborhoods and datacenters rising in their backyards.
But anger alone didn’t boost turnout. That required years of building coalitions, developing local campaigns and expanding movement infrastructure that turned frustration into organized action – and, eventually, votes.
Now, these same organizers are determining where to go next. The goal was never about any one party or politician. To continue to build power, movements must diversify their tactics, make clear demands, put pressure on the newly elected and keep building community-based networks, movement experts said. And they must be unrelenting.
“Elections themselves don’t achieve what it is that people want,” said Keeanga-Yamahtta Taylor, an African American studies professor at Princeton University and the author of From #BlackLivesMatter to Black Liberation. “They set the table for the possibility of change.”
Engaging beyond street protests
The national No Kings protests have been some of the most visible actions in the second Trump administration. The coalition, made up of dozens of groups and partner organizations, emerged in the middle of 2025 as intentionally leaderless and decentralized, its marches designed to be a container for the variety of grievances that millions of people wanted to express, from anger over gas prices and federal workforce cuts to frustration over war.
The marches provided an entry point for people who were new to activism, and now, after the midterms, the coalition is regrouping.
“One thing is clear: the work of protecting our democracy doesn’t begin or end with this election,” said Ezra Levin, co-founder of Indivisible, which helps power No Kings.
But drawing attention to injustice or sounding the alarm isn’t enough, said Jamila Raqib, executive director of the non-profit Albert Einstein Institution, which studies nonviolent action.
“People are more engaged than ever before,” said Raqib. “They’re taking action in response to the crises we face, but they’re less often achieving concrete objectives.”
Movements need to adapt tactics to keep up with authoritarian governments, she said. Many governments have learned that brutal crackdowns on nonviolent action tend to backfire, so they rely on “smart repression” – selective arrests, legal harassment, surveillance, disinformation, funding restrictions and job losses – to wait movements out. Governments simply outlast demonstrators who eventually have to return to school and work.
That’s why movements must map the “pillars of support” that any government depends on, including courts, businesses, media and religious institutions, Raqib said. They can then decide which of those pillars to win over, which to weaken and which to replace.
Activists should prepare to organize within workplaces, government agencies, businesses and congregations, where an opponent’s support actually lives, Raqib said. Mutual-aid networks, community defense groups and independent media can sustain a movement through a long fight, too. Preparing for smart repression also means treating digital security as a basic organizing skill, planning for the arrest of key leaders and training successors before a crackdown comes.
Several of those ideas showed up in Minnesota in January. A general strike, sit-ins at corporate headquarters and pressure on employers to speak out weakened Trump’s Operation Metro Surge in ways a single march could not. After federal agents killed two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, tens of thousands of people marched in subzero cold under the banner “No Work, No School, No Shopping”. Trump ended the operation the following month.
The response rested on years of labor, faith and community organizing, said Doran Schrantz, a longtime Minnesota organizer who founded the Organizing Lab. Thousands had trained as legal observers starting in January 2025 through immigrant rights groups like Unidos and the Immigrant Defense Network. Groups like Defend the 612 built an efficient rapid-response system to observe and document ICE agents, and the Ice Out Now coalition linked all groups on the ground, Schrantz said.
To resist, “not everyone has to march in the streets”, Raqib said.
Setting clear demands
The fight over datacenters has united Americans across party lines, showing what is possible when resistance is local and personal and outlines clear demands.
“There is an authentic local response to these datacenters,” said Schrantz. It was something that people felt they had agency over, she said: “It’s concrete: ‘I can stop that datacenter.’”
That clear target allowed groups that normally agree on little else to work together. The coalitions included environmental groups, farmers, retirees, school parents and “Maga moms”, Schrantz said. The tactics were simple and repeatable: residents packed council and county commission meetings, filed public records requests and gathered signatures for moratoriums and referendums. Across the country, the demands were clear enough to fit on a petition: pause construction until the impacts are studied, make developers pay the full cost of grid upgrades instead of passing it on to taxpayers, end tax breaks for the projects and give communities a vote before anything gets built.
On election day, the steady groundwork paid off. Voters weighed in on 41 datacenter measures in 10 states and sided against the industry in all but a single measure.
Another demand that people have rallied around during Trump 2.0 is “ICE out”. Executing that demand has proven more complicated. Still, organizers have remained steadfast to get justice for people killed by ICE and to pass legislative measures that would get officers off the street.
Three days after the Texas governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, claimed victory on election day, Houston mayor John Whitmire signed an executive order barring police from contacting ICE during vehicle stops when the drivers aren’t arrested, even if they have immigration warrants.
Whitmire’s order mirrors the ordinance activists first advocated for last year. Empowered by Republican governor Greg Abbott soon leaving office, three council members have filed a measure to write it into city law, said Jasmine Khadem González, the co-chair of the Houston Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).
“We’ve been going and having meetings with city council members, telling them, teaching them about the local police collaboration with ICE,” said Khadem González.
It took months of pressure – and the fatal ICE shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican immigrant who had lived in Houston for nearly 35 years, during a traffic stop – before city leaders publicly admitted the collaboration was happening, she said. Organizers canvassed businesses and helped them make safety plans for workplace raids, posting “employees only” and “ICE is not welcome here” signs . They met with faith leaders and held community teach-ins on how Houston police were delivering people to ICE, often through traffic stops. Now, the Harris county district attorney is taking the Salgado Araujo case to a grand jury.
“We can prosecute every single ICE agent who murdered people on our streets,” she said, “and so I’m excited to see some justice come to that family.”
Khadem González’s demands for the new Democratic majorities in the state go well beyond Houston. She wants lawmakers to repeal SB4, the state law that bans sanctuary cities, to end police collaboration with ICE across the entire state of Texas.
“Now that Democrats are in power, we have to show what good governance looks like,” she said.
Keeping pressure on electeds
This drives home the greater point: movements need to keep putting pressure on Democrats, newly elected or otherwise, to get their demands met.
Celebration can’t be the endpoint, Taylor, of Princeton, warned. “Everyone who is connected to an organizing project, to organization politics, must have a Wednesday agenda,” she said, noting the need to keep pushing after Tuesday’s election. “What are we doing now to push the political representatives who solicited our votes?”
Only sustained pressure will move anything, she said, and no elected official is off-limits.
The DSA has a slate of priorities it wants its affiliated candidates to push through when they get into office: an arms embargo on Israel; an end to foreign wars and on sanctions on Cuba, Venezuela and Iran; Medicare for All; abolishing ICE. The organization said its five nationally endorsed candidates, from Melat Kiros in Colorado to Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, will represent the largest bloc of democratic socialist candidates in Congress in the nation’s history.
“This election is a reminder that the electorate is not fixed and that organizing and investment can transform what’s possible,” said Katrina Gamble, a political scientist turned social impact strategist at Sojourn Strategies.
For example, in Mississippi, where Democrats just flipped a Senate seat and elected the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction, Black voters made up 3% more of the electorate than they did in 2024; nearly 21% of the state’s voters in this election didn’t vote in 2024.
But Gamble also warns that “these wins are fragile”. The work now is to keep engaging people and ensure electeds deliver on what they promised voters.
“It can’t just be that the blue wave comes and we’ve done our jobs,” Taylor said. “The blue wave is just the beginning.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Nvidia scandal: What’s next for the US tech company?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Nvidia scandal: What’s next for the US tech company?
What happens next at one of the world’s most valuable companies will have repercussions far beyond Silicon Valley.
The departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the 63-year-old cofounder and face of the chipmaking company which has become the backbone of the modern AI industry, has shaken the US’s Silicon Valley.
Nvidia, valued at nearly $4 trillion, is a critical pillar of the US economy where AI and tech companies make up some 40 percent of stock market valuations. The furore over Huang’s extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, has wiped hundreds of billions of dollars from the company’s market value, dragging down the S&P 500 and Nasdaq.
While CFO Colette Kress has temporarily stepped into the top job at Nvidia, the search for cofounder Huang’s successor continues.
What happens next at one of the world’s most valuable companies will have repercussions far beyond Silicon Valley. So, what’s next for Nvidia?
What has happened so far?
On October 29, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies suspected a Chinese businesswoman and executive associated with Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed International, Alice Huang, had been tapped by China’s Ministry of State Security to gather information from Nvidia’s Huang.
The newspaper reported that the two were involved in an intimate relationship, later confirmed by the cofounder of the company in an internal memo. Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.
“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote in an internal memo to Nvidia staff.
The business links go beyond just the affair, however, fuelling further concerns. Megaspeed purchased more than $4.8bn of Nvidia chips over roughly two years. Separately, The Information reported that Alice Huang facilitated at least $7.5bn in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese firms, raising even more questions about skirting US export controls.
Then, on Wednesday, the NYT reported a second alleged affair between Jensen Huang and Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reported directly to him.
The next day, Huang was forced out of the company and off its board.
Hours later, Reuters reported that Huang had allegedly been involved in a third affair with another Nvidia employee, citing two people familiar with the matter.
Why is Nvidia so significant?
In simple terms, if Nvidia sneezes, the AI industry and modern computing catch a cold.
Nvidia controls nearly 90 percent of the market for advanced AI chips which are used to train frontier AI models, giving it an extraordinary degree of influence over the global AI industry and the infrastructure powering it.
Observers say the company holds the keys to next-generation computing. Its customers include tech giants such as Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta, which rely on Nvidia hardware to build and operate their AI data centres.
That’s also why Washington has restricted Nvidia from selling chips to China.
Nvidia’s Huang has spent years lobbying in Washington against such restrictions, arguing that restricting sales would surrender a strategically important market to domestic Chinese competitors.
That puts him at odds with US lawmakers who view access to Nvidia’s advanced chips as a national security risk, particularly given their potential military applications.
How has China reacted?
A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said Beijing has “always opposed the abuse of export control measures”, as pressure gains momentum yet again in Washington. Beijing has rejected allegations that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as “baseless”.
In China, investors have been selling shares in Chinese AI-linked companies over worries that recent developments at Nvidia could deepen the technological divide between Beijing and Washington.
On Friday, shares in Z.AI, one of China’s top AI model developers, tumbled more than 10 percent in Hong Kong while shares in rival MiniMax hit record lows.
A Reuters review identified more than $3bn in Chinese computing projects built around Nvidia’s restricted processors – despite the American chipmaker claiming that US export controls effectively shut it out of the AI data-centre market in the world’s second-biggest economy.
The examination shows projects stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, and underscores how deeply Nvidia’s technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion.
What’s happened to Nvidia’s share price and will it recover?
Nvidia shares rose 1.8 percent in premarket trading on Friday after losing around 11 percent of their value this week up to Thursday, when Huang exited the company he built.
The company is on course for its longest streak of weekly losses since October 2012.
US President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, next week in Shenzhen at the APEC leaders’ summit.
Similarly, shares in Nvidia’s customers, such as South Korea’s Naver, fell more than 5 percent. Nasdaq futures and S&P 500 futures fell 0.4 percent and 0.15 percent, respectively.
“Jensen has obviously been a singular force in many ways so the impact will likely be felt far and wide,” UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri told Reuters.
“The company has become a key source of funds for a host of AI industry participants including neo-clouds, LLM developers, ecosystem partners, and suppliers, and we have always seen Jensen as a key driving force for this effort,” Arcuri said.
“Even if a new leader ultimately maintains a similar approach, there is likely to be some ‘pause’ in the company’s willingness and ability to continue pursuing these deals in the near term,” he added.
What’s next for Nvidia?
From washing dishes at a Denny’s to building a $4 trillion technology giant, Huang has led Nvidia for nearly 33 years – and made one of Silicon Valley’s defining entrepreneurial stories.
But the “cult-style” leaders at Silicon Valley – including Huang, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk – also reflect the concentration of market power that tech companies enjoy. Technology stocks now account for nearly 40 percent of the S&P 500’s total market value.
That is likely to rise when AI companies Anthropic and OpenAI also go public.
And in the absence of a clear succession plan, things could go awry, sending jitters among investors – a concern which Nvidia highlighted itself in its annual review for this year.
Under the risk factors dealing with its dependence on key personnel, Nvidia’s report noted that the company is “highly dependent on the services of our longstanding executive team”.
“Failure to ensure effective succession planning, transfer of knowledge, and smooth transitions involving executives and key employees could hinder our strategic planning, execution, and long-term success,” it said.
Nvidia’s board has begun searching for a permanent successor to Huang, tapping CFO Kress as interim CEO.
Meanwhile, President Trump, who has defended Huang as a “genius”, shared his two cents, too. He suggested former Apple chief executive Tim Cook could take over Nvidia. “A Legend replaces a Legend,” Trump wrote.
Nvidia has said it will consider candidates from both within and outside the company.

Israeli rabbi says politicians cooperating with Arab parties can be killed
A prominent rabbi in Israel has invoked a Jewish religious doctrine permitting the use of lethal force against politicians who cooperate with Arab parties, Haaretz reported.
Rabbi Gedalya Axelrod, a former head of the Haifa Rabbinical Court, said in a handwritten ruling that Jewish party leaders who support a government formed with the backing of Arab parties are subject to din rodef, or the “law of the pursuer”.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.title: Pride and no prejudice: how Tough Guy Book Club taught 10,000 men to be unashamed of reading
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Tim Byrne
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
“When did we decide that men and reading and toughness all had to be separate things?” Shay Leighton asks over a pint of Melbourne Black in his local Brunswick pub. “I don’t know about you, but I didn’t get a vote.”
For 14 years, Leighton has run the Tough Guy Book Club, a not-for-profit charity dedicated to encouraging men to read – although he’s quick to stress that they do more than just that. “We’re not a reading club, we’re a talking club,” he says. “The three goals of book club are: read more, talk more, have more friends.”
Leighton was once a tough kid himself but in 2012 he found himself in need of purpose: “I’d made some pretty bad choices and I was really unhappy. My partner had just left, my business had closed down and I didn’t have any friends.” A book club was a way “to get me out of the house cause I had pretty much fucked my life up”.
At the start, the club was just Leighton and his mate Tom Scott. As they sat discussing their first book – Ernest Hemingway’s The Old Man and the Sea – in the beer garden of a Collingwood pub, they had an encounter that would change everything. A stranger, “a big guy, a neck-tat dude”, approached and asked if they were in a book club. When Leighton confirmed they were, certain that he was about to get punched in the head, the man immediately asked, “Can I join?”
“We just invited people who didn’t think they were invited,” Leighton says. “And we invited people in places where they didn’t usually get invited.”
When they put fliers up in tattoo parlours, men’s barbers and boxing gyms, the interest was immediate: Tough Guy Book Club now runs chapters in 10 countries and has 10,000 members worldwide. Individual chapters are organised and run locally, meeting at 7pm on the first Wednesday of every month.
As for the name, several variations were tried out but “every time I said Tough Guy Book Club and someone laughed, I got more and more determined to call it that”, Leighton says. “Because those two things, toughness and reading, for some reason they’ve become so separate that, when you push them together, people think you’re doing comedy.”
Incongruity is a powerful weapon and a great recruitment tool but it can also reinforce cultural stereotypes around literacy and masculinity, something Leighton is fighting to change. “I’m not what a reader looks like,” he says. “I’m not invited to the local literary festival.” The typical Tough Guy Book Club member “is not telling you he wants to read more; he’s not walking around bookstores”. The focus is determinedly analogue, too; the club is only held “in person, at the pub and in your neighbourhood. We don’t want to do meetings online.”
For former NRL player and BookTok sensation Luke Bateman, the online space was an essential conduit to the world of reading and a lifeline when he was at his lowest. After a well-publicised breakdown brought on by a gambling addiction, Bateman retreated to his family farm, where a single book-related post on TikTok – recorded from his tractor – went viral. He clocks that down to incongruity, too.
“It’s unexpected that someone who looks like me and has my background would be so in love with reading and want to promote it so passionately,” he says, over the phone from Brisbane. “I’ve read since I was a child; it’s a genuine and authentic part of me. Reading transports me to somewhere I can exist without fear of ridicule. I just get to experience a deep sense of joy.”
It wasn’t always the case, though. As soon as Bateman was catapulted into the world of professional rugby, he learned to repress his love of reading, and certainly would never let a teammate see him with a book. “I had a lot of shame around my reading. I never saw men read. Reading was a feminine thing. Young boys need to see men read, see their heroes and role models share a love of literature.”
The biggest barrier to men reading is other men. And it happens early. In his podcast In The Good Books, Bateman talks to children’s author Scott Stuart about a study on boys’ reading that illuminates something essential about boys and their relationship with books. When boys are asked to choose a book for themselves, “gender doesn’t enter the equation”, Stuart explains. It can be pink, it can be about fairies, boys don’t care. “But when they are asked to choose for other boys, suddenly all the female main characters disappear.”
While reading rates are declining among men and women in Australia – gen X men are the only demographic that reads statistically less than women of the same age – Bateman believes passionately that we can turn those numbers around if we start in the home.
“If you want your kids to be readers, you have to be a reader. We can’t be placing the responsibilities of failing literacy rates upon children. As adults, that’s our responsibility; we’re the ones failing them. We live in a world that corporations and capitalism have wanted to make very easy for us, frictionless. But reading requires friction, a little bit more effort.”
Bateman thinks books are essential “if we want our children to grow and prosper and evolve into fully integrated and capable, competent human beings”.
Leighton sees the transformational effects of reading in men firsthand. He runs a book club in a prison – they also started with The Old Man and the Sea – and he encourages them to join Tough Guy Book Club once they’re out.
“When you’ve done 15 years, the only other guys you know are guys who’ve done 15 years. I just wanted to give them another option. They can come hang out with us.”
When men read, the whole community benefits. Bateman believes that reading lets young men see “that there are further possibilities for them outside the narrative they’ve been given”. For Leighton, men must actively tear down their own assumptions about reading and masculinity – because no one else can do it for them.
“Men are our own jailers and our own police officers on this,” he says. “Somewhere along the way we decided and then we just enforced it ourselves. We’re the only people who can help us out of that.”

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: German knives, English socks: 13 gifts beloved globally that Americans are missing out on
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Karen Yuan and Guardian staff
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
Our editors and writers have lived across the globe, from Abu Dhabi to Toronto to São Paulo. So when we asked them to share beloved gifts from outside the US, the answers were as varied as our home towns.
This is the stuff we bring home in our suitcases and press into friends’ hands. Take the “workhorse” German paring knives or the bright red tortilla press that makes homemade masa feel effortless. There’s a 3lb tub of Maldon salt that is absurdly whimsical yet practical, and a set of Australian linen sheets that get softer with every wash.
Some picks, such as El Dorado rum from Guyana, are a little piece of home. Others, including posters from Denmark’s Louisiana Museum, are just beautiful. And all of them are delightful discoveries that don’t require a plane ticket to bring home.
Germany
Mexico
Cast-iron tortilla press
There’s something really special about a fresh, homemade tortilla. They taste better than anything you can get at the supermarket and are shockingly (at least I was shocked) simple to make. To make your masa (dough), just add water to your harina (maize flour) and roll into little balls. Though you can realistically flatten these balls with a rolling pin and some parchment papers, a tortilla press gives you consistent thickness. Plus, the bright red finish brightens up any kitchen. Danielle Renwick
Australia
Hunter candles
I first discovered Hunter Candles when a colleague introduced me to their tucked-away storefront in Sydney’s tree-lined Surry Hills neighborhood. Their scents are fresh and never overpowering, with unique, earthy notes inspired by ingredients such as shiitake mushroom, river mint, blue gum trees, mountain ash and grapefruit rind (who would have thought!). I also love that customers in Australia can return empty candle glasses for refills. My favorite is Daisy, a bright scent with delicate florals and summery hints of peach. Maya Yang
Soft sheets from Dazed but Amazed
When I moved to Los Angeles, one of the first things that I bought was a linen sheet set from Dazed but Amazed, a small Australian company. The small-batch color combinations they offer are striking and unexpected; the sheets themselves get softer and softer with use. There’s a Pacific sensibility in everything the brand offers – they make my bedroom feel like it opens right on to the beach. Lois Beckett
UK
3lb tub of Maldon salt
For your friends with caviar taste on a McNuggets budget, let me introduce you to the 3lb container of the UK’s Maldon sea salt flakes. While small boxes of Maldon salt are widely available at grocery stores around the US, loyalists to the stuff (me) know that the 3lb tub is a whimsical necessity in any good kitchen. It’s not only a visually fun gift to receive (it comes with a cute little handle!), it’s absurdly practical! I use a smaller salt cellar on my counter, but knowing there’s plenty to refill it with at all times? A thrill! It’s also roughly $30, making it a cost-effective gift for someone desperately seeking seasoning in their life, a white elephant offering or a cheeky pre-holidays gift from you to you. Jenna Amatulli
Rock & Ruby socks
This sustainable knitwear brand, founded in east London during the pandemic, produces a beautiful array of striking, vintage-inspired socks. There are bold checks and tasteful stripes in a wide array of colors. I craved a pair as soon as I saw them. LB
Brazil
Pão de Queijo
I lived in Brazil in my 20s and 30s and to this day crave cheesy, gooey pão de queijo. This addictive treat, originally from the state of Minas Gerais, is a mix of tapioca flour, cheese and eggs. If I’m feeling particularly nostalgic I’ll pair them with some açai. I was delighted to find that this dry mix comes in bulk and tastes just like anything you’d find at a Brazilian padaria. DR
Italy
Bialetti Moka Pot
“Despite my Italian heritage, it took a temporary move to Rome to discover the magic of the moka pot. I instantly fell in love with this Italian coffee maker’s ability to brew a beverage on par with the $10 lattes found at my favorite cafes,” I wrote in my guide to achieving a perfect cup of iced coffee. In the chillier months, I rely on mine for achieving steaming cups of coffee, topped with frothed milk and a dash of cinnamon. It’s far less expensive than an espresso machine, but makes coffee nearly as strong.
 
While I own two sizes, the colored option would make for a particularly great gift (I have red). Lauren Gould
Canada
Mango puzzles
In the nearly 15 years I’ve lived in Toronto, I’ve never been more than 15 minutes by bike or streetcar from the city’s best outdoor spots: Trinity Bellwoods, or a ravine. These beautifully illustrated jigsaw puzzles that capture my favo(u)rite city scenes are a dream to play, each piece snapping easily into the next, and the poster is so lovely I have framed it. Jessie Willms
Canadian e-reader
If you’re looking for a non-Amazon alternative to the Kindle, let this be your sign to get a Kobo. (These e-readers are widely available outside Canada, but it’s nice to tell people that Canadian tech extends beyond the BlackBerry – RIP.) Then load it up with your favorite Canadian books, from Margaret Atwood to Rachel Reid to all the Emily St John Mandels. Does it also snow terribly from early December to May where you live? Get cozy under this quilt, in these sweatpants and this bunny hug (an endearing Saskatchewan regionalism for hoodie. Light a Province of Canada candle and read until spring. JW
Fable’s affordable ceramics
If you’re a millennial looking to (finally) upgrade and unify your tablewares, consider Fable. The Canadian company makes lovely ceramics that feel much more luxurious than their price point. The plates and bowls are a lovely foundation if you want to pair them with your existing eclectic tableware. While I would die to have all my tableware from Michelle Organ or Toni Darling Frank, budget (and my likelihood to drop breakables) prohibits it. A mix of makers big and small is the sweet spot. JW
Guyana
El Dorado rum
El Dorado rum comes from Guyana, where I’m originally from. Growing up, El Dorado was always a name we knew and took pride in. Guyana is known for its demerara sugar, and El Dorado rum is one of the great products that comes from the ingredient. When I give it as a gift, I love that I’m sharing a little piece of home and introducing someone to something special that represents my country. It’s a great rum. Keisa Caesar
Denmark
Posters from the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art
Scandinavia’s best contemporary art museum is tucked away in the Danish countryside, a short train ride outside Copenhagen. Luckily, its online store of stunning art prints ships to the US – and you can get them framed or unframed. There’s something for every art lover: reimagined maps and manuals of Dominican-American artist Firelei Báez, eerie figures of Kaari Upson, classic landscapes by David Hockney and more. For a holiday gift, I might choose one of these ocean plant cyanotypes by 19th-century British botanist Anna Atkins. LB
Other pieces you might enjoy from the Filter, the Guardian’s guide to buying fewer, better things:
- The 13 best Advent calendars for 2026
- The nine best personalized gifts
- This indulgent, self-heating ceramic mug has ruined all other mugs for me

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Trump the ‘biggest loser’ for scrapping climate action, John Kerry says at Cop31
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Oliver Milman in Antalya
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Donald Trump is the “biggest loser we’ve seen in a long time” for scrapping action on the climate crisis and ceding the clean energy race to China, former US secretary of state John Kerry has said.
Kerry, speaking at the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey, criticized Trump for withdrawing the US from the international climate process and axing measures that reduced planet-heating emissions. Unlike almost all other countries in the world, the Trump administration has sent no delegation to the resort city of Antalya for the annual UN climate talks, which started on Monday.
The US president, who has previously called climate science a “hoax” and called for countries to drill for more oil and gas, again expressed his hostility towards clean energy on Monday. “I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser,” Trump, who has long-held animus towards wind farms, said about potential new legislation that would make it easier to build new energy projects.
Asked about his comments by the Guardian, Kerry said: “[The] first thing they should do is hold up a really big mirror so he can look at a loser, because he’s the biggest loser we’ve seen in a long time on all of these issues.”
“He’s missing the point,” Kerry, a former climate envoy for Joe Biden’s administration, added. “He’s missing the competitiveness with China. He’s missing the marketplace for goods that could be produced in the United States. We could be the supply chain for some of these.”
Under Biden, the US passed sweeping climate legislation that gave tax breaks for clean energy and electric vehicle manufacturing in a bid to compete with China, which has dominated clean tech.
Republicans eliminated most of this support, however, with Trump instead imposing tariffs on various goods and pouring public money into propping up struggling coal-fired power plants. Coal is the dirtiest of fossil fuels, causing much of the pollution that is dangerously overheating our planet.
“He declared he wanted to beat China, be number one in X, Y, or Z, and he walked away from the battlefield,” Kerry said of Trump. “He totally took America out of that sector. So honestly, if you want to be number one, you don’t do it by literally blackballing an entire sector of the economy.”
Kerry, who ran as the Democratic candidate for president in 2004, has repeatedly urged the US and the rest of the world to follow China’s lead on green energy. The overall rapid growth in renewables has helped prevent a significant amount of fossil fuel power going online, with global emissions edging down slightly last year.
Far larger and deeper cuts to emissions will be needed for the world to avoid catastrophic climate change, however, with countries gathering at Cop told by António Guterres, the UN secretary general, it was “long past time” to phase out fossil fuel use.
The dawdling progress in years of talks to even discuss fossil fuels, the central cause of the climate crisis, has provoked ire from advocates. “Cops have become greenwashed circuses,” said Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, who arrived in Antalya on Tuesday. “That is the reality.”
Kerry acknowledged the ponderous progress and that politicians should talk differently about the climate crisis to engage the public. But he claimed that while it was not the central issue to the recent US midterm elections, concerns about global heating did overlap with alarm over rising energy costs and drove voters to the Democrats.
“I think we will have a number of candidates who will have this high on the agenda,” Kerry said of the victorious Democratic candidates. “And all of the analysis that I’ve seen, I mean real analysis, has said this was one of the issues that counted.”
The White House has dismissed the Cop 31 talks. “This summit rejects reality by failing to acknowledge that extremist climate policies are destroying countries around the world,” a White House official said, confirming that the administration would not send anyone to Cop31.

https://apache.be/2026/10/28/buitenspori.title: Buitensporig politieoptreden bij vreedzaam protest in Antwerpen: wie beschermt de kwetsbaren?
https://apache.be/2026/10/28/buitenspori.author: Abel Meers
https://apache.be/2026/10/28/buitenspori.text:
Het Antwerpse De Coninckplein gaat dezer dagen onophoudelijk over de tongen; het vormt het brandpunt van het debat over overlast en veiligheid in onze wijk, in onze stad. Midden oktober was dit plein het toneel voor een vreedzame betoging tegen de nieuwe ‘claimersmaatregel’ van waarnemend burgemeester Els van Doesburg (N-VA). De reactie van de politie was disproportioneel.
“Ik heb pijn! Waarom doen jullie dit? Jullie beschermen just niemand. Iedereen is bang van jullie!” schreeuwde een jongen, zijn gezicht bebloed, donderdagavond (15/10) uit tegen de undercoveragent die hem enkele minuten daarvoor had toegetakeld. Zittend op de dorpel van een koffiebar wat verderop wist hij in enkele zinnen de essentie van de avond te vatten. Daarna werd hij per ambulance afgevoerd om gehecht te worden in het ZNA Cadix.
Deze maatregel past in een politiek van symptoombestrijding; de maatschappelijke ellende in een stad los je niet op met willekeurige arrestaties
Ik was die avond aanwezig op het De Coninckplein bij het burgerprotest tegen de omstreden nieuwe maatregel. Die laat de politie toe om gekende daklozen, thuislozen en mensen met een verslavingsproblematiek voor maximaal twaalf uur bestuurlijk op te pakken, in het kader van de “strijd tegen overlast” in de Seefhoek.
Die preventieve arrestaties konden aanvankelijk zonder aanleiding gebeuren, wat op 12 oktober werd bijgesteld. Sindsdien moet er een ‘claimerfeit’ aan voorafgaan, of de voorbereiding ervan. De politie van Antwerpen heeft sinds 1 oktober al 615 van dit soort bestuurlijke arrestaties uitgevoerd.
Dat de uitdagingen in Antwerpen-Noord reëel zijn en maatregelen absoluut nodig zijn, staat buiten kijf. Maar de stigmatisering die dit beleid met zich meebrengt, is allesbehalve de oplossing. Het past in een politiek van symptoombestrijding; de maatschappelijke ellende in een stad los je niet op met willekeurige arrestaties.
Muur van blauw
Wie objectief naar de menigte op het protest keek, zag dan ook geen relschoppers. Het publiek bestond uit bezorgde buurtbewoners, medewerkers uit de daklozenopvang, eerstelijnshulp en zorgverleners. Zelfs de omliggende cafés stroomden vol met sympathisanten. Toch voelde de politie zich genoodzaakt dit vreedzame protest op te wachten met een buitensporige muur van blauw: acht arrestatiebusjes, bewapende eenheden, agenten in burger en een handvol reguliere agenten.
Waarnemend burgemeester Els Van Doesburg (N-VA) benadrukt in de media te pas en te onpas dat de politie altijd éérst inzet op dialoog en de-escalatie. Het bemiddelingsteam was inderdaad aanwezig en kwam ons vooraf melden dat we een halfuur gedoogd werden, waarna we verzocht zouden worden uit elkaar te gaan. Na dertig minuten doken onaangekondigd agenten in burger op die de groep hardhandig uit elkaar dreven. Vier mensen werden opgepakt. Twee mensen geraakten gewond door het politiegeweld. Eén jongeman kreeg daarbij zulke zware klappen in het gezicht dat hij bloedend per ambulance moest worden afgevoerd. Hij houdt er wellicht een litteken als levenslang aandenken aan over.
De aanwezigen waren bezorgde buurtbewoners, medewerkers uit de daklozenopvang, eerstelijnshulp en zorgverleners
Toen ik het bemiddelingsteam nadien vroeg waarom er niet, zoals ons was gezegd, eerst werd gevraagd om te vertrekken, kregen we nul op het rekest. “Wij moeten in de eerste plaats de veiligheid van onze eigen mensen garanderen”, klonk het. Op mijn repliek dat ik me zélf ronduit onveilig voelde door de disproportionele politiemacht op straat, viel een stilte. Mijn weg naar huis was versperd door agenten met wapenstok en schild. Op de vraag hoe ik dan veilig naar huis kon, antwoordde een van hen: “Probeer maar, we zullen eens zien wat er gebeurt als je langs daar loopt.”
Deze disproportionaliteit lijkt helaas structureel. Dat uitte zich niet alleen op die avond, maar weerspiegelt zich in alledaagse situaties op exact dit plein. Mijn broer werd hier onlangs tijdens een interviewopdracht voor de universiteit zonder enige aanleiding geviseerd en om zijn identiteitskaart gevraagd. Wie deed hij kwaad? Net als buurtbewoner Erik, die − als ik de VRT NWS reportage over het protest mag geloven − al vier keer zonder duidelijke reden werd gecontroleerd. Waarom mocht dit protest, georganiseerd en gedragen door onze wijk zélf, niet in dialoog doorgaan?
Dat deze alledaagse intimidatie snel kan omslaan in fysiek geweld, ondervonden velen van ons al tijdens een eerdere, vreedzame betoging van de Antwerpse Coalitie voor Palestina. Omdat ik op de Suikerrui “niet snel genoeg achteruit stapte”, kreeg ik toen zonder waarschuwing een matrak in mijn nek. Even later kwam een vriend met pepperspray in de ogen naast me schuilen voor het waterkanon. Die avond brak mijn vertrouwen in de politie, maar nog veel meer mijn vertrouwen in de politiek. Zeker wanneer Els van Doesburg kort daarna live op televisie de feiten op het terrein stelselmatig verdraaide om het hardhandige politieoptreden te verantwoorden.
Disproportioneel optreden
Ik schrijf dit stuk vanuit een comfortabele positie: ik ben een witte man, ik ken mijn rechten en heb de middelen en het platform om dit disproportionele optreden aan te kaarten. Ik doe dat bewust, omdat de publieke opinie zich vaak moet baseren op officiële politieverslagen die niet altijd stroken met de feiten op het terrein.
Als ordediensten zich al zo intimiderend opstellen tegenover geprivilegieerde burgers, studenten en hulpverleners, wat betekent dat dan voor de mensen in de marge?
De vraag die mij na donderdagavond het meest bezighoudt is deze: als ordediensten zich al zo intimiderend opstellen tegenover geprivilegieerde burgers, studenten en hulpverleners op een doodnormale donderdag, wat betekent dat dan voor de mensen in de marge? Wat betekent die 'claimersmaatregel' voor de verslaafde of de thuisloze die ‘s nachts op dit plein door diezelfde eenheden wordt benaderd?
Antwerpen-Noord is een buurt met uitdagingen die vragen om maatschappelijke en menselijke oplossingen. Repressie is geen zorg. Een stad – een samenleving – die de dialoog met haar eigen hulpverleners en buurtbewoners vervangt door groteske intimidatie, creëert geen veiligheid. Ze creëert wantrouwen, en verliest uiteindelijk haar menselijkheid.

https://www.cartooningforpeace.org/en/ca.title: Cartooning for Peace in Taiwan and South Korea
https://www.cartooningforpeace.org/en/ca.author: ADMIN-principal2026

Cartooning for Peace / Cartooning for Peace in Taiwan and South Korea	
From 11 to 20 November 2026 in Taiwan, and then from 24 to 26 November in South Korea, Cartooning for Peace is running an educational project on artificial intelligence and human rights in partnership with the French Office in Taipei, the City of Paris and the Institut français in Seoul.
On Thursday 19 November, Cartooning for Peace will take part in the ‘Night of Ideas’ organised by the French Office at Hsinchu University, focusing on issues relating to technological innovation, and will be hosted on 20 November by Le Pigeonnier bookshop for a book signing event in Taipei, featuring Kak and Stellina, as well as Pierre Haski, a journalist specialising in geopolitical issues and president of Reporters Without Borders.

https://www.cartooningforpeace.org/en/pr.title: « Propaganda Monitor », le rapport de RSF sur la géopolitique de la propagande du Kremlin, illustré par Cartooning for Peace
https://www.cartooningforpeace.org/en/pr.author: ADMIN-principal2026
https://www.cartooningforpeace.org/en/pr.text:
Cartooning for Peace / « Propaganda Monitor », le rapport de RSF sur la géopolitique de la propagande du Kremlin, illustré par Cartooning for Peace	
Reporters sans frontières (RSF) lance un nouveau rapport compilant l’ensemble des contenus de son projet “Propaganda Monitor”, un site dédié qui expose les mécanismes de propagande et de désinformation, pour mieux agir face à eux.
“Depuis longtemps, Moscou rêve de réduire au silence toute alternative à sa vision du monde. Et le contexte international favorise cette ambition. La décision du 14 mars 2025 de Donald Trump de démanteler l’Agence américaine pour les médias mondiaux (USAGM), a été accueillie avec satisfaction par le Kremlin : moins de voix indépendantes, c’est plus d’espace pour ses récits. Mais avec le Propaganda Monitor, l’idée est simple : nous devons reprendre la main face à la propagande. L’ambition est claire : donner aux citoyennes et citoyens des clés de compréhension pour ne pas subir un discours obéissant aux intérêts et qui se diffuse et se reproduit avec une agilité déconcertante.”
Thibaut Bruttin, Directeur général de RSF
Cette publication, consacrée aux stratégies du Kremlin en Russie et à l’international, est illustrée par des dessinateurs de presse du réseau Cartooning for Peace. Elle comporte également une interview exclusive du dessinateur de presse russe Denis Lopatin, exilé en France depuis 2018, qui témoigne de la gravité de la situation.

https://www.newyorker.com/culture/photo-.title: The Unclassifiable Talent of Hervé Guibert
https://www.newyorker.com/culture/photo-.author: Hilton Als
https://www.newyorker.com/culture/photo-.text:
Hervé Guibert’s ultimately unclassifiable talent brilliantly evokes the shadows, the moments of dread and paranoia, that are part of the experience of love. Doom lurks everywhere in Guibert’s world, in large part because love, as Guibert expresses it, is synonymous with longing, and what is longing but a pit stop on the way to hurt, loss, and the lover’s need to control the beloved?
Born in 1955, into a middle-class family in a suburb of Paris, Guibert, who wrote about photography in addition to taking pictures himself—he also published more than two dozen books of fiction, autofiction, and essays—was a gay man who came of age during the AIDS epidemic, a time of incalculable devastation. Guibert describes the epoch with what feels like a preternatural calm in his now classic 1990 novel, “To the Friend Who Did Not Save My Life,” in which we meet some of his friends, thinly disguised, including the philosopher Michel Foucault and the actress Isabelle Adjani. I remember reading about the book when it came out in the U.S. the following year—the year that Guibert died, at age thirty-six, of AIDS-related causes. Some people condemned the work for outing Foucault as a fellow AIDS sufferer. What right did Guibert have to tell someone else’s story? At some point, I read the book, and then I put the memory of reading it away: it was too potent, too sharp a reminder of what I had experienced during those years when quick and slow disasters were all around, and I felt ashamed of my helplessness and relative good health.
But then, about a decade ago, the writers Bruce Hainley and Jennifer Krasinski told me about a video that Guibert had made some months before his death. Titled “Modesty, or Immodesty” (1991), the hour-length work, shot by Guibert himself between June, 1990, and March, 1991, shows the artist going about his daily life in his final months, writing, talking on the phone, bathing, exercising, undergoing a medical procedure, then playing back the footage so that he can witness it, taking a holiday, and finally typing on a word processor, which continues to produce his text after he has moved on. This piece, Guibert’s single work on video, is an extraordinary film of self-dramatization: life and illness as a form of theatre. It is not a brave work—that’s too paltry a word for it. It is a powerful record of the isolating effects of AIDS, and of a patient who is running out of time and holding onto the act of creation as evidence that he has lived. As with “To the Friend Who Did Not Save My Life,” I did not want to remember the film after I had seen it; its solitude spoke of universal solitude, all those rooms filled with lost potential and the memory of the dead.
So it was with some trepidation, but also curiosity and not a little excitement, that I began looking at the volumes of Guibert’s photographs that were published recently, in elegant editions, by the Magic Hour Press. “The Only Face” is a version of the catalogue for a show that Guibert had in Paris, in 1984. The images are in black-and-white, and are romantic in a way that reminds one almost immediately of the photographer Duane Michals, another artist who worked with image and text. In the introduction to the original catalogue, Guibert wrote:
Love doesn’t necessarily make a good photograph, but the photographer’s interest, and the intelligence and imagination behind it, can contribute to the making of a picture that interests us. It’s important to remember that Guibert was a very young man when he was taking these photographs, because sometimes the romanticism of his vision draws out a kind of artificiality that feels distinctly Gallic in its love of surface beauty; one longs to go deeper, to be allowed to go deeper, into the image.
The photographs are titled—“The mother,” “The father,” and so on—and the dominant visual theme in the work is the photographer’s fascination with the play of light in black-and-white. Too often Guibert goes for mood, as in “The fiancé” and “Sienna.” In the former, we see a figure shot from the front, draped in tulle. At first it’s not clear what sex the person is, but, looking closer, you can make out black hair across his chest. It’s a self-conscious study in texture, the kind of Photography 101 assignment you’re proud of yourself for having carried to completion, but Guibert’s lyricism topples over into kitsch in “Sienna.” In that picture, we see light pouring through a window. There’s smoke in the light. Is it cigarette smoke, or angels’ breath? A thin, shirtless figure sits in a chair with arms and head bent over a table. Again, it’s not a photograph but an image about photography, and Guibert’s too-romantic love of it.
Guibert’s love of Michals-influenced gay narrative also plays out in a piece called “The friend.” A white male hand rests on a broad, darker-skinned chest. That is all we see, in medium closeup, and the contrasts are obvious—light and dark, older and younger—but the picture stops there; what we are meant to register is not so much the bodies, their stories, as the photographer in the act of becoming one. (Helmut Newton is another influence. In Guibert’s portrait “Agathe,” a wavy-haired young woman looks out at us, her open jacket exposing her small breasts.)
Sometimes, though, Guibert is helped by a subject who works with him to make an emotionally legible picture that succeeds graphically as well. I don’t think I’ll soon forget his terrific portrait “Isabelle,” in which we see Adjani lying on a bench, her face turned to the camera. She wears a light-colored garment; her right arm rests on her belly. Adjani’s dark hair, the openness of her gaze, feels less like a study in grays and blacks than like a photograph about stillness. You can see how in their time together, the time it took to take this picture, Guibert was able to move past his love of the art of photography to the point of understanding it as an instrument of connection.
Like Adjani, the subjects of Guibert’s brilliant book “Suzanne and Louise” are so extraordinary that you can’t look away from them, and neither can the artist. Guibert called this book, originally published in France in 1980 and now available in English for the first time, a photo-novel, and that’s fine, but the category seems too limiting for what “Suzanne and Louise” is: a work as great as Jean Genet’s “The Maids,” and just as chilling. We’re in another black-and-white world, this time in a hôtel particulier in the Fifteenth Arrondissement, where two sisters, Suzanne and Louise, have lived for more than forty years. The fairly reclusive ladies, Guibert’s great-aunts, have had different lives: Louise was a Carmelite nun until she was convinced to leave the order by Suzanne, a widow who was once married to a pharmacist. Suzanne has money, and Louise does not. They share a dog named Whysky, and a marriage of sorts: Suzanne is the dominant figure, and Louise her poor relation who waits on her. The prose in the book is written from the inside; when Guibert was a child, he and his family made weekly visits to these sisters, who ultimately fascinated him enough that he was able to sidestep his overly aestheticized sensibility and let these singular beings speak and act and be in ways that are constantly startling and new. “Five years ago, I proposed to my great-aunts that I make a film about them; I had started writing a script, but their refusals were so categorical that I lost of [sic] all hope of ever making it,” Guibert writes. He was able to take photographs, though, and, as the contact sheets piled up, he decided to print some of the images, “just to see, to show them.” In a book of astonishing acts of intimacy, the most revealing is in a series of pictures that Guibert shot of Louise taking down her hair—her “most intimate thing.” Long ago, a woman would send a missed loved one a photograph of herself taking her hair down. In this case, Louise’s washing of her long gray tresses is less an erotic image than an act of self-dramatization in the theatre of being. It’s not a statement so much as a reckoning, a way of showing love to the young relative behind the camera who refuses to let these women not be in the world and then leave it, forgotten. ♦
