Ernstige kwetsbaarheden blootgelegd in software voor gebruik eID
door Jan Walraven
Een Amerikaanse onderzoeker heeft veiligheidsproblemen ontdekt in de browser-extensie van Connective. Met dat stukje software van Nitro Software Belgium kunnen Belgen met hun eID online inloggen, documenten ondertekenen of ook Itsme activeren. De extensie in de Google Chrome-webbrowser telt twee miljoen gebruikers. Nitro heeft de problemen intussen opgelost, weliswaar bijna 150 dagen na de eerste melding door onderzoeker James Arnott van het Amerikaanse cyberveiligheidsbedrijf Bay Area Labs.
Arnott stelde zijn bevindingen voor op DEF CON, een jaarlijkse conferentie in het Amerikaanse Las Vegas, en in een uitgebreide blogpost. Via de door Arnott ontdekte kwetsbaarheden kon in principe elke website toegang krijgen tot de gegevens van de identiteitskaart − inclusief de pincode − wanneer die via de kaartlezer ingelezen werd. Arnott legde ook bloot dat een potentiële aanvaller via de Connective-extensie vanop afstand computercode kon uitvoeren op de computer van gebruikers, ook als de kaartlezer niet verbonden was. De potentiële impact hiervan is moeilijk in te schatten, want zo “kan het bijvoorbeeld gaan om spyware of ransomware die al wordt geladen door simpelweg de verkeerde webpagina te bezoeken”, schrijft Arnott in een e-mail aan Apache.
Onder meer bij de ingebruikname van Itsme, de authenticatie-app in handen van vier Belgische grootbanken en drie telecomoperatoren, moeten gebruikers de extensie van Connective gebruiken. Hetzelfde geldt ook voor onder meer het gebruik van je eID met Doccle, de tool waarmee particulieren, zelfstandigen en bedrijven online hun administratie kunnen regelen, en die naar eigen zeggen gekoppeld is aan meer dan 150 bedrijven en overheidsinstellingen.
In zijn blogpost legt Arnott uit dat de veiligheidsfout het in principe mogelijk maakte dat een aanvaller bijvoorbeeld een vals Itsme-account op naam van een slachtoffer kon aanmaken en dus in diens naam transacties en dergelijke zou kunnen uitvoeren, met alle mogelijke gevolgen van dien. Dat een stukje software dat zo belangrijk is voor Belgische burgers dergelijke kwetsbaarheden vertoont, noemt Arnott reden om de wettelijke veiligheidsvereisten te verstrengen.
In een officieel statement benadrukt Nitro dat het om “een kwetsbaarheid, geen inbreuk” ging. “We hebben geen aanwijzingen gevonden dat er misbruik is gemaakt van deze kwetsbaarheden. De kwetsbaarheden zijn gemeld aan het Centrum voor Cyberveiligheid België en we hebben gedurende het hele proces nauw met hen samengewerkt.” Volgens Nitro is het probleem nu verholpen en zijn klanten die de huidige versie gebruiken beschermd. Een woordvoerder van het Centrum voor Cyberveiligheid België benadrukt dat niet Nitro, maar wel de onderzoeker het Centrum op de hoogte bracht.
Aan Apache bevestigt Arnott dat ook hij geen aanwijzingen heeft dat er misbruik van de kwetsbaarheden is gemaakt, “maar dat komt alleen omdat we geen manier hebben om dit te controleren”. Hij voegt er nog aan toe dat het bij Nitro “ontzettend lang heeft geduurd” om deze problemen op te lossen, ondanks zijn aandringen en hoewel een oplossing volgens hem veel sneller geïmplementeerd had kunnen worden. Na de eerste melding duurde het volgens hem 146 dagen totdat Nitro de problemen effectief opgelost had. Nitro vroeg hem om zijn bevindingen pas wereldkundig te maken zodra ze de oplossing hadden doorgevoerd. Hij vroeg een ‘beloning’ (bounty) voor zijn werk en Nitro zou hem 200 dollar hebben aangeboden, maar hij wil die niet aanvaarden.
Om Apache te kunnen lezen moet je niet inloggen via eID, gewoon jaarlijks of maandelijks je abonnement betalen volstaat. Oef! En dat geld proberen we zo goed mogelijk te besteden. Bijvoorbeeld door niet langer elke maand een pakje euro’s over te maken aan Google. We hebben het er in deze blog al enkele keren over gehad, maar nu komt het stilaan in een stroomversnelling: de migratie van onze cloudopslag naar Nextcloud.
Wat we nu al zeker kunnen zeggen, is dat Google op dat vlak een beetje op Donald Trump gelijkt: het maakt migratie allesbehalve gemakkelijk. Om het overzetten van ruim 600 gigabyte aan documenten, e-mails, … toch zo vlot mogelijk te laten verlopen, rekenen we op de expertise van Tactic asbl. Deze vzw zal ook onze Nextcloud-omgeving ‘hosten’ en onderhouden.
Maar maakt Apache zich dan niet afhankelijk van Tactic, vraag je je misschien af. En dat is een terechte vraag. Hier ligt net het voordeel van opensourcesoftware als Nextcloud: als we niet meer tevreden zijn over de ene aanbieder kunnen we gewoon aankloppen bij een andere. Of kunnen we zelf de opensourcesoftware hosten op een eigen server – nu al doen we dat voor sommige zaken. De software blijft dezelfde, enkel de aanbieder verandert.
Rekening houdend met de vakantieplannen van onze ploeg, mikken we erop dat we vanaf midden september in Nextcloud aan onze artikels en nieuwsbrieven schrijven en schaven. Daarna openen we meteen enkele andere werven. Zo willen we onder meer het Amerikaanse Mailchimp, het programma waarmee we nieuwsbrieven versturen, vervangen door het opensource-alternatief CiviCRM.
En volgende week hebben we een videogesprek gepland met de mensen van Bonfire. Zij ontwikkelen opensourcesoftware waarmee we hopelijk de Apache-community een boost kunnen geven. Het Duitse magazine Jacobin toont nu al de mogelijkheden van dit “eigen sociale netwerk”. Daarover later hopelijk meer!
Om zijn afhankelijkheid van big tech af te bouwen werkt Apache aan een eigen app. Wil jij ons een zetje geven? Dat kan met een donatie op BE55 5230 8045 8444, of door een aandeel in onze lezerscoöperatie te kopen via apache.be/bouw-mee. Bedankt.
Ludieke luddieten maken verzet tegen big tech weer leuk
door Jan Walraven
“Fuck, fuck, fuck AI.” Veel duidelijker wordt een slagzin niet. Begin juli vierden actievoerders in New York een week lang The Summer of Ludd. En ‘vierden’ is wel degelijk het juiste woord, als we het verslag van Janus Rose voor technologieniewssite 404 Media mogen geloven.
Het festival was niet gewoon een zoveelste protestmars, maar wou eerst en vooral aantonen dat we geen sociale media en dominante techplatformen nodig hebben om elkaar te ontmoeten én plezier te maken.
De Luddite Renaissance kondigde de acties niet aan op sociale media, wel via affiches en mond-aan-mondreclame. Van het theatrale tribunaal en de vele getuigenissen tegen pakweg de “criminele praktijken” van OpenAI werden geen korte video’s voor TikTok of Instagram gemaakt. Want: The Event is the Medium, zoals de titel van het enkel op papier verkrijgbare manifest duidelijk maakt.
Ja, er verschenen wel nieuwsartikels met enkele foto’s, maar je moest er vooral écht bijzijn. Bijvoorbeeld om te zien dat de nieuwe generatie luddieten, die al enkele maanden onder verschillende namen actief zijn in New York, niet enkel haar inspiratie haalt bij de originele brekers van machinale weefgetouwen in het negentiende-eeuwse Engeland, maar ook bij de Nederlands-Belgische ‘kabouters’. Deze geweldloze, anarchistische protestbeweging voerde begin jaar 70 ludieke acties tegen onder meer consumentisme en voor natuur en milieu.
(Terzijde: als iemand ‘luddiet’ als scheldwoord gebruikt omdat je niet zomaar Claude gebruikt om te weten hoe je een potlood slijpt, laat die persoon dan dit artikel uit ons archief lezen.)
Zal een als kabouter verklede New Yorker die een iPhone aan grut slaat Mark Zuckerberg doen twijfelen of hij wel nog een giga-datacenter moet bouwen? Wie weet! Janus Rose ziet alvast in de kolderieke en absurdistische sfeer het onderscheidende karakter van deze nieuwe luddieten: geen cynisme, wel het pure plezier van protesteren tegen iets dat onontkoombaar lijkt. En een oude smartphone symbolisch offeren, is eens iets anders dan AI-ontwikkelaars als Anthropic die massaal tweedehands boeken opkopen om die in te scannen en tegelijk te vernietigen (de rug wordt ervan gesneden om ze makkelijker te kunnen scannen). Hoe ouder het boek, hoe liever, want daar staat zeker geen door AI gegenereerde nonsens in, in tegenstelling tot wat tegenwoordig op het wereldwijde web verschijnt. Zeldzame boeken zijn het meest gegeerd. Kwestie van hun taalmodel nog “slimmer” te maken. En eenmaal vernietigd, worden ze nóg zeldzamer.
Maar terug naar de nieuwe luddieten. Zij willen voorbijgangers geen complex aanpraten of veroordelen omdat ze werkelijk alles aan Google Gemini vragen of soms te lang door hun Instagram-feed scrollen, maar vooral tonen dat we ook zonder big tech kunnen. En dat dit verzet geweldig plezant kan zijn. Dat is misschien de beste overredingstactiek om zich bij deze onafhankelijkheidsbeweging aan te sluiten en mee te werken aan offline ontmoetingsplekken.
Het is een les die we bij Apache ook ter harte kunnen nemen. Uiteraard geven we onze onafhankelijkheidsstrijd tegen big tech niet op, maar dit gaat om meer dan technologie. Onze Franstalige collega’s van Médor en ook van het Portugese Fumaça hebben dat al langer begrepen: zij organiseren op regelmatige tijdstippen ook échte, offline ontmoetingen met hun lezers, zoals we in een artikel voor Apache Magazine schreven.
Ook de Europese Commissie lijkt er (althans soms) op gebrand om big tech het lachen te laten vergaan. De Commissie heeft Google (nogmaals) twee boetes opgelegd van in totaal 890 miljoen euro omdat de techgigant zijn machtspositie misbruikt. Ten eerste door in zijn zoekmachine voorrang te geven aan eigen producten en diensten, en ten tweede door het voor app-ontwikkelaars te moeilijk te maken om gebruikers naar goedkopere aanbiedingen buiten de Google Play Store te leiden.
Die nieuwe boete is Donald Trump wel (weer) in het verkeerde keelgat geschoten. Hij heeft al gedreigd met hogere importtarieven voor de EU, waarmee hij nogmaals de nauwe banden tussen de Amerikaanse techsector en het Witte Huis in de verf zet.
Het is lang niet de eerste (noch laatste) keer dat de Commissie Google aanpakt wegens oneerlijke praktijken. Begin juli bevestigde het Hof van Justitie een boete van ruim 4 miljard euro voor het misbruik van de dominante positie van zijn smartphone-besturingssysteem Android. Het beroep van Google mocht dus niet baten.
Ik schreef deze blogpost trouwens op een Lenovo Thinkpad X240, bouwjaar 2013, die stof lag te vergaren op onze redactie. Aangezien we met Apache op zoek zijn naar alternatieven voor de diensten van big tech en daarbij zoveel mogelijk willen kiezen voor opensourceoplossingen, moeten we ook af en toe experimenteren, bijvoorbeeld met een alternatief op Linux gebaseerd opensourcebesturingssysteem. Dat we zo een dertien jaar oud toestel nieuw leven kunnen inblazen, is mooi meegenomen.
Ik koos ervoor om Linux Mint te installeren ter vervanging van Windows 10. En dat ging verbazend vlot. De naar hedendaagse normen oeroude laptop doet weer wat hij moet doen. Gezien zijn ouderdom verwondert het niet dat hij soms wat hapert, maar dat is niet erg als je het toestel als een prikkelvrije computer beschouwt en gebruikt. Ideaal om zonder al te veel afleiding deze blogpost te schrijven.
Eerst had ik trouwens de meest geavanceerde versie van Linux Mint geïnstalleerd. Die bleek echter te zwaar voor de dertien jaar oude hardware. Met de lichtere Xfce-versie van Linux Mint loopt alles veel vlotter. Linux Mint wordt aangeraden als de beste Linux-optie voor gebruikers die Windows gewend zijn. Als Mac-gebruiker is het dus wel wat aanpassen aan de interface, maar door enkele simpele aanpassingen kan je de gebruikerservaring iets meer op die van een Apple Macbook laten lijken. Een simpel voorbeeld: de knoppen om een venster te sluiten of minimaliseren kan je links bovenaan zetten zoals op een Macbook.
Het zal nog even duren voor alle collega’s op een laptop werken die draait op Linux, maar dit experimentje toont alleszins dat het niet onmogelijk is. En dat opensourcetoepassingen ook een ecologische optie kunnen zijn: alweer een laptop van de schroothoop gered.
Vlaamse Microsoft-factuur verdubbeld tot 22,6 miljoen euro
door Jan Walraven
De Vlaamse overheid gaf vorig jaar ruim 22,6 miljoen euro uit aan Microsoft-diensten. Dat is een verdubbeling ten opzichte van 2023. Dat blijkt uit een antwoord van Vlaams minister-president Matthias Diependaele (N-VA) op een parlementaire vraag van Kris Verduyckt (Vooruit). De voorbije drie jaar spendeerde de Vlaamse overheid net geen 50 miljoen euro aan Microsoft.
Van de 22,6 miljoen euro die Vlaanderen in 2025 betaalde, ging bijna 8 miljoen naar clouddiensten. De resterende 14,6 miljoen euro ging vorig jaar naar de licenties om de programma’s van Microsoft te mogen gebruiken.
In die 14,6 miljoen euro zit ook de kost van 5.000 Copilot-licenties verrekend. In 2025 bedroeg het totaalbudget voor de uitrol van Copilot binnen de Vlaamse overheid 1,93 miljoen euro. Zoals Apache eerder schreef, komt daar dit jaar nog eens 3,65 miljoen euro bij voor de uitrol van 5.000 extra Copilot-licenties.
De uitgaven voor Microsoft gebeurden binnen de bestaande raamovereenkomsten, die nog lopen tot 2029, geeft minister-president Diependaele aan.
Terwijl Digitaal Vlaanderen een nieuwe aanbesteding voor de ICT-raamovereenkomsten voorbereidt, zet de Europese focus op digitale soevereiniteit de keuze voor Amerikaanse technologieleveranciers op scherp. Daar zit het bruuske optreden van Donald Trump voor iets tussen, maar ook een recente uitspraak van het Amerikaanse Hooggerechtshof zorgt voor onrust.
Is op vlak van gegevensbescherming het gebruik van Amerikaanse clouddiensten nog te verantwoorden, nu er eigenlijk geen onafhankelijke Amerikaanse toezichthouder meer is?
De geopolitieke context, maar ook de modus operandi en de daaruit vloeiende machtsconcentratie die big tech zo big maakt, noopt Apache tot een koerswijziging.
Zoals we een maand geleden hebben aangekondigd, wordt een overstap naar de opensource-toepassing Nextcloud in plaats van Google Workspace ons eerste wapenfeit. We gebruiken al een tijdje beide oplossingen naast elkaar, maar in de komende weken bereiden we een volledige migratie voor.
Dat zal wat voeten in de aarde hebben – en dat terwijl collega’s van welverdiende vakantie genieten – maar het is ook een goed moment om ons overstromende digitale archief op te ruimen. Hebben we echt nog een kopie van een draft van een artikel uit 2017 nodig?
De cloud mag dan wel efemeer klinken, het gaat wel degelijk om fysieke, energie- en waterslurpende infrastructuur, zoals ze onder meer in Henegouwen maar al te goed beseffen.
We gebruiken sinds kort de opensource-berichtenapp Signal om dagelijkse updates over onze onderzoeken te versturen. En dat wordt blijkbaar gesmaakt, want het aantal leden in onze Signal-groep groeit razendsnel. Op deze pagina leggen we graag uit hoe jij je ook kan aanmelden.
Verandering doet meestal wel een bitje pijn – pun intended – maar het helpt om te weten dat we er niet als enige mee bezig zijn.
Voor een artikel dat in het herfstnummer van Apache Magazine zal verschijnen, mocht jouw verslaggever langsgaan in de Brusselse hackerspace, waar digitale doe-het-zelvers tonen dat technologie ook leuk kan zijn en dat een door een AI-chatbot gegenereerde afbeelding niet het toppunt van digitale creativiteit is (alsof dat nog bewezen moest worden).
Ja, opensourcetoepassingen zijn plezant. Wie experimenteert nu niet graag met een robotstofzuiger?
Bij de meeste Belgen doet de naam Hyves wellicht geen belletje rinkelen. In Nederland ging de nostalgiemeter wél in het rood bij de aankondiging dat het sociaal netwerk een tweede leven krijgt. De Telegraaf had de primeur: met Hyves gaat moederbedrijf Mediahuis de concurrentie aan met de Facebooks en Tiktoks van deze wereld. Hyves was in Nederland begin jaren 2000 nog de populairste socialenetwerksite, maar gaf dertien jaar geleden de strijd tegen de Amerikaanse concurrenten op. Drie jaar eerder, in 2010, had Telegraaf Media Groep (TMG) nog 43,7 miljoen euro veil voor het platform. TMG werd inmiddels opgeslorpt door Mediahuis, de Belgische uitgever van onder ander Het Nieuwsblad en De Standaard.
Mediahuis ontkent dat de reanimatie door nostalgie werd ingegeven, maar probeert het te verkopen als ethisch alternatief voor big tech. De uitgever plaatst Hyves’ herrijzenis nadrukkelijk binnen twee trends. Enerzijds speelt het in op toenemende kritiek op de schadelijke effecten van de verslavende algoritmes van grote platformen, anderzijds surft het mee op de golven van de beweging die pleit voor meer Europese digitale autonomie.
“Hyves wil het anders doen”, klinkt het. Maar wie de gebruiksvoorwaarden en privacyverklaring leest, ziet meteen dat je dit best met een korrel zout neemt. Hyves wordt een zoveelste advertentieplatform voor Mediahuis, zoals elke ‘mediamerk’ dat eigenlijk is. De gegevens die Mediahuis over gebruikers van Hyves binnenhaalt, kunnen gebruikt worden om ook de advertenties op andere sites van Mediahuis op maat van gebruikers te snijden.
Of het nu van Mediahuis of DPG Media is: op basis van de gegevens die de uitgevers verzamelen, krijgen gebruikers ‘gepersonaliseerde’ reclame te zien: surveillance capitalism in de Lage Landen. Op kleinere schaal, maar in essentie blijft het hetzelfde verdienmodel als dat van Facebook, Instagram, … (Moederbedrijf Meta lanceerde tot grote tevredenheid van de beurs een ‘persoonlijke’ AI-agent voor zijn gebruikers en daarmee wil Meta uiteraard ook gebruikersgegevens opslurpen en gebruiken.)
Het Nederlandse platform voor onderzoeksjournalistiek Follow the Money ontdekte bovendien dat gebruikersgegevens van Hyves gewoon verwerkt worden via Amerikaanse software. Ondanks de belofte van “een overwegend Europese technische architectuur”.
Een commercieel mediabedrijf dat gebruikers wil insluiten op een commercieel sociaal medium. Denken we echt dat dit een oplossing is? Een stukje macht van vooral Amerikaanse big tech afknijpen en overdragen aan commerciële bedrijven van ‘eigen bodem’? Nochtans toont een andere krant van Mediahuis dat het ook anders kan. Lezers van NRC konden de voorbije weken de queeste van techjournalist Marloes de Koning volgen om de krant aan het open sociale web toe te voegen. Het leidde tot een plan om een NRC-server te openen op Mastodon, waarop “mensen van binnen en buiten NRC met elkaar in gesprek kunnen gaan, onder onze eigen voorwaarden en op onze infrastructuur”.
Mastodon is onderdeel van het fediverse, een verzameling van alternatieve sociale netwerken die onderling verbonden zijn. Zoals bij e-mail maakt het niet uit of je nu een account hebt bij NRC of bij een andere dienstverlener: je kan met anderen in gesprek gaan. (En van dienstverlener wisselen als je ontevreden bent.) Om dit mogelijk te maken, rekent dat fediverse op het ActivityPub-protocol; een set van regels over hoe systemen met elkaar moeten communiceren.

https://www.propublica.org/article/trump.title: On the Ground in the Final Days Before Trump’s Midterm Debacle
https://www.propublica.org/article/trump.author: Alec MacGillis
https://www.propublica.org/article/trump.text:
Jacob Hawk leaned over the plastic fencing to get Vivek Ramaswamy’s attention as the Republican candidate for Ohio governor moved down the line shaking hands at the Ohio University branch campus in Chillicothe, six days before the midterm elections. Hawk held onto Ramaswamy’s hand and started trying to tell him everything he was dealing with, everything he wanted the Republican candidates gathered there to help him with.
Hawk, 39, told him that he was a self-employed landscaper who was having a hard time with the high cost of fuel. He told him that he was raising three young kids from two different moms, mostly on his own. He told him of his worries for his 9-year-old son, who was autistic and underweight and suffered from a two-year delay in brain development.
Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire, nodded and offered some token reassurance and moved down the line, toward the arena where he would soon be appearing with President Donald Trump and Sen. Jon Husted and the rest of the Republican slate in a state that Trump had won by 11 percentage points two years ago, and which the party had dominated during the era of Trump. I had been at many Republican events in the state over that time, including a rally in an airplane hangar outside Dayton in March 2016, where a giant crowd had roared as Trump’s jet had rolled into view and where he had declared that he had come to save Ohio. “Our jobs are being sucked away,” he said then. “It’s unbelievable what’s happening.”
This event was different. Ten years had passed, and gone was the fierce bravado of Trump the conquering hero, bristling with retribution and promises. This rally was populated largely by the same sort of voters who had been particularly drawn to Trump all along, working-class Midwesterners who had not been engaged in politics before he came on the scene. But there were fewer of them — the campaign had chosen an arena that held only 2,000 — and their devotion had been subsumed by uncertainty. They were still with Trump, but they weren’t sure how to reconcile their own difficulties with the fact that he was the president during this trying time.
Take gas prices, which “are beating the hell out of me,” Hawk told me. He was trying his best not to hold them against Trump and his decision to go to war against Iran, instead faulting Congress for limiting domestic oil drilling. “The president has to go find oil in another country because Congress won’t let him find it in our country,” he said, overlooking the fact that Trump’s party has controlled both houses of Congress during his second term.
Nearby, Debbie Shock, a 57-year-old mail carrier, blamed the high fuel costs on “the stock exchange, the markets — they’re the ones that control it.” “We have oil right here in the U.S.,” she said. “Why are we buying it from other countries to begin with?”
Shock fit a profile I had gotten to know well in 2016: an Obama-Trump voter. She was loyal to Trump — “I like the man. Nobody’s perfect, you know what I mean?” — and told me she would never go back to Democrats now. Why not? I asked. “They’re covering up the child molestation,” she said. What did she mean by that? “I’ve heard stories about the sex trafficking. The Clintons are involved in it, Disney World, you know, all that.”
It would be easy to ridicule such murky talk, yet it was not much less coherent than what soon emerged on the arena stage, which was streamed on a large screen for the few hundred of us who were out on the lawn outside the arena. Trump has never been known for structured oratory, but it is hard to overstate the extent to which his digressive style has advanced since 2016, and to convey how surreal it is to experience firsthand, as the reality of what presidential communication has come to in 2026.
The rally opened with the customary introductory video of late-era Trump, an explicitly messianic framing: “God said, ‘I need someone who will be strong and courageous,’” the voice-over intones. “So God made Trump.”
Thus introduced, Trump opened his remarks with a lengthy disquisition on Husted’s body, which had newly become part of his routine. “I looked at Jon and studied his physique,” he cooed, after referring to his recent comments on Husted’s “ass.” “I studied the feet, the legs, the shoulders. I tapped him on the shoulder, and it was like hitting a piece of steel.”
When a protester inside the arena started shouting something — those of us outside couldn’t hear what — and was removed, Trump bid him good riddance: “Now he goes home and his boyfriend gets upset with him.”
There were protesters outside, too, and things were starting to heat up between them and the supporters. “What are you talking about, ‘boyfriend?’” shouted one protester, a young man. “He was just talking about Jon Husted’s ass! That’s not gay??”
A supporter in front of me, a bearded man in his 50s, stewed as he watched the protesters. “You’re going to see someone dropping like a bad habit,” he growled, as he started to move toward them, before being held back by the woman who was with him.
A moment later, Trump had moved on to Jeffrey Epstein, saying that the Democrats had protected him for years. “I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-a-Lago,” he declared. “I was the one who was totally exonerated from him. But they use it, because that’s what they do. They’re sick, weak people.”
This set off a new round of shouting outside, as cries of “pedophiles!” flew back and forth.
Suddenly, one Trump supporter near me rushed hard at a protester and knocked him to the ground, his head landing with such a thud on the blacktop that I initially thought it might be a suppressed gunshot. Dozens of officers swarmed to the spot. Cameras flashed.
A few moments later, a couple other protesters, also young men, began railing against the war against Iran. “We’re going to be the ones sent off to die for Israel,” one shouted. “‘America First,’ and you want me to die in the Middle East?”
Trump touched on the war — “they’re getting beaten very badly” — but spent far more time on his home renovations. “The White House has to be beautiful outside, it needs that exterior plaster. The bricks were falling, the stone was broken, the monuments were coming off, the beautiful windows were cracked, it looked terrible, and I fixed it very inexpensively, and now it’s more beautiful than ever,” he said. “And President Obama, who doesn’t understand cleanliness, who doesn’t understand broken cracked stone and sidewalks, who doesn’t understand that having asphalt going to your main entrance is not the right thing, we’d like to have granite and marble we’d like to have it look nice, you don’t use asphalt, you use asphalt for your streets. …”
On the ramble went. To the Haitians in nearby Springfield: “The town went from no crime to high crime,” but “they’re being moved out.” To a riff on Ramaswamy’s ad featuring his opponent Amy Acton’s mother calling her a liar, in apparent reference to Acton’s having accused her stepfather of raping her when she was 12, as he was subsequently charged with doing. The ad had met with widespread opprobrium, but Trump defended Ramaswamy. “The mother said that Amy Acton, the daughter, is a liar, that she is no good. … How the hell is that his problem?” To “O Canada, which has been ripping us off for years,” and Somalia, “which isn’t even a country,” and “transgender mutilization,” and his plan to rename the Strait of Hormuz for himself.
Finally, Trump ceded the stage to Husted and Ramaswamy. But by then, the lawn had emptied out as people drifted home, Jacob Hawk among them. A vendor was shouting out discount prices on his MAGA merchandise. “$10 special on hats! All the hats are $10! These are normally $25 hats. That’s a good hat for $10.”
The next day, the full Republican slate of statewide candidates appeared, sans Trump, at a small pep rally inside a former Delphi auto-parts factory in Vandalia, outside Dayton. It is an enormous building that employed more than 100 prior to its closing in 2009 and is now being used as a warehouse by a company that sells air conditioners, employing only 10 or so; Delphi announcements still remained on the bulletin boards, adding a ghostly feel.
The setting was an unintentional reminder of what Ohio has been through. Between 2000 and 2025, the state lost 300,000 manufacturing jobs, a devastation that had made it highly susceptible to Trump’s message in 2016. But Republicans have been in charge of the state since 2010, and so it was the task of the candidates gathered there, with an audience of just a few dozen, to cast the state as being on an upswing. Complicating this challenge is the fact that so much of the state’s recent growth has been concentrated in the Columbus area: countless data centers, defense contractor Anduril, a massive Intel plant under construction.
The bigger challenge, though, was the nationwide pall that hung over the event: the reality of stubbornly high inflation and high gas prices, the latter a direct consequence of Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. He had stood against costly foreign entanglements when he ran in 2016, in opposition to his party’s recent record, and carried that same banner again in 2024. But another aspect of his political persona had prevailed: a heedless swagger that, in this case, had been fanned by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. It had led him into this drawn-out conflict that has already cost U.S. taxpayers more than $47 billion.
And it had left a long row of Republican candidates standing in this giant building stacked high with made-in-China air conditioners all but pleading the small assemblage to save them from the political climate. “You can’t give up,” Husted said. “This is a Republican state, and the only way Democrats can win is if Republicans don’t vote.”
Five days later, I was in York County, Pennsylvania, which Trump had won by 25 points in 2024, and which was home to one of four Republican-held House districts targeted by Democrats. I chose to go to a precinct on the outskirts of York, thinking it would offer a diverse cross-section, in between more Democratic York proper and more Republican rural areas. But over 90 minutes of conversations, I didn’t encounter a Republican voter until I was about to call it a day.
The first person I spoke with, Bill, a 52-year-old state government employee who asked that I not use his last name for fear of losing his job, had voted for Trump three times. He hardly considered himself MAGA but was drawn in 2016 to Trump’s “drain the swamp” rhetoric and his disavowal of the war in Iraq. He voted for him again in 2020 and 2024 because he didn’t think much of Joe Biden and Kamala Harris.
But on this day, Bill was coming to vote against his Republican representative, Scott Perry, because he was too “Trump adjacent.” Bill had finally had enough of Trump, especially when it came to all the revelations of self-dealing involving his family and cronies. “I will not be falling for him again,” he told me. “Drain the swamp, no wars. … It was all a lie.”
He said he couldn’t understand how Trump had gone from America First to seemingly letting the country’s foreign policy be dictated by Israel. He said that he was voting for the Democrats mainly just for the sake of “gridlock,” as deliberate blockage. “Someone’s got to stop this,” he said. “It’s getting out of control.”
Each Democratic voter I spoke with after that was coming with their own motivation for voting against the Republican slate, like the cast of “Murder on the Orient Express.”
For Annie (who also asked that I not use her last name), it was for Trump’s social-welfare cuts, which had cost her and her disabled husband $300 per month in SNAP benefits and nearly cost them their Medicaid coverage.
For Desiree Edmonds, an elementary school teacher, it was high inflation, which was translating into anxiety among the working-class children in her classroom.
For Mark Castillo, a 19-year-old ironworker, it was for the sky-high cost of diesel.
For Jacqueline Jimenez, a native Puerto Rican who worked as a home-health aide, it was for the excessive harshness of ICE arrests.
For Shiri Kramer, a warehouse worker, it was for the general meanness emanating from the administration, which made her think of her grandfather, a Jewish American who had extended mercy to German POWs during World War II. “My grandfather would be writhing right now,” she said. “Nothing happening in our country is OK.”
By night’s end, Republicans had lost this Pennsylvania district by 10 points, as well as the other three in the state and more than 40 nationwide. They had lost at least seven Senate seats, even in states where Democrats hadn’t prevailed in decades — Kansas, Texas, South Carolina. Incredibly, even Mississippi was on the verge. In Ohio, Republicans lost the race for Senate and governor — only one of the seven statewide candidates on stage at the warehouse emerged a victor — as well as two Republican-held House seats, a stark reversal in a state that had seemed to be trending away from Democrats for good. In all, Democrats flipped five governorships and up to 12 state legislative chambers. The Democratic popular-vote margin in congressional races nationwide was 13 percentage points — nearly double the Republican margin in their own wave years of 2010 and 1994, and approaching the scale of the historic Democratic rout in the post-Watergate election of 1974.
The particularly stunning loss of the South Carolina seat brought to mind a warning issued in May 2016 by Lindsey Graham, whose death this July left the seat vacant. “If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed…….and we will deserve it,” Graham tweeted in 2016. For years, the Republican Party had avoided the catastrophic reckoning he warned of — through Trump’s narrow win in 2016, through the Jan. 6, 2021, assault on the Capitol, through Biden’s fateful insistence on running for reelection at age 81 in 2024. Along the way, much of the party, including Graham himself, had accommodated itself to Trump. One way of looking at the 2026 results was that the warning had finally come true. The reckoning had been delayed by a decade, but it had gathered more force over time, like a boulder rolling downhill.
There was a hint of such a reckoning in the words that Bill, the three-time Trump voter, left me with in York. After he returned from voting, he bade me farewell with a parting regret.
“You see what’s going on,” he said, “and you’re like, ‘What the hell did I do?’”

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/07/jane.title: How a Socialist Can Govern a City Under the Thumb of the Trump Administration
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/07/jane.author: Jessica Washington
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/07/jane.text:
Socialists will soon govern three of the United States’ most influential cities: Los Angeles, New York City, and the District of Columbia.
Janeese Lewis George joins Zohran Mamdani and Nithya Raman as part of a new wave of socialist local executives. But unlike Mamdani and Raman, Lewis George will govern a city under federal rule.
D.C. is a “federal district,” subject to the whims and micromanagement of the president and Congress. If the federal government doesn’t like the city’s legislation, it can override it. This poses additional challenges if Lewis George wants to change how things are done in the nation’s capital.
Lewis George, a current D.C. city councilmember, has promised to usher in sweeping reforms centered around affordability, including stronger tenant protections, investments in affordable childcare, and long-sought-after reforms on the city’s restrictive zoning laws. She rose to political prominence as the first socialist on the city council, winning her seat on a platform of defunding the police in the wake of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor protests in 2020. (She has since called for hiring additional Metropolitan Police officers.)
For Lewis George to fulfill her campaign promises is “going to require Janeese to use her position and her longstanding reputation as an organizer to convince members of Congress that we can exercise Home Rule and that we deserve the dignity of any other collective body, like a state, in this country,” said Kurtis Hagans, chair of Metro DC Democratic Socialists of America, which endorsed Lewis George in the primary.
All local D.C. bills are required to go through a congressional review period of 30 working days for civil legislation and 60 working days for criminal bills. If Congress doesn’t like the bill, it can either decide to let that review period lapse, allowing the legislation to go into effect, or pass a joint disapproval resolution in both the House and the Senate. If they pass a disapproval resolution, it goes to the president’s desk, where they can choose to veto and let the new law stand or sign it and override the legislation.
Speaking to The Intercept on Election Day, voters said they supported Lewis George because they wanted to elect someone who would fight for everyday Washingtonians.
“I was certainly motivated by wanting really strong leadership for D.C. and people who are going to put D.C. first, in the sense of the residents and the community members and not solely as our role as the capital city,” said Izetta Mobley, a voter in Ward 4, where Lewis George serves as a councilmember.
For Mobley and other voters, that primarily means tackling issues of affordability. “Affordable housing and the rise in unhoused folks, and making sure that unhoused folks have support and city resources …those were very important to me,” said Mobley.
Although Democrats took both houses of Congress on Tuesday, paving a clearer path for the district to flex its autonomy, Lewis George will still have to contend with Democratic leaders like Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries, both moderates, who are likely to lead the Senate and the House next session. Schumer and Jeffries were often critical of Mamdani when he was running for mayor in their home state of New York, though they seized primarily on his stance on Israel.
Hagans pointed out that Lewis George has the longtime support of former at-large councilmember Robert White, who was elected as Washington’s non-voting delegate on Tuesday. But Hagans said the DC Metro DSA is also preparing to organize residents to put pressure on Congress, given ”the relative powerlessness of the district in the face of Congress.”
Governing Washington has other pitfalls. The district is hamstrung by the fact that the D.C. Council is required to pass a balanced budget and is prohibited from carrying it over into the following year. (Congress also gets to approve it.) The city is already struggling to close a $1.1 billion budget deficit for the upcoming fiscal year — caused by Congress.
In order to achieve her agenda, Lewis George has suggested raising taxes on businesses and the city’s wealthiest residents. For that, she’ll need the support of the city council.
Lewis George is aided by the fact that Tuesday also ushered in a record number of socialists on the city council, adding two, Aparna Raj and Oye Owolewa. “A big part of the vision for the district is to have these organizers on the council as well as an organizer-in-chief at the executive level,” said Hagans.
Aside from bold economic policies, many voters who spoke to The Intercept said they want the new administration to prioritize resistance to the federal takeover of Washington, D.C., and ending the scourge of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. “We’ve seen ICE raids in our neighborhood, literally where our kids used to go to school,” said Jason Cherkis, another Ward 4 voter. “That’s one reason we voted for Janeese for mayor because she was out front and speaking about ICE in a way our current mayor never did.”
Despite the restrictions placed on a D.C. mayor, immigrant advocacy and civil rights groups concerned about the incursion of ICE in the district are pushing for Lewis George to take a stand.
“We want to see the next mayor doing everything possible to protect these most vulnerable communities from continued attacks,” said Peggy Ramin, policy counsel at the American Civil Liberties Union of the District of Columbia. “Whether that is legislation or the mayor ensuring that the administration’s agencies are well educated as to what that means in terms of limiting cooperation and even prohibiting cooperation.”
In particular, Ramin said that her organization is calling on the D.C. council and Lewis George to pass legislation that would allow residents to sue any officer — local or federal — who violates constitutional rights.
Ramin is aware of the challenges facing the district to pass this type of legislation without incurring interference from Congress or President Donald Trump — who has personally vowed to oppose Lewis George.
“No matter what Congress ends up doing, whether it disapproves or passes a disapproval resolution or not, I think people here in D.C. are really demanding and asking our council to step up and pass this sort of legislation,” said Ramin.

As evidenced by the record number of socialists winning power across the country, Hagans says it’s clear both D.C. and the nation are looking for fighters.
“Democrats have promised a lot for a long time, but they seem unwilling to stand up to Trumpism,” said Hagans. Voters are noticing “this new class of democratic socialists,” he said, concluding, “Maybe I don’t know what that means entirely, but let’s give it a shot.”

https://www.propublica.org/article/texas.title: Texas’ School Voucher Program Could Be “Unrecognizable, If Not Extinct,” Says Democratic Lawmaker
https://www.propublica.org/article/texas.author: Lexi Churchill, Jeremy Schwartz
https://www.propublica.org/article/texas.text:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s vision for education was finally coming together.
This year, the state launched a voucher program that allowed roughly 110,000 of Texas’ more than 5 million schoolchildren to get a private education using taxpayer dollars. Abbott’s loyal appointee at the Texas Education Agency, Commissioner Mike Morath, was leading the state’s largest takeover of public schools in recent history. And the Texas State Board of Education, with Abbott’s support, helped pass a controversial new social studies curriculum that required teaching Bible stories and shifted away from world history to focus on Texas and the United States.
On Tuesday night, as Democrats clinched nearly every office in the state, it all began to unravel.
In a speech after denying Abbott a fourth term, Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa called for a reversal of his education agenda. She pledged to fire Morath and to end the public school takeovers.
Perhaps most significantly, she doubled down on a campaign promise to erase one of Abbott’s biggest accomplishments: school vouchers.
“We will work tirelessly to repair the damage of the Texas voucher scam,” said Hinojosa, who did not respond to requests for an interview.
It is not clear how Hinojosa will deliver on that promise. While Democrats have the ability to restrict parts of the program, eliminating it would require legislative action.
But Hinojosa will have help.
Democrat Sarah Eckhardt, a former state senator who voted against vouchers and will now lead the state office charged with running the program, has said she will push changes to increase accountability and transparency.
Eckhardt, however, acknowledged the limitations of her office, saying that any big overhaul must come from lawmakers.
Democrats won back the Texas House for the first time in 24 years, but Republicans retained a majority in the Senate.
Rep. Diego Bernal, the Democratic vice chair of the House education committee, seemed confident that there is a path toward killing the program, at least as it now exists.
Bernal, whose district is in San Antonio, said some Republican colleagues previously told him privately that they had reservations about the voucher program, but were limited in what they could do because of pressure from leaders who have now been ousted.
“I guarantee that program is not going to be untouched, and it will be probably unrecognizable, if not extinct, by the time we’re done with it,” he said.
Rural Texas Pushes Back
Abbott spent years trying to pass a statewide voucher program. By 2024, he’d grown angry at rural Republicans who repeatedly blocked such legislation because, they argued, public schools were a vital part of their communities. So Abbott shelled out millions of dollars to oust them from office and elect pro-voucher Republicans instead.
He succeeded. And the following year, those Republicans helped pass the $1 billion state voucher program. This week, at least 13 Republicans who Abbott had previously endorsed or helped fund as part of his voucher push lost to Democrats or were trailing in close races.
Abbott’s office declined an interview request, referring ProPublica and The Texas Tribune to his campaign office, which did not respond.
His bullishness on vouchers turned off some Republican voters in rural communities that have historically been strongholds for his party, education experts and politicians said.
A Texas Tribune analysis found Democrats made striking gains in rural and semirural parts of the state, where concern over vouchers, along with issues like data centers, ran high. In rural counties, Abbott’s margin over Hinojosa fell 16 percentage points from his 2022 margin over former U.S. Rep. Beto O’Rourke, and it fell 20 percentage points in exurban counties.
Former state Rep. Dewayne Burns, an anti-voucher Republican from a mostly rural district south of Fort Worth who was defeated by an Abbott-backed primary challenger in 2024, said many of his constituents felt betrayed by the governor’s push for vouchers. “That’s the first time that I think rural Texans really kind of stepped back and said, ‘Are you guys really supporting us?’” he said. “I think they overestimated the loyalty that Texans, especially rural Texans, had to the governor.”
Former state Rep. Steve Allison, who represented a suburban San Antonio district before he was unseated in the 2024 primary, said he remains convinced his constituents never wanted the voucher system. Pro-voucher groups targeted him in a series of ads that attacked him for issues like border security and property taxes but said little about school choice. Polls at the time showed Texans held complicated views on school choice, with one University of Houston poll showing that while two-thirds of Texans supported voucher legislation, an equal number believed that vouchers would funnel money away from already struggling public schools.
“I know what I saw when my staff took very careful notice of what phone calls were coming in and what emails and texts and visits were coming in,” he said in an interview. “It was clear that the overall district was opposed to vouchers.”
Concerns about vouchers became key in several rural and suburban Texas districts this year where Abbott’s selected candidates had won two years ago. One of those races was for Allison’s old seat, which pro-voucher candidate Marc LaHood won in 2024 after Abbott spent at least $700,000 supporting him.
Another was in Bell County in Central Texas. There, the Abbott-backed incumbent, Rep. Hillary Hickland, conceded a close race Wednesday morning. She did not respond to a request for an interview. Her Democratic opponent, Amelia Rabroker, a former teacher, said the Republicans’ heavy-handed push for vouchers spurred her to challenge Hickland.
“A lot of money was pushed into her campaign to make that happen, and she delivered on those vouchers, and it was very upsetting to the people of Central Texas,” Rabroker said. “I think it was a huge concern. The biggest.”
Similarly, LaHood, who did not respond to requests for comment, faced a flurry of questions over his support of vouchers at a candidate forum for the District 121 race in October. His opponent, Democrat Zack Dunn, said vouchers and public education were second only to affordability in the minds of voters he met. On Tuesday night, Dunn defeated LaHood with 54% of vote.
“Across the board, overwhelmingly the sentiment was, ‘We need to fully fund our public schools,’” Dunn said in an interview. “The voucher scam, the voucher scheme, the voucher vote that was taken is hurting us. It’s hurting us definitely across the state, but it’s hurting us in 121. Yes, we heard that over and over and over again.”
What’s Next?
Dunn said he would support measures that ensure more transparency in how taxpayer dollars are used for private schools.
Ultimately, though, he wants to see the program repealed.
Some changes can come through administrative actions by Eckhardt, the new state comptroller. In a news conference the day after her election, Eckhardt said she planned to rigorously audit how taxpayer money is spent and to release more information about the program to the public.
Under her Republican predecessors, the comptroller’s office shielded information that included data detailing how much state funding certain private schools received and how many students most public schools lost to the program. The office argued that it was protecting student privacy.
“As the comptroller, my job is to vigorously follow the money and report back to the Legislature if their investment is not panning out,” Eckhardt said. She added, “That is part of the vigorous audit and performance evaluation of this program that any comptroller should be doing, and I certainly will be doing.”
One key supporter of vouchers in the Senate, the last Republican bulwark in the state, is taking a more measured approach on the program’s future.
Houston Republican Sen. Paul Bettencourt, who led the effort to approve vouchers that had failed in prior years, said the Legislature will need to review the outcomes from the 2026-27 school year and assess the benefits and families’ concerns. He pointed to the fact that vouchers were returned by some parents whose children required special education services.
“I think that it has helped students in many other states,” Bettencourt said. “We need to look at what’s happened here with this first cohort, and we need to make sure that we’re debating not the emotionality prior to passage of a bill, but the facts of what happened after the passage of a bill.”
Scott Schneider, an attorney who represents private schools participating in the voucher program, said the midterm results shocked private school leaders. Some were counting on the state funding to support their business. He said private school leaders could start a lobbying effort to grandfather in the families already benefiting from the program, but schools are also planning for what they will do if the state funding goes away altogether.
“It’s going to be a hot mess,” Schneider said.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/08/nith.title: The Pressure on LA’s First Socialist Mayor
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/08/nith.author: Jonah Valdez
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/08/nith.text:
On paper, the second-largest city in the country has its first democratic socialist mayor.
Los Angeles City Councilmember Nithya Raman declared victory on Thursday over the embattled incumbent Karen Bass, joining a list of socialist mayors who have risen to power in recent years, including Zohran Mamdani in New York; Seattle’s Katie Wilson; and most recently Janeese Lewis George in Washington, D.C., who won in a landslide this week.
Raman, however, did not campaign unabashedly as a socialist. Though she ran as an endorsed member of the Democratic Socialists of America’s Los Angeles chapter, the national DSA threatened to override the local chapter and rescind the endorsement over concerns around her stances on Israel and Palestine.
Unlike her counterpart in New York, to whom she draws most comparisons, Raman did not make sweeping socialist promises, such as free public transit, universal childcare, or taxing the rich. Instead, she focused on what’s wrong with the city. Riding a wave of resentment for Bass’s alleged mismanagements of the Palisades fire and the Lineage Logistics warehouse fire in Boyle Heights, Raman talked about filling potholes, fixing street lights, and making roads safer for pedestrians and cyclists.
In addition to DSA-LA support, she earned the endorsements of popular anti-corruption City Controller Kenneth Mejia and Unite Here 11, a major local hospitality workers union, whose large membership canvassed for her in the general. But she lacked endorsements from most key labor groups and social justice nonprofits, and the organizing base they provide. Her fellow DSA members on the Los Angeles City Council all pulled for Bass, forcing Raman to battle back the perception that she struggles to build coalitions.
While Mamdani, 10 months into his term, now finds himself under pressure from New York’s left for refusing to fire NYPD’s police commissioner, his massive base of organizer support offers a buffer to criticism. Raman won over the city’s voters, but it’s not clear how much time that will buy her to tackle the city’s most vexing problems once she takes office.
“Folks in New York are willing to cut Mamdani more slack on the movement side, because he was one of them on a bunch of issues,” said David Levitus, executive director of LA Forward, a progressive nonprofit that endorsed Raman in the general election. ”I think Nithya” — who did not come from the ranks of DSA organizing like Mamdani — “has more skepticism from parts of the left because of that.”
Raman will face scrutiny from LA’s progressive left on a host of issues: bloated police department spending amounting to roughly a quarter of the city’s nearly $15 billion budget; fear of collaboration between ICE and law enforcement agencies; the 2028 Olympics prompting an expansion of surveillance; rising homelessness; and failing infrastructure.
Weeks before the November election, Raman seemed less concerned with movement-based allegiances or ideological labels, saying she is “a capitalist and I’m also a democratic socialist.” Before the primary in June, she said she was “one of the most independent voices in City Hall” when asked about her membership with DSA. The statements and her votes in city council have prompted intense debate among DSA-LA’s members over whether Raman holds up to democratic socialist ideals.
While most Angelenos do not care about such fine distinctions, Raman’s measured embrace of socialist mantle has created among some activists the perception of a more responsive audience in city hall compared to previous administrations. Yet to others on LA’s progressive left, Raman’s ideological elusiveness reads as political unreliability.
“I don’t think Nithya Raman is accountable to anyone in the movement,” said Kris Rehl, an activist who volunteered for Raman during her 2020 city council run and now runs the mutual aid group LA Street Care. “If you do not subscribe to any ideology, you can’t be held accountable to it.”
Rehl, who advocates for abolishing anti-camping bans that criminalize homeless encampments near schools and daycares, expressed dismay over Raman’s previous votes on expanding the police department despite running on defunding the police in 2020.
Others like Tal Levy, a member of DSA-LA’s electoral politics committee, remain more optimistic about what Raman can deliver as mayor. While DSA-LA is pushing for reallocating funds from the police budget into social services, Levy sees the value of Raman’s pledge to support LA Forward’s initiative of citywide expansion of unarmed crisis response teams, which divert certain 911 calls to teams of social workers and clinicians, rather than police.
“Even if Nithya were a fire-breathing abolitionist, it would still be a long fight to make those changes,” said Levy, who has been organizing with DSA-LA for nearly a decade. “But I believe there is plenty of room for us to make material wins in the short term.”
Room to Push
While there is debate over how much power DSA-LA has within LA’s political landscape, the group provided Raman additional attention and credibility among leftist voters, which was only bolstered by the successes of other DSA-endorsed candidates in New York and in congressional races across the nation.
The DSA’s National Political Committee, however, spurred one of the biggest public rifts during Raman’s campaign. The committee held a vote to un-endorse Raman over her perceived lack of support for the Palestinian-led Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions movement, which hadn’t been included by the DSA-LA on its endorsement questionnaire. After a week of debate and dueling resolutions, and an email from Raman, in which she wrote, “the best way for working Angelenos to stand in solidarity with Gaza is through non-violent protest, legislative action, and diplomatic pressure, including BDS,” the national committee decided against rescinding its endorsement of Raman by a narrow margin.
Frances Gill, one of three DSA-LA members on the DSA national political committee, voted against rescinding the group’s endorsement. She opposed the idea of alienating the organization’s second largest chapter as “bad organizing and bad leadership,” especially in a high-profile race when the stakes for the regional and national chapters were so closely intertwined.
“The public ties us to one another,” Gill said of the DSA and Raman, “and there’s not a lot of other key players who have also played such a critical role in her being able to win. So I think that gives us an outsized seat at the table.”
She was a part of the faction among national leadership that instead called for a long-term pressure campaign on Raman on the issue of Israel and Palestine. The group is planning to push Raman on what she can do as mayor to halt the transportation of military hardware that makes its way through the Los Angeles International Airport to Israel. Organizers also plan to call for an end to real estate events in LA facilitating the sale of housing illegally built in the occupied West Bank. They will also examine whether the city itself is invested in companies that are profiting off Israel’s genocide in Gaza and apartheid rule of Palestinians.
“I think there is room to push,” Gill said.
Another major public spat between progressives and Raman took place in January before she announced her candidacy for mayor.
Catching housing advocates by surprise, Raman introduced a motion to reform the city’s “mansion tax” to make exemptions for developers. Raman claimed that the tax, known as Measure ULA, was inadvertently preventing construction of new multi-family housing. Organizers opposed the idea, since the tax generates funds for services to support existing affordable housing and keep people housed, and that carveouts for developers would only fuel displacement of low-income renters, possibly pushing more people to the streets.
LA Forward was among those blindsided by the motion, which she eventually withdrew. Before endorsing Raman, Levitus and the group met with the candidate alongside organizers in an activist’s home.
“She talked about, ‘The times when I’ve succeeded, it’s because I built a coalition, the times when I failed, it’s because I didn’t, and I didn’t bring people along,’” Levitus recalled from the July meeting. “She really owned her mistake. I don’t know how much her mind has changed intellectually about the policy, but think clearly she recognizes that she needed to do something different — and that might lead to her pushing for a policy that is different from what she had pushed for before.”
Police Chief Dilemma
Among Raman’s early tests progressives will be watching for is how she fulfills her pledge to fire LAPD police chief Jim McDonnell. Raman was among the councilmembers who approved his appointment in 2024, despite concerns around his track record of collaborating with ICE as LA County sheriff. She has since said she would fire McDonnell over his response to the ICE raids and his refusal to enforce a state law that banned federal agents from wearing masks.
Yet the pledge to replace McDonnell may present a political quagmire for Raman, given that the mayor in LA cannot unilaterally force out a police chief. The city’s police commission, consisting of five civilians appointed by the mayor, must make that decision. Raman first will need to assemble her own commission, but that process also requires approval from a city council that remains largely supportive of the police department.
William Gude, a vocal police accountability advocate who supported Raman in the election, said he planned to push the mayor to circumvent the process by asking McDonnell to resign. “I’m putting pressure on her from day one,” he said. “There’s some promises that she made, and those promises need to be kept.”
In her first press conference as mayor-elect, Raman sidestepped a question about whether she still planned to fire McDonnell, amid public threats from the police union warning of “Armageddon.” “Public safety is the most important service the city is delivering to its people,” said Raman, noting the chief was one of her first phone calls after winning.
Activist pressure could be a burden for Raman — or a tool she could use to force legislation through a city council she knows well, according to Gude. “Does she want to have activists coming after her, also while battling 15 council members?” said Gude, who goes by @FilmthePoliceLA on social media. “Or would she rather have the activist base going after the council members that are coming after her, to create a buffer, to do a lot of her heavy lifting? It’s a choice she has to make.”
Hamid Khan, who heads the Stop Spying LAPD Coalition, is among those who is closely watching who Raman appoints to her police commission. But he sees Raman’s pledge of firing McDonnell as “a band-aid” for the more glaring structural issues of the department. While crediting Raman’s opposition to automated license plate readers from Flock Safety and Axon, Khan also pointed to Raman’s historic support for expanding the police department.
While in city council, Raman voted to expand LAPD’s budget three times: in 2021, 2022, and 2023. But she also voted against police raises in 2023, and this year, she opposed a plan by Bass to hire 170 more officers. She has said on the campaign trail she does not wish to expand the police budget, but also said she would not cut into it either.
In the span of her time in city council, the LAPD has expanded its surveillance reach, Khan said. The department is slowly unrolling its Real-Time Crime Centers, which meld automated license plate reader technology, social media monitoring software, and CCTV cameras into a constant surveillance tool. He warned such a technology, while marketed to curb retail theft, will disproportionately harm Black and brown Angelenos.
“We have to situate the people’s expectations in Los Angeles that they’re not based upon the comment, ‘I’m gonna fire Jim McDonald,’” said Khan, who advocates for abolishing the budding police outposts. “What does that do? The fundamentals still remain the same.”
A True Outsider
There is a notion among some on the left that Raman is very much a part of the political machine that bred some of LA’s ongoing problems. She has served on city council for five years and was an ally to Bass, having endorsed Bass just weeks before jumping in the race herself. Yet Raman, a Harvard-educated urban planner and former entertainment director of Time’s Up, is in many respects an outsider to the political establishment.
Former City Councilmember Mike Bonin called Raman’s victory a “reordering of the governing class in Los Angeles.” For the past several decades, LA politics has been run by establishment Democrats, such as Bass or her predecessor, Eric Garcetti, son of a former LA County district attorney; the chambers of commerce; lobbyists; longtime city hall staffers; all riding the influence of homeowners.
For Lex Steppling, an organizer with Los Angeles Community Action Network and a critic of Raman’s time in city council, the “political recalibration” with her victory in city hall was a welcome sight.
Steppling grew up in a generation of LA political activists who got their start organizing with Community Coalition, which Bass founded in 1990 and for a long time was the only progressive organization in the city offering paid political work. He watched as his peers grew to leading campaigns on issues such as policing and mass incarceration, then began running for elected office. They brought with them their organizing chops, but also their relationships with the organizations that gave them their start. Steppling described this as a “relational ecosystem,” in which movements would be co-opted into electoral politics — in which scoring political points became more important than addressing the issues.
He blamed the lack of gains on policing and mass incarceration since the 2020 George Floyd uprising on such a relational ecosystem. A victory for Raman could mark a reset to such an establishment, and he hopes activists will capitalize on the opening.
“The right kind of openings to do the right kind of work will reemerge,” said Steppling, who helped lead a successful anti-incarceration measure in 2020. “It’s gonna once again start to be about the demands.”
Raman’s election evoked for Bonin memories of the last time an LA incumbent mayor was ousted. In 2005, then-state Assembly member Antonio Villaraigosa beat James Hahn, becoming the city’s first Latino mayor. Villaraigosa, previously director of Southern California ACLU, was seen as a progressive candidate at the time. That’s not how he governed. An early sign of his establishment politics was hiring a longtime political insider as his chief of staff.
Raman will also signal her governing priorities with the hires for her transition team and cabinet.
Some organizers were encouraged to see progressive figures added to her campaign, such as Faizah Malik, a civil rights attorney and former city council candidate also endorsed by DSA-LA, and Jamie York, an advocate for greater transparency in city politics whose high-profile rejection by the city council as an ethics commission appointee drew public scrutiny. It remains unclear what if any role they would play in city hall.
The LA Times reported that Rick Cole, former deputy mayor, is expected to supervise Raman’s transition team alongside Andrea Conant, Raman’s chief of staff in city council.
“How big is the table,” Bonin said, “and how much of the activist community is at the table?”
