https://theintercept.com/2026/11/09/impe.title: Impeachment Vote Looms for Hegseth
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/09/impe.author: Nick Turse
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/09/impe.text:
Calls for self-styled War Secretary Pete Hegseth’s ouster have grown louder on Capitol Hill as a possible impeachment vote looms this week. At the same time, Hegseth has shored up support at the White House and among MAGA faithful, according to dismayed Pentagon officials.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced articles of impeachment on the House floor Monday afternoon, charging Hegseth with “high crimes and misdemeanors.” Top Democrats have indicated a desire to join Massie’s effort since their midterm election landslide. “I am a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is poised to be the next House speaker, told ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday. Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., the current House Oversight Committee chair, told Newsmax on Friday it is “very possible” the votes exist to impeach Hegseth.
Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., one of the leading voices for Hegseth’s impeachment, agreed. “I think there’s a high chance that it will be successful,” she told The Intercept of Massie’s effort. In April, Ansari filed six articles of impeachment against Hegseth, including violations of the law of armed conflict and targeting of civilians, abuse of power, and obstructing congressional oversight. She called for a floor vote on his ouster this week.
“Hegseth has demonstrated that he is wholly incompetent. He’s committed what I believe to be war crimes in Iran and the Caribbean and he is ill-equipped for the job,” said Ansari. “My reason for introducing the articles of impeachment back in April had a lot to do with his conduct and the war crimes in Iran, including the bombing of the children’s school. But it’s refreshing to see that since then, more and more Republicans are also recognizing that his leadership has failed and that he’s putting all of us in danger.”
In the wake of a devastating election rout of the GOP that handed Democrats firm control of the House and the Senate, Congress begins a five-week lame-duck session on Monday. With dozens of Republican lawmakers ending their tenure in the House, it’s unclear how many will even show up for votes. Such absences, as well as outright defections in the GOP ranks, make it increasingly likely that Massie’s measure will pass, staffers on Capitol Hill told The Intercept.
On Sunday, GOP Rep. French Hill of Arkansas left open the possibility of backing the measure. “I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president,” he said on CBS News’s “Face the Nation.” Outgoing House speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., did not answer when asked by Politico if GOP leaders would whip the Hegseth impeachment vote. House leaders must take up the matter within two legislative days; opponents could table the resolution or refer it to committee instead of voting directly on impeachment.
After narrowly being confirmed by the Senate, which required Vice President JD Vance to break a 50-50 tie, Hegseth’s tenure has been marked by fiascos and failures beginning with Signal-gate, the sharing of secret war plans in a chat group with a journalist. In that case, according to the Pentagon’s own inspector general, “Hegseth violated security protocols and endangered U.S. troops and objectives.” Since then, Hegseth has been under perpetual fire for the unsuccessful Iran war in 2026, specifically a strike on an elementary school in Minab, Iran, that killed more than 150 civilians, most of them children. He faces pressure over his campaign of extrajudicial killings in attacks on so-called drug boats in the waters off Latin America. And questions continue to mount about his purge of top military leaders — many of them women and minorities.
“The fact that many career officials from the department have left citing his leadership, I think, is very telling,” said Ansari. Last week, The Intercept published an exposé quoting six current and former defense officials who currently serve or served under Hegseth and called for his ouster. “He is conducting state terrorism. He is 100 percent a war criminal. He needs to be prosecuted,” said Wes J. Bryant, one of those officials and, until last year, a senior targeting adviser and policy analyst at the Pentagon who was pushed out of his job for blowing the whistle on Hegseth’s efforts to undermine protections for civilians.
As calls for his ouster have grown louder, Hegseth launched a desperate bid to whip up support at the White House, including a nakedly obsequious video seeking Trump’s support that he posted on X. It was accompanied by a coordinated campaign of social media posts by Pentagon underlings tying Hegseth’s fortunes to the president with the text “STAND. FIGHT. DEFEND THE REPUBLIC.”
Hegseth’s hand was strengthened on Friday when Trump’s chief of staff Susie Wiles stepped down and was replaced by his hard-line domestic policy adviser, raging xenophobe, and illegal boat strike proponent Stephen Miller, according to two Pentagon officials. The embattled war chief was quick to offer “Huge CONGRATS” to Miller on X, and posted a photo of himself alongside Trump’s new consigliere. The same coterie of Hegseth devotees at the Pentagon followed with similar posts featuring Miller.
Wiles had reportedly soured on Hegseth, blaming his woeful management of the Iran war for flagging Republican fortunes. A senior Trump administration official also told MS Now that Miller and Hegseth “have been extremely close since the beginning of the administration.”
If the House impeaches Hegseth, removing him from office would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate — a high bar, even when Democrats take control of the chamber in January. Neither of the two Cabinet secretaries impeached by the House — William Belknap, the secretary of war, in 1876; and Alejandro Mayorkas, the secretary of homeland security, in 2024 — were convicted by the Senate.
An Armed Services Committee staffer who spoke with The Intercept was skeptical that Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., would bring the measure to a vote. Ansari held out hope. “Thune is very much aligned in terms of his view that Hegseth is not fit for the job,” she said, adding, “I do think that the resounding victories on Tuesday night will impact the way Republicans operate moving forward.”
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who is retiring at the end of the year, has said for months that he regrets his vote to confirm Hegseth and rebuked the war chief for his desperate video address aimed at Trump. “[C]abinet secretaries shouldn’t be wasting taxpayer dollars on campaign style videos. Kristi Noem learned that the hard way,” he wrote on X on Friday, also laying into Hegseth for “the incompetence you’ve displayed, the bad advice you’ve given to president, and your shameful and embarrassing episodes from firing our top generals to texting war plans to reporters.” Tillis had also previously said Hegseth “needs to go.”
Massie suggested his impeachment resolution is the legislative equivalent of a mercy killing, calling it “a much gentler version” of what Democrats will do when they take control of Congress in January. Congressional committees have broad investigative powers, and Ansari said that if Hegseth survives this year’s impeachment push, there were “many ways” for Democrats to hold him accountable in the next session, specifically compelling him to testify before the American people. “I would be surprised to see him last the next two years in this administration,” she told The Intercept. “I think that he is not only one of the most incompetent members of the administration, but also the most unpopular — and it’s on a bipartisan basis. So the pressure will continue to grow for there to be some change at the Pentagon.”
Trump expressed mild “confidence” in Hegseth in a “60 Minutes” interview taped on Friday, touting the U.S. victory over Venezuela, but stopped short of praising his Pentagon chief for it. Asked if he credited Hegseth for what he considers a major victory, Trump replied: “No, but he was a part of it.” On Saturday, Trump wrote on Truth Social that calls for impeachment of administration officials amounted to “extortion at the highest level” and ordered the Justice Department to investigate those making the push.
Attorney General Todd Blanche, himself a potential target of impeachment, said on Sunday that the Justice Department would represent Hegseth during any impeachment proceedings. He added that he “would be very worried” if he were a Democrat threatening to investigate administration officials. Asked if he considered those threats to be a crime, Blanche said, “It depends on what’s said. So yes, there could be.”
The White House did not respond to questions about Trump’s support for Hegseth.
Update: November 9, 2026, 2:50 p.m. ET
The article has been updated to note that Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced articles of impeachment against War Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday afternoon. 
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

https://www.propublica.org/article/gener.title: Watch: Where Do Our Generic Drugs Come From? We Dug to Find Out.
https://www.propublica.org/article/gener.author: Katie Nixdorf, Debbie Cenziper, Megan Rose, Brandon Roberts
https://www.propublica.org/article/gener.text:
These days, we know where almost everything comes from. Everyday items like food, clothes and pens all carry labels listing where things are grown, manufactured or even designed.
So why is it so hard to find where prescription drugs are made?
That question set off a 14-month investigation into where our medications are made, how the FDA polices drug manufacturers and what happens when inspectors report issues inside factories.
The vast majority of prescriptions filled in the United States are for generic drugs, which are often far cheaper than brand-name alternatives. 
For years, Congress, doctors and watchdog groups have questioned the quality of generic drugs made overseas. India produces about half of all generics used in the U.S., but the labels on pill bottles often don’t list where a drug is manufactured. Inspection reports describe unsafe manufacturing conditions at generic drug factories, but the Food and Drug Administration redacts the names of the medications made in those factories. That means if drugs made in errant factories wind up in your medicine cabinet, you’d have no way of knowing.
To better understand how the FDA regulates the generic drug industry, Debbie Cenziper and Megan Rose interviewed current and former factory inspectors, tested medications in a lab and sued the federal government for critical documents.
Here’s what they found:
- Birds defecated on boxes of sterile equipment. Inspectors reported finding dirty labs, mold and foul water at factories. Records referenced vials of medication that were “blackish” from contamination. Inspectors found what appeared to be metal shavings on equipment.
- Drug manufacturers manipulated and destroyed drug-testing records. At one factory, an analyst poured acid on records stuffed in a trash bin. At another, inspectors said in a report that records were “routinely manipulated” to cover up the presence of particulate matter —  which could include glass, fiber or other contaminants — in generic drugs.
- A lifesaving generic drug contained a lower amount of a key ingredient. We worked with an independent lab to test generic versions of tacrolimus, used to prevent organ rejection. We found some pills contained a lower amount of the key ingredient in the drug. Doctors and experts said that underdosing can leave patients vulnerable to organ rejection.
- The FDA allowed generic drug imports from banned factories — and didn’t inform the public. The agency gave some manufacturers a special pass to continue to ship drugs made in factories whose manufacturing practices were so bad they had been banned from the U.S. Over a dozen years, the FDA exempted at least 150 drugs or their ingredients from banned factories.
- A transplant patient’s lungs failed after she took generic versions of tacrolimus. Hannah Goetz had a double-lung transplant as a teenager and had to take tacrolimus twice a day. Her lungs failed in 2023, and she died at 21 years old, after years of relying on the generic drug made by two manufacturers with documented problems. Lawyers told Goetz’s mother that it was impossible to draw a straight line from Hannah’s death to a generic manufacturer, but her mother said she wonders if her daughter would still be alive if she took a different brand of tacrolimus.
In a response to ProPublica, a spokesperson for the FDA said in a statement that the exemptions given to banned factories are “thoroughly evaluated through a multi-disciplinary approach” but declined to say exactly what those evaluations entailed. The agency also said it requires manufacturers to conduct additional quality checks with third-party oversight before sending drugs to the U.S. The agency did not respond to questions about how it can know that generics are safe without a more robust testing program.
In statements to ProPublica, drug companies said that they take patient safety seriously, adhere to quality standards and are committed to working with the FDA on any regulatory issues.
ProPublica’s investigation, which went on to be a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for investigative reporting, published in 2025. 
Use our tool to find where your prescription drugs were made.
ProPublica’s Brandon Roberts and a team of data journalists made a tool called Rx Inspector that will show you the facility that manufactured your generic prescription drugs and any inspection reports, warning letters and import bans we have from the FDA. 
The data isn’t perfect; it’s possible the FDA hasn’t published everything it knows about a given facility, for example. Also, one company may have acquired another or moved the factory somewhere else. This tool also isn’t meant to provide you with medical advice: If you find something troubling, it doesn’t necessarily mean that your drug is compromised. Doctors and pharmacists advise that you not stop taking your medications. Instead, you should talk to your healthcare provider about any concerns.
Step 1: Enter the name of your prescription drug, as well as the company name found on your pill bottle or drug label.
Step 2: If there are multiple matches in our database, you can narrow your search using the markings found on a pill, for example.
Step 3: When you click on a drug, we’ll show you any manufacturing facilities we’ve been able to connect to it. Click on a facility to see any information we have from the FDA.
FDA inspections come with compliance outcomes, such as import alerts or warning letters. The best possible outcome of an inspection is “acceptable state,” which means the FDA took no compliance action and ProPublica found no issues documented by inspectors. Search your prescription here.
ProPublica described Rx Inspector and the methodology used to build it to the FDA, which did not comment. The agency previously told ProPublica that it doesn’t reveal where drugs are made on inspection reports to protect what it deemed to be confidential commercial information.
Read more of Cenziper, Rose and Roberts’ reporting from their series Rx Roulette or watch their video explainer.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: New centre for contemporary Indigenous art launches in upstate New York
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gabriella Angeleti
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Branchline, a new 10,000-sq.-ft arts centre focused on championing contemporary Native American art, opened its main gallery to the public on Saturday (7 November). Located in the town of Katonah in New York’s Westchester County, Branchline is an initiative of the Gochman Family Collection (GFC), a private lending collection established in 2021 by the philanthropist Becky Gochman, who has a longstanding interest in Native art, and the former gallerist Zach Feuer.
Branchline is located steps from the Katonah station on the Metro-North Railroad, around 45 miles from Manhattan, and takes its name from a term for points where railroad tracks diverge and begin. When it is fully completed next year, the complex will span three adjoining buildings—including multiple galleries, a ceramics studio, two apartments, a deck filled with sculptures and a café.
Laura Phipps, a former associate curator at the Whitney Museum of American Art, was appointed director of the GFC earlier this year. She is working alongside the creative director and curator Rachel Martin (Tlingít) and several other curatorial consultants at Branchline.
“Branchline builds on an extension of the ethos and the experience of the GFC, which is centring artists, supporting artists and sharing their work,” Phipps said at a preview of the centre on 5 November. “We were excited about all the ideas that Branchline conjures, both thinking about the metaphor of the train, the metaphor of trees, and what we can do to experiment and grow in this space.”
Organisers seek to explore innovative ways of activating the space in dialogue with the collection. The inaugural programme features a site-specific installation on the exterior of the main gallery building by the artist Matthew Kirk (Diné). The four-panel mixed-media work We Start To Think We’ve Got Someplace To Go (2026) features traditional Diné motifs made with construction materials.
The opening exhibition, Line Break, is curated by Branchline’s assistant curator Moonoka Begay (Ndee/Diné) with the collection associate Nicole van Brugge. It explores the concept of lines and borders figuratively and metaphorically through nearly 30 works by 18 artists—including Sara Flores, Jeffrey Gibson, Jaune Quick-to-See Smith, Kay WalkingStick, Marie Watt and Emmi Whitehorse.
A centrepiece of the opening show is the Diné artist Raven Chacon’s Storm Pattern (2021-24). It consists of abstracted musical scores that reference traditional Diné weavings while also evoking the sounds made by drones. The work is accompanied by isolated recordings Chacon captured of drones that hovered above the Standing Rock encampments during the Dakota Access Pipeline protests in 2016, with the lines in the work referencing the oscillating sonic waves of their erratic flight patterns.
Before establishing a dedicated exhibition space, some of the GFC’s holdings—totalling around 800 works—were displayed in private residences on Manhattan’s Upper East Side and in West Palm Beach, Florida. The GFC has loaned art to more than 100 exhibitions worldwide, with 260 works loaned to date.
Gochman and Feuer previously co-founded the Forge Project in 2021, an initiative similarly dedicated to the advancement of contemporary Native art and located around 70m north in Taghkanic, New York. That space also offers year-round exhibitions, artist residencies and workshops. It was converted from a private organisation into a Native-led nonprofit in 2024, when Gochman withdrew from the project. Candice Hopkins (Carcross/Tagish First Nation) is its current executive director and chief curator.
“We started Branchline and the Forge Project for social-justice reasons, and we are now separate from Forge, but we got the bug to collect Native art,” Gochman said at the preview. “The Branchline space functions as a free public space, which is a new concept for us. We are consistent, though, with the philosophy that artists and art come first, because we wouldn’t be here without them.”

https://citylimits.org/la-cultura-taina-.title: La cultura taína sigue viva: exposición en el Bronx celebra legado de Bobby González
https://citylimits.org/la-cultura-taina-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/la-cultura-taina-.text:
Share This Article
Una nueva exposición en el Museum of Bronx History explora la vida del poeta, narrador y educador puertorriqueño que dedicó casi cuatro décadas a preservar la cultura indígena y desafiar los estereotipos sobre el sur del Bronx.
Este artículo se publicó originalmente en inglés el 4 de noviembre. Traducido por Jacob Velez. Read the English version here.
Para Bobby González, la preservación de la historia indígena comenzó cerca de casa: en la bodega de su familia, ubicada en el sur del Bronx.
Mientras crecía cerca de las viviendas públicas Melrose Houses, González conoció a personas de diferentes comunidades indígenas que visitaban el negocio de sus padres. Esas conversaciones lo ayudaron a comprender mejor su propia herencia taína y despertaron en él un compromiso de por vida con la enseñanza de la historia indígena.
Ahora, tres años después de su fallecimiento, su trabajo es recordado en una nueva exposición en el Museum of Bronx History (Museo de Historia del Bronx).
La exposición, titulada “From the South Bronx Reservation: Bobby González, Taíno Indian” (“Desde la reserva del sur del Bronx: Bobby González, indígena taíno”), inaugurada el 8 de octubre y abierta hasta marzo de 2027, explora la vida del poeta, narrador y educador puertorriqueño que dedicó casi cuatro décadas a preservar la cultura indígena y desafiar los estereotipos sobre el sur del Bronx.
Nacido en 1951, González creció en una familia puertorriqueña cuyos padres emigraron a Nueva York después de la Segunda Guerra Mundial. Su padre trabajó como cocinero antes de abrir una bodega en la década de 1970, donde González y sus hermanos ayudaban a administrar el negocio familiar.
Según Stephen Payne, director de la Sociedad Histórica del condado del Bronx, la bodega desempeñó un papel importante en la formación de la identidad de González.
Entre los visitantes había personas de ascendencia cherokee, quechua, lenape y de otras comunidades indígenas. Sus conversaciones motivaron a González a aprender más sobre las comunidades indígenas de América y a explorar su propia ascendencia.
Esa experiencia influyó posteriormente en la expresión “South Bronx Reservation” (“Reserva del sur del Bronx”), que González utilizaba para describir la presencia indígena en su vecindario.
Payne explicó que la expresión también reflejaba similitudes entre el sur del Bronx y algunas reservas indígenas de Estados Unidos, incluidos problemas relacionados con la contaminación y la falta de recursos.
Para González, el vecindario era mucho más que el lugar donde había crecido. Se convirtió en la base de sus escritos, su poesía y su activismo cultural.
Su viuda, María Aponte González, lo recordó como alguien que siempre mantuvo una profunda conexión con su comunidad.
“Era una persona de espíritu muy amable”, dijo. “Nunca gritaba, nunca levantaba la voz”.
Describió a su difunto esposo como una persona accesible y tranquila, a quien los miembros de la comunidad acudían frecuentemente en busca de consejos.
González cofundó la organización cultural Taíno del Norte, organizó el festival anual Bronx Native American Festival y escribió varios libros, entre ellos The Last Puerto Rican Indian (“El último indígena puertorriqueño”). También viajó por todo el país para ofrecer charlas en escuelas, universidades y museos sobre la historia indígena.
Su misión era desafiar la creencia de que los taínos, un pueblo indígena que habitaba originalmente el Caribe, incluido Puerto Rico, habían desaparecido siglos atrás.
“Somos taínos, todavía estamos aquí”, dijo Payne, al recordar una frase utilizada por la organización que González ayudó a establecer.
Payne explicó que la exposición destaca cómo la identidad indígena continúa formando parte de las comunidades puertorriqueñas, particularmente en el Bronx, donde González se convirtió en una figura importante del movimiento de revitalización cultural taína.
La exposición también llega en un momento en que el Bronx atraviesa cambios demográficos. Payne señaló el aumento del costo de vida y cómo ha contribuido a que los residentes puertorriqueños abandonen el distrito o la ciudad, lo que resalta la importancia de que los miembros de la comunidad compartan sus historias.
“Es muy importante preservar esa parte de la historia mientras todavía haya personas en la comunidad que puedan hablar de ella”, dijo.
La exposición reúne pertenencias personales, escritos y otros materiales que González conservó a lo largo de su vida.
Aponte González, quien fue cocuradora de la exposición junto con el documentalista Edwin Pagán, seleccionó los objetos de su hogar.
“Todo lo que van a ver en la exposición es obra de Bobby”, dijo.
En lugar de centrarse en cómo otras personas describían a su esposo, quiere que los visitantes conozcan su legado a través de los materiales que él mismo había creado.
Entre sus contribuciones se encontraban talleres de poesía, incluida una serie de poesía recitada que ayudaba a poetas emergentes a desarrollar sus propias voces. También utilizaba títeres y narraciones para enseñar a los niños sobre la historia indígena y sus tradiciones culturales.
Aponte González puso en marcha el Proyecto Legado de Bobby González en 2024, después de conversaciones que había mantenido con su esposo sobre la preservación de su trabajo antes de que enfermara gravemente.
Describió la exposición como un proyecto que tardó dos años en desarrollarse, con el apoyo de Pagán y el Museum of Bronx History.
Para Payne, la exposición también refleja un desafío más amplio que enfrentan las instituciones históricas: preservar las experiencias de las comunidades trabajadoras, cuyos documentos y pertenencias personales suelen perderse debido a la inestabilidad de vivienda o la falta de recursos económicos.
Explicó que las familias que han sufrido desalojos o mudanzas frecuentes pueden haber perdido fotografías, documentos y otros materiales que ayudan a contar sus historias. En esos casos, las instituciones suelen recurrir a testimonios orales e investigaciones de archivo para recuperar historias que, de otro modo, podrían desaparecer.
La colección de González ofreció una oportunidad diferente, ya que él había conservado gran parte de su propio trabajo, que su viuda ha puesto a disposición a través del Proyecto Legado.
Más allá de celebrar sus logros, tanto Aponte González como Payne esperan que la exposición anime a las generaciones más jóvenes a conocer sus raíces culturales.
“Los jóvenes necesitan hacer espacio en sus mentes y estar abiertos a aprender”, dijo Aponte González.
Para Payne, el mensaje principal es que la historia indígena no debe entenderse únicamente como algo que pertenece a un pasado lejano.
Espera que los visitantes reconozcan que las comunidades indígenas continúan preservando, recuperando y desarrollando sus tradiciones culturales en la actualidad.
A través de los escritos, las narraciones y el activismo de González, la exposición ofrece a los visitantes la oportunidad de explorar esa historia viva mediante las experiencias de un hombre que dedicó su vida a compartirla.
La exposición estará abierta al público en el Museum of Bronx History, en 3266 de Bainbridge Avenue, en el Bronx, hasta marzo de 2027.

https://citylimits.org/nyc-to-expand-hom.title: NYC to Expand Homeless Outreach This Winter Following Last Year’s Deadly Cold
https://citylimits.org/nyc-to-expand-hom.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/nyc-to-expand-hom.text:
Share This Article
The city is earmarking an extra $25 million to hire 300 additional outreach workers and open more low-barrier shelter beds, officials announced Friday. It comes after a brutal freeze killed 18 New Yorkers last winter.
The city will spend an extra $25 million to expand its homeless outreach efforts when temperatures drop this winter—hoping to avoid a repeat of last year, when a brutal stretch of historically cold weather killed 18 New Yorkers, many of them unhoused.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the additional funding at a press conference on Monday, part of a sweeping package of winter preparedness reforms that will also include “supercharged” plows and new snow blowers.
The $25 million will go to beefing up the Department of Homeless Services’ “Code Blue” operations, which kick in when temperatures dip below 32 degrees Fahrenheit overnight.
It’ll pay for 300 additional outreach workers, including nurses, to canvas city streets and implore people to come indoors. It will also open more public warming facilities, including heated buses and vans, and to creating another 800 “low barrier” shelter beds—sites with fewer entry requirements and less stringent rules than typical city shelters.
Those beds will be in single- and double-occupancy rooms, officials said, offering greater privacy than crowded—and sometimes, dangerous—group facilities that many street homeless New Yorkers are reluctant to enter.
“When we speak to homeless New Yorkers, we will hear that if only there was a low barrier single room bed, they would then be willing to go,” the mayor said.
Mamdani was newly inaugurated when last winter’s emergency cold conditions hit—what officials say included the city’s first blizzard in a decade as well nine consecutive days of below-freezing temperatures.
The cold killed at least 18 people, including several unhoused residents.
“I wasn’t here in the heart of last winter, but I’ve reviewed it, and I know how it went, and I learned a lot from it,” said Department of Social Services Commissioner Erin Dalton, who oversees the Department of Homeless Services (DHS). Mamdani appointed her to lead the agency in February.
Dalton said DHS will be making key changes to its cold weather response this year, including having its street outreach teams adopt a “broad geographic canvassing approach.”
This breaks from previous winters in which homeless outreach teams focused their efforts on a list of about 350 known street homeless New Yorkers, visiting their usual spots and urging them to take shelter. On most nights, the city was only able to locate about 15 percent of the people on that list, Dalton said.
She added that workers are already engaging with those folks before very cold weather sets in, but that “an approach built around a vulnerable list leaves way too many people in the street that aren’t known to us, and only covers a small portion of people.”
Instead, Dalton says, outreach teams will “walk the streets, encampments, parks, and subway steps where we know the vast majority of people experiencing homelessness stay,” and “engage every vulnerable person along the routes.”
The commissioner said DHS tested this broader canvassing approach over the summer during heat waves, and were able to reach far more people—”more than 20 times as many as on a given day” compared to the summer before.
While homeless advocates applauded the additional resources, they said many of the changes are long overdue.
“These are smart responses that will save lives. But these are also well-known action steps that have been called for for years,” VOCAL-NY, a grassroots group that organizes low-income and systems impacted New Yorkers, said in a statement Monday.
VOCAL leaders called on the city to invest more in permanent solutions to getting New Yorkers off the streets, like with additional city-funded rental vouchers and supportive affordable housing.
“That’s kind of the the ideal. It’s moving people into permanent housing,” Charles King, the CEO of the homeless nonprofit Housing Works, told City Limits last week, when the organization held a funeral mass for nine of the unhoused New Yorkers who died of hypothermia in last winter’s extreme cold.
“At the end of the day, giving a person a decent place to live is what all of us need.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Hundreds protest US Senate bill that would gut key section of National Historic Preservation Act
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Emma Cieslik
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
On Monday (9 November), hundreds of protesters gathered on the West Lawn of the US Capitol in Washington, DC, to protest the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA, or senate bill S.5653), which would gut a key section of the National Historic Preservation Act. Representatives from more than 100 tribal nations, members of congress, leaders from the Association of African American Museums, the DC Preservation League, the American Institute of Architects and the Archaeological Institute of America gathered to protest a bill that would remove the requirement for federal agencies to notify and consult with the public and tribal nations about potential harms to historic sites, as stipulated in Section 106, Title III of the National Historic Preservation Act.
The BAAJA, described by New Mexico congresswoman Melanie Stansbury at the protest as a “dirty deal”, was created without tribal consultation or public input. According to California representative Jared Huffman, the 500 new pages of legislative text, which he described as “the most sweeping legislation we’ve seen on energy and environmental policy in decades”, was released just 48 hours before the Senate was set to vote on it Monday evening.
“They scheduled this vote for tonight to try to prevent something like this,” Huffman told protesters gathered on the Capitol lawn; organisers estimated around 800 people attended. “To try to prevent the American people from having a say, from looking under the hood of this sweeping legislation and understanding what’s actually it, but you came anyway.” Holding signs with illustrations of President Donald Trump’s planned Triumphal Arch in flames and “Nix 106”, protesters gathered for over two hours to listen to more than 15 speakers who argued that BAAJA would seriously threaten US history.
Greg Werkheiser, a leader of the Section 106 Coalition and co-founder of Cultural Heritage Partners, kicked off the protest. “We gather at the seat of American democracy, where the laws of this nation are written, to affirm one simple principle: the people deserve a voice in decisions that affect the places that we love,” he said. “That is the promise we have come here today to defend.”
Along with removing the requirement for federal agencies to engage with the public, the BAAJA would also make consultation with tribal nations optional, narrow what types of activity trigger a federal historic preservation review, restrict the definition of what constitutes a historic site, and remove any consideration of sensory, indirect and cumulative effects of changes to historic and sacred sites, essentially allowing federal agencies to take over tribal and state historic preservation offices that do not abide by limits and deadlines that the new bill would set. The BAAJA would even restrict what legal action people and organisations can take against the destruction of historic and sacred sites.
“For tribal nations,” Arizona congresswoman Adelita Grijalva said, “the fight is more than historic preservation. It’s about sovereignty. It’s about self-determination. It’s about the fundamental right to protect our ancestral homelands, culturally significant sites, and traditions that have existed since time immemorial.”
In its current form, Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act requires federal agencies to consider the impact of federally funded building projects and requires that people receiving federal funds or permits consult with tribal nations. If passed, S. 5653 would make that consultation—the requirement that tribal nations participate in decision-making—optional.
“Our sacred places are living places of prayer, our responsibilities to them do not end at the reservation boundary,” Harry Antonio Jr, the governor of the Pueblo of Laguna in New Mexico, said at the rally. “You do not have to share our prayers to understand why those places deserve respect. Section 106 gives our governments a way to bring those concerns into federal decisions.”
Senators in favour of the bill have argued that its passage would lead to more economic opportunities. Articulating a position held by most rally attendees, Grijalva said: “Economic development does not require sacrificing our history, our culture or our sovereignty. We can create jobs without destroying sacred places. We can create jobs without sacrificing Mother Earth, our land, our water.”
Rashida Tlaib, the congresswoman from Michigan, said the bill would be used to fast-track projects with severe environmental consequences, including data centres and gas pipelines. “This bill strips away what little tools we already have to defend ourselves from corporate polluters,” she said.
The senate’s vote on the BAAJA coincides with Trump’s push to build a 250ft-tall arch between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. On 5 November, protesters gathered at its proposed site and spoke against it during a National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) meeting. Although the NCPC voted to approve the arch, a Washington, DC judge then immediately blocked construction for 14 days.
“The court orders stopping construction of those projects would not be possible if this BAAJA legislation becomes law,” Huffman said. “If this becomes law, the administration will use that in those pending court cases to make it much, much harder to stop Trump from advancing those and other vanity projects.”
Speakers urged protesters to call their senators, and implored senators to vote down the bill or to table a vote until the newly elected members of congress are sworn in in January.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Aros museum in Aarhus, Denmark acquires sun-like Olafur Eliasson sculpture in new partnership with the artist
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Aros Aarhus Art Museum in eastern Denmark will acquire a major piece by the high-profile Danish-Icelandic artist Olafur Eliasson—a crowd-pleasing vast glowing yellow sphere that appears to hover in space (Presence, 2025)—as part of a new long-term partnership.
The initiative between the artist and the museum, called “Shared Futures”, also encompasses Thin Ice, a solo exhibition to open autumn 2027. “This exhibition presents key works from recent decades alongside new projects reflecting Eliasson’s growing engagement with the climate, ecology, and humanity’s relationship with its surroundings,” says a statement.
A new site-specific version of Eliasson’s installation Waterfall (2004) will meanwhile be installed on Aros’s Art Square from 9 October next year; Studio Olafur Eliasson will also create a publicly accessible library collection of books on Eliasson’s artistic production at Aros under the plans. In addition, the partnership includes a dedicated postdoctoral research position in collaboration with Aarhus University.
Eliasson says in a statement: “Aros has supported my work in Denmark for many years, so it felt natural to make my online archive and library available there… the ambition is to show that museums can offer depth and focus for engaging with an artist’s practice in a more detailed, granular way.” The museum is also home to Eliasson’s rainbow rooftop walkway Your Rainbow Panorama (2011).
Rebecca Matthews, the museum's director, tells The Art Newspaper: “I first met Olafur Eliasson when I was chief executive of the European Capital of Culture in 2017, when he created an extraordinary stage design for the performance Tree of Codes. We were supposed to have our photograph taken together, but it was pouring with rain, so we ended up standing in a colonnade, talking. I remember thinking: If I ever get to lead a museum, he will be the first person I call.” Matthews became director of Aros in 2022.
In December 2025, Eliasson appeared on The Art Newspaper podcast A brush with…. with Ben Luke. “His works can be deceptively simple or enormously complex, but often share a rigorous and reductive geometry, which may conversely produce expansive and multifarious perceptual, sensory and embodied effects,” wrote Luke.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: ‘I’m looking for faces which surprise me’: how Richard Avedon photographed the soul of his subjects
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: David Smith in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
Richard Avedon had only taken a couple of frames when he accidentally hit his head on a light being held above him. The Dalai Lama burst into laughter. That was when Avedon snapped two more frames and announced: “Oh, I got it!”
Avedon’s assistant, Sebastian Kim, was baffled. “I was like, what the hell happened? There’s only four frames out of a roll of 12 frames,” he recalls in a phone interview. “I realised he knew at that moment that something had happened, a mistake had happened: he hit his head and the Dalai Lama lit up.”
Kim, 52, now an eminent photographer in his own right, is among the interviewees who feature in a new documentary, Avedon, directed by Oscar winner Ron Howard, which premiered at the Cannes film festival and is released on Netflix this week.
The film explores the six-decade career of the fashion and portrait photographer renowned for white backgrounds that stripped away distractions and for capturing figures ranging from Marilyn Monroe and Charlie Chaplin to civil rights activists, anti-war protesters and working-class Americans.
Avedon was raised in New York City. His father, Jacob Avedon, co-founded a specialty store on Fifth Avenue, which was lost overnight during the Great Depression. Avedon struggled academically, flunking out of high school despite winning a citywide poetry prize.
He once said: “My father wanted me to be strongly educated, strong physically, and to make a living. But I always felt that I flunked. I grew up thinking I was certifiably stupid. I couldn’t graduate high school. I flunked everything.”
In the second world war, Avedon joined the Merchant Marine. Assigned to the photographic unit, he took more than 100,000 ID card photos and performed autopsy documentation. Observing endless faces against white backdrops taught him that no two faces are alike.
At the New School’s Design Laboratory, Harper’s Bazaar art director Alexey Brodovitch provided Avedon’s foundational philosophy: “Astonish me.” When Avedon struggled to design a neon sign using traditional media, Brodovitch suggested using pipe cleaners or spaghetti, teaching Avedon never to be blocked by technical limitations.
Commissioned by Harper’s Bazaar magazine, Avedon brought theatricality to fashion. Observing Christian Dior’s 1947 The New Look collection, Avedon captured models moving, swirling and laughing across Paris streets, transforming fashion photography from static posing into dynamic visual storytelling.
His approach to portraiture was no less distinctive. Avedon’s studio aesthetic relied on a stark, seamless white paper backdrop, bounded by a bold black film border. He once explained: “It’s the existential white. The only thing you see is the geography of the face. One of the functions of art is to eliminate in order to make more powerful or stronger what the artist wants to get across.
“I remember once that I fasted for three days. I fasted with a friend. And she and I decided after the fast, how will we break the fast? We decided on a peach. I never tasted anything like that peach in my life. Because everything, because of the fast, becomes so precious. That’s a little bit about getting rid of the background.”
For his picture of Monroe in 1957, Avedon waited through hours of joyful posing until the actor collapsed into quiet exhaustion. Monroe slumped into a corner, allowing Avedon to capture her unguarded melancholy – a portrait often called Sad Marilyn.
He believed that models were active creative collaborators rather than decorative props. He once said: “I know perfectly well what I want before I leave the house in the morning but if the girl doesn’t feel that she’s part of it, if she feels that she is someone that’s hired for an hour, a stick of wood that’s going to be told to stand over there and do that, that’s exactly what you get out of her.”
By engaging sitters through conversation, music and playfulness, he created an atmosphere of mutual trust. Models like Penelope Tree and Lauren Hutton recall in the film that working with him was liberating, allowing them to drop their guards and express vulnerability in front of the lens.
Dallas Brennan Rexer, 54, one of the film’s producers, said: “He was trying to get into their head and into their soul, in a way, through his photos. It was the same process for him regardless, and the models that we interviewed spoke about how they weren’t treated as a model who was just there to hold the clothes on.
“They were a human that he connected to and he asked them questions and he tried to understand what they were thinking about and what they were feeling and tried to help get something out of them that radiated and gave them an energy. That’s what made the photos special. It wasn’t just that they were pretty and their clothing looked nice.”
Avedon photographed the Duke and Duchess of Windsor in their hotel suite. Aware of their polished public persona, he broke through their guard by claiming his taxi had run over a dog.
Rexer elaborates: “He knew how he felt about their politics and he didn’t want to allow himself to be used to make another polite pretty picture of them. He wanted to say something much more pointed and important. He used the photograph in a very clever and specific way. He captured the moment that he thinks said everything that needed to be said about them.”
Though Avedon achieved commercial success – directing television campaigns for Calvin Klein – he channelled his resources into politically charged documentary work.
In 1963, Avedon reconnected with his high school friend James Baldwin, with whom he had co-edited a school magazine. Together they published Nothing Personal, combining Avedon’s portraits of civil rights leaders and mental asylum patients with Baldwin’s rich prose.
Rexer explains: “Dick was at a place in his life where he was ready to get involved in something political and he wanted to do something meaningful on civil rights. Nothing Personal is a phenomenal book. The text that James Baldwin wrote is poetic and beautiful, but it also is so resonant today.”
Avedon’s asylum photographs were deeply personal, influenced by his sister Louise, who suffered from severe mental illness. He said: “I photographed things that frightened me so that I could understand them.”
But when Nothing Personal received a withering review in the New York Review of Books, Avedon was crushed. He admitted: “That review simply stopped me from working for about a year because I began to question myself as an artist.”
Yet Avedon continued his political involvement. During the civil rights movement, he quietly supported activists. Rexer notes: “In the background very quietly, Dick was sending film down to SNCC [the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee] because they were using photography to keep people accountable to what was going on in the south. Then they would send the film back, and he would take it to the lab and process it for them, quietly on the side to just keep the movement going.”
These efforts culminated in In the American West (1979–1984), commissioned by the Amon Carter Museum of American Art in Fort Worth, Texas. Over five summers, Avedon photographed working-class Americans against white paper. Avedon stated of the project: “I’m looking for faces which surprise me. I’m looking for a face that will hold the wall.”
In 1992, at age 69, Avedon became the first staff photographer in the history of the New Yorker magazine, hired by editor Tina Brown. He produced portraits of global figures and controversial fashion essays, such as the Mr and Mrs Comfort portfolio.
In a statement provided by Netflix, Howard observed: “He had to learn to bridge his commercial success and his creative endeavors, using his own resources to underwrite far riskier projects. He figured out how to lean into the popular to make space for the unusual ... In many ways, Avedon defied the idea that there must be a division between art and commerce, highbrow and lowbrow, beauty and brutality.”
Avedon’s internal contradictions are at the heart of Howard’s documentary, which draws from unprecedented access to personal archives held by the Richard Avedon Foundation, including hundreds of thousands of negatives, contact sheets and behind-the-lens footage.
Rexer says: “The archive is daunting at first because there were 16,000 sittings, and that can only mean hundreds of thousands of images, and so it’s a bit overwhelming in the first couple of months.”
Among the production team’s most extraordinary discoveries was a cache of casual audio tapes recorded inside Avedon’s studio during the 1960s and 1970s with collaborators like Marvin Israel and Doon Arbus.
Rexer says: “They would put a recorder on the table and hit record and forget about it. So you could be a fly on the wall. He was working out a lot of questions about truth and identity and self and all of the big things like beauty. They would have these wonderful lunches with these abstract conversations about it but then he could turn that into something concrete.”
Despite all the success, the workaholic Avedon lived in a constant state of anxiety and self-doubt. His son, John Avedon, says in the film: “He had a bull-like confidence in himself. At the same time, he was totally insecure. He absolutely suffered from performance anxiety, but then he absolutely performed. I think he had to be anxious in order to perform.”
For Rexer, this is the key to unlocking much of Avedon’s work. She explains: “You need to have the confidence to walk up to Henry Kissinger and say: ‘I’m taking your portrait right now and no, we’re going to do it this way and put your hands down and look into my lens.’
“But also the insecurity or the lack of know-it-allness to be able to ask questions and connect with his subjects and explore and make people feel comfortable too. It didn’t just come in big in the room. He made space for the people he was photographing. That’s beautiful.”
Avedon suffered a cerebral hemorrhage and died in 2004, aged 81, while in San Antonio shooting a project titled Democracy for the New Yorker.
For Kim, his influence remains profound. He says: “I credit him for making me the person that I am. The way that he shaped the person that I am, the photographer that I am. He has had such an impact on so many people. It was difficult, but I look back and it’s the discipline that creates character.”
- Avedon is available on Netflix on 11 November

https://www.propublica.org/article/bill-.title: The Garbage Man: Bill Gates Has Earned Billions Investing in Climate-Polluting Landfills
https://www.propublica.org/article/bill-.author: Alex Cuadros
https://www.propublica.org/article/bill-.text:
Reporting Highlights
- A Little-Known Investment: Bill Gates has quietly accumulated a $29 billion stake in America’s No. 2 landfill operator, Republic Services.
- Climate Pollution: EPA inspectors have repeatedly found methane — a highly potent greenhouse gas — escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits.
- Undermining Climate Policies: Republic has lobbied against regulations that could make the waste industry cleaner, including by keeping organic garbage out of landfills in the first place.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
In November 2015, world leaders descended on Paris to negotiate a historic agreement to limit global warming. But on the summit’s opening day, attention turned to a private citizen slouched awkwardly in a chair on stage: Bill Gates.
Gates, with his characteristic flop of sandy hair, grinned impishly as President Barack Obama called him a “visionary” and a “driving force” behind a pair of pledges that both saw as key to the larger agreement. First the world’s largest economies would double their spending on research into clean-energy technologies. Then investors like Gates would back the startups that emerged. The Microsoft cofounder had already enlisted two dozen other billionaires to join the effort.
For Gates, who’d become increasingly consumed by this unprecedented threat to human well-being, the moment marked his arrival as a leading figure in the fight against climate change.
“If we back over 50 different breakthrough approaches, we know that several of those will give us the solution that we need,” Gates said during his own speech. He would invest at least $2 billion of his own money in companies developing geothermal wells, new kinds of nuclear reactors and machines that pull carbon from the air, to name just a few.
With much less fanfare, however, Gates has put more than double that amount into a very dirty, old-school industry. At the time of the Paris summit, he was already the dominant shareholder of America’s No. 2 landfill operator, Republic Services. He has since increased his stake to 38% of the company, a position worth $29 billion.
Bill Gates’ Stake in Republic Services, a Landfill Operator, Now Exceeds a Fifth of His Net Worth
While fossil fuels get most of the attention, scientists increasingly see landfills as a crucial climate issue. They’re responsible for as much as a fifth of the country’s emissions of methane, a highly potent greenhouse gas, studies show. Republic alone generates as much climate pollution as 3 million gasoline-burning cars each year, according to its own reports.
One might imagine that a landfill operator with Gates as its largest shareholder — and with three people closely linked to Gates on its board — would lead the way in tackling those emissions. Even after seemingly softening his stance on global warming in a controversial blog post last year, Gates remains one of the world’s most prominent voices on the issue. As he did in his bestselling 2021 book “How to Avoid a Climate Disaster,” he continues to advocate for cutting emissions, and he has called on his fellow business leaders to do their part.
Gates, though, has failed to make Republic live up to his own climate principles, a ProPublica investigation has found. Federal inspectors have repeatedly found methane escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits. The company has refrained from adopting the ambitious emissions-reduction goal embraced by its main competitor. Republic has even lobbied against policies that could make the wider industry cleaner, including by keeping organic waste out of landfills in the first place.
“It seems very likely that Bill Gates has the power to influence Republic’s behavior to make it more climate-friendly, even if that costs the company profits,” said Ann Lipton, a legal scholar who studies corporate governance at the University of Colorado, Boulder.
As for whether he should, in her words, “put his money where his mouth is,” Lipton said, “you can leave it to the reader to make the moral judgment.”
Gates’ Climate Awakening
Gates didn’t respond to repeated requests to discuss his landfill investments, and ProPublica couldn’t find any public comments he’s made about them. But the bet has proven wildly lucrative. Since November 1999, when he emerged as the owner of 5% of Republic’s shares — “It’s ‘Garbage In’ for Gates,” the New York Post headline read — the company’s stock price has soared thirtyfold. And Gates has personally received $2.6 billion in dividends, a ProPublica analysis of securities filings shows.
In those early days, Gates hadn’t yet awakened to the threat of global warming. It was a different time. Microsoft Windows ran on more than 80% of personal computers. Gates was the world’s richest person, and his bespectacled face graced the cover of Time magazine twice that year. He was simultaneously criticized for what a federal judge determined to be Microsoft’s monopolistic practices and admired for establishing what was soon to become the world’s largest charitable foundation.
A rare clue to why Gates made his foray into landfills can be found in an interview he gave to Fortune that year. To fund his plan to give away virtually his entire fortune, he said he’d given his personal money manager, Michael Larson, a simple remit: Sell Microsoft shares, buy safe, boring assets.
Republic’s then-chairman, billionaire Wayne Huizenga, had flown Larson by helicopter to his private golf course in Florida, according to the article. It’s unclear if Huizenga pitched Republic there, but it fit the remit. America would always produce trash, ensuring a steady stream of revenue. After that initial investment, Larson progressively increased Gates’ stake in Republic over the years that followed. Larson would also acquire a small chunk of Republic’s main competitor, Waste Management — which Huizenga also once led — on behalf of the Gates Foundation.
It was only in 2006, when he asked two climate scientists to educate him, that Gates started to grasp the potentially “catastrophic” effects of greenhouse gases, he later wrote. But he also saw that the poorest people in the world needed more energy to improve their lot. The solution, he concluded, was something climate activists often underplay: innovation that could make clean energy cheap enough to naturally displace fossil fuels. That was the idea behind Breakthrough Energy, the initiative he launched in Paris in 2015.
Around the same time, methane began to emerge as a focus of climate action. The gas can trap 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide in the near term, and it’s responsible for one-third of the global warming we experience today, according to the United Nations Environment Programme. But it also breaks down much more quickly, turning into CO2 and water vapor in about a decade — which means that cutting methane emissions now would reduce that warming within our lifetimes. This is especially urgent, scientists say, as the climate approaches tipping points that could doom rainforests, coral reefs and ice sheets.
In speeches and interviews, Gates has sometimes warned about methane, but usually from agricultural sources (“cow farts,” in his words). He has rarely mentioned landfills, even after Larson — who still runs Gates’ investment office, Cascade Asset Management — joined Republic’s board in 2009. Gates’ stake in the company, though, was a relatively small portion of his own net worth until fairly recently. And as Larson put it to Fortune, “I’ll call Bill about something I’m buying if he needs to know, but Bill might not have any idea what Cascade owns.” (Gates’ Republic holdings are publicly disclosed in securities filings.)
Elsewhere in Gatesworld, people started to home in on the climate threat posed by landfills. The root of the issue is that landfills store buried trash — and when organic waste decomposes underground, in the absence of oxygen, it generates methane. The Gates Foundation has funded research and advocacy aimed at solving that problem, and Breakthrough has backed at least two early-stage companies developing their own solutions. One, Windfall Bio, uses microbes to digest methane into fertilizer. Its product was actually tested last year at a Republic landfill in California, where the pink liquid was sprinkled on the soil covering the top layer of trash.
Windfall said the test worked, substantially reducing emissions, but the startup reportedly ceased operations after a Department of Energy grant was canceled. (Windfall didn’t respond to emailed requests for comment.)
On the surface, Republic has pursued a path consistent with Gates’ mission. In 2019, it became the first U.S. landfill operator to sign up for the Science Based Targets Initiative, promising to cut its emissions by 35% by 2030. Not that this was charity. Republic’s “climate leadership” became part of its pitch for garbage-collection contracts in progressive cities and counties. The company also won placements on stock indexes for businesses that meet certain environmental, social and governance criteria, attracting sustainability-minded investors.
Still, a fundamental tension remained — one at the heart of Gates’ vision. As Republic’s then-CEO Donald Slager put it on a 2017 call with investors, “You can’t have sustainability without profitability.”
A Not-So-Model Landfill
Each day, Americans throw away melon rinds, salmon skins and half-eaten drumsticks, paper towels, cheese that was too funky and eggs a day past their sell-by date. They discard greasy pizza boxes with crusts still rattling around inside and unthinkable amounts of leftover Chinese takeout. Not to mention the occasional dead pet.
Most of that trash — 240 million tons a year, enough to bury Manhattan under 100 feet of refuse — is hauled to one of the country’s 1,400 active landfills, where hulking vehicles with spiked wheels crush it into thin layers. At the end of each day, bulldozers typically spread soil on top, and for almost everyone who produced that trash, it will forever remain out of sight and out of mind.
People who live near landfills, though, describe smelling rotten cabbage, rotten eggs and rotten fish, as well as ammonia and skunk. Or as a neighbor to one Republic landfill put it: “I started smelling this stench like burning diapers. … It was foul.” Some describe burning throats, burning eyes, headaches and nausea. And while methane itself has no scent, those odors indicate that the gas is being released, studies show.
Still, modern landfills are an undeniable improvement over what came before. Open dumping and burning remained widespread until the 1970s. It was only in the ’90s that federal regulators started requiring operators to collect leachate (garbage juice, which can contaminate groundwater) and, at larger facilities, landfill gas (which is typically about half methane and half carbon dioxide but can also contain carcinogens like benzene).
Industry experts often compare landfills to living, breathing creatures. Underground trash inevitably shifts and settles, making it difficult to keep that gas from escaping. Managing such a beast is costly, which helps to explain why smaller operations have increasingly given way to corporations like Republic, which can turn a profit through economies of scale.
Republic declined to make executives available for interviews or to allow ProPublica to visit a landfill. But in May 2022 — around the same time Gates was lobbying for the passage of President Joe Biden’s historic climate bill — the company invited the Houston Chronicle to its local McCarty Road Landfill. Opened a half century earlier, the facility had passed through two corporate owners before being swallowed up by Republic, and now it was the site of a very Gatesian kind of project.
On the day of the visit, gulls circled hungrily as workers in neon vests gave a tour of the gas-collection system. Like at most other large landfills in the country, wells had been drilled deep into the trash below — five hundred of them in total. The top of each well sprouted from the grassy slopes in the form of a stubby black pipe fitted with a valve for adjusting the flow of underground gas. The workers also showed off large, bright blue, snail-shaped “blowers” — machines that suck that gas into a network of pipelines, then push it to the clanking, humming on-site plant that turns it into a salable product.
Most landfills that are required to collect gas simply burn it off. But they can also process it into “renewable natural gas,” which is functionally equivalent to the version pumped by oil companies. In part because this reuses the carbon from decomposing waste, it’s generally considered more climate-friendly. It also turns an environmental liability into a source of revenue — exactly the kind of win-win that Gates has long championed.
Yet the technology is no guarantee that the climate is being protected. In fact, it may be just the opposite.
In September 2024, the Environmental Protection Agency issued an “enforcement alert” saying that landfills across the country were “violating monitoring and maintenance requirements.” While the EPA didn’t name the operators, ProPublica obtained the corresponding spreadsheet through a public records request, and a fifth of the facilities targeted belong to Republic.
McCarty, far from being a model landfill, was among the worst offenders. It would soon earn Republic a formal “finding of violation” for allegedly failing to detect “exceedances” — methane escaping at levels above federal limits — for years on end. The EPA also noted repeated failures to address flooded wells, gullies formed by erosion and trash peeking through the surface of the landfill. Despite Republic’s economic incentive to capture methane, EPA inspectors found evidence of “poor maintenance” and “careless operation” of the gas-collection system as well.
And McCarty is hardly an outlier. Recent studies suggest that landfills with renewable natural gas facilities can actually emit more methane than those that only burn off the gas or use it to generate electricity. One possible explanation is that methane concentrations can vary across different parts of a landfill. According to researchers at Carbon Mapper, a NASA partner that measures emissions from various industries, some operators may prioritize collecting gas with higher methane content, which is cheaper to process — allowing more of the remaining methane to leak out.
Republic spokesperson Rob Litt declined to comment on whether that happened at McCarty, but said in a statement, “We employ hundreds of environmental managers and engineers. … If issues are identified, we work to resolve them.”
“Protecting the environment is part of Republic Services’ business,” he added.
The issues aren’t exclusive to landfills with natural gas facilities. Since 2020, EPA inspectors have used handheld methane detectors to sweep at least 39 of Republic’s roughly 200 landfills, according to inspection reports obtained by ProPublica. Including the issues at McCarty, they documented more than 1,400 problem spots — ranging from animal burrows to choked-off wells — spewing excessive amounts of methane.
In some cases, methane could be seen bubbling up through dark, fetid leachate pools. In others, so much methane was being released — with concentrations between 100 and 300 times the federal limit — that it was an explosion hazard.
Methane Bubbles at a Republic Services Landfill
What the Satellites Saw
Around the time of the Houston Chronicle visit, Republic’s CEO, a former McKinsey consultant named Jon Vander Ark, was promoting a new slogan: “Sustainability in action.” Meanwhile, though, Republic was quietly shying away from true climate leadership.
In 2021, two years after Republic signed on to the Science Based Targets Initiative, the SBTI made its minimum climate goal much more ambitious. Waste Management (where the Gates Foundation owns a small minority of the shares) would soon adopt it.
This was just months after Gates published “How to Avoid a Climate Disaster,” in which he exhorted private companies “to embrace the harder steps” toward solving global warming. Republic staff calculated that the new SBTI target could require more than $1 billion in additional spending on gas wells and other improvements, according to a former employee. Though that is less than half of what Republic has spent on dividends for Gates alone, it would leave less money for the company to redistribute to him and other shareholders. Republic has also spent more than $8 billion buying its own stock in the open market, ProPublica’s analysis shows, likely boosting the value of shares held by investors.
The matter was finally presented to the board around the second half of 2024, this person said. By then the board included Larson, Gates’ longtime investment manager — whose “insight into sustainability issues” is cited in company filings — and three other people with business ties to Gates (one has since left). While that is only four board members among a total of 13, Gates’ dominant shareholding means that, “as a practical matter, on any matter that gets voted on, he will almost certainly control the outcome,” said Lipton, the corporate-governance expert.
Republic never made the leap, and now it walks an awkward line. It continues to tout its affiliation with the SBTI while saying, in a note buried deep in one of its many sustainability reports, that the more ambitious target is “not an immediate strategic priority.”
Per SBTI rules, Republic has until the end of this year to submit an updated target. But when ProPublica asked if it would, the spokesperson said only, “We are reviewing our goals.” He declined to comment on the estimated cost or the board discussions.
There is, though, an even larger issue with Republic’s climate claims.
In line with its existing SBTI goal, Republic says it has already cut its landfill emissions by 20% since 2017. But that figure isn’t based on actual measurements of methane escaping from its facilities. According to the method cited in its sustainability reports, Republic instead typically measures the methane collected by its wells. Then it extrapolates how much it’s failing to collect — and how much is being emitted — based on the characteristics of each facility.
This method is based on an industry study that, as the EPA has noted, excluded data from gas-collection systems that were “not working well.” The EPA’s own reporting rules allow the same basic approach, which can cause companies collecting less gas due to a “malfunction or inefficiency” to “erroneously report decreasing emissions,” according to a 2025 study using satellite data by researchers at Harvard, NASA and Carbon Mapper. The researchers specifically examined two Republic landfills, and at one of them, the company reported declining emissions to the EPA even though satellite measurements showed they had risen over a four-year period.
The reporting gaps can be enormous. A study led by Hannah Nesser, now at Georgetown, found Republic facilities to be the No. 1 and No. 2 emitters among the roughly 70 large U.S. landfills the researchers observed over the course of 2019. The first, the National Serv-All Landfill in Indiana, was found to be releasing an astounding 13 times as much methane as what the company reported to the EPA. And that pattern repeated to varying degrees across three-quarters of the Republic landfills in the study. (McCarty wasn’t in the study, but according to measurements by Carbon Mapper, it emits more than twice what the company has reported.)
In response to questions about these studies, the Republic spokesperson said, “We stand by the sustainability results we’ve achieved.”
He also pointed to a letter from the National Waste and Recycling Association, a major trade group, questioning the accuracy of satellite measurements. It is a tactic from the playbook of another major climate polluter, the oil and gas industry, said Katherine Blauvelt of Full Circle Future, which advocates for cleaning up landfills.
“Satellites, peer-reviewed research studies and EPA inspectors on the ground all keep finding the same thing: unchecked and underreported methane emissions,” she said. “There’s a fire alarm going off and instead of getting out the extinguisher, the waste industry is blaming the smoke detector.”
Quietly Fighting Climate Policies
Last year, Gates published a blog post criticizing the “doomsday view” of global warming — a striking shift for someone who’d once warned of the failing ecosystems, mass migration and soaring mortality that could result from hotter temperatures. That led climate skeptics, including President Donald Trump, to say that Gates had admitted he was wrong. But Gates called that a “gigantic misreading.” While he believed more lives could be saved by improving global health, where he’d decided to shift his resources, he remained a “climate activist,” he told one audience.
Gates has tried to lead by example. In 2019, he sold his shares in oil and gas companies because, he later wrote, “I don’t want to profit if their stock prices go up because we don’t develop zero-carbon alternatives.” He kept flying by private jet, but he “offset” those emissions by buying credits from a company that removes carbon from the air. He has also called on other business leaders to “make sure that they’re not holding back” climate policies, even if those policies could cut into profits.
Republic has actively worked against such policies — and yet Gates, according to securities filings, has never sold a share.
In the final year of the Biden administration, the EPA announced a plan to update its landfill gas rules, which have changed little since the ’90s. Among other potential changes, the agency asked for comments on the newer technologies, such as satellites and drones, that research has found to be effective in monitoring and controlling methane pollution.
Some landfill operators were already experimenting with these innovations. But they wanted almost all of it to remain voluntary, according to a joint statement from the National Waste and Recycling Association and the Solid Waste Association of North America, both of which have Republic executives on their boards.
“We do not believe that any of these technologies are sufficiently developed,” the industry groups said, adding that the various innovations were “not cost-effective,” “reliable” or “transparent.”
The Republic spokesperson declined to comment on whether that lobbying goes against its climate commitments.
“A lot of the issue comes down to the profit of the corporate landfill operators and their resistance to do things that will eat into that,” said Darin Schroeder of the Clean Air Task Force, a climate advocacy group.
Gates’ press representatives didn’t respond to questions about whether he’s aware of the issues at Republic — or whether he has independently investigated the source of a fifth of his fortune. But ProPublica interviewed multiple former employees at Breakthrough Energy, Gates’ clean-tech investment arm, who all spoke on condition of anonymity. They each said they hadn’t even heard about his landfill holdings.
“I agree there’s a bit of a conundrum there,” said one high-ranking staffer who was laid off last year. But this person added, “Based on my time with him, I think he’s very serious about climate change. This isn’t a vanity thing for him.”
“My theory is that he probably doesn’t have much involvement in those investments,” said another laid-off staffer.
Gates’ investment managers, at least, can’t claim total ignorance. Larson and Thomas Handley, a Cascade senior adviser, both participate actively in Republic’s board discussions, according to a fellow director who spoke on the condition of anonymity to share details of those private discussions. The board also receives regular management briefings, including “high level” reports on the company’s lobbying and litigation over “practices we could do better,” this director said. (Larson didn’t return phone messages left by ProPublica at his office, and Cascade didn’t respond to a question about his and Handley’s involvement in Republic.)
It’s unclear if Gates himself ever learned of those reports. But he appears to have an even larger blind spot on the issue. The waste industry doesn’t fit neatly into his view of climate change as a problem to be solved mainly through technological breakthroughs. Innovations can help, but the root of the problem is the inescapable fact that, when organic waste decomposes in the absence of oxygen, methane is produced.
Properly managing the waste we’ve already buried is only the first step, said Riley Duren, the former NASA engineer who founded Carbon Mapper. “In parallel,” he said, “reduce food waste. Full stop. Then divert organic waste away from landfills to prevent future emissions.”
This isn’t a utopian fantasy. Germany started phasing out the landfilling of biodegradable waste in 1993, and its landfill methane emissions have plunged by more than 90%. (That compares to a decline of 40% in the U.S. over roughly the same period.) Within the U.S., California now requires food scraps and yard trimmings to be collected for composting or other uses, and state regulators found that the economic, climate and health benefits would ultimately outweigh the costs.
In its glossy sustainability reports, Republic says that “organics recycling plays an important role in our operations.” And in California, with its mandatory collection rules, the company processed close to a million tons of organic waste last year, much of that at composting facilities.
But that remains a small fraction of its business. Speaking to a different kind of audience — investors — Republic has described landfilling, along with dumpster collection, as its most profitable segments. So when the EPA floated a federal organics-diversion policy in 2024, the company, along with the rest of the landfill industry, opposed this, too. Their response invoked an argument often used by opponents to regulation: It should be left to the states to decide.
“It’s like you’ve got a mousetrap, and it catches mice,” said Robert Bullard, a Texas Southern University professor widely seen as the father of the environmental justice movement. “You’ve got a landfill, and it makes money — big money. So why tinker with it?”
