He was a billionaire politician who is maybe not so politically relevant; she was his girlfriend of 26 years, a financial executive, whatever that means. Can we make it any more obvious? 
That's right: Former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg and his longtime partner Diana Taylor finally tied the knot on Monday after more than a quarter century together. And what a quarter century it's been! 
"Twenty-six years after a chance seating assignment, Mike Bloomberg and Diana Taylor have married," a spokesperson for Bloomberg posted on the ex-mayor's X account. "The longtime couple exchanged vows today in a small, private ceremony at their home on the Upper East Side, joined by family, including his daughters, Emma and Georgina. The two first crossed paths when they sat next to each other at a Citizens Budget Commission meeting while he was first running for Mayor."
Extremely romantic origin story aside (we always thought it was strange that the Citizens Budget Commission only meets by candlelight at that cute hole-in-the-wall Italian spot down the block), Bloomberg and Taylor have been through a lot together over the last two and a half decades.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Bringing Billionaires to Account at the Ballot Box
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: David Futrelle
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Bringing Billionaires to Account at the Ballot Box
Last week’s midterms were a powerful repudiation of MAGA, but the fight against oligarchy will be a longer struggle.
The midterms were more than just a victory for Democrats—they were also a critical blow for democracy, as well as a powerful repudiation of President Donald Trump’s crass authoritarianism and of the Republicans who have enabled his worst impulses. But if we want to enable our still-fragile democracy to thrive again, we need not only to purge it of the baleful influence of MAGA but also to confront directly another dire, and continuing, threat to self-rule: that of the billionaires who are increasingly using their wealth and power to try to override the will of the people. In some cases, our moneyed oligarchy quietly (or not so quietly) bankrolls the worst among the Republicans; in others, it puts considerable rightward pressure on the Democrats it supports.
Do we the people have a chance against billionaire money? We just might, as two case studies from the midterms make clear: James Talarico’s successful Senate candidacy in Texas, and the failed campaign for a billionaire wealth tax in California.
On the surface, the two campaigns seem to offer radically different lessons. In Texas, Talarico was able to overcome some $200 million in spending from Elon Musk and deliver a decisive victory, one that Talarico touted as proof “that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas.”
But it was more than simply people power that enabled Talarico to win; he also responded to Musk’s intervention in the race with a certain shrewdness, ultimately recognizing that in many ways Musk and his money were more formidable opponents than the corrupt and uncharismatic Ken Paxton. (Even Trump, Paxton’s key political supporter, jokingly referred to him as a “pain in the ass” who didn’t know how to dress, or talk, properly.) Given that Talarico was essentially running against a tag team of Paxton and Musk, he made the world’s richest man one of his primary foils in the campaign—thereby turning the millions that Musk directed into the coffers of the Paxton campaign into a political liability. “In all likelihood, if you’ve seen an attack ad on your TV, that was Elon,” Talarico said on the campaign trail. “If you’ve gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon. If you’ve received a text message saying scary things about me, that was Elon, too.” Musk, Talarico said, clearly “wants his very own personal United States senator,” one who would do Musk’s bidding in the state where he lives in exchange for purchasing his office.
All in all, Musk spent close to half a billion dollars in the midterms and got close to zero return. Six of his seven Senate picks went down in defeat (with one race still too close to call), and only a small handful of the 43 House candidates he supported prevailed. But it was the Texas race that marked his most significant defeat. Talarico, not surprisingly, sees his victory as a major blow in the battle against billionaires in politics. “We’ve just sent a message to every millionaire mega donor, to every trillionaire mega donor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system,” he declared in his victory speech.
In California, the lesson seemed to be of a rather different sort. The backers of Proposition 40—the voter initiative to ratify a billionaire wealth tax—were unable to fend off a “no” campaign backed by billionaire money. One top staffer of the SEIU–United Healthcare Workers West, the union behind the ballot initiative, blamed the campaign’s likely defeat on “billionaire-funded propaganda” that misled voters.
There was indeed a torrent of such propaganda coursing through California’s airwaves. After the billionaire tax was first put forward by Dave Regan of the SEIU-UHW, a number of the state’s wealthiest residents began strategizing how to defeat it in a secret Signal group chat. Google cofounder Sergey Brin, worth a cool $219 billion even after the dip in Big Tech stock values last week, led the charge, cofounding an innocuously named group called Building a Better California. Brin’s outfit quickly amassed a $333 million war chest, plumped up considerably by a $102 million donation from Brin himself. The group quickly realized that its biggest backers could ill afford becoming the face of the campaign; its own polling showed that “billionaires are seen as having a net negative impact across issues,” as internal documents seen by The New York Times put it. (Ya think?) And so their “billionaire-funded propaganda” starred not Brin himself but an assortment of non-billionaire opponents of the measure, Anti-Prop 40 ads thus featured doctors, carpenters, firefighters, and teachers, and even the Democratic governor of California, Gavin Newsom.
As the casting decisions for these ads suggest, the story of Prop 40’s defeat was far more complicated than a simple blame-the-billionaires narrative would suggest. Regan is a divisive figure, to put it mildly—a publicity-hungry activist who’s considered something of an asshole not only by tech billionaires but also by some Democratic politicians; he has also, more significantly, been credibly accused of bullying and worse by union officials. He pushed the referendum largely on his own, without first making much of an attempt to build a coalition. He also sidestepped (some would say stepped on) an already existing campaign by the California Teachers Association (CTA) for another ballot proposition calling to make permanent an increased income tax on the wealthy (happily, despite all the confusion, this measure has passed). Prop 40 would have directed almost all of the proceeds of the wealth tax toward healthcare—a provision that alienated some union leaders who felt that at least some of the money should have gone to support their members as well. As a result, several leading unions, including CTA and the State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, came out against the tax.
In the end, the SEIU-UHW spent most of the $34 million it raised on gathering signatures, according to The New York Times, leaving only a small fraction of money on hand to counter the massive ad spending from Brin’s group. That enabled the “no” voices to define the terms of the debate. Weirdly, the union spent some of its paltry ad money on perplexing campaigns directed at Planned Parenthood, which had come out against the bill, and Newsom himself. (The anti-Newsom message was featured in ads that didn’t even run in California.) Why they went this way instead of pulling a Talarico and going directly after Brin I don’t know. When you’re fighting billionaires, you need to fight billionaires—not just in general but with great specificity, by name.
It didn’t help that Regan was not himself the best face for the Prop 40 campaign. The controversial and often volatile activist has long had a reputation as a bully. The issue came to a head in September when the press got hold of two investigative reports on his behavior sponsored by SEIU’s national union and its California council that substantiated accusations of threats and bullying of union officials by Regan—and a 2009 physical assault on a woman who was then SEIU California’s executive director. One of the reports concluded that Regan has a “propensity for bullying women and women of color.” (Regan dismisses the allegations as “politically motivated,” ginned up by opponents of Prop 40. A union hearing is set for December.)
And then in the final week of the campaign, as a sort of dysfunctional cherry on top, some 230 of SEIU-UHW’s own staffers went on strike, saying that the union wasn’t negotiating with them in good faith over a raise, derailing the union’s attempts to seal the deal with voters.
In the end, Prop 40 was defeated by more than all this internal dysfunction and a well-funded pro-billionaire agitprop offensive. Voters also appear likely to have passed a poison-pill measure bankrolled by the billionaire’s coalition, Prop 42, that bars future wealth taxes in California. Prop 42’s passage would leave proponents of a California wealth tax in worse shape than if the initiative had never been put forward in the first place. “What a waste of resources and what a squandering of an opportunity,” one prominent supporter of Prop 40 told Politico. “There was no coalition, they pissed off everyone, and so many of those natural allies that would’ve supported it refused.” Billionaires, in California and elsewhere, emerged from the fight not only with their wealth intact but feeling empowered. The apparent lesson for them was that they can win any future battles over wealth taxes by simply sacrificing a small sliver of that wealth to political donations.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
But the ongoing struggle to contain the damage wrought by the superrich is hardly as hopeless as Prop 40’s defeat might make it seem. Talarico’s win shows that even the world’s richest man can lose to a charismatic politician who knows how to mobilize the disgust most Americans feel toward the excessive power of money in politics. In Talarico’s case, it certainly didn’t hurt that Musk himself is an odious, cringey edgelord who has almost completely squandered whatever goodwill he once had as a supposed tech wunderkind; his favorability rating, as measured by recent polls, is in the 30s, right alongside Donald Trump’s. But the thing is, most Americans seem to have grown profoundly tired of our billionaire class as a whole; they’re not just sick of Musk. If you start looking at our other billionaires, particularly of the tech variety, you’ll find that some are as widely despised as Musk, if not more so. According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll from last year, Amazon’s bald, newly buff Jeff Bezos had a 29 percent favorability rating; Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg garnered a pathetic 26 percent.
In other words, the people, if not the billionaires, are on our side here. According to the most recent Harris Poll Americans and Billionaires survey, more than half of all Americans think billionaires are a threat to democracy. And they want something done about it: 69 percent say the ultra-wealthy should have less influence in politics, 71 percent think wealth taxes should be imposed on the rich and 53 percent that there should be actual caps on wealth. They’re right on all counts, of course. We just need to do a better job of convincing them to vote as if these opinions matter.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/ariz.title: Arizona Town’s Probe on Sex Abuse Claims Could Block Prison Firm Building New ICE Camp
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/ariz.author: John Washington
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/ariz.text:
This story was published in partnership with LOOKOUT News.
An official from Marana, Arizona, is seeking clarification from the private prison giant Management and Training Corporation about its handling of sexual abuse allegations at the former state prison in the town, following an investigation from LOOKOUT and The Intercept.
In an October 28 letter, reviewed by LOOKOUT and The Intercept, Marana Finance Director and License Inspector Yiannis Kalaitzidis asked MTC Senior Vice President Mary Calvin for a written explanation of what the town official called an “apparent inconsistency” between state records and the facility’s 2023 Prison Rape Elimination Act, or PREA, audit, a report required by the federal law.
The request is part of the town’s review of MTC’s October 1 application for a business license to “Operate Marana Detention Facility.” The company ran a former Arizona state prison in Marana and plans to reopen it imminently as a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention camp.
The letter cites a September 29 LOOKOUT and Intercept investigation about how state records reference three allegations of sexual misconduct at the prison in 2022 and 2023.
PREA audits — which are required for jails, prisons, and detention centers at least once every three years — must record all allegations of sexual misconduct at detention facilities, whether they are substantiated or not. Certified in December 2023, MTC’s report for the Marana prison, however, recorded none.
Kalaitzidis noted in his letter that the audit says the finding of zero incidents was verified by the warden, chief of security, PREA compliance manager, and internal investigator. He also wrote that, despite the apparent reviews by several company officials, the report “does not appear to be certified or signed by any MTC personnel.”
The letter says the town of Marana is requesting the explanation as part of an investigation into whether MTC “made a material false statement in conducting the business” of the state prison facility, which would be grounds for denial of a business license according to the town’s code.
“The Town of Marana is currently reviewing MTC’s business license application,” said Andrea De La Cruz, the assistant town manager, told LOOKOUT and The Intercept by email. “As part of our review process and due diligence, the Town has contacted MTC to request additional information. The application remains under review, and no final determination has been made at this time.”
MTC did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Changing Political Context
Local residents and officials say the state, the federal government, and MTC left them out of meaningful discussions about reopening the prison as an ICE camp, LOOKOUT and The Intercept previously reported.
For now, a town business license is among the few levers local officials have.
In an October 2 letter from the local group Pima Resists ICE, or PRICE, to a Marana official who specialized in licensure, organizers cited not only the discrepancies between state investigations into sexual abuse and the PREA audit, but also alleged violations involving an escape from an MTC prison in Kingman, Arizona, in 2010, as well as abuses in a New Mexico immigration camp run by MTC as revealed in a 2017 DHS Office of Inspector General report.
The inquiry comes as Arizona’s political landscape is shifting. The midterm election gave Democrats control of both chambers of the state legislature as well as the governor’s office — a historic change in state power. Republicans will be in the minority at the state Capitol for the first time in 60 years.
That has Democratic lawmakers talking about taking on one of the most contentious laws in recent Arizona history. Following protests across the state, Democrats took up the cause of repealing a controversial 2010 anti-immigrant law known as Senate Bill 1070. In 2012, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down three of its provisions, leaving a requirement that police check the immigration status of people they stop under certain circumstances.
“I would absolutely love to see a repeal of SB1070,” state Sen. Analise Ortiz, a Democrat from Glendale, told LOOKOUT and The Intercept. “There are still parts of that law on the books that are enabling cities to collaborate with ICE to rip families apart, and that needs to stop.”
State Rep. Betty Villegas, D-Tucson, echoed Ortiz: “We already have bills aligned to focus on what other states have done to control ICE from coming into private property.”
Following the lead of neighboring New Mexico’s prohibition on local jurisdictions entering into contracts with ICE for immigrant detention camps, Villegas said Democrats in Arizona see an appetite for doing something similar in their own state.
Ortiz agreed, saying there is “likely an appetite” for something similar in Arizona, and that the Latino Caucus would address the issue.
Local nonprofits said lawmakers should also conduct a review of no-bid contracts like the one inked between the Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, and MTC.
“This was literally handed to them with no review and no public input,” said Caroline Isaacs, the executive director of Just Communities Arizona, a nonprofit working on criminal justice reform. “We do not want the Democrats to wait until things get bad to investigate conditions.”
“We want them to do this now, before people get hurt.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/vance-maga-t.title: Trump’s Midterm Rout Didn’t End the Threat From J. D. Vance
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/vance-maga-t.author: Gilbert Achcar
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/vance-maga-t.text:
Trump’s Midterm Rout Didn’t End the Threat From J. D. Vance
President Trump’s midterm debacle has weakened the entire MAGA camp. But J. D. Vance, a more disciplined and more ideological far-right figure, is already positioning himself to inherit the movement in 2028.
Donald Trump may have foreseen another reversal of his political fortunes when he chose J. D. Vance as his running mate. For who would want to remove Trump if the result were Vance at the helm of US executive? After all, Trump is the ultimate opportunist, a man who can smile and shake hands with Zohran Mamdani while hurling outrageous anti-socialist and Islamophobic slanders at him; a man who can pose as a dove while acting as a hawk, and who is so obsessed with his own ego that he is ultimately his own most effective enemy — as he proved brilliantly in bringing about the Republicans’ midterms debacle. Vance, on the other hand, is a consummate far-right ideologist. True, he does not lack opportunism either. As Compact magazine’s editor Matthew Schmitz recently reminded readers in a New York Times op-ed: “He made his way from the Rust Belt to Yale Law, and from saying Mr. Trump might be ‘America’s Hitler’ to serving as his vice president.”
Yet this is closer to the cold-blooded careerism so common on the far right than to Trump’s crude, crowd-pleasing demagogy. Moreover, as The Washington Post’s George F. Will, a traditional conservative and longtime Trump critic, put it: “Trump’s deepening weirdness (e.g., repeatedly proclaiming his admiration for various men’s and women’s body parts) suggests he is residing in the suburbs of dotage. Vance has no such excuse.” Unlike Trump, Vance harbors intellectual pretensions and has been cultivating his own wing of the MAGA movement with close, personal ties to other far-right ideologues such as Steve Bannon and Tucker Carlson. In that sense, he would be an even more dangerous president than Trump. However, the resounding rebuke Trump suffered in the recent elections has also damaged his entire camp, including the ideological far right that Vance represents. Schmitz concludes: “Perhaps he can complete another unlikely journey, to the presidency. But he now seems farther from that office than he did just one week ago.” That is fair enough, but no one should assume that the vice president too has become a lame duck.
Vance’s Post-Mortem
Vance was visibly stunned by the scale of the electorate’s repudiation of Trump — which is also a repudiation of the MAGA craze by a clear majority of voters. Like a rat fleeing a sinking ship, the vice president hurried to disclaim responsibility for the debacle and distance himself from the president. His reaction is revealing, for it indicates what his ideological campaign will center on in the next two years, as he plainly seeks to become the next MAGA presidential candidate. On the afternoon of November 4, once the Republican rout was largely confirmed, he posted his break with Trump on X. Citing an unnamed pollster, “one of the smartest people I know in politics,” he listed what he described as the four main issues behind the rout — and, by implication, his four priorities for the next two years: “1) End the war; 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation; 3) Put America First; 4) Change our relationship to Israel.”
Let us consider these four points and what they leave unsaid. Trump’s war on Iran has obviously not gone down well with the US public. Not only did it flatly contradict the pacifist-sounding promises of Trump during his presidential campaigns — promises that, to be sure, reflected no real love of peace, only an appeal to the old far-right isolationist legacy long embodied by Pat Buchanan. More importantly, while Trump assumed that the US public would barely feel the consequences of the war, it came home to roost in the form of an inflationary surge fueled by gas prices. Yet the war accounts for only part of this surge, which — under the name of “affordability” — loomed far larger than war itself in the campaign. Hence, Vance’s second point on the cost of living. But he keeps mum about the squeeze’s root causes, above all Trump’s outrageously pro-rich budget and his ultranationalistic, wildly erratic tariffs. Vance would not say a word about these for the very good reason that he fully endorsed them, unlike the war on Iran, from which he tried, albeit timidly, to distance himself.
The Same Old Scapegoats
Then comes the old far-right refrain of “America First,” dear to Trump and the MAGA crowd. This hollow slogan serves only to stoke the basest ultranationalist sentiments among mostly poor white social layers that tend to interpret their economic hardship in a highly skewed, xenophobic, often racist way. It is a slogan whose clearest translation is Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). And one that obscures all the real problems that the US working class is facing, offering tariff fetishism as a universal panacea instead. For the section of the far right to which Vance belongs, and which he hopes to lead, this jingoism has typically gone hand in hand with antisemitism. It is their way of perverting the massive — and entirely legitimate — rise in popular antipathy toward Israel caused by the appalling genocidal war it has waged in Gaza with full US support, from Joe Biden to Trump: diverting it into a “blame it on Israel” stratagem. The aim is, of course, to deflect attention from the reality of US imperialism, including, in this case, the deeply corrupt interests of the Trump syndicate and its cronies, by resorting to the oldest of far-right scapegoating tricks.
As for Vance’s fourth point, his phrasing — “Change our relationship to Israel” — is deliberately vague, a far cry from the increasingly popular and unambiguous calls to end all US military support for Israel. The key issue is certainly not the $3.8 billion that Washington grants Israel every year under a memorandum of understanding concluded by the Obama administration. In a classic case of US taxpayers’ money being funneled to the US military-industrial complex, these funds were earmarked for Israeli purchases of US weaponry. The mercenary logic governing Trump’s foreign policy — which, by gutting the United States Agency for International Development, has inflicted severe damage on several countries of the Global South — had already led him to cut off the much larger US funding of Ukraine’s purchases of US military hardware, forcing Kyiv’s European backers to foot the bill themselves. Now Israel will have to pay for its deadly US imports on its own — hardly a big deal for the Zionist state. Trump presented the move as agreed upon with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who confirmed it, even boasting of what he portrayed as a shift in Israel’s relationship with its US godfather from dependence into equal partnership.
Peter Thiel’s Godson
That said, the most glaring blind spot in Vance’s account of the rout is his total silence on one of the issues that decided the elections: Big Tech, AI, and data centers. “There’s no question about how voters feel about data centers after Election Day, with restrictive measures across 10 states going 43–1 at the ballot box. The margins weren’t close, with an average of 75% of people favoring restrictions,” wrote Maria Curi of Axios. “America turns on Donald Trump’s tech cheerleaders,” declared a Financial Times headline in the elections’ wake. Polls indicate that public resentment of what is perceived as a Big Tech mafia has become one of the main channels through which Americans register the immense social inequality of their society, far greater than in any other economically advanced country. On this, of course, Vance — the political godson of Peter Thiel, who, along with Elon Musk, is the farthest right of the Big Tech tycoons — would not utter a single word, even though some of his most populist MAGA allies, such as Steve Bannon, have joined the anti–Big Tech chorus, which fits neatly with the anti-elitist rhetoric characteristic of their brand of far-right ideology.
Vance is being built up as the standard-bearer of MAGA continuity. While many expected a reshuffle that would oust the ultramasculinist, hyperarrogant “Secretary of War” Pete Hegseth, one of the administration’s most unpopular liabilities, Trump instead promoted his éminence grise, Stephen Miller — a sinister far-right ideologue, rabidly antimigrant (Mr ICE par excellence) and Islamophobic — to the key post of White House chief of staff. Vance immediately hailed the promotion on X: “Stephen Miller is an amazing patriot and will do great things.” Backed by Thiel, Donald Trump Jr, and others of their ilk, Vance is already poising himself to lead the MAGA current into the 2028 presidential election. It is vital not to underestimate the threat he represents, and to make the fight against this chief embodiment of the US far right as one of the priorities of the coming period.
Vance might have once been thought of as “Trump lite.” But it’s abundantly clear now that, if he somehow made it to the White House, he could possibly be even worse that the godfather of MAGA himself.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Tate Britain spotlights Bloomsbury artists Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant for the first time since 1999
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Andrew Pulver
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Bloomsbury Group seems to have been ever-present in UK culture since its inception in the early 20th century, just before the First World War. Lytton Strachey, John Maynard Keynes, Virginia Woolf, E.M. Forster, Vanessa Bell, Duncan Grant—their names are legion as representatives of a flowering of British intellectualism across the full spectrum of literary and artistic endeavours. While Roger Fry was arguably Bloomsbury’s most influential art-world voice, as the critic who essentially introduced European Post-Impressionism to Britain with a celebrated exhibition at the Grafton Galleries in 1910, Bell and Grant were the group’s most active and high-profile painters. The pair’s bracketing together for a new Tate Britain exhibition is also a result, no doubt, of their 40-year open relationship that saw them live and paint together—and each other—over many decades.
The Bloomsbury Group has largely retained its high profile over the decades, with feature films on many of its protagonists and even a BBC mini-series in 2015 called Life in Squares, named for the supposed Dorothy Parker gag that the group “lived in squares, painted in circles and loved in triangles”. Bell and Grant’s former home Charleston, near Lewes in East Sussex, has maintained a near-constant programme of exhibitions to keep the flame alive, the latest of which, Mad Bloomsbury (4 November-11 April 2027) examines the group’s engagement with mental health issues.
But the Tate show marks the first Bloomsbury-focused show at the national home for British art for over a quarter of a century. Thomas Kennedy, the curator of Modern British art at Tate Britain, thinks it is about time. “That means an entire generation of visitors have not seen an exhibition on Vanessa or Duncan’s work at Tate, and we felt that it was important for us to revisit their practices again after so long,” Kennedy says. “I don’t believe there’s ever been a major exhibition on Vanessa and Duncan together, and it’s so fascinating to see the ways they differ. We should recognise their individual accomplishments of course, but also the works they made together and how they influenced each other. We know about their relationship—she was married and he was gay—but this exhibition explores what that really meant in their artworks and in their life.”
Out of fashion
Looking back at that previous 1999 show, the cuttings files reveal that the turn of the millennium clearly marked a low point in critical opinion of the Bloomsbury artists; outright abuse might be the best description of some of the responses. The Guardian art critic Adrian Searle called them “a bit crap”, “lightweights” and “third rate”, while for the novelist Philip Hensher writing in The Independent, these “no-hopers” and their “rubbish” inspired simple “rage and loathing”.
But Kennedy is not having it. Bell and Grant, he says, “started experimenting with art in unique ways that hadn’t really been seen in Britain before”. He adds: “They created some of the first abstract works in Britain, which is sometimes very much overlooked. And they were creating these works together, and talking about art all day, every day, breaking the distinction between fine and decorative art with the Omega Workshops. What they were doing was really special.”
Bell, whose sister Virginia Woolf was even more celebrated in her field, is perhaps now the slightly more recognisable name of the two painters, though, as Kennedy points out, both Bell and Grant were considered leading figures during their lifetimes. Their close physical proximity, from when they moved to Charleston in 1918 to Bell’s death in 1961, meant their styles were often similarly adjacent, though Kennedy is clear on the differences. “Vanessa’s painting is more deliberate with very considered blocks of colour and very strong outlines, whereas Duncan’s is scratchier, more impulsive and it feels like he is experimenting more with more expressive techniques,” he says.
Kennedy adds: “However, later on, when they’re working on the Famous Women dinner service [a collection of 50 hand-painted plates], their styles are completely the same: the authorship has very much broken down and we can’t tell who did what. So much so that Roger Fry told them to paint in different studios to reassess their own way of making. It’s fascinating to see that push and pull between what they were taking from each other.”
In the end, it might be that the very thing that seemed to diminish the Bloomsbury Group for previous generations—their complex, near-incestuous love lives—is what is powering their current revival: to contemporary perspectives they now look like pioneers of unrepentantly queer lifestyles. Bell married fellow painter Clive Bell in 1907, then had a long relationship with Fry and had a daughter, Angelica, with Grant in 1918. Grant, for his part, had a string of male lovers while maintaining his domestic relationship with Bell. “They were looking towards non-monogamous relationships and accepting queer relationships. The latter, as you know, was illegal in the UK at the time,” Kennedy says. “Within the Bloomsbury Group they felt freedom—both artistically and the way they lived.”
• Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury, Tate Britain, London, 12 November-11 April 2027

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/kals.title: Kalshi Is Cozy With Trump — But It’s Ramping Up Dem Hires and Campaign Spending
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/kals.author: Matt Sledge
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/kals.text:
Since the start of the year, the prediction betting site Kalshi has two hired former officials from Joe Biden’s White House as a policy adviser and a top lobbyist.
The company’s co-founders have also spent nearly $1 million on donations to federal candidates, with more than a third, or $377,000, going to Democrats like Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., according to a new report.
Kalshi’s spending spree shows how much prediction market sites have ratcheted up their presence in Washington as regulators craft rules for the industry. While the sites’ close relationship with the Trump administration has drawn headlines, the report from the progressive group Demand Progress details how the industry’s influence operation crosses party lines.
The push for bipartisan relationships began months ago, but it could pay dividends as Democrats take over both chambers of a Congress, said Ella Fanger, the corporate power policy adviser for Demand Progress. A betting market critic, Fanger predicted that the companies will keep trying to win allies on both sides of the aisle.
“They’ve been hopeful that they can have Democratic champions for their policy agenda,” she said, “and not just have Trump’s cronies sticking out their necks for them.”
The hiring spree of former Biden officials and spending on Democratic candidates come as prediction markets are facing increasing scrutiny over betting on elections and a spate of suspicious trades from Washington about policy moves and even military action.
On Tuesday, Democrats on Capitol Hill called for Trump to bar White House staffers from using the betting sites and, with Democrats taking Congress, many observers expect investigations into their use in Washington.
In a statement, Kalshi said it was willing to work “across the ideological spectrum.”
“Kalshi has had substantive conversations with policymakers over the past year regarding legislation that protects consumers, keeps minors off our platform, makes insider trading bans standard across the industry, and ensures the CFTC” — the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — “has the resources they need,” said the company’s head of government relations, John Bivona, a former Democratic congressional staffer and Biden White House official.
“We’ve come out in support of legislation introduced by members across the ideological spectrum,” Bivona said, “and we’ve worked with dozens of lawmakers from both parties on these priorities.”
Hiring Republicans — and Dems
Kalshi and its rival Polymarket are the dominant players in the prediction market industry, which has flourished since Donald Trump became president thanks to his administration’s hands-off approach to regulation.
The ties between the prediction betting sites and Trumpworld go all the way to the president’s inner circle, as evidenced by Donald Trump Jr.’s financial stakes at both competitors.
Polymarket has also hired as a lobbyist a Republican former top official at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The federal regulatory body has, under the Trump administration, sued states for trying to regulate sports betting as gambling.
The Demand Progress report covers Trump Jr.’s ties to the industry, but it also shines a light on the role of former Democratic congressional and executive branch staffers.
Kalshi’s hires have tended toward establishment Democrats. Among them are Stephanie Cutter, a political strategist whose work spanned the Obama and Biden administrations as well as Kamala Harris’s campaign for president. Cutter was tapped as a policy adviser for Kalshi in April. Bivona was hired by Kalshi as its head of government relations in January.
Tripled Lobbying Spend
Overall, Kalshi has spent $1.8 million on lobbying in the first half of 2026, compared to $615,000 in all of 2025, according to the Demand Progress report.
Polymarket spent a relatively meager $180,000 during the same period this year, compared to $360,000 last year.
Fanger, whose group is critical of the prediction markets’ attempts to neutralize state sports gambling regulators, said she is worried that a pliant Congress could approve the Trump administration’s favorable regulations.
“The concern is basically just that we could get legislation that would codify the rulemaking that the CFTC has already begun,” she said, referring to the agency’s efforts to formally exercise jurisdiction over sports, political, cultural, and weather betting contracts. “And we think that it’s important for states to be able to regulate this industry as gambling, which is what it is.”
The industry may need all the lobbyists it can get if progressives gain power in the next Congress. Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., who is angling to chair the House Financial Services Committee, said in a letter last week that she wants to “rein in predatory lending and predatory platforms, including prediction markets, so that our constituents keep more of their hard-earned dollars in their pockets.”
Waters is also a longtime foil to the crypto industry. Crypto currency interests alienated Democrats by spending tens of millions of campaign dollars on Republican Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio, who lost his seat to Democrat Sherrod Brown in the midterm election.
While crypto has lavished money on campaign spending through a super PAC, the prediction market industry has opted for a quieter campaign of smaller donations routed through more traditional channels.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-wild-.title: Wild Horse Nine Skewers the Dangerous Fools Behind US Empire
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-wild-.author: Eileen Jones
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-wild-.text:
Wild Horse Nine Skewers the Dangerous Fools Behind US Empire
Wild Horse Nine is an irreverent portrait of the dopes who traffic in violence against democracy around the world, all in the service of US empire. But the connection between human callousness and evil has flown over the heads of some critics.
The climactic speech of Martin McDonagh’s dark comedy Wild Horse Nine is the “Kill ’em” monologue, delivered by an old Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) operative named Chris Carlisle (John Malkovich), who’s dying of cancer and whose mind is also starting to go. But after decades of habitual lying for professional reasons, he’s pledged to tell the truth to a Chilean college student and leftist organizer named Monica (Mariana di Girolamo) in what becomes an unlikely end-of-life friendship.
When Chris finally does tell her the truth as he knows it, after a life spent doing the worst, sickeningly violent, and incalculably harmful dirty work for US empire, it’s so terrible that it brings tears to her eyes. It’s about what you’d have to do to really achieve widespread democracy and human flourishing: eradicate those forces that are always going to support fascism, that will always be dedicated to upholding the power of dictatorial, money-grubbing, and colonizing monsters for all the typical reasons.
Chris includes himself in the roster of people who should be killed, or should’ve been, long before he could make this cold assessment of his own life’s work: “I’m a big shot at the CIA. A veteran of Guatemala 1954 — success. The Congo 1960 — success. The Bay of Pigs 1961 — less successful. Dallas 1963 . . . ”
It seems Chris played a key role in the John F. Kennedy assassination and is talking more and more freely about it, even including it in the memoir he’s dictating into a tape recorder. You may recall another CIA agent being evoked in Wild Horse Nine, also wonderfully played by Malkovich, who’s writing a memoir — or as Osborne Cox calls it in the Coen brothers’ comedy Burn After Reading (2008), a “mem-wah.” Malkovich has had a whole history of playing CIA agents experiencing various degrees of career turmoil and mental instability. He was the rogue assassin Booth, seeking to kill the current president in In the Line of Fire (1993) and tormenting Clint Eastwood’s aging Secret Service agent for failing to prevent the assassination of JFK.
In Wild Horse Nine, Chris has become such a loose cannon that his superior, MJ (Steve Buscemi), a CIA bureau chief overseeing South American operations, decides they can’t wait for Chris’s death by natural causes, no matter how imminent it might be.
The “kill ’em” speech alone is so powerful, though it’s delivered with such perfectly shocking casualness that it would probably get John Malkovich another Best Actor Oscar, except that his costar, Sam Rockwell, is equally fantastic as Chris’s only friend, the irascible longtime CIA protégé Lee Chesterfield. In all likelihood they’ll both be nominated and then split the Academy Award vote and lose.
They play old cronies in 1973 Santiago, Chile, who’ve just finished destabilizing the government of democratically elected President Salvador Allende, to the point that Chris can predict the exact time the coup d’etat by Augusto Pinochet’s military forces will occur, after which the roundup, torture, and murder of leftists will begin. Lee has agreed to a trip to the Chilean territory of Easter Island so that Chris can see the “big heads,” his last goal before he dies.
There’s no sugarcoating the fact that Chris is a hopelessly corrupt old spook, but the process of dying, plus his Catholic fear of going to hell for his innumerable mortal sins, has given him a certain melancholy sweetness and has also made him want to reckon, very loudly and publicly, with his god-awful past. Lee has been assigned by MJ to keep Chris in line and, if he can’t do that, to kill him on the island. Chris, who in his lucid moments knows this, carries a scrap of paper around reminding himself, “Don’t trust Lee!”
Chris also periodically forgets that he’s arranged to have Lee ease him out of life in a mercy killing on the island. The code word is “Arkansas.” As Chris reasons, he’d never casually say “Arkansas” because “no one wants to go to Arkansas.”
If you know Martin McDonagh’s film work at all, most famously In Bruges (2008) and The Banshees of Inisherin (2022), you recognize the elements of McDonagh’s favorite designs. They include, most prominently, two male friends bickering and bonding and betraying in shades of light humor and dark antipathy. Then there’s the heartbreakingly beautiful setting that creates the ironic backdrop to human viciousness, making the viewer wonder once again what the hell is wrong with us as a species. It’s always in an earthly paradise where people turn on each other and the shooting starts.
The title Wild Horse Nine is one that McDonagh shrugs off as far as any deep meaning, saying “I like numbers and I like horses.” But there’s no question that wild horses roaming free on gorgeously shot Rapa Nui are a key element of the film, especially the one particular horse with the distinctive white stripe on his forehead that keeps approaching Chris. “Are you a cancer-sniffing horse?” Chris asks.
The haunting attentions of the horse, like the odd, poignant friendship with Monica, takes on outsize importance as Chris tries to reckon with his own grim legacy. “I should’ve shot fewer people and spent more time with horses,” is one awkward, emotionally stunted conclusion drawn.
Wild Horse Nine doesn’t fail to include the almost nonexistent personal lives of Chris and Lee. McDonagh favorite Tom Waits gives a one-scene performance as Chris’s reclusive and estranged brother, a crusty old wreck who lives in a hut near Monument Valley — John Ford’s Monument Valley in Utah, where he shot all those celebrated Westerns — which serves to demonstrate how few and tenuous Chris’s links to life are anyway. And Lee is frequently on the phone with his wife Marge, played by Parker Posey. She’s an emotionally erratic alcoholic who has a very active sex life during Lee’s long absences from home. When Lee asks after the kids, Marge squawks, “The kids? Who cares!”
The message is pretty clear — what Chris and Lee have, personally, is each other, and that relationship, built on professional barbarism, is coming to a necessary end.
In an interview with Seth Myers, Malkovich called the two main characters “American jackasses,” just much more lethal than most.
The point is they’re still typical, on a continuum between ordinary chuckleheads and the dangerous chuckleheads in positions of power. If we find some of these jackasses dangerously likable, well, of course we do — we were raised with them, they’re our relatives, our neighbors, our old college pals we gave a pass to for a while before their malevolence became clear. And obviously McDonagh wants to connect these ordinary people with a harsh look at the United States and the simpleminded attitude of hero worship that’s been inculcated in the Western world since World War II:
The film explores a time when, seemingly, America’s place in the world was as the good guy, which is what most kids in the West — not just in the U.S. but in the U.K. and Ireland, Western Europe — are brought up to feel. The C.I.A. are the good guys and the K.G.B. are the bad guys; America is the good guy and Russia is the bad. But the more I read about what the C.I.A. were up to throughout the end of the last century, and particularly in Chile — to destabilize and help overthrow a democratically elected government, which ended up in fascist horrors for 15 years — it makes you think that you’re not being told the truth about the West and its moral outlook.
To those on the Left, this probably seems like a far too mild agenda. But we’ve got to keep in mind the extraordinary level of delusion that still prevails in the United States. For every leftist that knows all about what the CIA did in Chile in 1973, there are a hundred Americans who either don’t know about it or refuse to acknowledge the fact of it or what the fact means. There’s a reason McDonagh includes documentary footage of Chile ’73 in Wild Horse Nine, as well as actual footage of the capture of Patrice Lumumba, prime minister of the First Congolese Republic after having played a significant role in overthrowing the region’s Belgian colonizers. He was also taken out through a CIA-engineered coup — tortured, executed, body dissolved in acid.
In Wild Horse Nine, Chris claims blandly that “I liked Patrice.” When Lumumba told him the CIA would be responsible for the end of democracy in the Congo for at least a generation, Chris replied in tones of sympathetic reasonableness that of course it would. That was the whole point.
It’s interesting to note that among the many excellent reviews the film is getting, it’s also racking up a few prominent bad reviews from sites like NPR and the New Yorker. But what’s not mentioned in these reviews are such gutting interludes as the Lumumba footage. Instead the critics carp about the “tiresome bickering-and-bantering routine” of the two lead characters and McDonagh’s irreverent attitude, not making any attempt to consider the relationship between the two, the blandly callous rhetoric about horrors, the crude joking around, the hideous incongruence that we encounter every single day in the United States in the forms of blithering government edicts and banally evil pronouncements of the tech lords and brainwashed media commentary and sociopathic online f-ckery of all sorts.
We live among American jackasses, and there are big consequences that arise from the way they flourish here and around the world.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: London’s Photographers’ Gallery to launch exhibition programme for emerging voices
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Simon Bainbridge
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Photographers’ Gallery in London is launching a 10-year programme to platform emerging talent through a series of biennial exhibitions. The initiative has been made possible by what the not-for-profit gallery describes as “a very generous grant” from the UK-based John Kobal Foundation.
Shoair Mavlian, the director of the Photographers’ Gallery, declined to specify how much the grant is worth, but she tells The Art Newspaper that it will cover all the costs of staging the shows in its second-floor space, newly named the John Kobal Foundation Gallery.
The initiative will see one artist selected every two years for an exhibition. The first solo exhibition will be announced later this year and will run from 23 June to 26 September 2027.
“The whole idea of the programme is based around giving an opportunity to someone who hasn’t had an institutional solo show before,” she says. “The Photographers’ Gallery is in a similar situation to all other museums in the UK in that we are pressured into having to always do blockbuster shows [to generate revenue]. And what this programme allows us to do is to take risks.”
The gallery received a renewed three-year grant from Arts Council England in 2023, as one of the funding body’s national portfolio organisations (NPO). This grant represents around 20% of the gallery’s revenue, says Mavlian, however, it has remained the same throughout years of rising operational costs and high inflation, and so like other UK arts organisations, the gallery has become more reliant on other sources of income. Its accounts for the year ending 31 March 2025 report £620,573 in admissions income, which is more than two thirds the value of its NPO grant over a single year.
“We are under this constant pressure to sell tickets and bring people through the door—which, of course, is important. But what that means is we then don’t always see the full breadth of photography that is being made today. We are often looking at things that are historic rather than looking at the contemporary.”
The John Kobal Foundation was established in 1990 a year before the death of the eponymous film historian and photography collector “to advance the public appreciation and awareness of photography”.
“We are delighted to support this important new initiative," says Michael Mack, the co-chair of the John Kobal Foundation, “which honours John’s vision of nurturing creativity and innovation in photography.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: How Mona Chalabi Explains Income Inequality
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Naomi Elias
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
How Mona Chalabi Explains Income Inequality
An interview with the data journalist about how she uses numbers and design to illustrate how class weighs on the lives of Americans.
Iraqi British journalist Mona Chalabi is trying to convince the world that data visualization is cool—and it’s working. She has amassed a significant social following with her whimsically hand-drawn and boldly color-blocked figures that foreground what she calls data’s “human aspect” and make it more legible and engaging. Chalabi—who was formerly a data editor at The Guardian and is presently a lecturer of graphic design at Al-Quds Bard in Palestine—has come to be known for using these tools to make social issues the center of her work. The data journalist was awarded the 2023 Pulitzer Prize in Illustrated Reporting and Commentary for her New York Times series depicting the staggering wealth gap between Jeff Bezos and average Americans.
In her first book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are, she again turns her pen to the problem of money in America by mapping the country’s “economic universe”—i.e., the financial lives of 10 representative Americans of different income deciles. These include a woman working as a birth surrogate for supplementary income, a recent divorcée, a Gen Z rideshare driver recovering from gambling addiction, and a veteran conflicted about his need for disability assistance. She explores how much people have and don’t have, where it comes from, its relationship to their health and sense of identity, all with her trademark visual flair. (One figure from the book depicting mortgage denial rates by the race or ethnicity of applicants replaces the usual bars in a bar graph with upturned middle fingers that get progressively larger). She also weaves her own financial portrait with theirs, showing remarkable transparency about her career earnings and family history in recognition of how we’re all implicated in each others’ universes. The book reflects Chalabi’s personal commitment to not participating in the harmful but normalized practice of looking away from social inequities. Below, she talks to The Nation about the journalistic rules she’s happy to break, and how data can help reveal, and potentially overthrow, unfair systems.
—Naomi Elias
Naomi Elias:  Why did you land on money as the subject for your first book?
Mona Chalabi: At the start of Covid, when I was worrying about money, and I was thinking about the forces that had shaped my life. I mentioned in the book how on the one hand I felt precarious, but also I was not precarious at all, which is kind of a theme throughout the whole book, people feeling precarious even despite not necessarily being. I lived on the third floor of a Brooklyn brownstone at that point, and I remember seeing some of my neighbors, the people who owned their full brownstones, descending and climbing into their Range Rovers and just disappearing upstate. The streets literally emptied. And those of us that were left behind had a different kind of exposure to the pandemic because of class. And at the same time, we were also far less exposed than the people working in Amazon, for example, who were delivering our goods, the people who were stocking the shelves in the supermarket while we wandered around with our masks on. It was really clear to me that class really, really mattered.
NE: Why the focus on income and not wealth?
MC: Partly pragmatism. It would be really hard to extract that data from the people that I was interviewing, because sometimes their wealth actually isn’t even known to them. There are instances where people don’t exactly understand how much money their partner might have. And, for reasons I talk about in the book, I really focus on the household rather than the individual.
It also requires a different kind of honesty. I already found it so remarkable that people would just sit down for hours and hours detailing their finances to me. If I would have started to get into how much they were going to inherit from their parents, I don’t know if I could have relied on the same kind of honesty from them. And more importantly, the fact-checking would have been harder. It’s one thing to gain consent from them to tell me the story, but it’s another thing to then contact their parents and be like, “So, how much wealth exactly do you have?”
NE: When you narrowed down the responses to your questionnaire, in order to find “ten representative Americans,” what sort of demographics were on your mind?
MC: There were groups that I wanted to see represented, that I didn’t hear from. For example, I think it’s a failing of the book that I don’t have anybody who’s Native American in there. It’s not perfectly representative. I did know that I didn’t want these 10 people to be white; I didn’t want them to live on the two coasts. I did find that just because of the nature of my Instagram following—and by the way, obviously I didn’t find everyone through Instagram—but a lot of the people who responded were between 20 and let’s say early 40s, and I wanted a bigger age range than that. I did want to have some gender representation. I definitely wanted to include some disability representation. There were so many different boxes that I wanted to check, and what happened was that certain themes that I knew that I wanted to explore—like gambling addiction, like surrogacy—meant that I just set aside whoever was responding to me, and I went out looking for those people by going through nonprofits or through chat forums or whatever it might be to find someone who was navigating that particular world.
NE: Over the course of the years you worked on this book, subjects’ financial circumstances changed sometimes dramatically, which created really interesting storylines, as in the case of you meeting Chris Smalls before he became president of the Amazon Labor Union. How did that evolving data affect the story you were telling?
MC: That definitely wasn’t the plan. When I first sold the book, I was like, “Yeah, I’m going to have this written for you in 18 months.” Completely delusional and arrogant. And in a way that was actually a blessing, because if I just did three interviews with each person, a snapshot of their lives, I wouldn’t have seen that evolution. It’s because I struggled so much to find those 10 people, and each interview just led to so many more questions for me to understand them. Their lives did change. I mean, Chris’s a really dramatic one, but all of them. It’s depressing to me that when I met Tiffany [a 46-year-old Black goat farmer in Ohio representing the book’s poorest decile], one of the first times we spoke, she was like, “God, I would hate to be working in Burger King.” And then on one of our calls she’s like, “Yeah, I had to start working at McDonald’s.” So, yeah, their lives did change quite dramatically, as did mine. I think the book is stronger for it, and it changed the nature of our conversations. If I had done that snapshot approach, I don’t think there would have been that same kind of emotional investigation. There’s a vulnerability in disclosing numbers, and there’s also a vulnerability in admitting to working in Burger King when it’s the very thing that you said you never ever wanted to do.
NE: I’m interested in how you view hand drawing as a way of visualizing imprecision and why you think that’s important in data visualization.
MC: It’s fundamentally more honest. Many of the data sets that I’m looking at, the underlying information actually does have quite a big margin of error. So to present in these really clean charts is fundamentally a bit misleading. I was working with data that did have that degree of precision, but even then I want people to be able to see the respective scale of these bars as opposed to things with decimal places. Including these wobbly lines, the idea is that you see that the underlying data is imprecise, and it reminds me of this human aspect of the data, like, a human was responsible for choosing which variables to gather, what time period. It’s also about what is in vogue in terms of data collection. There’s so much bias that is involved. I hope that by presenting information in this way, I’m not hiding from that. It’s a bit more explicit: Here’s my hand and my pen and where my bias lies as I’m presenting this to you.
NE: All journalistic mediums (editorial, broadcast) are dealing with the attention span issue in their audiences. How does that influence your artistic choices?
MC: I’m much more familiar with how to navigate that on social media. I will often present an extremely simplified version of the statistics and then kind of gradually complicate it. And that’s obviously a really difficult line. You never want someone to have walked away with a version that is so simplified and abstract that it’s wrong, basically. And so, it’ll be a case of when I’m saying breaking it down into pieces, it might be that the title gives you the most simple takeaway, and then there’ll be one asterisk in the graphic and then another one. I’m trying to kind of guide where your eye goes in terms of how you’re consuming that information. I call that iterative storytelling. If you imagine on Instagram, it’s like each swipe is a different part of the story and I guess in a way, each chapter here is like another swipe and another complication.
NE: You break with some journalistic practices in this book by paying your interviewees and including yourself and your financial history in the story. What was behind that choice?
MC: I actually did more than that. Another practice that I broke with was I sent them the chapters prior to publication, which you don’t normally do. That felt really important to me, and I said that I would do that right from the start, even though nobody asked. And obviously the consequence of that was that not everyone was super happy with their chapter. Some of that actually did result in a little bit of a negotiation, which is why I did it. I’m willing to make a little sacrifice so that you don’t feel bad about this project.

Then to speak a little bit to the other principles that you mentioned that I parted with, disclosing my personal circumstances was really unpleasant, and it’s the reason why I’m very, very anxious about talking to you right now, why I’m anxious about the book coming out. I’ve done work in the past that has been a bit revealing, but this feels really different. I felt like there was no way I could make this argument that many of us are navigating shame about our finances and a lot of us are dishonest, and that actually we need to have much more frank conversation about class.… How could I do all of that without actually walking the walk? And because so much of the book is actually claiming a very important way to address inequality is redistribution, hoarding up all of the assets that I got from the book felt wrong. Look, I know it’s really complicated if we just change the journalistic norm and everyone can be paid for participating in journalism, but to write a book about class and to interview people who literally, in some cases, were really struggling, and to just take those stories and make money from writing those stories without paying them money, I kind of think it’s indefensible.
NE: You express a desire for this book to encourage people to make “collective economic demands on government that are more specific and more powerful than ‘tax the rich,’” which I found interesting because you once said data journalism is not suited to a radical agenda “because all it can do is show you the consequences of the system and not how it operates.” Do you still believe that and how does your work address that issue?
MC: I do think in a way the book is still showing you a lot of the consequences of how the system is operating. At least the charts are doing that. A lot more of the back and forth, the actual transcripts, are revealing more of the how. I still do think that there’s a lot of truth in that. I hope that this book is not solely a work of data journalism, because if it were just that, I don’t think it would be a radical book. I don’t even know if it’s radical. It’s funny, I was approached about writing a book for a few years before I undertook this and a lot of them were conversations about basically publishing a collection of my graphics, and that was so uninteresting to me. I have no desire to do a coffee-table book of my illustrations. I was really clear about this when we were really figuring out the design, but the illustrations and the charts are in service of the text. I still believe that data journalism alone is never going to assure a radical agenda, because when it’s done badly it can have this silencing effect on individual voices.
NE: And when done correctly?
MC: I just did a silly little chart yesterday about intergenerational mobility. It was about the percentage of people that earn less than their parents. And a few people said, “This makes me feel better.” I think really good data journalism actually galvanizes people to become more radical because it lets you know that there’s this tendency to internalize many things and assume that it’s our individual shortcomings.
I spoke to one of my closest friends this morning, she was my French professor, and one of the things that we have spoken about in the past is the fact that in France it’s illegal to collect data on religion. That’s because of the French concept of secularism, which they’re obsessed with, which I understand in theory, but what it means is that it’s virtually impossible to prove, on a systematic basis, Islamophobia in France. Now, Muslims in France aren’t like, “Oh, I don’t know if Islamophobia exists. I haven’t seen the data or I haven’t seen the chart.” They are well aware of the fact that Islamophobia exists, that anti-Arab racism exists. And I understand the arguments that some French people will make to me, that what does it do to let’s say a 17-year-old boy who is the child of North African immigrants, to see what his chances are of going to college? Is that massively demoralizing? Or does it contextualize their struggle and let them know that it’s not them? I think really good data journalism does reveal some of these systems.
I wrote an article for The Guardian ages and ages ago, and they never ended up publishing it. As soon as Trump took office, I went around and interviewed a bunch of people who worked at the Census Bureau, including the former Census Bureau director. And I was like, “Things are about to get bad, aren’t they?” And everyone was very clear on like, “Yeah, they’re about to get bad.” I think the fact that Trump, as is the playbook of authoritarian regimes, is interested in dismantling the data sets that reveal discrimination on a systematic basis means that it’s not for me to be sitting there pondering about the efficacy of these things. If he believes that those numbers matter, then I fucking believe they matter.
Like, this might feel like a stretch, but it’s something I’ve been thinking about. I wanted to create a chart on suicide rates in the Israeli military, and they stopped publishing those statistics a few years ago. And I’m like, OK, if you believe that those statistics are harmful, then I want them even more. I really, really want to understand what’s going on. I hope I’m communicating both that, yes, I believe that these data sets matter, that it matters to see.… One of the data sets that [Trump’s] stopping is the one that shows employment discrimination. I want that data set to continue to be able to see racial patterns in employment discrimination. And I don’t believe that relentlessly collecting that data, documenting that data, publishing the data is sufficient to overturn the systems that we have. So it’s both things. It’s not blind faith and adoration of numbers at all.

Whatever Centrists Say, the Left Won Big in the Midterms
Don’t allow centrists to change the terms of debate and the metrics of success. Last week’s midterms saw victories for socialists and other progressives that will allow the Left to grow in the months and years to come.
As recently as five years ago, the argument against the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and the Left from centrists and libs in the Democratic Party was this: Run left or socialist or progressive candidates, and you’ll lose; because the Trumpists are so terrible, you can’t afford to run that risk; give up your utopian plans and settle for reality.
Now the midterms happen, and many DSA and progressive candidates win, in both high-profile and low-profile races. Despite the Republicans trying to use individual leftist candidates as a way of beating the Democrats as a whole, the Democrats get their biggest win in fifty years. And how do centrists and moderates and libs respond? Well, the DSA and left candidates won with lower margins of victory than did the centrist candidates; moderates win better.
How does the Left respond? It recoils in fear and reacts in kind. It either tries to deny the truth or desperately searches for local variables and all sorts of quantitative nonsense that might salvage victory from the jaws of victory — thereby turning victory into defeat. The Left completely forgets its long-term project of building power; it forgets that a DSA or left candidate winning with fewer votes but still winning is not only a win but a very big win for the Left.
Let’s accept the centrist claim as true. Moderates win with more votes, progressives win with fewer votes. So what? The point is: a leftist won! Over the next six years, Michigan Senator Abdul El-Sayed will build an even stronger base while in office, he’ll push and vote for progressive legislation, inspiring other people to do the same elsewhere. That’s how the left wing of the possible, the slow boring of hard boards, works. You shed a point here, you lose a vote there, but you still win and are able to pass progressive legislation, building a base of support in the population for the long term. Without sacrificing an election.
Don’t just think this is special pleading for the Left. It applies across the board. Just consider some history. In her first race for Senate, self-styled Michigan moderate Elissa Slotkin won with a margin of victory of 0.34 percent. Her opponent? Mike Rogers, the very Republican who El-Sayed just defeated by 7 points. Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff’s margin of victory in his first Senate race? 1.23 percent. People invoke Ossoff and Slotkin today as if they are titans of the electoral map, but in their first victories, their margins were far smaller than those of progressive legislators. Yes, there were different variables in those elections, different electoral landscapes. But do you know what else is a confounding variable and a different electoral landscape? Being the first Muslim candidate for Senate in Michigan, which El-Sayed also is.
Former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell’s first margin of victory? 0.4 percent. Current Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s first margin of victory? 1.2 percent. Both of them turned into the the most powerful Republicans in the twenty-first century Senate.
So indoctrinated are we with ever-presentist, anti-historical, Nate Cohn/Nate Silver style of analysis, so beguiled are we by numbers and math, we completely lose sight of substance. We turn, or allow others to turn, victories into defeats. We forget to keep track of how the media and the centrists used to talk about the Left and fail to chart the way their propaganda changes over time. This, by the way, is why education in history and political theory is helpful: it keeps you attuned to how arguments are made, and how arguments change, and what’s behind those changes. It keeps you attuned to politics in a much deeper way than tracking the horse race of numbers does.
The problem with the ahistorical takes of our times is that they treat political reality as fixed, something like a natural fact. The foundation of all politics, going back to the ancient Greeks, is that there’s a difference between physis (nature) and nomos (law or custom, or what we call politics). Centrists and libs look at the world and see “battleground states” as some self-evident term of permanence and fixity, as facts of nature. They’re not.
I’m old enough to remember when California was a battleground state. It’s now the bluest of the blue. Likewise, Nevada and Arizona, once red, now purple, trending blue, and of course, there’s the big state of Texas. These things change, not in some Keynesian sense of “in the long run, we’re all dead” but in reasonably proximate notions of time.
Let’s look at the four anti-trans initiatives the Right put on the ballot this time. They won in three states: Colorado (blue state), Washington (blue state), and Arizona (purple state). The one state where an anti-trans ballot initiative went down? Missouri, a red state, which used to be purple. Why? Because the Right attached the anti-trans initiative to an anti-abortion initiative. A commitment to abortion rights, in other words, saved trans kids. In Missouri, a red state.
None of this would have been easily predicted from the past. It’s not that there are no risks with pushing a left platform. There are. And you have to be careful and not be reckless. But the idea that in an extremely fluid environment like this one, where North Carolina is suddenly talking about its long progressive heritage, where Georgia Democrats are, for the first time in decades, faced with the task of governing as opposed to merely resisting — the idea that, in an environment like this, we’d act as if we knew in advance, with 100 percent certainty, what is red, what is blue, what is purple, and so on, is what C. Wright Mills called “crackpot realism.” It’s not realistic. It’s reading the world through math.
And don’t just take it from me. Max Weber, considered by many to be the dean of realism, said it clearly, just a little bit more than a hundred years ago: “Certainly all historical experience confirms the truth — that man would not have attained the possible unless time and again he had reached out for the impossible.” Today we’re not even reaching out for the impossible. We’re merely advancing the left wing of the possible. It’s not an unreasonable project.
So, once again, the Left won. By how much or how little, it doesn’t matter nearly as much as the centrists would have us believe. Now we use that power to build more power, to expand our base, to show voters we can deliver. Don’t allow centrists to change the terms of debate and the metrics of success.

Letters From the December 2026 Issue
True progress… A willful blilndness… Correction…
True Progress
Your special issue on the US semiquincentennial brilliantly reminds us that America remains an unfinished project [“250 Years in Search of a More Perfect Union,” July/August 2026].
Contributors Simon Moya-Smith [“Murderers Most Foul”] and Gerald Horne [“Banquo’s Ghost”] expose the brutal truths underlying our national myths. In his review of Joseph Ellis’s The Great Contradiction: The Tragic Side of the American Founding, Horne writes, “Much like Macbeth and Banquo’s ghost, Ellis concedes, the nation cannot evade the tragedy preordained at its founding”—specifically, as Ellis puts it, the “failure to end slavery, and the failure to avoid Indian removal.” True progress requires confronting these foundational failures directly rather than erasing them from our narrative.
Brij Mohan
santa barbara, california
A Willful Blindness
I believe that The Nation erred by publishing an advertisement from the Citizens Commission on Human Rights (CCHR) [July/August 2026]. That ad promotes a very misleading video titled “Prescription for Violence: Psychiatry’s Deadly Side Effects,” which demonstrates a willful blindness to important facts. It decries gun violence by patients with a wide variety of mental illnesses but blames their medications for the violence. But what’s most problematic about the ad is that it fails to identify the real cause of increased shootings: the broad and easy availability of high-capacity-magazine firearms. Its video also omits researchers’ recommendation for a public-health approach to gun violence via limiting people’s access to such high-capacity firearms. Instead, the video features plaintiffs’ attorneys reading medications’ “black box” warning language as if the effects it describes are typical, when in fact it describes atypical outlier events and psychiatrists can successfully treat most of these patients.
My perspective is informed by more than three decades as a career “academic” emergency physician at urban trauma centers, where I’ve treated many patients whose psychiatric symptoms reemerged because they self-discontinued the very medications that were successfully remediating their psychiatric disorders. I’ve also treated many gun-violence victims.
It’s a bad idea to give matches to an arsonist. But that’s effectively what The Nation has done by publishing CCHR’s ad. It should not appear in future issues.
Gary Gaddis, MD, PhD
university city, missouri
Correction
Due to an editing error, the state represented by Jesse Helms was misnamed in “Our Unalienable Right,” by Regina Mahone [July/August 2026]. He was a senator from North Carolina, not South Carolina.
