https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Joshua B. Freeman
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
A Tale of Two Cities
How did New York go from a center of social-democratic experiment to one of neoliberal devastation?
How Did New York Become So Unequal?
A new history of New York examines how it went from a center of social-democratic experiment to one of neoliberal devastation.
In 2013, Mason B. Williams published City of Ambition, in which he told the story of New York’s transformation during the New Deal era, when federal dollars from Washington powered Fiorello La Guardia’s expansive vision for the role of municipal government in everyday life. La Guardia’s alliance with Franklin D. Roosevelt, supported by an expanding labor movement and a network of left and liberal organizations, laid the basis for the New York I grew up in. Federal funds allowed the city to build the high school I attended, the subway lines I spent a lifetime riding, the highways, bridges, and tunnels that whisked me around the city and sometimes congealed me in traffic jams, the innumerable parks, playgrounds, beaches, swimming pools, and health clinics, and the public-housing system that currently has more than a half-million residents.
Books in review
City of Fortune: Inequality and the Making of Contemporary New York
Buy this book
Williams’s new book, City of Fortune, chronicles a transformation just as profound: the post-1970s-fiscal-crisis replacement of the local New Deal order with a New York version of neoliberalism. Williams shows in devastating detail how, over the past half-century, the city’s economy and municipal capacity for governance have grown at the same time that it has developed levels of poverty and inequality unprecedented in its modern history. It is the relationship between these trends—how “the systems that made [the city] work for some imposed costs and violence on others”—that is the central focus of his book.
Williams has digested the vast literature on modern New York, of which these trends are only a part. To it, he has added a massive research effort of his own, in scores of archival collections and publications, giving his volume an authoritative quality. His wide-ranging knowledge might bring to mind comparisons to the late historian Mike Wallace—and they would not be entirely unjust. But unlike Wallace’s encyclopedic accounts of life and change in New York, City of Fortune focuses on three particular issues to tell its story: policing, education, and housing. All three profoundly affected the lives of New Yorkers; all three were political flash points; and all three were intertwined with changes in both material conditions and ideological assumptions.
Like many other American cities in the 1960s and ’70s, New York suffered a massive increase in crime and the sense of danger and disorder that came with it. By the mid-1970s, the New York Police Department had been diminished by cuts in funding and personnel and seemed utterly ineffective in countering the trend. (Those of us who had cars stolen or apartments broken into during those years can remember how the police considered the idea of investigating such crimes laughable.)
But starting under Mayor Ed Koch, a new generation of police leaders and new crime-fighting strategies, many coming out of the academic world, reshaped police activity and remade life for millions of New Yorkers, especially men of color. Pursuing various iterations of “community policing” and “broken windows” theory, the NYPD aggressively combated even minor acts of disorder in neighborhoods targeted as centers of drug activity and crime, arguing that doing so would allow the natural mechanisms of community self-regulation to reemerge.
In the early 1990s, the crime rate in New York began to fall, and it would continue to do so until Covid-19 hit in 2020. How much police strategy had to do with this is unclear, since crime would soon decrease in other cities as well. Still, the NYPD doubled down on its intense policing in high-crime areas, which tended to be neighborhoods with large African American or Latino populations. “Stop-and-frisk” became the favored mode of policing, a practice both deeply racist in disproportionately targeting non-white men for searches without legitimate cause and a clear violation of the Fourth Amendment. Even as crime continued to drop, the city refused to reduce the pressure: In 2011, it recorded an astounding 685,724 stops.
In some precincts, there were more stops than residents. If you were young and Black, the relentless harassment could lead to jail time for petty offenses, job loss, or far worse. The swagger and sense of omnipotence that came with the official veneration of aggressive policing resulted in a series of tragic murders of innocent people by police officers that tore the city apart. Yet, Williams notes, the NYPD would only become more “impervious to reform.”
****In education, the city faced two massive challenges: the extreme racial segregation in its schools (among the worst in the nation) and their failure to provide huge swaths of students with a decent education. Rather than confronting segregation head-on—a politically difficult approach—the city began experimenting with “magnet schools” to draw students from both white and non-white communities to superior schools with superior resources. At roughly the same time, progressive educators like Deborah Meier began creating public schools that broke from the older, more rigid and hierarchical approaches to pedagogy and drew interested students from across relatively broad areas to alternative learning communities.
The idea of school choice, which encompassed both developments, proved ideologically promiscuous: It soon became a favored approach of leftists, liberals, and free-market conservatives. By the early 1990s, it was also the official policy of the New York City Board of Education. New schools (some dubbed “academies”) popped up like mushrooms, both within the regular public-school system and as charter schools, supported by foundation as well as taxpayer money.
Some of these new schools proved to be excellent, although they often created conflicts as they took over the buildings of older schools the way hermit crabs take over the shells of other creatures. They also helped keep middle-class white students in the public-school system—an explicit goal of city leaders. But in doing so, critics argued, they siphoned away resources as well as many of the best teachers and students from the rest of the system and left behind those who could not (or didn’t know how to) get into selective schools. Regardless of the reasons it was initiated, Williams notes, school choice often ended up reinforcing and deepening segregation and inequality.
New York’s housing market was plagued by segregation and inequality as well. “Nothing animated the city’s business community quite like rent regulation,” Williams observes, framing his discussion of housing around the never-ending contest over whether to expand, diminish, or eliminate rent control.
These limits on rent increases—a legacy of federal price controls during World War II—helped preserve a city made up largely of working- and middle-class renters during the postwar years, when America’s other major cities mostly shrank in size and vitality. In 1970, 1.3 million apartments in New York City built before 1947 were covered by the state’s strict rent-control law, while another 375,000 units built later were regulated by a looser rent-stabilization system the city set up in 1968. Rent regulations, by design, limited landlords’ profits and challenged the idea that owners of property had the right to do whatever they wanted with it. Landlords knew there was little point in arguing that they should be allowed to make more money—but the claim that rent control made it impossible to properly maintain their existing buildings and discouraged new construction carried more weight.
In 1971, with the support of Governor Nelson Rockefeller, the New York State Legislature instituted “vacancy decontrol,” which removed the limits on what a landlord could charge for a previously rent-controlled apartment after the former tenant had vacated it. The backlash against this victory for building owners was so intense that, three years later, the Legislature required that apartments leaving the rent-control system be placed, after a onetime opportunity to hike the rent, under rent stabilization, gradually shifting housing from the older regulatory system to the newer one. But rather than ending the battle, the decision simply changed the terrain on which it has continued.
For one thing, the mayor-appointed Rent Guidelines Board, which determines each year how much stabilized rents can be raised, became the object of intense lobbying by tenants and landlords, with hearings that are famously epic, unruly affairs. For another, real estate interests continued to chip away at the system, eventually winning laws that removed apartments whose rent was above a certain cap or whose tenants made more than a certain income (“luxury decontrol”). In 1997, Governor George Pataki and Republicans in the Legislature were set to gut the system beyond recognition, until a massive mobilization of tenants, backed by organized labor, largely forced them to retreat.
Despite how heroically tenants and their organizations have dug their heels in to maintain these restrictions on rent, the housing-affordability crisis in the city has only worsened. The removal of hundreds of thousands of apartments from the rent-regulation system, the failure to build enough new housing, and a growing population have combined to accelerate gentrification and make finding a place to live a nightmare for all but the well-off. “By 2011,” Williams writes, “for the first time in the city’s modern history, the median New York rental household was officially rent-burdened, paying more than 30 percent of its income in rent—and a third of households paid more than half.”
The three stories that form the spine of City of Fortune will be familiar to longtime New York residents, if not to outsiders, but Williams tells them with an impressive combination of lucidity and granular detail. He also makes two very important points about their dynamics that are not often brought out.
The first is the centrality of state politics to what happens in New York City. The system of rent regulation, for example, comes primarily from state law, though city ordinances are involved too. Its fate has remained in the hands of a Legislature made up mostly of people elected outside of the city and governors who looked to the suburbs for swing votes to keep them in office. The mayor may press the Rent Guidelines Board to limit increases on regulated units, but the state, if it chooses, could get rid of the entire system. Tax-abatement programs to encourage housing construction likewise come from Albany, not City Hall. So do charter-school authorizations and many of the regulations (including the testing regime) that shape the city’s school system. More broadly, the ability of the city government to create and maintain programs of all kinds, from policing to transit to healthcare access, depends on legal and financial relationships with the state and federal governments. The city cannot even change its income-tax rates, which are controlled by the state, to the frustration of the current mayor, Zohran Mamdani. Even with a DSA-led campaign to “Tax the Rich,” he failed to win state approval for a higher income tax on wealthy residents or a boost in corporate tax rates, ultimately settling for a modest surcharge on real estate taxes on expensive second homes.

The second point that Williams stresses is the continuity of public policy across parties and mayors. Though packaged and sold differently from administration to administration, practices like aggressive community policing (including stop-and-frisk) and school choice have proved remarkably durable, even with the mayor’s office occupied by such seemingly dissimilar characters as Ed Koch, David Dinkins, Rudy Giuliani, Michael Bloomberg, and Bill de Blasio. Williams never steps back enough to ask why this is so, though he does mention some factors in passing, including the power of institutional interests like the NYPD and the continuing influence of various lobbies and advocacy organizations.
Williams’s concentration on particular policy areas allows us to see the expanding impact of neoliberalism on everyday life, but it also limits his portrayal of the larger structures of economic and political power that shaped the evolution of the city. For example, the post-fiscal-crisis New York economy is quite different from its earlier incarnation, with the virtual disappearance of manufacturing—once a mainstay—and the increased importance of services, finance, and real estate. The new robber barons in the city, though they may be extracting wealth from across the globe and bringing it into New York, are also more attentive to municipal matters than their predecessors. And they are much more ideologically engaged: Issues like charter schools and school choice have become vehicles for delegitimizing the state and promoting free-market ideas (though when it comes to policing, the same folks are all for strong government).
The 1975 fiscal crisis, widely interpreted by politicians, business leaders, and the press as a verdict on the flaws of expansive egalitarian government, led to years of austerity. It also laid the basis for a consensus on the importance of attracting and catering to wealthy companies and individuals and maintaining an orderly city that would not offend them. This became the new common sense, the hegemonic idea sustaining the power of New York’s financial and real-estate elite. In myriad ways, it shaped public policy no matter who headed City Hall.
What did not happen in the years after the post-crisis recovery is as revealing as what did. While billions of public dollars were devoted to subsidizing high-end office construction, not a single new unit of public housing has been built in the past 35 years. During the same period, cities all over the world have built mass-transit lines or whole new systems; New York added only four subway stops, all serving wealthy Manhattan neighborhoods. As economic inequality and homelessness soared, with nearly one in seven public-school pupils homeless, the government failed to build the housing and provide the services needed for the displaced and resourceless.
City of Fortune is shocking not only for the details it recounts but also for its disturbing picture of the moral and political failures of New York’s leaders. How can a city like New York, with a landscape now punctuated by palaces for the ultra-wealthy—such as the $238 million penthouse that billionaire Ken Griffin counts as a second home—have 420,000 children living below the poverty line? How can a society go so wrong so quickly?
Williams sees some hope in the future and gives us a hint of what that future might look like. Ending his book on an upbeat note, he recounts an October 2019 rally in the Long Island City neighborhood of Queens, where Bernie Sanders, after suffering a heart attack, relaunched his presidential campaign with Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at his side. In the crowd listening to Sanders’s moving appeal for solidarity across racial, religious, and national lines, Williams writes, was Zohran Mamdani, who had just launched his own campaign for the State Assembly.
Mamdani’s astounding election as mayor and his first months in office suggest that a new era might be beginning in New York. Unlike his opponents, Mamdani has a gut feel for the changes that took place in the city during the years Williams examines: the massive growth of inequality; the daily struggle of so many New Yorkers just to get by; the precarity of even young professionals in fields like higher education, culture, and the arts; and the extraordinary diversity of a city in which over 37 percent of the population was born outside the country (compared with 18 percent in 1970).
For progressives and ordinary New Yorkers, Mamdani is a breath of fresh air. Like Fiorello La Guardia, he is everywhere, filling potholes, shoveling snow, rallying with striking nurses, sharing iftar with city workers, riding his bike with Brooklyn parents taking their kids to school, and sitting in the nosebleed section of Madison Square Garden watching the Knicks. So far, he has been largely successful in avoiding pitfalls and inching toward fulfilling his campaign promises, which included freezing regulated rents, universal childcare, and free buses. But Williams’s account is a cautionary tale about the obstacles he faces: the limited power of the city in such crucial areas as tax policy and education; the fiscal challenges in an era when, unlike La Guardia’s, the federal government is determined to undermine blue-state cities rather than partner with them to better the lives of their residents; and the enormous power of the self-serving financial and real estate interests. It is too early to say if Mamdani and the movement that helped him win office will be able to break the link between the city’s growth and the grotesque inequality that Williams so ably chronicles. At stake is what it means to be a civilized society.

The Country Repudiated Bigotry in This Election. Will the Sports World Follow?
If we follow the lead of billionaire team owners, toxic cable news channels, and misguided athletes, it’s a resounding no. That just means we need to forge our own path.
The confetti had not even been swept up after last week’s historic electoral repudiation of Donald Trump when Democratic Party leadership made it clear that they would not try to, in the words of incoming Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries, “get even” with the assorted criminals that have been stripping this country for parts. But people don’t want to “get even,” as if this were all some childish tit-for-tat. They want justice.
The electorate voted for a reckoning, but the current Democratic leadership—including Jeffries and incumbent leader of the newly flipped Senate Chuck Schumer—are utterly unequal to the task. Their inadequacy is a huge liability. If they fail to live up to voters’ expectations, that avalanche of young people we just saw go to the polls might stay home in 2028 out of disgust, potentially sweeping into power a shrewder generation of racist authoritarians bleating about Democratic “broken promises.” It’s a movie we’ve seen before.
Concerns about their total absence of spines goes beyond squandering electoral gains, though. If they fail to provide the kind of reckoning voters went to the polls to endorse, they’re also signaling to the public that they accept the kind of racist political rhetoric we saw germinate over the past several months. From Trump on down, these midterms contained a measure of anti-Islamic bigotry that was beyond the pale. And while it face-planted electorally, that does not mean it didn’t also change the boundaries of how politicians feel like they get to speak and act toward our Muslim neighbors.
This has even infected our national pastime. After the election, Toronto Blue Jays player Anthony Santander posted anti-Muslim screeds on social media, including graphic memes—since taken down—that included the phrase, “America voted for Sharia Last Night!” overlaid on an image of Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, and “Islam is not peaceful.” In response, the Blue Jays issued a milquetoast statement that read, “Baseball is for everyone and the Blue Jays have created an inclusive experience where all fans feel welcome at our ballpark. Individual comments do not represent our organization’s values and beliefs.”
This is not nearly good enough. Shireen Ahmed, senior contributor to CBC sports and cohost of the Burn It All Down podcast, pointed out that the Blue Jays have a track record of diversity celebrations and a significant Muslim fanbase, which makes the response all the more disappointing. “The Blue Jays play in one of the most multicultural cities in the world,” she wrote. “According to a 2024 report from Statistics Canada, up to 57 per cent of Toronto’s population is racialized. The Blue Jays as an organization celebrate this diversity with cultural events and heritage themes throughout the season including Pride Night and Caribbean Carnival night.”
It’s true that the sports world may be one of the last to actually show some backbone and reflect the popular will: The conservative billionaire team owners and the news networks they watch (or own) love to mewl about the mythical—coded as white male—right-wing sports fan, whom they fear alienating above all. And it’s also true that the politics of the owner’s box, which is overwhelmingly reactionary, will always matter more than the political ideas of fans or players. Even so, it’s time for these institutions, which have cowered in the face of Trump’s poisonous white supremacy, to show where they stand in the wake of last week’s overwhelming repudiation.
There was a beautiful—and tragic—moment at the end of a recent game between the San Antonio Spurs and Dallas Mavericks. Spurs star Victor Wembenyama was caught on video whispering into Dallas Mavericks guard Kyrie Irving’s ear, “Free Palestine, my brother. I’m proud of you.” Irving, long a supporter of a free Palestine, has been wearing keffiyehs, Palestinian colors, and political shirts and bracelets to represent his solidarity since Israel launched a total war on the people of Gaza in 2023. That a star of Wembenyama’s stature feels he has to furtively whisper such a sentiment speaks volumes. It speaks to a sports world in 2026 where players are policed by right-wing blowhards on behalf of team owners, where outspoken athletes feel like they must hide in shadows, even when opposing a genocide.
Anti-Arab and anti-Islamic racism just got muzzled at the polls, but the dangerous rhetoric that produced such a backlash is now off the leash. It will be a collective task to make racists afraid again to speak their bile and sports owners to see that it doesn’t pay to be the great underwriters of the white revanchism that has scarred the political landscape for too long.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/hegs.title: Hegseth Survives Impeachment Attempt
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/hegs.author: Matt Sledge, Nick Turse
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/hegs.text:
Self-styled Secretary of War Pete Hegseth narrowly avoided impeachment Tuesday night, as solidarity from House Republicans blocked a bill introduced by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., charging Hegseth with “high crimes and misdemeanors.”
Though Democrats overwhelmingly joined Massie’s effort following their midterm election landslide, the House voted 211 to 204 to refer the charges to a committee, allowing Republicans to slow the process. With 11 Democrats absent, they lacked the numbers. Massie, however, dismissed the impact of Democratic absences to The Intercept. “No, there were enough Republicans to rally to get here,” he said.
The procedural vote spared Republicans a more difficult vote on whether to impeach Hegseth on Massie’s eight charges, including waging wars without Congressional authorization and undercutting measures to prevent civilian casualties. It followed a week of increasingly desperate efforts by the Pentagon chief to shore up Congressional and White House support, including a campaign-style video intended to influence Trump, a social media campaign by underlings, and a rare appearance by Hegseth himself before the Pentagon press corps.
Over half an hour on Tuesday morning, Hegseth wove a web of lies designed to refute or obfuscate Massie’s eight charges. He claimed that the effort to impeach him was a stunt by just “one disgruntled congressman.” That, too, turned out to be false as 203 members of Congress voted with Massie.
On Tuesday, a coalition of more than 40 civil society organizations – including Oxfam America, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), Common Defense, Demand Progress, MoveOn, and the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft – sent a letter calling on all House members to vote for every article of impeachment filed against Hegseth.
“Pete Hegseth’s time at the Pentagon has done grievous harm to the nation and to the Constitution,” said Demand Progress Senior Policy Advisor Cavan Kharrazian. “This is a man who ignored the will of Congress to execute an illegal war in Iran, kidnapped a foreign leader for oil, restarted war on Yemen, sent missiles to kill suspected drug traffickers and weaponized the Pentagon against a political enemy.”
The House has only impeached two Cabinet secretaries: William Belknap, the secretary of war, in 1876; and Alejandro Mayorkas, the secretary of homeland security, in 2024. In neither case did the Senate vote to convict.
After the vote, Massie called out the display of inaction from his Republican colleagues.
“They diagnosed why they lost the election,” Massie said of fellow Republicans following the vote on Tuesday night. “But tonight they were paralyzed to do anything about it. And that’s the story of Congress.”
Absent from the vote were Democratic Reps. Julia Brownley, Lou Correa and Nancy Pelosi, of California, Laura Gillen of New York, Steven Horsford of Nevada, Jonathan Jackson of Illinois, Brittany Pettersen of Colorado, Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico, Haley Stevens of Michigan, Marilyn Strickland of Washington, and Frederica Wilson of Florida. The absent Republicans were Reps. Monica De La Cruz of Texas, Neal Dunn of Florida, Russell Fry of South Carolina, Julia Letlow of Louisiana, Tom Tiffany and Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin, and Rudy Yakym of Indiana.
A senior Congressional staffer predicted that Hegseth would face a very rough road if he survived impeachment. “Oversight is going to come crashing down on his head,” that staffer said. “Will Hegseth continue to obstruct? Yes. But wait until the subpoenas start.”
Congressional committees have broad investigative powers, including the authority to subpoena administration officials to testify under oath and compel them to turn over documents. Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, who will head the House Armed Services Committee in the next Congress, said Hegseth and Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg would be first on the list to testify.
Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., one of the leading voices for Hegseth’s impeachment, told The Intercept there were “many ways” for Democrats to hold him accountable in the next session, specifically compelling him to testify before the American people. “I would be surprised to see him last the next two years in this administration,” she told The Intercept. “I think that he is not only one of the most incompetent members of the administration, but also the most unpopular — and it’s on a bipartisan basis. So the pressure will continue to grow for there to be some change at the Pentagon.”
Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda, D-N.C., told The Intercept that the incoming Democrats have Hegseth in their sights. “I want Pete Hegseth not just impeached. I want him prosecuted, They murdered people in the Caribbean. And we killed 163 little girls in Iran,” he said. “Everybody in my class is ready for him to go. We tried it, It didn’t work. Well do it again.”
In a Truth Social post, President Donald Trump celebrated the outcome while expressing confusion over the vote. Trump called it the “Democrats’ attempt to impeach” Hegseth, despite the fact the effort was introduced by Massie, a Republican, who he called “a major LOSER.” He claimed it was an “EXONERATION” of Hegseth and added: “The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America. They must be stopped!”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Peruvian senator calls for removal of large-scale replicas of Moche erotic sculptures from public park
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Graciela Ibáñez
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A controversy over 3m-tall erotic sculptures in northern Peru reignited recently after a senator requested that the cultural ministry remove them from a public area. Located in a park outside the city of Trujillo, the sculptures are replicas of ceramics from the pre-Incan Moche civilisation.
“What happens when children see these images? Neurological and psychological factors are affected, because they see body dimensions that are completely different from how they see themselves,” Milagros Jáuregui, a conservative senator from the Renovación Popular party, said in a speech on 26 October.
The sculptures are located in Parque de la Fertilidad (Fertility Park), a public space where in 2021 then-mayor Arturo Fernández of the Moche district began installing giant fibreglass reproductions of ceramic depictions of sexual acts to promote tourism.
Known as huacos eróticos, the much smaller original ceramics date from the 3rd to 8th century AD. No more than 30cm in height, they were placed in tombs as burial offerings. But the debate about their much larger versions in the park goes beyond political prudishness.
“It’s a complicated issue,” the Peruvian archaeologist Walter Alva tells The Art Newspaper. “There’s freedom to express or re-create themes from the past, but these ceramics were created to be placed as offerings to the dead, with a sense of revitalising life. They are associated with both fertility and an entire system of beliefs.”
The Moche civilisation covered 700km of the coast of what is now Peru, between the regions of Piura and Ancash, centuries before the Inca dominated the area. “Moche art is primarily ceramic, and these vessels depict erotic scenes or concepts of sexuality from that era,” Alva says. “The sculptures in the park were created outside of their historical context.”
One of the greatest archaeological discoveries from the Moche civilisation was that of the Lord of Sipán near the city of Chiclayo—a discovery Alva made in 1987. A 3rd-century monarch, the Lord of Sipán’s body was found covered with gold along with eight other people, a dog and two llamas and nearly 500 objects including ceramic vessels, ornaments and textiles.
The Moche have the largest number of erotic representations among pre-Hispanic civilisations. The most complete collection of its ceramics is in Lima, at the Larco Museum of pre-Columbian art, which celebrated its centennial in July. Before the 1960s, children were forbidden from entering the room that housed the huacos. Today, minors must be accompanied by an adult. The institution’s Erotic Gallery is one of its most popular attractions.
Jáuregui, an evangelical pastor as well as a senator, believes these Moche sculptures should only be in closed spaces. “Displaying these types of images in public is harmful to children,” she told congress. “We should have them in museums, where high-school students can observe a part of our culture that is a national treasure with the help of teachers or some kind of tutor.”

https://citylimits.org/nuevo-grupo-de-de.title: Nuevo grupo de demócratas latinos busca ampliar su influencia política en los cinco condados de Nueva York
https://citylimits.org/nuevo-grupo-de-de.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/nuevo-grupo-de-de.text:
Share This Article
La organización busca aumentar la representación latina en la política local, formar futuros líderes y fortalecer la participación comunitaria en toda la ciudad de Nueva York, según su fundadora, Jamey Battle.
Este artículo se publicó originalmente en inglés el 4 de noviembre. Traducido por Jacob Velez. Read the English version here.
Después de años de participar en clubes demócratas, organizaciones de mujeres y redes profesionales, Jamey Battle dijo que se hacía constantemente la misma pregunta.
“Pensaba: ¿dónde están los demás latinos?”, dijo Battle, quien antes trabajó en la Asamblea Estatal de Nueva York y en una compañía haciendo lobby. “¿Cómo puedo incorporarlos a este espacio? ¿Cómo podemos involucrarnos en este movimiento político?”.
En lugar de seguir buscando representación latina dentro de las organizaciones políticas existentes, Battle decidió ayudar a crear un espacio propio, centrado en las voces y experiencias de la comunidad latina.
El mes pasado, Latino Democrats of New York City (LDNYC por sus siglas en inglés) celebró su lanzamiento oficial como organización 501(c)(4). Fundada en octubre de 2025 como un grupo de organización voluntaria, LDNYC cuenta actualmente con casi 200 miembros, según un comunicado de prensa.
La organización busca aumentar la representación latina en la política local, formar futuros líderes y fortalecer la participación comunitaria en los cinco condados de la ciudad de Nueva York.
“Se me ocurrió la idea de Latino Democrats hace aproximadamente un año. Le envié un mensaje de texto a mi vicepresidenta, Evelin Vazquez, y nos comunicamos con personas de nuestra red que compartían dos valores: la integridad y el compromiso de poner a la comunidad en el centro”, dijo Battle, presidenta de la organización.
“Finalmente me di cuenta de algo: ¿por qué estoy dedicando tanto tiempo a intentar que los latinos encajen en un espacio que nunca fue creado para nosotros, que no está dirigido por nosotros ni para nosotros y que tampoco responde a nuestras necesidades?”.
El grupo celebró su reconocimiento como organización sin fines de lucro el 21 de octubre con una recepción inaugural llamada “Primera Noche”, realizada en Lighthouse Rooftop, en Long Island City, Queens.
La velada reunió a funcionarios electos, líderes comunitarios, organizadores y simpatizantes en una celebración que incluyó discursos, entregas de reconocimientos y conversaciones sobre la participación política latina.
Entre los asistentes estuvieron Claire Valdez, quien asumirá su cargo en el Congreso en enero para representar al Distrito 7 de Brooklyn y Queens; Brian Romero, recientemente elegido para representar a Woodside y Jackson Heights en la Asamblea estatal; además de los asambleístas de Queens Catalina Cruz y Steven Raga, entre otros.
Durante la recepción, los oradores compartieron historias personales sobre sus familias, sus trayectorias profesionales y las experiencias que los llevaron a involucrarse en el servicio público.
Uno de los participantes recordó haber crecido con una madre salvadoreña que llegó a los Estados Unidos sin documentos migratorios a los 12 años. También relató las historias familiares que escuchaba sobre explotación laboral, robo de salarios, prácticas policiales y operativos de las autoridades migratorias, experiencias que, según explicó, continúan influyendo en su manera de defender a la comunidad.
En el estado de Nueva York, los latinos representan 2.2 millones de votantes elegibles, lo que los convierte en el grupo racial o étnico más numeroso después de los votantes blancos, según el Pew Research Center.
Para Battle, el lanzamiento de la organización representa una oportunidad para incorporar a más neoyorquinos latinos a los espacios políticos y desarrollar una red más sólida de líderes comunitarios.
El lanzamiento ocurre mientras los demócratas celebran amplias victorias en todo el país en las elecciones de mitad de mandato del martes, incluidos los triunfos de varios candidatos respaldados por Latino Democrats NYC.
“Estoy muy emocionada por los próximos años, por la oportunidad de movilizar y entusiasmar a la comunidad latina de Nueva York y de construir poder político para todas las comunidades latinas de la ciudad”, dijo Battle.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: NYC Student Homelessness Declines but Remains Stubbornly High, Report Finds
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Amy Zimmer, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters.
One in eight New York City public school students experienced homelessness last school year, according to a report released Tuesday by the nonprofit Advocates for Children.
That meant more than 138,000 children lived in temporary housing, whether in shelters or “doubled up” with family or friends. The total dropped 10% from the previous school year — largely driven by a decline in the number of families living in shelters. Still, the figure remained staggeringly high, roughly equivalent to the population of Albany, and marked the 11th straight year the number topped 100,000, the report said.
Of those students, 37% lived in shelters, while 58% shared housing with other families because of economic hardship, the report said.
Students who are homeless, particularly those living in shelters, tend to fare worse academically than their peers in permanent housing. In 2025, about 27% of students living in shelters in grades 3-8 were proficient in reading, less than half the rate of students in permanent housing, according to state test results. About 59% graduated on time, compared with the citywide rate of 81%, and 14% dropped out of school, about triple the dropout rate of their peers.
A major factor contributing to these poor outcomes is that simply getting to school can be a challenge.
Nearly half of students in temporary housing and 63% of those living in shelters were chronically absent, meaning they missed at least 10% of the 2024-25 school year. That compares to about a third of students citywide. And 1 in 5 students in shelters transferred schools at least once during the year, more than four times the rate for their peers.
Jennifer Pringle, director of Advocates for Children’s Learners in Temporary Housing Project, said the city must do more to address these challenges, warning that people without a high school diploma are 4.5 times more likely to experience homelessness as young adults.
“Unfortunately, for too many families, being in shelter derails their education,” Pringle said. “I know this is the long game, but if we really want to address family homelessness, we have to focus on education now.”
Far-Flung Shelter Placements Keep Children Out of School, Advocates Say
While the Department of Homeless Services tries to place families in the borough where the youngest child attends school, that’s not always the case. About 37% of families in shelters are placed in a different borough from where their children attend school, Pringle said.
Because of that, many children in shelters rely on school buses, but Pringle said it typically takes more than a month to get assigned to a route. Even then, families can face delays and buses that fail to show up.
“The city has a lot of control over these systems,” Pringle said. “New York City Public Schools does not control where the Department of Homeless Services places families in shelters. But the Department of Homeless Services’ practices about shelter placements makes a tremendous difference to whether or not a child can be stably educated.”
Once a family is placed in a shelter, there is no mechanism to revisit that placement, Pringle said. She suggested that shelter case managers check in with families a week after they arrive to see whether they want to transfer closer to their children’s school.
Families remain in shelters for an average of 14 months, she added. For parents spending several hours a day getting their children to and from school, that leaves less time to work or look for permanent housing.
“It may be unrealistic to expect that the city can place all families close to kids’ schools. But let’s at least design a process that you know takes this into consideration and makes it a greater priority,” she said.
The city has been working to improve attendance strategies and has expanded Every Child and Family is Known, a program that pairs homeless students and their families with designated school staffers who build relationships and connect them with support and resources.
Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels said the Education Department has worked with other city agencies in recent years to improve policies for families, including eliminating a requirement that children attend all housing meetings and expanding community schools offering wraparound services such as eye care and housing support in districts with high concentrations of shelters.
“Supporting these students is both a priority and shared responsibility,” Samuels said in a statement. “As this report shows, this work is far from over, and we’ll continue to work in partnership to bolster resources, address ongoing challenges and ensure that our most vulnerable students have the support they need to receive a rigorous, high-quality education.”
Department of Homeless Services Commissioner Erin Dalton also pointed to declines in chronic absenteeism among students living in shelters and said the agency was expanding outreach to children who frequently miss school and working to help families transition to more stable housing.
Bronx Leads NYC in Student Homelessness Rates
The Bronx continued to have the highest rate of student homelessness, with nearly 1 in 6 students experiencing homelessness in the 2025-26 school year.
Manhattan had the next-highest rate, at 1 in 7 students, but saw the biggest year-over-year drop, at 18%, largely because fewer students enrolled in the borough’s schools were living in shelters. Staten Island had the lowest rate, with about 1 in 20 students experiencing homelessness.
At the school district level, the highest rates were in the South Bronx’s District 9, Brownsville’s District 23 and Bushwick’s District 32. More than 1 in 5 students in those districts experienced homelessness last year.
At the other end of the spectrum, fewer than 5% of students in District 26, which spans Queens neighborhoods including Bayside, Fresh Meadows and Jamaica Estates, experienced homelessness.
Amy Zimmer is the bureau chief for Chalkbeat New York. Contact Amy at azimmer@chalkbeat.org.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-bars-and-.title: NYC bars and restaurants say they're struggling and may raise prices
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-bars-and-.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-bars-and-.text:
New York City bars and restaurants are struggling to keep up financially amid rising operating costs and uneven customer spending, according to a survey by trade association NYC Hospitality Alliance.
Many bars, restaurants and nightlife establishments are considering raising menu prices or reducing staff, if they haven’t already, according to the NYC Hospitality Alliance’s quarterly survey. It found that among the 275 establishments represented in replies to the survey, half said they were breaking even or operating at a loss in the third quarter of this year. About the same amount said their sales were below expectations.
It was a dip in performance after a strong second quarter, in which operators received a boost from World Cup and Knicks game watchers, said Andrew Rigie, executive director of the New York City Hospitality Alliance. The group represents more than 3,000 restaurants in the city.
“These big events gave a lot of small businesses a big boost, he said. “Unfortunately, it seems that it was short-lived.”
According to the survey, 61% of restaurant operators said they had or were considering raising menu prices, and 57% reported reducing or considering reducing employee hours or staffing levels. Almost half of operators surveyed, or 45%, identified labor costs as a leading business concern. Other major issues cited were inflation and tariffs, liability insurance and commercial rents, according to the survey.
Rigie said the numbers speak to how widespread challenges like labor costs and rising cost of goods are in the industry, and a need for policymakers to step in to address them. He said one area of concern should be the city’s affordability crisis, which beyond affecting individual New Yorkers, also affects restaurant sales when people spend less money.
“The cost to purchase goods continues to go up, has stayed high, and there's really only so much that restaurants can pass the cost on to their customers in the form of increased menu prices,” Rigie said. “When you start to increase menu prices, you can deter customers from coming to the restaurant and spending money. Often, they will order differently. They'll order less. So even some restaurants that have experienced increased overall sales, they've reported decreased profitability. So it's a complex issue that's going on.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.title: Solstice Sonnet
https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.author: Zeina Hashem Beck
https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.text:
Poems
                                        
                                    
                                     / 
                                                                            November 10, 2026
                                    
                
        
                            
                
                                
    
The Litani banks fill with phosphorus.
Here, the cricket repeats, somewhere, somewhere,
with its dark wings, its five eyes, its toothed legs.
Don’t mistake me for a recovered heart,
fascinated by the longest sunsets.
I am a green permanent resident,
which rings more eternal than citizen.
The summer solstice is about distance,
angles. Pulsing with airports & amens
under the fog, I give up on endings.
You point, articulate: Ta-mal-pa-is.
Try mountains if you’re searching for soul. Break—
but don’t trust me on this. Most days, I don’t
venture out in twilight like hungry deer.
Venture out in twilight like hungry deer!
But don’t trust me on this. Most days, I don’t
try mountains. If you’re searching for soul, break.
You point: articulate Tamalpais
under the fog. I give up on endings,
angles. Pulsing with airports & amens,
the summer solstice is about distance
which rings. More eternal than citizen,
I am a green permanent resident,
fascinated by the longest sunsets.
Don’t mistake me for a recovered heart
with its dark wings, its five eyes, its toothed legs.
Here, the cricket repeats, somewhere, somewhere—
a litany. Banks fill with phosphorus.
    
    
        
     
            
                            
                    
                                        
                        Zeina Hashem Beck is the author of the mirror sonnet collection This Was Supposed to Be About Beauty (Penguin, March 2027) and Sublingual: Failing in an Other’s Language (Haymarket, fall 2027), her debut nonfiction book. Her collection O (Penguin) won the 2023 Arab American Book Award for Poetry and was named a best book of the year by Literary Hub and the New York Public Library. She’s also the author of Louder than Hearts and To Live in Autumn, as well as the chapbooks 3arabi Song and There Was and How Much There Was. Her work has appeared in LARB, Lit Hub, Poetry, and elsewhere. She grew up in Lebanon and currently resides in the Bay Area.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Mike Beggs, Ben Burgis, Bhaskar Sunkara
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Do Socialists Even Believe in Socialism Anymore?
The American left has a growing list of victories—and an unfinished argument about the society it wants to build.
We’ve all seen the cover. some of us even have a copy of it hanging in our living room: “The Red Apple.” The New York Post marked Zohran Mamdani’s November 2025 election with a Soviet-inspired cover that featured the incoming mayor carrying a hammer and sickle high above his head.
It was an image that those of us who grew up in New York during the Rudy Giuliani or Michael Bloomberg era couldn’t have imagined. The larger global context made it even more remarkable, demonstrating socialism’s advance in the United States even as it’s in retreat in much of Europe and Latin America. And since last year, Mamdani’s election has helped catalyze a string of socialist victories in congressional races. The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) has surged to over 120,000 members, and with the midterm results, the movement’s small congressional contingent is set to become dramatically larger.
What does socialism mean, though, to the socialists of our era? Their predecessors in early-20th-century socialist parties liked to talk about a “minimum program” of reforms within capitalism and a “maximum program” of reforms that go beyond capitalism entirely. Some even theorized a “transitional program” to bridge the gap between the two.
The “minimum program,” at least, is easy enough to see today. Socialist candidates for office talk about Medicare for All, jobs programs, and ending America’s wars overseas. In New York, Mamdani has conducted hearings on the misdeeds of negligent landlords, frozen the rent for millions of New Yorkers in rent-stabilized apartments, and established a Mayor’s Office of Worker Power to help people organize their workplaces. He’s worked to expand free childcare and taken the first steps to build public grocery stores in each of the city’s five boroughs. And through it all, the city’s economy has continued to boom.
To progressive allies of the DSA, these reforms are proof of the movement’s inherent pragmatism—in deeds, if not always in words. But others can reasonably ask if this generation’s socialists still believe in socialism at all.
When the leading DSA-affiliated politicians like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are asked to define socialism, they tend to talk about mitigating income inequality and giving everyone a dignified life. While these are certainly goals close to the heart of any socialist, it’s hard to see how they add up to socialism as a system, since they avoid the question at the core of socialism: the ownership of the means of production. Similarly, while the radicalism of some clauses of the DSA’s national platform—including the calls to abolish the Senate and to dismantle the carceral state—has been a lightning rod for criticism from the right, the document offers little detail about how a world beyond capitalism would work.
The DSA platform calls for public ownership of the largest corporations and essential industries. That would be a major transformation, but it could still leave much of the economy organized around private employers and wage labor. Even the section titled “Democracy at Work” is about trade unions, not who owns the means of production. And although the DSA declares a classless society its goal, it offers little explanation of how its demands for change within capitalism would get us there.
This blurriness about the “maximum program” can’t be chalked up to a lack of radical commitment or to strategic coyness. It reflects a real problem. On the one hand, capitalism is a brutally unequal system in which many struggle to take care of their families and spend much of their waking lives in jobs they despise. There are many good reasons to find it abhorrent. On the other hand, especially after the failures of state socialism in the Eastern bloc, many people who are deeply critical of capitalism aren’t entirely sure what an economically viable alternative to it would look like.
In light of that uncertainty, many progressives, and surely many readers of The Nation, wonder if it’s better to drop the socialism talk entirely. Politicians like Zohran Mamdani should abandon the historical baggage associated with socialism, their thinking goes, and just embrace social democracy and the great effort to tame, rather than replace, capitalism.
On one level, it’s easy to see their point. Social democracies like Denmark, Norway, Sweden, and Finland really were, at their peak, the most livable societies that human beings ever built. If the United States adopted the Nordic model in the coming years, it would be the greatest triumph of the American left since the Civil War and Reconstruction. That much should be obvious to anyone with progressive values. What might be less obvious is that it would still be a woefully insufficient response to growing levels of inequality and discontent.
Admittedly, one reason that socialists like ourselves stubbornly refuse to limit our horizons to social democracy is purely ideological. Even in the most expansive social-democratic welfare states, like Sweden in the 1970s, most of the working-age population worked for capitalist employers. Democracy stopped at the factory and office doors.
In the places where most adults spend their working days, we do not interact with each other as equals. The working-class majority have to do what they’re told by bosses or risk becoming unemployed. Often, workers’ best recourse against unreasonable demands is the power of exit. But even if they’re able to exercise that option, they will still have to find a new boss to submit to. They can choose their masters, but they can’t choose not to have a master. Meanwhile, some of their fellow citizens, due to nothing but accidents of birth, can live off trust funds without having to work at all.
For egalitarians, this is a deep injustice, and one that remains even when extensive public provision and a powerful labor movement have sanded off some of the system’s worst effects.
Even if we were willing to swallow this imbalance of power at the heart of the economy, though, there’s also a practical objection to stopping at social democracy. Thinking that’s as far as we can go sounds realistic, but it’s far from clear that capitalism as it exists in the third decade of the 21st century can sustain ambitious pro-labor policies and deep welfare-state commitments that would enable full employment and the truly comprehensive provision of public goods.
Michał Kalecki identified the underlying problem decades before it came to the fore. In his 1943 essay “Political Aspects of Full Employment,” Kalecki argued that while sustained full employment might be economically achievable under capitalism, it was politically unstable. Individual capitalists might occasionally welcome state policies to these ends in the short term to help restore demand for their products, but over time they would come to resist them. Tight labor markets weaken workplace discipline, strengthen workers’ bargaining power, and erode employers’ social authority—an environment, the business leaders feared, that would undermine capital accumulation.
Much of today’s progressive discourse ignores this lesson entirely. Full employment, expansive fiscal policy, and ambitious state investment are often presented by American progressives as stable end points within capitalism. Yet these policies will be bitterly contested by capital and, inevitably, will provoke crises.
Governments, for their part, can sometimes sustain such policies against the immediate wishes of business, especially when public order is at stake. But this autonomy is limited, since states remain dependent on private investment for growth, employment, and tax revenues. In an era of intensified global competition, and with aging populations already threatening the existing welfare states, it’s unclear that the Golden Age advances of the middle 20th century, when both labor and capital grew stronger, can return.
All this, of course, might sound like the case for an even more moderate reform program, one that avoids burdening capitalist job creators with excessive interference from labor but rewards workers with reasonable wages and protections in return. We draw the opposite conclusion. We think that people have the right to both the security of a welfare state and a voice in their workplaces. Precisely for that reason, socialists must not shy away from maximal demands: doing away with capitalism altogether.
The socialism of central planning and administrative allocation was a failure in the Soviet Union and similar societies. Learning from that history requires rethinking how egalitarian production and distribution can actually work.
If we need market mechanisms in at least some sectors of the economy, it doesn’t follow that we need capitalist property relations and the deep inequalities of power that go with them. We know that worker-owned and democratically governed firms can operate efficiently. Spain’s Mondragon Corporation, a federation of dozens of autonomous cooperatives, employs around 70,000 people. Its worker-members elect their governing bodies and participate in strategic decisions. If we could have a market sector where every company worked that way—where it was all Mondragons and no Amazons—we could have a prosperous modern economy without workplace authoritarianism and labor exploitation.
One reason cooperatives are rare under capitalism is that even relatively well-off workers who could pool their resources to start a business would be making a risky bet. It’s not rational for people with very limited resources to put all their financial eggs in the single basket of a venture that could go belly-up and leave them with nothing. Apologists for capitalism conclude that capitalist employment relations are morally innocent and mutually beneficial. Capitalists assume the risk and get the power, while workers surrender their power but get the security of a biweekly paycheck. We think that a better society would offer workers better options than the choice between economic insecurity and economic oppression.
In our vision of socialism, a large state sector provides universal public services such as education and healthcare, while a regulated market sector composed of democratic, worker-controlled firms produces ordinary goods and services in response to consumer demand. This means that workers do not have to risk their personal savings; public banks finance the companies, which must pay their members regular wages that meet minimum benchmarks. Worker-members also share any profits remaining after wages and other obligations have been paid.
Our model retains markets because prices, competition, and consumer choice solve real coordination problems. But it rejects capitalism on egalitarian and democratic grounds: A dynamic economy doesn’t require a separate class of owners with authority over production, investment, and the lives of ordinary workers.
This is no utopia. It wouldn’t automatically eliminate all forms of inequality, and it certainly wouldn’t eliminate all sources of political conflict. It would, however, be the first dominant form of human social organization since the Neolithic Revolution that did not divide society into a class of subordinated producers and a class of rulers living off the fruits of those producers’ labor. That’s the North Star that past generations of socialists understood themselves to be striving toward. It’s the vision that many of them died for, whether killed by strikebreaking Pinkertons or fighting as internationalist volunteers in the Spanish Civil War. We still think humanity has a chance to achieve that future.
DSA founder Michael Harrington used to say that radicals had to “walk a perilous tightrope.” We had to “be true to the socialist vision of a new society” and also “bring that vision into contact with the actual movements fighting not to transform the system, but to gain some little increment of dignity or even just a piece of bread.”
Harrington is not often invoked in DSA circles nowadays, but almost every socialist in the country is still trying to walk that tightrope, judging reforms both by the relief they bring and by the strength they give working people to fight for more. Universal healthcare would weaken workers’ dependence on employers for medical coverage. More public housing would reduce tenants’ dependence on private landlords. Stronger unions would give workers more power over their jobs. But turning these gains into steps toward socialism requires organizing and political agitation. That transformation won’t follow automatically from a popular mayor or a well-run sanitation department.
The New York Post cover was meant to be a warning about the society that Mamdani wants to build. We owe its readers a clearer picture of that society than a hammer and sickle can provide.
