https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.title: I Am Yusuf, My Father
https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.author: Mahmoud Darwish
https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.text:
I Am Yusuf, My Father
I am Yusuf, my father. My brothers do not love me,
Father, do not want me among them. They attack me,
pelting me with stones and words. They want me to
die, that they may say my eulogy. In my face they’ve
shut your door, and from the field they’ve driven me.
They’ve poisoned my grapes, Father. They’ve smashed
my playthings, Father. When the breeze blew and
ruffled my hair, jealous, they rose up against me, and
against you. But what have I done to them, Father?
Butterflies alighted on my shoulders, ears of grain
bent toward me, birds perched upon my hands. So
what have I done, Father? Why me? You named me
Yusuf, and they cast me into the well, but blamed the
wolf. The wolf is more merciful than my brothers…
oh, my father! Did I wrong anyone when I said that:
I saw eleven stars, saw the sun, and the moon, saw
them prostrate before me?
(Translated from the Arabic by Barbara Romaine)

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Rethinking the Early History of North America
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Ned Blackhawk
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Zones of Encounter
Rethinking the early history of North America
Rethinking the Early History of North America
Peter Mancall’s new book reframes the history of the American continent as a zone of encounters between Native peoples, European empires, and African societies.
On October 12, 1992, the commemorations for the 500th anniversary of Columbus’s landfall were uneven. Urban gatherings were moderately sized, but the mood was often less than celebratory. In Columbus, Ohio, the city’s $95 million floral and garden exposition drew roughly half the expected number of visitors. In Berkeley, California, the city defiantly reclaimed the date as Indigenous People’s Day, while in Nevada, an antinuclear gathering took place at a US Department of Energy test site, co-organized by Western Shoshone activists. Few festive events marked the quincentenary; fewer still generated national attention. By contrast, a century earlier, the 400th anniversary of Columbus’s arrival served as an occasion to celebrate—so much so that one of the country’s largest fairs ever was held in its honor, Chicago’s Columbian Exposition. But not so in 1992, when Columbus Day largely came and went.
Another date that has seen a dramatic shift in how it has been memorialized is 1776. Synonymous with the founding of the United States, 1776 has been treated by generations of Americans as part of a broader civilizational story: the westward expansion of European peoples, institutions, and political traditions. Within that framework, national commemorations form essential chapters in a single narrative linking European arrival to nationhood, thus blurring the distinction between the history of Europeans in what would become North America and the history of the United States itself.
Books in review
Contested Continent: The Struggle for North America, c. 1000-1680
Buy this book
But over the past 40 or so years, a remarkable shift has occurred. More recent interpretations attempt to disentangle the history of colonization from that of the US Constitution. In this view, the United States is understood less as the political expression of European settlement than as a particular constitutional project: one grounded in republican government, in the institutions and philosophies articulated in the Declaration and then codified in the Constitution. Such interpretations do not deny the centrality of European colonization to the nation; rather, they critically reexamine North American and US history to foreground the peoples excluded, displaced, or subordinated by it. Native nations, enslaved Africans, and non-Anglo populations claimed as well as rejected the United States. In this interpretive framework, the history of the United States is not reducible to the history of Europeans in North America, even if European settlement formed its precondition.
The 12-hour PBS series The American Revolution reflects this interpretive shift. Its opening episodes foreground historians of Native America, seeking to widen the traditional narrative beyond a familiar story of colonial resistance to Britain. In doing so, the series implicitly asks whether 1776 should be remembered primarily as the triumph of a particular people in its struggle toward self-government, or as the beginning of a contingent experiment in such government. With more than half a dozen historians of Native America foregrounding the latter, the series details how the republic was founded, witnessed, and carried forward by a range of peoples and perspectives—peoples and perspectives that became more diverse with continental expansion.
Into this interpretive fray comes the latest offering in the venerable Oxford History of the United States, a now 10-volume series that, in the words of its publisher, “blends social, political, economic, cultural, diplomatic, and military history into coherent and vividly written narrative.” Initiated under the coeditorship of C. Vann Woodward and Richard Hofstadter in the 1960s, the series has become in many ways the Cadillac of US historical production: tomes written by master craftsmen without a female or minority author among them (yet). The books are not necessarily flashy but instead reflect the boxy and somewhat stodgy assumptions of the postwar historiography from which the series was born: sweeping national narratives organized around the development of the United States as a political, constitutional, and national project.
Peter Mancall’s Contested Continent joins these celebrated studies while also subtly unsettling the framework on which the series was built. Covering the period from 1000 to 1680, Mancall’s book offers the broadest chronological and geographic coverage of any of the volumes to date, stretching across a vast Atlantic world that encompasses Native peoples, European empires, African societies, and the unstable zones of encounter connecting them. Rather than treating the United States as the inevitable center of the narrative, Mancall uses these landscapes to frame a history in continental rather than national terms: a far-reaching “struggle for North America.”
That shift in scale and perspective mirrors the broader changes in historical interpretation that are now shaping commemorative debates. Earlier volumes in the series generally operated within the gravitational pull of the nation-state. Their organizing assumption was that US history could be narrated as the development of a single political society that moved, however unevenly and even hypocritically, toward national consolidation. Mancall’s study instead reflects the growing influence of Atlantic history, Native history, and borderlands scholarship, all of which have challenged nation-centered narratives. Such studies emphasize movement, contingency, competing sovereignty, and the permeability of imperial borders. The result is a history less concerned with national origins than with the larger continental and imperial processes out of which the United States emerged.
In so doing, Mancall draws on a remarkable range of sources, an impressive command of the field, and a clear narrative style. Unlike many comparable works, Contested Continent is exceedingly well referenced. Sources are used so extensively that Mancall reveals how laborious an undertaking it is to tackle this bewildering, not exactly global, not exactly continental, not exactly national history—a notoriously vast undertaking that ranges across geographies, times, and climes. Nowhere do eventual national borders and boundaries offer analytical comfort.
To give structure to this seemingly boundless inquiry, Mancall leans on the political constructions and material limits of the time—charting the development of European empires across the natural limits that land and sea then imposed for the movement of peoples, flora, and fauna. Starting with the introduction of maize in Native America, and then venturing to the Nordic expansions across the North Atlantic before settling into the more familiar Atlantic empires, Contested Continent captures the forces of technological and human movement that wove together the four continents that became forever conjoined after 1492. This Atlantic world has defined the modern era. Its histories of exploration, settlement, missionization, plantation economics, and racial formation generated the eventual origins of what would become North America and the United States, doing so empire by empire, peoples by peoples, and ultimately death by death.
While its nearly 700-page narrative doesn’t reach 1776, Contested Continent illuminates the tensions between writing the history of the Atlantic world and attempting to connect that project to national history. Notably, the 400-year history of North America before 1492 is condensed into a single chapter. By contrast, Columbus receives such extended coverage in the second chapter that readers might forget Mancall’s earlier insistence that American history extends deep into the pre-Columbian world. Twenty pages aim to yet again reinterpret the famous mariner whose 1493 letter saw quick publication “in Strasbourg, Valladolid, Florence, Heidelberg, Augsburg, Nuremberg, Venice, Pavia, Lübeck, Ferrara, Bologna, Burgos, Brescia, and Milan, as well as continuing to appear in printers’ works from Rome and Basel.” The first European images of the Western Hemisphere also accompanied his writings, several of which are included to illustrate the seismic recalibrations unleashed after his first voyage. Although Columbus may no longer be celebrated as the “discoverer” of North America, Contested Continent squarely positions him as a central hand in writing the resulting history.
Though brief, the book’s opening chapter does set the analytical framework for interrogating the more traditional national histories that follow. One of Mancall’s most significant methodological moves is that he develops the book’s narrative within a frame of confrontation and conflict. Violence, gritty and repugnant, is a central if not defining force in Contested Continent.
If you’re unfamiliar with the loss of life after 1492, brace yourself. Taking a less deterministic and epidemiological perspective than Jared Diamond does in Guns, Germs, and Steel, Mancall examines European expeditions alongside studies of Indigenous history and culture. Chilling conclusions abound: From the Andes to the St. Lawrence and from Puerto Rico to the Mississippi, European explorers rushed across the hemisphere with a ferocity often forgotten by subsequent historians, particularly those in the United States. In this sense, Contested Continent stands apart from the other volumes in the Oxford series—despite many calls to broaden US history, too few view that history apart from its eventual or current territorial form. By immersing the reader in a nearly global history of the post-Columbian world, Contested Continent reveals the ubiquitous violence and suffering at its core.
Although it may be surprising to those who were raised on the celebratory Cold War version of US history, contemporaneous studies of early America remain as sobering as they are compelling. Slavery, Indigenous holocaust, and violent social relations characterize works in the field, especially those on the 17th-century world of exploration, settlement, and fracture. Several of Mancall’s concluding chapter titles convey such an emphasis—for example, “Enslavement” and “An Empire for Extraction.”
A second analytical contribution of Contested Continent lies in its treatment of imperial governance as inseparable from the intellectual, political, and legal resistance that it provoked. While specialists can point to comparable works, Mancall assembles hundreds of discrete studies into broader forms and then keeps on going, both chronologically and interpretively. By synthesizing the historical literature in this way, he demonstrates how instantly European imperialism became not only a global phenomenon but also a governing project formed in the face of open and reasoned resistance. Close studies of the writings of the Andean author Guamán Poma de Ayala, the Mexica scribes of the Florentine Codex, and (most indelibly) the 16th-century works of Bartolomé de Las Casas cement this effort, offering vivid contemporary accounts of European expansion and, ultimately, genocide. “To Las Casas,” Mancall observes, “writing a history was a form of bearing witness.” His Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies was among the 43 volumes published in Seville alone by 1552. The everyday ubiquity of the printing revolution, Mancall notes, became one of 1492’s most immediate legacies: “Once printers started spreading stories about the Western Hemisphere, they never stopped.” Las Casas’s text “would soon become the most influential European published work about the Western Hemisphere since the 1493 publication of Columbus.”
Read together, these anti-colonial writings—old and new—recast the violence of conquest not as an unfortunate by-product of cultural collision but as the result of deliberate choices made by imperial powers in full view of contemporary critique. As Greg Grandin has similarly suggested in America, América, Las Casas’s writings and his conversion from colonizer to priest and from participant to advocate offered what should be understood as the first condemnation of global colonialism. Such condemnation both preceded English colonization and was understood across Europe.
Another fierce critic of this emerging order was Guamán Poma. As he toured the Viceroyalty of Peru, Mancall writes, Guamán Poma was inspired to offer a bracing account of “the tragedy that had unfolded over the course of his own life.” Like Las Casas, he had witnessed cruelties and indignities. In his eventual but long-unpublished epic work, El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno (The First New Chronicle and Good Government), Guamán Poma lamented how “all the demons of hell had come forth in order to trouble the poor of Jesus Christ.” Andean leaders were routinely assaulted, whipped, beaten, and hanged. Urbanization and exile followed: Lima had become “full of Indians who had abandoned their communities and African slaves who had escaped from their masters and become servants, even officials.” Such heterogeneity took a particular toll on Indigenous women, often forced into economies of sexual exploitation that filled the vacuum left in the conquest’s wake. Violence shaped the foundations of the family as Indigenous women became, in Guamán Poma’s words, “loaded down with mestizo and mulatto children.” One wonders when the sexual violence against Indigenous women so evident on these pages will find a more central place in the history of the Americas.
Mancall ultimately carries the analytical frames of imperialism, violence, and disruption into the English colonial world, connecting the national narrative to the continental, imperial, and even interpersonal dynamics that produced it. In English plantation societies, indentured servants drawn from colonies closer to home, such as Ireland, supplied much of the earliest generations of laborers. From Virginia to Barbados, the demand in Europe inspired the introduction of new export products, particularly tobacco and sugar. Harsh disciplinary regimes followed. “I have seen such cruelty there done to Servants, as I did not think one Christian could have done to another,” reported an early writer on Irish laborers in Barbados. By 1660, Mancall writes, sugar had so revolutionized the island’s economy that English leaders “concluded that they could not attract sufficient indentured labor across Britain’s current colonies. The most reliable source of labor, the king believed, was captive Africans.” Only after 1492, then, did institutions of human enslavement begin to structure North America and the United States thereafter.
Deftly capturing large-scale economic and social dynamics, Mancall also remains attentive to everyday forms of resistance, particularly in the late 1600s, when multiple imperial regimes either fell or were challenged by social and anti-colonial revolts. He ends with the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 and highlights the fractures of empires rather than their totalizing outcomes. By 1680, along the Rio Grande, dozens of Pueblo Indian villages had endured generations of Spanish violence, religious persecution, and labor drafts. What at the time were—and still remain today—the oldest continually inhabited human societies in what would become the United States, Pueblo nations organized and revolted against the yoke of colonization, destroying Spanish colonial churches, symbols, and archives. It is within this dialectical encounter between cultures and communities that Mancall locates what would become North America: “Nowadays,” he writes, “scholars recognize that, even if most of the written evidence emphasized Europeans’ actions, Indigenous Americans and Africans, even those brutalized by enslavement, retained agency as well.” However violent, however fractious and agonistic, “Indigenous, Africans, and Europeans together created a new world.”
In certain respects, Contested Continent perfectly prepares the way for the rediscovery of this knowledge and a new American history to be written thereafter. Throughout his sweeping account, Mancall demonstrates that the continent was never a wilderness awaiting European discovery. It was a world of competing sovereignties, economies, and cosmologies that Europeans entered into unevenly and often precariously. By tracing the contingencies of conquest, diplomacy, migration, and survivance across the continent, he helps challenge the triumphalist narratives that still frame the United States as the inevitable product of an Anglo-American political tradition alone. In this way, Contested Continent’s strongest contribution lies less in proposing a revised commemorative framework than in revealing the instability of older ones.

At the same time, the book stops short of fully resolving the problem it so clearly identifies: If the North American continent and, with it, the republic that emerged rely on competing historical claims, then the question is not merely how historians recover neglected voices but also how those recoveries intervene in the broader scholarly and public conversations. Contested Continent gestures toward this challenge without entirely articulating what a rediscovered national story might finally look like. After chronicling more than 600 years of history, perhaps Mancall felt that he had covered enough, but he concludes somewhat abruptly in 1680, thereby ceding much of the telling of this story to the older volumes in the series. Because the interventions of Contested Continent are so persuasive, the book gives rise to the question of what a new history of the United States that begins with Mancall’s volume might look like—and it also raises the question of whether, in fact, the Oxford series, which began publishing in 1982, might be in need of a reset.
What would be the central themes and preoccupations of this new series of US histories? First, there would be a shift away from viewing the United States as a linear extension of European settlement and republican ideology and toward a more rigorous understanding of North America as a site of encounter among many peoples whose collective interactions shaped the continent’s subsequent development. Native nations, enslaved Africans, imperial rivals, missionaries, merchants, and migrants would no longer be peripheral actors in this new rendering of American history. Instead, they would be constitutive agents initiating the processes from which the nation emerged.
Second, there would be a more sustained focus on the contested nature of sovereignty in the development of the United States, thereby correcting the current, overly familiar accounts of state formation that portray US expansion as coherent, consensual, or inevitable. Empires and nations would be front and center, but so too would be the many who challenged and resisted them: local, Native, colonial, African American, all engaged in their own ongoing experiments in government.
Finally, this new account of US history would integrate the authoritarian dynamics of empire into the story of American modernity itself. Imprinted upon the globe in so many places—from the Philippines to Puerto Rico, Alaska to Hawai’i—unbridled US authority has governed millions of non-subject populations, often through force. Rooted in the suppression of Native resistance, the legacies of such anti-democratic practices are becoming more evident, and they inform current efforts to extend US authority into new colonial settings, from Venezuela to Greenland.
Histories of struggle and survival thus become essential means through which to understand our modern American life. Deep, immersive histories like Mancall’s offer contrasts with those that view modernity as the achievement of a unified liberal republic or the fulfillment of Enlightenment philosophies and capitalist economics.
Such a rediscovered American history would not dissolve the national history into fragmentation. Instead, it would recast the nation as a perpetually unfinished project, a “more perfect union” whose legitimacy depends on recognizing the many peoples who have sustained that experiment over time. In this light, the uneasy commemorations of the recent past would reveal less a collapse of national mythologies than a transformation in historical consciousness. The celebratory confidence that animated the Columbian Exposition of 1893 was undergirded by a presumption that establishing the nation was itself the accomplishment of progress, rather than marking these founding moments as the birth of experiments whose causes and consequences were yet to be determined.
Ultimately, Contested Continent suggests that moments of “discovery” and “founding” should not lend themselves easily to uncritical celebration. The American Revolution gave rise to an unprecedented experiment in government in North America, an experiment that has yielded many successes worth celebrating: the formal abolition of human enslavement, the extension of political rights regardless of gender, and the tenuous but exceptional, government-to-government relationship that exists between Native nations and the United States.
Perhaps, in the end, new histories, textbooks, and syntheses may reveal how the nation’s significant achievements did not emerge from the presumed certainty or righteousness of its beginnings, but from the continuing struggle to engage in that experiment. A global and Indigenous cast has played an immense historical role in that experiment, doing so in order to pursue visions of happiness and the good on a continent that many have long called home.

The Political Power of Seniors
In places like Wisconsin, campaigns can’t win without seniors. They are the second-largest, fastest-growing, and most reliable group of voters.
It feels so good to see: college students marching to the polls after their campus voting sites were shut down, young men and women dancing at El-Sayed’s watch party, 18-year-olds taking selfies with “Just Voted” stickers.
This midterm election, young voters swung dramatically toward more progressive candidates, helping fuel the midterm sweep. But young and first-time voters make up a critical but small portion of the electorate, with voters under 30 casting only one in 10 votes.
A much slower, less dramatic but promising trend is emerging among the most reliable voters in the country—senior citizens. Seniors always show up. Two out of three seniors vote in midterms, and even more vote in presidential elections. And the much-maligned “boomers” have been steadily trending left since 2016.
Progressives shouldn’t be wary of seniors. On the contrary, they should seek them out, explicitly lay out a progressive senior agenda, and engage them in their campaigns.
I’ve spent the last three years organizing with older adults in Wisconsin. I’ve sat in community meetings, talked with them in their homes, shared meals at church, and had hundreds of conversations about aging, caregiving, and politics. Here’s what I’ve learned: For candidates who want to put people over corporations, transform healthcare, fund public transportation, and raise wages for working people—especially care workers—seniors will help lead the way.
In places like Wisconsin, campaigns can’t win without seniors. They are the second-largest, fastest-growing, and most reliable group of voters. That’s serious political power.
Every election cycle, progressives work hard to generate new voters, engage young people, and promote new leaders and voices. This is necessary and smart. Yet if candidates and campaigns aren’t engaging seniors on the issues that matter most to them, in most times and places, it won’t be enough.
Wisconsin saw this during the Democratic primary this year. Progressive Francesca Hong was making headlines by leading in the polls. But a dramatic last-minute shift narrowly handed David Crowley the win. Had the polls failed again?
The polls weren’t wrong so much as misunderstood. Wisconsin’s gold standard, the Marquette Law School Poll, accurately measured Hong’s support but also identified the race’s wild card: a large share of undecided voters.
The poll found that 46 percent of voters age 60 and older remained undecided less than two weeks before the Democratic primary. In other words, seniors decided that primary at the last minute.
I believe Hong could have won their votes, but her message hadn’t reached them. As one senior voter told me: “The only thing I know about her is from the negative TV ads her opponents are running.”
Hong ran an inspiring campaign, and she was the first candidate to commit to the Small Town and Rural Seniors (STARS) candidate forum in July. For an hour, gubernatorial candidates answered questions from the elders who organized the event: What would you do about the caregiver shortage in our state? How would you support transportation for seniors in rural areas? How can we protect seniors from online and phone scammers?
Seniors in attendance sat in a tight semicircle around Hong and the other candidates, listening intently. As rural seniors posed questions, Hong’s answers became stronger, clearer, and more confident. You could see her realize she didn’t need to persuade people to support her progressive agenda; she needed to show them she could deliver it.
When asked about a manufactured homes bill of rights midway through the forum, she stated with conviction that she aimed to make Wisconsin hostile to private equity. The 70-to-80-year-olds in the room interrupted her with applause.
Hong’s responses impressed many seniors in that room. But Wisconsin has over a million seniors, hundreds of thousands of whom hadn’t heard her message.
When senior voters hear about—and are included in—progressive politics, they listen. In the Texas Senate race, voters 65 and older moved away from Trump and toward Talarico by nine points. It wasn’t the biggest swing in the midterm elections, but in a state where seniors make up 29 percent of voters, that’s a critical number of votes.
Back in Wisconsin, Representative-elect Rebecca Cooke’s campaign is a good example. She expanded her appeal in Wisconsin’s rural Third Congressional District by making aging with dignity a priority in her campaign, helping her seal her victory on election night. I suspect we’ll see this slow but steady senior impact everywhere as we continue to crunch the numbers from the midterms.

The seniors I organize with have been proving for years that elevating senior issues can move local elections, especially in rural areas. They have been organizing there to protect publicly owned nursing homes from sale to private buyers. Many have turned these local organizing campaigns into electoral victories. This spring, Sauk County seniors helped recruit candidates who opposed selling their county nursing home and won eight of nine contested races. In Lincoln County, nursing home supporters were inspired to run for office and won.
When candidates address senior issues, seniors turn out. And it’s not just nursing homes. In rural Walworth County, seniors have won investments in public transportation and are leading the charge for multigenerational care (senior care and childcare). Others are campaigning for reforms to protect manufactured housing from private-equity predators. These, too, can be winning issues for campaigns.
Seniors may or may not call themselves progressive, but the issues they care about and the solutions they favor often are. Seniors are strong proponents of government investment, even across party lines.
A 2024 Hart Research poll found that older voters in Wisconsin believe the government should do more to ensure access to quality, affordable long-term care. Majorities of Democrats, independents, and Republicans support policies including higher wages to attract and retain long-term care workers in smaller towns and rural communities, and expanded access to Medicaid.
I’ve learned a lot working with senior citizens. My assumptions have been challenged, and I’ve become clear-eyed that they are an important, even crucial, part of a progressive coalition. And perhaps most importantly, they are eager to hear from us.
The bottom line: Candidates who directly engage seniors and support a progressive senior agenda will win votes, and in aging states like Wisconsin, Michigan, and beyond, senior votes can push them over the finish line.

The Voters Who Saved Democracy Are Being Written Out of the Story
The media downplayed the importance of Black voters for Democratic victories.
Here are some media headlines and hot takes after last week’s Democratic midterm victories. See if you can catch what’s missing from their framing.
First, CNN ran an exit-poll explainer under the headline “Women, young voters and independents: See where Democrats made inroads.” Time said the “distinct gains came from young, rural, and Hispanic voters.” The Washington Post told readers, “Democrats have a surprising group of voters to thank”: namely, rural voters in Republican strongholds. And Reuters reported, “Latinos drive Democratic gains.”
While those shifts were real, and the shift among Latinos was critical to Democratic fortunes in Texas, what each outlet neglected to mention is the centrality of Black voters to the party’s wins. And yet, these voters were the most crucial part of the story.
In Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina, Ohio, Michigan, and Mississippi—where Scott Colom appears set to become the first Black senator since Reconstruction—only the Black vote secured Democratic victories and flipped the Senate. In each of those states, exit polls show that white voters supported Republicans and would have gladly kept the chamber in GOP hands.
Even in Texas, although Latinos are the largest group of voters of color, at 25 percent of the total, with only 72 percent voting for James Talarico, and only 39 percent of white voters doing so, he needed the 12 percent of the electorate that was Black to turn out big, and they did, with 91 percent of their vote.
The extent to which the media downplayed the importance of Black voters to Democratic victories was stunning. For instance, Newsweek highlighted rural voters breaking for Democrats in South Carolina, while only noting farther down in the story that those rural voters were Black, while white rural folks mostly stayed home.
And The Washington Post, rather than crediting Black voters for Annie Andrews’s win there, ran a graphic highlighting the “significant improvements” Democrats made with less-educated whites, as if to suggest that had powered her victory. But this “improvement” moved these only voters from a 42-point Republican margin to a 21-point margin—hardly the key to Andrews’s victory, since this group still overwhelmingly rejected her.
The New York Times followed the same pattern, running a story proclaiming “White, Working-Class Voters Shifted Left,” noting, almost as an afterthought, that they still rejected Democrats by nearly 20 points.
And it wasn’t only in Senate races where the Black vote made the difference. In House races, white voters mostly supported Republicans nationally, meaning that here too, African American voters led the way, however much the media appears to have missed it.
This is no minor mistake, but rather anti-Blackness that refuses to give credit where it’s due. To the political press, those who drift away and come back are a story. Those who never left are like humidity in New Orleans, always there and not worth a headline. That tendency punishes Black Americans for being right first, seeing what Trumpism was in 2016, and voting against it consistently for a decade.
And when we see Black movement in the numbers, as with increased turnout, they still struggle to get credit. During an interview in which he was crediting every other possible constituency for the Democrats’ victories, a Vox interviewer asked Democratic political consultant David Shor about Black turnout. Only then did Shor acknowledge that the Black share of the electorate had risen four points in Georgia compared with the 2022 midterms. But even then, he immediately changed the subject back to the Latino vote in Texas, which wasn’t what the interviewer had asked about, and which also ignored the importance of Black turnout in that state.
This kind of erasure also harms those who did swing, because it hides who their allies are. Working-class whites who voted for Democrats spent years hearing that their problems were caused by “Black crime,” “DEI,” or government handouts to Black communities. In the end, they got nothing from those who offered them scapegoats without solutions. When they finally woke up, they joined a coalition that Black voters had been holding down the whole time.
Popular

But if the coverage never says so, these new arrivals may fail to realize that the people they were taught to fear are the ones who kept the door open for them. Black voters are the base of any coalition that can beat authoritarianism. Leaving that out of the story is how the right keeps working people divided.
Perhaps the most dangerous effect of erasing the importance of the Black vote is on Democratic priorities. Parties respond to stories about why they won. If the official story is that white rural voters or independents delivered the majority, the party will cater to them and, once again, treat the concerns of its most loyal voters as something that can wait.
But Black voters cannot afford to wait. In April, the Supreme Court gutted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has dismantled much of the federal civil rights apparatus, and the Justice Department’s Voting Rights Section has been hollowed out.
Restoring the Voting Rights Act is the Democratic Party’s best strategy for concretizing its gains. It won Senate seats in three (and likely four) Southern states, flipped House seats throughout the region, and held on to others, despite Republican attempts to gerrymander them away. A South where Black citizens can vote freely, in fairly drawn districts, is a South where those gains can last. And a South that is competitive for Democrats, where the promises of Reconstruction can finally be realized, is the recipe for lasting multiracial democracy.
Yes, President Trump will veto a new Voting Rights Act. But Democrats should pass it anyway, and they should make the veto a central issue in 2028.
But that won’t happen if the party believes the media framing about their victories. In state after state, Black voters didn’t just save the Democratic Party; they saved democracy. The least we owe them is the courage to tell the truth about that, and perhaps a thank you.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Bryce Covert
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The EEOC Is Failing Workers While Hunting for Discrimination Claims From White Men
Investigators are rapidly closing out claims of workplace discrimination so that they can search for the kinds of cases chair Andrea Lucas most wants to find.
Earlier this year, Sebrina, a direct-care worker in Pennsylvania who works in group homes assisting clients with disabilities with everyday tasks, was discussing a client’s medications with a coworker. When she told her coworker that one of the clients does in fact need seizure medications, despite her coworker’s claim to the contrary, the coworker called Sebrina a “bitch,” she recalled. Another time, that same coworker called her “colored.”
Sebrina, who asked to use only her first name because she’s in the middle of legal action, reported the incidents, as well as the fact that one of her clients told her that he was being abused by a different caretaker, to her boss. That’s when she was abruptly suspended. She was accused of not following instructions for a particular client, but she says she had been begging to get the relevant instructions for months to no avail. Meanwhile, the coworker who called her the slurs was simply told to apologize to her. Eventually Sebrina was fired on July 13 for, she says, failing to attend a meeting scheduled for July 18.
On June 29, Sebrina filed an inquiry with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the federal agency tasked with protecting private-sector workers from discrimination, claiming she had been illegally discriminated against. An agency investigator started looking into it on August 14. When an EEOC investigator investigates a case, they typically spend months probing whether the case has merit, soliciting the employer’s response and gathering documents to either pursue an EEOC lawsuit or help the employee do so. Instead, five days later the agency sent Sebrina a “right-to-sue” letter, which closed out the EEOC case without any investigation and left her to pursue justice in the courts. “It just happened so fast,” Sebrina said. “I wanted him to investigate.” Instead, she was on her own with no more information than when she had started.
Related Articles
Three sources within the EEOC, plus three employment lawyers who regularly bring claims to the agency, told The Nation that what Sebrina experienced is increasingly common. Their comments and statements from the agency’s chair demonstrate that under the second Trump administration, the EEOC, created by the Civil Rights Act of 1964, has focused on representing aggrieved white men and people with anti-trans complaints while shutting out those whom it has historically served. Since she was appointed to lead the EEOC by President Donald Trump, chair Andrea Lucas has increased pressure on agency staff to field far more inquiries without growing the backlog of cases, three agency sources tell The Nation. At the same time, she’s pushed them to spend disproportionate resources on her personal priorities. The combination of those factors means that more and more people are experiencing what Sebrina did: Investigators in EEOC field offices are rapidly closing out claims of workplace discrimination without thoroughly investigating them so that they can search for and sink time into the kinds of cases Lucas most wants to find.
Democrats in Congress can hold hearings and bring Lucas in to testify about her priorities, but they aren’t empowered to change agency policies. In fact, Trump just nominated Matt Zandi, who most recently served as chief of staff to Harmeet Dhillon, until recently the head of the Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division, as an EEOC commissioner, which if confirmed will give the Republican members of the commission a quorum and majority for at least two more years. It would also allow President Trump to fire the remaining Democratic commissioner, Kalpana Kotagal, as he did with the other two Democratic commissioners, while still maintaining enough members for Lucas to set the agency’s rules and agenda.
Workers get only 90 days after receiving an EEOC right-to-sue letter to file a case in court. Sebrina spent sleepless nights googling and scouring TikTok and YouTube for someone who might take her case in time. “Any and everything,” she said. Over 20 attorneys turned her down. “I cried,” she said. “My little baby saying, ‘Mom, you got to close your eyeballs or they’re going to dry.’” With just 30 days left, she decided to go pro se and try to file the paperwork in court on her own, but she had to figure out how to get the $200 filing fee waived. Her blood pressure was sky-high from the stress; her psychiatrist recently advised her to take a break to protect her mental health. “I’m just trying to stop the timer from ticking,” she said. “It’s just a lot that’s dropped on me.”
Early last year, Lucas created a list of her own personal priorities for the EEOC—including claims from people who believe they were adversely affected in the workplace by so-called diversity, equity, and inclusion programs, such as white men who believe a woman or person of color unfairly got a promotion instead of them, and claims that are “defending the biological and binary reality of sex,” such as cisgender women who feel discriminated against for sharing a bathroom with a trans woman—and told agency officials to seek out cases that lined up with them. Prior EEOC commissioners said that violated the agency’s processes and exceeded her authority. Lucas has also prioritized religious bias and national-origin discrimination against American citizens who believe a foreign-born person unfairly got an opportunity instead of them. She posted a direct-to-camera video on X.com last year soliciting complaints from anyone who is “a white male who has experienced discrimination at work.”
In response to a request for comment, an EEOC spokesperson, “Under Chair Lucas’s leadership, the EEOC continues to deliver significant results for American workers.”
The EEOC, which has a budget of just $455 million to cover the country’s 136 million private-sector employees, has always had to prioritize some complaints over others. Before Lucas became chair, however, those priorities were determined by looking at data showing what kinds of discrimination were most prevalent, an EEOC staffer with knowledge said. “Historically, people of color and women file the greatest number of charges, because they disproportionately face discrimination in the workplace,” so those complaints were prioritized (though the EEOC has always pursued discrimination claims of all kinds). Now the determination is driven by the administration’s political priorities. But the focus on white men, for example, is “not what our body of data reflects,” the EEOC employee said.
According to The New York Times, cases from white men claiming so-called reverse discrimination have been “accelerated through the process,” and the director of at least one district (the EEOC divides the country into 15 districts) told staff that such cases should be designated as deserving the highest level of resources and time. The director also said that such cases can’t be sent to mediation—a process in which the EEOC helps try to broker a settlement—and require “special permission” to dismiss. The EEOC employee I spoke with has heard from people directly involved that Lucas has fought back against staff attempts to reach settlements in these cases because she instead wants to bring litigation. Cases involving DEI and gender identity are getting extra resources, the EEOC employee said, and are all being assigned attorneys. Lucas herself has gotten far more actively involved in them than previous chairs would get in specific cases, according to the EEOC staffer with knowledge.
And yet staff told the Times that they have struggled to find complaints Lucas wants that have merit or strong evidence. That requires them to spend even more time trying to put a flimsy case together. So complaints without merit that fall into Lucas’s priorities are now supplanting other kinds with merit, the staffer with knowledge said, and staff is focusing on the demographics of who filed the complaint instead of whether the complaint itself is worthy.
In addition to being directed to find cases that Lucas wants to focus on, expectations for field staff have been raised to unrealistic levels, the EEOC employee said. Beginning October 1, Lucas directed EEOC investigators in the agency’s field offices to complete five intake appointments every day, two EEOC staffers said. An effective intake typically takes an hour and a half to two hours to complete, the staffer with knowledge said. At the same time, Lucas and Thomas Colclough, the EEOC’s director of field management, have told the directors of the agency’s field offices that anyone who walks through their office doors must be served. The change appears at least in part to be Lucas’s attempt to make it easier for white men to access the agency. Lucas herself has assured people on X.com alleging the kind of discrimination she’s focused on that they can walk into EEOC field offices and get quick responses. In one post, she said she was “aware of & working to increase our interview availability.” In another, she said she was working on ensuring that “all field offices are equally welcoming and available to walk-in appointments.” Prior to Lucas’s becoming chair, goals for the number of intakes completed each day were set by each local field office based on their capacity, and most workers had to get initial online appointments to ensure that there was enough staff capacity for each. Outside of rare instances, employees have never before been asked to do five a day, the staffer with knowledge said.
In response to a request for comment, an EEOC spokesperson said, “Chair Lucas is proud of the agency’s efforts to serve more workers by expanding intake appointments and walk-in availability. In Fiscal Year 2026, charge inquiries reached an all-time high, while charge receipts increased 11 percent—the highest level in more than a decade. These results underscore the growing demand for the EEOC’s services and the importance of Chair Lucas’s commitment to evenhanded enforcement, expanded outreach, and ensuring all American workers understand their rights under federal civil rights laws.”
All the extra time diverted to intakes is less time that staff can spend investigating inquiries and charges or developing promising cases to litigate. “People are spending so much time putting out the immediate fires,” the EEOC employee said.
Meanwhile, staffing is at a nadir. The agency received 270,000 inquiries last fiscal year, a 9 percent increase over 2024, but it had the lowest number of staff to handle that work since at least 2005. Staffing has continued to decrease this year—the agency has just 1,693 employees to police discrimination in all private workplaces, a 26 percent decrease from its peak under President Joe Biden and down by a third since a high-water mark in 2010. Just a few hundred of those employees are the investigators who both handle new inquiries and investigate them if they become actual charges.
At the same time, aggressive goals have been put in place for making sure the backlog of inquiries and charges doesn’t grow beyond a certain length, the EEOC staffer with knowledge said, even as employees are being forced to field more inquiries. That’s led to a mass closure of inquiries—in which EEOC investigators don’t even look into a complaint and simply issue a right-to-sue letter—and the neglect of complaints with merit or even the potential to make systematic change.
“Staff are closing charges in order to meet the goals, in order to keep the inventory [of pending inquiries and charges] artificially low,” the EEOC employee said. “The agency has become sort of a right-to-sue machine.”
The impact on Americans who have experienced discrimination at work has been stark. Steve Auerbach, founding attorney at the Law Office of Steven T. Auerbach, and Rachel McElroy, an attorney at the McElroy Law Firm, say that clients have received right-to-sue letters before the agency has even asked their employers for a position statement, which is typically the first step in assessing all inquiries. Charges Auerbach has filed with the agency have been closed out incredibly rapidly. “We’re looking at days, when in the past it was months, if not longer,” he said. “It was rare for me to even hear back for six months.” One inquiry that he filed in mid-June was issued a right-to-sue letter 18 days later; another filed in early August got one in just eight days. McElroy has similarly seen clients get right-to-sue letters in a matter of weeks, while a previous case waited years.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Beginning last year, Nathan Simmons, an attorney at Kaplan Law Firm, would file an inquiry only to receive an e-mail demanding more information—information that had already been included in his inquiry on behalf of his client. The agency has sometimes ignored his response and then immediately issued a right-to-sue letter. “The new policy completely undermines the purpose of the EEOC,” he said.
“I can’t rely on them to do their job right now,” Auerbach said of the EEOC. And, he said, it’s happening even to cases that appear to have merit. “I’m seeing it in instances where it’s both clear-cut and a pretty good case,” he added. McElroy agreed that the cases getting closed out are surprising. “They’re just your average EEOC charges,” she said.
Both Auerbach and McElroy have simultaneously experienced a huge increase in calls from workers seeking legal help after being quickly issued a right-to-sue letter by the agency—the week we spoke, McElroy had gotten three, when before she would only get such calls “every once in a while.” Auerbach called it “frightening” given that workers only get 90 days to file a lawsuit after getting such a letter.
Even when the EEOC decides not to take a case, its investigation is a crucial component of getting justice for employees. Auerbach noted that he’s reluctant to file a lawsuit without having heard the employer’s side of the story—something the agency is skipping over now as it scrambles to issue right-to-sue letters. “I’m counting on that to see if this is a meritorious claim, and I’m being deprived of that,” he said. “Not every dispute belongs in front of a federal jury.” Meanwhile, without the agency’s having done any investigation of a charge, attorneys must compile all the necessary documents and evidence before the 90-day window closes, which is not always possible.
It’s already difficult for workers to find an employment lawyer to take a case like this. First, there just aren’t enough of them. “A lot of the big billboard attorneys, they’re personal injury attorneys and medical malpractice attorneys,” McElroy pointed out. There are far fewer lawyers who take civil rights cases, and those that exist can only take on so many cases at a time. Many won’t respond to every call that comes into their office.
Many workers also can’t afford to take their employers to court on their own, even if they can find lawyers. Few workers who represent themselves get a favorable ruling. If the EEOC isn’t even looking into whether to pursue their cases itself, they may end up with no recourse in a worthy case. “To be shut out and ignored by the agency that’s congressionally tasked with listening to them,” Auerbach said, “it’s insult to injury.”
“Workers that are most in need of the agency’s services can’t in fact benefit from those services and get left behind,” the EEOC employee said. “If you have no actual way to enforce your civil rights, are they meaningful?”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/11/f.title: Feds Characterize Trump As Mercurial King In Latest Bid to End Congestion Pricing
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/11/f.author: Dave Colon
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/11/f.text:
New court, same losing argument.
The federal Department of Transportation continues to insist that the president and his agencies can do whatever they want, whenever they want, as the Trump administration tries without success to destroy congestion pricing in New York City.
In June, U.S. DOT appealed Judge Lewis Liman’s March decision in favor of the MTA, which sued the federal government over President Trump’s attempt to kill the Manhattan toll. In their brief, the feds asked court, not for the first time, to endorse the idea that Trump’s whims, rather that the law, have the final say over his government’s actions.
The brief contained two main arguments. The first, which will be familiar to longtime followers of this increasingly absurd legal saga, is that Liman never had the authority to hear the MTA’s lawsuit because it involves a dispute over a financial contract. If that were true, the entire case should have been heard by the smaller and more specialized Court of Federal Claims, not the larger and more general Article III court system.
The second and newer argument is similar to what the Trump administration argued in lower court: that the FHWA can do whatever it wants at any time. But instead of arguing that the president is a de facto sovereign who enjoys unlimited powers, Department of Justice attorneys argued that the FHWA can simply change its mind at any time.
“[E]ven if the Agreement were considered in [Administrative Procedure Act] terms — not as a contract but as a ‘regulatory grant of approval to build toll infrastructure on a federal aid highway,’ or perhaps as a similar agency action granting a benefit or establishing a federal program—the agency would have the inherent power to reconsider and revoke it,” the attorneys wrote.
The argument is consistent with the federal government’s longstanding position from the moment President Donald Trump kicked off his attempt to kill congestion pricing: that the president has inherent king-like powers to do whatever he likes. After Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy sent his first letter demanding New York end the toll in February 2025, Trump dubbed himself the King of New York. Ever since, the rest of the federal machinery has scrambled to stand up his argument.
Last January, in a hearing before Judge Liman, DOJ lawyer Eric Hamilton argued unconvincingly that the president and his agents possessed an absolute power to cancel contracts or agreements the federal government signs with other parties. Liman described that argument as “breathtaking” and “wrong.”
So the brightest legal minds still willing to work for the Department of Justice tried once more to convince the judiciary that American law allows the federal government to be an unreliable partner. Instead of insisting that the president can cancel contracts, DOJ lawyers argued that federal agencies can just change their mind about previous approvals. “The government must be empowered to adjust to changing circumstances or to changed priorities,” they wrote.
The problem with the new argument, as one legal expert pointed out, is the very same problem that tripped up Duffy when he tried to end congestion pricing: the agreement that authorized congestion pricing, the Value Pricing Pilot Program, lacks a kill switch and the overall law authorizing the program lacks a “revoke whenever you want” clause. 
Among the cases the federal government cited as precedent was California Sea Urchin Commission v. Bean, which involved a dispute over sea otter relocation program. That program followed an agreement with a specific clause that allowed the program to end under certain conditions — an arrangement found nowhere in the VPPP.
“It’s a stretch to say they have any inherent authority just to change their mind,” said NYU law professor Roderick Hills, Jr. “I don’t know of any case that said an agency can just always change its mind, regardless of the statute under which the initial decision was made, regardless of the correctness of the original decision.”
Hills said that precedent does allow for an agency to reverse itself if it can prove that it authorized a program based on an actual error. But since the FHWA didn’t rely on Duffy’s very first argument — which is that the VPPP never actually authorized cordon pricing — Hills was perplexed as to why the government cited case law that’s hinges so strongly on human error.
“Almost all the cases they cite involve an initial agency decision that was a mistake, or that the agency claimed was a mistake,” he said. “Since they don’t claim or identify any error that was made in the initial decision here, it’s hard to see how they can claim they have power to correct an error that they don’t indicate. How can you correct an error that doesn’t exist?” 
The argument is also out of place because the federal government didn’t raise it when the MTA sued the FHWA in district court. A district court will hear all sorts of weird legal arguments that a plaintiff or defendant puts forward. But at the appeals court level, judges only consider whether there the lower court’s ruling committed a legal error. A requirement known as “appellate preservation” requires a party in a suit raise the specific issue if it wants to be able to raise it on appeal.
Since the government never suggested in the lower court that it ordered an end to congestion pricing because a federal agency can just change its mind, the judges hearing the case could decide to ignore the argument entirely.
“The simplest thing to do would be not to rule on the merits at all, but say on second argument, you didn’t raise it below. It’s waived,” said Hills.
Because of these discrepancies, the Second Circuit may choose to exclusively analyze the federal government’s argument that the original VPPP contract, between the MTA and the FHWA, should be reviewed by the Federal Court of Claims, which considers federal disputes over contracts for money. Liman rejected that argument in the lower court.
There is no strong evidence that shows the dispute over congestion pricing is a contractual dispute over money. Furthermore, the MTA has been levying the tolls for nearly two years now and New York City has yet to fall. Both of these elements bode well for the MTA and the future of congestion pricing.
“Sean Duffy is the one who’s trying to change the status quo,” said Hills. “For almost two years, the MTA has been chugging along, and Sean Duffy’s been on the sideline saying, ‘Judge, stop that guy.’ In general, judges, like everybody else, don’t like to get involved with something unless there’s a good reason to get involved and change the status quo. 
Hills continued: “In this case, the legal arguments are weak, and the policy here seems fine. The Second Circuit has to hear the case. They have mandatory review, so they’ll have to say something, but after two 100-page opinions, I imagine that they won’t think they need to say a whole bunch.”

What Ballot Measures Told Us About America
Last week’s votes on taxing billionaires, abortion and trans rights, and divestment from Israel offer a window into the American electorate’s political mood.
The blue tidal wave that swept congressional and local elections around the country is leaving a new political landscape in its wake. The generational scope of Democratic wins and unprecedented success of democratic socialist candidates notwithstanding, the president’s party almost always loses midterm elections, often by wide margins. How much do the election results reflect a shift in society’s politics, and how much do they reflect an extreme version of the standard two-party pendulum swing? And more importantly, where are the opportunities to push organizing to new horizons in this new terrain?
The results of ballot initiative votes are especially useful in analyzing the political realities on the ground. Ballot measures present a simple yes-or-no choice on a piece of legislation, making them excellent barometers of public sentiment. Between state and local ballots, Americans vote on hundreds of initiatives every cycle. Coming out of Election Day 2026, three ballot measures demand particular attention.
In California, a pioneering attempt to tax billionaires’ wealth to fund the hollowed-out health care system was drowned in almost $400 million in billionaire spending. Missouri saw the first Republican attempt to overturn abortion rights that were previously won at the ballot by packaging the rollback with transphobia; it was resoundingly defeated. And a whopping three-quarters of voters in Providence approved a measure to divest from countries and companies committing severe human rights abuses, making Rhode Island’s capital the largest US city to approve divestment from Israel.
Not Yet Taxing Billionaires in California
The California Billionaire Tax was as novel a proposition as it was consequential. Trump’s 2025 “One Big Beautiful Bill” made major cuts to Medicaid, with major coverage restrictions scheduled to take effect after the midterms, in January 2027. The cuts are expected to leave millions without insurance and put health care facilities at risk of closure. Billionaires’ fortunes have skyrocketed by hundreds of billions of dollars more since the bill’s passage.
In California, a union of hospital and health care workers put two and two together. In collaboration with leading progressive economists, the Service Employees International Union–United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW) proposed a first-of-its-kind, one-time 5 percent wealth tax on the two hundred–odd billionaires living in California. The union projected that it would raise roughly $100 billion. Ninety percent of the revenue was earmarked for health care, with the remainder for education, food assistance, and administration.
Proposition 40, as it was designated once it qualified for the ballot, was written to be applicable to billionaires residing in the state on January 1, 2026, anticipating the capital flight argument that billionaires would simply move out. With the mind-boggling amounts of money billionaires have been making in recent years, the 5 percent wealth tax would still have left California’s billionaires vastly wealthier than they were just a year ago, while the state’s health care system would avoid disaster. Seems like common sense — unless you’re a billionaire who thinks taxation is oppression.
Yet the billionaires were not the only ones opposed to Proposition 40. Labor was mostly aligned behind UHW in the push, including the California Labor Federation, Teamsters California, and California Nurses Association. But it wasn’t unanimous: the California Teachers Association and the State Building and Construction Trades Council of California opposed. SEIU California remained neutral, despite Proposition 40 being proposed by one of its largest locals. Some prominent progressive advocacy groups like Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California and the NAACP California/Hawaii State Conference joined unlikely forces with the likes of Peter Thiel against the billionaire tax.
The apparent split in left forces, particularly the elements of labor that opposed the billionaire tax, was prominently featured in ads from Building a Better California, a billionaire-backed organization opposing Proposition 40.
Many of Building a Better California’s attacks were focused on UHW president Dave Regan, who was on the receiving end of a litany of allegations, including resurfaced claims he used intimidation tactics in political negotiations seventeen years ago — all of which Regan frames as a transparent smear campaign aimed at distracting from the issue at hand.
Still, if the billionaire lobby’s goal was to sow mistrust around Proposition 40, the intra-left divisions and air of scandal around UHW certainly helped. To add insult to injury, UHW’s staff union declared a strike in the days leading up to Election Day, obstructing Proposition 40’s final get-out-the-vote push.
Ultimately, neither the measure’s necessity — even now, nobody seems to have an alternative plan for when the Medicaid cuts kick in — nor its meticulous construction ended up matching the unprecedented amounts of money the billionaire lobby dumped into this election. Opponents raised at least $378 million, overwhelming the pro-tax campaign and helping swing the popular vote away from Proposition 40. The billionaire lobby also financed two poison pill measures, Propositions 41 and 42, which could have blocked Proposition 40 even if it passed, provided they received more “yes” votes.
Proposition 40’s chaotic loss should not distract from its importance. The front line often doesn’t survive the battle, but in this case it opened an important new front. By organizing to put the issue directly on the ballot, UHW forced a public conversation about wealth taxes that put the idea on the political menu. Not only did Bernie Sanders and Ro Khanna wholeheartedly endorse the measure, they had already introduced legislation for an annual federal billionaire wealth tax. California governor Gavin Newsom, in his haste to kill the California billionaire tax, was forced to admit that America needs a national minimum tax on the ultrawealthy (as long as it didn’t start in his state). United Airlines’ millionaire CEO, Scott Kirby, recently chimed in, advocating for a national wealth tax.
Proposition 40’s hard-fought loss is at once an illustration of how hard many billionaires will fight being taxed and how important it will be to tax them anyway.
Defending Abortion Rights and Defeating Transphobia in Missouri
Alongside the demonization of immigrants, attacks on transgender people have been a staple of reactionary scapegoating in recent years. In September, Elon Musk reportedly authorized more than $100 million in midterm spending by his PAC, which launched transphobic ads, including in Texas, Tesla’s headquarters. That strategy failed, as targeted Democrats swept in the midterms.
However, transphobic attacks also made it directly onto the ballot in multiple states, where they were largely successful. Majorities in Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska, and Washington approved restrictions on transgender students’ participation on school sports teams aligned with their gender identity. Another Colorado measure, banning gender-affirming surgeries for minors, also passed. Niche an issue as it may seem to many, the Right has found a foothold in youth sports.
Nevertheless, the biggest test of how far conservatives can leverage transphobia failed in Missouri, where Republican legislators tried using it as a lever to overturn abortion rights. The victory against this tactic is instructive for how the Left can defeat transphobic scapegoating at the ballot moving forward.
In 2024, Missouri residents voted to enshrine abortion rights in the state constitution. That vote, titled Amendment 3, had been proposed as a citizen initiative and won narrowly but decisively with 52 percent of the vote. It didn’t take long for Republicans in the state legislature to hatch a scheme to countermand the popular vote. The result was Amendment 3, part two.
This year’s Amendment 3 was a legislatively referred repeal of the citizen-initiated Amendment 3 from 2024. It combined a rollback of abortion rights with a constitutional ban on gender-transition procedures for minors, including surgery, puberty blockers, and hormone treatment, subject to specified medical exceptions. Rather than trying to change majority opinion on abortion rights, the antiabortion campaign focused its talking points on transphobia.
Voters also had to wade through the confusion. Not only had they just voted on abortion two years ago, but when a majority of Missouri voters checked “yes” on Amendment 3, they were voting to support abortion rights. Now, a “yes” vote on Amendment 3 meant the opposite.
It’s not the first time Republican legislators have attempted this kind of ballot title shell game, to little effect. It didn’t work in Missouri either. On Election Day, Missouri voters decisively rejected the new Amendment 3 with 55 percent of the vote — an even higher percentage than voted for abortion rights in 2024. To cement their rebuke, voters also passed a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment to protect the ballot initiative process from legislative tampering.
Had Missouri Republicans been successful in overturning a popular vote for abortion rights by leveraging transphobia, the same tactic would have been rolled out across the country. It still might, but now there is both strategy and precedent to defeat it. The coalition against the new Amendment 3 had to balance a focus on abortion rights with addressing attacks on trans youth.
A contingent of the campaign headed by PROMO, a Missouri LGBTQ organization, leaned into the opportunity to move the needle on trans rights for the long term. They committed to an intensive deep canvassing program aimed at changing hearts and minds — an approach that has worked on gay marriage and trans antidiscrimination votes over the past decade and a half. Therein lies the lesson.
The political Right has a fast-evaporating pool of persuasive appeals to the public. Following the Right’s trouncing in the midterm elections, conservatives can be expected to double down on anti-trans arguments as a foot in the door to a popular audience. Missouri shows that the best defense against transphobia is a good offense, both pointing out that scapegoating is designed to distract and also engaging in proactive public education to stand in unflinching solidarity against all forms of bigotry.
Divesting From Genocide in Providence
If elections over the summer indicated that Palestine had changed US politics, November signed, sealed, and stamped that reality. Explicitly pro-Palestine candidates won across the country, most prominently Abdul El-Sayed, who won a US Senate seat in Michigan despite what he described as $42 million in AIPAC spending against him. These wins proved beyond a doubt that questioning US support for Israel — a nearly unthinkable stance in mainstream politics only a few years ago — calling the genocide in Gaza a genocide, and advocating for an arms embargo against Israel are no longer liabilities for elected leaders.
Still, it is difficult to distinguish those who voted for El-Sayed because of his stance on Israel from those who supported him in spite of that stance. Such is the nature of two-party elections, when voters must shoehorn or project a variety of wants, needs, and hopes onto a single personality and often hold their noses about the rest. But devil’s advocates will find no solace this year, because there was one vote last Tuesday that was about Palestine and nothing else, and the results were not ambiguous.
Providence, Rhode Island, is the first US city to enact a binding divestment law by popular vote, targeting investments in countries and companies engaged in severe human rights abuses like genocide, ethnic cleansing, and apartheid — a campaign explicitly focused on divesting from Israel. It won by a landslide, with 75 percent of the popular vote. The effort was led by a local coalition that included Jewish Voice for Peace; Democratic Socialists of America; Reclaim Rhode Island, a housing justice and generally progressive organization; and American Federation of Teachers Local 6516, representing graduate workers at Brown University. (You can read more about the initiative in this Jacobin piece by two organizers from the campaign.)
Following the initiative win, Providence becomes the largest US city yet to approve divestment from Israel. It will join at least six other cities around the country in passing some form of divestment legislation — Hayward and Richmond in California; Dearborn, Michigan; Medford, Massachusetts; Belfast, Maine; and most recently Cambridge, Massachusetts. Providence does not have a proportionately large Muslim or Arab population, but it does have a sizable Jewish population. The overwhelming victory for divestment at the ballot cements beyond a doubt the swing happening in the American public not only away from Israel but toward decisive action against its genocidal policies.
It is also worth noting, with the California Billionaire Tax in mind, that while Providence marks a triumphant success for the Palestine solidarity movement in a watershed election, it was not the first attempt to divest from Israel by direct democracy. The first two attempts, both in Pittsburgh, lost court challenges and never made it to voters. The third, in Somerville, Massachusetts, won majority support a year ago, but was a nonbinding initiative. Somerville’s City Council has committed to pursuing a binding ordinance, and an ethical procurement proposal remains before it. Sometimes it takes time for game-changing policies with deep-pocketed adversaries to succeed at the ballot.
Alongside Question 7, Providence elected a mayor who endorsed the divestment initiative, twenty-eight-year-old democratic socialist David Morales, as well as a slate of allied city council members. Should Question 7 survive the court challenges that have already been threatened, it will be implemented by the new city government.
But even if it is somehow beaten back in the courts, the Providence vote will echo across the country and well beyond, showing that after three grinding years of misery in Gaza and across Palestine, firm policy against genocide is not only a viable position but an asset for candidates and elected officials.
American politics is changing fast. To make the most of it, it is helpful to understand how majorities vote when they get a chance to legislate key issues directly. Our moment requires taking big swings in redistribution and economic justice. At the same time, the closer those moves get to billionaires’ money, the more severe the reaction will become. Going up against those kinds of resources, setbacks are to be expected, but the worst thing we could do would be to interpret losses as undermining the necessity or viability of taxing billionaires’ wealth.
As the Right’s bid for legitimacy falters, it will lean harder into scapegoating and demonizing marginalized groups. Contra antipopulist liberal fantasies, American society is not hopelessly bigoted. People can be won over to both economic and social justice, but only if movements commit to the protracted work on both fronts as part of the same political project. And policy positions that appear to be third rails, like divesting from Israel used to be, can be transformed through mass organizing and popular pressure.
