The Anti-Billionaire Midterms
Third Way says moderates won Democrats their majorities. But 25 of the party’s 32 Senate candidates explicitly ran against the billionaire class.
Within hours of last Tuesday’s shellacking of Republicans, the centrist think tank Third Way was claiming credit. Its November 4 memo, “Moderates Made Democratic Majorities,” declared that “the majority makers of 2026 were mainstream and moderate Democrats” and pointed to victories in Texas, South Carolina, Iowa, and Kansas as proof that the party should move toward the “center.” Meanwhile, the wins of left-wing candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine were treated as cautionary tales.
Our friends at Third Way are either confused or lying, because the evidence is clear: Bernie Sanders’s anti-billionaire message was widely adopted by Democrats in this election, including among the very candidates Third Way celebrates as “moderates.”
I spent the past week combing Democratic Senate campaign websites from 2024 and 2026 to quantify Democrats’ shift to economic populist rhetoric. The results were even more dramatic than I expected.
In 2024, “billionaire” or “billionaires” were referenced on six of 32 Democratic Senate campaign websites — only 19 percent. In 2026, the figure was 25 of 32 — a whopping 78 percent.
The change was greatest among challengers and open-seat candidates. In 2024, only two of 18 had websites mentioning billionaires, or 11 percent. Two years later, 20 of 23 did, or 87 percent. Among incumbents, the figure also rose, from 29 to 56 percent.
Compare this year’s campaigning with Democrats’ more conventional economic messaging in 2024. Last time around, Washington Senator Maria Cantwell’s website praised the state’s successful businesses and her work supporting its “unique and enviable culture of science, innovation, and economic growth.” As Democrats have done for decades, she called for shared prosperity without identifying the social class blocking it.
Several of the biggest 2026 winners were far more confrontational. Their attacks on the wealthy were prominent campaign themes rather than passing references buried in a press release.
Take James Talarico, the Texas senator-elect frequently hailed as a model for Democratic moderation. On the campaign trail, he denounced Democrats and Republicans alike for embracing “trickle-down economics” for close to half a century. And in his victory speech, he accused billionaires who control media and politics of keeping Americans divided while they enrich themselves. “The real fight in this country is not left versus right,” he declared. “It is top versus bottom.”
Texas’s Democratic governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, offered an equally direct argument. Her campaign asked: “Does Texas belong to the people of Texas, or is this the billionaires’ world and we just live in it?” In her victory speech, she promised to stop writing separate rules for working families and the wealthy.
In South Carolina, Senator-elect Annie Andrews made the point in an election-night message pinned to her X account. Voters had shown, she said, that even in “a politics dominated by billionaires, special interests, and insiders in Washington,” they would not bow down. Andrews campaigned on health care and affordability while refusing to treat big-money influence as an unavoidable fact of political life.
Nor were these isolated examples. Of the 11 victorious Democratic Senate challengers and open-seat candidates, all had websites mentioning billionaires: Talarico, Andrews, Josh Turek in Iowa, Adam Hamilton in Kansas, Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Sherrod Brown in Ohio, Chris Pappas in New Hampshire, Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, Juliana Stratton in Illinois, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, and Troy Jackson in Maine.
Democratic Senate candidates who ran on anti-billionaire messaging were spread across the country, and they won more frequently than candidates without documented mentions. Among the 20 non-incumbent Democrats whose campaign websites or linked policy documents mentioned billionaires, 11 have won, and seven have lost, with Alaska and Mississippi still unresolved and Democrats leading in both. All three candidates without a documented mention lost; among decided races, that was an 11-of-18 win rate (61 percent), versus zero of three.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
The pattern persisted in states Trump carried in 2024. Five of the 12 billionaire-mentioning candidates with decided races won, while all three candidates without documented mentions lost.
To be sure, these win rates are descriptive rather than causal: the samples are small, the contexts differ, and website mentions of billionaires aren’t a complete measure of a candidate’s economic platform (or of their willingness to challenge economic elites once in office). Nor can these numbers prove that attacking the 1 percent caused anyone to win.
It’s obvious that a powerful anti-Trump backlash was the main driver of the Democratic wave. But my findings do establish that candidates using this economic populist language won across the country, including in states where Democrats had struggled for decades and where Third Way–type consultants still wrongly insist that across-the-board moderation is the only possible path to victory.
A politician can sound like a centrist on some cultural issues while calling for a fight against the billionaire class. That distinction matters if we want to understand what Democrats actually ran on this time around. Some successful Democrats took positions on immigration or trans rights to the right of the party’s progressive wing. But none of that prevented them from running against wealthy donors, corporate interests, or the rules of an economy tilted toward the rich.
Third Way acknowledges that winning Democrats campaigned on lowering costs. But the memo downplays New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s role in bringing this message to the fore, and its ideological categories obscure whom these candidates blamed for the problem.
In one sense, the fact that politicians like Talarico and Andrews are now being called “moderates” is itself a victory for economic populism. After Sanders helped make the billionaire class a familiar political target, and after virtually the entire corporate elite cozied up to Trump 2.0, ideas once dismissed as too radical for ordinary voters have become standard campaign language among Democrats of all stripes. That’s what winning the argument looks like.
Yet this lesson can easily be lost if establishment pundits and politicians distort the mandate voters delivered last Tuesday. It would be a disaster for Democrats to forget the economic commitments their candidates made during the biggest Republican rout in five decades. To actually deliver health care, child care, and housing, Democrats need to take on the handful of oligarchs who benefit from the status quo.
Last Tuesday offers no proof that anti-billionaire rhetoric alone wins races. But it offers plenty of proof that such rhetoric is compatible with victory from Texas to South Carolina to Iowa and Kansas. Corporate donors and their defenders would prefer to make this lesson disappear. We can’t afford to let them.

https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-ai-hone.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-ai-hone.text:
On Tuesday morning, New York Governor Kathy Hochul announced another step in her mission to "rein in artificial intelligence" in lieu of federal regulation: The state is launching an academic research center focused on AI safety—the first one in the nation.
"They'll harness the highest computing power anywhere outside the private sector," Hochul said Tuesday. "Nobody can top this."
The New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research will employ about 80 "elite scientists" to independently test AI systems and bolster safety, Hochul said. Examples of their research includes developing methods to prevent AI agents escaping their sandboxes, like they did in the Hugging Face hacking incident, and working out how to best evaluate the safety guardrails that AI companies are deploying, said the Center's interim Co-Director Greg Morrisett. 
The Center will be powered by Empire AI, the state's $500 million AI computing center at the University of Buffalo, and is funded by a $30 million gift from Bloomberg co-founder and Empire AI board chair Tom Secunda, plus a $25 million research investment from SUNY and the state. It's set to launch by the new year. When the RAISE Act comes into effect January 1, AI companies will be required to submit detailed safety frameworks on their models to the state, which will also be assessed by researchers at the center.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Art Basel offers compensation to dealers after early closure of Paris fair due to protests
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Georgina Adam
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Art Basel will compensate dealers for the early closure of its Paris fair, held 20-23 October in the Grand Palais, the fair company announced today (11th November), on a French national holiday.
The fair was forced to shut down its Parisian outing two days early because of violent rioting in the French capital. Since then, dealers have been demanding compensation for their lost sales and booth fees. Indeed, soon after the closure the French Comité Professionnel des Galeries d’Art (CPGA) sent a strongly worded letter to the fair director, Karim Crippa. It accused the firm of not consulting with dealers—the CPGA represents 57 of the fair’s 211 exhibitors—and of showing “disrespect, even contempt” for them.
The closure hit the smaller dealers particularly hard, since the biggest galleries tended to make sales on the opening days, whereas the smaller dealers, mainly sited on the upper floor of the Grand Palais, depended on the two weekend days for business. The letter said it expected “concrete proposals” for this compensation.
Now Crippa has responded to the letter, with an offer of a reduction across the board of 20% of booth fees to all participants. He said: “We believe this approach offers a fair and considered way forward, reflecting our appreciation of the partnership we share and our commitment to strengthening it further.”
Philippe Charpentier of Mor Charpentier gallery, who is the president of the CPGA, tells The Art Newspaper that the compensation rate is what the committee expected.
Nonetheless, if one calculates in percentages, the fair was open for three-and-a-half days—it's ultra-VIP Avant-Première timeslot began 3pm on Tuesday 20 October, and the fair closed Friday—instead of the projected five and a half. The fair was therefore shortened by about 36%.
Speaking about the decision to close the fair early, Noah Horowitz, chief executive of Art Basel, tells The Art Newspaper: “We stand by the decision to close. We feel it was in the right interest of all the parties involved. It was a very difficult decision, but we stand by it.”
Asked about the decision to close for the two days—when unrest was only expected on the Saturday—he said: “Given the uncertainty surrounding the impact and the duration of the planned demonstrations and access to the Grand Palais, we simply couldn't be confident that conditions would allow us to reopen safely on Sunday. An event of this size and scale is incredibly complex, and some exhibitors had also expressed serious concerns about leaving artworks unattended in the Grand Palais on the weekend. We concluded that closing the fair early was in the best interests of the art, the staff and ultimately the visitors.”
Horowitz was not prepared to comment on other aspects of the closure, for example questions of insurance or the firm’s relationship with the Grand Palais, for which MCH paid €10.6m to rent the space for seven years in 2022. Horowitz said that MCH, the parent company of the Basel group of art fairs, was "fully committed to delivering the 2027 edition of the fair".

https://gothamist.com/news/wind-rain-may.title: Wind, rain, maybe snowflakes: It's about to get chilly around NYC
https://gothamist.com/news/wind-rain-may.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/wind-rain-may.text:
New Yorkers should prepare for temperatures to drop later this week, with meteorologists forecasting gusty winds, moderate rain and the potential appearance of snowflakes in the coming days.
The National Weather Service is warning New Yorkers of light to moderate rain starting Friday and potentially continuing into early Saturday, with a few wet snowflakes possible in areas of higher elevation on Friday evening.
Parts of Long Island and Western Sound could also see minor coastal flooding during the daytime high tide cycles from Thursday into Saturday.
A low-pressure system passing through the area is responsible for this, as it is expected to bring cooler air from the north, with temperatures dropping to the 40s from Friday through Sunday, according to Brian Ciemnecki, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.
That means New Yorkers will notice temperatures about 10 to 15 degrees colder than they’ve been for most of this week. Highs should remain about 60 through Thursday, before the sharp drop in temperatures begins.
Temperatures are expectedly to slightly increase into the 50s on Monday and Tuesday of next week.
Ciemnecki said this year has thus far been slightly warmer than last year, but New Yorkers shouldn’t assume they won’t get a repeat of last winter’s brutally cold weather.
“We’re not quite to wintertime yet, we’re still in fall,” he said. “Let’s see.”
Nearly two dozen people froze to death during last year’s wintry conditions, which saw record-breaking snowfall as temperatures plunged below freezing.

https://www.propublica.org/article/follo.title: A Newborn Died in a Faith-Healing Sect. The State — and One Ex-Believer — Stepped in to Save Her Twin.
https://www.propublica.org/article/follo.author: Noelle Crombie, Beth Nakamura
https://www.propublica.org/article/follo.text:
The deputy medical examiner thought the family was being evasive. Eric Tonsfeldt had been dispatched to the pistachio-green house in Oregon City on the night of March 5, 2017. Inside he found Sarah Mitchell in bed, her dead newborn in her arms.
Mitchell is a member of the Followers of Christ, a sect known for refusing medical treatment. She had received no prenatal care. Three women without medical training guided her delivery that afternoon.
Tonsfeldt listened as the family insisted that the baby, whom they had named Ginnifer, had seemed healthy for most of the afternoon, then suddenly stopped breathing. They couldn’t explain why the baby appeared so underweight. Their answers to many of Tonsfeldt’s questions were vague. Nobody would make eye contact with him.
Later, investigators would discover that 13 minutes after Ginnifer’s birth, Followers began exchanging a series of worried texts. “Not good breathing,” one wrote in a group chat. Another requested prayers: “She’s really bad.” (One person in the chat would later advise deleting the messages.)
No one had called 911 as the gaps between each breath increased. When asked why not, Ginnifer’s father later said, “Because it’s in God’s hands.” He anointed his daughter with olive oil and wept as he prayed that she would be OK. Ginnifer died in his arms at 7 p.m., four hours after she was born.
Tonsfeldt gently collected the newborn and examined her in another room. She weighed 3½ pounds, roughly half that of an average full-term infant. He found no signs of injury or trauma.
The medical examiner still felt that something was awry. To play for time, he asked if someone would make him a cup of coffee and headed to the kitchen. As Tonsfeldt waited, one of the baby’s grandfathers approached him and blurted out an unexpected question: Would it make a difference if Ginnifer had a twin?
There was another baby, a girl named Evelyn. She was alive.
In the dim light of a bathroom, Tonsfeldt found women huddled over a tiny newborn, who was barely making a sound. They were feeding her from an eyedropper.
He told the family to get her to a hospital. After Evelyn’s grandfather made it clear they weren’t going anywhere, Tonsfeldt summoned the police, who delivered an ultimatum: Take Evelyn to the hospital or they’d do it themselves.
Evelyn’s family relented. A patrol car followed to make sure they got there. She was admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit in Portland with respiratory distress syndrome. With the help of a breathing machine and a feeding tube, Evelyn began to stabilize. An autopsy would later conclude the same condition, common in premature babies, had caused her sister’s death.
The Mitchells were charged with murder by neglect, as well as criminal mistreatment for failing to get Evelyn medical care. That left authorities with another challenge: Who would care for Evelyn?
Her family assumed any custody arrangement would be temporary and suggested Marshall and Jennifer Phillips, a couple born and raised in the Followers. But Marshall was no ordinary Follower. Once, when his young son became gravely ill, he brought him to a hospital. In the eyes of the state, that made Marshall and his wife suitable candidates to look after Evelyn.
Evelyn’s family didn’t know then that Marshall’s choice to save his son had set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known. And that he would take Evelyn with him.
For more than a century, states have wrestled with how to address the deaths of children whose parents refuse them medical care for religious reasons. As early as 1901, a father in New York who believed in the “power of God to heal the sick through prayer” was prosecuted for failing to call a doctor for his young daughter who died from pneumonia. Since then, courts have repeatedly held — in cases where Christian Scientists refused treatment or Jehovah’s Witnesses declined blood transfusions — that adults are free to reject medical care for themselves.
Whether they can be compelled to provide medical care for their children is another matter, one that’s been left to states to decide. Courts have generally deferred to legislatures on this question.
Video: This Secretive Religious Sect Doesn’t Believe in Medical Care
Marshall Phillips was raised in the Followers of Christ, which forbids medical care. When his son fell gravely ill, he took him to the hospital. That choice set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known.
For decades, Oregon’s law gave latitude to faith healing and authorities did little to intervene. Between 1989 and 1999, 18 children of the Oregon City-based Followers died. (The sect numbered between 1,500 and 2,000 at its peak.) Most or all of those deaths were preventable, according to the state medical examiner at the time, who estimated that the child death rate in the sect was 26 times that of the general population.
The revelation of those deaths, in The Oregonian and other news outlets, prompted state lawmakers to act. In 1999, they removed spiritual treatment as a defense for second-degree manslaughter and criminal mistreatment. In 2008, prosecutors filed their first case against Followers parents after a 15-month-old died from untreated bronchial pneumonia and a blood infection. A jury convicted the girl’s father of a single count of criminal mistreatment, a misdemeanor, and acquitted her mother.
Two more children in the sect died without medical attention during this period, prompting the Legislature in 2011 to do away with the spiritual defense for any crime. Among those supporting the change: the Christian Science church, which by then had softened its stance amid a steep decline in membership. In a letter to lawmakers that year, a church official wrote: “Spiritual care should never be practiced at the expense of a child’s life.”
Changes in Oregon law — and prosecutors’ willingness to pursue parents who watched their children die — spurred a slow but perceptible shift: Deaths of children in the Followers have become an anomaly. Ginnifer Mitchell’s death in 2017 came amid that yearslong decline. Since then, one child has died due to lack of medical care.
During this same time frame in Idaho, where the laws protect parents who rely only on faith healing, reporting by ProPublica found at least 11 babies and children of Followers died from treatable conditions.
Still, Ginnifer’s death shows how the most entrenched elements of faith-healing communities resist aggressive enforcement. Sarah Mitchell chose to give birth without doctors or nurses, even as her sister was in prison for failing to provide medical care for her premature newborn, who died in 2009. And Sarah’s lack of prenatal care was such that she realized she was carrying twins only when her labor continued after her first baby emerged.
Evelyn might not have survived if police didn’t have the law on their side, allowing them to intervene and demand that her parents take her to the hospital.
The stories of Evelyn and Marshall Phillips — still the subject of legal proceedings today — offer a rare view into the closed community and reveal both the power and the limits of the state’s efforts to compel parents to seek medical care for their children.
Marshall’s ancestors were among the earliest members of the Followers, whose history dates to the late 1800s, when faith-healing sects were active in the Midwest. The faithful later migrated west, starting congregations in Idaho. In the 1930s, a charismatic Followers preacher named Walter White left Idaho for Oregon City, then a lively hub for the timber and paper industries. White’s emotional sermons earned him the moniker “the crying preacher.”
Followers believed the devout earned their place in the afterlife through good acts. They also believed that God heals. The doctrine stems from a passage in the Book of James, which proclaims “And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up.” Seeking medical care was viewed as an abandonment of faith. Those who visited doctors risked being shunned.
By the 1950s, White broke ties with other Followers congregations. He later said that Christ had visited him in a dream and told him the world would soon end and so would baptisms.
White died in 1969 at age 67. Baptisms ended after that, effectively sealing the faithful from the outside world. The Followers never identified White’s successor. To this day, the congregation has no pastor. The lack of a spiritual leader seems only to have intensified members’ influence on one another.
The sect’s practices include other unusual elements: The Bible doesn’t figure in their services, which consist mostly of congregants singing hymns.
In many respects, Followers lead conventional lives. As a boy born in 1975, Marshall rode his bike, ate sugary treats, watched TV and listened to 1980s rock bands like Van Halen. His parents took him and his siblings camping and saved up for trips to Disneyland.
But his life was also circumscribed by his faith. Several times a week, he accompanied his parents to functions at the beige meetinghouse set back from busy Molalla Avenue in Oregon City. Starting at age 7, Followers’ children are separated by gender and age into their own pews. Marshall understood that he would grow up, and grow old, with the kids seated around him. He was instructed not to befriend kids outside the church. Followers considered them “worldly,” the sect’s derisive term for those focused on terrestrial, rather than celestial, concerns.
Like his peers, Marshall never visited a pediatrician. He was never vaccinated. His mom anointed his forehead with extra virgin olive oil when his head throbbed. He endured chicken pox and whooping cough and eventually recovered from both — proof, he believed, of God’s healing powers.
His parents, like others in the sect, made exceptions for dental care. They accepted the use of Novocain but refused the ibuprofen the dentist recommended to address lingering pain after a procedure.
Marshall knew from a young age that his future would be determined by the church. He figured he’d work for a Follower. He’d marry one, too. Marshall and Jennifer went on their first date in a courtship ritual the Followers call a carload — small groups of teens who drive together to get ice cream or coffee. She was 14 and he was 18. They married when Jennifer turned 17, the age girls in the Followers typically wed.
Jennifer’s father had died the year before, surrounded by men from the church. Members were expected to care for the dying, with men tending to men and women to women. Her father never went to the doctor, and family members think he died from heart failure. He was 37.
Women typically give birth in their parents’ homes, and Jennifer was no exception. She delivered her first child, Mary, in the living room, attended by her mother, her mother-in-law, aunts and other women. Marshall was there, too. The rest of the men waited out of sight, smoke from their cigarettes drifting into the living room. She had two more children after that, both sons.
Today, at 50, Marshall looks like the epitome of a suburban dad. With his receding hairline, beard and broad physique, you could picture him browsing the aisles of The Home Depot. He possesses a gentle quality and doesn’t shy away from even harsh self-reflection.
The Followers abide by what they view as traditional gender roles, with men leading their households. Many male Followers work as contractors, electricians and plumbers; Marshall works as a consultant for a heating and air conditioning company. Women mostly focus on the home and their children. Jennifer cleans houses to supplement their income and homeschooled their kids for a time.
As a Follower, Marshall said he pressured his children to fit in at church. He believed the sect’s teachings about earning one’s way to salvation, and he spent many Sunday afternoons visiting the sick and caring for the dying. He and his wife never challenged the institution that shaped their lives.
The couple saw no reason to visit the doctor or take their kids to one. That changed in the summer of 2013. They watched as their energetic preteen son, Nick, suddenly turned lethargic. Walking even a few feet left him out of breath, and he was soon confined to the couch.
His symptoms worsened over a matter of hours. As his extended family gathered to offer support, one relative wondered whether he had diabetes. Millions of Americans manage the condition with medication, but for a Follower, it could amount to a death sentence.
Marshall remembered that his cousin Bo had suffered from the disease more than a decade earlier. Bo Phillips developed flu-like symptoms and within days lapsed into a coma. He died in his parents’ bed at 11 — Nick’s age. A sheriff’s detective arrived to find Bo in a diaper, his body gaunt from dehydration. His fever was so high that his body registered a triple-digit temperature three hours after his death. He never went to a doctor.
As Marshall pondered what to do about Nick, he knew his relatives expected him to rely only on his faith in God. For a Follower, going to the hospital was unthinkable.
He knew that Followers had been prosecuted for failing to seek medical attention. He panicked at the thought that he — or worse, his wife — could go to prison if he chose not to take Nick to the hospital. Marshall felt trapped between his faith and the law.
He could see his son was struggling to breathe. The boy lay on the couch, barely conscious.
Marshall decided to act. “I’m taking him to the hospital,” he announced. In the same breath, he apologized.
Some family members expressed disapproval as he carried Nick to the door. One urged him not to turn away from God. Another whispered the name of a hospital where he should take the boy.
Marshall and Jennifer, who agreed with his decision, sped north on Interstate 5 to Legacy Emanuel Medical Center in North Portland. “Can you help my son?” he begged as he rushed into the emergency department, his unresponsive boy in his arms. Medical staff whisked him into the back, where a team quickly assessed Nick’s condition.
He had acute onset Type 1 diabetes. His blood was turning acidic, his organs shutting down. The Phillipses had arrived just in time. Without treatment, the doctors later said, he was hours from death.
That Marshall dwelled on his own fate as his son lay dying would leave him with a searing shame. “I wish I could be the great dad who jumped up and saw that his kid was sick and ran into the hospital,” he would say years later. “But I was weighing out the consequences. That’s the truth. And I’m not happy to say that.”
Marshall quickly grasped the implications of his decision. Relatives who had poured into the house to pray for Nick as he lay near death stopped coming around as he recovered. When the Phillipses tried to make holiday plans, some relatives didn’t reply. Nick’s closest friend stopped talking to him.
Marshall descended into depression. He turned to the Bible, scouring passages for proof that God forbade medical care. He found only references that showed how doctors were held in high esteem, such as Luke, whom Scripture refers to as a “beloved physician.”
On his commute to work, Marshall started listening to sermons of preachers from other denominations. He was moved by their messages of grace, forgiveness and redemption, concepts he’d never heard much about at church.
Over time, Marshall came to believe that God did heal — and he could use doctors to do it. He also came to believe that by saving his son, he had freed himself. And eventually that choice placed him at the center of another family’s tragedy.
When Evelyn arrived at the hospital a few hours after her birth in 2017, she was small even for a premature baby. She had been born about eight weeks early and weighed less than 4 pounds. Her glucose level was perilously low. She needed a feeding tube and a machine to help her breathe and remained in the neonatal intensive care unit for 11 days.
As criminal authorities investigated her parents, Evelyn’s fate rested with child welfare workers and a Clackamas County circuit judge. At a hearing to decide who would take care of Evelyn, lawyers for the Mitchells argued that Evelyn should come home with them while the investigation played out.
For child welfare officials and prosecutors, the proposal was out of the question. “These parents let this child’s twin die in their arms without making any effort at all to seek medical care,” one prosecutor told the judge. “And simultaneously they failed to seek medical care on behalf of this child and placed her also at extreme risk of death.” She continued: “We send parents to prison for failing to adequately undertake their duty to their children.”
On the stand, Marshall testified about his decision to take Nick to the hospital. He told the judge that his son was thriving and pledged to make sure Evelyn received medical care. (Evelyn’s grandfather had called him the night before to ask whether he’d be willing to take her in.)
Evelyn would stay with the Phillipses for now, the state decided.
Two days later, the couple drove to the hospital to meet Evelyn. She was so tiny that Jennifer’s mother bought her outfits from the doll aisle of Fred Meyer.
A year later, in the summer of 2018, Sarah and Travis Mitchell pleaded guilty to criminally negligent homicide for Ginnifer’s death and criminal mistreatment for failing to get Evelyn medical help. The agreement called for the couple to spend six years and six months in prison — the harshest sentence ever handed down to parents in the sect.
The couple’s lawyer told the judge that the Mitchells grieved the loss of Ginnifer and loved Evelyn. “Travis and Sarah are utterly sincere, decent and caring human beings,” he told the judge. (The Mitchells and their lawyer did not respond to requests to be interviewed for this article.)
As part of their plea bargain, prosecutors insisted the Mitchells sign a statement. “We should have sought adequate medical care for our children,” it read, “and everyone in the church should always seek adequate medical care for our children.”
The district attorney instructed the Followers to post the message at their Oregon City meetinghouse.
The message was torn down later that day.
The Phillipses had begun attending services at an evangelical Christian church. The couple worried Followers would find out they were drifting away, so they picked a large out-of-the-way congregation where they figured it would be easy to go unnoticed. The church, like other mainstream evangelical congregations, encouraged its members to visit doctors.
Even then, Marshall didn’t sever the family’s ties with the Followers. He couldn’t face the prospect of walking away from his parents and people he’d known his entire life.
The Phillipses weren’t the only Followers questioning their faith. Around the same time, a loose network of men had been quietly meeting to pray and discuss the Bible. Starting in 2018, an estimated 150 to 200 people left the sect, an exodus spurred mostly by a desire to engage with the Bible. Many who walked away had also become disillusioned with the Followers’ rejection of medicine.
Like generations born into the sect after White’s death, Marshall had never been baptized. Doing so would offend the Followers.
But in the fall of 2018, he decided he could no longer ignore his desire to experience the rite. He saw it as a public expression of the spiritual shift he’d undergone. Jennifer did too.
One Sunday afternoon that October, the couple joined dozens of others on the muddy banks of the Willamette River. They waded into the water as a friend held a sleeping Evelyn, then 19 months old. By this point the state had made the Phillipses’ guardianship permanent.
The baptism spelled the end of Marshall and Jennifer Phillips’ time in the Followers. Before the ceremony, Marshall had texted his family to let them know it was happening.
Soon after, his mother texted him to say goodbye.
Earlier this year, Evelyn climbed into the back seat of the Phillipses’ car, a bouquet of tangerine-colored roses that she picked out resting on her lap.
It was March 5, her ninth birthday. Every year on this day, the couple drives Evelyn to the Followers cemetery to visit her twin sister’s grave.
Evelyn admired the stuffed bear she had charmed Marshall into buying. She especially liked the polka dot ribbon twirled around its neck. “I think if Ginny was here,” she said, “she would have liked this for her birthday.”
Marshall pulled up to the cemetery gate. The sect owns this land at the end of a rural two-lane road about 10 miles from downtown Oregon City. Generations of Followers are buried here. Among them: Evelyn’s great-great grandfather, Walter White, the sect’s founding pastor.
Ginnifer’s grave lies near a stand of evergreens. Evelyn knelt down. “I miss you, Ginny,” she said, placing the stuffed bear on the tombstone.
Nearby lay the grave of Hayden Edwards. He died two days after his birth in 2023. His parents were convicted of criminal mistreatment for failing to seek medical care for him, the most recent faith-healing prosecution in Oregon.
Marshall walked the neat rows, passing a fresh grave, one that showed the limitations of Oregon’s laws. The state had stepped in several years ago when parents had refused to get medical treatment for their teenage son, who was experiencing renal failure. After prosecutors intervened, the parents agreed to a plea deal and made sure he got care. But when the son turned 18 this year, he declined further treatment. He died within days.
Marshall paused when he came to his own father’s headstone. It had “Dad” etched into the granite. He learned of his father’s death last year from a friend who heard the news from someone else. One of Marshall’s relatives called to let him know he wasn’t welcome at the funeral.
The day after the visit to the cemetery, guests filled the Phillipses’ home for Evelyn’s birthday party. Three-tiered display stands held homemade carrot cupcakes topped with swirls of cream cheese frosting — treats Evelyn had requested. Evelyn, ebullient, pinballed (and later roller-skated, using one birthday gift) between friends, parents and grandparents. Her long hair spilled out from under a pink helmet. The family had invited Evelyn’s birth parents, who joined them in the living room to watch her open gifts piled high on a table.
Evelyn first got to know them while they were in prison, and she knows why they were there. The couple spends time with her twice a month, taking her on adventures to the Oregon Zoo, roller skating and the park. She is their only child.
At the party, the Mitchells kept their focus on Evelyn, smiling broadly as she tore the wrapping from packages. They pulled out their phones to record her delight.
“Daddy!” Evelyn exclaimed at one point, marveling over one of her gifts.
Marshall and Travis both swiveled toward her in response.
The Phillipses’ friends filtered back into the kitchen. The Mitchells stayed behind. Their birthday card lay at one end of a table in the living room. “Not a day goes by where you aren’t missed, loved and thought of,” it read. “We thank God every day that we get to be a part of your life.” They signed it: “All our love, Dad & Mom.”
Travis ducked into the other room to look for Marshall. He thanked him for the evening. His wife had already slipped out of the house.
These days, brief exchanges with Travis are as close as Marshall comes to interacting with other Followers.
The Phillipses still live in Oregon City, home to most members of the sect. Marshall sees them, including his extended family, around town. Some ignore him. Others offer an obligatory nod. Rarely do they stop to talk. The Followers continue to gather every Thursday evening and Sunday morning without him.
Still, there are hints of change, albeit invisible ones. One former Follower told detectives in 2023 that some younger parents are quietly taking their children to the doctor.
For now at least, Evelyn is an outsider to the Followers. Marshall raised her that way. In June, she took a step that could further alienate her from the sect: She was baptized.
Four months after that, in October, tensions flared between Evelyn’s two sets of parents. The Mitchells filed a motion in court effectively seeking to terminate Marshall and Jennifer’s permanent guardianship — they acknowledged that Evelyn opposed the move — then withdrew the filing in November. (The Mitchells also criticized the Phillipses for allowing Evelyn to participate in this article.) The Mitchells are now seeking expanded visitation time with Evelyn.
Marshall wants Evelyn to determine her own future — to marry when she’s ready, not at 17. He talks to her about college, a possibility he wouldn’t have broached with his children as a Follower. Today he regrets how rigid he was, during his years in the sect, with his older children. Evelyn has brought out a paternal tenderness in him.
Some months ago, Jennifer took Evelyn to the pediatrician for a checkup. Evelyn swapped her school uniform for an oversized hospital gown that brushed the floor when she stood.
A cheery medical assistant stepped into the room. “She’s up to date with vaccines,” the woman announced. “We do offer the HPV at age 9. Do you want to do that today?”
Jennifer and Marshall weren’t vaccinated as kids, nor were their other children. Jennifer, who visited a doctor for the first time in her mid-40s, hadn’t heard about the HPV vaccine, which can prevent most cancers caused by the human papillomavirus. But she trusted Evelyn’s pediatrician. If vaccines were recommended, she wanted Evelyn to have them.
A physician assistant looked in Evelyn’s ears and shone a light in her eyes. She tapped her knees to check her reflexes. All signs pointed to a healthy girl.
“Now,” she said, “I’m going to listen to your lungs.” She placed a stethoscope on the girl’s chest, the sound of the ventilation system humming in the quiet room. Evelyn, whose lungs once nearly failed her, took a deep breath.
How We Reported This Story
Reporter Noelle Crombie relied on records from the Clackamas County District Attorney’s Office and the Clackamas County Sheriff’s Office, including detectives’ interviews with Sarah and Travis Mitchell, their parents and other members of the Followers of Christ; photographs taken during the execution of search warrants; investigative summaries by detectives and records obtained by investigators; Oregon City Police Department reports; recordings of the March 16, 2017, circuit court hearing where Evelyn’s initial custody status was determined and the July 9, 2018, hearing in Clackamas County Circuit Court where the Mitchells were sentenced; Clackamas County Circuit Court records; Clackamas County Department of Communications 911 audio recordings; Oregon City Police Department body-worn camera footage; Evelyn’s medical records from the OHSU Doernbecher Children’s Hospital, which her legal guardian Marshall Phillips obtained at The Oregonian/OregonLive’s request; historical legislative records in the Oregon State Archives; and archival records from the Followers of Christ. Crombie observed many of the interactions she describes in the story. For others, she relied on official records and the memories of those who were directly involved.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Mamdani Budget Floats on Wall Street Cash as Momentum Grows for New Taxes
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Greg David
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
When the City Council and Mayor Zohran Mamdani agreed on a $127 billion budget last June, the story behind the story was obvious.
The numbers for the fiscal year beginning last July 1 added up to a balanced budget, thanks to a flood of state aid and some fiscal gimmicks. And the plan projected a worrisome $6 billion hole for the next budget.
But when the mayor updates his budget later this week, he will be the beneficiary of two major developments that will ease his budget problems and, at the same time, get him closer to his long-cherished goal of a tax increase on the wealthy.
First, the city has received a flood of tax revenue from Wall Street that will shrink the deficit. And last Friday, newly re-elected Gov. Kathy Hochul opened the door to a tax increase, making it likely the question to be decided in the next state legislative session will not be whether to raise taxes but by how much, on whom and for what reason.
“I will work hard to manage within our existing resources, but if we need more, we will find a path, as I’ve done before when there’s a particular need, a very specific need,” Hochul said at the annual post-election political gathering in Puerto Rico, linking any increase to the mayor’s plan for universal childcare, which carries a price tag of as much as $9 billion a year.
The mayor’s announcement this week, called the November budget modification, is primarily a way to see whether the city is on track to produce a balanced budget. The fiscal watchdog Citizens Budget Commission says a key issue will be whether the Mamdani administration will detail the $1 billion in savings it has instructed city agencies to find.
Another key issue will be whether the administration will be able to cut spending in the city’s housing voucher program and at homeless shelters, along with the cost of sending special education students to private schools, as it has pledged.
Mayors do not usually change their revenue forecasts, but there is little doubt the city is going to see an increase over what it expected to collect in the current year.
MORE: New York’s Pension Funds Soared in the AI Boom — and Could Crash With the AI Bubble
The state said last month that soaring Wall Street profits had boosted revenue for its current fiscal year, which ends March 31, by a whopping $8 billion more than projected. Hochul also said the expected deficit for the next budget had plunged to $3 billion from a little over $6 billion.
The governor put the windfall into reserves and paying down debt, though the Legislature could always decide to spend that money in the next budget and send some of that money to the city.
The city will not see as big a jump since income and corporate taxes comprise a smaller portion of local taxes than the state, but the numbers will go up. City Comptroller Mark Levine reported personal income taxes in the first three months of the city’s fiscal year were $500 million more than expected.
Since the revenue surge is almost completely dependent on Wall Street and because the profits it is generating are largely a result of the artificial intelligence boom, fiscal experts warn the windfall could disappear quickly.
“The rocky markets of the last few days serve as a reminder that the city needs to prepare itself to protect New Yorkers from the next bust,” said Andrew Rein, president of the Citizens Budget Commission.
He said he wants the city to follow the governor’s example and send extra money to its reserve funds in case tax revenue plunges.
With Hochul easing her opposition to tax increases, momentum for a hike seems irreversible. Both Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie and Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins have said they favor an increase on wealthy New Yorkers. New York City residents making more than $2 million currently pay a 14% tax on income, the highest in the nation.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/public-power.title: A Sewer Socialist Proposal for the Climate: PowerNYC
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/public-power.author: Batul Hassan, Michael Paulson
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/public-power.text:
A Sewer Socialist Proposal for the Climate: PowerNYC
PowerNYC, a public clean energy developer in New York, could be Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s climate engine, lowering costs and creating a more resilient, greener electricity grid for New Yorkers.
Two years ago, then Assemblymember Zohran Mamdani launched his campaign for mayor with a series of on-the-street interviews of Donald Trump voters on Fordham Road in the Bronx. In the course of the following year, the cost-of-living crisis solidified as the uniting theme of his mayoral campaign, anchored by a clear agenda to bring costs down and build a city where New Yorkers can “afford to dream.” Last week, a big tent of Democratic politicians used this same message to rout the Right across the country — potentially opening the door to a new kind of politics that embeds climate action within economic populist agendas.
New York City is already providing a governing framework for legislators across the country seeking to translate campaign slogans into material improvements for working-class people. Through initiatives like discounted groceries at municipal grocery store pilots and a public stake in New York University’s Quantum Institute, the Mamdani administration has begun to demonstrate that the public sector can and must play a critical role in tackling the affordability crisis and meeting people’s everyday needs.
In this approach, Mayor Mamdani is drawing on a rich history of public ownership in the United States catalyzed by the New Deal. But in the modern era, we can only ensure that all New Yorkers can “afford to dream” if we tackle the climate crisis — a core driver of economic instability, high costs, and the foreclosure of a stable future.
A new report from Climate and Community Institute, Public Renewables Project, and Public Power NY, PowerNYC Development Corporation: The Case for a Public Renewable Developer in New York City, lays out a clear path for New York City to lead on climate action. Drawing on a New Deal–inspired approach to the energy sector, authors Jason Kowalski and Johanna Bozuwa make the case for New York City to take charge of its own energy future via a city-owned development corporation called PowerNYC. By rapidly deploying solar, battery storage, and thermal energy networks (TENs) across the five boroughs, PowerNYC would accelerate decarbonization to lower utility bills, ensure more reliable service, and phase out the fossil fuels driving the combined affordability and climate crisis.
Since the New Deal era, public development has built systems to service common needs from international airports to water and sewage systems across the country. Many of these systems still stand as durable remnants of a more ambitious era of governance.
PowerNYC Development Corporation applies this formula to twenty-first-century needs: it would leverage the public sector’s ability to coordinate and plan at scale to create a glide path for renewable energy projects that might otherwise languish in the limbo of private markets. Such an institution would fill a clear gap in New York City’s renewable energy landscape, delivering climate and economic benefits in the form of lowered emissions and utility savings.
Overlapping Energy Crises
New York City currently faces multiple overlapping energy system crises that are on track to get much worse in the coming years.
First, utility rates are becoming unaffordable for New Yorkers, who are now paying 11 percent more for their electricity bills than they did just last year, largely due to the costs of fossil fuel infrastructure and volatile natural gas prices. Second, the city’s supply of energy is constrained by an outdated grid, power plants reaching the end of their lifespan, and lack of needed transmission lines to bring renewable power from upstate New York, leading to blackouts in the summer and even higher risk of service interruptions in the future. Third, the cascading effects of fossil fuel generation threaten the well-being of New Yorkers through dangerous air pollution and increasingly catastrophic weather events.
To address these crises requires tackling the root cause of continued reliance on volatile fossil fuel markets and transitioning to green energy sources.
To date, the state has relied chiefly on market incentives to spur renewable energy development, but this strategy has fallen well short of meeting the state’s climate targets. And New York City has fallen way behind the rest of the state, with 90 percent of downstate electricity still coming from fossil fuels rather than renewables.
The technology to tackle such challenges exists, and renewable energy provides a cheap and clean alternative to polluting fossil fuels. But bringing projects themselves into fruition faces technical, bureaucratic, and cost barriers. Thousands of viable sites for clean energy projects scattered across public schools, hospitals, affordable housing, and other sites are currently underutilized due to the significant amount of time, expertise, and up-front resources required to turn a promising site into an operating clean energy project. Clean energy development is rarely a core competency of institutions or organizations with other primary purposes. While some of this market is served by private developers, navigating transaction costs, small project sizes, complicated sites, and other requirements and economic considerations often means such projects are deprioritized in the short term.
The burden of such delays falls on ratepayers and the public. This summer, heat waves overwhelmed the grid and left thousands of New Yorkers without power during the hottest days of the year. With winter temperatures around the corner, heating oil costs have risen nearly 70 percent since last year. Too often, working-class households are forced to choose between keeping themselves safe or paying their utility bills — even as the climate collapses around them.
We are now facing a stark choice: continue business as usual and suffer the consequences, or embrace a new approach that mobilizes the economic strength of the public sector to ensure the job gets done. As timelines for implementation of Local Law 97 (which mandated strict caps on emissions on large buildings in New York City), broader climate mandates, and escalating climate chaos loom, the city needs a public developer like PowerNYC to rapidly expand the deployment of green technology to electrify existing systems.
Introducing PowerNYC Development Corporation
PowerNYC would use its position as a public developer to create a financially self-sustaining engine of decarbonization for New York City. While many of the component parts and projects exist across agencies and other institutional actors, PowerNYC would consolidate the support available at various levels and provide a means to ensure renewable energy projects move from the page to implementation.
One major benefit of PowerNYC would be its ability to recycle capital to create a financially self-sustaining engine of decarbonization. After initial capitalization, its ownership of revenue-generating assets would allow it to back funding for further rounds of development. Applying this model to thermal energy networks and other green technologies would leverage the power of aggregated planning to ensure the public sector can tap into the same low-cost revenue sources from which private utilities already benefit.
For example, through PowerNYC, deploying battery storage across the five boroughs would allow the city to package a fleet of batteries’ worth of power to sell back to the electricity grid at peak demand times to displace the fossil power on which the city currently relies. The contract for such a deal could then be leveraged to secure further financing for ongoing development of renewable energy assets.
By accessing long-term, low-cost, stable financing, public developers like PowerNYC can unlock the potential for large-scale infrastructure projects while ensuring benefits are democratically distributed. Instead of taking a project-by-project approach, it would maximize the government’s ability to coordinate at scale with the goals of multiplying affordability benefits for ratepayers and expediting urgent climate action.
Research shows that deploying an initial 200 megawatts of distributed batteries alone via PowerNYC could generate New York City’s Con Edison ratepayers at least $170 million of savings annually by lowering capacity market costs and distribution costs. And publicly developed thermal energy networks, an alternative to gas pipe replacement, could create savings for National Grid customers in Brooklyn, Staten Island, and Queens who are currently paying for unnecessary gas infrastructure investments. Over time, its development mandate could expand to other clean energy and grid infrastructure needed to support decarbonization and affordability.
A Green Era of Public Institution-Building
No single city or even country can take on the planetary scale of the climate crisis alone, but the establishment of PowerNYC is a major opportunity for the largest city in the country to chart a new era of public institution-building to rapidly scale up climate ambitions.
Cities and states across the country have already embraced the potential of green public development. Nearly a decade ago, the Connecticut Green Bank established a similar, successful model for solar that has driven the state to the top of the national list for its percentage of public schools with on-site solar projects. Countries from Costa Rica to Denmark are using strong networks of public institutions to accelerate the planning and development of public power.
Public development is a proven method for bringing public goods to fruition. PowerNYC would use it to accelerate the deployment of green energy systems and begin to fix our toxic, cost-burdening energy system.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Exclusive: Bernie Sanders on Why It’s Vital for Democrats to Replace Chuck Schumer
In an interview with The Nation, the progressive icon says that the Senate leader is “way out of touch with where the American people are at.”
Exclusive: Bernie Sanders on Why It’s Vital for Democrats to Replace Chuck Schumer
In an interview with “The Nation,” the progressive icon says that the Senate leader is “way out of touch with where the American people are at.”
US Senator Bernie Sanders, who inspired and helped to elect many of the young insurgent candidates who surfed this month’s Democratic “blue wave,” announced Tuesday that he will not support New York Democrat Chuck Schumer’s bid to lead the party’s majority Senate caucus in the next term of Congress.
The move by Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats and who jumpstarted progressive politics with two bids for the party’s presidential nomination, highlighted the need to break with status-quo agendas after a national election result that was broadly read as a cry for change from the American people.
While Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for a decade, retains significant support within the caucus, Sanders argued in an exclusive interview with The Nation that it is vital for the party to do more than simply oppose the administration of Republican President Donald Trump. He said that Democrats must offer a bold domestic and foreign policy vision that replaces Schumer’s cautious centrism with bolder progressive leadership from a senator such as Maryland’s Senator Chris Van Hollen, who says he has begun reaching out to fellow senators as part of a potential leadership challenge.
—John Nichols
THE NATION: You’ve known Chuck Schumer for a very long time. Obviously, you don’t have a lot of personal antipathy toward him. What made you decide to announce that you would not vote to make him majority leader?
SANDERS: Chuck and I grew up, literally, in the same [Brooklyn] neighborhood. I am older than Chuck, but we went to the same elementary school, the same high school. We were on the Banking Committee together when I was first elected to Congress. So I have known Chuck for a long time, and I like Chuck, personally. He’s a very nice guy.
But, I think, in this moment in American history, Chuck’s views are way out of touch with where the American people are at — and especially with where [the base of] the Democratic Party is. On issue after issue, I think he is just not in tune with where his constituents are at.
THE NATION: What issues stand out in that regard?
SANDERS: You can start off with US military aid to Israel. I think that’s a very emotional issue for people in the Democratic caucus. Many of us, including myself, think that [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu has committed genocide on the Palestinian people in Gaza, that Netanyahu is a war criminal, and that the United States should not provide another nickel of military aid to Israel, period.
And I think that basically on other issues Chuck is a guy who wants to tinker around the edges. Is Chuck prepared to fight for what the American people want, which is dealing with massive levels of income and wealth inequality by imposing a billionaire tax — a tax on a billionaire’s wealth so that we can adequately fund childcare, make public colleges and universities tuition-free, and build the millions of units of affordable housing that we need? Is that where Chuck is coming from? I don’t think so.
On AI, Chuck was the minority leader and did nothing significant to address what is the most transformational technology in the history of the world being pushed by a handful of multibillionaires. The American people are deeply concerned [about data centers and the rapid development of artificial intelligence]. The elections show that. Chuck was not there.
Those are just some of the issues that, I think, Chuck has not been leading on.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
THE NATION: The polls show that the Democratic Party is not all that popular. Donald Trump is very unpopular, but the Democratic Party is not all that highly rated.
SANDERS: The Democratic Party, in some polling, is less popular than Trump, correct?
THE NATION: That’s been the case. So, is it your view that it is important for the Democratic Party to show that it actually recognizes that there was a vote for change?
SANDERS: Absolutely, John, and I think for two reasons.
Number one, so many of our people are hurting. Sixty percent of our people live paycheck to paycheck. You have millions of elderly people who don’t know how they’re going to retire with dignity. We have the highest rate of childhood poverty of any major country.
And, number two, I’ll tell you this: Trumpism is not just an American phenomenon. All over Europe, they are seeing the growth of right-wing parties, and the collapse of center-left parties. And I think working people throughout Europe, throughout the United States, are looking at their governments and asking: Do you know that we exist? Do you understand the pain that we are experiencing?
To my mind, it’s not only a question of whether Democrats have to address the enormous economic pain that working families are now experiencing — and their concerns, as they look to the future, that AI may take their jobs, that their kids are likely to have a lower standard of living than they do. It’s not only that we have to deal with those economic issues to help address the pain and anxiety that people are feeling. It’s that if we do not address that pain and anxiety, I worry about the future of democracy. I think people will say: Trump failed us. We gave Democrats an opportunity. Now, they failed us. What we really need is a strong man who will get things right. That’s the history of fascism around the world.
So I think it’s not only the need to address economic pain. Government has finally got to address the issues that working families experience. And if we fail again, and more and more people give up on government, I worry about the future of democracy.
THE NATION: Do you have a candidate in the race for majority leader?
SANDERS: Chris Van Hollen has indicated he’s interested.
THE NATION: And you would support him?
SANDERS: Yes.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Venice exhibition tells the story of the man who brought together contemporary artists and Murano’s master glassblowers
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Emma Park
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
In 1952, Egidio Costantini, an entrepreneur based in Venice, had a brainwave: to take the designs of contemporary artists and, with the collaboration of master glassblowers on the island of Murano, to make artistic sculptures in glass. This was a different approach from that adopted by traditional furnaces like Venini in their decorative glassware, which, although it increasingly involved international designers, was often produced in large, commercially dictated series.
Three years later, Costantini established the Fucina degli Angeli gallery to exhibit the results of his experiment. From then until the 1970s, when other glassmaking companies began to compete, Costantini played a pioneering role in the evolution of glass in Venice, acting as interpreter for more than 100 international artists to Murano’s master glassblowers.
An exhibition opening at the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice this month, curated by the art historian Cristina Beltrami, will tell the Fucina’s story from the 1950s to the 1980s. It will also examine the little-documented but vital role played behind the scenes by Peggy Guggenheim herself, whose purchase of many items helped sustain the gallery financially and whose connections enabled Costantini to exhibit his glass across Europe and even in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. (As it happens, the collector is also the focus of an exhibition opening this month at the Royal Academy of Arts in London, about her Mayfair gallery of the late 1930s—Peggy Guggenheim in London: The Making of a Collector, 21 November-14 March 2027.)
More than 100 works, including glass, painting and sculpture, will be on display in Venice, as well as material from the Fucina’s archives, which have never before been studied in depth. These will be exhibited in 11 rooms organised by artist and theme, and will include glass translations of works by many luminaries of the period, from Max Ernst and Oskar Kokoschka to Lucio Fontana and Paul Jenkins.
Born in Brindisi in the south of Italy in 1912, Costantini established himself permanently in Venice, where he had been raised and educated, at the beginning of the 1950s. There he became a commercial agent for several of Murano’s glassworks. It was the time of Italy’s post-war economic boom and the city was teeming with creative energy. Costantini seems to have found no difficulty in assembling a group of Venetian artists to form the Study Centre for Painters in the Art of Glass, a collective that exhibited its work at the furnace of Ferro & Lazzarini in 1953.
A gift from Picasso
The next step was to involve international artists of even greater stature. Acting on his own initiative, Costantini had glass versions made of some ceramic sculptures by Pablo Picasso and then travelled to Picasso’s house in Vallauris, near Cannes, to show him the results. In return, Picasso gave Costantini a copy of the book Faunes et Nymphes de Pablo Picasso (1952). This survives in the archives with markings on the images of ceramic figures that were later reinterpreted as glass sculptures at the Fucina. But who made the markings remains a mystery.
The name “Fucina degli Angeli” (smithy of the angels) was proposed by the French writer and artist Jean Cocteau, a long-term friend and collaborator, apparently in reference to Costantini’s large family. The Austrian Expressionist artist Kokoschka contributed an emblematic sketch of two angels holding up an anvil, which he dedicated to the gallery and its founder, “who first succeeded in making me fascinated with the glass of Murano”.
Cocteau enjoyed designing extravagant mythological heads for the Fucina, as well as visiting the furnaces and discussing his ideas with the maestri. Both he and Jean Arp, the German sculptor and painter whose work also features in the exhibition, were “seduced by the colour” of glass and its richness, Beltrami says.
The results, though, may not have pleased everyone. The Swiss artist Walter Bodmer allowed his sketch Asymmetric Cat (1955) to be transformed into an oversimplified glass vessel. But after this, for reasons unknown, he never participated again.
The exhibition looks set to offer a fascinating insight into a very personal approach to collaborations between artist and craftsman, as well as an evocative record of an under-appreciated chapter in Venetian history.
• Fucina degli Angeli: Peggy Guggenheim and 20th-Century Artistic Glass, Peggy Guggenheim Collection, Venice, 14 November-29 March 2027

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-sanitatio.title: NYC sanitation supervisors keep speeding on the job, data shows
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-sanitatio.author: Liam Quigley
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-sanitatio.text:
New York City sanitation department supervisors who oversee trash collection and issue tickets have a need for speed, an analysis of ticketing data shows.
A Gothamist review of thousands of license plates belonging to the sanitation department shows 763 SUVs and passenger vehicles assigned to supervisors and other non-trash collection staff have racked up at least 2,375 speed camera tickets since 2023. Those employees drive cars and are tasked with making sure trucks collect trash on schedule. Supervisors also issue tickets to home and business owners who don’t comply with city regulations for putting out their garbage.
Transportation activists say the hasty driving demonstrates the need to accelerate a rollout of devices in city-owned vehicles that limit how fast the cars can go, something Mayor Zohran Mamdani has championed.
Sanitation officials said the agency requires employees to pay back fines from automated camera tickets out of their own pockets, or face disciplinary action. Sanitation employees have paid back nearly $199,000 in fines they got while driving department vehicles since 2023, according to city data.
The agency employs around 10,000 people, but fewer than 1,700 of them are supervisors, superintendents or enforcement agents.
Alexa Sledge, a spokesperson for the street safety advocacy group Transportation Alternatives, said the department’s supervisors need to slow down on the job.
“There’s no world in New York City where the kind of vehicles that we're relying on to serve and protect New Yorkers should also be traveling recklessly around the five boroughs,” spokesperson Alexa Sledge said.
Sledge said the city should put speed limiters on the vehicles and change how streets are designed to make it untenable for drivers to do so in the first place.
“By far the most effective thing that New York City can do is ensure that no city vehicles have the ability to speed, [that] they all have speed limiters, and then designing the kinds of streets and intersections that make it very, very difficult and unappealing to speed,” she said.
Roughly 77% of the sanitation department’s garbage trucks have not received a single speeding ticket since 2023, city data shows.
The large vehicles have at times been a source of traffic deaths. Last month, a 30-year-old woman was killed in Brooklyn when she was run over by a DSNY garbage truck driver. The investigation into that crash is ongoing. Police arrested the sanitation worker and issued him a desk appearance ticket, prosecutors said.

It was a stark and forbidding vision for those who followed the righteous path. Scorn, the preacher told his congregation, was a person’s lot if they led an “honest, clean, pure, godly life.” The world hated “people that live like that,” he said.
“They want you to be just as ungodly and filthy as they are,” he said in a rare audio recording, obtained by The Oregonian/OregonLive, of a 1958 sermon.
The preacher was Walter White, who led an Oregon City offshoot of the Followers of Christ, an Idaho sect that spurns medical treatment as a show of faith. White was a grocer, originally from Picabo, Idaho, whose congregants came to view as a prophet. He rambled at times during his sermon but always returned to simple and severe messages about choosing righteousness rather than the ways of the world. A trim figure in wire-rim glasses and dark combed-back hair, he spoke in a voice that evoked the stentorian tones of an old newsreel announcer. In the scratchy recording, people cough and babies cry as he preaches.
White was uneasy about being taped, according to a note by the congregant who made the recording. White didn’t want his message to fall into what he thought were undesirable hands. He viewed disbelievers with disgust. They put their trust in human experts, such as doctors, rather than in God. People like that, he told the faithful, “want to be somebody.” They want “the wisdom of the world and admiration.”
Today, nearly 60 years after White’s death, his pronouncements continue to influence the faithful. For many Followers, White remained “the highest authority,” said Mark Shaw, who left the sect in 2019 and keeps in touch with some Followers. Members invoked his teachings to settle disagreements. “It was used as the trump card,” he said. “It was the discussion-ender.”
To understand the modern-day Oregon City congregation, it’s essential to examine White’s role. No pastor ever succeeded him, leaving the sect all the more reliant on his teachings.
The Oregonian/OregonLive and ProPublica have published a series of articles in recent months about the Followers of Christ in Oregon and Idaho, focusing on the long history of parents in Followers congregations declining to seek medical care for their critically ill children and the sometimes fatal consequences.
Little has been publicly known about White, likely due to the Followers’ culture of isolation and secrecy. The Oregonian/OregonLive was able to piece together details through documents we obtained, including biographical sketches, a transcript and the recording of the sermon, along with written accounts of dreams White purported to have and records of baptisms he performed. Among the documents was a list of his prophecies and even a sex guide he disseminated.
White was born into the Followers, whose members migrated to Idaho from the Midwest around the turn of the 20th century. Men in White’s family preached, and he joined them in his 20s, the story goes, after he dreamed that worms would devour him if he didn’t.
In the early 1930s, White joined two church elders on a journey from Idaho to Oregon City to minister to a dying man. After talking with them, the man readily discarded his medications and was relieved to see White, an avid smoker, roll a cigarette because the man didn’t want to kick the habit. For the next five years, White traveled between Idaho and Oregon to preach and by 1938, he had moved to Oregon to lead a fledgling congregation.
Followers at the time were led by a constellation of preachers and elders, all men. Notes from one of their meetings in 1937 revealed that Followers believed White possessed the “gift of prophecy.” It also recorded the debates that simmered among them — whether women should be allowed to cut their hair, for instance. They talked about the value of dictionaries, which some classified as “worldly” items to be avoided, and determined that women assisting with home births should not “look under the cover” as women labored. One account written years later by a Follower suggested that White split with a prominent Idaho preacher after revelations that the man had sexual contact with a 15-year-old girl.
Some of those values still shape the Followers today. Congregants tend to stay out of what they view as the worldly affairs of politics and civic life, and they generally don’t pursue education beyond high school or vocational training. The Followers remain patriarchal; men are expected to lead their households.
White was known among Followers as “brother Walter.” An undated black-and-white photograph shows him baptizing a child in what appears to be a baptismal pool, his arm raised in prayer. In another image dated 1951, he wears a suit jacket and tie, a mug in one hand and a cigarette in the other.
As much a ruler as a spiritual leader, White enjoyed near-absolute authority. Followers believed he possessed such divine power that he knew their thoughts and secrets. They turned to him for approval on matters both consequential and mundane, from marital advice to appliance purchases. (White even weighed in on where to shop: He owned a local market and made it clear he expected to see Followers there.)
White’s earthly teachings extended to a perhaps unexpected realm: Couples on the cusp of marriage received a sex guide, which continued to be distributed as recently as 2018. Complete with explicit detail and anatomical diagrams, the 15-page manual includes chapters titled “the ideal love act” and “the control of climax.” And, in a seeming exception to the prohibition on medical treatment, it goes so far as to recommend that women who feel inhibited should consider seeing a doctor “who has given the sex problems sincere study.”
White preached the Oregon City sect’s singularity: His flock was spiritually superior to other Follower congregations, he contended, including ones in Idaho and Grants Pass, Oregon. By the 1950s, he had cut off ties to those groups.
In 1965, White told his congregation of his prophecy that the end times were near. He recounted a dream, which he said was set against the backdrop of the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, that involved walking with Jesus Christ, according to one account. He dreamed they climbed a launchpad, and White noted he was impressed with Christ’s physical agility. Days before White shared his vision, NASA launched Gemini 3, the first U.S. mission to send multiple astronauts into space.
White told the faithful that it was during this dream that Christ said the world would come to an end in six years. He said Christ warned that baptisms among the Followers would end even sooner. That his apocalyptic prophecy fizzled didn’t shake Followers’ faith.
White died in 1969. He was seen as irreplaceable. A handful of elders divided his leadership duties but lacked White’s authority. The faithful never tapped a successor, believing only a man called by God could fill the role. No one was ever deemed worthy enough to take his place.
But one element of White’s prophecy did come true. Given that he was the only person who could perform baptisms, his passing also meant that the ritual ended. As a result, the flock, which former members say numbered 1,500 or more at its peak, today consists solely of generations of the same families who were members in 1969.
Like other elders in the early days of the Followers, White saw illness as a test of faith. During the 1937 meeting, about 18 elders and preachers from congregations in Idaho and Oregon gathered at the Oregon City meetinghouse to settle the rules that would shape the church, according to a written account compiled by sect members years later.
The men discussed the Book of James in the New Testament, which says, “And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up.” Followers interpret the lines as an edict to rely only on faith when faced with illness. The passage would be “strictly enforced to show faith,” according to an account of the meeting compiled years later. They believed that death, if it came, was God’s will.
Years later, in 1965, when the state investigated the case of a teen in the sect whose broken ankle had gone untreated, White said, “faith can heal,” according to a story in The Oregonian at the time. “We believe that God comes before man. If a person’s faith doesn’t go far enough, then he can seek help from man.”
The consequences of this belief system still reverberate. For years, the Oregon City Followers suffered multiple child deaths, many from treatable or preventable conditions. The deaths prompted the Legislature in 1999 to chip away at legal protections for parents whose children died without medical care. Then in 2011, lawmakers removed all protections for faith healing.
The faith-healing doctrine would affect White’s own descendants. Two of his great-granddaughters spent years in prison for failing to seek medical care for their premature newborns who died. In 2017, one of his great-great-granddaughters, Evelyn, suffered respiratory complications related to her premature birth. Authorities attribute her survival to the intervention of law enforcement officials who ordered her parents to get her to the hospital. Evelyn’s life and journey out of the Followers is the subject of a story and documentary published by The Oregonian/OregonLive and ProPublica.
