Capitalism Is More Than a Legal Regime
Katharina Pistor argues that capitalism is a legal regime we can transform by rewiring private law. But a reform program that ignores the wage relation and the exploitation of labor will leave the core of capitalism untouched.
“Capitalism is a legal regime, not just an economic system as conventional wisdom has it.” With this opening sentence, Katharina Pistor takes the argument of her previous book, The Code of Capital, a step further. There she showed how lawyers turn assets into capital through property, contract, collateral, trust, corporate, and bankruptcy law. Her new book extends the argument to capitalism as a whole.
If law so thoroughly constitutes capitalism, she asks, why is it “so resistant to legal governance”? And how might we transform it?
Pistor has much to say about the legal powers of capital, and her account deserves serious attention. Yet I find two fundamental problems with her argument. Although she insists that capitalism is legal to the core, she has remarkably little to say about the wage relation and the extraction of surplus labor in the production process. Without these, we can understand neither capitalist production nor its capacity to reproduce itself.
This omission carries over into her proposals for transforming capitalism. Her project of democratizing private law leaves the basic relations of production intact. The result is a reform program that may constrain some of capital’s powers but offers little prospect of overcoming capitalist exploitation.
The second, related problem concerns the economic foundations of her argument. Pistor describes her approach as “imbued with a strong dose of political economy.” Yet she makes claims about the redistributive achievements of the welfare state and the sources of capitalist profit without engaging with a substantial body of Marxian theoretical and empirical research that bears directly on both questions.
At the heart of Pistor’s account is a definition of capital by its tradability. For her, capital is any asset that law has coded so that it can be “mortgaged or sold for profit.” Without such coding, she writes, ordinary assets “will not produce wealth on the scale that legally coded capital assets can.” Three things follow.
Capital becomes an asset that law codes for trade at a profit. Capitalists become “traders in any asset that promises financial returns,” and capitalist ownership becomes a matter of “maximizing pecuniary gain from an asset.” Capitalism thus becomes the legal regime that creates such assets and gives their holders privileged access to the coercive power of the state through private law. Conspicuously absent from this triad is the capitalist as employer of wage labor, a point to which I return below.
Drawing on Evgeny Pashukanis, Pistor locates a defining feature of capitalist law in the separation of private and public law. Each rest on a different normative foundation. Public law concerns constitutions, democratic self-government, and limits on state power; private law, by contrast, revolves around individual autonomy and freedom of contract. Yet private rights, no less than public ones, depend on the coercive power of the state for their enforcement.
This arrangement enables capital to exercise considerable power through private law while escaping many of the constraints that public law imposes.
Pistor develops this argument through three mechanisms. The first is legal empowerment: property, contract, and the corporate form confer powers on private actors while limiting their accountability. The second is access to legal coercion, through which private parties can call on the state to enforce their claims. The third is legal arbitrage: capital can move between jurisdictions and choose favorable legal arrangements, whereas workers and other individuals face the restrictions that immigration and nationality laws impose.
In Pistor’s account, these mechanisms also help explain why earlier reforms proved so vulnerable. The New Deal introduced substantial changes in finance, housing, labor relations, and social security, but “did not alter private law and its normative foundations.” Capital subsequently found ways around these reforms, including the outsourcing of labor and the creation of new financial instruments. Pistor therefore argues that regulation alone cannot do the job; we must rewire private law itself and place it on a different normative foundation.
Production and Exploitation
My principal difficulty with the book concerns its treatment of production, or rather its failure to examine it. In the opening paragraph, Pistor lists several phenomena that Karl Marx and Joseph Schumpeter regarded as economic: trade, labor relations, private ownership of the means of production, corporations, banking, and money. She then declares that “these matters are legal to the core.”
Given this claim, one might reasonably expect an examination of the legal relations that govern capitalist production, particularly the employment contract. Surprisingly, there is almost none of it.
The terms “surplus value,” “surplus labor,” and “labor power” do not appear in the book, and the index contains no entry for “exploitation.” Production enters the discussion mainly through the ownership of the means of production, with little attention to what happens when workers put those means to use in the production process.
Pistor does refer to labor exploitation on three occasions, but none of them leads to a sustained discussion. She notes that recently some Marxist scholars have questioned “the exploitation of labor as the source of surplus that capital extracts.” But she reports this disagreement without a reference, without saying who these scholars are, and without stating her own position.
In a related passage, she appears to endorse the view that, “as Marx and [Friedrich] Engels argued, owning the means of production allows capitalists to extract surplus from labor.” That idea, she adds, “economic models have more recently confirmed.” These “economic models,” however, turn out to be a single model, that of Oliver Hart and John Moore, which is a far cry from confirming Marx’s theory of exploitation. For these authors, “surplus” refers to the gains from trade that relationship-specific investment generates, which the parties then divide through bargaining; it has nothing to do with Marx’s surplus value.
Pistor also observes that one-sided contracts have long characterized labor relations, and that this “inspired Marx’s analysis of the exploitation of labor through capital.” She recognizes, moreover, that ownership of the means of production gives capital “the power to set the terms for the contractual relation with labor.” This could have been the starting point for an analysis of capitalist exploitation, but she does not pursue the subject further. The discussion turns instead to unionization, the National Labor Relations Act, and gig workers, largely in terms of bargaining power, before moving on to social media contracts.
Finally, she remarks that “labor exploitation has never been recognized as grounds for asylum.” Here “exploitation” refers to abusive working conditions rather than to the specific social relation that Marx analyzed.
This neglect of exploitation matters for Pistor’s own argument, because the wage contract is surely among the most consequential legal relations in capitalist society. Workers and capitalists enter into it as formally free and equal parties, yet the contract gives the capitalist command over the use of labor power for a specified period. The worker’s separation from the means of production is what makes this arrangement possible and, for most wage earners, necessary.
Marx’s analysis of the sale and purchase of labor power is particularly relevant here. In the sphere of circulation, the exchange happens between equals. Exploitation takes place in production, where the use of a unique commodity, labor power, creates more value than its own reproduction requires. The wage contract provides the legal form of this exploitative relation.
Pistor’s engagement with Marx follows a consistent pattern. She either sets aside central elements of his materialist analysis or reworks his categories into new ones. The first move shows in the weight she gives to power, intangible property, and data ownership. These largely take the place of the material constraints that, for Marx, the economic structure imposes on social and legal relations.
The second move is clearest in her claim that law is “a productive force in its own right, because it is the means that allows holders of assets to extract their pecuniary value.” Pistor knows that she is departing from historical materialism here, and she says so against G. A. Cohen and Jeremy Kessler. The difficulty is her criterion. In Marx’s framework, the capacity to extract value does not make something a productive force.
That capacity belongs to the relations of production, the social relations that organize production and determine who appropriates its results. She calls law a productive force, but extracting and appropriating value is precisely what relations of production do. Law adds nothing to a society’s capacity to produce; it organizes who controls production and who claims its results. By her own criterion, then, law belongs among the relations of production, not the forces.
Profit on Alienation and the Legal Appropriation of Wealth
One Marxian concept could help clarify much of what Pistor describes: profit on alienation, or profit upon alienation, a term Marx took over from James Steuart. It refers to profit that arises from transfers and unequal exchange rather than from the production of surplus value.
Anwar Shaikh discussed profit on alienation as a secondary but significant source of profit. Shaikh and I subsequently used the category in our book Measuring the Wealth of Nations, and Shaikh reiterated its significance in his treatment of the transformation problem. Costas Lapavitsas drew on a related conception in Profiting Without Producing to analyze the profits banks extract from workers’ income.
In a recent study, Alper Duman and I examined profit on alienation in Turkey between 2010 and 2019, focusing on real estate and finance. The first case involved the privatization of public land. When the state transfers land to a private developer at less than its market value, the developer gains the difference as profit, although the transaction creates no new wealth; public wealth simply passes into private hands.
The second case concerned bank lending to working-class households, which pay the interest out of wages rather than out of surplus value from production. We estimated profit on alienation over the decade at $9.31 billion in real estate and $57.23 billion in finance.
These examples are closely related to the processes Pistor investigates. The enclosure of land, data, and knowledge; the privatization of public assets; and the socialization of financial losses all involve legal arrangements that enable private actors to appropriate existing wealth. The law is an indispensable participant in these processes, and Pistor is right to insist on its importance.
An account of how assets acquire legal protection and become sources of private profit does not, however, by itself tell us where that profit comes from. It may come from the production of new value or from the reappropriation of existing wealth through unequal exchange. We can understand much of what Pistor calls the legal coding of capital as the legal organization and enforcement of profit on alienation. This is especially apparent in privatization and in financial claims on household income.
The distinction between surplus value and profit on alienation would allow Pistor to address a question that remains unresolved in her account. So would the related distinction between productive and unproductive activities, which Shaikh and I developed, and which I have extended to the digital sector. Under what circumstances does the legal coding of assets facilitate the production of new wealth, and when does it merely enable the transfer or reappropriation of wealth that already exists?
This question is especially relevant to The Code of Capital, whose subtitle promises to explain “how the law creates wealth and inequality.” Pistor provides a compelling account of the legal construction of claims to wealth. But the distinction between the production and the redistribution of value is essential if we are to understand the economic significance of those claims.
This also brings us back to the absence of the labor process. If the law helps constitute capitalist social relations, the employment contract and the property relations underlying it ought to occupy a central place in the analysis. Without them, we learn a great deal about how capital acquires, exercises, and protects its legal powers, but very little about the legal conditions under which workers produce surplus value.
The Welfare State and the Net Social Wage
Pistor’s case for rewiring private law also rests on a particular understanding of the welfare state. Countries have “experimented with social welfarism,” she writes, but the success of this reform agenda “has often been only temporary.” The New Deal, she argues, “aimed to restore the balance between the working class and the upper class.” Her explanation for the eventual erosion of the welfare state’s achievements emphasizes capital’s capacity to circumvent public regulation through private law.
This account takes for granted something that deserves closer examination: How much did the welfare state actually redistribute from capital to labor?
For several decades, Marxian researchers have investigated this question using the concept of the net tax and, later, that of the net social wage. They define the latter as the government expenditures on social services that workers receive minus the taxes they pay. The results are much more nuanced than the conventional picture of the welfare state as a sustained transfer of income from capital to labor.
Shaikh and I studied the United States and found that, between 1952 and 1997, the net social wage seldom moved outside a range of ±4 percent of employee compensation. It averaged only 0.6 percent, effectively zero. During the postwar expansion of 1952–1969, it was negative: workers paid more in taxes than they received in social expenditures.
The Ronald Reagan–George H. W. Bush period, which we described as a “counterattack by capital and the state,” pushed it down again. Our conclusion was that, by and large, “it is the taxes of the working population that essentially pay for the corresponding state expenditures.”
Shaikh’s subsequent multicountry study reached a similar conclusion for countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD): “In effect, workers paid for their own social benefits.”
Katherine Moos extended the US estimates through 2012 using two methods. On the narrower measure, the net social wage averaged 1.3 percent of GDP; on the more comprehensive measure, which attributes a larger share of taxation to labor, it averaged -3.8 percent. She also identified a shift after 2001, when the net social wage turned positive for more than a decade.
Moos did not, however, interpret this development as evidence of renewed redistribution from capital to labor. She linked it instead to mass unemployment and underemployment, rising health care costs, and the expansion of wage subsidies such as the Earned Income Tax Credit. As she argues, “subsidies to labor are also subsidies to capital.”
Public expenditures, which governments often finance through deficits, increasingly make up for wages and benefits that employers no longer provide. In this context, a positive net social wage can be “evidence of the decline in conditions for the working class, not improvement.” Yakup Karabacak and I found a different pattern in Turkey from 1980 to 2019: the net social wage was negative in all but five years and averaged -1.13 percent of GDP. Turkish workers, in other words, paid more in taxes than they received in social benefits.
These results bear directly on Pistor’s explanation of the welfare state’s limitations. Her argument implies that public law reforms initially restrained capital, but that capital later undermined them because the foundations of private law remained unchanged.
Taxation and social security are themselves legal institutions, and public law largely constitutes them. The net social wage studies suggest that these institutions have often redistributed income within the working population rather than producing a substantial net transfer from capital to labor. More recently, some forms of social expenditure have effectively subsidized employers by compensating for inadequate wages and benefits.
This does not mean that welfare state programs were unimportant to workers or that they brought no improvement in living standards. Public health care, education, pensions, and unemployment protection can have enormous social value; however, governments finance them. But we should not confuse their existence with a net redistribution from capital to labor.
Pistor’s account of the welfare state would be considerably stronger if it engaged with this evidence. Public law was not necessarily the counterweight to capital that her argument seems to assume; it has also helped reproduce capitalist relations, including through the taxation of wages and the public subsidization of labor costs. Capital’s ability to escape into private law therefore cannot by itself explain the failure of welfare state reform.
For a book whose central concern is the difficulty of governing capitalism through law, engagement with this literature would have provided a direct test of its central claim.
Reform and the Question of Political Agency
The problem with Pistor’s program is not simply that her proposals are modest. Reforms can matter, and there is no reason to dismiss them because they fall short of abolishing capitalism. What is difficult to understand is why Pistor expects reforms of this kind to transform a system whose underlying relations of production would remain unchanged.
Consider the place of workers in her program. They appear as possible beneficiaries of greater participatory rights and as weaker parties who might gain access to public courts if restrictive arbitration clauses no longer stood in the way. Both changes could be worthwhile, but they leave the employment relation itself largely untouched.
Nor does Pistor propose changing the ownership of the means of production, which, as she herself acknowledges, gives capital the power to set the terms of labor contracts. Martha Nussbaum’s “capability of being able to work as a human,” which Pistor draws on, comes closest to addressing the conditions of work, but it does not confront the social relation through which capital appropriates surplus labor.
There is a further difficulty. Pistor says remarkably little about the social and political forces that might bring about the changes she advocates.
Pistor recognizes the rise of “populist” discontent, but she treats it primarily as a danger to channel before it becomes “difficult to control.” She does not seriously consider whether the conflicts that give rise to such discontent might also provide a basis for collective political action.
One might object that a book about law need not offer a comprehensive theory of political organization. But once Pistor moves from explaining capitalism’s legal structure to proposing its transformation, the question of agency becomes unavoidable. Through what organizations and struggles could anyone achieve and defend the proposed changes?
Treating law as constitutive of capitalist relations is not the problem (what is objectionable, as I argued above, is treating it as a productive force); indeed, Marx’s analysis of the wage contract provides ample grounds for doing so. But accepting the material significance of law does not settle the question of which social relations to transform. Pistor’s stated aim is to “chart a path beyond capitalism,” yet the economy she envisages is a “genuine market economy” without capital’s legal privileges. If the objective is to move beyond capitalism, a serious program cannot leave out the legal relations governing wage labor and the ownership of the means of production.
Transformation Without Transformation
The neglect of production and of collective agency also shapes Pistor’s strategy for transforming capitalism. She explicitly rejects revolution: “Traditionally, Marxists have called for revolution, a violent overthrowing of the ruling class. This has never happened in advanced capitalist countries, seems unlikely, and is also undesirable.”
Her preferred approach draws on Nicos Poulantzas’s image of “walking on a tightrope,” a gradual process of change within existing institutions. She mentions Andre Gunder Frank’s call for a “revolutionary Marxist strategy” only in passing, observing that “Obviously, this has not happened.”
For Pistor, the existing legal system “cannot simply be undone”; instead, “law needs to be rewired from within.” She returns to this position in the epilogue: “The transformation of the existing system will not happen in a single leap. Rather, transformation happens as the cumulative effect of a myriad of smaller steps.”
This preference for incremental “rewiring” rests partly on the claim that revolution has never occurred in advanced capitalist countries. Pistor does not analyze revolutions elsewhere — in Russia, China, Cuba, and Vietnam, and in the anti-colonial struggles — as revolutions; they appear only as “disappointing” outcomes or as instances of convergence on capitalism. Moreover, her own examples of law’s capacity for transformation, from feudalism to republicanism and from colonialism to a new international order, include several revolutionary ruptures. This sits uneasily with her claim that history has never moved “in a single leap.”
Pistor’s proposal to “democratize private law” rests on a theory of the state that is more sophisticated than the strategy she builds on it. She rejects both the liberal picture of the state as a neutral arbiter and the classical Marxist picture of it as an instrument of the ruling class. Following Poulantzas, she treats the state as a “condensation of the relations of forces,” a terrain of struggle that private law has caught “in its own trap.” She concludes that “calling for the state to free society from the excesses of capitalism is therefore misguided.”
However, her proposed transition still runs almost entirely through the state’s institutions. A binding “Just Private Law” code would require action by legislatures or a revision of the EU treaties. The precautionary principle, an expanded duty of care, and a broader doctrine of veil-piercing would depend on judges willing to apply them. Ending the banks’ money franchise, she admits, “rests in public hands”: legislatures, central banks, and finance ministries, the very bodies her own analysis shows to be most exposed to the influence of finance.
Capital has shaped each of these tools, and it has long influenced the processes that staff them. Her own evidence shows these institutions reworking or reversing reforms, from the New Deal to the civil procedure reforms of 1938. It is therefore unclear why a democratized private law would escape the same fate.
Pistor’s selective use of Poulantzas makes the problem worse. She takes over his relational conception of the state and, as we have seen, his tightrope image of gradual transformation. But she leaves aside what, in Poulantzas’s own framework, made any change from within the state conceivable at all: an organized social force outside it, capable of shifting the balance of forces that the state condenses.
One need not accept Poulantzas’s strategic conclusions to see the inconsistency. If the state is a condensation of class forces, then a reform program that names no force able to change that condensation has no road to realization, even on its own terms. Pistor offers no such force. No class, party, trade union, or movement appears as the agent that would push a reformed private law through captured legislatures and courts and defend it afterward.
Instead, she relies on deliberation, on crises as moments of decision, on judges, legislatures, and citizen tribunals, and on the hope that small steps will accumulate. When she anticipates the charge of naïveté, she answers that law is itself part of the raw material of capital, so normative change can act as a material lever. This shows that law can be a lever, but not one that anyone could pull in a state whose topography capital has shaped.
Without a theory of collective agency, her proposal risks being less realistic than the socialist alternatives she sets aside, not more. If we go beyond the limits Poulantzas imposed on his own approach, the main way out lies in a struggle by that collective agent to abolish the capitalist (or bourgeois) form of the state. That form of the state allows the private law system to function as a source of profit when capitalism finds itself in great crises. In its place, the struggle would establish a public law order that takes care of the collective interest of the whole society: socialism.
An Analysis Without a Strategy
Pistor has written an important book about the legal organization of capitalist power. Her insistence that law is constitutive of capitalism challenges the tendency of mainstream economics to treat legal institutions as an external framework within which economic activity takes place. Her account of the dismantling of New Deal reforms persuasively shows how private law arrangements enabled capital to circumvent public regulation. The net social wage evidence suggests, however, that we need to assess the redistributive achievements of those reforms more critically.
Her discussion of central banks and the socialization of financial costs since 2008 is also valuable. Her observation that contracts are “only rarely expressions of bargains” and more often “instruments of control” is especially striking. This insight could provide the basis for a much richer examination of the employment relation.
My disagreements concern the economic foundations of Pistor’s analysis (production, profit on alienation, and the net social wage) and the political conclusions she draws from them.
These gaps matter for her proposed reforms. The democratization of private law may restrain corporate power and strengthen the hand of weaker parties, and these are worthwhile objectives. But wage labor and capitalist ownership of the means of production would remain in place, and Pistor barely discusses the political forces capable of bringing about even the reforms she proposes.
I therefore find The Law of Capitalism more convincing as an analysis of the legal powers of capital than as an account of how we might transform capitalism. Pistor has considerably enriched our understanding of the former. A theory of the latter would need to address the production and appropriation of surplus value, the role of the state in reproducing class relations, and the social struggles through which working people might change those relations.

A month after closing its Berlin exhibition space, the Julia Stoschek Foundation, a nonprofit arts organisation set up by the German collector and businesswoman Julia Stoschek, announced it will reopen its Dusseldorf headquarters in April 2027.
The Dusseldorf space closed for renovation in 2025. The inaugural exhibition in the newly revamped space, called Selfish in Bed, is curated by Krist Gruijthuijsen, formerly the director of the KW Institute for Contemporary Art in Berlin, and features works by 43 artists from the foundation’s collection. The foundation’s more than 1,000-piece collection is focused primarily on time-based art—including video, film, moving-image installations, multimedia work, performance, sound work and virtual reality work.
“Seeing the collection continue to grow and welcoming new audiences two decades on brings me enormous joy,” Stoschek said in a statement. “And I can think of no better home for it than Düsseldorf, a city where art has been part of everyday life for generations.”
Stoschek’s Berlin space operated for ten years from June 2016 to October 2026. It hosted 22 exhibitions and drew 500,000 visitors. In April, the foundation said the closure was the result of a “strategic realignment” and that it would “now focus on international projects in order to make the collection accessible to a global audience.”
The Dusseldorf reopening marks the foundation’s 20th anniversary.
Selfish in Bed, which will run from 10 April to 19 December 2027, takes its name from a 2000 self-portrait by Sarah Lucas. Other artists who will feature in the exhibition include Wolfgang Tillmans, Bill Viola, Simon Fujiwara, Rosemarie Trockel and Tracey Emin.

https://gothamist.com/news/mamdanis-rede.title: Mamdani’s redevelopment plan for NYCHA complex in Chelsea spills into DSA
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdanis-rede.author: Elizabeth Kim
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdanis-rede.text:
The fight over the redevelopment of a NYCHA complex in Chelsea is playing out inside Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s political machine, pitting holdout tenants and leftwing democratic socialists against allies of the mayor and pro-housing advocates.
Tenant activists at Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea Houses have joined the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, arguing that the redevelopment of their homes amounts to privatization of public housing. The plan would allow private developers to build mixed-income housing on the NYCHA property in exchange for replacing roughly 2,000 units of public housing.
Mamdani and other high-profile DSA members in his administration counter that the aging buildings are in such bad condition that a teardown is cheaper than renovations. The $1.2 billion project could serve as a model for rebuilding other NYCHA complexes.
The escalating conflict has created uncomfortable optics for the mayor. The newly minted DSA members accuse Mamdani, who campaigned as a champion of working class New Yorkers fighting wealthy interests, of abandoning his values.
“What's happening here doesn't fall under socialist principles,” said Celines Miranda, a 51-year-old tenant activist who grew up in an apartment at the Elliot-Chelsea House. “If you're a socialist, then you support socialist housing.”
“We have no interest in being privatized. We have no interest in being demolished,” she added.
Cea Weaver, who leads the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants, said the tenant activists do not represent the broader opinion of residents.
“Just as everybody in DSA does not agree, everybody who lives on the Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea campuses do not agree,” Weaver said. “My experience working for the mayor and being on the ground in this project over the last few months has been that there are many, many tenants who are very eager for this to move forward.”
Miranda rejected the notion that a new building built by a private developer is actually an upgrade.
“I don't want the fake Gucci bag just because it glitters and it looks pretty,” she said.
On Saturday, Miranda will join two fellow tenant activists at a DSA convention where members will decide whether to take a formal stance against the city’s plan for the NYCHA properties.
The debate centers on ideological questions about what constitutes public housing, and what a progressive city can and should do to fix NYCHA with dwindling federal funding.
Nicholas Bloom, a Hunter professor who has written about the history of NYCHA, said leftists inspired by social housing programs in Europe pitched the idea of the housing authority in the aftermath of World War II. He said today’s democratic socialists now face a tough choice over political priorities.
“We definitely are entering some era, at least at the city level, of more social democratic politics,” he said. “But the question is, where do you want to put your effort? Building new public housing or permanently affordable housing?”
City officials have promised existing tenants at Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea new apartments, which would come under private management. Rents would remain at 30% of their income.
But rather than falling under the federal Section 9 program, the developments would be converted to project-based Section 8, in which the government subsidizes rent through vouchers.
The shift to private-public partnerships has made some tenants uneasy. A group of holdouts are refusing to leave the NYCHA buildings, slowing the project.
“We're trying to save public housing,” said Savasiah Gardner, a 41-year-old tenant who joined the DSA earlier this year. “Public housing is a human right. Period.”
The debate spilled online last month after some accused Layla Law-Gisiko, a local district leader who opposes the redevelopment, of trying to recruit new DSA members to stack votes against the city’s plan. Some questioned her socialist bona fides, noting her hobby as an equestrian and her physical proximity to Republicans Curtis Sliwa and City Councilmember Vickie Palandino during a press conference last year.
“Apparently, defending public housing now requires surviving a forensic examination of your political contributions, photographs of your summer meals, and G_d forbid you had a Maryland blue crab,” Law-Gisiko wrote on X.
Law-Gisiko declined to comment.
Weaver, a DSA member, downplayed the internal strife.
“One of the reasons why I love being in DSA is that reasonable people can debate, and I think a robust culture of debate, including debate that happens in public, is part of being a socialist,” she said.
Weaver said the city’s plan — which had been in the works across two prior mayoral administrations — is consistent with DSA principles.
“Keeping our public housing in disrepair as it is today is not acceptable to me given my socialist values,” she said.
The city has yet to close on the deal with the developers. Under the first phase, two buildings have been designated for demolition. More than two dozen families, including a large group of seniors who fear they won’t outlive the redevelopment, are refusing to move.
City officials, including Weaver, have offered to meet with the tenants opposed to the plan.
But the tenants say they want to meet with the mayor.
Jackie Lara, who has lived in the Fulton Houses for 24 years, has circulated petitions, filed lawsuits and even appeared in a documentary that drew the attention of DSA members. Last year, she ran unsuccessfully for City Council.
The 63-year-old said she joined the DSA in hopes that she and other tenants could finally get a meeting with Mamdani.
“He should come speak to the residents that have been fighting this and listen to our story,” Lara said. “That’s all I ask.”

https://www.propublica.org/article/east-.title: “We Have No One”: How Trump’s Dismantling of the VA Left a Veterans Hospital in Crisis
https://www.propublica.org/article/east-.author: Eric Umansky, Joel Jacobs, Hokyoung Kim
https://www.propublica.org/article/east-.text:
This was not normal. But nothing had been normal at East Orange since President Donald Trump returned to office last year and set his sights on the VA.
The behemoth agency, which traces its roots to the Civil War, is both the country’s largest healthcare system and one of its most effective. It provides 9 million veterans what is essentially socialized medicine, often for free, under the cover of the American flag. The doctors, nurses and other staff are employed by the government.
Despite the occasional scandal and persistent short-staffing, studies have shown that the VA — where the doctors coordinate with one another and have deep expertise on veterans’ needs — has better outcomes than private care.
But in his second term, Trump has moved aggressively to upend this system, embracing a decades-long conservative campaign to effectively kneecap the VA’s government-run healthcare and shift veterans toward private doctors and hospitals.
Under Trump, the VA has increasingly acted like an insurer, paying doctors in the community for vets’ care. This, the reasoning went, would allow the government to cut thousands of needless bureaucrats while giving veterans more choices if the VA can’t provide the care.
Do You Have Information About the VA That We Should Know?
We’re still reporting. If you know more about this topic, please contact our reporting team.
Eric Umansky
I’m looking for tips on the VA’s care of veterans, and I’m particularly interested in hearing from healthcare providers and others who work at VA hospitals. Contact me with tips by email or securely on Signal. I take confidentiality seriously.
“We love our veterans,” Trump said during an Oval Office photo op shortly after his inauguration. “We are going to take good care of them.”
Days after that pronouncement, a memo leaked showing the administration was considering sweeping job cuts at the agency. “Things need to change,” warned Doug Collins, Trump’s new VA secretary, in a video message to staff.
After pushback from vets groups and others, the administration retreated from its threat of mass layoffs. But it found another, less attention-getting way to shrink the VA.
If Trump’s appointees couldn’t lay off employees, they would make work conditions so untenable that staffers would leave on their own.
The administration canceled the contracts of the agency’s unions — citing national security concerns. They ordered remote staffers back to the office. Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency demanded employees report what they had accomplished each week. And the administration offered staffers early retirement packages and other incentives to quit.
Throughout it all, the VA’s leadership said front-line medical workers would be immune from any cuts. But amid the upheaval, many left anyway.
Six months after Trump entered the White House, the VA had 3,800 fewer doctors, nurses and other “mission critical” staff than it did at the start of his term, according to the department’s own data. While the losses made up a small percentage of overall employees, the drop compounded longstanding shortages — and contrasted sharply with a hiring spree under President Joe Biden that had begun to address them. Many of the front-line workers who quit in Trump’s early days have never been replaced. Instead, the VA has eliminated thousands of open positions, including doctors, nurses and other providers.
The administration has denied that it is hurting veterans’ care. “There’s actually an excitement about what’s going on,” said Collins, a former personal lawyer for Trump, in congressional testimony this spring. A spokesperson said the eliminated jobs for healthcare providers were simply “not needed.”
That is not what we have found. Over months of reporting, ProPublica has watched the East Orange VA Medical Center — a typical agency facility — spiral downward. The hospital and its affiliated facilities in New Jersey lost nearly a tenth of the staff they had when Trump took office.
Over the past two years, a VA watchdog report shows, the number of roles with “severe shortages” in East Orange has tripled, from around 30 to roughly 90. Among them: oncologists, radiologists, surgeons, cardiologists, anesthesiologists, critical care doctors, nurses, mechanics, cleaners — nearly every job that makes a hospital run.
“It’s scary,” one East Orange administrator said in a meeting this year. “We have no one.”
It’s not just there. According to the VA’s watchdog, nearly all VA hospitals — 97% — reported having severe shortages of doctors. (The agency argues that the report — titled in part, “Staffing Shortages” — is simply about shortages of candidates and not actual staffing.)
The exodus of healthcare providers has increasingly forced veterans into the private care program — called Community Care — that the Trump administration has pushed. Amid soaring caseloads there and what a government report describes as “insufficient staffing,” many vets have been facing interminable waits.
ProPublica and other outlets have previously detailed problems with particular areas of VA care under Trump, such as mental health. But our reporting suggests far more care for veterans is being put at risk.
At East Orange, the damage wrought by the administration’s approach has cut like a scythe across nearly every area of the hospital.
Wound care is harder to get, since the nurses who specialize in it have mostly gone. The standard tests for blood clots weren’t available for most of the year, because there were no technicians. Even radiation treatment was stopped for months, after one of the key specialists left.
“Care has gotten worse for the patients,” said one doctor. “The services available. The wait times. We’re not providing the care that we wish we could.”
Another doctor, who recently quit, recalled how vets coming in with chest pains couldn’t get cardiac tests for months. “It felt dangerous practicing in a place like that,” said the physician, who, like others, declined to be named for fear of retribution. “That’s something you don’t want on your conscience.”
VA employees across the country told ProPublica they are seeing remarkably similar issues at their hospitals.
In Albuquerque, New Mexico, short-staffing forced the hospital to take many of its beds offline and stopped it from operating on severe heart attacks. Surgeries — on lungs and spines — have also been suspended for months at the VA hospital near St. Petersburg, Florida. At both hospitals, government reports found, Trump’s touted private care program was also overwhelmed and understaffed, further fueling delays in care.
Surgeries and other critical care have also been delayed at the Minneapolis VA. A staffer there shared a friendly looking notice tacked to a bulletin board in May: “No SOD coverage” — meaning, no surgeon on duty — “until further notice.” Radiation treatment was also suspended there because one of the machine’s operators quit. A Minneapolis doctor recalled that meant having to put a vet with cancer-riddled bones on a rattling ambulance ride every day, rather than simply wheel him down the hall. The doctor said each bump on the winter roads caused the vet excruciating pain: “It was miserable.”
A longtime oncologist who works with VA hospitals around the country told me, “Care is collapsing from the inside.”
Starting in July, ProPublica repeatedly asked the VA about evidence we’d found that short-staffing is hurting veterans’ care. We asked to interview Collins and the leadership of East Orange. The VA did not make them available. Nor did it address the specifics ProPublica shared on care.
In a general statement, the VA said care has improved under Trump. “This Administration is solely focused on measuring VA’s success by how well it serves Veterans,” said agency spokesperson Quinn Slaven. He cited a record number of appointments for both direct and private care over roughly the past year. Slaven also noted that the private care program began under the first Trump administration and was also embraced by the Biden administration.
As for East Orange, Slaven said the facility is outperforming private hospitals on certain metrics, such as diabetes care and some cancer screenings. Slaven also said more appointments were completed in fiscal year 2025 — which ran from October 2024 through September last year — than in any year of the Biden administration.
Citing privacy law, the VA noted it could not address individual cases without a waiver from the patient or appropriate family member. While ProPublica spoke with veterans’ family members and loved ones, none chose to sign.
We did, however, also ask the VA about the general issues surrounding those cases — such as East Orange’s OR being closed — and the agency did not respond.
In speaking to us, family members expressed surprise about their loved ones’ care. Falchetto’s brother, Tony, knew his brother had appendicitis, but hadn’t known that the OR in East Orange was closed. “Oh my god,” Tony exclaimed when I told him that his brother didn’t get timely care.
This story is based on internal documents, emails, agency data, recordings and interviews with more than two dozen current and former VA staffers, along with veterans and their families.
Contrary to the administration’s rhetoric, what emerges is a portrait of an institution in trauma.
“It Felt Like Bullying”
As soon as Trump was reelected, healthcare providers and other staffers at East Orange could feel the barometric pressure plummeting and the storm arriving.
The incoming administration’s plans for federal employees had long been clear. “We want to put them in trauma,” said Russell Vought in 2023, before he became Trump’s chief of the Office of Management and Budget. “We want them to not want to go to work.”
Just days into the new administration, officials imposed a rigid return-to-office policy, even as many staffers — from schedulers to radiologists reading digital scans — had shifted to remote work in recent years. An internal agency watchdog later wrote that the edict caused a “system shock” at East Orange, whose outdated infrastructure and long-mothballed rooms couldn’t handle the influx.
“I love working with vets, and I’ve never wanted to work anywhere else,” said one medical provider at East Orange who rattled off a list of edicts. “You’re this little person, and the full weight of the federal government was on you. It felt like bullying. It was very, very stressful.”
That May, Collins appeared before Congress and promised that the administration would not cut care: “We’re going to maintain VA’s mission-essential jobs, like doctors, nurses, claims processors, while phasing out nonessential roles, like interior designers and other things — DEI.”
Two months later, the agency touted the loss of nearly 30,000 staffers. “VA is headed in the right direction,” Collins said in a statement announcing the losses. It was hard to know if the remaining staff agreed, since officials canceled the VA’s employee satisfaction survey.
Among the most essential staff at VA hospitals have long been the specialty doctors, with their years of extra training. Recognizing their importance — and their potential to earn far more in the private sector — bipartisan legislation, which Biden signed into law in January 2025, allowed the VA to pay top-notch doctors more than the standard government rate.
But under Trump, the department didn’t use that authority for more than a year — even as more and more specialty doctors were leaving.
So, amid the departmental tumult, East Orange’s doctors began to exit, and they often weren’t replaced.
Six months into the administration, East Orange was down five psychologists, two of its four general surgeons and 18 nurses, among others, according to data obtained through a public records request.
Winter Comes to East Orange
A half dozen oncologists and surgeons told me that delaying treatment by more than a month and a half was problematic. At the least, they said, the delays almost certainly made his last weeks more painful. One told me he gives patients in Dennis’ condition radiation “within hours.” (ProPublica is withholding the veteran’s last name at the request of his family, which wants to maintain their privacy.)
Other veterans at East Orange faced the same dynamics: They were shunted to private care after their VA doctors and others left — and then they got stuck in the system since the office that handles private care — Community Care — was so overloaded. “That volume just keeps going up,” one administrator said at a meeting last November. The reason for the increased referrals to Community Care? She explained: “We just do not have the providers to provide the care.”
That winter the short-staffing and its effects spread across East Orange.
Staff were told via email that because of “urgent nurse staffing levels,” eight of the hospital’s roughly 60 general admission beds were being “taken out of service.”
“That was a big chunk of our beds,” said one of East Orange’s doctors. “I don’t recall ever having to close that many.” Without beds, the doctor explained, veterans often “stay in the emergency room, which is not ideal.” Indeed, studies have shown that leaving patients in the ER is dangerous and results in higher mortality rates.
A vet at one of East Orange’s campuses wrote to Trump complaining about short-staffing. He soon received a response signed by the president. “Every American owes our veterans an eternal debt of gratitude,” Trump said in the one-page letter, “and under my leadership, they will always have the loyalty, respect, and support they have earned and so dearly deserve.”
Around the same time, the hospital also had to shutter its operating room.
In December, part of the operating room’s air flow system had malfunctioned, contaminating the surgical instruments. Breakdowns like this weren’t unusual. East Orange was built 70 years ago, and its infrastructure showed it. But now the hospital mechanics who kept it all running were quitting. In interviews, they cited the same downward spiral that healthcare staffers did: As coworkers left, the staff who remained had to pick up the load, further increasing the strain of their jobs.
This put even more strain on a department that was already “severely understaffed” before Trump, said Irvin Webb, who worked as an air systems technician before he left the VA in May 2025. As a result of the departures, he said, repairs ended up taking longer. (Air conditioning equipment mechanic and air conditioning equipment operator were both among the many East Orange positions categorized as having severe shortages in this year’s VA survey.)
Medical staff felt the impact. One doctor calculated that the OR has been down nine times over the past year — compared with once the year before.
After the air flow malfunction in December, the OR was out of action for roughly three weeks. It then reopened for planned surgeries but remained closed for emergency and off-hours surgery for more than another month.
Then, on Feb. 12, Falchetto came to East Orange with a burst, gangrenous appendix.
He arrived in the early evening. Doctors noted that he had abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhea, and described the results of Falchetto’s CT scan as “worrisome.” The doctors wrote that Falchetto needed surgery, but, as one physician noted, there was a “lack of OR capability.” And so, despite his life depending on quick intervention, Falchetto had to leave the hospital that was treating him.
At about midnight, East Orange arranged for Falchetto to be transferred to the VA hospital in Manhattan. It’s less than an hour away. But Falchetto ran into yet another problem: Instead of arranging an emergency transfer, the administrators scheduled him to be moved when the transport unit started its morning shift around 7.
“Imminent Risk to Patient Care”
It’s impossible to say for certain whether short-staffing caused Falchetto’s death. He was severely ill when he arrived at East Orange and may have died even if he got proper, timely treatment. But he didn’t get that.
“If I were the family, I’d sue everyone,” one of the doctors involved in Falchetto’s case told ProPublica. “He should have been operated on immediately.”
By last spring, managers at East Orange were sending increasingly dire alarms internally. One email in March — just a few days after Falchetto died — warned that the shortages were preventing proper care.
The crises began coming in quick succession, one more desperate than the next.
Both of the hospital’s orthopedic surgeons left. And wound care became a particular problem. The East Orange VA previously had three nurses who specialized in the area. By this spring, just one remained, according to East Orange staffers. She would have to commute dozens of miles between East Orange’s hospital and its satellite clinics and nursing home.
“I’m not going to have time for anything,” the nurse told colleagues in a meeting about the changes.
A few months later, a veteran arrived at East Orange with a diabetic ulcer — essentially an open wound — on his left foot. His records state that the wound “significantly increased in size” but that he hadn’t been seen by a wound care specialist amid shortages.
It was the VA’s nearby nursing home — which the agency calls a community living center — that raised the starkest alarm. A message to the staff on April 10 warned of an “extreme shortage of CLC nursing staff with an imminent risk to patient care.”
An administrator wrote in the message that the nursing home was taking emergency action to cut the number of veterans allowed at the facility from 192 to 180. Soon the cap was reduced again, to 170.
What that meant is that vets who qualified for spots would be mostly turned away.
Typically, the East Orange hospital could function as a kind of temporary overflow facility for the nursing home. And the nursing home could do the same for East Orange, taking some patients when the hospital was full.
But now neither could handle any more. On May 20, a notice went out to staff saying the hospital couldn’t accept patients from the nursing home that day.
What’s more, 17 veterans who needed admission were instead housed in the ER. Other hospitals also sometimes do that, but at East Orange the problematic practice went from rare to “far more common,” one doctor involved recalled. They were stuck there at least a day. “They’re in bed all day,” said the doctor. “It’s essentially a cot.”
“People Are Falling Through the Cracks”
The day after the ER pileup, Collins, the VA secretary, arrived on Capitol Hill to testify again. He bristled when he was asked about how staff cuts and eliminated positions were affecting care.
“There is nothing they cannot hire,” Collins told the lawmakers. If hospitals need a doctor, “they hire the doctor.”
Soon after, Collins quietly imposed staffing caps. What’s more, even when hospitals do have the authority to hire, the pall hanging over the agency now has impacted recruiting. As ProPublica reported last year, many doctors have turned down VA job offers amid the ongoing turmoil. Nearly 4 in 10 of the roughly 2,000 doctors offered jobs from January through March last year rejected them. That is quadruple the rate of doctors rejecting offers during the same time period in 2024.
At the time of Collins’ testimony, the VA had around 5,100 fewer doctors, nurses and other “mission critical” staff than it did at the start of the Trump administration, a 3.4% drop. Under Biden, by contrast, the VA had been staffing up.
At East Orange, staffers told me the hospital had no vascular techs for most of this year, meaning there was no one to run tests on arteries and veins. And on the oncology ward, internal records show the team assigned to help patients navigate their treatment was down to just one nurse.
The providers who have stayed have been overwhelmed by vets’ needs — a dynamic that employees say is playing out in VA hospitals across the country. “People are falling through the cracks, and now they’re not getting help,” said one primary care physician at a VA clinic in Missouri.
“I’ve been working from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.,” she said. “I’ve had to take mental health breaks because I’ve been so stressed. I’ve been near suicidal. It’s not normal.”
Coins, Not Care
On a late August morning, a smattering of black SUVs and police cars pulled up to a VA campus near East Orange. Collins and a gaggle of aides stepped out of the caravan and went inside.
The VA secretary visited two departments. One was the chaplains’ unit, which, like so many units within East Orange these days, is “severely understaffed,” according to an internal presentation. (Collins is an ordained Baptist minister and once served as a Navy chaplain.)
The other was the residential PTSD unit. Staffers had arranged for Collins to meet with veterans, messages show. The event was not open to the media, but, according to staff and a vet who were there that day, Collins sped through the visit and did not stay long to speak with the vets.
On his way out, Collins stopped for a moment to talk to a veteran without legs in a wheelchair. After Collins strolled away, I asked the veteran what they discussed. “He just thanked me for my service and gave me one of these,” said Willie Johnson, showing me a commemorative coin that says, “Secretary of Veterans Affairs, Douglas A. Collins.”
I asked Johnson whether he had noticed changes in care since Trump returned to office. “Oh yes,” he said, noting that even food has gotten worse (among the positions with severe shortages at East Orange: food service worker).
The day after Collins’ visit, an email went out to staff. A “particularly meaningful part” of the visit, the email from a top administrator said, was the opportunity to recognize the service of five employees with Collins’ coin.
Among the recipients was the head of the maintenance department — the diminished unit that’s struggled to keep the operating room open.
Last week, as we were preparing to publish this story, a doctor at East Orange told me of a development: a backup generator had failed, and the OR was closed yet again.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-col.title: Trump Is Still Attacking Vets’ Health Care
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-col.author: Steve Early, Suzanne Gordon
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-col.text:
Trump Is Still Attacking Vets’ Health Care
Unlike other Trump administration officials who have gotten, or may soon get, the axe, Veteran Affairs head Doug Collins seems safe in his position. In the absence of legislative and grassroots pushback, he is set to continue dismantling the VA.
If any Donald Trump appointees lose their posts as part of a midterm cabinet reshuffling, Secretary of Veterans Affairs (VA) Doug Collins is not likely to be among them. Unlike controversial former colleagues already sacked as the heads of the homeland security, justice, and labor departments — or Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, perhaps the next to go — Collins is good at keeping his head down. He does the president’s bidding without personal drama or political scandal.
This low-profile Air Force Reserve chaplain is a clean-living Southern Baptist minister, small town lawyer, and former congressman from Georgia. When the Senate confirmed him last year, there was no need for a tiebreaking vote like the one J. D. Vance cast to push Hegseth across the finish line as secretary of defense; Collins won Senate approval with the bipartisan support of twenty-two Democrats.
Busting VA Unions
Yet Collins has proved to be Trump’s worst VA secretary ever; his main goal is faster privatization of the nation’s largest public health care system. The likelihood that he will control the third-largest federal agency budget and second-largest departmental workforce for another two years is not good news for nine million VA patients.
By the time a Democrat potentially replaces Trump in the White House in January 2029, Collins will have diverted far more than $46 billion annually from their direct care budget to a network of 1.7 million private sector providers and four health care companies who administer it. Just two months ago, he awarded new contracts to the latter worth $1 trillion over the next decade (if not canceled or curtailed by a future administration). As a result, industry giants like United Healthcare and Humana will be profiting from further outsourcing of VA care that is costly, unnecessary, and disfavored by veterans themselves.
VA defenders, inside and outside the Beltway, need a damage control agenda, one that will restrain rather than enable further White House attempts to defund and dismantle the United States’ best working model of socialized medicine. Otherwise, more VA staffing and budget cuts, plus facility closings, in the VA’s own system of 1,380 public hospitals and clinics around the country will be happening soon.
Reinforcements on the Way
Those most motivated to lead the charge against Secretary Collins on Capitol Hill in 2027 are newly elected pro-labor progressives with personal experience in public health care systems, either as patients or family members of patients, caregivers, or administrators.
Thanks to their successful campaigns against MAGA supporters, these VA defenders now include: former Army paratrooper Richard Ojeda in North Carolina; former Marine drill instructor JoAnna Mendoza in Arizona, who has been treated for military sexual trauma at the VA; former Army surgeon Adam Hamawy, a Gaza war critic from New Jersey who once operated on a helicopter pilot injured in Iraq named Tammy Duckworth, now senator from Illinois; and Fred Wellman from Missouri, a West Point graduate who began rallying fellow vets against Trump six years ago through the Lincoln Project.
Last but not least is VA privatization critic Mitchell Berman, “who spent over a decade serving veterans, active duty service members and their families as a VA nurse” — and now represents conservative Republican Paul Ryan’s old district in Wisconsin. All of the above could help energize a House Veterans Affairs Committee, where playing footsie with Collins (and his predecessor in the Biden Administration) has gone on for too long to the detriment of real agency oversight.
On the Senate Veteran Affairs Committee, the Democrats’ defense of our nation’s largest public health care system would be much improved by adding new senators from either Michigan, Maine, and Iowa. Dr Abdul El-Sayed, the just-elected Michigan public health specialist and Medicare for All advocate, would be following in the footsteps of his longtime ally Senator Bernie Sanders.
El-Sayed could be joined by Troy Jackson, the former logger who ousted five-term Senator Susan Collins with Sanders’s support in Maine; as a state legislator, Jackson long championed the cause of Maine National Guard members who suffered Agent Orange exposure during their Vietnam War–era training but were later deemed ineligible for compensation and health care.
In Iowa, newly elected Senator Josh Turek is not only the son of Vietnam veteran but one who suffered birth defects due to his father’s Agent Orange exposure. As a wheelchair athlete, Turek played alongside disabled vets and worked with them in sports rehabilitation programs. He has pledged to “end unnecessary wars that put American lives at risk” and insure that “veterans exposed to toxic substances during their military service get the care and benefits they need.”
Ready, Fire, Aim
A recent report from Democracy Forward by two former VA officials provides plenty of ammo for new members of Congress to use in a long-overdue counteroffensive against Collins. Josh Jacobs, a former VA undersecretary under Joe Biden and Nicole Nedd, a past director of the agency’s national workforce management program, write:
The VA has lost approximately 30,000 employees through attrition, early retirements, deferred resignations, firings, and other departures. These staff had institutional knowledge and skills that cannot be quickly replaced. The staff who remain are bearing an unsustainable burden. Morale has deteriorated, and there is growing evidence that employees feel unable to raise safety concerns without fear of retaliation — a condition linked to more errors and worse patient outcomes.
In their indictment of Collins, entitled “Ready, Fire, Aim,” the authors warn that “the choices being made now by the Trump-Vance administration — at the White House and within VA’s own leadership — will adversely shape veterans’ care for a generation.”
Road Map for Fighting Back
Nobody new or old inside the Beltway — whether in Congress or veterans’ advocacy organizations — will get much done by themselves, without the pressure of grassroots opposition to cuts in VA care and benefits.
Paul Rieckhoff, an Iraq War veteran who helped found Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America (IAVA) two decades ago, believes that “both parties are looking for quiet ways to control VA disability spending, which now tops $118 billion a year for 5.1 million disabled veterans.” This fall, Rieckhoff’s new group, Independent Veterans of America (IVA), backed candidates like Navy Veteran and former National Guard member Dan Osborn, who distanced themselves from both major parties. Unfortunately, Osborn suffered a second narrow defeat running as a labor-backed independent candidate for the US Senate from Nebraska.
Rieckhoff fears that “career political operatives” in Washington are still floating “budget options” that include “cutting benefits and raising minimum disability rating thresholds.” To stop these changes, veterans have to “build the media and organizing muscle to mobilize fast when veterans’ benefits are on the line.”
Fortunately, veterans’ groups across the political spectrum had a major victory earlier this year when they blocked the deceptively named “Take Care of America’s Veterans Act” (TACVA). Veterans Service Organizations (VSOs) like the Veterans of Foreign Wars, Disabled American Veterans, and Progressive Veterans of America all sounded the alarm about this Collins-backed bill pushed by Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson.
TACVA would have helped fifty thousand former service members whose careers were cut short due to medical problems collect both their military pensions and VA disability benefits. But as Common Defense Political Director Naveed Shah warned last summer, this multipart bill was heavily booby-trapped. If enacted, hundreds of thousands of other veterans would have been adversely affected.
According to Shah, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, it would have “cut $57 billion from our future tinnitus and sleep apnea claims, tripled the VA home loan fee, allow[ed] disability appeals to be decided in bulk rather than on the merits of each veteran’s record, enable[d] more lay-offs that threaten the quality of VA care, and [laid] the groundwork for handing VA facilities over to private operators.” (Lame-duck Republicans may make a second attempt to pass TACVA before January.)
Grassroots Defense of VA Care
Veterans for Peace (VFP) has long been the most reliable first responder whenever veterans’ care has been threatened. VFP’s “Save Our VA” campaign has generated thousands of letters to members of Congress about privatization-related problems, too often downplayed or ignored by VSOs that take health care industry donations. VFP members have personally lobbied many members of Congress or their staffers on VA issues.
A newer Common Defense (CD) campaign — called “VA Not for Sale” — has sponsored VA-focused lobby days in Washington, DC, and town hall meetings in Iowa, Wisconsin, Illinois, and other states. CD and the Veterans Healthcare Policy Institute (VHPI) also collaborated on a just-issued report called “The Privatization Playbook,” which documents the sorry history of bipartisan support for costly and unnecessary VA outsourcing since 2014.
In California, members of the Vietnam Veterans of America (VVA) and VFP have joined forces with active and retired VA caregivers to conduct weekly anti-privatization picketing and rallies at their local facility in Sonoma County.
In 2027, there should be hundreds of events like this, in far more locations across the country. And before it’s too late, more protests should target the costly and defective overhaul of VA medical recordkeeping that’s occurring on Collins’s watch.
Stopping Oracle’s Rollout
As Ace Allen, a now retired VA medical oncologist, warned last spring in The Kansas City Star, in every place where the VA’s existing system has been “modernized” by health information-technology corporation Oracle Health, the result has been serious disruption of patient record handling and widespread demoralization among VA caregivers forced to use an inferior system. As a result, “huge numbers have quit or retired early.”
During the president’s first term, Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner helped Oracle (formerly Cerner Corporation) get a no-bid contract to replace what Allen calls a “custom built, publicly owned electronic health record (EHR) system that was refined over decades by VA clinician-coder teams to support clinical care, not maximize revenue.”
A contract originally estimated to cost $10 billion has now ballooned to $32 billion in the same “cost-overrun” fashion as infamous Pentagon projects like the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter. That’s why Steve Friday, an Air Force veteran, VFP member, and former VA social worker in Michigan, is helping to rally foes of Oracle around the country through StopTheRollout.org. According to Friday, this grassroots initiative “brings together clinicians, VA employees, veterans, advocates, union members, and others who understand what is happening and are willing to act.”
They are scouring contracting records, publicizing inspector general and Government Accountability Office reports on Oracle system failures and sharing whistleblower information from patients and providers with members of Congress willing to hold Collins responsible for already occurring patient safety threats.
As Friday explains his involvement and the stakes of the fight for everyone: “the VA, for all its problems, still demonstrates that we can publicly fund and deliver health care rather than turning every patient into a source of profit. Losing that,” he says, “would hurt veterans, workers, and the larger struggle for health care as a human right.” Thanks to last week’s midterm election results, this caregiver perspective will soon be much better reflected on Capitol Hill.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: What We Can Learn From Lula’s Seismic Win
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: David Adler
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
What We Can Learn From Lula’s Seismic Win
The Brazilian president looked headed for defeat. The Brazilian people had other ideas.
On Saturday, October 24, the Avenida Paulista in central São Paulo became a vast red sea of hats, flags, and crimson shirts declaring support for President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s Workers’ Party. Joyful activists sang movement songs, raised banners supporting Lula, and cried out against right-wing favorite Flávio Bolsonaro’s illicit campaign to capture the country’s presidency. The mobilization was reported to be the largest in Brazilian history, and it would prove to be critical to the stunning come-from-behind victory the following day for Lula’s bid to stop the march of the right in Latin America.
Yet such a mobilization would have been unthinkable just a few weeks earlier. Throughout the campaign, we had watched Brazil’s far-right forces rise and rise so far and so fast that their return to the country’s presidential Palácio do Planalto at times felt all but inevitable. Bolsonaro’s party had crushed its conservative adversaries to dominate both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate in the country’s legislative elections. And the son of the jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro had finished ahead of Lula in the election’s first round.
Going into the runoff, the cards were stacked against Lula—and Brazilian democracy. President Trump hit Brazilian goods with 50 percent tariffs last year as punishment for the prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro, and then he piled on another round this past summer. On top of the economic warfare came technological attacks, with widespread reports that Meta was suppressing pro-Lula content on its platforms in a flagrant effort to help Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign. Brazilians battled back on social media: A supportive congressman built a WhatsApp channel called Lula’s Army that attracted over 10 million followers.
Many commentators will tell you that this digital campaigning made all the difference, on the theory that the left finally learned to master the algorithm. We can, the new narrative goes, simply defend democracy by posting, sharing, liking, and subscribing.
But that’s the wrong lesson to take away from Brazil. Sure, social media can capture lightning in a bottle. It can put a message in front of millions of faces in a single afternoon, and that matters enormously in the final days of a campaign. But it is simply too weak an instrument for the kind of sustained social mobilization that will be necessary to restrain the far right, let alone vanquish it.
Far more important to the fate of Brazilian democracy, I would argue, is the fact that students, workers, and families filled the streets of every major city in this country, over and over, with joy and love and an unflinching spirit of resistance to the fascists arrayed against them.
On that same Saturday before the election, Lula marched with crowds on the beachfront at Copacabana before flying to join us in São Paulo. People felt the energy, and they responded. Between the two rounds of voting, abstentions fell by some 3 million votes—and given that abstention rates are generally highest among the poorest voters, those who had cast blank ballots on October 4 likely broke overwhelmingly for Lula.
I have worked on elections in countless countries, and I have never seen a people rally like this. Brazilians came to understand fascism not as an abstract concept but as something concrete and close at hand: a threat to their wages, their families, and the basic texture of their daily lives.
This mobilization against the right and for the promise of a better future made all the difference in the election. And it must continue. Lula will return to power facing a National Congress in which right-wing parties control 276 of the 513 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 49 of the 81 seats in the Senate.
Against this daunting congressional arithmetic and threats from the opposition, people power will be the critical instrument for driving Lula’s popular agenda forward. No politician in Brasília should be able to sleep at night without knowing that their constituents expect them to respect their rights as workers, as women, and as citizens of this great democracy—and that millions are prepared to take to the streets to defend those rights.
That brings us back to social media. It is great that people can join WhatsApp groups or watch videos on TikTok. But we cannot win back the world without rebuilding the community that’s been shredded by these same technologies. The Bolsonaro project has always depended on hyper-individualism: the idea that each of us is alone, competing against everyone else, with nothing to rely on but ourselves. Lula countered with a movement that made people feel less alone, reminding them that they belong to a society and to one another.
The people responded by giving Lula a victory that upended the political calculus for a country that had been told for months that its future was already decided. His victory proves that there is nothing inevitable about the rise of the reactionary right. It is a cliché to say that the people united will never be defeated, but it is impossible to walk away from Brazil now without believing it.
