https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: As war continues, local people mobilise to salvage southern Lebanon’s history
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Sarvy Geranpayeh
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
“Wow. Can you hear the bombing?” Riad Al-Assaad asks The Art Newspaper, speaking from his village of Zrariyeh in southern Lebanon. An Israeli strike on a nearby village cuts short a conversation about his efforts to save what remains of the heritage in the country’s south: scanning its old buildings, recording its oral history and now rescuing its libraries. Despite a ceasefire, south Lebanon remains under Israeli occupation and at war, and its people say their history is being erased.
The south has lived with Israeli invasion and occupation for nearly half a century. Israel invaded in 1978 and pushed north to Beirut in 1982, the year Hezbollah formed to fight it, and it did not withdraw from the south until 2000. In 2006, the two fought a month-long war after Hezbollah captured two Israeli soldiers in a cross-border raid.
The present conflict began on 8 October 2023, the day after the Hamas attacks on Israel, with exchanges of fire between Hezbollah and Israel. It escalated in September 2024 into full-scale war, with an Israeli ground invasion and strikes on Beirut, before a ceasefire that November. Fighting resumed in March 2026, when Hezbollah fired on Israel after the US and Israel attacked Iran; a ceasefire agreement reached in US-led talks in June has not ended it. Strikes continue daily, and Israeli forces occupy around 600 sq. km of the south, reaching up to 10km into Lebanon, behind what the army calls the Yellow Line.
Zrariyeh has around 2,000 houses, Al-Assaad estimates. By his count, 65 have been destroyed in this war and more than 100 damaged. His father’s house, in the middle of the village, was hit twice: first by shrapnel, then by blasts that “levelled” neighbouring buildings and blew out its windows and doors. Like others who have repaired their homes “once, twice, three times”, he now covers the openings with plastic. “We are living in the nylon era,” Al-Assaad says. But what is at stake, he adds, is “our historical existence”.
The most visible part of that history is the south’s ancient monuments, and international protection has not kept them safe from the war. Since 2024, Unesco has granted 73 sites across Lebanon enhanced protection, which prohibits targeting them or using them for military purposes. In July, it inscribed the five castles of Mount Amel, all of them granted enhanced protection, on its World Heritage List and its list of sites in danger. Three of the castles, Beaufort, Dubieh and Chama’, are under Israeli occupation. Days after the inscription, the Israeli military detonated 700 tonnes of explosives about 800m from Beaufort, claiming it was destroying Hezbollah tunnels. In Tyre, a World Heritage Site since 1984, strikes have damaged columns, mosaics and the site’s offices and stores.
Ali Badawi, the ministry of culture’s regional director for south Lebanon, says his teams cannot reach the occupied sites and rely on low-resolution satellite images and footage released by the Israeli army. One broadcast showed Israeli soldiers in Beaufort’s historical halls watching the Fifa World Cup on televisions he believes were taken from the castle’s information centre. Unesco has allocated some funding for the restoration of Tyre, but elsewhere donors are holding back while the war continues. “We cannot do anything at the moment,” Badawi says. “We have to wait.”
Badawi lives in a village south of Tyre, close to Al Mansouri, an area that he says Israeli forces strike daily. “Sometimes at night we don’t sleep, because it is just explosion after explosion,” he says.
‘Constantly afraid, unsettled and distracted’
His colleague, Mohana Chahine, who manages the artefact stores at Tyre’s Al-Bass site, was seriously injured in an Israeli drone strike on 14 August 2024, weeks before the war escalated. She was driving home with her husband when a missile was fired at a motorcycle behind them, shattering the car’s windows and leaving her unable to move. Her husband pulled her from the car, and a second strike threw them both clear of it. After a month in hospital and further treatment in France, Chahine has completed her PhD and returned to work. “I go to work actively, but I am constantly afraid, unsettled and distracted,” she says. “I am constantly anxious about another war or being injured again.”
Beyond Tyre and the castles lies heritage that appears on no Unesco list: the old houses, mosques, churches and cemeteries of southern Lebanon’s villages. Joanne Farchakh Bajjaly, an archaeologist and former journalist, is the founder of Biladi, a heritage organisation that has monitored the south since October 2023. In 2025 it recorded 389 historical buildings in five villages—according to Biladi, 85% of them are now destroyed. It was preparing to publish a report last March, but the return of war halted that project and Biladi widened its survey instead. With architecture students from the Lebanese University, the organisation logged around 850 sites across 105 villages, occupied or under threat, from archaeological ruins to houses built before 1950. The full findings are being held for its delayed report, but Biladi shared some of them with The Art Newspaper. Among them: the loss of the area’s Shia religious sites—mosques, shrines, mausoleums or husseiniyas (halls for religious gatherings)—stands at around 98%.
In July Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said the army had completely destroyed 24 villages that were “hundreds of years old”, totalling 15,000 to 20,000 homes, by his estimate. Lebanese counts are higher.
“We have 38 villages that have been bulldozed to the ground. Nothing remains,” Bajjaly says, adding that villages still under attack, such as Al Mansouri, have not yet been assessed and the figure could rise. Badawi puts the total number of villages destroyed at around 50. Each village has an ancient centre built over older remains, he notes, some of them Byzantine, Roman or Phoenician, so the loss cannot be counted in homes alone. “It is not just a matter of number of houses. The historical fabric itself is destroyed.”
According to both Badawi and Bajjaly, historic cemeteries across southern Lebanon have also been bulldozed by Israeli forces. At shrines, Bajjaly says, the earth has been turned over and the dead dug up. “This is total desacralisation, and these are well-calculated gestures,” she says.
Olive trees have been destroyed, too. After seeing images of trees being uprooted, Badawi went to Naqoura in early 2025 and found a field stripped of its old trees. In September a French Lebanese businessman filed a lawsuit in France accusing the Israeli military of war crimes, alleging that 600 trees his family had cultivated for 250 years were uprooted and taken to Israel. “When they remove 500-year-old olive trees, this is not anymore an issue of security,” Al-Assaad says.
The aim, Bajjaly believes, is “to kill the relationship between the people and their land and their history, and therefore to make it clear for them that there’s no return”.
The artist Oussama Baalbaki knows all too well what that means. His late father, the renowned painter Abdel Hamid Baalbaki, began building the family’s house in their ancestral village of Odaisseh, close to the border, in 1984, two years after Israel’s invasion of Beirut displaced them. With the village under occupation, his parents built it “over a very long period, with limited financial means and amid occupation, recurring war and displacement”.
His father, an amateur collector, hoped the home would become “something like a museum, or a cultural centre for literature and poetry”, and filled it with manuscripts, rare books, sculptures, paintings and antiquities. “Most important of all, the house shelters, beneath the trees of its garden, the tomb of my mother and father,” Baalbaki says.
In October 2024 the house was “rigged with explosives, along with every neighbourhood of the village, in a systematic, annihilating manner”, Baalbaki says of the detonation, which was captured on video. His siblings visited the ruins in February 2025 to salvage what they could, but the village is now occupied and out of reach. “We lost our connection to the land of our ancestors,” he says, “and were left wandering in a torn space of imagination and time.”
The house had looked out over a valley towards a bare plateau, a view that shaped two generations of paintings. “This natural horizon imprinted itself on my father’s paintings and, in time, passed into my own,” Baalbaki says.
In Al Qantara, the family village of the artist and film-maker Ahmad Ghossein, the landscape itself has gone. His father returned there when the Israeli occupation ended in 2000, built a house and retired among his olive trees and chickens. When fighting began in 2023, he refused to leave, answering his son’s pleas from Beirut with photographs and videos.
“He was sending me all the time images of the sunrise, every morning, to say, ‘I’m fine’,” Ghossein says. He held out until September 2024, and even then went back whenever a ceasefire allowed. This March, Ghossein says, the village was blown up by Israeli forces and the hill it stood on levelled. “It’s not that you don’t find your house, you don’t find the land. It became white sand.”
Ghossein has made his father’s daily photographs, videos and WhatsApp voice notes into a four-screen video installation, The Sound of Silence. It was shown at the Beirut Art Center and at Frieze London in October, and is due to be shown at Art Jameel in Jeddah. The footage is as his father shot it: the garden, the chickens, the road to the village, never the war. The question behind the piece, Ghossein says, is: “Can you do something about a place that doesn’t exist anymore?” His father, who now lives in Beirut, is “lost, more or less”, facing the reality that he may not go back for a long time.
But Ghossein refuses to be cast as a victim. “Yes, it’s horrible. Yes, it’s a disaster. Yes, they are erasing,” he says. “But I’m just continuing. This is a resistance by itself.”
Rescuing private libraries
Al-Assaad’s answer is to save what can still be carried or recorded. He owns a construction company, which in wartime becomes “like a civil defence company”, handing out food, medicine and fuel. Working with the culture ministry, he supplies architectural scans of old mosques and houses in the border villages. “We can’t remove them. We can’t sandbag them,” he says, but they can be documented for future generations.
With Biladi he is now also rescuing private libraries: family collections handed down through generations. In Zibqin, known as the village of poets, they have found around 20. The two largest were lost under rubble; one of them, with around 6,000 books, was burned by an incendiary bomb, he says. From another damaged home the team is recovering up to 2,000 volumes, many of them handwritten. Each book is cleaned, photographed, catalogued and moved to safe storage until its owner can reclaim it. He is appealing to anyone in the south with a library at risk to get in touch. “We don’t have the luxury of time,” he says. “We don’t have the luxury of doubt.”
Bajjaly fears what happens to a people’s past when nothing physical is left to hold it. “Is the history of south Lebanon going to turn into a myth? ‘We had a house here. We had a mosque here’,” she says. Documentation is her answer, a way “to give back to the population a proof of their own existence”. Biladi’s survey will go to the ministry of culture, which she says is pressing for heritage to be part of any rebuilding. “Any plan of reconstruction for south Lebanon that does not include heritage would be a continuity of the destruction,” she says.
Baalbaki says the uprooting will be temporary. “We will return to our land. But with what imagination will we return, and to what landscape?”

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: We Have Invited Insane Surveillance Into Our Homes
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Kate Wagner
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
We Have Invited Insane Surveillance Into Our Homes
Aggregated property listings are being weaponized by insidious intelligence outfits. We have ourselves to blame.
In October, 404 Media uncovered yet another AI spy ring, one that truly brings the surveillance state home. The “visual intelligence” platform Raven, formerly GeoSpy(!), makes it possible for cops to geolocate a building based solely on interior images (or even pixels from images) fed into the platform’s AI software. Raven’s software uses the property listings that real-estate agents and homeowners post on Zillow and Airbnb to pinpoint locations with terrifying precision, and the company boasts that it allows authorities to “capture dangerous individuals faster than ever before.” The comically shadowy “frontline intelligence” AI lab Graylark developed this software, which Raven has licensed to the Miami-Dade and Los Angeles police departments. This means that if you have ever uploaded a photo of the inside of your apartment to one of these listing sites, police could identify your exact location. Airbnb has said it has no relationship with Graylark, while Zillow said scraping its site violated its terms of use, making it unclear where the company is obtaining this data.
If the AI era has taught us anything about the tech industry and its billionaire overlords, it’s that there is no limit to how far they will go to steal and profit from the information that billions of people have contributed to the Internet since the dawn of its existence. The art we’ve made is transmogrified into ChatGPT slop. The help we’ve provided to others on forums and blogs is pilfered—and often misconstrued—by Google Gemini (which has cut off websites’ ability to generate ad revenue from search-engine traffic). Even our most personal posts on Instagram and Facebook are being mined for God knows what purposes.
More From Kate Wagner
These technologies have always been insidious. We all oohed and aahed at the premiere of Google Earth in 2005 (I certainly spent hours exploring it) and crowed with excitement when we saw a Google Maps car on the street. Now satellite and street-view data of all kinds provide the scaffolding for a surveillance state we all participate in, to ends both innocuous (like tracking how busy a restaurant is) and sinister (like supplying pretexts to detain our neighbors when Flock cameras misread their license plates). Just as we chose social media as a means to connect with one another, we accepted geolocation as a technology of convenience—who doesn’t use Google Maps every day?
Every time we photograph our surroundings or ourselves and others, we leave behind a digital trail that is extremely desirable to data brokers, police departments, and AI companies. While passersby are still blurred in Google Street View, companies like Graylark are rendering intimate details of our lives visible to law enforcement or private interests. The sense of security we feel in our neighborhoods—and now even in our own homes—is being undermined in ways that once existed only in spy movies. There is no longer a true “public” to speak of, because we can’t have collective autonomy if we don’t have individual autonomy. We may have largely accepted that our phones are bugged, but the fact that we’ve allowed the routine commercial processes of renting and selling our homes to enable such grotesquely invasive surveillance should send a chill down all our spines.
Of all the companies that are ensnared in this collective affront against privacy, Zillow is perhaps the most interesting. In its own way, Zillow has always been a technology of surveillance. The company’s broad goal has always been to disrupt the real-estate industry. Launched in 2006, it aimed to make individual property records widely accessible, enabling people to see an estimate (“Zestimate”) of the value of their home—and that of their neighbors. Undercutting appraisers, people flocked to the site to see where they stood on the financial ladder at the zenith of the housing bubble. Keeping up with the Joneses would never be the same again.
As the company continued to accumulate data, it began providing image-hosting space (at a time when it was in short supply) and later a map-based view of listings, aggregating and publicizing information that real-estate agents once kept under lock and key. Soon agents found their sales flagging if they didn’t list their properties on Zillow, and they lost their exclusive access to multiple-listing services (MLS), private databases of homes for sale and their prices. Once local MLS sources capitulated to sharing their data with Zillow, the need to go directly to a real-estate office when searching for a home was largely replaced by shopping online and then contacting the agent attached to the property. (Zillow is still trying to conquer the entire home-buying process, though it has faced major legal troubles as a result.)
Real-estate aggregators like Zillow (or Redfin or PropertyShark) have blurred the boundaries between a dwelling and a commodity, between curiosity and nosiness, between minding one’s own business and spying. The ability to look into so many houses at the press of a button has changed interior design itself (by creating market-driven hype for certain types of renovations and fixtures) as well as our relationships with our neighbors and cities, and it has furthered our conception of a home as an asset rather than a place of shelter. Zillow puts us in the driver’s seat of a vehicle designed to accelerate speculation and diminish the power of individual taste and judgment. It was only a matter of time before the tables turned.
We are barreling toward a new normal where there is no longer such a thing as private space. This development goes hand in hand with the commodification of the built environment as a whole. Real estate is not just illiquid capital anymore. It’s even more abstract than that: It’s now digital capital as well, and we are not the ones who are profiting.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Prize dedicated to African women artists expands to Senegal, announces 2026 winners
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gameli Hamelo
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Ghanaian-French artist Kwama Frigaux and the Senegalese Fatoumata Sy have been announced as the joint winners of the Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize. The prize, founded by the London and Accra-based Gallery 1957 in 2021 to support women artists in Ghana and its diaspora, has this year expanded to include artists from Senegal, in partnership with Institut Français du Sénégal. Frigaux and Fatoumata have been awarded $5,000 each, as well as a three-month residency (in Senegal for the Ghanaian and in Ghana for the Senegalese), and solo exhibitions.
The prize is named after the former Ashanti queen mother, renowned for her anticolonial resistance when Ghana was under British rule. The call for applications for this year’s edition opened in June and ran until September, and was open to Ghanaian and Senegalese women artists aged 18 or older, based either in their home countries or in the diaspora. The winners were announced during Accra Cultural Week (29 October -2 November), which is organised by Gallery 1957. On view there until 5 December 2026 is The Lore of Care: Maternal Acts of Devotion, a solo show by Theresah Ankomah, the winner of the 2025 Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize.
Frigaux and Sy were selected by a jury comprising Touria El Glaoui, the founder of the 1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair; the Ghanaian artist Serge Attukwei Clottey; Marie Hélène Pereira, a senior curator at Berlin’s Haus der Kulturen der Welt; Jeanne Barral, a curator at the Fondation Cartier; the collector Alexa Waley-Cohen; and Dominique Heyse-Moore, the senior curator of contemporary British art at Tate Britain.
Runners up of the prize participate in a mentorship programme, which provides support on topics such as grant applications and entrepreneurship. Mentors this year include the Nigerian artist Modupeola Fadugba and Aisha Ayensu, the founder of the Ghanaian luxury fashion brand Christie Brown.
"I think [it's] an incredible programme that helps drive the longevity of [the prize's] impact,” Leila Zakhem, the director of the Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize, tells The Art Newspaper. “And it really creates a beautiful community.”
Zakhem explains that her team considered several countries for the expansion, including Nigeria. A key part of this search was finding a "very good implementing partner." The Institut Français du Sénégal, which is "a non-commercial space [has] a lot of credibility,” she adds, “and they were very excited to partner with us on the prize.” Zakhem says that she hopes the expansion will help develop and create a bridge between art communities in English- and French-speaking West Africa.
The planned next steps for the Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize are to expand further into West Africa, and then potentially beyond, with winners selected from different regions of the continent. “The goal is eventually to be the leading Pan-African female art prize on the continent,” Zakhem says.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: The One Issue to Rule Them All
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Elie Mystal
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The One Issue to Rule Them All
To win in 2028, Democrats must commit to doing a full Supreme-Court Press—and breaking the power of the court for good.
The 2028 Democratic presidential primary season has officially begun. With the midterms officially in the rearview mirror, but with the Democrats’ strong showing buoying the party from Georgia to Texas and beyond, we can expect an energetic primary full of people eager to ride the blue wave straight to the White House.
The last time there was an open primary for the Democratic nomination, in 2020, 29 candidates tried to convince voters they could defeat Donald Trump by defeating inequality, student debt, and climate change (though I think one guy was just trying to sell us coffee). Then Covid arrived, followed by the mass marches for Black lives, and the focus shifted to the once-in-a-generation deadly virus and the daily reality of deadly racism.
It is impossible to predict which combination of policy proposals, violent assaults, and global crises will prove dispositive to voters this time around. Will it be data centers, gas prices, and ICE? Healthcare, democracy, and the Iran War? Smoky eyeliner, American-flag cuff links, and GLP-1s? It’s hard to say. But no matter which combination dominates, there is one issue that must be championed by any Democrat serious about rescuing the country from the depths of Trumpism: Supreme Court reform.
Reforming the court is, in many ways, the skeleton key that unlocks the entire Democratic agenda. It’s the issue upon which all other issues depend. That’s because without reforming the Supreme Court, no other Democratic policy matters. Without reform, a Democratic president will hold power in name only. Without reform, the Democratic legislative agenda will never be implemented. The current Supreme Court has been designed by Republicans to make winning elections irrelevant, to give them ultimate control over federal law and policy regardless of who happens to win the White House. A Democrat who is unwilling to break the power of the Supreme Court is a Democrat who is wasting all of our time.
I know that for many politicians, and the political consultants they trust with our lives, “the Supreme Court” and “issues that matter to regular people” can sound like two vastly different things. But in practice, they’re the same. You cannot, for instance, have Medicare for All if the Supreme Court is going to strike it down. You cannot have a Green New Deal if the court will immediately declare it unconstitutional. You cannot implement meaningful restrictions on AI if the court is unwilling to enforce those restrictions the moment the tech-bro mafia unleashes a barrage of lawsuits to try to stop them. And this is true of nearly every issue Americans talk about at their kitchen tables. There is simply nothing the current Supreme Court will allow Democrats to do—unless the court itself is reformed first.
Think about it this way: Trump will be gone in 2029, unless the Supreme Court rules that he, or his chosen successor, can stay. That is its real power—not to be a king, but to make one out of thin air. If Democrats do not address the court, they will address none of the damage Trump has done to this country.
Unfortunately, the current assumed front-runners for the Democratic nomination have yet to get the memo. They’re still treating Supreme Court reform as a niche issue to be sidestepped, instead of the key to the return of liberal self-government. California Governor Gavin Newsom is perhaps the saddest example of this failure. Newsom likes to talk tough—at least to defenseless trans kids. He’s got all kinds of smoke for trans girls who want to play sports, but when it comes time to deal with John Roberts and the cabal of Republicans who took away the rights of women and girls to control their own bodies, Newsom becomes cautious. In September, he told Don Lemon that he was “evolving” on court reform, but he was still unwilling to commit to the biggest reform of all: Supreme Court expansion. “I normally have very clear conviction on things. I’ve been open to argument and interested in the evidence on this,” Newsom said. But while he considered two potential reforms—term limits and ethics reform—to be “a no-brainer,” he still felt “caution” (but also “an openness”) about expanding the court.
Right, so Newsom has very clear convictions about things like who should be allowed to play girls’ field hockey, but he still needs more evidence as to whether the right-wing Supreme Court can play with our lives? Good to know.
Newsom isn’t the only one, of course. J.B. Pritzker, the tough-talking Illinois governor and billionaire, also needs the Supreme Court to bash us over the head for a few more years before he finds enough “evidence” to act. “I think I want to see, you know, a little more out of this Supreme Court before I would make a judgment [about expanding the court],” he told Politico in May. “But I will say that if that is what is necessary in order to restore our Republic to what it was, you know, which is standing up for individual rights the way it was before Donald Trump, then that may be what we need to do.”
Since 2020, the Supreme Court has overturned abortion rights, affirmative action, and most of the Voting Rights Act. It has adopted a pro-gun-rights view so extreme that it’s even struck down Republican-backed gun restrictions. It’s allowed the GOP to gerrymander at will and given wealthy Republican donors the nearly unfettered ability to buy victories for their preferred politicians. Pritzker’s insistence that he needs to see more from this Supreme Court before advocating for reform is like Abraham Lincoln saying, “We should let this Confederacy thing play out a little longer before I make a judgment on restoring the Union.”
The progressive wing of the Democratic Party has been a little bolder about court reform. Potential presidential contenders like Ro Khanna and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have come out in favor of both court expansion and ethics reform. Pete Buttigieg had the most aggressive Supreme Court–reform plan during the 2020 cycle, so we know he takes the issue seriously. The entire party seems to be behind 18-year term limits, which is a reform that polls well but fundamentally fixes nothing in the short term. But even when Democrats support court reform, they frame it as a secondary issue, something to be addressed separate and apart from the affordability crisis or healthcare or whatever else.
This is the critical mistake. Democrats treat the Supreme Court as an issue for nerds, policy wonks, and elites. Republicans, by contrast, use the Supreme Court to mobilize voters and win elections. The Supreme Court is the reason that so-called “Christians” had no problem supporting a godless, thrice-married sexual predator. They knew that, despite his many “sins,” Trump would provide them with the justices they needed to achieve victory over the secular state and allow them to practice public bigotry under the guise of private religion. And he has.
Democrats are losing on issue after issue because they have not focused on the Supreme Court, and because they have not told their voters to focus on the Supreme Court. The rise of the white wing over the past 20 years tracks neatly with 20 years of Democratic malpractice when it comes to the courts. This generation of Democratic failure was captured most famously by Rahm Emanuel, Barack Obama’s first chief of staff, who, when asked if Obama would prioritize nominating and confirming judges, responded: “I don’t give a fuck about judicial appointments.” Since then, presidents and presidential contenders—from Obama to Hillary Clinton to Joe Biden to Kamala Harris—have consistently failed to pay more attention to the court than the Republicans pay to Greenland.
This decades-long political and moral malfeasance must end. Now. The 2028 primary cycle should not be a question of whether a Democratic candidate has a plan for the Supreme Court. It should be a knock-down, drag-out fight over whose plan is best.
The first step for Democratic presidential hopefuls who want to be taken seriously on Supreme Court reform is simply to talk about the court at every opportunity. You can’t lead on an issue if you’re afraid to mention it. Talking about the court should happen organically whenever these candidates talk about literally anything else on their legislative agenda, because there is no legislation that can or will survive a Republican Supreme Court.
Take abortion rights. Every single Democrat on the presidential-debate stage will say they want to “restore Roe.” But Trump didn’t overturn Roe, nor did the Republican Congress. The Supreme Court did that. When you are talking about restoring Roe, you are literally talking about overruling a Supreme Court decision.
So how do candidates intend to do that, exactly? Democrats should be expected to answer that question, which means not only laying out their plan but telling voters how they intend to get it past the six robed theocrats who think the fallopian tubes are stairways to heaven.
There are four potential ways to do that, four elements of any Supreme Court–reform plan, and 2028 candidates should have proposals for all of them. These elements target the court’s corruption, its excessive power, its immutability, and its conservatism, and they do that through a combination of methods: creating a code of ethics, stripping the court of its right to rule on certain cases, imposing term limits on justices, and, most important of all, adding justices to the court.
Let’s start with the code of ethics, because that’s the lowest-hanging fruit. The Supreme Court is corrupt. Everybody has seen it. Everybody feels it. Even if wealthy Republican interests aren’t directly buying votes, they’re most certainly buying access and the influence that access provides. And yet the Supreme Court is the only court in the land that operates without an ethics code that is enforced by a separate body.
Politicians and policymakers have discussed at length the idea of passing a Supreme Court ethics code through Congress. Those efforts have failed in part because the court claims that only it can police itself. Letting any other branch do so violates the separation of powers, according to the court.
I happen to think the court’s constitutional interpretation is wrong, but I’m not on the Supreme Court, so I can’t make the justices listen to me, or to Congress. But Congress could potentially get the court to abide by a legislative ethics bill by pulling on the lever that is unquestionably within its constitutional powers: the budget. The Supreme Court’s budget, like every other budget in the federal government, is controlled by Congress. Democrats running for office should promise to cut that budget—“defund the court,” if you will—unless the court agrees to be bound by an ethics code administered by some other body. The Constitution says there will be a Supreme Court; it doesn’t dictate how Congress must fund it. It doesn’t say that Congress has to give the justices a fancy courthouse to hold their hearings in. It doesn’t say that Congress has to give the justices clerks and assistants to do all of their research. It doesn’t say that Congress has to provide the justices with security. The Supreme Court can do its work from Clarence Thomas’s RV parked outside a Walmart, for all the Constitution cares.
If you cut the court’s funding to change its decisions, it looks like a form of bribery. But if you cut its funding until the justices agree to stop taking bribes, it just looks like a win.
The next reform Democratic candidates should promise to pursue is “jurisdiction stripping,” although Democrats shouldn’t call it that on the campaign trail unless they want to put their audiences to sleep. I’d call it “reclaiming the Constitution from the Supreme Court.” The basic idea here is that Congress has the power to limit the Supreme Court’s ability to overturn laws, to deem them unconstitutional, and this reform would allow Congress to do just that.
To understand how, it helps to remember that the word unconstitutional appears nowhere in the Constitution, which means the power to declare laws unconstitutional was given to no specific branch of government. Instead, the Supreme Court took that power for itself and dubbed it “judicial review” in the landmark 1803 case Marbury v. Madison. But Congress can take that power back, because Article III of the Constitution gives it the authority to restrict which kinds of cases the courts can review and thus limit the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction.
Congress can’t tell the courts how to rule, but it sure as hell can tell the courts what they’re allowed to rule on. Democrats could say, for instance, that the Supreme Court is not allowed to rule on political-redistricting cases and then pass a national anti-gerrymandering law. They could say the court is not allowed to rule on campaign-finance laws, and then pass a law negating Citizens United and restoring meaningful restrictions on campaign contributions. Taking power away from unelected elites and giving it back to the people is always a winning electoral issue.
Getting rid of Citizens United, courtesy of jurisdiction stripping, would be popular. So would forcing Clarence Thomas to pay for his own vacations by imposing a code of ethics. Still, the most popular Supreme Court reform is term limits. Nearly all Democrats already support imposing 18-year term limits on Supreme Court justices.
The question I have for Democrats promising term limits is: How? I have explained the political and constitutional levers Democrats can pull to get other Supreme Court reforms over the line, but on term limits, the Constitution is pretty clear that federal judges serve “during good behavior,” which has consistently been interpreted to mean “for life, unless impeached.” Many legal scholars have made arguments for how term limits can be imposed without a constitutional amendment, and I think those arguments are brilliant. But the people who get to decide whether those arguments are correct are the very justices whom we are trying to kick off the court.
As of this writing, the justices who have served for more than 18 years are Thomas, John Roberts, and Samuel Alito. How, Democrats, are you going to convince them that it’s time to leave? My response to Democrats promising term limits is to cite my forever president Josiah Bartlett’s “next ten words” speech, in which he effectively argues that a sound bite of support for a policy is useless without an explanation of how that policy can be accomplished. Or as he says: “How are we going to do it?” If Democrats have a compelling case for how term limits can be implemented over the objection of the justices who would be required to leave, I’d love to hear it.
This brings us to the reform that is the most essential—and also, somehow, the most controversial. All three of the reforms mentioned so far do a lot of important work. But at the end of the day, none of them—not term limits, jurisdiction stripping, or ethics rules—will change how the Supreme Court’s conservative supermajority rules. These reforms put up important guardrails, limiting the justices’ power and the time they have to abuse that power, but they don’t prevent the court from scuttling the liberal agenda. If you want different decisions to come out of the Supreme Court—decisions that allow the Democrats to enact their programs and policies—then you’re going to have to increase the number of justices who believe that liberal priorities are constitutional.
That means we’re going to have to add members to the Supreme Court. There’s no other way. We need a majority of justices who believe in liberal, multiethnic, multi-faith democracy. We need a majority of justices who believe that women are people who deserve equal-people rights. We need a majority of justices who believe guns are not people and do not have an inalienable right to kill us all. We don’t just need more justices, we need liberal justices committed to undoing, overturning, and reversing the precedents laid down over the past 50-plus years. The last time a majority of the Supreme Court’s justices had been appointed by Democratic presidents was… 1969. That stat alone should tell you why we’re now at the point where court expansion is the only reasonable solution.
And expanding the court is reasonable. It is also easy, constitutionally speaking. Court expansion can be accomplished through simple legislation passed in the House, passed in the Senate with 51 votes (or 60, if Democrats lack the courage to abolish the filibuster), and signed by the president. That is literally all it takes to add justices—no complicated constitutional hocus-pocus required. If you want national single-payer healthcare or abortion rights or gun-safety laws, then you simply have to have a majority of justices who are willing to uphold those laws as constitutional.
If I were running for president, I would tie Supreme Court expansion directly to gun reform. That’s because the Republicans currently on the court are even bigger gun extremists than mainline Republican voters. There is no way to keep our children and our society safe from gun violence without expanding the Supreme Court to include more members who want the rest of us to live. There is no way to get real background checks, to close the gun-show loophole, to ban bump stocks and ammunition drums, and to enhance licensing and safety requirements without expanding the Supreme Court.
That has to be the message from all Democratic Party candidates. Moderates who are squeamish about court expansion should be asked if they are perhaps more squeamish about wiping the blood off the blackboard after the next school shooting. Show the people that the court is getting us killed and must be stopped.
A line I have often heard from people who think of themselves as “pragmatists” is that Democrats should focus on winning the election first, and worry about fixing the Supreme Court only after they’ve secured power. The theory, as I understand it, is that Democrats should campaign on broadly popular kitchen-table issues, like affordability, instead of focusing their campaigns on something as esoteric as the Supreme Court.
I agree with half of that. Obviously, winning is paramount. There can be no Supreme Court reform unless Democrats actually win. If Democrats can win by promising to lower the price of eggs, they should do that. If Democrats can win by promising to fight data centers with water guns, they should do that. If Democrats can win by promising every single voter in the country a universal basic income and a new puppy, they should do that. If Democrats can win by doing all of the above while walking backwards and chewing gum, in heels, they should do that.
My argument is that Supreme Court reform must be put front and center while the Democratic candidates are promising all the other things. Because if they don’t do that, everything from regulations on price gouging to free puppies will be overruled by the Supreme Court. Democrats must build the conditions under which Supreme Court reform doesn’t just become preferred but inevitable. The Democrats running and winning on the presidential nominee’s coattails must similarly know that court reform is inevitable. Again, that’s because court reform is the first step, not the last, in unlocking the rest of their agenda. Democrats can do nothing unless they win, but that victory will be meaningless without court reform.
If you will forgive the classical reference, I would handle the balance between so-called kitchen-table issues and the overwhelming need to reform the court the way Cato the Elder pressed for his signature obsession in ancient Rome. Famously, Cato ended every single speech he made in the Senate, regardless of the topic, with the line Ceterum censeo Carthago delenda est: “Furthermore, I think Carthage must be destroyed.” That is the bare minimum we should demand of Democratic candidates in the 2028 cycle. “We’re going to have Medicare for All. We’re going to keep AI data centers out of your communities. We’re going to get guns off our streets and out of our schools. Furthermore, the Supreme Court must be destroyed.”
Cato, it must be said, got his way, and I’m confident that Democrats could mimic his success. Today’s voters, and particularly Democratic-primary voters, are hungry for candidates who will take back our power from the Supreme Court. The court is extremely unpopular—just 34 percent of adults (and only 23 percent of Democrats!) approve of what the institution is doing. But voters like the idea of Supreme Court reform. According to a September poll by Marquette Law School, 89 percent of adults approve of enforcing an ethics code for justices; 79 percent favor term limits; and 53 percent like the idea of increasing the number of justices. Or as Josh Orton, the CEO of Demand Justice (disclosure: I’m a board member), told me, “In 2028, a Democratic presidential candidate won’t be taken seriously unless they have a clear plan to break up the Roberts majority within two years of taking office.”
This isn’t hard. In my lifetime, I’ve seen Democrats go from “marriage is between one man and one woman” to Gene Hackman in The Birdcage in one election cycle. Democrats must be leaders here, whether they get there through rational self-interest or idealistic good government. The people are ready for candidates who take the fight for our rights and democracy all the way to the Supreme Court.
I want Democrats to win. I want to win the campaign season and the governing season. I want to win the battle and the war.
Supreme Court reform is how Democrats win. It’s an unpopular institution, staffed and protected by elites, that has made itself the enemy of the popular will. If Democrats want to fight for individual rights, market regulations, environmental justice, healthcare, and fair taxes on the impossibly wealthy, then they have to fight the Supreme Court.
If they don’t, we’re looking at another cycle of failure, regardless of who happens to win.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Collector Elie Khouri to create physical home for his private foundation in Dubai
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Melissa Gronlund
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Dubai-based art collector Elie Khouri is building a space in the city for his eponymous foundation. The Elie Khouri Art Foundation (Ekaf) will be located in the coastal district of Jumeirah 1, in a villa renovated and redesigned by Counterspace, a firm led by the architect Sumayya Vally. The space, expected to open in 2028, will host public exhibitions and educational programmes.
Khouri is one of the Unite Arab Emirates (UAE)’s biggest and best-known collectors. Originally from Lebanon, he made his name as the chief executive officer of Omnicom Media in the Middle East and North Africa, and has been based in Dubai since the 1990s.
He began making plans for the foundation around five years ago, as one of the London-based Deflina Foundation’s collectors-in-residence, a programme launched in 2017 that considers collecting as a practice and seeks to support more ambitious implementation. With them he conducted feasibility studies to better understand what Dubai needs.
“The whole idea is to give back and foster exchange of ideas, challenge thinking and bring new perspectives,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “Dubai is about entrepreneurship. They support people like me, people coming to fulfil their ambitions. And what Dubai needs is private institutions, because that's how they will build their own version of culture.”
Despite Dubai’s large number of artists and galleries, it has never had a major museum, and private foundations have become a significant part of its infrastructure. The Jameel Arts Centre and Alserkal Avenue, each backed by individuals, are the two pillars of the art scene, in addition to smaller foundations such as Ishara, which focuses on art from South Asia.
Ekaf has an emphasis on global contemporary art, though one in which art from the Middle East will play an important role.
“We are here to support talent internationally,” says Khouri. “We're not about the region, but since we are in the Middle East, we also look at the best talent here. We have a responsibility to the ecosystem and the galleries.”
Ekaf will take Khouri’s collection, comprising works by more than 300 artists, as its starting point, drawing from it for initial exhibitions. Later shows will increasingly involve loans and collaborations. Ultimately, Khouri intends to establish an Ekaf collection that is separate to his personal holdings.
The veteran art strategist Caroline Louca, who was formerly at Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism and Christie’s Middle East, has been appointed as the director of the foundation. Louca and Khouri are looking to hire a curatorial team closer to the completion date for the museum.
Louca underlines that community engagement will be a major part of the foundation, with plans for talks, lectures and education streams. The foundation’s location, in Jumeirah 1, is a bonus in this respect. Jumeirah 1 is one of the oldest neighbourhoods in Dubai, where many affluent long-time residents live. Ekaf’s villa was home to an Emirati family in the 1980s, and Vally’s designs retain the elements of old-school Gulf architecture that is a source of nostalgia for many in the UAE.
"We are focusing on how we can make a place become part of the community—and not just focus on what we’re showing,” says Louca. “You can see beautiful artworks everywhere, but we want people to be a bit daring. We want them to walk in and ask questions—and not be embarrassed to ask questions—and then come back and ask more. If we can achieve that, it will be our barometer of success.”

The Fugitive From Brazil
The implications of Trump’s red-carpet rollout for Flávio Bolsonaro.
As millions of Brazilians celebrated President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s come-from-behind reelection, the defeated candidate was secretly preparing to flee the country. On October 27, two days after the runoff vote, Flávio Bolsonaro arrived in Miami aboard a private jet, having slipped out of Brazil in a furtive journey involving multiple countries and, as would later emerge, assistance from officials close to Donald Trump. Within hours he declared himself “president-elect,” then “leader,” then head of the Brazilian opposition-in-exile, insisting that Lula’s victory was illegitimate. Flávio’s apparent hope was that Trump, an ally of the Bolsonaro family who has aggressively criticized Lula’s government, would support his efforts to challenge the legitimacy of Lula’s win.
“I want to make it clear: I did not flee Brazil. I left for the sake of Brazil,” Bolsonaro proclaimed in a slapdash statement that had to be rescinded and reissued several times. If his intention were to dictate the course of the resistance to Lula’s unprecedented fourth term, Flávio obviously would have stayed in Brazil. But his electoral defeat meant losing the parliamentary immunity that came with his Senate seat, leaving him more exposed to police questioning and possible prosecution on various counts.
It is now clear that for Flávio the 2026 campaign was a high-stakes, last-chance gambit. There was no Plan B. What compelled him to run away was the fear of being arrested in connection with a host of illicit activities. And by coming to the United States there was always the possibility that his patron, Donald Trump, might aid and abet the Bolsonaro family’s quest to return to power.
The Banco Master Scandal
Credible accusations of criminal wrongdoing have swirled around Flávio for years. But his immediate legal exposure centers on three investigations currently before Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court.
The most serious concerns the financing of a planned film about his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overthrow the election he lost to Lula in 2022. Flávio negotiated a $24 million investment from Daniel Vorcaro, then the owner of Banco Master, a Brazilian bank that collapsed amid revelations of massive alleged financial fraud. Vorcaro, who has been arrested in connection with the scheme, is suspected of orchestrating fraudulent financial operations involving billions of dollars and bribing political figures across the ideological spectrum. Unlike Lula, Flávio is directly implicated in the scandal.
According to the Federal Police, approximately $12.3 million of the promised $24 million was routed to an account in the United States linked to associates of Flávio’s brother Eduardo, a former congressman who relocated to the United States last year. Investigators suspect that some of the money may have been diverted for other purposes, including possibly funding Eduardo’s lavish lifestyle in the United States. The production company has yet to provide a detailed accounting of how the funds were spent. Flávio was formally placed under investigation in July 2026 for suspected money laundering, corruption, and illegal transfers of funds abroad.
A second inquiry concerns Flávio’s relationship with lawyer and businessman Willer Tomaz, whom police suspect of helping him conceal a financial interest in an online betting business. Investigators found e-mails suggesting Flávio had been registered as a privileged user on a bank account belonging to Alcazar Holdings, a company controlled by Tomaz, which is linked to the holding company behind the online betting platform Rede Loto. Police also found that companies linked to Tomaz paid for private flights taken by Flávio and his family. A third investigation concerns Flávio’s social-media accusation that Lula was involved in drug trafficking and money laundering—statements of slander that have prompted a criminal defamation inquiry.
So far, none of these investigations have resulted in any prosecutions. But they presented Flávio with the prospect of prolonged police scrutiny and potentially serious legal proceedings. “You already know where they are going with this, right?’” the former president reportedly told his son during a meeting the day after the election, to which Flávio responded: “Dad, I already know. And I am prepared, I know what I have to do.” The next day, he ran.
Trump and Bolsonaro
The Trump administration has offered Bolsonaro a warm welcome. After Lula’s victory, Trump baselessly questioned the legitimacy of the election, alleging that it had a “very bad look.” The president subsequently said he had approved Flávio’s arrival in the United States and that the defeated candidate could stay “as long as he wants.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio recommended that Flávio and his family be admitted under humanitarian parole, a temporary immigration arrangement that Trump immediately approved.
Indeed, Trump’s administration has spent much of the preceding year attempting to boost the Bolsonaro family to power, beginning with efforts to shield Jair Bolsonaro from the legal consequences of his 2022 coup attempt. Flávio’s brother Eduardo spoke openly about his sustained effort to push Trump to punish Brazil for daring to prosecute his father. In July 2025, Trump levied a 50 percent tariff on Brazilian imports as an explicit demand that Jair Bolsonaro be set free, despite his being charged with coup plotting that included a plan to assassinate Lula. “The way Brazil has treated former President Bolsonaro, a Highly Respected Leader throughout the world during his Term, including by the United States, is an international disgrace,” Trump wrote in a letter to Lula, posted on his Truth Social platform. “The trial should not be taking place. It is a Witch Hunt that should end IMMEDIATELY!”
Washington’s overt interference in Brazil’s judicial proceedings not only failed—the former Brazilian president was sentenced and duly incarcerated—but also gave Lula a potent rhetorical weapon to wield against the opposition in the form of a defense of national sovereignty.
Flávio campaigned as a MAGA acolyte, criticizing Lula’s independent streak on the world stage and promising to join the Shield of the Americas, Trump’s haphazard effort to create a militarized law enforcement coalition among like-minded hemispheric leaders. If elected, Bolsonaro insisted, pardoning his father would be among his first acts.
For its part, the Trump administration harbored no doubts that Flávio would be much more amenable to US dominance of Brazilian rare earth minerals and other resources than Lula, who insists on conditions for foreign involvement in key areas. Flávio visited the United States six times in 2026, meeting with conservative activists, attending the Conservative Political Action Conference in Texas, and making repeated trips to Washington.
On May 26, Trump received him in the Oval Office, where he also met Secretary Rubio, Deputy Secretary Christopher Landau, and presidential adviser Jason Miller, who reportedly assisted Bolsonaro’s escape to the United States. The White House offered no official account of the meeting. But by posing in the Oval Office with the presidential hopeful Trump signaled a personal bond that Bolsonaro implied would translate to policy wins for Brazil if he won.
Implications for US-Brazil Relations
So far, the Trump administration has been unwilling to back Flávio’s absurd claims that he is the legitimate president of Brazil; but Washington evidently wants to show the world that it takes care of those who offer their allegiance.
Using the United States as a base, Flávio can continue lobbying American officials, cultivating conservative media, and portraying the Brazilian judiciary as an instrument of political persecution. There is always a grift to be had for a reactionary Latin American politician in Miami.

Moreover, Flávio’s presence serves the Trump administration’s apparent goal of keeping the Lula government on its heels. The energized far-right opposition is already preparing to challenge the Supreme Court, particularly Alexandre de Moraes, whose prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro and supporters involved in the January 8, 2023, insurrection in the Brazilian capital remains a central grievance of the movement. This agenda offers the opposition a way to keep the country in a state of political confrontation independently of Flávio. While his congressional allies can obstruct and confront Lula at home, Flávio and Eduardo can cheerlead from abroad and cultivate support for their cause in Washington.
Unsure of what exactly Washington might do next, Lula’s government has, so far, simply ignored the pronouncements of the defeated candidate-in-exile. The strategy is clearly to avoid turning Flávio’s departure into a diplomatic crisis with Trump, particularly while the two governments are negotiating on trade and tariffs. The Foreign Ministry did summon Argentina’s diplomatic representative to explain the circumstances of Flávio’s passage through that country, but has left the question of his departure and possible legal consequences to Brazil’s courts and the Federal Police. To date, no formal extradition request to Washington has yet been reported.
For his part, Lula has mocked Flávio’s escape, drawing a connection between his arrival in the United States and Trump’s historic midterm defeat days later. Lula also delivered a pointed prediction: “You’ll have to come back to Brazil to face the cases against you.” After losing the 2022 race, Jair Bolsonaro also came to Florida with the hope of returning to power by hook or by crook. The former president ultimately went back to Brazil, where he ended up on trial and in prison instead. Flávio insists that he will not repeat the mistake of returning.
The shifting political landscape in the United States adds to the uncertainty of Flávio’s presence. Overwhelming Democratic victories in the midterm elections last week delivered a stunning rebuke to Trump. The president is likely to face congressional investigations, including challenges to the “Donroe Doctrine” of maximum US control in the region that Trump’s interventionist efforts in Brazil have sought to advance.
“Trump is convinced that Brazil is no longer a full democracy,” Flávio told The Washington Post last week, implying that further aggressive action from Washington was still possible. Trump’s decision to elevate Stephen Miller to be White House chief of staff—Millier is a rabid defender of the “might makes right” principle of US power in Latin America and an extremist with ties to several Bolsonaro allies—has offered a rare bit of good news for Flávio’s future.
Still, the dramatic change in Trump’s political fortunes has forced Flávio to change his tune on the US assistance in his fleeing Brazil. When Bolsonaro arrived in the US, he thanked Trump for his support. But, perhaps in anticipation of increased scrutiny, he now claims that his presence in the US owes very little to Trump. His escape was entirely his own doing, he told The New York Times: “It was all me. There was help from absolutely no one, from no government.” When it came to “how I got here,” he would “take that to the grave with me.” In the same interview, Flávio praised Trump for staying out of Brazil’s election, claiming that the president had done the right thing by not taking sides—presumably notwithstanding that campaign photo op in the Oval Office.
So far, Trump officials have been publicly noncommittal on Bolsonaro’s efforts to overturn Brazil’s election. Members of the administration may have their own reasons to keep some distance. After all, a White House operation to extract a defeated foreign presidential candidate facing criminal investigations and supporting his aspirations to overturn a free and fair election in Latin America’s largest nation are precisely the sort of scandals a newly empowered Democratic Congress might decide to investigate. It also threatens to complicate relations with Lula at a moment when Washington has considerable economic and strategic interests in Brazil.
Trump has consistently favored the Bolsonaro family. But his willingness to protect them will be tested if doing so begins to carry a political price at home.
Flávio, meanwhile, has little choice but to tie himself to the mast of a MAGA ship taking on water. As Lula plans his fourth administration, he may well find that the most consequential postelection development is not Flávio’s flight to Miami but the diminishing political prospects of his American host.
