https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: As Route 66 shifts into its centennial year, preservation efforts accelerate
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Allison C. Meier
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
US Route 66 officially started on 11 November 1926 with the launch of the nation’s first federal highway system. With the spread of affordable automobiles after the Second World War, it became a destination. A unique vernacular culture formed along its almost 2,500 miles running through eight states from Chicago, Illinois to Santa Monica, California, from neon signs enticing travellers to themed motels to roadside attractions with concrete and fibreglass sculptures.
Route 66 was decommissioned in 1985, with the new highways bypassing its Art Deco service stations and mid-century diners. Now, 100 years after its debut, there are efforts across the country to preserve what survives from what was once the “Main Street of America”.
Linking diverse cultures
“We want to let people outside of Route 66 know that it’s more than what you think it is,” says Rhys Martin, manager of the Preserve Route 66 Initiative at the National Trust for Historic Preservation. “Most people think of ’57 Chevys and cheeseburgers and Marilyn Monroe, and there’s a lot of that, but there’s so much more. It ties together so many diverse cultures, from Native American to African American. In my home state of Oklahoma, it goes through the Asian District [in Oklahoma City], which sprung up around Vietnamese refugees during the war. In West Hollywood, Route 66 has a huge LGBTQ presence.”
Grants from the Preserve Route 66 Initiative reflect that range of history, which is often overlooked in the nostalgia for its Americana. There are structural repair needs, like at the Fanning 66 Outpost in Cuba, Missouri, which hosts a 42ft-high rocking chair (the world’s largest until 2015), as well as storytelling projects, such as mapping Native American experiences along the corridor, as it passes through many tribal and ancestral lands yet has had little representation of their voices. Care for the road extends to the scarce sections of its original pavement. Through local advocacy, what is known as the Ribbon Road in Ottawa County, Oklahoma, which has the last segment of a 9ft-wide design made for Model Ts, was partially protected from resurfacing this year.
These are the same roads that the Model Ts went west on during the Dust Bowl to seek a better life Rhys Martin, Preserve Route 66 Initiative
“You might think a pavement’s not art, but when you get out and look at it, especially compared to what it is today, it is very different,” Martin says. “I have come to really appreciate it from a craftsmanship perspective, but also a longevity perspective. These are the same roads that the Model Ts went west on during the Dust Bowl to seek a better life, and the fact that I get to drive these same roads tells a story.”
Advocacy is under way to give National Historic Trail designation to Route 66, with a bipartisan bill introduced last year. Martin notes that Route 66 is now similar to how it was before 1926, when it was a loose network of roads, and this legislation would help bring together its fragmented parts.
“It gets people to sit at the same table, like the state Route 66 associations, the National Park Service and the Department of Transportation, so that we can find ways to work together for corridor-wide initiatives and to help elevate preservation needs,” he says. “The corridor continues to evolve, and buildings are threatened all the time with demolition or augmentation beyond recognition, and being designated as a National Historic Trail is not a roadblock. But it is something to say, this is important and we need to take care when the fabric of the road might be forever altered.”
Local groups, municipalities and individuals are stewarding Route 66’s relics. Martin is also the president of the Oklahoma Route 66 Association, which is restoring a U-Haul painted by the late artist Bob Waldmire, who illustrated maps and postcards of the road’s built and natural wonders. The city of Catoosa in Oklahoma acquired the beloved roadside Blue Whale in 2020 from the family of Hugh S. Davis, who in 1972 sculpted the 80ft-long attraction from concrete as a gift for his wife. Last May, a new Blue Whale Visitor Center opened with retro illuminated signage.
The city of Albuquerque opened a Route 66 Visitor Center last April and its park features a collection of restored roadside signs. Among them is the first major project from the Friends of the Orphan Signs (FOS), an organisation that since 2010 has worked on revitalising abandoned signs, particularly in Albuquerque’s underserved neighbourhoods.
Lindsey Fromm, the executive director of FOS, says that many of these signs are for places that were razed during the city’s removal of derelict buildings: “There were areas of Route 66 with dozens of towering empty signs.”
Most Route 66 sign restorations return them to their former glory; FOS reimagines them as public art. Revivir (2012) at the new visitor centre was created with students who designed visuals responding to local nature that were bordered with purple neon.
“While artists lead these sign projects, they will collaborate with communities, archives, the surrounding environment, or will collect histories and stories to create the work that is displayed, so that it speaks to the immediate moment and surrounding community who live, work and travel by the sign,” Fromm says.
Projects like this are not just about preserving places for tourists but Route 66’s role in daily life. These grassroots and national efforts recognise that even though it is no longer a main thoroughfare, it is still a vital place of connection from the Midwest to the Pacific, for communities both urban and rural, and between the visitors and residents brought together on their journeys.

https://gothamist.com/news/manhattans-ea.title: Manhattan’s East Side loses another movie theater to development
https://gothamist.com/news/manhattans-ea.author: Hannah Frishberg
https://gothamist.com/news/manhattans-ea.text:
Months after news broke that the Kips Bay AMC will shutter at year’s end, another East Side movie theater announced it has projected its last film.
Cinema 123 by Angelika closed on Oct. 30 after more than 60 years of business near the Queensboro Bridge on East 60th Street.
“As our final credits roll, we thank you for being part of our story,” the theater wrote in a social media farewell post with vintage photos of its 1976 marquee and line for “Rocky” and a 1986 photo that includes its former neighbor, the classic consumer electronics chain Crazy Eddie.
Cinema 123’s building was sold by owner Reading International to developer Roger Equities for $41 million in a deal that, according to public record, closed on the same day of the theater’s announcement.
Roger Equities currently plans to redevelop the approximately 8,000-square-foot, 1001 3rd Av. lot – located between East 59th and East 60th streets, and across from Bloomingdale’s flagship – into multifamily rental housing, the Commercial Observer reported.
A change of property ownership also caused the expected closure of the AMC Kips Bay 15, which was purchased by NYU Langone and is likely to be developed into a medical facility. That plan has prompted pushback from local elected officials who are seeking to preserve the theater.
Cinema 123’s sister locations, Angelika Film Center & Cafe on W. Houston St and Village East by Angelika on 2nd Ave. in the East Village remain open.
When Cinema 123 opened in 1962, it was the nation’s first ever twin-screen cinema. Following its initial success, it added a third screen in the 1980s. In more recent years it was beloved for still offering 70-millimeter film screenings.
Cinema 123’s closure will leave the AMC Orpheum 7 as the Upper East Side’s last remaining movie theater.

https://www.propublica.org/article/elect.title: A Tool Built by Election Deniers Said These Voters Were Dead. We Found Them Alive.
https://www.propublica.org/article/elect.author: Doug Bock Clark, Max Blau, Misty Harris
https://www.propublica.org/article/elect.text:
Ahead of the midterms, conservative election activists discussed plans to wield a powerful new weapon in the war against fraud: a data tool built by one of their own that could identify suspicious voters and help with contesting their ballots.
The system was put to the test this week in Forsyth County, Georgia, where a member of the county’s election board provided other officials with what he suggested was evidence of wrongdoing: four allegedly dead voters.
But it turns out all four are alive and well, ProPublica determined. The board rejected the attempt to challenge their ballots.
The effort, though, shows that even after last week’s blue wave, those who believe the 2020 election was stolen have continued to relentlessly search for ways to contest Republican losses. In Georgia, Democrats swept statewide offices.
The board member who initiated the Forsyth County challenge, Max Clavijo, is a member of the Election Integrity Network, a group led by conservative lawyer Cleta Mitchell that works to restrict voting and tighten election laws and rules. Mitchell worked closely with Donald Trump in his attempt to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election and, since he retook the presidency, has been central to his push to assert greater federal control over voting.
In the run-up to the midterms, on right-wing media and on private organizing calls, EIN participants outlined plans to search voter rolls with a software tool known as ELLY’s Election Monitor and contest ballots the tool deemed suspicious.
ELLY was developed by EIN member Rick Richards. It aggregates public data from state voter files, federal change-of-address records, tax documents, obituaries, property websites like Zillow and other sources. In Georgia, State Election Board members and top staffers have urged counties to use the tool to search their voter rolls for signs of fraud.
Richards talked about ELLY’s national potential on a podcast in late September, on which right-wing media personalities and activists touted its capacity to help GOP candidates contest their defeats. “We can prove the fraud that’s gone on in every state,” one commentator said. “This data will be able to set up challenges to those who lose.”
The following month, on a private call with EIN members and other conservative activists, Richards promised to provide data from more than 3,000 counties to “citizen monitors” and GOP candidates to try to prove fraud, according to a recording reviewed by ProPublica.
In an interview, Richards told ProPublica that he gave Clavijo data on Forsyth County at Clavijo’s request. He said in a subsequent email that their actions were meant to inform the board and remain confidential. Clavijo didn’t respond to questions from ProPublica.
Richards refused to answer questions about whether Clavijo’s effort was part of a wider EIN campaign to contest votes cast in the midterms.
“That’s irrelevant,” he said. “The data is the data. People can use it for what they want to.”
Mitchell, EIN’s leader, didn’t respond to questions about the group’s plans related to ELLY, either in Georgia or nationally.
In the months since some on Georgia’s State Election Board started promoting ELLY’s use, its accuracy has been much debated. The tool doesn’t have access to personal identifiers such as voters’ Social Security or driver’s license numbers or full dates of birth, which increases the potential for mismatches involving people with the same names.
Voting rights groups have called ELLY error-prone. The Cherokee County election director complained to the state board after the tool falsely flagged a county board member’s spouse as dead.
State Election Board members and Richards have defended ELLY. Accusations that the data is unreliable were “horse hockey,” Richards told ProPublica, explaining this was “a Southern colloquialism for B.S.”
Late last week, according to several people familiar with the matter, Clavijo circulated documents to board members and Forsyth County’s election director. Based on data from ELLY, Clavijo questioned whether the names of more than 22,000 people on the county’s voter roll were correct and disputed the eligibility of 69 voters. In addition to four he claimed were deceased, he alleged others had moved out of the county or state, had voter ID irregularities or had registered under fictitious names, giving an initial as their first name.
During the meeting, Clavijo claimed that he was not trying to disrupt the election’s certification or formally challenge the voters, a process outlined in statutes that can lead to ballots being tossed or voters removed from the rolls. (Richards also said they had not formally challenged ballots.) Clavijo said he was merely seeking “to clean the voter rolls” and inform the board so officials could investigate further.
But other board members accused him of doing an end run around the formal challenge process. Barbara Luth, the board chair, said she felt “sorry for” Clavijo because activists were bypassing the challenge procedure “by coming to you and having you submit it.”
Under fire from fellow board members, Clavijo admitted he could not vouch for the data’s accuracy.
“I did not make any explicit accusation that the information was 100% correct,” he said.
The cover letter Clavijo submitted with the challenges said that they had not been verified with any “human review,” according to sources familiar with the matter.
Richards and Clavijo submitted obituaries for the voters they claimed were dead, but there were discrepancies between the information in them and the voters’ records. All of the obituaries said or suggested the deceased lived outside of Forsyth County, which would have made it impossible to vote there. One said the person lived in Arizona.
ProPublica confirmed that all four are actually alive.
Alexis Ramirez, a night-shift nurse, told ProPublica that she cast her ballot during early voting. She was surprised to hear her vote had been contested — and why.
“It’s kind of crazy that they attempted to do that without trying to prove it first,” she said.
Saramma George, another voter Richards and Clavijo claimed was dead, said she was “really angry” to have the validity of her ballot questioned.
In the third case, ProPublica spoke with a voter’s son, who said she was alive but didn’t want to talk to ProPublica. Her “ballot is valid,” he said.
The fourth voter, Chris Strickland, said, “I don’t know where they’re getting their information from, but it’s false. I’m alive. I’m here.”
The majority of the challenges — 38 of them, according to people familiar with the matter — involved voters who’d registered using an initial.
One voter, Alexander Knight, told ProPublica that he goes by his middle name and that the information in voter records mirrors how Department of Driver Services officials suggested he be identified on his driver’s license.
“I am real,” he told ProPublica.
Four other challenged voters said they, too, abbreviated their first names. A. Joseph Guntherberg confirmed he routinely used the same formulation of his name, adding that blocking his ballot would not help the challengers: “My candidate didn’t win.”
Richards said it was up to county election workers to check ELLY’s data — he merely gathers it to facilitate efforts to maintain accurate voter lists.
But at the meeting, Joel Natt, a Republican board member, said the responsibility lay with challengers to justify their accusations. “This has no relevance to anybody here until” they provide solid evidence, he said, “through the proper channel.”

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: The space rocket I could have been aboard explodes: Rhiannon Adam’s best photograph
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Interview by Charlotte Jansen
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
This photograph was taken on 20 April 2023 from the VIP section of SpaceX’s launch viewing area, looking out from South Padre Island, Texas, towards Boca Chica, a nature reserve near the Mexican border which is home to SpaceX’s Starbase launchpad.
 
In 2021, I and seven other civilians were selected from an open call to go around the Moon on a free SpaceX Starship flight funded by the Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa. The dearMoon Project included myself and another photographer. For me, the story also became about being plucked from obscurity and planted in this very surreal world I could never have imagined being a part of in a million years. At the time, only 24 white American men had orbited or landed on the moon. Being selected for something like that changes your life and your perception of your worth in the world. The flight, originally scheduled for 2023, completely took over my life. It took the air out of every room – I couldn’t talk about anything else. People stopped commissioning me because they assumed I was busy going to space; every conversation I had was about it. This was going to be the rest of my life.
That day in April was pivotal. We were there to watch SpaceX’s Integrated Flight Test 1. After four minutes, following a relatively successful liftoff, the vehicle experienced what they call in space terms an “RUD” – Rapid Unscheduled Disassembly – and broke apart in the air. We put on a brave face but secretly I was thinking: “Wow, the risks are no longer theoretical. I could have been on that.”
 
The dust cloud in the image emerged from the concrete launchpad and tower – obliterated by the power of the raptor engines. The debris ended up all over the local houses and SpaceX closed the launch facility for reconstruction for four months while they conducted a huge clean-up operation. Going to space feels futuristic and grandiose but there are still the practical problems – like people wiping dust off their windows.
Unbeknown to me, this photograph marked the beginning of the end of dearMoon. We didn’t know at that time there was trouble in paradise and a loss of faith in the project and its viability. Maezawa had gone back to Japan after the first launch attempt had been scrubbed the day before, and so missed this launch. Eventually, in mid-2024, we all received an email invite to a Zoom call. We were told that they were not continuing the project, but it was made to sound like the disappointment should be only equal to finding out your favourite TV show was cancelled. But it was completely flooring. This wasn’t just a project – it had become my whole identity. I still dreamed about it every night. It was a poisoned chalice and it obliterated my career as I knew it.
This photograph is now part of my Rhi-Entry project, which is my version of a modern-day tragic cycle. I am Icarus, who flew too close to the sun and my wings melted. It is both tongue-in-cheek and deadly serious, moving through bathos, pathos and hamartia. The exhibition combines the visual tropes of the space museum, brings together facts and fiction, a reflection on the past and my fears for the future, with my personal story as its spine. The irony is, all of my work is about calling out structural abuses of power, and I was blinded by the wild promise of an almost impossible dream.
 
I wanted to change how we collectively feel about who is selected to go to space. I’m a 5ft 2in, gobby, messy queer who grew up on a sailing boat. Living in a tin can floating with blackness above and below, surviving with what you have – it was the closest thing on Earth to going to space, and uniquely prepared me for potentially leaving our planet. We still think of people who go to space as untouchable superheroes. The chiselled-jaw GI Joe lookalike with a wife at home. I wanted to break that mould. It was also about exploring ideas and debates around the colonisation and ownership of space, and who has the right to explore it – and to craft our collective future.
 Rhi-Entry is at the International Centre for the Image, Dublin, until 23 December. Rhiannon Adam’s work is also part of Space @ Fotografiska Tallinn until 17 January. Her book Polaroid: The Missing Manual is published by Thames and Hudson. See more @rhiannon_adam
 
Rhiannon Adam’s CV
Born: Cork, Ireland, 1985
 
High point: Being selected for dearMoon. Strangers coming up to me to tell me that my book Big Fence changed the way that they move through the world
 
Top tip: It never gets easier, so don’t expect it to! Remember that we’re all in the same boat; you can win the biggest award at 20 or at 85, and whichever way it happens, don’t count your chickens. Be nice to everyone, be generous with your time, treat others as you want to be treated – being a diva isn’t a good look. No matter how much success you have, remember half of it was luck and being in the right place at the right time. Listen to Baz Luhrmann’s Everybody’s Free to Wear Sunscreen at least once a year

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: NYC Overhauls Homeless Outreach for Freezing Weather After Last Winter’s Cold Deaths
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Kaitlyn Schwanemann
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
New York City is revamping its homeless outreach programs for Code Blue weather emergencies, when real-feel temperatures outside drop below freezing overnight and become potentially lethal.
The move follows a brutal winter at the start of the year where at least 18 people died from cold exposure outdoors during a weekslong arctic stretch in January and February that posed an early crisis for the Mamdani administration and put unsheltered New Yorkers at risk. At the time, city officials scrambled to get vulnerable people indoors through increased outreach around the clock and opening more warming sites and low-barrier shelters.
As part of a $25 million investment, the administration is looking to hire 300 additional outreach workers who during frigid weather will fan out across zones where unsheltered people tend to stay, including encampments, parks and subway steps. Officials did not specify these areas, but said they represent about 75% of “known unsheltered locations” citywide.
Department of Social Services Commissioner Erin Dalton said her agency identified the zones based on 311 calls for homeless outreach and encampment responses, along with intel from canvassers who scour the streets throughout the year. She said DSS tested the approach last summer during extreme heat periods and recorded more than 2,000 “engagements” with people, more than 20 times as many on a given day compared to the previous summer.
“We’re going to implement this and then continue to improve. There’s no perfect plan,” Dalton told The City Reporter in an interview. “Weather is changing rapidly, and so we want to make sure that we can continue to innovate there.”
The overhaul includes hundreds more low-barrier beds in single- and double-occupancy rooms that New Yorkers can access through a relaxed intake process, as well as hiring dozens more nurses for outreach teams during freezing temperatures.
The city is also soliciting for on-demand transportation to speed up getting people into shelters, warming centers and drop-in sites, where they can get free food, showers and case management services. That is in addition to 50 NYC Health + Hospitals vans, each staffed with a nurse or nurse practitioner so people can get checkups, and 20 DSS warming buses at peak levels, officials said.
Not all 300 new canvassers will be deployed during every Code Blue event, according to the department, but they will be on standby for the most dangerous weather. Dalton added the city is interested in hiring more outreach workers with personal histories of street homelessness who can connect with unsheltered New Yorkers, and DSS will train them before they deploy into the field.
Advocates Hopeful for Retooled Strategy
Homeless advocates said they are pleased the administration plans to do more to find people in need who do not know about or trust city resources, including shelters. Some street-homeless people say they stay out of the shelter system due to concerns about safety and strict rules, even if that means living outside and risking the elements.
Andrew Chappotin, an activist with the nonprofit Safety Net Project who lived on the streets for three years until last winter’s fatal cold stretch, said he entered a Safe Haven shelter at the end of January even though he had negative experiences in local shelters before.
“I just couldn’t take the cold anymore,” Chappotin said. “This was the coldest weather I’ve ever experienced. My body did not do well this past winter.”
He said street outreach teams still need to build stronger relationships with unsheltered residents and better inform them about accessing help.
Adolfo Abreu, housing campaigns director for the advocacy organization VOCAL-NY, said he is excited about the revamped Code Blue program and hopes it is part of a broader effort to expand homeless outreach year-round.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Abreu said, has “outlined a very bold vision of a city that works for working families and as many people as possible. And a big gap in that vision has been how we’ve been kind of executing, delivering vital governmental services to our most vulnerable New Yorkers.”
Nearly 5,000 people were estimated to be living unsheltered in the city during an annual official count in March, an 11% jump from 2025. The survey is usually conducted in January, but was postponed because of the extreme cold.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Jim Jordan’s MAGA Comeback
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Chris Lehmann
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Jim Jordan’s MAGA Comeback
The Ohio representative was once too extreme for GOP leadership. Not anymore.
It was no great surprise that, in response to the historical drubbing the Republican Party suffered in last week’s midterm vote, President Donald Trump resisted even a semblance of any accommodation to a new political order. In lieu of shaking up his cabinet or announcing a new ethos of bipartisan deal-making, Trump elevated racist edgelord policy savant Stephen Miller to chief of staff, pretended (or unsuccessfully attempted) to appoint UFC Dana White as his new press secretary, and cheered on his murderous and incompetent defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, who survived an impeachment vote in the House on Tuesday.
What did prove somewhat surprising is that the House GOP conference voted to anoint Ohio Representative Jim Jordan, the present chair of the Judiciary Committee, as its new leader in the 120th Congress. Jordan previously put in for the GOP speakership in 2023, after Kevin McCarthy was cashiered for making a deal with Democrats to keep funding the government, but lost to all-purpose bobblehead Mike Johnson. Jordan, a fierce MAGA demagogue in his own right, was undone in part by his divisive role in fomenting rancor in the party; long before his rise to the ranks of senior leadership, former speaker John Boehner—a longtime Buckeye State colleague—dubbed him a “legislative terrorist.”
Yet, in today’s GOP, that description is a credential. It was indeed Jordan’s bomb-throwing profile as a leader of the House Freedom Caucus that earned him a top slot on the leadership team McCarthy assembled during his short-lived tenure as speaker in 2023: Jordan was plumping for the chair of the Oversight Committee, but McCarthy instead set him up as the head of the chamber’s new manufactory of persecution agitprop, aka the Select Committee on the Weaponization of the Federal Government. As the panel’s title indicated, its brief was to gin up any and all hints of the Deep State’s mania to undo the virtuous forces of Trumpian governance—including the campfire tale of the 87,000 IRS commissioners that Joe Biden sought to unleash on the MAGA faithful, the phony charge that Attorney General Merrick Garland designated activist parents in the right’s crusades against critical race theory and DEI as “terrorists,” and various January 6 fantasies too wooly to recount in detail. When Jordan lost out in his bid to succeed McCarthy, he was rewarded with the chairmanship of the House Judiciary Committee—a post that allowed him to continue flogging the same demented tales of Deep State perfidy from a bigger stage, unruffled by his own failure to honor a subpoena from the House Select Committee on the January 6th Attack on the US Capitol. Charging a law-defying purveyor of MAGA lies like Jim Jordan with oversight of law enforcement and the judiciary was something like designating William Burroughs drug war czar.
Jordan also carried a more troubling résumé entry that today’s GOP also feels entitled to disregard: a serious role in a far-reaching and repellent sexual-abuse scandal. When he served as assistant wrestling coach for Ohio State University from 1987 to 1995, the squad’s doctor, Dr. Richard Strauss, was sexually abusing the wrestlers in his charge; during Strauss’s tenure, which ran from 1979 to 1996, he abused more than 177 team members. Jordan has denied any knowledge of Strauss’s predations, but at least half a dozen former wrestlers have publicly claimed otherwise. “There’s no way unless he’s got dementia or something that he’s got no recollection of what was going on at Ohio State,” former OSU wrestler and UFC fighter Mark Coleman, who was Jordan’s roommate on many wrestling team road trips, told The Wall Street Journal. Jordan disingenuously claims that the state’s inquiry into the Strauss scandal exonerated him, but it simply didn’t mention him—and it did stipulate that discussion of Strauss’s predations was widespread among people in the team’s orbit.
That the House GOP conference has named Jordan its leader is further evidence, if any were needed, that there will be zero postelection introspection on the MAGA right. Jordan’s elevation is the same lurch into fuck-you impunity that the House GOP assumed in anointing Mike Johnson—a key architect of the bid to overthrow the results of the 2020 election in Congress. With Johnson at the helm, the party has lost 42 seats (and counting) with little in its policy playbook that could arrest its hemorrhaging. In lieu of using its leadership votes to chart a new course, the Republican conference pinned its hopes on the same leadership candidate who was too divisive and scandal-plagued to prevail over Mike Johnson.
In addition to keeping the MAGA right on a collision course with public opinion, Jordan’s win poses an important test for the leaders of the new Democratic majority, who are already signaling a reversion to caretaker form and unleashing stale gusts of bipartisanship and “kitchen-table” rhetoric. Exit polls in the wake of the midterms blowout saw voters naming corruption as a key issue driving their decision—a factor only outstripped by the skyrocketing cost of living. That’s a signal that the opposition overlooks at its own risk. Jim Jordan is the very avatar of Trump-era corruption—which is why his Democratic counterparts need to make Dr. Richard Strauss as much of a household name as Jeffrey Epstein and continue reminding voters that the man who turned a blind eye to that scandal will continue stonewalling Trump’s own well-documented Epstein fraternizations. Like Trump’s postelection embrace of Stephen Miller and Pete Hegseth as his spirit animals, the House’s decision to throw in with Jim Jordan is a confession of utter moral bankruptcy. If Democrats on Capitol Hill are serious about consolidating their election gains into a long-term governing majority, they can’t afford to let voters forget it for one minute.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: Long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe painting found in East Village closet
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Hannah Frishberg
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
“Oh, by the way, there's a Georgia O'Keeffe in the closet,” a woman casually called to her niece, who was over at her East Village home, helping her get her affairs in order shortly before she passed away.
The niece knew her aunt collected art but was still shocked when, in a wooden box buried behind coats in the apartment’s front closet, she subsequently discovered the 10-inch by 24-inch landscape painting “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I,” O’Keeffe’s signature “OK” clearly visible on the original backboard.
The team at Christie’s auction house was also shocked when they got the niece’s email about it.
“We have a very large inbox that gets a lot of stuff sent to it, as you can imagine, and the vast majority of those things are…not that compelling,” Tylee Abbott, senior specialist and international director of American Art at Christie's, said in a phone interview. “From time to time we get something pretty good. This was obviously exceptional. As soon as it came in we all kind of immediately jumped to our feet and ran together and huddled around a computer screen and looked at it, and then started pulling books off the shelves and finding it in published literature to confirm that it was the real deal, and then quickly gave them a call and said we'd be right over.”
The existence of “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” was previously known solely through a 1931 photograph. When the aunt – an “incredibly accomplished” world-ranked bridge-master, Foreign Service member, multilinguist and “extremely private” individual whose family has requested anonymity – earned her master’s degree in 1963, her mother bought the work from the Downtown Gallery on 51st Street, O’Keeffe’s Manhattan dealer, as a graduation gift.
For years, “Near Abiquiu” hung in the woman’s East Village apartment until, during a bridge game in the mid-1980s, she noticed a guest “eyeing it a bit too closely” and decided to pack it up in its original box and hide it in the closet, where it sat until the niece unearthed it.
The woman’s mother paid $3,800 for the piece in 1963. Christie’s, which is including the long-lost work in its 20th Century Evening Sale in New York on Nov. 17, estimates the piece is today worth in the region of $3 million.
It is likely the first in a series of three works depicting New Mexico’s Lobo Peak, the second of which hangs in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and the third of which was formerly in the collection of David and Peggy Rockefeller.
O’Keeffe painted the series in 1930, a year after her first trip to New Mexico, the American Southwest freshly seeping into her mind’s eye.
“This is the Lobo Mountain…I want to paint this mountain,” she wrote at the time in a letter to her husband, Alfred Stieglitz, “but it is quite impossible.”
A 1935 Stieglitz photo of Radio City in the morning light is also part of the sale, which is on view to the public through Nov. 17 at Christie’s New York. The Stieglitz, however, is an iconic print of well-documented provenance far less delightfully unexpected than the depths of one woman’s East Village coat closet.
“You know, we can get a little bit jaded, seeing art so often coming across our desks,” said Abbott of the charming surprise the O’Keeffe’s inclusion has brought to this month’s sale. “It's really kind of re-inspiring to know that there are still treasures hidden away.”

https://gothamist.com/news/suspect-arres.title: Teen arrested for fatal shooting of 15-year-old Bronx boy walking to school, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/suspect-arres.author: Hannah Frishberg
https://gothamist.com/news/suspect-arres.text:
A teen suspect is in custody for the murder of 15-year-old Javits Frimpong, who was shot and killed on his way to school in the Bronx, police said.
The NYPD did not release the name of the suspect, who is 17 years old and accused of murder and other charges.
Javits' sister, Millicent Frimpong, said Wednesday morning by telephone that she was glad the suspect was off the street. When asked whether the arrest brought her any relief, she said “not really.”
Javits Frimpong was shot in the stomach around 9:30 a.m. on Oct. 29 near Crotona Park as he walked to DreamYard Preparatory School.
Frimpong’s father, Thomas Frimpong, 60, told Gothamist his son immigrated from Ghana to live with him last year.
“It’s not easy for me,” Thomas previously said. “I’m here with him alone.”
The suspect’s motive was not yet clear.
Thomas noted that two DreamYard students were fighting with Javits a few days before the shooting, and that both were suspended.
NYPD Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny said four days after the shooting that the police were investigating bullying as a motive, while also considering that the case may be a case of mistaken identity or robbery.
DreamYard Preparatory School students held a walkout and a memorial for Javits after his murder.
Soon after the shooting, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced that President Donald Trump had agreed to grant an immediate travel visa to Javits' mother in Ghana.
This story has been updated.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: France’s Left, Divided at the Worst Possible Time
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Harrison Stetler
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
France’s Left, Divided at the Worst Possible Time
Years of progressive infighting weigh on Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s presidential ambitions.
A lot should be playing in the French left’s favor this autumn. With the country engulfed by one of the most intense cycles of social protest in years, public attention has turned to the needs of high school students and financially stressed households—and away from the culture-war issues that have made the fortunes of far-right firebrand Marine Le Pen. But it most of all adds up to a rebuke for outgoing centrist President Emmanuel Macron, whose erstwhile allies are being forced to run against a legacy that counts fewer and fewer defenders by the day.
“Everyone hates the Macronist regime,” left-wing candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon told supporters at a campaign rally this Saturday, six months from presidential elections that could well sign the death certificate for the country’s traditional political class. On November 9, Macronist Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu conceded to an accelerated rise in the minimum wage, the latest bid to calm the anger.
So where does it all leave the left? In many respects, this fall’s crisis is the dreamed-of preelection scenario for Mélenchon’s party La France Insoumise (LFI). Having long billed itself as the party-political companion to French social movements, LFI hopes to emerge as the natural electoral outlet for the pent-up frustration that has spilled onto the streets since September.
“The France of rebellions and revolutions—our dear country, we’re all well at home here,” Mélenchon boasted to the packed audience gathered in Le Bourget, a suburb just north of Paris. “France has reached a boiling point. In demonstrations and then elections, our people are looking for and will find a solution to its problems.”
For LFI, which currently leads the pack of progressive contenders for next spring’s vote, this Saturday’s rally was a showcase for its sprawling policy platform. The party is calling for a radical social-democratic program, including a jump in the minimum wage to €1,700 per month, or just over $1,900. Among the over 1,000 measures in the platform are a massive injection of funds for public services, a lowering of the pension age, price freezes on gasoline and food, and a program of reindustrialization through “ecological planning.”
With France’s budget deficit hitting well over 5 percent of GDP, a platform like this is predicated on confronting the European Union over the bloc’s stringent fiscal rules—something the left-wing force does not shy away from. The party also wants broad wealth redistribution, namely a cap on inheritances at €12 million, or nearly $13.5 million, and the creation of a so-called “Zucman tax,” a 2 percent annual charge on the country’s largest fortunes. Named for the French-born Berkeley economist Gabriel Zucman, it’s France’s version of the wealth tax that California voters defeated in a referendum last Tuesday.
“I only have one thing to propose, something that is ultimately quite reasonable: We must change everything,” Mélenchon summed up on Saturday, arguing that the country needed a politics adapted to what he called a “global crisis of human civilization.”
For the more than 10,000 people in attendance, the November 7 rally was also a reminder that the party knows how to put on a show. Beyond the candidate’s undeniable rhetorical talents, the convention featured a genre-bending display of political communication. Preceding Mélenchon’s headline speech was a video montage of scripted vignettes highlighting the party’s main proposals, scenes that drifted into onstage dramatizations featuring leading party MPs. As far as pedagogical political theater goes, Bertolt Brecht could hardly have done better.
And yet, the palpable enthusiasm among the left-wing base for Mélenchon’s candidacy, his fourth since 2012, is difficult to square with the many roadblocks on the way to power next spring. French progressives are marginalized and divided in a country tilting dramatically to the hard right, as Le Pen’s grip over a wide swath of the electorate shows few signs of giving way.
For the April 18 first-round vote, well over 30 percent are estimated to back the far-right front-runner. That’s a double-digit lead over Mélenchon, who currently finds himself in a distant second place, benefiting from the dispersal of candidates to his right—something that’s likely to change before Election Day. For now, however, the veteran left-winger is ahead of both the weak field of other progressive contenders and even Macron’s centrist and conservative allies, who are caught in their own factional fights and reeling from the outgoing president’s stark unpopularity. The runoff looks similarly dire. Polling has been proven wrong before, but the most drastic predictions have Le Pen leading Mélenchon in a hypothetical second-round vote by over 30 points, a wider gap than Le Pen’s lead over other potential runoff opponents.
The story of how France got here is a long one, and there’s plenty of blame to go around. Most goes to Macron, who has devoted much of his presidency to catering to hard-right priorities on subjects like immigration and public order. Propelled by drastic shifts in France’s media landscape, in particular the sudden rise of a television and news pole owned by hard-right billionaire Vincent Bolloré, the culture of French politics has undergone nothing short of a counterrevolution in the last 10 years.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
But the left has also inflicted far too many wounds on itself. Its current weakness is downstream of the various failed attempts at cross-party coalition building in recent years, starting with the Nouvelle Union populaire écologique et sociale (NUPES) formed after Macron’s 2022 reelection as president. Long gone, too, are the days of the Nouveau Front populaire (NFP), the revamped left-wing alliance that delivered a surprise first-place finish in the snap parliamentary elections called by Macron in June 2024.
Stemming the tectonic shifts dragging France rightward was the best argument for progressive unity. But powerful forces opposed just that very strategy. Mélenchon’s sworn enemy since he bolted from the party in the late 2000s, the centrist Parti socialiste (PS) has lent its institutional stamp to the reckless pillorying of the radical left. This October, the party selected the anti-LFI media personality turned politician Raphaël Glucksmann as its candidate, confirming the center left’s definitive break with the Mélenchonists. Glucksmann and the various center-right figures now battling over the remnants of Macron’s coalition disagree on many things, but they seem to see eye to eye on the spurious idea that “Mélenchonism” represents as grave a danger to the country as Le Pen.
LFI has also painstakingly worked to undermine left-wing unity. Since the crack-up of the NFP and the NUPES before it, the open secret on the left is that the other main adversary of coalition politics was Mélenchon himself, who feared that a durable alliance would evolve into the institutional framework for a multiparty primary that might jeopardize his presidential candidacy. “My aim is not to unify the left,” the candidate told journalists shortly before taking to the podium this past Saturday.
Instead, LFI’s defining strategy has been to maintain hegemony over a left-wing electorate, itself reduced to a shrunken third of the political space amid the tripartite division of the French party system since 2017. There’s plenty of racist dog-whistling in the attempt to discredit Mélenchon’s appeal to what he calls the “new France” represented by the country’s diverse urban areas. But beyond these electoral strongholds, LFI has struggled to build out support in rural parts of the country and in smaller towns, a share of the electorate potentially requiring other types of candidates, messaging, and campaigning than those perfected by Mélenchon and his allies.
On international politics, possible allies have also long accused Mélenchon of foot-dragging when it comes to condemning Russia’s invasion of Ukraine since 2014. After Saturday’s rally, progressive and moderate critics were again up in arms at Mélenchon’s call for a referendum in the Donbas to decide control over the territory, currently largely occupied by the Russian military. Add on top of that the party’s often loose standards for fiery communication, which have landed it in a now-lengthy series of antisemitism scandals. They have had the combined effect of distracting from LFI’s otherwise principled—and often courageously solitary—defense of the Palestinian cause.
“Clarity” is the response from many France Insoumise supporters when they’re pressed on the infighting that has derailed the various attempts at left-wing coalition building. With their standard-bearer now positioned as the left’s lead contender for 2027, they also argue that it’s not too late to make up for lost time. Nonaligned factions in a progressive camp divided between Mélenchon and Glucksmann will have little choice, they claim, but to take sides as Election Day approaches. Then there are the abstentionists. And given Mélenchon’s undeniable knack for debating, many confidently assume that their candidate can trounce Le Pen in a head-to-head debate before the May 2 runoff.
For that matter, Mélenchon has long argued that the breakdown of France’s party system would lead to a decisive battle royale between what LFI calls the “left of rupture” and Le Pen. But if the cards fall hard next spring, one wonders just how much virtue there’ll really be in clarity.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Victor Gaetan
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
Pope Leo Goes to War—Against the Department of War
The growing divide between Rome and Washington.
Over the last year, a divide has widened between Rome and Washington. It is one based on radically different views of diplomacy and war. It has compelled leading American bishops, encouraged by the Chicago-born Pope Leo, to take public positions at odds with the administration’s bellicose worldview.
Pope Leo XIV’s recent declaration, for example, that military spending enriches a few while diverting billions from peoples’ authentic needs, is in sync with the message of so many candidates who were swept to office in the blue tsunami, especially in Texas, where the arrest by ICE of a nun on her way to Mass galvanized the faithful.
What deserves more attention though, is Vatican suspicion of the US Department of War’s casual normalization of “tactical” nuclear weapons, when there are few codified international restraints.
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth recently announced a new decision-making structure linking robotic, drone, and AI capabilities known as Autonomous Warfare Command or AutoWarCom. Leo’s major focus on artificial intelligence includes the conviction that AI-enabled weapons of war, deployed with devastating effect in Gaza and Iran, pose an unacceptable global risk.
Longtime Critic
Since 1945, the Vatican has been a consistent critic of nuclear arms, especially considering that the atomic bomb dropped on Nagasaki obliterated much of Japan’s Catholic community.
Pope Francis ratcheted up Vatican engagement in the anti-nuke movement, first by negating the ethics of deterrence, then by outright condemning these arms. To an audience in Hiroshima, he declared, “Possessing nuclear weapons is immoral,” a statement crystallizing Vatican support for the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear States (TPNW), which bans developing, testing, producing, acquiring, possessing, or using nuclear weapons.
The TPNW went into force in 2021, once 50 countries had ratified it. To date, 75 countries have affirmed the treaty, excluding all nine nuclear powers, namely, China, France, India, Israel, North Korea, Pakistan, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States. But without their support, the treaty can’t have any meaningful effect, which is why the Trump administration’s entertainment of new forms of nuclear weaponry is so dangerous, in the Vatican’s view.
Unilateralism
According to the Vatican’s former nuncio (ambassador) to the United States, Cardinal Christophe Pierre, the pope’s advisers saw “disturbing things” in the Trump administration’s 2025 National Security Strategy, especially an emphasis on military solutions and a dismissal of multilateral consultation.
Then, while the Vatican was negotiating for their removal to a third country, President Nicolás Maduro and his wife were abducted by US forces from their Caracas residence and thrown into a Brooklyn jail. Regardless of offenses committed by the Venezuelan strongman—and local Catholic bishops largely opposed him for violating human rights—the US military had no right to trample Venezuela’s sovereignty, as Pope Leo swiftly pointed out.
American bishops were also increasingly agitated at evidence of illegality by US officials: ICE agents attacking people born abroad, many of them faithful Catholics, and speedboats being bombed in the Caribbean, supposedly for transporting drugs. The first practice violates domestic due process and the second international law.
When Pope Leo spoke to diplomats accredited to the Holy See, an annual New Year tradition, he lamented, “War is back in vogue and a zeal for war is spreading.’”
The Department of War took offense and summoned Pierre before Elbridge Colby, undersecretary of defense for policy—an unusual scenario. If Colby, a Catholic, thought he could silence the Vatican by delivering a “might makes right” lecture to a priest-diplomat of 50 years, he was wrong. The encounter seemed to trigger a more combative Catholic clergy.
On Easter Day, Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who serves a global diocese of Catholics in the US military (comprising 1.8 million service members and their families), told Face the Nation that the war against Iran can’t be called “just,” a theological category requiring wars to be defensive. The following Sunday, three American cardinals appeared on 60 Minutes reiterating criticism of the Trump administration’s “war of choice” and protesting “indiscriminate mass deportation.”
The Iran War inspired a public feud between Leo and Trump, who called the pope “terrible for foreign policy.” The next day, Leo pledged to “continue speaking out loudly against war,” including the use of AI targeting, blamed for obliterating an elementary school in southern Iran on the first day of bombing. Around 175 people were killed, most of them girls ages 7 to 12. Parents asked Pope Leo be a voice for the tragedy; he emphasized that international law requires belligerents to protect innocent lives.
Pierre told me, “The real history of America is that it built institutions for dialogue. But now you say no to dialogue? You destroy people then offer to engage in dialogue after that? It will never happen. Trump wants to isolate America and make America great against the others. Before, America became great with the others.”
Pope Leo’s geopolitical critique was formalized with the May 25 release of Magnificat Humanitas: On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence. It describes a “culture of power” ignoring dialogue and diplomacy, promoting war as an instrument of international politics, and advancing a false realism that conflict is inevitable. Though he never mentions a specific country, the narrative reads like an indictment of American foreign policy.
The document became the basis for an assembly of Nobel laureates in July at the pope’s summer residence, Castel Gandolfo, then at City Hall in Rome where laureates signed the Rome Declaration on AI and Nuclear Weapons. The Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists called it the first gathering of experts and activists tackling dangers of the “AI-nuke nexus.”
Former president of Colombia Juan Manuel Santos, a Nobel Prize winner, helped organize the event. Echoing the pope, he declared, “We are seeing the erosion of ethical restraints in favor of the pursuit of raw power. The development of increasingly advanced artificial intelligence adds additional unpredictability.”
At Castel Gandolfo, Dr. Ira Helfand, a cofounder and past president of Physicians for Social Responsibility who helped win two Nobel Peace Prizes related to nuclear arms, confirmed the Vatican as a longtime ally, adding, “Unfortunately, many people, including many practicing Catholics, are unaware of the Vatican’s clear and uncompromising position that nuclear weapons must be abolished. It has been clearly stated in diplomatic settings, but not in most parish churches.”

Vatican Deployment
A major reason for Pope Leo’s visit to the city of Metz, France in late September was to highlight a historic picture of goodwill reversing hatred: The European Coal and Steel Community, which evolved into the European Union, was founded there. Flying back to Rome, he again challenged Trump, this time insisting that safety concerns about AI are not “fake news.”
While Leo was in France, his secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, used a UN speech to reiterate: “The control of these powerful tools must not remain in the hands of a select few; they must serve humanity, not the other way around. In particular, the development of lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS) raises profound moral questions.” Last month, the Vatican’s new representative to the UN, Lebanese-born Archbishop Christophe-Zakhia El-Kassis, spoke of “additional risks” caused by the integration of AI into nuclear systems.
A major motivation for Rome’s thematic repetition is the evidence that the Trump administration intends to expand its arsenal, including “tactical” nuclear options. Colby revealed this in a speech to military brass, as reported by the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists. The Vatican sees an upcoming opportunity to flag US irresponsibility at the first UN review of the TPNW, to be held in New York, November 30–December 4.
Meanwhile, advisers close to the American pope say he is encouraging a new movement against the AI-fueled, nihilistic nuclear arms race.

https://gothamist.com/news/1-dead-10-inj.title: Brooklyn building collapse: 2 dead, 7 children among at least 19 injured
https://gothamist.com/news/1-dead-10-inj.author: Elizabeth Shwe, Hannah Frishberg, David Brand, Liam Quigley
https://gothamist.com/news/1-dead-10-inj.text:
A three-story building fully collapsed in Flatbush, Brooklyn Wednesday, killing two people and injuring at least 19, including seven children, FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said at a press conference at the collapse site late Wednesday.
"We do not know how many people are still in the collapse zone," she said. "We will likely not be finished for some time."
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said ten of the victims had been transported to local hospitals with both critical and non-life-threatening injuries.
"This has been an incredibly challenging and fast-moving situation, with precarious wreckage to navigate and dangerous voids beneath the surface," he said. "DOB and our law enforcement partners will be leading an investigation into the cause of this building collapse."
The FDNY said it received a call about the collapse at 2625 Bedford Ave. just after 4 p.m.
The building collapsed into a hole where construction workers had been excavating for a new building on an adjacent lot earlier in the day, according to the city's buildings commissioner Ahmed Tigani. A developer has submitted plans to the department for a nine story building that have yet to be approved.
FDNY Cheif of Department John Esposito said the agency's emergency responders arrived one minute after the three-story residential building collapsed and that rescue workers are using dogs to search for victims in the pile of debris.
In an interivew with WNYC, Councilmember Farah Louis described a chaotic scene late Wednesday evening with rubble strewn along Flatbush and Bedford Avenues.
"We've seen infants, toddlers being pulled out of the rubble on stretchers into ambulances to be rushed to the hospital. We've seen a husband who was desperately waiting to see if his wife would be pulled out of the rubble, who was also six months pregnant," Louis said. "They did find her, and she is in critical condition. It's just a horrific scene for our community and the constituents that live in this building."
A photo from the scene at the intersection of Flatbush and Bedford avenues showed firefighters at a construction site filled with debris. The images appeared to show nearly all of the building had collapsed into an adjacent construction site, exposing a stairway and clothes stored in a closet in a neighboring residential building.
"You see the building next to it is sheered off in part," former FDNY Commissioner Laura Kavanagh told WNYC, who warned that Thursday's forecast for storms could further complicate the rescue effort and the collapse site. "Rain and wind can cause further instability."
Mamdani said Flatbush Avenue was closed between Clarendon to Bedford Avenues and urged New Yorkers to avoid the area as rescue work continued into the night.
New York City's Office of Emergency Management said it has coordinated with the Red Cross to open a reception center for impacted residents at the Flatbush YMCA at 1401 Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn.
Department of Buildings spokesperson David Maggiotto told Gothamist that buildings officials were at the scene and would investigate the cause of the collapse.
This is a developing story that will be updated.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/11/open.title: OpenAI Fooled by Russian Pranksters Into Thinking They Were Speaking to Ukrainian Official
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/11/open.author: Sam Biddle
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/11/open.text:
A Russian internet comedy duo tricked three of OpenAI’s highest ranking military and national security staff into a candid conversation about arming Ukraine. The online pranksters posed as officials from Ukraine’s government, according to a recording of the meeting posted online.
The Russian comedy duo known as Vovan and Lexus have pulled off a long string of prank telephone calls to famous figures since 2011, with victims ranging from Elton John to John McCain. The group, whose pranks have often aligned with Russian foreign policy priorities, have been accused of working in league with its government, a charge they deny.
The latest to fall for their routine were Sasha Baker, who runs national security policy at OpenAI; the company’s lead for strategic initiatives, Caroline Zier; and Ben Crampton, who leads the country’s forays into European national security matters. All three have extensive government experience, with Baker and Zier taking high-level postings in the Department of Defense, and Crampton working in the European Union and United Nations.
“Weeks ago, we launched a thorough investigation into the call’s authenticity,” OpenAI spokesperson Nate Evans said in a statement to The Intercept. “We acted internally and with the relevant authorities to conclude that it was a prank conducted by individuals with a history of targeting officials and other companies. We took action to prevent similar situations from happening in the future.” (The Ukrainian Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)
The Russian prank duo said they arranged a high-level meeting with OpenAI by pretending to be Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service. During their 17-minute video conversation, a recording of which the Russian group uploaded to Rumble, the participants discussed OpenAI’s military support to Ukraine to aid its ongoing defense against Russia, including the possibility of providing offensive capabilities.
“There’s no question, I think, from our perspective that we want to have as deep a relationship as we possibly can with Ukraine,” Crampton said when asked about selling such offensive military AI services to the country. “But it may not be possible to get to where we want to be straight away.”
“There’s a general reluctance on the part of many people who are senior in the company to get too involved in offensive uses of our technology in a military context,” Crampton continued. “Part of our job is to explain that offense and defense are not necessarily distinguishable from each other under certain circumstances.”
OpenAI’s ongoing $200 million contract with the U.S. Department of War says it provides artificial intelligence applications aimed at “warfighters” that will “improve military advantage, military utility, or enhance military decision making,” according to contract documents obtained by The Intercept.
In the conversation with the Russian pranksters, Baker added that the company has been in contact with the Pentagon about aiding Ukraine.
OpenAI officials also mentioned ongoing work with the Ukrainian government based around the company’s Daybreak Blue AI model, a system for fixing computer vulnerabilities, as well as a nascent “partnership” with the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense.
“There has been some contact with the Ministry of Defense,” Crampton said. “It’s primarily through a colleague of ours based in Washington as well, who previously had worked with the Delta team in your Ministry of Defense. I think in this field we are interested to partner in as many ways as we can.”
During the video call, both Baker and Zier commented that they had met Umerov previously and were pleased to be speaking to him again. The faux-Umerov appears to have kept his camera turned off for the duration of the meeting.
Vladimir Kuznetsov, the member of the Russian comedy duo known as Vovan, told The Intercept the prank was simple to arrange.
“We initially contacted a senior Ukrainian official in San Francisco, posing as Mr. Umerov,” Kuznetsov said. “It turned out that he had been working to establish connections with OpenAI through the Ukrainian diaspora in California. He was already in touch with Sasha Baker, especially since she had maintained close ties with Ukraine during her time at the U.S. Department of Defense. Believing he was speaking with Umerov, the official offered to arrange a meeting with OpenAI.”
The conversation touched on other topics, including whether OpenAI could help protect against the influence of Elon Musk, and President Donald Trump’s sentiments on the war.
“I’m afraid we probably can’t help you with Elon Musk,” said Baker. “He’s not a fan of our CEO either, if it helps you at all. So, we’re in the same boat.”
Of Trump’s increasingly icy stance on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Baker said, “It’s unfortunate. Of course, we’ve been reading in the news the back and forth and the comments from the U.S. president. But I do want to reassure you that I think the majority of the U.S. government, the U.S. people certainly, and our researchers are very supportive of Ukraine.”

A Sprawling CIA Plot
Forty years ago, on the evening of October 5, 1986, I sat conferring with members of my local Nicaragua solidarity organization. We were trying to understand the implications of the day’s events in San Carlos, a small town in southern Nicaragua. A young Sandinista soldier had fired a shoulder-launched missile, bringing down a plane in a wreck survived by one Eugene H. Hasenfus. The plane contained U.S.-supplied weapons destined for the Contras, the counter-revolutionary force illegally supported by the CIA to overthrow the Nicaraguan government.
Hasenfus was captured, tried, and convicted of terrorism, and then, in a clever PR move by the Sandinista government, pardoned and released in time to spend Christmas at home with his family in Wisconsin.
Hasenfus’s capture — along with his planeload of AK-47s, 50,000 rifle cartridges, some shoulder-mounted missiles, and grenades — provided concrete evidence of something we’d known for a while: The Reagan administration was actively defying Congress by illegally funding and supplying the Contras. In those years, the Boland amendments (addenda to laws funding U.S. intelligence agencies) prohibited the CIA from using appropriated monies to support the Contras. Hasenfus’s capture not only demonstrated that those amendments were being violated, but also eventually led to the unraveling of a much bigger plot, known today as the Iran–Contra affair.
Oliver North, Iran, and “The Enterprise”
The trail from Hasenfus led to a military aide at the National Security Council, Oliver North, who was running a project to fund the Contras — with money from congressionally outlawed missile sales to Iran. Iran needed the military hardware for a brutal war of attrition with neighboring Iraq. The Reagan administration wanted to free U.S. hostages held in Iran and by Iran’s ally Hezbollah in southern Lebanon. So the arms-for-hostages deal was cooked up. Ollie North saw a way to use that one illegal deal to enable a second one. He would funnel unappropriated funds for the Contras by charging Iran a steep markup on the weapons and stashing the difference in Swiss bank accounts, outside U.S. government control.
At the suggestion of CIA Director William Casey, North had recruited Richard V. Secord, a retired Air Force major general, to establish what they called “the Enterprise.” North would later describe the Enterprise as an “off-the-shelf, self-sustaining, stand-alone entity that could perform certain activities,” i.e., covert overseas operations. The congressional committee that eventually investigated the Iran–Contra affair reported:
The Enterprise, functioning largely at North’s direction, had its own airplanes, pilots, airfield, operatives, ship, secure communications devices, and secret Swiss bank accounts. For 16 months, it served as the secret arm of the N.S.C. staff, carrying out with private and non-appropriated money, and without the accountability or restrictions imposed by law on the CIA, a covert Contra aid program that Congress thought it had prohibited.
North became something of a comic figure in U.S. history, especially after the escapade in which he choked a government office shredder during a late-night document “shredding party.” He and the coterie of implicated officials both above and below him all received pardons from incoming President George H. W. Bush, who’d served as Reagan’s vice president.
There is no way of knowing just how large North’s Enterprise might have grown had Hasenfus’s plane not been shot down, or what other sorts of dirty money-making businesses it might have spawned. Perhaps today we’d be living in a country with a largely self-funding, and therefore (even more) unaccountable, national security apparatus.
Big, “Dirty” Business in Venezuela
I thought about the Iran–Contra affair and North’s Enterprise for the first time in years when I read that Pete Hegseth’s Defense Department is getting into the oil business in Venezuela. Under the new arrangement, the Department of Defense would receive “penny warrants” for an ownership stake in at least one company developing Venezuelan oil fields. These warrants, according to the New York Times, “would give the Pentagon the option to take up to a 35 percent stake in the parent company” of North American Blue Energy Partners.
The company, which is legally registered in Barbados, is run by Alejandro Betancourt López, a Nicolás Maduro crony, around whom corruption rumors have swirled for at least a decade. The deal would also provide the Defense Department with the right to purchase up to 20 percent of the company’s oil output “at production cost” and first refusal on the remaining 80 percent, presumably at market rates.
There are a number of issues to consider here: The U.S. invasion’s legality, the logistical difficulties of extracting and using Venezuela’s “dirty” crude, and, of course, the human folly of pouring even more oil on the climate fire. But what especially caught my attention in the Times story is that the Pentagon taking an equity stake in a private oil company looks a lot like a new edition of North’s off-the-shelf operation from the 1980s.
The Pentagon isn’t alone among federal agencies acquiring ownership stakes in a variety of companies. Perhaps most notable is the Commerce Department’s purchase of an almost 10 percent interest in the chip manufacturer Intel for $8.9 billion, a stake that’s now reportedly worth $42 billion. As the Center for Strategic and International Studies reported in February, “the Trump administration is acquiring a strategic portfolio of investments in companies directly related to national security, spanning minerals, nuclear energy, and semiconductors, among other sectors.”
The CSIS report lists several smaller — though still enormous — Defense Department equity investments, among them:
- Vulcan Elements, a manufacturer of rare earth magnets: warrants to purchase equity at an undisclosed fixed price; $620 million loan against a $50 million equity stake
- MP Materials, a rare earth magnet manufacturer: 15 percent stake for $400 million
- Korea Zinc, a joint venture with Commerce and private investors in a Tennessee smelting installation; Defense Department to take 40 percent ownership, total cost $1.9 billion
- ReElement Technologies, a rare earth magnet recycler: warrants for future stock purchase; $80 million from Defense “matched by private capital”
- Trilogy Metals, a Canada-based company with Alaskan mining rights: 10 percent stake purchased for $35.6 million, with warrants to purchase another 7.5 percent
Since that report was published, DoD has continued to expand its portfolio with other equity purchases, which seem to be aimed at least in part on restocking American weapons reserves depleted by the Iran war:
- L3Harris Missile Solutions: $1 billion direct equity investment for solid rocket motor and missile production
- The Elmet Group: $450 million preferred equity investment in the only U.S.-based tungsten producer. Tungsten is crucial in the production of Patriot missiles, an essential defense against incoming missiles and drones, and a much-depleted armament in U.S. stores because of the Iran war.
- Hertha Metals: an apparent $65 million investment — for an undisclosed number of shares — in a steel manufacturer. The libertarian Cato Institute, which generally opposes federal ownership stakes in corporations, called the investment with Hertha an “apparent” deal, as only the company, not the DoD, has announced it publicly.
Beyond taking direct ownership shares in corporations, DoD continues to diversify its loan portfolio beyond traditional military materials. For example, President Donald Trump recently promised a $100 million Pentagon investment to rebuild a pharmaceutical factory in Winchester, Kentucky — but only if Republicans won the midterms in that state.
How Does Government Ownership of Corporations Work?
The federal government has taken temporary partial ownership of U.S. corporations before Trump’s current string of acquisitions. What makes this round of purchases different is that it seems the Pentagon intends to make them permanent. In the past, when the federal government acquired warrants or corporate shares, the move was part of a program to shore up failing institutions in the midst of a more general financial disaster.
This was the case with the Troubled Assets Relief Program, which formed part of the Obama administration’s response to the 2008 fiscal crisis, and more recently when airlines faced bankruptcy during the 2020-21 Covid pandemic. In neither case did the government retain permanent ownership of the entities it bailed out.
The evidence is that this time around, the Trump administration envisions permanent ownership stakes in companies it deems essential to military preparedness and national security. In the case of the Pentagon, two related offices are responsible for overseeing DoD’s equity investments.
The Office of Strategic Capital was established in 2022 during Joe Biden’s administration and funded under the National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2024. The OSC’s initial purpose was to facilitate Pentagon loans to industries it deems crucial to national security. Other parts of DoD use grants or purchases to get money to defense industries. Only OSC can lend those corporations money. Still, neither the NDAA for 2024 nor subsequent NDAAs permits the OSC to buy shares in companies.
The OSC received a huge funding boost under Trump’s 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act. While simultaneously meting out drastic cuts to programs that support Americans’ actual everyday security — such as Medicaid, nutritional assistance, housing, and student loans — the One Big Beautiful Bill Act awarded OSC $1.5 billion in additional funds.
The other entity tasked with overseeing Defense equity investments is the Economic Defense Unit. Established this year through an internal DoD memo, the EDU offers a hint that the Pentagon isn’t ready to give up on capital. Like the Office of Strategic Capital, the EDU is overseen by Defense Department Undersecretary Stephen Feinberg, a billionaire, major Trump donor, and co-founder of the private equity firm Cerberus Capital Management.
EDU’s ostensible purpose is to coordinate U.S. economic competition with adversaries such as China, Iran, Russia, and North Korea. But reporting suggests another reason Feinberg established the unit. Quoting a knowledgeable inside source, The American Prospect says that the EDU “operates as a ‘venture capital firm-type entity that looks at deals, what the government’s going to do and evaluates them,’” determining what the government’s ownership stake should be.
The Cato Institute says of the EDU:
Available information points to an investment apparatus being created within the Pentagon, staffed by financiers connected to the same private-equity world that stands to benefit from it.
It sounds like another attempt by the administration to construct a pseudo-sovereign wealth fund controlled by the executive branch.
In other words, the Economic Defense Unit looks like the beginning of a Defense Department investment bank.
As of today, no law explicitly permits the Pentagon to own pieces of corporations or to develop its own pseudo-investment bank, but the 2027 NDAA may change that.
In the meantime, what happens to any revenue derived from DoD’s investments? Such income could include interest on loans, share dividends, or proceeds from the sale of equities. Legally, any such income should be deposited to the U.S. Treasury within three days, according to the U.S. legal code section § 3302(b), perhaps in the Pentagon’s Industrial Base Fund at Treasury.
History tells us North sent the Iran–Contra money to Swiss banks, not the U.S. Treasury. Can we trust Hegseth — who just this week survived an impeachment vote — and his boss not to do something similar with the Pentagon’s earnings today? How would we even know if that trust were violated?
Just Like Egypt and Iran?
The prospect of a metastasizing U.S. Defense Department may seem far-fetched, but it’s already happened in a number of other countries. In Egypt, popular demonstrations brought down President Hosni Mubarak, the country’s effective dictator, during the 2011 Arab Spring. After a brief period under an increasingly unpopular elected president, the Egyptian military staged a coup and has ruled the country directly ever since.
But Egypt’s army is more than a military force. It’s the most powerful economic entity in the country as well. As the Carnegie Middle East Center describes the situation, the Egyptian military has its tentacles in every aspect of Egypt’s economy. Members of the military:
… deliver massive infrastructure projects, produce consumer goods ranging from food to household appliances, manufacture industrial chemicals and transport equipment, and import basic commodities for civilian markets. They have expanded into new sectors as diverse as steel production, pharmaceuticals, gold prospecting, and managing religious endowments and pilgrimage.
At the same time, “thousands of retired senior officers have benefited from the powerful political influence of the military to occupy senior positions throughout the state’s civilian apparatus and public sector companies, securing extra postretirement incomes for themselves while complementing the formal military economy in return.”
(This sounds a lot like the egregious post-service opportunities promised to the investment bankers being recruited to work in the Pentagon’s EDU. After serving on the Pentagon’s new 30-person investment team, where they would have “unmatched access to top-level government officials and privileged information flow,” the recruitment pitch goes, “if you ever want to raise your own fund, you will gain access to fund-raising channels that include royal families and foreign sovereign contacts,” according to the New York Times.)
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which has emerged as Iran’s most powerful economic force, plays a similar role, according to CSIS:
The IRGC now owns businesses in the oil and gas sectors, as well as land, marine, and air transportation. The IRGC-owned company, Khatam al-Anbiya, established as the IRGC’s arm in the construction sector, currently controls 812 officially registered Iranian companies which have a total of some 1,700 governmental contracts. Another IRGC-owned company has also recently bought a 51 percent stake in the Iranian Telecommunications company that was privatized at a value of $5 billion.
Can It Happen Here?
Could the Pentagon really emerge as an economic power in its own right, one that operates in tandem with, but parallel to, the federal government? Not tomorrow, certainly, but now is the time to step on the brakes to prevent that scenario.
The prospect of an economically independent U.S. military would be frightening under any circumstances. But it becomes both more frightening and more likely with a Pentagon that Hegseth is reshaping in his own white Christian nationalist and misogynist image. He’s already removed many of the potential human guardrails by purging long-serving top military leadership. As long as DoD doesn’t threaten any of the enterprises of the Trump family and friends — including those of Don Jr. and Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, and Steve Witkoff — we can expect little resistance from the demented relic in the White House.
Fortunately, Hegseth is not the sharpest bayonet in the armory. As with many aspects of this nightmare administration, we may yet be saved from a metastasizing Pentagon by the ineptitude of its leader. Let us work to make it so.
