https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: A good bet: New Yorkers are lining up to become casino dealers
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Hannah Frishberg
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
The odds seem to be in their favor.
On the sixth floor of a NoMad office building, an hour’s drive from New York City’s first full-scale casino in Jamaica, the Big Deal Casino Academy has been scaling up to keep pace with demand.
During a recent Thursday morning class at Big Deal, a diverse array of students practiced the card game Baccarat. Cocooned from Manhattan’s busy streets within a narrow office building, the windowless space was quiet but for the clicking of cards and chips.
Big Deal founder Wendy Rubin is a poker player who said she “saw the writing on the wall” for the city’s impending need for dealers. She poured her life savings into starting the first incarnation of the Academy, the boroughs’ only Department of Education-licensed dealer school, back in 2014, soon after the New York legislature passed resolutions permitting casino gaming in the city. She didn’t anticipate that it’d take over a decade for the casinos to actually arrive.
Then at last, this April, Resorts World Casino launched live table games. A second casino, adjacent to Citi Field, and a third in the Bronx are both slated to open in 2030.
“I've kinda hung in there like a dog with a bone, waiting, waiting, waiting — and here we are,” Rubin said. Now, “We get people calling all the time looking to take classes. After so many years of waiting, it’s really rewarding.”
“It’s become a hotter job,” said Brooklyn native and Bed-Stuy resident Tony Hall, 28, a dealer manager at Resorts World who teaches at Big Deal. “Growing up, I never heard anyone say, ‘hey, I wanna be a table games dealer. I wanna work in a casino.’”
Now, though, friends and family often contact him about what it takes to get the gig after seeing him making good money without having to do grueling physical labor.
“It's never too hard to take someone’s bet, or to pay someone out, or to flip a card,” Hall said. It’s a far cry from the work that was expected of him during his days driving trucks for FedEx, loading boxes for UPS and cleaning up schools as a custodian for the Board of Education. It's better money too, not to mention a more reliable schedule. After switching to be a dealer, “I didn’t have no back pains. I’m not going home with no headaches, no nothing, no stress. It’s a real easy labor job.”
Dealing is also appealing for its relatively low bar for entry: It takes approximately nine weeks and $2,780 to get certified. No high school diploma is necessary. Those who’ve been convicted of certain felonies — fraud, perjury, embezzlement — or have been found to demonstrate financial instability through failure to pay child support or unpaid taxes are ineligible.
Since the house always wins, employment is relatively secure, and for now jobs are plentiful and unionized. Those who are promoted to be pit bosses and floor managers lose their union cards but often make six figures annually.
To become certified and hirable, aspiring croupiers must formally learn blackjack and one other table game of their choice. Right now, Rubin said, Resorts World is looking for craps dealers. Craps is a notably challenging game to play and deal, so she and her team have been keeping an eye out for students who seem well-suited for it, no matter their know-how entering the Academy.
The school, meanwhile, is being challenged by the casinos themselves, which teach dealers in-house, creating something of a competition for both students and teachers. (Unlike the DOE-licensed Big Deal, casinos’ internal education programs are overseen by the Gaming Commission.)
“In fact, the casino hired all of our teachers,” she said, a fact she acknowledged was “certainly a little challenging.”
But she’s rehired and is confident that “in a year or so I imagine everything will shake itself out — there’ll be enough teachers, there’ll be enough dealers, everybody will be happy.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/pete.title: Humanitarian Orgs Demand Answers on Yemen War After Hegseth Impeachment Fails
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/pete.author: Nick Turse
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/pete.text:
With Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth temporarily safe from impeachment, a dozen humanitarian groups are calling on Congress to investigate one of the eight shelved charges lodged against him: his role in the deaths of hundreds of people during the “unauthorized war in Yemen.”
“We urge members of Congress to conduct robust oversight into Operation Rough Rider and the resulting human toll,” reads a new letter shared exclusively with The Intercept, using the Pentagon’s term for its war against Yemen’s Houthi government. The 12 groups — including Airwars, Amnesty International USA, the Center for Civilians in Conflict, and Mwatana for Human Rights — seize on civilian harm prevention efforts that Hegseth’s War Department slashed, demanding “more information about how and why civilian harm incidents occurred, what lessons the Department learned from these operations, and the status of ongoing civilian harm assessments and investigations.”
The push for accountability follows last week’s electoral rout of the GOP and immediate calls by top Democrats for scrutiny of war powers abuses by the Trump administration. But with Democrats taking the gavel in both chambers next year, a defense official told The Intercept that the Trump administration’s failed 2025 conflict in Yemen risks becoming a “forgotten war” amid a push for accountability focused on higher profile conflicts.
Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the House Armed Services Committee’s incoming chair, announced last week that the committee’s “top priority will be to conduct vigorous oversight of the Department of Defense and the Trump Administration,” specifically singling out “the illegal war against Iran” and “unauthorized military strikes in the Caribbean and Latin America.” Smith did not mention Yemen, and his office did not respond to repeated queries about whether Yemen would also be a priority. The office of Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I., who is slated to head the Senate Armed Services Committee, also did not immediately respond to questions about whether oversight of Rough Rider would be a focus.
Over just 52 days, from March to May 2025, Rough Rider caused “extraordinarily high numbers of civilian casualties,” the groups noted. As The Intercept first reported in August, the Pentagon’s annual report to Congress on civilian harm acknowledged almost 400 civilian casualties — 153 deaths and 243 injuries — from just three attacks in Yemen: a strike in Sanaa on April 6, a strike on the Ras Isa Port on April 17, and a strike on a migrant detention center in Saada on April 28.
Amnesty, one of the signatories, spoke with five survivors of the strike in Saada who cannot work because of their injuries. “If I don’t take a painkiller, I feel hopeless and wish to die,” said a 22-year-old Ethiopian man who sustained a serious arm injury in the U.S. attack. “I think about how at such a young age I can’t even support myself and still rely on help from others. The metal rod inside me is very painful and uncomfortable. It drives you insane.”
A U.S. official called the Pentagon’s civilian casualty count “lowball numbers.” According to the Yemen Data Project, the estimated toll was higher: at least 238 civilians killed and 467 injured.
“It’s striking that the Department acknowledged nearly 400 civilian casualties from just three incidents — a staggeringly high rate — without any explanation whatsoever about what happened and why, how they’ll respond to victims and their families, and how they’ll prevent it from happening again,” Annie Shiel, the U.S. director of Center for Civilians in Conflict, told The Intercept.
More than a year after Operation Rough Rider ended, 15 additional attacks were still under assessment, according to the civilian harm report. One official told The Intercept in August that the backlog would likely carry over several years. Under Hegseth, the 10-person civilian harm mitigation team at Central Command, or CENTCOM, has been reduced to just one individual.
This lack of attention doesn’t bode well for understanding civilian harm in Hegseth’s longer-running and even more destructive war efforts, officials said.
“How will they get through hundreds of cases for Iran if their one civilian harm person still hasn’t finished Yemen?” a U.S. official asked in August.
At present, CENTCOM claims that the U.S. attack on the Shajarah Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab, Iran – that killed more than 150 people, most of them children — is the lone civilian harm incident of that burgeoning forever war. For months, CENTCOM has failed to answer questions about that attack and additional Iranian civilian casualties, including eight members of a family — the youngest, a 20-day-old infant — killed in a strike documented in an investigation by The Intercept.
Shiel highlighted the connections between the civilian casualties during Rough Rider and those in Iran.
“There is a through-line here from Yemen. We’ll never know if the devastation of Minab would have been prevented through a fully staffed civilian protection program and a more robust inquiry into what happened in Yemen, but it’s clear that important reckoning didn’t happen,” she said. “This is part of a broader trend of focusing on ‘lethality’ over civilian lives, ignoring hard-learned lessons in the process.”
A group of Democratic lawmakers told Hegseth in a July letter that his “gutting” of Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response efforts has left the Pentagon unable to “comply with the law and its congressionally-mandated CHMR responsibilities.” Sent by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and nine other lawmakers, the letter echoed concerns raised by a War Department inspector general report that described civilian protection efforts as largely “inactive.” The May missive by the Pentagon’s top watchdog says cuts to civilian harm mitigation and response efforts have been so severe under Hegseth that the United States cannot adequately protect civilians in conflict zones or track harm when it occurs.
These criticisms were echoed in an another report, first revealed by The Intercept in July, that found Hegseth’s Pentagon gutted its premier center devoted to preventing civilian casualties in war zones. The War Department’s Civilian Protection Center of Excellence slashed its staff from 40 personnel in January 2025 to just nine by the end of the year, according to the report.
Last week, The Intercept published an exposé quoting six current and former defense officials under Hegseth who called for his ouster, including a former senior adviser at that center. “He is conducting state terrorism. He is 100 percent a war criminal. He needs to be prosecuted,” said Wes J. Bryant, who was pushed out of his job for blowing the whistle on Hegseth’s efforts to undermine protections for civilians.
The 12 humanitarian groups called on Congress to “fully restore” the Pentagon’s civilian harm mitigation program, “including by mandating minimum staffing levels and earmarking funding in annual appropriations and maintaining robust oversight over DoD implementation of congressionally-mandated policies.” The groups also specifically requested the release of the Civilian Protection Center’s lessons-learned study on Operation Rough Rider, which has been bottled up for months.
During a rare Pentagon press conference on Tuesday, ahead of the impeachment vote, Hegseth celebrated Rough Rider, claiming the Houthis “cried uncle.” But a post-mortem of the operation in the CTC Sentinel — published by the Combating Terrorism Center at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point — said that because of Rough Rider, the Houthi leadership “will have the confidence that, like the Taliban in Afghanistan, it can simply outlast the United States.”
The U.S. has, to date, failed to come to the aid of its staunch ally Saudi Arabia as the Houthis have battered that country’s airports and energy infrastructure for weeks. On Monday, an attack on the financial district in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, damaged an office of Aramco, the state oil giant.
The White House failed to respond to questions about the Yemen war from The Intercept. CENTCOM did not reply to a request for information on the status of civilian harm assessments or formal investigations stemming from Rough Rider.
Shiel was emphatic about the necessity of accountability, telling The Intercept, “Congress needs to step in and force that reckoning through oversight over civilian harm incidents and by mandating and funding the restoration of the civilian harm mitigation program.”
In their letter, the 12 humanitarian organizations urged the U.S. to make amends to survivors and the families of victims.
“The Department’s 2025 report also stated that ex gratia or condolence payments to victims and survivors were ‘determined to not be appropriate’ in the three Yemen incidents. This decision is premature and seemingly arbitrary,” they wrote. “Rather than dismissing amends out of hand, the Department should undertake a good-faith effort to understand families’ needs and preferences for responses.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Mamdani’s White Knight for Troubled Buildings Has Dismal Record of Violations
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Greg B. Smith
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani recently celebrated the transfer of ownership of three long-neglected rent-stabilized buildings in Brooklyn from Rubin Dukler, an owner who’d made frequent appearances on the city’s worst landlord list, to a new landlord named Mark Schwartz.
Schwartz is the mayor of Teaneck, New Jersey, and owns rent-stabilized apartment buildings across the city. Under the landlord swap that was cheered by the mayor and subsidized by the city, Schwartz has pledged to fix up the three Dukler buildings and provide tenants with decent living conditions they had long been denied.
In a Sept. 3 statement, Mamdani called the transfer “a new chapter” for the tenants and promised to work with the new owner “to put these 88 homes on a path toward stability and make clear that every New Yorker deserves a safe, well-maintained and stable place to call home.”
What the mayor did not mention was that Schwartz and his partners have racked up more than 1,400 open housing code violations deemed hazardous or immediately hazardous in the 28 buildings they now own or manage across the city, according to an internal city document obtained by The City Reporter.
Records show that the city Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) — the agency that will monitor Schwartz’s upgrade of the Dukler properties — has repeatedly cited Schwartz’s buildings for a sobering variety of squalid conditions. In the last four years alone, they have sued him or his partners 15 times to force required repairs.
And HPD has had to hire contractors to remedy conditions at their buildings because the owners failed to complete required repairs. The internal city document notes Schwartz and his partners currently owe the city $1.3 million for this work.
Of Mice and Mold
Tenants at 3569 Dekalb Ave., a 54-unit tenement near Woodlawn Cemetery in The Bronx that Schwartz and his partners have owned for many years, know all about this.
As of Nov. 2, that building had accumulated 268 open violations for conditions inspectors deemed hazardous or immediately hazardous, including 30 citations issued Aug. 26 for rat and mice infestations, non-functioning smoke detectors and toxic mold. Since Schwartz took ownership in 2018, the city has spent $21,500 to hire contractors to perform required repairs there.
“The roaches and the rats are crazy,” Maritza Diaz-Sanchez, 40, recently told The City Reporter, recalling a recent encounter when she said rats and mice ran through the lobby and up the staircase across her path. She pointed to a patch the building super had installed over a hole in the lobby floor to try and block additional furry guests.
“Two mouses and two rats,” she said. “It was a family.”
‘A Ton of Care’
In an interview, Schwartz admitted he was “embarrassed” by conditions at Dekalb Avenue, but insisted he’s aggressively moving to address all outstanding violations there and at his other properties across the city.
He said he’s had varying degrees of oversight of his buildings, relying at times on partners and third-party entities to stay on top of building conditions. This arrangement, he said, has not always obtained optimal results.
“When I handle it myself, they’re very clean. When, over the past years, over time in past years when others handle it, they don’t get taken care of as well as they should,” he said. “Every few years we give buildings back and forth to partners and third parties and it just doesn’t for the most part work out.”
“If I screw up I will say I screwed up,” he added. “If you rely on other people, you can’t say that.”
Last month Schwartz said he took control of 11 rent-stabilized buildings in which he says he had a small stake because he says he wants to better assist Mamdani’s efforts to preserve existing affordable housing.
“This administration and myself are getting very heavily involved in preservation. The rent-stabilized industry is a mess right now. The buildings need a ton of care,” he said. “I want to make sure our buildings are taken care of before I work with others. I’m very proud of our internal track record and the buildings we took over.”
Schwartz insisted he has “hit the ground” to remedy open citations: “We immediately began attacking all the violations and have made great progress.”
He has his work cut out for him. At one of those properties, a four-story property at 2044 Bergen St. in Crown Heights, a mile away from the Dukler buildings, Schwartz said he had been a “small partner” there for years but on Oct. 1 took full charge.
‘A Profitable Business Model’?
One of his first orders of business will be to address a lawsuit HPD filed last month. At the time there were 92 open violations in a building with 16 units, including 76 deemed hazardous. That represented a per-dwelling average of 4.75 hazardous violations — far in excess of the citywide average for rent-stabilized buildings of 0.05 violations per dwelling. Hazardous violations cited this year included roach and mice infestations and non-functioning self-closing doors and smoke detectors.
HPD alleged the owners had falsely certified that dozens of other violations had been remedied when inspectors discovered they were not. And they pointed out that the address of the building’s registered agent, Brian Dulitz, was a mail drop in a UPS store in Lower Manhattan. Dulitz has served as a registered agent on multiple Schwartz properties, including the Dukler buildings on Eastern Parkway.
HPD characterized the pattern of failure to address repair requests as deliberate, alleging the owners had “turned deferring maintenance of rent-stabilized buildings into a profitable business model.”
How Schwartz became the go-to guy in the Mamdani-supported landlord swap starts with him purchasing the mortgage on the Dukler properties in late 2024. Since then he said he’s moved to foreclose, but Duckler has continued to be the registered agent responsible for managing the three buildings.
Schwartz said in the summer of 2025, frustrated residents who had formed a tenants union after years of inaction from Dukler approached Schwartz about stepping in. Schwartz said he then began working with HPD — first under Eric Adams, then under Mamdani — seeking city subsidies to help him preserve and upgrade the 88 rent-stabilized apartments in the three buildings.
Rent Strike
On Sept. 4, the Dukler Tenant Union announced they’d reached an “agreement in principle” with Schwartz to rehabilitate their buildings with a long-term goal of converting them to co-ops that tenants would have the option to purchase.
The union said Schwartz agreed to cancel all arrears accumulated during a years-long rent strike in protest of Dukler’s failures, and that tenants will have some oversight over the upgrades to “ensure high quality renovations.” HPD will monitor contractors performing the rehabilitation.
“HPD is very hands-on,” Schwartz said. “The city is trying to expedite this for months. The city is begging to get this done by June. That would be a dream. I’m not going to lie to you. It is pressuring us.”
Asked to comment on Schwartz’s track record, the mayor’s office sent a statement from Cea Weaver, who runs Mamdani’s Office to Protect Tenants.
“Working alongside new ownership, the Dukler Tenant Union has negotiated a strong Memo of Understanding with Mark Schwartz so that they have another tool in their toolbox to hold building management accountable,” Weaver said. “As we do with any building, we will use each and every mechanism at our disposal to enforce the city’s Housing Maintenance Code and support both building owners who come to the table in good faith, and tenants who fight for their right to live in a safe, stable home.”
Schwartz said tenants were aware of his track record when they signed the memorandum of understanding, but when The City Reporter visited the Dukler buildings on Monday, tenants universally declined to comment about their soon-to-be new landlord.
Arielle Hersh, director of policy at the nonprofit Urban Homesteading Assistance Board, which helped organize the Dukler tenants, said she would not discuss Schwartz’s portfolio on the record.
Schwartz, for his part, said he’s enthusiastically working with the Mamdani team to make his takeover of the Dukler buildings work, but he noted the administration’s plans to greatly expand this tactic to other in-need buildings will require ample funding.
He estimated repairs alone at the Dukler buildings are expected to cost $150,000 per unit.
“I love their approach. I want to work with them on their approach,” he said, adding that “the Eastern Parkway package, it’s several hundred thousand per unit. That’s three buildings. How do you do this with hundreds of buildings? I don’t know where they’re going to get the money.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/enviro.author: Jimmy Tobias
https://www.thenation.com/article/enviro.text:
Is America Headed Toward A New “Nuclear Golden Age”?
As the attempted revival of a nuclear plant in Michigan is revealing, actually running a nuclear reactor is a risky, and expensive, proposition.
In 2022, Jigar Shah, a clean-energy entrepreneur who was serving as the director of the Loan Programs Office (LPO) at President Joe Biden’s Department of Energy, reached out to Kris Singh, the multimillionaire founder and CEO of Holtec International, with a bold question. Holtec was in the process of buying the Palisades Nuclear Generating Station, an aged 800-megawatt nuclear plant in southwestern Michigan, to decommission it. Would Holtec consider resurrecting it instead? The company, which makes nuclear-waste storage casks and provides other industry services, had never operated a nuclear facility before. Nor had a shuttered nuclear plant that was due for decommissioning ever been revived in the United States.
“Well, sell me,” Singh replied, according to an interview Shah gave to the Odd Lots podcast in 2024. In March 2022, before Holtec had even finalized the purchase of Palisades, Shah sent Singh an e-mail that outlined the subsidies Holtec might receive from the federal government if the plant was refurbished, including tax credits from Biden’s Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. Shah estimated that the plant would require as much as $1 billion to bring it up to operating standards. The LPO “is committed to exploring the full range of financial structures under our authorities to support the refurbishment and potential uprate of the Palisades plant,” Shah wrote.
Singh, evidently, was sold. Roughly a week after Holtec closed its purchase of the plant in late June 2022, the company applied for federal subsidies for the restart effort. According to e-mails obtained from a public-records request, Shah and Singh corresponded many times and scheduled meetings and meals together in the following years. “We appreciate the diligent efforts being made by the LPO office to engage with us,” Singh wrote to Shah and his DOE colleague in 2023. “The whole world is watching if America can pull off the restart of Palisades.”
In March 2024, the Department of Energy announced that it would provide a conditional $1.5 billion loan guarantee to Holtec to support the Palisades restart. Biden’s Department of Agriculture also awarded a total of $1.3 billion to subsidize two Midwestern power cooperatives that agreed to purchase the electricity from the revived Palisades plant. And the State of Michigan, under Governor Gretchen Whitmer, provided Holtec with $300 million in additional subsidies. Holtec plunged headfirst into the challenging task of reviving Palisades, promising hundreds of jobs and “clean energy reliability, 24/7/365.” Should its efforts succeed, the company stands to gain a major cash-generating asset for decades to come.
But now, several years later, Holtec has blown past its self-declared timeline. It is not clear when exactly Palisades will restart or, when it does, whether Holtec can achieve financial sustainability while maintaining safe and reliable operations over the long term. Meanwhile, some local residents, nuclear critics, and at least one former high-ranking Palisades employee have raised questions about both the safety and the economic viability of the plant, which is one of the oldest nuclear facilities in the country. “We are desperate for ways to protect ourselves,” said Karen Davis, whose home sits just a few hundred yards from the plant’s property line on the shores of Lake Michigan.
The resurrection of Palisades comes amid a resurgence of proposals for new nuclear-energy projects all over the United States. Its supporters say that it is a safe and steady source of low-carbon baseload energy—the kind that runs around the clock—and thus something to be encouraged. But the industry poses unique challenges, including highly complex and costly systems; a history of accidents and unmet ambitions; and the ever-present specter of radioactive contamination, which can linger in the environment for hundreds or even thousands of years and cause lethal disease. Given that the industry rests on huge public subsidies, it would likely take just one high-profile failure in the US to plunge it back into a dark age.
Fully operational by the early 1970s, with a single-unit pressurized water reactor, the Palisades plant for decades provided enough electricity to power as many as 800,000 homes in Michigan. Its long life of supplying low-carbon energy to the state came to an end in early 2022, after the plant’s owner at the time, the behemoth electric utility Entergy, decided to shut it down amid fierce competition from cheap natural gas and looming maintenance expenditures. When Holtec acquired the facility to decommission it later that year, the plant’s fate seemed sealed.
That is certainly how it seemed to Karen Davis and her husband, Bruce, residents of a small Michigan community just south of the nuclear plant. Known among its denizens as Palisades Park, it is a tightly packed collection of some 200 cottages along a small creek and connected to the outside world by a single dirt road with a gate at the entrance. Though it has full-time residents, the community is mostly a summer retreat, a place where families from all over the Midwest have been coming for generations to enjoy the woods and beaches that line Lake Michigan.
The Davises were relieved when Entergy announced the Palisades closure. Decades of summers spent next to a nuclear-power plant were quite enough. Karen, her sister, and her mother have all suffered from thyroid tumors in recent years, and her daughter and daughter-in-law also struggle with thyroid dysfunction. The thyroid—a gland that is part of the body’s endocrine system—is uniquely vulnerable to radiation exposure, and Karen attributes the family’s diagnoses to their neighbor to the north. All of them have had a “lifelong proximity” to the nuclear plant, she said of her family. “One hundred percent.” Karen had her own thyroid removed in 2004, when she was 41 years old.
With the nuclear plant’s closure assured, or so they believed, the Davises decided to move full-time to Palisades Park. But then Holtec pivoted. By early 2023, Holtec had officially filed paperwork with the federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission to begin the process for the plant’s resurrection. The Davises were stunned. Bruce and some of his neighbors protested at a press conference in March 2024 in southwestern Michigan, during which Governor Whitmer and Biden-era Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm celebrated the loan guarantee for Holtec’s restart efforts. Holtec also received a $400 million award from the Department of Energy in late 2025 to help it start deploying new small modular reactors, or SMRs, a type of advanced nuclear reactor that many see as the future of the industry, at Palisades.
After Holtec’s plans were made public, similar proposals followed. In 2024, the nuclear-energy giant Constellation announced that it would restart a reactor at Three Mile Island that sits adjacent to the site of the infamous 1979 partial meltdown that shocked the nation. “The decision here is the most powerful symbol of the rebirth of nuclear power as a clean and reliable energy resource,” Constellation CEO Joe Dominguez said at the time of the announcement.
Holtec’s lavish public funding stems primarily from Biden’s aggressive agenda to promote green energy. Biden officials saw nuclear energy—which emits minimal greenhouse-gas pollution—as an essential strategy in the pursuit of the administration’s commitment to achieve net-zero emissions in the United States no later than 2050. The federal government showered the industry with loans, tax credits, and favorable legislation. Palisades “was operating safely for decades and was shut down prematurely due to economics above all else,” said Katy Huff, the chair of the nuclear-engineering department at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and a former assistant secretary at Biden’s Department of Energy. “That is antithetical to what we are trying to do, which is increase the amount of reliable carbon-free electricity on the grid.”
Though the Trump administration has eviscerated most of Biden’s green-energy agenda, it has kept the money spigot turned all the way on when it comes to nukes, promising “more nuclear power than ever before.” Last summer, the Department of Energy announced $17.5 billion in conditional loans to help facilitate the development of 10 new large reactors across the country. Trump himself has business interests in nuclear power. Last year, the Trump Media and Technology Group announced a merger agreement with a nuclear company called TAE Technologies, which has received financial support from the DOE. And Trump’s current energy secretary, Chris Wright, formerly sat on the board of the nuclear-energy company Oklo, which has also received federal largesse.
According to Gallup, public support for the industry is near record highs. Demand for electricity is surging, driven in part by the insatiable energy needs of the emergent artificial-intelligence economy, and grid operators are struggling to meet the enormous demand while keeping costs down. Some tech giants, like Microsoft and Meta, are striking stand-alone deals with nuclear plants to power their data centers.
Nuclear energy also boasts a smaller land-use footprint and higher reliability than other green-energy sources, making nuclear plants an important resource within the dual context of the climate crisis and the country’s increasingly overtaxed transmission grid, said Huff, the former DOE official. She notes that greenhouse-gas emissions from nuclear energy are similar to those from wind energy, citing figures from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.
The nuclear industry benefits too from an increasingly vocal and well-funded movement. And many state-based prohibitions on nuclear-power generation have recently fallen; last year, Illinois lifted its 40-year moratorium on the construction of large nuclear plants. Meanwhile, Russia and China are pursuing their own expansion of nuclear energy, fueling domestic arguments that the United States must keep up if it hopes to compete with its principal adversaries.
With Trump in the White House, the nuclear industry has been transformed by more than just subsidies. In May 2025, Trump issued an executive order directing the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to undertake a sweeping revision of its structure and regulations in collaboration with Elon Musk’s DOGE. Among other things, the NRC was ordered to effectively speed up the approval of new plants and advanced technologies. Since then, the agency has unveiled a stream of regulatory changes, including loosening its implementation of the National Environmental Policy Act, a key environmental law. And in early 2025, Trump issued an order that effectively abolished the independence of regulatory agencies like the NRC, which had previously been structured to prevent political influence.
These maneuvers have greatly troubled some former NRC officials and other industry observers. “There has been a policy sledgehammer to destroy government oversight and regulation,” said Edwin Lyman, a physicist who works as the director of nuclear-power safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “Through the executive orders, they have fully compromised the independence of the NRC and have made it another tool of administration policy.”
“I don’t feel so confident anymore about what is being regulated and what isn’t,” said Allison Macfarlane, a former chair of the NRC under Barack Obama. The NRC had “a great mission to ensure public health and environmental health and the security of these facilities and nuclear materials. And now I don’t know what it is.”
In a statement published in September, Trump’s NRC chair, Ho K. Nieh, wrote that the agency’s “mission remains unchanged: protect the public, protect the environment, maintain security—and enable nuclear technology to serve the nation.”
Nothing, of course, would halt the current nuclear momentum more quickly than an accident on American shores. But skeptics of the current renaissance argue that it is more likely to founder due to the cost of generating nuclear energy, and that the huge public subsidies flowing into the industry would be better spent elsewhere, including on solar, wind, and battery-storage projects. A plant like Palisades was abandoned because it wasn’t a good asset, said Greg Jaczko, a physicist and another former NRC chair under Obama. Without subsidies, such plants “are nowhere close to being economic, and probably aren’t economic even with the subsidies.” Even with the favorable macroeconomic conditions of today, he questions whether newly built plants will fare any better.
“You have got Bill Gates building a reactor,” Jaczko added, referring to an advanced reactor being built by Gates’s company TerraPower in Wyoming. “You’ve got X-energy building their thing down in Texas. But one reactor does not an industry make.”
“People can wish all they want. I think it is misguided,” said Mark Jacobson, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at Stanford and a prominent critic of nuclear power. “There have only been two reactors built in the last 30 years, and they took 17 or 18 years, cost $35 billion, and produce electricity for $16 a watt. And new solar and wind are $1 a watt, and they take only two to five years from planning to operation. So you are waiting around 15 years for something that costs 16 times more.”
Huff, the former DOE official, argues that a grid dominated by wind and solar, which are intermittent power sources that can vary depending on the weather, requires an expensive “combination of storage, expanded transmission, dispatchable generation, and substantial excess generating capacity…. The cost and performance of the complete system required to deliver sufficient electricity at every hour of the day and throughout the year is improved by including nuclear energy.” But she acknowledges that she shares the anxiety about obstacles that could derail the nuclear revival. Noting her apprehensions about the changes that could undermine the NRC’s independence, she said, “I certainly wonder if we will truly realize this dream.”
In December 1953, as the Soviet Union and the United States raced to expand their nuclear arsenals and the awesome devastation of Hiroshima and Nagasaki still thrummed in the zeitgeist, President Dwight Eisenhower delivered his famous “Atoms for Peace” address to the United Nations General Assembly, seeking to reshape public perceptions about the purpose of humankind’s dalliance with the split atom. Though acknowledging the grave danger of nuclear war, Eisenhower extolled the peaceful civilian promise of the new atomic era, envisioning a future in which nuclear technology would “provide abundant electrical energy in the power-starved areas of the world.”
His bright vision was echoed by other powerful figures in the early nuclear period, including Lewis Strauss, the chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission, who in 1954 said that “it is not too much to expect that our children will enjoy in their homes electrical energy too cheap to meter.”
Just days before Strauss’s speech, the United States broke ground on the Shippingport Atomic Power Station along the Ohio River northwest of Pittsburgh. The first full-scale civilian nuclear-power plant in America, Shippingport was designed as a pressurized water reactor, in which heat from nuclear fission is transferred via pressurized water running through metal tubes to a secondary source of water that produces steam, spins turbines, and generates electricity. Such plants also use massive amounts of water to cool their reactor cores, which is why they are located near lakes, rivers, or oceans. Shippingport’s design became a prototype for most of the civilian nuclear-power plants in the US today.
By 1974, there were 54 nuclear reactors operating within the United States and more than 190 proposed, planned, or ordered. It was around this time that Herbert Kouts, who led the reactor-safety division of the Atomic Energy Commission, told the Associated Press, “Preliminary results suggest there will never be a major accident in a nuclear power plant.” Not long after, disaster arrived.
On March 28, 1979, at the Three Mile Island Nuclear Generating Station on Pennsylvania’s Susquehanna River, the cooling system of one of the plant’s two reactors malfunctioned, flooding the containment building with hundreds of thousands of gallons of radioactive water and releasing radioactive gas into the environment. Fear and panic set in as more than 100,000 people evacuated the area. The disaster, the worst nuclear accident in US history, was front-page news across the country.
Even before Three Mile Island, the civilian nuclear industry faced mounting challenges, from inflation, rising interest rates, and shifting electricity demand to intensifying local opposition, including an effective moratorium on new nuclear plants enshrined in California law in 1976. Construction costs for nuclear facilities had risen fivefold between 1967 and 1978. Though no one died at Three Mile Island, and later reports found that the release of radioactivity had been minimal, the incident greatly exacerbated the nuclear industry’s woes. Support for the industry cratered across the United States.
Closer federal oversight of the nuclear industry was one consequence of this high-profile disaster. By 1975, the Atomic Energy Commission had been dissolved amid fears that its dual mandate of both promoting and regulating nuclear energy amounted to a conflict of interest. It was replaced by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, charged with maintaining the safety of the civilian nuclear-reactor fleet, and the Energy Research and Development Administration, which later merged with the Department of Energy, tasked with advancing the development of nuclear energy across the nation. In the aftermath of Three Mile Island, the NRC overhauled many of its regulations, upgrading plant-design requirements, strengthening the inspection regime, imposing new emergency-planning mandates, and revamping staffing protocols. The industry itself established the Institute of Nuclear Power Operations, or INPO, which worked to infuse the civilian nuclear sector with a stricter safety culture. Growing public opposition pushed states and localities to impose moratoriums on the construction of new facilities or other restrictions on the industry. New York, for example, saw a massive protest movement against the Shoreham Nuclear Power Plant on Long Island in 1979. Fierce public opposition ultimately forced the closure of the multibillion-dollar plant before it ever entered commercial operation.
The combination of escalating construction costs, soaring interest rates, public backlash, increased regulatory scrutiny, and diminished investor support whittled away the industry’s grand ambitions. Of the 197 nuclear reactors on order in 1974, more than half were never completed. Since 1990, around 20 reactors have shut down in the United States. The 94 reactors operating in the country today are, on average, 44 years old, and the vast majority were proposed, planned, or ordered before 1974, including Palisades, according to a study by Lucas W. Davis, a professor of economics at UC Berkeley.
Strauss’s “too cheap to meter” never materialized; indeed, the cost of electricity from newly built nuclear plants is generally more expensive than energy from new gas, coal, solar, or wind facilities. But the nuclear industry was never moribund in America. The United States currently generates more power from nuclear energy than any other country in the world. The industry provides roughly 20 percent of the nation’s electricity and nearly half of its low-carbon power. In some states, like Illinois, it is a dominant energy source. The industry has also made great strides in efficiency in recent decades, becoming much more adept at keeping its reactors running without lengthy outages. And the government has continued to pour money into nuclear research and development.
By the early 2000s, amid high gas prices and global concern about carbon pollution, the industry seemed ready for a revival after roughly a decade without the completion of a new reactor in the United States. Both the George W. Bush and Obama administrations provided loan guarantees and subsidies to new nuclear facilities. Proposals for more than 20 new reactors were submitted to the federal government between 2007 and 2009, but again the expectations did not bear out. Among other obstacles, the industry struggled to compete with the sudden influx of cheap gas produced by the emergent fracking boom. The vast majority of the proposed plants were canceled or paused. Those that moved forward, including a proposal to build two new reactors at Georgia’s Vogtle Electric Generating Plant, ran into major problems, including long delays and massive cost overruns. After more than a decade, the Vogtle reactors finally entered commercial service in the mid-2020s at a cost of more than $30 billion.
And here we are in another supposed nuclear renaissance. Indeed, according to a recent announcement from Trump’s Department of Energy, “The Golden Era of American Nuclear Energy Has Arrived.” We shall see. The revival of Palisades, itself a relic of the industry’s past, is an early test of such proclamations.
Despite the massive federal loan, the subsidies for its customers, surging energy demand, and the favorable regulatory interventions of the Trump administration, Holtec has struggled to reopen the Palisades plant. A company that has never operated a nuclear facility before seems to be learning in real time about the costly and complex nature of the undertaking. In a July 2022 application sent to the Department of Energy, Holtec said it would take as much as $1.9 billion and one to two years of work to bring the plant up to operating standards. The company subsequently blew past its self-declared reopening target of October 2025. This fall, it postponed a planned IPO on the NASDAQ, attributing its decision in part to “a perfect storm of adverse developments, driven primarily by uncertainty over data center development.” If it is to meet its contractual deadlines, Holtec has until March 2027 to get things up and running at Palisades. One Holtec official recently admitted to The New York Times that the company “didn’t take the time to really plan out the whole project before we started doing work. It’s like building a fire truck on your way to the fire.” Regarding the delays, Holtec said in a statement to The Nation and Type Investigations: “Since acquiring Palisades, Holtec has undertaken extensive engineering, inspections, equipment maintenance and refurbishment…and operational testing. As that work progressed, the scope of the project was further developed and refined based on the condition of the plant.”
Much of the trouble stems from the fact that Palisades is more than 50 years old, and at the time it was shuttered, it was not being maintained in a manner that was amenable to its revival. A plant like Palisades houses thousands of steam-generator tubes that are filled with radioactive water and are used to transfer heat from the reactor vessel to the main steam system, which spins turbines and produces electricity. Steam-generator tubes serve as a key safety barrier in reactors but are prone to corrosion and cracking.
Flawed steam-generator tubes played a major role in the early closure of the San Onofre Nuclear Generating Station in Southern California in 2013. In February 2000, 25 miles outside of New York City, a steam-generator tube at the Indian Point 2 nuclear reactor ruptured, causing superhot radioactive water to leak from the reactor core into other parts of the plant. The accident forced the reactor to temporarily shut down and ignited fear and outrage in the local community. Ultimately, the Indian Point power plant was permanently shut down in 2021.
Alan Blind, a nuclear engineer and 40-year veteran of the industry, was the vice president for nuclear power at Indian Point 2 when the steam-generator tube ruptured. “I know how bad they are,” he said of such accidents. In 2006, Blind took a job at Palisades, where he served as engineering director. He is now retired and lives about 30 miles south of the plant. Despite his support for nuclear energy, he has been outspoken about his misgivings with the Palisades resurrection. His most pressing concern centers on the plant’s steam generators. Not long after Holtec took over the plant, the company discovered that the facility’s steam-generator tubes were more seriously degraded than anticipated. Made of antiquated materials, they were nearing or even at the end of their service life, according to Blind. But rather than replace them, the company decided to plug the most defective tubes and installed thousands of metal sleeves over other tubes in order to keep them in service. The maintenance effort delayed the project by months.
Blind believes that the steam generators should have been fully replaced, as was done at Indian Point, and he has made known his concern about the situation, speaking to the press and sending letters to government officials. In a letter last year to Gretchen Whitmer, he highlighted the degraded conditions of the steam-generator tubes and explained that a rupture would likely result in a release of radiation into the environment that would force nearby residents to evacuate.
Since Blind’s letter, an NRC-sanctioned assessment of the plant’s repaired steam-generator systems found that they would need frequent safety inspections. Normally, a plant like Palisades would run for at least 18 months and then temporarily shut down to replace its fuel supply. But the Palisades reactor will need to temporarily shut down after about 14 months so that its steam generators can be assessed again to ensure their integrity. Blind thinks that the repaired generators could run safely if the company adheres to frequent inspections, but “the expense of maintaining [the steam-generator tubes] could be so high that you can’t operate the plant with a profit,” he said. Replacing the steam generators could cost as much as $510 million, according to Holtec’s own estimates.
Asked about Blind’s letter, a spokesperson for Holtec said in a statement that “Palisades conducted extensive inspections of the steam generators, which were scheduled early in the restart effort to account for potential discovery and repair. Upon identifying tubes that required corrective action, the company…undertook a comprehensive repair campaign using established industry methods, including tube sleeving and plugging…. Each repaired tube is subject to rigorous inspection and testing before being returned to service.” The company would not say how much it had spent to restart the plant or whether it was over budget, stating: “Holtec does not disclose detailed project expenditures beyond information contained in publicly available filings and financing documents.”
When asked for comment by The Nation and Type, the NRC pointed to a letter it published in September stating it had determined that the extensive inspection and repair of the tubes, the agency’s oversight, and other evaluation and maintenance activities “provide reasonable assurance that tube integrity will be maintained.”
Jigar Shah, the former Biden official who helped back Holtec’s efforts, said he does not believe the plant is over budget or behind schedule. The costs of maintaining or even replacing the steam-generator tubes were all anticipated, he said, and the DOE’s Loan Programs Office expected the plant to open by the end of this year and no sooner. As for safety concerns, he said nuclear power is the “safest form of energy we have ever had on planet Earth. I get it has been part of a lot of scary movies, but it objectively has the safest track record in the history of electricity.”
On a warm morning last spring, a group of Palisades Park residents met around picnic tables not far from the lapping waters of Lake Michigan. The group included families who had owned homes in the community for generations and were deeply distrustful of the Palisades restart. Some residents already have experience with the plant malfunctioning, including in 2013, when diluted radioactive water leaked from the plant into Lake Michigan, and in 2008, when plant employees were subjected to undetected radiation exposure. Some residents questioned whether Holtec, which has a spotty ethical reputation, was up to the job of reviving a nuclear plant. In 2024, Holtec agreed to pay a $5 million fine to defer criminal prosecution after New Jersey investigated the company for using faulty documents to obtain tax credits from the state. In 2023, Holtec’s former CFO filed a whistleblower complaint alleging that he had been fired after refusing to sign off on false statements about the company’s finances. For Bruce Davis and some of his neighbors, Holtec’s conduct at Palisades has also not inspired confidence. Davis said the company shut down a system of loudspeakers on the plant’s property that was meant to alert residents in the event of an accident and replaced it with a cell-phone-based text-alert program that does not work well. “All they have been doing is kicking the can down the road throughout this whole ordeal and getting exemptions from the NRC, and only fixing what they absolutely have to,” Davis added. (Holtec refused my requests to visit the Palisades site.)
Residents recently established a committee to monitor the plant’s activities. Some have bought new Geiger counters to do their own radiation monitoring. Some are stocking up on potassium-iodide pills, which help prevent the uptake of radiation into the thyroid gland, in the event of a nuclear emergency. And the community is pushing for a new road out of the area to facilitate a speedy evacuation if the worst should occur. A recent study by public-health researchers at Harvard suggests that their concerns are warranted, finding that “counties located closer to operational nuclear power plants have higher cancer mortality rates than those farther away.” In a statement to The Nation and Type, an NRC spokesperson said that “the recent papers from Harvard researchers do not demonstrate radiation dose or establish causation. Decades of environmental-monitoring data required by the NRC consistently show that routine releases from operating reactors result in extremely small public radiation doses.”
Holtec, meanwhile, suffered a significant mishap while loading fuel into the plant this fall. One of the fuel assemblies containing fissile material tilted from its upright position inside the reactor core, forcing the company to suspend fuel loading and build a retrieval device to remove the faulty fuel assembly and discard it in a spent fuel pool. Holtec eventually informed the NRC and said that “a root cause evaluation has been initiated to determine the cause of the event and identify any resulting corrective actions.” Alan Blind told a Michigan news outlet that in his “40-year career, I never experienced anything like that.” (In a statement, a Holtec spokesperson said: “Plant personnel evaluated the incident and determined that it did not trigger the safety reporting requirements under NRC regulations. The fuel assembly remains intact, with no identified fuel damage, no release of radiation, and no injuries associated with the event.”)
Critics of the plant believe that the incident may have been a cause of the company’s postponed IPO. “It is not a coincidence that Holtec’s IPO, years in the planning, could not go forward with pending bad news of a major refueling SNAFU at the end of August,” said Michael Keegan, chair of Don’t Waste Michigan, a local group opposed to the Palisades restart. In a statement, Holtec said that it delayed its IPO “based on market conditions.”
Shah remains excited about the nuclear industry’s prospects in America today. “There are genuinely 20-plus companies reaching for the stars right now, and that is awesome,” he said. “Do I think that will turn into a nuclear renaissance? Hell if I know. But they are genuinely trying their best.”

https://projects.propublica.org/us-citiz.title: More Than Numbers: Portraits of U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
https://projects.propublica.org/us-citiz.author: Sarahbeth Maney, Nicole Foy
https://projects.propublica.org/us-citiz.text:
More Than Numbers
The Department of Homeland Security says it’s not detaining Americans.
In written statements, it has said that “allegations that ICE is arresting and deporting U.S. citizens is FALSE.”
It has said that “when individuals are briefly questioned under ‘reasonable suspicion’ and are found to be U.S. citizens, they are immediately released.” And it has said that “U.S. citizen agitators are only held while they actively remain a safety threat to our officers and the public.”
But ProPublica has identified more than 500 citizens detained since President Donald Trump returned to office.
They are not just numbers.
Among them is an elderly car wash owner whom agents repeatedly knocked to the ground as they detained several of his workers. A 6-year-old whose mother says still has nightmares after agents pointed guns at him and his siblings. A high school senior who was detained after she tried to stop officers from questioning her autistic younger brother. A dad who was held for several days and missed his daughter’s third birthday.
Over the past year, several of these people shared the lingering effects of what happened to them with ProPublica.
“We have so much trauma just from the 30 minutes we were held.”
In their own neighborhood
Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan
In September 2025, Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan learned that ICE agents had intercepted members of her family as they drove one of her uncles to a court hearing. Ramirez Sanan, then 17, said she rushed to the scene and discovered agents had broken the car windows and pulled her two uncles, her mother and her younger brother out. Video of the incident showed agents kicking and slamming Ramirez Sanan’s mother to the ground and then twisting her arms to handcuff her. Ramirez Sanan said she saw other agents questioning her brother against a fence, threatening to arrest him if he couldn’t prove he had legal status.
Both she and her brother are citizens.
“Him being a 13-year-old with autism, he doesn’t understand these things like we do. He didn’t know what ‘a legal status’ is. He’s not able to tell them: ‘Yes, I have a legal status. I’m born here,’” Ramirez Sanan said. She said that when she rushed toward her mom and brother, begging agents to let them go, they detained her. “It was really scary thinking that they might have taken us and deported us to Guatemala, where we don’t have anything.”
DHS said that its agents intercepted the car in order to detain the uncle who was going to court that day, and that they “used the appropriate force necessary.” He was facing charges of sexual assault on a child and remains in ICE custody. He has pleaded not guilty.
As for Ramirez Sanan, her mother and her brother, they were released the day of the incident. Her mother, who has lived in the United States for 20 years and has a green card, was treated at a hospital for a concussion, bruising and nerve damage in one of her arms.
DHS denies that they were ever detained.
“We have so much trauma just from the 30 minutes we were held,” said Ramirez Sanan, who struggled with anxiety and depression after the incident. “I lost my whole senior year fighting this. My brother isn’t the same either.”
On her way to work
Andrea Velez
In June 2025, Andrea Velez was dropped off at work at a shoe company in downtown Los Angeles and inadvertently walked into an immigration raid on street vendors. She said one of the masked agents rushed toward her, grabbed her and slammed her to the pavement. Velez said she attempted to shield herself with her work bag.
“Throughout the whole time, I kept saying I was a U.S. citizen,” Velez recalled, saying that agents called her an “alleged U.S. citizen” even after they checked her ID. “They kept saying how many ‘bodies they got’ that day.”
Velez said that she was detained for two days, and that she was denied an opportunity to call family or a lawyer for most of that time. The government charged Velez with assault. DHS said she “made physical contact” with agents and tried to impede them. A judge ultimately dismissed the case.
After her arrest, Velez said she was so afraid of being detained again that she worked remotely and avoided going outside.
At the end of his school day as a teaching assistant
Quentin Williams
In January, not long after immigration agents in Minneapolis had shot and killed an American woman named Renee Good, Quentin Williams, a teaching assistant at nearby Roosevelt High School, was guiding students toward buses when more agents arrived outside his building.
Williams said that agents began confronting students and staff. At some point during the commotion, he said, the agents threw him to the ground and choked him so hard he couldn’t breathe.
“They didn’t even know what they were doing — just kind of being reckless [with] assault rifles out and pepper-spraying staff after they took me down,” Williams recalled.
Agents drove Williams to the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building, where they detained him for several hours.
Later, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi published his photo on her social media accounts, describing him as a “Minnesota rioter.” Federal authorities issued a warrant for his arrest for assaulting officers. The charges against him were eventually dismissed, and he’s filed a claim against the government for damages over his arrest.
Williams said he’s still haunted by the idea that he came close to meeting the same fates as Good and George Floyd, who was killed by a Minneapolis police officer in 2020. “I didn’t leave the house for at least up to a week,” he said. “I felt lucky to be alive.”
Attending a horse race
Anabel Romero, John Carter, Juana Rodriguez and their children
In October 2025, some 200 federal agents and local police officers in armored vehicles, a helicopter and on horseback conducted a raid on a racetrack in Wilder, Idaho, and detained hundreds of people, including dozens of children. Among them ProPublica identified at least 30 U.S. citizens.
Anabel Romero had left her kids eating in the car while she went to look at the horses. They were on opposite sides of the track when the raid began.
Romero said the agents wore camouflage and had their guns drawn. She had no idea who they were. So she ran and tried to hide. “They didn’t identify themselves,” Romero said. “I didn’t know who they were.”
She said unidentified officers tackled her, zip-tied her and threatened to “fucking blow your head off.”
On the other side of the track, Romero’s 14-year-old daughter, SueHey Tello, said officers surrounded their car, pointing guns at her brother, 6, and sister, 8. When Tello refused to exit the car without her younger siblings, agents pulled her so roughly out of the car that she fell, leaving bruises. She said agents zip-tied her hands.
Romero and Tello said the agents refused to remove the zip ties for hours, despite Tello’s age. The teenager said the incident has affected her view of law enforcement. Her mother says that the 6-year-old still has nightmares. Officers are meant “to keep us safe,” Tello said. “But yet they treated all of us like that.”
John Carter was working security at the track when the raid started. He had brought his girlfriend and his two children along with him. He recalls officers throwing a flash-bang near him and his son, and then the officers detained them. “They cinched the zip ties down as tight as they could,” Carter said. He said the officers also zip-tied his 14-year-old daughter but removed the restraints when he complained.
Carter explained that he is active in the local Republican Party and a strong supporter of law enforcement. But he said that what he saw officers doing that day was wrong.
“Things are supposed to be done humanely and correctly,” he said. “This wasn’t.”
The agents also detained Juana Rodriguez, who attended the event with her family. She said that she was zip-tied beside her 3-year-old son, which left her unable to pick him up and comfort him during the long hours they waited to prove their citizenship. “He wanted me to hug him, to hold him,” Rodriguez said. She and her son are both U.S. citizens and lead plaintiffs in an ACLU of Idaho lawsuit alleging the raid illegally targeted Latinos. ICE, the FBI and several Idaho agencies have denied the charge and asked that the lawsuit be dismissed.
DHS did not respond to any specific allegations made by Rodriguez, Romero, Carter or their families. Instead, a spokesperson wrote in an email statement that the raid successfully helped dismantle an illegal gambling operation, and that ICE officers “didn’t zip tie, restrain or arrest any children.” The FBI declined to comment to ProPublica but told local media no “young children” were zip-tied. DHS, the FBI and multiple Idaho law enforcement agencies have refused to share the number of U.S. citizens held that day.
“I didn’t want to walk to my apartment by myself; I didn’t want to be out in the dark by myself.”
Monitoring ICE operations
Amanda Trebach
In August 2025, Amanda Trebach, a nurse and volunteer with an immigrant advocacy organization, said she was monitoring ICE activities outside a facility that the agency was using to stage operations when agents grabbed her and pinned her to the ground, kneeling on her neck and back. They shoved her into the back of a van and held her for several hours until taking her to a federal detention facility in Los Angeles. She was not given the opportunity to speak with an attorney during the 33 hours that she was in custody. She said agents took her phone and never returned it.
DHS said Trebach was detained because she attempted to physically impede its agents’ operations by jumping in front of moving vehicles, hitting their cars with her protest signs and shouting obscenities at agents. She denies this.
She said that after the incident she felt paranoid that she was being followed.
“I didn’t want to walk to my apartment by myself; I didn’t want to be out in the dark by myself,” she said. “I didn’t know if they were going to come get me.”
Driving to work
George Retes
George Retes, a U.S. Army veteran who served in Iraq, was driving into work at a cannabis farm in July 2025 and arrived to find the place being raided by immigration agents. Protesters had gathered outside the farm. He found himself trapped between the agents and the protesters. The agents broke his car window, pepper-sprayed him and pulled him out onto the ground. He was detained for three days, missing his daughter’s third birthday. Retes said, agents refused to explain why he’d been detained or to let him call relatives or a lawyer.
When ProPublica published Retes’ story last year, he said agents knew he was a citizen.
“They didn’t care,” he recalled. “They still sent me away to jail.”
DHS officials made statements claiming Retes had assaulted their agents. But he was never charged.
Working at his auto shop
Javier Ramirez
In June 2025, immigration agents conducted a raid on an auto shop owned by Javier Ramirez and his family. He said agents swept him up as they were detaining his workers. He recalled hearing one of the agents yell: “Hey, just get him! He’s Mexican.” He said agents tackled him and one of them put a knee on his face. He recalled hearing the agents boasting about the numbers of immigrants they were detaining across the city that day, saying: “How many did you get? I got 10, I got 15.” According to a lawsuit that Ramirez filed against DHS, he said he was held in federal custody for four days and was denied medication he needs for diabetes. DHS has not filed a response to the lawsuit, but previously the agency said that Ramirez was arrested for obstructing law enforcement, and that it never denied him medication.
“I was begging them, ‘Just let me breathe!’”
Working at his car wash
Rafie Ollah Shouhed
Rafie Ollah Shouhed, 79, was born in Iran, moved to Los Angeles after the Islamic Revolution and became a U.S. citizen. On Sept. 9, 2025, Shouhed, owner of Valley Car Wash, watched with alarm as immigration agents stormed into his business and attempted to detain his employees. He rushed outside to see what was going on. Security video of the incident shows agents knocked Shouhed to the ground repeatedly. He told agents that he had just had heart surgery. “They were sitting on me,” he recalled. “I was begging them, ‘Just let me breathe!’” He said in an ongoing lawsuit that the agents kept him handcuffed for 12 hours and left him with injuries to his arm, elbows and ribs. Shouhed said that he’s still receiving treatment for his injuries, and that he has quit working. DHS said Shouhed was arrested for interfering with and assaulting officers and did not answer questions about his lawsuit. He was released without charges.
Monitoring ICE operations
Jeane Wong
When Jeane “Bleu” Wong, an operator of a daycare center and activist, heard in July 2025 that ICE agents had arrived at a nearby apartment complex, she rushed to the scene to provide assistance to people who were being detained. Agents detained her when she tried to remove one of their masks.
She was held in the San Ysidro Port of Entry, the largest and busiest land border crossing in the Western Hemisphere, and later moved to a federal prison. Wong said that during her time in custody she was strip-searched and shackled in chains that restricted her from using the restroom. Federal authorities charged Wong with assaulting a federal agent. She eventually pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor.
A little over a year later, Wong received a notice from the California Department of Social Services that her license to care for children had been revoked because of the assault. She and her wife are selling their home and relocating outside of Southern California.
“We could totally fight, and I’d probably win,” she said. “But we don’t have the money, time, energy.”
Working construction
Leonardo Garcia Venegas
Leonardo Garcia Venegas was laying concrete with his construction crew in Alabama in May 2025 when immigration agents arrived at the site without a warrant and began detaining his co-workers, including his brother. Garcia Venegas pulled out his phone to film the agents. Videos he and other workers recorded show agents approaching to arrest Garcia Venegas while he filmed, tackling and arresting him while he yelled that he was a U.S. citizen. Garcia Venegas said that he told the agents he had his REAL ID on him, but that they dismissed the document as fake. They held him in handcuffs for an hour before finally releasing him without charges. DHS said he was impeding officers. After that first incident, immigration agents detained Garcia Venegas two more times, each time ignoring statements and identification documents that prove he is a U.S. citizen.
Garcia Venegas filed a lawsuit against DHS over its warrantless raids on construction sites. DHS responded to the lawsuit, saying that its agents didn’t need warrants to operate at construction sites because they’re open to the public. The agency also said that brief stops like Garcia Venegas’ were “reasonable.” Until the case is resolved, a judge ordered a temporary halt to the operations.
“I just want to live in peace,” he told ProPublica after his third arrest.
“Nobody ever asked me for ID, my name or my citizenship.”
Driving to the doctor
Aliya Rahman
Aliya Rahman, who is autistic and disabled, was driving to a doctor’s appointment in January when she reached an intersection where protesters were confronting immigration officers. She said several agents swarmed her car and yelled at her to move out of the way. They broke her window and pulled her from the car.
“Nobody ever asked me for ID, my name or my citizenship,” Rahman said.
DHS said agents detained Rahman because she ignored their instructions. She denied that, saying that she was confused and saw no way to move without hitting someone.
She said agents then shackled her feet and held her in a detention cell at the federal building. She passed out and awoke in a hospital room. She was released without charges later that day.
Sleeping in her bedroom
Jeyli Salguero
In January, Jeyli Salguero awoke when she heard someone banging on her door and then the sound of the door breaking open. Federal agents, their guns drawn, rushed inside and told her family they were looking for her brother.
“We told them yes he lived here, but he doesn’t live here anymore,” Salguero said she told the agents. “They started getting a bit more angry and were like, ‘Since you’re not collaborating, we’re gonna start checking your status.’” An agent grabbed Salguero’s phone and ordered Salguero to face a wall. In an ongoing lawsuit, Salguero has said that the agents entered the home without a valid warrant. DHS said that agents were searching for a fugitive, and that it has suspended the policy of entering homes without a judicial warrant.
Her father has temporary protected status but had not received paperwork showing that his status had been renewed. He was handcuffed and then detained for a month. Salguero’s older sister, who was undocumented, was handcuffed and deported to El Salvador. The rest of her family is now planning to sell their home and move to El Salvador. “It’s been a mental toll — a very big mental toll on all of us.”
Protesting the Broadview ICE Detention Center
Juan Muñoz
Juan Muñoz, an elected member of the Board of Trustees that governs Oak Park Township outside of Chicago, was participating in an October protest outside the Broadview ICE Detention Center when he said that he was knocked to the ground by the commander of the Border Patrol. “When I looked up,” Muñoz recalled, “it was Commander Greg Bovino who was standing over me.” In depositions, Bovino denied tackling Muñoz, saying videos of the arrests showed no “reportable uses of force.”
Muñoz said agents knocked away his phone and zip-tied his hands. “Every agent that I encountered, I told the same thing, ‘I’m an elected official.’ No response.”
Muñoz was held inside of the detention center for eight hours before agents dropped him off at a gas station, without explaining why he’d been held. “They were over capacity, keeping people for way longer than that facility was intended for,” he recalled about the detention center. “It was filthy. They don’t have proper hygiene products or are able to feed people properly,” Muñoz said. DHS did not comment on his specific detention. But, referring to Muñoz and other protesters detained with him, it posted a comment on social media, saying, “We will NOT allow violent activists to lay hands on our law enforcement.”
Responding to ICE in a hospital
Jessie Fuentes
In October 2025, Chicago Alderperson Jessie Fuentes said she rushed to a local emergency room because she’d been told that ICE agents had been spotted inside. She identified herself to the agents as an elected official and began asking them whether they’d obtained a warrant. Video taken of the incident shows that agents grabbed and handcuffed her. Fuentes was held for 15 minutes, during which time members of her staff posted the video online and her supporters gathered outside the hospital to demand her release. DHS, in a written statement, told ProPublica that Fuentes was put in “handcuffs but NEVER placed under arrest.”
“These individuals are operating above the law,” Fuentes said. “They’re operating with impunity.”
Monitoring ICE operations
Caitlin Arwen
Caitlin Arwen was scrolling through a Facebook group for moms in October when she noticed a shared post that said immigration agents were detaining people in her town, which is about an hour’s drive outside of Chicago. Later that day she saw some of the vehicles that had been posted on Facebook and began following them, honking her horn to alert residents of their presence. One of the vehicles slammed on its brakes. U.S. marshals who were working with ICE surrounded her car, broke her window and pulled her out.
“They threw me on the broken glass, and they were all on top of me. I couldn’t breathe,” she recalled. Arwen estimates she was kept handcuffed face down on broken glass for roughly 35 minutes. “They taunted me, took photos of me, called me names, berated me and acted like I was somehow deserving of this.” DHS referred questions about Arwen’s arrest to the U.S. Marshals Service. A spokesperson for the service said Arwen’s arrest was a “task force arrest” and declined further comment.
Arwen was taken to a hospital, where marshals handcuffed her to the bed. After she was discharged, agents shackled her and moved her to a DHS detention facility, where she was not allowed to contact a lawyer or anyone else for help. “I didn’t have access to water or food the whole time,” said Arwen, adding that she was held for several hours. “Nobody showed me their badge all day. No one identified themselves. No one once read me my Miranda rights.”
Though federal officials declined to prosecute Arwen, state authorities charged her with traffic violations and obstruction of law enforcement. She has pleaded not guilty.
