https://gothamist.com/news/north-brookly.title: North Brooklyn street redesign paves the way for NYC's 'low-traffic neighborhood' plan
https://gothamist.com/news/north-brookly.author: Liam Quigley
https://gothamist.com/news/north-brookly.text:
A new street design seeks to slow drivers and force traffic away from McGolrick Park in north Brooklyn.
The city transportation department in late October finished installing new road markings and chunky plastic bollards at two intersections of Driggs Avenue that force drivers to turn. The traffic diverters now in place on Driggs Avenue at Monitor and Sutton streets aim to stop drivers from speeding through Greenpoint to bypass gridlock.
Crews this year have also extended curbs to shorten crosswalks, added bike corrals and reduced parking spaces on the streets around McGolrick Park. It’s the type of “low-traffic neighborhood” treatment that a group of city lawmakers wants to implement across the city. And the city may be able to make such changes more quickly due to a ballot measure approved by voters last week to fast-track street redesign projects.
Some drivers are still adjusting to the new bollards. Soon after they were installed last month, cars smashed them up. The transportation department installed replacements.
“These are our plastic little soldiers in the street. They're gonna get run over. That's fine with me,” said local parent Chris Roberti, who helped organize his neighbors to call for the redesign. He said drivers spilling from the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway onto local streets need to be forced to slow down.
“This has been a major dangerous intersection. And there was no stop sign here. So now cars are stopping, they're turning. There's not that conflict anymore,” he said. “It’s like night and day.”
Transportation officials said similar equipment was installed in Sunnyside, Queens, in 2021. Crews eventually upgraded the redesign using stronger concrete barriers.
Katie Denny Horowitz, the executive director of the North Brooklyn Parks Alliance, worked with city officials to bring dozens of heavy planters to the area around the park on Sunday to fortify the plastic bollards and reduce drivers ability to barrel through them or speed around them.
“You might be less inclined to run over a planter filled with beautiful plants than you are one of these bollards that kind of flips back and forth,” she said.
Roberti said two people killed in car crashes near McGolrick Park over the past three years show why the street changes are necessary. One of the deaths was at Monitor Street and Driggs Avenue, which now has the new bollards.
Diego Flores, who uses his personal car to deliver packages for Amazon, gingerly drove through the bollards on Monday morning. He said the devices make his hard job even harder.
“It complicates the routes a lot,” Flores said. “It is too complicated to work.”
Noel Hidalgo, who lives at that intersection, photographed a heating oil truck driving right over the new barriers Monday morning.
“This weekend was the most quiet weekend that I have been in the neighborhood,” he said, adding that trucks running over the plastic bollards make a “very distinct sound.”
The truck’s owner, Ferrantino Fuel Oil, said through a spokesperson that the company was looking into the incident.
“We understand and support the city's efforts to improve traffic and pedestrian safety,” Ferrantino spokesperson Michael Alba said. “However, the continued narrowing of city streets presents challenges for larger commercial vehicles.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/trum.title: Trump Taps Campaign Lawyer and Pardon Adviser for Top U.S. Intel Agency
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/trum.author: Matt Sledge
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/trum.text:
As a lawyer on President Donald Trump’s 2024 reelection bid, Gary Lawkowski filed a complaint against the Washington Post for supposedly making an in-kind contribution to the Kamala Harris campaign by buying social media advertising for its articles.
In the White House, he played a pivotal role in the pardons process that rewarded Trump cronies and donors.
Now, Lawkowski could serve in an obscure but crucial role within the nation’s top intelligence agency, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. On Monday, Trump nominated Lawkowski to serve as general counsel of ODNI.
It is unclear when Lawkowski will appear before a confirmation hearing or whether Democrats will look favorably upon him when they take control of the Senate in January. His nomination is already drawing pushback, however, from a progressive group that says it represents another attempt to politicize the ODNI after Trump’s bid to install loyalist Bill Pulte as its director fizzled.
“Lawkowski has been a key player in Trump’s corrupt pardon scheme and his nomination tells us that the administration is trying to stack the intelligence community with cronies so they can further weaponize it against their perceived political opponents and innocent Americans,” Hajar Hammado, senior policy adviser at Demand Progress, said in a statement. “Senators must oppose his nomination.”
The ODNI is a relatively small agency, and it doesn’t hoover up its own raw data. As the only intelligence body operating at the Cabinet level, however, it is tasked with coordinating and overseeing intelligence collection and analysis at other spy agencies like the CIA and National Security Agency.
Under former Director Tulsi Gabbard, the ODNI took an unusually prominent role in declassifying information that cast a negative light on Trump’s enemies or fed into right-wing obsessions, such as the Covid lab-leak controversy.
The general counsel plays an important role in interpreting spying law — meaning that Lawkowski could either facilitate or block intelligence community abuses.
In recent months, Trump has displayed an unusual interest in the ODNI, installing housing czar Pulte to replace Gabbard before bipartisan pushback forced him to tap former prosecutor Jay Clayton as a permanent replacement.
In his current role at the White House, Lawkowski serves as deputy assistant and deputy counsel to the president, according to his most recent ethics disclosure, and it is unclear whether he has relevant national security experience.
There is ample evidence that he is a loyalist to Trump. As a lawyer on the Trump campaign, he blasted off a complaint to the Federal Election Commission claiming that the Washington Post’s online advertisements about stories on Trump represented an in-kind contribution to Harris’s campaign. Campaign finance law experts said the claim was baseless. Lawkowski also represented Trump in litigation over the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.
In the White House, he has helped decide who does and does not receive pardons, according to reporting last year in the New York Times. Under Trump, the White House has asserted authority over a pardons process that traditionally flowed through the Department of Justice.
Trump’s blanket clemency for January 6, 2021, insurrectionists preceded a parade of pardons for people who donated to his campaign or causes, or Republican officials who had been convicted of corruption, drawing widespread criticism.
One of the many who received a Trump pardon was former Tennessee state senator Brian Kelsey, who had been represented by Lawkowski before the lawyer went to the White House. Lawkowski did not respond to a request for comment on whether he recused himself from that pardon.
It is unclear whether Senate Select Committee on Intelligence Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark., will push to have Lawkowski confirmed before the next Senate is sworn in on January 3. The Senate is dealing with a cramped calendar before the end of the year. (Cotton’s office declined to comment.)
The likely incoming intelligence chair, Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., was harshly critical of Trump’s temporary appointment of Pulte at the ODNI. He ultimately voted against Clayton’s nomination after touting him as a more acceptable alternative to Pulte. (Warner’s office did not respond to a request for comment.)
Lawkowski was tapped to replace John “Jack” Dever, who was confirmed by the Senate to serve as general counsel a little over a year ago. Dever joined the government-backed mortgage finance company Freddie Mac as its executive counsel and vice president in September, according to its website. (Dever left the ODNI with Director Jay Clayton’s blessing and remains well-respected at the agency, an ODNI spokesperson said.)
Dever’s resume included extensive work in the national security realm as a Korean linguist for the U.S. Army, an assistance general counsel at the FBI, and a counter-terror prosecutor in Illinois.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘I railed against the stereotype of the humourless lesbian’: the cheeky, feminist photography of Jill Posener
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Philippa Kelly
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
If it were a lady it would get its bottom pinched. If this lady was a car she’d run you down.” These are the words that Jill Posener immortalised in November 1979, when she picked her way through traffic on London’s Farringdon Road to photograph something most would have overlooked: a graffitied billboard. The first sentence was there by design – a sexist attempt at wit intended to promote a new Fiat. The second she has since been repeatedly accused of adding herself.
In reality, the image-maker, playwright and nonprofit founder explains from her home in California, the now infamous phrase had been daubed by two women working at the nearby offices of the socialist newspaper Morning Star. “They had seen the billboard go up and were so incensed that they came up with this solution,” Posener recalls. “They didn’t think anything of it until they saw the postcard. I sent them a whole bunch and we all had a good laugh.”
It was in a small West End print shop that Posener first produced about 100 postcards featuring her image of the defaced – or, to use her preferred term, refaced – Fiat advertisement. In the years since, she estimates that more than 1m have been sold. Although, she hastens to add, she has never made much money from them.
Not that profit was ever Posener’s goal: the postcards were simply a way to disseminate what would become her signature brand of political satire. They were created at a time when the women’s liberation and gay rights movements were at odds with Margaret Thatcher’s socially conservative vision for Britain, and explicitly railed against the stereotype of what Posener describes as “the humourless lesbian or humourless feminist”. As with much of the photographer’s work, they also carried another message: “a big fuck you to the establishment”.
More than 40 years after it was taken, in 2023 the Fiat image enjoyed a somewhat unexpected revival when it featured in Tate Britain’s landmark exhibition Women in Revolt. For Posener, who had shifted her professional focus to animal welfare more than a decade earlier, the experience was cathartic. “I had absolutely walked away from photography,” she recalls. “So I do credit the Tate show with – and I don’t mean to sound dramatic – giving me my old life back.”
The show also sparked renewed institutional interest in her work, and eventually led to a new Glasgow School of Art retrospective, Jill Posener: Stage and Street. The exhibition looks far beyond that one well-timed photograph, traversing the image-maker’s years as a member of Britain’s first professional gay theatre troupe, Gay Sweatshop, exploring her time photographing party conferences for the Daily Mirror, and re-examining her influential 1987 series, Dirty Girls Guide to London. It also features several less famous – though equally deserving – examples of wry billboard graffiti.
Together, these works make Stage and Street Posener’s most significant UK solo show to date, and the first to recognise, in its entirety, a 50-year career dedicated to cultural production and social justice. Now 73, she is stoic about the overdue nature of the honour. “I think part of it is that I’m not a particularly gifted photographer,” she says, “and I’m not being self-deprecating. But I am somebody that sees things, and it’s possible that I can see things others don’t.”
This was certainly the case in November 1979, when Posener first caught sight of the graffitied Fiat billboard. Does she worry that, even now, this remains the defining moment of her photographic career? “I think, if you have one image that so encapsulates a moment, a movement, then embrace it,” she says. “I have no problem being a one-hit wonder.”
Casts, creches and kisses: Posener’s political pictures
Join Lesbians United, London, 1981 (main picture)
  
“I’m not sure how I came upon this one, but I think it was in north London. You can’t help but laugh when you see it. Maybe because I’ve lived with a lot of anger in my life, I loved that we could respond to these things with humour, and that other people could then recognise and take pleasure from that.”
Promotional photo for Posener’s play Any Woman Can, performed by the Gay Sweatshop theatre company, 1976
  
“At the time, there was a lot about it that resonated with people,” says Posener. “The last line was: ‘You’re looking at a screaming lesbian, and I’m looking right back at you.’ For me, as a young woman, this was both a reflection of my own coming out and my confrontational nature toward the world.”
Margaret Thatcher at the Conservative Women’s Conference, London, 1987
  
“I took some photographs at the Tory party women’s conference that really made fun of that audience, and sometimes I feel embarrassed that I did that. On the other hand, they were showing who they were, and I was identifying that and photographing it. Thatcher in the creche was just the most hilarious thing I could possibly imagine.”
From A Dirty Girls Guide to London, 1987
  
“It’s called A Dirty Girls Guide to London because it was like a tourist brochure. But instead of just icons of British culture, there’s two women kissing, basically saying: ‘We can do this right here, in front of everybody.’ It’s about not hiding, and it’s about saying: ‘You cannot control our lives and you cannot control our bodies.’”
Drew Griffiths performs in Jingleball, a Gay Sweatshop production, eight years before his murder, which remains unsolved, 1976
  
“When Sweatshop had its first press conference, Drew actually couldn’t face the press. He was too ashamed to face the media, so he had his back to them, even though he’d started the group. And I think that’s what we all felt: this terrible fear, and yet this hope and possibility of something new.”
Jill Posener: Stage and Street is at Reid Gallery, The Glasgow School of Art to 9 January

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/12/g.title: GET OUT: E-Bike Battery Fires are a Crisis We Can No Longer Ignore
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/12/g.author: Charles Komanoff
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/12/g.text:
Back-to-back mass-death fires in Brooklyn and the Bronx have rocked the city these past two weeks, taking ten lives and ripping apart countless more, as reported in the Times, News, Post, Hell Gate, City Reporter, Gothamist, and of course Streetsblog. Substandard e-bike batteries likely triggered both conflagrations, an all-too-common occurrence that should shock street-safety and cycling champions into action.
Over the past decade, e-bike battery fires in New York City have killed dozens of residents and injured many more. They have rendered hundreds of apartments uninhabitable. Yet micromobility advocates have had little to say, treating this as an anomaly and not a core problem.
City government is complicit, too. On Oct. 28, three teens and their mother died from burns after their father’s e-bike erupted in flames in their Mott Haven apartment. The next day, Mayor Mamdani and Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore offered up pablum: don’t leave e-bikes in doorways, don’t charge them overnight and try to store them outdoors. We might just as well dispense with highway lane markers and beseech drivers to take it easy.
Officials took a similar tack after the Nov. 5 Brooklyn disaster, when another fast-moving fire, also apparently sparked by an e-bike battery, killed six residents of a two-story frame house in Sunset Park. The blaze marked the greatest loss of life from a single fire in New York City since the 2022 Twin Parks fire in the Bronx. Mamdani vowed to find a solution but omitted any specifics. Bonsignore was out of town and did not comment.
Even before the Mott Haven and Sunset Park blazes, e-bike-related fires across the five boroughs rose 41 percent from 2025. Batteries caused at least 406 fires this year, versus 241 over the same period in 2025 — a 68-percent increase. 
“Every single New York City resident should be furious,” said Brooklyn-based street-safety advocate and battery-swap entrepreneur Baruch Herzfeld. He’s right. We cyclists assert the moral high ground as we battle car and truck drivers and their elected enablers. We solemnly memorialize New Yorkers whom motorists kill on our contested streets. Yet this adjacent conflagration finds us largely silent.
This problem has persisted for so long that multiple mayors have “cracked down” on it, at multiple times in multiple ways, with little evident change. Between August and mid-September, the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection inspected more than 200 bicycle and micromobility shops and issued 136 violations that led to 77 summonses. But it was insufficient: the agency’s sweep primarily targeted vehicles equipped to exceed the city’s speed limit of 20 mph for scooters and 20 mph for e-bikes — not hazardous batteries.
This infernal calamity traces to the uncertified lithium-ion batteries that power thousands of e-mobility devices on the city’s streets. Extravagantly distant food delivery — enabled by the lack of a mileage surcharge — compounds the disaster by requiring longer and more frequent charging cycles. 
What Sets UL-Certified E-bike Batteries Apart
We think of batteries as mundane pieces of technology. Nobody fears the small metal disc that powers their wristwatch or the slightly larger cylinder in their television remote. E-bike batteries, by comparison, are complex devices that must operate over variegated conditions for long periods of time. That led Underwriters Laboratory to publish their first light-vehicle electric-battery safety standard, known as UL 2271, in 2013.
William Henry Merrill, an M.I.T.-educated electrical engineer and electrical inspector for the Boston Board of Fire Underwriters, founded UL in 1894. Now a multinational conglomerate with $3 billion in annual revenue, UL maintains safety standards for e-bike batteries. It is one of a few firms authorized by the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration to certify their safety.
To win UL certification — those upper-case initials in a circle you’ve probably seen a thousand times but never really noticed — batteries must demonstrate that they can interrupt overheating, cut off power to battery elements in the event of over-charging or over-discharging, and prevent short circuits from triggering high-energy fires or explosions. In contrast, many uncertified batteries lack automatic shutoff controls or employ generic chargers that can overpower battery cells. They’re also less protected from damage from road jostling, moisture ingress and everyday wear-and-tear.
Many deliveristas ride cheaper e-bikes and scooters manufactured by obscure Chinese brands with cheap and swappable batteries. New York City has never recorded a fire caused by a UL-certified e-bike or other micromobility device. From all appearances, replacing the off-brand batteries with UL-certified batteries is both necessary and sufficient for fire-safe micromobility.
How to rid the city of substandard e-bike batteries
I propose a two-step solution:
- Enact a municipal ordinance authorizing the immediate seizure and confiscation of non-UL-certified lithium-ion batteries from residential, commercial and institutional buildings in the five boroughs. 
- Impose a steep surcharge on food deliveries administered by food-delivery app companies such as Doordash and Uber Eats. The levies will pay for a new FDNY-DCWP task force to hunt down the non-compliant batteries.
How big a surcharge? I approached this question by estimating the annual societal cost of e-bike battery fires and dividing that figure by the number of annual deliveries via e-bike. The result is a fee of $15 per delivery. (Yes, there would be parallel surcharges for deliveries by car or truck; and yes, the charge should graduate by distance.) 
To be sure, my $15 estimate is much less finely drawn than is my wont, owing to inexact figures on the frequency and societal costs of e-bike battery fire deaths, injuries and dwellings destroyed. It’s also a broad-brush figure, since not every e-bike is used for food-delivery. Case in point: the burning e-bike in Mott Haven was apparently gifted to the father — who remains in a medically induced coma — and probably wasn’t used for business purposes. 
Still, most deadly New York City e-bike fires are tied to the delivery sector. Moreover, that industry’s pockets are deep enough to pay for a municipal strike force to ferret out the thousands of non-compliant lithium-ion batteries used for micro-mobility — commercial or otherwise. The policy question is whether the entire calculated $15-per-delivery “fire externality” should be added to delivery prices, or a smaller amount.
Surcharge Calculations and Assumptions
If passed on to customers, a $15 surcharge would translate to a 40-percent rise from the average pre-tip, pre-tax price of $35-40. An increase of that magnitude would cut the demand for food delivery by half.1 That would be tough news for deliveristas, but good tidings for most New Yorkers, who for years have endured enormous collateral damage — both fire-related and street safety-related — from the sector’s unpriced dangers. Lesser surcharges would soften both the customer price increase and the impact on the delivery sector.
My calculations, assumptions and data sources are spelled out in a simple Excel sheet, available here, covering the past three years. For 2026, the largest damage cost, $144 million, stems from the 10 fatalities in the Mott Haven and Sunset Park fires. I arrived at this figure by multiplying U.S. DOT’s standard measure for the “valuation of a statistical life” — which was $14.2 million last year ($14.4 million with inflation) — by the number of deaths.
The second largest cost, $67 million, covers the far greater number of injuries. For the purposes of my calculation, I assessed the cost of each injury as five percent of the cost of a fatality, corresponding to U.S. DOT’s assessment of “moderate” injury costs. (The agency assesses serious, severe and critical injuries at roughly 10, 27 and 60 percent of fatal injury costs, respectively.)
The third largest cost, $16 million, concerns lost housing. I derived this figure from a 2024 report on “the economic, human and community toll” from e-mobility battery fires in New York City by Oxford Economics for UL Standards and Engagement, the non-profit arm of Underwriters Laboratory that devises safety standards.2
The three categories sum to $159 million for 2024, $193 million for 2025, and $227 million for this year. I have used the middle (2025) figure of $193 million and divided it by the annual rate of 13 million food deliveries. The result is $14.85, or $15 rounded.
If New York City were to surcharge app-operated food deliveries by that amount, the annual take would be close to the $193 million figure. That level of revenue could staff a thousand-person enforcement office, assuming fully loaded costs of $200,000 per employee. (The surcharge, and the task force, would shrink as the number of non-certified batteries diminished.) Alternatively, some of the revenue could support a trade-in program (as has been done with guns). The City could buy certified batteries at a bulk discount and give them to deliveristas in exchange for uncertified ones. 
Would this throw deliveristas under the bus?
In the short run, deliverista work-hours would surely shrivel along with the size of their industry. That shrinkage would be temporary, pending the eventual bounceback as non-UL-certified batteries disappear and the gross fire-damage figure dwindles — and, with it, the delivery surcharge. Authorities should press for a federal ban on the manufacture and importation of uncertified batteries, but that likely would take years — time the city doesn’t have.
Admittedly, this scheme is unabashedly draconian, at least at the “full price,” and stands in marked contrast to the “essential” designation of food-delivery in the Covid pandemic. As the strike force retrenched, the city could redirect some of the surcharge revenue to retraining and resettlement.
But when the smoke clears, we should see the facts clearly: what arose as a pandemic-era stopgap has transformed our streets to service some of the wealthiest New Yorkers. Requiring them to bear the true costs of their expensive and maladaptive habit isn’t exactly the French Revolution. It’s a way of prioritizing a safer city over extreme convenience.
Externality pricing can be a stern taskmaster. But what’s good in the case of congestion pricing should also be good for snuffing out e-bike fires that are hurting, and haunting, New Yorkers.

https://taz.de/Abgewendete-Sozialkuerzun.text:
Abgewendete Sozialkürzungen : Zur Abwechslung mal: Danke, SPD!
Die SPD hat die schlimmsten geplanten Sozialkürzungen verhindert. Zeit, ihre Hartnäckigkeit in der Koalition einfach mal zu loben.
G elegentlich ist die SPD noch für eine Überraschung gut. Im Bundeshaushalt gibt es weniger zu verteilen, und bis Mittwochabend war zu erwarten, dass ein unverhältnismäßig großer Teil der Rechnung an diejenigen geht, die am wenigsten haben: Kürzungen bei Grundsicherung, Wohngeld und Kindersofortzuschlag standen in den vergangenen Monaten im Raum und zum Teil auch schon auf dem Papier. In Zeiten steigender Lebenshaltungskosten sollten die ärmsten Schichten am meisten sparen.
Mit dem SPD-Mantra der vergangenen Jahre hätte sich das durchaus gedeckt: Man sei die Partei der „hart arbeitenden Mitte“, die zwar nicht exakt definiert ist, zu der die Empfänger*innen der genannten Transferleistungen zum großen Teil aber nicht zählen. Es ist also erstaunlich, dass sich die Sozialdemokrat*innen in den Verhandlungen mit der Union doch ernsthaft für sie eingesetzt (und am Ende ein Stück weit durchgesetzt) haben.
Das Paradies bricht mit der Einigung natürlich nicht aus. Erstens sinken Grundsicherung und Co zwar nicht, die Regierung erhöht sie aber auch nicht. Inflationsbedingt wird das Leben für die Betroffenen also trotzdem härter. Zweitens bezahlt für die abgewendeten Kürzungen zum Teil die breite Mittelschicht, die die steigenden Preise ebenfalls spürt, jetzt aber weder bei der Strom- noch der Einkommensteuer entlastet wird.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Drittens kommen natürlich keine neuen Steuern auf große Vermögen, die zwar auch nicht alle Haushaltsprobleme lösen, die Wohlstandsverluste aber zumindest breiter verteilen würden. Die Koalition gestaltet mit diesem Haushalt auch nichts Neues, sondern führt im Wesentlichen den Status quo unter großen Mühen noch ein Jahr weiter. Eine Lösung für die 2030er Jahre, in denen die explodierten Militärausgaben absehbar nicht mehr allein mit Krediten bezahlt werden können, bereitet sie erst recht nicht vor.
Die Sozis wird das nicht retten
All das war in der konkreten Situation und in einer Koalition mit der Union aber auch nicht zu erwarten. Für die SPD war nicht viel zu machen, und zumindest das wenige hat sie gemacht: Sie hat die gravierendsten Auswüchse eines Sozialabbaus abgewendet, vor dem Opposition und Sozialverbände über Monate gewarnt hatten.
Ihre Krise wird die Sozialdemokratie zwar auch damit nicht überwinden. Parteien punkten für gewöhnlich nicht damit, für die einen nichts herausgeholt und für die anderen das Schlimmste verhindert zu haben. Aber da sich die Gelegenheit an dieser Stelle sonst nicht oft bietet, kann man ja zumindest heute mal sagen: Danke, SPD!
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

A bronze sculpture by renowned French German artist Hans (Jean) Arp valued at €145,000 ($160,000) was stolen from Galerie Ludorff’s booth at Art Cologne on November 8, the last day of the fair’s run. The Düsseldorf-based gallery has filed a criminal report with the police and is asking the public for assistance in finding the sculpture. Titled S’élevant (Rising), 1962, and standing just under a foot high, it is typical of the artist’s late oeuvre, which is characterized by smooth organic forms.
According to a press release on the website, the work was taken sometime between 4:55 and 5:10 p.m. “If you visited our booth during this period and took any photographs, we would be very grateful if you could share them with us,” wrote the gallery, which urged fair visitors and the broader art community to keep an eye out for the sculpture. “If you are being offered for sale the work described below at any point in the future or if you have any information regarding its whereabouts,” the gallery wrote, “please contact us or the police directly.”
Artnews reports that the work had been displayed unbolted on a plinth for the duration of the fair’s November 4–8 run, and that there had been four attendants on duty the day it was taken. Maya Hanke, Galerie Ludorff’s publicist and art fair manager told the platform that the fair’s security measures were inadequate. Among her complaints were a lack of security staff in high-traffic areas, and inconsistent bag checks on entry and exit. Fair representative Judith Leyendecker told the publication that fair officials were in contact with the gallery and were supporting the police investigation.

https://hellgatenyc.com/eight-dead-in-br.title: Disaster in Brooklyn: Building Collapse Kills at Least 8, Including 2 Kids
https://hellgatenyc.com/eight-dead-in-br.author: Nick Pinto
https://hellgatenyc.com/eight-dead-in-br.text:
Six adults and two children were killed Wednesday afternoon when a three-story building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue collapsed into a construction site next door. Eighteen other people were injured in the collapse or responding to it. One of them remains in critical condition, Mayor Zohran Mamdani reported at a press conference Thursday afternoon.
Many of the people impacted by the collapse are immigrants, the mayor said, including from Trinidad, Colombia and Mexico. One victim was a 26-year-old father from Ecuador, Today reported. José Luis Caguana Cosquillo leaves behind his pregnant wife and their first child.
"A tragedy of this magnitude demands a comprehensive and thorough investigation that includes both the construction site and the building which collapsed," Mamdani said. But at this time, City officials said, the cause of the collapse has not been determined. It could well have something to do with the demolition and excavation of the building site next door at 2625 Bedford Avenue, work that was permitted and ongoing when 1321 Flatbush collapsed, taking with it one side of the neighboring building.

https://gothamist.com/news/developer-at-.title: Developer at Brooklyn collapse site had record of flouting orders from city agency
https://gothamist.com/news/developer-at-.author: David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/developer-at-.text:
The developer of the property adjacent to the fatal Brooklyn building collapse had a record for cutting corners at the construction site, according to records from the city buildings department.
Those documents show that owner Robert Fischman sent a letter to neighboring landlords in June of this year to inform them of an upcoming disturbance: his company would begin excavating the empty lot at 2625 Bedford Ave. to make way for a new apartment building. It was one of many similar projects set to rise in the rapidly gentrifying neighborhood.
Five months later, the excavation site was the scene of a fatal disaster, after one of the apartment buildings next door at 1321 Flatbush Ave. crumbled into the dirt pit below. At least eight people have been pronounced dead as a result of the collapse and many more were injured, including multiple children on a day that public school students had off for the Veterans Day holiday. Rescue workers were still digging through the rubble Thursday morning for survivors.
The letter Fischman sent neighboring landlords lists the same phone number as his company, Berkoff Supply, an industrial hardware store in Brooklyn. A person who answered the phone at a number listed for Fischman hung up when contacted late Wednesday. An employee answered the phone at Berkoff Supply on Thursday but said Fischman was not available.
By the time Fischman had sent the excavation notice, the project team had already ignored commands from the Department of Buildings, according to records from the city buildings department.
The agency had previously issued the stop work order at the lot during demolition of an existing one-story building in March after determining that contractors had failed to install required safety precautions, including netting and sheds, said Department of Buildings spokesperson Andrew Rudansky. A month later, a buildings inspector found the owners had continued demolition work in violation of the order and issued another penalty.
At a press conference Thursday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the Brooklyn District Attorney's office is involved in investigating the collapse and that building inspectors had been dispatched across the five boroughs to check other related construction sites.
"A tragedy of this magnitude demands a comprehensive and thorough investigation. That includes both the construction site and the building that collapsed, that has already began with the Department of Buildings and law enforcement leading it," Mamdani said. "There are five main entities involved with this construction site who are associated with approximately 100 other sites across the city. Our Department of Buildings is commencing sweeps of those sites today."
Construction workers had been digging in the empty lot Wednesday before the adjacent structure collapsed, Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said at a press conference late Wednesday.
The lot is owned by a limited liability company tied to Fischman and Judy Swimer, according to property records. Swimer did not respond to a phone message. Architectural drawings filed in December last year reveal plans for a three-story complex on what was once a single-story commercial building. The developer later submitted new plans for a nine-story structure in September. Tigani said the buildings department had yet to approve those new plans. A permit was in place for the excavation work.
Structural plans filed by engineer Jeiming Wang of the firm LMW Engineering Group call for extensive excavation and bracing work to prevent neighboring buildings from collapsing, including steel, timber and concrete shoring. They also require the excavation contractor to use seismic monitors to track vibration and install crack gauges on surrounding buildings to monitor movements. Visual inspections were required, along with various oversight and reporting requirements under the supervision of a special inspector.
It’s unclear whether these precautions were taken. The Department of Buildings said it is still investigating what caused the collapse. Wang and the special inspector, MD Islam of Queens-based RI Consulting Services, did not respond to calls and emails on Wednesday.
The company Townhouse Builders was contracted to carry out the shoring work, according to a building permit issued to its owner, Mordchai Waisbrod, in September. Neither he nor the company responded to requests for comment.
This story has been updated with comments from Mayor Mamdani.
Other problems plagued the three-story apartment at 1321 Flatbush Ave., which is owned by a separate landlord, prior to Wednesday's disaster.
City records show inspectors documented a raft of hazards and that the owner Olufemi Falade had a long track record of deplorable building conditions. A judge sent Falade, to jail for 12 days in 2006 for violations at a different building, including vermin and exposed wiring.
Before its collapse, the building had 98 open housing code violations for unsafe electrical wiring, inadequate water supply to the sprinkler system, a lack of smoke detectors, water outages and a bed bug infestation among other problems, according to city data.
The property has cycled through the city’s tax lien sale process at least five times since 2017, due to its unpaid municipal debts, according to court and city property records.
Falade did not respond to a phone message.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/hud-.title: New Trump Rule Threatens Immigrant Families With Separation or Homelessness
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/hud-.author: Jessica Washington
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/hud-.text:
The Trump administration is preparing to kick nearly 80,000 people, about half of them children, off federal housing assistance over their family’s immigration status, threatening to drive thousands into homelessness.
On Thursday, the Department of Housing and Urban Development published a final rule that’s on track to effectively bar families of mixed immigration status from receiving most federal housing assistance, which allow people to receive housing vouchers to reside in privately owned rental homes or in government-owned or -assisted public housing units.
As it stands, undocumented immigrants and temporary non-residents in the United States already are barred from personally receiving most forms of federal housing assistance. But if some members of the family are eligible, the eligible members can receive prorated assistance to help cover their housing, and the non-eligible family member can live with them.
The new rule, which goes into effect in mid-December, would disqualify an entire family if one member is ineligible after a temporary grace period, forcing them to choose between separation and eviction.
Families are “going to be faced with the impossible choice of deciding whether they want to split up so that some people can stay housed, or to stay together and risk homelessness and eviction,” said Marie Claire Tran-Leung, Evictions Initiative Project director at the National Housing Law Project.
Children will bear a disproportionate burden, Tran-Leung said. Of the nearly 80,000 people who could be affected, according to estimates from Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, nearly 37,000 are children.
Many families have one parent who doesn’t qualify, one parent who’s a citizen or otherwise eligible immigrant — i.e. a permanent resident — and kids who hold U.S. citizenship. According to Tran-Leung, the typical mixed-status family in HUD housing is a family of four that fits that profile.
This rule is “going to tear families apart and take adults away from their children,” said Deborah Thrope, chief program officer at the National Housing Law Project.
Beyond potentially leaving tens of thousands of families and children homeless or separated, the change could cost the already beleaguered federal housing agency hundreds of millions of dollars, housing experts told The Intercept. This would likely worsen conditions across the board for the roughly 9 million people in federal housing, who would now be subject to onerous documentation requirements.
“The impacts are not just limited to mixed-status families,” said Renee Williams, senior advisor for public policy at the National Low Income Housing Coalition.
Currently, both U.S. citizens and non-citizens are required to submit a declaration under penalty of perjury attesting that their citizenship or immigration status makes them eligible for housing assistance. Non-citizens under age 62 must submit a document that proves their immigration status. And additional documentation can be requested by local housing agencies or landlords.
The rule change would upend the current system. U.S. citizens would have to go through the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program, also known as SAVE, to verify their eligibility status.
“It’s a system that hasn’t been used to verify citizenship before but now is because of the work that DHS and DOGE did together on a very expedited timeline at the beginning of the Trump administration,” said Tran-Leung. “This causes a lot of concern for us about the very significant risks of residents who are citizens being caught up in verification issues and potentially losing their housing.”
If SAVE cannot verify someone’s eligibility, the new rule requires the person to provide documentation proving their status. The rule would give families 30 days to obtain evidence of immigration status, in addition to the initial 30-day grace period where families can receive pro-rated assistance before having to go through verification.
Tran-Leung and other experts worry that the new documentation requirements could make it harder for low-income tenants — particularly older immigrants over the age of 62, who were previously exempted from verification requirements — to access the program.
Older people, low-income people, and people who’ve experienced homelessness are far more likely to lack access to proof of citizenship such as a passport, valid photo ID, or birth certificate. That means an untold number of the millions of eligible people in federal housing programs could lose assistance just for lack of documentation.
“For folks who may not have easy documentation accessible, who may not have access to a birth certificate, who may not have access to a passport, we’re really worried,” said Williams.
The changes would also burden housing agencies financially by requiring their staff to review documents that were previously not required by federal law.
It is unclear just how expensive these additional administrative costs will be for HUD. But an analysis from HUD itself found that because mixed-status families receive assistance prorated, it would cost the federal government $300 million in additional funds to serve the same number of families as it does now.
For example, a family of four with one ineligible member currently receives 75% of a full household subsidy. A family of four that is not mixed status receives 100% of the subsidy, making it more expensive for the agency to house the non-mixed-status family even though the two families have the same number of people.
“At the same time, HUD is requesting fewer funds from Congress to end homelessness,” said Kayla Blackwell, senior housing policy analyst at the National Low Income Housing Coalition. President Donald Trump recently proposed cutting $3.8 billion from the agency’s affordable housing, homelessness, and community development programs.
HUD Secretary Scott Turner has justified the rule by claiming that mixed-status families are “pushing aside hardworking U.S. citizens” for housing. But experts said the changes will make the system worse for everyone.
“This is scapegoating immigrant families, and HUD is doing less,” said Blackwell.
For the families who either are forced out of the program or leave willingly due to fears around their status, the road ahead is difficult. The majority of mixed-status families live in California, Texas, and New York, where the cost of living can be incredibly high.
“It’s going to be really difficult, I think, for families to be able to stay in their communities and not be displaced if they lose their access to HUD assistance,” said Blackwell.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/cultural-mar.title: How Cultural Marxism Became a Right-Wing Obsession
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/cultural-mar.author: A. J. A. Woods
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/cultural-mar.text:
How Cultural Marxism Became a Right-Wing Obsession
The term “cultural Marxism” has become one of the main rallying cries for the international right. This lurid conspiracy theory about the influence of the Frankfurt School has little connection to reality, but that doesn’t make it any less dangerous.
In December 2021, the term “cultural Marxism” was added to the Oxford English Dictionary. It was, according to the OED, a phrase with a sinister and controversial past. Its etymology could allegedly be traced to 1930s Nazi propaganda; its first recorded English-language use was in a 1938 issue of a British Union of Fascists magazine.
Despite its dark history, this expression has recently surged in popularity. College campuses and city streets have been plastered with stickers that urge passersby to “smash” cultural Marxism. Prominent US Republicans, such as Texas Senator Ted Cruz and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, have written book-length polemics to blame America’s decline on cultural Marxist ideologies.
Leaders in Latin America, like Brazil’s former President Jair Bolsonaro and Argentina’s President Javier Milei, have vowed to rid their governments of this left-wing scourge. In the United Kingdom, Conservative Party MPs have said that cultural Marxists are “destroying” children’s souls and “snuffing out” the right to free speech.
Even the world’s richest man, tech-mogul-turned-Trumpian Elon Musk, has voiced concerns about a Wikipedia article that dismisses cultural Marxism as a “conspiracy theory.” This buzzword has now become a fixture in the lexicon of the contemporary Right — but what does it mean?
The Long March
“Cultural Marxism,” or the “cultural Marxism conspiracy theory,” is the political right’s attempt to explain why the culture of Western societies has changed over the past sixty years. According to this theory, a group of German thinkers known as the Frankfurt School (or the Institute for Social Research) invented the “ideologies” of multiculturalism, feminism, and environmentalism to trigger the demise of Western civilization.
When Theodor Adorno, Herbert Marcuse, and other Frankfurt School theorists fled Nazi Germany, they traveled to the United States and successfully injected their ideas into the 1960s student movement — or so the story goes. In the late twentieth century, their indoctrinated disciples performed a “long march through the institutions” (a phrase coined by German New Left activist Rudi Dutschke) to promote cultural Marxism in education, the media, the government, and the church.
More recently, right-wing activists and conservative pundits have used this theory to understand the rise of the Black Lives Matter movement, the increased visibility of LGBTQ+ communities, and the efforts to tackle the climate emergency. Even in countries outside the United States, conservatives have engaged in a “culture war” to defend their societies from this supposed menace.
What is cultural about this cultural Marxism? What is Marxist about cultural change? Conservative critics speculate that the Frankfurt School developed a fresh strategy of communist subversion in the 1930s. Instead of building a vanguardist party or seizing the factories, the Frankfurt School decided to infiltrate the cultural apparatus of bourgeois society to undermine Western capitalism.
Once ensconced in these positions of power, the critics maintain, cultural Marxists catered to the petulant demands of various minority groups — Black people, LGBTQ+ people, feminists — and dismantled the civilizational inheritance of the (white) majority. The Frankfurt School apparently believed that this strategy would cause a Marxist egalitarian utopia to emerge from the ruins of Western culture.
As the art historian Sven Lütticken observes, this alternative intellectual history relies on a theory of culture that mixes “conservative essentialism” with “schematic superstructuralism.” Culture, according to this right-wing conception, naturally reflects the values of a native populace. These values fuse a nation’s citizens into a harmonious unity that annuls antagonism and difference.
Yet this essentialist notion of culture cannot account for the drastic social changes that have taken place since the 1960s, because it treats the subordination of minorities as “natural” (or even as virtuous). Consequently, conservatives must conclude that an outside agent has seized the organs of cultural production to destroy the West.
In an act of self-defense, the opponents of cultural Marxism propose to eliminate every instance of “political correctness” or “wokeness” in public life through legislative reform, lifestyle changes, or violence. In this version of global events, the Frankfurt School and their devotees are blessed with a magical level of agency that can overcome all contradictions and countervailing forces.
A New Concept
Of course, no one can deny the historical existence and importance of the Frankfurt School. But why does this narrative of cultural degeneration focus so much on a collective of German Marxists? How does it continue to convince and excite the forces of political reaction? What is the genealogy of this idea we call the “cultural Marxism conspiracy theory”?
Some scholars suggest that “cultural Marxism” is simply an updated version of older antisemitic conspiracy theories like “Judeo-Bolshevism” or “cultural Bolshevism.” Of course, there are some eerie parallels between these earlier ideas and “cultural Marxism.” The British Union of Fascists translated Kulturbolschewismus as “cultural Marxism” in 1938, even if their use of the term was long forgotten by the time it was “recoined” in the early 1990s.
Contemporary far-right activists and authors tend to emphasize that several members of the Frankfurt School were Jewish, as if to suggest that these thinkers were genetically predisposed to operate as agents of cultural degeneracy. Even more damningly, the fascist online encyclopedia Metapedia once maintained an entry on cultural Marxism that presented the term as interchangeable with “cultural Bolshevism.”
It is ahistorical, however, to claim that “cultural Marxism” is nothing more than a rebranding of these previous tropes. This argument presupposes that Judeo-Bolshevism, cultural Bolshevism, and cultural Marxism are substantially identical, as though they share a transcendental essence that precedes their historical manifestations. It ignores the distinct trajectories of these ideas and implies that all right-wing politics are fundamentally the same.
The phrase “cultural Marxism,” as well as the conspiratorial narratives about the Frankfurt School that it often denotes, had its own bizarre history long before it ended up in the neo-Nazi thesaurus as a synonym for cultural Bolshevism. Where do we start? While I recognize the parallels between cultural Bolshevism and cultural Marxism, I do not think that the story begins in the 1920s or 1930s. For me, the 1960s is a better starting point for our analysis.
The history of cultural Marxism cannot be understood unless we reflect on the many overlapping shifts and realignments that stemmed from the ’60s. We must remember not to limit our notion of that decade to the spectacular images of May 1968 or Woodstock. As many scholars now agree, the 1960s were long — some claim that the 1960s lasted from 1955 to 1974 — and global.
It was a conjuncture that opened possibilities for revolution, dissent, and counterculture. However, it also involved the exercise of vast political power to defend social and racial hierarchies, control subversive energies, and protect modes of domination and exploitation.
Decades of Struggle
In his groundbreaking essay “Periodizing the 60s,” the cultural critic Fredric Jameson argues that the beginning of what would become known as the 1960s can be traced back to the struggles for national liberation and decolonization that broke out in 1950s Africa. Events in the Global South, such as the independence of Ghana and the Algerian War, ignited nearly two decades of struggle that shook the postwar global order.
Radicals in America and Western Europe drew inspiration from the successes of revolutionary and anti-imperialist movements around the world. They read Frantz Fanon’s The Wretched of the Earth, Mao Zedong’s The Little Red Book, and Che Guevara’s Guerrilla Warfare. Students in the American New Left marched in the streets, held teach-ins, and occupied university buildings to protest their government’s military interventions in Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos.
The truly global nature of this 1960s revolt, with all its fissures and contradictions, gave rise to the hope that the “marginalized” and “minoritized” of the earth would be at the forefront of an unstoppable worldwide revolution. The days of an all-supreme Western civilization looked like they were coming to an end.
The 1960s saw the flourishing of new social and political categories of race, gender, and sexuality. Traditional modes of class-based struggle had lost their radical edge. The Taft-Hartley Act of 1947, as well as the merger between American Federation of Labor and the Congress of Industrial Organizations, tamed the labor movement in the United States and integrated unions into the anti-communist Cold War consensus. Uprisings against bureaucratic communism in the Soviet Bloc — Hungary, Poland, Czechoslovakia — demonstrated the need for a non-Stalinist and antiauthoritarian left.
New ways of doing politics were tested and elaborated. The slogan “The personal is political,” popularized by second-wave feminism, emphasized the importance of finding the links between individual experiences and wider structures of repression. Movements for Black power, women’s liberation, and gay liberation introduced a vibrant politics of identity that fused potent critiques of the existing order with daring visions of a liberated future.
They exposed the social exclusions, subordinations, and restrictions that underpinned the status quo of postwar capitalist societies. In the United States, these movements fought for the establishment of women’s studies, Black studies, and ethnic studies departments in American universities. Racial, sexual, and gender identities were embraced as epistemological bases for developing new forms of knowledge that could identify the multiple dimensions of power and oppression.
In the decades following the 1960s, many countries experienced something of a social and cultural revolution as women, racial minorities, and LGBTQ+ people acquired civil rights and started to play a more active and visible role in the public sphere. While these forms of equality and inclusion were usually partial and contradictory, they represented a significant liberalization of social life and an unsettling of old hierarchies.
The Cultural Turn
One of the most significant developments of the 1960s was the drastic expansion of “culture.” In the middle of the twentieth century, many “developed” countries transitioned from a predominantly industrial model of production to a largely service-and information-based one. During the rise of the postindustrial economy, culture burst into the foreground of day-to-day life.
The mass media — film, television, music, fashion, advertising, newspapers, and magazines — started to exert tremendous power and influence over the rhythms of everyday existence. The growing demographic of teenagers and young adults became an eager audience for the offerings of a new and exciting “youth culture.” The rise of this youth-oriented popular culture even altered conventional habits of speech, dress, and behavior.
These rapid changes spurred a “cultural turn” in humanities and social sciences scholarship. The thinkers of British cultural studies drew on the resources of Gramscian theory to rethink the nature of cultural production and consumption in postwar capitalist societies. Instead of assuming that mass culture turned people into passive consumers, these cultural theorists suggested that popular culture, especially youth subculture, constituted a site of potentially subversive political struggle.
As the forces of Western Marxism cut ties with Moscow, these intellectuals engaged with other radical causes and movements to promote a broad and populist form of cultural politics. Since the 1960s, cultural questions have become increasingly central to political debate.
It would be a mistake to believe that the 1960s were nothing but an outburst of liberal acceptance and youthful rebellion. From right-wing coups and neocolonial economic policies to police repression and state surveillance, the 1960s featured the use of extraordinary force to preserve arrangements of power and privilege.
Various right-wing and reactionary political movements ventured into this conjunctural terrain to defend the existing hierarchies of a supposedly pristine Western civilization. These forces required intellectuals who could explain away the causes of perceived cultural decline, organize their supporters into a coherent political identity, and offer compelling visions of conservative revival.
All cultural Marxism narratives derive from these efforts to resist and reverse the social changes that started to unfold in the long and global 1960s. It is important to understand how these intellectuals operated within their own political movements. How might we investigate the function and activity of these intellectuals? What kind of theory would illuminate the specific ideological practices that shaped their approaches to this cultural tumult? What this task requires, I suggest, is a return to Antonio Gramsci’s theory of intellectuals.
The Formation of Intellectuals
A central theme of Gramsci’s Prison Notebooks is a sustained and innovative rethinking of the concept of the intellectual. In a letter to his sister-in-law Tatiana Schucht, Gramsci remarked that he wanted to extend this concept beyond the limits of “the current notion that refers only to the preeminent intellectuals.” Instead of sticking to this abstract notion, Gramsci examined how specific types of intellectual were formed historically and how they functioned politically.
The sociologist Jerome Karabel describes this reorientation as a shift from a normative framework, which “treats intellectuals not as they actually are, but as they should be,” to an analytical one that identifies “the conditions and processes that shape the actual political consciousness and actions of different groups of intellectuals.” In the Prison Notebooks, Gramsci started from the “immediate, direct, and vivid impression” — the details of social practice and material circumstance — to reveal larger historical patterns.
His entries on intellectuals included several reminders about the importance of grounding one’s research in material reality. He specified that the formation and elaboration of intellectual strata did not “take place on the terrain of abstract democracy, but in accordance with very concrete traditional historical processes.”
The elements of cultural Marxism have been deconstructed and reconfigured time and time again as reactionary political forces across the world search for new ways to justify their opposition to equality, democracy, and justice. We will never understand these stories if we cling to the language of individual pathology.
Our approach to cultural Marxism must be rooted in the institutional, the conjunctural, and the structural. As Gramsci once put it:
Ideas and opinions are not spontaneously born in each individual brain: They have had a center of formation, of irradiation, of dissemination, of persuasion [that] has developed them and presented them in the political form of current reality.
It would be impossible — and uninteresting — to refute all the claims that every critic of cultural Marxism has made. After all, most cultural Marxism narratives include several factual observations, such as Herbert Marcuse’s endorsement of the “long march through the institutions” as a potential strategy for the post-1960s New Left. Yet these little facts are rarely used to provide us with an accurate account of either the Frankfurt School’s influence or contemporary social realities. Instead, they are mobilized to fuel political campaigns that seek to denigrate and disempower certain groups.
The Right has declared war on cultural Marxism. Only when we understand the practices — and weaknesses — of those reactionaries who have signed up for this war can we hope to resist their attacks and fight for a better future.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120385.title: Polizeigewalt in Berlin | Rassistischer Angriff: Polizeischüler bekommt nur Verwarnung
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120385.author: Jule Meier
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120385.text:
- Berlin
- Polizeigewalt in Berlin
Rassistischer Angriff: Polizeischüler bekommt nur Verwarnung
Ein Polizeischüler beleidigt einen Mann rassistisch, schlägt und tritt ihn bewusstlos. Das Gericht sieht eine Jugendverfehlung.
Ab welchem Alter ist die geistige Reife erreicht, die einen befähigt, jemanden nicht rassistisch zu beleidigen, nicht zu schlagen und nicht zu treten? Das ist Gegenstand eines Verfahrens, in dem sich ein ehemaliger Polizeischüler am Donnerstag vor dem Amtsgericht Tiergarten verantworten musste. Der 21-Jährige Ryan S. wurde wegen gefährlicher Körperverletzung und Beleidigung schuldig gesprochen.
S. hatte einen Mann mit dem N-Wort beleidigt, ihm mit der Faust ins Gesicht geschlagen und gegen den Kopf getreten, als dieser schon bewusstlos am Boden lag. Trotzdem kam der frühere Polizeischüler mit einer Verwarnung und 60 Stunden gemeinnütziger Arbeit davon. Der Grund: Das Gericht wertete die Tat als »Jugendverfehlung«.
Treffen sich drei Polizeischüler am Alex
Doch was war eigentlich passiert? Am Freitag, den 8. August 2025, treffen sich die Polizeischüler Ryan S. (damals 20), Max L.*(damals 18) und Tobias G.* (damals 17) am Rosenthaler Platz und trinken gemeinsam eine Flasche Whisky, wie L. und G. als Zeugen vor Gericht berichten. Alkoholisiert steigt das Trio in die Bahn und am Alexanderplatz wieder aus.
Dort treffen sie auf den Geschädigten Ayo M.* und seinen elfjährigen Sohn Malik M. Wie genau die drei Polizeischüler auf ihn trafen, daran will sich keiner von ihnen so recht erinnern. L. und G. hören nur irgendwann Schreie und sehen den Geschädigten am Boden liegen. Auch eine Beleidigung soll irgendjemand in der »Pöbelei« gerufen haben. Aber auf keinen Fall das N-Wort.
Das Trio entfernt sich nach dem Übergriff schnell, wird jedoch von Kolleg*innen aufgehalten. Passant*innen hatten die Polizei gerufen, nachdem sie die Auseinandersetzung beobachtet hatten. Nachdem die Polizei die drei vernommen hatte, leitete das Landeskriminalamt (LKA) Ermittlungen ein. Neben strafrechtlichen Konsequenzen wurden auch dienstrechtliche Konsequenzen geprüft.
Treffen sich drei Rassisten am Alex?
Der Angeklagte S. und der Zeuge G. wurden daraufhin aus dem Dienst entlassen. Nur der Zeuge L. ist weiterhin im Dienst. Vor Gericht präsentiert er sich als Schlichter. Er habe versucht, »dazwischen zu gehen«, wie er sagt. Auf den Stress mit S., der bereits auf dem Weg zum Alexanderplatz einen Obdachlosen angepöbelt haben soll, habe er keine Lust gehabt.
Seine weiße Weste bekommt jedoch ein paar Flecken. So fand das LKA auf seinem Social-Media-Kanal einen Beitrag, den er von einem anderen Kanal geteilt hatte. In dem Beitrag wurde gefordert, alle Menschen, die mit dem N-Wort bezeichnet werden, zu erhängen. Außerdem sagte der Sohn des Geschädigten vor Gericht aus, er habe in Erinnerung, dass einer der beiden anderen Polizeischüler, eventuell gar der angehende Polizist L., seinen Vater festgehalten habe, bevor der Angeklagte S. ihm ins Gesicht geschlagen hatte.
Sowohl die Staatsanwältin als auch der Richter bezweifeln, dass sich die Zeugen Max L. und Tobias G. wirklich nicht erinnern können. Zum Teil widersprechen sie sich außerdem bei der Frage, ob sie nach der Tat nochmal über den Abend gesprochen hätten und ob sie noch mit dem Angeklagten Ryan S. in Kontakt seien.
Treffen sich drei Unreife am Alex?
Obwohl der Angeklagte S. zum Tatzeitpunkt bereits volljährig war, kann er nach Jugendstrafrecht behandelt werden. Das ist möglich, wenn er entweder in seiner sittlichen und geistigen Entwicklung reifeverzögert ist oder wenn es sich bei der Tat um eine sogenannte Jugendverfehlung handelt.
Laut Staatsanwältin sprechen die 2,1 Promille des Angeklagten für eine »Jugendverfehlung«. Dennoch erkennt sie eine »ganz klar rassistisch motivierte Tat«, wie sie im Plädoyer sagt. Der Verteidiger des Angeklagten will seine Unreife darin erkennen, dass der 21-Jährige häufig in Begleitung seiner Mutter zu den Anwaltsterminen erschienen sei und noch zu Hause lebe. »Er ist jetzt eine andere Person«, verteidigt er seinen Mandanten und weist darauf hin, dass sein Mandant bereits fünf Einheiten in einem Anti-Gewalt-Training zum Thema Rassismus absolviert habe.
Folgen der Tat für Vater und Sohn
Dem Gericht reichen die fünf absolvierten Einheiten aus, um den Angeklagten nicht zu weiteren Trainings zu verpflichten. Ryan S. muss neben den Arbeitsstunden zusätzlich 3000 Euro Schadensersatz an den Geschädigten zahlen. Das sei für ein Verfahren nach Jugendstrafrecht eine vergleichsweise hohe Summe, sagt die Nebenklagevertreterin Leonora Arslani im Gespräch mit »nd«.
In ihrem Plädoyer hebt die Rechtsanwältin die rassistische Komponente der Tat hervor. Der Angeklagte habe ihren Mandanten »gezielt aufgrund der Hautfarbe herabgewürdigt«. Ihrer Meinung nach handelt es sich bei der Tat nicht um eine »Jugendverfehlung«. Vor allem die jüngere Generation benutze das N-Wort nicht einfach so. Vielmehr reihe sich das Verfahren eine Reihe rechtsextremer Vorfälle bei der Polizei ein und zeige den starken Korpsgeist in der Behörde. Für Arslani ist es ein »Skandal«, dass Max L. weiter im Dienst ist.
Ayo M. und seinem Sohn Malik sitzen der Sommerabend im August tief in den Knochen, wie man den beiden vor Gericht anmerkt. »Ich weiß nur noch, dass ich und mein Vater zu Burger King wollten«, berichtet der inzwischen zwölf-jährige Malik über den Beginn des Abends.
Auf die Frage seitens des Richters, wie es ihm nach der Tat ergangen sei, überlegt er kurz. »Ich habe darüber nachgedacht«, sagt er. Mit seiner Mutter hat er auch über eine Therapie gesprochen. Vor allem habe er sich für seinen Vater schlecht gefühlt, weil dieser verletzt worden sei.
Die zwei werden vor Gericht von etwa zehn solidarischen Prozessbeobachter*innen begleitet. Gerechtigkeit habe er an diesem Tag nicht bekommen, sagt Ayo M. nach der Verhandlung gegenüber »nd«. Die drei Polizeischüler hätten gelacht, als er am Boden lag – und auch noch als er bereits in den Krankenwagen getragen wurde. »Ich habe Angst, halten Sie Abstand«, soll er zu dem Polizisten gesagt haben, nachdem er geschlagen und getreten worden war. Der Polizei, so Ayo M., vertraue er seit diesem Tag nicht mehr.
* Namen von der Redaktion geändert
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
