https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Ekow Eshun outlines his curatorial vision for the next Site Santa Fe biennial
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Constanza Ontiveros Valdés
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Under the curator Ekow Eshun, the upcoming 13th edition of the Site Santa Fe International Biennial, There Are Other Worlds (11 June 2027-10 January 2028), will aim to reflect how artists open up new ways of understanding the world, potentially inspiring connection and kinship amid the complexity of our times. The exhibition’s citywide programming will span more than six venues, bringing together more than 40 artists from over 15 countries. The biennial is due to include new commissions by the US artists Cauleen Smith, Sanford Biggers and Edgar Arceneaux, the New Mexico-based Diné artist Raven Chacon and the Canadian artist Lotus Kang.
Founded in 1995, Site Santa Fe is one of the US’s key contemporary art events, showcasing international artists while building on New Mexico’s history and social fabric. Eshun—who chairs the Fourth Plinth in London’s Trafalgar Square and is the curator of the touring British Art Show 10: A Chorus of Strangers (touring the UK until June 2028)—is drawing inspiration from the region.
“New Mexico has a layered history, including colonial settlements, but also in the 20th century it had artistic communities that found something here that allowed them to think with expansiveness,” Eshun tells The Art Newspaper. “It is the site of settlement, world-making and self-discovery.”
Beyond New Mexico, Eshun’s vision explores how artists challenge, interpret and shape reality. “We live in a time of divisiveness, uncertainty, inequality and environmental crisis,” he says. “I am inspired by how, in contrast, artists hold complexity and contradictions, inviting us to look beyond binary positions and consider other ways of seeing the world.” These might include imaginative, psychological, emotional and sensory worlds.
The sprawling exhibition is structured into three sections, the curator explains, conceived as “interlocking territories”. The first, “Worlds Beyond”, explores sensory and psychological perception, drawing on the legacy of the Transcendental Painting Group that was active in New Mexico in the 1930s and 40s. “I am interested in how artists look beyond the physical world and can be inspired to think metaphysically, psychologically and emotionally,” Eshun says. He cites the participating Danish Icelandic artist Olafur Eliasson, who thinks with scientific precision while creating works that have both sensorial and emotional impacts.
The exhibition’s second section,“Worlds in Common”, draws on New Mexico’s history of utopian settlements to explore “how artworks may enable us to move beyond hierarchies of power or status and conjure connection or kinship, finding imaginative ways in which we can relate to each other”, Eshun says. He cites the work of Chacon as an example, which uncovers histories of displacement in the Americas, but also turns to connection and memory as routes to reimagining assertions of place.
The exhibition’s third section,“Worlds Alive”, will focus on interactions with nature, considering “the planet as a living territory where all the creatures may have a say in how we live collectively”, Eshun says. He is particularly interested in artists who imagine a relationship with the planet beyond extractivism and grounded in connection across organisms. The participating Colombian artist Delcy Morelos, for instance, reflects on the earth as a physical and ethical territory and a space for aesthetic adventure.
The line-up of participating artists, spanning generations and geographies, reflects the curator’s intention to create a locally rooted biennial with an international scope. “The biennial exists in conversation, not isolation,” Eshun says, adding that community programming will be key. Nearly half the artists are from the US, including Arthur Jafa and Nan Goldin, while five, such as the Indigenous artists Rose B. Simpson and Cannupa Hanska Luger, are based in New Mexico. The exhibition will also include a large contingent of international participants, such as Louise Giovanelli (UK), John Akomfrah (Ghana/UK), Sandra Vásquez de la Horra (Chile), Shilpa Gupta (India) and Tavares Strachan (Bahamas), among others.
While touching on pressing issues, Eshun hopes the biennial will also carry a sense of possibility, empathy and even optimism. Artists, he says, “offer no answers but may open new ways to see, imagine and engage with the present”.
- 13th Site Santa Fe International: There Are Other Worlds, 11 June 2027-10 January 2028, various venues, Santa Fe, New Mexico

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: 8 Dead in Brooklyn Building Collapse As Search and Rescue Continues, Mamdani Says
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Andrew Giambrone, Samantha Maldonado
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Eight people have died and 18 were injured after a three-story building in Flatbush, Brooklyn, collapsed into an adjacent construction site Wednesday afternoon, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday as rescue operations continued.
“There are no words for a loss of this magnitude,” Mamdani said in a statement. “My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we have lost, those who are injured and everyone grieving today.”
Those who died include six adults and two children, the mayor said at a press briefing Thursday afternoon. Two of the dead were workers at the construction site, and one person remains hospitalized in critical condition, he added.
City officials urged people to avoid the area where the building collapsed, at Flatbush and Bedford avenues. They said New Yorkers unable to reach someone they believe may have been affected by the catastrophe should call 311, while those outside of the city should call 212-639-9675.
Authorities were working to determine the cause of the collapse of the building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. into the open-pit construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave. around 4 p.m. Wednesday. A third building, at 1323 Flatbush Ave., was damaged in the incident, with footage from the scene showing the side of that building ripped off and rubble from the collapsed building below.
“We have immediately launched a full investigation into how exactly this happened with our law enforcement partners, and we will be looking into all aspects of the building and the neighboring construction site,” Department of Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said in a video statement late Wednesday.
Officials said Thursday they have issued vacate orders on three buildings on Flatbush Avenue and are sweeping other locations where the companies on the construction site were working when the building toppled. Regulators and the Brooklyn District Attorney’s office are probing the incident.
The city has not yet released the names of the victims.
At a church across from the disaster site Thursday morning, an anguished woman sobbed as she learned her husband, a construction worker, had died in the collapse. While exiting the church, she fell onto the sidewalk and others helped her get up.
“Mi esposo!” she cried.
Jose Gutierrez, a construction worker who came to the church to support the woman and the family, said he knew her husband from working at the same company. Gutierrez said the man’s body was extracted from the construction site around 6 a.m.
“We stayed here all night,” he said. “I came here to see my friend. I wish the situation was good.”
Officials said they were conducting structural stability inspections of nearby buildings. Multiple people were trapped when first responders arrived Wednesday at the scene, which drew more than 250 fire and emergency medical personnel.
Emergency management officials and the Red Cross have opened a reception center for displaced residents at the Flatbush YMCA at 1401 Flatbush Ave., authorities said.
Authorities said they shut down water mains around the site to facilitate the search and rescue operations, with about 100 buildings affected.

https://citylimits.org/more-than-138000-.title: More Than 138,000 NYC Students Experienced Homelessness Last School Year, New Data Shows
https://citylimits.org/more-than-138000-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/more-than-138000-.text:
Share This Article
Though student homelessness declined by 10 percent from the previous school year, advocates warn that tens of thousands of children continue to face housing instability, transportation barriers and educational challenges.
More than 138,000 New York City public school students experienced homelessness during the 2025-26 school year, roughly one in every eight students, according to data released Tuesday by Advocates for Children of New York (AFC).
The figure represents a 10 percent decline from the previous school year, when student homelessness surpassed 150,000 for the first time. Still, it marks the 11th consecutive year that more than 100,000 city students lacked permanent housing.
Of those students, more than 50,700, or 37 percent, spent time in shelters, while approximately 81,100, or 58 percent, were “doubled up”—temporarily sharing housing with relatives, friends or others because of housing loss or economic hardship, according to the report.
The decline was largely driven by a 22 percent decrease in the number of students living in shelters, though that population remained 41 percent higher than a decade ago.
“While it’s encouraging to see that student homelessness is declining after reaching historic highs in 2024-25, today’s data is no cause for celebration,” said Maria Odom, executive director of AFC, in a statement Tuesday.
The Bronx recorded the highest student homelessness rate among the five boroughs at 16.4 percent, followed by Manhattan at 14.1 percent, Queens at 11.9 percent, Brooklyn at 11.6 percent and Staten Island at 5 percent.
Rates varied significantly across the city’s 32 school districts. More than one in five students attending schools in District 9, covering Highbridge and Grand Concourse in the Bronx, District 23 in Brownsville, and District 32 in Bushwick experienced homelessness.
In Brownsville, more than one in eight students spent time in shelters, approximately three times the citywide rate.
Housing instability also creates challenges for students trying to attend school regularly and succeed academically.
According to AFC, nearly half of students living in temporary housing and 63 percent of those in shelters were chronically absent during the 2024–25 school year, accounting for at least 1.1 million missed days of instruction.
In 2025, only 27 percent of third through eighth grade students living in shelters demonstrated reading proficiency on state tests, less than half the rate of their permanently housed peers. Just 59 percent of students in shelters graduated high school on time, while 14 percent dropped out.
Transportation remains another obstacle. During the 2025-26 school year, 37 percent of families were initially placed in shelters in a different borough from their youngest child’s school. Additionally, 1,775 students living in shelters ended the school year waiting for bus service.
Jennifer Pringle, director of AFC’s Learners in Temporary Housing Project, called for improvements to school transportation and greater coordination among city agencies to address shelter placements far from students’ schools.
Nearly 40 percent of homeless families with children are placed in shelters outside the borough of their child’s school, forcing long commutes, early mornings, and strained community ties, as City Limits previously reported.
Christine C. Quinn, president and CEO of Win, a nonprofit providing shelter and supportive housing to homeless families, also urged city officials to address the crisis.
“Students experiencing homelessness are fighting an uphill battle, battling chronic absenteeism while routinely struggling to reach the benchmarks achieved by their housed peers,” Quinn said in a statement Tuesday. “In the wealthiest city in the world, we cannot accept this as normal.”
Quinn called for expanding affordable housing, strengthening rental assistance programs such as CityFHEPS and improving educational support for students experiencing homelessness.
“It’s time for our leaders to be bold and bring forward innovative solutions that put families in permanent homes and bring this crisis to an end,” Quinn said.

https://www.thenation.com/article/econom.title: How Nvidia’s CEO Flirted With Oblivion
https://www.thenation.com/article/econom.author: David Futrelle
https://www.thenation.com/article/econom.text:
How Nvidia’s CEO Flirted With Oblivion
A tech titan’s dopey affair with a suspected Chinese agent could upend the economy.
Will the AI boom that currently powers the stock market—and pretty much the whole economy—be brought low by one tech exec’s inability to keep it in his pants? Nervous investors sent Nvidia’s stock skittering downward after hours Wednesday in the wake of reports that the already scandal-infected company CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an executive who reports to him—and that Nvidia’s board was about to send him packing. Huang wound up sparing them the trouble by announcing his resignation Thursday.
This was all, of course, on top of his recent admission that he’d had an affair with a Chinese executive at the tech firm Megaspeed with the same last name who the US government says is a Chinese spy. Many observers thought that Huang would somehow survive the revelation of the Chinese spy affair, but evidently two affairs is one too many to overlook.
A CEO having a fling with a subordinate is an egregious HR nightmare, to be sure, but it was the affair with apparent Chinese Ministry of State Security employee Alice Huang that raised actual geopolitical concerns. Had the Nvidia CEO (knowingly or unknowingly) passed along information to her or lobbied for an easing of restrictions on plans to export chips to China at least in part on her behalf? Was he so gullible that he didn’t realize she was a spy? Or could he have known, and thus committed some light (or possibly heavy) treason?
But the whole Huang fiasco looks like it could be far more than a sex scandal with a side of espionage. Some company critics are suggesting that Nvidia’s “China problem” goes well beyond Huang’s bad spy romance. We know that Nvidia sold some $4.6 billion worth of chips to a Megaspeed subsidiary, ostensibly intended for a Malaysian data center. But Culper Research, a small short-selling shop that produced an explosive report on Nvidia back in May, says that this is just the tip of the iceberg: Culper estimated that at least 20 percent of the company’s compute revenue in the 2026 fiscal year may have come from illicit sales of its most advanced chips to a network of sketchy companies in Southeast Asia that have in some instances diverted the chips to China, contravening the US export ban.
According to Culper, “Numerous experts told us that Nvidia has long possessed the means to detect diversions”—including post-sale technical tests of server IP addresses and latency time, which could prove that the chips were physically in China. The implication is clear: Either Nvidia knew about the diversions and did nothing, or it didn’t even bother to check, almost certainly because company leaders didn’t want to know. (Culper Research acknowledged in its report that it was shorting Nvidia stock, which means that it benefits if it goes down.)
Ed Zitron, a tech muckraker and AI-boom skeptic contends, based on Culper’s research and his own, that “Nvidia is an untrustworthy company inflating its revenues with deals that range from dodgy to outright illegal.”
Culper’s broad-ranging accusations haven’t exactly been at the center of the media coverage of the scandal. A Wednesday New York Times profile of the man behind Culper mentioned them only glancingly, but you can rest assured that reporters at the Times and elsewhere are hard at work trying to corroborate the Culper research—and so are congressional investigators. In other words, as big as the Nvidia scandal is now, it could get a lot bigger.
And of course there’s the not-inconsiderable political angle. President Donald Trump was first informed of Huang’s affair with a spy about a year ago, and was reminded again by Marco Rubio just prior to a trip Trump took to Beijing back in May. Trump was evidently so unbothered by the fact that the CEO running the firm that provides the essential infrastructure for the AI boom, whose most powerful chips are so cutting-edge that it is forbidden to sell them to China, might be compromised by Chinese intelligence that he went ahead and invited Huang on his trip. As the Times put it, in its deadpan prose, “Mr. Trump has been wary of disrupting Nvidia’s chip sales, which are helping to drive the economy and the stock market.” (Trump also harbors his own conflict of interest, having brokered a deal for the United States to share between 15 and 25 percent of Nvidia’s revenues derived from China sales.)
Trump continues to insist that he knew nothing of any of this until “not too long ago.” As far as he’s concerned, Huang is “an amazing guy” who, as far as Trump knows, hasn’t “done anything wrong.” He went on to offer the perplexing explanation that Huang “dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else.” On Sunday, after Huang had publicly confessed to having an affair, Trump assured reporters that the CEO was “an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”
It’s unlikely that Huang has even one convincing explanation for his actions. But what Huang did have was a crisis PR firm—run by Risa Heller, who famously also represented former (and greatly disgraced) Democratic Representative Anthony Weiner, and which he hired around the time the Times first raised questions about his association with Alice Huang in an article more than a year ago. Presumably, Huang (Jensen, that is) thought that he was about to be enveloped in a scandal of his own making. The Times article, titled “A Mystery C.E.O. and Billions in Sales: Is China Buying Banned Nvidia Chips?,”not only featured several photos of Huang and Huang, er, networking in Taipei; it also made a pretty convincing case, if an implicit one, that Nvidia should have known that Megaspeed was not exactly on the up-and-up. The article closed with a memorable vignette, noting that when a Times reporter visited the headquarters of Megaspeed’s subsidiary Speedmatrix in a Malaysian mall, “three employees inside did not answer despite repeated knocks. A woman eventually emerged for lunch and identified herself as an administrator. She said she had no contact with her bosses. When asked what the company did, she said, ‘It’s not clear.’ ”
You might have thought that this report, which sketched out many of the basic elements of the scandal that now saturates the financial media, would have been a huge deal at the time. But the world only really stood up and took notice when we learned last week that Huang was literally fucking someone who seems to be a Chinese spy.
But the scandal’s salacious aspects aren’t the key issue here, largely because of who Jensen Huang is. He wasn’t just any CEO, just as Nvidia isn’t just any company. Huang was the de facto “key man” of the second-biggest company in the world by market cap, after Apple. Many tech industry observers regarded him as an indispensable figure in the rolling AI boom, and he apparently concurred, having made no effort to groom a successor. Oops.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
As for the $4.2 trillion company he cofounded, it isn’t just a supplier of the chips that make the AI boom possible; it’s widely considered the “central bank of AI.” Its outsize market valuation has left it deeply entangled in a web of circular finance with companies ranging from tech giants like Meta and OpenAI to smaller companies like the cloud-computing rentier CoreWeave. Nvidia will often invest billions of dollars in companies that in turn buy billions of dollars worth of chips from it. It’s all a bit reminiscent of writer Brandy Jensen’s definition of “modern friendship [as] just sending the same $20 back and forth via venmo, forever.” The Economist, noting that Nvidia pledged more than $70 billion in investments in start-ups over three years and offered $300 billion in financial support to customers, warns that “the more of this boom they finance, the more of any bust they will have to bear.”
And the more of this boom they finance, the more likely that a scandal like the one they now face could trigger an AI market crash that could quickly spread to other stocks and take down the economy itself. As Charlie Warzel of The Atlantic notes, “Nvidia has much of the financial system in a hostage situation. Huang is too big to fail.” And now he has.
But Nvidia isn’t the only company that is, as Warzel and Matteo Wong put it in an Atlantic essay last year, “load-bearing” for the economy. So are the other giant firms at the top of America’s corporate heap, many of which have become monstrously large in recent years. Concentration of economic power has increased dramatically. At the end of 2015, the top 10 firms in the S&P 500 represented roughly 19 percent of the market cap of the total index, according to RBC Wealth Management; by the end of last year the top 10 represented nearly 41 percent, a record. (My own back-of- the-envelope calculations suggest the number is a few percentage points higher today.)
Meanwhile, the diversity of these top firms has decreased as the AI boom has inflated the top tech firms and pushed older stalwarts like GE and Johnson and Johnson off the list. Currently, after Apple and Nvidia, the next five-largest US companies by market cap are all tech firms, with most of them, including Alphabet (the parent company of Google), Microsoft and Meta, heavily invested in AI—and all are large customers of Nvidia. If Nvidia falls, so will they, and we’ll all suffer the collateral damage. Hey ChatGPT, are we all screwed?

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/12/a.title: As NYC Debates Amazon’s Delivery Model, Its Partner Fires 200 E-Bike Workers
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/12/a.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/12/a.text:
As NYC Debates Amazon’s Delivery Model, Its Partner Fires 200 E-Bike Workers
Just as the City Council debates reining in Amazon's business practices, the delivery giant threw workers of the job after canceling its contract with a Manhattan subcontractor.
An e-quad bike used to make deliveries in SoHo. Photo: Sophia Lebowitz
This just isn’t working.
Amid a heated Council debate over reining in Amazon’s business practices, the delivery giant threw 200 e-bike delivery workers off the job this week after canceling its contract with a Manhattan subcontractor, Streetsblog learned from one of the laid-off employees.
Employees of Kaizen Management Solutions, a Delancey Street delivery service partner contracted by Amazon to fulfill same-day deliveries on electric cargo bikes, got the news on Wednesday night.
“Approximately 200 employees will be impacted,” said a letter sent to workers, which Streetsblog has seen. The positions will be terminated on Nov. 18. Employees will receive benefits until Jan. 31.
One of the laid-off employees told Streetsblog that Kaizen owner Ezra Tilaye said the firings came after Amazon terminated its contract with the company, one of Amazon’s many delivery service providers. Tilaye did not immediately respond to Streetsblog’s request for comment.
Amazon confirmed to Streetsblog that it did indeed terminate Kaizen’s contract, prompting the mass layoff.
The sudden layoffs could be a violation of the state’s WARN act, which requires employers with more than 50 employees to either provide severance or give workers at least 90 days written notice before layoffs affecting more than 25 people.
The closure of one of Amazon’s contracted Delivery Service Partners is not new for the e-commerce giant, which, despite its omnipresent company branding, does not directly hire delivery workers, but instead relies on a network of small companies to hire workers to fulfill deliveries. Workers are often seen on e-bikes or in vans blazoned with the Amazon logo, but they are not directly employed by Amazon but by companies like Kaizen.
Since 2018, Amazon has terminated contracts with 35 DSPs in the state, resulting in the loss of over 3,500 jobs, a report from the Teamsters Union found.
The firings come at a critical moment for Amazon’s business model in the city. The City Council is currently debating a bill, the so-called Delivery Protection Act, that would require Amazon to directly hire its delivery workforce. Supporters, who include Mayor Mamdani, believe the change is necessary to prevent these types of sudden layoffs.
“Mass layoffs and WARN Act violations at … captive DSPs highlight that they are not bona fide independent businesses but pawns of a giant corporation that needs to be held accountable for their operations,” said Paul Sonn, state Policy Program Director at National Employment Law Project, which worked with the Teamsters on its report. “New York City’s proposed Delivery Protection Act would do just that — and the City Council should act swiftly to approve it.”
The union, which has been pushing hard for the bill’s passage, said the situation at Kaizen is a prime example of why the Council should “close the loophole” allowing Amazon to evade responsibility for such firings.
“Amazon has spent millions of dollars on ads falsely claiming that this law will kill jobs. In fact, Amazon is New York’s biggest job killer,” said Teamsters spokesperson Matthew McQuaid.
Mayor Mamdani has released two videos this month in support of the bill, which a super-majority of Council members support.
City Council Speaker Julie Menin (D-Upper East Side) is still not ready to bring the legislation to vote. She told reporters at a press conference last month that she was still working through the bill’s “legal issues” with the city’s law department.
The bill has major street safety implications. Supporters say direct employment would hold Amazon accountable for what happens on the street while workers are delivering packages.
The Alliance for a Greater New York, which supports the bill, created an interactive tool that shows that Amazon-associated delivery vans drew 14,290 tickets from cameras and traffic enforcement agents between July 2021 and June 2025. And Amazon’s vehicles can be seen parking illegally and obstructing bike lanes all over the city.
On the other hand, Amazon is also one of the leading companies transitioning from dangerous trucks to safer electric cargo quads. But the company has threatened to pull its e-bikes out of the city if the bill passes, Streetsblog reported last month.
Amazon told Streetsblog it terminated its contract with Kaizen because of safety issues. Company spokesman Steve Kelly sent over the following statement only after Streetsblog inquired:
The safety of our employees, partners, and the communities we operate in is our top priority. Over the past year in New York City, we’ve talked a lot about the steps we and our partners take to support safety, the high standards we hold ourselves and our partners to, and the progress we’ve made together.
When a partner doesn’t put safety first, we take action. An investigation found that Kaizen Management Solutions put several e-cargo bikes back on the road before necessary repairs were done. That put its employees and others at risk. The investigation also found multiple breaches of contract involving fraud, including failure to accurately record drivers’ hours worked.
As a result, we’ve ended our partnership with Kaizen. We’re supporting the company’s affected employees by connecting them with other DSPs in the area.
Ninety percent of people living around the proposed bike route get to work without a car, but lazy reporters would rather write a "neighborhood divided" piece with no context.

https://www.artforum.com/columns/on-site.author: Thomas Patier

"This is the posture of a child: thrown into an already furnished world, in need of shelter yet wary of the rules on which shelter depends"
TO ENTER TOLIA ASTAKHISHVILI’S solo exhibition “Figure of the Child” is to descend beneath the surface. Curated by Fatima Hellberg and Manuela Ammer, the artist’s first solo museum exhibition does not merely inhabit two of MUMOK’s lower levels—it rebuilds them from within using drywall, tarpaulin, pipework, and light. The route begins in the foyer of Level -4, where Astakhishvili’s twenty-channel video Their own small gardens (2026) includes footage of the building’s inaccessible cellar and boiler room, and continues through a red polypropylene tunnel, Singing out of doors (2026), to the main exhibition space. Level -4 alone contains fifty-eight of the artist’s works, which often double as shelters for other artworks: huts and shelves that host pieces from the MUMOK collection, as well as contributions by members of the artist’s family and long-standing collaborators. In other words, the exhibition is like a house that has opened its door to everyone at once. Such generosity is the show’s first argument, and its first difficulty: Amid such a density of works, one may wonder whether each piece can be registered as itself, or whether it dissolves into an undifferentiated accumulation.
In such a situation, one has little to go on but their body. A museum ordinarily teaches the body to be quiet, upright, to keep a respectful distance from the object; here the works and their architecture unsettle that sense of discipline. With art everywhere the eye can see, even the floor becomes a display, and Astakhishvili’s dwellings and hiding places almost oblige the visitor to wonder, stoop, kneel, even crawl in order to see what else is there. This is, as the exhibition title suggests, the posture of a child, naming less a subject than a predicament: that of being thrown into an already furnished world, dependent on others yet capable of invention, in need of shelter yet wary of the rules on which shelter depends. The dwellings that thus command the body stand in loco parentis to more than the visitor. Hut 2 and Hut 3, like other architectural interventions elsewhere in the exhibition, were built to display the collection’s works—among them Nan Goldin’s Cibachrome print Honeymoon Suite, Nürnberg Eck, Berlin (1988), Picasso’s bronze Fernande (1906), and Medardo Rosso’s posthumous bronze cast Ecce Puer (1960).
Elsewhere, the shelter turns fully domestic. My emptiness (2025–26) re-creates the most intimate room of a house: a bathroom filled with excavated pipes, a bathtub, a shower tray, a light, and, hanging on one wall, a photograph in greenish tones by Kaucyila Brooke, taken from the series “Vitrinen in Arbeit’” (2002–2005), which documents Vienna’s Natural History Museum during renovation. One can walk in; mirrors add one’s figure to the scene so as to partake in the room’s intimacy. A wall seems to have once divided the bathroom into two parts; now gone, that division can still be felt via traces left behind. On the other side of that vanished line, Astakhishvili’s Hidden dreamer (2019–22)—a canvas worked in papier-mâché, pen, and paint—hangs on the wall.
The exhibition continues on Level -2, which adopts a lighter touch. From the staircase, one enters the space through a temporary corridor whose right side is a wall left standing from the preceding group exhibition, “The World of Tomorrow Will Have Been Another Present” (2025–26). Indeed, on the left, a wall text declares this floor to be a public space given over to events and invites visitors to make themselves at home, to play with what lies at hand, and to take care of the space as they would their own. Nearby are a wooden cabinet by Michael Kleine (Vitrine of dinner menu for June 19, 2026) and Heimo Zobernig’s shelf (2026), which itself holds small-scale sculptures by Veronica Brovall and Jonas Kuck together with several objects left over from the public programs of “Figure of the Child,” making it unclear which works belong to whom.
The corridor opens into a main room, sparer than the display downstairs, an environment in flux. Further remnants of the previous exhibition, along the right-hand side, carve out semi-secluded subspaces. On some days these spaces are occupied by public programs; on others they are left empty. In the open-plan part of the room, a table with paper and markers, benches left over from the opening dinner, and other material echoes from the ongoing events give the space the feel of a venue between special occasions. In one corner stands what appears to be a partial replica of a house, built at the start of the exhibition using plain construction board. Over the course of the show, the work, titled ideas are everywhere and in everything, 2026, has been filled with drawings and paintings by children. At the center, another unfinished house structure (the others are inside us, 2026) invites the audience in and, on occasion, is inhabited by visitors and by invited artists. A projector mounted on top of the structure casts nothing but a vast white field onto the wall, as though a film were about to play or had just ended.
This is all part of the “Tolia Curriculum,” a program that grew alongside the exhibition and unfolded both on this floor and in the museum’s cinema. Curated by Astakhishvili with Hellberg and realized with Marie-Claire Gagnon from MUMOK’s Exhibitions Department, these events began in May, while the installation was still under way, launching weeks of readings, screenings, movement sessions, and workshops for children and adults. During the first events, this space was little more than an armature, a world still coming into being. Once the show opened, the architecture was finalized, though still open to revision: Each event has given the floor a different spatial grammar.
Among the staggering thirty-one events, many bear the exhibition’s concerns closely. At Open Studio (May 23), visitors were invited to continue drawings the artist had started, authorship passing from hand to hand. On June 10, Simon Lässig’s presentation Microdrama traced, through texts and images, the emergence of the distinction between self and other in early childhood, and the ways it can be destabilized. James Richards’s film screening (June 18) carried a title, We came into this world wanting milk—everything else was made up as we went along, that read like a metaphor for the recurring child figure. Later events organized after the June opening extended that filial line of inquiry. Düsseldorf-based artist Keta Gavasheli’s First Utter, a listening/screening session in September, included cassette recordings, voice, movement, and acoustic guitar, growing out of the artist’s long-distance readings with her mother in Georgia. The performance circled motherhood, distance, and the unstable ground between memory and voice. Finally, the October screening of Jeff Preiss’s STOP, a film that follows his child’s growing up and transition over sixteen years, brought the exhibition’s titular figure to the screen in its most literal form.
Throughout the “Tolia Curriculum,” Astakhishvili’s most incisive gesture was to treat time, not space, as artistic material. The installation period, ordinarily compressed into as few days as possible and kept from public view, was entrusted to other artists and to the public as an open, durational event. Even for an artist whose practice has long been collaborative, to turn that interval into an open process meant forgoing authorial finality: making the work contingent on the program and the program on the hosting institution. Yet the plurality of perspectives assembled by the Curriculum was not confined to Level -2. Each program tacitly mediated how a visitor could encounter the exhibition below, drawing attention to its material and immaterial registers alike. A visitor who returned to Level -4 found its huts and hiding places inflected, after the fact, by what had been heard, drawn, or screened in the interim.
The mediation at work here differs from typical Kunstvermittlung (German for “art mediation”), which usually takes the finished exhibition as its point of departure and brings audiences into it by way of tours, talks, and workshops. The practice’s virtue is care; its limit is a tendency to leave the audience in the position of passive recipients, partaking in something already decided. Public programming, in the sense the Curriculum proposed, inverts that dynamic. Its premise suggests that the exhibition is incomplete without its public and that artistic practices can be shared as actively developing work rather than explained as finished concepts. Such a mode is scarcely visible in Vienna, where the repertoire of public programs seldom extends beyond the aforementioned lecture or guided tour, formats that transmit knowledge about a work while leaving its conditions untouched. The case for another approach to exhibition programming has never been stronger. At a time when public life is increasingly conducted through screens, and spontaneity is treated as a liability, the chance to draw, listen, or sit alongside strangers, and so to enact an exhibition together, acquires something close to political weight. An opening, with its glamour and free drinks, supplies the image of a community; the Curriculum materialized it, week after week.
In Deleuze and Guattari’s account of the wasp and the orchid1, two dissimilar beings become entangled: The orchid takes on the likeness of a female wasp, and the wasp, drawn to the flower, carries the orchid’s pollen onward. Neither imitates the other, but rather, each becomes a function of the other’s reproduction. What results is an arrangement neither could have produced alone. Something comparable took place at MUMOK. The installations turned into a venue, and the guests’ events entered the fabric of the work itself, each acquiring a vital function in the other’s apparatus. This kind of becoming is a process, however, and processes can be interrupted. Institutional critique has a habit of ending where it began: The museum temporarily accommodates the episodic, “childlike” disruption and then resumes its “adult” routines. The question now is whether and how MUMOK adapts this approach to its future programming now that the exhibition has closed, or lets it end here.
Michał Leszuk is a codirector of Kunstverein Kevin (Vienna) and a visiting lecturer in expanded museum studies at the University of Applied Arts Vienna.
“Tolia Astakhishvili: Figure of the Child,” and the accompanying “Tolia Curriculum,” ran from June 20 to November 1, 2026 at MUMOK, Vienna.
NOTES
1. Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari, A Thousand Plateaus: Capitalism and Schizophrenia, trans. Brian Massumi (University of Minnesota Press, 1987), 10–12.

So when two completely unrelated Beantown hotspots opened outposts here within days of each other last month, both with pretty much just a single item on their respective menus—one serves chicken cutlet sandwiches, the other bowls of udon noodles—and both instantly attracting sidewalk-lining hordes to their new neighborhoods (the East Village and NoMad), it was a coincidence too unusual not to check out.

https://gothamist.com/news/death-toll-fr.title: Mamdani: Brooklyn building collapse kills 6 adults, 2 children with rescue work still underway
https://gothamist.com/news/death-toll-fr.author: Brittany Kriegstein, Verónica Del Valle
https://gothamist.com/news/death-toll-fr.text:
Eight people, including two children, are dead, and 18 others are injured after a three-story apartment building collapsed in Flatbush on Wednesday afternoon, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday. More than 250 firefighters and emergency service workers responded to the scene; they continue to search the rubble for survivors.
The building, located near Bedford and Flatbush Avenues, collapsed around 4 p.m. Wednesday into a lot where construction workers had been excavating earlier in the day for a new building, officials said. Six people died at the scene, and two others succumbed to their injuries at nearby hospitals, the mayor said. Two of those who died were construction workers. At least seven of the injured are children. Most of those still hospitalized are in stable condition, though one person is in critical condition, Mamdani said.
Though rain threatened to complicate the rescue effort, FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said it would not “stop our operations.”
“ This type of an emergency is something our members train extensively for, and we will be here until we are one hundred percent sure there are no more people trapped,” she said.
The devastation puts the collapse among the worst such disasters in recent city history. The Department of Buildings and law enforcement have begun an investigation into what caused the building to collapse. The developer of the new construction appears to have flouted orders from the buildings department in the past.
Mamdani said five entities were involved in the construction site and are associated with about 100 other projects across the city. The Department of Buildings began a sweep of those sites Thursday, he said.
“If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them fully accountable,” Mamdani said.
The scene was chaotic Thursday morning as firefighters, emergency service workers and police officers moved around the site. A demolition excavator worked through the rubble, piling the debris on one end of the lot — a mattress, a refrigerator, wood floor panels — while bricks, clothing and dozens of music records lay scattered across the site.
Families who had spent the night on the sidewalk wrapped in blankets waited for any information about the fate of their loved ones.
One woman collapsed to the ground after learning her husband was among the dead.
“My husband, he died,” she yelled in Spanish.
Segundo Iza stood at the site of the collapse. He said he knew one of the construction workers who had died. They’d grown up together in Ambato, Ecuador. They’d met playing soccer.
Iza said his friend had moved to the U.S. four or five years ago. He had one son and another child on the way.
“He was someone who came here to achieve many dreams, to find better days for our children and our parents,” Iza said. “So it’s sad that our friend died here in New York.”
Assiah Bah, 23, said she and her family were waiting outside all night for news of their two cousins who lived in the collapsed building and were cooking dinner at the time of the disaster.
“We don't know what is going on, if they're still alive or if they passed, we don't know,” Bah said Thursday morning, saying her family immigrated from Guinea.
The extent of injuries and location of those who were caught in the wreckage has been changing throughout the rescue operation.
“We've seen infants, toddlers being pulled out of the rubble on stretchers into ambulances to be rushed to the hospital,” Councilmember Farah Louis said from the scene Wednesday night.
Katie Stevens, a teacher who lives down the block, said she was home, doing her laundry when she heard what sounded almost like a car crash. A few minutes later, she heard sirens and helicopters overhead. She said she found a family with a young boy standing on the sidewalk next to the rubble, crying. “ Can I do anything for you right now?”
“We need everything right now,” Stevens recalled them telling her. She took the young boy to a nearby clothing store to use the restroom. He kept asking her when he could go back home.
“I don't know, love,” Stevens told him. “I don't know. I don't know, but you are safe. Your family is safe. You're gonna be okay.”
The building collapsed into a hole where construction workers had been excavating for a new building on an adjacent lot earlier in the day, according to the city's buildings commissioner Ahmed Tigani.
“I actually watched it. I was in my room when the building fell down. You could hear it.” Antione Vines said, Wednesday night from the scene. “ Before they build a new building and you're connecting it to another building that’s been up since the 1700s, you gotta look at the structure of the building. You can't just build a new building and connect it.”
Nearly all of the building had caved into the adjacent construction site, shearing off the side of the neighboring residential building, exposing a stairway, a closet full of clothes and a bedroom set.
“We’ve been waiting here all night. We went to four hospitals, and they haven’t given us any information,” Luis Siguencia said of his son, 22-year-old construction worker Gabriel Siguencia, as he anxiously waited at the scene Thursday morning.
“He wanted to get ahead. Because we all come here with the dream of getting ahead. He had his papers and everything.”
Gabriel, who recently arrived from Ecuador, had been working on the foundation at the site for the last two weeks.
New York City's Office of Emergency Management said it has coordinated with the Red Cross to open a reception center for impacted residents at the Flatbush YMCA at 1401 Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn.
As of 6 a.m., the Red Cross has registered seven households (14 adults and five children) for emergency assistance, including temporary lodging.
Mamdani said anyone searching for a loved one should call 311 or 212-639-9675.
Liam Quigley, Ryan Kost and Catalina Gonella contributed reporting.
This is a developing story and has been updated.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/el-sayed-spo.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s Sports Fluency Is a Political Asset
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/el-sayed-spo.author: Sean Jacobs, Ivan Pech
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/el-sayed-spo.text:
Abdul El-Sayed’s Sports Fluency Is a Political Asset
Abdul El-Sayed’s ease in talking sports built rapport with skeptical voters and defies the stereotype of progressives hating what average people find fun. His knack for finding common ground is central to his broad political appeal.
One of Abdul El-Sayed’s greatest skills is his ability to deploy the language of sports to make his case. His fluency in sports allows him to find common ground with interlocutors and audiences, complicating the stereotype that progressives are anti-sports.
What makes him convincing and harder for his opponents to dismiss is that he played competitive team sports: El-Sayed was a hockey goalie in middle school. At Bloomfield Hills High School in the suburbs of Detroit, he played football and lacrosse and wrestled, becoming football team captain. These are sports conservatives embrace or consider quintessentially American. At the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, he continued playing sports at the club level, which is more competitive than intramural sports but separate from varsity athletics. As a Rhodes Scholar, he also played on and captained the University of Oxford men’s lacrosse team.
In a now-viral interview with Fox News’s Jesse Watters, El-Sayed did what so few progressive politicians manage: he disarmed a skeptical, even hostile, interlocutor not with talking points but with sports camaraderie. “We both played football and lacrosse. We both love America. We both love freedom,” he responded to the first question, before bantering about football ticket prices and ribbing his critics. The next night, Watters admitted to viewers, “I actually like Abdul. I probably shouldn’t like him, but I do.”
Hearts and Minds and the Home Team
By leaning into the language of sports, El-Sayed flips the script on the “bro culture,” especially among young men, that has long fueled right-wing politics and Trump-era masculinity. Rather than ceding that terrain, he claims it on his own terms. He repeatedly cast his opponent Mike Rogers as a subordinate “beta” in Donald Trump’s “alpha” orbit, turning the hierarchy of masculine posturing against them. Some skeptics, drawn in by his athletic bona fides, may find themselves unexpectedly receptive. It’s as if El-Sayed is saying: sports don’t belong exclusively to conservatives.
One of his most effective rhetorical strategies was to draw on the local loyalties and rivalries that shape Michigan’s fandom.
El-Sayed repeatedly invoked the long-standing rivalry between the University of Michigan Wolverines and the Ohio State Buckeyes, particularly their annual college football matchup, in which Michigan has the upper hand, sixty-two total wins to Ohio State’s fifty-three wins. His jabs at neighboring Ohio — and at J. D. Vance in particular — may seem strange and personal to outsiders, but they make perfect sense within Michigan’s political and cultural landscape. He was directing the taunt at Vance, an Ohio State alumnus who had repeatedly attacked El-Sayed with inflammatory racist and Islamophobic rhetoric. By turning the rivalry into a political jab, El-Sayed displayed local cultural fluency.
Some athletes agree. One high-profile supporter of El-Sayed is San Diego Padres pitcher Lucas Giolito. Front Office Sports previously reported that Giolito donated $1,250 to El-Sayed’s campaign. On election night, journalist Eli Kronenberg wrote on X that Giolito told him, “Although I don’t live in Michigan, I believe he’ll be a great progressive voice in the US Senate.”
On his book tour, Colin Kaepernick was asked which politicians he was most excited about. He answered quickly: “The ones that are interesting to me are obviously Mamdani in New York . . . [and] Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. I really like the approaches they’re taking. They’re staying very focused on the needs of the people. They don’t seem to be bought or swayed,” he said, adding that they represent a growing rejection of the establishment.
From the Field to the Campaign Trail
A few days before the election, former Michigan State long snapper Taybor Pepper, who played in the NFL for seven seasons, interviewed El-Sayed. After speaking with El-Sayed, Pepper wrote on X:
I understand why people want sports to be an escape from politics, but the reality is that throughout history, sports and politics have been deeply intertwined. From breaking racial barriers to fighting for equality and civil rights, athletes have played a pivotal role in pushing society toward meaningful social change.
Like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, El-Sayed supports English football club Arsenal FC, whose large, diverse global fan base has much in common with the New York Knicks, another of Mamdani’s passions.
This is not the first time El-Sayed has weighed in on sports’ cultural and political significance. In an April 2021 post on his now private Substack, The Incision, he analyzed the influence of big money on European football and fans’ successful resistance to major clubs’ attempts to commercialize the game further through the European Super League. He drew a parallel to the exploitation of the health care system back home: “If English soccer fans can stand up to fight for their soccer clubs, perhaps we too can fight for our healthcare, our prescription drugs, our schools, and our lives.”
In another post in October 2021, following the firing of former Raiders coach Jon Gruden over racist, homophobic, and misogynistic comments, El-Sayed argued that the problem was more systemic: “The toxic masculinity at the heart of America’s most popular sport — and men’s sports culture more generally — is way deeper than a few emails or a Jay-Z turnaround.”
Finally, about a month ago, El-Sayed’s campaign posted a short video on his social media in which one of his former high school football teammates, Nikita Sanches, speaks about El-Sayed as a teammate. Sanches, who was born in the Soviet Union and was a shy teenager when they first met, recalls how El-Sayed befriended him and took him under his wing. He also described how El-Sayed negotiated Islamophobia in the wake of 9/11. Sanches, now a chef, explains how, a year later, “we elected him our leader and our captain. Not just because he was our friend and our classmate, but because of the way he carried himself.” The same qualities that made El-Sayed a trusted teammate now help him use sports to connect with audiences beyond his political base.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120385.title: Israelischer Rüstungskonzern | Elbit sagt Sangerhausen ab – aber baut Präsenz in Deutschland aus
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120385.author: Matthias Monroy
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120385.text:
- Politik
- Israelischer Rüstungskonzern
Elbit sagt Sangerhausen ab – aber baut Präsenz in Deutschland aus
Einer der größten israelischen Rüstungskonzerne will nun doch nicht in Sachsen-Anhalt produzieren. Sein Geschäft floriert dank Abgeordneten trotzdem.
Die Ansiedlung des israelischen Rüstungsunternehmens Elbit Systems in Sangerhausen ist offenbar gescheitert. Der Standort sei keine Option, berichtet die in Halle erscheinende »Mitteldeutsche Zeitung« unter Berufung auf einen Firmensprecher. Für die Bedarfe des Unternehmens erfülle der Standort nicht die nötigen Voraussetzungen. Konkreter wurde Elbit nicht. Allgemein hieß es lediglich: »Faktoren wie die Größe der Liegenschaft, zeitnahes Baurecht, Verfügbarkeit von qualifizierten Arbeitskräften und die verkehrliche Anbindung sind für uns dabei ausschlaggebend.«
Über Monate hatte Elbit Systems Deutschland mit der Stadt über eine Ansiedlung auf 140 Hektar in einem neuen Industriegebiet direkt an der Autobahn 38 verhandelt. Die Rede war von der Schaffung von 400 Arbeitsplätzen. Gegen das Projekt mobilisierte das Bündnis »Keep Elbit Out – Keine Waffenfabrik in Sangerhausen«, das von Organisationen aus Sachsen und Sachsen-Anhalt getragen wird. Im August organisierte das Bündnis eine Demonstration mit 500 Teilnehmer*innen. Auch lokale Unternehmer und Landwirte stellten sich gegen die Ansiedlung, weil sie einen verschärften Fachkräftemangel, unfairen Lohnwettbewerb und den Verlust wertvoller Ackerflächen befürchten.
Bis zu acht neue Standorte angekündigt
Die Absage an Sangerhausen ist keine Absage an den Ausbau in Deutschland. Elbit Systems Deutschland will nach Angaben seines Deutschland-Chefs Marian Rachow gegenüber der »Zeit« innerhalb von drei Jahren deutlich über 1000 Mitarbeiter beschäftigen und bis zu acht neue Standorte errichten. Dazu gehören Fabriken für Kamikazedrohnen, Artillerie-Raketensysteme und Munition. Neben dem Hauptsitz in Ulm sind Niederlassungen in Koblenz und Wilhelmshaven bekannt. Ein Büro in Berlin wurde nach nd-Recherchen aber 2026 geschlossen.
Im März 2026 gab Elbit mit dem deutsch-französischen Rüstungskonzern KNDS die Gründung des Joint Ventures Europuls GmbH bekannt, das seinen Sitz in Kassel hat. Dort soll das gleichnamige Artillerie-Raketensystem hergestellt werden. Die Bundeswehr hat fünf Europuls-Startgeräte für die erste Einsatzbefähigung bestellt. Weitere Kooperationen von Elbit Systems Deutschland bestehen mit Rheinmetall über ein automatisiertes 155-Millimeter-Radhaubitzensystem, mit dem Start-up Cucuyo über militärische Laserkommunikation sowie mit Diehl und Thyssen Krupp Marine Systems.
Deutsch-Israelische Gesellschaft im Fahrersitz
Schon jetzt ist Elbit Systems eng mit der Politik in Deutschland verzahnt. Im Juni besuchten drei CDU-Bundestagsabgeordnete die Ulmer Zentrale. Im September wurde dann ein fünfköpfiger Beirat unter Vorsitz von Peter Tauber angekündigt, dem ehemaligen CDU-Generalsekretär, einst als Mitglied des Bundestags auch parlamentarischer Staatssekretär im Verteidigungsministerium. Weitere Mitglieder des Elbit-Beirats sind der frühere Marinechef Andreas Krause, Generalmajor außer Dienst Wolfgang Köpke und Grisha Alroi-Arloser, Vorsitzender der Deutsch-Israelischen Gesellschaft und bis 2023 Leiter der israelisch-deutschen Industrie- und Handelskammer. Der Beirat berät Elbit Systems Deutschland zur Unternehmens- und Industriestrategie.
Eine heikle Personalie ist Marcus Faber von der FDP. Er leitete von 2024 bis zu seinem Ausscheiden aus dem Bundestag im März 2025 den Verteidigungsausschuss, acht Monate später wurde er Vizepräsident für politische Angelegenheiten bei Elbit Systems Deutschland. Faber ist zudem Vizepräsident der Deutsch-Israelischen Gesellschaft.
Im Lobbyregister des Bundestags ist Faber als eine von drei Personen benannt, die direkt für Elbit lobbyieren. Für 2025 gab der Konzern 520.001 bis 530.000 Euro Lobbyausgaben an. Nach eigenen Angaben will Elbit Systems Deutschland auch ein Büro in Brüssel einrichten.
Empfänge im Bundestag
Erstmals veranstaltete Elbit Systems Deutschland am vergangenen 4. November außerdem einen »parlamentarischen Abend« auf dem Dach des Bundestags. Nach Angaben des Unternehmens auf der Berufsplattform Linkedin kamen fast 200 Gäste und zahlreiche Abgeordnete. Auf den Bildern zu sehen sind unter anderem der Chef des israelischen Mutterkonzerns, Bezhalel Machlis und Deutschland-Chef Rachow. Die Keynote hielt demnach Vizeadmiral Thomas Daum, Leiter des Cyber- und Informationsraum-Kommandos der Bundeswehr.
Derartige Veranstaltungen sollen auch Verkäufe des Unternehmens fördern. Sie werden von Lobbyorganisationen wie Naffo angebahnt, die unter höchster Verschwiegenheit den grünen stellvertretenden Fraktionsvorsitzenden Konstantin von Notz dafür gewann, den Ex-Mossad-Chef David Barnea zu einem »parlamentarischen Frühstück« am kommenden 25. November einzuladen. Menschenrechtsorganisationen sehen ihn Barnea einen mutmaßlichen Kriegsverbrecher und fordern von der Bundesregierung seine Festnahme.
Nach seinem Abgang beim Mossad im vergangenen Sommer ist Barnea zum israelischen Rüstungskonzern Ondas gewechselt und dort für internationale Verkäufe zuständig. Naffo beantwortet dem »nd« keine Fragen zum geplanten Frühstück mit früheren Geheimdienstchef – nicht einmal, ob die im Lobbyregister des Bundestags angegebene Mailadresse für den Verein korrekt ist.
Dietmar Bartsch bei »Elnet Awards«
Eine weitere Lobbyorganisation für Israels Interessen und die Rüstungsindustrie des Landes ist nach eigener Aussage Elnet. Die Organisation wird unter anderem über einen Förderverein Elnet (Felnet) finanziert, in den laut Lobbyregister auch Elbit einzahlt.
Am Mittwochabend vergab der eingetragene Verein zum wiederholten Male seine »Elnet Awards«, unter anderem an Persönlichkeiten, die sich für israelische Regierungspolitik in Deutschland einsetzen. Ausgezeichnet wurde etwa der Chefredakteur der »Jüdischen Allgemeinen«, Philipp Peyman Engel.
Zugegen war auch wieder der Linke-Politiker Dietmar Bartsch, der in der Vergangenheit hohe Ämter in Partei und Bundestagsfraktion bekleidete. Er überreichte einen »Kulturpreis« von Elnet an die Konferenzreihe »Voices after Auschwitz«.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: New York auction houses hope single-owner collections will fuel $2.4bn week of sales
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Carlie Porterfield
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
New York’s major auction houses are heading into the November marquee sales next week with a sustained sense of confidence, as the global art market continues to show signs of recovery and a set of significant single-owner collections comes on the market. Sotheby's, Christie's, Phillips and Bonhams expect to bring in at least $2.04bn collectively from their auctions in the Big Apple this month, with sales potentially exceeding $2.4bn, slightly above last year’s estimates for the period.
The confident estimates for this month’s top lots—and strong results for New York’s May sales—resonate with an ArtTactic report released earlier this year, which found the top auction houses made strong recoveries during the first half of 2026. Global auction sales were up 70% year on year at Christie's, Sotheby's and Phillips in the first six months of the year, thanks in part to the enduring appeal of single-owner collections and major estates.
That consignment strategy will be on full display at New York’s blockbuster auctions next week. Single-owner collections allow the houses to rebrand regular seasonal auctions as can’t-miss, once-in-a-lifetime events, and craft marketing campaigns around not just the works on sale but also the legacies of the collectors.
Sotheby’s boasts the highest collective estimate of the auction houses, projecting more than $1.1bn, which would be a house record for a marquee sale season. Around 40% of that total is attributed to the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, a fully guaranteed group of 12 Impressionist, Post-Impressionist and Fauvist paintings expected to sell for around $450m, making it the highest-value single-owner collection on offer this season across the city.
The collection was assembled by the Argentine sugar magnate Carlos Pedro Blaquier and his wife, María Elena “Nelly” Arrieta de Blaquier. Blaquier faced charges relating to the kidnapping of suspected left-wing activists during Argentina's 1976-83 military dictatorship. He denied the allegations and died in 2023 without standing trial. The 12 paintings have been consigned by the couple’s five children; the auction on 18 November will immediately be followed by Sotheby’s multiple-owner evening sale of Modern art.
“The market is very much moved by these collections,” says Allegra Bettini, Sotheby’s head of Modern evening auction. “Collectors today like to understand a narrative and see where works are coming from to understand the taste of how they all hung together.”
When the works in the Blaquier-Arrieta hoard were acquired, mostly in the 1960s and 70s in Europe, collectors could still purchase museum-quality works by Modern masters from commercial art galleries. That is no longer the case, Sotheby’s specialists say, even with a seven-figure budget. The Blaquier-Arrieta family rarely, if ever, loaned works for public display. Until Sotheby’s put them on view in its galleries at the Breuer Building on the Upper East Side, few of the 12 consigned works had been on public exhibit or offered on the market in decades.
The trove’s headline lot is Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (1890), one of the final works the artist painted in Auvers-sur-Oise in the months before his death. It carries a staggering estimate of around $180m and, because it has been guaranteed, is sure to exceed the current auction record for a Van Gogh of $117m (including fees), set by Orchard with Cypresses (1888) at the Paul Allen sale at Christie’s New York in 2022.
“It’s hard to not want to just touch and feel these brushstrokes because it is so alive,” Bettini says, gesturing to the leaves of the trees in the painting. “There's an intensity to it that really brings us into this landscape with the artist.”
Another possible recordbreaker is Arlequin (1888–90) by Paul Cezanne, which is estimated to sell in the region of $120m. The late harlequin painting is the only example from Cezanne’s series still in private hands, according to Sotheby’s. The current auction record for a Cezanne work, also set during the Paul Allen sales at Christie’s, is $137.79m.
Other standout works from the Blaquier-Arrieta collection include paintings by Camille Pissarro, Claude Monet and Pierre-Auguste Renoir. Sotheby’s will also offer works from the collections of oil tycoon Armand Hammer, Seattle property developer Richard Hedreen and his wife Elizabeth Hedreen, and cable television pioneer Theodore Baum and his wife Ruth Baum.
In Midtown at Christie’s, the leading lot of the season is Wassily Kandinsky's Betonte Ecken (1922-23), from the artist’s Bauhaus period. Once part of the Guggenheim collection, it was purchased by its current owners—reportedly the billionaire, art-dealing Nahmad family—at Sotheby’s in 1986. It is estimated to sell for between $60m and $80m during the 20th-century evening sale on 17 November.
With the same estimate and on offer during the same sale, Gustav Klimt’s landscape Litzlbergkeller (1915-16) was once part of the collection gathered by Serge Sabarsky, the late art dealer who co-founded the Neue Galerie in New York (the beloved Austrian restaurant on the museum’s ground floor is named for him). Leading the 21st century evening sale is an untitled 1983 work by Jean-Michel Basquiat that references a drawing on paper by Leonardo da Vinci and is estimated to sell for between $30m and $50m.
Christie’s is also offering a wide variety of works from the holdings of well-known collectors, among them the music executive Clive Davis, the billionaire businessman William Koch, and more works belonging to the late Museum of Modern Art trustee Agnes Gund that will benefit her foundation. Also on offer is a group of seven works including Old Master, Modernist and post-war artists understood to have been consigned by Jeff Koons. Altogether, the auction house expects to take in between $823m and $1.1bn during its November sales in New York.
Despite recent stock market volatility following the “blue tsunami” during the US midterm elections earlier this month and concerns over a Democrat-controlled Congress’s regulation of artificial intelligence and datacentre development—heightened by recent revelations about chipmaker Nvidia’s president Jensen Huang being embroiled in a spy scandal—stocks show early signs of stabilising. Christie’s specialists are similarly optimistic ahead of the November auctions.
While fluctuations in the stock markets can influence the art market over the longer term, the immediate impact on high-end auctions tends to be limited. Particularly for evening auctions, where lots are estimated to sell for seven-, eight- and nine-figure sums, potential buyers are often wealthy enough to be insulated from the day-to-day fluctuations of the stock market.
“The art’s quality is going to supersede any day in the market. People aren’t day-trading Picassos,” says Kat Widing, Christie’s senior vice president, senior specialist in post-war and contemporary art, and head of the 21st-century evening sale.
Collectors are “looking at these works over months, and they’re thinking through these major purchases”, she adds. “These would be additions to major collections that are quite significant. With those two things in mind, I’m still very optimistic.”
Phillips expects to bring in between $80.4m and 128.7m in New York this month, with its auctions led by Amedeo Modigliani’s limestone sculpture Tête (1911-12), estimated to sell for between $28m and $35m after having been in the same private collection for more than 50 years.
Bonhams estimates it will sell at least $40m worth of art in November in New York, with most of that total coming from a collection of five fresh-to-market Constantin Brâncuși bronzes that were held in the same private collection for decades after being acquired from the artist’s estate. Collectively, they are expected to fetch $25m.

The Palace of Westminster, which has housed the British Parliament since the thirteenth century, is at risk of a catastrophic fire if restoration work is not performed.
Dezeen reports that the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) has determined that maintenance costs for Parliament, a UNESCO World Heritage site, will rise from £1.5 million to £2 million a week if delays around the building’s renovation continue. The government voted in 2018 to vacate the structure for restoration, but disagreements about how fully the House of Commons and House of Lords should leave during the potential decades-long renovation has suspended the work.
Two strategies have been recommended. PAC has asked MPs either to decamp fully from the building while the project is carried out—expected to take up to twenty-four years and cost up to £15.6 billion—or to “decant” gradually, which would result in the renovations taking sixty-one years with a cost up to £39.2 billion. Either option requires the approval of parliament.
“All options ahead involve extremely high figures with very big ranges,” PAC chair Geoffrey Clifton-Brown said. “At a time of national fiscal constraint, we would expect the parliamentary authorities to examine these figures extremely carefully to see how they can be reduced before the vote.”
Clifton-Brown warns, however, that current fire risks could result in “Notre Dame-like flames” at the Gothic Revival-style palace, which was assessed to be at “constant risk of fire” in 2023. “Consider the impact of global rolling news footage of Notre Dame-like flames licking out of the building’s roof,” Clifton-Brown said, “resulting in the destruction of our heritage, or worse, injuries or loss of life.”
According to the Guardian, ongoing maintenance to the Gothic Revival Palace has barely held at bay myriad issues: Leaking roofs; crumbling masonry protected by a maze of scaffolding; and a persistent risk outdated electronics causing a fire, necessitating round-the-clock fire patrols.

Big-box retailers jack up the price of goods between the time you set foot in the parking lot to when you get to the shopping aisle. Airline companies mine your personal data so they can squeeze as much fare money from you as possible. A grocery delivery app used what they called "price rounding" to arbitrarily increase the cost of a box of crackers by 23 percent. For-hire vehicle apps scrape your phones for reasons why you'd pay an extra $10 or $20 for a late-night ride home.
This kind of rotten, insidious, algorithm-boosted surveillance capitalism has become routine across most industries.
On Thursday, the City Council is expected to vote on a bill that aims to ban the practice in New York City.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: An expert guide to navigating the Fulton Center subway frankenstation
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Elizabeth Shwe, James Ramsay
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
This column originally appeared in the Looped In NYC newsletter. Sign up here.
Here’s a fun New York City puzzle: If a friend told you they were “getting off the train at Canal Street,” where exactly are they?
For a variety of reasons, it’s not uncommon for two or more subway stations to share the same name but not the same location. “Canal Street” is guilty of this, as is “86th Street” and “Wall Street.” And for much of the 20th century, “Fulton Street” was in that camp. (And it’s still true if you hop boroughs — there’s a Fulton Street station in Brooklyn.)
The Fulton Street 4/5 station came first, in 1905. Then the 2/3 station was built in 1918. The J/Z Fulton station opened in 1931. And finally, the A/C station arrived in 1933. By then, you had four stations, built and operated by three different train companies.
Fast forward to 2014, when the MTA — which has operated the city’s entire subway system since 1940 — opened the Fulton Center, one massive train hub that unifies all these lines and makes everything simpler. Except when it really doesn’t.
My Looped In co-host, Elizabeth Shwe, recently visited the eight-line, multi-level complex on a quest to cut through the confusion and become a Fulton Center super user.
She explains all the tips and tricks in this week's video, which you can watch here.
I had some questions of my own for her too:
James: Does the Fulton Center factor into your daily commute?
Elizabeth: Only when I have to transfer to the J/Z lines, which is unfortunate because the J/Z lines are the hardest to find. That’s because the J and Z platforms were built stacked on top of each other because Nassau Street they’re under is so narrow.
So, you really have to be careful and take the right stairs to get to the correct J/Z platform. My tip is to start on the A/C platform. If you want to go to the Brooklyn- and Queens-bound J/Z trains, you have to take one of the staircases closer to the west side, where you see a connection to the 4 and 5 trains. If you want to go the Broad Street bound J/Z trains, you have to take one of the staircases closer to the eastern 2 and 3 train side.
Another thing that trips people up: Unlike the rest of the lines at Fulton, the “Downtown” J/Z trains do not take riders to Brooklyn — those lines end at Broad Street. If you want to get to Brooklyn or Queens on those lines, you need to take an uptown train.
I once had a meltdown here trying to find the Brooklyn-bound J train. I kept ending up on the Broad street bound platform … which only takes you farther into the Financial District. That mix-up motivated me to study up on this cursed station.
James: Is the short answer to “why is this so confusing?” that the MTA combined three separate train lines into one superstation, and there’s only so much they move around
Elizabeth: Exactly. Fulton Center we know today is actually four separate subway stations built by three separate train companies at different times. Jodi Shapiro, a curator at the Transit Museum, told me that train companies didn’t want to make it easy for a commuter to transfer to a competitor line, which explains why the transfers feel so awkward.
And the Financial District has some of the oldest and most narrow city streets that twist and turn in ways that other parts of the Manhattan grid doesn’t, which meant train companies were pretty limited in where and how wide they could construct their subway lines. That explains why each subway line sits under different streets at different depths.
All those stations were pushed under one roof when Fulton Center opened in 2014.
James: I’ll admit I had never been to the Fulton Center until you told me about this project. It just never fit the patterns of how I move about town. But I took an inconvenient route one morning this week just to pass through, and my main takeaway was that there’s a Dunkin’ Donuts on one of the lower levels, but don’t fall for it; there’s a Krispy Kreme a couple levels up, if you’re willing to hike.
Elizabeth: Great tip, because I only saw the Dunkin' Donuts, since it’s on the first floor where you pass to get to the other subway stations.
James: Okay back to getting around: At some point I thought I was exiting through a turnstile and was confused when it didn't let me pass. Then I realized that somehow I had already left the subway system and needed to tap again to get back in. Is that a common mistake, or was I just not paying attention?
Elizabeth: You wouldn't know this if you don’t commute here often. Even though you can technically walk from Fulton Center to the World Trade Center station completely underground, it’s not a free transfer. So if you need to get to the E, R or W lines, expect to exit through a turnstile and pay the fare again.
James: What else should I know before returning?
Elizabeth: To me, the most confusing part of Fulton Center is that instead of the traditional mezzanine being the connection point to all transfers like at many other big stations, the A/C platform is usually a better place to orient yourself. My biggest tip is to think of the A/C platform as the backbone of the station. The J/Z platforms sit at their own levels and cut through the mezzanines, so going from the 4/5 trains to the 2/3 means heading down to the A/C platform, walking its length, and coming back up.
That means you might have to walk through a platform for a train you aren’t taking in order to get to the line you’re trying to ride.
James: You talked with people who’ve made 3D maps of the Fulton Center, do you look at one of those and think, "ah, I get it now?”
Elizabeth: Yes, they really did help! You can lose your orientation easily just walking up and down stairs and walking down the long corridor. But seeing a 3D map made it easy for me to conceptualize that the A/C platform is perpendicular to all the other lines, so it’s helpful to think of the A/C platform as your homebase where you can get to any transfer.
James: Is there anything else the MTA could do, in your opinion, to make it easier to navigate? Or is it one of those things where you as a commuter put in the work to really learn it, and then you get to feel smug about it, which every New Yorker loves?
Elizabeth: One suggestion for the MTA is to put a version of 3D maps and a “you are here” sign that may help people better situate themselves. Or even placing stickers on the floors pointing to the right direction for each different transfer.
But when I visited Fulton Center again, I noticed there’s plenty of signage, and they’re technically correct. It’s just that you have to stop and read them carefully.
When I reached out to the MTA about how confusing Fulton Station is to some commuters, they told me signage is present throughout the station and reminded me that there are station agents posted throughout the complex outside of the booths to help confused commuters.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/israeli-elec.title: Self-Determination Is the Core Palestinian Demand
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/israeli-elec.author: Bashir Abu-Manneh, Ryan Tfaily
