Self-Determination Is the Core Palestinian Demand
In Israel’s recent elections, Palestinians in Israel voted in unprecedented numbers — using one of the last remaining means at their disposal to challenge Israeli Jewish politics.
- Interview by
- Ryan Tfaily
The parliamentary elections held in Israel on October 27 failed to produce a bloc with the sixty-one seats required to govern on its own. Although it remains in the lead, Benjamin Netanyahu’s camp has fallen from sixty-eight to fifty-three seats, while the opposition, led by Gadi Eisenkot, has made gains but secured only forty-eight seats. The two Palestinian lists achieved a historic breakthrough, winning nineteen seats, thanks to an unprecedented mobilization of Palestinian citizens of Israel. Coalition negotiations remain deadlocked, however, as the opposition is reluctant to accept any form of cooperation with the Palestinian parties.
How should these results be understood at a time when the genocide in Gaza and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank are ongoing. and as Benjamin Netanyahu and Donald Trump threaten to resume a regional war? Bashir Abu-Manneh, the author of Disposable Palestinians: Israel’s War and Genocide in Gaza, sees these elections as reflecting Israel’s supremacist nature. He argues that militarism and the shift to the right are long-term phenomena that extend far beyond electoral cycles.
- Ryan Tfaily These elections were marked by historically high turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel. How can this mobilization be explained, and what are the two main political currents representing this community?
- Bashir Abu-Manneh The main reason is a strong political desire to bring down Netanyahu’s government, the most right-wing in Israeli history, and to punish it for several things: First, for its genocidal war and total destruction of Gaza and for its intensifying colonization of the West Bank, which is undergoing “Gazafication” as we speak. Second, for its endless attacks on collective Palestinian life. Third, for its racism, contempt, and systematic humiliation of Palestinians, and for the consolidation of fascist norms in Israel. These are usually referred to as Kahanist, following their most extreme Jewish fundamentalist proponent, Meir Kahane, who was banned from running for the Knesset for his extremist views — views that have now been normalized in Israel by Netanyahu’s government. There are also more specific factors related to Palestinian society inside Israel: house demolitions by the state, destruction of communities in the Naqab (Negev), Israel’s effective encouragement of crime and mafia killings of hundreds of Palestinians a year, and the deep sense of lawlessness this produces by forcing small businesses and professionals to pay protection money and subjecting them to extortion (a deliberate policy advanced by Itamar Ben-Gvir as minister of national security). As a result, there is a deep sense of fear and social uncertainty that is compounded by daily incitement and violence against Palestinians in the Israeli labor market, whether they are doctors, nurses, or bus drivers. Some commentators in Israel have openly blamed Ben-Gvir and his endless provocations against Palestinians for their high turnout in the elections. But he’s in reality a crude symptom of government-wide policies. October 7 also generated a clampdown against political organization, demonstrations, and free speech as part of a policy of delegitimizing Palestinians in Israel — which, most recently, led to the disqualification of Sami Abu Shehadeh from running for the Knesset. In this ultrarepressive context, the act of voting became the only remaining mode of political expression for Palestinians. First, to affirm Palestinian presence and belonging in their own homeland, however twisted are the means of doing it as second-class citizens in a state that excludes them by its basic laws and definitions. Palestinians resoundingly said to Israeli Jews: we are here, we are going nowhere, and you must accept and adapt. Second, Palestinians understood the mathematics of voting. The more they come out to vote, the larger the number of votes needed by smaller extreme right-wing Jewish parties to meet the 3.25 percent electoral threshold for entering the Knesset, and the more likely they would block them. This succeeded. Weakening the right wing electorally is a Palestinian achievement. Third, Palestinians in Israel worry that they are next on the fascists’ list — that if Kahanist Smotrich and Ben-Gvir stay in power, they’ll make good on their promise of Judaizing the Galilee and the Naqab even more intensively, and that this will become a major part of new government policy. This is a realistic worry. Religious fundamentalist activism would have real adverse effects on Palestinian communities in terms of stealing their remaining lands, blocking their access to the labor market, and further degrading their livelihoods. Most Palestinians voted for either the Joint List or Ra’am. Let me briefly describe their main differences. The Joint List is a nationalist-left coalition of the Jabha (the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality), an Arab-Jewish left-wing formation closely associated with the Communist Party and led by Yousef Jabareen; Ta’al (the Arab Movement for Renewal) led by Ahmad Tibi; and Balad (the National Democratic Assembly) led by Sami Abu Shehadeh. Its broad platform has historically been to end the Israeli occupation of 1967 and push for equality in Israel. But because of wanting to halt the growing degradation of Palestinian life in Israel and to shoo out this extremist right-wing government, its campaign has focused on civic demands and its willingness to do everything in its power to end Netanyahu’s chaotic and dangerous reign. I do find the singular focus on Netanyahu a problem, though, because it could end up justifying compromises that are politically unacceptable. One should distinguish between blocking Netanyahu from continuing his Kahanist policy and actively supporting an opposition that, on most Palestinian national and on regional issues, is quite like him. There are limits to electoralism, and Palestinian politics in Israel cannot be reduced to influencing government civic policy at the expense of equal national and political rights. But those limits are not impediments for the second strand of Palestinian politics, Ra’am (the United Arab List led by Mansour Abbas). This religiously and socially conservative Palestinian strand in Israel has intentionally excluded the Palestinian question and collective national rights from its platform. I see it as a Palestinian “Shas,” the religious party that represents Mizrahi Jews. Like Shas, Ra’am has avidly joined Israel’s electoral horse-trading business, and all it seeks to get is funding and state budgets to spend on local constituencies, while also trying to address Palestinian civic concerns over crime and house demolitions. In an atmosphere of fear and shrunken political horizons, Ra’am’s shameless opportunism does get support precisely because it feeds on cynicism and narrow self-interest. But the price of its policy of wielding influence at any cost is a denationalization of Palestinians and the inflation of religion in civic and political life. To facilitate acceptance by Zionist parties in any future government negotiation, Abbas has also appointed a Jewish Zionist legislator as number two on his list. This brazen maneuver, in which you compel your supporters to vote for a Zionist politician with a law enforcement background, just shows how low Abbas is ready to go for Zionist crumbs, all in the name of resolving the crime wave that the state itself has created.
- Ryan Tfaily Does the marginalization of Palestinian parties by the majority of the anti-Netanyahu bloc, alongside the fierce accusations leveled against them by the pro-Netanyahu bloc, not demonstrate the unequal nature of Israel’s political system?
- Bashir Abu-Manneh The hate campaign waged against the Palestinian parties is hardly surprising. Does anyone really believe that Israel is a normal liberal state? How can you, when ethnonational Jewish supremacy is codified as basic state law? You can see how the state has conducted itself since its forcible foundation in Palestine: dispossessing, expropriating, and denationalizing Palestinians. Even the requirements of eligibility to run for the Knesset (such as the prohibitions on rejecting Israel’s Jewish and democratic mantra and on supporting armed struggle by Israel’s enemies) are ideological and Zionist. Since Sami Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification from running for the Knesset, these criteria have evolved. It now also means writing one article that is deemed insensitive to Jewish feelings in Israel after October 7 and being uncritical of (rather than supporting) Palestinian armed struggle. I must say that I find Abu Shehadeh’s apologetic discourse in front of the Israeli Supreme Court to avoid disqualification unacceptable. It sets a very bad political precedent for the Palestinians in Israel. Here you have the leader of a Palestinian nationalist party apologizing for one article in which, even under Israel’s restrictive laws, nothing illegal is said. Abu Shehadeh did so in front of the same judges who have aided and abetted Israel’s genocide in Gaza and its brutal occupation policies for decades. Since Abu Shehadeh insisted on going to the court when the outcome was preordained, what he should have done was use the global limelight to expose Israel’s crimes of conduct and the court’s own pathetic clampdown on one speech act in an era of Israeli state genocide and rife genocidal incitement. Let’s be clear: Israel is a democratically racist state — what David Ben-Gurion called during the days of Jewish labor-led colonization “a dictatorship of the Hebrew worker.” Winning seats in its house of representatives does not change its basic ethnonational character. Embarrassing it by saying “look, it is not a liberal democracy” is missing the point. What the Palestinians in Israel have achieved by voting in unprecedented numbers in these elections (close to 80 percent) is using one of the last remaining means at their disposal to challenge Israeli Jewish politics and push for change. The pressure should now be on the Israeli Jewish opposition to develop a new policy toward Palestinians that doesn’t compel them to deny who they are as a ticket of entry. Eyes should be on Israel’s opposition to do better than running on a ticket that denies Palestinian rights and affirms Jewish supremacy and apartheid. This is a longer process than one election. But the Palestinians have made a huge contribution to it by teaching Israeli Jews a lesson in real democracy.
- Ryan Tfaily How would you describe the areas of convergence and divergence between the anti-Netanyahu and pro-Netanyahu blocs regarding policy in Gaza and the West Bank, and, more broadly, regional issues (Lebanon, Syria, Iran, and the Abraham Accords)?
- Bashir Abu-Manneh For any progressive or democrat, this is the real problem. The opposition shares the government’s extremist agenda over national security, the key issue in Israel. The differences are marginal, though not insignificant for Palestinians inside Israel over crime and civic peace or for how the legacy of the 1967 conflict with Palestinians is managed. Let’s take some examples. Gadi Eisenkot (the leader of the largest opposition party, Yashar) is the ex-head of the army and author of the Dahiya doctrine, which is the deliberate targeting of civilians in an indiscriminate and disproportionate way as collective punishment for acts committed by militants and in violation of international law. Eisenkot ran on a ticket of personal integrity, national and personal sacrifice (his soldier son and two soldier nephews died fighting in Gaza), and a state inquiry into October 7. His campaign was strong in emphasizing Netanyahu’s failure to provide security to Israelis and his being unfit to lead Israel. Yet his views on Iran, Gaza, the West Bank, and the region are hawkish and basically like Netanyahu’s. The one main difference is epitomized in his vocal criticism of soldier Elor Azaria’s conduct back in 2016 for killing a wounded and immobilized Palestinian militant in cold blood with a bullet to the head. In addition, in the context of what some army leaders see as settler rioting and disorder in the West Bank (in which army commanders also participate), Eisenkot believes in the sole right of the Israeli army to injure and kill Palestinians. This statist emphasis also pertains to settlement policy, which, Eisenkot believes, should be less chaotic, provocative, and friction-seeking, and should be organized by the state. During his campaign, he did thus suggest that he would clamp down on Jewish settler terror in the West Bank (rather than fueling it like the Netanyahu government) and that he would rein in the settlers. What he doesn’t support is changing the fundamental character of the occupation or granting Palestinians any rights beyond disaggregated and autonomous enclaves under Israeli sovereignty. In Gaza, Eisenkot is committed to achieving Israel’s war aims, which he shares with Netanyahu, and destroying Hamas. In essence, that means more war and more risk of expulsion and forcible removal for the Palestinians. This policy is supported by other opposition figures like Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid, and Avigdor Lieberman — who plan to continue Israel’s genocidal policy in Gaza. Most opposition parties have also voted in the Knesset against establishing a Palestinian state. No doubt removing Ben-Gvir as a government minister would alleviate the daily torture of Palestinians in Israeli prisons, who are subject to a cruel regime of repression, punishment, and systematic health degradation. An opposition government might, thus, take the extreme edge off some of Israel’s post–October 7 practices while sustaining the underlying state policies that would still constitute a threat to the existence of Palestinians in their homeland.
- Ryan Tfaily Likud remains Israel’s largest party, and Netanyahu’s bloc has held its ground despite losing seats. What is the sociological composition of the Likud electorate, and how can we explain this enduring loyalty to Benjamin Netanyahu despite the various legal cases in which he is involved?
- Bashir Abu-Manneh Likud has cannibalized its right-wing partners as the bloc shrank from sixty-eight to fifty-three seats. Without scalping support from the opposition camp, Likud cannot secure the sixty-one seats needed to form a government. The basis of its support is peripheral towns and communities across the country where it receives a significant percentage of the vote (with a higher percentage among non-Ashkenazi Jews). Likud voters are quite tribal. Support for the party by economically marginalized communities is rewarded by transfers of state funds for investment and development. Settlements also play an economic role here in providing cheap land, mortgages, and handouts in ’67-occupied areas. But you cannot discount the effect of Likud’s anti-Arab racism that succeeds in inciting hatred and contempt for Arabs precisely because they are seen as competitors with Mizrahim over jobs in the labor market. If the heyday of the Labor Party gave a more Ashkenazi and kibbutz aura to the state, Likud has changed that by being the political home of marginalized Mizrahim who need state support and remain tribally loyal to the party. Netanyahu’s Likud thus aims to protect Mizrahim from the exact same neoliberal policies it institutes. An economic dependency sits at the base of this electoral loyalty as neoliberalism is alleviated by Israeli colonialism. Israeli historian Guy Laron makes this link in a recent Catalyst piece.
- Ryan Tfaily In your latest book, Disposable Palestinians, you use the concept of “disposability” as a key analytical framework to describe the restructuring of the Israeli colonial regime in the aftermath of the Oslo Accords. How do you explain, over the long term, the dehumanization of Palestinians within Israeli society and the broader rightward shift of Israeli society?
- Bashir Abu-Manneh To put it briefly, the Oslo deal and regime produced an economically disposable Palestinian population living under Israeli occupation. Palestinians were cut out of Israel as cheap labor and subjected to closure and curfew. Separation was also merged with continued domination and colonization. In a word, Israel in Oslo transformed Palestinians from being exploited black South Africans to dispensable Native Americans, weakening their leverage to challenge their subordination. I chart this development through the concept of disposability and its intensifying forms in colonization, warfare, and genocide. Since 2000, the Israeli army has turned the Oslo process into a war process against the Palestinians and has unleashed one war after another, not just to crush Palestinian society but also to discipline Israelis and return them to the war mentality of 1948. This has succeeded. Since then, Israel’s wars have had overwhelming support in Israeli Jewish society, up to horrific percentages of 95 or 96 percent. War thus turns Palestinians from being economically disposable to being morally disposable and a killable population, a process culminating in the Gaza genocide. The question of the moral disposability of Palestinians is an important one. The Israeli army, in its increasingly permissive rules of engagement, fueled the killing of civilians as a deliberate policy. In the eyes of Israeli soldiers from 2000 onward, Palestinians became people to be killed with impunity — mainly because of the way the army organized war by systematically offloading its costs from Israeli soldiers to Palestinian civilians. You must step back and imagine what this does not only to a conscript army but to the society it returns to and calculate its effect generationally. It boosts Jewish supremacy and ethnic narcissism in Israel and consolidates the fundamentalist, rightward shift of Israeli society. Palestinians become unpeople, less than human. Come the catalyst of October 7, Palestinians become mass-killable now. I spend time on explaining the roots, catastrophic nature, and effects of October 7 and the genocide that has followed.
- Ryan Tfaily The religious-nationalist parties led by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich have also retained seats. How can we explain the rise of this messianic current in Israeli society, and should we expect it to grow in the coming years, particularly among young people?
- Bashir Abu-Manneh This is another big story: the growing power of religious Zionism as a direct outcome of the 1967 occupation and its colonization project. Bezalel Smotrich and the Iraqi-descended Ben-Gvir represent a new strain of activist, messianic Zionism that is openly fascist. It advances settlement expansion and wars, utilizes the state to promote settler interests, and actively turns Palestinians into unwelcome guests in their own homeland. The message to the Palestinians is that everything in Eretz Yisrael belongs to the Jews (even your olive trees), and that Israeli Jews are overlords who must be obeyed. Because of Netanyahu (and Bennett before him), this worldview is now a core part of Israel’s governing bloc, and it advances extremely aggressive policies against the Palestinians — seeking their dispossession, annihilation, and expulsion. To survive politically, and because he believes this ideology, Netanyahu has played a crucial role in boosting religious nationalist power and its hold over state ministries, including the economy, security, and the civil administration of the West Bank. In fact, he has turned the Likud into a Kahanist party that utilizes its rule to instill authoritarian norms in Jewish society and to undermine the rule of law. Indeed, to stay in power (and to resolve his own personal legal problems), Netanyahu has unleashed a judicial overhaul that is a cover for his increasingly thuggish rule. There is no doubt that Netanyahu is Israel’s most successful Machiavellian politician and a global master in cynical manipulation. Everything is twistable in his acrobatics for power.
- Ryan Tfaily Benjamin Netanyahu has severely damaged Israel’s image abroad, first among public opinion and then, gradually, among certain European leaders. In the event of a change of government, should we expect a recalibration of Israeli policy toward its allies? What implications would this have for the emerging international pressure on Israel?
- Bashir Abu-Manneh Yes. But that is no reason not to wish him out. My perspective here is that there are benefits that are not insignificant to his departure from government, and that wishing him to stay because Israel might be worse off in international public opinion is perverse. It ignores the costs for Palestinians of his continued rule. If he stays, worsening conditions are guaranteed and will constitute an existential emergency for Palestinians, both those occupied in 1967 and made citizens in 1948. This outcome is not a guarantee with Eisenkot. And some of his statements seem to acknowledge the fact that Palestinian presence, though not national, should be accepted. He might also be more susceptible to external pressure and might stymie the rabid, messianic forces that did everything to prolong the war and genocide in Gaza — the reason why he himself left Netanyahu’s war cabinet in June 2024. European state behavior might also be more susceptible to the growing support for the Palestinian cause in the West. It is, therefore, not just up to Israeli politics. The US November midterms are a good example. They might well be more consequential in determining Israel’s regional behavior than its own internal politics. My fear is that war on Iran will resume, with Israel joining in again, and that this becomes an occasion for a national unity government in Israel, thus prolonging Netanyahu’s reign. Netanyahu is hoping for that. He’s great at running forward to resolve contradictions. This might be a good chance for him to come out of the stalemate of the elections and hope for a better chance at victory down the line. His sole aim is to stay in power and advance his agenda. Another round with Iran is a good opportunity to increase his support. But that depends on the Trump administration, where the Iran file sits. Because of its regional ramifications for US dominance and primacy, Iran is not and never has been in Israel’s own hands to determine for itself. To think otherwise is to believe the Israel Lobby twists and distorts American policy against US interests — which has no empirical basis. The Iran issue is not the Palestinian issue, where the US is only ever keen to support and protect its ally. To read US Mideast policy through the Palestine prism is to misread it, as the Palestinians have no strategic significance for the United States, nor a Strait of Hormuz to leverage regionally and globally. That is why Donald Trump endorsed Netanyahu: to tell the Iranians that a bigger blow is in the cards. Even though the attack on Iran has broad support across the Israeli political spectrum, it is indelibly connected with Netanyahu and is seen as Bibi’s baby. Trump knows what it means to endorse him now.
- Ryan Tfaily Since change is not going to come through these elections, what would it take to make a peace based on justice possible?
- Bashir Abu-Manneh The challenges for anyone seeking justice and peace are massive. I’ll name two. First, to roll back Israel’s permanent war society and disposition to use force at every opportunity. That should involve an Israeli opposition, for example, that argues for shrinking the army in Israeli national life, not one doing the opposite and seeking to recruit ultra-Orthodox Jews to the army (who are vehemently against that proposal) in the name of the equal sharing of the national burden. You cannot want peace and continue to increase army conscription and army budgets. To end Israel’s wars, you must weaken the Israeli army’s hold on society. After all, Israel is the most militarized society in the world. The only way to get there is through the second issue I want to raise: the occupation. The lever to changing Israel as a settler-colonial state and forcing on it a new political reality is ending the occupation of the West Bank and Gaza. It is by activating the new and enormously significant International Court of Justice decision on the illegality of Israel’s occupation. To restore international legality, numerous forms of sanctions against the Israeli state should be activated, as the court states. It must also involve a new Palestinian liberation struggle that puts democratic mobilization at the heart of the confrontation with Israel. To get there, catastrophic Palestinian elite failures like indiscriminate violence and subservient negotiations in contravention of international law must end, precisely because they accelerate rather than stem disposability. The Palestinian struggle after the Gaza genocide is a long one that involves essentially rebuilding the Palestinian national movement from scratch. By putting Palestinian politics everywhere on a new democratic foundation and activating huge assets like international law and global solidarity, the aim is to overcome today’s national emergency and end Palestinian disposability in Palestine. What is now clear is that the nature of Israel must change structurally to allow for Palestinian self-determination. Self-determination (upheld by the International Court of Justice decision and international law) is the core Palestinian demand that should sit at the center of both Palestinian and global solidarity politics. Anything else is simply a distraction. Or worse, it could undercut effective political work and prolong Palestinian disposability.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Newark Museum of Art restores ownership of David Drake jug to artists’ descendants
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Eileen Kinsella
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
This past summer, the Newark Museum of Art in New Jersey initiated a dialogue with the family of David Drake (around 1801-74), the enslaved potter from South Carolina, regarding a large brown ceramic jug in its collection, dated 1852. Just a few months later—lightning speed in museum time—The Art Newspaper has learned that the institution has reached an agreement with Drake’s heirs to restore ownership of the work and purchase it back for its permanent collection.
The arrangement comes just over a year after the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston reached an historic agreement with Drake’s family to return two major stoneware vessels, one of which the museum purchased back. Momentum built from there and return agreements were reached with institutions including the Telfair Museums in Savannah and the Georgia Museum of Art in Athens, Georgia, the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts, and others.
“What happened this July was really special,” says George Fatheree, an adviser to the Drake family. A letter the Newark Museum sent to the artist’s descendants and shared with The Art Newspaper states: “We acquired a jug by your ancestor in 2022 to help us more powerfully teach the history of enslavement and enslaved labour, as part of the 2023 reimagining and reinstallation of our American art galleries, Seeing America: 18th and 19th Century.” Noting the MFA Boston partnership, the museum extended the opportunity to meet and “identify ways we might collaborate”.
According to Lisa Funderburke, the Newark Museum’s director and chief executive, it was the museum’s senior director of registration and collections management, Amber Germano, who first approached her over the summer and asked if she would be willing to sign a letter.
“It’s not uncommon for curators to visit my office with a stack of papers of things that are either for consideration or ongoing engagement on articles of repatriation,” Funderburke says. “Always my first question is: ‘Can you articulate to me what we’re doing here and what the impulse behind that is?’”
According to Yaba Baker, one of Drake’s fourth great-grandsons, Funderburke credited her staff with the initial action. “Lisa understood immediately what needed to be done,” Baker says. “One thing my family all agreed on: Dave is such a powerful figure in art history and Black history that to take the pots out of public view would be a disservice.”
Things moved quickly after that, with additional family meetings and Funderburke’s conversations with board members and other leaders at the museum. “I felt like this would be a strong north star for our board about where we are and where we want to be, and position ourselves as a museum into the future,” the director says.
After the museum commissioned several appraisals of the ceramic vessel, a value of around $135,000 was decided on. Numerous Drake pots have sold for five- and six-figure prices; the current record at auction for one of his works is the $1.65m paid for his 25-Gallon Poem Jar (1858), achieved at Crocker Farm Auctions in Maryland in 2021.
“Our approach is this should not be a zero-sum game,” Fatheree says, describing the outcome in Newark as a “win-win”.
Baker concurs, stressing the enduring lessons of Drake’s legacy. “He was a slave. He was considered three fifths of a person by the US constitution,” Baker says, adding that anti-literacy laws in South Carolina at the time forbade teaching enslaved people to write.
“For our family, it’s telling the story of someone who was considered by a lot of people to be nothing, but he conducted himself with such excellence,” Baker says, before quoting a famous inscription Drake wrote on another of his vessels that begins, “I wonder where is all my relation”, and concludes: “Friendship to all.”

Never Let Trump’s Elite Enablers Forget What They’ve Done
Universities, scientists, law firms, and many other powerful institutions are about to start pretending they never rolled over for the president. But we know better.
Just before sunrise on the day after the midterm elections last week, progressive journalist Walker Bragman posted this: “Many people, institutions, and companies sacrificed their integrity because they thought Trump’s power grab was inevitably going to succeed and he’d be the American Orban. Don’t forget their names.”
Bragman is right. One of the most remarkable, and despicable, things about the last two years is how many so institutions—the law firms, the tech companies, the universities, the august scientific and professional societies—swiftly, completely, and indeed eagerly “obeyed in advance.” Meanwhile, ordinary Americans with much less money and power were left to both shoulder the burden of the attacks from the Trump administration and lead the resistance to those attacks.
If the midterms showed us the resolve and determination of the American people, the preceding two years demonstrated the fecklessness, cowardice, and selfishness of American elites—many of whom would frankly do anything to remain “on top,” even if it meant bowing down to fascists. These folks are a portrait of “upper-middle‐class decadence” straight out of Bertolucci’s The Conformist. They are a type that always rises up under authoritarianism— not so much true believers as true opportunists—and they always survive, no matter whom they step on in their rush for the exits when things go badly.
I’ve written many times about these acts of collaboration, large and small, over the past two years. But in the wake of the drubbing that the Republicans took last week, it’s worth reviving the greatest hits of appeasement, now that these truly bad choices made by so many are running up against the sunshine of a new day.
As a university scientist, watching the decay of American science, public health, and higher education up close has been painful. The entire infrastructure of these sectors is so damaged and compromised that, even with a new Congress and potentially a Democrat in the White House in 2028, we will be digging out of this mess for decades to come.
But the collaborators who helped create this crisis engender a whole set of other feelings: scorn, disgust, anger. Now that Trump is headed toward political oblivion, get ready for them to tell us how they were always against this, trying to do their part, to ingratiate and rehabilitate themselves with the rest of us—and don’t believe a word of it.
When I think back to November 2024, I still remember my shock when two political scientists at Princeton with no expertise or experience in biomedical research, Frances Lee and Stephen Macedo, penned an over-the-top encomium pushing for Jay Bhattacharya to run the National Institutes of Health, claiming he would bring: “a strong dose of fresh thinking and institutional reform from experts prepared to challenge the reigning consensus and renew our commitment to the basic values of science and liberalism.” Ahem. No. Now, as the NIH sits as a smoking husk of its former self, I wonder if they have even an ounce of buyer’s remorse. Not likely. And even within public health, we had people making craven pronouncements to keep themselves in the story. “I think @MartyMakary at FDA, @DrOz at CMS and @DrJBhattacharya at NIH are all pretty reasonable,” tweeted former dean of the Brown University School of Public Health Ashish Jha weeks after Trump’s reelection. Ahem. No. Again.
Then, I think of people who cozied up to MAHA influencers as if they were tribunes of the people. Some were just making a buck with their Substacks and podcasts by blaming public health. Outlets like Why Should I Trust You propped up purveyors of vaccine misinformation like RFK Jr.’s bestie Del Bigtree and gave a platform to people like Bret Weinstein who have fantasized about hanging public health officials. As writer and podcaster Michael Hobbes snarkily said:
The argument is always the same: rather than judge MAHA supporters on what they do, we should judge them on what they say. This is dangerously uninformed about how conspiracy movements work…. the second MAHA took power it started gutting basic science, promoting quack treatments and loosening health regulations. *This* is what the movement is. Yet it’s up to critics not to conclude or predict anything from these actions and bend over backward to find common cause.… It’s not the anti-science movement’s fault that public opinion has shifted against public health, it’s the public health authorities they’re constantly lying about!
Others took bad-faith MAHA arguments at their word, and became credulous to a fault, which sent them into the embrace of the indefensible. Despite wanting to maintain that MAHA wasn’t all bad, they elided the fact that the single most reliable indicator of supporting the MAHA movement is political affiliation, and identification with the MAGA movement most of all.
Then, think about the champions of free speech and expression on university campuses—as long as that speech doesn’t involve discussions of race, gender, or sexuality, and anything they might consider “woke.” These are the denizens of the heterodox academy, the good ol’ boys touting viewpoint diversity for me, not for thee. I remember one academic at Harvard writing to me after the abrupt removal of Mary Bassett, the university’s director of the FXB Center for Human Rights. He wondered where economist Larry Summers, psychologist Steven Pinker, and law professor Alan Dershowitz and the Harvard Council on Academic Freedom had disappeared to during this show trial for a physician who had devoted her life to the improvement of health for the most vulnerable, run the health departments in New York City and New York State, and worked for the Rockefeller and Doris Duke Foundations over a long, distinguished career. Not a peep. Because, of course, under the guise of championing fundamental rights, they were simply protecting their own, not others they considered expendable. It made them little different from the Trump administration officials attacking universities around diversity, equity, and inclusion, yet no one called them out as they used their seniority in academia as a shield for their behavior.
Finally, here at Yale, where I teach, students, faculty, alumni, and staff are locked in a battle with an administration and set of trustees who have been absolutely unwilling to talk about the decay of the rights to free speech and assembly on campus, the erosion of academic freedom, and the long game of footsie they’ve been playing with the Trump Department of Justice over admissions policies.
Yale decided at the start of the Trump administration that appeasement was the play to make. The university clamped down on protests; issued a self-flagellating report on trust that mirrored conservative critiques of higher education, which was praised by none other than Secretary of Education Linda McMahon; took down resources on DEI and anti-racism from its website devoted to a five-year campaign on Belonging at Yale; and changed the names of DEI and disability offices to ones that were more palatable in the political climate of the day.
While the president of the university and the trustees stonewall their own community, they constantly maintain the need for open dialogue on difficult topics on campus. It is a doublespeak that is just shocking to watch and reflects an unvarnished disdain for everyone here. Like the good old boys at Harvard, Yale leaders see everyone but themselves and big-name donors as incidental to their mission and the success of the university. Students, faculty, alumni, and staff are treated as a set of irritants, as a recent hot-mic episode with the president and the dean of Yale College exposed.
So what are we supposed to do now? The first thing is: write it down. We’ll soon be awash in revisionist history, or rather, as the historian Henry Rousso calls it, “historical negationism,” where the past is deliberately distorted for contemporary ends. So again: Just keep the receipts. They are the primary sources for truth-telling. No detail is too small. And as Bragman says: Don’t forget.
Long after Trump is history, you’ll run into people who will be all too happy not to have tales of their capitulation restated, rehearsed again and again. It’s what they depend on, so they can slip into new roles, without any consequences or accountability. And yes, the country will move on; it’s a national pastime to sweep things under the rug.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
But the election last week was about more than science, public health, and higher ed, the arenas in which I spend most of my time. While it may have been “the affordability election,” it also showed that the pillars on which Trump’s political empire rests—like democratic backsliding, white supremacy, and Christian nationalism—can be toppled. As conservative New York Times columnist David French, said, it was the Ozymandias election too, and for all his inflated aspirations, Trump’s legacy is dust.
Repairing science, public health, and higher education requires that we make this so, as so much of the motivation for what Trump has done to our fields is tied straight to these noxious underpinnings of his movement. It thus points us to a more fundamental mission tied to the future of a fair, multiracial democracy in America. It connects scientists, clinicians, and academics to those fighting for democracy in the US. It calls us towards the need for what my Yale colleague and fellow Nation correspondent the Rev. Dr. William J. Barber II has called a Third Reconstruction in America, and what he has called a moral policy agenda for this country.
As I watched election returns in my hotel room in San Antonio, Texas, last week, tears streamed down my face, from relief and from joy. I have no doubt that the fight has only begun and that difficult times are still ahead, but the size and scope of the rout shows that something else is possible. Even in places that seemed locked into the past, from Texas to Mississippi, from Kansas to Georgia, change is afoot. We have to do our part to keep it going, not simply for science, public health, and education’s sake but for our shared humanity and the future of this planet.

Wolfgang Tillmans has been named the winner of this year’s Henri Cartier-Bresson Lifetime Achievement Award. The award coincides with the Paris Photo fair, which opened today. Tillmans was recognized for his “outstanding contribution to the photographic medium.”
The German photographer is known for his intimate documentation of youth culture, first coming to prominence in the early 1990s. Tillmans previously won the Turner Prize in 2000, and was the first photographer and non-British artist to do so. His work is ubiquitous, appearing not only on album covers by artists like Frank Ocean and the Pet Shop Boys, but also in major retrospectives at the Tate Modern and the Centre Pompidou. Recently, his work has also appeared on the covers of books by the political theorist Anton Jäger and the novelist Vincenzo Latronico.
Tillmans is the third recipient of the Henri Cartier-Bresson Lifetime Achievement Award, following Sophie Calle and Susan Meiselas. In an interview with Ocula, Tillmans’s gallerist Maureen Paley said that he has “proven to be an impressive artist, visionary and thinker.” Tillmans shared in a video on Instagram that he is “very proud to be part of the lineage,” adding ”Even though I work in the larger field of contemporary art and my practice spans from installation to sound to video, it is almost always touching and centred around the lens, and photography is really at the heart of what I do.”
“I sometimes think I’m actually just taking pictures, doing it so others don’t have to, but that’s only half the truth,” he continued, “I get pleasure from the experimentation of ‘Can I take a picture of this? . . . Is it possible to take a picture of this?’ That is an ongoing challenge and that is never answered.”

https://gothamist.com/news/homeless-new-.title: Homeless New Yorkers’ healthcare costs plummeted after getting housed, study finds
https://gothamist.com/news/homeless-new-.author: Caroline Lewis
https://gothamist.com/news/homeless-new-.text:
An NYC Health and Hospitals initiative to help homeless patients find housing is paying off in the form of fewer emergency department visits and lower Medicaid costs, according to a new study by the public hospital system and its insurance subsidiary, MetroHealthPlus.
The study tracked Medicaid claims for 259 New Yorkers who received help finding apartments or supportive housing from NYC Health and Hospitals. Their healthcare costs dropped by an average of nearly $17,000 per person in the first two years after getting housed as they visited the ER and got admitted to the hospital less frequently, according to the study, conducted with the Wakely Consulting Group.
At the same time, the group’s spending on doctors’ visits and other non-emergency services such as substance use treatment increased, suggesting they were getting more preventive care.
The small study adds to a growing body of evidence suggesting that housing can help reduce emergency healthcare spending and utilization among people who were homeless, and comes as the city’s public hospital system continues to expand its housing efforts.
Under the Housing for Health Initiative, started by the Adams administration, the hospital system has been helping patients find permanent housing, while also using its land to build supportive housing developments and creating new transitional housing options for people leaving inpatient hospital stays who have nowhere to go.
“We have to think about our robust patient population that experiences homelessness,” said Leora Jontef, who leads NYC Health and Hospitals’ Housing for Health initiative. “This patient population is sicker than housed New Yorkers.”
NYC Health and Hospitals serves more than 60,000 patients a year who are homeless or unstably housed and many of them are what those in the healthcare field refer to as ‘frequent flyers’ — patients who visit the emergency department or get admitted for inpatient care over and over.
Among the study cohort, emergency department visits declined by about 40% in the first two years after getting housing placements, while inpatient stays dropped 36%.
The average number of days study participants spent in the hospital each year also got cut in half, dropping from an average of 10 days before finding housing to five days after being placed.
The biggest savings came from the decline in spending on inpatient care, which dropped from a monthly average of $1,278 per person before finding a housing placement to $492 during the first year of being housed.
The study also compared the cohort of newly housed patients with a group of New Yorkers enrolled in MetroHealthPlus who started out with similarly high levels of healthcare spending and utilization but remained homeless. Over time, healthcare costs for the group that received housing dropped below the group that did not.
However, healthcare spending among those that got housed was not lower than the broader homeless population enrolled in MetroHealthPlus overall, the study found.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ai-anthropic.title: The Real AI Misalignment Problem Is Capitalism
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ai-anthropic.author: Nick Couldry
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ai-anthropic.text:
The Real AI Misalignment Problem Is Capitalism
Figures at top AI firms says that their frontier models are running out of control. It points to a problem Big Tech finds harder to admit: the rise of a predatory computational power driven solely by profit-seeking.
This September, some rather technical issues regarding artificial intelligence, or rather their upshot, made headlines. The reason lay in two resignations from companies leading the development of frontier AI models, namely David Robinson, OpenAI’s Safety Officer, and Jacob Coxon, a developer at Anthropic. Each resigned because they no longer believed the companies were taking seriously the risks that frontier models’ recent “advances” pose to the survival of humanity. So, not just what most of us would call a “technical issue.”
Those fears were not hype. They were based on careful argument: a September 6 blog by Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, serves as an example. It’s worth looking more closely.
One fear the blog expressed was that frontier models are on the brink of “recursive self-improvement” (or RSI): the ability to take autonomous control over their future refinement. This could mean that, very quickly, humans lose all control over where advanced AI’s development is headed, even if it involves concentrations of computational power that by themselves pose a threat to human life.
Another fear — perhaps more alarming because the danger is already baked into our future, whatever decisions about future development are made now — is that Big Tech companies are fast losing the ability even to evaluate whether their current models (without RSI) are in fact aligned to the values they were designed to serve or aligned to completely different values that don’t serve human interests at all.
The reason for this second fear sounds technical. Until now, as Pachocki explains, OpenAI relied on assessing a model’s so-called chain-of-thought (CoT) to assess what that model was doing and with what values it was attempting to align. But, as Pachocki notes in chilling language: “Unfortunately our evaluations indicate [that] our ability to rely on chain-of-thought monitoring is progressively diminishing.” Why? Because out on the “frontier,” AI models are getting ever better at hiding what they are actually doing and the values that actually guide their processing, or at least are getting better at not revealing them in their CoT.
Luckily, in the case of OpenAI’s latest model, researchers at the UK’s AI Safety Institute were able to find alternative evidence of how the model was going rogue. But the issue goes far beyond technicalities. In simple terms, OpenAI has fashioned a machine that is now smart enough to undermine our belief in anything it tells us, because, as Pachocki puts it, AI is getting better at “manipulating its own reasoning process.”
In any reasonable world, that should be reason enough not just to halt further AI advances (that is, the rush to RSI) but to stop their current development, because we can no longer reliably align them to what humans need and want. Can it be scientific or even business “progress” when, as Pachocki coolly says, “progress in generalizable alignment may not sufficiently outstrip [technological] progress in general model intelligence”? And yet Pachocki’s blog did not call for a halt in AI development. He merely proposed that RSI should be “paced,” using words echoed by Dario Amodei of Anthropic. The reason given was economic competitiveness: RSI, Pachocki wrote, “is the only way to remain at the AI frontier.”
Admittedly, OpenAI concluded three weeks later that its GPT-6.1 Astra model, which had been slated for release as the public debate raged, should be pulled for now. Rather than just sighing with relief (and hoping for similar judgement calls when the pressure is even greater, say, on the eve of Anthropic’s mooted $2 trillion flotation), it’s more prudent to ask: What is the disease of which the reasoning of OpenAI’s chief scientist is the symptom?
The disease is capitalism or, more precisely, the inevitability of a profound misalignment with the broad goals of human life — including the basic goal of continued existence — when extraordinarily powerful computation is developed almost exclusively to serve economic ends: corporate profit, national economic competition, and abstract efficiency. This is the deeper misalignment problem that Big Tech can’t openly talk about: the conflict between a technological will to power always aligned to optimizing profit and a tolerable life for humans. Fail to confront this conflict as societies, and we guarantee that AI will become predatory on humanity’s future.
This is only the most dramatic way in which today’s commercially driven AI is becoming predatory on human life. Three other ways are also crucial.
The first is the most obvious: AI is predatory on human life by taking human-produced content (almost all of it) as the inputs to train its models. This data grab was clear almost from the start, and legal disputes with the cultural industries over copyright and compensation continue. Meanwhile, other forms of data grab have emerged: the exploitation of Global South workers to train AI’s early functioning and, most recently, the enticing of professionals (once privileged but now precarious) into literally showing specialist AI how, for example, medical reasoning works. The latter work can pay well until the AI has been trained, in which case the human expertise expended becomes redundant.
AI is predatory in a second, more subtle way: by shaping our habits of thought and imagination as we get better at prompting AI and start to reframe our questions about the world in forms that predictive text machines (that is, AI) are suited to answer.
And there is a third way in which, over time, predatory commercial AI threatens to capture the human mind: by changing our understanding of what intelligence is. We are progressively overvaluing the outputs of AI’s disembodied intelligence while progressively undervaluing our own embodied intelligence — and that of other sentient animals too. Behind this third form of capture lies a deep philosophical error going back to René Descartes, so that resisting the corporate capture of the human mind will require us to forge a different philosophical language from the one currently fashionable in Big Tech.
For now, though, the challenge is more immediate, and it absolutely cannot be left to those few brave insiders in Big Tech corporations willing to sacrifice their salaries to reveal the dangerous compromises their employers are making.
It is for workers in every workplace, and in every network of freelance workers, to start to assert their capacity to say no to commercially imposed AI. After all, the reason why AI is being forced on society so fast and with so little consultation is because, without widespread and deep adoption of their products, Big Tech corporations will never recoup their huge up-front investment and start making reliable profits.
Start seriously resisting commercial AI’s adoption and a different AI future becomes possible, as Evgeny Morozov has argued: a future where communities, rather than rejecting AI outright, start getting together to decide the social goals for which they might want to use AI, on what terms, when, and where. Clearly, for workers to claim such power to determine the direction of AI adoption, some radical changes will also be needed in how work institutions currently function.
But maybe realizing that is the start of a larger recognition of the unlivable contradiction that capitalism currently forces AI to inhabit. For sure, without the boldness to imagine radical alternatives, the outlook for the “AI era” is bleak.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Women finally start to get pride of place with central London sculptures
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Louisa Buck
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
London bristles with sculptures of men. Only 4% of public monuments in the city are devoted to named women, according to the charity Art UK. It says something about the national psyche that there are twice as many animal statues in the city as there are sculptures devoted to specific women. But right now a pair of radical new works depicting and made by women—Tschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue in Trafalgar Square, and Nicole Eisenman’s Stack outside the Royal Academy of Arts (RA) on Piccadilly—are making their presence powerfully felt in two of the most male-dominated locations in the capital.
In Trafalgar Square, surrounded by depictions of monarchs and militia and across from Admiral Nelson atop his 51m-high column, Self’s Lady in Blue painted bronze cuts a distinctive dash on the empty plinth to the northwest of the square that, since 1999, has hosted a programme of contemporary sculpture commissions. Head held aloft with her vivid blue dress clinging to her ample curves, she strides forth in high heels, exuding purposeful confidence and optimism. As with all Fourth Plinth sculptures, this impressive female will be in situ for two years, before going to a permanent home in Fornebu in Norway.
“She’s not an idol to venerate or a historic figure to commemorate, she’s an everyday young metropolitan woman much like those who use the square every day,” Self declared at the work’s unveiling, adding: “Lady in Blue is not static, she’s in motion… and I hope she inspires all who see her to find the optimism to move forward in community with all those around them.” In this spirit, Self sees her sculpture as an attempt to redress both racial and gender imbalance in public art whether in her native US, the UK or Norway. “In most cities there’s an underrepresentation of sculptures that depict women, and especially women of colour, so I think that it is important to add more images and visual representation,” she said.
Meanwhile, a few streets away outside the RA, which in 258 years has shown only two living women in its main galleries, New York-based Eisenman has erected Stack, a towering work at over 8m tall. This totem of figures and objects made from an assortment of materials, including bronze, oak, brass, steel, nylon, acrylic resin and tin, is currently having a friendly face-off with Alfred Drury’s grandiose bronze sculpture of Joshua Reynolds, the RA’s first president, who brandishes his paintbrush and easel just outside the main entrance. In 2021 Eisenman got to the shortlist for Trafalgar Square’s Fourth Plinth and now with Stack, she has created her own column, impressive in its scale and magnitude, but also irreverently anti-monumental.
Eisenman’s column
At its base hunches a craggy, androgynous figure shod in Birkenstocks and with a wooden barrel strapped to its back. A stand-in for the artist, perhaps, abject and emphatically earthbound, clutching not a paintbrush but an empty wine glass. On top of the barrel, rising out of a puddle of what looks like gooey melted cheese is a giant potato, over which lolls a rusty leonine cat modelled on Edie, Eisenman’s studio companion. Rather than a posturing war hero, Stack is topped off by the amiably smiling seated figure of the late artist Phyllida Barlow, rendered in gleaming sky-blue aluminium and jauntily balancing a vase of flowers on her head.
Barlow, who died unexpectedly in 2023, was a Royal Academician. Given where this work is situated, it is hard not to see Stack as a memorial to this much loved and greatly mourned artist. Eisenman is a huge admirer of Barlow, whose colossally ambitious but always defiantly anti-hubristic sculpture she first encountered when they were both in the Carnegie International in 2013. They subsequently became friends to the extent that an apparently amused Barlow went to Eisenman’s New York studio in 2022 to be 3D-printed for this work—“She was really good humoured about it,” Eisenman recalled in a recent talk at the Royal Institution. But while undoubtedly honouring Barlow, Stack is also more than a tribute to one person.
Eisenman is reluctant to offer specific interpretations but in her talk she revealed that the work was conceived with London in mind, declaring: “It’s amazing to me that it is at the RA. I hope it can stay in London.” She also stated that Stack emerged during the pandemic and forms a personal testament to when, as she put it, “life got pared down to the basics: food, wine, art, my cat”.
In strikingly different ways but with similar underlying intent, Stack and Lady in Blue offer alternative monuments to aspects of all our lives that rarely get acknowledged, and most notably the power of great women of all ages and from all origins. May we see more of their kind in all our cities.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: The Unpardonable Malpractice of Pete Hegseth
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Michael T. Klare
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The Unpardonable Malpractice of Pete Hegseth
Yes, the defense secretary has committed impeachable offenses. But he’s also just really, really, really bad at his job.
The offenses cited by Representative Thomas Massie (R-KY) in commencing impeachment proceedings against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth—that he initiated and sustained the war with Iran without required congressional approval, conducted military operations in Yemen and the Caribbean without such approval, and eroded protections for civilians trapped in overseas war zones—are all valid and fully justify his removal from office in accordance with constitutional precepts. But however worthy, they fail to capture his essential, unpardonable offense: strategic malpractice when commanding troops in battle.
Hegseth himself has been very outspoken about the need to cleanse the armed services of incompetent generals and admirals (many of whom, he claims, received their promotions as the result of some sort of affirmative action process) and to retain only those able to fight and win. “The previous administration wanted politically correct generals,” he told an assembly of junior officers on September 30. “We only want the top performing generals. It’s not just pass or fail…. The best move on, the worst do not.”
Secretary Hegseth wants us (and every member of Congress) to believe that he ranks among the successful generals and so should be retained. After berating Massie (“a disgruntled and defeated congressman”) and others during his unapologetic Pentagon press conference on November 10, Hegseth sought to defend his record as the ultimate commander of US forces. “By every measure,” he said of the war against Iran, “we achieved a historic military victory.”
But this is sheer fabrication. Were Hegseth to hold himself to the same high standards he supposedly set for his generals, he would have to say: “By every measure, we achieved a total fiasco in Iran,” and hand in his resignation.
To fully appreciate the magnitude of Hegseth’s incompetence, let’s recall the tasks he was assigned when ordered by President Trump to commence hostilities against Iran on February 28. As indicated by Trump in a prerecorded video address that morning, Hegseth was given four overriding objectives: (1) to eliminate, forever, Iran’s ability to construct a nuclear weapon; (2) to eliminate Iran’s ability to manufacture and launch long-range ballistic missiles; (3) to eliminate Iran’s ability to project power in the region, whether with its own military or via proxy forces like Hezbollah and the Houthi rebels; and (4) to eliminate the Iran problem altogether, by killing off Iran’s top leadership and igniting a popular rebellion.
Hegseth set out to achieve these goals with unrestrained vigor. The US military alone struck 13,000 targets in Iran during the first 38 days of fighting, and its Israeli partners struck many thousands more. From the administration’s perspective, it was a total win. In a press statement released on April 8, following the announcement of a ceasefire (that was to prove temporary), the White House declared that “the greatest fighting force the world has ever known has met those objectives with overwhelming strength and lethal precision.”
Among the war’s ostensible accomplishments: “Iran’s ballistic missile arsenal and production capacity has been razed…eliminating its ability to project power.” Also, “Iran can no longer arm terrorist proxies.” And, although the regime was still clinging to power: “What’s left of [it] is desperate, dejected, and in denial.”
For Hegseth, this was a “decisive military victory.”
But, in fact, it wasn’t: Not one of Trump’s stated objectives was achieved by Hegseth and the forces under his command. Not one.
To begin with, the Iranian regime has remained intact and (so far as can be determined from afar) remains as entrenched as ever, with no signs of an imminent popular rebellion.
Although the Iranians have made no visible move to reconstitute their uranium enrichment program (a prerequisite for manufacturing a nuclear bomb), they have demonstrated no inclination to surrender their existing stockpiles of highly enriched uranium or to renounce their enrichment efforts entirely.
And Iran’s regional clout—now buttressed by its apparent capacity to disrupt the Persian Gulf oil flow at will—appears enhanced, not diminished.
Most significantly, Iran’s ability to project power with missiles and long-range drones remains robust, as demonstrated by repeated strikes on US bases in the region. As if to prove this point, the Iranians struck Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on July 17, killing three US Army service members and destroying or damaging vital military equipment.
The Iranians have also continued to strike tankers attempting to traverse the strategic Strait of Hormuz without their approval, sharply constricting the world’s oil trade and keeping diesel and gasoline prices high.
From any perspective, then, the Hegseth-run war on Iran has been a total fiasco, failing to achieve a single one of its stated objectives. For these reasons alone, the self-styled “secretary of war” should resign. But the war was more than a failure: It entailed a massive strategic disaster, one whose vast dimensions are only beginning to be calculated.
The Strategic Calculus
How do you measure a strategic disaster? We begin, properly, with an intelligence failure, followed by military miscalculation and geopolitical retreat—all adding up to an astonishing contraction of America’s global clout.
Let’s start with intelligence failure, the origin of so much of the sorrow to come. Hegseth and his top lieutenants began with the assumptions that (a) the Iranian military was no match for the technologically superior US military, and (b) the Iranian regime was fragile and would be swept away once its top leaders were killed. Neither assumption has proved even remotely accurate: The Iranian military has demonstrated a remarkable degree of resilience under fire, able to inflict far more damage on US forces than was ever thought possible; and the regime has proved equally resilient, able to reconstitute itself after the loss of its top leadership on the first day of fighting.
Some of this leadership myopia can be attributed to Trump’s ebullience after the successful January 3 US seizure of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in Caracas, and to the overly optimistic assessment of the regime’s fragility given to Trump on February 11 by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a pivotal White House meeting. From the accounts by Jonathan Swan and Maggie Haberman of The New York Times, we know that Vice President JD Vance and Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, warned of possible risks in starting a war with Iran, but that Hegseth assured the president of a rapid US victory. With this assurance, Trump took the plunge.
But this is only part of the story. Hegseth was clearly so blinded by his faith in “the greatest fighting force the world has ever known” that he failed to consider the potential strengths of his adversary—the very first responsibility of a capable commander. The Iranians may have possessed a third-rate navy and air force, but they had also developed a substantial missile- and drone-production capacity and had hardened their launch facilities against possible attack. More importantly, the Iranians had clearly studied US military tactics and prepared for Hegseth’s air and missile bombardment by decentralizing their command and combat capabilities around the country, allowing them to absorb a massive US-Israeli assault and still conduct punishing retaliatory strikes.
By predicting a swift US military victory, moreover, Hegseth saw no need to account for the possible consequences of Iranian retaliatory strikes against Persian Gulf oil shipping. Why worry about oil tankers’ safety if the war would be over in a matter of weeks? Evidently, no one in Hegseth’s inner circle foresaw the possibility of recurring Iranian drone strikes on vital ships and oil infrastructure, depriving the world of approximately one-fifth of its daily petroleum supply and sparking economic hardship around the world.
Surely, those responsible for such a mammoth intelligence failure should be removed from their posts—including those at the very top.
From intelligence failure we move to military miscalculation, another lethal command deficiency. If, like Hegseth, you believe you command the greatest fighting force that ever was, you might be forgiven for a touch of overconfidence when going into battle against a demonstrably weaker power. But when your hubris endangers the lives of your soldiers and their ability to fight, you are unfit to lead.
Most egregious, of course, is Hegseth’s failure to learn from Ukraine about the devastating impact of one-way attack drones on contemporary combat. Anyone who has followed the Ukrainian conflict—and this should have included every senior US military official—knows that drone warfare has transformed the battlefield, placing any unprotected asset at extreme risk of being targeted and attacked by long-range assault weapons, like the Iranian Shahed-136 drones employed by Russia in great numbers.
Yet Hegseth deployed tens of thousands of US soldiers, along with some of America’s most advanced military systems, at bases in the Gulf area within easy range of Iran’s own fleet of Shahed drones. Yes, those troops and weapons were protected by America’s advanced interceptors, such as Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missiles—but never in sufficient quantities to knock down all of the drones and missiles pitted against them. The unsurprising result: 18 US lives lost, over 800 wounded, and billions of dollars in damage to weapons and equipment.
And then there is the critical issue of interceptor use. To defend US facilities in the Gulf (along with the energy assets of US allies in the region), the Pentagon fired off a substantial share of its available supply of Patriot and THAAD air-defense missiles, leaving US bases elsewhere at greater risk of potential attack. According to a report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a Republican-leaning Washington think tank, the US fired between 1,000 and 1,400 Patriot interceptors during the first weeks of the war, representing about half of the total US inventory at that time; it also expended 190–290 THAAD missiles, or two-thirds to three-quarters of its prewar inventory.
To stem the losses at US bases in the Middle East, Hegseth reportedly ordered US commanders in Europe and Asia to ship scarce Patriot and THAAD batteries from their areas of responsibility to the Gulf, substantially weakening US air and missile defenses in other likely hot spots.
Replacing all those expended missiles and bolstering US air defenses around the world will cost this country tens of billions of dollars and take years to accomplish, Pentagon officials acknowledge.
Add all of this up, and the outcome includes what should be termed geopolitical retreat, or reduced US political clout in the Gulf and elsewhere. As Trump and Hegseth made clear in the opening days of the war, a major US objective was to demonstrate that America’s global reach and power were greater than ever. “[The Iranian] regime will soon learn that no one should challenge the strength and might of the United States Armed Forces,” Trump declared on February 28. A victory there, coming on top of the seemingly cost-free intervention in Venezuela, would again demonstrate Washington’s capacity to project power and overcome adversaries worldwide. But the Iran venture failed, severely damaging US credibility.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
It will take a long time to calculate all the consequences of this geopolitical setback, but we can begin with Washington’s apparent failure to eliminate all Iranian threats to the untrammeled flow of Persian Gulf oil. Ever since the world economy became dependent on the Gulf’s oil output, in the early Cold War era, protection of the Gulf oil flow has been viewed in Washington as a vital US interest. Following the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979, President Jimmy Carter told Congress in 1980 that Soviet forces were now “close to the Straits of Hormuz, [thereby posing] a grave threat to the free movement of Middle East oil.” Any attempt by Moscow or some other power to block that flow, he asserted, “will be regarded as an assault on the vital interests of the United States of America, and such an assault will be repelled by any means necessary, including military force.”
In accordance with this edict, Carter established the US Central Command (currently responsible for the fighting with Iran) and installed a permanent US military presence in the region. His successors, beginning with Ronald Reagan and continuing with the two Presidents Bush, have cited this so-called Carter Doctrine to justify repeated US military intervention in the Gulf. Over time, the US role in safeguarding “the free movement of Middle East oil” has become a defining feature of America’s global dominance, along with the US military presence in Europe, Japan, and South Korea. But the Iranians have demonstrated an invincible capacity to disrupt that flow, throwing into question a core component of America’s claim to global hegemony.
The US failure to subdue Iran has also undermined America’s dominant status in the other major foci of its hegemonic sway, Europe and Asia. Not only has Iran demonstrated that a medium-sized power can, under the right circumstances, hold a much more powerful force at bay—a feat no doubt being closely studied by Russia and China—but also, by eliciting such a wanton expenditure of advanced US munitions, it has actually left the US less well-equipped to counter those rivals in any future conflicts. According to that same CSIS study on US missile use, the Pentagon consumed a large share of its offensive strike weapons during the opening weeks of the war, including approximately one-third of its prewar inventory of Tomahawk cruise missiles and one-fourth of its Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles.
No doubt there will be other negative consequences from this geopolitical retreat, some possibly of equal concern, but we already know enough to conclude that Hegseth’s combat malpractice has resulted in a severe strategic debacle.
This, combined with his intelligence failures and combat miscalculations, would, in other countries and at other times, result in his forcible removal from office. With this not in the immediate offing, despite calls for his impeachment by prominent Democrats and Republicans in Congress, Hegseth should pay homage to the martial ideals he holds so dear, take personal responsibility for the debacle, and resign.

Renowned Indian painter Arpita Singh, whose dreamlike depictions of floating women earned her comparisons to Marc Chagall and influenced generations of artists, died on November 9 in a New Delhi hospital. She was eighty-nine. Drawing from traditional Indian folk art, miniature paintings, and weaving, Singh centered Indian women in crowded, festive paintings filled with flora and fauna and occasionally tinged with violence. Despite the efforts of many to affiliate her work with a feminist or political belief system, Singh refused categorization. “Things happen on their own,” Singh told The Guardian in a 2025 interview. “The affairs of political and social life come into my painting like the way light comes as color and breeze comes as movement.”
Arpita Singh was born Arpita Dutta on June 22, 1937, in Baranagar, in what is now West Bengal. In 1946, she moved with her parents to New Delhi, where she would remain all her life. The following year, the Partition of India took place; the violence of the event, which divided the British-ruled country into the independent nations of Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan, would shape her artistic output over six decades to come.
In 1954, on the advice of a high school teacher, she enrolled in Delhi Polytechnic’s School of Art, where she studied under legendary Indian modernists Biren De and Sailoz Mookherjea and was introduced to the work of Wassily Kandinsky and Paul Klee. Shortly after graduating in 1959, she went to work at the Weavers Service Centre, a government agency that promoted the craft of weaving. Tasked with evaluating shawls, she began investigating clothmaking traditions, and gained an understanding of pattern and technique—including pattachitra scroll painting and kantha embroidery—that she would soon bring to bear in her painting.
As the 1960s dawned, along with a handful of former art school classmates, she helped to found the Unknown, a progressive artists’ collective that experimented with various visual vocabularies, and with whom she first exhibited at group shows. That same decade, Singh, now married to fellow artist Paramjit Singh, began to gain national attention as a modernist painter, originally embracing a faux-naïve figurative style and eventually receiving her first solo show in 1972, at New Delhi’s Kunika Chemould Gallery.
At the exhibition’s close, feeling that she was not “moving naturally on canvas,” as she told The Guardian, she switched to painting or drawing dots and lines, often in black and white. Typical of these works is the hypnotic Untitled, 1976, a cliff of tiny black lines and X’s—their tight formation suggesting a textile’s weave—that grows slightly narrower at the bottom, where several key-like shapes drift in a stack, perhaps having fallen from its top. Another Untitled, this one from 1981, shows a packed field of black needle-like shapes, in whose midst floats a band of what look like minuscule, gun-shaped forms. “It was like practicing handwriting before I found my voice again,” she later explained.
By the 1980s, in response to the nearly two-year-long state of emergency declared by Indian prime minister Indira Gandhi in 1975, she had returned to narrative figuration, this time adding text fragments to her busy renderings of gravity-defying scenes. Also in the ’80s, Singh, alongside compatriots Nalini Malani, Nilima Sheikh, and Madhvi Parekh, mounted a traveling exhibition of women artists, titled “Behind the Looking Glass.”
The following decade would see Singh create some of her best-known works. Among these are Devi Pistol Wali, 1990, and My Mother, 1993, both featuring the impassive-seeming women and cartoonish men that characterize her output. In the earlier canvas, the subject, clad in filmy white and possessed of five arms, aims a gun at a diminutive male figure who appears to be dropping out of the sky. In the later work, made in the wake of the 1992–93 Bombay riots sparked by the destruction of the Babri Mosque, an older woman gazes stoically at the viewer, male bodies littering a road bisecting the canvas, soldiers gesturing wildly behind them as they dodge bicycles and cars.
The spread of cable television brought the Gulf War into Singh’s works, as Meera Menezes pointed out in a 2019 issue of Artforum, and her canvases seemed to become increasingly jumbled and vibrant, as evinced for example by 2007’s Buy Two Get Two Free, depicting a pair of binocular-wielding male figures gazing at two scantily clad women accompanied by a duo of vultures and a couple of freakish mushrooms. Similarly entrancing is 2005’s My Lollipop City: Gemini Rising, a fantastical map of New Delhi arrayed with masculine bureaucratic figures, overhung with dozens of tiny airplanes, and festooned with text, one fragment of which reads “THE MAP IS FAULTY DO NOT FOLLOW IT.”
In 2010, Singh achieved the highest price ever paid at auction for a work by a living female Indian artist with the $2.24 million sale at Saffronart of her sixteen-panel mural The Wish Dream, 2001. In 2019, she was the subject of a major retrospective at New Delhi’s Kiran Nadar Museum of Art. Though her work appeared in numerous group shows in museums around the world for decades, she only began to achieve real acclaim outside India in the last years of her life, receiving her first solo institutional show outside the country—a survey at the Serpentine in London—in 2025. A US solo show, “Unfolding,” is on view at New York’s Talwar Gallery though February 27, 2027.
Singh’s work is held in the collections of the Peabody Essex Museum, Salem, Massachusetts; the Victoria and Albert Museum, London; and the Kirin Nadar Museum of Art and the National Gallery of Modern Art, both in New Delhi. Her only daughter, artist Anjum Singh, died in 2020. She is survived by her husband.
