https://jacobin.com/2026/11/kurds-uk-mig.title: Kurds Have Become Britain’s Latest Demonized Migrants
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/kurds-uk-mig.author: Matt Broomfield
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/kurds-uk-mig.text:
Kurds Have Become Britain’s Latest Demonized Migrants
During the war against ISIS, the Kurds were feted in Britain as heroes. Today the stateless Kurdish population is increasingly demonized as a source of illegal immigrants and people smugglers.
A decade ago, the Kurds briefly figured in Western public consciousness as the feted heroes of the war against the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria (ISIS). In Britain as worldwide, audiences were fascinated by fetishized, orientalized images of “badass” Kurdish female fighters battling the Islamist terror group on the ground, backed by the UK and US militaries. Today the most populous stateless people in the Middle East are making headlines in the UK once again, but this time depicted as people smugglers, organized criminals, and unwanted illegal immigrants.
Broadly speaking, both migrants themselves and the smuggling networks who profit from their need to travel are hysterically depicted as united in highly organized, criminal, Islamic gangs that need to be “smashed” by the UK government. And a recent slew of right-wing media commentary has specifically focused on the Iraqi Kurdish groups, who are admittedly the current top dogs profiting from migrants seeking to make the treacherous journey between Calais and Britain.
This newfound attention feeds into BBC investigative journalism targeting Kurdish criminal networks in the UK allegedly running hundreds of illegal barbers and vape shops, which in turn leads to right-wing attacks on migrant-run high-street barbershops by Nigel Farage and Richard Tice of the far-right Reform UK party, and Robert Jenrick of the even further-right Restore UK. At the extreme, this discourse even leads to incidents like the attempted decapitation of one Kurdish barber by a Bristol neo-Nazi. As Western sympathy toward the Kurds occasioned during the ISIS war finally expires, media commentary and government policy is gradually setting up another marginalized ethnic group as the migration villains du jour.
Another Anti-Migrant Wave
For sure, it’s unlikely that axe-wielding fascists could or would distinguish a Kurd from a Turk or Arab. Likewise, the far-right politicians peddling anti-migrant narratives in Westminster have tended to refer conspiratorially to networks of “Turkish barbers.” Indeed, for better or worse, the Kurds — who number around forty million but have never had a recognized state of their own — have more often remained invisible in British public discourse.
The Kurdish ethnicity only made it onto the UK census for the first time in 2021, meaning that while official figures suggest there are around a hundred thousand Kurds in the UK, community representatives estimate the true figure is several times higher. Some Kurds are assimilated or prefer to refer to themselves as Iraqi, Iranian, Turkish, or Syrian for reasons of personal security or simple brand recognition: many of the UK’s nominally “Turkish” barbers or “Mediterranean” restaurants are actually Kurdish-owned.
On one level, the Kurds are thus simply being swept up in the latest broad wave of anti-migrant sentiment, targeting small boats in the English Channel and small businesses at home. And the same story is repeating itself elsewhere. There are rather fewer Kurds in the United States than in the UK or Europe, but there too recent Kurdish migrants report being caught up in new waves of anti-immigration sentiment. In Germany, cases of anti-Kurdish racism more than doubled in the past year, though this was primarily driven by Turkish, Iranian, and Arabic migrant communities themselves discriminating against the Kurds. Even Japan has seen its own tiny population of around three thousand Kurdish migrants become the key target of a specific xenophobic hate campaign spearheaded by the Asian country’s own far ight.
Kurdish Blame Game
The latest hysteria in the UK can’t be ascribed to the Kurdish ethnicity in particular. After all, the channel crossing has successively been controlled by groups from various nations: Iran, Iraq, Afghanistan, Albania. But this is just why increasingly frequent British media mentions of the Kurds in connection with organized crime are worth tracking.
While terms like “people smuggler” are weaponized by prosecutors and the media to smear and criminalize innocent migrants, Kurdish criminal organizations certainly do profit from the trade, sometimes on an exploitative basis. The Kurds’ long-term statelessness and the occupation of Kurdish-majority regions by Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Syria has left many of the Middle East’s estimated forty million Kurds occupying impoverished borderlands. Unsurprisingly, some turn to the grey- and black-market trade in legal or illegal goods to survive, including the Kurdish kolbar porters trekking through remote mountain passes between Iran and Iraq who are killed in their dozens every year. Decades of (legal) Kurdish migration have allowed these networks to extend to Europe, laying the foundation necessary to facilitate continued migration amid increasingly tough policing of UK and European borders, and create a profit for certain Kurdish individuals at the expense of others.
Throughout the Middle East, state violence against Kurds has often been linked to racialized depictions of Kurdish minorities as backward, uneducated mafiosos — as in the universally popular Turkish soap operas that frequently represent Kurds as villainous people smugglers and drug traffickers. Related negative stereotypes of Kurds are already somewhat more prominent in continental Europe, influenced by propagandistic Turkish depictions of the country’s domestic Kurdish opposition as narcoterrorists profiting from the European heroin trade, and may now be leaching into UK public policy. The shift recalls the vitriol previously directed toward Albanians during a prior surge in anti-small-boat rhetoric after 2022, and which academics argue directly contributed to UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) policy targeting migrants from the beleaguered Eastern European nation.
While the Albanians at least have a government that can robustly challenge Farage’s salvos, the stateless Kurds are left even more exposed. Ben Judah, the former adviser to Foreign Secretary David Lammy and centrist critic of UK migration policy, has suggested the Kurds’ weak geopolitical position should make it easier for Westminster to crack down on Kurdish migration networks. For Judah, despite the semiautonomous Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI) “being under a de-facto Anglo-American security umbrella since the first Gulf War, there has been an unwillingness to put [people smuggling] first in our relations. . . . For Britain, the relationship as we know it should be on the line unless these authorities take this gravely seriously.”
In truth, this work is already being done. The FCDO has funded an anti-migration media campaign in the KRI, copying methods it previously deployed in Albania. More significantly, the BBC’s investigation into Kurdish migration networks led to the arrest of a leading Kurdish people smuggler in the KRI in coordination with the Iraqi Kurdish authorities. When I visited the KRI this summer, an official from the governing Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) stressed their ongoing cooperation with the British authorities to curb illegal migration, which was also the headline when Britain’s National Security Advisor visited the KRI earlier this week.
Though never numbering more than a few thousand per year, migrants from Iraq (most of them Kurdish) figured in the top five nationalities arriving in the UK via small boats from 2021 to 2023. They have since dropped out of the rankings. Relatedly, the latest figures suggest overall irregular migration out of the KRI has fallen by half in the past six months. None of this suggests an unmanageable crisis so much as the latest bout in the game of whack-a-mole in which one migration network loses control to another, and another set of desperate people are driven to seek a new life abroad, whatever the risks.
Expiring Partnership
In fact, the UK’s domestic shift against the Kurds comes amid related developments on the international stage. Judah correctly notes that the geopolitically isolated KRI, which was established by Western diktat following Saddam Hussein’s genocide against the Kurds and subsequent US-Kurdish cooperation during the two Gulf Wars, has long been reliant on these partnerships in order to survive. But rather than a cozy, mutually beneficial relationship, the Iraqi Kurdish authorities are currently being placed under severe security pressure by Westminster and Washington.
The US has withdrawn all its troops from the KRI and cut all security, essentially terminating the decade-old partnership that saw Kurdish ground troops defeat ISIS in coordination with Western air strikes, intelligence, and logistical support. The UK has unsuprisingly followed suit, withdrawing its own troops long stationed in the region. These moves repeat recent developments in neighboring Rojava (Syrian Kurdistan), where Kurdish forces that had lost twelve thousand fighters battling ISIS were this January forced to capitulate to the rule of a new Islamist government in Damascus after the United States finally terminated its cooperation with the Syrian Kurds. The Iraqi Kurds are now being left similarly exposed — not only to a potential ISIS resurgence but also to violent attacks by Iran-aligned militias in a febrile Iraq that is set to be the Middle East’s next battlefield and cross-border attacks from Iran itself.
Alongside their newfound status as migrant criminals, some Kurds are still making headlines as key Middle Eastern players — but no longer as heroic Western allies. Tehran has long repressed its own Kurdish population, executing hundreds in recent years. As the United States and Israel launched their disastrous war on Iran, US officials signaled and then rapidly aborted plans to arm unspecified Kurdish opposition groups. Donald Trump subsequently distanced himself from the proposal, announcing he was “very disappointed” with “the Kurds” who just “take, take, take,” adding “I think it’s a disgrace. . . . I’ll remember that,” and claiming that Kurdish forces illegitimately intercepted weapons shipments. As ever, these allegations were leveled at “the Kurds” in general, painting a whole people represented by a diverse range of political movements as mercenary and untrustworthy.
When I was in the KRI, both the governing authorities and exiled Iranian Kurdish armed groups stationed in the region strongly denied these allegations, with KDP spokesperson Hoshyar Siwaily telling me: “Although we are partners of the US, we would like to stay neutral, because this war is bigger than us. We don’t want to be part of it.” That hasn’t stopped Iran from launching more than seven hundred retributive strikes against the KRI, killing dozens of people — more than any other noncombatant country. The West is gradually closing the door on its erstwhile allies, even as Iran revenges itself on the Kurds.
Anti-Kurdish Alignment
With the Kurds abandoned by the West and targeted by the East, it’s little wonder that many still need to flee the region. The structural factors that drive Kurdish migration to the UK — and occasional involvement in criminality — are only likely to worsen in the coming years. Seriously tackling Kurdish migration to the West would mean tackling these regional “sources of conflict and insecurities” at their root. Conversely, however, the stage is being set to demonize those Kurds who flee future bouts of instability driven by the West’s regional interventions and repeated instrumentalization of the Kurdish cause. Western governments and right-wing media will find it increasingly convenient to join the likes of Iran in vilifying the Kurds, the one issue on which everyone in the Middle East seems to concur.
Below the line, commenters on right-wing news sites like the Daily Express and Daily Mail still generally confine themselves to the usual diatribes against migrants in general. But some are clearly picking up on the Kurds’ newfound prominence within this familiar rhetoric. Commenting on a story blasting the Kurdish networks between Calais and the UK as “brutal criminal kingpins,” one writes: “Saddam had the right idea about how to deal with these lot. . . . ” It’s a call to repeat the Iraqi dictator’s 1987–89 massacre of around a hundred thousand Kurds, a crime officially recognized as genocide.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Botticelli painting saved from leaving UK goes on view in Oxford
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A painting by Sandro Botticelli at risk of leaving the UK earlier this year has gone on display at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford where it was first shown in the 1930s.
The Virgin and Child Enthroned (1470s) was bought by the London-based private collection Klesch Collection, which announced plans in May to loan the painting to the Ashmolean for three years. The painting was previously exhibited at the museum in 1934–35 when it was attributed to Botticelli's workshop.
The UK government placed an export bar on the Botticelli painting, valued at £10.2m, in May 2025. The UK Department for Culture, Media and Sport said that the painting had a recommended price of £9,960,000 (plus VAT of £272,000, which can be reclaimed by an eligible institution). The work was sold at Sotheby’s London in late 2024 for £9.7m (with fees).
The painting underwent conservation over the summer to remove discoloured varnish and later retouching, revealing well-preserved details of the Virgin and Child and restoring the original cooler tones, says an Ashmolean statement. The painting is also unusual for its generous use of gold leaf, “although earlier Italian painters regularly applied gold to the backgrounds of their devotional works, it was less widely used by Botticelli's time”, add the statement.
The Botticelli painting was housed in the Convent of San Giuliano in Florence in the early 19th century, and was later transported to a small chapel attached to a group of farmhouses in a nearby village. It then passed into the family of Giovanni Magherini Graziani, who sold it in November 1903 to the Italian dealer, Elia Volpi. Harriet Sarah Jones Loyd (Lady Wantage) bought the work in May 1904 for £5,000. The Botticelli painting had been kept at Betterton House, near Wantage, Berkshire, since 1944.
Founders A. Gary and Dr. Anita Klesch started the Klesch Collection with the acquisition of a set of Four Seasons by Giuseppe Arcimboldo in 2014. The collection of 15th-to-17th-century European art, which also includes works by Caravaggio, Sofonisba Anguissola and Rubens, is regularly loaned to museums and institutions worldwide.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-bill-woul.title: NYC bill would require food delivery firms to fund fixes to the e-bike 'crisis'
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-bill-woul.author: Arya Sundaram
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-bill-woul.text:
One East Village block has transformed over the past few years into ground zero in the battle over delivery e-bikes in New York City.
On any given day, hundreds of bikes line the curb of East 11th Street, between First Avenue and Avenue A, near a mosque where many workers congregate. The scene has drawn the ire of nearby residents, who complain of clogged streets. City officials have installed bike corrals and hired a contractor for extra street cleanings, and the NYPD has repeatedly confiscated bikes it says are parked illegally.
But none of the attempted fixes have reduced the crowds of e-bikes, nor solved the underlying problem, according to City Councilmember Harvey Epstein, whose district includes the block: Workers need a safe place to park their bikes and pass the time in between deliveries.
Many workers continue to park their bikes at the controversial site in part because they feel their property is less likely to get stolen in the presence of their peers and the mosque’s cameras, according to advocates for delivery workers.
A new bill Epstein is set to introduce on Thursday would shift the burden of solving the issue onto third-party food delivery companies. It would require the companies to create rest areas for delivery workers, including bathrooms and e-bike charging and storage areas.
The bill raises a central question: Who should pay for the infrastructure that powers the city’s food delivery industry — specifically, in this case, e-bike storage and charging? Currently, that responsibility lies in the hands of the city’s estimated 80,000 e-bike workers, largely working-class immigrants who often lack safe, secure storage facilities.
“This is an infrastructure crisis our city has,” said Ligia Guallpa, the co-founder and executive director of the Worker's Justice Project, an advocacy group for working-class immigrant laborers, and its subsidiary Los Deliveristas Unidos, which supports delivery workers.
She added: “Since the explosion of e-bikes across the city, the city hasn’t really caught up with that evolution.”
As food delivery has become a fixture of city life, other blocks across the East Village neighborhood and the city in high-delivery zones have also emerged as informal delivery worker hubs, drawing complaints from neighbors.
Meanwhile, fire-related deaths have doubled in the past year, in part driven by fires from lithium-ion batteries, which commonly power e-bikes. Such batteries have been found at the site of recent fires, including in Sunset Park where six people died, and at a Bronx apartment fire last month where an an 11-year-old boy died.
After decreasing last year, death and injuries from lithium-ion battery fires are on the rise in New York City. So far this year, nine people have died from lithium-ion battery fires and 71 people have been injured, according to data provided by the fire department.
The Mamdani administration has attempted to address the concerns of workers, safety advocates and peeved neighbors alike by creating the city’s widely used first delivery worker hub near City Hall in April. The years-in-the-making, federally funded project includes e-bike charging stations and worker rest areas. Guallpa said the site is popular — but it’s just one location.
The administration has yet to officially announce if any other delivery worker hubs are in the works. But mayoral spokesperson Cassio Mendoza said in a statement, “The administration looks forward to reviewing this legislation and working with the Council to continue to expand protections for delivery workers.”
Mendoza added: “Delivery app companies must do more to support the workers that make their companies possible."
Under a plan developed by former Mayor Eric Adams’ administration, and with $3 million in state funding, the city Department of Transportation is set to start installing 25 e-bike charging stations across the city late next year, according to a department spokesperson.
The agency was also previously awarded $25 million in federal funding under former President Joe Biden’s administration to build battery charging stations at public housing facilities, but the federal government never obligated the money, and the city has yet to receive any of the funding, the spokesperson said.
“ I think, just a much better way to do it is to say to the companies, ‘Hey, this is your obligation and your responsibility. Don't rely on government to fix your problem. Fix it yourself,’” Epstein said in an interview.
Spokespeople for prominent food delivery app companies, including Uber Eats, Grubhub, and DoorDash, did not respond to a request for comment about the proposals. However, Epstein said he contacted their representatives in crafting his bill.
Epstein said he also considered similar offerings, deployed by Amazon and the urban delivery bike company JOCO, both of which have indoor spaces where workers can rest and store bikes overnight.
“ Amazon, JOCO, it's exactly the same model that we're trying to really make the industry standard,” Epstein said.
He added about food delivery companies: “All we are doing is basically paying for the cost of what a private company is putting into the market.”
The city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection would set many of the specifics, including the number and location of the rest and storage areas. The agency would have to create the new rules within a year of the bill taking effect.
Guallpa, the delivery worker advocate, said she’s still hoping City Hall will pitch in some way to expand delivery worker hubs, given Mamdani’s vocal support of delivery workers on the campaign trail and in office.
“We need every public official to understand that the root cause of the problem that exists in our city is not the workers,” Guallpa said. “Let's address this micromobility infrastructure crisis by delivering what workers actually need on the ground to stay safe.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: German museum returns Slevogt painting to heirs of Nazi-persecuted collector
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Anzhela Khachaturova
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A painting by the German Impressionist painter Max Slevogt, which has been restituted to the heirs of Eduard Fuchs—a collector, Communist and writer who fled Nazi Germany with his Jewish wife—will be auctioned next month. Slevogt's Paradiesvögel (Birds of Paradise, 1900), was acquired by the Von der Heydt-Museum in Wuppertal, western Germany, in 2006 and following an investigation that began in 2020 was approved for restitution by the Wuppertal city council on 13 July 2026. Paradiesvögel will be offered at Ketterer Kunst's 5 December Day Sale with an estimate of €40,000–€60,000.
Given the large number of heirs a sale was the only option, Ketterer Kunst's head of communications Anja Häse tells The Art Newspaper. The heirs consigned the painting once the restitution was completed, she adds. Another work by Slevogt from Fuchs’s collection, Don Quichotte und die Schafherde (Don Quixote and the Flock of Sheep, 1907) is also included in the auction with an estimate of €20,000–€30,000. According to Ketterer Kunst's provenance information, a settlement was reached between the current private owners and Fuchs's heirs in 2026, allowing the work to be offered at auction free of restitution claims. The terms of the “amicable restitution” have not been disclosed.
Fuchs's collection was confiscated by the Nazis but later released. In 1937, he was forced to sell works from the collection to pay a punitive emigration tax imposed by the Nazi authorities. Paradiesvögel was auctioned in Berlin in June 1937 and acquired by the art dealer Hildebrand Gurlitt, passing to Fritz Slevogt in 1939.
Paradiesvögel was included in a sale at Kunsthaus Lempertz in December 2004, estimated at €100,000-€120,000, but went unsold. According to Meyer, the work remained in the auction house’s custody afterwards and was subsequently exhibited at the Von der Heydt-Museum in 2005. The museum then purchased the painting through the auction house in 2006 for €120,000. Meyer says that while the painting's provenance was documented in the 2004 auction catalogue, the museum can no longer establish whether a provenance check was carried out before the acquisition or how thoroughly it was assessed. She also confirmed that the museum is not considering any legal action against Kunsthaus Lempertz regarding due diligence on the painting.
The provenance investigation began after Fuchs's heirs contacted the institution in 2020, the museum's press officer Marion Meyer tells The Art Newspaper. The research drew on a wider project, supported by the German Lost Art Foundation, to reconstruct Eduard and Margarete Fuchs's collection.
“Restituting Max Slevogt's Paradiesvögel means losing a painting, but we gain something far more important: the certainty that we have acted responsibly towards history,” the Von der Heydt-Museum's director Roland Mönig says in a press statement. He describes provenance research as “an essential part of our work”.
In 2024, the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart restituted Slevogt's Der verlorene Sohn (The Prodigal Son, 1899) to Fuchs's heirs. The triptych was sold at Ketterer Kunst later that year.

https://gothamist.com/news/exclusive-vid.title: Exclusive video shows shocking moment Brooklyn building collapsed
https://gothamist.com/news/exclusive-vid.author: David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/exclusive-vid.text:
Anderson Velez had just arrived in the Bronx for a painting job when he received a frantic phone call from his wife.
She was screaming, he said, begging rescue workers to pull their two sons from the rubble of their Brooklyn apartment building, which had collapsed minutes earlier.
All three survived, but his 9-year-old son was in intensive care after undergoing surgery on his skull and his wife has serious injuries to her ribs, spine and collar bone, he said Thursday.
Velez was left caring for his 2-year-old son. A video recorded by an in-home surveillance camera in the family’s apartment shows the boy being swept up in the rubble as a wall beside him gives way, revealing bright day light outside. He was pulled from the wreckage with scrapes to his forehead and legs.
“I am still in shock,” Velez said in the small lobby of a Brooklyn hotel the city is using to house people displaced by the disaster. “The truth is, I’m trying to be strong for my son, but I feel terrible.”
The shocking video reveals the moment his wife and their two children realized the building was collapsing.
The 9-year-old boy is seen holding a baby bottle and retrieving a gallon of milk from the refrigerator while the 2-year-old plays on the floor of the small third-floor apartment. Moments later, Velez's wife opens a door to the room screaming. The 9-year-old runs to his mother. A candle on a table can be seen visibly shaking and moving across the table’s surface. The younger boy moves slightly away from the wall before it caves in and the video cuts off.
“That movement, in my opinion, saved his life,” Velez said in an interview in Spanish.
Velez said he immediately returned to Brooklyn after his wife’s call.
“Everything was going through my mind. I was thinking about my children, hoping they were okay and that nothing serious had happened to them,” he said. “God heard me because I prayed so much for their health and well-being.”
Velez said he and his family had moved into the $1,500-a-month apartment at 1321 Flatbush Ave. earlier this month, after living in a homeless shelter.
He said his 2-year-old son “was completely covered in dirt” when rescue workers pulled him from the debris pile.
“His ears were full of dirt, his nose, his little mouth, his back — his entire body was covered in dirt,” he said.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said two of the eight people pronounced dead in the catastrophic collapse were kids, and several more were left injured.
Velez said his family knew the two children, who lived one floor below them.
A spokesperson for the Department of Buildings is still investigating the cause of the collapse of the three-story building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. The near-century-old structure crumbled into an adjacent construction site, where the buildings department had previously penalized the development team for cutting corners and ignoring a stop work order.
Mamdani said buildings inspectors would conduct safety enforcement sweeps at more than 100 other projects linked to five companies involved in the botched construction project.

https://hyperallergic.com/protesters-urg.title: Protesters Urge Steven Spielberg to Boycott MoMA Over Leon Black’s Epstein Ties
https://hyperallergic.com/protesters-urg.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/protesters-urg.text:
Protesters Urge Steven Spielberg to Boycott MoMA Over Leon Black’s Epstein Ties
Activists rallied at the museum ahead of a benefit for the Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center, decrying the board member’s Epstein connections and his pro-Israel support.
Ahead of the Museum of Modern Art's (MoMA) annual benefit for its Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center tonight, November 12, about 20 protesters assembled outside the institution to call on the gala's honoree, Steven Spielberg, to reject the recognition. The protest comes amid growing calls to oust Leon Black from the museum board over his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
A letter sent to Spielberg by the feminist campaign group We Are UltraViolet, reviewed by Hyperallergic, urges the Academy Award-winning director to boycott MoMA until the institution severs ties with Black and renames the film venue.
“MoMA has benefited so handsomely from Black that they have named the very room you will be honored in, the Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center, in his honor,” reads the missive to Spielberg, authored by Elisa Bautista, campaign director of UltraViolet. For the past four iterations of the benefit, MoMA has funneled all proceeds into the film center, which was created in 2019 in recognition of a $40 million gift from the private equity tycoon.
“Mr. Spielberg, you do NOT want your legacy connected to accused abuser and Epstein associate Leon Black,” Bautista continues.
The letter makes reference to three sexual assault and misconduct accusations brought forth against the billionaire, all of which Black denies. One of the lawsuits was discontinued by the plaintiff, and an earlier lawsuit was dismissed by the court. A third lawsuit was allowed to move forward after a judge imposed a sanction. UltraViolet said it has not received a response from Spielberg's representatives.
Black left his role as CEO of his private equity firm Apollo Global Management in 2021, when news broke that he paid Epstein $158 million for financial advice from 2012 to 2017, after Epstein’s first conviction for soliciting sex from a minor. Even though he stepped down as MoMA board chairman that same year, after Hyperallergic published an open letter signed by over 150 artists calling for his removal, Black remains a MoMA board trustee.
Public scrutiny of Black intensified in September, after the US House of Representatives unanimously approved a resolution to hold the MoMA trustee in contempt of Congress for defying subpoenas in an Epstein investigation. This month, Black sued California Representative Robert Garcia for defamation over public comments such as "Leon Black is at the center of Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.”
Playwright and theater artist Gracie Gardner, who initially posted an open letter to Spielberg on her Instagram, said she was “amazed” by the public response.
“Steven Spielberg has made his career making stories about the dignity of women and children,” Gardner told Hyperallergic at tonight's protest. “It's totally disgusting that he's accepting an award [at the film center named after Leon Black], who's currently in contempt of Congress for not producing NDAs and his involvement in the Epstein files.”
Last month, Gardner co-performed a staged reading of former Barclays CEO and JP Morgan executive Jes Staley's deposition on Epstein to the United States House Oversight Committee in July.
At this evening's protest, others carried signs pointing to Black's connections to pro-Israel and Zionist organizations. Black has reportedly donated money to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which denies that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, and Birthright Israel, which is accused of serving as a propaganda campaign for the Israeli government.
“I can personally say I'm Jewish and it's specifically because of my Jewish values that we're here. Never again means never again for anyone,” one demonstrator, Janet Goodman-Clarke, told Hyperallergic. “Leon Black not only is a Zionist, but he's also named ad nauseam in the Epstein files.”
MoMA has not replied to Hyperallergic's request for comment.
Artists, activists, and Epstein survivors have repeatedly gathered in front of MoMA demanding his ousting. Among those in attendance at today's action was Katie Fuller, arts educator and founder of the Time and Memory Project, who staged a separate protest calling for Black's removal in front of the museum with her sister in September.
Last month, Fuller teamed up with Epstein survivors, UltraViolet, and the Epstein-Trump Reading Room, created by the Institute for Primary Facts, to illustrate the extent of Epstein's network. The free, mobile installation displayed a timeline of President Donald Trump’s relationship with Epstein and contains thousands of books' worth of the released so-called “Epstein Files,” in which Black was mentioned over 8,500 times.
That protest included Dani Bensky, a dancer, educator, and Epstein survivor from 2004 to 2005. A few weeks after the action, Bensky wrote an op-ed for Hyperallergic condemning Black’s board position as “one of the starkest examples of institutional ignorance — a head-in-the-sand, look-the-other-way mentality that will inevitably give abuse of power a dark corner to grow and fester in.”
Besides his investments in MoMA, Black has held enormous sway in the art world. In a newly released book by William D. Cohan, Black disclosed plans to convert the Woolworth Mansion into a tax-beneficial art foundation, which is expected to house works from his estimated $5 billion art collection, an asset that Epstein helped leverage as bank collateral.
Gardner said she had one simple message for the attendees of tonight’s benefit gala: “If you know, you're human garbage. And if you didn't know, you can't say that after tonight, because we're out here saying hi to everybody with our signs.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Companies at Center of Brooklyn Building Collapse Have a Record of Safety Violations, Ignoring City Orders
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Greg B. Smith, Katie Honan, Claudia Irizarry Aponte, Andrew Giambrone
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
As city officials scramble to figure out who is to blame for the stunning collapse of a Brooklyn apartment building into an adjacent construction site this week, questions are surfacing about the troubled track records of two of the contractors doing work there.
The three-story apartment building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. collapsed Wednesday afternoon into an empty lot next door at 2625 Bedford Ave. that was being dug out to make way for a planned apartment building. The city Department of Buildings said workers were down in the pit doing excavation when the late afternoon collapse occurred.
City officials said Thursday that eight people — including two children aged 9 and 10 — died and 19 more were injured, seven kids among them. Firefighters searched for survivors, braving treacherous conditions made worse by a torrential downpour, but wrapped up their mission late Thursday after concluding the search was complete. The dead included two construction workers, officials said.
At a press conference near the site, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the Buildings Department had identified five companies working at the collapse site that are “associated with 100 sites across the city.” The agency launched a sweep of those locations to ensure they’re in compliance with the city’s building code.
“If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city who is responsible for this, we will hold them accountable,” the mayor vowed.
On Thursday evening, the Police Department released the names of the victims: Nicole Daniela Salvada Rodriguez, 9; Kevin Santiago Reyes Gonzalez, 10; Gabriel Siguencia, 22; Barry Mamadou, 23; Jose Luis Caguana Cosquillo, 25; Edgar Sapon, 26; Ndiaye Mamdou, 31; and Juan Daniel Salvada Guzman, 31.
Elite Concrete’s Record
Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani would not name the companies who had been working at or near the site, but records and interviews with workers revealed two: Elite Concrete, which was handling the excavation, and N Tech Design of America, which had performed demolition of the one-story building that existed at the empty lot before construction began.
Records reviewed by The City Reporter show Elite has been cited by the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration, the federal agency that regulates construction safety, two times in the last four years over serious construction accidents.
In April 2023 an Elite worker fell 12 feet at a site at 32-03 39th Ave. in Long Island City after a steel deck collapsed, records show. OSHA accused Elite of failing to ensure workers had adequate fall protection and did not “determine if the walking/working surfaces in which its employees were to work on had the strength and structure integrity to support employees safely.”
Then, in August 2025, OSHA cited Elite again after a worker at a Jersey City, N.J., site was electrocuted using a steel trowel near a power line that wasn’t properly grounded. OSHA issued another violation, charging that workers at the site were exposed to empalement dangers because protruding steel bars known as rebar were not adequately covered.
In the Long Island City case, OSHA hit Elite with $32,000 in penalties which they reduced to $15,000 after the company contested the sanctions. In the New Jersey case, OSHA issued more than $11,000 in fines which Elite is contesting, records show.
Elite’s CEO, Eli Friedman, did not immediately respond to The City Reporter’s request for comment Thursday.
Defied Stop-Work Order
Another firm working the site was N Tech Design of America which did the demolition of a one-story building there that preceded the excavation work.
Last spring the Buildings Department slapped N Tech with $10,000 in fines after city inspectors discovered they were doing demolition without a permit, and then defied a stop-work order and continued working. The company paid the fine and work resumed in April after DOB granted them a permit.
Two years ago N Tech was sued by the owner of a Fenimore Street building in Brooklyn adjacent to where the firm was performing excavation work. The owner, James Farah, alleged that he found significant water and structural damage at his building that he blamed on N Tech’s excavation work.
Aramis Brown, who is listed as the licensee for N Tech, declined to comment.
On Thursday Crain’s New York reported that they had reviewed a Buildings Department document that said unsafe construction work at 2625 Bedford had caused the three-story building next door at 1321 Flatbush to collapse. After Crain’s inquired about that, however, DOB retracted the finding and said the cause of the collapse remained under investigation.
City Objections to New Building Plan
In addition to the two contractors, the buildings department has raised questions about plans by the owner, a limited liability company owned by Robert Fischman called W6 Facility X LLC, to erect a nine-story building at the site.
Buildings Commissioner Tigani said the department had earlier this year approved plans to build a three-story structure there, but last month Fischman amended his plans and sought approval for a nine-story structure that would rise 85 feet above the street.
In city records, the agency noted it has raised “objections” to this plan. But DOB spokesperson Andrew Rudansky said the department could not provide specific details about its concerns until the owner’s registered design professional — the developer’s architect — had a chance to respond.
Property records have also raised questions about the owner of the building that collapsed.
The building was built in 1930 and is owned by Isolag Realty Corp., tied to Brooklyn-based landlord Olufemi Falade. The building had 98 open housing violations as of Thursday, including 21 “immediately hazardous” and 40 “hazardous” violations for various conditions, according to city records.
The property appeared on the city’s tax lien sale list multiple times in the past decade. Falade was jailed for 12 days in 2006 for civil contempt for failing to fix reams of violations at other Brooklyn buildings he owned, the New York Times and New York Post previously reported. Public Advocate Jumaane Williams named him on the city’s “worst landlords” list, based on housing code violations, as recently as 2024.
‘An Excellent Young Man’
A Bushwick-based soccer club told The City Reporter one of its athletes died in the collapse.
José Luis Caguana Cosquillo was a construction worker at the Flatbush Avenue site. He leaves behind a pregnant wife and 4-year-old son, said Club Deportivo La Bahía leader Rodrigo Tubón. Caguana Cosquillo’s wife is due to give birth Friday, Tubón said.
Tubón, 50, hails from the same Ecuadorian village as Caguana Cosquillo and said he’d known his parents and relatives for many years. The young father would often come to games with his own burgeoning family, who lived in Bushwick.
“He was an excellent young man,” an emotional Tubón said in Spanish. “We lost the best guy on the team.”
The soccer club is discussing turning its scheduled championship game on Saturday into a fundraiser for Caguana Cosquillo’s family.
“Anything we can do to help,” Tubón said. “We’re all very shaken up by this. It’s unbelievable.”

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘Hurry, hurry, get your tickets now!’ The last of the great Australian showmen – photo essay
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Words by Tereasa Trevor and photographs by Liz Ham
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
My uncle Teddy Trevor remembers Casey Nelson, a fellow showman, spruiking his double-jointed horse to sideshow punters in the 1960s. The horse, Nelson warned, was “showing here for the last time”. “Too late, too late will be the cry, when Happy Harry has passed you by,” he called. The act continued for another two decades.
I’ve been hearing stories like this my whole life. Ted laughs at Casey’s line as he pours another cup of tea and passes the biscuits at the kitchen table of the family home in Brisbane. At 91, after a lifetime in Australia’s travelling shows, he has no desire to quit the showgrounds yet. While their mid-century heyday may have passed, these grounds are still the lifeblood of his friendships and family.
Ted feels blessed, he says, to belong to two great show families: the Trevors, circus people on his father’s side, and the Fosters, sideshow people on his mother’s. Born on the showgrounds in 1935, he comes from more than eight generations of show folk.
Ted’s grandmother Cora Trevor performed an iron-jaw act, hanging upside-down and spinning grown men by her teeth, including her 14-stone (88kg) acrobat father. My great-grandmother Alice Foster, known as LuLu, arrived in Australia in 1913. She was a widow with six sons and a daughter. Lulu kept her whole family fed while running a dancing duck as a sideshow act.
Uncle Teddy’s own entry into work coincided with the second world war, which brought the showgrounds to a halt. He started his career selling fabric door to door from my grandmother’s vardo caravan. As a young man in the 1950s, he worked with my uncle Frank Foster, promoting Slim Dusty’s tent show on the sideshow alley. Those days were hectic. “You start at nine in the morning, you don’t finish till after 11 at night, and you do a show every 20 minutes,” Ted tells me.
“The show was a big event for the town,” Ted says – the biggest day of the year for some places. The men wore suits, hats and ties, the women their best dresses. “Now they go in a pair of shorts and thongs,” he says.
Teddy says the atmosphere of the sideshow was what everyone came to the show for. He can still recite the lines they used to entice the crowds: “The Slim Dusty show is just about to start! Australia’s top country-and-western recording star, the only Australian to top the hit parade in England, our only gold record-holder, is on this next big program. Hurry boys, hurry girls, get your tickets now! The cowboys, the cowgirls, the knife-throwers, the jugglers, you’ll see and meet them all on the inside.”
Uncle Teddy says that between the advent of TV, RSL clubs offering sideshow talent a new touring strategy, and state-based showground permits hindering showpeople from pivoting beyond the scope of their trade (for example, a clown joint can only do clown business), the landscape of the showgrounds drastically changed in the early 1970s.
Performers could sing half a dozen songs at an RSL, Ted tells me, “for what three or four days and hundreds of songs paid them on a sideshow”.
Participator numbers also declined, while costs climbed, he says. The big rides came in, worth millions. “The showgrounds are saturated with equipment now,” he says. “There’s no more ground available, so there’s no permits for the young showman.”
The cost escalated, too. “They’re charging $12 for a game on the clown joint. It’s all ridiculous,” he says. In Ted’s day, it used to be “only four bob [40 cents] to go and see the show”. Some shows were three shillings, and a shilling for a child. As he puts it: “The money was sort of nothing.”
In the last couple of years, I had seen Uncle Teddy posting diary-like entries on Facebook, sharing his memories along with photographs It led me to ask him some more questions.
Uncle Teddy often says: “I’m sorry you were born a bit late to see the action.” It’s clear he thinks I’d have loved it. He describes the camaraderie of the sideshow community, with everyone pitching in when they were needed. “Everyone’s got to do their own thing,” he says. “The stars have got to get out in the middle of the night and knock pegs in if a storm’s coming up.”
“I always loved the showgrounds because of the people,” Ted says.
 
My cousins still travel the showground runs, working joints, food trucks and rides. The skills of a modern showman are totally different from the past.
“Today you buy a $2m ride and you don’t have to be a showman,” he says. “People either like the ride or they don’t. It’s just got to be a spectacular ride, a thrill ride, and they’ll queue up and go on it … it’s a different ballgame.[Showpeople] don’t have to get up and tell a tale. They just say, ‘Next ride, hurry now, get your tickets for the next big ride,’ and that’s it.”
These days, Uncle Teddy visits his friends and family at the Beenleigh or Brisbane shows, and chats on the phone to his friends across Australia. “You get friends in different towns. You meet their kids, and when you get old, you meet their grandchildren, and they all become like family.”
I take my own child to the Royal Easter Show when it’s on in Sydney, and the moment I spot a laughing-clown joint, I half expect to see Uncle Teddy come around the corner, his eyes sparkling, a joke on his lips and coins jingling in his waist pouch. I tell them the stories Ted told me, alive with dancing ducks and my iron-jawed great-grandmother. Their eyes widen the way mine did at Ted’s kitchen table, and the show rolls on to another generation.

https://citylimits.org/mayors-office-bac.title: Mayor’s Office Backs Two New Hell’s Kitchen Tenant Unions, As Residents Push for Repairs
https://citylimits.org/mayors-office-bac.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/mayors-office-bac.text:
Share This Article
Tenants organizing across 31 Manhattan buildings in foreclosure are the latest to see support from Mamdani’s newly reinvigorated Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants.
Since January, the newly reinvigorated Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants has made it its business to support tenant unions across the city.
Now, city-employed tenant leaders are working with two new tenant unions in Hell’s Kitchen, where residents are asking for help in securing repairs and stewarding their troubled rent stabilized properties through a potential future sale.
The majority of tenants in the impacted buildings have come out in support of the union effort—a milestone, organizers say, that helps them get the attention of both their landlords and the city—and could represent another chance for the Mamdani administration to steer distressed affordable housing into the hands of tenants’ preferred buyer.
One of the unions represents tenants in 31 buildings owned by Arthur Haruvi and Peter Hungerford, which launched on Saturday, where tenants stood with city leaders outside 408 W. 56th St., where they say cooking gas has been out for 722 days. The residents are demanding repairs and a seat at the table when it comes to the future of their dilapidated buildings, now in foreclosure and bankruptcy.
“The two years without cooking gas has had a big toll. My family, and especially myself, like to cook during the holidays. We can’t cook Thanksgiving and Christmas meals on a hot plate,” said Luis Pelaez, who has lived in the building for 34 years.
There are 357 open housing code violations across the 478 units facing foreclosure, according to analysis by Housing Conservation Coordinators.
Tenants say that Peter Hungerford has responded to their request to meet, and they hope to go to the bargaining table in the coming weeks. Hungerford did not respond to City Limits’ requests for comment.
On Saturday, tenants of landlord David Ohebshalom will launch their own tenant union for nine buildings (including both rent stabilized and market rate units) on West 47th Street, alongside the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants head Cea Weaver.
Ohebshalom’s brother Daniel has made headlines before: he did jail time in 2024 for failing to comply with court orders to repair hazardous conditions at two buildings in Washington Heights.
Can tenants influence a sale?
Third time’s the charm?
Since January, the newly reinvigorated Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants has tried to influence the sale of two major portfolios of rent stabilized housing in New York. But each time, efforts to steer the buildings to preferred buyers have stumbled.
Early this year, officials intervened too late to stop the bankruptcy sale of 5,000 units from prior owner Pinnacle to private landlord Summit. And in July, housing officials backed the bid of preservation group Spatial Equity to buy 850 units in East Harlem, only to see their offers turned down and the portfolio go up for foreclosure auction this week.
Tenants in the Haruvi-Hungerford buildings say that their immediate concerns are securing repairs and maintenance, including restoring cooking gas and addressing pests. Some of the buildings are also included in a class action suit by Housing Rights Initiative against Peter Hungerford’s PH Realty Capital, which accuses the company of overcharging tenants in 18 buildings by $15 million.
But residents know they face a precarious position with their buildings in foreclosure. “If our buildings go up for sale we need a say in who buys them and the terms of that purchase,” said Joseph Di Salle, a resident at 450 57th St.
Tenants and their allies in city government have limited control over what ends up happening to their buildings in such scenarios. But some have credited the work of unions with pushing new landlords into concessions, like when Summit real estate forgave back rent for former Pinnacle tenants shortly after taking over.
The mayor’s housing plan includes some measures that can help tenants assert more control over their buildings when they go up for sale. Tuesday, he signed the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act into law, a measure that would give some city-approved buyers first dibs on distressed rental properties before they hit the wider market.
Those attempts to influence ownership, and the city’s overt support for tenant unions, has rubbed some property owners the wrong way, saying it “vilifies” them. And at least one developer that the administration championed recently, in the sale of three debt-riddled rent stabilized Crown Heights buildings, has a less than stellar maintenance record of its own, The City Reporter reported Tuesday.
But others see a clear role for City Hall to play.
With the Hell’s Kitchen buildings, Charlie Dulik of the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants said that the city could coordinate code enforcement, come to the bargaining table with tenants, or liaise with the landlord for the Haruvi-Hungerford tenant union.
The tenants have not, as of yet, asked for support in steering their homes to a preferred buyer. If they asked, “we would absolutely talk about it and see what we can do,” said Dulik.
To get traction, get the majority of tenants on board
The Hungerford-Haruvi buildings fit the profile for the kind of properties most likely to get City Hall’s attention. The portfolio is vast, mostly rent stabilized, and connected to a former member of the city’s worst landlord list. It also has a tenants union.
And its members on Saturday, wearing freshly pressed royal blue T-shirts, said that a majority of tenants across 10 Hell’s Kitchen buildings in the Haruvi-Hungerford portfolio had signed on with the union.
Ten blocks south, the West 47th St. Tenants Union also declared that it has the majority support of tenants in nine buildings between 8th and 9th avenues, and are calling on their landlord Ohebshalom and his management company to address rat, mouse, and pest infestations, as well as ongoing maintenance needs.
The 50 percent threshold—getting at least half of a building or buildings’ tenants on board with the union—is key, tenant leaders said, indicating that they will have significant bargaining power.
“Supporting tenant unions and majority tenant unions is incredibly important,” said Dulik, wearing a freshly screenprinted Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants jacket.
Getting to a majority of tenants has become standard practice in the field, advocates say, in part to a growing national tenant movement. The Mamdani administration has been exploring ways to give tenant unions official legal status and recognition and allow them to sue, similar to how the National Labor Relations Board recognizes labor unions.
“There’s going to be more of an emphasis on majority unions for sure, but there’s also going to be an emphasis on portfolio-wide organizing because that’s when you can make the most changes,” said K Agbebiyi, director of communications at Housing Justice for All.
Hell’s Kitchen is one of the city’s most expensive neighborhoods, with smaller walk up buildings nestled between luxury towers.
“Neighborhood tenant unions and community-based organizations are anchors for neighborhood stability,” said Alejandro Coriat, director of borough organizing for Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal. “It is what kept Hell’s Kitchen, some parts of Chelsea, and some parts of the Upper West Side affordable for working class people for a very long time.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/rich.title: Oklahoma Drops Murder Charge Against Richard Glossip, Avoiding Third Trial
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/rich.author: Liliana Segura, Jordan Smith
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/rich.text:
Less than a month before he was scheduled to stand trial a third time, accused of a murder he has always sworn he did not commit, Richard Glossip on Thursday agreed to plead guilty to a lesser charge, a final step toward bringing his three-decade legal saga to an end.
Glossip, 63, was twice convicted and sentenced to death for the 1997 murder of his boss Barry Van Treese inside Room 102 of the rundown motel the Van Treese family owned on the outskirts of Oklahoma City. A 19-year-old maintenance man named Justin Sneed admitted to killing Van Treese, but he insisted Glossip put him up to it. Sneed, who is currently serving a life sentence, escaped the death penalty by becoming the star witness against Glossip.
During a brief hearing that was originally scheduled to address pretrial matters, Oklahoma County Court Judge Natalie Mai instead accepted a plea from Glossip to accessory after the fact and dismissed the murder charge against him. With members of Van Treese’s family looking on from their seats in the jury box, Glossip stood to answer a series of routine questions to confirm that his plea was voluntary. Mai did not ask any specific questions about the crime itself.
Under Oklahoma law in place at the time of the killing, the maximum punishment for accessory after the fact was 45 years. Taking into consideration the decades Glossip spent on death row and credits earned for good behavior, Glossip’s attorneys say he would have been eligible for full release in 2016 and should serve no more time behind bars. But defense lawyers did not reach an agreement with the state as to a proposed sentence. In a statement released after the hearing, Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond, who once expressed deep concerns about the state’s case against Glossip, made clear that his office will be seeking additional prison time.
Ultimately it will be up to Mai to decide if Glossip should be sentenced to time served or if any additional punishment is warranted.
The contours of Glossip’s plea are remarkably similar to a behind-the-scenes agreement made in 2023 between Drummond and Glossip’s lead attorney Don Knight. At the time, Drummond told Knight that if a court were to overturn Glossip’s conviction, he would resolve the case by accepting a plea to accessory after the fact in exchange for time served – and a promise that Glossip would not sue Oklahoma for anything related to his arrest and incarceration.
But after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Glossip’s conviction in 2025, finding that it was rooted in false testimony and prosecutorial misconduct, Drummond, who by then was running for governor, did an abrupt about-face, announcing he would once again prosecute Glossip for first degree murder.
In the year and a half since then, it has become glaringly apparent that prosecutors from Drummond’s office are grossly ill-equipped to take Glossip’s case to trial. Since his original trial in 1998, the state has lost or destroyed evidence, numerous witnesses have died, and prosecutors have conceded that their own star witness — who has sought to recant his testimony multiple times — can’t actually be expected to remember what happened the night of the killing.
“For 30 years, Richard Glossip has maintained his innocence,” Knight said in a statement after the hearing. “After nearly executing him 9 times, the State of Oklahoma has now dismissed the murder charge against him. This morning, to finally put this matter to rest, Rich pleaded guilty to being an accessory after the fact. We believe Rich has more than paid his debt to society.”
Glossip had originally been charged as an accessory after the fact for initially failing to give police information about the killing. The night Van Treese was killed, Glossip said, Sneed woke him up around 4 a.m. by knocking on the wall of his apartment, which was adjacent to the motel’s office. Standing outside with a black eye, Sneed told Glossip he had chased off some drunks who had broken a window in one of the motel rooms. According to Glossip, he asked Sneed about his black eye, and Sneed flippantly replied, “I killed Barry.”
According to Glossip, it wasn’t until the next morning, when Van Treese was missing, that he realized Sneed might have been serious. Still, Glossip didn’t tell the cops right away; he said his girlfriend suggested waiting until they figured out what was going on.
But Sneed told police Glossip was the mastermind behind the plot to kill Van Treese, and, with no other evidence tying Glossip to the crime, Sneed’s statement became the basis of the state’s case. At Glossip’s 1998 trial, prosecutors said that he had taken advantage of the younger, more vulnerable Sneed, offering him money to kill their boss so that Glossip could take over the motel. “Glossip encouraged, aided and abetted and sent Mr. Sneed off to do his dirty work,” then-prosecutor Fern Smith told the jury.
But this story began falling apart not long after Glossip arrived on death row. A video of Sneed’s police interrogation cast serious doubt on the state’s version of events, revealing coercive questioning by Oklahoma City detectives who pressured Sneed into implicating Glossip.
Glossip’s defense failed to present the tape to the jury, which led an Oklahoma court to overturn Glossip’s first conviction based on ineffective assistance of counsel. Although a second jury convicted him and sent him to die in 2004, doubts over Glossip’s guilt continued to grow.
Glossip subsequently came close to execution many times and may well have been executed if Drummond hadn’t intervened upon taking office in 2023. He ordered an independent investigation into the case, which concluded that rampant prosecutorial misconduct had infected Glossip’s conviction. Drummond asked the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals to overturn the case. When that failed, joined Glossip in asking the Supreme Court to intervene, arguing that Sneed – whom the state has described as its “indispensable witness” – had lied on the witness stand.
Drummond’s concessions about the flaws in the state’s case and his unprecedented advocacy on Glossip’s behalf made his announcement in June 2025 that he would seek to retry Glossip for murder all the more shocking. According to Glossip’s lawyers, the decision also betrayed the long-standing agreement with Drummond to resolve the case and set Glossip free.
After that, Drummond essentially washed his hands of the case to focus on his ultimately failed attempt to become Oklahoma’s next governor, handing off prosecutorial duties to other lawyers in his office. Prosecutors declared that they intended to use the same discredited evidence to try Glossip a third time and spent months fighting to keep him in jail. Despite those efforts, Mai ordered Glossip’s release.
With a December 2026 trial date looming, tensions between the two sides have ratcheted up. Glossip’s lawyers have complained about prosecutors failing to turn over evidence as required under the law. Prosecutors have tried to limit what the defense can present to jurors at trial regarding the history of the case – including asking Mai to bar any mention of Drummond’s previous advocacy on Glossip’s behalf.
Glossip’s sentencing hearing is scheduled for December 17.
Since his release, Glossip has “been living a peaceful and law-abiding life,” Knight said in his statement. “We look forward to an opportunity to show why returning him to custody would not serve the interests of justice, and to ending this nightmare for Rich and all concerned.”
After the hearing, Glossip and his wife, Lea, stood with Knight to address reporters. Glossip thanked Knight and Lea for their support. “It was a hard day,” Lea told The Intercept, “but Richard and I are both people of faith.” She expressed that “today marks a meaningful step toward finally bringing this case to an end. We are both deeply grateful for the tireless efforts of his legal team.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Philadelphia city council investigates sudden closure of oldest natural history research institution in the Americas
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Adam Schrader
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Academy of Natural Sciences, a 198-year-old public museum in Philadelphia run by Drexel University, shuttered in September because of rising costs. The university’s president will now testify under subpoena before Philadelphia’s city council on 16 November, answering questions about the sudden closure and what will happen to the museum’s valuable collection of more than 19 million specimens.
While many of the Academy’s workers have been laid off, collection managers still on staff have faced an “astronomical increase” in emails and calls, says Amber Redfield, a former geosciences collection manager and fossil preparator at the Academy who was recently laid off and is now volunteering there. She says that people have been asking: “Is this safe?” “Can I see it?” “Can I book an appointment?”
Isa Betancourt, a former curatorial assistant in the entomology department and an organiser with the Save the Academy coalition, says the number of curators has dropped from 11 to five. The invertebrate palaeontology collection manager recently left for a job at the American Museum of Natural History. “There is no plan to replace her," Betancourt tells The Art Newspaper. Endowed curator posts in entomology and palaeontology have gone unfilled for years, she adds.
Founded in 1812, the Academy describes itself as the oldest natural history research institution in the Americas. It opened its museum to the public in 1828 and, in 1868, put Hadrosaurus foulkii on view as the world’s first mounted dinosaur skeleton. Its millions of specimens include plants collected on the Lewis and Clark expedition, John James Audubon’s birds and Thomas Jefferson’s fossils.
The Academy became a Drexel affiliate in 2011, while retaining its status as a separate non-profit with its own board. Drexel recently told the city council it had “stepped in as a partner” that year, when the Academy “faced severe financial distress”.
The city council passed a resolution on 17 September to investigate the Academy’s closing. The resolution calls institutions like the Academy “part of the cultural fabric of the city” and says its shuttering would especially affect area residents “for whom the museum is a fixture of the neighbourhood”. An initial hearing took place on 26 October, which Drexel’s president did not attend.
At the hearing, representatives for Drexel cited the building's "substantial capital needs" and told the city council that public exhibitions need a new model, "almost certainly in a different location".
Sarah McAnulty, a squid biologist and Save the Academy organiser, says city council members asked Drexel representatives to check their numbers. "If all you need to keep the public museum open is a million dollars, what the hell are we doing here?" she says, describing the city council’s reaction.
Staff learned of the Academy’s closure at a morning meeting on 1 September, Redfield says. Most staff were laid off by 1 November, and many people "found out they were let go in a report by The Philadelphia Inquirer", she adds.
Redfield says the museum drew more than 60,000 visitors in its final 12 days of public hours. "That's not enough time to shut down a lifetime of scientific and educational work," she adds. "I planned to retire at the Academy and don't have any backup plans." Now she is volunteering.
"Unfortunately, volunteer labour is essential to most natural history collections, but it’s not sustainable,” Betancourt says. “The fact that the volunteer manager was initially slated for termination and had to be reinstated shows Drexel has no idea how these collections function."
Betancourt adds that the Academy's social media accounts have been inactive for two months and staff do not have access because Drexel controls them. The Academy's director of marketing and communications was let go with the closure. Betancourt says the university may not realise that communications and education staff connect the collections with the public and potential benefactors, "otherwise, the collections work in darkness”.
The William Penn Foundation has offered a year of funding to replace Drexel's subsidy for the museum. "The foundation has not received a response to our offer," a spokesperson told the Inquirer. Drexel later stated that it had not received a "formal proposal with a defined level of financial support".
Betancourt says Save the Academy wants Drexel to explain "why no capital campaign was undertaken" and "why the scientific community has been shut out of behind-the-scenes negotiations. The closed-door negotiations got us a closed museum. Natural history collections tied to a financially haemorrhaging university are not safe natural history collections.”

The National Gallery of Art has announced part two of its Across the Nation lending program, which will bring masterworks from its collection across the United States. The initiative began last year to commemorate America’s 250th anniversary. The new cycle follows a $116 million gift from the Mitchell P. Rales Family Foundation.
In its first year, Across the Nation traveled to ten states. In its second iteration, it will expand to Alabama, California, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Texas, and Wisconsin. Its goal is to lend work to museums in all fifty states within the first decade of the program. Partner museums for this cycle are the Crocker Art Museum (Sacramento, CA), Dayton Art Institute (Dayton, OH), El Paso Museum of Art (El Paso, TX), Gilcrease Museum (Tulsa, OK), Madison Museum of Contemporary Art (Madison, WI), Mobile Museum of Art (Mobile, AL), South Dakota Art Museum (South Dakota State University, Brookings, SD), and the Westmoreland Museum of American Art (Greensburg, PA).
Each institution will receive important works from the National Gallery collection, including historical and contemporary pieces spanning painting, sculpture, video, and installation. The loans will include works by artists such as Claude Monet, Mark Rothko, Donald Judd, Georgia O’Keeffe, Sol LeWitt, Henri Matisse, Rembrandt, and Susie J. Lee. Works will go on display as early as summer 2027 and will be on view through 2029.
“Everyone deserves to experience the awe-inspiring power of art. Through Across the Nation, we are proud to extend the reach of the nation’s art collection by bringing incredible works of art from throughout history directly into American communities together with our partner museums. It is an honor for the National Gallery to partner with our valued colleagues from museums located in communities across America,” said Kaywin Feldman, director of the National Gallery of Art, in a press release. “This would not be possible without the generosity of Mitchell P. Rales, whose historic gift will allow the program to continue expanding access to defining works of art for generations to come.”
