https://jacobin.com/2026/11/snyc-youth-c.title: The Southern Negro Youth Congress’s Bold Push for Equality
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/snyc-youth-c.author: Robert Greene II
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/snyc-youth-c.text:
The Southern Negro Youth Congress’s Bold Push for Equality
Founded in 1937, the Southern Negro Youth Congress was a key player in the radical wing of the early phase of the civil rights movement.
“Behold the land, the rich and resourceful land, from which for a hundred years its best elements have been running away, its youth and hope, black and white, scurrying North because they are of each other, and dare not face a future of equal, independent, upstanding human beings, in a real and not a sham democracy.” This line was spoken by W. E. B. Du Bois near the end of arguably his greatest speech, titled “Behold the Land.” It was delivered on October 20, 1946, at a convention hosted by the Southern Negro Youth Congress (SNYC), where Du Bois thundered from the dais at Antisdel Chapel at Benedict College in Columbia, South Carolina. He and the SNYC had, for a brief moment, made the Palmetto State the center of the struggle for global human rights in the post–World War II years.
Founded in 1937, the SNYC represented the radical wing of the early phase of the civil rights movement. Its radical politics lay in the organization’s recognition of the links between racial and class problems in the US South and throughout the nation. At times, it made alliances on the ground with various Communist Party USA organizations in the South. While many historians have come to see the civil rights era as extending longer than the “classic” phase of 1954 until the mid-1960s, what makes the SNYC unique is how many of the issues they attacked would come up again during both the 1960s and the early decades of the twenty-first century.
As part of the youth wing of the National Negro Congress (NNC), the SNYC went well beyond organizing the black youth of the Jim Crow–era South. It offered them an opportunity to voice and do something about the growing frustration many of them felt living in the grip of Jim Crow segregation.
Through the course of the Great Depression and World War II, the SNYC pressured political and social leaders throughout the South. As they pressed for greater freedom for all people in the former Confederacy, the SNYC became a beacon of hope during the fight against fascism at home and abroad. The SNYC always linked the struggles against Jim Crow segregation at home to the rising tide of fascism, Nazism, and militarism abroad, even before the advent of the better-known “Double V” campaign among black Americans during World War II, pushing for victory over fascism abroad and Jim Crow at home.
The bread and butter of the organization was the organizing of previously disenfranchised workers in the South. Their earliest campaigns included the organizing of black tobacco farmers outside their first headquarters of Richmond, Virginia. At other points, the SNYC would participate in voter registration drives and work with unions to increase labor organizing across a region that, by the Great Depression, had earned a staunchly anti-labor reputation. Other efforts included the investigation of cases of murder in the South via private investigators, such as the case of William Daniel’s 1946 murder by Birmingham police. In short, like the NNC and other radical organizations of the Great Depression and World War II eras, the SNYC used virtually every method at their disposal to fight against Jim Crow segregation.
But the challenges facing the SNYC were more dangerous after America’s triumph in World War II. A rift formed between liberals and leftists after the war; the wartime exigency of the American-Soviet alliance gave way to fears of another world war, this time between the United States and its allies against the Soviet Union and a growing postwar Communist bloc. At the same time, anti-colonial campaigns were spreading like wildfire across Asia and Africa. This, coupled with black frustration at home due to renewed white backlash to civil rights, gave the SNYC ample reason to step up their efforts in a place like South Carolina.
Ahead of Its Time
By 1946, South Carolina already had a growing movement for radical human rights. The Progressive Democratic Party (PDP), led by black South Carolinians Modjeska Simkins, John Henry McCray, and Osceola McKaine, built a progressive black alternative to South Carolina’s white-supremacist Democratic Party of South Carolina. Registering black South Carolinians to vote, putting up their own slate of candidates for state and national office, and even traveling to the 1944 Democratic National Convention to challenge the legitimacy of the South Carolina Democratic Party, the Progressive Democratic Party presaged the better-known Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party (MFDP) by twenty years in using grassroots democratic traditions to attempt to upend the old system.
Their efforts to overturn the ironclad rule of the white-supremacist Democratic Party did not result in electoral victory. Osceola McKaine, the black nominee of the PDP who campaigned against incumbent Olin Johnston in 1944, fell short in his campaign. But McKaine’s own personal story is a reminder of why black South Carolina, in 1944, was so thoroughly galvanized to fight back against Jim Crow.
McKaine, a native of Sumter, South Carolina, served in the United States military during World War I. After his term of service ended, McKaine, tired of the hypocrisy of American calls to “make the world safe for democracy” abroad while not doing so at home, settled in Ghent, Belgium, and opened a successful nightclub. Forced to flee Belgium due to World War II, McKaine returned to Sumter determined to fight for democracy in his home state. He was defeated in 1944 by Johnston, who was governor of South Carolina when the state condemned to death fourteen-year-old George Stinney, who some believe is the youngest person condemned to death in US history.
The PDP, like the MFDP twenty years later, was important not due to victory at the polls but due to the organization’s ability to give voters hope who had had none for generations. Thousands of new black voters became part of South Carolina’s voting process for the first time since the immediate aftermath of the collapse of Reconstruction. Meanwhile, growing pressure to restore the right to vote for black citizens in the South was also enhanced by the 1944 Smith v. Allwright Supreme Court decision, which declared the all-white primaries of Southern Democratic parties unconstitutional.
Again, South Carolina played a crucial role in resisting this, with Governor Johnston himself calling a special session of the state legislature in 1944 to pass new laws to continue the white primary. It was not until another federal court case, Elmore v. Rice, originating with the challenge of black South Carolinian George Elmore and decided in 1947, that the white primary was broken.
What SNYC Represented
South Carolina, therefore, had already made itself the nexus of domestic political battles over racism and citizenship. But the state was also important as a site of international debate over the future of peace in the post–World War II landscape. One of the chief architects of the post–World War II foreign policy, which quickly became antagonistic toward the Soviets, was South Carolinian James Byrnes.
Often overlooked in twentieth-century American foreign and domestic policy history, Byrnes holds the unique distinction of being one of the few politicians in American history to hold virtually every possible office in the federal government. He served as congressman, and later senator, from South Carolina in the 1920s and 1930s. As a close friend to President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Byrnes briefly served on the Supreme Court before being named director of the Office of Economic Stabilization, and later director of the Office of War Mobilization during World War II. In that role, Byrnes became one of the most important people in America’s war effort. Afterward, under President Harry Truman, Byrnes was named secretary of state in 1945.
But Byrnes coveted the presidency. As was the case with another South Carolinian, John C. Calhoun, in the nineteenth century, Byrnes’s ties to South Carolina and white-supremacist ideology became the chief impediments to higher office. Most notably, liberals and progressives within the New Deal–era Democratic Party stymied efforts to make Byrnes the vice president under Franklin Roosevelt during his 1944 campaign. Still, Byrnes remained a powerful force within Southern and national politics. And as the Cold War intensified, a massive campaign for social change in his home state made perfect sense.
The SNYC, committed as it was to racial justice at home and peace abroad, knew that targeting Byrnes’ home state was a major rallying point for the radical wing of American politics in the post–World War II years. Also, the fact that South Carolina was home to a growing radical movement for human rights helped make it a logical choice for the SNYC’s annual convention.
Bringing both foreign and domestic crises together, finally, was the saga of Isaac Woodard, which galvanized activists and brought global attention to South Carolina. A black World War II veteran blinded by police on February 12, 1946, in Batesburg-Leesville, South Carolina, Woodard’s case became a symbol of the brutal attacks on black veterans and their allies that occurred throughout the South after World War II. A backlash similar to the Red Summer of 1919, the post-1945 political and social environment was incredibly difficult and reactionary, but also presented incredible opportunities to SNYC leaders.
The SNYC needed a place to not only bring together their members but a location where a new, militant human rights movement was evolving on the ground. Columbia became that place, due in large part to the work of Modjeska Simkins in welcoming the organization to her hometown.
The 1946 convention in Columbia, South Carolina owed a great deal to Modjeska Simkins. A human rights activist born and raised in Columbia, Simkins had become, by 1946, one of the leaders of a radical human and civil rights movement in the Palmetto State. She became secretary of the South Carolina State Conference of the NAACP in 1941 after working tirelessly in black communities across the state as director of negro work for the South Carolina Tuberculosis Association, and after playing a pivotal role in the formation of the state conference in 1939.
Many years later, in an oral history interview with Jacquelyn Dowd Hall, Simkins argued that the SNYC represented something unique and powerful in the broader human and civil rights movements of the twentieth century. “The power structure,” Simkins stated, “has always feared the combining of the forces of black and white masses.”
This was what the SNYC represented. On the first insert page of the 1946 conference program, the Southern Youth Legislature, which was the organizing body within the SNYC that spoke for the organization, made their demands clear. “We meet in solemn session,” they began, as “militant, courageous Negro youth of the South. Youth. . . . which must and will be served. Youth. . . . dedicated to the struggle for freedom. Youth determined to achieve that freedom in its lifetime.” For members of the SNYC, the opportunity arose to finally make a serious blow against segregation. Or, as the title of Erik Gellman’s groundbreaking 2012 work on the National Negro Congress goes, a “death blow to Jim Crow.”
Some of the leaders of the 1946 conference, like Modjeska Simkins or Dorothy Burnham, would become better known throughout the twentieth century for their work in various strands of the civil and human rights movements. Others, such as Columbia SNYC leader Harold H. Poole or Benedict College student Ethel Bigby, are not as well known nationally or even regionally. But they all were pivotal leaders in a movement that, in 1946, seemed poised to tackle the crises that Dr Martin Luther King Jr so eloquently described a generation later: militarism, racism, and capitalism.
Alas, the Second Red Scare at home and the Cold War abroad destroyed the SNYC. The organization was constantly harassed by the FBI and local police forces in the South. Ultimately, the organization was also brought down, like others, due to its alliance with the 1948 Progressive Party campaign of Henry Wallace. Eugene “Bull” Connor — better remembered for his vicious treatment of activists in Birmingham in 1963 — created havoc for left-wing activists in Birmingham.
Its 1946 convention remains the high point of the organization’s history, leaving behind a legacy of activism in South Carolina and throughout the nation. Many of the members of the SNYC, or those affiliated with the organization, continued to be involved in activism deep into the twentieth century. For example, several of the founders of the legendary Freedomways magazine, which between 1961 and 1985 served as a key periodical for the black left, were veterans of the SNYC. Editors and writers such as Esther Cooper Jackson, Louis Burnham, and even Du Bois himself all had significant ties with the organization.
In that sense, the SNYC is part of the larger connective tissue of twentieth century radical social movements — and the 1946 convention in South Carolina was its moment of triumph.

https://taz.de/Experte-zu-Prognosemaerkt.title: Experte zu Prognosemärkten: „Diese Märkte können Desinformation antreiben“
https://taz.de/Experte-zu-Prognosemaerkt.author: Simon Wörz
https://taz.de/Experte-zu-Prognosemaerkt.text:
Experte zu Prognosemärkten: „Diese Märkte können Desinformation antreiben“
Wetten auf sogenannten Prediction Markets sorgten bei den US-Midterms ganz leicht für ein künstliches Wahlkampf-Momentum. Die Trump-Familie verdient mit.
taz: Herr Hornsby, sogenannte Prediction Markets haben bei den US-Midterms eine große Rolle gespielt. Deren Daten wurden von CNN und anderen Medien für ihre Prognosen genutzt. Worum geht es hier überhaupt?
Michael Hornsby: Prediction Markets sind Prognoseplattformen, auf denen Menschen mit Verträgen handeln, wie wahrscheinlich ein bestimmtes Ereignis ist. Anbieter wie Polymarket oder Kalshi wirken auf den ersten Blick wie Wettseiten, funktionieren aber anders. Es gibt keine Buchmacher, die die Quoten festlegen, sondern die Leute handeln direkt miteinander: Die eine Seite setzt faktisch auf „Ja, das tritt ein“, die andere auf „Nein, das passiert nicht“. Beide schließen einen Vertrag zu einem Preis ab. Wenn das Ereignis vorbei ist, wird der richtige Vertrag ausgezahlt.
Michael Hornsby ist Co-Direktor des Anti-Corruption Data Collective (ACDC). Die Non-Profit-Organisation untersucht, wie Technologien wie Kryptowährungen und Prognosemärkte Korruptionsbekämpfung und Demokratie beeinflussen.
taz: Warum setzen viele Leute Geld bei solchen Plattformen und nicht bei klassischen Wettanbietern?
Hornsby: In den USA werden Prediction Markets eher als Finanzinstrumente, denn als Glücksspiel behandelt und können neben Sport auch Märkte zu Wahlen, Politik oder Kultur anbieten. Und Polymarket, das seinen Sitz offshore in Panama hat, bietet sogar Märkte zu militärischen Fragen an. Viele Menschen finden das spannend, weil sie Informationen aus den Medien, von anderen Personen oder aus ihrem beruflichen Fachwissen nutzen können, um zu versuchen, ihren vermeintlichen Informationsvorsprung gegenüber dem Rest des Marktes in Geld umzuwandeln.
taz: Ihr Kollektiv hat jetzt beobachtet und analysiert, wie die US-Zwischenwahlen auf Prediction Markets abgebildet wurden. Mit welchem Ergebnis?
Hornsby: Wir konnten in unserer Analyse etwa 28.000 verschiedene Märkte für die Kongresswahlen sehen. Nach unserer eher konservativen Berechnung flossen insgesamt über 440 Millionen US-Dollar in Prediction Markets zu den Midterms. Andere Schätzungen sprechen von über eine Milliarde.
taz: Auf welche Ereignisse konnte gewettet werden?
Hornsby: Die Fragen auf diesen Märkten können ganz einfach sein, zum Beispiel: „Wie wahrscheinlich ist es, dass Kandidat*in X die Wahl gewinnt?“ Es gibt aber auch sehr detaillierte Wetten, etwa darauf, ob eine Nachrichtenagentur die Wahlergebnisse bis zu einer Uhrzeit verkündet, ob Obama für eine*n Kandidat*in im Wahlkampf auftritt oder wen Trump bis zu einem bestimmten Datum unterstützt.
taz: Welche Gefahren haben Prediction Markets für Wahlen?
Hornsby: Wir haben uns Prediction Markets zuerst vor allem mit Blick auf Insiderhandel angesehen. Die Gefahr, dass Menschen mit vertraulichen Informationen auf diese Märkte setzen, so wie bei der Maduro-Festnahme. Als wir sahen, wie viele einzelne Märkte bei den Midterms eröffnet wurden, wurde klar: Viele dieser Märkte haben sehr wenig Volumen, sprich es wurde wenig darin investiert. Diese Märkte sind anfällig dafür, dass Einzelne mit viel Geld den Preis und die angezeigte Wahrscheinlichkeit eines Ereignisses verschieben können. Unsere Sorge ist, dass rund um Wahlen gezielt Desinformation betrieben werden kann.
taz: Wie funktioniert das?
Hornsby: Bei 96 Prozent der von uns untersuchten Midterms-Märkte ließ sich der Preis mit weniger als 3.500 US-Dollar um fünf Prozentpunkte Wahrscheinlichkeit verschieben. Wenn eine Seite im Wahlkampf oder Medien das aufgreift und sagt: „Schaut, hier gibt es ein Momentum, diese Person liegt vorne“, beeinflusst das die ganze Informationslandschaft rund um die Wahl und möglicherweise sogar, wie Menschen am Ende abstimmen.
taz: Gab es solche Vorfälle im Vorfeld der Midterms?
Hornsby: Das Problem ist, dass wir Preisbewegungen nur schwer einer klaren Absicht zuordnen können. Ein konkretes Beispiel ist die Bürgermeisterwahl in Los Angeles mit Kandidat Spencer Pratt, eine Reality‑TV‑Star. Dort gab es eine Art Fanbasis auf Prediction Markets, die seine abgestürzte Prognose nach schlechten Umfragen schnell wieder hochgekauft hat. Solche Dynamiken zeigen, dass Märkte nicht nur Informationen widerspiegeln, sondern auch gezielte Versuche hervorheben könnten, die Chancen eines Kandidaten sichtbar hochzuhalten.
taz: Bei den Präsidentschaftswahlen in Brasilien lagen die Prognosen der Plattformen ziemlich daneben. Bei den Midterms waren sie ziemlich treffsicher. Polymarket und Kalshi feiern sich dafür, richtige Ergebnisse besonders schnell verkündet zu haben.
Hornsby: Prediction Markets lagen bei den Midterms recht häufig richtig, aber das gilt genauso für viele Umfragen. Was man klar sieht, ist ein Beschleunigungseffekt. Prediction Markets greifen Stimmungen und Trends in der Wahlnacht früher und manchmal stärker auf. Wenn der Eindruck entsteht, das ist ein riesiger Sieg für die Demokraten, investieren viele Leute schnell. Die eigentliche Frage ist daher, ob Prediction Markets wirklich zusätzliches Wissen geliefert haben oder vor allem das widerspiegelten, was ohnehin schon bekannt war.
taz: Wer gewinnt am Ende bei Prediction Markets?
Hornsby: Ein kleiner Prozentsatz der Nutzer*innen verdient den Großteil des Geldes. Zahlreiche Studien zeigen, dass das oberste ein Prozent die Mehrheit der Gewinne abschöpft. Was kostet es die Gesellschaft, wenn wir für eine etwas schnellere, vielleicht ein bisschen genauere Wahlvorhersage in Kauf nehmen, dass viele Menschen dafür auf diesen Plattformen Geld verlieren?
taz: Donald Trump Jr. ist Berater von Kalshi, hält Firmenanteile und sitzt im Beirat von Polymarket. Welche Rolle spielt er?
Hornsby: Die politische Rückendeckung durch die Präsidentenfamilie für diese Märkte muss man vor allem mit Blick auf Regulierung sehen: Der Vorsitzende der zuständigen Behördenaufsicht, ein Trump‑Ernannter, verfolgt einen sehr industriefreundlichen Kurs. Gleichzeitig führte eine Investmentgesellschaft, an der Donald Trump Jr. beteiligt ist, eine große Finanzierungsrunde für Polymarket an.
taz: Was könnte sich durch die neuen Mehrheiten im Kongress hinsichtlich Regulierung für die Plattformen ändern?
Hornsby: Es gibt bereits zahlreiche Gesetzesvorhaben mit Unterstützung aus beiden Parteien, die aber kaum vorangekommen sind. Einige wollen die Zuständigkeit zurück an die Bundesstaaten geben. Andere zielen darauf, Beteiligung von Militär und politischen Insider*innen einzuschränken. Mit der Kontrolle der Demokraten über zentrale Aufsichtsgremien ist zu erwarten, dass die Rolle der nationalen Aufsichtsbehörde genauer untersucht wird.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: This Guy Could Change the Direction of the Supreme Court
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Elie Mystal
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
This Guy Could Change the Direction of the Supreme Court
Texas’s newly elected attorney general, Nathan Johnson, has the power to end the state’s role as a pipeline for the most toxic high-court cases.
The most important legal development from the midterm elections happened in Texas. Nope, I’m not talking about the election of James Talarico, or the Democrats’ newfound power to block Donald Trump’s judicial appointments. That stuff matters, of course, but the single biggest change to what happens in the courts over the next two years probably comes down to Democrat Nathan Johnson, the new attorney general for the state of Texas.
The Texas AG’s office has been ground zero for many of the most destructive legal battles Republicans have fought and largely won over the past generation. The outgoing Texas AG is the guy who lost to Talarico for the Senate, Ken Paxton. Paxton has been suing abortion providers who send mifepristone (the “abortion pill”) to his state. He has attacked trans people, immigrants, and the environment. He tried to single-handedly block Joe Biden’s agenda from ever being enacted in Texas, and has generally been a despicable menace who uses the law to promote bigotry. Paxton has been at the post since 2015. Before him, the Texas AG was Greg Abbott (the Texas governor who just lost to Gina Hinojosa). Before him, John Cornyn held the role; he’s the outgoing Republican senator whom Paxton beat in the primary. Cornyn replaced Democrat Dan Morales as AG in 1999. Republicans have literally controlled this post this whole century.
What makes the person who occupies this post particularly influential is that the Texas attorney general is always backed up by the Texas solicitor general, who has the job of arguing the AG’s cases in court. The Texas AG, rather than the governor, is also the one who appoints the SG. Past Texas solicitors general include Johnathan Mitchell—who is the guy who had the bright idea to set bounty hunters on abortion providers—and… Senator Ted Cruz.
All of this matters because a disproportionate number of this Supreme Court’s worst, most corrosive cases originate in Texas. That’s because of a quirk in Texas’s judicial structure that allows for easy and flagrant judge-shopping. In other states, the initial judge presiding over a federal lawsuit is chosen by lottery from among the available judges in the district where the lawsuit is filed. In Texas, the presiding judge is whoever happens to run the courthouse in the place where the case is filed. That means that the Texas AG can pick the judge who will rule on any given case by filing the case in the right mailbox. For the past few years, the judge of choice for culture-war issues has been the “emperor of Amarillo,” the reactionary misogynist Matthew Kacsmaryk. For the past 20 years, the judge of choice for immigration issues has been reactionary bigot Reed O’Connor.
Sometimes, a case might end there, with a favorable ruling from one of these handpicked judges. But if the losing party appeals—and, the Texas AG and SG are often counting on this—they can defend their case in front of the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals. The Fifth Circuit is the most conservative appellate court in the country, by some margin. It is full of people openly auditioning for Supreme Court appointments, and in the Trump era that audition has devolved into judges’ ruling in the most insane way possible. Fifth Circuit judges like James C. Ho, Stuart Kyle Duncan, and Andy Oldham are truly some of the worst people the system has to offer.
From there, once the next inevitable appeal arrives, it’s a straight shot to the Supreme Court, where whatever legal monstrosity the Texas AG cooked up is often enshrined into national law by the six Republican justices. What starts in Texas rarely stays there.
This is why replacing the Texas AG with a Democrat is so important. It stops a bunch of lawsuits before they even start. It greatly diminishes the evil the people on the Fifth Circuit can do. It deprives the conservatives on the Supreme Court of some of the cases they need if they want to change the law. Other Republican attorneys general who survived the blue tsunami will surely try to pick up the slack for Texas, but because other states lack the unique judge-shopping structure available in Texas, those surviving AGs are unlikely to be as effective as the Texas AG has been. Moreover, as Ian Millhiser points out, the attorney general offices in other states (like Louisiana and Mississippi, which are the other two states in the Fifth Circuit) are fundamentally smaller than Texas and don’t have as much money. “[T]hey will likely only have the resources to bring a fraction of the number of partisan lawsuits filed by Paxton.”
You don’t have to take our words for it. Just listen to conservative legal commentator Josh Blackman bemoaning the loss of the position in a post-election article in Reason:
I would suspect that all of the conservative strategic litigation cases brought by Attorney General Paxton will be dismissed. Indeed, it is conceivable that the new Texas Attorney General would not defend the Texas Ten Commandments Law if cert is granted.… The Texas Attorney General will also not bring original jurisdiction actions before the Supreme Court of Texas. Going forward, all of the strategic forums in Texas will be severely underutilized.
To de-jargonize some of the gobbledygook: “original jurisdiction actions” refer to cases where Texas sues some other state for, say, “election fraud”; “strategic forums” refer to the judge-shopping Texas AGs traditionally do; and “strategic litigation” is whatever antidemocratic cultural nonsense people like Josh Blackman can think up next. As Sean Rankin, head of the Democratic Attorneys General Association, put it in an interview with Politico, “We took the head of the snake.”
With that head gone, the Texas AG will no longer be the force for pure evil that it has been. There’s a lot of bad stuff the office will cease to do. The other side of the coin is the good stuff the AG can do. Nathan Johnson has already said he will end the out-of-state prosecutions of abortion providers and restore a “respect for the rule of law,” which was something that was severely lacking under his predecessor. But I will dare to hope for a little more than a mere restoration of respect. Texas is the corporate home of a number of companies that haven’t been regulated or investigated at the state level during this century, among them: ExxonMobile, McKesson Pharmaceuticals, AT&T, Oracle… and the entire Elon Musk cinematic universe, including Tesla, SpaceX, and Twitter.
That’s right, Nathan Johnson is poised to become Elon Musk’s worst nightmare: a Democrat with jurisdiction. Musk and his companies fled California after Tesla was sued for civil rights violations there. Do we think he stopped allegedly violating workers’ civil rights when he got to Texas? I don’t think so, and I bet Johnson doesn’t think so either. The judge-shopping door swings both ways, and all Johnson needs is one favorable district court judge in, say, Austin, and he can haul Musk before a jury of his new neighbors.
Think about all the work New York Attorney General Tish James (who won a third term last week) has done trying to hold the Trump crime family accountable. Think about all the work Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison has done trying to hold police accountable. Think about all the work California Attorney General Rob Bonta (who just won a second term) has done trying to hold ICE accountable. Now think about the fact that we added new Democratic AGs in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, and Kansas (defeating Republican Kris Kobach, who would have been the worst AG in the country if Ken Paxton did not exist).
And now we’re adding Johnson in Elon Musk’s home state of Texas to the illustrious array of Democratic crime-fighters. This, my friends, is a full-on “Avengers, Assemble” moment—and they are “on your left.”

https://gothamist.com/news/why-brooklyni.title: Why Brooklynites Jeffries and Schumer are still favorites to lead Democrats in Congress
https://gothamist.com/news/why-brooklyni.author: Brigid Bergin
https://gothamist.com/news/why-brooklyni.text:
This column originally appeared in The Politics Brief, our weekly newsletter on the people, power and policies that shape New Yorkers' lives.
Sign up to get the full version where you can ask questions, share news tips and weigh in on the conversation. Hits inboxes on Wednesdays.
Outside the Beltway, there’s been an outpouring of pushback against electing House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries as speaker and Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer as majority leader. But political observers say it’s what happens inside the Beltway that counts, and that the two Brooklyn-based politicians are unlikely to be knocked off their leadership perches.
One big reason: no one has formally stepped up to challenge either lawmaker.
In the House, Jeffries' election as speaker would mark historic firsts. He is poised to become the first Black speaker of the House and the first speaker from New York City. While a handful of newly elected Democrats have not committed to supporting him — including incoming local Reps. Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier — no other lawmaker has emerged to challenge him.
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who sits decidedly to Jeffries’s ideological left but has said she will support him, went on Instagram on Monday to explain how the internal leadership election works. The real vote takes place in a private Democratic caucus meeting through a secret ballot, she explained. If no one is challenging Jeffries, then members have no one else to vote for.
“ When you vote, it’s not this person's name, ‘yes or no’. That's not how this ballot looks,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “ The question needs to be, ‘Who do you actually want for the speakership? Who is running?’”
The behind-closed-doors process stands in contrast to how recent Republican House speaker elections have played out, spilling into acrimonious debate on the floor fueled by ideological divisions within the party and their razor-thin majority. In January 2023, it took 15 ballots to elect Rep. Kevin McCarthy speaker of the House, and then four ballots to replace him in October of that year with Rep. Mike Johnson.
Democrats are expected to hold nearly 260 seats when the next session begins in January. Jeffries only needs 218 to be elected Speaker. That means he has three dozen seats worth of negotiating room — a much more comfortable margin than House Republicans had in recent years.
“I think anything over 230 makes Hakeem’s life a lot easier A) in terms of getting elected, and B) in terms of passing bills without having to cater to the left wing of the caucus as much,” said Adam Carlson, head of the progressive polling firm Zenith Research.
In the Senate, Schumer’s prospects are more complicated.
Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, the de facto leader of the left, said he would not be supporting Schumer and that “the time is now for change.” He held a press briefing Tuesday with Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who said she was undecided.
There are rumblings that the 75-year-old veteran lawmaker may face a challenge from Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who told reporters this week that he was in “listening mode” and had not ruled out running against Schumer.
“ If Van Hollen really throws his hat into the ring and goes full bore, I think he's the only one who can theoretically put together a coalition that could work, because he's an insider,” Carlson said.
New York’s junior Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, who served as chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, said she was not "privy" to any conversations with Van Hollen and was standing firmly by Schumer.
“ He's done a great job marshaling our caucus these past two years to be laser-focused on cost, corruption and chaos,” Gillibrand said. She credited him with supporting candidates across the country who flipped at least seven Senate seats from red to blue, raising over $500 million for candidates.
“ I think people have a lot of gratitude towards Senator Schumer,” Gillibrand said, “and I think he'll win any Majority Leader race he has.”
Schumer would need a majority of the Democrats 54 to 56-member caucus to elect him majority leader. That’s roughly 29 votes.
Jeffries voiced strong support for his fellow Brooklynite.
“ Chuck Schumer was the quarterback of a team effort led by Senate Democrats and incredible candidates who ran all across the country,” said Jeffries, citing wins in Texas, Maine, Michigan, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina, Georgia and potentially in Alaska and Mississippi.
“I think the results of that election, the outcome, the decisive victory speaks for itself,” said Jeffries.
We want to hear from you
Do you support Jeffries for speaker and/or Schumer for Senate majority leader?

https://hyperallergic.com/print-center-a.text:
Print Center and Women’s Studio Workshop Name New Leaders
Plus, SITE Santa Fe artists announced, awards for Lorna Simpson and Wolfgang Tillmans, and Penske Media partners with Amazon … because of course.
Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.
Yukiko Yamagata to Helm NYC's Print Center
New York's Print Center, home to programs and exhibitions celebrating all the art that's pressed, proofed, and published, announced Yukiko Yamagata as its new executive director this week.
Her professional profile doesn't immediately scream “print nerd”: Yamagata most recently served as deputy director at Creative Time and previously worked at the Open Society Foundations, where she led a $15.8 million arts and culture fellowship program for socially engaged artists. But one of her earliest roles in the 1990s was as a senior curatorial assistant in the photo department at the Whitney Museum of American Art, and she is a current board member of Women Photograph, an organization focused on equitable practices in photojournalism and visual media.
Yamagata succeeds Judy Hecker, who announced her decision to step down earlier this year after a decade in the role, and is now executive director emerita.
Natalie Renganeschi to Lead Women's Studio Workshop
The Women's Studio Workshop in Rosendale, New York, dedicated to the printing arts as well as papermaking, bookbinding, photography, and more, has named Natalie Renganeschi as its fourth-ever executive director in the organization's 52-year history.
Renganeschi's career at WSW began in 2018, when she joined as a part-time employee while working as a high school art teacher. Now, she will oversee the nonprofit's major campus expansion, including the relaunch of its ceramics center.
“My path to leadership hasn’t been a traditional one, but it’s rooted in the ethos of WSW,” Renganeschi said in a statement. “Just as our mediums are steeped in process and the history of craft, working here is a sustained act of communal learning that allows for growth to come from below and within.”

https://citylimits.org/tras-una-decada-n.title: Tras una década, Nueva York abrió su lista de espera para licencias de venta ambulante. Esto es lo que debes saber.
https://citylimits.org/tras-una-decada-n.author: Daniel Parra
https://citylimits.org/tras-una-decada-n.text:
Share This Article
La ciudad añadirá 10.500 nuevas licencias de venta ambulante de mercancías el año que viene —que otorgan a los vendedores el derecho a vender legalmente productos, pero no alimentos— tras haber limitado el número a tan solo 853 durante décadas. “Dije: ‘Dios mío, esto está pasando de verdad’”, comentó Calvin Baker, un veterano vendedor ambulante de Harlem que fue uno de los primeros en presentar su solicitud.
Este artículo se publicó originalmente en inglés el 10 de noviembre. Traducido por Daniel Parra. Read the English version here.
Hay oportunidades que solo se presentan una vez cada década.
Para los neoyorquinos que se ganan la vida como vendedores ambulantes —un sector en el que predominan los inmigrantes, entre ellos muchos latinos—, una de ellas es entrar en la lista de espera para conseguir una codiciada licencia municipal.
Por primera vez en una década, la alcaldía abrió la semana pasada su lista de espera para las licencias de venta ambulante de mercancías, que otorgan a los vendedores el derecho a vender legalmente mercancía como joyas, juguetes y ropa, pero no alimentos.
“Dije: ‘Dios mío, esto está pasando de verdad’”, comentó Calvin Baker, un veterano vendedor ambulante de Harlem, describiendo cómo se sintió cuando por fin pudo aplicar la semana pasada.
Por décadas, él y otros vendedores han luchado contra el limitado número de licencias de la ciudad, restringido a 853 licencias desde 1979. Desde entonces, estas licencias para vendedores que no son veteranos solo estaban disponibles cuando un titular de licencia existente renunciaba a una, lo que ha llevado a que miles de personas vendan mercancías en las calles sin licencia, arriesgándose así a costosas multas y posibles cargos criminales.
A principios de este año, el Concejo Municipal anuló el veto del exalcalde Eric Adams y aprobó el proyecto de ley que creaba 10.500 nuevas licencias de venta ambulante, y la semana pasada comenzó a aceptar solicitudes para una nueva lista de espera.
“Fue maravilloso ver a gente que había estado en la primera línea, luchando conmigo en las calles para conseguir estas licencias, sentada allí esperando su turno para rellenar la solicitud”, dijo Baker, de 64 años, quien vende gorros, guantes y otras prendas de vestir. “Fue una bendición para mí, tío. Sentí la paz de Dios. Me sentí satisfecho”.
Anteriormente, cuando quedaba libre una licencia, el Departamento de Protección del Consumidor y del Trabajador de la ciudad de Nueva York (DCWP por sus siglas en inglés) se ponía en contacto con los solicitantes de la lista de espera existente, que se cerró en 2016.
Según la nueva ley, la ciudad agregará 10.500 licencias más —entre ellas, 3.478 licencias generales para toda la ciudad, también denominadas “blancas”, que permiten vender en cualquier lugar de la ciudad, y 7.875 licencias para los condados periféricos, o “verdes”—, que estarán disponibles a principios del próximo año.
“Es muy difícil de predecir, pero es justo decir que estimamos que se presentarán miles de solicitudes”, afirmó Mohamed Attia, director del Street Vendor Project (SVP por sus siglas en inglés), el grupo de defensa que impulsó la ampliación de las licencias.
En agosto, el DCWP comenzó a dar prioridad a los solicitantes que ya figuraban en la lista de espera de 2016 y empezó a ponerse en contacto con ellos, enviándoles cartas en las que se describían los siguientes pasos. Tenían hasta el 29 de octubre para presentar una solicitud de licencia, explicó un portavoz del DCWP.
Después de eso, la nueva lista de espera para 2026 se abrió el 2 de noviembre y se cerrará el 16 de diciembre. Los vendedores deben presentar una solicitud para inscribirse en la lista y, a continuación, esperar a que el DCWP les comunique qué deben hacer a continuación.
Baker fue uno de los primeros solicitantes el pasado lunes.
“Es como correr la Maratón de Nueva York y decir: ‘Dios mío, ¿cómo voy a hacerlo? ¿Podré terminar esta carrera?’. Pero luego te lanzas a ella y la terminas. La satisfacción que sientes al lograrlo. Esa es la satisfacción que sentí al completar la solicitud”, describió Baker.
Un portavoz del DCWP no especificó cuántas personas han presentado su solicitud hasta el momento.
“El DCWP está trabajando intensamente para garantizar que la puesta en marcha de las nuevas licencias generales para vendedores ambulantes se lleve a cabo de forma clara, ordenada y accesible”, afirmó un portavoz. “Sabemos que los vendedores ambulantes son un elemento imprescindible de la comunidad, y nos enorgullece apoyar a estas pequeñas empresas mediante los mejores servicios de concesión de licencias, formación empresarial proactiva y reformas para reducir la burocracia”.
¿Dónde y cómo aplicar?
Si aún no figuras en la lista de espera de 2016, puedes presentar tu solicitud para la nueva lista por Internet o por correo y, en circunstancias muy limitadas, como en casos de “dificultad severa”, en persona.
Los vendedores pueden solicitar una licencia blanca o verde, o ambas, en una sola solicitud.
Si necesitas ayuda con tu solicitud, puedes ponerte en contacto con la Oficina de Servicios a los Vendedores Ambulantes del Departamento de Servicios a la Pequeña Empresa (SBS) llamando al 888-SBS-4NYC (888-727-4692).
También puedes obtener ayuda en persona acudiendo a los Centros de Soluciones Empresariales de Nueva York (NYC Business Solutions Centers) en horario de oficina (de lunes a viernes, de 9 a.m. a 5 p.m ) en las siguientes ubicaciones:
- El Bronx: 400 East Fordham Rd., séptimo piso, Bronx, NY 10458
- Brooklyn: 9 Bond St., quinto piso, Brooklyn, NY 11201
- Bajo Manhattan: 14 Wall St., decimoséptimo piso, Nueva York, NY 10005
- Alto Manhattan: 361 West 125th St., segundo piso, Nueva York, NY 10027
- Washington Heights: 560 West 181st St., segundo piso, Nueva York, NY 10033
- Queens: 90-27 Sutphin Blvd., cuarto piso, Jamaica, NY 11435
- Staten Island: 120 Stuyvesant Pl., tercer piso, Staten Island, NY 10301
Los solicitantes también pueden concertar una cita con el Street Vendor Project por correo electrónico o por teléfono (646-602-5679).
“Hay mucha desinformación y mucha confusión sobre qué es esta licencia”, explicó Attia.
“Esta licencia permite a las personas vender productos en la calle, en las aceras públicas, sobre una mesa, y hay muchas normas que la regulan”, añadió. “Por lo tanto, si eres vendedor de comida, esta licencia no es para ti. Si tienes un negocio minorista y quieres ampliar tu actividad a algunos eventos privados o a mercados temporales, esta licencia tampoco es para ti”.
¿Cuáles son los requisitos para aplicar?
La información que se solicita a los solicitantes es información personal básica, como nombre, dirección, número de teléfono y correo electrónico. Además, se pregunta si la persona ha estado vendiendo mercancías generales desde enero de 2025 hasta el 2 de noviembre de 2026.
Aunque la mayoría de los vendedores ambulantes de la ciudad son inmigrantes procedentes de diferentes partes del mundo, la solicitud sólo está disponible en inglés. El SVP ha indicado que está prestando asistencia a los solicitantes en siete idiomas.
El formulario también exige la presentación de un documento de identidad con fotografía, que puede ser un carné de conducir, un permiso expedido por un organismo público, un pasaporte o un documento de identidad municipal, entre otros.
Un aspecto irónico del proceso: las multas civiles o criminales anteriores emitidas contra el vendedor pueden servir como prueba de su experiencia en la venta ambulante (además de fotografías en las que se vea a la persona vendiendo, recibos de compra de mercancía o una carta de un político electo, un líder comunitario o una organización sin ánimo de lucro en la que se acredite su actividad anterior como vendedor ambulante).
Los defensores de SVP ven esto como un reconocimiento de que el sistema anterior dejaba a muchas personas sin una forma de vender legalmente, y como un recordatorio de lo difícil que era obtener una licencia bajo el antiguo límite máximo.
“La solicitud fue muy fácil”, dijo Baker. “Tardé 10 minutos”.
¿Y luego qué?
La solicitud para la lista de espera es independiente de la solicitud de licencia, por lo que inscribirse en la lista de espera no garantiza automáticamente la obtención de una licencia.
El DCWP revisará las solicitudes, asignará un número a cada una de ellas y se pondrá en contacto con los solicitantes para informarles sobre los siguientes pasos a partir de febrero de 2027.
“Quiero llegar a lo más alto. Quiero mi licencia”, dijo Baker. “Me sentiré mucho mejor. No tendré que estar siempre mirando a mi alrededor y preocupándome de que la policía de Nueva York venga a por mí y tire mis cosas como les dé la gana, sin siquiera respetar lo que es mío”.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Artist captures the saga of Luigi Mangione in tweets
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Hannah Sage Kay
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
On the morning of 4 December 2024, the Los Angeles-based artist Stanya Kahn opened X (formerly Twitter) to get her daily news digest, when she, like many Americans, was inundated with a mass chorus of tweets—ranging from celebratory snark to unbridled vitriol—about the assassination of United HealthCare’s chief executive Brian Thompson.
“The compression of anger and joy that I was seeing people write that day was astonishing,” Kahn tells The Art Newspaper; she immediately felt compelled to capture the torrent of reactions. “At first I was bookmarking them, and then [screenshotting] them, and fairly quickly my thought was to gather these up because the algorithm might start shutting them down.”
Fairly quickly, the Trump administration announced that any celebration of the killing could be criminalised. But with an ever-growing archive and a long-held practice as a time-based media artist, Kahn decided to create a film that chronologically presented the public’s rapidly unfolding response to this now-infamous event.
Titled Deny Defend Depose (2026)—a play on the words scrawled on three shell casings from bullets fired in the shooting, and the strategy invoked by major healthcare providers to reduce payouts and increase profits—Kahn’s film is now screening across the country at artist-run-spaces, cinemas and galleries. The New York non-profit space Participant Inc will screen it on 13 November, with more showings to come.
Originally, Kahn planned to release the film in the lead-up to 9 September, when the state trial of Luigi Mangione was due to take place in New York. Now that Mangione’s 14 August guilty plea—an attempt to avoid double jeopardy—has postponed the state hearing until 10 December, with a federal hearing to follow on 18 December, Kahn plans to continue updating the film with more responses from the public as the saga continues unfolds.
When it all began, she had considered turning the project into a coffee-table book, which would afford a funny inversion of X’s quippy, short-form format. But switching to a film, her primary medium, afforded an opportunity for in-person film screenings, which enabled the originally solitary experience of watching the commentary unfold online to be transformed into a collective viewing experience.
Set to a dramatic soundtrack of acid and jungle, the 30-minute film takes viewers on an emotional rollercoaster. Watching the tweets unfold in sequence together, the audience collectively holds its breadth as anticipation builds to the moment the suspect is revealed as Mangione, laughs as tweets comment on his attractiveness or the Monopoly money found in his backpack, and sighs at the devastating state of healthcare in the United States when statistics regarding industry salaries and investment patterns, or personal anecdotes about life-threatening denials, are shared.
Just like Kahn was glued to X that morning in late 2024, viewers of her film are often transfixed as they relive their reactions to the still-unfolding story at top speed.“The poignancy of such a broad spectrum of the American public responding in kind to what was basically a public political assassination felt like a rupture, especially in party-based politics,” Kahn says. “It cut across the entire political spectrum and the common ground that suddenly emerged in this flashpoint seemed like a new beacon for potential mass movement, because it was a unity that emerged spontaneously and instantaneously, it wasn’t something that got hammered out in time.”
The outpouring of affection for Mangione has been staggering, Kahn says. “Without blinking,” she adds, “people were in full-throat applause of [an alleged] murderer.”
Attention from the media and public has remained steady since the early days of the manhunt, Mangione’s arrest and the trial, with comparisons to Robin Hood, lookalike contests and wanted posters for other healthcare company executives. While the extent of the public’s celebration of Thompson’s killing took many by surprise, Kahn sees this reaction as evidence of just “how deep the pain and anger and frustration is in this country about the evilness of the healthcare system and its inaccessibility”. (Per capita spending on healthcare in the US is double the average of other wealthy countries, and has been increasing faster than inflation for decades.)
Thompson’s killing and its aftermath are hardly a black-and-white tale of righteous moral vengeance. Though some originally attempted to paint Mangione as disaffected and radicalised, his Ivy League education and privileged upbringing told a different story. And the responses to the event “weren’t just coming from more radical spaces”, Kahn says. While capturing their reactions in real time and reviewing the posters’ profiles, she found, “it was literally just ‘every man’—people with five followers and five million. It was regular people because they were pissed.”
- Stanya Kahn’s Deny, Defend, Depose screens on 13 November at Participant Inc, New York and on 12 December at Slash Art, San Francisco

The organizers of SITE Santa Fe have revealed the theme and named the forty-two artists participating in the New Mexico biennial’s thirteenth iteration, to take place June 11, 2027–January 10, 2028. Titled “There Are Other Worlds,” the Ekow Eshun–curated exhibition aims to show how art might offer “Alternative ways of seeing, relating, and imagining,” per a curatorial statement.
The event will be divided into three sections: “Worlds Beyond,” inspired in part by the Transcendental Painting Group; “World in Common,” which will explore community-building among artists; and “Worlds Alive,” which will center the connections between flora, fauna, and humans.
Visitors can expect to see new commissions by Edgar Arceneaux, Firelei Báez, Raven Chacon, Lotus L. Kang, and Cauleen Smith. Among the other participating artists include John Akomfrah, Sanford Biggers, Frank Bowling, Olafur Eliasson, Nan Goldin, Shilpa Gupta, Sky Hopinka, Arthur Jafa, and Tavares Strachan.
“Uniting these practices is a shared sense that the world is never singular or fixed, but continually reshaped by how we perceive, imagine, and relate to one another. There Are Other Worlds invites us to look beyond existing realities to consider how alternative ways of being might come into existence.”
