https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Scott Colom’s Historic Victory
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Michele Goodwin
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Scott Colom’s Historic Victory
The Mississippi Democrat’s win is more than a joyous occasion—it’s redemption.
On Wednesday, Scott Colom was declared the victor in the hotly contested United States Senate race in Mississippi. Colom, a lawyer and district attorney, will become the first Black person from Mississippi to hold a US Senate seat in more than 140 years. Colom’s victory against the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith was declared after close ballot-counting. Upon learning of this, I sat in my office and wept, reflecting on childhood summer visits to Mississippi, where my maternal great-grandfather lacked running water and electricity. He died while I was in law school—never having had running water.
Pundits will point to Colom’s important win as particularly noteworthy for several reasons. For example, in 2023, Hyde-Smith blocked his candidacy to become a federal judge by withholding the “’blue slip’ required under Senate Judiciary Committee practice to advance Colom’s judicial nomination, despite support from fellow Mississippi Republican Sen. Roger Wicker,” reported The Advocate. And in 2024, Donald Trump swept the state, defeating Kamala Harris by almost 23 points—a jump in voter support from his 2020 and 2016 victories in the state. Commentators will also likely frame Colom’s victory as a response to the very real economic hardship Americans are facing given Trump’s disastrous policies. All are true.
However, Colom’s victory means something much more profound and earthshaking—perhaps even greater than the presidential victory of Barack Obama, who failed to receive more than 43 percent of the vote in the state in both of his elections—especially for many Black Americans with a legacy tied to Mississippi. For those of us who share this lineage, Colom’s victory is not only a repudiation of Donald Trump but also of the horrific political and social machines that drove American slavery and Jim Crow. For centuries—not decades—Mississippi was a proud “slave state.” It embraced and profited from the enslavement of Black people and fought hard to keep its status quo.
In its 1861 declaration of secession—“A Declaration of the Immediate Causes which Induce and Justify the Secession of the State of Mississippi from the Federal Union”—state lawmakers affirmed, “Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery—the greatest material interest of the world. Its labor supplies the product which constitutes by far the largest and most important portions of commerce of the earth.” Mississippi referred to enslaved Black people as “products” that were “peculiar to the climate verging on the tropical regions, and by an imperious law of nature, none but the black race can bear exposure to the tropical sun.”
Mississippi saw enslaved Black people as essential to its economy and ways of being. Its declaration of secession points to a degradation in being denied owning people rather than the immorality of human bondage, rape, forced pregnancy and childbearing, and the cruelties of family separation and the whip. Even after the Civil War, in which Mississippi’s losses were high (all of its enlisted Ole Miss students died fighting for the Confederacy), the state refused to ratify the 13th Amendment, which abolished slavery and involuntary servitude. In fact, it wasn’t until 2013 that the state did so—148 years later.
Even while it could not block Black people’s newly ratified constitutional freedoms, Mississippi erected barriers nonetheless. It was the first state to enact notorious Black Codes, barring Black people from freely engaging in labor contracting. It passed harmful apprenticeship policies, snatching Black children away from their parents on dubious claims of neglect. These practices condemned Black children to slavery under the guise of apprenticeship to plantation owners. Mississippi lawmakers also imposed fines on Black people who traveled and stood together on public streets, calling this vagrancy.
Despite all of these barriers to equal participation in society, newly freed Black Americans in Mississippi came into office, helping to enact policies that resulted in public education for all and even property rights for married women. That window was closed abruptly when the United States Supreme Court dismantled Reconstruction by upholding segregationist laws and granting its imprimatur to “separate but equal” strategies.
Mississippi welcomed the end of Reconstruction and profited from it with coercive sharecropping practices and convict leasing. Aspects of those legacies linger. For example, it must be noted that Black Americans today represent more than half of Mississippi’s prison population, while representing only 38 percent of the state’s entire population.
The horrors of Mississippi’s Jim Crow–era are hard to turn away from. Featured in award-winning documentaries like Eyes on the Prize, detailing among other things Mississippi’s brazen and violent citizens’ councils that organized against Black voting rights; in films like Mississippi Burning, which narrates the tragic killings of three young civil rights workers—Andrew Goodman, Michael Schwerner, and James Chaney; in song, Nina Simone’s Mississippi Goddam comes to mind, as well as Billie Holiday’s Strange Fruit, capturing the chilling terror of lynchings; in the testimony of Fannie Lou Hamer at the 1964 Democratic National Convention, when she spoke of being arrested and beaten by law enforcement after attempting to vote—and in the terrifying image of Emmett Till on the cover of Jet magazine after his bloated, beaten, and tortured 14-year-old body was lifted from the Tallahatchie River. His murderers, Roy Bryant and J.W. Milam, were acquitted in barely an hour by an all-white jury. They later confessed in Look magazine.
Colom’s victory must be understood against a complex backdrop, where Black people fled Mississippi during the Great Black Migration to never return given a legacy of cruelty and hate. And one where so many remained like Colom and his forebears, committed to fighting for democracy in a state that they toiled to build and where quite literally, the blood of their ancestors was spilt.
For me, Colom’s victory is a balm or salve on scars carried across generations—on the backs of grandparents and great grandparents. Of my grandmother’s siblings who fled Mississippi, she was the only one who would cross the Mason Dixon line, to drive south to visit family. Sadly, this took courage. Several of her siblings simply could not. My summers in the South, especially the visits to Mississippi, left an indelible mark.
Whether they are residing now in the state or are the offspring of the hundreds of thousands who fled north in the greatest migration, Colom’s win is more than a joyous occasion for the Black Americans who remain connected to Mississippi. It is the closest to redemption that the state and perhaps the United States has come to in modern times.

https://gothamist.com/news/bronx-grand-j.title: Bronx grand jury to weigh charges against teen in fatal shooting of 15-year-old
https://gothamist.com/news/bronx-grand-j.author: Samantha Max
https://gothamist.com/news/bronx-grand-j.text:
A Bronx grand jury will consider Monday whether to indict a teen arrested in connection with the killing of 15-year-old Javits Frimpong, who was shot on his way to school last month, according to the district attorney’s office.
Prosecutors said Thierno Jalloh, 17, and two others were involved in Javits Frimpong's killing. Javits Frimpong was shot in the stomach as he walked to DreamYard Preparatory School around 9:30 a.m. on Oct. 29. The two others are still at large, officials said.
Jalloh briefly appeared in court Thursday on murder, manslaughter and weapons charges. He is being held in detention without bail and is expected back in court Monday.
According to the criminal complaint, someone who knows Jalloh identified him in surveillance footage connected to the crime during an interview with police several days later. Prosecutors said ballistic evidence and information from witnesses also tied Jalloh and two other people to the shooting. Those people had not been arrested as of Thursday afternoon.
Bronx Defenders, which is representing Jalloh, declined to comment after the court appearance.
Family members previously told Gothamist that the 15-year-old recently moved to New York from Ghana, following his father, who immigrated here in 2000. Prominent civil rights advocates, including the Rev. Al Sharpton and attorney Ben Crump, have condemned the killing and rallied around Javits Frimpong’s family.
Dozens of supporters for Frimpong’s family filled the sixth-floor courtroom for Jalloh’s brief appearance Thursday afternoon. Outside the courthouse, they shouted, “Justice for Javits.” Someone held a framed photograph of the 15-year-old with angel wings.
Thomas Frimpong, the boy’s dad, previously described his son as quiet. He said two students fought with his son a few days before the shooting and were suspended. The school told him his son was not to blame, he said.
Crump, who is now representing Frimpong’s family, said after the court appearance Thursday that prosecutors told his clients they do not believe the shooters went to Frimpong’s school or were involved with the bullying incident a few days earlier.
“Young people being able to get access to guns and cause irreparable harm — not only to Javits’ family, but also to themselves — I mean, it is a tragedy upon tragedy that everybody loses in this situation,” the attorney said. “It has to be a teachable moment to lead to a greater discussion about stopping gun violence in our community.”
Police arrested Jalloh Wednesday. Javits Frimpong’s sister, Millicent Frimpong, told Gothamist after the arrest that she was happy a suspect had been apprehended but that it did “not really” bring her any relief.
This story has been updated with a comment from Ben Crump.

https://hyperallergic.com/how-to-free-th.title: How to Free the Art World From Its Neoliberal Capture
https://hyperallergic.com/how-to-free-th.author: Nitasha Dhillon
https://hyperallergic.com/how-to-free-th.text:
How to Free the Art World From Its Neoliberal Capture
In “The Battleground of Art,” curator and activist Marco Baravalle dissects the art establishment's co-optation of radical politics and uplifts the stories of collectives that resist it.
We first met Marco Baravalle in 2015 at the 56th Venice Biennale, All the World’s Futures, when we were organizing with the Gulf Labor Coalition. The group and our autonomous direct-action wing, Global Ultra Luxury Faction (G.U.L.F.), had been invited by curator Okwui Enwezor to present our research and organizing against migrant worker exploitation in the construction of the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi. An artist boycott was underway, direct actions were escalating, and days earlier, on May 1, we had shut down the Guggenheim Museum in New York City.
Through Baravalle, a longtime researcher, curator, and activist, we encountered a network of autonomous spaces in Venice and Milan. These were not simply cultural centers; they formed the infrastructure for collective organizing, resistance, and enacting other worlds.
Eleven years later, The Battleground of Art: Radical Curating in the Crisis of Neoliberalism (2026) extends this praxis into an important and timely call to action. Drawing on his two decades of experience, Baravalle offers what we have called movement-generated theory and practice, rooted in the dialectic of doing and knowing. The book confronts the neoliberal capture of the art world, while also excavating histories and practices of abolition and autonomy that offer other possibilities.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Staff petition against major restructuring plans at Sydney's Chau Chak Wing Museum
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Elizabeth Fortescue
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A Sydney University proposal to restructure its prestigious Chau Chak Wing Museum has shocked and angered the museum’s curators, who fear the world-class collections in their custody will be put at risk. A petition circulating in the Australian cultural sector decries the planned cuts to eight positions across curatorial, collections and public engagement teams.
”The loss of these roles, and changes to organisational structure, risks diminishing the museum’s capacity to care for and develop its collections, deliver educational experiences, support academic research and maintain its standing as a leading university museum,” the petition says.
According to the petition, the proposed new management structure is “top-heavy”, with three executive-level salaried directors in an organisation with only about 30 staff. The key position of head of collections would also be removed.
The Art Newspaper understands morale at the Chau Chak Wing Museum has plummeted. But John Buchanan, the branch president of the National Tertiary Education Union at the University of Sydney, says the museum’s staff members were strongly unionised and would fight the changes.
“They’ve got deep expertise, and they’ve basically been told: ‘there’s going to be a spill-and-fill change process and get in line to apply for your job again’,” Buchanan tells The Art Newspaper. ”This is an unhelpful way of dealing with a complex problem in the creative workforce, and [the staff] are showing their creativity by being so effective in organising.”
According to a university statement in response to the petition, the proposed changes aim to strengthen the museum’s educational and exhibition programme. “They include realigning positions in education and public programs and curatorial work, while creating a more sustainable staffing structure to meet growing demand,” the statement says. It adds that the proposed overall number of full-time equivalent roles would remain unchanged.
Craig Barker, an archaeologist and the head of public engagement at the Chau Chak Wing Museum, believes that the proposal would refocus staff attention towards education and engagement. While he was generally in favour of that idea, Barker tells The Art Newspaper that this will swing staff attention away from curatorial and collection management. Academic research and international expert connections would suffer, Barker adds.
Barker says his role’s title would become “deputy director of business, education and experience”, and that he believes the focus would be on business. ”Our big frustrations are not that there’s a refocus towards public engagement. It’s something that we want, but it’s at the cost of what we have done so well and where we’ve built our reputation, which is in highest-quality curatorial research,” Barker says. “The fundamental question is: does the University of Sydney want an internationally recognised, world-class research and object-based teaching facility? Or do we just want a nice shiny building with pictures hanging on the wall?”
Ann Stephen, a senior art curator of the university art collection at the Chau Chak Wing Museum, says her job is under threat. She adds that curatorial knowledge is vital for collection care, research, publications and advising on acquisition and deaccession of works. ”Without recourse to such knowledge, artworks can be misattributed, over or undervalued, or simply not understood in terms of any wider context,” Stephen says. ”Exhibition programmes not informed by curatorial knowledge can become merely dumbed-down spectacles lacking historical research or insights.”
According to the University of Sydney's statement, formal consultation began in July and “feedback and proposed alternatives” are welcomed.
The modernist Chau Chak Wing Museum opened to the public on the university’s main campus in 2020 and is free to enter. The museum amalgamated the university’s three main collections: antiquities, natural history and art. The director of the Chau Chak Wing Museum is Michael Dagostino, who was chosen as the curator for the Australian pavilion at the 2026 Venice Biennale. The Chau Chak Wing Museum was also a venue of the 2026 Sydney Biennale.

https://gothamist.com/news/tornado-watch.title: Tornado watch in effect for 11 NJ counties, flash flood warning in Queens
https://gothamist.com/news/tornado-watch.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/tornado-watch.text:
A tornado watch was in effect for 11 New Jersey counties, and parts of Queens were under a flash flood warning until early Thursday evening.
The National Weather Service said that in addition to the possibility of a few tornadoes, also in Pennsylvania and Delaware, there was the potential of scattered hail up to the size of a ping pong ball and wind gusts reaching up to 70 mph.
The agency’s advisory about the tornado watch included areas as far north as Warren, Hunterdon, Somerset and Middlesex Counties, as well as several other areas in Central and South Jersey. As of mid-afternoon, the watch was in effect until 7 p.m.
The Garden State has seen an increasing number of tornadoes this year. So far, there have been five tornadoes in New Jersey, compared to two in all of 2025, and one in 2024, according to data from the New Jersey State Climate Office at Rutgers University.
A tornado warning had also previously been in effect for Southern Queens but expired after 2:30 p.m. However, the area was under a flash flood warning until 5:15 p.m. due to heavy rainfall in the area, according to the agency.
“We issued the warning as a potential heads up in case there are conditions that end up materializing with the heavy rain that is materializing over Queens right now, “ said David Stark, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service headquartered in New York.
Stark said that there wasn't a flash flood warning in effect for other parts of the city.

https://hyperallergic.com/after-the-midt.title: After the Midterms, the Real Work for Arts and Culture Begins
https://hyperallergic.com/after-the-midt.author: Jasmine Wahi
https://hyperallergic.com/after-the-midt.text:
After the Midterms, the Real Work for Arts and Culture Begins
Democratic leaders need to understand that cultural funding cannot stop at large museums and institutions; it must reach the people whose labor makes it possible.
In the afterglow of the blue-nami, those of us who make, organize, fund, and sustain cultural life are feeling a twinge of hope. But I find myself slipping into a spiral of anxiety as the everyday reality of economic precarity sets back in. Our newly elected Democratic congressional leaders have an opportunity to change that reality — pushing back against Trump is necessary — but it cannot be the full extent of their ambition.
As a curator and the co-director of an arts nonprofit, I’ve been asked what the results mean for the so-called “art world.” My first response was cynical: “not much.” At least not immediately. An election does not directly restore a canceled grant or pay an artist’s rent. And even a return to the funding landscape that existed before Trump took office in 2025 would leave us with a system that was already failing the people expected to sustain it.
Instead, the midterm election results should serve as an opening to hold Democrats in Congress accountable for making arts and cultural life materially sustainable, not simply to defend an inadequate system from further attack. That mandate concerns whose histories are told, who gets paid to make art, and who gets to define the country’s future. It also concerns whether the people doing that work can afford to keep going.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Could Firenze Lai’s first UK solo show signal a shift in global market recognition for Hong Kong artists?
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Vivienne Chow
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
In mid-October, coinciding with Frieze London and nearly four years after she relocated from her native Hong Kong to London, the artist Firenze Lai opened her first UK solo exhibition at White Cube Mason’s Yard. Featuring new works created in her adopted home, North and True North (until 14 November) is not just a milestone for her career, it also signals a potential shift in major galleries’ approach to Asia.
Lai is among a handful of Hong Kong artists represented by major Western blue-chip galleries today. Born in 1984 and educated in Hong Kong, the artist has exhibited internationally, including in the main exhibition of the 57th Venice Biennale in 2017. Her current show marks the first solo exhibition White Cube has staged by an artist originating from Hong Kong since it opened its outpost in the city in 2012.
The shift suggests the maturity of this generation of mid-career artists from Hong Kong, several of whom have relocated abroad fairly recently. It also raises hopes that Western blue-chip galleries are finally adopting a less siloed approach to Asia, in which global art markets were approached from a simplistic geographical perspective. This mindset of “keeping Asians in Asia” kept transnational relationships rare, the cultural strategist Adeline Ooi notes, but this is starting to change.
“People are much more cosmopolitan and international today. They are not just rooted within their region and bounded by their geographies,” says Ooi, the former director for Asia at Art Basel.
Taking a wider view
Major international galleries are taking a more sophisticated approach, rather than simply placing Asian artists in front of Asian collectors, says the Taipei- and New York-based art adviser Gladys Lin. “It’s about integrating that artist into the wider language of the gallery programme, so that collectors from different backgrounds can understand the work in relation to other artists, histories and conversations.”
Hong Kong has long been Asia’s biggest art market hub, with headline-grabbing auction sales for over half a century joined, since the 2000s, by a lively landscape of galleries and fairs catering to local collectors, and those from mainland China and the wider region. The city has hosted Art Basel Hong Kong since 2013, and Asian outposts of blue-chip galleries proliferated after the launch of the ArtHK fair in 2008. Artists from the city, however, have struggled to receive much attention in the global market, or even at home.
Leading multinational Western blue-chip galleries such as White Cube, Hauser & Wirth, David Zwirner, Gagosian and Pace have shown Asian artists internationally, but they tend to concentrate on bolstering their rosters with established names from Asian cultural powerhouses like mainland China, South Korea and Japan.
Hongkonger artists are increasingly exhibiting abroad, but primarily with smaller galleries. The Taipei-based artist Lee Kit works with galleries including Massimo de Carlo in London and ShugoArts in Tokyo. The UK-based Chris Huen Sin-kan showed with the now-defunct Simon Lee in New York and London, and more recently with Matt Carey-Williams.
While diaspora and émigré Hongkongers have more opportunities to cultivate overseas networks, artists based in the city are also widening their reach. Chang Ya Chin held her first solo show with Perrotin in New York in 2025, while Stephen Wong Chun-hei exhibited with Unit London in 2022 and Mother’s Tankstation in 2025, which also represents Lee Kit. The sound artist Samson Young performed his work Canon at Art Basel Unlimited in 2016, presented by Cologne’s Galerie Gisela Capitain and the now-closed Team Gallery. Wong Ping held a solo show at Tanya Bonakdar Gallery in New York in 2021, while Mak2 had her European gallery solo debut in 2023 with the now-defunct Peres Projects in Berlin.
However, representation by one of the global “big five” galleries remains rare for Hong Kong artists. White Cube began working with Lai in July 2025. “Her paintings have a singularity that speaks to the human condition, a universal theme that audiences everywhere can appreciate,” a spokesperson for the gallery says.
Lai was born and raised in Hong Kong, and has lived in London since 2022. Her visual language nonetheless remains rooted in her lived experience of her densely populated hometown. “We are not 100% Chinese, nor are we 100% British,” Lai says.
Moving to London changed how she approaches the canvas. The painter recalls that during her time in Hong Kong—where she built a solid career and a following for her dreamlike figurative paintings through a long-term and continuing collaboration with Guangzhou gallery Vitamin Creative Space—she tended to work on smaller canvases.
‘I needed a bigger canvas’
“After moving to London, I felt that I needed a bigger canvas. I have a lot more to say,” Lai says. Much of her poignant new work draws from deep emotional responses to her changing environment before and after relocating.
Lai says the current timing for global market recognition for Hong Kong artists makes sense. Those of her generation, born between the late 1970s and 90s, needed time to establish themselves and explore which galleries would be a good fit for their career. “I am proud of the fact that Hong Kong has produced a generation of artists who can have solo shows in London,” she says. “I’ve been told to give up many times. But I can now tell a 15-year-old [aspiring artist] that this is possible.”
It remains unclear how much long-term benefit a solo exhibition at a global gallery can bring to an artist’s career. “Who are the people paying attention to Firenze right now? If they are private collectors, who are they and what are their demographics? If it’s an institution, who are they?” Ooi asks. Expanding the following for her work will take time as much as exposure.
Lin says Lai’s move to London put her into a different art world, where she offers galleries a “compelling combination”. “She already comes with a collector base in Asia, an institutional history and more than a decade of critical exposure,” Lin says. “It’s not simply about bringing in Asian collectors, but about adding an artist who connects different collectors, institutional and geographical systems. For a global gallery today, geography can still be a useful entry point, but it cannot be the final framework.”

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-p.title: NYC Council passes ban on 'surveillance pricing' that relies on personal data
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-p.author: Elizabeth Kim
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-p.text:
The City Council passed a bill Thursday that bans companies in New York City from using surveillance pricing, which charges different prices based on algorithms or shoppers’ personal data.
Surveillance pricing means shoppers see a price based on their personal data like demographics, credit, browsing history or purchasing history. The bill prohibits surveillance pricing both online and in stores, although the practice is mainly used on the web.
Speaker Julie Menin described surveillance pricing as an “insidious and predatory corporate practice” that erodes privacy and fairness.
“It's a practice that worsens the affordability crisis, and today it's a practice that we are going to be ending,” she said during a press conference ahead of the vote.
In one investigation cited by the Council, Target shoppers saw a jump in pricing based on location data showing whether they were inside or outside a store. Shoppers found that a 55-inch SmartTV cost $499 on the Target app when inside a store, and $599 when in the store parking lot.
Uber, Lyft, Target, Instacart and airlines are among the companies that have faced scrutiny for alleged surveillance pricing. Many of the companies have denied using the practice.
Under the bill, the city would be able to issue fines of up to $1,000 for each transaction that violates the ban.
Menin’s proposal follows legislation approved by Albany lawmakers in June that prohibits surveillance pricing online and in stores, with some exceptions.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement that he supports the ban. He called surveillance pricing “just another way corporations are finding to squeeze working people.”
“New Yorkers’ personal data should never be used as a weapon against their own pocketbooks,” he added.
Business groups have warned that the ban could hinder discounts or loyalty programs for customers.
“If enacted, this law will make it harder for small restaurants with limited marketing budgets to reach customers, putting them at a disadvantage against national chains,” said Josh Gold, a spokesperson for Uber.
The company operates Uber Eats, which allows restaurants to offer discounts based on search history and previous orders.
Menin said the legislation would not affect discounts.

https://hyperallergic.com/human-rights-o.title: Human Rights Orgs Denounce Egypt's Arrest of Mada Masr Editor Lina Attalah
https://hyperallergic.com/human-rights-o.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/human-rights-o.text:
Human Rights Orgs Denounce Egypt's Arrest of Mada Masr Editor Lina Attalah
Attalah was accused of publishing false news and operating without a license amid Egyptian authorities’ extensive crackdown on independent press.
Prominent Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah, co-founder and editor-in-chief of Egypt's independent news outlet Mada Masr, is facing a one-year prison sentence among other penalties in a targeted crackdown on press freedom.
Summoned to court in Cairo last month on charges of publishing false news and operating the news site without a license, Attalah learned during the proceedings that she had been handed a year-long sentence in absentia on similar charges in 2024 without her knowledge.
Human rights and press freedom organizations, including Reporters Without Borders, Human Rights Watch, and the International Federation for Human Rights, have publicly condemned the charges against the journalist and Mada Masr, decrying her prosecution as a “Kafkaesque miscarriage of justice.”

https://gothamist.com/news/feds-say-gang.title: Feds say gang members killed 12-year-old in East Flatbush drive-by, targeting a rival
https://gothamist.com/news/feds-say-gang.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/feds-say-gang.text:
Federal prosecutors have charged three men in the 2022 drive-by shooting that killed 12-year-old Kade Lewin in East Flatbush — saying the men were targeting an associate of a rival gang and fired into the wrong car.
Ousmane Diallo, Mayel Bussereth and Jonah Luc are members and associates of a Brooklyn gang called ICG Babiez, prosecutors wrote in court papers Thursday. A letter from prosecutors asks a federal magistrate judge to keep all three locked up until trial.
Court records showed none of the three had been assigned a lawyer as of mid-day Thursday.
“The senseless killing of a 12 -year-old boy in March 2022 is just one example of the violence ICG members and associates commit that endanger the lives of Brooklyn residents,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella, Jr. and prosecutors wrote in the letter.
Lewin was in the front passenger seat of a sedan parked near East 56th Street and Linden Boulevard when shots were fired into it from a black Mercedes-Benz on the evening of March 31, 2022, according to the letter. The boy was hit in the head and chest and died within 10 minutes, according to prosecutors.
A woman in the car was shot multiple times and survived, prosecutors said. An 8-year-old girl in the back seat was not hurt.
The men “misidentified the car that they believed the rival gang associate was in,” the letter states.
Prosecutors allege Diallo and Bussereth fired the shots. Each is charged with murder in aid of racketeering, along with assault and firearms charges, and faces a mandatory life sentence or death if convicted.
Luc is charged with assault and firearms counts, including causing Lewin’s death with a gun. Prosecutors say Luc admitted he was inside the Mercedes at the time of the shooting. He faces between 10 years and life imprisonment, and could face the death penalty.
A fourth person, identified in the letter only as “CC-1,” got into the driver’s seat of the Mercedes, prosecutors wrote. That person is not among the defendants.
Surveillance video followed the car from a Crown Heights apartment used by the gang, according to the prosecutors. They say it caught the car circling the block before the shooting and showed the men returning with their faces apparently covered.
Diallo, whom prosecutors call a leader of the gang, was on probation for a robbery when Lewin was killed.
He is now serving 14 years in state prison after pleading guilty to two attempted murders in Brooklyn, one of them about a year after the drive-by.
Luc is in New Jersey state custody for a probation violation. A jury convicted him in June of stealing government funds in a separate federal case.
Bussereth was on pretrial release in a gun case at the time of the shooting, according to prosecutors.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: China rules out hosting Cop33 climate summit in 2028
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.
The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts, who had hoped the world’s biggest emitter would take the lead on the global stage, as the US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate.
Al Gore, the former US vice-president, was among those left disheartened by the decision. “I would be very much in favour of that idea [of China hosting the summit],” he told the Guardian. “It’s too bad.”
China is in the midst of an economic transformation, from being heavily dependent on coal to becoming an “electro state”. John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, told the Guardian that China was leaving the rest of the world behind in forging and using the low-carbon technologies of the future.
Renewable energy generation capacity has now outstripped coal in China, and its greenhouse gas emissions appear to have declined slightly this year.
Sales of electric vehicles in the country have also taken off, making up nearly two-thirds of the market last month, and China’s clean energy industries drove more than 90% of the country’s investment growth last year.
The rules of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) mean an Asian country should host in 2028.
Gareth Redmond-King, the international lead at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank, said China’s position as an industrial powerhouse would have made it a formidable contender to hold the summit.
“It would undoubtedly be significant for the world’s biggest emitter and second-biggest economy to host a climate Cop,” he said.
“They’re leading the world on investment, manufacture and deployment of clean energy tech, and their emissions have started to tick down. As a leadership story, China hosting Cop33 would be a big deal.”
It is not clear why China has decided against hosting the conference, but several experts that spoke to the Guardian suggested that the US electoral cycle was likely to have been a factor. The next US presidential election will take place on 7 November 2028, and Cop33 is scheduled for 6 to 17 November that year.
After the strong showing by Democrats in the recent midterm elections, in which voter concern over the climate crisis was thought to be a factor, the Democrats will be hoping to elect a climate-friendly president in 2028. But even if they succeed, Trump will still be in office until the following January.
The US president rejects climate science and withdrew the US from the Paris agreement, and is also withdrawing from its parent treaty, the 1992 UNFCCC.
China seeks to be seen as a leader among developing countries, but has been wary of stepping into the gap left by the US. Under the Democratic presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, the US and China enjoyed a close partnership on climate issues, setting joint targets on reducing methane and developing clean technology.
Cop33 will be an important meeting because it will include the “global stocktake” – a mechanism under the 2015 Paris climate agreement that examines countries’ progress on cutting emissions in line with the goal of limiting global temperature rises to 1.5C.
That limit is now certain to be surpassed, but experts say countries should now try to minimise the temperature “overshoot”, to avoid worse ravages from extreme weather.
India’s government considered offering to host Cop33 for several months earlier this year, but also decided against it. India’s coal use has been increasing, even as the country exceeds its own renewable energy targets.
The Guardian understands that other countries mulling a bid to host Cop33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand.
No decision on a host is likely to be made at this year’s Cop31 meeting, which is ongoing in Turkey, with the Turkish and Australian governments jointly presiding over the summit.

https://taz.de/Das-bisschen-Bundeshausha.title: Verhandlungen über Bundeshaushalt: Das bisschen Haushalt macht sich nicht von allein
https://taz.de/Das-bisschen-Bundeshausha.author: Anna Lehmann
https://taz.de/Das-bisschen-Bundeshausha.text:
Verhandlungen über Bundeshaushalt: Das bisschen Haushalt macht sich nicht von allein
In der Union ist der Unmut nach der Haushaltseinigung groß: keine weiteren Entlastungen. „Vertrauensbruch“ gegenüber den Bürger:innen, sagen die Grünen.
„Das bisschen Haushalt kann so schlimm nicht sein“, sang Johanna von Koczian ironisch lächelnd in den 70er Jahren. Die Ampelregierung aus SPD, Grünen und FDP erfuhr, wie schlimm der Haushalt sein kann, und zerbrach vor genau zwei Jahren endgültig am Streit um diesen. Union und SPD sind also gewarnt, so weit will es keine der drei regierenden Parteien kommen lassen. Vor der entscheidenden Bereinigungssitzung des Haushaltsausschusses am Donnerstag wurden die Fraktionen daher auf Kompromisse eingeschworen, die insbesondere für die Union schmerzhaft sind.
Anders als Kanzler Friedrich Merz vor einem Monat nach einer Sitzung des CDU-Präsidiums angekündigt hatte, wird die Stromsteuer für private Haushalte und kleine Unternehmen wohl nicht gesenkt. Merz hatte zwar damals eingeschränkt, eine Steuersenkung könne es nur geben, wenn es Spielräume im Haushalt dafür gibt. Auf Nachfrage hatte er sich aber zuversichtlich gezeigt, dass die nötigen 5 Milliarden Euro aus zusätzlichen Steuereinnahmen leicht zu beschaffen seien. Offenbar hat er sich erneut zu weit vorgewagt.
Das Geld fehlt nämlich nach wie vor. Und zwar auch, weil die Koalition auf neue Einnahmen vorerst verzichten will. So soll die Einführung der Zuckersteuer auf Getränke verschoben werden und die geplante Steuer auf Plastikverpackungen soll ganz entfallen. Auch eine Erhöhung der Sektsteuer, also auf Schaumweine, ist vom Tisch.
Ein schwacher Trost für die Unionsabgeordneten. Die SPD hat hingegen erreicht, dass die Kürzungen beim Wohngeld weitgehend rückgängig gemacht werden und Kinder aus armen Haushalten weiterhin 25 Euro monatlich vom Staat erhalten. Asylbewerber:innen sollen diesen Kinderzuschlag allerdings nicht mehr bekommen.
SPD-Fraktionschef: Gerechtigkeitscheck erreicht
Der Fraktionsvorsitzende der SPD, Matthias Miersch, versuchte, nicht zu zufrieden zu schauen, als er am Mittwochabend kurz vor Mitternacht zusammen mit Unionsfraktionschef Thorsten Frei und CSU-Landesgruppenchef Alexander Hoffmann im Reichstagsgebäude die Einigung verkündete und sich zunächst bei seinen Unionskollegen bedankte, bevor er fortfuhr: Die SPD habe einen Gerechtigkeitscheck versprochen und erreicht, dass die Einsparungen für Familien rückgängig gemacht werden.
Frei und Hoffmann stellten vor allem die Tatsache heraus, dass man sich geeinigt hat. Das sei schon der dritte Bundeshaushalt, den man zusammen beschließe, lobte Frei. Hoffmann räumte ein: „Dieser Regierungsentwurf führte zu viel Gesprächsbedarf in der Fraktion.“
Das ist milde ausgedrückt. Während die SPD schon ihre Social-Media-Kanäle bespielte mit Kacheln wie: „Einigung mit der Union: Keine Kürzungen beim Wohngeld“, diskutierten die Unionsabgeordneten noch. Der ursprünglich für 21 Uhr angesetzte Auftritt vor den Medien verschob sich immer weiter. „Da hat’s auch ordentlich geknallt“, gab Vizefraktionschef Matthias Middelberg am Donnerstagmorgen im Interview mit dem Deutschlandfunk zu. Nach Informationen der Bild-Zeitung sollen sich mehr als 30 Abgeordnete zu Wort gemeldet haben, unter anderem der Generalsekretär der nordrhein-westfälischen CDU, Paul Ziemiak. Das Einzige, was man gewollt habe, die Stromsteuersenkung, komme nicht. „Wir verlieren jede Glaubwürdigkeit“, soll Ziemiak gesagt haben.
Paul Ziemiak, CDU-Generalsekretär NRW
Die Wut der Union richtet sich gegen Klingbeil
Der taz wurde diese Äußerung aus Teilnehmerkreisen bestätigt. Die Wut der Unionsabgeordneten soll sich demnach vor allem gegen die SPD und Finanzminister Lars Klingbeil gerichtet haben, der den Kanzler auflaufen ließ. Doch zur Wahrheit gehört: Auch in der Union waren zuvor schon Zweifel aufgekommen, ob sich Merz’ vollmundige Ankündigung, die Stromsteuer zu senken, überhaupt umsetzen lässt. Denn darüber hinaus will die Union ja auch noch die kalte Progression ausgleichen, also verhindern, dass inflationsbedingte Lohnerhöhungen dazu führen, dass die Arbeitnehmerinnen in eine höhere Steuerklasse rutschen und dadurch am Ende doch wieder weniger Geld im Portemonnaie haben. Denn auch der Progressionsausgleich würde etwa 4 Milliarden Euro kosten – und ob sich das nötige Geld findet, ist fraglich.
Die Einigung sei eine schwere Niederlage für die Union, aber auch kein triumphaler Sieg für die SPD, urteilt der haushaltspolitische Sprecher der Grünen, Sebastian Schäfer, gegenüber der taz. „Die Fraktionen von Union und SPD haben sich vor allem gegen die eigene Regierung durchgesetzt. Die im Regierungsentwurf vorgesehenen Steuererhöhungen und Kürzungen werden nun rückgängig gemacht.“
Dass die vom Kanzler ins Schaufenster gestellte Stromsteuersenkung nicht komme, findet Schäfer „fatal“, denn es wäre wichtig, die Bürger sowie kleine und mittlere Unternehmen zu entlasten. „Diese Art von Vertrauensbruch schadet uns allen.“
Linke: An Subventionen rangehen
„Wenn man wollte, könnte man sowohl die kalte Progression ausgleichen als auch die Stromsteuer senken“, meint Linken-Haushälter Christian Görke. „Die Union müsste bereit sein, an Subventionen ranzugehen, die sie selbst eingeführt hat, wie die ermäßigte Steuer für die Gastronomie und für Agrardiesel.“
Noch hat die Union die Hoffnung nicht ganz aufgegeben. „Wir halten an der Stromsteuersenkung fest“, sagte Middelberg im Deutschlandfunk und verwies auf den Koalitionsausschuss, der sich nächste Woche Dienstag trifft. Miersch, der dem Ausschuss als Fraktionschef angehört, ist allerdings wenig zuversichtlich, dass es in der Spitzenrunde noch zu einem Durchbruch kommt. „Alles wünschenswert, aber ich muss es solide gegenfinanzieren.“ Bislang gebe es diese Finanzierung nicht.
Forderung nach Mehrwertsteuererhöhung
Derweil kursieren in den Reihen der Union zunehmend Forderungen nach einer Erhöhung der Mehrwertsteuer. Steigt sie um 1 Prozentpunkt, hätte der Staat auf einen Schlag 16 Milliarden Euro mehr in der Kasse, bei 2 Prozentpunkten wäre es schon 32 Milliarden Euro. Ein schönes Polster für die sich abzeichnenden Haushaltsprobleme im Jahr 2028. Darauf angesprochen, schloss Unions-Haushälter Middelberg diese Möglichkeit zumindest nicht aus.
„Ich halte das für falsch, gehe aber fest davon aus, dass die Koalition zu diesem Mittel greifen wird“, meint Grünen-Politiker Schäfer. Das würde Menschen mit kleinen und mittleren Einkommen überproportional belasten – wirke sich allerdings nicht so stark auf die Konjunktur aus, weil es etwa die Exportwirtschaft nicht treffen würde. Görke von der Linkspartei findet eine Mehrwertsteuererhöhung „verheerend“. „Sie würde vor allem Menschen mit niedrigen Einkommen bestrafen und der Wirtschaft Kaufkraft entziehen.“
Zunächst allerdings muss die Koalition den Haushalt 2027 beschließen. Die dritte Lesung im Bundestag ist für den 27. November angesetzt. Allerdings verfügten Union und SPD nur über 12 Stimmen Mehrheit. Ob die Mehrheit steht, wird wohl auch davon abhängen, ob die Union bis dahin noch etwas rausholen kann.

https://taz.de/Rot-Rot-Gruen-in-Mecklenb.title: Rot-Rot-Grün in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern: Timmy-Flüsterer Till Backhaus verliert Wal-Kompetenz
https://taz.de/Rot-Rot-Gruen-in-Mecklenb.author: Rainer Rutz
https://taz.de/Rot-Rot-Gruen-in-Mecklenb.text:
Rot-Rot-Grün in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern: Timmy-Flüsterer Till Backhaus verliert Wal-Kompetenz
Nach langen Verhandlungen einigt sich Rot-Rot-Grün in MV auf die künftige Verteilung der Ministerien. Ein SPD-Urgestein muss Abstriche machen.
Deutschlands dienstältester Minister Till Backhaus wird gerupft: Das SPD-Urgestein ist in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern seit fast drei Jahrzehnten für Landwirtschaft zuständig, später wurden ihm auch noch die Bereiche Umwelt und Klimaschutz zugeschlagen. Letzteres hat sich nun erledigt.
Wie SPD-Ministerpräsidentin Manuela Schwesig am Donnerstag in Schwerin bekannt gab, bleibt Backhaus in ihrem künftigen rot-rot-grünen Kabinett nur noch die Landwirtschaft. Umwelt und Klimaschutz muss der 67-Jährige an die Grünen abgeben, den neben SPD und Linke neuen dritten Koalitionspartner. Ausgerechnet an jene Partei also, denen der ehemalige LPG-Abteilungsleiter seit jeher in besonderer Abneigung verbunden ist.
Für bundesweite Empörung sorgte im September 2022 Backhaus’ Äußerung über die damalige Grünen-Chefin Ricarda Lang: „Früher waren Dick und Doof zwei Personen.“ Für – je nach Sichtweise – bundesweite Begeisterung oder Irritation sorgte in diesem Frühjahr sein missglückter Rettungseinsatz für die gestrandete Walkuh Timmy. In der neuen Regierung wird er auch die Zuständigkeit für die Wale an die Grünen verlieren.
Schwesig versüßte Backhaus die grüne Landnahme mit dem einprägsamen Leitsatz: „Es gibt in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern eine Regel, eine einfache Regel: Landwirtschaftsminister ist Till Backhaus.“ Wobei an der Stelle selbst die sonst so streng wirkende Ministerpräsidentin kurz auflachen musste.
Staatsgeheimnis Ressortverteilung
Die Frage, welche Partei welches Ministerium bekommt, wurde bis zuletzt wie ein Staatsgeheimnis behandelt. Erst müssten schließlich die inhaltlichen Schwerpunkte der künftigen Koalition geklärt werden, hieß es immer wieder. Am Dienstag wurde mit der Vorstellung des 130-seitigen Koalitionsvertrags dann zwar ein Haken hinter die Inhalte gesetzt. Die sogenannte Struktur blieb aber weiter ungeklärt. Bis jetzt.
Demnach werden die erstmals in der Landesregierung vertretenen Grünen zwar nur ein einziges der insgesamt acht Ministerien übernehmen. Das wird dafür umso größer. So wird die Grünen-Politikerin Claudia Müller nicht nur Ministerin für Umwelt, Natur- und Klimaschutz. Aus dem bisherigen Wirtschaftsministerium wandern zusätzlich die Bereiche Mobilität und Energie zu Müller. Auch die Gleichstellungsbeauftragte wird in ihrem Haus angesiedelt.
Müller selbst ist zufrieden. Sie hätte sich zwar auch über ein zusätzliches Ressort für die Grünen gefreut, sagte sie im taz-Interview. „Wir hatten aber auch einen klaren Fokus, und zwar auf die Zuständigkeiten. Wir haben gesagt, Zuständigkeiten und Gestaltungsspielraum sind uns wichtiger als Köpfe. Und das haben wir erreicht.“
Die Grünen stellen im 71-köpfigen Parlament nur 5 Abgeordnete. Gleiches gilt für den zweiten Juniorpartner von Schwesig, die bei der Landtagswahl am 20. September arg geschrumpfte Linkspartei, mit der die SPD bereits die vergangenen fünf Jahre zusammen regiert hat.
Linke behält zwei Ministerien
Die Linke ihrerseits hatte schon vor Beginn der Koalitionsverhandlungen auf – wie bisher – zwei Ministerien gepocht. Die hat sie auch bekommen. Wie in der rot-roten Vorgängerregierung wird die Partei auch im künftigen Kabinett die Zuständigkeit für Justiz behalten. Hinzu kommt neu das Arbeits-, Sozial- und Gesundheitsministerium.
Dafür geht das bislang von der über Parteigrenzen hinweg anerkannten Linken-Politikerin Simone Oldenburg geführte Bildungsressort an die Sozialdemokrat:innen, die im Landtag mit ihren 29 Sitzen fast dreimal so stark sind wie Grüne und Linke zusammen. Dementsprechend erhält – oder genauer: behält – die Partei von Manuela Schwesig dann auch die verbliebenen großen Ministeriumsschiffe Wirtschaft (inklusive Wissenschaft), Finanzen, Inneres (inklusive Bau) – und eben Till Backhaus (ohne Wal).
Mit Blick auf das Gesamtkabinett mahnte die alte und neue Chefin Schwesig nach der Vorstellungsrunde noch: „Die Erwartung ist, dass die Minister gut zusammenarbeiten.“ Da lachte sie dann aber nicht mehr. Die neue Regierung soll am kommenden Montag vereidigt werden.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120386.title: EU-Einsatz Eunavfor Med Irini | Bundestag verlängert Bundeswehr-Beteiligung an Mittelmeer-Einsatz
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120386.text:
- Politik
- EU-Einsatz Eunavfor Med Irini
Bundestag verlängert Bundeswehr-Beteiligung an Mittelmeer-Einsatz
Das Parlament hat die Beteiligung an der EU-Militärmission Eunavfor Med Irini verlängert. Scharfe Kritik kommt von Seenotrettungsorganisationen.
Berlin. Der Bundestag hat die Beteiligung der Bundeswehr an der EU-geführten Militärmission Eunavfor Med Irini im Mittelmeer verlängert. Die Abgeordneten billigten am Donnerstagnachmittag die Fortführung des Einsatzes um ein Jahr bis Ende November 2027. Der Militäreinsatz soll »Menschenschmuggel« und illegale Ölexporte aus Libyen unterbinden. Zudem soll gegen die sogenannte russische Schattenflotte vorgegangen werden. Die Bundeswehr übernimmt dabei Aufgaben wie die Seeraumüberwachung und -aufklärung. Wie bisher soll sie dafür bis zu 300 Soldatinnen und Soldaten entsenden können.
Die Mission hatte ursprünglich auch den Auftrag, ein Waffenembargo der Vereinten Nationen gegen Libyen durchzusetzen und dazu Schiffe zu inspizieren. Die entsprechenden UN-Resolutionen sind aber mittlerweile ausgelaufen.
Eunavfor Med Irini sei aber »weiterhin integraler Bestandteil des UN-geführten Friedensprozesses zur langfristigen Stabilisierung Libyens«, heißt es in der Begründung der Bundesregierung für die Mandatsverlängerung. Gleichzeitig zeige die EU mit der Operation »dauerhaft Präsenz im Mittelmeer«. Deutschland beteiligt sich seit Beginn im Jahr 2020 an dem EU-Einsatz. Die voraussichtlichen Kosten für die Bundeswehr belaufen sich für ein weiteres Jahr auf 16,6 Millionen Euro.
Die Seenotrettungsorganisationen Sea-Watch, SOS Humanity und Ärzte ohne Grenzen haben den Bundestagsbeschluss am Donnerstagabend scharf kritisiert. Die Bundesregierung trage damit »die Neuausrichtung von Irini mit, die der sogenannten libyschen Küstenwache als Partner mehr Gewicht gibt«. Davon würden auch Einheiten des ostlibyschen Milizenführers Khalifa Haftar verstärkt profitieren. Dies, obwohl die UN libyschen Einheiten wiederholt Menschenrechtsverletzungen bis hin zu Verbrechen gegen die Menschlichkeit an Migrant*innen und Geflüchteten vorgeworfen hätten, heißt es in einer gemeinsamen Pressemitteilung.
Abweichend vom ursprünglichen Zweck sei die Mission über die Jahre »zunehmend zu einem Instrument europäischer Abschottungspolitik ausgebaut« worden, so die Organisationen. Dazu zählten die Ausbildung und Unterstützung der sogenannten libyschen Küstenwache. Diese schlage und bedrohe Menschen in Seenot mit Waffengewalt, bringe sie gegen ihren Willen zurück nach Libyen oder »wirft sie ins Wasser und lässt sie dort zurück«. Auch zivile Rettungsschiffe werden von ihr nachweislich zunehmend mit Schusswaffen angegriffen.
Nach Libyen zurückgebrachte Menschen seien dort »Folter, sexualisierter Gewalt, Versklavung und Zwangsarbeit ausgesetzt«, erklärte Felix Braunsdorf von Ärzte ohne Grenzen. »Eine Mission zu verlängern, die solche Strukturen weiter stärkt, ist hochproblematisch.«
Marie Michel von SOS Humanity wies darauf hin, dass die UN dem Regime von General Haftar »nicht nur Gewalt gegen Geflüchtete, sondern auch Menschenhandel und Schmuggel von Waffen für den Sudankrieg« vorwerfen. »Seine Einheiten durch Irini zu unterstützen, ist untragbar und steht im Widerspruch zu der Durchsetzung des UN-Waffenembargos«, so Michel.
Die Organisationen weisen darauf hin, dass Irini-Schiffe schon heute Informationen über Boote in Seenot mit Behörden von Mittelmeerstaaten sowie mit der EU-Grenzagentur Frontex teilen, deren Rolle bei illegalen Rückführungen nach Libyen derzeit Gegenstand eines Verfahrens vor dem Gericht der Europäischen Union sei. Sie kritisieren zudem, dass sich Deutschland mit der Verlängerung des Irini-Mandats vorbehält, die sogenannte libysche Küstenwache durch Bundeswehrangehörige selbst auszubilden. Bis 2024 hatte die deutsche Bundesregierung das noch ausdrücklich ausgeschlossen. nd/AFP
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.
