https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: How Frieze became the latest step in Abu Dhabi's cultural masterplan
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Melissa Gronlund
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Frieze Abu Dhabi (19-22 November) debuts next week to a crescendo of cultural development in the emirate. As 2026 draws to a close it brings the launch of the long-awaited Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, which joins three other museums in the Saadiyat Cultural District that have opened in the past 18 months. Meanwhile, the second editions of the Public Art Biennial and Nomad Abu Dhabi art and design fair take place this month, while plans continue for Miza, the creative quarter in Mina Zayed.
While most of Abu Dhabi's cultural projects are newly launched, the city’s art fair has been running under various guises for nearly 20 years. It began in 2007 as ArtParis Abu Dhabi, held first at Emirates Palace, the luxury hotel on the Corniche, before later rebranding to Abu Dhabi Art and moving to Manarat Al Saadiyat, where it remains today. In those early years, galleries looked towards the newly announced Saadiyat museum projects. Heavyweights such as Gagosian, White Cube and Hauser & Wirth sold works primarily by Western artists at high prices and with institutional buyers in mind. As acquisition strategies shifted in the 2010s, many of the larger galleries left Abu Dhabi Art and the fair turned towards the Arab region and the Global South.
Regional stalwarts stayed, among them Green Art Gallery and the Third Line from Dubai, and Elmarsa from Tunisia, and it is thanks to the sustained efforts of the region's scene that art from the Arab world is gaining stature, institutional backing and international recognition. For example, the three artists on the stand of Dubai gallery Lawrie Shabibi—Mandy El-Sayegh, Shaikha Al Mazrou and Hamra Abbas—all now have international profiles. Meanwhile Dala Nasser, the inaugural winner of the Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, arrives fresh from solo shows at Nottingham Contemporary in the UK and Kunsthalle Basel in Switzerland.
This market, nonetheless, has conspicuously lagged. Art from the Arab world remains comparatively underexposed and relatively inexpensive. According to Dyala Nusseibeh, who joined Abu Dhabi Art as director in 2016 and now directs Frieze Abu Dhabi, the UAE accounted for 45% of all buyers of Mena (Middle East and North African) art in 2025. Collecting is rising among the younger Gulf generation, and the number of private collectors in Abu Dhabi has grown over the past decade, among Emiratis and foreign residents alike. Yet most Mena artists still sell to people with a connection to the region, a pattern both Frieze and the emirate are keen to break.
"We got to a point where we’d stretched as far as we could within our existing framework in building the market," Nusseibeh says. “We’re now ready for that next step outward—integrating the local and the regional market far better into the global market."
That step is a "marriage", Nusseibeh says, between the international fair giant and Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT), which ran Abu Dhabi Art. “The fair is a celebration—you’re coming to the wedding,” she says, framing the arrangement as an evolution of the fair rather than a takeover.
Frieze's chief executive Simon Fox describes the company following a growing market. “Our last new fair was in Seoul, and we just had our fifth edition, which was very successful,” he says. “We’ve been looking at how the art market is evolving, where collectors are, where there is growth. Unsurprisingly, this region is of great interest and becoming more so.”
Frieze’s offer is twofold. First, it promises greater international exposure for galleries and artists from the region, and not only through the curators and collectors it brings to Abu Dhabi. The Third Line, for example, secured a slot at No. 9 Cork Street—Frieze’s year-round London outpost—during Frieze London, on top of its place in Abu Dhabi. Second, the fair offers its regular Western galleries, facing a faltering market, entry to a new collecting cohort.
New structure, new horizons
Despite Fox’s Seoul comparison, Frieze Abu Dhabi represents a different arrangement: it is a partnership with a state entity, behind which lies a web of capital and longstanding business relationships. Frieze was previously owned by Endeavor, the company run by Ari Emanuel. When Endeavor was taken private by the investment firm Silver Lake and its assets bought back in 2025, it was split into three: what Fox calls the “fighting assets”, the Ultimate Fighting Champion (UFC) and World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE), combined as TKO; the talent agency William Morris Endeavor (WME); and the live-events businesses, Frieze among them, under a new company founded by Emanuel called Mari.
Mubadala, one of Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth funds, is a key backer of Silver Lake, having put in $2bn in 2020 and signed a 25-year strategic co-operation agreement. Mubadala has also invested directly in Mari, as has the Abu Dhabi media group IMI. That builds on a close relationship dating to the 2010s between Emanuel and Mubadala chief executive Khaldoon Al Mubarak, the brother of DCT director-general Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak.
This multifold investment by Abu Dhabi into Frieze should mean the fair is well supported, even as its first edition takes place amid regional instability. It should also ensure Frieze's plans align closely with those for the emirate as a whole. Nonetheless, the decision to not align the opening of Guggenheim Abu Dhabi with the fair will likely mean fewer international visitors for Frieze.
Luxury destination
The arrival of Frieze, and the rest of Emanuel's portfolio, chimes with Abu Dhabi’s embrace of luxury and high-end events—which is, of course, another way to describe an art fair. Mari's holdings include elite tennis, such as the Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open. The sovereign wealth fund ADQ’s $1bn investment in Sotheby’s in 2024 has produced a second year of auctions at the five-star St Regis hotel, where the auction house is selling jewellery as well as art. Next door to Manarat Al Saadiyat, the fair’s venue, sits not only the museums but the luxury Saadiyat Grove Mall, where its developer, Aldar, also chaired by Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak, has commissioned major works by serious artists. Emanuel has often called this the entertainment and experience ecosystem: a synergistic portfolio spanning live events, luxury and leisure.
How measurably this will touch the fair itself remains to be seen. When Endeavor, then WME-IMG, took a stake in Frieze in 2016, pundits predicted crossovers between celebrities and artists that never materialised, and WME was later reconfigured as a separate entity. Frieze maintains that it retains full creative control, although with input from DCT, and has no plans to alter the art-centred formula that has served it well.
The luxury connection matters less for the fair than for what it reveals about Abu Dhabi’s positioning as a city for global elites. The private-equity and investment firms that have been arriving at pace until Iran's missile strikes on the Gulf earlier this year tell the same story. As does the commitment to an event-driven lifestyle, with calendar points throughout the year that drive business to the emirate. This week, Frieze; next month, the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, Abu Dhabi Collectors’ Week and Guggenheim Abu Dhabi.
Rebalancing the canon
Stepping back, Frieze Abu Dhabi represents one part of a longer, grander plan for the emirate. Accordingly, its success will be measured not only in sales, but whether the artists at its heart will eventually launch onto the global stage. The Guggenheim's arrival is expected to further propel Abu Dhabi's efforts to canonise not only the UAE’s contemporary scene, but also the history of Arab Modernism, which unfolded largely further west in the Maghreb, Egypt, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq.
The fair’s geography has also widened since its early editions, most notably with the growing importance of South Asian artists and collectors. Some of the most successful stands in recent years at Abu Dhabi Art have come from the subcontinent, and Frieze boasts a significant South Asian contingent, including Experimenter, Galerie Isa, Jhaveri Contemporary, Nature Morte and Project 88. South Asia shapes the non-commercial programme too: the curator Tarini Malik anchors her section, Global Futures, in the Arabian Sea, which connects South Asia and the Arabian Peninsula, and positions Abu Dhabi at the heart of a re-ordered world.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120386.title: Ebola | Hunger, Krieg und Misstrauen
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120386.author: Ulrike Henning
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120386.text:
- Wirtschaft und Umwelt
- Ebola
Hunger, Krieg und Misstrauen
Der Ebola-Ausbruch im Kongo ist auch nach sechs Monaten nicht unter Kontrolle – die humanitäre Krise breitet sich aus.
Ungeachtet der Geschäftigkeit von Hilfsorganisationen und in WHO-Gremien: Der aktuelle Ebola-Ausbruch in der Demokratischen Republik Kongo ist nach einem halben Jahr Dauer weder bewältigt noch sind die Aussichten dafür besonders gut. Zuletzt war von mehr als 11.000 erfasste Fällen und rund 5500 Toten die Rede. Die schlechten Nachrichten reißen einfach nicht ab. An diesem Freitag mussten WHO und mehrere UN-Organisationen (darunter Unicef) vor einer zusätzlichen Hungerkrise in der Region für Anfang 2027 warnen.
Der Teufelskreis von bewaffneten Konflikten und Krankheitsausbrüchen würde dann noch akuten Hunger bei mehr als 30 Millionen Menschen umfassen, davon 4,2 Millionen auf Notfallniveau. Dabei ist auch das nicht neu: Bereits im ersten Halbjahr 2026 waren 26,5 Millionen Menschen von der Hungerkrise betroffen. Besonders schlimm sieht es im Osten der DR Kongo aus, in eben den Provinzen, die auch am stärksten mit der Ebola-Epidemie zu kämpfen haben.
Angriffe von den diversen beteiligten militärischen und paramilitärischen Kräften führen zu Fluchtbewegungen in der DR Kongo selbst, von denen im Osten des Landes schon mindestens fünf Millionen Menschen betroffen waren. Unter diesen Bedingungen wird Landwirtschaft immer schwieriger, da Wege unsicher und Felder verwüstet werden. Von Ackerbau und Viehzucht leben konnten (oder müssen) 70 Prozent der Bevölkerung. Militärische Checkpoints behindern jegliche Mobilität zusätzlich, eben auf die von Hilfslieferungen.
In einer solchen Situation steht die Gesundheitsversorgung hinten an, zumal auch deren Einrichtungen häufig attackiert werden. Einige der Vorfälle zählte dann selbst der äthiopische WHO-Generaldirektor Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus in einer Rede in dieser Woche vor Vertretern der WHO-Mitgliedstaaten auf.
Er erwähnte einen Angriff auf die Ortschaft Cantine-Aloya in der Provinz Nord-Kivu. Hier wurden in der Woche zuvor 66 Zivilisten getötet, darunter drei Mitarbeiter des Gesundheitswesens. Drei Gesundheitseinrichtungen wurden geplündert und niedergebrannt. Für die Ebola-Bekämpfung hieß das auch, dass der Kontakt zu mehr als 1000 Personen, die mit Infizierten in Berührung gekommen waren, abriss. Drei Menschen mit bestätigter Infektion seien unauffindbar, so der WHO-Politiker.
Neben getöteten Gesundheitskräften auch an anderen Orten seien Angriffe, Brandanschläge, Steinwürfe auf Einrichtungen und sogar auf speziell gesicherte Bestattungsfahrzeuge zu beklagen, überdies auch Drohungen gegen alle, die sich hier engagieren.
Die humanitäre Krise, die unter anderem die Hilfsorganisationen Help und Ärzte ohne Grenzen beklagen, ist also umfassend. Ungelöst ist auch das Problem, die Helfenden selbst zuverlässig zu bezahlen. Die WHO bedauert verzögert ausgezahlte Gehälter, was teils schon zu Streiks führte und für noch mehr Spannungen sorgte.
Einfacher materieller Mangel tritt auch schon bei ausreichend Treibstoff für Fahrzeuge und eben auch für Krankenwagen auf. Die Nachverfolgung von Infektionsketten geschehe nur auf dem Papier, kritisiert unter anderem Ärzte ohne Grenzen; es fehlten Telefone und mobilies Datenvolumen zur Weitergabe von Warnungen, ganz abgesehen von medizinischer Grundausstattung.
Im Effekt sterben immer mehr Infizierte in ihren Dörfern und nicht in Behandlungszentren. Und in der Folge tritt das bekannte Problem auf, dass die Toten unter strengen Schutzmaßnahmen beerdigt werden müssten, ansonsten werden Beerdigungen Hotspots für weitere Ansteckungen. Das dringend nötige Vertrauen lässt sich auch nicht so einfach aufbauen oder wiederherstellen, wenn private Gesundheitsanbieter (darunter Kliniken, Apotheken und traditionelle Heiler) bei den Hilfsmaßnahmen übergangen würden, so ebenfalls Ärzte ohne Grenzen. Die Organisation gehörte zu den ersten Unterstützern der kongolesichen Behörden nach Ausrufung des Ausbruchs am 26. Mai dieses Jahres.
Dabei wissen die internationalen Akteure und Experten durchaus, mit welchen Mitteln der Ebola-Ausbruch eingedämmt werden könnte. Der WHO-Generaldirektor hat es in seiner Rede zusammengefasst: Jeden Ansteckungsfall zügig identifizieren, Isolierung und behandeln, alle Kontaktpersonen nachverfolgen, um die Übertragungsketten zu unterbrechen. Auch sichere und würdevolle Bestattungen gehören dazu.
Dass das alles im Zusammenspiel funktionieren kann, wenn nur stabile Bedingungen herrschen, zeigt Kenia. Der Staat hatte am 6. Oktober seinen ersten Ebolafall registriert. Der letzte Patient konnte jetzt aus dem Krankenhaus entlassen werden. Zudem war keine der Kontaktpersonen von neun Infizierten erkrankt. Am 23. Dezember, nach Ablauf von 42 Tagen, was zwei Infektionszyklen entspricht, könnte Kenia für ebolafrei erklärt werden.
Für die DR Kongo ist es vermutlich bis dahin noch ein weiter Weg. Der im Mai gemeldete Ausbruch ist der sich am schnellsten ausbreitende in Bezug auf Ebola. Innerhalb von 40 Tagen nach Einleitung von Gegenmaßnahmen waren schon 1000 Fälle bekannt. Bei dem Ausbruch 2018, ebenfalls hautpsächlich im Ost-Kongo, dauerte das mehr als 200 Tage. In der Epidemie von 2014 bis 2016, die vor allem drei westafrikanische Staaten betraf, wurden 28.000 Infizierte und über 11.000 Todesfälle registriert.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/pete.title: Hegseth Dodges Impeachment, for Now. And Tom Morello on Fighting for the World You Want
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/pete.author: The Intercept Briefing
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/pete.text:
Secretary of defense Pete Hegseth narrowly avoided impeachment on Tuesday, but his future is anything but secure as an enraged Democratic caucus prepares to take control of both the House and Senate in January.
“Tick, tock! Get ready, asshole, because we’re coming,” Congress member-elect Richard Ojeda, D-N.C., warned Hegseth at a press conference on Wednesday. Ojeda told The Intercept that he planned not only to impeach Hegseth but also to bring criminal charges against him.
On Tuesday, the House declined to move forward with impeachment proceedings introduced by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., which accused Hegseth of multiple “high crimes and misdemeanors.” Massie accused Hegseth of illegally waging war against both Iran and Yemen and of overseeing extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean.
This week on The Intercept Briefing, co-host Jessica Washington speaks with Nick Turse, Intercept senior national security reporter and editor of Tom Dispatch, about Hegseth’s legacy as “secretary of war.”
“Hegseth can spin it any way he likes,” says Turse. “He can use the troops as a shield, claiming that indictments of him are indictments of them. But in the end, he’s got a lot to answer for on his own, and none of it’s because he’s doing a good job.” Turse adds: “It’s because he’s committing high crimes.”
Co-host Jordan Uhl also sits down with musician and guitarist Tom Morello to talk about his new album “Everyone Gets Everything They Want” and his decades-long fight against forever wars and his resistance to fascism.
“My career has basically been rebellion as self-care,” says Morello. “But in this day and age, every act of art is an act of resistance. Every truth spoken is a light in the gathering darkness. And every song sung has the potential to be a trumpet of a bulwark against the rising tide of authoritarianism to help sound the bell for current and future generations to continue to fight for a more just and peaceful and decent planet.”
For more, listen to the full conversation of The Intercept Briefing on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, or wherever you listen to podcasts.
Transcript
Jessica Washington: Welcome to The Intercept Briefing, I’m Jessica Washington, politics reporter for The Intercept.
CNN: Republicans banded together and they killed this effort to impeach Pete Hegseth and largely stayed united. And the final vote here was 211 to 204.
NBC: Republicans uniting to block them from moving forward following Hegseth’s fiery rebuke of the outgoing congressman who introduced them, Thomas Massie.
ABC: The Republicans sticking together have essentially tabled or moved this resolution to the House Judiciary Committee, where it’s expected under Republican control these articles of impeachment will die. Pete Hegseth, for the moment, will not be impeached by the House of Representatives under this effort by Kentucky Republican Congressman Thomas Massie. Not a single Republican colleague joined him. All the Democrats stuck together, but there were not enough.
JW: On Tuesday night U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth narrowly avoided impeachment as House Republicans blocked a bill introduced by Republican Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky.
Rep. Thomas Massie: We’re not indicting him for being bad at his job. In fact, he was very effective at killing school children in Iran. He was very effective at extrajudicial killings. There’s no argument in these impeachment articles that he’s ineffective. The argument here is that he’s broken laws and he’s violated the Constitution.
JW: That’s Congressman Massie speaking at a press conference about the articles of Impeachment he introduced against the embattled Cabinet Secretary. This is how Hegseth responded:
Pete Hegseth: As for the articles themselves, Iran, the cartels, Maduro, Yemen, every one was a lawful operation ordered by the commander-in-chief, then ordered by myself, notified to congress and executed by American warriors who did their jobs. We destroyed terror regime’s capabilities. We sank the boats carrying poison into our communities. We put a narco dictator into handcuffs. These are not high crimes. This is the job. And it is a job well done.
Joining me now to break it all down is Nick Turse, senior national security and foreign policy reporter for the Intercept and editor of Tom Dispatch.
Nick, welcome back to The Intercept Briefing.
Nick Turse: Thanks for having me on. It’s great to be here.
JW: Before we dive in, I also want to let listeners know we have a special interview with Tom Morello, the musician and original member of Rage Against the Machine.
Tom Morello: My job from day one is to try to make one guitar sound like a riot and to have my music be a contributing factor to social justice movements at home and abroad.
JW: So stay tuned for that conversation
All right, Nick, to start. What’s your reaction to Secretary Hegseth dismissing Massie’s impeachment articles, claiming:
Pete Hegseth: What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability. It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.
JW: and that Massie is punishing him for a, “job well done”? What is your response?
NT: To start, it’s laughable. For half an hour at a press conference on the morning of the impeachment vote, Secretary Hegseth wove a web of lies designed to refute or obfuscate Massie’s eight impeachment charges. He repeatedly claimed that the effort to impeach him was just a stunt by one disgruntled congressman.
But, as we came to see, more than 200 members of Congress voted with Massie. So no, this wasn’t one man’s vendetta. When the new Congress is sworn in I think we’re going to find that the number in favor of impeaching him is only going to grow. And consequently, I think the list of high crimes and misdemeanors against him is also going to grow.
There’s almost a limitless list of high crimes that Hegseth can be charged with, and there are crimes within crimes. Waging unlawful wars in Iran and Yemen and Venezuela and specific war crimes within them that Hegseth may also be culpable for.
The boat strikes in and of themselves are criminal, and then there is, for example, the double tap strike on the first attack on a so-called drug boat, which is a crime in its own right.
Hegseth can spin it any way he likes. He can use the troops as a shield, claiming that indictments of him are indictments of them. But in the end, he’s got a lot to answer for on his own, and none of it’s because he’s doing a good job. It’s because he’s committing high crimes.
JW: High crimes and misdemeanors to a layperson, even to me, is not exactly indicative of what these actual crimes are. So what were the actual charges that Massie leveled against Hegseth?
NT: There were three charges for illegally waging war against Iran in violation of the War Powers Resolution. There was a charge related to Operation Rough Rider, which is the 2025 war in Yemen, which caused a tremendous number of civilian casualties. It’s become a forgotten conflict at this point.
The boat strike campaign which experts say are extrajudicial killings. There’s also a charge related to Hegseth’s efforts to undermine efforts at minimizing the possibility of civilian casualties. So these are some of the high crimes and misdemeanors of eight charges that Massie put forth.
JW: You just mentioned the drone strikes on so-called “narco terrorist” boats in the Caribbean and the Pacific, which to your estimate have killed more than 240 civilians. Those strikes, from my perspective, have gotten far less media attention than the Iran war, and obviously part of that is that much of what the U.S. is doing and who they’re targeting in open waters is shrouded in secrecy. But, how unprecedented are these strikes, and are these actions considered war crimes?
NT: The boat strikes, as you said, have largely been overtaken by the Iran war. But during his Pentagon press conference, Hegseth made a full-throated defense of his actions that actually drew attention to the unprecedented nature of the boat strike campaign.
Hegseth said that the charges that the American military targets civilians are a lie, and that the only people that target civilians are the terrorists that the U.S. hunts down. That itself is an outright lie. The U.S. boat strike campaign has only targeted civilians. Only. Not some, not inadvertently, not maybe. These are all civilians, period, full stop.
These summary executions of more than 240 people are a significant departure from the standard practice in the long-running U.S. war on drugs, in which law enforcement agencies detained suspected drug smugglers and then brought them to trial on criminal charges.
Experts in the laws of war, Pentagon officials that I’ve spoken with, and members of Congress from both parties say that Hegseth’s boat strikes are illegal, that they’re extrajudicial killings. The military is not permitted to deliberately target civilians, even suspected criminals.
Interdiction in these cases is possible. It’s preferable. It’s legal. We don’t execute suspected criminals in this country, or when the police do, it’s supposed to be a crime. If there was a declared war, these boat strikes might be war crimes, but no war exists, and there is no plausible legal justification for the strikes. And outside of armed conflict, the legal term for premeditated killing is murder. That’s what’s happening. That’s what Hegseth is responsible for, outright murder.
JW: Massie has not called Hegseth a war criminal or used the term murder like you have, but he did have this to say about Hegseth when discussing the articles of impeachment.
Thomas Massie: You won’t find a reference to war crimes. What I do say, though, is because he’s violated the international norms of war and violated our own conventions of war, he’s put our own soldiers and sailors at risk. When you go back for a second kill on people who are clinging to wreckage, you’re encouraging our adversaries to do the same. That’s why those laws — those international laws — are on the books.
JW: Nick, what did you make of Massie’s response just now?
NT: We were the first outlet to report that double tap strike in September 2025. It caused a firestorm in Congress for the very reason that Massie’s talking about.
He’s right. Double tap strikes on helpless shipwrecked people, they’re in contravention of the U.S. military’s own law of war manual, and they undermine respect for the laws of war and encourage enemies to give Americans no quarter, which is a war crime, and a war crime that Secretary Hegseth has openly called for and advocated.
I’m going to out myself as a lapsed historian here, but to emphasize that this is a longstanding norm in armed conflict I’d mention that a great rallying cry of the Revolutionary War — the American Revolution —was “Remember Paoli.” It’s a town in Pennsylvania where British Redcoats reportedly offered no quarter and massacred American forces.
Back in 1777, this was considered a major breach of the laws of combat. This is what Secretary Hegseth has advocated [that] we are doing in these types of double tap strikes, executing those who are injured those who are surrendering. That’s outright barbarism.
JW: We were just discussing civilian casualties in the boat strike —intentional civilian casualties. I also wanted to talk about what happened in February when the United States conducted an airstrike on an elementary school in Minab, Iran. That strike killed at least 150 people, most of them children.
Now, U.S. officials said the strike was caused by a “targeting error” where the military mistook the elementary school for an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval base. What did this horrific incident tell us about how the military has been operating under Hegseth when it comes to civilian casualties?
NT: This horrendous attack — a massacre of children — was the predictable result of Pentagon policies that The Intercept has been spotlighting since the spring of 2025, just after Pete Hegseth came to office. Hegseth made it inevitable that something like this mass killing of children would happen.
We reported that immediately upon taking office, he began dismantling what is known within the military as CHMR, the shorthand for Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response, basically undermining everything he could that restrains the military in favor of his favorite dictum, which is lethality.
A group of Democratic lawmakers told Hegseth in July in a letter directly to him that this gutting of CHMR had left the Pentagon unable to comply with the law and also its congressionally mandated responsibilities to protect civilians. This is precisely what military officials told us would happen months earlier, and it all came to fruition.
These criticisms were echoed in another report that we revealed in July that found that Hegseth had gutted the premier center devoted to preventing civilian casualties in war zones, the Pentagon’s own Civilian Protection Center of Excellence. Its workforce was slashed from 40 personnel in January of 2025 to just nine at the end of last year.
Last week we published an exposé that quoted six current and former defense officials who served under Hegseth, and one of them was the former senior advisor to this Civilian Protection Center of Excellence. This former official Wes Bryant, served eight combat deployments calling in airstrikes on ISIS and other post-9/11 entities.
Then he served under Hegseth until he was pushed out for blowing the whistle on policies that would undermine protections for civilians. Bryant told me that Hegseth is conducting what he called, “state terrorism.” He said Hegseth is “100 percent a war criminal,” and that he needs to be prosecuted.
JW: To that last point, and I really don’t like to play devil’s advocate, but from my understanding, you choose to refer to Hegseth by his self-styled title, Secretary of War, and if I understand you correctly, your argument is that there’s no need to sugarcoat what the U.S. military is doing. The Army is not in the business of defense. It’s in the business of war.
Is there an argument to be made that Hegseth is simply stripping back the facade of the U.S. military as anything other than a war machine, or is he really changing how the U.S. operates in the theater of war and in the world?
NT: I take a lot of heat from from readers on social media and in my email inbox about this, and readers plead with me not to bend to Hegseth’s will and call him the Secretary of War, which is, as you said his preferred title.
But I’ve really jumped at the chance for the reasons that you mentioned. When Hegseth unilaterally renamed the department, it gave me license to do what I’d wanted to do for years to call it as it’s seen, as it’s experienced in the world. For years out in the field, I found it grating whether I was in Vietnam or Cambodia or Libya and Somalia, to talk to victims of U.S. military violence about the so-called Department of Defense. The DoD says this. The DoD spokesman says that. I don’t think these people cared about it, but I absolutely did.
The Defense Department made war on the world, killing, wounding, and displacing millions of people not in the defense of anything. It was an aggressive war-making organization, plain and simple.
I hate using milquetoast euphemisms, but journalistic conventions handcuffed me. I couldn’t go off on my own and start calling it “Department of War.” But when they freed me up to give readers a more accurate assessment of what they do now under Hegseth and what has been done since they changed the name going back to the 1940s, I took the opportunity that I was afforded.
Attacking an elementary school in Iran is an act of war and maybe a war crime. It’s not a defense of the United States or in defense of the United States. That’s the reason why I use that title.
JW: Do you think that Hegseth has changed what the department is? Did it becoming the Department of War change something fundamental about it, or is that what it’s always been? And then is Hegseth changing anything about the actual way it operates?
NT: Hegseth has pulled the veil off of what the department does. I think in a very real sense, he’s undermined protections on civilians that were only just starting to perhaps take hold. The Center of Excellence that I mentioned earlier only just came into existence and was needed because the Pentagon has a long history of attacking civilians whether purposefully or inadvertently as “collateral damage.”
So the Defense Department always did what the Department of War does now, but there were some measures that were perhaps just starting to take hold, and Hegseth has undermined them completely.
JW: I think to your point, yes, Hegseth has lifted the veil off of what this department does. It is a department that makes war on the world. But he’s also made that worse and deadlier for civilians around the world.
And, obviously on Tuesday, Republicans killed the possibility of Hegseth being impeached by the current Congress. But come January, there’s going to be a new Congress dominated by Democrats. Now, before the vote on Massie’s articles of impeachment, Massie had this really interesting argument actually for why Republicans should join him in impeaching Hegseth. Let’s hear that clip.
Thomas Massie: I’m being polite here. What is an impeachment? An impeachment is just firing somebody, really. You don’t go to prison. You don’t go to jail. You don’t pay a fine. OK, when the Democrats get in charge, they are going to be very vicious.
JW: He went on to say.
Thomas Massie: The Democrats are going to bring people in here who have served under him and with him, give them protection. They’ll be able to say what he’s actually done, the things that he has ignored, the things that he did that caused civilian casualties, the way he’s ignored the laws, and then there’ll be a full, robust trial over in the Senate.
JW: Nick, what do you make of Massie’s remarks, the failure of this vote now, and what do you think might be coming in the next Democratic-led House and Senate?
NT: So Hegseth was very fixated on Massie having a grudge against Trump, which he had transferred over to the war secretary. But Massie, as we heard there, throughout the process, was very vocal that he was doing Hegseth a huge favor. Massie suggested that his impeachment resolution was the legislative equivalent of a mercy killing, calling it a much gentler version of what the Democrats would do when they take control of Congress in January.
The Democrats can rain down relentless hellfire on Hegseth. Congressional committees have broad investigative powers including the authority to subpoena administration officials to testify under oath and compel them to turn over documents. They can paper the Pentagon with subpoenas.
Representative Yasmin Ansari, who filed articles of impeachment against Hegseth in the spring, told me that Hegseth surviving Massie’s impeachment only opened him up to a plethora of ways for Democrats to hold him accountable in the next session. Specifically compelling to testify under oath before Congress and before the American people.
She emphasized that he’s “not only one of the most incompetent members of the administration,” her words, “but also one of the most unpopular” on a bipartisan basis. What she believes is going to happen is that Hegseth is going to be hauled up before Congress, and he’s just going to be battered incessantly.
This is probably going to grow so great that he’s going to become toxic to the administration. Representative-elect Richard Ojeda of North Carolina told our colleague Matt Sledge just after the impeachment vote the new Democrats are spoiling for a fight with Hegseth. He said “I want Pete Hegseth not just impeached, I want him prosecuted.”
I personally think that Hegseth might relish this rhetorical combat on Capitol Hill as a prelude to a potential presidential run. But, I think at some point it’s going to become untenable for him to actually preside over the Pentagon.
JW: I was at a press conference where Richard Ojeda was as well, and he had even more colorful language for Hegseth.
Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda: Make no mistake about it, the 120th Congress, he will not be so lucky. Tick, tock! Get ready, asshole, because we’re coming.
JW: They certainly seem to have plans to really target Hegseth and Massie might have been right that he was trying to offer a mercy kill. But we’re going to have to leave it there.
Nick Turse, thank you so much for joining me on the Intercept Briefing.
NT:: Thanks so much for having me.
JW: After the break, my co-host Jordan Uhl speaks to musician and guitarist Tom Morello about his new album “Everyone Gets Everything They Want” and using his platform to fight fascism.
[Break]
Jordan Uhl: “Every act of art is an act of resistance,” says the legendary musician Tom Morello. Fighting for social justice and against fascism has been a staple of his art and career, from his work with The Nightwatchman to Rage Against the Machine to Audioslave.
And he’s at it again with his new album “Everyone Gets Everything They Want.” The track “Adjourn it” denounces the rising tide of racism and anti immigrant bigotry.
The song features Serj Tankian of System of a Down and Morello’s 15 year old son, Roman.
Tom Morello joins me now.
Tom, thanks so much for joining us on The Intercept Briefing.
JU: Tom Morello, it is an honor. Thank you so much for joining us on the Intercept Briefing
Tom Morello: It’s my pleasure. Thank you very much for having me
JU: Tom, you have a long history of activism, infusing that into your music and your art, and creating space for activism-oriented concerts and events like Power to the People. Your new album follows that tradition. It’s called “Everyone Gets Everything They Want.” Can you tell us about this new album, the themes that you explore on it, and if there are plans for future Power to the People festivals as we head into the presidential cycle?
TM: My career has basically been rebellion as self-care — rock and roll, especially in these troubled times. But in this day and age, every act of art is an act of resistance. Every truth spoken is a light in the gathering darkness. And every song sung has the potential to be a trumpet of a bulwark against the rising tide of authoritarianism to help sound the bell for current and future generations to continue to fight for a more just and peaceful and decent planet.
“Everyone Gets Everything They Want” is the 22nd album of my career. All 22 of those records have been built around a single purpose: that history is not something that happens, history is something that we make. Standing up in your place, in your time, in your place of work, whether it’s in a recording studio, whether it’s at the carpenter’s union, whether you’re a student, whether you’re an unhoused person, whether you’re a politician, is doing what you can with what you’ve got to try to be an advocate and an agent for a more just and peaceful planet.
JU: We are coming off of a massive rout in this election. Voters made it clear how they feel about this growing fascist movement in this country. But coming out of it, while some people are relieved, some people are happy, there are already intra-party debates over the policy priorities and leadership.
Unsurprisingly, we are seeing the pundit class rush to quell people’s enthusiasm, insisting the left does not have a mandate and that the moderate policy is the answer. What is your response to that?
TM: I was the scheduling secretary for United States Senator Alan Cranston for two years, so I got to see how the sausage is made from inside the sausage factory, and it is worse than you could possibly imagine. While it is encouraging that here and in Hungary and in Serbia and in Brazil that the people have resoundingly said no to fascism but the idea is not to have a kinder, gentler oligarchy. The idea is the liberation of humanity. The idea is securing a planet — a healthy planet — for our children and grandchildren, generations to come.
One thing that is encouraging in those other countries and in our most recent election is in addition to the terrible corporate Democrats who are also represented, there’s a new breed of politician. We have a socialist mayor in New York City. We have a socialist mayor in Los Angeles, the two biggest cities in our country.
The young people are once again the hope of the future. Rather than having me, a musician of a certain age saying, “This is what you should do,” I think that the main thing I can do is listen to what they have to say and encourage them in their efforts to build that more just and more peaceful planet.
JU: Do you have any thoughts on who should lead in the House and the Senate? We’re seeing calls for Schumer to step aside. Maybe if it’s new blood, maybe it’s Chris Van Hollen. Do you have any thoughts on who should lead Democrats in the Senate?
TM: My thoughts of people who should lead in the Senate are not elected in politics. And likely your show would be thrown off the air if I were to name them. [Laughter.]
Obviously the Chuck Schumers and Hakeem Jeffries are just awful continuations of the awful policies that got us in this to begin with. You can trace it back to Clinton with the crime bill and with NAFTA, and the abandonment of the working class that got us in this mess to begin with.
But again, I also think that it’s important to aim for the world you really want without compromise, without apology, and to not just go, “OK, well this is going to be better than the slippery slope to obvious this 50 percent clown show, 50 percent fascism that is the Trump administration.”
But what is the world you really want, and how do you build that? Not just what is a glazed-over version of what we’ve had, a reheated version of the terrible policies of both parties that got us in this situation of nearly environmental collapse and right-wing white Christian nationalism.
One thing I will say is that, there has been some reckoning that needs to be pushed even further of dealing with America’s original sin. The paradox of this country, which is demanding liberty while embracing white supremacy. That is the story of our country from day one in that some people’s lives just matter a lot more than other people’s lives, both at home and abroad. And a full rejection of that we’ve seen in some other countries, we’ve seen in part of the electorate here, and in some of the elected officials.
In my view, Election Day is harm reduction. I always vote. I vote my conscience, unless it is a contested election, and then I vote for the absolute most harm reduction.
To go beyond that and be like, “What’s the world you really want, and how do we fight for it?” That doesn’t just happen on Election Day. That happens the day after Election Day, and the day after that.
Since I was 17 years old, I have been in the trenches of grassroots organizing via rock and roll to try to do what I can in my small way with a Marshall half stack to liberate humanity. And that work has only just begun.
JU: I want to touch on that. I live in Los Angeles, and we just watched California voters reject a billionaire tax. This was a fight you were directly involved in. You performed at a rally here in Los Angeles in the spring. How do you make sense of that? You’re talking about these socialist gains, and we’re seeing this—
TM: It’s easy to make sense of it. It’s money in politics. I’m a fan of sports. Every World Series game, every football game had 72 ads paid for by tech billionaires and featuring the heroes of the California Democratic Party saying, “Please don’t tax the billionaires, whatever you do.”
This is a firsthand account. I was the scheduling secretary for a U.S. senator. Let me tell you what I scheduled. I scheduled phone calls for him to ask rich dudes for money. That’s what the schedule was.
We would go to a hotel, and there were like 10 payphones in a row. I would commandeer them, and I would call up the first guy and say, “Can you hold for the senator?” He’d get on the phone and ask that rich dude for money. Nine more calls in a row, Republicans, Democrats, corporate people, whatever.
Then they would start again, and we would spend the whole day doing that. Those guys are bought, sold, and totally beholden to the oligarchs that have their hands on the lever of power. So the reason why that tax failed was because how much money did they spend? If they had put as much money into healthcare for Californians as they did in trying to reject the billionaire tax, we’d be a lot better off.
JU: Over $300 million by a handful of billionaires. It’s absolutely staggering.
I want to look ahead. You and through your music, you’ve always been ahead of the curve waiting for folks to catch up. So what are the emerging fights that you see now that people need to get plugged in on? Is there something that stands out?
TM: I would say one thing is to not sink into a complacency when there’s a euphoria in the aftermath of a in my view somewhat surprising rejection of to the level that we’ve seen of Trumpism. But that’s just the beginning. We’ve already seen, as you mentioned, the right-wing of the Democratic Party asserting their hold on, like, “Hold on now. Hold on now.”
What people need to realize is the world isn’t going to change itself. That is up to you. That is up to me. While that may sound like a daunting sentence and a daunting task, the good news is whenever the world has changed in progressive, radical, or even revolutionary ways, it has been changed by people who didn’t have any more money, courage, power, intelligence, influence than anyone listening or watching this right now. The world is changed by average, everyday, ordinary people standing up in their time, not just at the ballot box, but in all that intervening time. Change comes from below. When change is real, it comes from below. It comes from you and me. That’s what I’ve been singing about and screaming about in my songs for an entire career. But I think that just that realization that we are agents of history, not just on election day, but beyond.
JU: The song “Unconquered” on your album features Kneecap, the Irish rap trio who have been very vocal at their shows for the liberation of Palestine, and they faced backlash, losing gigs, revocation of visas. Macklemore, same thing, speaking out about Palestine. We are in a moment right now where artists are using their platform for a critical human rights issue, a moral issue, and they are being punished.
What do you make of this backlash from the industry, from venue owners, from the billionaire class?
TM: First of all, welcome to my life. There’s nothing new about that. From Rage Against the Machine to my own political organizing, the pushback is real when you threaten centers of power and established orthodoxy in that regard.
The one thing that artists should remember is that you don’t put down your First Amendment rights when you pick up a microphone or a guitar. A lot of people are like, “Just shut up and dribble in sports,” or, “Just shut up and play music.” I would encourage all artists, don’t leave behind who you are and what you do.
But not just artists. As journalists, whatever your job is, don’t leave behind your convictions in your vocation. Those artists, Kneecap and Macklemore, have done it, and they’ve paid a price. Well, thank God. If you are making music that everyone can like hold hands to and skip around, you’re probably making pretty shitty music.
But those artists have stood up at a critical juncture. They are the Rage Against the Machine of now, fearlessly standing up for an oppressed people in a time where the world pushes back, and they don’t give a fuck. That should not just be Irish rappers and Pacific Northwestern rappers, but everybody should be emboldened by that and realize that they’re on the right side of history.
JU: Tom, before we let you go, we know you’re pressed for time. Any final thoughts?
TM: Thank you for your service, and The Intercept’s service in doing what you do. I think that you guys are upholding a long tradition of confrontational journalism, which the world needs now more than ever.
And also I’ve just started. I had hoped maybe around this time in my career we’d be living in the anarcho-syndicalist utopia that perhaps we imagined in the pre-choruses of some Rage Against the Machine songs long ago. That not being the case, though, I’m in it to win it. And I’ve only just started. My job from day one is to try to make one guitar sound like a riot and to have my music be a contributing factor to social justice movements at home and abroad.
JU: Tom, thank you so much for joining me on the Intercept Briefing
TM: Thank you very much.

https://www.propublica.org/article/georg.title: Members of Georgia’s Election Board Have Been Coordinating With Cleta Mitchell’s Network
https://www.propublica.org/article/georg.author: Doug Bock Clark
https://www.propublica.org/article/georg.text:
In the run-up to the midterms, members of Georgia’s State Election Board and much of its professional staff were coordinating with an activist group led by Cleta Mitchell, the conservative attorney who worked with President Donald Trump to try to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election.
The board sets the swing state’s election rules, oversees the conduct of its election officials and investigates allegations of fraud.
Recordings of private calls and events reviewed by ProPublica show current and former state board members working with the Election Integrity Network and allied organizations on shared priorities. Among them: advancing the use of a controversial, error-prone software tool known as ELLY to search voter rolls for purportedly suspicious voters.
The state board’s current vice chair, Janelle King, and her predecessor, Janice Johnston, have both attended meetings of EIN or VoterGA, an aligned organization whose membership and goals significantly overlap with EIN. Johnston retired in June but still plays an active role in state election matters behind the scenes.
At an August 2025 fundraiser for VoterGA, Mitchell declared she loved Johnston and King, who were both present. “You know, we’ve worked so hard together,” Mitchell said.
At least three members of the state board’s eight-person professional staff have participated in EIN meetings, including people who handle allegations of voter fraud and misconduct by election officials.
The board’s executive director, James Mills, likewise has worked closely with members of the EIN, according to five sources with knowledge of these interactions, board documents and EIN communications shared with ProPublica.
EIN’s close ties to the board and its staff have given it extraordinary influence over how elections are run in Georgia, experts said. In particular, the group has been able to enlist the board’s help in getting counties to remove voters from their rolls based on information from ELLY.
“Trump allies captured the State Election Board to keep claims of a stolen 2020 election going and tilt Georgia elections toward Republicans,” said Max Flugrath, a director at Fair Fight Action, a voting advocacy nonprofit that has closely tracked the board’s and the network’s actions. “EIN was the behind-the-scenes driver spearheading these changes.”
The board’s chair, John Fervier, told ProPublica he had not known about EIN’s sway over the board or its staff, but said he’d long sensed that an outside force was shaping the board’s actions.
“The more I look into this, the more I’m realizing that the Election Integrity Network has been having an undue influence on the State Election Board, and that needs to cease,” he said in an interview, though he declined to go into specifics about personnel matters. “I’m looking forward to changes in how the election board operates.”
Fervier has called a special meeting for Friday, in part to discuss personnel matters.
In response, Garland Favorito, an EIN leader and head of VoterGA, called on social media for his followers to inundate state board members with messages defending Mills and other staffers associated with the group.
“There is a significant possibility that these members will vote to terminate the Executive Director, investigators or possibly even staff members, any of which would destroy the SEB as we now know it,” Favorito wrote on Wednesday, referring to the State Election Board. “As most of you know, the SEB staff has made remarkable historical progress this year in … accountability for election corruption and much more. The Executive Director and staff deserve raises for amazing performances, not threats of termination.”
In interviews in late September, Johnston did not directly answer questions about her relationship to EIN. “I’m all about election integrity, wherever it comes from,” she said. She acknowledged she had remained involved with board affairs after her retirement. “It gets in your blood,” she said. Two days later, she posted on social media that “Cleta Mitchell, Election Integrity expert has the right ideas” about how elections should be run.
Johnston did not answer detailed questions about her relationship with EIN and affiliated groups.
King acknowledged she spoke about election matters with activists from EIN and VoterGA, but said they did not influence her decisions. She also said she saw no problem with EIN activists working for the board, though the staff is supposed to be independent and nonpartisan.
“As long as they are representing the SEB well, fine,” she said in an interview. “If they choose to become members of an organization in their private time, that is their choice.”
When a reporter recounted instances in which staffers had worked to advance EIN goals in their official capacity, she said she was unaware of this. “That is the first I’ve heard about it,” she responded.
Mills declined to answer questions from ProPublica about his relationship to EIN.
Mitchell did not respond directly to ProPublica but, after receiving detailed questions, put a post on X celebrating EIN’s work with the election board. “An election integrity group is working with election officials to oversee elections,” she wrote. “Wow! What a discovery!!! Pulitzer anyone?”
Favorito called the idea that the board and its staff had been working secretly with the EIN and VoterGA a “patently false conspiracy theory.”
EIN has been deeply entwined with conservatives’ efforts to reshape Georgia elections since at least 2024.
That year, ProPublica’s reporting revealed, EIN members secretly pushed a rule through the State Election Board allowing local officials to potentially delay certifying the state’s vote count. A court subsequently struck down the change, which experts had warned could enable county election boards to disrupt certifying the election if Trump had lost.
In late 2025, the board played a role in instigating the Trump administration’s unprecedented effort to reinvestigate alleged 2020 voting irregularities, formally asking the Justice Department to obtain Fulton County election records subsequently seized by the FBI. It was a move pushed by the EIN. The affidavit authorizing the raid cited Johnston and King as witnesses. The affidavit also cited a report put together by an EIN researcher compiling activists’ debunked allegations of fraud.
In recent months, EIN’s allies and participants at the state board pushed counties to use ELLY, a tool developed by an EIN member, to search voter rolls for signs of fraud and purge suspect registrants.
ELLY aggregates public data from state voter files, federal change-of-address records, tax documents, obituaries, property websites like Zillow and other sources, but doesn’t have access to personal identifiers such as Social Security numbers or full dates of birth. As a result, voting rights groups have said, ELLY often erroneously flags legitimate voters.
Nonetheless, before the midterms, the State Election Board’s investigative staff pressured Chatham County, a Democratic stronghold, to purge more than 200 registered voters that the tool identified as questionable, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported.
After the election, a Forsyth County election board member who is also a member of EIN submitted ELLY data questioning the validity of over 60 ballots, including four cast by people who were supposedly dead. ProPublica found that all four were, in fact, alive. The board rejected the challenges.
EIN members and state board officials have defended ELLY’s accuracy.
The EIN’s connections to the board carry additional importance in light of last week’s election results, in which Democrats wrested control of all statewide offices and the state House from Republicans. The House appoints a member to the State Election Board, opening the door to change.
Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms ran on a platform that promised a new approach to the election board.
“The State Election Board has become mired in political games, conspiracy theories, and partisan interference,” the platform stated. Bottoms’ platform pledged that she would “work with the General Assembly to eliminate the current State Election Board and replace it with a stronger, more independent election oversight structure that is insulated from partisan manipulation.”
Fervier is part of the board’s four-member Republican majority, but he has clashed repeatedly with Johnston, King and Mills and has effectively been relegated to a member of the minority at times.
Emails and communications between board members and staff obtained by ProPublica via public records requests show that Fervier and other board members who oppose steps supported by the EIN have been excluded from some board hiring decisions.
Earlier this year, Fervier publicly accused Mills of going beyond what the board had authorized in calling for the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security to intervene to assess the security of the state’s voting machines.
“Activists should not control the board,” he told ProPublica. “I’m really looking forward to this meeting because I think that we’re going to address some issues that should have been addressed awhile ago.”

A Toolkit for a Liberated Art World
Amin Husain and Nitasha Dhillon on Marco Baravalle’s new book, plus Jasmine Wahi on the continued fight for arts and culture after the midterm elections.
“Radical politics,” “marginalized communities,” “feminist art” … If you see these terms peppering wall labels at a major museum, there’s an excellent chance the institution behaves in direct opposition to those values and groups. Scholars Amin Husain and Nitasha Dhillon, who were also among the organizers of the historic Strike MoMA protests in 2021, know this pattern all too well. It’s part of the neoliberal capture of art institutions, which Italian curator and activist Marco Baravalle lays bare in his new book, The Battleground of Art. Read on for a review by Husain and Dhillon, who write that it’s a toolkit for building a better, freer art world.
Meanwhile, in the United States, that art world finds itself at a crucial turning point. In the wake of the midterm elections, longtime nonprofit arts leader Jasmine Wahi reminds us that the fight is only beginning. She opines today about the importance of holding Democratic officials accountable not just for redressing the damage inflicted by the Trump administration, but also for taking its responsibility to artists and culture workers seriously. “Rebuilding the same inadequate baseline is not enough,” she explains.
More in the news today, including public backlash against Egypt’s arrest of the editor of an independent publication and San Francisco-based painter Hiroshi Sato’s resistance against Silicon Valley and enshittifcation through his quietly subversive art. Heaven knows we could all use more of that.
—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books
After the Midterms, the Real Work for Arts and Culture Begins
In the afterglow of the blue-nami, those of us who make, organize, fund, and sustain cultural life are feeling a twinge of hope. But I find myself slipping into a spiral of anxiety as the everyday reality of economic precarity sets back in. Our newly elected Democratic congressional leaders have an opportunity to change that reality — pushing back against Trump is necessary — but it cannot be the full extent of their ambition. | Jasmine Wahi

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: NYC Juvenile Lockups Packed Beyond Capacity as Overtime Soars: Audit
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Reuven Blau
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The city’s two juvenile detention centers are operating far beyond capacity, staff overtime has quadrupled and the average length of detention has nearly doubled, according to a new state audit.
The 69-page review also found that the number of probation officers declined by one-third between 2020 and 2026, even as juvenile caseloads increased.
“New York City is spending more money to keep young people in detention, and they are staying there longer,” state Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli said in a statement.
“The city needs to address staffing shortages and overcrowding and also invest in prevention efforts, including after-school programs, mentoring and summer jobs, to give young people more opportunities and help keep them out of the juvenile justice system.”
Overcrowding at the two facilities has gotten so bad the city has been forced to use classroom space as housing units. Earlier this month, a state oversight agency stopped issuing waivers to allow ACS to use those common areas for housing.
The report — which covers 2019 through fiscal year 2026 — comes weeks after the Mamdani administration announced a series of changes aimed at addressing problems at the beleaguered facilities, Horizon and Crossroads.
The Administration for Children’s Services, which oversees the centers, says it is expanding alternatives to detention, increasing staffing and investing in educational and recreational programming.
Among the initiatives is a new intensive community monitoring program through the Department of Probation that will combine closer supervision with clinical assessments, family engagement, educational and employment assistance, and other community-based services. The program is intended to serve 150 young people who are transitioning out of secure detention or at risk of being placed there.
The administration is also increasing funding for community-based programs, expanding access to family therapy and making nonsecure detention available to some young people whom judges determine are appropriate candidates for a less restrictive setting.
ACS also announced plans to hire 56 additional youth development specialists and 85 employees dedicated to emergency response at Horizon and Crossroads.
The agency said it is investing in scanners, metal detectors and cameras to prevent contraband from entering the facilities, while expediting renovations and the installation of temporary classrooms to create more room for educational programming.
The state audit comes nearly ten years after state lawmakers passed the Raise the Age Law to transition 16- and 17-year-olds from the adult to juvenile criminal justice system.
In New York City, that meant transferring them from Department of Correction-run adult housing units on Rikers Island to the two secure detention centers operated by ACS.
But the department has struggled to staff and operate the centers as the number of young people facing criminal charges has ballooned over the past several years, according to a series of oversight reports and court filings.
In October 2024 the city’s Department of Investigation concluded that ACS’s point-based system to reward and punish the behavior of incarcerated youths, known as a behavioral management tool, had failed to adequately deter violence and contraband smuggling.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/counter.title: The Enemies List
https://inthesetimes.com/article/counter.author: Alberto Toscano
https://inthesetimes.com/article/counter.text:
The Enemies List
The Trump administration’s war on the Left is designed to suffocate dissent.
Alberto Toscano
One year ago, in the wake of the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, the White House ramped up its campaign against left-wing dissidence.
The government weaponized the legally dubious category of “domestic terrorism” when, on Sept. 22, 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order against “Antifa,” designating it as a domestic terrorist organization. Three days later, Trump issued a national security memorandum declaring that the “‘anti-fascist’ lie has become the organizing rallying cry used by domestic terrorists to wage a violent assault against democratic institutions, constitutional rights and fundamental American liberties.” It instructs federal agencies to devise a national strategy to preempt, disband and prosecute those “networks” and “conspiracies” that supposedly seek to undermine and overthrow the U.S. government.
This strategy framed the prosecution in the “Prairieland” case, in which nine activists were charged in relation to a solidarity noise protest outside an ICE detention center at which an officer was shot, in circumstances that remain disputed.
But as Adam Federman reported for In These Times and Type Investigations in March, FBI records obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request show that the bureau investigated an alleged Dallas-area antifa group years earlier, in 2018, and closed that investigation after finding it posed no threat to national security.
In June, eight of the Prairieland defendants were sentenced to a cumulative 450 years in prison. The sentences were largely for actions deemed “material support” for terrorism. Perhaps most egregiously, Daniel Rolando Sanchez-Estrada, who was not present at the demonstration, was given 30 years for moving a box of anarchist zines, which was construed as conspiracy to corruptly conceal documents.
The same month the protesters were sentenced, antifa was again invoked in the federal charges levied against 15 members of Direct Action Minnesota for their role in anti-ICE protests. Just as Prairieland prosecutors depicted black clothing at demonstrations as evidence of terroristic intent, the use of the messaging app Signal was understood as proof of conspiracy in the Minneapolis case.
These cases demonstrate the grievous effects of applying the legal and ideological arsenal of counterterrorism to left-wing activism, imagined as a vast conspiratorial network (“Antifa”). They are also one front in something larger: a counterterrorism crusade that functions as a miniature version of the economic warfare that has been deployed against nation-states such as Cuba, Iraq and Iran. Its aim: to suffocate any opposition — abroad and at home.
The Trump administration’s efforts to repress opposition have always been international in scope. While domestic terrorism is not covered as such by any existing law, designation as a foreign terrorist organization or specially designated terrorist group has momentous consequences — not least for U.S. citizens or residents accused of providing material support. The desire to paint antifa as an heir to the fantastical Soviet-managed “terror network” that preoccupied the CIA in the 1980s explains the decision to designate four marginal European groups as terrorists in November 2025.
The economic siege against Cuba has also been accompanied by an effort to link the U.S. Left to nefarious foreign puppet masters. In an improbable regurgitation of high Cold War propaganda, contemporary Cuba has been reimagined as America’s dystopian nemesis.
The State Department released a 100-page report, widely suspected to have been produced by the AI platform Claude, under the bombastic title “Cuba: The Capital of 21st Century Communism.” The transparent aim is to tie the effort to turn Cuba into a docile dependent through economic (and eventually also military) warfare to the mounting campaign to persecute political dissidence at home.
Turning history on its head, the report’s first lines declare: “For nearly seven decades, the Cuban regime has waged a sustained campaign of subversion against the United States.” The conspiratorial imagination is on overdrive: despite its poverty and almost total asymmetry of power vis-à-vis the United States, Cuba has orchestrated “a vast hemispheric network.” It has infiltrated “the highest reaches” of the United States and established “a revolutionary infrastructure designed to turn America against itself.” This infrastructure has co-opted everyone from Karen Bass to Barack Obama, the Black Panther Party to the People’s Forum, Amy Goodman of Democracy Now! to myriad university departments and civil society organizations.
As scholar Charisse Burden-Stelly has argued, this pastiche of red scares past is a form of “anti-communist governance” — one that combines public authority and self-censorship “to penalize, regulate, censure and criminalize ideas and beliefs that challenge racial oppression, economic inequality and class antagonism by labeling them ‘communist.’”
These increasingly delirious declarations are not trying to consolidate or manufacture consent; they seem meant for internal consumption within the echo chambers of the White House Situation Room and the MAGA mediasphere.
Unfortunately, without commensurate resistance, force without consent can go a long way. Behind the fantastical façade is the as yet unimpeded project — nationally and regionally — to maximize the impunity of capital while suppressing any alternative vision of collective life and welfare.
That international reach was on full display at the “Ministerial on the Resurgence of Political Terrorism,” a conference hosted by Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Washington, D.C., in July. In his keynote remarks, Rubio lambasted a media and academic establishment that he presented as treating left-wing violence as a “protected class unto itself” and declared: “It is time to crush this evil forever.” He launched into a vituperative portrait of violent leftists as resentful enemies of Western greatness and civilization.
For Rubio, the menace to be snuffed out is “a revolt of the worst against the best, a revolt of the weak and the cowardly against the strong and the good … perpetrated by those who cannot build, who cannot create, who cannot achieve great things, and take their revenge upon the world for their own inadequacy by seeking to destroy those who can.”
The sentiment was echoed with characteristic shrill hyperbole by White House Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy Stephen Miller, who asked the audience to reflect on why no one attending antifa protests looks “normal”. His answer contained a familiarly fascistic theory of leftist ideas manifesting as physical degeneracy: “Every one of them … has scarred their body and their appearance in many different ways, to the point in which their outer appearance becomes a manifestation of their inner hatred.”
But behind the rhetoric about the revolt of the weak — which, like the anti-communist pastiche of the Cuba report, is of very old vintage — lies a focused, and terribly contemporary, strategy of repression. Miller emphasized the need to “disrupt, identify, defund, debank, arrest, and prosecute” the nodes of the new terror network.
This counterterrorism architecture projects any single act of so-called left-wing violence as linked to all others both ideologically and materially. Its latest target is the Italian anti-fascist hacktivist collective and digital service provider Autistici/Inventati (translated as Autistic/Invented), also known as A/I.
A/I was founded in 2001, in the context of the antiglobalization movement and the mobilization against the G-8 in Genoa, and provided services like blogs, mailing lists, email and website hosting to groups and individuals with whom it felt a broad political affinity.
On August 26, A/I was named a specially designated terrorist group by the State Department, alongside Palestine Action — the direct action group whose designation as a terrorist group by the UK government has been the object of sustained protest and challenge — and the Palestinian Alternative Revolutionary Path Movement (Masar Badil). But the designation does not concern any actions the collective has carried out. There are no indictments pending against it in either the United States or Italy. Rather, the State Department alleges that its digital infrastructure facilitated acts of “left-wing violence,” from railway sabotage in Europe to the resistance against Cop City in Atlanta, as well as communications among groups ranging from Rose City Antifa to the Kurdistan Workers’ Party.
The designation’s effect, as intended, was swift and drastic. In Italy, where a U.S. designation has no legal standing, A/I was debanked by Banca Etica. The bank declared that notwithstanding its opposition to this campaign against its client, it could not risk the consequences to its other 130,000 accounts should the Treasury Department’s secondary sanctions affect the bank’s access to Visa, Mastercard, Nexi and dollar exchanges.
The outsize power of the U.S. government and the dollar in the international financial system, specifically in monetary transactions, means banks exercise anticipatory overcompliance to avoid risk. The effect is to turn any opponent into an economic nonperson, with all the social and political consequences that entails.
A/I disbanded to shield its former clients from persecution. Shortly before, the collective said the Trump administration had targeted it in a kind of “hybrid warfare.”
Perhaps the most worrying aspect is the absence of any concerted effort by Italian or European institutions to defend the collective’s right to free expression, which is also a right to the digital infrastructures that make it possible. As the collective Sabot Media observed, U.S. sanctions create a “perimeter of fear” around those they target, one that operates in advance of and in lieu of the law.
This crusade builds upon the anti-Palestinian, anti-migrant and anti-Muslim legal provisions that were crystallized by the so-called “war on terror” — when the terror lists were born.
As the academic Lisa Bhungalia rightly notes in her work on the “asphyxiatory violence” of contemporary imperialism, the current wave of repression is “a depository of past decades that build one upon the other rather than … a radical departure from that which came before.”
To face this moment, an internationalist Left must maintain and repair the infrastructures of resistance. The threat is not only a frontal assault or Trump and Miller’s fascist verbiage, but also the kind of suffocation that uses the silent violence of money and law to snuff out any liberatory alternative to the status quo.
Thank you for reading this story. At a time when corporate media is dominating the web and our airwaves, independent journalism is more important than ever, and that’s what we provide at In These Times. We offer some of the best reporting, investigations and analysis on the growing movements for justice in the U.S.—and our work is firmly pro-labor and anti-fascist. To continue producing it, we need your support.
If you believe in the power of an independent press, please make a donation to In These Times today. By becoming a sustaining member, you can ensure that our work reaches even more readers.
And if you become a sustainer right now, you'll get a free year-long print subscription and a special subscribers-only print from artist Molly Crabapple.
Thank you.
ALBERTO TOSCANO is the author of Late Fascism: Race, Capitalism and the Politics of Crisis (Verso) and Terms of Disorder: Keywords for an Interregnum (Seagull). He lives in Vancouver.
