https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/mi.title: Microsoft Outage Disrupts Global Operations and Art World Too, Undercover Investigation Busts Fake UK Artist Visas, and More: Morning Links for November 13, 2026
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/mi.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/mi.text:
To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.
Good Morning!
- As Microsoft’s global outage stretches into its second day on Friday, the art world, like everyone else, is feeling the pain.
- An undercover investigation has found that companies are helping migrants create fake art portfolios, complete with fake published art criticism and art news, to help them apply for UK visas.
- The Kennedy Center began negotiations under its former president, Richard Grennel, to switch ticketing platforms to Ticketmaster, whose parent company, Live Nation, is also tied to Grennel, raising concerns about a conflict of interest.
The Headlines
INBOX UNOPENED. As Microsoft’s global outage stretches into its second day on Friday, the art world, like everyone else, is feeling the pain. In fact, there’s no telling when many of you will receive this message, typically sent via e-mail around 9 a.m. ET. ARTnews’s own e-mail system relies on Microsoft Outlook, so if you’re trying to write us there, let this be a warning: We have no way to read it. Meanwhile, not everyone is peeved; the British Museum has taken the opportunity to have a little fun with a host of playful memes drawn from its historic collection, which you can enjoy here. The French, at Musée d’Orsay, say that if Outlook is down, “it’s time to relax.” On Friday, Microsoft said its services were improving, according to the New York Times, and by 6 a.m. ET traffic was restoring in the Asia Pacific region. Businesses, airlines, and government agencies, such as police and intelligence services, have all been disrupted. And for now, Microsoft said it has “no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident.” Nor have they received any e-mails about it.
A FOR ART. F FOR FAKE. An undercover BBC investigation has found that companies have been helping migrants create fake art portfolios, complete with fake published art criticism and art news, to help them apply for UK visas under the government’s Global Talent program. The program launched in 2020 and was designed to attract creative workers, including scientists and artists. But wealthy migrants are also being courted by companies to pay thousands in exchange for help with cheating the system. According to the BBC, visas for two Nigerian men have been revoked because the Home Office believes they were not the fine art photographers they claimed to be. “There is a real problem whereupon fake articles are being implanted onto newspaper websites using bylines of reputable culture journalists,” said Molara Wood.
The Digest
The Kennedy Center has delayed issuing tickets for its annual December Honors gala because of negotiations, begun under its former president, Richard Grennel, to switch ticketing platforms to Ticketmaster, whose parent company, Live Nation, is also tied to Grennel, raising concerns about a conflict of interest. [NPR]
Jenny Holzer has a solo installation of quotes about queer love and loss coming to Times Square in time for World AIDS Day on December 1. [Artnet News]
After a Nazi-looted painting by German Impressionist Max Slevogt was restituted to Eduard Fuchs’s family in July, it will head to auction next month at Ketterer Kunst’s December Day Sale, with an estimate of €40,000 to €60,000 ($44,250 to $66,370). [The Art Newspaper]
Los Angeles’s famous, graffiti-art-covered towers, or Oceanwide Plaza, were just washed clean, prepping the stalled real-estate development for acquisition. [Los Angeles Times]
Next year, 450 years will have passed since the birth of Flemish painter Peter Paul Rubens, and his native Antwerp is planning a host of exhibitions. [The Brussels Times]
The Kicker
FRIEZE FORGES AHEAD. Ahead of Frieze’s debut in Abu Dhabi November 19 to 22, exhibitors discuss jitters about traveling to the region amid uncertainty about the ongoing US war in Iran and recent attacks by Houthi militants in Saudi Arabia, reports the Financial Times. “Anyone saying that they are not concerned in some way is either lying to themselves or to each other,” said Frieze exhibitor Niamh Coghlan, director of Richard Saltoun gallery in London. Nevertheless, “there are some incredible collectors and institutions in Abu Dhabi, and it is important to be seen to support them, as they support us,” Coghlan added. Around the same time as Frieze, the Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial opens, along with the design and art fair Nomad. Or, as Katia Nounou Boueiz, chair of Sotheby’s Middle East, put it, for now, “We are checking the news and obviously attuned to what could happen. We are all in the same boat … and we’ve decided to carry on.”

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/dublin/a-d.title: À Dublin, l’Europe se lance dans la bataille de l’IA et sa filière militaire

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/dublin/a-d.text:
En Irlande, ce vendredi, le sommet des Vingt-Sept est entièrement consacré à l’intelligence artificielle. Une technologie aux applications militaires qui change de plus en plus la donne avec la guerre d’Ukraine et sa mine de données sur les champs de bataille. Au forum de la Coopération économique pour l’Asie-Pacifique en Chine les 18 et 19 novembre, Pékin, Washington et Moscou pourraient annoncer un protocole sur l’IA dans les arsenaux nucléaires.
À Dublin, les 27 pays membres de l’Union européenne ont consacré un sommet à l’intelligence artificielle, ce vendredi. Les dirigeants veulent combler leur retard par rapport à l’Asie, et la Chine en particulier, ainsi que sur les États-Unis. La seule exception au niveau européen, le Français Mistral qui s’est imposé dans cette course entre les deux principales puissances.

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: A sweet treat every day: the best chocolate Advent calendars in 2026
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Marian Bull
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
When I think of Advent calendars, I think of chocolate: tiny treats meted out day by day, and intended to increase, with their sheer volume and delight, the recipient’s level of festive cheer. Luckily for the chocolate obsessive among us (myself included), the Advent calendar landscape is vast. Whether you’re looking for classic nostalgia or bean-to-bar extravagance, you’ll be able to find a chocolate Advent calendar to match your tastes. I’ve done the hard work of testing a bunch of them, and am here to outline the best, brightest (literally, one lights up), and classic favorites for 2026.
- Visit our ultimate holiday gift guide for more gift guides and holiday shopping ideas for everyone on your list.
Chocolate that teleports you to Tokyo:
Tokyo Choco Club 12-Day Japanese KitKat Advent Calendar
Opening this Japanese KitKat Advent calendar transported me back to the Tokyo convenience stores that defined my recent trip to Japan that I will never shut up about. It features 12 varieties of KitKats, from a dark matcha to an intriguing sweet potato. I appreciate that each door is filled with multiples of a flavor, so that you can try each variety with friends or family. If you don’t want to give the whole thing to one person, you could also split these into stocking stuffers far more unique than a candy cane or Hershey’s bar. Lauren Gould
Small batch chocolate, with a side of folk tales:
Dandelion Chocolate 2026 Advent calendar
This Advent calendar from San Francisco’s favorite bean-to-bar chocolatier is a lush gift full of considered details. Its circular box holds bonbons and treats from 24 chocolatiers from North America and Japan; it also includes a folding paper star to adorn your house, and a book of Nordic tales, one for each night, that inspired the box’s design. It’s really an exploration of what chocolate can be – from bonbons to caramels to praline. The standout, to me, was a genmaicha praliné, which you can also get in their sublime Japanese Tea Bonbon Collection.
A box of chocolates that reads like a cereal box:
Tony’s Chocolonely Advent calendar
Tony’s is hands down my favorite grocery store chocolate brand, so I was thrilled to dig into their calendar, which carries the brand’s signature playfulness: when you open it up, one side offers a “guide” to each day, and reminds me of reading the back of a cereal box. We get six flavors here, including my absolute favorite: dark milk chocolate with pretzel and toffee. They are even educating us about ethics in the chocolate industry while feeding us our daily treat – there’s a QR code you can scan to learn more about this topic that’s a big part of the brand’s identity.
A European classic:
Toblerone Advent calendar
If you have ever picked up the XL Toblerone bar at duty free, this one is for you. The Toblerone calendar includes mini bars in white, milk and dark chocolate. They emerge from a narrow gold box printed with a Christmas tree that will make you think, hey, the Christmas tree and the Toblerones are kinda the same shape! And this sort of whimsy is what Advent calendars are all about.
A luxury ski chalet, full of chocolate:
Vosges 2026 Haut-Chocolat Advent calendar
This has got to be the most tricked-out edible Advent calendar on the market. Luxury chocolatier Vosges has made an Advent calendar that not only looks like a ski lodge and opens up to offer you a world of chocolate – it also plays an instrumental rendition of Deck the Halls, lights up and comes with its own USB-C charger. Inside the “Grand Cacao Lodge” you will find all sorts of unexpected confections, such as pumpkin seed brittle and chocolate dipped gingersnaps. On the final day, you get all the fixings for a cup of “haute” chocolate: drinking chocolate, plus two types of marshmallows.
Another European classic:
Ritter Sport Advent calendar
Here we have an Advent calendar from perhaps my second favorite grocery store chocolate brand, Ritter Sport. Hiding inside the Christmas tree-emblazoned box are a whimsical assortment of Ritter flavors, from the classic to the nouveau: dark chocolate marzipan, milk chocolate with crispies, milk chocolate caramel and milk chocolate pistachio. These squares are the perfect size for snacking, whether it’s post-dinner or during a mid-afternoon slump.
Justice for milk chocolate:
Lindt Teddy Advent calendar
Listen, I ride for dark chocolate and I always will, but this teddy bear-shaped Advent calendar from Lindt reminded me how right milk chocolate can taste, especially during the holidays. I loved this jaunty bear and all the many shapes of milk chocolate he held. Obviously there’s the classic Lindt truffle, as well as teddy-shaped milk chocolates, and mini milk chocolate balls (that come in pairs). If only they offered a sweater so I could match the bear …
Bon bons that are beautiful inside and out:
Cacao and Cardamom Advent calendar
As you might guess from its name, Cacao and Cardamom specializes in chocolate crafted with creative, bold flavors. This box comes shaped like a home – with a pair of women baking in the windows – and opens up, bureau-style, to reveal Technicolor boxes full of chocolate delights. Cacao and Cardamom is based in Houston, and I loved the Texas flavors imbued into these treats, particularly the Texas-shaped chocolate filled with a subtle barbecue-flavored caramel.
Classic cookie, crazy flavors:
Oreo Advent calendar
There’s something incredibly charming about an Oreo Advent calendar shaped … like an Oreo. (With smiling penguins in front of it!) Each day offers a new flavor of chocolate-dipped Oreo – not exactly the flavors you are used to finding at your local grocery store. My favorites were the caramel and pretzel, and peppermint. Give this to your sugar-deprived niece and don’t tell her parents.
 
***

https://taz.de/Umstrittener-Gast/!622985.title: Umstrittener Gast: Issa Remmo besucht Veranstaltung im Europaparlament
https://taz.de/Umstrittener-Gast/!622985.text:
Umstrittener Gast: Issa Remmo besucht Veranstaltung im Europaparlament
Als Issa Remmo bei der Wahlparty der Linken in Berlin auftauchte, löste das viel Wirbel aus. Nun war er im Parlament in Brüssel.
dpa | Ein führendes Mitglied der Berliner Großfamilie Remmo hat eine Veranstaltung im Europaparlament besucht. Im Anschluss an die Podiumsdiskussionen unter dem Motto „Demokratien im Kampf gegen den Islamismus: Aufrütteln, Widerstand leisten, wiederaufbauen“ sagte Issa Remmo der Jüdischen Allgemeinen unter anderem, Antisemitismus möge man „vernichten“, er solle nicht mehr existieren. Zugleich zeigte er sich enttäuscht von der Linken.
Die Veranstaltung am Donnerstag war unter anderem von dem bekannten französischen Imam Hassen Chalghoumi ins Leben gerufen worden. Eingeladen hatte auch die französische Abgeordnete Céline Imart aus der konservativen EVP-Fraktion, zu der auch CDU und CSU gehören. Einen Teil der arabischstämmigen Remmo-Großfamilie ordnet die Polizei dem kriminellen Clanmilieu zu.
EU-Linksfraktionschef Martin Schirdewan sagte dem Spiegel zu Remmos Teilnahme: „Das ist schon ein starkes Stück!“ Er halte den Vorgang für „zutiefst verstörend“ und fordere Aufklärung von EVP-Fraktionschef Manfred Weber. Schon den Verdacht, „dass das Umfeld der Organisierten Kriminalität Zugang zu einem Parlament bekommt“, halte er für „zutiefst problematisch“, sagte der Linken-Politiker.
Berliner Linke wegen Remmos unter Druck
Remmo hatte im September nach der Wahl zum Abgeordnetenhaus in Berlin eine Wahlparty der Linken in Neukölln besucht und damit großen Wirbel ausgelöst. Der Linken-Abgeordnete Ferat Koçak geriet zudem unter Druck, weil er freundschaftliche Chatnachrichten mit einem Sohn von Remmo ausgetauscht hatte. Koçak selbst hatte das als Fehler bezeichnet und um Entschuldigung gebeten. Schließlich zog er sich aus der Öffentlichkeit zurück und gab seinen Sitz im Innenausschuss des Bundestages ab.
Als Reaktion auf die Ereignisse schlossen Linke, Grüne und SPD eine Vereinbarung: Kontakte zur organisierten Kriminalität seien strikt zu meiden und bei Verstößen zu ahnden. Der Begriff Clankriminalität ist umstritten, weil er nach Ansicht von Kritikern Menschen mit Migrationshintergrund allein aufgrund ihrer Familienzugehörigkeit und Herkunft stigmatisiert und diskriminiert.
Issa Remmo: Eigene Partei gegründet
Der Jüdischen Allgemeinen sagte Issa Remmo nun, er sei „sehr enttäuscht“ von der Linken. Er habe eine eigene politische Partei namens „Der Weg zum Licht“ gegründet, die die Brüderlichkeit zwischen den Menschen fördern solle, so Remmo.
Im Europaparlament in Brüssel finden immer wieder Veranstaltungen statt, zu der einzelne Abgeordnete und Organisationen einladen.
Die beteiligte Abgeordnete Imart sagte der Bild-Zeitung, sie und Imam Chalghoumi hätten erst im Nachhinein von den Vorwürfen gegen einen Teilnehmer erfahren. Sie entschuldige sich „bei allen, die sich durch die Anwesenheit dieser Person verletzt gefühlt haben könnten“. Bild berichtete weiter, die Teilnehmerliste sei aufgrund der Sicherheitsanforderungen vorab der Polizei übermittelt worden.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Seleção Argentina de Futebol perde oportunidade de fazer ‘racism washing’ com Kiki Ramos ao abandoná-lo no último momento
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Jackson Jean
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Dias antes do dia 8 de novembro, data em que a Argentina comemora o Dia Nacional dos Afro-argentinos e da Cultura Afro, uma decisão da Associação do Futebol Argentino (AFA) voltou a colocar em pauta uma pergunta incômoda: quem é reconhecido como parte da identidade futebolística do país e em que condições?
A data foi instituída pela Lei 26.852, sancionada em 2013, em homenagem a María Remedios del Valle, capitã afrodescendente do Exército do Norte e figura importante das lutas pela independência. Todos os anos, essa é uma oportunidade para rever o lugar ocupado pelas pessoas afrodescendentes na história nacional e na Argentina contemporânea.
Nesse contexto, a trajetória de Stephen Oscar “Kiki” Ramos merece atenção. Ele nasceu em Porto Príncipe, no Haiti, em 2009; cresceu na Argentina e se formou futebolisticamente no Vélez Sarsfield. Diego Placente o convocou para a seleção argentina Sub-17 neste ano. Kiki estreou internacionalmente contra o Equador e marcou um gol. Em agosto, ainda integrava o grupo de preparação. No entanto, deixou de aparecer nas convocações seguintes e não fez parte da delegação que disputou a Vertex Cup, em outubro.
A AFA não apresentou publicamente uma explicação técnica que permita conhecer os motivos dessa descontinuidade. A decisão chama a atenção quando se considera o desempenho que o atacante vinha mostrando no Vélez: não era um jogador alheio ao processo de seleção, mas alguém que já havia vestido a camisa argentina, marcado um gol e mantido uma produção expressiva de gols em sua categoria.
Em novembro, a Federação Haitiana de Futebol (FHF) anunciou a incorporação de Kiki à seleção haitiana Sub-17, que se preparava no Brasil para disputar a Copa do Mundo no Catar. A escolha de representar o Haiti partiu do próprio jogador. A federação o recebeu oficialmente na família dos Grenadiers e agradeceu a colaboração de seu representante e do Vélez Sarsfield.
O anúncio chegou poucos dias antes de 18 de novembro, data em que o Haiti comemora a Batalha de Vertières, de 1803. Naquele episódio, as forças revolucionárias haitianas derrotaram o exército expedicionário francês, em um dos momentos decisivos do processo que culminou com a independência, proclamada em janeiro de 1804. O dia 18 de novembro também é o Dia das Forças Armadas do Haiti.
Entre 8 e 18 de novembro se cruzam, assim, duas memórias afrodescendentes: a de uma Argentina que, ainda que tardiamente, reconhece oficialmente sua herança africana e a do Haiti, que comemora uma vitória decisiva da revolução antirracista. Nesse intervalo, Kiki passou de ser excluído das últimas convocações argentinas a ser recebido pela seleção do país onde nasceu.
Essa história tem uma dimensão que ultrapassa o resultado de uma decisão esportiva. A Argentina perdeu a possibilidade de manter em seu projeto um jovem jogador com raízes africanas, nascido no Haiti, criado no país e formado em um de seus clubes. Também perdeu a oportunidade de mostrar, por meio de ações e não apenas de discursos, que a identidade nacional pode reconhecer a diversidade das trajetórias que a compõem.
Um desempenho que merecia continuidade
As realizações de Kiki não desmerecem. Em 15 de setembro de 2026, o Vélez Sarsfield informou que Ramos havia marcado 17 gols em 23 partidas pela Sexta Divisão e era o artilheiro de sua equipe. Também registrava 30 gols em 68 partidas desde a Nona Divisão. Mais tarde, a revista El Gráfico publicou um balanço atualizado de 20 gols em 29 jogos.
As estatísticas das categorias de base, por si só, não permitem afirmar que um jogador seja superior a todos os seus concorrentes. Juan Cruz Policella, Facundo Salinas, Tobías Goytía e Alan Alcaraz também tiveram atuações internacionais de destaque. Mas os números de Ramos justificavam, no mínimo, uma explicação sobre os critérios esportivos que levaram a deixar de convocá-lo.
Não houve declaração pública de Placente sobre essa decisão. Não cabe lhe atribuir uma decisão que não foi justificada. A falta de informação, porém, tampouco deveria encerrar o debate: quando uma decisão afeta um jogador afrodescendente em um contexto marcado por controvérsias raciais, exigir transparência é legítimo.
O racismo que a Argentina ainda não terminou de discutir
A controvérsia em torno de Kiki havia começado antes de sua saída do processo argentino. Quando sua convocação provocou comentários racistas nas redes sociais, Placente declarou que o jogador estava na seleção porque jogava bem, e não porque era negro. Também afirmou que, em sua avaliação, o racismo na Argentina era principalmente uma questão cultural e defendeu o uso de apelidos como “Negro”, comparando-os a designações como “Polaco” ou “Ruso”.
É possível que o treinador quisesse defender o jogador. Mas reduzir o racismo a uma questão cultural ou a uma forma de familiaridade deixa sem resposta uma parte importante do problema. O racismo não aparece apenas nos insultos explícitos; também se expressa na invisibilização histórica, nas representações sociais e nas hierarquias que determinam quem é considerado parte legítima de uma comunidade.
A historiadora Lea Geler pesquisou a persistência do racismo estrutural na Argentina, especialmente em Buenos Aires, e a relação entre afrodescendência, direitos e igualdade. Por sua vez, o relatório do Centro de Estudos Legais e Sociais (CELS), apresentado ao Comitê das Nações Unidas para a Eliminação da Discriminação Racial, documentou padrões de invisibilização e desigualdade racial na Argentina. Ou seja, essa discussão não nasceu nas redes sociais e não pode ser descartada como uma questão de sensibilidade individual.
Kiki declarou que nunca se sentiu discriminado na Argentina e que se sentia parte do país. Seu testemunho merece respeito. Também merece ser ouvido sem que seja transformado em uma resposta geral sobre as experiências de toda a população afrodescendente. O fato de um jovem ter se sentido acolhido não significa que tenham desaparecido as desigualdades vividas por outras pessoas. Kiki podia se sentir argentino, gostar do país onde cresceu e desejar vestir sua camisa. Reconhecer isso não exige deixar de examinar as estruturas raciais dessa mesma sociedade.
Uma decepção que também foi sentida no Haiti
Para muitos haitianos, a Argentina não é apenas mais um país no mapa do futebol sul-americano. Sua seleção ocupa um lugar especial entre aqueles que acompanham o futebol argentino, admiram seus jogadores e reconhecem sua tradição em Copas do Mundo. Por isso, a possibilidade de ver um jovem nascido em Porto Príncipe vestindo a camisa da AFA tinha um significado particular. Para uma parte da torcida haitiana, essa imagem teria sido motivo de orgulho e uma forma de se reconhecer em uma das seleções mais admiradas do planeta.
A expectativa deu lugar à decepção quando Kiki deixou de integrar as convocações argentinas e teve de se incorporar à seleção haitiana para a Copa do Mundo. O episódio reabriu questionamentos enquanto as controvérsias sobre o racismo na Argentina já fazem parte da conversa pública no Haiti.
Não cabe atribuir uma opinião uniforme a todo um povo: a sociedade haitiana é plural e seus torcedores têm visões diferentes. Mas tampouco seria sério ignorar que a representação racial e as experiências de discriminação influenciam a maneira como muitos haitianos observam seus vínculos com outros países.
Nesse contexto, as boas-vindas da Federação Haitiana de Futebol tiveram um significado que foi além do anúncio de uma convocação. Sua mensagem foi direta: “Kiki, você está em casa!”.
A oportunidade perdida do ‘racism washing’
Aqui está a ironia política dessa história. A Argentina teve a possibilidade de mostrar que seu futebol reconhece e celebra a presença afrodescendente que faz parte de sua história. Não era necessária uma campanha institucional nem um discurso diplomático. Bastava manter um critério esportivo consistente: convocar com base no desempenho e dar continuidade quando as condições futebolísticas justificassem.
A expressão “racism washing” nomeia o uso de uma inclusão visível como recurso para projetar uma imagem de diversidade e abertura, sem que necessariamente mudem as práticas que produzem desigualdade. A presença de Kiki na seleção poderia ter se tornado uma imagem internacional poderosa: um jovem afrodescendente nascido no Haiti, criado na Argentina e reconhecido por seu talento com a camisa nacional. Mas essa possibilidade se dissipou quando ele deixou de ser convocado.
No plano político, o contraste merece atenção. O presidente Javier Milei busca projetar a Argentina como referência de uma corrente internacional da nova direita. Suas intervenções em fóruns como Davos geraram controvérsias por suas posições sobre imigração, diversidade e políticas identitárias. Em seu discurso de 23 de janeiro de 2025, questionou a imigração em massa e criticou as políticas de diversidade e reconhecimento.
O futebol tem um peso singular na representação nacional. Uma camisa pode funcionar como ferramenta de diplomacia cultural e como sinal de pertencimento. Por isso, a Argentina perdeu a oportunidade de mostrar que sua identidade não se esgota em uma narrativa homogênea e que é capaz de reconhecer as diferentes raízes de quem a integra.
Poderia ter feito um “racism washing” exemplar. Mas a inclusão não deveria servir para limpar uma reputação: exige rever as práticas e os critérios que sustentam a exclusão.
O Haiti não é um plano B
A incorporação de Kiki à seleção haitiana não deve ser interpretada como um fracasso pessoal nem como uma derrota esportiva. O Haiti o recebeu quando surgiu uma oportunidade concreta de disputar uma Copa do Mundo. A federação reconheceu sua trajetória e abriu espaço para que representasse o país onde nasceu.
O Haiti não é uma alternativa de emergência nem uma camisa de consolação. É uma nação com uma história decisiva de emancipação e resistência anticolonial. Foi a primeira república negra independente do mundo e surgiu da única revolução de pessoas escravizadas que conseguiu fundar um Estado independente.
Sua história não começa nem termina em suas dificuldades econômicas, políticas ou humanitárias. Também compreende vitórias, produção cultural, criatividade e resistência. Hoje, o futebol oferece outro palco para que o país se faça presente diante do mundo.
A trajetória de Kiki reúne uma experiência pessoal transnacional e duas formas de pertencimento que não se excluem. Um jovem que cresceu na Argentina pode valorizar o que esse país lhe proporcionou e, ao mesmo tempo, reencontrar a terra de suas raízes. Não há contradição nisso.
Senhor Kiki Ramos, a Argentina ainda tem uma oportunidade
Não é tarde para que Kiki volte a jogar pela seleção argentina. Sua participação na Copa do Mundo Sub-17 pelo Haiti não significa, por si só, que tenha que ficar definitivamente vinculado à FHF por toda a carreira. O regulamento da Fifa prevê condições específicas para mudanças de país em categorias juvenis. Qualquer cenário futuro dependerá dessas regras e da decisão do próprio jogador.
Também serão necessários vontade esportiva e respeito por sua escolha. A Argentina poderia reconhecer que deixou escapar uma oportunidade e voltar a avaliar um jogador cujo talento já havia considerado suficiente para convocá-lo, fazê-lo estrear e lhe dar minutos com a Albiceleste.
Enquanto a Argentina pensa na oportunidade que deixou escapar, o Haiti se prepara para uma nova experiência em uma Copa do Mundo. Kiki levará consigo a história do país que o formou e a da terra que o recebeu de volta. O Haiti não é apenas a primeira república negra independente: também é uma nação que disputa a Copa do Mundo, com uma história de luta, dignidade e futebol.
De volta à terra natal. Desta vez, com a camisa dos Grenadiers.
*Jackson Jean é um jornalista haitiano.
**Este é um artigo de opinião e não necessariamente representa a linha editorial do Brasil de Fato.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Portugal vs Denmark: UEFA Nations League – predictions, how to watch, teams
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Portugal vs Denmark: UEFA Nations League – predictions, how to watch, teams
Playing their first game since Cristiano Ronaldo announced his retirement, two-time champions Portugal face Denmark at home.
Who: Portugal vs Denmark
What: UEFA Nations League, Group A4
Where: Braga Municipal Stadium, Braga, Portugal
When: Saturday, November 14, at 7:45pm (19:45 GMT).
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 16:45 GMT before our live text commentary stream
A new chapter in Portuguese football starts on Saturday, as the national team moves on from the departure of their record scorer and longstanding captain, Cristiano Ronaldo.
Ronaldo ended his 23-year association with the Selecao last week, announcing his retirement in a lengthy video on social media, weeks after a public rift with Portugal coach Jorge Jesus.
The 41-year-old, a polarising football icon who wore the much-adored No 7 shirt for his country, said it was now time to “pass it on to the future”.
Playing their first game without their biggest star, Portugal face Denmark in Saturday’s home fixture, having already confirmed their spot in the quarterfinals.
With three goals each, forwards Goncalo Ramos and Joao Felix have orchestrated Portugal’s attacking play in Ronaldo’s absence, while Denmark’s charge has been led by Rasmus Hojlund, who has netted three of his team’s seven goals so far.
Two-time holders Portugal will be confirmed as group winners if they avoid defeat against Denmark, who are second in the standings.
The Danes have a bit more complicated path to secure their spot in the last eight on Saturday – they need to win against Portugal and hope that neighbours Norway do not beat third-placed Wales in a clash of the bottom two.
How have Portugal played in the Nations League?
Portugal have a perfect record in the competition, with four wins out of four.
They began their title defence with a 1-0 home win over Wales before beating Norway 2-1, a game in which Ronaldo was an unused substitute.
Shortly afterwards, Ronaldo stormed out of the national camp, but his absence did not trouble the team as they thrashed Denmark 4-2 in another away game before winning 2-1 at home against Norway to reach the quarterfinals.
How have Denmark played in the Nations League?
Denmark have won two games and lost two.
Their campaign started with a 3-2 loss in Norway, but they bounced back with a 2-0 home victory against Wales.
The third match saw them fall 4-2 at home to Portugal before they beat Wales 1-0 away.
What happened when Portugal and Denmark last met?
Goals from Joao Cancelo, Goncalo Ramos, Vitinha and Felix gave Portugal a 4-2 win over Denmark on October 1.
Mikkel Damsgaard and Rasmus Hojlund scored for the hosts in that game at Copenhagen.
Portugal vs Denmark: Predictions
Opta’s supercomputer has given Portugal a 59.4 percent probability of victory, while Denmark’s odds stand at 19.4 percent.
There is a 21.2 percent chance the game ends in a draw.
Head-to-head
- Matches: 19
- Portugal wins: 13
- Denmark wins: 4
- Draws: 2
Form guide
(Last five matches, latest game first)
Portugal: W-W-W-W-L
Denmark: W-L-W-L-D
Team news and predicted lineups
Portugal
Cancelo and Francisco Conceicao are suspended, while Rafael Leao, Nuno Mendes and Nuno Tavares are out with injuries.
Probable Portugal XI: Diogo Costa; Diogo Dalot, Ruben Dias, Renato Veiga, Flavio Nazinho; Ruben Neves, Vitinha, Bruno Fernandes; Joao Felix, Goncalo Ramos
Denmark
Denmark will be without Patrick Dorgu, and they will have to be cautious with six players one booking away from suspension.
Probable Denmark XI: Mads Hermansen; Rasmus Kristensen, Joachim Andersen, Oliver Provstgaard, Joakim Maehle; Morten Hjulmand, Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg; Gustav Isaksen, Mikkel Damsgaard, Mohamed Daramy; Rasmus Hojlund

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: A Mumford & Sons member is opening a new venue in Williamsburg's Domino Sugar Factory
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Sonia Rao
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
Williamsburg was Ben Lovett’s gateway to New York. The British multi-instrumentalist, known for cofounding the folk-rock band Mumford & Sons, fell for the city immediately upon playing his first show here at an art gallery on North 6th Street.
It was 2008, and the indie music scene was thriving. He moved to the city a couple years later and began frequenting the edgy music venues scattered throughout the neighborhood.
“I have some great memories of crowd-surfing to Twin Peaks at a Glasslands show,” he told Gothamist.
Glasslands closed in 2015. A considerable number of Williamsburg dance clubs and concert venues followed. While Lovett still finds much to admire in places like Baby’s All Right, he said the continued closures strengthened his desire to “protect” the music scene.
“These spaces are essential to our humanity,” he said. “I don’t think people would want to live in New York if all you did was live here and work here. What you do with your third amount of time, your third space … is really important to consider.”
And so, Lovett said, he decided to do something about it: He’s opening an all-ages venue on the Williamsburg waterfront called Domino. Set to open in April 2027, the 750-capacity space will occupy the ground floor of the historic Domino Sugar Refinery building. Visitors will enter on River Street and walk through its preserved structures, such as a 240-foot-tall chimney, to attend concerts, comedy shows, film screenings and other planned events.
Domino was already in the works when Lovett learned that another beloved venue, Music Hall of Williamsburg, would be closing its doors at the end of 2026. The musician, who is developing his new space through his company tvg Hospitality, said he hopes for it to help foster the city’s creative community. He said Domino is the eighth venue that he has either built or operated. He is partnering on it with Emerson Hospitality, which opened the West Village steakhouse Graciela over the summer.
“In the hospitality and entertainment industry, you’re providing a centerpiece for people’s lives,” Lovett said. Music venues like Domino are “where they’re going to go to form a new friendship or fall in love or hear a lyric that suddenly unlocks a feeling. I’m all about protecting these spaces as best as we can and not allowing them to become the next, like, Gucci store.”
Major developers have flocked to the Williamsburg waterfront over the years, sparking accusations of gentrification and public debates over who gets to use the space and how. Two Trees, the management company that owns the Refinery building, landed a state tax break on a different waterfront housing complex earlier this year.
Lovett said he believed Domino would be the final tenant in the Refinery building, which otherwise houses office space, a glass-domed penthouse for events and an Equinox fitness club. He wants his venue to be an accessible space amid Williamsburg’s ever-evolving landscape.
“We need to make sure that we’re not losing the cultural side of Williamsburg,” Lovett said. “So we’re going to work really hard to put a stake in the ground at Domino and make sure that people know Williamsburg is culturally as relevant … and important to the city as ever.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/uk-labour-is.title: Andy Burnham’s Criticism of Israel Is All Bark and No Bite
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/uk-labour-is.author: Jamie Maxwell
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/uk-labour-is.text:
Andy Burnham’s Criticism of Israel Is All Bark and No Bite
Andy Burnham and his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, have adopted a more critical tone toward Israel in a bid to win back progressive voters to the Labour Party. But the fundamentals of Britain’s close alliance with Israel remain largely unchanged.
In September, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced that his government was going to impose sanctions on British trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Miliband also referred to “ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists.”
The Israeli authorities responded by downgrading the 180-year old British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem — it is now merely a “mission” — and expelling twenty British diplomats, including the consul general.
Miliband’s announcement came two months after Andy Burnham replaced Keir Starmer as Labour Party leader and prime minister. He billed it as part of a “comprehensive reset” of Britain’s approach toward Israel: Britain would no longer “acquiesce in the destruction of the two-state solution,” Miliband pledged.
In reality, there has been no such reset: the fundamentals of Britain’s relationship with Israel remain largely unchanged.
Extraordinary Lengths
Naturally, Miliband’s move provoked a roar of condemnation from Israeli political elites. Israel’s president Isaac Herzog, who has been credibly accused by multiple organizations of aiding and abetting war crimes in the Gaza Strip, said that he was “disturbed” by the new sanctions. The Israeli foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar accused Miliband of “outrageous lies.”
Israel’s British supporters were also indignant. Britain’s Chief Rabbi Ephraim Mirvis denounced Miliband’s program, claiming that it was “a dark day for Britain’s Jews,” and that Miliband was seeking to appease “those who harbour a dangerous obsession with the Jewish state.”
This is not the first time Mirvis, an indefatigable defender of Israel, has attacked the Labour government. In September 2024, he denounced a move by Miliband’s predecessor as foreign secretary, David Lammy, to limit the supply of British arms for the Israeli military: “This announcement feeds the falsehood that Israel is in breach of International Humanitarian Law, when in fact it is going to extraordinary lengths to uphold it.”
On that occasion, events proved that Mirvis had little reason to be concerned. The following year, British arms sales to Israel soared to reach the highest level on record. If we look more closely at the details of Miliband’s announcement, a similar picture of tough talk combined with very limited actions reveals itself.
Red Line, Green Line
The sanctions focus on the banning of imports into the UK of goods produced in “illegal” Israeli settlements, an expansion of UK licensing refusals for arms exports to Israel, and the nonspecified “strengthening” of penalties against settlers who “support or incite acts of violence against Palestinian communities.”
If we assume that all of these sanctions are actually implemented — Miliband opted for a grace period of up to nine months before the changes take effect — their impact on Israel’s economy would still be very limited. An Al Jazeera investigation found that, since Miliband’s announcement, his government has awarded more than $14 million in public sector contracts to firms that profit from West Bank settlements.
Miliband coordinated his sanctions package with eleven other Western countries, including Canada, Ireland, France, and Denmark, ten of which have recognized a Palestinian state. In theory, if those countries applied the sanctions in a maximal way, they could hit the sprawling and internationally connected network of Israeli finance, fin tech, and construction firms that facilitate the spread of Jewish settlements in the West Bank.
But that seems unlikely. In his Commons statement, Miliband made clear that his quarrel was with the settler movement and its sponsors in Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, not with Israel itself. “We will continue to support valued trade with green line Israel precisely because we support the two state solution,” he said. “For this reason, I wholeheartedly oppose the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions campaign.”
This argument draws a convenient distinction between “illegal” Israeli settlements outside the 1967 borders and Israel proper. (In fact, in line with Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention, which prohibits the transfer of civilian populations into occupied territories, all Israeli settlements are illegal under international law). By doing so, Miliband has carefully shielded the infrastructure of British support for Israel from the damage that a broader and more robust UK economic boycott could inflict.
A Lucrative Relationship
That infrastructure is substantial, because the UK is Israel’s largest European trading partner. Israeli companies supply billions of pounds worth of medicines to the National Health Service every year. Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest defense electronics manufacturer, operates multiple factories throughout the UK, while its subsidiaries export engine components to the Israel Defense Forces.
Israel’s state-owned defense giant, Rafael, owns and operates factories in Newcastle and Hampshire. Through Lockheed Martin and BAE Systems, the UK defense sector manufactures approximately 15 percent of the machinery present in every operational F-35 fighter jet, the aircraft of choice for the Israeli military as it has laid waste to Gaza. None of these economic linkages will be negatively impacted by the sanctions.
Israel even maintains investments in the North Sea through Ithaca Energy, which is owned by the Delek Group, a multibillion-dollar Israeli energy conglomerate. Ironically, it may benefit from those investments in the future if the Burnham administration gives the go-ahead for exploitation in the Rosebank oil field, a highly controversial, potentially climate-wrecking development west of Shetland. Ithaca owns a 20 percent stake in Rosebank; a decision on the field’s future is due imminently.
There is also a strong case that the UK has colluded directly on an institutional level in Israel’s campaign of slaughter in the Gaza Strip. As the investigative journalism organization Declassified has exhaustively archived, between December 2023 and March 2025, the Royal Air Force flew a minimum of 518 intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance flights over the Palestinian Occupied Territories, including Gaza.
Successive UK governments have insisted that these flights were part of a broader effort at “hostage location.” However, given Britain’s long history of intelligence cooperation with Israel, there is good reason to suspect that the Israeli military could also have used the information gathered during these sorties for other purposes. Miliband has made clear that British-Israeli intelligence sharing will go on despite the sanctions. “I’m confident that our security co-operation with Israel will continue,” he told the BBC in September. “We have important intelligence and security relationships with Israel.”
Burnham’s Pivot
Miliband’s discretely designed sanctions system performs a domestic political function as well as an external strategic one. By publicly picking a fight with Netanyahu ahead of the Israeli elections, and by criticizing his annexationist policies, Labour sent a signal to left-wing voters who had turned away from the party during the Starmer period, when UK criticism of Israel was, to say the least, less forthcoming.
Starmer was a latecomer to Westminster life who appeared to be largely devoid of the ruthless intelligence needed to succeed in the Westminster snake pit. He thought he could build a lasting coalition in the crumbling center ground of British politics. When it became clear that he couldn’t, Burnham stepped in with a plan to reinvigorate Labour by convening a progressive bloc of voters in opposition to the reactionary one rapidly coalescing around Nigel Farage and Reform UK.
In order to do this, Burnham needed to win over the young, left-wing, and vigorously pro-Palestinian parts of the UK electorate that had peeled off in recent years toward Zack Polanski’s “ecopopulist” Green Party. Hence the Labour government’s new and heightened anti-settler rhetoric and its willingness to characterize Israel’s actions against the Palestinians as “war crimes.”
Yet the superficiality of the rhetoric grates against the reality of Labour’s inertia in other areas. In 2025, Starmer’s government imposed a draconian ban on Palestine Action, a campaign group that targeted Israeli defense firms on British soil with acts of civil disobedience and vandalism. It is now legally defined as a terrorist organization, on a par with al-Qaeda and the Irish Republican Army. Since then, the British authorities have arrested more than 3,500 people and formally charged more than 2,250 for peacefully protesting against the ban.
Burnham has not committed to repealing the ban, which the UN Human Rights Commissioner Volker Türk has described as a “disturbing misuse of counter-terrorism legislation.” Last month, his Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood strongly defended the arrest of Palestine Action supporters, comparing them to “a group of skinheads standing outside a mosque.”
“Systematic Duplicity”
In fact, there are growing signs that Burnham may extend authoritarian restrictions on the expression of support for Palestine in British public life. This would include a prohibition on the display of pro-Palestinian symbols by teachers in schools. His government is also urging schools and colleges to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism, which conflates criticism of Israel with antipathy toward Jewish people.
In contrast to Miliband, who is Jewish and thought to be genuinely sympathetic to the Palestinian cause, Burnham is by instinct a classic Labour Atlanticist who views Britain’s relationship with Israel as a core component of the UK’s strategic loyalty to the United States.
As a junior minister in the Tony Blair government, Burnham was a supporter of Blair’s Iraq adventure who later voted against parliamentary inquiries into the war (though he has since recanted on both fronts). He has also been a member of Labour Friends of Israel since 2015: during his first pitch for the party leadership that year, he dismissed the campaign to boycott Israel as “spiteful.”
None of this will be sufficient to quell Israel’s anger in the face of a remarkably modest set of British sanctions, nor to persuade a skeptical and exhausted Palestinian public that the UK has suddenly become an ally. But British double-dealing on the issue is hardly new.
In his 1993 book Culture and Imperialism, Edward Said reflected on Britain’s pattern of double-talk in the early twentieth century, promising independence to the Arab inhabitants of Mandatory Palestine while simultaneously committing itself to the creation of an autonomous Jewish homeland in the region.
“The history of British imperial policy in the Middle East is a history of systematic duplicity,” Said wrote. “Making promises to all sides that could never be kept.” Time, as they say, is a flat circle — nowhere is this maxim more true than when it comes to the British role in Palestine.

Image of the week
We found Tate Britain’s new exhibition, Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury, an “epic yet flaccid roam through the complicated lives and desperately mediocre paintings” of the co-habiting modernists. Read the full review
What we learned
The brilliantly bolshie artist Ryan Gander lambasted practically everyone
Jill Posener’s cheeky, feminist photography served as a rebuttal to 80s misogyny
Epstein survivors were overwhelmed by messages of support at pop-up art exhibition
The Vatican houses a collection of Indigenous treasures questionably ‘gifted’ to it
Masterpiece of the week
Head of Christ Crucified by the Master of Liesborn (Johann von Soest?), probably early 1480s-1490
The blood streams over Christ’s deathly white face in a vivid, almost Hammer horror contrast between gore and pallor. It flows in thick rivulets from the crown of thorns that has been mockingly forced on to his head. The initials INRI on a piece of paper fixed to the cross stand for “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” in Latin, and the cruel crown rams home the barb. Christ bears the laughter and the physical pain with patience and dignity, lowering his eyes in sorrow as he waits for his earthly body to die. The stark, simple shock of this image comes from an age in which Europeans were encouraged to identify with Christ, to imagine themselves suffering alongside him. At the same time this artist’s explicit focus on flowing blood may serve a theological function: the central moment of the medieval Mass was the miraculous transformation of bread and wine into the actual body and blood of Christ. According to the philosopher Thomas Aquinas this took place literally: the bread and wine kept their “accidental” appearance while changing their “essential” nature. This painting is part of an altarpiece from Germany, but not all Germans were convinced by such ideas. In the early 1500s Martin Luther would rebel against the miracle of transubstantiation, and against art like this which he regarded as idolatry.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Tate’s Bloomsbury group exhibition throws fresh light on early British enthusiasm for Van Gogh
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Martin Bailey
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Tate Britain’s exhibition Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury, which opened yesterday (12 November), emphasises how early 20th-century British artists were inspired by Van Gogh.
Vanessa Bell (1879-1961) and Duncan Grant (1885-1978) lived together for more than 50 years in a very Bloomsbury fashion, each having other lovers. The Bloomsbury group, named after the London quarter where they lived in the early 20th century, began as an informal collective of progressive artists, writers and intellectuals.
As the Tate show’s curator, Thomas Kennedy, points out: “When Bell and Grant were doing new and exciting things, individuals like Van Gogh—who were creating something wildly different from other artists of the time—were very much an inspiration for them.”
Bell and Grant were both also very close to the art critic Roger Fry, who in 1910 curated the pathbreaking London exhibition Manet and the Post-Impressionists, inventing the term Post-Impressionism. This show introduced Van Gogh to a British audience.
As so often with the Bloomsbury group, sexual relationships were complex and intertwined. In 1907 Vanessa had married the art critic Clive Bell, but it was always an open marriage. Two years later she started a relationship with Duncan Grant, producing a daughter, and they then continued to live together.
Duncan Grant, however, was homosexual, having numerous lovers, including a male cousin and Vanessa’s brother. To add to the complications, Vanessa later had a brief relationship with Roger Fry. The quip about the group was that they were “living in squares [in Bloomsbury], painting in circles and loving in triangles”.
The Bloomsbury relationships may seem bewildering to outsiders, but the key point to bear in mind with the current Tate exhibition is that Bell and Grant shared a home for over 50 years. Initially they lived in London, and, from 1916, partly at Charleston farmhouse in rural Sussex.
It proved to be an enduring artistic partnership. They influenced each other, and they, in turn, were influenced by modern European artists, such as Van Gogh, along with Paul Gauguin, Paul Cezanne, Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso.
Grant, who studied art in Paris in 1906, may have then come across the work of Van Gogh. What is more certain is that Bell discovered Van Gogh in 1909, in a group exhibition at London’s New Gallery, which included a single painting by the Dutchman. She once described it as “a lovely little Van Gogh of flowers in a jug”.
The still life had been lent by Thomas Fisher Unwin, a London publisher who, with his wife Jane, had in 1896 been the first Briton to buy a Van Gogh after the artist’s death. This was a flower still life, probably one with a black background which has always been in private collections.
Post-Impressionism and Provence
But what was most influential for Bell and Grant was Fry's first Post-Impressionist exhibition in 1910. Including around 30 works by Van Gogh, it was the first chance for Londoners to see more than an odd painting by the artist.
This was a heady time for the Bloomsbury group. Bell later recalled: ”That autumn of 1910 is to me a time when everything seemed springing to a new life - a time when all was a sizzle of excitement, new relationships, new ideas, different and intense emotions all seemed crowding into one’s life.”
In 1912 both Bell and Grant had paintings in Fry’s second Post-Impressionist exhibition. They also co-designed the catalogue with Fry, and Bell helped hang the show. This time there was only a single Van Gogh, but it was again the Fisher Unwin flower still life, which Bell had known from four years earlier.
Bell, Grant and Fry all loved the south of France, where Van Gogh had also worked, and they visited regularly from the 1920s. Fry helped a friend buy a farmhouse in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, just a few hundred metres from the asylum where Van Gogh had stayed in 1889-90. On one occasion Grant visited Bell, who had bought a house just outside Cassis, on the Mediterranean coast. Grant described the surrounding landscape as “far more extraordinary than St Remi [sic]”. Both artists were well aware of Van Gogh's connection with Provence.
How then did Van Gogh’s art inspire Bell and Grant? They never set out to simply imitate his style, but were nevertheless powerfully influenced by his work and that of the other Post-Impressionists. The two British artists began to paint with heightened colours, simplified forms and strong lines.
The links can also be seen in individual pictures. Bell’s View into a Garden (1926, Bolton Library & Museum Services) includes two empty chairs, which were probably a reflection of Van Gogh’s pair of paintings of his own chair and the armchair of Gauguin (the picture of his own chair had been bought by London’s National Gallery three years earlier, so would have been well known to Bell).
In 1911, the critic Frank Rutter described Bell’s Chrysanthemums (1920, Tate, although not in the current exhibition) as “undoubtedly influenced by Van Gogh”. Its dark background echoes the Van Gogh still life which Bell had seen some years earlier.
Decades later, in 1946, Grant wrote to Bell about visiting a Van Gogh exhibition in Copenhagen, “a splendid show”. He added: “I really feel that artists should resist to the death having their works reproduced in colour. It really has been the death of Van Gogh. It’s only when one sees the originals that one realises what a very lovely & personal colour sense he had… I really do not believe in his madness as an artist at all.” Van Gogh remained in the minds of the couple for the rest of their lives.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Holding Trump Accountable Is Not Optional for Democrats
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Sasha Abramsky
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Holding Trump Accountable Is Not Optional for Democrats
Yes, the party must focus on the economy. But that is inextricably linked to a focus on corruption.
Heading to the airport Tuesday morning, I lucked out on my Lyft driver. He was a middle-aged African American man, listening to the news coverage of the impeachment proceedings against Pete Hegseth. He was horrified that a man like Hegseth—someone willing to embrace clearly illegal orders to, for example, turn the military against civilians, and eager to deny people promotion based on the color of their skin and/or gender—had so much power; and he was salivating at the prospect of the self-proclaimed “Secretary of War,” whom he denounced in fiery language as a dyed-in-the-wool racist, finally being held to account. To restore America’s global reputation, he insisted, there had to be accountability. And that accountability should begin, but not end, with Hegseth’s impeachment.
I asked if he thought that the incoming Democratic majority should focus on investigations and impeachments, or on legislation intended to provide an economic boost to struggling Americans? “Do both!” my driver exclaimed. “You can chew gum and walk down the staircase at the same time.”
Amen to that.
Polls showed that two issues were dominating voters’ minds in the midterm elections. The first, more “normal” concern, was bread-and-butter economics: inflation, high interest rates, job insecurity, the destabilizing impact of AI, the difficulty in finding affordable housing, the increasing cost of healthcare. But the second was different: corruption and its degrading effect on our democracy, as well as the damage done to government institutions by the incompetent and cruel leadership of men such as Hegseth.
After 10 years of the Trump cult, America’s voters, in overwhelming numbers, finally saw through the con. They intuited, at long last, that their government was being shamelessly tapped for private profit, and that a man elected as the ultimate outsider was, in fact, consolidating a new elite strata, in large part propped up by unqualified hires such as Hegseth, infinitely more venal and brutal than the “establishment” they had replaced.
These two issues, of course, are intertwined. In the sort of sultanistic kleptocracy that Trump is running—backed up by mediocre loyal foot soldiers, such as Hegseth, who owe their status solely to their undying fealty to Trump and Trumpism—the suffering of ordinary Americans as a result of, say, high tariff-induced and war-induced inflation, represents a glittering set of opportunities for grifters to move in and capitalize on the crisis, for influence-peddlers to sell their wares, for backroom deals that exempt companies from tariffs in exchange for lining the pockets of Trump and his princelings. Addressing one without the other will never lead to the sort of cleansing moment that America so desperately needs—and is demanding—in order to truly enter the post-Trump era.
Come January, of course, Democrats should focus on rolling out a new social compact. They need to offer voters an expanded social safety net—a new Fair Deal—paid for by appropriately taxing America’s emergent oligarchy and its ill-gotten gains. Make Elon Musk, Zuckerberg, Altman, and the other tech-lords pay their fair share, and suddenly—precisely because wealth is so grotesquely concentrated—you have a whole lot more money to stabilize Social Security, move toward healthcare access for all, build more public housing, expand nutritional programs, and much else besides.
But simultaneously, Democrats must also be relentless in hammering home to Americans that, while they are fighting the good fight, Trump and his shrunken claque of GOP congressional enablers, with the ludicrous Jim Jordan at the helm, are still mired in extremism—stonewalling, grifting, or simply prattling on about vanity projects such as the (now-not-so) Triumphal Arch. That means holding public hearings on all the corruption and criminality, all of the unconstitutional, violent actions, and all of the self-dealing of this gang of crooks.
There is debate over exactly which members of the administration can be impeached, but at least some legal analysts think that in addition to elected officials and cabinet members, high-ranking, non-Senate-appointed officials can be subject to this sanction too. On that assumption, Democrats should start by aggressively investigating new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller’s white nationalist ties; his orders for ICE to meet arrest quotas, which have resulted in an epic level of violence against noncriminal immigrants; his decision to send shock- troops into cities such as Minneapolis, Chicago, Charlotte, Portland and Los Angeles; his vastly cruel project of ramping up deportations—more than 25,000 to date—to third countries with atrocious human rights records; and, court orders notwithstanding, the shipping of people, via third countries that are a party to the scheme, back to homelands where they could well be tortured or killed.
With the exception of Trump, there is no man more dangerous to the ongoing viability of the multiethnic, diverse, American democratic experiment than Miller—no man more willing to push the country toward civil conflict to pursue his fanatical political ends. Democrats should lay this all out for the American people to see—that Miller isn’t just a shmuck but that he is a shmuck on a Constitution-wrecking mission—and then impeach him. Dare the GOP survivors in the Senate to not convict this odious man and drive him from office; and, if they take up that dare, make them wear their spineless decision as a scarlet letter heading into the 2028 and 2030 election cycles.
Similarly, since the GOP-led Congress failed to impeach Hegseth this week, impeach him in January. Add to the list RFK Jr, Todd Blanche, and Kash Patel, all of whom have flagrantly abused their offices—whether through promoting quack medical cures at the urgings of financial donors or siccing the vast investigative and legal powers of the DoJ and FBI on Trump’s “enemies”—and then force the Republicans in the Senate to choose sides. These men are all low-hanging fruit, as strong candidates for impeachment as any public officials in US history. If the Republicans remaining in the Senate come 2027 can’t muster the strength to pick off these cabinet members, the public will, I suspect, be entirely unforgiving over the coming years’ election cycles.
And, above all, Democrats need to investigate Trump and his family’s endless self-dealing. Lay out in easy-to-understand detail how the con works: how the billions of dollars flow in via crypto scams; corrupt real estate deals; illegal “gifts”; strong-arm, mafiosi-like tactics deployed against corporations and overseas governments; the endless demanding of tribute; the pay-to-play understandings with companies looking to secure government contracts.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Document all of this and convict the Trumps beyond any reasonable doubt in the court of public opinion. But don’t immediately trigger an impeachment vote; don’t give the GOP an excuse to say this is all Trump Derangement Syndrome. Instead, let the Trump clan twist on the end of the investigative rope for a while as the full scope of their criminal actions is laid bare for the world to see. And then force the Republicans themselves to take the initiative, as—when push came to shove—GOP senators in 1974 did in pushing Nixon to resign: force them to either make their peace, even after the midterms drubbing, with who and what Trump and his self-dealing family is, with all the electoral fallout this will likely lead to for the GOP in 2028 and 2030, or to finally and definitively cut ties with Trump’s mobster government and agree to vote to convict him. Make those Republicans with capacious ambitions for high office—the Josh Hawleys and Ted Cruzes, for example—beg to be allowed to turn a corner on the Trump era that the party’s cravenness and opportunism have inflicted on the world.
In short, make the GOP cry uncle. Make the party that brought us Trump be the one that has to deliver the coup de grâce to the man and his kleptocracy.

Abhörskandal erschüttert Indonesien
Im größten Land Südostasiens kommt der Vizepräsident durch Rücktritt seiner Amtsenthebung zuvor. Die Unzufriedenheit mit Staatschef Prabowo nimmt zu.
Die Ankündigung erfolgte schon tags zuvor, am Donnerstag vollzog Gibran Rakabuming Raka den Schritt offiziell: Indonesiens erst 39-jähriger Vizepräsident ist zurückgetreten. Mit dem freiwilligen Schritt, der für die Regierung als kleiner Befreiungsschlag wirken mag, kam er einer möglichen Amtsenthebung zuvor. Nachdem unlängst sogar das Verfassungsgericht geurteilt hatte, dass seine bei der Kandidatur eingereichten akademischen Abschlüsse aus dem Ausland nicht regelkonform seien, wäre wohl in Kürze die Einleitung eines formellen Impeachment-Verfahrens erfolgt. Gibran erklärte jedoch, sein Rücktritt habe nichts mit dem Diplom-Streit zu tun und sei »kein Eingeständnis mangelnder Eignung«. Vielmehr habe er damit dem Team von Präsident Prabowo Subianto den Rücken freimachen wollen, sich mit größerem Zusammenhalt und Fokus den Herausforderungen des Landes zu widmen. Prabowo dankte seinem bisherigen Stellvertreter für die Unterstützung seit dem Wahlkampf. Die beiden hatten mit knapp 59 Prozent die Präsidentschaftswahl im Februar 2024 gewonnen.
Der Rücktritt steht gleichwohl nicht für sich. Er ist eingebettet in umfangreiche politische Turbulenzen, die den bevölkerungsreichen Inselstaat, größte muslimische Nation der Erde und führende Volkswirtschaft der Staatengemeinschaft ASEAN, seit Monatsbeginn erschüttern. Trotz vier Tatverdächtigen, die festgenommen wurden und im Polizeihauptquartier in U-Haft sitzen, sind die Hintergründe eines Abhörskandals bislang unklar. Den ranghohen, aktiven und ehemaligen Polizeioffizieren wird vorgeworfen, das Telefon des Präsidenten angezapft zu haben. In welchem Umfang, mit welchem Motiv und Ziel und vor allem, in wessen Auftrag – darüber kann vorerst nur spekuliert werden. Ein Name, der dabei mindestens am Rande auftaucht, obwohl ihn noch niemand offiziell einer Beteiligung beschuldigt hat, ist der von Ex-Präsident Joko Widodo alias Jokowi. Es handelt sich um Prabowos unmittelbaren Amtsvorgänger. Er löste ihn im Oktober 2024 ab und ist der Vater des jetzt zurückgetretenen Gibran.
Von Rivalen zu taktischen Partnern
Das Verhältnis zwischen Jokowi und dem rechtskonservativen Ex-General Prabowo ist äußerst komplex. Jokowi vollzog seinen Aufstieg bis an die Staatsspitze noch in der liberalen Demokratischen Partei des Kampfes (PDI-P), bevor er sich in seiner zweiten Amtszeit immer mehr von seiner politischen Heimat entfremdete. Prabowo ist der ehemalige Schwiegersohn des verstorbenen Diktators Mohamed Suharto. Früher waren sie Rivalen: Bei den Präsidentschaftswahlen 2014 und 2019 hatte Jokowi über seinen Kontrahenten gesiegt, diesen aber schließlich als Verteidigungsminister ins Kabinett geholt. Obwohl Jokowi im Amt offiziell neutral blieb, hatte Prabowo – mit Gibran an der Seite – vor zwei Jahren dann mindestens seine unterschwellige Unterstützung.
Jokowis jüngster Sohn Kaesang Pangarep wiederum ist Vorsitzender der Indonesischen Solidaritätspartei (PSI), als deren Mitglied seit 2025 sich vor einiger Zeit auch der Ex-Präsident geoutet hat. Die PSI verfehlte zur jüngsten Wahl zwar abermals den Parlamentseinzug, gehörte mit einigen Vertretern aber dem Regierungsteam an. Zu Wochenbeginn gaben der Forstwirtschaftsminister sowie die beiden Vizeminister im Kultur- beziehungsweise Familienressort ihren Austritt aus der PSI bekannt. Im Zusammenhang der übrigen Ereignisse wirkt der Zeitpunkt nicht mehr ganz zufällig.
Abhörfall gibt Rätsel auf
Was den Abhörskandal angeht, stehen die Ermittlungen noch ziemlich am Anfang. Gleich nach den ersten Enthüllungen am 3. November waren Listyo Sigit Prabowo, Ahrie Sonta Nasution und Eko Hadi Santoso festgenommen worden. Ahrie leitete bis dahin die Justizabteilung der Polizei, Eko war leitender Ausbilder am Polizei-Trainingszentrum. Im Visier stand aber vor allem Listyo, der bis 1. Oktober nationaler Polizeichef war, bis er von Prabowo zum Leiter der Präsidialverwaltung gemacht und damit sozusagen an die kurze Leine genommen wurde. Da er schon 2021 von Jokowi ernannt worden war und bereits zuvor als Polizeichef in dessen größter Bastion Surakarta (Solo) wirkte, gilt er bis heute als dessen Mann. Zwei Tage später wurde Slamet Uliandi, zuletzt Chef der Technologieabteilung der Criminal Investigation Agency, so etwas wie Indonesiens Bundeskriminalamt, als vierter Tatverdächtiger präsentiert.
Zumindest offiziell ist im Abhörskandal zu weiteren Beteiligten im Netzwerk noch nichts bekannt. Der Fall gibt einige Rätsel auf. Derweil gilt der eigentlich machtvolle Prabowo, der sich im Parlament mit Ausnahme der PDI-P auf eine »Supermehrheit« aller anderen Parteien stützen kann, mehr denn je als angeschlagen. Er appellierte bei Gibrans Rücktritt abermals demonstrativ an Einheit und Zusammenhalt des riesigen Landes mit seiner so vielfältigen Bevölkerung. Prabowos Zustimmungsrate liegt derzeit bei nur 44,5 Prozent. Einen niedrigeren Wert hat ein Präsident seit Beginn der Meinungsumfragen in Indonesien nie erreicht.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/pete.title: Next Time, Impeach Pete Hegseth for Press Censorship
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/pete.author: Seth Stern
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/pete.text:
Seth Stern is the director of advocacy for Freedom of the Press Foundation.
Before the effort to impeach him failed Tuesday, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth lashed out at a group he despises even more than “beardos” and “weirdos”: the press. His security team threatened to physically remove journalists from a news briefing, Hegseth’s first in several months, if they didn’t maintain decorum.
It’s nothing new for Hegseth. He may want to pump soldiers up with testosterone, but he’s spent the last couple years trying to neuter the Fourth Estate. It’s unfortunate that his unconstitutional attacks on journalists were not part of the official case for removing him. Next time, they should be. And Congress should not stop with Hegseth.
The impeachment resolution Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., brought against Hegseth included eight articles, alleging that the so-called Secretary of War acted illegally in military campaigns in Iran, Venezuela, and the Caribbean, among other things. The resolution touched on free speech violations – Article VI is about Hegseth’s retaliation campaign against Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., for reminding troops of their right to refuse illegal orders – but it didn’t mention the press.
A recap is in order: In February of 2025, Hegseth’s Pentagon evicted the New York Times, NBC, Politico, and NPR from their dedicated workspaces in the building, replacing them largely with sycophantic right-wing outlets like Breitbart and One America News Network. Some elements of the fawning right-wing press were on full display during his Tuesday press conference: “How does it make you feel,” asked a reporter from an outlet called Real America’s Voice, “when our own politicians don’t support taking out the narco-traffickers that kill their own constituents?”
Months later, Hegseth concocted a requirement that journalists who wish to access the Pentagon pledge not to solicit unauthorized information from the government, under threat of losing their credentials. Dozens of reporters from outlets across the political spectrum turned in their access badges rather than comply. They were replaced, once again, by loyalists who could be counted on to treat Hegseth and his fragile ego with kid gloves.
A judge soon struck down the pledge policy as an unconstitutional effort to force out disfavored journalists. The Pentagon immediately issued new restrictions on unauthorized disclosures that were, in some ways, even worse than the originals. The judge rejected that policy too. Hegseth also imposed a requirement for reporters to be escorted around the Pentagon, which is still working its way through the courts.
Hegseth’s Pentagon cracked down on the military’s newspaper, Stars and Stripes, barring it from briefings and demanding it stop publishing “woke” content. After all, it used to run columns from that well-known leftist Ann Coulter. His Pentagon then fired key personnel and otherwise did everything it could think of to try to turn Stars and Stripes into a propaganda organ unrecognizable to its readership – mostly troops, veterans, and their families.
It gets even pettier: Hegseth’s staff barred press photographers from briefings after they published pictures of him that he found unflattering.
Hegseth’s illegal war on transparency has extended not just to reporters but also to their sources. He forced staff to take unreliable polygraph tests to identify leakers until the White House itself halted the effort after a Trump loyalist complained about being targeted. He’s formed a joint task force with the Justice Department to push for prosecution of leakers and adopted President Donald Trump’s alarming habit of equating national security reporting to “treason.”
There will almost certainly be another effort to impeach Hegseth in the next Congress, if not sooner. Censorship may not be the lede — alleged international war crimes understandably tend to take the spotlight over other infractions — but it also shouldn’t be an afterthought.
While Congress is at it, remove Brendan Carr too
And while they’re impeaching wartime censors, Congress shouldn’t forget about FCC Chair Brendan Carr. He has defied federal law, the First Amendment, and the FCC’s own rules and guidelines in his incessant efforts to turn the agency into Trump’s journalism police. And critical reporting on the Iran war – which the Republican party now apparently agrees deserved criticism all along – has been one of Carr’s most frequent targets.
At the beginning of the war, after Trump fumed at accurate coverage he disliked, Carr – who wears Trump’s gilded face as a lapel pin and sips from a mug depicting himself as Trump’s pit bull – promptly reposted the president’s attack. He warned that broadcasters airing “hoaxes and news distortions” should “correct course before their license renewals come up.”
An emboldened Trump responded the same night, posting that outlets spreading “fake news” about the war should “be brought up on Charges for TREASON,” adding that he was “thrilled” Carr was investigating the licenses of media outlets across the country.
Then, after April’s purported ceasefire, CNN reported a statement from Iran’s Supreme National Security Council claiming victory. Trump took to Truth Social to announce a purported investigation into whether CNN committed some unspecified crime by publishing the quote. Carr piled on, accusing CNN, which the FCC does not regulate, of pushing a “hoax headline” that “requires accountability,” implying that licensees who aired similar reporting would face his wrath. But the statement was real. Trump just would’ve preferred CNN air a different one.
Of course, Carr’s censorship campaigns are myriad and many have little to do with the war. But his arguably most egregious (and impeachable) offense did, albeit indirectly.
Last year, Carr inexplicably stalled the FCC’s consideration of then-CBS News parent Paramount’s merger with David Ellison’s Skydance until Paramount paid $16 million to settle Trump’s frivolous lawsuit over “60 Minutes’” editing of an interview with Kamala Harris. He approved the merger two days after Trump said he’d received his dirty money. Essentially, he aided Trump in laundering a bribe through the courts.
Carr – who knows better, having once written that editorial judgment “should be beyond the reach of any government official” – also used his leverage over the merger to give himself and his delegates a seat at CBS’s editors desk, extracting unconstitutional editorial concessions from Ellison’s team. CBS has since been widely criticized for softening its coverage of Trump’s agenda, including (among other things) echoing administration narratives on the U.S. military operations like the war in Iran and the abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
Facilitating likely bribery is the epitome of an impeachable offense. Republicans might not vote for impeachment, but after all the backlash Carr has received from the right, they also can’t credibly accuse Democrats of some kind of partisan witch hunt. Congress should not let the opportunity to hold Carr accountable pass them by.
Lawmakers need to acknowledge that the reporters the administration called traitors got it right all along, and that those who attempted to censor wartime journalism did a disservice to the Constitution and the American people. Hegseth and Carr should both be impeached, with the press they tried to muzzle freely reporting on every minute of the proceedings.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.propublica.org/article/follo.title: His Church or His Child? A Sixth-Generation Member of a Faith-Healing Sect Had to Choose.
https://www.propublica.org/article/follo.author: Teresa Mahoney, Noelle Crombie, Beth Nakamura, Samantha Swindler
https://www.propublica.org/article/follo.text:
What if you had to pick between your deeply held faith and the life of your child? That’s the gutting choice that faced Marshall Phillips, an Oregon dad who was born into the Followers of Christ, a sect whose creed bars medical treatment. When his 11-year-old son was stricken with a dire health crisis, Phillips became caught between his faith, his family and the state of Oregon, which had begun cracking down on faith-healing parents who don’t seek medical help for their minor children. A decade later, Phillips was pulled into another one of his church’s life-or-death dramas when he was asked to care for a newborn whose twin had died because her parents had refused to seek medical attention.
Read More
To examine the power of faith-healing churches and the toll of their teachings, The Oregonian investigative reporter Noelle Crombie, senior staff photojournalist Beth Nakamura and videographer Samantha Swindler spent months with Phillips and his family, piecing together rare accounts from inside the deeply shuttered world of the Followers of Christ and of the state officials who fought to protect children who need medical treatment. The documentary, produced by The Oregonian’s managing producer of video, Teresa Mahoney, not only lays out in visceral detail the agonizing choices that families like the Phillips have to make, it also chronicles how they overcame the clash with their religious beliefs.
Go inside the secretive Followers of Christ sect and watch the extraordinary journey.
Read more in this riveting print narrative, and meet the man who dominated and shaped the sect.
