https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120386.title: Nahverkehr | Berliner S-Bahn weniger schlecht als im Jahr 2025
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120386.author: Nicolas Šustr
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120386.text:
- Berlin
- Nahverkehr
Berliner S-Bahn weniger schlecht als im Jahr 2025
Zuletzt 2022 war die S-Bahn pünktlicher als im laufenden Jahr. Große Schritte für einen stabileren Betrieb sind jedoch vorerst nicht zu erwarten
Die Berliner S-Bahn hat in den ersten zehn Monaten des laufenden Jahres eine stabilere Leistung erbracht als im Vorjahreszeitraum. Im Durchschnitt waren 2026 von Januar bis Oktober 94,3 Prozent der Fahrten pünktlich oder weniger als vier Minuten verspätet. Im gleichen Zeitraum im Jahr 2025 war dies nur für 92,9 Prozent der Züge der Fall.
»Nachdem wir im letzten Jahr ja berichten mussten, dass wir in allen Dimensionen schlechter geworden sind, können wir in diesem Jahr berichten, dass wir in allen Dimensionen teilweise deutlich besser geworden sind«, kommentiert S-Bahn-Chef Heiko Büttner das Zwischenergebnis. Die DB-Kantine am Nordbahnhof, in der der vom Berliner Fahrgastverband Igeb organisierte Fahrgastsprechtag am Donnerstag stattfindet, ist mit über 100 Interessierten gut gefüllt.
Positiv entwickelt hat sich auch das Ausfallgeschehen bei den Zügen. Von Januar bis Oktober 2026 fielen 3,82 Prozent aller Zugkilometer aus. Im Vorjahreszeitraum lag diese Quote noch bei 5,14 Prozent.
»Das ist am Ende nicht das, wo wir wirklich sein wollen. Wir wollen noch besser sein«, sagt Heiko Büttner. »Aber es ist auch im nationalen Vergleich tatsächlich aktuell der beste Wert.« Dabei vergleicht er die S-Bahn Berlin mit den anderen S-Bahn-Netzen. Zuletzt war die Gesamtpünktlichkeit im Jahr 2022 mit 95,1 Prozent besser.
Weniger Rückzahlungen an den Senat
Für die Haushälter einer möglichen künftigen rot-grün-roten Koalition sind das eher betrübliche Nachrichten. Zwar könnte die S-Bahn die im Verkehrsvertrag vereinbarte Pünktlichkeitsquote von 96 Prozent für 2026 nicht mehr erreichen, selbst wenn im November und Dezember 100 Prozent aller Züge pünktlich fahren würden. Aber die Rekord-Rückforderungen von 53 Millionen Euro für Schlechtleistungen aus dem Jahr 2025 dürften für das laufende Jahr nicht mehr erreicht werden.
Im Januar, Februar und Juni des laufenden Jahres lief es besonders schlecht. »Was uns zu schaffen macht, sind Wetterextreme«, sagt Büttner. »Man kann auch deutlich sehen, dass am Jahresanfang mit den langen kalten Temperaturen, aber auch im Juni, wo es so besonders heiß war, die Ausfälle deutlich nach oben gehen.«
Im Januar fielen fast sechs Prozent aller Zugkilometer aus, im Juni waren es 5,5 Prozent. Bei den Verspätungen war der Juni mit nur noch 92 Prozent pünktlichen Zügen der Tiefpunkt des Jahres. Im Januar und Februar waren 92,6 beziehungsweise 92,8 Prozent aller Fahrten weniger als vier Minuten verspätet.
Grob gerechnet geht etwa ein Drittel der Ausfälle auf das Konto der S-Bahn Berlin als Betreiberin der Züge. Ein weiteres Drittel ist durch Probleme mit der Gleis- und Signalinfrastruktur in Zuständigkeit der DB Infrago verursacht. Der Rest sind externe Einflüsse durch Notarzt- und Polizeieinsätze oder in zunehmendem Maße durch Personen im oder am Gleis.
Alternde Fahrzeuge als Problem
Für seinen Bereich macht Büttner hauptsächlich das zunehmende Alter der Bestandsbaureihen 480 und 481 verantwortlich. Die zusammengenommen 1130 Wagen sind zwischen 1990 und 2004 gebaut worden.
Für die 1000 Wagen starke Baureihe 481 läuft Anfang 2027 das Programm »Langlebigkeit II« an, bei dem zunehmend störungsanfällige Verkabelungen und Elektronikbauteile getauscht werden. Die letzten Fahrzeuge müssen noch bis 2037 durchhalten. Dann soll die Nachfolgebaureihe komplett ausgeliefert sein. Der nötige Verkehrsvertrag für die Stadtbahn- und Nord-Süd-Linien konnte diesen Sommer nach jahrelangem juristischem Tauziehen endlich unterzeichnet werden.
Die restlichen Fahrzeuge der Baureihe 480 werden bereits Anfang der 2030er Jahre auf den Schrott wandern. Lange war unklar, ob sie so lange durchhalten. Einige der heute bereits 32 bis 36 Jahre alten Wagen dürften aber bereits früher den Weg alten Eisens antreten.
S15 erweist sich als Musterlinie
Entgegen den Befürchtungen im Vorfeld hat die Inbetriebnahme der S15 zwischen Hauptbahnhof und Gesundbrunnen am 15. Juni 2026 nicht zur Verschlechterung der Betriebsqualität beigetragen. 97,4 Prozent aller Fahrten sind pünktlich, etwas unter zwei Prozent aller Fahrten sind ausgefallen – der Spitzenwert aller Linien.
Grund der Sorge war, dass die Linie einen Teil der Strecke mit den notorisch instabilen Ringbahnlinien S41 und S42 teilt. Besonders das Entleeren der Züge am Ringbahnsteig in Gesundbrunnen und die Signalisierung bei Fahrt in das Wendegleis wurden als potenzielle Hindernisse ausgemacht.
S-Bahn-Chef Büttner berichtet, dass DB Infrago im Vorfeld ein zusätzliches Signal in Gesundbrunnen eingebaut hatte, damit die durchgehenden Ringbahngleise beim Wendemanöver möglichst kurz blockiert sind. Statt den schwächer motorisierten Zügen der Baureihe 481 kommen inzwischen Fahrzeuge des neuesten Typs 483/484 zum Einsatz. Die steilen Rampen zwischen Ringbahnstrecke und dem Tunnelbahnhof am Hauptbahnhof hatten sich unter gewissen Konstellationen als problematisch erwiesen.
»Bis dato läuft es wirklich sehr stabil«, sagt Heiko Büttner über die S15. »Auch die 13 000 Reisenden an Werktagen sind durchaus nennenswert.« Er sei »persönlich ein bisschen zurückhaltend«, ob »so eine Stummelbahn« nachgefragt werde. Einen Teil zum Fahrgastzuspruch dürfte die noch bis zum Fahrplanwechsel Mitte Dezember anhaltende Sperrung der Stadtbahn für den Fern- und Regionalverkehr beitragen.
Mit dem Fahrplanwechsel am 13. Dezember dünnt die S-Bahn ihr Angebot im Berufsverkehr aus. Die Verstärkerzüge auf S1 und S5 sollen nur noch halb so oft wie bisher fahren. Statt eines planmäßigen Fünf-Minuten-Takts werden auf den Abschnitten abwechselnd alle fünf und zehn Minuten Züge fahren. Das liegt an den für das Langlebigkeitsprogramm zusätzlich in der Werkstatt stehenden Fahrzeugen.
Im Gegenzug sind die Verstärkerfahrten der S1 nicht mehr nur auf die Strecke zwischen Zehlendorf und Potsdamer Platz beschränkt. Sie fahren künftig weiter durch den Nordsüd-Tunnel bis zum Nordbahnhof. Die S-Bahn verspricht sich davon mehr Stabilität auf den Tunnellinien. Denn am Potsdamer Platz blockieren endende Züge das durchgängige Streckengleis, was am Nordbahnhof nicht der Fall ist.
Großer Tausch bei S1 und S2 Ende 2027
Eine langjährige Forderung des Fahrgastverbands Igeb dürfte tatsächlich Ende 2027 umgesetzt werden, wie Heiko Büttner bestätigt: S1 und S2 werden ihre Nordäste tauschen. Die S1 fährt dann nach Bernau, die S2 nach Oranienburg.
Mehrere Gründe sprechen dafür. Der lange eingleisige Abschnitt auf der Strecke nach Bernau ist sehr verspätungsanfällig. Die Verspätungen lassen sich besser ausgleichen auf der durchgehend zweigleisigen Strecke nach Wannsee als bei der ebenfalls eingleisigen Strecke nach Blankenfelde. Außerdem bekommt die S2 am neuen Endpunkt Oranienburg eine direkte Anbindung an eine S-Bahn-Werkstatt.
Bisher mutieren regelmäßig Züge der S2 Richtung Süden am Potsdamer Platz zur S1 Richtung Wannsee, um die dortige Werkstatt zu erreichen. Fahrgäste müssen in einen bereitstehenden Ersatzzug wechseln. Das Manöver sorgt für Verspätungen und kann mit dem Asttausch entfallen. Auch die S-Bahn Berlin GmbH hatte sich bereits in der Vergangenheit dafür stark gemacht. Doch lange verschloss sich das Land Berlin als Besteller einer solchen Lösung.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/subp.title: Trump Subpoenas Teachers Union for Info on Pro-Palestine Students
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/subp.author: C. Frances
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/subp.text:
The Trump administration quietly broadened its crackdown on campus pro-Palestine protests over the summer, moving to ensnare one of the largest unions in the country in a case revolving around alleged incidents of vandalism.
The national headquarters of the American Federation of Teachers, or AFT, received a grand jury subpoena in August as part of an ongoing federal investigation into protests at the University of Michigan. Twelve pro-Palestine activists have been charged with felonies in the case.
The subpoena against the AFT, which has not been previously reported and was obtained by The Intercept, shows the administration casting a wider net in its investigation into student protesters than was previously known.
The Graduate Employees’ Organization, or GEO, an AFT local at the university, also received a notice to provide information and testimony to a grand jury around the same time, according to a copy of the previously unreported subpoena obtained by The Intercept.
The effort to draw a powerful, liberal union into a case that revolves around spray-painting charges represents a dramatic escalation in Donald Trump’s war on the left.
“They’re using this language around conspiracy and trying to draw in all of these different organizations that are taking stances against fascism, against the government, and anything that’s counter to their ideology,” said Natalie Chen, who serves as GEO’s communications director. “This is perhaps another ‘in’ for them to broaden their attack
on labor.”
Subpoenas to Crush Dissent
As pro-Palestine protests swept campuses across the country in 2024 and widespread demonstration broke out against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement this year, the Trump administration has sought to paint left-of-center protest, nonprofit work, and labor organizing as a nefarious far-left conspiracy, even labeling some activists and groups as terrorists.
Critics of the administration’s crackdown on Palestine solidarity and protests against ICE see moves like the ones against AFT and GEO as part of an effort to silence dissent.
“Historically, federal grand jury subpoenas have been used against social movements and political dissent to gather information, to isolate individuals, and of course to try and prosecute people,” said Xavier de Janon, executive director of the National Lawyers Guild. “What is different in politicized cases is the extent of people and places that get subpoenaed, which many people see clearly goes way beyond what they’re supposedly trying to prosecute.”
Activists at the University of Michigan said the effort to extract information about students from the union was an attempt to further target pro-Palestine protesters and their relationships with labor organizers.
The grand jury subpoenas came as part of a case that has seen a dozen protesters become caught up in serious federal charges against the students, dubbed “the Michigan 12.” They allege that protesters committed illegal acts like vandalism as part of a pressure campaign seeking to push university officials to divest school holdings tied to the Israeli genocide in Palestine.
The subpoenas against the GEO and AFT were requested by federal prosecutor Margaret Smith with assistance from FBI agent Kara Phipps — two federal officials deeply enmeshed in the investigation into the Michigan 12. (The Department of Justice declined to comment for this story.)
GEO Under Fire
The subpoenas were issued as the GEO was already reeling after its president, Hiab Teshome, was charged with felony embezzlement by local prosecutors working in conjunction with the University of Michigan Police Department.
Authorities alleged that Teshome, who was a bargaining team member in the middle of intense contract negotiations between the union and the school, misused organizational funds to purchase laptops for a campus club.
In a statement, the GEO called the charges meritless and characterized them as an attempt to limit protected union activity. Teshome was later cleared of any wrongdoing by the university’s student government, and the charges against her were thrown out by a judge.
Federal prosecutors issued the subpoenas the same day the charges against Teshome were dismissed, leaving activists little time to regroup.
Although GEO is not mentioned in the federal indictment against protesters, the AFT chapter is a prominent member of the Tahrir coalition, a pro-Palestine student collective that is referenced repeatedly in federal filings and characterized by prosecutors as having ties with defendants.
Broad in Scope
The scope of the information requested of the unions by the federal government is broad. GEO and AFT are being compelled, according to the subpoenas, to surrender information including complete membership rolls, payroll records on officers, reimbursement policies, audit reports, and all transcribed minutes on membership and executive board meetings of the University of Michigan local since January 2023.
The American Federation of Teachers has more than 1.7 million members and more than 3,000 local chapters.
After receiving the subpoena, GEO immediately obtained attorneys and filed a motion to quash the order. The national office of the AFT, however, has not publicly acknowledged receiving the directive or stated whether it intends to comply. (AFT did not respond to requests for comment about the subpoenas, including whether the union would be complying.)
Teshome, the GEO president, believes that the subpoena against the AFT may be an attempt by the federal government to circumvent the local union and force the national organization to comply.
“GEO has taken the stance that we will do everything in our power to protect the data and the information of our membership,” Teshome said. “I think that this is a strategy that the federal government is using in order to try to actually receive the information that they are trying to get by usurping us as a local union and going instead to AFT national.”
Additionally, Teshome likened the GEO’s case to similar surveillance activities conducted by federal agents against trade unionists in Minnesota as part of the Trump White House’s National Security Presidential Memorandum-7, a presidential directive that attempts to criminalize leftist political organizations.
“All of the repression we are seeing across the country is the federal government’s attack on anyone who has political thought,” Teshome said. “Michigan is no different than all of these other cases in that we are one of the testing grounds for NSPM-7 and how much oppression can be applied through the federal government in order to demobilize and disorganize.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.propublica.org/article/offsh.title: How Trump’s War on Offshore Wind Upended a “Limitless” Future for Thousands of New England Workers
https://www.propublica.org/article/offsh.author: Ben Berke, John Moritz, Anastasia Lennon
https://www.propublica.org/article/offsh.text:
On a hot July day in 2022, then-President Joe Biden gave a speech from the ruins of a coal-fired power plant on the southern coast of Massachusetts.
Standing where ships once delivered coal for combustion, he said the same dock would soon launch components for wind power out to sea.
He praised an Italian company’s plans to build a new factory there, set to create 250 jobs and supply American-made undersea power cables to what was then a line of offshore wind projects waiting to be built along the coast.
Four years later, weeds and tall grass have reclaimed the dirt lot on which Biden spoke.
The company never came.
A 20-minute drive east, in New Bedford, hundreds of workers who helped assemble wind turbine parts from Canada and Europe over the last three years have given way to seagulls and geese. The birds shuffle along the now-empty pier the state of Massachusetts spent $140 million to build for offshore wind development.
In nearby Providence, Rhode Island, a newly built factory that manufactured offshore wind turbine foundation platforms has emptied out.
Amid the Trump administration’s multifront war against offshore wind, the cost on the ground in New England, the launchpad of the country’s offshore wind industry, can be seen in empty warehouses, silent marine terminals and ledgers recording hundreds of millions of dollars of state investment that may not be recouped.
ProPublica partnered with Ocean State Media, The Connecticut Mirror and the New Bedford Light to document the consequences of the administration’s efforts.
Many offshore wind projects faced a precarious future before President Donald Trump retook office. Rising construction costs driven by inflation and supply chain shortages forced some developers to back out of contracts to build wind farms and supply electricity to states. Various groups have also fought construction of projects saying they disrupt marine ecosystems and mar coastal views.
But last year, the administration temporarily forced five projects to stop construction, further clouding the horizon. Courts allowed the developers to proceed, but that has not eliminated the threat. Last month, the U.S. Department of the Interior asked a court for permission to reconsider a key permit for one of those five projects, Revolution Wind, which is already up and running and can power more than 350,000 New England homes at maximum capacity.
The administration also has frozen future development on all offshore wind farms, including a cluster of projects that haven’t been built but proposed to power up to 1.7 million New England homes. It has blocked or is seeking review of the permits that would allow these to be built. Meanwhile, the administration is paying other wind developers billions of dollars to sell back their leases and walk away.
At a press conference Monday, Trump said he supports a bipartisan bill that would accelerate U.S. energy development. When a reporter pointed out that the bill includes wind energy, Trump said he would not approve “wind turbines ’cause wind turbines are a major loser.”
The upheaval has had ripple effects. The cable company Biden touted decided not to build its factory, citing “long-term trends in the U.S. market.”
Port cities like New Bedford, Massachusetts, and New London, Connecticut, are left trying to hold onto the economic gains they have made building wind farms.
As recently as last winter, New Bedford, a historic whaling and textile manufacturing center, had hotels, offices and piers buzzing with offshore wind workers. Local businesses from caterers to cleaners to fuel suppliers landed new contracts servicing the wind industry.
In New London — another port once central to the whaling industry — officials worked with one of the world’s largest wind developers to pump more than $300 million of public and private funds into a state-owned pier. Despite significant cost overruns and some early construction challenges, the effort transformed the pier into a staging area for the wind industry.
Over the last four years, the pier has been a hive of activity. Hundreds of workers were employed loading and offloading turbine parts — with blades the length of a football field — from specially designed ships, some with names drawn from Greek mythology. Local companies also found work supporting the industry, including one that offered water rescue training for people working on construction sites offshore.
“I think the future just looked limitless,” said New London Mayor Michael Passero.
Before wind, Passero said that officials tried for years to attract different industries to the pier, which is overshadowed by larger port facilities in New York and Boston. It was often used to import and store large piles of road salt.
The most recent wind project based at the pier is scheduled to finish work next year. Port officials have yet to find a tenant to occupy the space.
“They’ll be back to the old days of trying to lure cargo here,” Passero said.
Amid Trump’s war on wind, a frontline of union and nonunion workers watches opportunity disappear. One project alone, Vineyard Wind, directly employed a total of more than 3,700 full- and part-time workers — most of them from Massachusetts — over eight years of development and construction, according to the developer.
During peak construction activity, as many as 300 union members worked onshore in southeastern Massachusetts for the project, the first large offshore wind farm fully permitted by the federal government. The wind farm was completed this year.
Longshoreman Onix Vazquez, 34, worked full-time tying up barges and moving turbine components on and off New Bedford’s wind pier. He grew up a few blocks away and said he had struggled to find lucrative work until Vineyard Wind began hiring from his union.
Vazquez’s hourly wage of $50 was nearly double what he previously earned unloading occasional shipments of tangerines and juice concentrate. It allowed him and other members of his historically Black union to make down payments on houses, pay off medical bills and for the first time take their families on out-of-state vacations.
“Most of us have to get other jobs for now or collect unemployment,” said Kevin Rose, president of New Bedford’s longshoremen union, which put about two dozen members to work on the project.
The union had been planning to rebuild its nearby meeting hall, which was demolished a decade earlier when work grew scarce. But the next developer to lease New Bedford’s wind pier has delayed its project indefinitely. The union members have put the plans for their new hall on hold.
Vazquez said he now works a seasonal job in the cranberry industry for much lower pay.
“They don’t see that it affects us, the ones that work the projects,” he said.
In response to questions about the impact of the administration’s actions on American offshore wind workers, a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of the Interior repeated criticisms of offshore wind as an expensive and unreliable source of energy.
“The reality is that the Biden administration lured companies into these projects with the promise of millions of taxpayer dollars in subsidies to make these offshore wind projects viable,” the spokesperson said in an email.
The view is more nuanced on the ground. New Bedford’s fishing industry is generally critical of wind farm development because fishermen worry about disruption to fishing grounds.
But fishing catch limits keep boats tied to docks for much of the year. Work for wind farms gets them out to sea and helps pay the bills.
Over the past few years of construction, Vineyard Wind paid about $11 million to 55 fishing vessels from New England and an estimated 60 to 70 fishermen, according to the developer. (The figure also covers fuel.) The fishermen look out for protected species, guard exposed underwater cable as it’s being laid and log information for the developer.
Some fishermen say they will work in offshore wind for as long as they can.
“The scallop boats need the extra revenue,” said Patrick Walsh, 37, a fifth-generation fisherman who plans to rejoin his father’s fishing business when wind work wraps up. “The worst thing for a boat is to sit. Those boats are made to work.”
Wind farm work made it possible for him to buy his first house, he said.
“Fishing would pay bills, and wind was going in the bank.”

https://inthesetimes.com/article/massage.title: Seattle’s Massage Workers Demand Safety and Solidarity—Not Stigma
https://inthesetimes.com/article/massage.author: Kim Kelly
https://inthesetimes.com/article/massage.text:
SEATTLE—On September 7, 1885, three Chinese hop pickers were shot dead in their camp outside Seattle. That night, their attackers snuck up to the tent of sleeping laborers and opened fire. Three died and three more were wounded, yet their assailants were never convicted or punished for their bloody crimes.
The attack marked the beginning of a years-long campaign of harassment and violence toward Chinese immigrant workers in what was then called Washington Territory.
Two months after the Squak Valley murders, a white mob, led by the town’s elected leaders, descended upon Tacoma’s then-thriving Chinatown neighborhood, drove out 700 of its inhabitants and burned the entire district to the ground. This pattern of white supremacist, anti-Chinese violence was repeated across the Northwest, including in Seattle, where more than 200 Chinese residents were expelled at gunpoint in 1886.
“It was not looked at with shame, but with pride by the anti-Chinese vigilantes and the state — so much so that it had a name: the Tacoma method,” said J.M. Wong, a member of the Massage Parlor Organizing Project (MPOP), during a press conference in late May.
Ahead of the summer 2026 World Cup, police raided more than 50 Asian massage parlors in the Seattle area, costing workers their jobs and homes. The workers and their advocates at MPOP responded by demanding an end to the raids and emphasizing the need for a state licensing path that recognizes their cultural expertise.
The press conference, held outside the Wing Luke Museum of Asian Pacific American Experience in Seattle, was part of MPOP’s ongoing Safety Not Stigma campaign. “Anti-Asian stigmatization and racism is still here with us today,” Wong said. “Today’s model chases after immigrant women and workers in the name of stamping out trafficking and rescuing the very people they want to silence and exclude from the city’s future.”
The raids came as Seattle prepared to host six World Cup matches in June and July — and news of increasingly violent ICE raids on immigrant communities continued to spread throughout the country. Police and fire departments in King and Pierce counties raided the parlors as part of a “cross-agency anti-trafficking initiative”; but in the eyes of these workers, and their advocates, they weren’t being “saved”; they were being punished.
“Police and fire tell us in the media that these women were victims who needed to be rescued,” Wong said. “But this is not what we heard from the workers who were in distress outside their places of work, afraid to get their belongings.”
As a result of the raids, many workers lost their livelihoods and their housing in one fell swoop.
In response to the raids, MPOP and its allies in the Asian Pacific American Labor Alliance (APALA) publicly called for a moratorium on anti-Asian police raids of King County massage parlors. The Martin Luther King, Jr. County Labor Council — the county’s central labor organization — passed a historic resolution in support of the workers.
The vote marked “the first time a resolution has passed supporting an active campaign pushed by Asian massage workers (Safety Not Stigma), instead of memorializing those lost to police or white supremacist violence,” according to an MPOP press release.
The increased frequency of police and ICE raids and the dramatic uptick in anti-immigrant rhetoric from the political class have contrived to make these workers’ jobs even harder. Many immigrant massage workers, especially those who speak little or no English, struggle with the licensing process. Applicants must complete 625 hours of training at a state board approved massage school, for which tuition varies wildly, and in many said schools, training materials are only offered in English or Spanish. MPOP says workers regularly spend thousands of dollars and months of training at schools whose programs turn out not to qualify for licensure, forcing them to start over. “Some of us have experienced this multiple times,” said an MPOP speaker at the press conference. Fraud in the massage-school industry is well documented: A 2021 USA Today investigation identified two dozen schools with alleged ties to fraud or prostitution, including operators accused of selling fake credentials. In 2012, lawmakers removed language accommodations from the state’s massage and reflexology licensing framework that would have provided alternatives for non-English speakers.
Since the licensing framework only recognizes state-approved institutions, it fails to account for previous work experience or training acquired in traditional Chinese medicine and other cultural practices. MPOP is calling on the city and state to create an alternative licensing pathway for Asian massage workers by establishing a “cultural bodywork” category. “The industry is so stigmatized by the government officials that they just deem all the professional work you do, especially the Chinese medicine part, not proper massage,” Sally told me in Mandarin, while an MPOP staffer translated. She’s a Chinese-born massage worker who has lived and worked in Seattle’s Pike Place neighborhood since 2013. In her view, the current licensing system only accepts “Westernized medical massage.”
It’s a catch-22: It’s extremely difficult to acquire a license, but without one, workers are at risk of arrest, and those with complex immigration statuses are in further danger of detainment or deportation. This climate of fear has also emboldened bad actors to take advantage of these vulnerable workers: Some customers have threatened to report workers to the police or ICE to avoid paying, have sexually harassed workers or even robbed them. “Because workers fear arrest and deportation,” said an MPOP spokesperson, “they will not call the police or report incidents of violence or exploitation within their workplace.” Trapped in a vicious cycle by the current system, there is little workers can do right now to defend themselves. But they’re trying to change that.
Sally (who asked to use a pseudonym for her safety and privacy) originally moved to the Seattle area in 2011 with her American husband, leaving behind a career managing a shopping mall in her home province, Sichuan. When he died of cancer in 2013, she scrambled to find whatever work she could. A friend recommended she look into the massage business. “I actually didn’t do massage back in China; in China I was the one receiving the massage!” she said. “But at the time I did feel like, Oh, this is so relaxing for me, this is a helpful kind of work.”
Over the next fifteen years, Sally learned from coworkers in the massage field, perfected her technique and now sees herself as almost a mother to many of her customers. She listens to their problems, checks in on their health and recommends exercises for them to do at home. “We provide services for both really rich engineers and also the low-income customers who really need the massage to relieve their muscle pain,” she said. “I have a lot of customers who are doing heavy lifting work, and they can’t afford really expensive medical massages or don’t have health insurance in that way. … This is really important care labor.”
Now Sally is fighting alongside MPOP to break down barriers preventing other immigrants from safely working in the industry and to end the stigma against Asian massage workers. She is especially disappointed in the lack of respect she feels she and her coworkers receive from the government, the media and those who want to “rescue” them. Her stern recommendation for them: “If you really want to talk about trafficking, go listen to the real workers who are in this industry, instead of believing some biased news.” That’s what MPOP and APALA are doing, and that’s why massage workers like Sally are involved in their collective push for reform. MPOP was formed in the wake of the 2018 police raids on Asian massage parlors in the Chinatown-International District in Seattle. It has since grown into a powerful resource for legislative and community organizing. Its members are Asian immigrant workers who are often excluded by the dominant labor movement and criminalized under existing laws.
In a region with such a deep and ugly history of anti-Asian violence, righting these historic wrongs will take action, not just words. “Once again, we see this region’s legislators, industry bodies, neighborhood groups, the city, and the country’s police and safety systems attack the most vulnerable Chinese workers in our communities under the guise of stamping out social ills and bad business that undercut struggling professionals,” J.M. Wong said during the May press conference. Since lawmakers and the powers that be have continually failed them in favor of top-down “anti-trafficking” initiatives, these workers are determined to make it happen for themselves.
“The government doesn’t listen to us migrant workers,” said a Seattle massage worker who spoke during the press conference. “They speak for us and make laws based on stereotypes and biased views of Asian women. What is truly good for us? We need to be able to report wage theft and violence without fear of being criminalized or deported. We need translators, lawyers, doctors and affordable housing. If police raids and shop searches only make us poor and more silent, then they are not helping us.”
Safety, not stigma, is both the demand and the goal. Massage workers “are really a part of this society,” Sally said. “We’re contributing, we’re also taxpayers, so just give us enough respect and value our work.”
Thank you for reading this story. At a time when corporate media is dominating the web and our airwaves, independent journalism is more important than ever, and that’s what we provide at In These Times. We offer some of the best reporting, investigations and analysis on the growing movements for justice in the U.S.—and our work is firmly pro-labor and anti-fascist. Les cookies et technologies similaires que nous utilisons sur Mediapart sont de différentes natures et nous permettent de poursuivre différentes finalités. 
Certains sont nécessaires au fonctionnement du site et de l’application mobile (vous ne pouvez pas les refuser). D’autres sont optionnels mais contribuent à faciliter votre expérience de lecteur ou de lectrice et d’une certaine façon à soutenir Mediapart. Vous pouvez les refuser ou les accepter ci-dessous, selon leurs finalités. 
Acceptez-vous que Mediapart utilise des cookies ou technologies similaires pour les finalités suivantes ? 
Vous pouvez faire votre choix, pour chaque catégorie, en activant ou désactivant le bouton interrupteur.
                    
                            
                                Nécessaires au fonctionnement
du site ou de l’application
                            Connexion des abonné·es, mesure d’audience anonymisée, envoi des notifications push, suivi des pannes, mise en avant de nos services : ces outils sont nécessaires au suivi de l’activité de nos services et à leur bon fonctionnement.
                                    Voici les différents cookies et technologies similaires compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Cookies d’authentification : connexion des abonné·es.
- Batch (uniquement sur l’application) : envoi de notifications push et de messages in-app.
- Affichage de contenus éditoriaux multimédias : vidéos (YouTube, Dailymotion, Vimeo, INA), réseaux sociaux (Facebook, Instagram, Pinterest, Twitter), documents (Scribd, Document Cloud, Slideshare), sons (SoundCloud, Spotify, Deezer), cartes (Google Maps, Mapbox, CartoDB, uMap), infographies (Highcharts, GitHub, Datawrapper, Flourish, Infogram, ThingLink, jQuery, Google Fonts, Bootstrap), live blogs (24liveblog, CoverItLive), aide à l’intégration de média dans les publications Journal et Club (Embedly).
- Datadog (uniquement sur le site web) : indicateurs techniques et équilibrage de charge.
- Firebase Cloud Messaging (uniquement sur l’application) : nécessaire au fonctionnement des notifications push sur Android.
- Microsoft App Center (uniquement sur l’application) : système de mise à jour et de suivi des pannes de l’application.
- Piano : mesure d’audience anonymisée
- Selligent (uniquement sur le site web) : communication avec l’abonné·e, mise en avant des services, offres et avantages.
- Typeform : questionnaires facultatifs pour recueillir les avis des lecteurs sur nos produits numériques.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Ces outils nous permettent de recueillir des statistiques de fréquentation du site et de l’application mobile pour comprendre les usages, détecter d’éventuels problèmes et optimiser l’ergonomie de nos produits.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Batch (uniquement sur le site web) : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- CrazyEggs (uniquement sur le site web) : analyse de parcours client.
- Nonli (uniquement sur le site web) : permet à notre équipe des réseaux sociaux de publier les contenus Mediapart sur les réseaux sociaux.
- Piano : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- Qiota (uniquement sur le site web) : gestion du système de datawall.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Il n’y a pas de publicité sur Mediapart. Mais nous faisons la promotion de nos contenus et services sur d’autres sites et réseaux sociaux. Pour cela, nous utilisons les technologies mises à disposition par certains acteurs publicitaires.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Facebook (uniquement sur le site web) : ciblage d’audience sur les réseaux sociaux pour faire la promotion de Mediapart.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                                Gestion de l’accès aux contenus
                            Nous utilisons le service Qiota d’Opper Marketing Suite pour configurer l’activation d’un datawall sur certains de nos contenus (uniquement sur le site web). Ce dispositif destiné aux utilisateur·ices non abonné·es requiert la saisie d’une adresse email pour accéder aux contenus concernés. En fournissant cette information, l’utilisateur consent à sa collecte, son stockage et son utilisation à des fins statistiques. Conformément à la réglementation en vigueur, les utilisateurs disposent d’un droit d’accès, de rectification et de suppression de leurs données, qu’ils peuvent exercer en contactant dpo@opper.io.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Marlon Brando cool to Jensen Huang joke: how the black leather jacket became a meme
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Chloe Mac Donnell
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
For nearly two decades a black leather jacket has been a key part of Jensen Huang’s look. Now it has become a punchline.
As the founder and chief executive of Nvidia resigned this week after reports of multiple affairs, his affinity for a leather jacket, an item of clothing typically associated with a man in midlife crisis mode, has become widely mocked.
The Cut ran a story suggesting a clear line between his penchant for a luxury leather jacket and his extramarital affairs. “Jensen Huang’s leather jackets confessed before he did” read the headline. Writing in the New York Times, the author Anand Giridharadas asked “is an expensive leather jacket on a middle-aged man the new symbol of a honeypot victim?”
Meanwhile, the internet is rife with memes, including an AI-generated image of a leather jacket flying at half mast outside Elon Musk’s rocket company SpaceX. There was also another fake image, this time of Huang in a studded leather jacket, that many people believed was real.
Elsewhere, there are plenty of divorced dad jokes doing the rounds. “Jensen leather jacket discourse reminds me of the time two years ago when I wore my beloved moto jacket to a party and my good friend said “great jacket, sorry you got divorced”, wrote one user on X.
Similar to Steve Jobs’s black rollneck and jeans or Mark Zuckerberg’s Latin-sloganed T-shirts, Huang’s black leather jacket has become a visual trademark. He likes to pair a leather jacket (always black) with a black T-shirt and black jeans.
In September, in an interview with CBS, Huang explained he had 30 to 40 leather jackets. He credited his wife, Lori Huang, with choosing them. They vary from motorcycle-inspired jackets with a tighter fit and plenty of zips to collarless croc-embossed jackets and clean-cut tailored versions. He has worn them to trade shows, to parties and to give keynote speeches at developer conferences. In 2021 he appeared on the cover of Time magazine in a black leather jacket from Tom Ford. In July, another Tom Ford jacket worn and signed by Huang sold at a charity auction at Sotheby’s for $960,000, more than 10 times its original price.
“The leather jacket is Huang’s way of borrowing some cool,” says Peter Bevan, a writer and stylist. Bevan points to the leather jacket’s “rebel history” as part of the appeal.
Marlon Brando led his biker gang wearing an asymmetric zip jacket in 1953’s The Wild One; James Dean zipped around off-screen in a similar style while following his Berlin era; David Bowie wore a black leather jacket on the cover of his Heroes album in 1977. Patrick Swayze in Dirty Dancing, John Travolta in Grease and Harrison Ford as Indiana Jones also made a leather jacket an enduring symbol of Hollywood style.
By choosing a black leather jacket rather than a corporate suit, it suggests that Huang is unconventional, a leader rather than a conformist.
“It’s basically Huang saying: ‘I’m not a regular billionaire boss, I’m a cool billionaire boss’,” Bevan says.
When asked by CBS in October why he wore a leather jacket day in, and day out, Huang said it helped him avoid decision fatigue. “Black is the absence of choice,” he said. “It’s nice to wear the same thing every day because no surprises. For everybody else, they probably have to make three or four decisions. I took that off my plate. The moment I wake up, I could be thinking about important things.”
It’s a look that has not gone unnoticed by his fellow tech giants. In 2024, Zuckerberg posted a photo of Huang swapping jackets. Later in the year, at a Siggraph conference in Colorado, Zuckerberg presented him with another jacket. “It’s black and leather and shearling,” Zuckerberg said describing the coat. “It’s a vibe. I mean, get this guy a chain.” In return, Huang gave him the black leather jacket he was wearing, explaining that Lori had bought it for him to commemorate that year’s conference. “This is worth more because it’s used,” Zuckerberg said as he slipped it on.
Bevan says that while Huang’s choice of designer jackets are “the kind that most fashion insiders would rate”, a box-fresh leather jacket “feels try hard” and as a result, “tips into midlife crisis territory fast”.
The biggest mistake men make when buying a leather jacket Bevan says is choosing one that is “too shiny, too new and too tight.”
The list of those who get it wrong is long – including Jeremy Clarkson, who likes to wear a black leather jacket with bootcut jeans.
For Bevan, the men who have mastered a leather jacket are those who “look like they’ve owned it for ever”.
Lenny Kravitz who, like Huang, is in his 60s, prefers a battered leather jacket. John Malkovich, who is a decade older, likes a brown oversized leather jacket, while the rapper A$AP Rocky, who is in his 30s, has made a bomber leather jacket his style staple.
For those without youth or “rock-star DNA” on their side, Bevan suggests ditching a leather jacket for a cotton Harrington style that he describes as “having the same cool but none of the leather-clad midlife baggage”.
As for Huang, he may have to reconsider his default wardrobe for next week. While he managed to pull off a leather jacket at tech conferences, it may be harder to pull off at a congressional testimony.

https://taz.de/Mordanklage-gegen-Partner.title: Sechsfachmord in Stade: Mordanklage gegen Partnerin des mutmaßlichen Schützen
https://taz.de/Mordanklage-gegen-Partner.text:
Sechsfachmord in Stade: Mordanklage gegen Partnerin des mutmaßlichen Schützen
Ende Juni erschoss ein Mann in einer Jugendeinrichtung sechs Sozialarbeiter:innen. Zwei Frauen sollen von der Tat gewusst und den Schützen unterstützt haben.
dpa | Nach den tödlichen Schüssen in einer Jugendhilfeeinrichtung im niedersächsischen Stade könnten zwei Frauen bald vor Gericht stehen. Viereinhalb Monate nach der Tat erhob die Staatsanwaltschaft Anklage, wie die Behörde mitteilte. Sie legt der Partnerin des mutmaßlichen Schützen sechsfachen Mord aus Heimtücke und niedrigen Beweggründen zur Last, der Fahrerin des Fluchtautos Beihilfe zum Mord.
Bei dem Angriff am 29. Juni kamen sechs Menschen ums Leben. „Die Opfer waren arglos und haben nicht mit einem Angriff während des Gesprächs gerechnet“, teilte die Staatsanwaltschaft mit.
Was in der Jugendhilfeeinrichtung passiert sein soll
Ein Mann soll bei einem Gespräch in der Mutter-Kind-Einrichtung westlich von Hamburg vier Frauen und zwei Männer getötet haben. „Der Schütze hatte während eines Gesprächs in der Jugendhilfeeinrichtung plötzlich mit einer mitgebrachten halbautomatischen Pistole auf die anwesenden Mitarbeiter geschossen“, teilt die Staatsanwaltschaft mit.
Drei Opfer arbeiteten in der Einrichtung. Bei den anderen handelte es sich um Beschäftigte des Jugendamts der Region Hannover, die nur für das Gespräch nach Stade gefahren waren. Nach der Tat stieg der 45-Jährige als Beifahrer in ein Auto und flüchtete. Die Polizei verfolgte den Wagen und feuerte Schüsse ab. Sie nahmen den Schützen und die Fahrerin fest.
Der 45-Jährige kam nach seiner Festnahme in Untersuchungshaft. Drei Wochen später, am 21. Juli, fand ihn ein Mitarbeiter der Justizvollzugsanstalt Bremervörde tot in seiner Zelle. Die Ermittlungen gegen den mutmaßlichen Schützen wurden daraufhin eingestellt.
Die Ermittler gehen nach früheren Angaben davon aus, dass ein Streit um das Sorgerecht das Motiv für die Tat war. Den Eltern war das Sorgerecht entzogen worden, weil ihr drei Monate altes Baby eine Hirnblutung hatte. Ärzte vermuteten ein Schütteltrauma, ein Gutachten bestätigte später die Diagnose. Ein Gericht entschied daraufhin, dass die Mutter mit ihrem Kind in der Stader Einrichtung leben soll. Beide Eltern gingen juristisch dagegen vor.
Welche Rolle spielten die Frauen?
Die Staatsanwaltschaft nimmt an, dass die Partnerin des mutmaßlichen Schützen in dessen Pläne eingeweiht war. Die 34-Jährige mit türkischer Staatsangehörigkeit soll „von den Absichten des mutmaßlichen Täters gewusst, sein Motiv geteilt und ihn sowohl bei der Vorbereitung als auch während der Tat aktiv unterstützt zu haben“, teilten die Ermittler mit.
Auch die Fahrerin des Fluchtwagens soll vorab im Bilde gewesen sein. Die Staatsanwaltschaft wirft der 65-jährigen Deutschen vor, den Mann bei der Vorbereitung unterstützt und anschließend mit einem Auto vom Tatort weggebracht zu haben. Die Ermittler werten das als Beihilfe zum Mord in sechs Fällen. Nach Angaben der Staatsanwaltschaft befinden sich beide Frauen weiter auf freiem Fuß, Haftbefehle gegen sie liegen momentan nicht vor.
Auch mutmaßlicher Waffenverkäufer angeklagt
Die Staatsanwaltschaft klagt nach eigenen Angaben auch den mutmaßlichen Verkäufer der Tatwaffe an. Der Mann wurde bereits Ende August festgenommen und sitzt seitdem in Untersuchungshaft.
Demnach soll ein 49 Jahre alter Kioskbesitzer aus Berlin dem späteren Schützen wenige Tage vor der Tat sowohl die Pistole als auch 21 Schuss Munition verkauft haben. „Aufgrund der näheren Umstände des Kaufes musste er davon ausgehen, dass mit der Waffe zeitnah auf Menschen geschossen werden würde“, teilt die Staatsanwaltschaft weiter mit.
Die Behörde wirft dem Mann deshalb vor, durch den Waffenverkauf zu dem Tod der sechs Menschen beigetragen zu haben. Auch unerlaubter Waffenbesitz und Waffenhandel werden dem 49-Jährigen zusätzlich vorgeworfen.
Wie es nun weitergeht
Beide Verfahren sollen nach dem Willen der Staatsanwaltschaft miteinander verbunden werden. Die Schwurgerichtskammer am Landgericht Stade muss nun über die Eröffnung des Verfahrens entscheiden. Bis zu einer Verurteilung gilt die Unschuldsvermutung.

Olá! Mesmo derrotado nas urnas, o mercado quer ficar com a picanha.
.Papagaiada. O giro de Lula pelo exterior foi ofuscado pela pauta monotemática do mercado nos jornalões brasileiros. Enquanto a população afiança o projeto vencedor nas urnas, com a defesa de políticas públicas como o fim da escala 6×1, valorização do salário mínimo e isenção de tributos sobre a cesta básica, o que se refletiu no aumento da aprovação do governo e no otimismo em relação ao futuro, o mercado repete a ladainha do ajuste fiscal. A novidade é a reação do Planalto. Depois de tergiversar, o governo acabou cedendo para a gritaria do mercado, com uma proposta paliativa feita pelo senador Jaques Wagner em dobradinha com o ministro do Planejamento, Bruno Moretti. A promessa é economizar até R$ 60 bilhões em 2027, focando no corte de isenções fiscais concedidas a grandes empresas e altos salários, preservando o orçamento destinado às políticas públicas. Porém, o projeto também limita o uso do imposto extraordinário sobre o petróleo, o que pode ter impacto futuro sobre o piso da saúde. O problema é que, abusando da malandragem, a proposta não agradou nem ao mercado, que pede cortes de gastos e não aumento na arrecadação, nem à esquerda, que desconfia que as medidas possam comprometer as despesas obrigatórias, as políticas sociais e o programa do governo eleito nas urnas. Além disso, a medida chega exatamente no momento em que os dados sobre a inflação desmentem o terrorismo econômico de Gabriel Galípolo de que há aumento de risco, possibilidade de choque cambial duradouro e escalada inflacionária. Ao contrário, o IPCA de outubro ficou abaixo das expectativas do mercado, desmentindo os argumentos do Banco Central e mostrando que o aumento da Selic definido na última reunião do Copom contraria a vida real da economia brasileira.
.Reorganizando a casa. Os impasses do novo governo vão além da política econômica e incluem também o cenário internacional e as relações com o Congresso. No exterior, por ora, Lula pode comemorar um clima de coexistência pacífica com os Estados Unidos depois da derrota dos Republicanos nas eleições legislativas. A ida do presidente brasileiro para a COP 31 na Turquia foi a primeira viagem internacional após as eleições de outubro. Conforme o esperado, ao tratar da questão climática, Lula reiterou as críticas aos países ricos e a defesa de mecanismos de equidade; também reafirmou a liderança de Marina Silva em relação ao tema; e o governo brasileiro pôde apresentar resultados positivos, como a diminuição do desmatamento na Amazônia e a significativa redução da emissão de gases de efeito estufa. Dentro de casa, no entanto, a situação é mais complexa. Além dos privilégios concedidos pelo governo federal ao agronegócio — um dos grandes responsáveis pela destruição ambiental e para quem nunca há corte de gastos. Enquanto isso, o governo de São Paulo se tornou o bastião do negacionismo ambiental: Tarcísio de Freitas indicou como seu secretário da Justiça nada mais, nada menos que Ricardo Salles, o homem da boiada, ex-ministro do Meio Ambiente de Bolsonaro e atualmente réu por contrabando de madeira. A boa notícia é que a direita está com dificuldades de se reorganizar depois da derrota e fuga de Flávio Bolsonaro. A pretensão do PL de comandar a Câmara e o Senado esbarram nas discordâncias internas. Já o Planalto trabalha para constituir sua própria base parlamentar para os próximos quatro anos. O primeiro passo deve ser a escolha dos ministros que, por enquanto, está a cargo do senador Camilo Santana e do presidente do PT, Edinho Silva. Lula, no entanto, não quer repetir o mesmo erro de entregar cargos sem receber a contrapartida de apoio parlamentar, especialmente na relação com o centrão e a direita, como o MDB, o PSD e o União Brasil.
.Velhos problemas. Não é só o Planalto que passa por mudanças. Por motivos diferentes, os outros poderes também precisam pôr a casa em ordem e resolver suas pendências. Especialmente o STF, em que uma toalhinha esconde um elefante chamado Master na sala. Depois de sete anos, Edson Fachin finalmente encerrou e arquivou o esdrúxulo inquérito das fake news, no qual o STF era investigador e juiz. Necessário, mas pouco efetivo para resolver o verdadeiro problema, que são quatro ministros com relações pouco republicanas com um banqueiro preso. Além de estar longe de ser resolvida na Corte, a crise respinga e dá combustível para outro conflito, desta vez na Polícia Federal. No centro, estão as divergências no relatório sobre o envolvimento dos ministros no caso Master, solicitado por Fachin, que levaram ao afastamento dos dois delegados responsáveis. O diretor-geral Andrei Rodrigues ainda pediu sua desfiliação da Associação Nacional de Delegados, acusando a entidade de servir ao bolsonarismo. A disputa ocorre justamente quando a Polícia Federal começa a tratar dos assuntos pendentes da eleição, como a suspeita de financiamento internacional na campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro, as ameaças aos povos indígenas durante a eleição e a prisão de um servidor do STJ, suspeito de vazar informações para o sócio de Flávio, Willer Tomaz. Aliás, só agora o TSE decidiu multar a Meta/Facebook pelas irregularidades cometidas. O descumprimento de decisões judiciais durante cinco dias da última semana de eleição ficou pela bagatela de R$ 7,5 milhões. No Congresso, ainda que as pautas do governo estejam andando, como a prorrogação da proibição da Bets, isso não significa que o cenário seja mais tranquilo. Numa amostra do que devem ser os próximos quatro anos, os parlamentares, atendendo aos empresários, tentam adiar a adoção da reforma tributária, tentando postergar os novos impostos, assim como o fim da escala 6×1. Enquanto isso, não se sabe qual será o destino da proposta de reforma eleitoral, desengavetada às pressas para instituir o voto distrital misto, e da redução da maioridade penal, temas sem consenso no plenário do Congresso.

https://gothamist.com/news/new-york-city.title: New York City wind and rain make way for a cool and cloudy weekend
https://gothamist.com/news/new-york-city.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/new-york-city.text:
New York City will see a cold and gloomy end to the week, with wet and blustery weather expected to continue through much of Friday.
According to the National Weather Service, rain is expected to keep falling until Friday evening — though not with the same intensity as Thursday’s storms, which mainly affected parts of Brooklyn and Queens.
“We actually did have multiple reports of flash flooding in Southern Queens, with that thunderstorm that kept kind of training over the area for a couple of hours,” said meteorologist Matt Wunsch. “With that, JFK [airport] actually saw their second wettest day in November on record, with just over three and a half inches of rainfall for the day.”
Wunsch said a tornado warning went into effect at one point, though by the end of the day he said there were no reports of a tornado materializing anywhere in the five boroughs.
Though gusty winds are expected to persist throughout much of Friday — especially out at sea, where a gale force wind warning is in place — Wunsch said the forecast is looking less volatile than Thursday. He said snow is not likely.
“We should still see on-and-off rain pretty much through the day; anywhere from another quarter to a half an inch of rainfall is possible across the entire city, before the rain starts to kind of taper off as we get into the overnight tonight,” he said.
Temperatures will only reach the low to mid-40s, which is a lot chillier than the last several days.
The air will stay cool into Saturday and Sunday, with highs in the low-to-upper 40s, Wunsch said. Skies are expected to be dry with a mix of sun and clouds.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Exhibition explores how the fisherman-turned-artist Alfred Wallis inspired leading British artists
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Maev Kennedy
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Pallant House Gallery in Chichester, southern England, does not own any paintings by the self-taught Cornish artist Alfred Wallis (1855-1942). But it does own many works by the early 20th-century artists who were heavily influenced by the former fisherman and rag-and-bone merchant, who first took up painting with pots of house paint and sheets of cardboard as a lonely widower aged 70.
Alfred Wallis: an Artists’ Artist gathers together works by Wallis and by artists who visited, lived in or worked in St Ives, including Barbara Hepworth, Peter Lanyon, Margaret Mellis, Adrian Stokes, John Wells, Wilhelmina Barns-Graham, Ben and Winifred Nicholson and Christopher Wood. It was Ben Nicholson and Wood who first befriended Wallis in 1928 when they peered in astonishment into his tiny dark cottage stuffed with paintings.
Many of the Wallis paintings—of tilted houses and harbours, ships and stormy seas, under lowering grey skies—originally acquired as gifts or bought for a few shillings, are now being borrowed from private collections and museums including the Tate, Kettle’s Yard in Cambridge and Aberdeen Art Gallery. A private collector is loaning a unique collaborative work: a half-finished view of a Brittany quayside by Christopher Wood, which Wood gave to Wallis who then completed it.
A record price of £184,000 was set at a Christie’s auction last year for a work by Wallis, who once said to a buyer: “gimme what you like for ’em”. Ben Nicholson, barely earning himself and with a young family, bought his first Wallis painting for half a crown; Wallis once sent a bundle of paintings to the collector and curator Jim Ede for ten shillings. When the artist died in 1942, a roll of uncashed postal orders was found on his mantelpiece. He was only saved from a pauper’s grave by the St Ives artists.
The exhibition is curated by James Scott, an orthopaedic surgeon, who first discovered Wallis when, as a bored medical student, he spent days in Sotheby’s auction rooms, watching sales and afterwards tracing the buyers out of curiosity.
Scott insists there was neither condescension nor exploitation in the relationship between Wallis and Nicholson and the other art school educated artists. Hepworth wrote that Wallis never knew “how much we all learnt from him”.
The St Ives artists “discovered him when they were looking for a new direction, experimenting with a restricted palette and flattened picture plane,” Scott says, “and they found he was already doing it and doing it better.” Wallis learned nothing from them, continuing his own unmistakable style until weeks before his death.
Scott treasures two works by Wallis. “I’ve often thought maybe the time has come to sell them, and then I come downstairs and see them on the wall and think no, I can’t, I love them more and more.”
• Alfred Wallis: an Artists’ Artist, Pallant House Gallery, Chichester, 21 November-2 May 2027; Penlee House, Penzance, 15 May 2027-9 October 2027

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Who Will Lead the New Congress?
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Robert L. Borosage
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Who Will Lead the New Congress? Van Hollen vs. Schumer
Can the bluenami clean its own house?
A stunning realigning election. Previously unimaginable Democratic majorities in both the House and Senate. Stark repudiation of Trump and his Republican enablers and a loud demand for dramatic change. Every swath of voters moved left. Economic populism drove the debate. Democrats won across the country. Hell, Texas went blue top to bottom. And Mississippi, goddamn.
Donald Trump is visibly discombobulated by the rout. But beneath him, MAGA is girding for war. The loathsome Stephen Miller has been named chief of staff. Russell Vought is arming OMB to control the power of the purse. House Republicans chose the MAGA zealot Jim Jordan as their leader. Their gloves are off.
So, who will lead the newly empowered Democrats for the next two years? Who can galvanize the new majorities, lay out a bold vision, champion aggressive reforms, and drive the battle against Trump and the MAGA remnants?
Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries?
Really? It is hard to conjure up a pair less suited for the time. Both are cautious and compromised, more comfortable plotting tactical retreats than launching full-force offensives. Both are wooden speakers. Both are too close to Wall Street, to Big Tech, to Israel and AIPAC. Both are practitioners of small-bore, big-money politics, not populist insurgencies.
In revealing ways, both have already failed the moment. As House Democratic leader, Jeffries could have crystallized the insurgency. The head of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, Greg Casar, presented it to him on a plate. Last April, the CPC put out a 10-point affordability agenda of popular reforms that could unite Democrats. Jeffries could have imitated Newt Gingrich when he led Republicans to capture Congress for the first time in 40 years against Bill Clinton. Put out a clear platform, line up 300 candidates to commit to passing it in the first 100 days. Democrats would now be armed with a clear mandate to move from the get-go, so they wouldn’t end up enmeshed in investigating Trump’s crimes while they cast about for positive reforms. Jeffries chose to set up “working groups” instead.
Then this week, in the lame-duck session, Jeffries demonstrated that his competence may be as questionable as his charisma. He inexplicably failed to mobilize all Democrats to show up and vote on the Hegseth impeachment resolution, giving MAGA a cheap win. A missed opportunity and a failure of basic responsibility—hardly an auspicious start.
Schumer boasts that he gave Democrats their message of “costs, corruption and chaos,” and defines that as his charge as Senate majority leader. But a message is not an agenda; alliteration is not a plan. In fact, the election victory was launched by popular mobilizations—No Kings, anti-ICE, anti-AI—and framed by the populism of the Bernie Sanders–AOC anti-oligarchy tour. With voters squeezed by Trump’s wars and rising prices, appalled by brazen corruption and big money, revolting against AI and Big Tech’s swagger, and young voters particularly appalled by the Gaza horrors, Schumer’s record lines up too often on the wrong side of the barricades.
Even as Jeffries and Schumer basked in the victory, a revolt against their ascension was brewing. Indivisible and other organizers of the No Kings demonstrations inundated congressional offices with calls for new leadership. A Change.org petition against Jeffries has garnered over a million signatures since its launch in September. The International Association of Machinists (IAM) called for Schumer to step aside. But in both the House and Senate, the deck is stacked against change.
Jeffries
Of the two, Jeffries is the more structurally vulnerable and the more politically secure. To be elected speaker of the House requires a majority vote of the entire House. Despite the remarkable Democratic Party margin, the active base of the 110-plus members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus could in theory join the unified Republican opposition to block his candidacy.
But there is no alternative candidate—and Democrats will choose their leader and candidate for speaker next Tuesday. Few Democrats will want to usher in a new era by defeating their own candidate for speaker.
Also, Jeffries would be the first African American speaker of the House, a milestone that many will be reluctant to oppose, particularly in the face of Trump’s race-baiting politics. Add to that the support any Democratic leader garners by raising funds for candidates and the power the leader has to punish insurgents by denying them prized committee assignments, threatening them with ostracism and more—and Jeffries’s election is assured. Even a former vocal opponent, Representative-elect Will Lawrence, cofounder of the Sunrise Movement and former member of the Democratic Socialists of America, now plans to vote for Jeffries. The CPC’s leadership is focused on defining reform priorities, not on leading a coup attempt.
Schumer
Schumer, in contrast, is more structurally secure and more politically vulnerable. He only must win a majority of the Democratic caucus to become Senate majority leader. Most of the caucus are incumbents who weren’t even up for reelection this year.
Schumer confidently predicted victory: “I’ll be reelected as majority leader,” claiming he had the votes in hand. Turns out that may be only another indication of how removed he is from the moment.
From Maine to Texas, the newly elected senators—El-Sayed of Michigan, Talarico of Texas, Hamilton of Kansas, Andrews of South Carolina, Stratton of Illinois, Pappas of New Hampshire, Flanagan of Minnesota, and Jackson of Maine—declared they were not ready to commit to Schumer.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Then, in a stunning press conference, Bernie Sanders, the populist independent who caucuses with Democrats, joined with Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin, an ambitious centrist Democrat, to announce that they wanted a full debate before a leader was chosen. Sanders said it was “time for a change,” and that he was a “no” on Schumer. Slotkin called for a debate, saying that this wasn’t about left or right, but a choice between “team fight vs. team flight,” intimating that Schumer was on the wrong team. “You can’t lead people,” she said, “if you can’t lay out where you’re going.”
Then, after canvassing many members, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced he would run for majority leader. The election, he declared, “wasn’t only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption, and his wars and his cruelty.” It was also a call to “take on a broken economic system that’s rigged in favor of the very wealthy against working people.… The call was to reject…business as usual, and to do that, I think we need new leadership.”
Van Hollen, a respected progressive, earned acclaim for his courageous opposition to ICE and its criminal wilding, and his demand that the US stop arming and abetting Israel’s military, given the horrors in Gaza. Sanders and Abdul El-Sayed, the newly elected senator from Michigan, immediately voiced their support for Van Hollen.
Although even Van Hollen recognizes that Schumer at this point is still the odds-on favorite, a serious challenge is assured. Whatever the outcome, the contest will have important effects. Van Hollen will drive commitments from the caucus on bold reforms. Both party posts beneath Schumer in the Senate—the party whip and the chair of the steering and policy committee—are open. Long-overdue changes in caucus planning, coordination, and communication strategy might also open new positions. Van Hollen’s challenge will open the way for new leaders from the younger generation to emerge.
The press tends to dismiss the leadership fights as either destructive or a distraction. In fact, this is a direct product of the transformative election. A new generation of economic populists has been elected. They don’t outnumber the centrists yet, but the incumbents have been put on notice. If real change is to come, activists must continue to ratchet up pressure on legislators. The challenge to Schumer lays down a marker: Business as usual will no longer be acceptable.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120386.title: Infektionskrankheiten | Streit um die »Hoffnung« in der Ebola-Epidemie
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120386.author: Kurt Stenger
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120386.text:
- Wirtschaft und Umwelt
- Infektionskrankheiten
Streit um die »Hoffnung« in der Ebola-Epidemie
Die WHO lässt in der DR Kongo drei Impfstoffe auf ihre Wirksamkeit gegen das Bundibugyo-Virus testen. Nicht alle sind glücklich über das Verfahren.
Tumaini bedeutet auf Swahili Hoffnung. Seit einigen Wochen hat das Wort aus der in Ostafrika weitverbreiteten Sprache, die auch eine der Amtssprachen in der Demokratischen Republik (DR) Kongo ist, eine weitere Bedeutung: So heißt die von der Weltgesundheitsorganisation (WHO) Ende Oktober gestartete Plattformstudie, um zu testen, ob Impfstoffe sicher und wirksam gegen das im Land grassierende Bundibugyo-Ebola-Virus sind. Der Vorteil: Dank bestehender Infrastruktur können verschiedene Vakzine gleichzeitig getestet werden. Die Zeit drängt, denn die Zahlen steigen von Woche zu Woche ungebremst weiter, während auch noch zwei weitere Länder erste Fälle gemeldet haben.
Mit dem schweren Ausbruch in der DR Kongo wurde die internationale Gemeinschaft auf dem falschen Fuß erwischt. Zwar rief die WHO im Mai die internationale Gesundheitsnotlage aus, doch es gab weder Medikamente und Diagnostik noch Impfstoffe gegen Bundibugyo. Dabei hat dieses Virus schon vor fast 20 Jahren für einen Ausbruch gesorgt. Zur Verfügung stand aber lediglich das 2019 für die Zaire-Variante des Ebola-Erregers zugelassene Vakzin Ervebo des US-Pharmakonzerns Merck, mit dem zwei Jahre später eine globale Notfallreserve etabliert wurde, die eine Koordinierungsgruppe unter dem Dach der WHO verwaltet. 336.000 Dosen sind hier gelagert.
Nun endlich sind Tests gestartet. Geleitet wird Tumaini vom Institut National de Recherche Biomedicale in der Hauptstadt Kinshasa und der Uni Antwerpen, beteiligt sind neben der WHO unter anderem die Afrikanische Union und Ärzte ohne Grenzen. Los ging es mit Ervebo. Tierversuche und Labortests hatten bei dem Lebendimpfstoff auf Vektorbasis erste Hinweise gebracht, dass er womöglich einen Kreuzschutz mit Bundibugyo bieten könnte.
Kontrovers diskutiertes Studiendesign
Bei Tumaini handelt es sich um eine kombinierte Phase-2 und -3-Studie, für die insgesamt 20.000 Ervebo-Dosen bereitstehen. Getestet werden also sowohl Nebenwirkungen und die richtige Dosis als auch die Wirksamkeit. Probanden sollen ermittelte Kontaktpersonen Infizierter sein. Vorgesehen ist, dass eine Gruppe sofort eine Dosis bekommt, Menschen aus der Kontrollgruppe erst ein Placebo (einen Typhus-Impfstoff) und am 29. Tag ebenfalls eine Dosis Ervebo. »Es ist das ethischste Studiendesign, das möglich ist – jeder, der daran teilnimmt, erhält einen Impfstoffkandidaten gegen das Bundibugyo-Virus«, sagt Ko-Leiter Jean-Pierre Van Geertruyden. Mit ersten Ergebnissen wird nicht vor Anfang 2027 gerechnet.
Das Studiendesign wird allerdings unter Fachleuten kontrovers diskutiert. Vor allem angesichts des akuten Bedarfs: Allein in der Provinz Ituri, dem eigentlichen Epizentrum, leben mehr als vier Millionen Menschen. Mittlerweile betroffen sind aber sogar 66 Gesundheitszentren in acht Provinzen des riesigen zentralafrikanischen Landes. »Wir sprechen aktuell von Dutzenden einzelner Ausbrüche«, sagt Daniel Bausch, Experte für Tropenmedizin und globale Gesundheit.
Die Regierung der DR Kongo hat daher gefordert, Ervebo auch ohne klinische Tests für reguläre Impfkampagnen freizugeben. Auch Hilfsorganisationen fordern eine schnellere Reaktion, da der Impfstoff sicher sei. Ihn jenseits der Studie zurückzuhalten, sei fahrlässig.
Die WHO lehnt das ab: Eine Beratergruppe erklärte, nach jetzigem Erkenntnisstand sei eventuell ein Schutz vor tödlichem Verlauf möglich, nicht aber vor Erkrankung und Übertragung. Eine Massenimpfung könnte erhebliche negative Folgen für das ohnehin schwache Gesundheitssystem in den betroffenen Gebieten haben. Eine Impfung mit einem Vakzin, das sich als möglicherweise unwirksam herausstellt, könnte zudem leichtsinniges Verhalten auslösen und am Ende nur die ohnehin bestehende Impfskepsis vor Ort weiter schüren. »Derzeit läuft alles gut – die Menschen wollen geimpft werden«, plädiert Geertruyden für das strenge Studiendesign. »Wir müssen dafür sorgen, dass wir diese Dynamik aufrechterhalten.« Die WHO trägt dem Druck aber insofern Rechnung, als zusätzlich 50.000 Dosen außerhalb der Studie für das medizinische Personal vorgesehen sind.
Nichtsdestotrotz haben Ärzte ohne Grenzen (MSF), die in allen Gegenden mit besonders hohen Übertragungsraten aktiv sind, im September eine eigene Studie namens »Bundibugyo: Répondre Avec la Vaccination« (BRAVO) gestartet: Bei dieser »Antwort mit Impfung« werden in Zusammenarbeit mit lokalen Partnern bis zu 20.000 Gesundheitsmitarbeiter geimpft. Kommt es in den Behandlungszentren später zu Ebola-Symptomen beim medizinischen Personal, wird über den PCR-Status (positiv vs. negativ) und den dokumentierten Impfstatus die tatsächliche Wirksamkeit ermittelt. MSF geht es mit diesem »test-negativen Design« weniger um eine saubere wissenschaftliche Studie als um schnellen Schutz für das gefährdete medizinische Personal »an der Front«. Bravo werde »Erkenntnisse aus der Praxis darüber liefern, ob Ervebo vor durch das Bundibugyo-Virus verursachten Erkrankungen und Todesfällen schützt«, so die NGO.
Gleichzeitig warnt Ärzte ohne Grenzen vor Produktionsengpässen bei Ervebo: Merck müsse »alle in den kommenden Monaten produzierten Dosen dem globalen Impfstoffvorrat zur Verfügung stellen«., fordert Julien Potet, MSF-Experte für den Zugang zu Impfstoffen. Gleichzeitig sollten Länder mit hohem Einkommen darauf verzichten, Dosen über ihren unmittelbaren Bedarf für den öffentlichen Gesundheitsschutz hinaus zu reservieren. Und angesichts der beträchtlichen öffentlichen Mittel, die für die Entwicklung von bundibugyo-spezifischen Impfstoffen bereitgestellt werden, müssten diese für alle Bevölkerungsgruppen, die von Ausbrüchen betroffen sind, »zugänglich und erschwinglich gemacht« werden.
Tatsächlich setzten bei internationalen Organisationen nach Ausrufung der Gesundheitsnotlage hektische Aktivitäten ein. So investierte die »Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations« mehrere zehn Millionen US-Dollar in eine schnelle Impfstoffforschung und -entwicklung. Die Impfstoffallianz Gavi wiederum stellte 50 Millionen US-Dollar unter anderem für die Ausweitung der Produktion bereit.
Mindestens vier Impfstoffe speziell für Bundibugyo sind aktuell in der Pipeline, zwei von ihnen wurden vor wenigen in die Tumaini-Studie aufgenommen: Ein von der Universität Oxford gemeinsam mit dem Serum Institute of India entwickeltes Vakzin, das dem Vektorimpfstoff von Astra Zeneca aus der Corona-Zeit ähnelt, und ein mRNA-Impfstoff der US-Firma Moderna. »Ein Problem ist, dass eher Monate als Wochen vergehen, bis Phase-I-Daten vorliegen, Impfdosen produziert sind und die Impfstoffe in die Studie aufgenommen werden können«, erklärt Jürgen May, Vorstandsvorsitzender des Bernhard-Nocht-Instituts für Tropenmedizin in Hamburg. »Ein breiter Einsatz im aktuellen Ausbruch ist kaum früher als Mitte 2027 realistisch. Im besten Fall stehen sie für künftige Ausbrüche bereit.« Die Hersteller ließen verlauten, sie könnten jeweils rund eine halbe Million Dosen kostengünstig bereitstellen.
Die Strategie lautet Ringimpfungen
Bei Ebola werden nicht alle Menschen in einer Region prophylaktisch geimpft. Bewährt haben wie bei Mpox sich sogenannte Ringimpfungen von Kontaktpersonen Infizierter und deren Kontaktpersonen. Eigentlich sind Ebola-Ausbrüche auch ohne Impfstoffe beendbar, wie seinerzeit bei der Epidemie in Westafrika 2013-15: mit einem wirksamen System der Kontaktnachverfolgung. Das Virus hat zwar eine extrem hohe Todesrate – sie liegt im Kongo derzeit bei etwa 50 Prozent –, aber es verbreitet sich nicht über die Luft, sondern nur durch direkten Kontakt mit Körperflüssigkeiten Infizierter.
Allerdings funktioniert die Nachverfolgung derzeit maximal zu 80 Prozent, wie aus dem Kongo berichtet wird. Und ein Großteil neuer Fälle stammt aus gänzlich unbekannten Übertragungsketten. Dafür gibt es vielerlei Gründe: bewaffnete Konflikte mit zahlreichen Milizen, die zum Teil große Mobilität der Bevölkerung und das schwach ausgestattete Gesundheitswesen. Viele meiden auch Gesundheitsstationen aus Furcht vor Ansteckung. Das alles ist gleichzeitig auch ein Nachteil beim Einsatz von Vakzinen.
Das muss auch WHO-Generaldirektor Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus einräumen, auch wenn er die neuen Vakzine als »Beweis für die Kraft der Wissenschaft und der Zusammenarbeit« bezeichnet. »Impfstoffe allein werden diesen Ausbruch nicht beenden«, sagt Tedros, »aber sie könnten zu einem wirkungsvollen neuen Instrument werden, um ihn unter Kontrolle zu bringen«. Insofern ist die mit der Tumaimi-Studie verbundene Hoffnung wohl eher ein Hoffnungsschimmer.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.
