The Class War Midterms
The legacy of Bernie Sanders’ presidential runs was on full display in Democrats’ titanic midterm election results. The message from voters is clear: deliver on economic populism.
Miles Kampf-Lassin
The day after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) released a video that encapsulated the left electoral movement he helped bring to life.
Set to David Bowie’s iconic song “Starman,” the video shows Sanders clasping hands with many of the candidates he endorsed this cycle. Not only did Sens.-elect Adbul El-Sayed (D-Mich.), Troy Jackson (D-Maine) and Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) — along with more than 50 U.S. House and downballot victors backed by Sanders — win their races, they were instrumental in delivering Democrats’ sweeping tidal wave in this year’s midterms.
Far more than just a flex, the video served as a reminder of how deeply Sanders — the iconoclast democratic socialist leader — has transformed U.S. politics over the past decade. After more than 30 years of shouting his message from the sidelines, Sanders’ call to take on the billionaire class, tackle wealth inequality and guarantee universal healthcare is now the incandescent core of a new economic populism that is redefining how candidates run and govern.
The incoming class of Sanders disciples — along with a legion of newly minted winners who embraced key aspects of his platform — will hold greater sway in Congress than progressives have seen in a lifetime. Democrats took back control of both the House of Representatives and Senate in dramatic fashion, with a mandate to turn the page on Trumpism and enact an agenda squarely focused on uplifting the working class. 
For President Donald Trump and Republicans, the outcome was ruinous. As Ryan Grim of Dropsite News pointed out, it turns out starting an illegal war in Iran that drives up gas prices while covering up a child sex predator ring and engaging in never-before-seen levels of corruption is not a successful gameplan for retaining power — especially when you promised during your campaign to end foreign wars and bring consumer prices down.
But that’s not all voters were furious about. Sending armed gestapo-like forces into cities to kidnap and kill U.S. residents shocked the country and led to a nationwide resistance movement that coalesced labor and grassroots organizations. The colossal buildout of data centers in communities across the country, along with the unchecked development of artificial intelligence (AI) by hyperrich tech oligarchs on a mission to rule over our lives, sparked widespread anger and opposition. And voters are reeling from the impact of a full-scale war on working people — epitomized by the GOP’s “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which is ripping away lifesaving food and healthcare programs to enrich the wealthiest Americans and supercharge Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
Trump made this all possible, and his party paid the price.
But now the real fight begins. There is a push and pull between every election, with the party in power losing seats and the other gaining, until the cycle repeats itself. The only way out of continuing this historical trend is for Democrats to use their newfound leverage to make clear they’re unafraid to bring about real fundamental change.
When it comes to bringing legislation to the floor, as Democrats will be able to do in both houses of Congress next year, Sanders’ policy program is a good place to start. The majority of Americans support Medicare for All, a billionaire wealth tax, expanded Social Security, a $20 per hour minimum wage, a national data center moratorium, free public college, enhanced union rights and an end to U.S. military aid to Israel.
Even if Republicans try to block such attempts, or President Trump promises to veto them, showcasing Democratic backing of these massively popular measures would help polarize the country and show which party is actually out of step with what Americans want from the government. As Sanders told MS NOW’s Chris Hayes two days after the midterms: “Our job is to be bold. Trump wants to veto stuff? It’s his privilege. We’ve got to distinguish ourselves from the Republicans.”
The emphasis on corporate greed and a rigged economic system has trickled down from Sanders to all levels of Democratic politicians. In his victory speech, Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) said, “We just sent a message to every billionaire megadonor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system: in this state, in this country, power belongs to the people.” That wasn’t simply a winning message — Talarico smoked his Republican opponent by 12 points in a state where a Democrat hadn’t won a Senate seat since 1988.
Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-endorsed candidates also had a historic showing, with more than 50 scoring wins up and down the ballot. That includes newly-elected members of Congress Claire Valdez (D-N.Y.), Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-N.Y.), Chris Rabb (D-Penn.), Donavan McKinney (D-Mich.), Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) and Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif). They’ll join fellow DSA members Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.), taking the total number of socialists in the House up to eight — the most in U.S. history.
And this new crop of socialists is following the path being laid by New York City Zohran Mamdani, a DSA member who has helped reorient the Democratic Party around a politics of affordability. Following the results, Mamdani told reporters that voters gave Democrats “a mandate to lower the cost of living, to build not bomb, to never betray the working people who entrusted them with power.” 
But taking bold action will require real leadership, something elites in the party establishment have shown themselves unwilling (or unable) to adopt. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), in line to become House Speaker and Senate Leader, respectively, have both expressed caution about moving too fast or putting forward bills that could be considered too ambitious, including Medicare for All.
At least seven incoming Democratic senators have so far refused to commit to supporting Schumer in the upcoming leadership vote, and even incumbent Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) told Bloomberg, “no one should be committing to anybody as the next Democratic leader” unless they put forward a plan to enact an aggressive progressive agenda, adding: “we need commitments.”
With the incoming Democratic House caucus swelling to more than 250, socialists and left-wing members will hold less sway than if there had been a narrower margin, yet that shouldn’t impact the urgency of demanding the party take a fighting approach that shows which side it stands on. The donor class set aflame billions of dollars over the midterms and still couldn’t blunt voters’ hunger for a break from the status quo.
The pro-corporate Third Way set is already calling for Democrats to rush to the center, but it’s clear that class war-style populism came out on top this election — and points the way forward to building a durable coalition that can replace the failed authoritarian old guard clinging to power in the White House.
It will take a revitalized labor movement and energetic, broad-based grassroots organizing — not just more sympathetic elected officials — to steer U.S. politics in the direction of working people’s interests. But there’s no doubt the terrain has moved in favor of such a shift.
While Sanders didn’t win when he ran for president, he inspired a generation that’s now taking power. Let’s not blow it — he’s proven, as Bowie sang, that he knows it’s all worthwhile.

                            Ces outils nous permettent de recueillir des statistiques de fréquentation du site et de l’application mobile pour comprendre les usages, détecter d’éventuels problèmes et optimiser l’ergonomie de nos produits.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Batch (uniquement sur le site web) : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- CrazyEggs (uniquement sur le site web) : analyse de parcours client.
- Nonli (uniquement sur le site web) : permet à notre équipe des réseaux sociaux de publier les contenus Mediapart sur les réseaux sociaux.
- Piano : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- Qiota (uniquement sur le site web) : gestion du système de datawall.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Il n’y a pas de publicité sur Mediapart. Mais nous faisons la promotion de nos contenus et services sur d’autres sites et réseaux sociaux. Pour cela, nous utilisons les technologies mises à disposition par certains acteurs publicitaires.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :

                            Nous utilisons le service Qiota d’Opper Marketing Suite pour configurer l’activation d’un datawall sur certains de nos contenus (uniquement sur le site web). Ce dispositif destiné aux utilisateur·ices non abonné·es requiert la saisie d’une adresse email pour accéder aux contenus concernés. En fournissant cette information, l’utilisateur consent à sa collecte, son stockage et son utilisation à des fins statistiques. https://taz.de/Juedisches-Leben-in-Deuts.title: Jüdisches Leben in Deutschland: Hasspost mit Pulver zwingt Gießener Synagoge zur Räumung
https://taz.de/Juedisches-Leben-in-Deuts.text:
Jüdisches Leben in Deutschland: Hasspost mit Pulver zwingt Gießener Synagoge zur Räumung
Ein antisemitischer Drohbrief mit unbekanntem Pulver hat die Räumung der Gießener Synagoge ausgelöst. Immerhin steht jetzt fest: Die Substanz war ungefährlich.
dpa/kna | Der Fund eines verdächtigen Briefes mit antisemitischem und bedrohendem Inhalt hat am Donnerstag die Räumung der Gießener Synagoge und einen größeren Polizeieinsatz ausgelöst. Beim Öffnen des Briefes war am Mittag ein bislang unbekanntes Pulver freigesetzt worden, teilte die Polizei mit. Sie hob die weiträumigen Sperrungen am späten Nachmittag wieder auf, doch blieb die Synagoge selbst nach Angaben einer Polizeisprecherin zunächst weiter gesperrt.
Am Freitag wurde dann klar: Das Pulver aus dem Drohbrief war nach Angaben der Ermittler weder gefährlich noch giftig. Die Substanz sei im Handel frei erhältlich, teilten das hessische Landeskriminalamt und die Staatsanwaltschaft Gießen mit.
Zu der Substanz und zu den Inhalten des handschriftlich verfassten antisemitischen Drohschreibens wollten die Behörden aus ermittlungstaktischen Gründen aber keine weiteren Angaben machen.
Zum Zeitpunkt des Vorfalls befanden sich 26 Personen in der Synagoge. Sie wurden vorsorglich ins Freie geleitet. Vier Menschen hielten sich beim Öffnen des Briefes in unmittelbarer Nähe auf. Rettungskräfte untersuchten sie vor Ort, eine ärztliche Behandlung war nicht nötig.
„Die weiteren Ermittlungen werden intensiv geführt, um den oder die bislang unbekannten Täter zu identifizieren und die Hintergründe des Geschehens umfassend aufzuklären“, hieß es.
Für den Hessischen Innenminister Roman Poseck (CDU) ist der Fall sei ein weiteres erschreckendes Beispiel für die Angriffe auf jüdisches Leben. „Das ist eine Schande“, erklärte Poseck. „Wir werden weiter alles dafür tun, jüdisches Leben bei uns wirkungsvoll zu schützen.“
Eine Gefahr für die Allgemeinheit habe nicht bestanden, erklärte die Polizei. Neben Kräften des Polizeipräsidiums Mittelhessen waren auch Angehörige der Berufsfeuerwehr sowie des Rettungsdienstes vor Ort.
Ministerpräsident Rhein kündigt „volle Härte“ an
Hessens Ministerpräsident Boris Rhein (CDU) nannte die Bedrohung der jüdischen Gemeinde und deren Synagoge „unerträglich“. „Wer Jüdinnen in Juden in unserem Land mit Hass überzieht und bedroht, wird mit voller Härte bestraft. Gut, dass unsere Polizei schnell reagiert hat.“
Der Gießener Oberbürgermeister Frank-Tilo Becher (SPD) sprach von einem niederträchtigen Akt der Bedrohung: „Wir verurteilen diese ungeheure antisemitische Tat aufs Schärfste. Wir stehen in voller Solidarität an der Seite der Gemeinde.“ Es handele sich um puren antisemitischen Hass, dem sich die Stadt mit aller Kraft entgegenstelle.
Zuvor hatte der Hessische Rundfunk (HR) über das Thema berichtet. Das Gebiet rund um die Synagoge in der Gießener Innenstadt wurde vorübergehend abgesperrt. „Die Sicherheitsvorkehrungen in diesem Kontext sind ohnehin sehr hoch“, sagte ein Polizeisprecher. „Wir nehmen solche Vorfälle sehr ernst.“
Ein Studio des HR, das sich in unmittelbarer Umgebung befindet, musste nach Angaben des öffentlich-rechtlichen Senders ebenfalls geräumt werden. Wie der HR berichtete, baute die Feuerwehr unter anderem ein Zelt zur Dekontamination auf. Darin können Einsatzkräfte, die mit Gefahrstoffen in Kontakt kommen, anschließend gereinigt werden.
Die Gießener Synagoge mitsamt Gemeindezentrum wurde nach Angaben der Jüdischen Gemeinde Gießen auf ihrer Homepage 1995 wiedereröffnet. Die Gemeinde selbst besteht seit 1978. Die Synagoge ist das jüdische Gotteshaus und zugleich religiöses wie kulturelles Zentrum.
Drohschreiben auch an Jüdische Gemeinde in Speyer
Einen möglicherweise ähnlichen Fall hatte es Mitte Oktober in Speyer in Rheinland-Pfalz gegeben. Dort war per Post ein Drohschreiben bei der Jüdischen Kultusgemeinde eingegangen. Der Verfasser drohte damit, die Synagoge in die Luft zu sprengen. In dem Brief befand sich ein Pulver, das Experten des Landeskriminalamtes nach einer Untersuchung als ungefährlich einstuften. Die Kriminalpolizei nahm Ermittlungen auf, der oder die Täter wurden bislang nicht gefunden.
Unter anderem der rheinland-pfälzische Ministerpräsident Gordon Schnieder (CDU) hatte die Drohung damals scharf verurteilt. „Der Vorfall an der Synagoge in Speyer erschüttert mich. Wer eine jüdische Gemeinde mit Hassbotschaften und Einschüchterungsversuchen bedroht, greift jüdisches Leben in unserem ganzen Land an“, sagte er im Oktober.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.title: Nossos irmãos são nordestinos — e nossos algozes também
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.author: Victor Moura
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.text:
No alto do morro, cresci observando a chegada de cruzeiros no porto do Recife e os arranha-céus em seus bairros nobres. E pensava: como podemos estar tão próximos e tão distantes ao mesmo tempo? Por que nossos irmãos, com oportunidades e recursos, parecem não se importar com a nossa dor?
Temos uma briga externa, inter-regional, pautada pela xenofobia. E isso é evidente. Faz parte de um projeto. Mas, antes dela, dentro das cidades, enfrentamos desafios ainda maiores. E quem tem a caneta na mão, pasmem, também são nordestinos.
Esta semana, ouvi gente do meu entorno falando dos sudestinos, em resposta às exibições de uma novela. Falavam de um Recife moderno, tecnológico, ao contrário do que é proposto pelos estereótipos. E como um morador de favela que virou repórter, fiquei sem reação. A galera esqueceu que o Recife está sempre entre as cidades mais desiguais do Brasil?
Vira uma defesa que, honestamente, não se sustenta a partir da realidade concreta, da literatura e dos dados públicos. No Recife, temos uma “elite” que sequer conhece a própria cidade, seus 94 bairros e 545 comunidades. E, para piorar, vive em privilégios coloniais e quer se vender como nordestino oprimido.
Minha avó, Dona Amara, migrante do Agreste pernambucano e lavadeira nos prédios dos Aflitos, me dizia que costume de casa vai à praça. A partir da sua história, pude entender como tanta gente pobre acabou sendo expulsa do centro do Recife, no pós-abolição, pela perseguição policial e demolição de mocambos. A partir da sua história, descobri que não dava para mudar o Brasil se eu não procurasse mudar, primeiro, a minha comunidade.
Sim, a cabeça pensa onde os pés pisam. Já vi pessoas influentes da capital viajarem centenas de quilômetros para visitarem o Sertão, mas que nunca tem tempo de colarem na periferia, que fica bem ao lado. Andam pela cidade, vivem em bolhas e não conversam com os trabalhadores nordestinos, não visitam os terminais integrados, escolas públicas, UPAs. Não têm qualquer noção de realidade.
E o Recife, enquanto capital mais antiga dentre as capitais nordestinas, dá aula de como fazer mal ao seu próprio povo. Seu bairrismo megalomaníaco nada mais é do que uma ferramenta de manutenção das desigualdades locais. Uma cidade onde nordestinos ricos exportaram a “democracia racial” para o Brasil.
Do que adianta ter um grande polo de inovação e tecnologia, se a internet nos espaços públicos da periferia mal funciona? Do que adianta ter a maior avenida em linha reta e sei lá das quantas, se continuamos tendo um dos piores trânsitos do Brasil? Do que adianta ter o maior polo médico do Norte-Nordeste, se precisamos acordar às quatro horas da manhã para pegar uma ficha no postinho do bairro?
Do que adianta ter o maior shopping center do planeta, se os trabalhadores do comércio popular mal conseguem se sustentar? Do que adianta ser referência na produção cultural, se nossos mestres e mestras ainda precisam viver de aluguel? Do que adianta ser a “Veneza brasileira”, se nossos rios estão morrendo e mais da metade da cidade sequer tem saneamento básico?
Precisamos arrumar a casa e fazer da proximidade um valor prioritário. Mas parece que só viramos leão quando um carioca fala mal do Nordeste.

https://gothamist.com/news/with-search-f.title: With search for victims over, NYC officials look to what caused fatal building collapse
https://gothamist.com/news/with-search-f.author: Ryan Kost, Catalina Gonella, Brittany Kriegstein, David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/with-search-f.text:
It was a mild Veterans Day afternoon, and Katie Stevens, a teacher, had the day off. She’d left her windows open to let the cool fall air into her Flatbush apartment as she did her laundry.
At about 4 p.m., she heard what sounded like a car crash. A few minutes later came the sirens and then helicopters overhead.
Just down the block, near the corner of Bedford and Flatbush Avenues, a three-story apartment building had collapsed into a lot that construction workers had been excavating for a new development. Nearly all of the building had caved into the lot, shearing off the side of the neighboring building, exposing a stairway, a closet full of clothes and a bedroom set.
As Stevens approached the scene, she found a family crying on the sidewalk: “We may need everything right now,” they told her.
In the hours that followed, more than 250 firefighters and emergency service providers responded to the scene. Construction workers who had barely escaped themselves turned back to dig victims out of the rubble, Mayor Zohran Mamdani would later say. Councilmember Farah Louis described infants and toddlers being carried out on stretchers.
By Thursday afternoon, eight people were dead, including two children, and 18 others were injured. One person remained in critical condition. The rescue operation continued as a storm soaked the area in rain. By 4 p.m just as skies were clearing again, the FDNY declared the search and rescue operation over.
City officials said they began an investigation immediately after the collapse, one of the worst such disasters in recent city history. Gothamist reported Thursday that the developer of the site had a record for cutting corners on the project, according to records from the city buildings department.
The agency had issued a stop work order at the lot during demolition of an existing one-story building in March after determining that contractors had failed to install required safety precautions, including netting and sheds, officials said. A month later, a buildings inspector found the owners had continued demolition work in violation of the order and issued another penalty.
The five entities involved in the construction project are tied to about 100 others across the city, the mayor said, and building inspectors were beginning sweeps of those sites.
“If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them fully accountable,” Mamdani said.
In the immediate aftermath of the collapse, families gathered with their neighbors and loved ones on the sidewalk near the place that was once their home. Stevens, the teacher, said she took one young boy to a nearby clothing store to use the restroom. He kept asking her when he could go back home.
“I don't know, love,” Stevens recalled telling him. “But you are safe. Your family is safe. You're gonna be okay.”
Anderson Velez said he got a panicked phone call from his wife at home after he arrived for a painting job in the Bronx. She was screaming, he said, begging rescue workers to pull their two sons from the rubble of their Brooklyn apartment building, which had collapsed minutes earlier.
All three survived, but his 9-year-old son was in intensive care after undergoing surgery on his skull and his wife has serious injuries to her ribs, spine and collar bone, he said Thursday. Velez provided Gothamist with video of his apartment as the building collapsed.
“I am still in shock,” Velez said in the small lobby of a Brooklyn hotel the city is using to house people displaced by the disaster. “The truth is, I’m trying to be strong for my son, but I feel terrible.”
The Red Cross opened a reception center at a nearby YMCA for residents displaced by the destruction. At least seven households registered, though many spent their night on the sidewalks, wrapped in blankets, waiting for word about their loved ones.
The city’s public advocate, Jumaane Williams, described coming across a man on the sidewalk who appeared to be staring into space. The man was trying to find his wife. And so Williams and the local pastors asked if they might pray with him. He agreed, and they did.
“And so it was just amazing when his wife was found and taken out alive,” Williams said. “I'm hoping that that blessing, that miracle continues.”
But many were still left waiting.
On Thursday morning, rescuers continued the search as the community looked on. A demolition excavator worked through the rubble, piling the debris on one end of the lot — a mattress, a refrigerator and wood floor panels. Clothing and dozens of music records lay scattered across the site.
One woman collapsed to the ground after learning her husband was among the dead. “My husband, he died,” she yelled in Spanish.
“We’ve been waiting here all night. We went to four hospitals, and they haven’t given us any information,” Luis Siguencia said of his son, 22-year-old construction worker Gabriel Ariolfo Siguencia Yupa, who had recently arrived from Ecuador.
“He wanted to get ahead,” Luis Siguencia said. “Because we all come here with the dream of getting ahead. He had his papers and everything.”
It wasn’t until Thursday afternoon that the Ecuadorean consulate general could confirm Gabriel had died in the collapse.
Kayla Chimborazo, who said she was Gabriel's stepsister, said her family spent the night “jumping from hospital to hospital, showing pictures, telling his name, his date of birth, to see if anybody has him.”
“We didn't even get a chance to see him,” Chimborazo said. “Even if there was that one possibility that he was still alive, we didn’t get to see him.”
Chimborazo described her stepbrother as “a sweet soul,” who was working to be able to provide for his wife and son in Ecuador. Chimborazo said she'd just seen him two weeks ago, at a family church gathering in New Jersey.
“He was really stepping up and starting a new start in life,” she said.
José Luis Caguana Cosquillo, 26, another construction worker from Ecuador, was also among the dead, the consulate reported.
His friend, Segundo Iza, stood vigil at the site of the collapse Thursday. He said he and Caguana Cosquillo had grown up together in Ambato, Ecuador. They’d met playing soccer.
Iza said his friend had moved to the U.S. four or five years ago. He had one son and another child on the way.
“He was someone who came here to achieve many dreams, to find better days for our children and our parents,” Iza said. “So it’s sad that our friend died here in New York.”
Eventually, the storm moved in, and with it, a heavy rain. The mayor spoke to reporters under a tent.
“These were our friends and our neighbors, parents and children, young families building their lives in our city, and immigrants from Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador, Trinidad and beyond,” Mamdani said. “ Let us continue to hold close those who have been plunged into unimaginable grief and pray for a full and rapid recovery for every New Yorker injured.”
The FDNY said late Thursday afternoon rescue operations had completed, and that it had determined there were no further victims.
An aunt to two of the men confirmed dead, Mamadou Bhoye N’diaye and Mamadou Bhoye Barry, gathered with her family that evening and grieved at the news.
“Right now my emotions are not good,” Kadidiatou Diallo said. “I just lost my nephews.”
Charles Lane contributed reporting.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Group biography follows Lee Miller, Pablo Picasso and friends on holiday in the South of France
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Matthew Gale
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A group biography balances between a choir and a cacophony. Each person lies at the heart of a network, opening the potential for an exponential chain of many walk-on parts. Rooted in the photographs of what author Anna Thomasson rightly terms the “fleeting community” of a late summer holiday in 1937, A Vast Horizon succeeds remarkably in marshalling a complex tapestry of egos, events, ideals and disappointments.
The individuals gathered in the Hotel Vaste Horizon in the French village of Mougins formed the chain of couples constituting this community: Eileen Agar and Joseph Bard, Nusch and Paul Éluard, Ady Fidelin and Man Ray, Dora Maar and Pablo Picasso, Lee Miller and Roland Penrose. They were drawn to the South of France by their inter-linked friendships and by “le peintre soleil”, Agar’s witty characterisation of Picasso. As Picasso urged everyone to work, half the witnesses took photographs. Maar, Man Ray and Miller were the relaxing professionals; snapshots were added by Agar and Penrose. Thomasson has searched through this rich, if scattered visual archive of a moment through which photography (as Roland Barthes recognised in Camera Lucida) “mechanically repeats what could never be repeated existentially”. Their hedonism caught in this moment defied the political instability and totalitarianism, with civil war already a year old in Spain.
Plunged into war
From this carefree and creative escape, Thomasson’s narrative plunges its participants into the war. For each of them it constituted a restructuring of values—not as hoped for by the Surrealists, but as enforced by the destructive triumphalism of Nazi extremism. Here the account turns to Paul Éluard’s transformation of a love poem for Nusch into a litany for “liberty” that captured the spirit of resistance (copies were even dropped over Occupied France by the RAF). Equally powerful was Miller’s reportage of the savagery of combat and, eventually, the revelations of the concentration camps. In this way, the book touches upon the transience of bodies captured in photography: those at Hotel Vaste Horizon were willingly posed for the camera and exchanged in partnerships, before growing fragile through wartime deprivation.
There was no reciprocal gathering in the post-war period. As a result, Thomasson traces the endgames, as each of the participants ages in varying degrees of dignity, creativity and despair. Those bodies displayed on the beach in southern France become the distant, optimistic opposite to the tragic, haunting corpses of Buchenwald; it is little wonder that Miller, the photographer in both cases, would never fully recover from the experience of witnessing such deliberate inhumanity.
While the lives of many of these central figures are, to varying degrees, familiar—from autobiographies (Agar, Man Ray, Penrose) and biographies (Éluard, Miller, Picasso)—Thomasson’s synthesis draws on recent research and extensive reading. A particular strength is the rebalancing of longstanding gender biases and assumptions. The repositioning of Ady Fidelin, the double-marginalised Guadeloupean woman, is especially timely; drawing on fresh scholarship, she is given greater presence and somewhat rescued from simply being Man Ray’s model. Nusch Éluard is also brought more sharply into focus. Substantial traces of these women’s own voices remain to be found, however, confining them to an unknowability ascribed to their devotion to their partners, although this may be overstated in the suggestion that, in 1946, Nusch Éluard “died in the service of Paul [Éluard]’s pursuit of freedom”.
Words over pictures
Late on Thomasson cites Emily Dickinson’s belief that veracity is “more affecting, if told indirectly”. This emerges as a foundational conceit in a volume inspired by photographs but in which only four are reproduced. Instead of showing, the author presents often highly evocative descriptions of what she sees in a wide range of images that the reader is not shown. This is a surprising decision for a narrative stimulated, as we are told, by the author being drawn into “their distant world by their photographs”.
With such a limitation on images, the book’s cover photograph assumes disproportionate significance. Where the British edition favours Agar’s photograph of Maar, Picasso and the Éluards at Juan-les-Pins, Miller’s picnic photograph of “half-naked women sitting among fully clothed men”—the jarring nature of which introduces the whole narrative—appears on the cover of the US edition. Although unaltered when reproduced inside the volume, on the cover the half-naked torsos are rather ineptly airbrushed. That the publishers chose to manipulate a famous 90-year-old image seems an unfortunate undermining of an otherwise compelling narrative of artists embracing freedom before disaster struck.
ª A Vast Horizon: Artists and Lovers, Freedom and War, by Anna Thomasson, published by Pegasus Books, 304pp, 4 b/w reproductions, $29.95 (hb), 7 July

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120386.title: Handball | Bundesliga mit Kickstart: Zwei Spitzenspiele und neue Favoriten
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120386.author: Christoph Dach
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120386.text:
- Sport
- Handball
Bundesliga mit Kickstart: Zwei Spitzenspiele und neue Favoriten
Nach der Länderspielpause geht es zwischen Berlin und Kiel sowie Magdeburg und Flensburg schon um Entscheidendes – unter veränderten Voraussetzungen.
Zuletzt waren Andreas Wolff, Julian Köster, Lukas Zerbe, Lasse Ludwig, Matthes Langhoff und Tim Freihöfer wieder für ein paar Tage Teamkollegen. Die sechs Handballer vom THW Kiel und den Füchsen Berlin zählten zum Nationalteam von Bundestrainer Alfred Gislason, das in der vergangenen Woche mit einem Sieg gegen Belgien erfolgreich in die EM-Qualifikation gestartet ist – und darüber hinaus ein viel wichtigeres gemeinsames Projekt für den Handball verfolgt: die WM in Deutschland im kommenden Januar. Bis zum zweieinhalbwöchigen Heimspiel auf größter internationaler Bühne stehen für die Nationalspieler allerdings noch zahlreiche Verpflichtungen mit ihren Vereinen an.
Nach der Länderspielpause legt die Bundesliga an diesem Wochenende gewissermaßen einen Kickstart mit zwei bedeutenden Begegnungen hin, die gar entscheidenden Charakter im Kampf um den Meistertitel haben könnten: Zum Auftakt am Sonnabend empfangen die Füchse Berlin mit ihren Nationalspielern Ludwig, Langhoff und Freihöfer das Kieler Trio Wolff, Köster und Zerbe. Keine 24 Stunden später gibt es am Sonntag in Magdeburg den nächsten Gipfel, wenn der amtierende Meister und aktuelle Tabellenzweite SCM den Dritten aus Flensburg empfängt.
Allerdings haben sich die Vorzeichen in dieser Spielzeit dahingehend verändert, dass die Kieler nach den bisherigen Eindrücken wieder ein ernstes Wörtchen im Kampf um den nationalen Titel werden mitreden dürfen. Zur Erinnerung: In der vergangenen Saison legte der Rekordmeister die schlechteste Saison seit Ewigkeiten hin und landete in der Endabrechnung auf Rang sechs. Damit ist der THW erstmals seit mehr als 30 Jahren in keinem internationalen Wettbewerb vertreten.
Diese verheerende Bilanz kostete Trainer Filip Jicha den Job und brachte die Vereinsspitze des THW zu dem Entschluss, die sportliche Verantwortung auf den neuen Coach Børge Lund zu übertragen. »Unser oberstes Ziel ist es, eine starke Mannschaft zu entwickeln und im kommenden Jahr wieder international dabei zu sein«, sagte der Norweger vor dem Saisonstart und ergänzte: »Die Jungs wollen zweimal in der Woche spielen, nicht nur einmal. Das merke ich in jedem Training, und das geht mir natürlich genauso.«
Nach nunmehr elf Spieltagen liegen die Kieler auf Kurs. Seit Lund seinen Posten an der Ostsee im Sommer angetreten hat, liest sich die Bilanz auch wieder angemessen für den erfolgsverwöhnten Klub aus Schleswig-Holstein. Lediglich einmal musste sich der THW bisher geschlagen geben: Ende September verloren sie in Magdeburg, also in einer der am schwersten zu bespielenden Hallen der Bundesliga. Allerdings hat Kiel in dieser Saison – abgesehen vom SCM-Spiel – noch keine der ganz hohen Auswärtshürden nehmen müssen. Die Kieler waren noch nicht in Flensburg, Gummersbach, Melsungen oder Berlin zu Gast. Letzteres wird sich am Sonnabend ändern.
Bei den Füchsen sieht die Lage ein wenig anders aus. Während Kiel im Sommer mit Köster und Domen Makuc zwei Weltklassespieler verpflichtet und sich damit wieder konkurrenzfähig gemacht hat, prognostizierten den Berlinern die meisten Experten ein Übergangsjahr – weil sie mit Torhüter Dejan Milosavljev und Rückraumshooter Lasse Andersson zwei elementare Bausteine ihrer großen Mannschaft der vergangenen Jahre abgegeben und nicht adäquat ersetzt haben.
Die Folgen sind bei den Füchsen im Grunde alle paar Tage sichtbar: Zwar spielt die Mannschaft von Trainer Nicolej Krickau weiterhin hochattraktiven, schnellen und mitunter mitreißenden Handball. In der Breite fehlt dem Berliner Kader aber die Qualität der Vorjahre, in denen der Klub 2025 erstmals Deutscher Meister geworden war sowie zweimal in Folge das Finale der Champions League erreicht hatte. Mit sechs Minuspunkten liegen sie in der Bundesliga aktuell nur auf Tabellenplatz fünf. Wenn Ausnahmekönner Mathias Gidsel & Co. die Tabellenspitze perspektivisch nicht gänzlich aus den Augen verlieren wollen, ist ein Heimsieg in der Max-Schmeling-Halle gegen den THW praktisch Pflicht.
Andererseits muss sich in der Hauptstadt niemand Sorgen um die Zukunft des lokalen Handball-Bundesligisten machen. Im kommenden Sommer wechseln mit dem Franzosen Dika Mem und dem Dänen Simon Pytlick zwei der besten Rückraumspieler der Welt nach Berlin. Füchse-Manager Bob Hanning hat überdies weitere spektakuläre Verpflichtungen angekündigt.
Beim THW Kiel haben sie ebenfalls vorgesorgt – und mit Justus Fischer von der TSV Hannover-Burgdorf eines der aktuell größten Kreisläufer-Talente schon für die nächste Saison verpflichtet. Es ist also keine gewagte Prognose, dass sich Berlins und Kiels Handballer in naher Zukunft wieder häufiger um nationale wie internationale Titel streiten werden – ganz unabhängig vom Ausgang der Partie an diesem Sonnabend.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/mayor-j.title: “Sewer Socialism” is Ascendant in America’s Big Cities
https://inthesetimes.com/article/mayor-j.author: Rebecca Burns
https://inthesetimes.com/article/mayor-j.text:
“Sewer Socialism” is Ascendant in America’s Big Cities
As the next mayor of Washington, D.C., Janeese Lewis George will join other local leaders who say they’ll look to the public sector to help solve their cities’ housing crises.
Rebecca Burns
Following a night of historic victories for Democrats in Congressional and state races, you’d be forgiven for overlooking a stunning development in local politics: Beginning in January, multiple major American cities will be governed by self-described democratic socialists.
In Washington, D.C., City Council member Janeese Lewis George will become the city’s first new mayor in more than a decade, after winning a June Democratic primary to succeed retiring three-term Mayor Muriel Bowser. In Providence, Rhode Island, 27-year-old State Representative David Morales will become the city’s youngest-ever mayor, after beating incumbent Brett Smiley in a September primary. In Ann Arbor, Michigan, County Commissioner Yousef Rabhi handily defeated incumbent mayor Chris Taylor in the city’s mayoral primary and was elected in a landslide on Nov. 3.
And in Los Angeles, City Council member Nithya Raman is expected to oust Mayor Karen Bass. (Like Lewis George, Morales and Rabhi, Raman is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, although the group’s national body nearly voted to revoke her endorsement over her ambiguous support for the Palestinian Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement.)
Along with New York’s Zohran Mamdani and Seattle’s Katie Wilson, this new generation of left-wing municipal leaders are reviving the moniker of “sewer socialism,” a label embraced by early 20th century socialist office-holders in Milwaukee who built modern sewage and wastewater treatment systems, public parks and the nation’s first municipal public housing. Like their forbears, today’s sewer socialists say they’re laser-focused on demonstrating that the public sector can deliver everyday necessities — including housing.
Just days before the November election, Lewis George hosted a packed tenant town hall in a church on the city’s northwest side, where she invited renters to share their housing horror stories.
The crowd obliged, detailing stories of bedbug, roach and even raccoon infestations, as well as dangerous elevators and retaliatory property managers — including in affordable housing subsidized by the city.
“We know we can’t allow negligent landlords to operate in D.C., and we certainly can’t allow them to operate on the government’s dime,” Lewis George responded to applause from the crowd.
In order to deliver dignified and affordable apartments to those being priced out of the nation’s capital, Lewis George has proposed creating a new municipal office of social housing, similar to that now operating in Seattle. Where federally funded public housing is reserved for low-income residents — and can’t be significantly expanded without changes to federal law—local governments are exploring new avenues to build publicly owned, mixed-income housing with stable rents. “Social housing” is more of an umbrella term than a singular model, but many advocates take inspiration from Vienna, where nearly 50% of the population lives in apartments owned or subsidized by the city.
In April, the Washington Post editorial board denounced spending taxpayer money on social housing as “untenable in this economy,” calling instead for a rollback of eviction protections and other safeguards for renters in order to coax wary developers into building more.
Lewis George has maintained that boosting private-sector building is important, too: In an April editorial for Greater Greater Washington, she wrote that while once skeptical of new construction in the name of affordability, she now believes that “increasing supply, paired with policies to protect residents, really is critical.” Alongside new social housing, her housing platform calls for reforms to zoning restrictions and permitting in order to meet her overall goal of building 72,000 new homes in the city over the next five years.
But Washington currently spends more than a billion dollars annually on affordable housing, much of that going to subsidize private-sector landlords promising to build and maintain apartments for low-income residents. Key programs like the city’s Housing Production Trust Fund have faced accusations of inefficiency and favoritism toward political insiders. A 2021 report from the city’s Office of Inspector General found that D.C. officials had misspent nearly $82 million in funds earmarked for extremely low-income residents, including by overpaying certain private developers.
Meanwhile, the city has a dearth of more than 37,000 rental homes available and affordable to very low-income households, according to the National Low-Income Housing Coalition. While D.C. has an overall housing shortage — the worst in the nation as a percentage of its total housing stock, according to Freddie Mac’s estimates — that gap also reflects apartment construction tilted towards luxury housing.
Could the public sector prove a better vehicle for providing truly affordable housing at the scale required?
Will Merrifield, a housing attorney who ran for D.C. City Council in 2020, believes that incentivizing the private market to provide enough affordable housing is a “losing battle.” In order to build, developers often rely on private equity investors who expect hefty returns, pushing project costs up higher. When local governments step in to provide “public equity” instead, investors’ foregone profits can translate into greater affordability — and keep publicly subsidized housing in the hands of the public. Now the director of the non-profit Center for Social Housing and Public Investment, Merrifield hopes to help map out how Washington could provide a “public option” for renters.
One influential model exists just outside the city, where in 2021, Montgomery County, Maryland, created a $50 million revolving loan fund backed by municipal bonds. Drawing on that fund, the county provides low-cost construction loans to developers in exchange for an ownership stake. Once a project is completed, the developer repays the loan, and the county reinvests the money in new projects. Some 6,000 units are in various stages of development; because the projects are mixed-income, rents from higher-income tenants subsidize lower ones. While this approach keeps ongoing costs down, the lack of additional subsidies means fewer affordable units.
Merrifield emphasizes that Washington and other municipalities must grapple with those trade-offs in order to design social housing programs that balance speed, scale and deep affordability.
“Social housing is expensive because it’s expensive to produce housing in this country,” he says. “But it’s necessary if we’re going to reclaim economic development from the real estate investor class.”
At the October tenant town hall hosted by Lewis George’s campaign, renters living in buildings owned by one of the city’s largest affordable housing landlords made the case that the city is not getting its money’s worth — and that residents are paying the price.
Since the spring, tenants in buildings owned and managed by prolific developer Buwa Binitie have been organizing a citywide campaign, pushing for repairs in their buildings as well as an end to new public dollars or contracts for their landlord.
“One of the things we want this new administration to realize is that [Binitie’s company] has been cited for hundreds of thousands of dollars [in fees for violations],” said William Bates, a resident of a senior building managed by Binitie, during the town hall. “What we want is for him not to be able to get more properties.”
In September, D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb sued Binitie over “shocking” conditions at another one of his buildings, including broken elevators in the 10-story building, exposed electrical wiring and stairwells contaminated with human waste and debris. The 166-unit Delta Pearl building was rehabbed and re-opened in 2023 as “luxury affordable housing,” using $18 million from the city’s Housing Production Trust Fund.
The Dumas Collective, the real-estate conglomerate Binitie founded in 2006, comprises a development company that has secured a total of $444 million in public subsidies, encompassing “financing from nearly every public capital source available,” according to the firm’s website. A property management arm oversees more than 1,000 apartments in D.C., which have collectively racked up more than 1,600 code violations between them, according to a review by City Cast DC.
A major donor to outgoing Mayor Muriel Bowser, Binitie served for eight years as the chair of the D.C. Housing Finance Agency, which awards tax-exempt bonds and low-cost financing to affordable housing developers. While Binitie has said that he recused himself from decisions involving his own projects, he appears to have been investigated for an alleged conflict of interest, according to reporting by the Washington City Paper.
A separate investigation by the paper revealed that the District forfeited $3 million of federal low-income housing tax credits in 2024, in part due to a swap of newer credits used to “bail out” one of Binitie’s older projects, which had suffered delays and budget shortfalls.
Binitie’s political connections also created a bizarre scene this fall, when the lawyer defending him, former D.C. Attorney General Karl Racine, crashed a press conference where tenants were urging the City Council not to grant public land to the developer for a new project. The council tabled the bill that would have awarded Binitie development rights.
Binitie did not respond to a list of questions from In These Times. In a September statement to WUSA9, a representative of the Delta Pearl acknowledged the serious conditions but said that “prolonged court delays and widespread rent delinquency have pushed this affordable housing property into a severe financial crisis.”
Nathan Hunter-El, a former resident of Binitie’s Capitol Vista apartments and a leader in Empower DC, a tenant organizing coalition, says the campaign is “not just about one bad actor.” Tenants are also fighting to overhaul a system they say lets scofflaw landlords stay in business.
For example, they are advocating passage of legislation that would make it easier to hold serial bad actors accountable, including by wresting control of properties through the courts when owners refuse to address conditions threatening tenants’ health and safety.
That’s where a new office of social housing could play a role, says Damiana Dendy, a housing organizer for D.C. Jobs with Justice who is working with tenants in buildings owned by Binitie’s companies. City intervention to acquire and preserve troubled affordable housing portfolios could actually represent a more effective approach than continuing to throw taxpayer money at emergency intervention and enforcement in subsidized buildings.
“Right now, we’re just hemorrhaging money to these slumlords,” Dendy says.
While a transformation of the private housing market may sound quixotic, the public sector we take for granted today is, in part, the legacy of yesterday’s municipal socialists, says labor historian Shelton Stromquist.
The provision of basic services like clean water and sanitation were part of a struggle to put “a new kind of floor under what people could expect in daily life,” says Stromquist, whose book, Claiming the City: A Global History of Workers’ Fight for Municipal Socialism examines the legacy of local left-wing governments in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Today’s municipal socialists have an “inheritance,” Stromquist says, and an opportunity to “expand that public sector in new directions, beyond the limits that it faced in the past.”
Thank you for reading this story. At a time when corporate media is dominating the web and our airwaves, independent journalism is more important than ever, and that’s what we provide at In These Times. We offer some of the best reporting, investigations and analysis on the growing movements for justice in the U.S.—and our work is firmly pro-labor and anti-fascist. To continue producing it, we need your support.
If you believe in the power of an independent press, please make a donation to In These Times today. By becoming a sustaining member, you can ensure that our work reaches even more readers.
And if you become a sustainer right now, you'll get a free year-long print subscription and a special subscribers-only print from artist Molly Crabapple.
Thank you.
Rebecca Burns is an award-winning investigative reporter whose work has appeared in Business Insider, the Chicago Reader, the Intercept, ProPublica Illinois and other outlets.

https://gothamist.com/news/all-us-airpor.text:
The Federal Aviation Authority on Friday issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue affecting air route traffic control centers, according to U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
Duffy wrote in a social media post just after 4 p.m. that the ground stop is “following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”
Calls to New York’s airports and the Port Authority were not immediately returned. The websites for the airports’ have not yet listed any advisories.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/ndaa.title: Congress Might Sneakily Use Lame Duck to Deeply Intertwine the U.S. and Israeli Militaries
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/ndaa.author: Josh Ruebner
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/ndaa.text:
Josh Ruebner is policy director of the IMEU Policy Project and author of the forthcoming book The United States and Palestinian Nakba: A Transnational History, 1947-1950.
After President Biden’s unrelenting support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza helped pave the way for President Trump’s reelection in 2024, Trump’s own foolish decision to launch an Israel-backed war against Iran played a large role in putting Democrats back in control of both chambers of Congress — a fact Vice President JD Vance diagnosed in no uncertain terms.
Now Democrats and Republicans alike have the opportunity to demonstrate they’ve finally learned the lesson voters have tried to deliver to both parties over the last three years: The American people do not want to be entangled and complicit in Israel’s aggression and atrocities. Their first opportunity to heed that call is arriving sooner than one might expect.
Right now, the House Armed Services Committee and Senate Armed Services Committee are engaged in an informal but highly consequential conference to finalize the text of the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which sets policy for the Pentagon. A disturbing provision in current versions of the texts passed by the House and Senate committees would integrate Israeli weapons companies into the Pentagon procurement process at an unprecedented level — opening a back door to almost untraceably send billions of taxpayer dollars to Israeli weapons makers without congressional oversight. The House bill would create a new “executive agent” position within the Pentagon to steer this integration—a level of amalgamation that exceeds collaboration with nations in NATO.
Members of Congress on both sides of the aisle are opposing this provision. On Tuesday, Sen. Chris Van Hollen and nine other Democratic senators, plus independent Bernie Sanders, demanded it be removed. In the House, Democrat Ro Khanna and Republican Thomas Massie have made clear they will also try to strip the NDAA of this measure. In doing so, they are representing what the vast majority of Americans want—and their colleagues should take note.
In our August polling with Data for Progress, 75 percent of Democratic voters oppose this provision, as do 58 percent of independents and 42 percent of Republicans. In addition, polling shows a majority of Americans now want to see taxpayer funding to Israel reduced or ended. Passing the NDAA with this measure would mean that even if Congress zeroed out annual weapons funding to Israel, currently at $3.3 billion per year, in the State Department budget — earlier this year, 103 Democratic representatives joined Massie in a move to do just that — there could still be a major increase in actual dollars flowing to Israeli companies that the American people never hear about.
The negative repercussions extend beyond funding Israeli weapons makers (some of which are government-owned) with our tax dollars. This sort of integration could allow for Israeli weapons and surveillance technology that have been tested on Palestinians to be used in the U.S. to advance the Trump administration’s cruel mass deportation program. Israeli weapons maker Elbit Systems’s U.S. subsidiary is expected to install more than 300 surveillance towers along the U.S.-Mexico border, developed from its technology deployed along portions of Israel’s apartheid wall in the West Bank.
Melding Israel into our government procurement process should also set off alarm bells in the U.S. national security world. The Washington Post reported earlier this year that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vetoed Biden’s decision to send U.S.-Israeli co-produced missile systems to Ukraine three years ago for Ukraine’s war against Russia, even though the missiles were paid for by American taxpayers. The integration measure proposed in the NDAA would massively expand the scope of weapons over which the Israeli government could exercise a unilateral veto.
Congress should be unwinding intelligence cooperation with Israel, not only on the moral grounds that no part of the U.S. national security apparatus should assist in genocide, but also because Pentagon officials raised the threat of Israeli spying to its highest possible level earlier this year. But instead of diminishing our intelligence sharing with Israel, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence’s FY27 Intelligence Authorization Act, which is typically incorporated into the final NDAA version, includes a provision (Sec. 618) actually mandating the president engage in even more intelligence cooperation.
This should give us pause because of the faulty nature of Israeli intelligence and the way Israel used this intelligence to build a case for dragging the United States into war. It was reportedly Israeli intelligence that claimed the Iranian government could be overthrown within weeks, if not days, of Trump launching the war. Instead, Trump and Netanyahu are now stuck in a quagmire, and the war has imposed a terrible cost on the American people, U.S. servicemembers, and people across Iran and the region. Energy prices around the world have skyrocketed, the cost of the war has already exceeded $2,000 per U.S. household on average, and the U.S. is running low on interceptor missiles that will take years to replenish.
None of this seems to concern the main backers of U.S.-Israel military and intelligence integration, like Foundation for Defense of Democracies President Mark Dubowitz. In a column published in Israel Hayom, the right-wing newspaper owned by the Israeli-American GOP megadonor Miriam Adelson, Dubowitz said: “Israel and the United States should deepen their military, technological, intelligence, and economic integration to such an extent that inflicting financial harm on Israel would also carry a significant cost for Washington.”
In an interview, Dubowitz added that the U.S. and Israel should be so intertwined that any accountability measure against Israel, such as sanctions being enacted by American allies in Europe, would “impose costs on the U.S. itself.” In no uncertain terms, advocates for the integration envisioned in the NDAA want to try to make it impossible for the U.S. to disentangle itself from a regime that is increasingly perceived by many as a rogue actor.
The NDAA is usually considered a “must pass” bill in Congress — in fact, Congress has passed annual defense authorizations for 65 consecutive years. But Congress is under no statutory obligation to pass it this year, and doing so without stripping these provisions to become even more entrenched with supporting Israel would be an immediate betrayal of the will of voters. At a time when even Republicans are openly admitting the midterm election was a referendum on U.S. support for Israel, it would be an unforgivable choice for Congress to pass an NDAA with these integration provisions. If Republicans use their committee majorities to force their inclusion in the bill’s final text, Democrats have every bit of leverage to filibuster and block the bill’s passage in the Senate, which requires 60 votes.
Saying no to bringing the U.S. into a closer relationship with Israel in just about the most expensive, opaque, and dangerous way imaginable should be the easiest political decision Congress makes during its current lame-duck session.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/so.title: Sotheby’s Hedreen Auction Proceeds Will Repay Loan, Not Fund University Museum: Report
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/so.author: Tessa Solomon
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/so.text:
A $300 million art donation to Seattle University has been revealed to be more complex than originally reported.
On Monday, Sotheby’s will begin selling approximately 50 works from the collection amassed by Seattle real estate developer and philanthropist Richard “Dick” Hedreen, previously billed as the “largest art gift ever” to a US university. Hedreen said in September that the sale did not mean the promised gift was falling through. Rather, he suggested, the proceeds would help furnish Seattle University’s new art museum, where the collection was eventually expected to hang.
Records newly reported on by The Seattle Times, however, tell a different story: The works are being sold not to fund the museum, but to pay off a debt secured against the collection — a debt Hedreen says stands between him and fulfilling his pledge to the university.
What was originally framed as a donation, in reality, was a pledge: Hedreen, whose firm R.C. Hedreen Co. owns the Grand Hyatt among other Seattle properties, retained the right to buy and sell works from the collection until the gift was finalized. The Sotheby’s auction is expected to generate at least $100 million across a series of sales. As of writing, the overall value of the artwork set for Seattle University is unclear.
The sale spans an expansive sweep of art history. Works by Willem de Kooning, Rashid Johnson, Amy Sherald, and Jonas Wood will be offered alongside Old Masters by Bronzino, Jacopo Pontormo, Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, and Thomas Gainsborough. Leading Sotheby’s offerings is Roy Lichtenstein’s Reflections on “Painter and Model” (1990), estimated at $20 million to $30 million. Cecily Brown’s 12-foot-wide Untitled (Shipwreck) (2017), estimated at $7 million to $10 million, is another highlight.
A news release from Seattle University stated: “Hedreen has given the university the renowned Hedreen Collection (named for himself and his late wife Elizabeth ‘Betty’ Ann Petri Hedreen, a Seattle University alumna) valued at $300 million, along with $25 million in seed funding to develop the museum.”
However, the Seattle Times reported that records show that the “seed funding” was actually provided through the private sale of a de Kooning painting. Estimated in 2024 to be worth $25 million, the work fetched $17 million.
The Sotheby’s sale proceeds will instead go toward paying off an outstanding loan secured against the collection. The borrowing dates to 2012, when Hedreen first pledged several artworks, including a pieces by Francis Bacon, de Kooning and David Hockney, as collateral for a Goldman Sachs loan. In 2025, that financing was replaced with a Bank of America loan secured by approximately 44 major artworks.
R.C. Hedreen Co. President David Thyer confirmed that the Sotheby’s sale is tied to financial pressures in the hotel and real estate markets. Income generated by the company’s properties, he said, is insufficient to repay the loan “in any reasonably foreseeable time frame.”
ARTnews has contacted Sotheby’s for comment.
Richard Hedreen’s son, Guy, said in a statement that his family’s “commitment to Seattle University has not changed.” His father, Guy added, “is not selling works from his collection in order to spend money on himself” or his business. Rather, the auction reflects his commitment to the university “by removing a debt that prevents him from translating his pledge intentions into an outright gift.”
Construction on the new art museum, originally scheduled to begin this past summer, has been pushed to 2027 as the project awaits permits. Designed by local architect Tom Kundig, the museum is intended to permanently house the Hedreen collection, alongside rotating exhibitions and academic programming.
Scott K. McClellan, Seattle University’s vice president for university affairs, said the school continues to believe the collection “presents a significant opportunity for the university, community and our broader vision for the arts.” He reiterated the “shared intention of Mr. Hedreen and the university” that Seattle University ultimately receive a collection of museum-quality works commensurate with the collection that formed the basis of the original commitment.
McClellan added that it had been “reasonable” for the university to expect Hedreen’s loan to be paid off by 2028, when the museum was originally scheduled for completion.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Cidade de São Paulo tem mais de 28 mil imóveis sem luz após tempestade
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A tempestade que atingiu a cidade de São Paulo pouco depois do meio-dia desta sexta-feira (13) ainda causa consequências na vida dos paulistanos. Mais de 28 mil imóveis estão luz na capital paulista. Em toda a região metropolitana são mais de 33 mil locais sem energia, segundo dados da concessionária Enel.
Logo após a chuva, chegaram a ser 104 mil imóveis sem energia.
A Defesa Civil emitiu três alertas severos devido à tempestade, abrangendo as zonas sul, leste, oeste e central de São Paulo. Em seguida, a tempestade se deslocou, atingindo também a cidade de Guarulhos.
O Centro de Gerenciamento de Emergências (CGE), da prefeitura de São Paulo, indicou que a capital registrou pelo menos 11 pontos de alagamento. Já o Corpo de Bombeiros recebeu 22 chamadas para quedas de árvores, 17 para inundações e duas para desabamentos na região metropolitana.
Entre os pontos alagados estão a avenida Professor Luiz Ignácio de Anhaia Mello, em diversos pontos, inclusive no acesso à avenida Salim Farah Maluf. A Marginal Tietê também ficou alagada na altura da avenida Aricanduva. Todos esses pontos ficam na Zona Leste da cidade.
As avenidas Regente Feijó, no Jardim Anália Franco, Cassandoca, na Mooca, e a Radial Leste registravam pontos de alagamento. Semáforos foram desligados nas regiões do Tatuapé, Vila Prudente e Mooca. Na Zona Oeste, o túnel Dirce Camargo, no Itaim Bibi, chegou a ficar interditado.

New Orleans cruise ship and tanker collide in Mississippi Rover
A tanker has collided with a river cruise liner carrying more than 130 people in New Orleans, authorities have said.
The governor of Louisiana has confirmed an incident in the Mississippi River. Jeff Landry said on X he was in contact with local officials and law enforcement.
The cruise liner was taking on water, local media reports said, and rescue efforts are under way.
The Port of New Orleans press secretary said the tanker collided with the American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage around 12:30 pm local time on Friday.
There were about 129 passengers onboard as well as crew, Port authorities told local media.
This is breaking news story. We’ll bring you the latest updates as we get them.
A video circulating around social media shows a different angle during the moment the ship was falling on its side into the water. Passengers can be seen climbing onto the balconies’ railing to avoid sliding into the river as the ship turned horizontally. Several uniformed people can be seen running away from the scene, likely to gather equipment that would help rescue efforts.
Martin J Davies, a maritime expert at Tulane University, told local news outlet Fox 8 that he suspected the incident was caused by either steerage failure or engine failure.
“This ship is headed upriver and for it to have lost the ability to avoid the moored vessel, there must have been some fairly substantial failure, with the steering gear or the propulsion of the ship to prevent them from avoiding the vessel on shore,” Davies said.
“Given that the pressure of the water going down river is sufficiently strong that the upbound ship would have been going fairly slowly,” he said. “So that’s my first thought upon looking at the footage.”
Davies also noted how close the vessels appear to be to the bridge above, suggesting the ship was lucky to have avoided also hitting the bridge. He said: “This is obviously a really bad incident, but it could also have struck the bridge, which it didn’t.”
Photos show ongoing rescue efforts at the site of the crash
Julius Constantine Motal
Pictures are now coming in from the news wires. Emergency personnel and crews can be seen on the scene after a tanker crashed into a river cruise in New Orleans. The cruise liner can be seen lying on its side:
Officials said they will be holding a news conference at 3pm CST, to begin in about ten minutes, providing further updates on the collision. We will bring you those latest updates as they come.
A statement from the US coast guard also announced that the river “is closed to all vessel traffic between mile markers 93 and 96,” encompassing the area where Friday’s crash occurred. That is so to assist responders as they “assess the situation and conduct response operations”, the coast guard’s statement said.
The New Orleans Regional Transit Authority said in a statement on social media that ferry service across the Mississippi River has been temporarily suspended as a precaution following the collision. Travelers are encouraged to seek alternate routes.
Multiple people rescued from river, says New Orleans mayor
New Orleans mayor Helena Moreno’s communication team said multiple individuals have been rescued, and search-and-rescue operations remain ongoing, according to a local Fox News affiliate.
Photos are circulating on social media of people climbing out and onto the balconies of the ship that is now turned completely on its side.
Local media is reporting that multiple people have already been rescued, and helicopters were seen in the air along with ambulances waiting nearby. Several people can be seen in the river wearing life jackets.
Videos circulating across social media appear to show the moment the Atlantic Asphalt tanker crashes into the side of the American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage while the cruise ship is docked on the Mississippi River. The ship then falls to its side towards the open water and begins sinking rapidly.
An emergency response source said that there were efforts underway to rescue people from the water. That source said it was possible the tanker had lost power before striking the American Heritage.
Images on social media showed the American Heritage on its side. It was docked on the Mississippi River outside the port of New Orleans’s administrative building when it was hit.

The Art Dealers Association of America’s chummy five-day show returns to the Upper East Side after quietly canceling last fall’s edition.
There are many art fairs in New York City, but perhaps none are friendlier than the one hosted by the chummy Art Dealers Association of America (ADAA).
“We all know each other very well,” Dorsey Waxter, former president of the ADAA and partner at Van Doren Waxter gallery, told Hyperallergic. “We’ve vetted each gallery that comes into the association for levels of excellence and standards. And it’s not so big you can’t have conversations with dealers and find out things about what you’re looking at.”
Jovial conversations about pathbreaking newcomers and long-dead modernists abounded inside the Park Avenue Armory, which provided a needed refuge from the cold nor’easter pummeling Manhattan for Thursday night’s VIP preview.

Activists demand end to transfer of military materials to Israel through New York's JFK Airport
Activists, joined by New York State Senator Jabari Brisport, gathered outside the World Trade Center on Thursday, protesting against the transportation of military-related materials through JFK International Airport (JFK).
The protest, organised under the “Break the Chain” campaign led by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), comes amid reporting from The Intercept that Challenge Airlines cargo flights have transported materials including nitrocellulose, bomb casings and guidance kits from JFK to Israel.
Open-source data documented in the report reveals weapons flown out of JFK are tied to mass casualty attacks in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran.
Challenge Airlines is an Israel-based cargo airline and logistics company founded in 1976.
The Intercept reported that thousands of pounds worth of parts for "bunker-buster" bombs went through JFK during the height of the US-Israeli war on Iran. The war began on 28 February.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Break the Chain says that military cargo bound for Israel passes through JFK Airport regularly, sometimes multiple times a week, and that civilian infrastructure should not be used for the benefit of the Israeli military.
Protesters, including members of Jewish Voice for Peace, Palestinian Youth Movement, Democratic Socialists of America, and Brooklyn for Peace called for an end to the shipments and greater accountability from the Port Authority, which has jurisdiction over JFK Airport.
Palestinian Youth Movement activist Ibtihal Aboussad brought up the possibility that the weapons shipments contributed to the recent bombing of Nasser Medical Complex in southern Gaza that killed at least six people, including Dr Rizk Abu Shaira.
“The precision bomb Israel used to strike this hospital now for the seventh time was an American bomb manufactured by Boeing, paid for by American taxpayers, and perhaps shipped out of JFK - an airport that functions mere miles away from us.”
As of March 2025, at least 1,722 healthcare workers have been killed by Israel in the war on the enclave, according to the United Nations. The war has been deemed a genocide by the UN and Holocaust scholars. Over 74,500 Palestinians have been killed since October 2023.
Public safety
Senator Brisport believes civilians travelling through JFK face a public safety risk. Jabari spoke at the Port Authority board meeting on Thursday, with his main concern being the nitrocellulose being shipped through JFK to Israel, according to The Intercept report.
Brisport cited an explosion that involved nitrocellulose in a China port around a decade ago that killed around 170 individuals. He believes that this safety concern should be grounds to halt these shipments.
“In your own airport rules and regulations, Section 13, part A, it states that any material defined by a federal regulation, or the international civil aviation organization, as hazardous, poisonous, explosive, or radioactive, may not be handled without the prior permission, but the port authority. So, I'm asking you to publicly release your agreements related to Challenge Airlines, that is the airline that carried nitrocellulose and other explosives at JFK Airport, as well as any other airline passenger or cargo that is shipping and handling hazardous materials.”
A spokesperson for the Port Authority told Middle East Eye that it is doing all it can to ensure public safety and defers responsibility to individual airlines and the federal government for what is allowed to be shipped on aircraft.
Ibrahim Mossallam, a commercial airline pilot, testified before the Port Authority board on Thursday.
“As a commercial airline pilot, I do not know exactly what is being transported on my passenger flights. Not all military parts and supplies are categorised as hazardous material to be reported. Learning that we are indeed transporting this material, that may also be explosive in nature, to aid one side or another in an active military zone is extremely unsettling.”
Mossallam told MEE that he feels betrayed by the US government and the airlines, saying pilots and passengers are at risk when dangerous materials are transported in the same aircraft.
As a Palestinian and a pilot, the issue hits close to home.
“You almost feel like you're being forced to be a part of this onslaught that's being done by our government to our policy and counterparts there.”
Mossallam is demanding that the Port Authority stop allowing airlines to ship weapons through both JFK and Newark Airport on all planes bound for Israel.
