https://jacobin.com/2026/11/carchedi-mar.title: Guglielmo Carchedi Was a Pathbreaking Marxist Economist
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/carchedi-mar.author: Joseph Choonara
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/carchedi-mar.text:
Guglielmo Carchedi Was a Pathbreaking Marxist Economist
Guglielmo Carchedi, who died in October at 85, was one of the great Marxist thinkers of our time. His early work on the new middle class and his later work on value theory and crises still offer the Left powerful tools.
In October, the radical left lost Guglielmo Carchedi — “Mino” to his friends and comrades — who died in his sleep at the age of eighty-five. He was one of the great Marxist thinkers of our times.
I first met him in London a few years after the economic meltdown of 2007–9, at a conference I organized for the journal International Socialism to explore the dynamics of that crisis. He spoke patiently and calmly, setting out his views with authority and an unwavering confidence in the power of Marxist theory. I heard him many more times over the next few years, always speaking with the same measured style. On occasion, he ended his presentations with a shy smile and the Latin “QED,” quod erat demonstrandum: “that which was to be demonstrated.”
It was always a delight when our paths crossed. Often I would encounter him in conjunction with Michael Roberts, with whom Carchedi would form a close personal and intellectual relationship.
The partnership was a fitting one. Roberts, himself a fine political economist, complemented Carchedi’s theoretical subtlety with a keen eye for a potential audience and a flair for showmanship, qualities long evident on Roberts’s indispensable blog. In turn, for Roberts, Carchedi was a mentor in the realm of dialectics and Marxist value theory. Together they produced a stream of articles; an edited collection, World in Crisis: A Global Analysis of Marx’s Law of Profitability; and a coauthored book, Capitalism in the Twenty-first Century Through the Prism of Value.
Carchedi was a kind and modest man, generous with his time when younger Marxists sought advice from him. He was refreshingly uninterested in whether those he spoke to worked in the academy or were simply left militants with a thirst for theory, as I was when we first met. He saw his work not merely as addressing a series of intellectual puzzles but as a contribution to the struggles of the working class.
It is a great boon that new generations can continue to benefit from his wisdom through his writings. Here I will focus on some of his early contributions, which deserve broader appreciation.
Middle-Class Problems
The writing partnership with Roberts has helped win Carchedi a new readership. However, few among the younger generation of Marxists are aware of his early contributions to class theory, especially on the nature of the middle class.
One of his first articles, “On the economic identification of the middle class,” appeared in 1975 in the journal Economy and Society. A second piece, “Reproduction of social classes at the level of production relations,” appeared in the same publication a couple of issues later. They would form two chapters of a book, On the Economic Identification of Social Classes.
After much searching, I managed to get hold of a battered secondhand copy that North Staffordshire Polytechnic had marked “discarded from stock.” As with many niche academic texts of the period, the printers made the plates from the output of an electric typewriter. Only in 2024 did the publisher, Routledge, again make a facsimile of the text available.
Carchedi’s contribution to class theory appeared in the shadow of better-known works by two authors grappling with similar problems. The first was the Greek-French Marxist Nicos Poulantzas, whose Classes in Contemporary Capitalism appeared in English in 1975. The second was Erik Olin Wright, whose first major foray into class theory, Class, Crisis and the State, appeared in 1978. Carchedi’s account, I would argue, offered a more convincing resolution than either of its major rivals.
The new middle class has been a thorny problem for Marxist theory. Karl Marx saw capitalists and workers as the major contending classes within capitalism. He saw the former as the rulers of such societies and the latter as their potential adversaries, capable of overthrowing the rule of capital and beginning the process of forging a communist society.
There was, Marx acknowledged, a substantial petty bourgeoisie, consisting of smallholders of capital, such as shopkeepers or artisans, along with their rural counterpart, the peasantry. Yet as capitalism came to predominate, it would, as Marx put it, “cut up” members of these groups “into two persons,” forcing them to adapt to the new society by operating as both capitalist and worker.
There was no reason to imagine the petty bourgeoisie would vanish, but over long periods of time, the two key classes of capitalist society could begin to absorb such groups. This happens, for instance, when a peasant becomes successful enough to start hiring and exploiting wage labor. Conversely, it happens when a peasant can no longer reproduce themselves without turning to wage labor and subjecting themselves to exploitation at the hands of a capitalist.
But where did this leave the new intermediate layers that modern capitalism created, such as the managers and supervisors that large enterprises required, or technicians and engineers? They worked for a wage, just like workers, but their role set them apart from the mass of wage labor. For some, this called into question the whole Marxist approach to class — or at least blurred beyond recognition the lines demarcating the classes of capitalism.
Poulantzas had sought to resolve this issue by presenting a very restrictive conception of the working class, focused on “productive” workers (those who generate profit for capital) involved in creating material commodities. He assigned anyone who did not meet these criteria — service sector workers, those working in the sphere of circulation, and so on — to a “new petty bourgeoisie” on the grounds of their economic position. To this, he added “political” criteria, allowing him also to thrust managers into this new class, and “ideological” criteria, allowing him to add mental laborers.
As Wright complained, Poulantzas’s approach would make about 70 percent of the US labor force of the time petty bourgeois, many of them on the grounds of ideology and politics. To regard, say, teachers or nurses as petty bourgeois seems particularly out of tune with today’s reality: such groups are clearly subject to the degrading power of capital and are often at the forefront of workplace struggle.
Wright’s own alternative was to deal with these ambiguities through a notion of “objectively contradictory class locations,” avoiding forcing groups such as managers into either the class of capitalists or workers. However, Wright’s approach introduced a complication. He sought to apply his approach both to groups caught between capitalists and workers in the workplace, such as managers, and to other groups — semiautonomous wage-earners and small employers — he identified as lying between the traditional petty bourgeoisie and either workers or capitalists.
This unnecessarily complicates the position of the petty bourgeoisie, whose very nature allows them to shade into the two major classes. The new middle class is a distinctive type of formation, requiring a different approach.
Wright himself would come to reject elements of his earlier contribution. In his later work, he suggested that he had previously overemphasized criteria such as autonomy in identifying class locations at the expense of exploitation.
However, from the mid-1980s, Wright increasingly drew on analytical Marxist thinkers such as John Roemer rather than on Marx’s own approach to exploitation. Roemer was skeptical of the value theory Marx developed in Capital, recasting exploitation as a matter of the different assets that individuals possess. As well as capitalist property, such assets could, in Wright’s new class model, be “organizational assets” or “skills.” The result was a fragmentation of the class structure, leading to myriad different class locations.
Carchedi’s Alternative
Carchedi offered a way out of this morass, drawing on Marx’s Capital. Groups such as managers in modern enterprises must perform two contradictory functions within capitalist production. These are not simply different technical functions; they are social functions, reflecting the imperatives of rival classes.
On the one hand, managers perform some functions of the “collective worker,” including coordinating the labor process, something necessary in any large, complex workplace, in any type of society. On the other hand, they also perform “global functions of capital,” roles of control and surveillance necessary because the workplace sits within a class-divided society. As Carchedi wrote, they are a special group of waged employees forming a “hierarchically organized ensemble, “who collectively perform what used to be the function of an individual capitalist” alongside activities appropriate to the collective worker.
These contradictory functions combine differently in different concrete jobs, influencing whether sections of the new middle class side with workers in struggle or align with their capitalist employers. The configuration of these functions is not static; it shifts with technological change, management culls, and restructurings.
For those Marxists who paid attention, notably Bob Carter, Carchedi’s theory would form the basis for later work, both theoretical accounts of the new middle class and empirical studies of workplaces. It provided a missing link between the labor process analysis that Harry Braverman pioneered in the early 1970s and a sophisticated Marxist class theory.
From Class to Value
Carchedi’s early work on class may superficially seem disconnected from his later work on political economy. However, there are clear links. These become apparent in an exchange with Wright in 1989, which appeared in the collection The Debate on Classes.
Here Carchedi criticized two elements of Wright’s methodology. The first was Wright’s embrace of analytical Marxism’s claim that there is no distinctive Marxist method, that the methods of mainstream social science will suffice. In place of this, Carchedi emphasized a dialectical approach.
This meant acknowledging the crucial roles of social structures, which develop independent of the will of particular individuals. However, these structures are not static but subject to dynamism and change.
This concern with method would persist. It is no coincidence that his 2011 book, Behind the Crisis, opens with a heading: “The need for dialectics.” Almost all of Carchedi’s major writings contain a discussion of method, emphasizing Marx’s dialectical standpoint.
Second, Carchedi reasserted the centrality of Marx’s value theory. Here he would offer another pioneering contribution, as one of the progenitors, along with Alan Freeman and Andrew Kliman, of what its proponents came to call the Temporal Single System Interpretation of Marx.
When analytical Marxists such as Roemer and Wright claimed Marx’s value theory was flawed, they were scrutinizing a modified version of the theory.
For Carchedi, their approach drew heavily on an approach pioneered by figures such as Piero Sraffa, which revived elements of the approach of to the labor theory of value of Marx’s predecessor, David Ricardo.
This “neo-Ricardianism” treated production not as a social and historical process but as a primarily technical one, in which a set of commodities gives rise to another set of commodities. The exploitation of labor ceases to play any distinctive role in creating new value. Neo-Ricardians, conceiving of the economy in this way, could model it through a set of simultaneous equations.
As Carchedi pointed out, one of the key weaknesses in this approach was its neglect of the concept of time. Neo-Ricardians unrealistically assumed that the prices of the outputs of a given cycle of production were the same as the prices of the equivalent inputs into that cycle. Carchedi insisted on reintroducing time, following Marx in resisting seeing capitalism as a system in static equilibrium.
One advantage to this approach was that it helped Carchedi to resolve what Marxists call the “transformation problem.” Marx’s Capital proposes that the value of commodities reflects the labor time that their production typically requires. This includes both the “living labor” of the workers producing them and the “dead labor,” the labor that workers expended in the past to create the material means of production that the process uses up.
This had implications for the rate of profit, the ratio between profit and investment. For Marx, living labor had the distinctive role of creating new value. Because labor can do so in excess of the cost of its reproduction (the wage), this gives rise to profits.
But because the ratio of living and dead labor varies between branches of the economy, Marx’s approach implied a different rate of profit in each. Yet even in Marx’s day, economists observed that profit rates tend to converge over time. Marx reconciled theory with reality through his transformation of values into “prices of production.”
Capital migrates toward branches of the economy where profit rates are high, disrupting the price level as social demand and supply shift. Were this process to reach its conclusion, it would redistribute value between capitalists such that each receives the same average rate of profit on their investment. In fact, as Carchedi showed, this was only a tendency, and new disruptions upset any potential equilibrium long before the system could reach it.
Many critics, starting with Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk in 1896, followed by Ladislau von Bortkiewicz, Paul Sweezy, and Ian Steedman, have faulted Marx for considering only how this transformation of values into prices of production affects the outputs of production, without also transforming the value of inputs. For those working with an atemporal, equilibrium model, such as the neo-Ricardians, making this further transformation allowed them to detach the system of prices of production from value theory altogether.
Carchedi argued that no such detachment was necessary. When capitalists obtain inputs for a new cycle of production, the value they advance is simply the price of production with which they left the previous cycle. This was what Carchedi termed their “social value.” Prices of production are, he proposed, not merely “determined by values but rather are their concrete form of existence.”
Falling Profit Rates
The hallmark of great Marxist political economy is to synthesize the often rather abstract discussions of value theory with an empirical understanding of a dynamic, changing, and crisis-prone system. This was very much on display in what I consider Carchedi’s finest work, Frontiers of Political Economy. Here Carchedi clarified and extended Marx’s approach in Capital while seeking to apply it to contemporary capitalism.
The result is dazzling. Carchedi’s book deals with the intricacies of price formation in the context of uneven and complex processes of intercapitalist competition, first on the national terrain and then on a global scale, where, for instance, wage levels differ sharply. Besides the transformation problem discussed above, he investigated a range of controversies, such as precisely which forms of labor do and don’t produce value and how to account for different skill levels among workers.
At the center of the book, a chapter on “Growth, crises, inflation and crashes” develops themes that would become prominent in his work. Here he focused on Marx’s “tendency of the rate of profit to fall” (TRPF).
Capitalists must advance an ever-greater mass of capital, in the form of dead labor, to grab their share of the pool of profit that the system generates. But because only living labor generates new value, the scale of the employed workforce and the extent of its exploitation ultimately limit the size of this pool. The more dynamic capitalism is in mobilizing a greater amount of dead labor through automation and the expansion of capital, the more this tends to choke off future profits relative to investment, helping pave the way for crises.
The TRPF has been a source of considerable controversy among Marxists. For some, it is an unnecessary distraction from value theory. For others, it is so hedged with counteracting tendencies that no one can grasp an overall pattern. For others still, the empirical evidence has falsified it.
Carchedi argued that the TRPF should remain at the center of crisis theory. It was, he maintained, the ultimate expression of the contradictions of capitalism. This was because, as Marx had proposed, the very processes that impel capitalism forward — exploitation, competition, accumulation — can, through the TRPF, begin to undermine future accumulation.
In his account, Carchedi acknowledged various counteracting tendencies, such as the intensification of exploitation from the 1980s, but argued that, in the long run, the TRPF overpowered these. It might also appear that financial expansion had injected new dynamism into capitalism. Yet for Carchedi, this reflected how the TRPF in productive sectors encouraged capital to shift into the sphere of finance, feeding speculative bubbles and ultimately financial crises. The meltdown of 2007–9 was not, in this account, a purely financial phenomenon but one ultimately rooted in the productive economy, the realm of workers’ exploitation and the site where their potential power concentrates.
Carchedi’s Legacy
I have only touched on a few elements of Carchedi’s contribution. His career saw him explore many other themes, ranging from the class nature of European integration to the relationship between value theory and artificial intelligence. It is far better that the interested reader consults such works for themselves to understand their richness and diversity. Doing so will also make clear the passion that motivated him.
On that, let the final word go to Carchedi himself, from his acceptance speech on receiving the World Marxian Economics Award in 2021. Contrasting the 1960s and ’70s, a time of great hope for those on the radical left, with the present period, he said:
An economic and financial crisis of major proportions is again knocking at the door; the destruction of our natural habitat proceeds unchecked; the divide between the poor of the world and the absurdly rich has never been so great; the dark clouds of a new world war are gathering on the horizon; right-wing ideologies resurrect and even fascism is raising its ugly face again. These are the dangers the new generations will have to face. The difficulties ahead for them will be immense. But the contradictory nature of the system is such that each time capitalism wins, the anti-capitalist forces regroup and counterattack with new forms of resistance. My hope is that my work will be of some help in their struggle.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Paris Photo’s digital sector offers ‘soft photography’ and vital context
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Sarp Kerem Yavuz
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Two weeks after an abbreviated edition of Art Basel Paris, the 29th edition of Paris Photo has taken over the Grand Palais (until 15 November), where digital art is enjoying a moment in the spotlight.
The world of fine art photography is no stranger to controversies involving digital art, and it is heartening to witness the leading photography fair’s commitment to technological excursions within the medium. Featuring 12 exhibitors this year, the fourth iteration of Paris Photo’s digital sector has been curated by Marco De Mutiis of the Fotomuseum Winterthur, taking over from Nina Roehrs, who had helmed the first three editions.
This year, the digital sector is accompanied by a pedagogical exhibition programme titled Soft Photography, organised by the École Cantonale d'Art de Lausanne in Switzerland and devoted to contextualising the place of AI and CGI within photography. Spanning an interactive exhibition and talks, Soft Photography aims to offer some much-needed dialogue between the medium’s analogue and digital wings.
The digital sector certainly contains some AI-generated imagery, such as New York- based Heft Gallery’s presentation of Alkan Avcıoğlu’s Disreality series, which is an expansion of the surreal landscape aesthetic he first introduced in a collaboration with Edward Burtynsky. But there are also plenty of analogue images throughout the sector, even photograms, enough to make one wonder just how much of a separate section this really is. A similar dynamic played out in the Zero 10 sector of Art Basel’s Swiss fair last June, where the term “digital art” was used so broadly that it begged the question whether a separate area was really warranted.
Noteworthy presentations at Paris Photo include the Venezuelan gallery Carmen Araujo Arte, which is showcasing Alejandro Cartagena’s mosaic-cut collages. Created from found photographs, the series is a manual interpretation of how images are made by generative AI by gathering found pixels. The works ask timely questions about authorship while also, in a rather sweet, analog gesture, highlighting just how much our art-making inevitably differs from that of algorithmic processes. The results are genuinely magnetic and intimate.
Palo Gallery’s installation of works from the artist duo Adrea Orejarena and Caleb Stein’s American Glitch series interrogates simulation theory as well as the nature of our screen-filled reality. Oscillating somewhere between the tone of David Lynch’s series Twin Peaks and surveillance footage, the presentation is a highlight, particularly Glitch Typologies (2020-24), the seven-channel sequence of floating images projected on the walls of a 3m-by-3m glass cube, the projectors hanging on a rod at its core, reminiscent of CCTV cameras. At a time of growing cultural cynicism, Orejarena and Stein offer a welcome reminder that the intersection of photography and technology can be whimsical, conspiratorial and surprising.
Yumo Wu’s solo stand with Licheng Ling Projects spans AI and darkroom analogue manipulation, with the images interspersed in such a manner that technique—though it inspires a certain sense of wonder—becomes secondary to the impact of the image. It is perhaps the best example at the fair of a presentation that moves beyond our fixation with what might be real and how it may have been created, with the artist instead asking her audience to quietly behold the images’ abstract textures. Wu is an emerging artist whose skill and willingness to experiment drowns out the noise, and the results are rather wonderful to behold. In addition to the stand marking her first solo presentation in Europe, one of her images is included in Paris Photo’s selection marking the bicentennial of the invention of photography.
Vincent Fournier’s Flora Incognita, presented by Au Cube, features large-scale portraits of speculative flowers derived from existing flora and manipulated to depict what may happen to them on another planet, exposed to different kinds of radiation or gravity. The photos may at first register as AI-generated images, but were in fact created with CGI using Houdini, a comparatively old-school software. Each image is presented in a wooden frame with a golden plaque on the bottom featuring the name of the plant, evoking the kind of 18th- or 19th-century botanical illustration that particularly benefits from the aesthetics of the Grand Palais, whose architecture harks back to a time of earnest scientific fascination and discovery.
The New York gallery Nguyen-Wahed’s solo stand devoted to the Los Angeles-based photographer Summer Wagner contains unframed, romantic, large-scale photographs featuring grainy, densely-textured and coolly-lit portraits. The presentation, only digital insofar as the images were shot on a digital camera, deals with our relationship with reality as "we’ve collectively succumbed to the tsunami or cultural and technological changes that have thrown image-making into an existential crisis”, according to the artist.
Meanwhile, facing the digital sector is Ruttkowski 68’s solo stand devoted to François Hallard’s large-scale Polaroid prints of flowers, with the title “Conversations avec Claude” written by the artist in bold letters at the top of the booth. On the second day of previews, Hallard added “(Monet) not IA” to the title, after countless visitors had presumed the works were related to AI. Evidently Anthropic’s AI engine has eclipsed one of the most consequential painters of the 20th century—at least in its claim to the first name Claude.
Given how much of an impact the nascent field of AI-generated photography has had on photography at large, it is unsurprising that we continue to add disclaimers and coin terms to differentiate the medium’s analogue lineage from its technological step-cousins. Several years ago, the dealer Howard Greenberg told me he favours the term “lens-based” to differentiate the two, and this seemed adequate at the time. But since then, plenty of artists (myself included) have incorporated photographic lenses, enlargers and other analogue tools and processes to experiment with and human-wash digital imagery, so “lens-based” may no longer be up to the task of distinguishing between an image taken with a camera and an image generated with a computer. “Synthetic photography” does have a nice ring to it, although the word itself makes one think of things like latex and carcinogenic sunscreen. Perhaps “soft photography” is the best term, for the moment.
Paris Photo’s digital sector and the Soft Photography programming deftly and quietly tackle the discipline’s ongoing existential crisis by demonstrating that digital art predates many of the technologies we are debating today, and its applications in contemporary photography today are legion.
- Paris Photo, until 15 November, Grand Palais, Paris

https://hellgatenyc.com/a-new-film-festi.title: A New Film Festival Looks at Life Beyond Rikers
https://hellgatenyc.com/a-new-film-festi.author: Max Rivlin-Nadler
https://hellgatenyc.com/a-new-film-festi.text:
Shortly after Edwin Santana was released from prison in 2017, he picked up his phone and began making what would become his first-ever documentary: "Closing the Last Penal Colony."
The last penal colony in question was Rikers Island, where Santana had spent time as a young man. While in prison, he didn't know much about the movement to close Rikers, and now that he was a free man, he started filming a movement that was urgently trying to shut down a place that had wounded him deeply. 
"I know the horrors firsthand, but it was only when I came home did I see that there was a massive movement centered around the issues I experienced, even all these years later," he told Hell Gate. "It was amazing to see people like myself, the formerly incarcerated, people who felt like they didn't have a voice, that they should even be ashamed of their own voices because they were incarcerated, leading this movement."
Santana had seen Rikers Island depicted in film, either glorifying the violence or as this unimaginable hellhole. But he'd never seen anything that actually put Rikers in the context of a long history of incarceration and bondage in New York City. 
"I wanted to see where Rikers came from," Santana said. "How did it even get here?" 
His documentary, which traces the history of Rikers Island—from a military training ground during the Civil War (including New York's segregated regiment of Black soldiers), to a modern massive jail complex literally built by prisoners, to the movement to close it—isn't the most polished documentary. Santana knows, two years after its release, that it would be a lot better if he made it today. But he also knows it reflects the mindset and experience of someone who just came out of a system that had inflicted harm on thousands of young people like him, and which still, stubbornly, hasn't closed. 
Santana's film is now one of the centerpieces of A Future Beyond Rikers Film Festival, which is taking place this weekend at the Maysles Documentary Center in Harlem, beginning Friday evening.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: The McGuinness Boulevard Redesign Is Finally Complete
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Katie Honan
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
A long-awaited Brooklyn street redesign was finally completed Friday, after years of starts and stops and a supporting role in the bribery case of a former top aide to Mayor Eric Adams.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani and other elected officials celebrated the changes along a one-mile stretch of McGuinness Boulevard by cutting a ceremonial ribbon under the Pulaski Bridge in Greenpoint to cheers.
The changes, from Meeker Avenue to the bridge, add protected bike lanes, shorten pedestrian crossings and force turning vehicles to slow down. 
Mamdani vowed to restart the project three days into his term as mayor, and on Friday he thanked the advocates – many who lost loved ones to crashes – who kept pushing for it. 
“Even as the long pattern of wealthy interests trumping those of working people in this neighborhood repeated itself over and over, today that belief is finally vindicated,” he said. “My friends, we have completed the redesign of McGuinness Boulevard.”
The ceremony marked the end to a years-long back and forth on the street overhaul, first introduced by former Mayor Bill de Blasio and then squashed by former Mayor Adams, whose top aide, Ingrid Lewis-Martin, said the plan was only supported by outsiders. 
The City Reporter previously investigated the role siblings Gina and Tony Argento, owners of film production company Broadway Stages in the neighborhood, played in ending the project. The Argentos feared the reduction of traffic lanes would affect their trucks driving to and from the sound stages. 
More was revealed in a series of August 2025 indictments that alleged Lewis-Martin received cash, catering and a cameo on “Godfather of Harlem,” filmed at Broadway Stages, in exchange for stopping the redesign. 
Lewis-Martin and the Argentos were criminally charged over the scheme to influence City Hall. 
The largest push for a redesign of McGuinness Boulevard came after beloved teacher Matthew Jensen was struck and killed as he crossed McGuinness Boulevard just after midnight on May 18, 2021. 
He had just celebrated his birthday with seven friends, his cousin John Ogren said at Friday’s briefing.
“He was the happiest I’ve ever seen him. He had his dream job, he had his dream home,” he said. Jensen was struck by a speeding driver and thrown 75 feet with such a force his house keys were damaged, Ogren said, as he thanked everyone for the work to make the street safer.
“We gather as community because we care,” he said. “And because we care, we do.”

https://citylimits.org/local-leaders-dem.title: Local Leaders Demand Accountability in Deadly Building Collapse, And What Else Happened This Week in NYC Housing
https://citylimits.org/local-leaders-dem.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/local-leaders-dem.text:
Share This Article
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Friday that the city has identified six “entities” involved in the construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave., and that inspectors are checking roughly 160 other work sites across the city where those companies are also involved.
City officials are promising a full investigation into the cause of the deadly building collapse in Flatbush, Brooklyn, which killed eight people and injured 18 others earlier this week.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Friday that the city has identified six “entities” involved in the construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave., where officials say crews were doing excavation work Wednesday afternoon when the three-story apartment building next door, at 1321 Flatbush Ave., collapsed.
The Department of Buildings (DOB) is now inspecting roughly 160 other construction sites across the city where those six entities are also doing work, according to the mayor—part of a “comprehensive and thorough investigation” into both properties.
“If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them fully accountable,” Mamdani said in a briefing Thursday.
A City Limits review of public properties records found two previous building violations issued to the Bedford Avenue construction site: one in March for crews doing demolition work without required “overhead protection,” and another in April for continuing construction while a stop work order was in place. The contractor named in those violations, N Tech Design of America, did not immediately return a request for comment.
The site is owned by two limited liability companies, FF1632 LLC and JS1024 LLC, which bought the property for nearly $4 million in 2024. The owner and developer of the site, Robert Fischman, did not respond to voicemails left at his place of business Friday.
Fischman had city approval to demolish a one-story building on the site and construct a new three-story building, according to DOB records. He had also submitted plans to build a nine-story building, which were not yet approved.
“If there’s any changes to either the excavation that’s done, the foundation that would be in place for a larger building, those adjustments would have to be made as part of the longer-term approval,” said DOB Commissioner Ahmed Tighani at a press conference Friday.
The adjacent three-story apartment building that collapsed into the construction site, 1321 Flatbush Ave., had 98 open violations on record with the city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development, including for things like unsafe electrical wiring and a leaking ceiling.
Attempts to reach the owner—listed on city records as Isolag Realty Corporation, which is registered with the state under the name Olufemi Falade—were unsuccessful.
Local leaders, including Flatbush City Councilmember Farah Louis and civil rights activist Rev. Al Sharpton, planned a vigil near the scene of the tragedy Friday to demand accountability for the disaster.
The eight fatalities included two children, officials said.
“This could have been any one of us,” Sharpton told reporters, according to a video of the event shared online. “This should not go for two or three days of mourning, and then we go about our business. We don’t know when the next house will collapse.”
Here’s what else happened this week in housing—
ICYMI, from City Limits:
- The number of homeless students attending the city’s public schools declined by 10 percent during the 2025-2026 school year compared to the year before, but remains stubbornly high, with more than 138,000 kids who went without stable housing.
- The city is earmarking an extra $25 million to hire 300 additional outreach workers and open more low-barrier shelter beds this winter, after a brutal freeze killed 18 New Yorkers last year.
- Tenants organizing across 31 Manhattan buildings in foreclosure are the latest to see support from Mamdani’s newly reinvigorated Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants.
ICYMI, from other local newsrooms:
- A Columbian father and his 9-year-old daughter were among those killed in the Flatbush building collapse, according to Gothamist, which spoke to relatives about how the family had been fearful of federal immigration enforcement in recent months.
- The Brooklyn District Attorney’s Office has opened an investigation into the collapse, the New York Times reports.
- Councilmember Farah Louis introduced a bill that would require the city to come up with a plan for addressing vacant rent-stabilized apartments, according to The Real Deal.
- Mayor Mamdani signed the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act into law, amNY reports.

The Clark Art Institute in Williamstown, Massachusetts, has appointed Caroline Shields chief curator. A specialist in nineteenth-century French art, Shields joins the Clark following her position at the Art Gallery of Ontario (AGO), Toronto, where she has served as curator and head of the European art department since 2019. She will step into her new role this January; the exhibition “Pointillist Politics: Neo-Impressionism, Anarchy, Utopia,” which she co-curated, will go on view at the museum in June 2027.
“In Caroline Shields, we have found an excellent leader and a talented manager of curatorial projects. Caroline is well known to us for her exhibitions and scholarship, and we are confident she will expertly steward our ever-evolving collection,” said Clark director Esther Bell in a statement.
Shields arrived to AGO in 2017 as assistant curator of European art before rising to her current position. While at the museum, she notably curated a major exhibition pairing the works of American Impressionist Mary Cassatt with those of Canadian Impressionist Helen McNicoll. Before coming to AGO, she held curatorial roles at the National Gallery of Art, Washington, DC; the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston; and the Musée d’Orsay, Paris. Shields holds a BS in geology and art history from Boston College and a Ph.D. in art history from the University of Maryland.
“I am deeply inspired by the Clark’s institutional commitment to audience engagement, art historical scholarship, and its world-class collection,” said Shields in a statement. “It is an honor to join the Clark’s extraordinary team of curators and staff across the Institute as it moves into its next chapter.”
Shields joins the Clark as it prepares to break ground on a new wing to house the collection of European art it received as a gift from late philanthropist Asa O. Tavitian.

https://taz.de/Sophie-Calle-Ausstellung-.title: Sophie Calle Ausstellung in Berlin: Könnte es besser sein?
https://taz.de/Sophie-Calle-Ausstellung-.author: Hilka Dirks
https://taz.de/Sophie-Calle-Ausstellung-.text:
Sophie Calle Ausstellung in Berlin: Könnte es besser sein?
Zum 30-jährigen Jubiläum des Hauses zeigt der Hamburger Bahnhof in Berlin eine Schau Sophie Calles. Die Kuratierung entpuppt sich dabei als verkopft.
Am Ende erscheint sie dann doch noch: Die wagemutige, lustige, und voyeuristische Sophie Calle. „Because I wouldn’t want anyone squatting in my zygomatic arch. Because I wonder whether T and K still love each other or whether their love has died. Because one day only the padlock will remain.“ („Weil ich nicht möchte, dass sich jemand in meinem Jochbeinbogen einnistet. Weil ich mich frage, ob T und K sich noch lieben oder ob ihre Liebe erloschen ist. Weil eines Tages nur noch das Vorhängeschloss übrigbleiben wird.“) steht weiß auf violettem Filz gestickt. Am Rahmen befestigt, verdeckt er ein Foto. Die Besuchenden dürfen ihn lüften, das hat die Künstlerin in feiner französischer Schreibschrift mit Bleistift an die Wand geschrieben.
Hebt man den dicken Vorhang an, erscheint ein dunkelgrau verfärbtes Konvolut menschlichen Gebeins. Allerlei Knochen und Schädel. Sofort hofft man, dass es sich um eine irgendwie religiös geartete Ansammlung handelt und nicht um die Überbleibsel eines Massengrabs. Im darauf zentral abgebildeten Schädel hat jemand im Jochbein ein Vorhängeschloss angebracht. „T+K“ steht darauf mit dickem weißen Edding. Eine Geste der vermeintlich ewigen Liebe, wie sie sich in den letzten Jahrzehnten rasant an Brücken und vermeintlich romantischen Orten auf der ganzen Welt verbreitet hat.
Man schluckt kurz hilflos, gefangen zwischen Pietät, Humor und Neugier. Der Tod und die Sehnsucht und die Liebe und die Ausweglosigkeit und die Radikalität, für das Experiment oder das Ergebnis irritierend weit über Grenzen zu gehen, sowie die Kombination von Text und Fotografie liegen in dieser kleinen Arbeit – und die steht damit exemplarisch für alles, wofür Sophie Calle bekannt wurde.
„Is it Better“ heißt die Ausstellung der 1953 geborenen französischen Künstlerin, die der Hamburger Bahnhof anlässlich seines 30-jährigen Bestehens am Freitag in Berlin eröffnet. Während in der Haupthalle noch immer lärmende Schulklassen inmitten der von Chanel gesponserten Bauklötzen Lina Lapelytės Türme bauen und wieder einreißen, muss man, um Calles Werk zu bestaunen, in den ersten Stock des ehemaligen Bahnhofsgebäudes klettern, wo der hölzerne Baulärm sofort verstummt. Und doch steht man auch hier sofort zwischen Abriss und Wiederaufbau.
Auch Calle arbeitete vor 30 Jahren das erste Mal in Berlin
1996, im Jahr der Eröffnung des Hamburger Bahnhofs – Nationalgalerie der Gegenwart, begann auch Sophie Calle ihre Beziehung mit Berlin, wie Kuratorin Lisa Hörstmann es beschreibt, und fertigte in der Nachwendestadt die Serie „Die Entfernung“ an. Die Konzeptkünstlerin fotografierte Orte im öffentlichen Raum, wo Denkmäler und Insignien der DDR entfernt wurden, und zeigte die Bilder der darauf sichtbaren Leerstellen Menschen, die ihre Erinnerungen an ebenjene mit Calle teilten.
Das daraus entstandene Buch – eins unter dutzenden in ihrem Œuvre – dokumentiert Fotografien, die entfernten Objekte sowie die kurzen Texte. Es bereitet Freude, die Verschwommenheit und Indifferenz sowie die Verwobenheit des Individuums mit dem Politischen in der zwölfteiligen Serie zu entdecken, die als Leihgabe der Kunstsammlung des Deutschen Bundestags sonst nur den Parlamentarier:innen zugänglich ist.
Berlin hat es schon früh verstanden, seine Dysfunktionalitäten, Klüngeleien und Fehlentscheidungen für Eigenwerbung zu vermarkten. Auch der Hamburger Bahnhof war mit dem Drama um die Rieckhallen und die Kontroverse um den Sammlungsabzug der Friedrich Christian Flick Collection selbst häufiges Beispiel für die verfehlte Kultur- und Immobilienpolitik des Landes. Vielleicht liegen also auch Prisen von Mut und Selbstironie in der Kuratierung des Museumsdirektors Sam Bardaouil und Lisa Hörstmanns darin, anlässlich des Jubiläums die eindeutigen Berlin-Werke Calles zu zeigen.
Ist es besser?
So auch „Is it Better?“ die titelspendenden Arbeiten, die nach ganz ähnlichem Prinzip verfahren. Zweimal fertigte die Künstlerin sie an. Einmal 2012 und nun 2026, extra für die Schau. „Ist es besser?“, fragte Calle für die zweiteilige Serie Stadtbewohner:innen, bezogen erst auf den einstigen Palast der Republik, wo nach dem Abriss ab 2006 bis 2012 eine Rasenfläche die Grundfläche bedeckte, und später auf das neugebaute Berliner Schloss, welches ab 2013 auf ebenjener Rasenfläche errichtet wurde.
Auf Textbildern erscheinen die Zitate anonym neben Ortsaufnahmen, Postkarten zeigen den Zustand vor der Veränderung. Calle nimmt die Befragten ernst, die Meinungen scheinen durchaus exemplarisch für die Debatten in der Stadt zu sein. Große Poesie jedoch entsteht hier eher nicht. Und fragt man Hörstmann, wie die Kolleg:innen aus dem Humboldt Forum, das im Berliner Schloss residiert, auf die Arbeit reagierten, winkt diese ab: Die Debatte sei nun wirklich alt.
Die Ausstellung
Sophie Calle. „Is It Better?“, Hamburger Bahnhof – Nationalgalerie für Gegenwart Berlin, bis 04.04.2027
Das Werk der Autodidaktin Calle, die unter anderem 2007 Frankreich auf der Venedig-Biennale repräsentierte und deren größtes Publikum aus jungen Frauen besteht, wie sie in einem Interview mit der Zeit jüngst preisgab, fasziniert insbesondere durch die Illusion radikaler Selbstentblößung und der Unterwerfung der Künstlerin vor dem Projekt.
So begann sie als junge Frau einen fremden Mann zu verfolgen, reiste ihm bis nach Venedig hinterher und dokumentierte dies in detektivischen Fotos. Sie schickte einem Fremden regelmäßig anonym Kleidungsstücke zum Geburtstag, von denen sie meinte, sie würden ihm gut stehen, kopierte ein gefundenes privates Adressbuch, kontaktierte die Menschen darin, erstellte so ein Porträt des Besitzers und filmte das Sterben ihrer Mutter.
Das was fehlt
Fast immer drehen sich die Arbeiten um das Geisterhafte, um eine Lücke oder Erinnerung. Oft gehen diese einher mit von der Künstlerin notierten Projektionen, mit Selbstoffenbarungen und Sehnsüchten, mit Sinnlichkeit, mit Leidenschaft und Leidensbereitschaft. Was dabei tatsächlich autobiografisch und was Fiktion ist, bleibt im Unklaren, wodurch die Künstlerin nur noch stärker zum Symbol ihres Werkes wird: Die Leerstellen des Privatlebens füllen die Betrachtenden mit ihrer Projektion, wie Calle die Sehnsüchte in ihren Arbeiten selbst. Im Zeitalter des autofiktionalen Booms kann es da schon verwundern, dass ihre Arbeiten seit mehr als 20 Jahren nicht umfänglich in Deutschland präsentiert wurden.
Die Ausstellung im Hamburger Bahnhof wiederum steht eher im Namen der vom Selbst distanzierteren Werke der Künstlerin. Zwar präsentiert die Schau auch die Serie „The Ghosts of Orsay“ (Die Geister Orsays) von 2022, in der die Künstlerin sich mit ihren Jahren im verlassenen Hotel d’Orsay auseinandersetzt, einem Grand Hotel im gleichnamigen Pariser Bahnhof, der seit den 1980er Jahre das Musée d’Orsay beherbergt und in welchem sich die Künstlerin Ender der 1970er Jahre bis zum Beginn der Umbauarbeiten unbemerkt aufhielt und Unterlagen und Objekte einsammelte, doch ist diese weit weniger selbstoffenbarend als ihr frühes Werk.
Gästekarten aus den 30er Jahren, Zimmernummern und technische Objekte lässt die Künstlerin für diese Arbeit, die sie für eine Ausstellung im Musée d’Orsay anfertigte, von einem Archäologen interpretieren, die Texte dazu sind sorgfältig gerahmt.
Vom Museum im Bahnhof zum Museum im Bahnhof ist diese nun nach Berlin gewandert, und auch eine weitere Arbeit, die ursprünglich für das Musée national Picasso-Paris angefertigt wurde und Fotos verhängter Meisterschinken während des Coronalockdowns zeigt, ist zumindest in Teilen zu sehen.
Am Schluss kommt die Sinnlichkeit
Nach so viel Institutionsreferenzen tut es gut, die letzten beiden Räume der Ausstellung zu besichtigen. Für die dort gezeigte, fast schmerzhaft berührende Video-Arbeit „Voir la mer“ (Das Meer sehen) filmte Calle in Istanbul lebende Menschen, die zum ersten Mal das Meer sehen. (Die zuerst eingeblendete Rückenansicht wird natürlich auch hier im Text auf den sich in den Berliner Sammlungen befindlichen Caspar David Friedrich bezogen, dies lässt sich jedoch getrost ignorieren.).
Ein paar Schritte weiter darf man schließlich unter die Filzvorhänge schmulen und T’s und K’s morbide Liebe entdecken. Eingestickt im Textil notierte die Künstlerin, warum sie die Motive fotografierte. Darunter entdeckt man eine Wolke wie Gedärm. Oder eine Frau, die ins Nichts fotografiert, der Körper gekrümmt im schwarzen Kleid. Oder Hemd, Krawatte und letzte Rechnungen, die Worte auf dem Vorhang: „Because of the Pangs of Sadness“ (Wegen der Qualen der Traurigkeit). Und plötzlich kann man die sehr deutlich fühlen.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.mediapart.fr/journal/culture.title: L’actualité du Front populaire, avec Ludivine Bantigny
https://www.mediapart.fr/journal/culture.author: Edwy Plenel
https://www.mediapart.fr/journal/culture.text:
« Par la joie qu’il a embrasée, le moment 1936 a affirmé que le bonheur est aussi une affaire publique. C’est un acquis immense en même temps qu’un vivier où puiser : l’espoir d’une société émancipée. Dans ses continuités souterraines, le Front populaire ne saurait se figer en relique. Si l’histoire se tient à bonne distance du mythe pour approcher la vérité qu’on lui doit, elle sait aussi que cette joie est un trésor commun, dont nous avons toujours besoin. »
La fin de La Bourse ou la vie (La Découverte), ce livre où Ludivine Bantigny revisite le Front populaire comme une « histoire pour aujourd’hui », fait écho à notre actualité récente de soulèvements joyeux, généreux et rassembleurs, partis de la jeunesse lycéenne, dont l’Orchestre du Nouveau Monde est devenu l’un des formidables animateurs, communiquant son énergie collective par la grâce de l’enchantement musical.
L’unité nécessaire, face à la menace de l’extrême droite, de forces politiques hier irréconciliables, la tension créatrice entre le mouvement de la société à la base et l’action gouvernementale au sommet, la convergence des luttes autour de causes communes dans la recherche d’une vie bonne… : autant de questions qui résonnent avec nos débats d’aujourd’hui.
Dans le prolongement de ses travaux précédents, notamment sur Mai-68, sur la Commune de Paris et sur les luttes féministes, l’originalité de la démarche de l’historienne est de nourrir ces interrogations par une approche sensible, au plus près de ce qu’ont fait et vécu actrices et acteurs de cette invention collective.
Provisoirement vaincu, puisqu’il ne put empêcher le déferlement du nazisme sur l’Europe et la revanche du pétainisme en France, le sursaut du Front populaire nous a légué un héritage finalement victorieux, puisque repris par le Conseil national de la Résistance et officialisé après-guerre : une exigence de démocratie sociale issue de lois fondatrices, obtenues grâce aux revendications des grèves ouvrières, qui instaurèrent les congés payés, la semaine de quarante heures et les conventions collectives.
Ludivine Bantigny s’arrête particulièrement sur ces trois réformes qui, face au conservatisme patronal, furent à l’époque de véritables révolutions sociétales. Elle le fait avec autant de rigueur que d’empathie, ne cachant pas son engagement auprès des opprimé·es de tous bords, au point d’avoir volontairement quitté, en 2020, la position de surplomb que lui offrait un poste universitaire pour choisir d’enseigner dans le secondaire.
Ayant ce goût de l’archive qu’a célébré sa collègue Arlette Farge, elle s’attache ainsi aux anonymes, ces « obscurs et sans grades » dont Jean Maitron, le fondateur du dictionnaire biographique du mouvement ouvrier et social, faisait le cœur des mouvements émancipateurs. Mais elle réussit aussi à nous faire vivre les tourments du dirigeant socialiste Léon Blum, le président du Conseil du Front populaire, ce tiraillement dont il rend compte lui-même, non sans sincérité, entre la conquête du pouvoir et sa gestion, ces contradictions avec les idéaux et les principes qu’entraînent son légalisme et sa quête de respectabilité.
« Cette histoire, elle nous sert : sur les enjeux du front commun antifasciste, sur la présence de l’auto-organisation populaire », confie Ludivine Bantigny dans cette « Échappée » enregistrée dans un lieu qui en est une butte-témoin : la Maison des métallos à Paris. Ancienne manufacture d’instruments de musique, le bâtiment fut vendu en 1936 à l’Union fraternelle des métallurgistes, dont le militant de la CGT Jean-Pierre Timbaud, futur martyr de la Résistance, était l’un des dirigeants.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120387.author: Jana Frielinghaus
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120387.text:
- Politik
- Geheimdienstreform
Geheimdienstreform: Volle Beinfreiheit für Agenten
Der Bundestag hat Gesetzesänderungen beschlossen, die BND und Verfassungsschutz weitreichende Befugnisse geben und ihre Kontrolle weiter einschränken.
Die Mehrheit der vom Parlament im Vorfeld geladenen Sachverständigen hatte große Teile der von der Bundesregierung geplanten Geheimdienstreform als verfassungswidrig eingestuft. Unter anderem, weil die Unverletzlichkeit der Privatsphäre wie auch die vorgeschriebene Trennung zwischen Polizei- und Geheimdienstaufgaben damit teilweise aufgehoben wird.
Der Bundestag hat das Gesetzespaket am Freitag dennoch beschlossen. Die Überwachungsbefugnisse des Bundesamtes für Verfassungsschutz (BfV) und des Bundesnachrichtendienstes (BND) werden damit massiv ausgeweitet. Politiker*innen der Regierungsparteien betonten jedoch, Bedenken seien in zahlreichen Änderungen des Gesetzentwurfs berücksichtigt worden.
Das Paket aus dem Bundesinnenministerium, das Ressortschef Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) als »Jahrhundertreform« pries, erhielt mit 308 Ja-Stimmen die erforderliche Mehrheit aus den Koalitionsfraktionen. 190 Abgeordnete, vor allem jene von Linkspartei und AfD, votierten dagegen. 71 enthielten sich, 61 waren bei der namentlichen Abstimmung nicht anwesend.
Die Grünen enthielten sich nahezu geschlossen, weil ihre Anträge zur Teilung der Abstimmung und zur Streichung von Gesetzespassagen nicht durchkamen. Ihr Geheimdienstexperte Konstantin von Notz lobte die Reform dennoch: Vieles sei »gelungen«. Doch die Änderungen im Verfassungsschutzgesetz könne man nur mittragen, wenn die »verfassungsrechtlich bedenklichen Teile« gestrichen würden. Das lehnte das Parlament mit der Mehrheit der Regierungsfraktionen ab.
Von Notz monierte, die Gesetzesänderungen ermöglichten dem Verfassungsschutz einen »direkten Eingriff in das Leben von Bürger*innen weit im Gefahrenvorfeld«. Die Regelungen seien »völlig konturenlos, ohne Transparenz und Rechtsschutz«. Von Notz ist stellvertretender Vorsitzender des Parlamentarischen Kontrollgremiums (PKGr) zur Kontrolle der Nachrichtendienste.
Grüne als Speerspitze des »wehrhaften« Staates
Die Ausweitung der Befugnisse des BND befürwortet die einstige Anti-Geheimdienste-Partei ohnehin. Von Notz lobte: »Heute ist ein guter Tag für die Sicherheit in diesem Land.« Die Grünen hätten den Gesetzgebungsprozess »konstruktiv begleitet«, denn seine Partei wolle nicht, dass »Putin Deutschland zu einer russischen Einflusszone macht«. Im Abwehrkampf gegen den russischen »Schattenkrieg« seien die Geheimdienste die »erste Verteidigungslinie«.
Von Notz hob hervor, dass es seine Partei war, die durchgesetzt hat, dass die Ausnahme von der Schuldenbremse im Grundgesetz im Rahmen der »Zeitenwende« auch für die Ausstattung der Nachrichtendienste gilt.
Harte Kritik übte der Grünen-Politiker nicht nur an der AfD. Der Linken warf er »komplette Realitätsverweigerung« vor, weil sie die hybride Bedrohung nicht wahrnehmen wolle. Angesichts der Sicherheitslage sei die »Fundamentalopposition« der Linken »parlamentarische Arbeitsverweigerung«.
Linke-Innenexpertin Clara Bünger hielt dem entgegen, ihre Fraktion habe immer wieder Gesetzesvorschläge zur Reform der Geheimdienste gemacht. Es brauche »einen echten Schutz der Verfassung«, den das BfV nicht leiste und nicht leisten könne. Dafür sei eine »unabhängige Stelle« nötig, die »menschenfeindliche Bestrebungen« dokumentiert. Die Trennung zwischen Polizei und Geheimdiensten sei auch im überarbeiteten Gesetzespaket nicht gewährleistet, weshalb sie bei ihrem Vorwurf bleibe, es werde eine neue Geheimpolizei geschaffen. Wenn der Verfassungsschutz künftig heimlich und ohne gerichtliche Kontrolle Wohnungen betrete und eine flächendeckende KI-Überwachung nutze, entstehe »ein unkontrollierbarer Apparat, der die Grundrechte mit Füßen tritt«.
Gegen das Paket stimmte mit Ulle Schauws eine Grünen-Politikerin, mit Jan Dieren ein Abgeordneter der SPD – und mit der Brandenburgerin Saskia Ludwig eine CDU-Politikerin. Bei Letzterer könnte dies mit ihrer politischen und persönlichen Nähe zur AfD zu tun haben. Die Rechtsaußen-Partei hatte unter anderem beklagt, die sogenannte Resilienzklausel, über die Landesämter des Verfassungsschutzes aus dessen Informationsverbund ausgeschlossen werden können, sei eine »Lex AfD«.
»Lizenz zum Zurückschlagen«
In der Debatte folgten die meisten Abgeordneten dem Narrativ Alexander Dobrindts von der enormen Bedrohung, die die Reform alternativlos mache. Der Bundesinnenminister betonte, Deutschland sei »Operationsraum für Terrorismus, Extremismus, für fremde Mächte«. Zudem würden die Grenzen zwischen staatlichen und nichtstaatlichen Akteuren immer mehr verschwimmen. Um »wieder Sichtbarkeit zu erreichen« und offenzulegen, hinter welchen Ereignissen Angriffe stecken, brauche es leistungsfähige Nachrichtendienste. Linkspartei und AfD wollten »den Verfassungsschutz in einem Moment schwächen, in dem ein Schattenkrieg die Demokratie bedroht.«
Bisher sammeln Deutschlands Nachrichtendienste vor allem Informationen. Künftig sollen sie wie Geheimdienste anderer Länder auch »operative« Befugnisse bekommen, um Gefahren abzuwehren. So sollen BND und BfV künftig auch Hackerangriffe ausführen können, um Daten zu manipulieren oder zu löschen. Offiziell sollen sie das nur zur Abwehr einer laufenden Cyberattacke tun dürfen. In der Debatte hieß es folgerichtig, es gehe um die »Lizenz zum Zurückschlagen«. So ließen sich etwa Anleitungen zum Waffenbau verändern oder IT-Systeme von Drohnenfabriken oder Chemiewaffenlaboren sabotieren.
Auch die Befugnisse zur Sammlung und Auswertung von Daten werden erweitert. Dies betrifft auch die Auswertung großer Datenmengen mittels Künstlicher Intelligenz und den Abgleich biometrischer Daten durch KI-gestützte Online-Recherche. Unter bestimmten Voraussetzungen dürfen Verfassungsschutz und BND auch heimlich Wohnungen und Geschäftsräume betreten, um Überwachungsmaßnahmen vorzubereiten.
Zur Kontrolle der Dienste soll beim Unabhängigen Kontrollrat gebündelt werden, den mehrere Abgeordnete als »gerichtsähnliches« Gremium darstellten.
Bedenken aus der Zivilgesellschaft
Kritiker befürchten eine Aushöhlung des Datenschutzes etwa in Arztpraxen, mögliche Eingriffe in die Privatsphäre der Bürgerinnen und Bürger sowie eine »digitale Massenüberwachung«. Der Hartmannbund forderte einen »absoluten Vertrauensschutz für Ärztinnen und Ärzte« ein. Der Vorsitzende Klaus Reinhardt kritisierte, dass Mediziner*innen bei nachrichtendienstlichen Maßnahmen gegenüber anderen Geheimnisträgern wie Rechtsanwälten, Geistlichen oder Abgeordneten benachteiligt werden, indem das Vertraulichkeitsinteresse im Einzelfall gegen das Aufklärungsinteresse abzuwägen sei. Eine Petition, in der der Schutz von Ärzt*innen und Psychotherapeut*innen vor Überwachung gefordert wird, hatten bis Freitagnachmittag mehr als 71.000 Menschen unterzeichnet.
Am Donnerstag hatten noch einmal 28 Nichtregierungsorganisationen in einem offenen Brief an die Abgeordneten appelliert, den Gesetzesänderungen nicht zuzustimmen. Initiiert wurde das Schreiben von der Humanistische Union zusammen mit dem Komitee für Grundrechte und Demokratie, dem Republikanischen Anwältinnen- und Anwälteverein (RAV) und der Vereinigung Demokratischer Jurist:innen (VDJ).
Die Verfasser des Briefes beklagen die Aufweichung des erwähnten Trennungsgebots zwischen Polizei- und Geheimdienstaufgaben ebenso wie die Ausweitung der Möglichkeiten zur Überwachung und zum massenhaften Eingriff in Persönlichkeitsrechte. Gerade durch »weitreichende Zugriffe auf Videoüberwachung des öffentlichen Raums« und die KI-gestützte Auswertung enormer Datenmengen werde »ein weiterer Schritt hin zum Überwachungsstaat« gegangen, heißt es in dem Schreiben.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

We Just Witnessed a Populist Blowout
In Tuesday’s midterm elections, voters rejected Trump’s billionaire-backed politics and attacks on working people. The winners need to show that a different kind of politics can deliver.
Peter Certo
For years, Americans have been viciously divided according to race, religion, immigration status and gender identity by politicians dead set on making us fight each other rather than them. In a year where real people’s struggles were impossible to ignore, that effort fell short.
It’s hard to overstate the scale of Democratic victories in this year’s midterm elections.
Voters broke for Democratic candidates by margins scarcely anticipated by even the party’s rosiest polls—often in deep red states and congressional districts that few seriously thought were competitive. Democrats will now control a commanding House majority and hold a significant edge in the Senate as well.
This was a decisive rejection of Trumpism — and it happened on a significantly tiited playing field.
Before the election, Supreme Court justices aligned with President Donald Trump gutted what remained of the Voting Rights Act, only the latest in a series of rulings limiting fair access to voting and representation. At Trump’s urging, Republican-led statehouses unleashed an unprecedented flurry of mid-decade gerrymanders designed to maximize their partisan advantage and disenfranchise their critics. Billionaires poured vast sums into races — and trillionaire Elon Musk spent over $400 million alone, more than George Soros has spent on elections his entire life.
And that’s not even getting into the concerns, often stoked by leading Republicans themselves, that the administration would try to cancel results, deploy National Guard or Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to cities, or otherwise meddle in the election.
None of it was enough for voters who’ve spent years now watching events in their lives spin out of control.
Trump’s tariffs made life miserable for farmers, manufacturers, and consumers while his allies slashed safety net programs to fund tax breaks for billionaires. The war in Iran, which Trump launched shortly after promising no new wars, sent the price of fuel skyrocketing.
Lawless ICE agents terrorized immigrants and citizens alike and shocked the conscience of people across the political spectrum. And a data center boom spiked power bills and disrupted communities across the country, all to power a technology CEOs vowed to use for replacing people’s jobs and surveilling their day to day life.
In the races that mattered most, populist candidates spoke to these concerns directly.
Candidates who backed data center restrictions and moratoria flipped red governorships and/or Senate seats in Ohio, Texas, Georgia, South Carolina, and beyond—while voters directly passed their own local moratoria in dozens of communities.
In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed defeated a shockingly Islamophobic opposition by focusing relentlessly on taking U.S. foreign and domestic policy alike back from billionaires. In Maine, Troy Jackson toppled longtime Sen. Susan Collins by embracing his working class identity and supporting Medicare for All. And in a state that became emblematic of ICE’s abuse, Peggy Flanagan ran away with a victory in Minnesota calling to “rip ICE apart.”
But to sustain these gains, these winners — and the leaders of their party — will need to follow through on the promises voters entrusted them with.
In the two years Trump has left, they’ll need to be held accountable to claw back the enormous funds Trump and the GOP have set aside for ICE and Pentagon and put them back into programs to make sure struggling Americans have food and healthcare—areas which are only set to see further cuts as more provisions of the “Big Beautiful Bill” take effect.
They should embrace their powers of investigation not only to crack down on the administration’s unprecedented corruption, but also to make tech CEOs answer for foisting AI and data centers on Americans and to hold corporate price gougers accountable for raising the cost of groceries, healthcare and rent. And they’ll need to rapidly repair our civic infrastructure to get money out of politics and put ordinary people back in it.
If our next leaders can’t deliver as promised, the politics of scapegoating will come roaring back. It won’t be easy, but the voters are watching. And this November they spoke loud and clear.

https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-decli.title: Mamdani declines to back fellow New Yorker Schumer as Senate majority leader
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-decli.author: Brigid Bergin
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-decli.text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has declined to endorse Brooklyn native U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer as the next Senate majority leader, a signal that New York’s senior senator is facing increased pushback within the ranks of the Democratic party, including in the Empire State.
Mamdani was asked during a news conference on Friday if Schumer, who currently leads the Senate minority, deserved another term as leader when Democrats take majority control of the chamber in January. Instead of responding directly, the mayor said the American people voted for change in the midterm elections.
“They sent a message that they want Democratic leadership across the board that will deliver material improvements for the working class. And as the mayor of New York City, that's exactly what I want to see for New Yorkers across our five boroughs,” Mamdani said. “So I care less about who it is, and I care more about what they do with that power.”
Mamdani’s decision not to back Schumer is reminiscent of the senator’s own refusal to endorse Mamdani last year after Mamdani won the Democratic nomination for mayor. Even on the day of the mayoral election, Schumer would not tell reporters who he voted for and would only say he looked forward to “working with the next mayor.”
Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders have all said they would not support Schumer as their party leader.
Schumer led the Senate in 2021 and 2022, when Democrats held a slim majority with then-Vice President Kamala Harris serving as the tiebreaking vote. During that period, Congress passed several major pieces of legislation including the COVID-19 stimulus package and the bipartisan infrastructure law, which earmarked billions of dollars in aid to New York.
Late Thursday, Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen officially announced he planned to challenge Schumer for Majority Leader. In a statement posted to social media, Van Hollen said the American people demanded new leadership.
“In this election, Americans called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption. To deliver, we need new leadership,” Van Hollen wrote on X. “This isn't about any one person — it’s about answering that call. That's why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”
On Friday, the Working Families Party said that it was supporting Van Hollen for the Senate leadership post.
Schumer responded to Van Hollen’s announcement on Thursday night.
“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” Schumer wrote on X. “I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”
A spokesperson for Schumer referred to his existing statement when asked for a response to Mamdani’s comments.
Senate leadership elections are scheduled to take place in December.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/isra.title: Israel Used a U.S.-Made Missile to Kill Six at Gaza’s Nasser Hospital
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/isra.author: Jonah Valdez
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/isra.text:
Throughout Israel’s war on Palestine, doctors Thaer Ahmad and Feroze Sidhwa spent months at Nasser Hospital in the southern Gaza city of Khan Younis, where they provided care as volunteers and survived a raid and an airstrike on the complex. On Wednesday evening, they were in an Uber in New York headed to a screening of their film about their time in Gaza when they realized Nasser was the target of another Israeli airstrike.
“They just hit Nasser again,” Ahmad said, turning from the front seat toward Sidhwa. “I think Rizk is dead.”
He was referring to Dr. Rizk Abu Shaaira, an experienced surgeon and fixture of the Palestinian medical community whom both had worked alongside at the hospital and who appears in their film “American Doctor.” When Israel attacked Nasser Hospital on Wednesday — for at least the seventh time since the genocide escalated in 2023 — Abu Shaaira was one of the six people killed.
As the doctors arrived at a theater in Westchester for their screening, they received a flood of messages, photos, and video from their colleagues at Nasser, showing smoke-filled departments and wrecked operating rooms. The attack forced the closure of the hospital’s emergency, surgery, radiology and laboratory departments, hospital officials said.
Six people were killed in the airstrike, according to Gaza health officials, and 52 others were wounded, said Médecins Sans Frontières/Doctors Without Borders. Israel said it had used a precision-guided missile to target a Hamas commander.
One video showed a body bag holding Abu Shaaira, who had been working a night shift in the surgical ward, one of several floors severely damaged in the airstrike. Sidhwa, who worked directly with Abu Shaaira during his time volunteering at Nasser, described the 52-year-old father as a colleague who was “enthusiastic about everything” and “loved surgery.”
Another image showed unexploded ordnance launched at the hospital that medical workers had placed atop a stretcher, bearing the label “GBU-39/B” – a model of guided missiles manufactured by U.S. company Boeing. Israel purchases this precise missile model using funds from the U.S. State Department.
“That’s not complicity,” said Feroze when asked about the U.S.-made missiles used in the attack. “That’s active participation in the murder of physicians and other healthcare workers.”
Wednesday’s attack on Nasser Hospital, which serves a population of about 1.3 million people, is the fourth Israeli strike on a hospital since the so-called ceasefire agreement in October 2025. It is the seventh on the Nasser complex, including a double-tap strike in August 2025 when Israeli warplanes struck the hospital twice within minutes, killing first responders and journalists. Sidhwa had been volunteering at Nasser during an earlier airstrike on the complex in March 2025 violating an earlier ceasefire. That strike killed multiple people, including a 16-year-old boy.
When Ahmad volunteered at Nasser in early 2024, a part of the hospital’s pediatric ward was still damaged from an Israeli tank shell that flew through a window, killing Donia Abu Mohsen, 12, while she received care from a previous airstrike that killed her family. During his stint, Israeli soldiers raided the complex and detained several doctors with whom he worked; they remain imprisoned without charge. Ahmad said his colleagues at Nasser told him that upon hearing the first booms on Wednesday, they knew immediately, due to familiarity, that they had been hit by an Israeli attack.
“Something that has troubled us so much is how normalized the targeting of these hospitals has become for Palestinians serving their communities,” Ahmad said. “They knew what was going on right away.”
Since returning from their time treating patients in Gaza, both Ahmad and Sidhwa have lobbied members of Congress to support the Block the Bombs Act, a House bill that seeks to prohibit the sale of certain arms to Israel that are tied to violations of U.S. and international human rights law. Among the weapons subject to the ban is Boeing’s 250-pound GBU-39. With a new Congress soon to be controlled by Democrats, many of whom ran campaigns touting support for the bill, both Ahmad and Sidhwa called on lawmakers to act.
“If our Congress upheld international humanitarian law, as well as U.S. domestic law, Dr. Rizik would still be alive,” Ahmad said, “and there wouldn’t be a surgeon who lost both of his legs in this bombing.”
The Israeli military claimed in a series of statements posted to social media that it had targeted a senior Hamas commander and other Hamas members who were “hiding” in the hospital and that the strike was meant to “eliminate the threat they posed.” The military did not specify the actual threat nor address the killing of Rizk, patients, and other civilians by “precision-guided missiles” it claims to have deployed to mitigate civilian harm. Israel alleged Hamas was operating out of the hospital’s second floor, but provided no evidence beyond a computer-rendered video. At least six Israelis have been killed in Gaza since the start of the so-called ceasefire, the Israeli military has said. Israel has killed more than 1,400 Palestinians in that time, according to Gaza health officials. The United Nations said that among those reported dead are at least 340 children.
In a statement to The Intercept, the Israeli military repeated its claim that Wednesday’s strike was targeting a Hamas commander, but it declined to confirm whether the alleged target of their strike was killed or comment on the civilians killed in the attack.
President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, tasked with rebuilding Gaza, called Wednesday’s attack a “tragic loss of life” but went on to repeat the Israeli allegation that Hamas carries out “continued exploitation of hospitals and other critical civilian infrastructure for military purposes.”
Sidhwa called the Board of Peace statement on Hamas’ alleged embedding in hospitals “bullshit,” adding that he has seen no evidence of Hamas embedding its fighters within any hospital in Gaza, a recurring observation by international doctors who volunteer in the strip.
“Show me one example,” Sidhwa said. “I would love to see a single photo, a single video, a single testimony from a Palestinian. Literally anything. It’s just completely absurd.”
Médecins Sans Frontières/Doctors Without Borders said in a statement that it was “appalled and outraged” by Israel’s attack, adding that its doctors had to operate on two of their colleagues and another patient injured in the strike. The group referred to its earlier decision in January to temporarily halt its teams’ operations at Nasser, citing reports of “armed men in different areas of the large compound of the hospital,” and said similar incidents have taken place more recently. Even so, the group said, this does not justify Israel’s attack.
“Under international humanitarian law, hospitals must be respected and protected,” the group said. “In no conceivable circumstances can attacks on functioning hospitals in Gaza be treated as normal or acceptable.”
The strike came days after the board issued a rare condemnation of the Israeli government for its blockade of humanitarian aid from entering Gaza in the aftermath of a storm that wiped out thousands of tents, killing four people. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rebuffed the criticism and blamed Hamas for not disarming. Israel, meanwhile, continues to occupy about 70% of the Gaza strip, extending beyond the yellow line, a border drawn in the ceasefire agreement that is meant to mark where Israel can operate its military, and launches attacks on the strip on a weekly basis, all violations of the agreement.
“The same military who’s blocking the necessary supplies, as a middle finger to you, decides that they’re going to bomb a hospital,” Ahmad said. “I’m sure behind closed doors everybody is fuming and reeling, but unless people are ready to actually hold the Israelis accountable, actually use their leverage, nothing is going to change.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
