https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ke.title: Manhattan Landlord Sues Kehinde Wiley, Claiming He Owes $36,000 in Unpaid Rent
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ke.author: Harrison Jacobs
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ke.text:
Artist Kehinde Wiley returned to the New York art scene last week with his first show in the city since he was accused of sexual assault in 2024. Now the famed artist and Obama portraitist faces a legal dispute of a different kind: real estate.
In a complaint filed in New York County Supreme Court, 115 West 11th Street LLC accuses Wiley of failing to pay rent on his apartment in its building since October 1. According to court documents filed November 6, the rent is $18,000 a month, and the landlord is seeking $36,000 in total.
Per the documents, Wiley has lived in the building since September 2023 and signed a lease renewal in July 2025, which was later extended through the end of September. The landlord contends that Wiley did not vacate the apartment when the lease ended and has continued to live there without paying the agreed $18,000 a month.
Wiley has not yet responded to the complaint. A summons, also filed November 6, requires the artist’s attorneys to respond within 20 days.
The complaint was filed on the same day Wiley’s new exhibition, “What the Light Becomes,” opened at Sean Kelly Gallery in New York. The show features a new series of portraits of contemporary New Yorkers. According to the exhibition text, the show is “conceived of as a love letter to New York and a return to the subject of the city that launched Wiley’s career.”
Sean Kelly Gallery did not respond to a request for comment from ARTnews by press time.
Wiley is one of the art world’s brightest stars and one of the few artists who are household names, thanks to his beloved official portrait of President Barack Obama. He has been tied up in the courts since 2024, when five people accused him of sexual assault or rape. Wiley has denied the allegations. He has said that his encounters with some of the accusers were consensual and that he did not know others. Only one accuser, Ogechi Chieke, has sued the artist, and that case is ongoing.
In a New York Times profile published last week, Wiley said of the allegations, “I’ve been through more pain—it’s really hard to imagine what it’s like to have people believe that. To look at you and think you’re a predator.” He added, “In my life, there has always been, by hook or by crook, some sense of grace that comes out of even the most challenging situations.”
Jennifer Barrett of Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, Wiley’s attorney in the Chieke lawsuit, did not respond to a request for comment by press time.
	The Daily Mail first reported the new lawsuit on Wednesday.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ”Dark Horse’ é mais que um filme, é um esquema de lavagem de dinheiro’, avalia cientista político
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Ana Rosa Carrara
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A segunda fase da operação da Polícia Federal (PF) que apura desvio de emendas parlamentares para uso no filme “Dark Horse”, cinebiografia do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, agrava ainda mais a situação do deputado federal Mario Frias (PL-SP). A ação da PF teve como alvo Raphael Augusto Azevedo, ex-assessor de Frias.
Ao Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, o cientista político Mateus de Albuquerque, professor da Universidade Federal de Juiz de Fora (UFJF), avalia que cada fase da operação da PF ajuda a compreender o tamanho da engrenagem do esquema e evidencia que “‘Dark Horse’ é um filme, mas é, principalmente, lavagem de dinheiro”.
“É um esquema de transferência de verba pública para manutenção da família Bolsonaro”, resume.
Nesse sentido, Albuquerque destaca que os envolvidos lançaram mão da justificativa de que estariam realizando uma obra cultural para realizar os desvios de verba pública e tinham um nome forte para isso: Mario Frias. “Ele é ator, chefiou a cultura durante o governo Bolsonaro, deve ter mais intimidade com o ecossistema da cultura, que é cada vez mais profissionalizado, para mimetizar a forma com que se faz esse financiamento para transferir esse dinheiro para o seu fim, que fica cada vez mais evidente que era para sustentar [a moradia dos Bolsonaro] nos EUA”, argumenta.
O episódio, segundo o analista, também reforça a necessidade de rever a questão das emendas no Brasil. “É mais um exemplo de como o dispositivo de emenda, da forma como está no Brasil, pode ser usado para fins escusos”, continua.
Mateus de Albuquerque observa que há uma certa ironia quando se analisa a parte operacional do esquema, que, em sua lógica, se assemelharia à Lei Rouanet, tão criticada pelos bolsonaristas com base em desinformação. “Eles fizeram uma corruptela nefasta da Lei Rouanet, que não é um mecanismo de financiamento direto do Estado para produções culturais. Ela é um mecanismo de isenção fiscal para que empresas possam financiar obras artísticas”, afirma.
“O que o ‘Dark Horse’ faz: a busca por financiamento privado de maneira ilegal, irregular e, na prática, é um financiamento privado, porque a sua irregularidade se sustenta no elemento nocivo desse dinheiro privado que, na verdade, é público e foi roubado, convertido em dinheiro privado, através do Banco Master”, explica.
Para ouvir e assistir
O jornal Conexão BdF vai ao ar em duas edições, de segunda a sexta-feira: a primeira às 12h e a segunda às 17h, na Rádio Brasil de Fato, 98.9 FM, na Grande São Paulo, com transmissão simultânea também pelo YouTube do Brasil de Fato.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Microsoft outage shakes up companies, schools and local governments across US
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Gaya Gupta in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
The Microsoft Outlook outage has shaken up companies and local governments across the US that use its suite of email, calendar, video conferencing and cloud storage systems.
Even as Outlook started to resume normal operations Friday morning, local leaders from across the country, including in Miami, Maryland and Los Angeles, warned residents that certain staff or services were still unavailable due to the outage that started around 1pm ET on Thursday.
In Colorado, one local detention facility in Arapahoe county said that they were unable to take online bond payments to release detainees because of the outage.
“Until Outlook email is restored, anyone needing to post bond for immediate release must do so in person at the jail,” the office said in a social media statement.
The Los Angeles county sheriff’s department also warned that it was experiencing disruptions in its email and other communications platforms.
Emergency management services in Fredericksburg and Gillespie county in Texas said they were unable to receive emails and encouraged residents and partners to call instead.
Around Maryland, the Washington suburban sanitary commission, which provides safe drinking water and sewer treatment to parts of Maryland, said that its technicians may be delayed due to the outage, and some customers may have trouble making their water bill payments.
In Washington DC, congressional staffers continued to lament the outage’s impact during the lame duck session of Congress. Some told Politico that the disruptions were particularly disruptive as their offices were in the middle of negotiating pending legislation before the end of the year and planning for the next Congress.
“Shall we start conducting all official business via DM?” wrote Sharon Eliza Nichols, the director of communications for congresswoman Eleanor Holmes Norton of Washington DC.
Some school districts in Richmond, Virginia, and Port Washington, New York, also told parents on Friday morning that they were experiencing outages, and asked them to reach out by phone or through other online educational platforms to reach their child’s school, while the Albany school district said that it had restored its services.
The Colorado School of Mines encouraged “faculty to be flexible with assignment deadlines and understanding of students who cannot complete assignments due to unavailability of Microsoft tools”, though many of its systems were on unaffected platforms such as Google Workspace and Canvas.
Claude, whose developer, Anthropic, is gearing up for its upcoming stock market debut with a valuation of up to $1.4tn, also said that it was starting to see signs of recovery from the Microsoft outages, but warned that some users may still receive errors. OpenAI also said it was still investigating issues with “Microsoft connectors” that were degrading performance.
“We’re investigating an issue with Microsoft connectors where new connections may be broken and tools are not working as expected. We’ll share an update when we know more,” the company said.
On Wall Street, Workhorse Group, an industrial manufacturer, rescheduled its Q3 earnings call that was scheduled for Thursday afternoon because of the outage.
In a social media post, Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said late Thursday that “there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity”.
On Friday morning, Microsoft noted “improvements in service availability” but noted that “some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as a recovery continues”.
By the end of the day, most of the issues seemed to be ironed out. Schools and businesses appeared to be coming back online, congressional staffers reported “improvements to Outlook’s functionality”. The Colorado detention facility said it is “now receiving email notifications when online bond payments are made”.
And the emergency management services in Texas said they were starting to see emails trickle back in, saying: “Thanks for your patience with the worldwide outage!”
Dara Kerr and Johana Bhuiyan contributed reporting

https://hyperallergic.com/45-of-us-indep.title: 45% of US Independent Arts Publications Face Existential Crisis, Report Finds
https://hyperallergic.com/45-of-us-indep.author: Valentina Di Liscia
https://hyperallergic.com/45-of-us-indep.text:
45% of US Independent Arts Publications Face Existential Crisis, Report Finds
In addition to declining funding, the survey identified a disturbing correlation between censorship concerns and financial precarity.
Nearly half of independent publications covering arts and culture in the United States said their business models will not be sustainable without “profound changes” to the current funding landscape, according to a report from Critical Minded and the Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation released this week.
The new survey notably identifies a disturbing correlation between censorship concerns, including external pressure from advertisers and sponsors, and financial precarity. The 41% of respondents who said they faced free-speech pressures or threats in the last two years were more likely to report funding declines, throwing into stark relief how what outlets choose to cover — or not — may determine whether they can pay staff and contributors, or keep the lights on altogether.
“Support for Arts and Culture Journalism: A Survey of Independent Publications in the United States” polled 141 independent outlets that cover the arts on issues impacting the field and strategies used to address them. The anonymized respondents are based in 34 states and the District of Columbia, with the highest concentration (38.2%) in the Northeast, and reach an average annual audience of about half a million.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/bernie-democ.title: Democrats Did Their Best Bernie Impression in the Midterms
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/bernie-democ.author: Branko Marcetic
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/bernie-democ.text:
Democrats Did Their Best Bernie Impression in the Midterms
Put their 2026 midterms side by side with previous campaigns, and it’s clear: Democrats won in red states by sounding less like Democrats and more like Bernie Sanders.
The 2026 midterms saw historic gains for socialists and progressives. So, perhaps unsurprisingly, the Democratic Party’s corporate wing is hurriedly spinning the result as a victory for centrists and “moderates.”
Largely lost in this is the way that the Left has transformed what it actually means to run as a Democratic moderate or a centrist. Because looking at this year’s campaigns, there is no doubt that even the most uninspiring “moderate” candidates were taking several pages — whole chapters, really — from the books of Bernie Sanders, Zohran Mamdani, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
It’s worth recalling that before 2025, standard Democratic campaign rhetoric was all about “defending democracy,” railing against extremism and authoritarianism, and advocating for abortion rights — all good things on their merits, but (with the exception of abortion rights) largely abstract ones that are not as animating or as high a priority for the majority of voters as their basic pocketbook concerns.
Just look at former President Joe Biden’s big kick-off speech for his reelection campaign, which was almost completely devoid of an economic message but heavy on talk of “MAGA extremists” and the “soul of America.” In fact, the absence of an economic message was a constant left-wing criticism of the party through the Biden era, including from this very magazine.
This has now completely shifted. While Democratic candidates in 2024 ran by far most of their TV ads on abortion, with immigration coming a distant second, this year, the overwhelming focus of their ad spending was “affordability,” dropping $401 million on the topic — a full quarter of their $1.5 billion total spend.
And where did the “affordability” frame come from? Well, both Democratic and Republican members of Congress happened to start spamming that word in their emails to constituents right after socialist Zohran Mamdani won the New York City Democratic primary with a campaign that put affordability at its very center.
But it’s more than just coming up with a pithy new word describing voters’ struggles with the economy. A number of the moderate candidates who won in red states sounded oddly like Bernie Sanders, railing against billionaires and the ultrarich, the corrupting influence of money in politics, and swearing off corporate money.
The clearest example of this was Texas Senator-elect James Talarico, who said that the fundamental divide in US politics was “top versus bottom,” called billionaires “the only minority destroying America,” charged that “for fifty years, billionaire megadonors have been buying politicians” like his opponent who then “rig the rules of the economy,” and who said that “we already have class warfare in this country” in the form of “the billionaires waging war against the rest of us” — a line almost directly borrowed from Bernie Sanders. He was rewarded for it by winning by one of the biggest margins of the night and doing it in one of the reddest states in the country.
The corporate center has tried to square this by simply retconning Talarico as one of them, a moderate, as Matthew Yglesias dubbed him. They point to the fact that he moved away from some of his support for trans rights, embraced an “all-of-the-above” energy policy, and eschewed Medicare for All in favor a public option (though the idea that’s a “centrist” or “moderate” policy would be surprising to anyone with a memory longer than five or six years).
But even if Talarico wasn’t viewed by nearly half of all Texas voters as “very liberal” on the eve of the election (and as “somewhat liberal” by a further 27 percent), this is a pretty hard sell.
To see why, look at Colin Allred. Just two years ago, Allred, a former NFL player, civil rights lawyer, and congressman, launched his own Texas Senate run with a campaign widely characterized as a “centrist” one against Republican Ted Cruz.
What did that campaign involve? Allred cast the GOP as having become too extreme and told conservatives who believed in the rule of law and the Constitution that they should vote for him. He proudly touted his US Chamber of Commerce endorsement. He “was unable to successfully develop” an economic message against Cruz and made abortion and reproductive rights “central to” and the “banner of” his campaign instead. During their debate, he hammered Cruz for supporting an abortion ban and being soft on the January 6 rioters, calling him a “threat to democracy” and only offhandedly mentioning he cut taxes on the rich. Again, these are all important issues but were unconnected to voters’ economic struggles.
The result: Cruz won by 8 points, nearly quadrupling his winning margin from six years earlier.
Going Red in Red States
This was not something unique to Texas and Talarico’s “moderate” campaign there. It was the case in every red state that Democrats just won a Senate seat in.
Take a look at Annie Andrews’s campaign that made her the first Democrat elected to a South Carolina Senate seat in twenty-eight years. Andrews hammered her initial opponent, the late Lindsey Graham, for “sell[ing] out to big money” and for being “willing to take food off our kids’ plates” and gut Medicaid “just so he can deliver tax cuts to billionaires,” and called on him to refund donations from Jeffrey Epstein–linked billionaires. She swore off “corporate PAC money” and pledged to “rein in the influence of corporations and billionaires in our elections.”
When Graham died and was replaced by his sister, Darline, Andrews hammered her for the same thing. Andrews called her “handpicked and bought by big corporations,” attacked her for doing the bidding of a data center industry spending millions of dollars of dark money to get her elected, and pointed to the $27 million that “outside Super PACs” had spent to support her. She won by nearly 5 points.
This was a very different campaign than the one former corporate lobbyist Jaime Harrison ran against Lindsey Graham six years ago. Since Harrison was relying on corporate bundlers and billionaire donors to raise obscene amounts of money to outspend Graham, he couldn’t and didn’t launch any of these attacks — in fact, Graham turned it around on him, complaining that outside dark money was flooding in to support the Democrat. Harrison’s attacks on Graham were focused on the idea that voters couldn’t trust him, because he had gone back on his word in supporting Donald Trump’s 2020 Supreme Court pick. He lost by 10 points.
Or look at Josh Turek, who won Iowa by four points against GOP candidate Ashley Hinson. Turek constantly talked about how Washington was full of millionaires “looking out for billionaires” and that he was “not one of them,” nor did he take corporate PAC money or was “owned by billionaires” (even as he quietly did take money from some billionaires). Iowa’s Republican senators and, he implied, his opponent, were “just looking out for billionaires and large corporations.”
During a debate, in attack ads, and in a Des Moines Register op-ed, Turek took aim at Hinson’s personal wealth, complaining that she had “gotten richer in her time in Washington” while slashing social spending on working-class Iowans, slamming her for her stock ownership, and saying that “we have a corruption crisis that’s leading to an affordability crisis because we’re sending people like Ashley Hinson up to DC” to line their pockets.
Not even Sanders went this hard against his wealthy opponents.
Then look at Michael Franken’s campaign for an Iowa Senate seat four years earlier. Though Franken prominently swore off corporate PAC donations, there was no talk of billionaires or wealth inequality. Franken appealed to “that middle segment who want logical, pragmatic, smart, dedicated, national servants to work for them,” and ran on a message that “we need to put country over party” and “people over politics.” He jabbed at his opponent’s age and long tenure in office, framed himself as defending democracy and minority rights, particularly those of women, whose right to an abortion he frequently brought up. And he ended up losing by 12 points.
Over in Mississippi, where prosecutor Scott Colom eked out a shock win to become the state’s first black senator, he did it by similarly assailing his Republican opponent Cindy Hyde-Smith’s donations from “millionaires and billionaires” out of state and accusing her of throwing tens of thousands of Mississippians off their health insurance “to look out for people in California and New York,” specifically “billionaires and millionaires” there, by giving them a “billionaire tax break.” He ran on raising taxes on the rich and getting rid of corporate subsidies for billionaires, and hit his opponent for staying silent on data centers being pushed by “AI billionaires” while being backed by a pro-AI super PAC.
This did not happen two years earlier, when Ty Pinkins (who ran, to some controversy, as a third-party candidate this year) ran for the other Mississippi US Senate seat, once again eschewing any kind of bold economic message in favor of warning that “our very democracy is being threatened” by people attacking its “institutional safeguards,” in his announcement. Pinkins said his platform revolved around the vague motto of, “You talk, I listen, we do,” which he explained (in even vaguer terms) meant, “I can listen and hear what’s important to their communities,” and then “do what’s necessary to move these communities and our state forward.” That campaign lost by nearly 30 points.
A particularly instructive example is Sherrod Brown in Ohio, who lost reelection to his Senate seat by nearly 4 points in 2024, then won the other Senate seat this year by just under 5 points. Despite a long-standing and deserved reputation as a populist, Brown said very little about millionaires and billionaires two years ago, other than that they should “pay their fair share” into Social Security — even as they were spending massive amounts to defeat him, which they did.
In 2026, more or less the official motto of Brown’s campaign was “Workers Before Billionaires,” a phrase he put in press releases, merchandise, tweets, Substack posts, reels, TikToks, and video after video. Compare his demure response two years earlier to a question about Republicans backing personally wealthy candidates — “That’s who they are . . . I guess I’m not surprised by that” — to what he said about his 2026 GOP opponent, Jon Husted: “The disdain, the contempt they have for work and for workers tells you everything.”
This time Brown, who called for a tax hike on billionaires, went in on Husted’s connection to the ultrarich and what the campaign characterized as his “corruption”:
- “Clevelanders have seen time and time again how Husted bows down to billionaires and corporations while leaving hardworking Ohioans behind.” (August 29)
- “Jon Husted’s for sale and the billionaires and corporations pouring millions into this race know it.” (September 21)
- “Ohioans have watched Jon Husted put billionaires and corporations before working families time and time again.” (October 3)
- “From Elon Musk to Donald Trump, billionaires are spending hundreds of millions of dollars against me because they know they can buy Jon Husted’s votes.” (October 29)
For good measure, Brown ran at least three separate TV ads hitting Husted for taking more money from Les Wexner, the disgraced Epstein-connected Ohio billionaire, than anyone else in Congress.
It is hard to make the case that nothing has changed when the same candidate ran a completely different campaign just two years later.
Finally, take a look at North Carolina, home to the second largest US financial center after New York, and where former governor Roy Cooper beat the Republican candidate by nearly 20 points. “Time to elect a senator for everyday people, not billionaires,” Cooper said after winning the primary, a theme he came back to over and over again, whether saying that “we don’t have the billionaires they do,” that his opponent was “fighting for the billionaire friends he made while working as a Big Oil and utility company lobbyist in DC,” or hitting Trump’s bill “that gave tax cuts to billionaires” and had “driven healthcare premiums up.”
Again, Cooper has a well-established reputation as a moderate, but this kind of rhetoric simply bore no resemblance to the Senate campaign run by another moderate, former state Supreme Court Chief Justice Cheri Beasley in 2022. Beasley centered her campaign on abortion rights and health care generally, and talked about diversity and reforming the criminal justice system to fix the “disparities” that exist within it while touting her support from law enforcement. There was no talk of billionaires or dark money, since Beasley herself was backed by twenty-three billionaires and won her primary by being boosted by various out-of-state PACs. She lost by 3 points.
This is borne out by research by Eric Blanc. Going through candidate websites in 2024 and 2026, he found that while billionaires were referenced in only 19 percent of candidates’ websites two years ago, this year they featured in 78 percent. Meanwhile, research by the Center for Working Class Politics found that less than 20 percent of the candidates in 2024 attacked corporations, billionaires, or Wall Street for their role in the affordability crisis.
Admitting Defeat in Victory
The fact that these candidates used populist rhetoric doesn’t necessarily mean they are populists, or even progressive. A number of these candidates have taken money from the billionaires they decry, including Talarico, and did not necessarily run on very ambitious policies. Meanwhile, Cooper is a multimillionaire himself, and like several others, did not run on taxing the rich, for all the class-war-style rhetoric that was thrown around.
But it does mean that Democratic moderates have tacitly accepted what voices on the Left have been saying for years, which is that the Bernie Sanders pitch — of a corrupt, rigged system pitting billionaires and corporations against working Americans — has broad appeal that cuts across geographic, racial, and, yes, sometimes even partisan lines.
Whatever they may tell you now, centrists did not always feel this way. Third Way cofounder Matt Bennett, for instance, was one of the corporate centrists insisting that there was nothing remarkable about any of this, because Sanders was not “the first Democratic (adjacent) candidate to use populist rhetoric in the modern era.” This will be news to Third Way circa 2016, whose president celebrated Sanders’s loss in the Democratic primary that year, because if “liberal populism doesn’t win Democratic primaries,” then it can’t “be the path back for a party” in a general election, and showed that “voters are angry, but they don’t want to focus mainly on billionaires.”
Likewise, Matthew Yglesias today may mock clueless young people thinking “Bernie Sanders invented the idea of campaigning on economic fairness themes.” But back in 2016, he listed Sanders’s plans to “soak the rich to a much greater extent” as one of the supposedly risky, radical ideas that made “the vast majority of the party’s elected officials and interest group leaders” worry about him. Stances like that were “not popular,” Yglesias wrote, and made him unelectable, compared to Hillary Clinton’s “relatively modest, overwhelmingly popular tweaks to the tax code.”
Something interesting is happening here. For years, frustrated socialists and progressives have been arguing that opposition to billionaires, soaking the ultrarich, and getting money out of politics are the centrist positions: that Americans across all walks of life — white or black, college-educated or not, liberal or conservative, in blue, red, or purple states — were pretty united on this, regardless of their exact views on things like immigration, guns, or trans kids in sports. Whatever the pundits are saying, centrist candidates seem to have finally acknowledged that’s the case.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Healthcare company opens art gallery near Los Angeles
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Scarlet Cheng
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
AltaMed Health Services, a major healthcare provider in Southern California, is opening an art gallery, library and cultural centre to house its art collection in the Los Angeles suburb of Montebello. AltaMed’s collection, more than 50 years in the making, includes works by Laura Aguilar, Graciela Iturbide, Gabriel Orozco and others. Its new 30,000-sq.-ft space, The Alta, opens to the public on Sunday (15 November).
AltaMed began collecting art in the 1970s, based on a belief that art is an integral part of holistic well-being. Since then, its collection has grown to some 4,000 pieces, with about 1,400 of them currently placed in its offices and clinics.
“Our collection focuses on Chicano art," Cástulo de la Rocha, the president and chief executive of AltaMed (and founder of the collection), said in a statement. "Because AltaMed was founded as part of the Chicano Movement in the 1970s, because I was active in the Chicano Movement, and because our patients and employees can connect culturally with the art.”
In recent years, AltaMed has been converting a warehouse on the edge of a shopping mall in Montebello to house its collection. The space will have regular hours for visitors to tour its gallery, see works on shelves and sliding racks in open storage, and watch behind-the-scenes processes of digitisation and conservation. There is also studio space for artist residencies on site.
“The collection is here to serve the communities that AltaMed is focused on in Los Angeles and Orange County, primarily Latino communities,” Pilar Tompkins Rivas, AltaMed’s chief curator and vice president of arts, tells The Art Newspaper. “So we think about art that is relevant and celebratory of those populations.”
Some recently acquired and commissioned works also address health and community—such as Sonia Romero’s mural The Fence-Pomona (2026), made expressly for the central communal space in a senior-care facility in nearby Pomona. The mural is 6ft high and 10ft wide, depicting a white lattice fence festooned with roses and the San Gabriel Mountains behind it. It ioverlooks a space used for meals, artmaking and gathering for patients.
AltaMed’s collection runs the gamut of media and spans more than 100 years, although most of the work was made after the Second World War. Early pieces include those of Hernando Gonzallo Villa, a commercial artist who famously designed ads and posters for the Santa Fe Railway. More recent works include drawings, prints and paintings by Carlos Almaraz, Judy Baca, Camille Rose Garcia, Gronk, Frank Romero, Eloy Torrez, John Valadez and Linda Vallejo.
The first exhibition in the gallery is Patssi Valdez: LA LA LA (until 9 April 2027), featuring photo-based and collage works by a pioneer of Los Angeles’s Chicano art movement. For this show, Valdez re-created some of her photography from the 1970s and 80s—portraits of friends that helped define punk and goth glamour.
She says she had discussed doing something “out of the box” with AltaMed, and several of the framed work have coloured strips of paper flying out from the frame. To highlight some of her portraits, Valdez added Swarovski crystals to the prints, such as in Divine Dede (2026) and Hot Pink (Mario, Charlie & DeDe) (1983/2025). She also co-created work in collaboration with two younger artists, rafa esparza and Gabriela Ruiz.
It has been more than a decade since Valdez had a solo exhibition. “AltaMed has been a collector of my work for quite a while and has been very supportive," she says. The company has purchased Valdez’s paintings and photography, and even one of her signature full-size paper dresses. One of these dresses is in a glass case in The Alta’s open-storage area.
Down the hall are the residency studios. The artist Rubén Esparza is working in one of them, where he has been making multimedia pieces featuring his "ongoing exploration of the cultural significance of Latinx, Chicano and Queer diasporas".
The other studio has been transformed into an educational apothecary by Felicia Montes and her collective Mujeres de Maíz. La Botánica del Barrio (2026) features displays of samplable traditional herbal teas and tinctures, as well as a decorated pushcart. In the hallway, The Wellness Wall lets visitors put up cards with their own home remedies and healing practices. Visitors have suggested some very practical cures—from "talk to friends" and "travelling" to "Vicks" and "a good mezcal".

https://hellgatenyc.com/the-luigi-mangio.title: The Luigi Mangione Protest Documentary You Need to See
https://hellgatenyc.com/the-luigi-mangio.author: Julianne Escobedo Shepherd
https://hellgatenyc.com/the-luigi-mangio.text:
During the trial of Luigi Mangione, much of the coverage was focused on three women called the Mangionistas: Whether they are extremists, whether they should have press passes, whether they are simply bubbleheaded fangirls swooning over an objectively hot convicted killer. But much of the sensationalist, often sexist coverage has obscured the deeper issues that the murder of United Healthcare CEO Brian Thompson has pushed to the surface: The fact that in a nation as wealthy as the U.S., citizens are regularly dying or, at best, going into debt, due to the exorbitant cost of healthcare—and will, as of next year, be left even more vulnerable thanks to Trump's Medicaid cuts, which threaten coverage for nearly a million New Yorkers and institute work requirements to obtain basic coverage. 
"Bigger Than Luigi," Miléna Mikael-Debass's short documentary showing this week at DOC NYC, hones in on this topic so cogently it's a feat that the Emmy-winning director was able to fit so much in its 16-minute runtime, capturing snapshots of the lives of four people from the demonstrations outside Mangione's hearings in lower Manhattan. There is Shane, an ER doctor whose activism extends beyond the City courthouse to Albany, where he advocates for single-payer healthcare system and rallies at the state legislature to pass the New York Health Act; Breigh, a paralegal and true-crime fan from Philadelphia who is adamant about Mangione's right to a fair trial; Jonni, an activist and organizer who lost his brother due to inadequate healthcare; and Celeste, an Italian American New Yorker and grad student with a similar spinal affliction to Mangione.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: ‘A Joke’: Missing State Aid Leaves CUNY Students Stressed
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Aisha Baiocchi
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
More than halfway through the Fall semester, some CUNY community college students are still waiting on financial aid awards from the state — weeks after officials said the problem was being solved.
The delayed funding is from the New York State Opportunity Promise Scholarship, the state-supported component of the City University’s Reconnect program, and covers tuition, fees and books for students at community colleges pursuing certain degrees. Last month, Gov. Kathy Hochul announced an expansion of the program to include new degree pathways and campuses.
One student at Kingsborough Community College told The City Reporter they had been reaching out to their university’s financial aid office about the funds since they first noticed the delays. The office told them the money had not yet been disbursed by CUNY’s central office.
GET THE CUNY SCOOP: Subscribe to our new weekly newsletter covering the City University of New York
The student included a screenshot of an email from the office saying they “still do not have confirmation” of when the money will be disbursed.
Students have taken to online message boards to complain about the missing funds — and the stress of not knowing when it will arrive. The money is a “last dollar” scholarship, meaning it makes up for shortfalls after other sources of aid have been exhausted.
A CUNY spokesperson echoed last month’s promises that the funds were one their way.
“NYSOP funds were distributed to campus accounts in the University’s Student Financial Aid system over the past month and will begin appearing in students’ accounts starting Monday,” Noah Gardy, CUNY press secretary said in a statement.
The university did not say how many students are still affected by delays in disbursements. Last month, a university official said hundreds of students had not received their scholarships.
“Nope, I called my Financial Aid office again today and was told that they still don’t have a date they can give me and that they actually haven’t heard ANYTHING from CUNY since the 7th last month,” one student wrote in a Nov. 5 Reddit post. “This entire situation is a joke.”
MORE: Past Due: Why CUNY Adjuncts Can’t Get Paid On Time
A Queensborough Community College student shared emails from their financial aid office from Nov. 10, saying they do not have a date for NYSOP disbursement yet but “expect it to be soon.”
Gardy said the university was working to prevent additional hold-ups. “While these delays will not affect registration, we regret any stress or uncertainty they may have caused,” he said. “We are reviewing our internal processes to prevent such delays in the future.”
CUNY Reconnect received $18.8 million from the most recent state budget. The program covers the cost of enrollment in 220 high-demand associates degrees at community colleges for adults between 25 and 55. It serves 10,000 students across the seven CUNY community colleges.

Pathbreaking artist Lorna Simpson, known for her photographic works eschewing racist and sexist stereotypes and interrogating race, class, gender, politics, and history, has been revealed as the winner of the thirty-third Wolfgang Hahn Prize, presented by the Society for Modern Art at the Museum Ludwig in Cologne. The museum, which sponsors the prize, will put €100,000 (about $110,000) in member donations toward purchasing a work by Simpson for its collection. A solo exhibition of the artist’s work will go on view at the institution next year, and will be accompanied by a publication.
Born in Brooklyn in 1960, Simpson was the first African American woman to have her art exhibited at the Venice Biennale, in 1990. That same decade, she gained acclaim for works pairing text fragments with layered photographs, frequently of women with their faces obscured, forcing viewers to confront their own perceptions of Black women. She has since expanded her practice to include painting, drawing, film, collage, and installation, through which she continues to explore symbolic systems and the divide between the self and others’ perceptions.
Simpson was selected for this year’s prize by a jury comprising Naomi Beckwith, deputy director and chief curator of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York and artistic director of Documenta 16, and the Museum Ludwig board. The jury in a statement posited Simpson’s oeuvre as “a bridge” to the practices if contemporary artists including Carolyn Lazard and Diamond Stingily, whose works “reflect[ing] on the self-image of African American women” have recently entered the museum’s collection.
Inaugurated in 1994, the Wolfgang Hahn Prize honors established contemporary artists who are internationally recognized but are not yet considered to be as well known in Germany as they deserve to be. Previous winners include Francis Alÿs, Frank Bowling, Trisha Donnelly, Isa Genzken, Mike Kelley, Kerry James Marshall, Betye Saar, Cindy Sherman, Rosemarie Trockel, Lee Ufan, and Haegue Yang.

https://taz.de/Friesenjunkies/!6224385/.title: „Friesenjunkies“: Glamour in der Suchtklinik
https://taz.de/Friesenjunkies/!6224385/.author: Ambros Waibel
https://taz.de/Friesenjunkies/!6224385/.text:
„Friesenjunkies“: Glamour in der Suchtklinik
Wie lustig ist es auf Sylt? Die neue Serie der „Discounter“-Macher hat witzige Momente, doch das Setting überzeugt nicht.
Nein, richtig lustig sind diese „Friesenjunkies“ leider nicht. Auf jeden Fall nicht auf die Art, wie die „Discounter“ lustig war: bekannt lustig, fremdschämlustig, überraschend lustig, grenzwertig lustig – und was es eben noch so in den Regalen der erfolgreichen Serienmacher gab.
Das heißt nicht, dass es hier, im Setting einer exklusiven Klinik für Suchtkranke auf Sylt, nicht was zu sehen gäbe. Martin Brambach ist wie immer groß, hier als alkoholkranker Dauergast, obwohl der Eindruck bleibt, dass selbst dieser Duracelplayer nicht 100 Prozent gibt. Shadi Eck als Erzähler und Dauerkiffer hat natürlichen Charme und Lässigkeit vor der Kamera. Und Sylvie Meis ist keine Großschauspielerin, aber wenn sie ihren kleinen Töchtern mitteilen muss, dass Mami noch länger in der Klinik bleibt, dann rührt das an. Man könnte noch andere nennen, am Cast liegt es, trotz kleiner Ausreißer nach unten, nicht, dass die Sache so wenig zündet.
„Friesenjunkies“, 8 Folgen, ARD-Mediathek
Vermutlich ist es schlicht mangelnder Realismus. Den von studentischen Aushilfskräften und Schülerpraktikant:innen zugrunde gerichteten Discounter um die Ecke kennt jeder Großstadtbewohner. Den gibt es; und auf dieser Grundlage kann man anfangen rumzuspinnen. Bei den „Friesenjunkies“ ist der Eindruck, man habe erst rumgesponnen und sich dann ein Setting dazu überlegt. Nicht: Was ist lustig, an dem, was wir sehen? Sondern: Wie erzählen wir irgendwas Lustiges, und dann schauen wir mal, wo wir das hinpacken.
Jetzt kann man sich fragen, wie das sein kann, wenn doch die Macher von „Friesenjunkies“ die selben sind wie die von „Discounter“. Ganz einfach: In der Kunst muss man riskieren und ausprobieren. Das machen die Brüder Emil und Oskar Belton als Autoren und Regisseure. Und wenn man bei der Klinik Isebek auch nicht so mitgeht, dann lässt sich trotzdem anerkennen, dass hier mangelndes Talent nicht das Problem ist.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

Dans le Pas-de-Calais, la mairie proposait des obsèques deux fois moins chères, dans une ville où près d’un habitant sur trois vit sous le seuil de pauvreté : la nouvelle mairie RN a fait fermer ce service dès cet été. L’opposition conteste les comptes de la municipalité d'extrême droite et dénonce l’opacité entourant la vente du matériel au privé.
Environ 1 500 euros pour enterrer un proche, contre 3 000 à 3 500 dans le privé, selon les montants recueillis par l’Humanité. C’est cette offre que supprime la maire RN de Grenay, Daisy Duveau. Élue en mars, elle avait annoncé à La Voix du Nord la fermeture du service à la fin de l’année, invoquant notamment une concurrence déloyale envers les entreprises privées. Le RN promet de défendre le pouvoir d’achat. Sa majorité supprime ici un service créé par les communistes pour réduire la facture des familles endeuillées.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Democrats Should Not Give an Inch to the Lame-Duck Congress
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Elie Mystal
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Democrats Should Not Give an Inch to the Lame-Duck Congress
In this week’s Elie v. U.S., our justice correspondent makes the case for Democrats to block Trump’s attempt at judiciary-stuffing. Plus, boycott Harry Potter!
Donald Trump and the Republican Congress have confirmed 57 new federal judges over the last two years. Now, with Republicans on the way out, Trump is demanding that Congress confirm another 25 judges during the lame-duck session.
That’s a tough ask. Confirming judges takes a lot of Senate time and resources, both of which the Republicans might prefer to use for whatever other fell priorities Republicans may have before they are removed from power. It’s also worth remembering that the government runs out of funding (again) on December 11, and figuring out how to avoid (another) government shutdown should probably take priority for Republicans over confirming lame-duck judges.
Adding to the challenge is the question of whether Democratic minority leader Chuck Schumer will be in a deal-making mood when it comes to judges. On the one hand, Schumer allowed a number of Republican-aligned judges to be confirmed at the end of Joe Biden’s term in order to give Biden the “record” for the largest number of judges appointed in one presidential term. On the other hand, Schumer is facing increasingly loud questions about his leadership, and his ascension to majority leader is far from assured. If Chuck caves now—on the budget, on judges, on anything—the calls for his head will only get louder. I don’t think it’s in Schumer’s best interest to help Trump confirm 25 judges in the lame duck and then turn around and ask Democrats to give him the gavel in the new Congress.
Of course, outgoing Senate majority leader John Thune doesn’t need the Democrats to confirm a slate of new judges. He has the votes in his own caucus to do this, assuming retiring or defeated Republican senators are willing to give Trump a parting gift even though he’s ruined their careers.
But I do think if Republicans confirm 25 new federal judges in the lame-duck session, that becomes another data point to convince Democrats to confirm no new federal judges for the last two years of Trump’s term.
Now is the time for judicial hardball, and I hope Democrats get this memo.
The Bad and the Ugly
- Scott Colom defeated Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 3,000 votes in their Mississippi Senate race. Hyde-Smith conceded, saving us all from a weeks-long court battle to confirm her defeat. My mother is a Black woman who was born in Clarksdale, Mississippi, in 1950. Watching her react to a Black person being elected as senator from her home state for the first time in 145 years has been one of the joys of my life.
- In Alaska, Senate candidate Mary Peltola now has more votes than both Dan Sullivans combined, further obviating the Department of Justice’s antidemocratic lawsuit aimed at overturning the election, and making even more of a mockery of Trump’s wild claims that all of one Dan Sullivan’s votes should be given to the other. Peltola still hasn’t quite breached the 50 percent barrier, which is the point at which the state shuts down the ranked-choice voting process, but there are still more votes to count.
- Remember when Trump said he would accept the results of the election after his party got walloped? Yeah, that didn’t last a week. On Monday, Trump asked on Truth Social, “Does anybody really believe this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote.” An authoritarian goon does not change his spots so easily, and everybody who thought he did deserves another time-out in the dunce chair.
- The Kennedy family joined the lawsuit to block Trump’s arch, saying that the monstrosity would disturb and diminish John F. Kennedy’s gravesite at Arlington. I have watched enough movies to know that you should never disturb the ancestral burial grounds if you can possibly avoid it.
- Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault. At the sentencing hearing, Justice Joel Bennathan said, “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent.” I don’t have a joke here. This is just a perfect and true statement.
Inspired Takes
- Not gonna lie, I have enjoyed the Pope Leo experience. In The Nation, Victor Gaetan writes about how Pope Leo has gone to war—against war. Specifically, Pete Hegseth’s wars.
- In The New Republic, Perry Bacon makes the point that the “groups” that centrists and Democratic consultants maligned over the past few years are the reason Democrats won the midterms.
- Jamelle Bouie has a great article on the new “Southern Strategy” that helped the Democrats win in the South. Maybe next time the Democratic Party could actually invest in that strategy and give these candidates some money.
Worst Argument of the Week
OK, I think I understand what happened with the Pete Hegseth “impeachment” situation, and I think there‘s a lot of confusion out there that’s causing Democrats to get criticized unnecessarily. TLDR: This wasn’t the real Hegseth impeachment effort. The real one will be coming in the next Congress.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Here’s what happened. Representative Thomas Massie submitted articles of impeachment for Pete Hegseth on eight charges (mostly relating to the war in Iran and the extrajudicial killings Hegseth has overseen). Massie is a Republican from Kentucky who has been vocal about the Epstein files—so vocal that Trump backed Massie’s primary challenger, Ed Gallrein, who defeated Massie in the primary and won Massie’s seat last Tuesday. Massie is on his way out, and the impeachment articles were a parting gift to an administration he hates.
Trying to impeach Hegseth now, in the lame-duck Congress, was a stunt. And a stupid one.
In any event, there was a procedural vote this week on whether to send the articles of impeachment to the full House (which is still controlled by Republicans) or leave it with the House Judiciary Committee (which is still controlled by Republicans). The option to send it to the full House (which is what Democrats ostensibly wanted) was defeated 211–204, with only Massie breaking party ranks and joining Democrats in the losing effort. Eleven Democrats and seven Republicans “missed” the vote. Many people have pointed out that if the 11 Democrats had shown up, the measure would have passed (many of these people skip over the fact that if the seven Republicans had shown up to counter the Democrats, the measure would have failed). Since the Democrats have a history of snatching defeat from the jaws of victory, a firestorm over weak Democratic leadership erupted online.
Here’s the thing that I think is important to remember: Hegseth was never going to be impeached by this Republican-controlled Congress, and there were two legitimate dangers in trying to force it:
- No investigation
- Double jeopardy
There is a lot of potential evidence that Pete Hegseth has committed high crimes and misdemeanors, but Massie, acting on his own, was not in a position to provide any of it. Hegseth needs to be investigated by the House Judiciary Committee; that will not happen as long as Republicans control Congress. But I will bet all the money in my grabbable area that he will be investigated, once Representative Jamie Raskin is in charge of the Judiciary Committee. Impeaching him now, without that investigation, looks like a political stunt spearheaded by a bitter politician because it is. After Raskin gets ahold of the gavel, it will look a lot different.
And that might matter, legally speaking, because we might get only one shot at this. Look, I don’t believe that “double jeopardy”—the prohibition against prosecuting somebody twice for the same crime—should apply to impeachment proceedings. But, as I must regularly remind people, I don’t happen to have a seat on the Supreme Court. If you impeach Hegseth now, and he gets acquitted, can you impeach him six months from now for the same crimes? I think so. But I don’t know so. And I don’t want to give John Roberts, Clarence Thomas, and Samuel Alito an opportunity to answer that question for me.
Is it a bad look for 11 Democrats to “miss” a vote on impeachment so soon after the midterms? Sure. The optics are not good. The communication from the Democratic leadership on what really happened is worse. But by the same token, the “optics” around doing a rushed impeachment—a rushed impeachment that is destined to fail in front of a Republican-controlled House—are arguably worse.
If I were in the leadership chair (and I’ll note that’s yet another job I don’t have), I’d have told all my members to opt out of Massie’s vainglorious charade.
Democrats will impeach Pete Hegseth when they have their ducks in a row. They don’t need a Republican who has been booted out of Congress to lead the charge.
What I Wrote
Soo… I have the cover story in the December issue of the magazine. You can read it online here. It’s about how Democratic presidential hopefuls should campaign on court reform in 2028, and what will happen to their entire agenda if they do not.
I also wrote about how Texas has a new Democratic attorney general who will become the regulator of first resort of Elon Musk and his companies.
In News Unrelated to the Current Chaos
I’m not going to watch the new HBO Harry Potter series. I’m not going to watch it because the creator of Harry Potter, J.K. Rowling, is a drooling transphobic bigot.
There are a lot of artists and creators who are problematic in some obvious and heinous way. Rowling has committed no crime, but where she stands out to me is that she’s made being a bigoted scumbag her entire personality. It’s not that she’s said a few anti-trans things, here or there. It’s that she’s happily become the face of the anti-trans movement in the UK. It’s that she uses her money and power and influence to fund anti-trans organizations that try to erase trans people from public life. She works, tirelessly it would seem, to menace trans people and manipulate the laws against them. When you support a J.K. Rowling project, you are directly supporting her financial efforts to hurt trans people. Why would you do that?
And here’s the thing about boycotting Rowling media products: It’s easy. There are so many evil people in the world whose products have been integrated into our lives in ways that make it almost impossible to excise them. I hate Jeff Bezos, for example, but pretending Amazon and The Washington Post don’t exist is really hard. I don’t support the actions of the Saudi Arabian government, but it has major investment stakes in Uber and the company that makes football video games. And, speaking of football, I believe I’ve already discussed my ongoing issues with loving a sport that is based on my favorite athletes’ getting repeatedly concussed into early oblivion.
But Harry Potter? A Harry Potter television show? I can cut Harry freaking Potter out of my life with almost no downside. If the question is, “Watch a television show or stand with transgender people?,” it’s the easiest call in my otherwise complicated journey of trying to be a moral person in an immoral world.
“What’s on HBO tonight, honey?”
“Transphobus Maximus!”
“Umm… what else is on HBO?”
“Well, John Oliver comes on in about an hour.”
“Cool, let’s watch LITERALLY ANYTHING ELSE until then.”
It’s not hard. Just don’t watch Harry Potter and let trans people live their best lives.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120387.title: Internationale Arbeitsorganisation | Rumoren, Rotstift, Richtungswahl
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120387.author: Felix Sassmannshausen, Genf
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120387.text:
- Politik
- Internationale Arbeitsorganisation
Rumoren, Rotstift, Richtungswahl
Kürzungen bei der UN-Arbeitsorganisation ILO: Vor der Führungswahl ringen Amtsinhaber Gilbert Houngbo und Linkssozialistin Yolanda Díaz um den Kurs.
Die Internationale Arbeitsorganisation (ILO) steht vor einer historischen Richtungswahl, während sich vor ihrer Genfer Zentrale Protest regt. Der 56‑köpfige Verwaltungsrat – das oberste Exekutivorgan aus Regierungen, Unternehmensverbänden und Gewerkschaften – entscheidet am kommenden Montag über die künftige Leitung. Zur Wahl stehen die linkssozialistische spanische Arbeitsministerin Yolanda Díaz und der parteiunabhängige amtierende Verwaltungschef Gilbert Houngbo aus Togo. Letzterer führt die UN-Sonderorganisation derzeit durch eine beispiellose Finanzkrise. Weil Pflichtbeiträge säumiger Staaten – allen voran der USA – von über 360 Millionen US-Dollar ausbleiben, klaffen enorme Haushaltslücken.
Die Defizite lähmen das Tagesgeschäft der ILO spürbar: Fachkonferenzen können nicht stattfinden, Regionalprojekte laufen aus und Entwicklungsprogramme schrumpfen drastisch. Zudem streicht Generaldirektor Houngbo als Reaktion auf die roten Zahlen 120 Vollzeitstellen. Seit 2025 mussten wegen der US-Finanzblockade insgesamt rund 600 Beschäftigte die Organisation verlassen. Gewerkschaften sehen das Fundament der ILO bedroht, weil Teams wegbrechen, die weltweit die Einhaltung internationaler Arbeitsnormen überwachen. »Schützt die Menschen, schützt das Mandat«, forderte daher Daniel Bertossa, Generalsekretär des 30 Millionen Mitglieder zählenden Gewerkschaftsbunds der öffentlichen Dienste in einer Solidaritätserklärung mit den Beschäftigten diese Woche.
Hunderte ILO-Angestellte hatten am Dienstag erstmals in Genf gegen das rigide Sparprogramm protestiert. Ihre Wut entzündet sich vor allem daran, dass das Management alternative Sparvorschläge der Gewerkschaften bislang ignoriert. Der Personalverband hatte konkrete Maßnahmen für Energieeinsparungen und verwaltungsinternen Bürokratieabbau vorgelegt. Selbst der Kanton Genf bot finanzielle Überbrückungshilfen an. Doch Houngbo schickte zu den Gesprächen lediglich seine Büroleiterin. »Das Konsultationsverfahren hier, in einer Institution, die weltweit ein Vorbild sein sollte, genügt den Ansprüchen nicht«, kritisierte der Genfer Regionalsekretär der Schweizer Gewerkschaft Unia, Yves Defferrard, die Verhandlungsführung der Direktion. Auf eine Anfrage von »nd« reagierte die ILO vor Redaktionsschluss nicht.
Spardiktat gegen Systemwechsel
Für Houngbo, der 2022 als erster Afrikaner an die ILO-Spitze gewählt wurde, kommt die Revolte im Haus so kurz vor der Neuwahl zur Unzeit. Er verteidigt seine Sparpolitik in der Öffentlichkeit als alternativloses Krisenmanagement. Dabei verweist der frühere Premierminister Togos auf seine Stationen als Wirtschaftsprüfer bei Pricewaterhouse Coopers sowie auf Führungsposten beim UN-Entwicklungsprogramm und Internationalen Fonds für landwirtschaftliche Entwicklung. »Finanzverwaltung und Krisenmanagement sind seit vielen Jahren mein tägliches Brot«, warb Houngbo für seine Wiederwahl. Mit seinem Programm will er die Agentur künftig auf Kernaufgaben beschränken, administrative Dienste in ein günstigeres Zentrum außerhalb Genfs verlagern und Arbeitsnormen verbindlich an Kredite von Internationalem Währungsfonds und Entwicklungsbanken knüpfen.
Díaz nutzte indes den Unmut über Houngbos Krisenmanagement für sich. »Ich kann nicht verstehen, wie man einen Kürzungsplan ohne echten Dialog durchsetzen konnte«, erklärte sie. Díaz fordert stattdessen eine Demokratisierung der Führungsstrukturen und zusätzliche Finanzquellen über regionale Entwicklungsbanken. Zugleich verlangt sie mit einer neuen Charta der Arbeitsrechte existenzsichernde Mindestlöhne sowie verbindliche Schranken für künstliche Intelligenz und Algorithmen im Betrieb. Zudem pocht die Spanierin auf volle Arbeitsrechte und soziale Absicherung für Pflege- und Hausangestellte, die global noch immer millionenfach informell beschäftigt sind. »Die ILO muss beim weltweiten Pflegesystem voranschreiten – das ist eine epochale Herausforderung«, unterstrich Díaz ihr dezidiert feministisches Programm.
Rumoren im Gewerkschaftsflügel
Obwohl Díaz mit ihren Vorschlägen vielen Gewerkschaftsforderungen inhaltlich nähersteht als Houngbo, bleiben die Hürden für ihren Erfolg enorm. So dürfte der amtierende ILO-Chef auch rechte Stimmen einsammeln, da der peruanische Rechtsaußen-Kandidat Javier González-Olaechea Anfang November seinen Rückzug ankündigte. Zuvor sagten der internationale Arbeitgeberverband und die Führung des Internationalen Gewerkschaftsbunds (ITUC) Houngbo offiziell ihre Unterstützung zu. Der ITUC begründete seinen Schritt mit Verweis auf konkrete Erfolge des amtierenden ILO-Chefs trotz Finanzkrise – etwa neue Standards für Plattformarbeit sowie die Einstufung von Arbeitsschutz als Grundrecht. Zudem benötige die ILO in Zeiten globaler Krisen und Konflikte vor allem eine stabile Führung, erklärte ITUC-Generalsekretär Luc Triangle.
Unter den Gewerkschaften sorgt dieser Schritt der ITUC-Spitze für Empörung. Während insbesondere afrikanische Gewerkschaftsbünde hinter Houngbo stehen, werfen europäische und lateinamerikanische Verbände Triangle vor, die Entscheidung ohne formelle Urabstimmung durchgesetzt zu haben. Eine nd-Anfrage an den ITUC blieb bis Redaktionsschluss unbeantwortet.
Da die 14 Gewerkschaftsdelegierten ihre nationalen Bünde vertreten und das Votum geheim bleibt, kann Díaz auf Abweichler*innen in der Wahlkabine hoffen. Für einen Sieg benötigt die Herausforderin am Montag eine absolute Mehrheit von mindestens 29 Stimmen im 56-köpfigen Gremium. Weil die Unternehmensvertreter*innen geschlossen für Houngbo stimmen dürften, bräuchte Díaz aus den verbleibenden 42 Stimmen von Regierungen und Gewerkschaften eine satte Zweidrittelmehrheit.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/midterm.title: Organizing Beat Out Democratic Conventional Wisdom
https://inthesetimes.com/article/midterm.author: Hamilton Nolan
https://inthesetimes.com/article/midterm.text:
Organizing Beat Out Democratic Conventional Wisdom
Democrats’ sweeping victory in the midterms showed why the old playbook should be thrown out of the window—and that the Left is on the march.
Hamilton Nolan
A decade ago, I went to Texas to write a profile of the Democratic candidate running in the reddest congressional district in the United States. He was a local gadfly, and had been given no resources from the national Democratic Party beyond a handshake. The story was meant to be a lark — a farcical, lighthearted tale of mankind’s capacity to forge ahead into impossible tasks.
Yet that is not the lesson I found. As I wandered the dusty neighborhoods of Amarillo, I began to wonder why this place was assumed to be intractably, unchangeably Republican. This was a town with a lot of immigrants and working people trying to stay on the right side of the poverty line. It was a place where you could imagine plenty of people being attracted to the Democratic platform. The folly I saw was not the man who took on the uphill task of running, but the party that had written this place off as a lost cause, unworthy of any effort. What that deep red Texas district needed was not resignation — it needed organizing.
This is why political consultants will never change the world. They look at the seething ball of humanity that makes up a political district — a writhing mass of hopes and dreams and desperation, covered in fluctuating layers of repression and ignorance and inspiration — and they see a neat column of numbers. They see a set of fixed quantities. They see politics as the art of running towards the favorable numbers and away from the bad ones. They do not see that that entire grand edifice of numbers can be reversed. It can be smashed, with breathtaking speed, if the real people in the real places change their minds.
The data-driven model of politics that rules the United States, that governs the spending of the Democratic Party, that starts with the status quo and cautiously wonders if it can move a single space on the policy chessboard, is vulnerable to those who understand that all of that data can be changed. It is vulnerable to those who know how to organize. 
The Democrats’ sweeping victory in the midterms was, in one sense, no surprise — President Donald Trump is historically unpopular and dismissive of political advice, and he carried his entire party to doom like an insane mother who jumps off a bridge with her baby clutched to her chest. Democrats have taken back control of both the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate, where they will hold firm majorities, and a new class of socialists and progressives is headed to Congress.
The most striking element of the whole thing, to me, was the natural experiment that was carried out between the states of Texas and Florida. Both are huge states that have been Republican strongholds for so long that they became deep red-coded in conventional wisdom, despite the fact that their populations are racially and economically and culturally diverse. They are both places where the raw material of Democratic political power has been suffocated by a lack of adequate resources and organizing.
Last night, we saw what adequate resources could do. James Talarico turned Texas blue by winning his Senate race against Ken Paxton after the most expensive non-presidential race in U.S. history. Talarico’s campaign raised nearly $150 million and took advantage of maximal support from the national Democratic Party to overcome an even more grotesque sea of spending by Tesla CEO (and world’s richest person) Elon Musk in support of Paxton, his debased opponent. In Florida, by contrast, former union organizer and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) member Angie Nixon upset the party’s handpicked candidate in the primary, and then came within three points of winning the general election (the best performance by a Florida Democrat in a Senate race since 2018) by pursuing nonstop ground-level organizing while being significantly outspent the whole time.
In Texas, deemed by conventional wisdom to be a macho Republican stronghold, a decidedly non-macho Democrat won with the help of a flood of national resources. In Florida, deemed by conventional wisdom to be a stronghold of Trumpian racists and rabid anti-communists, a Black woman DSA member who knew how to organize came shockingly close to winning. What’s the difference there? The difference is that one candidate got the resources and the other didn’t. Angie Nixon did not win, but with time we may admit that she performed an even greater service for the Democratic Party by proving that their idea of what is and is not possible in red states is wrong. 
As soon as Election Day is over, the battle to write the narrative begins. Whoever is able to persuade the bulk of the party and the public of their own narrative can take control of the direction of the party as we turn towards the next presidential election. This battle for control of the Democratic vision is more pronounced right now than it has ever been in my lifetime. Now, for the first time in decades, the left wing of the Democratic Party is not a bunch of fringe outsiders begging for scraps. The Left is surging and ascendent. The next two years will not just be about thwarting the deranged and retrograde ambitions of MAGA world; they will be a fight for the steering wheel of the Democratic steamroller.
For centrists and moderates, there is always the same narrative: Centrism was vindicated. We must run to the middle. The path to victory lies in extending a hand to disaffected Republicans. This is the story they will tell about what just happened. But in fact, the real narrative, the one that follows the surges of political electricity, is this: Trump squeaked into office after the last Democratic president seemingly went senile and withdrew his candidacy abruptly. Two years of raving lies, fascist insanity, blatant corruption, and a violent racist purge carried out by Nazi-esque White House officials has left people pissed off. The need for real change, deep change, structural change, is obvious.
Zohran Mamdani’s election as mayor in New York City has energized a socialist movement inside of the Democratic Party that is getting stronger, more widespread, and better organized with each passing day. This group arises not from the business world or the consulting world but from social movements, from unions, from activism — and it therefore approaches politics with an organizing model that the “raise corporate money and pour it into negative advertising” model of campaigns struggles to defeat. More than any time in living memory, The Political Left as broadly understood is organized, popular, smart, and determined.
The Left is not confined to coastal big cities. It’s everywhere. The legacy of the wheezing Democratic establishment is that they lost to Trump and got us here. The Left is cleaning up their mess — thanks in large part to a capacity for ignoring conventional wisdom and doing things that politicians are not supposed to do, lest they isolate the fabled suburban swing voters who seem to grow less and less real with each passing election.
The real problem for the Democratic establishment is that U.S. democracy requires deeper changes than they are willing to countenance, and their failure to support the pursuit of those changes will ultimately result in the further erosion of Democratic power. The 2026 midterms were worthy of celebration for all of us. They were a sign of hope for America’s future. But for the Left, they are not going to be a ceiling. They are going to be a trampoline. 
Thank you for reading this story. At a time when corporate media is dominating the web and our airwaves, independent journalism is more important than ever, and that’s what we provide at In These Times. We offer some of the best reporting, investigations and analysis on the growing movements for justice in the U.S.—and our work is firmly pro-labor and anti-fascist. To continue producing it, we need your support.
If you believe in the power of an independent press, please make a donation to In These Times today. By becoming a sustaining member, you can ensure that our work reaches even more readers.
And if you become a sustainer right now, you'll get a free year-long print subscription and a special subscribers-only print from artist Molly Crabapple.
Thank you.
