https://gothamist.com/news/mayor-mamdani.title: Mayor Mamdani appoints ex-DSA chair as new NYC nightlife director
https://gothamist.com/news/mayor-mamdani.author: Elizabeth Kim
https://gothamist.com/news/mayor-mamdani.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced his pick for the so-called nightlife mayor Friday: a freelance web developer who recently served as cochair of New York City’s chapter of the Democratic Socialist of America.
Eric Thor’s appointment to lead the Office of Nightlife was announced in a Paper Magazine profile portraying him as a familiar figure in the city’s lefty political scene and a regular clubgoer in East Williamsburg and Bushwick.
The role has gained increasing prominence as other cities establish similar offices focused on nightlife. But Thor’s hiring came as a surprise to Andrew Rigie, the executive director of the influential New York City Hospitality Alliance.
Rigie serves as the chair of advisory board for the Office of Nightlife, which was established to work with the director and administration on nightlife matters.
“It’s strikingly bizarre that they wouldn’t reach out to the Office of Nightlife Advisory Board,” he said.
Rigie said the job of nightlife mayor serves as both an ambassador for the city’s diverse hospitality scene and government liaison who can help establishments cut red tape and mediate disputes with residents.
Following a boost from the Knicks historic playoff run and World Cup, many establishments say they are struggling. A recent survey of 275 bars and restaurants by Rigie’s hospitality alliance found that owners were either breaking even or operating at a loss during the third quarter of this year.
Thor, an Astoria resident who works as a freelance web developer, worked on both Mamdani’s state assembly and mayoral campaigns. His LinkedIn profile states that he “guided the mayoral endorsement process of Zohran K. Mamdani” for the NYC-DSA. His website cites a digital affordability calculator he created for his campaign that shows how much New Yorkers might save under Mamdani.
His online resume does not include any experience working in the nightlife industry.
In a press release, Mamdani described the city’s nightlife as a “lifeline for small businesses” and praised Thor’s experience as a political organizer.
“Eric has spent years organizing alongside working people and he will bring that same commitment building a nightlife economy that works for everyone,” Mamdani said.
Ariel Palitz, the city’s first nightlife mayor, said Thor reached out to her on Friday.
“Although it’s not yet clear to me what his nightlife experience is, I’m sure he and I will be having many conversations,” said Palitz, who now runs a consulting group on nightlife policy.
“I’m just grateful that the mayor sees the value in this office,” she added.
Thor referred questions to the mayor’s press office. The mayor’s office did not respond to Gothamist’s inquiry about the appointment process and Thor’s salary.
Jeffrey Garcia, the previous nightlife director appointed by then-Mayor Eric Adams, earned $146,000, according to data compiled by the Empire Center.
Garcia, who declined to comment, was a former NYPD detective. He previously owned a coffee and wine bar in the Bronx.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/hake.title: The Hegseth Vote Was Jeffries's First Big Test. He Failed.
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/hake.author: Eoin Higgins
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/hake.text:
Eoin Higgins is the author of “Owned: How Tech Billionaires on the Right Bought the Loudest Voice on the Left.”
Democrats rolled into Washington this week fresh off a generational sweep election on the promise of affordability for Americans and accountability for the Trump administration.
But on Tuesday night, Democrats in the House failed the first test of their incoming majority. An impeachment resolution introduced Monday by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., targeting Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, one of the main architects of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, provided Republicans with a chance to score an early victory.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and the chamber’s Democratic leadership failed to take advantage, as 11 Democrats missed a critical vote that would have kept the resolution alive. The attempt failed by a slim margin, 211 to 204; Massie told The Intercept on Wednesday that even if the missing Democrats showed up he was sure House Speaker Mike Johnson could have rallied his members and made up the difference anyway. Until the new term begins, the chamber is still controlled by the GOP.
Nonetheless, the vote was a chance to send a message to the White House. One was sent: that of a disorganized, dysfunctional caucus. Other Democrats sought to take advantage of the misstep, noting that they were unwilling to miss the vote—Rep. Jasmine Crockett of Texas said she rerouted around traffic, and Rep. Pat Ryan of New York made it the day after back surgery.
“No matter what, I wasn’t going to allow traffic to keep me from that vote,” Crockett told MS NOW. “It was just that important to me.”
When asked about the absences, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who was present for the vote, offered only “someone may have had a health issue” as an explanation.
House members who missed the vote blamed a number of factors for their absence, including traffic. On Wednesday, all of those same House Democrats save Rep. Haley Stevens (Mich.) began to offer explanations. Rep. Jonathan Jackson (Ill.) told TMZ DC that his “traffic jam”-related absence was “inexcusable.” He wasn’t the only one to blame traffic — Reps. Marilyn Strickland (Wa.) and Laura Gillen (N.Y.) also cited D.C. gridlock as the reason they missed the vote; Rep. Julia Brownley (Calif.) said she was “rushing” to the vote but missed it. Reps. Nancy Pelosi (Calif.), Lou Corea (Calif.), and Frederica Wilson (Fla.) were all out of town.
Rep. Melanie Stansbury (N.M.) offered a front-facing video apology to constituents. Rep. Steven Horsford (Nev.) took “full responsibility” in a floor speech. And Rep. Brittany Pettersen (Colo.) acknowledged that she was at a super PAC event and said there was “no excuse” for missing the vote.
Expressing regret is a good start. It shows these lawmakers are aware that their actions are antithetical to where their voters are at this moment and are adjusting accordingly. It’s not enough.
Leadership was asleep at the wheel. As whip, Rep. Katherine Clark should have kept the caucus in line. (It’s worth noting that Clark officially launched a bid for majority leader last week.) A number of reps who blamed traffic were previously at an event hosted by the group Elect Democratic Women, which receives some of its funding from AIPAC. The event overlapped with the impeachment resolution vote; Clark is a cofounder of the group.
“Republicans just blocked the House from impeaching Pete Hegseth,” Clark posted on X after the vote—failing to take responsibility for her party’s own lack of discipline.
Democrats missing a vote to hold one of the main figures in the war on Iran accountable so they could attend a fundraiser is so tailor-made for progressive complaints over the state of party leadership, it’s hard to believe.
Jeffries tried to spin the vote as only a temporary reprieve for Hegseth, but he didn’t telegraph much willingness about holding his caucus to account.
“I haven’t had a conversation with anyone on the floor team about what may or may not have happened in terms of the Hegseth resolution, but this is not the end of it. It’s just the beginning,” he told Politico. Most critically, he accepted no responsibility for the stunningly bad optics of having members of his caucus no-show, even if it likely wouldn’t have moved the needle.
This never should have happened in the first place. It was the result of a series of decisions by Jeffries and Clark about the vote that made clear it wasn’t important.
Momentum lost can’t be regained. If Jeffries doesn’t understand that, he’s not the man for the job purely on tactical grounds, and he should lay no claim to being a party standard-bearer to steer us through the next two years of Trump’s America.
Jeffries and his party seem doomed to repeat the past. In 2009, when President Barack Obama came into the White House on the back of a change election that gave Democrats huge majorities in Congress, including a filibuster-proof supermajority in the Senate, the party hobbled itself out of the gate by preemptively declining to pursue justice for the many crimes of eight straight years of George W. Bush.
“We need to look forward as opposed to looking backwards,” Obama told ABC News’s George Stephanopoulos in January 2009, effectively ending any hope of accountability for the outgoing administration’s torture program and myriad other misdeeds. The ramifications of that decision arguably led to the war on Iran, a bipartisan immigration-deportation regime, and the end of Roe.
Now, with a Republican president who is hated even more than W—something that would have seemed impossible to imagine almost 18 years ago—the Democratic Party’s establishment wing appears ready to repeat those failures. Taking on Trump and his corrupt, violent administration was one of the main messages that flipped House and Senate seats across the country but the party’s current leaders are allergic to action.
Entrenched Democrats also don’t seem interested in any sort of accountability. Stevens, the Michigan Democrat who broke ranks with her party and endorsed Republican Mike Rogers for Senate rather than back Abdul El-Sayed, was under pressure in the days before and after the election, with even establishment kingmaker Rep. Jim Clyburn signaling openness to expelling her from the caucus. By Tuesday morning, Pelosi — always in touch with party leadership — seemed to throw cold water on the idea: “I’m not supporting kicking her out…. Let’s focus on the very positive.”
This is such a complete misunderstanding of the mood of the electorate, one wonders if it’s intentionally obtuse. Democratic voters don’t want the party to rest on its laurels, they want blood. Anyone who’s been to a liberal rally since the start of the second Trump term can tell you that the signage is calling for, at minimum, accountability, not immediate compromise.
If Democrats rubber-stamp Jeffries as speaker and fail to adopt a more aggressive legislative and investigative approach, frustrations within the caucus and among the base will only continue to mount.
Jeffries is downplaying dissent, but this is more than just a battle between two wings of the Democratic Party. Democrats in New York have been looking to unseat the leader for years, frustrated with his closeness to AIPAC and financial institutions. He’s the kind of Democrat the base is fed up with, and that exasperation is widespread; polling shows just how deeply unpopular he is.
Now, multiple incoming and incumbent Democratic reps have told reporters that constituents and activist groups are demanding they not vote for Jeffries as speaker.
There is an alternative gaining steam: Rep. Ayanna Pressley, the Massachusetts progressive and member of the original “Squad” who were first elected in 2018. Pressley has an uphill battle and has not yet announced that she’s interested in the job. The left is interested.
Voters gave Democrats a clear mandate on Election Day for what they want to see in Washington. Holding this administration accountable should be one of the top priorities. If the party fails to do all it can to advance that goal, it will once again earn its reputation for preferring failure to action. We should all push the next Congress to act as the exception to that rule—and they can start by picking a new speaker to meet the moment.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/lo.title: Long-Lost Charles Le Brun Painting Returns to the New Palace in Potsdam
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/lo.author: Anne Doran
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/lo.text:
Lost for more than 75 years, a painting by French Baroque artist Charles Le Brun (1619–1690) is now returning to the New Palace in Potsdam’s Sanssouci Park. The news was reported first by the German Press Agency (dpa) following a statement by the Prussian Palaces and Gardens Foundation Berlin-Brandenburg (SPSG).
Court painter to Louis XIV after 1661 and the designer most responsible for the opulent style of the French monarchy, Le Brun created the work, a depiction of a sleeping Christ Child with the Holy Family, around 1655. It was acquired in the 1700s by King Frederick the Great (Frederick II) of Prussia for the New Palace, where it hung in one of the guest apartments.
In 1942, to protect it from Allied bombings, much of the art at the Picture Gallery of Sanssouci and the New Palace, including Le Brun’s painting, was evacuated some 60 miles northwest to Schloss Rheinsberg.
On April 29, 1945, the Red Army entered Rheinsberg. Russian troops occupied the building, and a short time later the majority of the paintings housed in the Schloss Rheinsberg were sent to the Soviet Union. However, according to the SPSG, not all of the works arrived there, with some entering private collections in Rheinsberg under “convoluted circumstances.”
Le Brun’s painting was documented as being at Schloss Rheinsberg until July 30, 1945. After that, according to a spokesperson from the foundation, the painting vanished—until it resurfaced at a Berlin auction house in 2021.
The return was made possible by the support of the Ernst von Siemens Art Foundation and the Friends of the Prussian Palaces Association. On November 18, 2026 at 2:30 p.m., the “Holy Family” will be unveiled in the Upper Red Chambers of the New Palace.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ‘É preciso regular o modelo de negócio e o monopólio das Big Techs’, afirma pesquisador
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Quem decide o que vemos nas redes sociais? Quem controla, armazena e monetiza as nossas informações pessoais? E que risco a concentração de poder das grandes empresas de tecnologia representa para a democracia? Essas perguntas motivam o trabalho do jornalista James Görgen, autor de “Notas da floresta digital – Geopolítica e desenvolvimento tecnológico em tempos de transição”, que já está nas livrarias.
O livro surge após quatro anos de análises sobre o avanço e a ameaça das big techs. A obra aborda a dependência do Brasil em relação aos gigantes da tecnologia sediados nos Estados Unidos e o que isso representa para a soberania nacional. Görgen é mestre em Economia Política da Comunicação e acompanha a agenda digital desde 1998.
Na conversa, o entrevistado comenta a necessidade de regular a atuação das plataformas e a resistência a essa regulação no Congresso. Também fala sobre a possibilidade de o Brasil construir a sua própria arquitetura digital e sobre alternativas como acordos com a China com transferência de tecnologia. Outros temas são a pressão dos Estados Unidos sobre o Pix e o papel do “Exército do Lula” em um governo sem maioria no Congresso.
O podcast De Fato é uma produção do Brasil de Fato RS em parceria com o SindBancários de Porto Alegre e Região.
Todo sábado, um entrevistado ou uma entrevistada debaterá os principais fatos em destaque no Rio Grande do Sul, no Brasil e no mundo.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Across racial lines, Americans celebrate Scott Colom’s historic election: ‘The times they are a-changin’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Democrat Scott Colom made history this month, becoming Mississippi’s first Black senator since the Reconstruction era after defeating incumbent Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.
The 43-year-old’s win also contributed to a Democratic majority of at least 55 seats in the Senate – the party’s largest midterm gains since 1986.
Voters across the US reflected on the significance of Colom’s victory, with many older voters expressing hope that it could signal a new chapter for a state and region marked by a long history of racism and segregation. Others looked to Colom and a new generation of Democrats to deliver on key campaign promises, from tackling the cost of living and ending the US war with Iran to addressing the Trump administration’s hardline immigration policies.
Dye Bailey, a Black older adult in Grenada, Mississippi, said: “It makes me so proud to see Scott Colom win the Senate because Mississippi has been trying to [prevent] Black people from voting for our rights for so long. Mississippi is so racist, but I’m proud that all [of] Mississippi can [come] together as one people.”
Bailey added that she hopes Colom will fight for healthcare for all Mississippians, “feed[ing] the needy” and protect voting rights.
For Greg P, a 71-year old retired professor based in Chicago who spent most of his childhood and young adulthood in Mississippi, Colom’s victory offers hope.
“My father was an Episcopal priest, and my family was active in the civil rights movement in the 1960s and 70s. Our family had a cross burned into our rectory’s front lawn in 1971, and I was assaulted several times in my mid-teens by racists incensed by our activism,” he said.
“What gives me hope is that Colom was able to speak to Black and white Mississippians, convincing Black voters that this time they could actually win, and persuading a significant percentage of whites that a Black senator would actually do better by them than a white one had for years.”
He continued: “Whites in Mississippi would often tell me of the awful things they believed would happen to them ‘if the Blacks ever take over’, showing an absolute clarity about what whites had done to Black people there over the decades and centuries. They believed that revenge would be the first order of business. Now, it appears that a significant number of them have overcome that fear, which gives me great hope that others will come along that way in the future.”
Like Greg, Catherine Park, a 64-year-old hospital lab director based in Newark, Delaware, sees Colom’s victory as a sign of change. Park grew up in south Mississippi in the 1970s, when the “KKK was a real presence in the state”.
“I am so proud and excited for senator Colom. I have been watching the news daily over his growing lead. The times they are a’ changin’,” Park said. She added that she hoped he “makes a difference in one of the nation’s poorest states” and that “his example becomes a shining light to bring Mississippi out of the 19th century and into the 21st”.
Pat Crimm, a 72-year-old retired electrical engineer who grew up in Jackson, Mississippi, during the segregation era, said that he registered to vote on his 18th birthday, casting his first ballot against Richard Nixon. He sees Colom’s victory as ushering in a new political chapter for Mississippi.
“Besides Dixiecrats, I have only voted for one Democrat who carried Mississippi and was elected – Jimmy Carter,” Crimm said, adding: “Scott Colom seems like a good man who will help us recover from the current administration. His predecessor in the Senate was against poor people and an ardent Maga. My hope is that there is a new sheriff in town who will fight for Mississippi and America.”
For Sherri Vacarella, a 75-year-old retired teacher based in Portland, Oregon, who grew up in Alabama during the 1950s and 1960s, Colom’s victory “is the most exciting change in southern politics in my long lifetime”.
“The idea that he will represent Mississippi, a state that has tried to prevent Black representation since Reconstruction, is particularly sweet to this progressive Democrat elder. I pray for his success and fully expect he’ll do an excellent job as Senator of Mississippi,” she said. “I’m optimistic that senator Colom will focus on affordability and offer legislation that will reduce costs and provide a more trustworthy national government, putting an end to ICE horrors, the Iran war, and Pete Hegseth.”
Similarly, JJ Amaworo Wilson, a 57-year-old writer based in New Mexico who identifies as Anglo-Nigerian-American, said: “In the most racist state in a deeply racist country, this is an extraordinary result, a seismic shift. In the arena of modern electoral politics, it’s comparable only to [Barack] Obama’s ascension to the presidency. Colom knows his history. He knows his achievement comes in the aftermath of the civil rights struggle of Fannie Lou Hamer, Martin Luther King, John Lewis, and many others.”
Wilson continued: “Colom has earned his place in history. Now he must focus on the present, particularly the cost of living and corruption. I hope he succeeds in improving the lives of everyone in Mississippi, including those who voted against him, because that’s his mandate and that’s how he’ll stay in office.”
Charmaine Rehg, 74, who lives in Eugene, Oregon, and is originally from St Louis, Missouri, said Colom’s victory will “mean much more respect for Mississippi, which has been belittled for being ‘backwards’ and ‘redneck’”.
Rehg recalled what she witnessed growing up and traveling through the south on family vacations to Florida, saying: “We saw separate drinking fountains for ‘white’ and ‘colored.’ We saw separate bathrooms on a train we took one year. In Florida, Black people weren’t allowed on the public beach. So I’m ecstatic to see this win, especially in Mississippi. This fits in with much other change in the south.”
Looking ahead, Rehg said she hopes Colom will pursue a range of policy changes, including a “healthcare system more in line with those in Europe”.
“We have a vastly overpriced and fragmented system. Also, housing is overpriced, which I hope he addresses. And I hope he addresses environmental degradation. His state is on the Gulf coast, where there is a history of offshore oil spills and pollution, in particular fertilizer runoff from the land carried by the Mississippi River to the Gulf, causing dead zones due to algae blooms,” she said.
“And I want him to help get this country to stop the war with Iran, to not support [Benjamin] Netanyahu, and to help Ukraine,” Rehg added.

https://hyperallergic.com/the-secret-lif.title: The Secret Life of Hockney's Beverly Hills Housewife
https://hyperallergic.com/the-secret-lif.author: Matt Stromberg
https://hyperallergic.com/the-secret-lif.text:
The Secret Life of Hockney's Beverly Hills Housewife
Taking David Hockney’s painting of arts patron Betty Freeman as his subject, James Cahill tells the engrossing story of two friends who shaped the cultural landscape of 1960s Los Angeles.
In the summer of 1966, David Hockney began work on one of his most iconic paintings: “Beverly Hills Housewife,” a portrait of the arts patron Betty Freeman. She is depicted on her garden patio in front of her sleek, modernist house, which is framed by strips of blue sky and green lawn. A few status symbols surround her — a William Turnbull sculpture, a zebra-skin lounge designed by Le Corbusier, and a mounted antelope head— but the focal point is Freeman in her bright pink dress, gazing wistfully beyond the confines of the canvas.
Critic and novelist James Cahill uses the painting as a jumping off point to expound on the intertwined lives of both artist and muse, as well as to provide a fragmentary snapshot of Los Angeles in the 1960s, in his new book. With The Beverly Hills Housewife: Hockney’s Californian Muse and the World Beyond the Pool (2026), Cahill bounces between formal analysis of the painting, historical anecdotes, and inferences about the broader culture, zigzagging as if driving across LA without a map. Some of the detours prove less relevant to his central narrative than others, but they are nonetheless diverting pit stops on a thoroughly engrossing journey about the friendship between two complex individuals who played formative roles in shaping LA’s cultural landscape.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.title: Houthis say they attacked Riyadh airport and Saudi oil pipeline
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Houthis say they attacked Riyadh airport and Saudi oil pipeline
Yemen's Houthis said they attacked Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and a pumping station on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, which carries crude oil to the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted the airport with a drone, and a pumping station east of Riyadh with two drones.
The group also fired two ballistic missiles at what Saree described as Saudi troop concentrations in the al-Tuwal area of Jazan, in southern Saudi Arabia, he said.
The group's statements came hours after Saudi civil defence issued an all-clear for the province, which is home to a Saudi Aramco refinery with a capacity of 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day.
Inside Yemen, Saree said the Houthis struck Saudi weapons depots at the Ras Abbas camp in Aden with ballistic missiles and drones.
He added that they also fired missiles at forces under the command of Saudi officers in Lahj and al-Jawf provinces, claiming they caused many casualties.
Saudi Arabia did not immediately confirm the Houthi claims.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/possible-lov.title: Possible Love Is a Cinematic Masterpiece About Class
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/possible-lov.author: Kap Seol
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/possible-lov.text:
Possible Love Is a Cinematic Masterpiece About Class
Lee Chang-dong doesn’t have the same profile as fellow South Korean directors like Bong Joon-ho and Park Chan-wook, but his latest film should change that. Possible Love is a powerful study of class in the wake of a shattering real-life strike defeat.
Possible Love is yet another masterpiece that South Korean director Lee Chang-dong has brought to us, after an eight-year hiatus since his last film Burning (2018). Unlike his younger Korean peers, such as Bong Joon-ho (Parasite) or Park Chan-wook (Old Boy and No Other Choice), Lee, now seventy-two, has often found himself confined to the independent film scene outside South Korea, where he has usually enjoyed modest commercial success.
Deeply rooted in humanity and class relations, Lee’s films deserve a wider audience beyond the ranks of art house aficionados (including Barack Obama, who named Burning among his favorite movies of 2018). Lee’s 1999 film Peppermint Candy weaves the life of a young man into the breakneck pace of South Korean capitalism, showing how innocence loses ground to violence, avarice, and lust. Burning explores the ways in which capitalism preys on and consumes poor young men and women.
Netflix’s funding and global distribution of Possible Love will likely expand Lee’s global reach. However, it has also revealed the maestro’s inability to raise further funds in South Korea, whose media giants — mostly outgrowths of chaebol conglomerates such as CJ ENM or Lotte Entertainment — no longer appear to be willing to bankroll Lee’s bold and unapologetic portrayal of South Korea’s economic system.
The Living and the Dead
For Netflix, Possible Love is a prestige project: an opportunity to bring home an Oscar with a highly accomplished director while reversing a viewership slump and enhancing its brand. Possible Love premiered theatrically in South Korea in September, meeting the Academy’s country-of-origin eligibility deadline. The streaming platform has also made Lee’s previous films available for its subscribers.
Possible Love is set against the aftermath of the 2009 brutal crackdown on the seventy-seven-day strike against massive job cuts at SsangYong Motor (fictionalized in the film as SP Heavy Industries). After crushing the strike, management and the government pushed through one of the country’s first massive layoffs by slashing 50 percent of SsangYong’s blue-collar workforce. In the film as in real life, workers refer to their laid-off colleagues as “the dead” and those who managed to escape the cull as “the living.”
Through the crackdown, corporations and the conservative government set a precedent for mass layoffs. After the defeat at SsangYong, corporations could cut jobs by invoking broadly defined criteria of managerial exigency. The repercussions of the strike and its vivid suppression resonated deeply throughout South Korea.
The strike even became part of the backstory of Squid Game, Netflix’s gamified portrayal of capitalist suffering. In his review of the series, Lee Chang-kun, a leader of SsangYong’s labor union, summed up the experience of an agonizing and prolonged factory occupation:
Out of the blue, we were left with no option but to squat at the factory. We first attempted to turn to each other to survive together. However, we were thrown into a life-or-death situation, often with no other option but to betray and dupe each other. At least once, as in Squid Game, we each had to hurt our closest friends.
Many workers or their family members have since died by suicide or from stress-related conditions such as cardiac arrest. There was probably no better place for Lee to begin Possible Love than the funeral of one such worker.
Anger and Betrayal
In the film, Ho-seok (played by Peppermint Candy star Sul Kyung-gu) was one of the remaining seven hundred striking workers who faced the violent police raid. He had been a welder, proud enough to name his son “Iron.”
Having been injured in the crackdown and subsequently jailed, he has been drained of his blue-collar mettle and sense of purpose, leaving him with simmering feelings of anger and betrayal. His wife, Mi-ok (Secret Sunshine star Jeon Do-yeon) is a good-hearted, innately resilient former seamstress who does her best to hold the family together against all odds in the wake of her husband’s layoff.
At this point, documentary director Ye-ji — played by Cho Yeo-jeong, almost typecast as the seemingly innocuous upper-class woman after her similar role in Parasite — encroaches on Ho-seok and Mi-ok’s fragile universe with her camera lens. A daughter of a small-business owner turned parvenu, Ye-ji is married to Sang-woo (Hope star Zo In-sung), a private equity investor born into generations of wealth and power.
Ye-ji attempts to love Mi-ok and Ho-seok because she believes herself to be a good person. While she is probably sympathetic to Ho-seok and his family, she is strikingly lacking in empathy for their situation. Her superficial innocuousness is pernicious.
Ye-ji’s interest in laid-off workers from SP Industries began during a vacation at a resort in the middle of the Qatar desert, maintained by workers who, her husband tells her, labored hard behind the scenes. Ho-seok is a subject Ye-ji wants to capture through her camera before he disappears into obscurity.
Ye-ji’s husband, Sang-woo, is kind and well-mannered, probably because he has little reason to be otherwise. In his line of business, everything seems impersonal, reduced to numbers and valuations. Although he possesses greater worldly insight than his wife, he need not concern himself with the consequences of his spreadsheets for people like Ho-seok, who remain invisible to him.
There seems to be nothing Ho-seok can do better than Sang-woo. The latter is the better husband, always supportive of his wife, both morally and financially. He is also the better athlete, having tutored the welder’s son in tae kwon do, the sport in which Ho-seok was once a varsity athlete.
To add insult to injury, he is even a superior musician who can play the oboe while Mi-ok sings at karaoke. Ho-seok keeps his guard up around Sang-woo, but he seems to be free of personal jealousy toward him, as though he instinctively feels that the rift between them is one of class rather than individual attributes.
Rather, what has traumatized Ho-seok is the experience of his coworkers, who are now divided into the living and the dead. He has feelings of envy toward the living; they can still throw a fancy birthday party for their children. Emotionally overwhelmed, Ho-seok cannot open up during a group therapy session, where one of the dead laments that they were defeated despite being on the right side.
Impossible Love
It is painful to watch Ho-seok, especially if you understand how strikes and campaigns are defeated — how they implode before they can fizzle out or are violently crushed. We do not walk away from our collective struggles because we abruptly come to fear or love our adversaries. We walk away because we have grown disillusioned or lost trust in the people beside us.
It is before Ye-ji’s camera that Ho-seok finally breaks down in tears and confesses his deepest fear that his wife and former coworkers will discover the anger and sense of betrayal he has kept deep inside. Words like “solidarity” or “resistance” have been reduced to hollow shells of what they used to mean to him.
It is also when Ye-ji finally lowers her intrusive camera, perhaps stunned by the scene, or perhaps realizing she can never genuinely understand (or love) her subjects. Her very innocuity is a form of violence against Ho-seok and Mi-ok. “That’s enough!” both Ye-ji and Mi-ok yell after Ho-seok’s moment opening-up. The two couples part ways.
Director Lee appears to have built the narrative around one of the Ten Commandments, “You shall not covet,” which appears at the beginning of the film. Ye-ji has even coveted Ho-seok’s agonies. For Ho-seok, that suffering still constitutes part of his own dignity. After opening up, he appears to regain part of his strength.
When Mi-ok asks for the first time in the film about their future, “What shall we do?” he answers, “We will keep living on.” “It will rain tomorrow,” his wife says. “It hasn’t today,” her husband replies, as if that were how he has put himself together day by day since the strike was crushed.
Possible Love is difficult to watch because it relentlessly makes you uncomfortable, if not downright pained. Ho-seok is not an idealized figure: he is a wavering worker, trapped in divisions within his own class, rather than a bold and brave militant taking on his boss and the system. However, this makes his character all the more real: like Ho-seok and the film itself, we are all multilayered beings defying any simple definition.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: New contemporary art centre coming to University of California, San Diego
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Angella d'Avignon
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The University of California, San Diego will open a 12,000-sq.-ft contemporary art space on its campus in spring 2027. Housed in the university’s new Triton Center, the Strauss Family Gallery will include four indoor exhibition spaces and an outdoor sculpture terrace. Free and open to the public, the Strauss will host exhibitions, commissions, artist residencies and public programmes that encourage collaboration between artists and UC San Diego researchers and scholars.
Jessica Berlanga Taylor, UC San Diego’s chief campus curator, tells The Art Newspaper that the university is aware of the challenges other San Diego cultural institutions are facing and believes investing in art and culture is essential. "The Strauss represents a long-term commitment that the university is making to contemporary art and sees it as an integral part of the university's intellectual and public life," she says.
In 2023, the local philanthropists Matthew and Iris Strauss gave more than 100 works form their art collection to UC San Diego. (Matthew, who made his money in real estate, died the following year.) Represented artists in the gift include Carrie Mae Weems, Fred Wilson, Zhang Huan and Sabine Moritz.
The Strauss’s new David and Claire Guggenheim Gallery will serve as the public entrance and a space for exhibitions, gatherings and an artist-in-residence programme focused on digital artists, while the two-story Gray Box will accommodate large-scale sculpture, moving-image installations and performances.
The 3,043-sq.-ft Black Box will be equipped for immersive video, sound, sculpture and performance; and the White Cube will provide a more conventional gallery setting for works from the Strauss Family Foundation, travelling exhibitions and collaborations with collections in San Diego and beyond.
Taylor calls the Strauss the first "ground-up museum" at UC San Diego. Pointing to existing spaces on campus like the Mandeville Art Gallery (open for nearly 60 years) and a black-box theatre in the music department, she says the Strauss will strive to be part of the landscape of both the campus and San Diego at large. But the Strauss will play a unique role—with commissions, curatorial research and exhibitions in collaboration with artists from across the globe.
UC San Diego’s Stuart Collection, which includes sculptures installed across campus, has already established a public art presence at the university. The Strauss will now give artists a dedicated space for exhibitions, commissions and research.
“We’re connecting art inside with art outside now with the Strauss and the Stuart Collection, but we also want to distinguish very clearly what Stuart is about and what the Strauss will achieve," Taylor says. "The Strauss is very much about perception and experience, but it’s also about expanding our ways of knowing and presenting different forms of knowledge that you wouldn’t necessarily encounter in the classroom."
Taylor's greater vision is to engage the community through public programming and student involvement. The Strauss plans to engage both established and emerging artists, particularly in the digital space, and support the development of their work. "We're looking at how we can bring artistic inquiry into university teaching and research," Taylor says.
This could include incorporating exhibitions and artistic methodologies into existing courses, giving students opportunities to participate in curatorial research and creative projects, and developing collaborations across the university. Taylor points to potential partnerships with UC San Diego’s Qualcomm Institute, the Interdisciplinary Computing and the Arts programme, the Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the Goeddel Family Technology Sandbox as examples of the range of possibilities.
"We see the Strauss as more of a platform than a container for a collection," Taylor says. "We do have a collection, but our goal is to be a platform for research and critical inquiry—and for challenging assumptions."

The Newark Museum of Art (NMOA) has agreed to restore ownership of a large brown jug made in 1852 by the enslaved South Carolina potter David Drake, also known as Dave the Potter, to the artist’s descendants. According to a press release, NMOA will purchase the work back for its permanent collection.
Amber Germano, NMOA’s senior director of registration and collections management, initiated a conversation with the family about restitution. “When I read about the family’s efforts to reunite Drake’s work with his descendants, I immediately knew it was important that we return the vessel in our collection,” she said. “Within a week of reaching out to the family, we were meeting with them. Hearing from them deepened my understanding of the artwork and the importance of restitution.”
“This is what moral leadership looks like,” said George Fatheree III, advisor to David Drake’s descendants, “and we invite other institutions with Mr. Drake’s work to engage with his family so we can move together towards justice.”
David Drake created the stoneware vessel at the Lewis Miles Stoneware Manufactory in Horse Creek Valley, near Edgefield, South Carolina, while enslaved by Miles. It is one of around forty known works by Drake associated with the manufactory and bears three fingertip impressions along the base and another on the applied strap handle. NMOA acquired the vessel at auction in 2022 and has had it on view in the long-term installation “Seeing America: 18th & 19th Century.”
The family began reaching out to institutions about restitution Drake’s work following the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s exhibition “Hear Me Now: The Black Potters of Old Edgefield, South Carolina” in 2022. To date, they have reached agreements with the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the Telfair Museums in Savannah, the Georgia Museum of Art in Athens, Georgia, and the Virginia Museum of Fine Art.

Polit-Affären: Entwarnung: Deutsche Machtmänner zu unsexy für Spioninnen
Spionage-Thriller wie der um Jensen Huang versüßen den Medien-Alltag ungemein. Nur schade, dass solche Geschichten hierzulande so selten vorkommen.
D er Gewinner der Woche heißt Andy Byron. Sie erinnern sich: der Tech-CEO, der nach einem Coldplay-Konzert zurücktreten musste. Nicht direkt wegen Coldplay – auch wenn hier geschmackliche Grenzen überschritten worden sein mögen. Sondern weil er dort eine Frau umarmte, die nicht „seine“ Frau war. Die Kiss-Cam hielt die Szene samt kläglichem Versteckversuch fest und lieferte perfektes Meme-Material.
Doch künftig wird die Welt bei den Suchbegriffen „CEO“ und „Affäre“ nicht mehr zuerst an Byrons Schammoment denken. Jetzt ist da Nvidia-Chef Jensen Huang, die chinesische Spionin und die sogenannte Honey Trap. Ob Huang seiner Frau zu Hause schon versprochen hat, dass dies garantiert Nnn-vi-dia, ähm, nie wieder vorkommt?
Solche Affären, gewürzt mit einer Prise Agententhriller, liebt das Publikum. Im taz-Titelressort dachte man bereits fieberhaft über Überschriften wie „KI – Koitus Interruptus“ nach. Verworfen wurde sie nur, weil ungeklärt blieb, ob Koitus nicht eigentlich mit C geschrieben werden müsste.

Aber Entwarnung für Deutschlands Elitemänner: Hierzulande muss niemand Angst vor einer intriganten Liebschaft haben. Die chinesische Führung interessiert sich kaum noch für das wirtschaftlich und technologisch abgehängte Deutschland. Und mit wem sollten Spioninnen auch ernsthaft anbandeln?
Hierzulande ist alles echt
Mit Friedrich Merz? Der seiner Frau Charlotte und den erwachsenen Kindern zu Weihnachten vier Thermomix schenkt und seinen Geburtstag lieber ganz familiär beim Italiener feiert, statt zur Weltklimakonferenz in die Türkei zu reisen?
Oder mit Mercedes- und Volkswagen-Managern, die der chinesischen Konkurrenz bei E-Autos ohnehin wenig entgegenzusetzen haben? Unangenehme Stelldicheins auf einer Parkbank in Wolfsburg oder nahe der Stuttgart-21-Baustelle bleiben so immerhin aus.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Why Progressives Are Backing Chris Van Hollen
The senator netted key endorsements from progressives, activists, and unions in his quest to oust Chuck Schumer. But he still faces an uphill battle.
Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen jumped into the race for Senate majority leader Tuesday night, providing a clear progressive challenge to what New York Senator Chuck Schumer had hoped would be a smooth transition into the leadership post following big Democratic gains in the midterm elections.
Even as Schumer—who has led Senate Democrats since 2017—claimed that he maintains more than enough support to prevail in an expected early December caucus vote, Van Hollen indicated in a Thursday night interview that at least 10 of his colleagues had already expressed interest in his bid. And he said he hopes to have serious conversations in coming days with senators of every ideological bent, background, and region.
Van Hollen received immediate support from Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, one of the highest-profile newcomers to a Senate Democratic caucus that now has 55 members—and could grow to 56 if Mary Peltola wins in Alaska. Peggy Flanagan, the new senator-elect from Minnesota, added her endorsement of Van Hollen on Friday morning. The Marylander also attracted support from activist groups, a key union, and prominent progressives such as Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent who had already signaled his preference for Van Hollen, and who celebrated the Marylander’s announcement as a step that would help build “a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families.”
Van Hollen, a Capitol Hill veteran and savvy election strategist who had been exploring a 2028 presidential bid, has emerged as a progressive favorite in the leadership race with Schumer for a variety of reasons, including his vow to provide “not a penny” of funding for the war in Iran. He has also argued that Senate Democrats should push for wage hikes, taxes on the rich, reining in AI, and a new approach to campaigns that rejects money from AIPAC, crypto interests, and influence-purchasing billionaires.
Reflecting on the 2026 election results—which saw Democrats take control of the House and Senate and make huge gains in states that as recently as two years ago had backed President Trump and right-wing Republicans—Van Hollen declared on Thursday, “In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies—but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people.”
“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership,” added the senator. “This is not about any one person—it’s about answering the call of the American people.”
Van Hollen followed that message up with interviews in which he promised to challenge a rigged system that has stalled progress on everything from Medicare for All healthcare reforms to a foreign-policy shift that would “end the American taxpayer blank check to the government of Israel.” In particular, he focused on the role that big-money influence on politics plays in undermining workers and unions while benefiting billionaires and expanding wealth inequality.
“We saw a huge outburst of democracy on Election Day—red states, blue states, purple states—and it wasn’t only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption and his wars and his cruelty,” the senator told MS Now. “It was also about a call for a larger change to take on a broken economic system that’s rigged in favor of the very wealthy against working people, led by a corrupt political system.”
El-Sayed, for whom Van Hollen campaigned in an August primary where the Michigander beat centrist Haley Stevens, has long encouraged Van Hollen to mount a leadership bid. And he was quick to jump on board Thursday.
“Michiganders demand money out of politics, money in pockets, and Medicare for All,” said El-Sayed. “Senator Chris Van Hollen offers both the courage to go toe-to-toe with the Trump administration to deliver for working people and the experience to maneuver the Senate caucus. It’s why he has my full support to lead our caucus.”
Flanagan also cited sentiments in her home state to make the case for Van Hollen. “Minnesotans are demanding change. Democrats need to deliver. That starts with new voices in our leadership,” she said. “I believe Chris Van Hollen is the leader and fighter we need to bring about real change, so no American is left behind.”
The Working Families Party, which is influential in the politics of Schumer’s New York State, has expressed opposition to his leadership bid. So have high-profile progressive and activist groups such as MoveOn and Indivisible. And climate activists with the Sunrise Movement called Thursday for Schumer to “STEP ASIDE as Senate Majority Leader in favor of Senator Chris Van Hollen.”
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
The 600,000-member International Association of Machinists union, which had previously called on Schumer to stand down, gave Van Hollen’s bid an enthusiastic boost.
Describing Van Hollen as “a proven champion of working people who will fight to unrig an economy stacked against working families,” Machinists International Union president Brian Bryant said, “Senator Van Hollen understands this is a fight of Workers vs. Billionaires and has the courage to deliver the change voters demanded. Workers did their part on election night. Now it’s Senate Democrats’ turn. Senator Van Hollen is the right choice.”
The momentum for Van Hollen is real, but the final choice rests with Democratic senators, many of whom remain closely tied to Schumer. The Maryland senator acknowledges that he has a lot of work ahead of him, but he continues to argue, “We shouldn’t have a coronation.”
