https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120387.title: Geheimdienste / BND | Geheimdienstreform als Teil eines »autoritären Staatsumbaus«
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120387.author: Peter Nowak
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120387.text:
- Politik
- Geheimdienste / BND
Geheimdienstreform als Teil eines »autoritären Staatsumbaus«
Linke-Politikerin Bünger erläuterte vor der Bundestagsabstimmung Hintergründe des Umbaus von BND und Verfassungsschutz. Sie warnt vor den Folgen.
Während der abschließenden Debatte unmittelbar vor der Abstimmung über das, was Bundesinnenminister Alexander Dobrindt eine »Jahrhundertreform« nannte, musste sich Clara Bünger am Freitag scharfe Vorwürfe anhören. Sie kamen nicht nur von den Koalitionsparteien, sondern auch von den Grünen. So befand der Grünen-Bundestagsabgeordnete Konstantin von Notz, Die Linke 
betreibe »Fundamentalopposition ohne jeden Gestaltungswillen«, indem sie die massive Ausweitung der Befugnisse für das Bundesamt für Verfassungsschutz (BfV) und den Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) pauschal ablehne.
Doch die Innenexpertin der Linksfraktion im Bundestag blieb bei ihrer Einschätzung, dass insbesondere mit dem Umbau des BfV eine neue »Geheimpolizei« geschaffen werde, die sich wirksamer staatlicher Kontrolle entziehen könne. Warum sie dies vertritt, hatte die Politikerin am Donnerstagabend noch einmal auf einer Veranstaltung des Vereins »Helle Panke« erläutert, der Berliner Landeszentrale der Rosa-Luxemburg-Stiftung.
Büngers Hauptkritik am Gesamtvorhaben ist auch nach den von der schwarz-roten Koalition aufgrund zahlreicher verfassungsrechtlicher Bedenken von namhaften Juristen vorgenommenen Änderungen, dass damit das Trennungsverbot zwischen der Arbeit des Verfassungsschutzes und der Polizei aufgehoben werde. Dieses wurde nach den Erfahrungen mit dem NS-Terror von den Westalliierten nach 1945 in der alten Bundesrepublik durchgesetzt.
Als weiteren Kritikpunkt nannte Bünger die Ausweitung der Befugnisse für den Auslandsdienst BND, der dann auch Wohnungen betreten darf. Zudem kann die Bundesregierung mit Zustimmung des Parlamentarischen Kontrollgremiums (PKGr) des Bundestages den »besonderen Feststellungsfall« ausrufen. Dann würden die Befugnisse des BND nochmals massiv ausgeweitet und die parlamentarische Kontrolle weiter beschnitten. Das PKGr ist derzeit nur mit Mitgliedern der Regierungsparteien CDU, CSU und SPD sowie der Grünen besetzt. Bünger als Linke-Kandidatin scheiterte trotz mehrerer Anläufe, auch ein AfD-Vertreter sitzt nicht in dem Gremium.
Auch um August Hanning ging es am Donnerstagabend, denn der ehemalige BND-Präsident war Anfang Oktober verhaftet worden. Denn er steht unter dem Verdacht, als Pensionär einen schwunghaften Handel mit internen Daten der Behörde betrieben zu haben, die ihm sein ehemaliger Büroleiter beschafft haben soll. Dass von Ehemaligen wie ihm eine große Gefahr für die Arbeitsfähigkeit der Dienste ausgeht, war im Bundestag am Freitag kein Thema.
Fabian Kunow von der Hellen Panke verwies auf ehemalige führende Beamte von BfV und BND, die sich nach ihrem Ausscheiden aus dem Amt im rechten politischen Spektrum tummeln. Dazu gehören neben dem ehemaligen BfV-Präsidenten Hans Georg Maaßen der ehemalige Leiter des Thüringischen Verfassungsschutzes, Helmut Röwer, und der Vizepräsident des BfV, Klaus-Dieter Fritsche. Letzterer war später Berater des kurzzeitigen österreichischen Innenministers Herbert Kickl von der extrem rechten FPÖ.
Für Bünger sind solche Aktivitäten kein Zufall. »Hierarchische Behörden, wie es die Geheimdienste sind, ziehen Menschen an, die sich in extrem konservativen bis ultrarechten Kreisen zu Hause fühlen.«
Die Politikerin bekräftigte, dass Die Linke weiterhin die Auflösung des Verfassungsschutzes fordert. So liege es auf der Hand, dass die AfD eine ultrarechte Partei sei. Für diese Feststellung brauche es das BfV nicht. Und stichhaltige Argumente für ein Verbot habe die Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte in einem Gutachten erarbeitet, so Bünger.
Zur Diskussion waren rund 20 Interessierte gekommen, unter ihnen auch einige sehr junge Menschen. Dabei war das Interesse insbesondere am Wirken und an der Geschichte des BND groß. Viele Gründe wurden benannt, die zum Widerstand gegen das neue Gesetz herausfordern müssten. So würden die Lehren aus der NS-Zeit bewusst missachtet und ein »autoritärer Umbau des Staates vorangetrieben«, sagte Bünger. »Zudem werden hier einer möglichen künftigen AfD-Regierung Instrumente in die Hand gegeben, die sie zur Verfolgung von Oppositionellen nutzen könnte«, mahnte sie. Aber auch die Parteien der selbsternannten Mitte könnten die Gesetzesnovelle zur Einschränkung der Rechte Oppositioneller nutzen.
Ein Aspekt wurde nur am Rande angesprochen: Der autoritäre Umbau wird in einer Zeit vorangetrieben, in der täglich die Kriegsfähigkeit Deutschlands propagiert wird. In der Bundestagsdebatte am Freitag spielte dieser Aspekt eine umso größere Rolle. Alexander Dobrindt und zahlreiche weitere Politiker*innen sprachen davon, dass Russland einen »Schattenkrieg« gegen »unsere Demokratie« führe, weshalb die Dienste zum effektiven Abwehrkampf befähigt werden müssten.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/voting-.title: The Hour Before Dawn
https://inthesetimes.com/article/voting-.author: Jesse Hagopian
https://inthesetimes.com/article/voting-.text:
The Hour Before Dawn
With the Voting Rights Act gutted and education under attack, building democratic power must reach beyond the ballot box—and into classrooms and the streets
Jesse Hagopian
In 1980, conservative strategist Paul Weyrich made a startling declaration during a speech in Dallas: “I don’t want everyone to vote.”
Weyrich, a leading strategist of the modern conservative movement and co-founder of the Heritage Foundation, explained, “Elections are not won by a majority of people. They never have been from the beginning of our country, and they are not now. As a matter of fact, our leverage in the elections quite candidly goes up as the voting populace goes down.”
Weyrich’s battles over political power did not end at the ballot box. He also saw education as a crucial battleground. In a 1999 op-ed, he claimed “political correctness” ruled schools and universities with “totalitarian ambitions.” His solution was for conservatives to build a “complete, separate, parallel structure” of “schools, universities, media, entertainment, everything.”
More than 40 years after Weyrich’s infamous voting remarks, Donald Trump has waged battles on these same two fronts. In 2020, on conservative talk show Fox & Friends, Trump warned that greater “levels of voting” would mean “you’d never have a Republican elected in this country again.” His administration has also sought to restrict what students can learn, threatening to withhold federal funding from schools that teach about systemic racism in ways it opposes and attempting to prohibit DEI programs in schools. Trump has simultaneously worked to dismantle the Department of Education while directing more public money toward private schools through voucher programs.
The message is clear: Limit who can exercise democratic power in the present, and limit what people learn about how previous generations expanded it.
The Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v. Callais represents the latest chapter in a centuries-long effort to restrict political participation whenever it threatens the existing distribution of wealth and power. The tactics have changed — from literacy tests and poll taxes to racial gerrymandering and voter suppression laws — but the goal of limiting political participation remains.
The case began when Black voters challenged a Louisiana congressional map that created just one majority-Black district out of six, despite Black residents making up nearly one-third of the population. A federal judge found that the map likely violated the Voting Rights Act by diluting Black voting power, prompting the Republican-controlled legislature to draw a second majority-Black district. But a group of self-described non-Black voters challenged the new map, arguing that creating the second majority-Black district amounted to unconstitutional racial gerrymandering. 
In a 6 – 3 decision on April 29, the Supreme Court struck down the new map and effectively gutted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, which prohibits racial discrimination in voting. As voting rights journalist Ari Berman explained, the ruling served to “effectively kill the last remaining tool of the Voting Rights Act,” following earlier Supreme Court decisions in 2013 and 2021 that weakened its protections.
The consequences have reshaped the 2026 midterm elections. Following Callais, Republican-controlled legislatures in Louisiana and Tennessee redrew congressional maps to eliminate majority-Black districts, including the district representing much of Memphis.
In Alabama, the Supreme Court allowed the state to use a map that eliminated a second district in which Black voters had an opportunity to elect their preferred candidate. Florida enacted a new congressional map designed to shift four Democratic-leaning districts toward Republicans. Meanwhile, a federal appeals court in Georgia overturned a 2023 ruling that the state’s electoral maps discriminated against Black voters, ordering the case reconsidered under the new, more restrictive standard. With additional redistricting battles already taking shape for 2028, the struggle over who gets to exercise political power is far from over.
In her dissent, Justice Elena Kagan warned that “The Voting Rights Act is — or, now more accurately, was — one of the most consequential, efficacious and amply justified exercises of federal legislative power in our nation’s history.”
The Callais decision arrives amid a broader assault on democracy. Across the country, lawmakers are redrawing electoral maps to dilute Black and brown political power, erecting new barriers to voting, attacking independent election administration, criminalizing voter registration efforts and undermining public confidence in elections themselves. These attacks are part of a broader effort to prevent the vast majority of people from exercising meaningful political power.
But democracy is about more than casting a ballot every few years. It depends on people having the freedom to learn, deliberate, organize, protest, advocate, and govern collectively. Achieving a democratic society requires a public empowered to decide not only who holds political office, but also how to govern the wealth, resources and institutions created by our collective labor.
It’s no wonder then why attacks on voting rights and education so often travel together. Limiting teachers’ ability to show students how social movements have expanded democratic rights and challenged concentrated political and economic power constrains the possibilities people can imagine for the future.
As veterans of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) warned in their response to the Callais decision, these attacks are part of a long historical effort to “control the vote. Control the outcome. Control the future.” Few people are better positioned to remind us why. SNCC organizers risked — and, in some cases, gave — their lives to secure the right to vote.
But “voting alone has never been sufficient,” they said. The movement that won the Voting Rights Act never imagined democracy as something that happened only every few years inside a voting booth. Voting mattered because it was one tool — among many — that ordinary people could use to build democratic power. As the SNCC veterans explained, movements must also “build power beyond” the vote through organizing, coalition building, political education and institutions capable of challenging unjust laws and holding those in power accountable long after Election Day. Voting rights have never been gifts handed down by enlightened leaders. They were victories won through collective struggle.
During Reconstruction, formerly enslaved Black communities and their allies fought to transform emancipation into political power. Their organizing helped secure the 15th Amendment in 1870, prohibiting states from denying the right to vote based on race. Reconstruction demonstrated that voting rights were inseparable from broader struggles for public education, economic opportunity, safety and full participation in society.
For a brief period, the United States moved closer to becoming a multiracial democracy. Black voters helped elect Black legislators across the South, establish public schools, expand public services and reshape political life. Yet Reconstruction was ultimately defeated by a campaign of racial terror and political reaction led by former Confederates and their allies. 
Today’s battles over voting rights are the latest manifestation of that counterrevolution.
Nearly a century later, the Civil Rights Movement launched what many historians have called a Second Reconstruction.
In 1964, SNCC helped lead the Mississippi Freedom Summer campaign through the Council of Federated Organizations, a coalition that brought together SNCC, the Congress of Racial Equality, the NAACP, and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. Alongside thousands of Black Mississippians who had been organizing for years, they built Freedom Schools, organized voter registration drives, developed local leadership and helped establish the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party to challenge the state’s all-white Democratic delegation. They faced bombings, beatings and jail cells, and the murders of James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner.
Yet the movement persisted.
Freedom Summer helped expose the brutality of Jim Crow to the nation and laid crucial groundwork for passage of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. But its lessons extended far beyond voting.
Freedom School students studied Black history, examined social inequalities, debated current events and imagined a more democratic future. Organizers recognized that people needed not only the right to vote but also the knowledge, confidence, and political understanding necessary to exercise power.
Reflecting on the movement decades later, SNCC veteran Courtland Cox explained that the struggle was never simply about access to the ballot. Rather, it sought to create “space for millions of Americans to participate in the political and economic life of this country.”
Voting rights are about more than elections. They are about who has the power to shape the conditions of their lives. They are connected to struggles for quality schools, affordable housing, healthcare, labor rights, clean air and water, public investment and economic justice. This is precisely why attacks on voting rights are so often accompanied by attacks on education.
Those seeking to restrict popular power understand the power of history education and see it as dangerous. When students learn about Reconstruction, they discover that formerly enslaved people fought to dramatically expand democratic rights in a nation that had never lived up to its democratic claims. When they learn about Freedom Summer, they discover that ordinary people challenged systems of oppression that seemed permanent. When they learn about the Civil Rights Movement, they discover that rights are rarely granted voluntarily by those in power; they are won through, as SNCC puts it, “courage, radical imagination and readiness to act.”
If young people understand these histories, they may begin to see themselves not simply as spectators to politics but as participants in shaping the future. That is precisely why educators must refuse to lie about the past and teach honest history about the Black Freedom Struggle and movements for collective liberation. Through the growing Teach Truth movement, educators, students, and communities across the country are organizing against book bans and curriculum censorship. Teachers are refusing to surrender to laws and political intimidation designed to erase the history of systemic racism and its enduring impact on American society. Instead, they are teaching the truth about the long struggle for voting rights and the grassroots movements that challenged slavery, segregation, and racial injustice. They are helping students understand that democracy has never simply been handed down from above. It has been expanded by ordinary people organizing together to demand it.
Paul Weyrich’s call for a “complete, separate, parallel structure” of schools and media lives on in today’s MAGA movement, with its push for school privatization through charter schools and private school vouchers while restricting the teaching of systemic racism in public schools. Yet decades before Weyrich’s declaration, SNCC and other Freedom Summer organizers had built their own parallel institutions from below — not to privatize public education, but to challenge the segregation and white supremacy of Mississippi’s schools and society. The irony is striking: Today’s MAGA movement champions alternatives to public schools while seeking to suppress the alternative education that SNCC’s Freedom Schools were created to provide — teaching that white supremacy can be challenged, that ordinary people can transform society and that education should empower young people to fight for a more democratic world.
In this time of rising authoritarianism, the lessons of SNCC veterans are vital. “We have seen darker nights than this one,” the SNCC veterans’ response to Callais reminds us, but “we do not pretend that this moment is ordinary.”
This metaphor from SNCC veterans is a fitting one for our own time:
Yes, it is late, and it’s dark outside. But it is 3 a.m. This is the hour when the body is most vulnerable. The hour when the future feels uncertain. The hour when many lose their way. But it is also the hour before dawn. A new world isn’t guaranteed. But it is possible. And it’s already being imagined, organized and fought for.
The hour before dawn has never belonged to spectators. It has always belonged to those willing to organize despite uncertainty and to imagine a freer society before it seems possible. That is the inheritance the veterans of SNCC have entrusted to us.
Jesse Hagopian is a Seattle educator, an editor for Rethinking Schools magazine, a founding steering committee member of Black Lives Matter at School and serves as the director of the Teaching for Black Lives Campaign for the Zinn Education Project. His most recent book from Haymarket Books is Teach Truth: The Attack on Critical Race Theory and the Struggle for Antiracist Education. Jesse is editor of More Than a Score: The New Uprising Against High Stakes Testing and co-editor of the books, Teaching for Black Lives, Black Lives Matter at School and Teachers Unions and Social Justice.

https://gothamist.com/news/first-code-bl.title: First Code Blue of the winter season arrives in New York City
https://gothamist.com/news/first-code-bl.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/first-code-bl.text:
New York City activated its first Code Blue of the season on Friday, opening warming centers overnight and relaxing shelter intake rules as temperatures and wind chills are expected to approach freezing, officials said.
The cold weather emergency runs from 4 p.m. Friday to 8 a.m. Saturday, according to the city Department of Emergency Management. Temperatures in Central Park are expected to fall to about 36 degrees, with windchills as low as 34, but colder air moving in after a storm could push both closer to freezing, the agency said, citing the National Weather Service.
It’s the first Code Blue since Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced an expanded plan this week, after more than two dozen people died outdoors or in their homes during a stretch of freezing weather last winter. The city promised $25 million in new funding, 300 more outreach canvassers, 800 more beds and 20 warming buses for the season, aimed to help New Yorkers sleeping on the street.
But last winter showed the danger isn’t limited to people living outside. Gothamist found that at least five of the people who died outside during the cold stretch that began in January had housing.
On Friday, six warming buses are scheduled to run overnight, from midnight to 5 a.m. Saturday at Bellevue, Elmhurst, Harlem and Lincoln hospitals and at Penn Station, according to city officials. Eight drop-in centers are open, and three of those hospitals are serving as warming centers from 4 p.m. to 8 a.m.
“When Code Blue is in effect, we make it as easy as possible for anyone to come inside,” Department of Social Services Commissioner Erin Dalton said in a statement.
Anyone who walks into a city shelter or drop-in center will be let in without the usual intake steps, she said.
NYC Emergency Management Commissioner Christina Farrell urged New Yorkers to check on older neighbors “and anyone who lives alone.”
She also warned that fire is the biggest risk of staying warm at home.
Officials are asking anyone who sees someone outside who may need help to call 311, and to call 911 if a person is in danger, seems confused or appears very cold. Warming locations are listed at on.nyc.gov/warm.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.title: The ADAA Fair Is Back, and Sometimes Smaller Really Is Better
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.author: Daniel Cassady
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.text:
Art fairs should do two things: let visitors see art, ideally stuff they haven’t seen before, and help dealers sell that art to people who want to buy it. Simple enough. And yet, somewhere along the way, fairs became so enormous that seeing everything on offer began to feel like an endurance sport.
That’s one reason the newly rechristened Art Dealers Association of America Fair, which opened Thursday night at the Park Avenue Armory, was such a pleasure. With just 63 exhibitors, it’s small enough to navigate without a map, manageable enough to spend time actually looking at the art, and varied enough to reward a little wandering. These may sound like modest achievements, but anyone who’s spent six hours trudging through a convention center will appreciate them.
The setting helps. The Park Avenue Armory still has plenty of its old New York charm, something that’s increasingly hard to come by in an art fair. Organizers have also moved the bar to the center of the exhibition hall, improving the sightlines and making the whole affair feel more open. You can actually see what’s going on across the room, rather than navigating a maze of booths.
Of course, the fair’s return wasn’t entirely straightforward. Last July, the AADA abruptly canceled its 2025 edition, calling the decision a “strategic pause.” The organization subsequently retired the Art Show name and ended its decades-long fundraising partnership with the Henry Street Settlement, which had received more than $38 million through the fair’s benefit previews. The Whitney Museum of American Art is now the beneficiary, and the fair has returned with 12 fewer exhibitors and what seems to be emphasis on its national membership.
The reasons behind the sudden cancellation remain something of a mystery (and there were no shortage of rumors percolating about what happened with the fair’s old partner, Henry Street) but whatever the circumstances of its reinvention, the result is a fair that gets at least one of those two basic things right.
As for the selling, well, that’s up to the dealers.
Kinsey Robb, the ADAA’s executive director, was spritely and in good spirits at Thursday’s gala, quite literally shining even, thanks to her skirt, which was decorated with what she described as little chandeliers. It was a new purchase and even spent some time at the tailor before the evening’s debut. Organizing a fair, she explained, comes with plenty of highs and lows. Sometimes a little retail therapy helps.
Robb, who took over the association in September 2024, has spent much of the past year talking about making the fair more valuable to its members. But when I asked whether that meant exhibitors were actually paying less to participate, she offered a rather different definition of value.
“I think it’s sales, sure,” she said, “but the real benefit was the connections dealers make with one another and with collectors.” She described a collegial atmosphere during installation, with dealers more than pleased to see old friends and actually interested in what their neighbors were showing.
That might sound a little sentimental, but Robb makes a reasonable point. The association represents a large network of galleries, many of them small businesses whose concerns are rather different from those of the industry’s multinational behemoths. The fair, she argued, gives them somewhere to meet, exchange ideas, and share their expertise.
“It’s not my fair,” she said. “It’s the members’ fair.”
Fortunately, there was evidence that the members were doing business, too.
According to sales figures released by the ADAA following Thursday’s preview, Jonathan Boos reported two of the evening’s biggest transactions: Agnes Pelton’s The Well of Peace (1932), with an asking price of $2.4 million, and a Beauford Delaney painting priced at $1.6 million.
The action wasn’t confined to the million-dollar end of the market. AH Arts sold a Helen Frankenthaler work on paper for a reported $75,000, while James Barron Art placed works by Beverly Pepper, Kenneth Noland, and Kikuo Saito, with asking prices ranging from $40,000 to $85,000.
Contemporary art found buyers as well. Jessica Silverman reported selling eight works by Julie Buffalohead, priced between $22,000 and $50,000, while Charles Moffett sold all four of its Lily Stockman paintings at $20,000 apiece and four works by Julia Jo priced between $30,000 and $40,000.
Kraushaar Galleries, meanwhile, reported two six-figure sales alongside several works priced below $2,000. That’s a fairly remarkable spread, and perhaps a better illustration of the ADAA’s appeal than another speech about the importance of community.
Of course, these are dealer-reported sales, and asking prices don’t necessarily reflect what buyers actually paid. Still, they suggest that at least some collectors came to do more than admire the art and enjoy the open bar.
And there was plenty worth admiring. Here are five booths that caught my eye.
Gavlak
At Gavlak, two generations of artists offer very different takes on light, color, and the cosmos. Lita Albuquerque, a veteran of California’s Light and Space and Land Art movements, presents a series of luminous paintings in which gold-leaf discs appear to float against fields of saturated blue, black, and crimson.
In Goya’s First Breath (2025), a pale gold oval glows against a black background, looking something like a distant planet glimpsed through the darkness.
Across the booth, Jessica Cannon takes a more intricate approach. Her paintings are built from overlapping geometric forms and thousands of tiny marks that create shimmering, almost woven surfaces. In August Radii (2026), bands of peach, orange, pink, and green spiral around a central point, while Razor Moon (2026) offers a cooler composition of blues and purples.
The two artists make an excellent pairing. Albuquerque’s paintings seem to radiate light from within, while Cannon’s appear to catch and scatter it. They’re also the sort of works that reward seeing them in person, changing subtly as you move around them. Albuquerque’s paintings are priced between $90,000 and $125,000, while Cannon’s range from $25,000 to $40,000.
Peter Blum Gallery
Alex Katz is one of those artists whose work is so instantly recognizable that it’s easy to forget how much thinking goes into making something look so effortless.
Peter Blum’s booth, devoted entirely to Katz’s works on paper, offers a particularly enjoyable reminder. Spanning roughly seven decades, the presentation brought together early cut-paper collages and later charcoal and graphite drawings.
One particularly charming little collage, Untitled (ca. 1957–58), shows four figures relaxing on a nearly deserted beach. A thin strip of dark green landscape cuts across the horizon, while the figures, rendered in tiny scraps of colored paper, occupy only a fraction of the composition. Most of it is simply sand.
It’s all very Katz, despite measuring just five by eight inches. There’s something wonderful about how little he needs to establish a scene.
The more recent drawings, including studies of flowers, reveal the same economy of line. Very little unnecessary information, yet somehow everything you need is there.
Eric Firestone Gallery
Eric Firestone, as usual, put together an excellent booth of seven women associated with the New York School, including Helen Frankenthaler, Pat Passlof, Elise Asher, Miriam Schapiro, Sari Dienes, Adaline Kent, and Jeanne Reynal.
It’s a compelling collection of artists whose contributions to postwar American art were frequently overshadowed by those of their male contemporaries. More importantly, the works themselves are terrific, and the presentation makes a convincing case for how much experimentation was happening beyond the familiar names of Abstract Expressionism.
Among the highlights is a small, previously unexhibited 1951 landscape by Frankenthaler, made with oil and pencil on a piece of palette paper. It’s a fascinating glimpse of the artist before the breakthrough that would transform her practice the following year.
There’s also Dienes’s Burnt Totem (1961), a monumental assemblage made from discarded wooden hat forms, and Passlof’s Keeping Still Mountain, a large, restless abstraction whose title comes from the I Ching.
The booth is a firm nod to the fact that there is a lot of art history that remains to be reconsidered, even when the period in question has been studied to death.
Cristin Tierney Gallery
Maureen O’Leary’s paintings at Cristin Tierney are wonderfully strange. At first glance, her bright colors, simplified figures, and seemingly cheerful domestic scenes suggest something almost storybook-like. Spend another minute looking, though, and things become considerably less straightforward.
In Spring (2026), a backyard gathering unfolds around a barbecue, with children, animals, and plants crowded into a busy, brightly colored landscape. Flames leap from the grill while the surrounding figures seem to inhabit slightly different versions of reality. There are echoes of the Nabis and Post-Impressionists in the flattened perspective and improbable colors, but O’Leary’s world is distinctly her own.
What makes the paintings work is the tension between their familiar subject matter and the peculiar atmosphere she creates. These are scenes of ordinary life, but ordinary life as remembered in a particularly vivid dream.
The presentation coincides with The Linden Trees, O’Leary’s second solo exhibition at the gallery, which runs through December 19.
Piero Atchugarry
Sculpture can be a difficult proposition at an art fair, where space is limited and paintings tend to get most of the attention. But Piero Atchugarry’s solo presentation of Brazilian artist Túlio Pinto is worth seeking out.
Pinto works with stone, steel, and glass, arranging materials in configurations that appear to defy the laws of physics without actually doing so. A heavy stone rests on a chain made of glass. Elsewhere, an enormous steel beam appears to depend on another delicate glass chain to remain upright.
In Complicity #52, rust-colored steel beams grip enormous amber glass forms, while a large piece of rose quartz hangs precariously from one end. The whole structure looks as though it ought to collapse, which is precisely what makes it so compelling.
The four works on view span several years of Pinto’s practice, including pieces from his Complicity Vectors series and more recent Gravitas sculptures. They share an interest in balance, resistance, and the sometimes surprising strength of materials we ordinarily think of as fragile.
It’s a smart, physically engaging, and exactly the sort of thing that makes a smaller art fair worth visiting.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: PF apura suspeitas de fraude em contratos emergenciais na enchente em Canoas e Cachoeirinha
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A Polícia Federal (PF) deflagrou, nesta sexta-feira (13), a Operação Deságue para investigar possíveis fraudes em contratos emergenciais de locação e operação de motobombas durante as enchentes de 2024 em Canoas e Cachoeirinha, na região Metropolitana de Porto Alegre. Segundo a corporação, o sobrepreço estimado nos contratos de Canoas é de pelo menos R$ 7 milhões.
Foram cumpridos 13 mandados de busca e apreensão em sete municípios gaúchos — Pelotas, Porto Alegre, São Leopoldo, Cachoeirinha, Gravataí, Capão da Canoa e Canoas — e em Itapema, em Santa Catarina. A operação resultou no bloqueio de mais de R$ 10 milhões em ativos financeiros e na apreensão de três veículos.
Os contratos investigados foram custeados com recursos federais destinados à resposta ao desastre climático. As motobombas utilizadas para retirar a água das áreas inundadas teriam sido contratadas de uma empresa sem estrutura operacional compatível, que, segundo a PF, teria sido favorecida e repassado a execução dos serviços a empresas especializadas por valores inferiores aos cobrados das prefeituras.
Em Canoas, a investigação aponta cobranças entre nove e dez vezes superiores aos custos reais em determinados serviços. Em Cachoeirinha, o serviço investigado envolveu duas motobombas entre 13 de maio e 13 de junho de 2024. Segundo a PF, também foram identificados orçamentos fraudulentos, elaborados ou assinados após o início ou mesmo depois do encerramento dos serviços.
A corporação informou ainda ter identificado saques em espécie e transferências para pessoas físicas e jurídicas sem vínculo aparente com a operação dos equipamentos. Os investigados poderão ser indiciados por crimes como fraude em licitação ou contrato, corrupção ativa e passiva, associação criminosa e lavagem de dinheiro.
A Prefeitura de Canoas confirmou nesta sexta-feira (13) a exoneração do secretário-geral de Governo, João Batista Portella Pereira. A administração informou que a decisão ocorreu após tomar conhecimento de que Pereira, secretário da Fazenda à época das contratações, é um dos alvos da operação.
Em nota enviada ao Brasil de Fato RS, a Prefeitura de Cachoeirinha afirmou que os fatos investigados ocorreram durante as enchentes de 2024, na gestão anterior, “não possuindo qualquer vínculo com a atual Administração Municipal”. Informou ainda que não houve buscas nas dependências da prefeitura, mas exclusivamente em residências de investigados da gestão anterior, e se colocou à disposição para colaborar com as autoridades.
Procurada pela redação, a Prefeitura de Canoas não enviou resposta até o fechamento desta matéria.
Confira a nota da Prefeitura de Cachoeirinha na íntegra
A Prefeitura de Cachoeirinha esclarece que a operação deflagrada pela Polícia Federal nesta sexta-feira (13) refere-se a fatos ocorridos em 2024, durante a gestão anterior, não possuindo qualquer vínculo com a atual Administração Municipal.
Ressaltamos que não houve nenhuma ação ou busca da Polícia Federal nas dependências da Prefeitura, tendo os mandados sido cumpridos exclusivamente nas residências de investigados da gestão anterior.
Pautada pela lisura, transparência e responsabilidade, a atual gestão reforça que está totalmente à disposição para colaborar com as autoridades competentes para o completo esclarecimento dos fatos.
Prefeitura Municipal de Cachoeirinha

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Mamdani and Trump agree to 90-day delay on new food assistance rules for corner stores
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Shrai Popat
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, has struck a deal with Donald Trump to secure a 90-day delay on new rules for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (Snap), so that bodegas and corner stores across the country have time to comply.
The extension, Mamdani said, starts Friday as a result of conversations he had with Trump and Brooke Rollins, the agriculture secretary.
The new guidelines, implemented by the US agriculture department, which retailers would have had to meet by 4 November, require stores to stock at least seven varieties within each staple food category: dairy, grains, protein and fruits or vegetables. Retailers would also have to ensure that they offer perishable items in three of the staple food categories.
The new guidelines threw the lives of “more than a million New Yorkers” and “tens of milllions more across America” into “chaos”, the mayor said at a press conference on Friday.
“People already reckoning with a shortage of affordable places to buy what they need for their home, soaring costs at the register, and food deserts across the five boroughs, now feared that the few places they could shop would no longer be able to accept their benefits,” Mamdani said.
Several advocates were concerned that the new rules would mean people relying on Snap would be unable to buy groceries at their only accessible store. According to the Food Research and Action Center, bodegas, convenience stores and small grocery stores make up roughly 70% of Snap retailers.
Given the tight timeframe to adjust their stock and meet the new requirements, small retailers ran the risk of going out of business if they couldn’t accept Snap benefits, the mayor said.
“For so many of our fellow Americans, whether they shop at a general store in Michigan or a convenience store in Missouri, would have struggled to use their benefits and feed those they love.”
More than 100 bodega owners reached out to Mamdani’s office with concerns about the new rule. According to the New York City department of city planning, there are more than 10,000 bodegas and corner stores across the five boroughs.

https://hyperallergic.com/tribal-groups-.title: Tribal Groups Urge Congress to Halt Bill That Threatens Sacred Sites
https://hyperallergic.com/tribal-groups-.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/tribal-groups-.text:
Tribal Groups Urge Congress to Halt Bill That Threatens Sacred Sites
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would speed up permitting for major projects and could impact Indigenous sovereignty over culturally significant land.
Tribal organizations are urging legislators to halt the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a bill that would speed up the permitting and review processes of major infrastructure projects and could severely undermine tribal sovereignty over sacred and culturally significant sites.
The United States Senate advanced the controversial bill for further debate on November 8 amid mounting criticism from Indigenous groups and historic preservation advocates, largely due to the act's narrowing of Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966.
The law mandates federal agencies to weigh the impact of projects on historic properties, oftentimes with required tribal consultation, though BAAJA removes tribal nations from much of the review process. The bill text also curtails several other environmental acts, such as the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act, and pushes for shorter review timelines, the loosening of protections of sacred lands, and less federal oversight.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.title: Israeli forces detain Palestinian groom in wedding raid as settler attacks continue across West Bank
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Israeli forces detain Palestinian groom in wedding raid as settler attacks continue across West Bank
Israeli forces and settlers carried out a series of attacks across the occupied West Bank on Friday, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
In Jaba’, south of Jenin, Israeli forces stormed the town, firing live ammunition and tear gas, and shot a young Palestinian man in the thigh, the Palestinian Red Crescent Society said.
Near Ramallah, Israeli forces raided a wedding hall in the village of al-Mughayyir, firing tear gas at around 150 guests and detaining four people, including the groom, Wafa said, citing Palestinian residents.
In the same village, troops stormed the home of Palestinian man, Hamed Abu Naim, seized keys and forced the family out.
In Beit Ummar, north of Hebron, several Palestinians were treated for tear gas inhalation after Israeli forces fired tear gas at residents and their homes.
According to residents, troops had entered the town to protect Israeli settlers who had chased children near its entrance and tried to assault them. Soldiers also stopped a vehicle at the entrance and beat its driver.
South of Yatta, in the Hebron governorate, settlers besieged the home of Yousef Shannaran for the 40th consecutive day, media activist Osama Makhamra told Wafa.
He said settlers had put back up a tent next to the house that Israeli forces had previously removed, so the family can only come and go by coordinating with nearby troops. Settlers also threw stones at the home, smashed its windows and doors and poisoned the family’s water well, he added.
Near Khirbet Srouj, west of Jenin, settlers attacked Palestinian families harvesting olives and stole harvested olives and equipment.
In occupied East Jerusalem, two Palestinian brothers were forced to demolish their own homes in Sur Baher after the Israeli municipality said they had been built without permits.
Israeli forces also detained a Palestinian child and a woman in the southern Hebron area, Quds News Network reported.
Israeli occupation soldiers joined Israeli settlers in dancing and singing outside the home of Palestinian Yousef Shanaran, which has been besieged for 40 consecutive days in Wadi al-Rakheem, south of Yatta in the southern Hebron hills. The settlers have besieged the family inside the home for 40 days with daily attacks and a poisoned water well, all in the presence of Israeli occupation soldiers. The soldiers also aid the siege by refusing to remove the settlers’ tent and by requiring the Palestinian family to obtain a permit to bring in food and water.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Pope thanks crowds on emotional return to ‘second home’ in Peru’s Chiclayo
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Pope thanks crowds on emotional return to ‘second home’ in Peru’s Chiclayo
The Chicago-born pope was welcomed by huge crowds in the coastal city, on the final leg of his South America tour.
Pope Leo has made an emotional return to his former diocese of Chiclayo in Peru, where large crowds welcomed their former bishop exactly one month after he had lung cancer surgery, and he thanked them for their support during his recovery.
“As I look at your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life,” he said.
About 500,000 people gathered for Mass at Pampas de Pimentel, a desert park just outside of Peru’s fourth-largest city, according to estimates from the Vatican, while another million lined his motorcade route.
Before he was elected pope, Leo had spent about two decades working in Peru as a missionary priest and served as bishop of Chiclayo, where he is still known as “Padre Roberto” and where his image is ubiquitous, from 2015 to 2023.
In Chiclayo, a coastal city of about 620,000, Leo earned a reputation for staying close to poor communities during times of crisis, including when the region was hit with devastating floods and the COVID-19 pandemic.
Some had camped overnight to see him, while others walked in the hot sun to avoid bumper-to-bumper traffic to get to the open-air Mass.
As he rode in his popemobile, people in the crowd waved yellow and white Vatican flags and shouted, “The pope is from Chiclayo.”
“What a joy it is to return to Chiclayo,” said Leo at the start of his homily.
Originally from Chicago and formerly known as Robert Francis Prevost, Leo also holds Peruvian citizenship and declared the country his homeland on Wednesday.
Peru is the final stop of his 12-day, three-country South America tour, coming after visits to Argentina and Uruguay. Approximately 12 million people have come to see him at public events so far.
Last month, he underwent surgery for lung cancer, amid fears that the trip would have to be cancelled. But doctors have said the cancer was localised, had not spread, and would not require further treatment.
Leo will stay in the Chiclayo area until Sunday, leading eight events, including a private dinner with the priests he oversaw during his time as bishop.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-lowre.title: US Government Bureaucracy Is Designed to Punish the Poor
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-lowre.author: Kelly McKowen
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-lowre.text:
US Government Bureaucracy Is Designed to Punish the Poor
In The Time Tax, journalist Annie Lowrey ably documents the myriad ways US public services harm poor and working-class people and alienate them from the government. Yet she downplays the class interests that benefit from these Kafkaesque arrangements.
For several years, I lived in Norway and enjoyed the privileges associated with membership in Folketrygden, or the National Insurance Scheme. One privilege that I still think about often is the relative frictionlessness of interacting with the Norwegian government.
Seeing a doctor, for example, was effortless, and once my low annual deductible (as of 2026, ~$300) was paid, all testing and treatment for the year was covered without my involvement or input. My taxes were — without my prompting — prepared for me and sent for my amendment and approval. There was never anything to amend, of course. And because of the country’s leveringsfritak, or “silent acceptance” law, I did not even have to sign or submit a return.
The great difference between how things are typically done in Norway and how they are done in my home country, the United States, was never clearer to me than it was one day when I had to visit the US embassy in Oslo to handle some paperwork. At that time, the embassy was housed in an angular, charcoal-colored Eero Saarinen building across the street from the Royal Palace. It was not only conveniently located but, despite its popular reputation as a “fortress,” simple and straightforward to access — entering the compound required flashing my passport and was about as easy as doing anything else in Norway.
Imagine my surprise, then, when I arrived at the office where I was to complete my task: from the uncomfortable seating and oppressive lighting to the interminable wait and general feeling of disaffection, it was such an uncanny recreation of an underfunded Department of Motor Vehicles or post office that it could have been a movie set. There was even a small, cheaply framed photo of the president. The juxtaposition of this experience — which seemed designed to frustrate — and my happy dealings with Norway’s bureaucracies was, in its own way, radicalizing.
I sense that Annie Lowrey, author of The Time Tax, has been similarly radicalized, albeit through extensive personal and journalistic exposure to the myriad forms in which people in the United States have their time wasted and disrespected — or “taxed,” as she puts it — in almost every conceivable interaction with the government. She is clearly and justifiably pissed, and her book endeavors to show that the problem is, though widespread and deeply rooted in a particular national history of racial exclusion and class oppression, fixable. There is a world, she argues, beyond our current patchwork of fool’s errands and wild-goose chases.
The Time Tax and Its Origins
But it is to this patchwork — and its associated “time taxes” — that most of the book is devoted. Through a mix of reporting, social scientific research, and reflecting on her own experience with an autoimmune condition, Lowrey has collected a cabinet of maddening curiosities: impenetrable forms, inexplicable rejections, multiyear wait times, and more. Page after page finds ordinary Americans trying to navigate a twisted institutional terrain seemingly designed by Franz Kafka or M. C. Escher. In the United States, you can buy, bid, and bet with the click of a button. Yet paying your taxes, voting, and getting benefits for which you qualify requires you to do American Ninja Warrior — with the proper forms of ID in hand.
Having cataloged the challenges people face when using public services in the United States, the first section of The Time Tax concludes with a tantalizing glimpse at the Estonian case, which, in many ways, resembles the Norwegian one with which I am more familiar (sans generous welfare state and strong labor rights). The story, as told by Lowrey, is that the small Baltic country, battered and bereft after exiting the Soviet Union, lacked the time, experience, infrastructure, and resources to recreate the comprehensive service architectures of other countries. So it didn’t. Instead, a generation of young and enterprising leaders leaned into speed, convenience, and digital integration to build an innovative e-government. In Estonia, Lowrey has seen the almost frictionless future of navigating government — and it works!
The Time Tax is at its most interesting and convincing when Lowrey is detailing the diabolical busy boxes that occupy millions of Americans. After the brief field trip to Estonia, the book could — and probably should — have ended with her proposals. It doesn’t.
Perhaps drawing inspiration from her subject, Lowrey decides that she requires more of her reader’s time to make her point. After a section break, we leave Estonia and arrive at . . . Fort Pillow in 1864? With Confederate general and future Ku Klux Klan Grand Wizard Nathan Bedford Forrest? It was disappointing to discover that The Time Tax was not in fact beginning its descent to a satisfying landing — it had been diverted to another destination: the past.
The middle third of the book draws on the extensive historical and social scientific scholarship devoted to the United States’ welfare system to recapitulate a story that will be familiar to anyone who knows the tortuous history of social provision in the United States. All the beats are there: Civil War pensions, Jim Crow, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and the Great Depression, Lyndon Baines Johnson and the Great Society, Ronald Reagan’s “welfare queens,” Bill Clinton and the “end of welfare as we know it.” Lowrey provides some useful context for twenty-first-century annoyances but breaks no new ground here, and the long historical detour saps the momentum of her opening chapters.
I worry that it also leads her to draw the wrong conclusions about her time taxes. She laments, for instance, that “diversity creates time taxes” and suggests that we are not Estonia due to “racial makeup.” Could it not be instead that time taxes transform diversity into inequality and hierarchy?
Cutting the Time Tax?
In any case, the final part of the book picks up the threads of the first to make a final appeal and offer Lowrey’s solutions. This appeal takes for granted that the reader has not been entirely swayed by their own experiences or by the book’s emphasis on aggravation, injustice, racism, and inequality. Instead, Lowrey makes a persuasive closing argument that time taxes also hurt our health, teach us the wrong lessons about citizenship and government, and undermine social trust.
She concludes with her blueprint for change. Her proposed fixes include measuring time taxes via “sludge audits,” federalizing what are today state-run programs, reducing the use of means-testing in favor of universalism, and abolishing work requirements and pro forma interviews. These changes would, in the aggregate, make using public services faster, easier, more convenient, more empowering, and ultimately more fulfilling.
But I hesitate to call these proposals “solutions,” because I do not think that they actually address the problem at the heart of The Time Tax. This problem is not time taxes per se but the success of actors who weaponize bureaucracy to undermine our access to the goods and services of the social citizenship for which previous generations have fought and even died. The status quo in the United States is a nightmare not because elites are unaware of the fact that universalism promotes greater public investment and trust in government — it is a nightmare because they are aware. The history of many hitherto existing time taxes is also the history of class struggles.
Lowrey knows this — I think. She condemns TurboTax for helping to kill Direct File, Florida Republicans for fighting the reenfranchisement of convicted felons, and Donald Trump for the disaster of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)–related cuts. She tells us that “time taxes are not just policy failures, but deliberate tools of social control.” And yet The Time Tax’s antagonist is without question “Uncle Sam” (her chosen shorthand for the government) and his “bureaucratic excesses.”
The issue is that while she lambasts “Uncle Sam” again and again, she is hesitant to center the private interests for whom that control is useful and profitable. In her long historical excursus, she can acknowledge that poll taxes and other discriminatory laws were used by racist white elites to exclude black people, make their lives precarious, and destroy governmental alternatives to foster dependency on actors who rarely had their best interests in mind. But while the past has opponents, for Lowrey, the present only has design flaws.
A smaller rhetorical point: Lowrey undermines her cause with the book’s core metaphor. Calling the problem the “time tax” might sell books to tax-wary Americans, but it could reinforce the pernicious idea that taxes do not benefit ordinary people. This is odd, as Lowrey herself acknowledges that a sustainable remedy to “the headaches, snafus, and frustration imposed by Uncle Sam” requires the expansion and improvement of administrative capacity — a development that would almost certainly require, well, greater taxes.
Finally, there is a problem of conceptual imprecision, which becomes apparent in the book’s first pages. Lowrey opens The Time Tax with a montage, juxtaposing disconnected scenarios for the purpose of creating a connective thread — the time tax — between radically different people, places, and challenges. But as she moves from losing the right to vote, to trying to get insurance to cover therapies for an autistic child, to attempting to open a soft-serve ice cream shop, to practicing cosmetology without a license, to handing out burritos to the homeless without a permit, I began to question whether each of these is in fact an example of the same problem. After a while, she more or less abandons any attempt to persuade you that a given obstacle is or is not a time tax. Instead, she just asserts it, identifying one or more annoyances and then adding something like “ — a time tax,” as if it were obvious.
All in all, The Time Tax is laudable as a collection of curios. It is less useful as a blueprint. Though Lowrey knows — and sometimes says explicitly — that this maddening status quo reflects the desires of certain powerful and well-resourced actors, she offers no proposals for organizing to muzzle, defang, or otherwise diminish their influence. She writes that “change does not happen without awareness, and awareness is not possible without numbers and stories.”
But it also does not happen without an awareness of who or what benefits from keeping you trapped in a thousand purgatories and a strategy for organizing against them. The path to a Norwegian-style welfare state is not just a matter of design — it is one of politics, and class politics in particular.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Shanghai’s art week finds buyers in a selective market
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Alex Wang, Lisa Movius
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Shanghai’s two leading art fairs, West Bund Art & Design and Art021, opened this week against a backdrop of slowing economic growth, subdued confidence in China’s art market and an increasingly crowded international art calendar. While the city no longer commands the same international panache it enjoyed before the pandemic, galleries report encouraging early sales, suggesting that committed collectors remain active despite a more cautious market.
“I think the serious people who have a long-term idea of what they want to do, they keep collecting,” says René Meile, director of Galerie Urs Meile, which has a location in Beijing. He adds that younger collectors increasingly favour artists of their own generation. While established artists continued to attract buyers, collectors were taking longer to commit to expensive works. Meile attributed the shift partly to the departure of speculative buyers from the market.
Meanwhile this year’s art week brings an explosion of art events city-wide and boasts many newcomers both in terms of industry visitors and new spaces, including three new galleries. Hangzhou’s longtime fair regular Inna Art Space just opened Inna Front Room in the Lujiazui business district, making it the first significant gallery on the Pudong side of the river. Chen Yongwei, the former director of nonprofit Pond Society, has opened Shanghai Industry atop the Suhe House art cluster. PTT Space, a rising star gallery from Taipei, meanwhile this week opened an outpost at the M50 gallery complex.
“Even though the Chinese market is at an all-time low, Shanghai is still a vibrant international city with many art institutions,” says Robert Hsu, who founded PTT in 2020. “Considering the past art week, the number of openings parties and fairs is still through the roof, surpassing Seoul Art Week and coming close to Hong Kong Art Week.”
Hsu says he also has existing “base infrastructure” in the city with staff and relationships with local artists and collectors. “As a second generation gallerist, I feel we have to keep moving in this new era. The market, the business, the people have all changed. To survive, I have to step out of our comfort zone and explore.”
Along with the gallery, Hsu is part of the team organising the new boutique fair Art Fusion Canton in the southern Chinese city Guangzhou next month (3-7 December). In Shanghai, the popup fair Hang Over (11-15 November) is going strong in its second year. Moving from last year’s restaurant to an event space in a new lifestyle complex on Donghu Lu, it this year features 18 galleries including Tokyo’s Misako & Rosen, Seoul’s Cylinder along with Shanghai’s Antenna Space, Vanguard and Linseed, owned by Hang Over founder Zhuang Lingzhi.
The 13th edition of West Bund Art & Design (10–15 November) brought together 85 galleries, including Hauser & Wirth, Perrotin, Thaddaeus Ropac and White Cube. Meanwhile, the 14th Art021, hosting 111 galleries at the Shanghai Exhibition Centre, has introduced a new acquisition initiative with the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (Lacma), supported by Chinese collectors, aimed at bringing works by Asian and Asian diaspora artists into the museum’s collection.
At West Bund, Thaddaeus Ropac reports several opening-day sales, led by Megan Rooney’s That Sky (Atlas) (2026), sold for £400,000 to a Chinese foundation. Other transactions included a painting by Martha Jungwirth for €200,000, a Robert Longo work for $90,000 and a painting by Han Bing for €55,000, acquired by an Asian museum. A work by Joan Snyder was also sold to a Chinese museum.
Dawn Zhu, the gallery’s Asia director, praises the enthusiasm of collectors, noting that the gallery had made early sales to both institutions and private collections. “We are seeing collectors who have travelled from across South East Asia and even a few from Europe,” she says.
Hauser & Wirth also reports significant sales at West Bund, led by Louise Bourgeois’s bronze sculpture Point of Contact (1967–68, cast 2006), which sold for $450,000 to a museum in Kuala Lumpur. Other transactions include Lee Bul’s Perdu XXXIII (2020), sold for $260,000 to a private collection in China, and another Bourgeois work, Femme (2008), acquired by a Chinese private collector for $165,000. The gallery also reports the sale of George Condo’s Black and Red Composition (2026) for $200,000.
At Art021, Galerie Urs Meile reports sales of works by Xie Nanxing for approximately RMB 1.2m and Ju Ting for RMB 400,000, alongside works by younger artists Chen Zuo and Miao Miao priced between RMB 100,000 and RMB 150,000, and a smaller painting by Vietnamese artist Mai Ta for RMB 40,000.
Also at Art021, Shanghai-based gallery Bank reports strong early sales of Liang Hao’s works, priced 60,000 to 300,000 RMB, and of a large Jiang Cheng painting for over 500,000 RMB. The gallery reports that Lacma may acquire a video work made in 2000 by Los Angeles-based artist Patty Chang.
Despite the more subdued atmosphere, some galleries remain optimistic about the depth of China’s domestic market. Liang Xiao, a spokesperson for Perrotin, which has operated a Shanghai space since 2018, says that the slowdown had given collectors more time to select works they genuinely appreciate.
He suggests that the growth of new art fairs in Yokohama, Seoul and elsewhere would not fundamentally undermine Shanghai’s position, given the size of China’s domestic collector base. “Even after all these years, there are still many collectors we have yet to reach,” Liang says, adding that Shanghai remains an important entry point for collectors from across mainland China.
Hsu says the feedback for PTT Shanghai has been “quite positive” in the debut week, but “the market is not at its best.” Transactions have been slow, but included some successful placement of works with established collectors. “As the old saying goes, the gallery business is a marathon, not a sprint.”

The Philips Collection in Washington D.C has received its largest ever individual gift. The $10 million donation comes from the Beatriz and Graham Bolton Global Vision Fund. According to a press release, it will be used to “strengthen the Phillips’s international presence as a world-class art museum.” This will include exhibitions, loans, and international partnerships with not only other museums but also embassies and cultural organizations. The gift will also support the Education and Responsive Learning department and will endow the Beatriz and Graham Bolton Chief of Education and Responsive Learning. The museum’s education and community engagement gallery will be named the Peggy Bolton Community Gallery, in memory of Graham Bolton’s late mother. The Boltons have been patrons of the Phillips for years. They’ve previously supported exhibitions and programs like the Intersections installations by Los Carpinteros and exhibitions of work by Zilia Sánchez, Daniel Canogar, and Bernardí Roig. Beatriz Bolton joined the Phillips Board of Trustees in 2022 and chairs its Institutional Culture and Civic Responsibility Committee. “Graham and I are thrilled to support the Phillips’s mission of being a welcoming home for all, especially its ability to bring people together through the universal language of art,” said Beatriz Bolton in a press release. “We are inspired by how the Phillips makes art accessible and meaningful to people from all walks of life, including through exhibitions and programs like Creative Aging. We are proud to support an institution that harnesses the power of art to enrich lives in ways that are deeply personal and lasting.” “This exceptional gift from Beatriz and Graham represents intentional and personal philanthropy at its finest, grounded in a spirit of deep partnership and responsiveness to the museum’s ongoing work and future potential,” said Elizabeth Racheva, the institution’s Chief Advancement Officer. “Their tremendous generosity—as global citizens themselves—will elevate the museum’s impact and international profile for generations to come.”

https://taz.de/Regierungskrise-in-den-Ni.author: Tobias Müller
https://taz.de/Regierungskrise-in-den-Ni.text:
Regierungskrise in den Niederlanden: Offener Dissens von Anfang an
Die Suche nach den Ursachen für die aktuelle Regierungskrise in den Niederlanden führt zur Entstehungsgeschichte der Minderheitsregierung von Rob Jetten.
Die Ereignisse dieser Woche sind selbst im chronisch wechselhaften politischen Klima Den Haags außergewöhnlich. Zwei von drei Koalitionspartnern – D66 und CDA – verhandeln mit den zwei Oppositionsparteien Pro und Volt über Unterstützung für ein Steuerreformpaket. Mit ihnen will die dritte Partei VVD in der Regierungskoalition partout nicht zusammenarbeiten. Wohlgemerkt: Den Koalitionären war freigestellt worden, einzeln Gespräche zu führen, um zu einer Mehrheit zu gelangen.
Offenbar beschwerte sich die VVD über die erzielte Einigung. Sie sei reichlich spät informiert und so vor vollendete Tatsachen gestellt worden. Nach einem ganzen Tag hitziger Debatten stimmte sie daher am Donnerstagabend gegen das eigene Steuerpaket – ein einzigartiger Vorgang. Spätestens da hing die Regierung angezählt in den Seilen.
Einzigartig ist aber auch die Konstellation, die zu solchen Zerwürfnissen geführt hat: Sie geht zurück auf den Status der Minderheitsregierung, der mit 66 von 150 Parlamentssitzen strukturell mindestens zehn Mandate zum Regieren fehlen.
Die Wahlsiegerin D66 hätte am liebsten die progressiven Parteien PvdA und GroenLinks, die sich im Sommer zu Pro zusammenschlossen – mit ins Boot geholt. Für die VVD freilich war dies freilich ausgeschlossen – sie wäre gern mit der rechten JA21, wie man hierzulande sagt, in See gestochen. Das wiederum war für die D66 ausgeschlossen.
Versuch zu dritt
Aus Mangel an rechnerischen wie inhaltlichen Alternativen versuchte man es also zu dritt. Dabei zeichnete sich von Beginn an ab, dass anstatt einer Mehrheit just dieser ursprüngliche Dissens präsent sein würde bei der Suche nach Unterstützung aus der Opposition, auf die man fortan angewiesen war.
„Permanente formatie“, so bezeichnet man auf Niederländisch die Phase der Koalitionsgespräche“ – nannte Pro-Chef Jesse Klaver diesen Vorgang mehrfach, wohl wissend, dass seine Partei dabei eine zentrale Rolle spielen würde. „Über rechts oder über links?“, diese Frage wurde seit dem Antritt der Regierung Ende Februar zum geflügelten Wort in Den Haag.
Dabei schwingt mit, dass es die jeweilige Unterstützung auf dem Weg zu einer Mehrheit in beiden Fällen nicht für umsonst gab. Und so verharrte die Regierung Rob Jettens, im Herbst 2025 überraschender und umso strahlenderer Wahlsieger, in diesem Zustand begrenzter Manövrierfähigkeit.
Symbol der Hoffnung
Vor Jahresfrist war Jetten ein Symbol der Hoffnung, die tiefe Polarisierung in der niederländischen Gesellschaft und Politik nach 20 Jahren hartem Populismus überwinden zu können. Seinem Wahlspruch „es ist möglich“ hing gar eine Prise des Obama´schen „yes we can“ an. Mittlerweile steht seine programmatische Ankündigung, Gräben zu überwinden und die Menschen wieder zusammenzubringen, hilflos vor der Realität eines stark fragmentierten Parteienspektrum, das sich in einem Parlament mit 17 Fraktionen widerspiegelt.
Erschwerend hinzu kommt, dass die Machtverhältnisse im Senat gänzlich andere sind, was auch ein Ergebnis der volatilen, hektischen Wählerwanderungen der vergangenen Jahre ist, als Symptom vieler schnelllebiger Hypes um neue Parteien, die teils bald wieder abstürzten. Just in dieser Konstellation versuchten D66 und CDA durch einen Deal mit Pro, dort stärkste Fraktion, der Koalition eine Basis zu verschaffen.
Und dann wäre da noch ein letzter Punkt, der überall in Europa eine Rolle spielt: Das seit Monaten anhaltende zähe, lähmende Tauziehen in Den Haag steht auch für die Verteilungskonflikte, die sich in Zeiten wachsender sozialer Probleme und stetiger Mehrausgaben für Rüstung und Verteidigung rasant zuspitzen.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/guerre-en-.author: La rédaction
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/guerre-en-.text:
Les nouveaux bombardements qui ont visé la capitale ukrainienne, ce vendredi, dévoilent une volonté russe de plonger les habitants dans un hiver 2026 critique. Les coupures d’électricité, de communication et de chauffage se multiplient alors qu’un établissement médical a été touché.
À Kiev, un cinquième hiver se profile avec le quotidien d’une guerre qui s’éternise. La capitale ukrainienne vient d’essuyer un nouveau bombardement, ce vendredi, qui a touché un établissement médical. Il s’agit de l’Institut de traumatologie et d’orthopédie, situé dans l’arrondissement Chevtchenkivsky, en plein centre, à quelques mètres des ambassades du Danemark et de la Roumanie.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: The Midterms Were a Revolt Against ICE. Democrats Need to Remember That.
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Felipe de la Hoz
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The Midterms Were a Revolt Against ICE. Democrats Need to Remember That.
Voters made their disgust with Trump’s war on immigrants clear. Now, with the fanatical Stephen Miller given even more power, Democrats must take on the administration.
With the final votes being counted in the 2026 midterms, electoral contests have given way to the usual and infinitely more annoying postelection debate over what the results mean. Did the Democrats triumph purely because of anger at the high price of gas? Was it because Black voters rose up against the Trump administration’s efforts to disenfranchise them? Was it a nationwide repudiation of MAGA on economic and cultural fronts? Do the people want another FDR?
These discussions, fun as they are for commentators (I know, glass houses), rest on the shaky premise that an election in an ultra-diverse, vast country of over 340 million people electing politicians at every level of government can speak with anything like a unified voice. But the rush to form a consensus that voters are driven above all by one singular factor also tends to paper over a host of other significant factors. For instance, most of the postelection analysis so far seems to have largely glided past one of the most directly visible examples of Donald Trump’s authoritarian excesses: the broad crackdown on immigration, speech, and political organizing helmed by ICE. This is despite the fact that revulsion at the crackdown can probably help explain not only the complete reversal of Republicans’ 2024 gains among Latinos but also broader Democratic turnout across the board.
It would be a mistake not to see the ICE invasion of Minneapolis, and the killings of Alex Pretti and Renée Good, as an inflection point in the country’s political thinking—not only in terms of the attack on immigration itself but also as such an open and militarized display of the administration’s authoritarian designs that it could no longer be ignored. Conversely, the resistance to ICE also proved that the administration was not invincible and was vulnerable to bleeding public support—and led to the biggest revival of the movement to abolish ICE since Trump’s first term.
Trump himself was questioned on this by Ross Douthat, Bari Weiss’s latest smooth-brained acquisition at the shell of 60 Minutes, where he said he might have been “too tough” on immigration enforcement. This unsurprisingly appeared to be a manifestation of Trump’s reflex to just agree with whomever he’s in front of, as almost immediately afterward he named Stephen Miller, the architect of this barbaric effort, the new White House chief of staff—a move not unlike replacing the control rods in a nuclear reactor with just more plutonium to see what happens.
The thing about Trump is that he is intrinsically, fundamentally a racist and has been for his whole life—an attitude learned from his developer father, who was infamously named alongside Donald in a federal civil rights case for refusing to rent to Black New Yorkers. He is, however, a different type of racist than Miller. Trump is the prototypical white Queens uncle racist, the sort who latently believes that Black people are less intellectually capable and Mexicans are simple, good workers who are exploitable and expendable, but is ultimately happy to transact with anyone as long as they serve his direct material interests. Miller, on the other hand, is a blood-and-soil racist, a man whose every impulse and action is warped through the prism of his deep, ideological bigotry.
In making Miller the chief of staff, Trump is ensuring that the latter approach wins out, if only because a matchup between relative indifference and zealotry will almost always result in a victory for the zealot. Trump can spend the next two years keeping the grift spigot going and enriching himself while letting Miller et al. mind the store. He’s in such a hermetic information bubble that he almost certainly does not and could not grasp the volume of disgust at Miller’s crackdown, particularly since the media narrative is already downplaying its importance to this enormous electoral loss.
No matter what, it will be hard to dislodge Miller. Trump, over a decade in public life, has proved mainly that he is committed to certain overarching tenets—his enrichment, his vanity, petty grievance and retribution, social hierarchy—but otherwise completely erratic in decision-making and personnel decisions. Apart from his family, other people do not seem entirely real to him, so he can command absolute loyalty from wretched underlings but is always prepared to toss them by the wayside the moment he thinks it’s advantageous. He has already dumped several people involved with his unpopular immigration actions, including former DHS secretary and noted puppy slaughterer Kristi Noem and fun-size Nazi Greg Bovino, the one-time Border Patrol commander responsible for the aggressive occupations in cities like Chicago and Minneapolis.
Miller, though, has been a remarkably consistent presence by Trump’s side since his first campaign, far outlasting Miller’s own former boss Jeff Sessions, who spent about a year and a half as attorney general (a long tenure in Trumpworld, as it would turn out). He seems to have entered that rarefied inner circle status just below family (the Tiffany tier, if you will).
For his part, Miller, who, if nothing else, is a tactical operator, must realize that the time he has to see through his vision of a paramilitary-enforced white America is dwindling. There will be significant pressure for Democrats to at the very least launch inquiries into ICE’s conduct. There are rumors about growing support for Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen as Senate majority leader. If his name rings a bell, it might be because Van Hollen made headlines for traveling to El Salvador to demand to see his constituent Kilmar Ábrego García at the notorious CECOT gulag at a time when no one had seen him—or indeed the other dozens of men unlawfully sent there—alive since their rendition. A majority leader Van Hollen is not likely to forget about ICE.
Whatever guardrails still exist, Miller is liable to try to remove them completely and let the authoritarian train run unimpeded until Congress and the courts actually throw some obstacles on the tracks. He has at least the financial ability to do so, given the MAGA Congress’s mammoth appropriation for immigration enforcement just earlier this year. Yet we’re already seeing centrist pundits and party apparatchiks performing a sleight of hand, saying that the new majority must prioritize “kitchen-table” issues rather than accountability work—a prospect that will only get more ridiculous if and when ICE and its corollaries do not moderate, and perhaps just get more sadistic. As with the other questions of accountability, corruption, and weaponization of government, it should be easy to make the case not just that they are just as needed as economic justice but are inextricably tied together with it.
I don’t think that the millions of voters that handed Democrats historic victories will need much convincing that the $70 billion handed to ICE and CBP—as the Iran War was in its fourth month and after the killings of Good and Pretti—could be better used elsewhere, or that the administration’s current enforcement posture has torpedoed industries from agriculture to construction to biotech, imposing long-term costs on the American economy writ large. Not that the argument has to or should be purely an economic one; there was true, tangible, national rejection of the administration’s targeting of longtime residents and contempt for constitutional principles and basic decency. Articles in the vein of “I supported Trump’s deportation efforts, and then my wife was detained” have become so common as to basically be a trope now.
Dragging DHS officials from the secretary down before congressional committees; having a Church Committee–style dedicated investigative team uncovering the extent, mechanics, and executors of DHS abuses; referring some to criminal prosecution or civil penalties, including the prospect of impeachment; and both clawing back DHS funding and putting some stricter limits on the spending that still exists (while broaching the conversation of full abolition) are not only moral and constitutional imperatives but at this point likely political slam dunks.
The post-2024 pundit consensus that the slim Trump victory had definitively indicated a popular appetite for mass and indiscriminate deportation and the unrestrained surveillance and enforcement apparatus to support it has been proved pretty conclusively wrong. Even those voters that ostensibly did support it were backing a version of it that existed mainly in their own imaginations. As the election showed, many of them have come to detest or at the very least disavow the operations in practice.
Miller, like all dogmatists, will stop only when he’s stopped. As they settle into power, the new Democratic majorities must understand this as part of their mandate.
