https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120387.text:
- Kommentare
- Bundeshaushalt
Die gute alte Hintertür
Klar, zugunsten der Aufrüstung kürzt die Regierung den Sozialetat. So manche Maßnahmen gegen Umverteilung fallen aber erst auf den zweiten Blick auf.
Was ist gesellschaftlich akzeptabel, wo zieht die Bundesregierung lieber die Samthandschuhe an? Geradeheraus streicht sie im neuen Haushalt den Sofortzuschlag für Kinder von Asylsuchenden. Das sind 25 Euro im Monat – für Menschen, die bereits unter dem menschenwürdigen Existenzminimum leben müssen, macht das einen Unterschied. Ganz nach dem Motto »Mit ihnen kann man es schon machen« geht Schwarz-Rot hier in die Offensive.
Bei anderen armen Personen geht die Regierung etwas vorsichtiger vor. Zwar kürzt sie die Grundsicherung nicht, friert den Regelsatz aber bis Mitte 2028 ein. Seit Januar 2024 gab es keine Erhöhung. Lebenshaltungskosten steigen jedoch weiter. Personen in der Grundsicherung können sich schon jetzt mit dem gleichen Geld weniger leisten als vor zwei Jahren, haben also auch so weniger zum Leben.
Noch mehr um die Ecke denken muss man mit Blick auf die Rente. Im Änderungsantrag zum Haushalt legte die Bundesregierung drastische Kürzungen des Zuschusses zur gesetzlichen Rentenversicherung für Leistungen wie die Mütterrente vor. Satte drei Milliarden niedriger soll der Erhöhungsbetrag sein. Damit kürzt die Regierung dreimal so viel wie vor dem Haushaltsbeschluss verlautbart.
Ein weiterer Versuch, hintenrum zu sparen. Zwar sinken so nicht automatisch die Renten. Ein geringerer Zuschuss kann jedoch nach der Rentenformel spätere Erhöhungen dämpfen. Die Kürzung verschärft außerdem die Lage der Kassen, was wiederum dazu führen kann, dass die Beiträge steigen. Tja.
Zusammengefasst bedeutet das alles: weniger Umverteilung, auf ganzer Linie. Flott durchgewunken durch die gute alte Hintertür.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/labor-u.title: It’s Time for Labor to Join the Fight Against Data Centers and Tech Oligarchy
https://inthesetimes.com/article/labor-u.author: Stephen Lerner
https://inthesetimes.com/article/labor-u.text:
It’s Time for Labor to Join the Fight Against Data Centers and Tech Oligarchy
There’s no room for dithering—the U.S. labor movement has to choose now whether to be on the right side of history.
Stephen Lerner
We just experienced a once-in-a-generation political earthquake as President Donald Trump’s authoritarian administration and the broader Republican Party were dealt massive defeats at the polls, even in once solidly red states like Texas. Over the course of the midterm election season, data centers became a key issue, and the growing revolt against them and their Big Tech owners played a key role in Democrats’ “bluenami.” Yet as opposition to data center construction is beginning to reshape politics, giving rise to one of the most sweeping social movements of our time, the U.S. labor movement is currently split on the issue. For unions, incoherence around this issue could be toxic.
I have been an organizer in the labor movement since I dropped out of high school to join the United Farm Workers union on the grape and lettuce boycott in 1974. Over the past 50 years, I’ve lived through numerous moments forecasted as the labor movement’s decline or revival. With the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) reorganizing wealth, power, and work on an unprecedented scale, none compare to the moment we’re currently living through.
Across all of my organizing — from supporting a year-long strike for the International Ladies’ Garment Workers’ Union in the South to the Justice for Janitors (JFJ) campaign that organized more than 100,000 workers in the 1980s and 90s — one lesson has held true: unions grow when they are part of something larger than themselves. Movements for justice — whether it be economic, racial, or immigrant rights — give organizing what it needs most: hope, unity, and a vision of a world we can win. Workers join unions for more than a raise. They join to realize aspirations for justice and dignity.
Today, a massive buildout of data centers and a planned string of IPOs inflating the AI bubble are further concentrating wealth and power among a handful of Silicon Valley billionaires who back President Trump, while soaring costs of living, surveillance, and job insecurity weigh on the rest of us. Yet as we face these existential threats to workers, labor, democracy — and, as some experts and safety researchers warn, humanity itself — the labor movement is divided over whether to oppose the forces driving the coming upheaval when the AI bubble bursts.
Some unions have stayed silent on the issue, despite growing backlash against data centers and the tech oligarchy. At the June AFL-CIO convention, delegates approved a resolution that acknowledged the harms and threats to workers posed by AI, while maintaining that “responsible data center growth” was possible if done with union labor.
Seduced by the promise of high-wage union construction jobs, other building trades leaders have championed data centers as the best opportunity for blue collar workers in decades. In a New York Times op-ed titled “Electrical Workers Love Data Centers. You Should Too.,” Don Slaiman, community relations director of IBEW Local 26 — which represents electrical workers in the Washington, D.C. area — argued that data centers are beneficial in their provision of good union construction jobs, calling them the equivalent of the Roman “aqueducts of our era.” That promise may turn out to be a dangerous mirage.
The record of trade union density also informs the current moment. At the end of World War II, 80% of construction workers in the United States were unionized, most under master contracts. Only 11% of building trades workers are unionized now. The issue isn’t a shortage in construction jobs — it’s a shortage in unionized construction jobs. While the sector has grown by almost 7 million jobs since the end of World War II, union membership has continued to hover around just 1 million.
As density has declined, Project Labor Agreements (PLAs) have replaced master agreements, causing unions to focus on staffing the highest paying jobs covered by PLAs. The jobs — and therefore membership density — ride the waves of economic recession and prosperity. They lose union members when union work dries up and regain fewer when work picks back up. The migration of the limited number of unionized workers to the highest-paying PLA-covered jobs allows formerly unionized work to go non-union.
In the 1970s and 80s, construction of the Washington, D.C., Metro system absorbed the labor of unionized trades workers and accelerated the deunionization of non-mega-project construction. The building trades face the same danger with the data center buildout: a short-term boost leading to a long-term bust.
History suggests that it would instead be wiser for labor to make common cause with the anti-data center movement. Labor now faces a choice that may well decide its fate for the foreseeable future: to support one of the biggest and most broadly based popular movements in recent history — the fight against data centers and the tech oligarchs funding their development — or remain at odds with it. A recent poll found nearly two-thirds of Americans oppose data center development in their communities. In 10 states across the country this election, voters endorsed restrictions on data centers or opposed their development in 40 out of 41 ballot measures.
Protests against data centers have spread like wildfire over the last two years. Over 340 protests erupted across 42 states since January 2025, and some 220 new grassroots anti-data center organizations emerged within the span of only three months in 2026. That activism helped fuel the Democrats’ victories in Texas, Georgia and Ohio, three of the top six most data-center-heavy states. Candidates like Texas Gov.elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat who beat a three-term incumbent, and U.S. Rep.-elect William Lawrence, who faced down the most expensive House race in the country this cycle, made opposition to data center construction core planks of their campaigns. 
By recognizing and joining hands with this movement, and standing together against the tech oligarchs who seek to define our future, labor can set the stage for its revival. By failing to do so, or, worse yet, allying with pro-data center forces against this metastasizing grassroots movement, labor risks accelerating its decline into irrelevance.
After all, labor’s great surges in membership, density, and power have come when it was in sync with broader social movements. In the 1930s, the children of sharecroppers and immigrants flocked into industrial unions because the Congress of Industrial Organizations (CIO) was bound up with the New Deal and its promise of dignity for workers. In the 1960s and 70s, workers inspired by the civil rights and women’s movements flooded into public sector unions. Those gains stabilized overall membership even as the private sector sank to its current 6%, down from a postwar peak of 35% overall. Nor is this pattern confined to the United States. Abroad, labor movements in Brazil, South Korea, and South Africa found that opposing authoritarianism sparked surging growth.
I’ve seen up-close how this kind of dynamic can play out. The success of the Justice for Janitors (JFJ) campaign we launched in the 1980s can be seen only in the context of the larger movement for liberation that thousands of immigrant workers rallied behind. Hundreds of thousands of janitors galvanized after the Los Angeles Police Department viciously attacked immigrant janitors who were striking to improve working conditions in Century City in June of 1990. Many attribute the movement’s success to its strong organizing in immigrant communities. Immigrant workers were fighting not only for their rights on the job, but for their dignity as human beings. JFJ was carried forward on the shoulders of communities that demanded to be seen.
The same dynamic played out earlier this year when the Trump administration sent armed immigration enforcement agents into Minneapolis to terrorize neighborhoods as part of its mass deportation plans. When unions joined in coalition with community organizations to resist, a movement culture started to coalesce. This model offers an alternative vision of how labor can approach the growing fight against AI data centers, and the tech oligarchy. Such deep alliance-building sets the table for mass organizing and growth through joining up with broader resistance.
I have seen what happens when workers feel like they’re part of something larger, and I have watched what happens when unions retreat to protect what they have. The first builds power, the second depletes numbers.
After this resounding election, we have now entered a “which side of history are you on” moment, one more consequential than any I’ve seen in the last 50 years. It is the labor movement’s task to act decisively in order to make sure it’s on the right side. Such an opportunity will not soon come again. 
Thank you for reading this story. At a time when corporate media is dominating the web and our airwaves, independent journalism is more important than ever, and that’s what we provide at In These Times. We offer some of the best reporting, investigations and analysis on the growing movements for justice in the U.S.—and our work is firmly pro-labor and anti-fascist. To continue producing it, we need your support.
If you believe in the power of an independent press, please make a donation to In These Times today. By becoming a sustaining member, you can ensure that our work reaches even more readers.
And if you become a sustainer right now, you'll get a free year-long print subscription and a special subscribers-only print from artist Molly Crabapple.
Thank you.
Stephen Lerner is the architect of the Justice for Janitors campaign. Lerner is a labor and community organizer and helped found the Bargaining for Common Good network.

https://gothamist.com/news/former-nyc-ja.title: Former NYC jails chief testifies about Adams adviser's push to hire friend’s daughter
https://gothamist.com/news/former-nyc-ja.author: Samantha Max
https://gothamist.com/news/former-nyc-ja.text:
When Eric Ulrich asked then-Department of Correction Commissioner Louis Molina to consider hiring his friend’s daughter for an open position in February 2022, Molina said he set up a meeting that same week.
Ulrich, then a senior adviser to Mayor Eric Adams, called Molina to recommend the daughter of his friend Michael Mazzio, according to a recording played in court on Friday. By the end of Molina’s one-on-one “exploratory conversation” with the recent college graduate, Mazzio’s daughter had a conditional job offer for an entry-level analyst position.
“She had the job if she wanted it,” Molina testified in court Friday.
Prosecutors have since accused Mazzio of bribing Ulrich with premium season tickets to the New York Mets in exchange for favors, including helping to secure the job for his daughter. A trial is ongoing in Manhattan against both men, who have pleaded not guilty.
Phone calls played in Manhattan court on Friday reveal new details about how Ulrich convinced Molina to interview Mazzio’s daughter and followed up to ensure the hiring process was moving along.
“Mazzio’s the priority,” Ulrich said in a recorded phone call played in court on Friday.
“You got it,” Molina replied.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.title: Lightsaber Brandished by Darth Vader Auctioned for $4.9 M., Breaking Record for Star Wars Sales
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.author: Andy Battaglia
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.text:
A lightsaber wielded by none other than Darth Vader sold for $4.875 million in a Heritage Auctions sale, breaking the record for Star Wars–related memorabilia.
The treasure was used in Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back (1980) and Star Wars: Return of the Jedi (1983), and also holds the special distinction of having been the weapon central to the former’s famous “I am your father” scene, in which Luke Skywalker learns some surprising news from the figure who had long been his nemesis.
Heritage reported that the sale exceeded that of “Luke Skywalker’s lightsaber and severed hand effects rig” last year (for $3.75 million) and a poster painting for Star Wars: Episode IV—A New Hope in 2025 (for $3.875 million).
About the sale of the lightsaber, one of 27 offered up by Heritage, Brian Chanes, the auction house’s senior director of Hollywood and entertainment, told Los Angeles’s ABC7 Eyewitness News, “I’ve been doing this for 35 years and I’ve never seen a compilation of screen-used lightsabers like this; you know, from the original franchise to the sequels.” He continued: “It’s the one on the set. It’s from the most iconic sequence of the entire franchise. From a memorabilia standpoint this is like the holy grail.”
	About sales of the kind in general, Chanes added, “I always tell people that memorabilia, the m-e-m portion is your memories, what you remember when you first saw the first Star Wars film. It basically takes you to the happy place when you first saw it, and it’s a feel-good thing!”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Milton Leite se torna réu por suspeita de ligação com o PCC
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Odair Braz
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A Justiça de São Paulo acatou denúncia do Ministério Público e tornou Milton Leite e mais 13 pessoas réus por suspeita de ligação com a facção criminosa Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC). Leite é ex-vereador e ex-presidente da Câmara Municipal de São Paulo e está preso.
O político filiado ao partido União Brasil foi para a cadeia em setembro, após uma operação da Polícia Civil junto com o Ministério Público que investigava a atuação do PCC no transporte coletivo paulistano.
Com a decisão da Justiça tornada pública na quinta-feira (12), Leite teve a prisão temporária convertida em preventiva. Outros 11 denunciados também tiveram prisões preventivas decretadas.
No documento que torna Leite réu, a denúncia informa que ele e todo o grupo de investigados “agiram sob a orientação de lideranças da organização criminosa, como Antônio José Muller Junior, vulgo ‘Granada’, e Marlon José de Souza Rosa, vulgo ‘MR’ e ‘Murilo’, denunciado em fase anterior desta investigação. Os denunciados atuaram para infiltrar e perpetuar a facção na exploração do transporte público, em procedimentos licitatórios e no poder público, bem como para movimentar e ocultar recursos da organização criminosa”.
Influência
Sobre Milton Leite, especificamente, o documento diz que o ex-presidente da Câmara Municipal de SP “promoveu interesses da organização criminosa, valendo-se de sua expressiva influência política e da condição de proprietário de fato da concessionária Transwolff Transportes e Turismo Ltda., empresa sabidamente vinculada à facção criminosa e destinatária de aportes ilícitos, exercendo atos de gestão, controle e ingerência em favor da permanência e favorecimento do grupo criminoso no sistema de transporte coletivo urbano da capital paulista”.
A decisão ainda aponta que Leite era informado sobre a rotina e os negócios da concessionária Transwolff Transportes por meio de “vídeos e informações sobre a implantação dos ônibus elétricos, o fornecimento de carregadores pela Enel, o treinamento de técnicos e o Projeto Aquático, explorado pelo grupo econômico na região do Bororé”.
Após a decisão da Justiça, os réus têm agora o prazo de dez dias para apresentar a defesa às acusações. Milton Leite está preso no Centro de Detenção Provisória II de Guarulhos, na Grande São Paulo.
A Agência Brasil tentou contato com a defesa de Milton Leite e não obteve retorno até a publicação deste texto.

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: I’m a semi-competitive shopper. These are my 12 favorite finds for someone who has everything
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Angela Serratore
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
The “has everything” person is, in some ways, the easiest person on your list to shop for: you know they like lip balm or bath salts or interesting spices, so why not get them more of those things and be done with it? Speaking as both a “has everything” person and a semi-competitive shopper, what I’m looking to get and give in this category is anything that solves a problem I didn’t know I had, anything that makes the most mundane parts of my day a little more special and anything that makes me laugh. I asked friends, relatives and experts to weigh in, and together we came up with 17 gifts that do all of those things and then some.
- Visit our ultimate holiday gift guide for more gift guides and holiday shopping ideas for everyone on your list.
KEVA Bonjour Mahjong Art Pop and Gallery Tray
Ali Linkov, owner of Foxy Red boutique in Lambertville, New Jersey, stocks an eclectic mix of housewares that feel of-the-moment without veering into “too obvious” territory. Right now, that means a carefully-curated assortment of mahjong-related pieces, and for the friend who’s made mahjong their entire personality, this colorful design by artist Jessi Raulet is a winning gift. Available as an interchangeable insert for KEVA’s gallery trays, it can brighten up game night or hang on the wall afterward.
Retrospekt Snoopy’s Beagle Scouts CP-81 Cassette Player
Speaking of things that feel of-the-moment and also, somehow, completely timeless, this Snoopy-themed portable cassette player is the kind of thing 80- and eight-year-olds will be equally delighted by (and if anyone shopping for me is reading this, I’d be pretty excited to get this myself). Make 2027 the year of physical media and throw in a few cassette tapes to get their collection started.
Ban.do Game Night! Peg Game
For the friend who wants to do more hanging out and less scrolling phones, Drew Zandonella-Stannard, a writer and creative, suggests this colorful peg game from Ban.do, which doubles as a cheerful coffee-table accessory, making it an ideal gift for design-conscious friends who love a little friendly competition. It’s also a clever housewarming party present, since it also makes for an instant activity.
Nostalgia 3-Tier Party Fountain
Speaking of party-themed gifts: “A friend is having a divorce party and I bought her this,” said Zandonella-Stannard. A recent divorcee isn’t the only person who would love this – anyone who prides themselves on being a good host will also welcome this into their party repertoire.
Glasshouse Fragrances Kyoto in Bloom Candle and Spinning Carousel
It is a truth universally acknowledged that every gift guide must have a candle on it – I don’t make the rules, but I do follow them! Even devoted candle collectors probably don’t own one that moves. This Glasshouse Fragrances set features a gold carousel that spins above the flame, and has a floral fragrance with notes of camellia, lotus, amber and sandalwood. This is the kind of gift I’d give to an aspiring fancy person – someone who wants to dip their toes into being indulgent, one high-end candle at a time.
John Derian Flowers Coloring Book
This floral-themed collection brings John Derian’s distinctive vintage-inspired aesthetic to a wonderfully low-stakes creative activity. Pair it with a beautiful set of colored pencils for the friend who doesn’t have the attention span for needlepoint.
Olipop Crisp Apple Soda
I’m something of a beverage expert – self-proclaimed, I haven’t gone to beverage school or anything. Of all the drinks I’ve tried over the last 12 months, nothing has come close to the flavor of this soda (it’s healthy!) that somehow perfectly captures the essence of Martinelli’s Sparkling Apple Cider, but with prebiotics. Stick a red bow on the box and bring these to every party you’re invited to from now until Valentine’s Day.
Line Phono Magic Audio Brush for Records and Gear
Over the last several years more and more corners of my living room have been devoted to record storage – I wasn’t kidding about physical media! My husband, the librarian and custodian of our collection, pulled out this brush one day and our LPs have been dust-free ever since. Its approximately 100,000 soft synthetic bristles remove debris from records, turntables and audio equipment, making for a smoother listening experience.
Fishs Eddy Butter Stick Butter Dish
Has anyone else noticed that everything is butter now? Seriously: socks, hair clips, stuffed animals – they’re all shaped like butter, probably because of a TikTok trend I am too old to know about. That’s why I’m tickled by this butter dish from gift-guide standby Fishs Eddy, who excels at crafting kitchen accessories that take themselves just seriously enough.
Gammarelli Mid-calf Socks
Another gift-guide staple? Socks, of course! There are many directions you could go in here, but as they say, all roads lead to Rome, so I picked the fine lisle variety made by Gammarelli, also known as the place where the Pope gets his socks.
Marvis Cinnamon Mint Toothpaste
As the proprietress of a popular shop in a Hallmark-y town, Linkov is no stranger to people rushing in to search for last-minute stocking stuffers, and for that there’s nothing better than a tube of Marvis’s Cinnamon Mint toothpaste. Yes, toothpaste is not the most obvious gift, but that is precisely the appeal, and this one comes with a beautifully retro tube that makes an everyday routine feel surprisingly luxurious. At about $12, it’s an affordable treat for someone who appreciates a little indulgence first thing in the morning.
Haflinger Roots Slippers
Slippers might seem like an uninspired gift until you’ve tried a really good pair. These Haflinger Roots slippers offer the kind of cozy comfort that makes staying home feel like an occasion. Their understated design – those sweet embroidered vegetables! – will put a smile on the face of anyone who can’t wait to get back into the garden as soon as the frost melts.
Serrano Shoulder Ham by Fermín
The best part of any historic house or castle tour is getting to visit the kitchens--there’s always a huge fireplace, gleaming copper kettles, and an array of meats hanging from the ceiling, to give you a sense of what it was like to be rich in Ye Olden Times. This ham has a similar vibe, and it ensures your recipient will always have an easy snack on hand!
Kitsch Satin Sleep Scrunchies
Modern life is hard enough these days--no one has time to be carefully combing knots out of tangled hair! Enter these silky-smooth scrunchies, which somehow prevent nighttime knots from forming for even the most restless sleepers. I’d put these in a stocking, and also keep a pack on hand for the friend who “just couldn’t resist” getting you a little something even though you’d already said this was a no-gifts year.
The Six Bells Cloved Orange Garland
For the grown-up American Girl doll on your list, who has always wanted to make her own pomander balls but never found the time.
Harris Tweed Hip Flask Keyring
For the Scotch aficionado (or Outlander superfan), this cheeky keyring flask holds a wee nip of whatever drink you like, and the tweed wrapping is hand-woven in the Outer Hebrides.
Real Accordion for Kids
As a DINK, I am always on the hunt for gifts that will delight the children of my friends while also annoying said friends just a little bit. This accordion is a noise-maker for sure, but it’s also screen-free, so everyone wins!

https://hyperallergic.com/the-alchemical.title: The Alchemical Possibilities of an Artist-Poet Collaboration
https://hyperallergic.com/the-alchemical.author: Phillip Pyle
https://hyperallergic.com/the-alchemical.text:
In 1982, Puerto Rican artist Papo Colo installed a book-shaped sculpture in the courtyard of El Museo del Barrio in Harlem. Commissioned as part of David Hammons’s Art in the Park program, it unfurled like an accordion across a series of 8-by-4-foot plywood panels co-authored by nearly 40 invited New York artists and poets. Four decades later, seven of those panels form the basis of Octopus and Others, an exhibition that addresses the porous boundary between the word and the image within the more experimental scenes of production from the ‘80s through today.
The first panel in the exhibition is by Colo himself and gestures toward the alchemical, even transcendent possibilities unleashed through the collaboration of artists and poets across distances, languages, and generations. “English Spanish $ Spanglish,” Colo scribbles in white paint against the black-coated plywood. “Vivas poetas individuales X-formed by Colo’s ceremony into collective.”

New Turkey-Qatar pact pledges joint stance against external attacks
Turkey and Qatar have pledged a unified stance against any external armed attack on either country, according to a joint statement issued after they signed the defence agreement.
The statement said the pact aims to strengthen collective defence and promote regional security.
Under it, the two countries will consult on threats to their security, regional and global security issues, and defence policy.
They will also expand cooperation through joint military exercises, defence industry projects and personnel training exchanges.
The statement added that the agreement reflects both countries’ commitment to safeguarding their sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as their shared vision of a more secure and stable regional order.
The two sides also said they were ready to pursue energy cooperation, particularly in liquefied natural gas trade.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Paraguay’s ex-president Pena faces new charge over Ueno bank collapse
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Paraguay’s ex-president Pena faces new charge over Ueno bank collapse
The criminal association charge over his alleged role in the collapse of the bank comes a week after his removal.
Paraguayan prosecutors have charged former president Santiago Pena with criminal association over his alleged role in the collapse of the digital bank Ueno, a week after Congress removed him from office.
The prosecutor’s office announced the new charge on Friday, adding to the breach of trust and self-dealing charges already facing Pena, who is being held in pretrial detention at a military facility.
The 47-year-old former leader is accused of using his position to direct millions in government funds to Ueno and concealing or downplaying its financial troubles, despite warnings of risky lending practices, while having financial ties to the bank.
He denies all charges.
Pena, who entered office in 2023, held a stake in the bank’s holding company until last year.
On Thursday, investigators raided his official residence in the capital, Asuncion. The prosecutor’s office said agents from the economic crimes unit were extracting data and gathering relevant information for the investigation.
Last week, Pena tried to step down as president, but Congress rejected his resignation, instead removing him from office through impeachment. Pena was arrested shortly after his removal.
The collapse of Ueno left customers locked out of their accounts, prompting huge protests across the country as thousands demanded accountability and their money back.
Prosecutors had been looking for missing funds and said on Friday that assets had been located abroad, although they did not specify in which countries. They had previously asked the United States, Luxembourg and Argentina for help locating the missing money.
“The necessary steps are under way to request that they be frozen,” prosecutor Francisco Cabrera told reporters.
Three former central bank officials were also arrested on Friday, accused of having known about Ueno’s issues since late last year.
The bank, which held more than $800m in public funds, grew quickly under Pena’s presidency from a financial technology company into a large firm handling state pensions and the accounts of several government entities.
The credit ratings agency Fitch has placed Paraguay’s sovereign rating on watch for a possible downgrade, which would make it more expensive for the government to borrow money.
On Thursday, the Central Bank said it had returned savings to more than 1.8 million people who had deposited money at the bank.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Museum heists on the rise: are new criminal markets, motives and tactics evolving?
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Riah Pryor
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Europol’s warning that museum thefts are becoming more violent and frequent could hardly have been better timed.
Published on 24 August, its report, Changing Tactics, Changing Targets: The Evolving Nature of Museum Heists, was followed within days by a string of high-profile thefts. On 27 August thieves stole a “priceless” Bronze Age hoard from Spain’s Museum of Villena; the same day a robbery at Vienna’s Museum of Applied Arts netted a diamond necklace worth several million euros. On 8 September thieves broke into the Musée Renoir on the French Riviera, with two works by the artist still missing.
There are plenty of regulations. The real problem is the lack of effective enforcement
“We have observed a clear and steep increase in the number of museum robbery cases since around 2022/2023,” says Jean-Yves Goriou, the head of the EU Organised Crime Unit, within Europol’s European Serious and Organised Crime Centre (ESOCC). Precious metals and stones, as well as Chinese cultural artefacts are identified in the report as increasingly popular targets, a trend which the report argues can be attributed to the objects’ high financial value.
“Some buyers in China will bid on these objects—sometimes to astronomical levels—but when they cannot acquire them legitimately, there appears to be a market for stolen Chinese treasures,” says Christopher Marinello, the founder and chief executive of Art Recovery International. He disagrees however, with the report’s claim that they “are likely to be easily sold on the art market”, arguing that “there are plenty of regulations on the books, many of which place significant burdens on honest dealers. The real problem, in my view, is the lack of effective enforcement of those regulations.”
Louvre’s €88m loss
The concentration and visibility of attacks, particularly against museums holding exceptionally valuable jewellery and precious metals, certainly feels prominent on the public agenda—boosted perhaps by the recent anniversary of the 2025 heist of €88m worth of jewels from the Musée du Louvre in Paris.
However, given that many museum thefts have historically remained unreported—often due to embarrassment or to prevent highlighting security vulnerabilities—“the lack of substantial consistent data has long made it a challenge to establish a workable sample size”, says Julian Radcliffe, the director of the Art Loss Register.
“In the sense of volume of crimes [against museums], there’s not been a change,” says Robert Read, the head of art and private clients at Hiscox insurance. He adds that around 50% of insurance claims continue to stem from accidental damage but adds that there does appear to be a shifting set of motivations at play. “Whereas financial value has long been understood as the key driver of such crimes, there is a sense that items could be being stolen to order, used as collateral, or even just to embarrass public institutions or governments,” he says.
Europol’s research describes a shift from the “traditional trafficker” towards an “emerging aggressor”. The former is characterised as a specialist, non-violent offender operating within a structured criminal network focused on cultural property. The latter is an ad hoc and decentralised perpetrator, prepared to use high-risk violence and operate across criminal markets, rather than concentrating exclusively on cultural property.
Organised networks
“A lot of these trends [in the Europol report] are not new, but they’re arguably occurring on a more pronounced or regular scale,” says Julian Radcliffe.
Certainly, the possibility of items being stolen to order by organised networks and with an eye on art market trends (notably the surge in demand for Chinese antiquities) has drifted in and out of public debate over museum thefts before. In 2016, for example, members of an organised gang were jailed for £57m worth of Chinese and rhino horn thefts from several UK museums and auction houses. Similarly, there is established understanding that the illicit trade in antiquities can involve networks spanning multiple types of criminality.

The Whitney Museum of Art has deaccessioned Willem de Kooning’s Yellow River and put it up for sale at Christie’s 20th-century evening auction on November 17. The 1958 painting is estimated to sell for $12 million to $18 million.
The sale is intended to support future acquisitions, Artnet reports, and follows the museum’s rare move in 2023 to deaccession seven works from its collection, including a major painting, Cobb’s Barns, South Truro (1930–33), by Edward Hopper. At the time, the Whitney justified the sale in part by stating that the works were “duplicative within the collection.” It’s not clear how the museum arrived at the decision to part with the de Kooning.
David M. Solinger, who became a trustee of the Whitney in 1961, purchased the painting from Sidney Janis Gallery in 1959, where it was on view in a hotly anticipated solo show of de Kooning’s canvases and works on paper. Nineteen had sold by noon of the opening day. These works marked a critical moment in de Kooning’s development, when he began painting monumental, gestural compositions that the editor and curator Thomas B. Hess dubbed de Kooning’s “abstract parkway landscapes.”
Fairfield Porter wrote of this period in de Kooning’s career, “It is as though his painting reached a different level of consciousness than painting that refers to a theory of aesthetics.”
Solinger’s widow, Betty Ann Besch Solinger, gave Yellow River to the museum as a gift in 2023. Christie’s lot essay includes an anecdote from Frank Robinson, former director of Cornell University’s Herbert F. Johnson Museum of Art, that the painting hung for a time at the foot of Solinger’s bed so that it was the first thing he saw upon waking.

https://taz.de/Einigung-ueber-den-Bundes.title: Einigung über den Bundeshaushalt 2027: Die richtigen Verteilungskämpfe stehen erst noch bevor
https://taz.de/Einigung-ueber-den-Bundes.author: Anna Lehmann
https://taz.de/Einigung-ueber-den-Bundes.text:
Einigung über den Bundeshaushalt 2027 : Die richtigen Verteilungskämpfe stehen erst noch bevor
Nach der Einigung im Haushaltsausschuss steht der Bundesetat für das kommende Jahr. Aber die Lücken werden in Zukunft nur größer.
D ie Stromsteuer elektrisiert Deutschland: Wird sie gesenkt oder nicht? Zweimal haben der Kanzler und die schwarz-rote Koalition bereits eine Senkung auch für Privathaushalte und kleine Unternehmen versprochen – zweimal haben sie dieses Versprechen gebrochen. Selbst wenn die Menschen die Entlastung am Ende kaum spüren würden – es geht um 6 bis 8 Euro pro Monat – der Schaden ist groß. Jedes Kind weiß: „Wer zweimal lügt, dem glaubt man nicht.“
Dabei dürfte es doch gar nicht so schwierig sein, die nötigen 5 Milliarden Euro in einem 560- Milliarden-Haushalt aufzutreiben, oder? Dass es in den Haushaltsverhandlungen bislang nicht gelungen ist, die fehlenden Milliarden zu finden, zeigt, wie klein die Spielräume in Wirklichkeit sind und wie groß die Verteilungskämpfe werden. Die Stromsteuer ist ein Menetekel für kommende Auseinandersetzungen.
Denn die Lücken, die in den nächsten Jahren im Staatssäckel klaffen, werden immer größer. Darauf wies in dieser Woche auch der Sachverständigenrat Wirtschaft, die sogenannten Wirtschaftsweisen, hin. Sie sehen einen „Handlungsbedarf von historischem Ausmaß“.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Ein Grund dafür ist, dass Deutschland und Europa sich selbst um ihre Sicherheit kümmern müssen. Noch finanziert Deutschland seine wachsenden Verteidigungsausgaben – im nächsten Jahr sind es knapp 140 Milliarden Euro – zu einem guten Teil durch Schulden. Die Wirtschaftsweisen haben nun empfohlen, die Kreditaufnahme zu reduzieren, was darauf hinausläuft, dass entweder die Einnahmen anders verteilt – also irgendwo gekürzt werden muss – oder zusätzliche Steuern erhoben werden. Wahrscheinlich sogar beides, das heißt, uns erwarten perspektivisch keine Entlastungen, sondern vielmehr zusätzliche Belastungen.
Solidarität in Deutschland anders organisieren
Längst denkt man in der Koalition über eine Erhöhung der Mehrwertsteuer nach. Wenn die um 2 Prozentpunkte steigt, hätte der Staat auf einen Schlag 32 Milliarden Euro mehr. Ein schönes Polster. Doch wenn die Menschen dann mehr für Butter und Brot, Klamotten und Benzin ausgeben müssen, wird auch die Frage lauter werden: Können wir uns die Unterstützung für die Ukraine noch leisten, seit 2022 immerhin 100 Milliarden Euro?
Wir können und wir müssen, aber das zu begründen, wird schwieriger. Solidarität für die Ukraine zu garantieren und in die eigene Sicherheit zu investieren, wird nur gelingen, wenn Solidarität in Deutschland insgesamt anders organisiert wird. Hochvermögende müssen endlich wieder besteuert werden und Topverdiener:innen einen größeren Beitrag leisten.
Die Union will beides um jeden Preis verhindern und pocht auf eine Senkung der Sozialausgaben. Auch wenn sie damit durchkäme, allein die Bedürftigen zu schröpfen, wird nicht reichen. Selbst die Wirtschaftsweisen halten eine weitere Erhöhung der Reichensteuer für denkbar. Wenn immer nur die ärmere Hälfte der Gesellschaft draufzahlt, kippt nicht nur der Haushalt, sondern auch die Stimmung.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Trump and Vance Are Using War to Enrich Their Cronies
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jeet Heer
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Trump and Vance Are Using War to Enrich Their Cronies
A new report shows how the pair is robbing Venezuela blind on behalf of one of their donors.
On Monday, while laying out his case for impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Kentucky Representative Thomas Massie made the grave accusation that Hegseth was deploying the military not for national defense but for plunder. “I do have a message to the troops. This secretary has used our troops to go seize oil for large corporations in America. You shouldn’t be used like that. You signed up to pledge your life for this country if need be, and that obligation shouldn’t be diminished to stealing oil for big corporations,” Massie said.
On one level, this indictment seems hardly noteworthy; Donald Trump has repeatedly gushed about the riches the United States is gaining from controlling Venezuelan oil since he kidnapped Prime Minister Nicolás Maduro at the start of this year. Speaking at the United Nations in September, Trump boasted that the US had signed with Venezuela “the biggest oil deal in world history,” guided by the philosophy “to the victor belongs the spoils.”
Massie’s accusation of theft is merely an acknowledgement of Trump’s own words. What’s more notable is Massie’s reference to the accomplices in the theft—the big corporations.
On Wednesday, Reuters published an explosive report offering more evidence of what Massie was talking about. The investigation focuses on the relationship between Vice President JD Vance and John Addison, an executive at the trading giant Vitol.
Addison is a patron of both Vance and Trump. In 2020, he donated $300,00 to a super PAC supporting Vance’s successful Senate run in Ohio. Two years later, Addison and his wife gave $7 million to PACs working to elect Trump and Vance to the White House.
According to Reuters, Vance and Addison met at a resort in Montana on December 27, 2025, one week before the United States invaded Venezuela to kidnap Maduro. The news service reports:
Vance and Addison talked about Venezuela, according to the person, who was given an account of the meeting from Addison. Vance was particularly interested to know how quickly Venezuelan crude could be sold if the US hypothetically gained control of the country’s oil supplies, the person said. Addison assured Vance that Vitol was uniquely placed to do that job.
Vance and Addison deny that this meeting took place, although flight records show they were in Montana at the same time. Prior to the meeting, Vance had commended Addison to Energy Secretary Chris Wright. Reuters notes that Addison has confirmed “that on Jan. 5—two days after the operation that unseated Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and killed up to 100 people—US Energy Secretary Chris Wright called him at his desk in Houston with an irresistible offer.”
Wright circumvented normal rules for government contracts designed to ensure competitive bidding and transparency. Instead, according to Reuters, he quickly signed a sweetheart deal that gave “Vitol and its rival Trafigura…special licenses to sell Venezuela’s oil.… the companies have since earned hundreds of millions of dollars marketing the crude.”
On the very day Reuters published this blockbuster report, Trump, displaying his characteristic freedom from shame, tasked Vance with investigating corruption in states and cities governed by Democrats.
Vance as a corruption fighter is a bad joke. His ties with Addison and Vitol cry out for congressional investigation.
California Representative Mike Levin posted on X.com that
Congress has a duty to act. We should bring Secretary Wright, Vitol, and Addison in to testify under oath. We should demand the phone records, emails, and flight logs. We should find out whether anyone got a heads-up about a military operation. And we should require open, competitive bidding before any company profits from our foreign policy.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
This is a reasonable demand, but should be extended to Trump’s entire foreign policy. With former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang engulfed in a scandal over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, the salient question becomes whether the Trump administration gave him protection and turned a blind eye to Nvidia’s circumvention of a US export ban to China. Huang and Nvidia have been major donors to causes near and dear to Trump’s heart, such as his inauguration and his garish White House ballroom.
The backroom deals behind the war with Iran also demand congressional scrutiny. Speaking to sports broadcaster Stephen A. Smith on Thursday, Trump justified the war by saying “the people we are looking to protect,” which is “basically the Middle East,” are “tremendous investors in our country. They spend trillions of dollars in our country.”
One of the biggest beneficiaries of these investments from the Middle East is Trump himself. In an interview for 60 Minutes that aired on Sunday, columnist Ross Douthat asked about the seeming corruption inherent in the fact that Trump’s sons Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump help “manage a cryptocurrency company called World Liberty Financial” that is “also partially owned by investors connected to the government of the United Arab Emirates.” Trump responded by saying “every president has a problem…going back to George Washington.” Very gently, Douthat noted that the sheer scale of Trump’s conflicts of interest dwarfs previous presidents’.
In 1935, Maj. Gen. Smedley Darlington Butler wrote a book titled War Is a Racket, a title that has a new resonance in the Trump era. Trump’s foreign policy is rancid with corruption. He is clearly setting policy, including the wars he’s launched, to benefit cronies who have lavished largesse on him and his inner circle. The incoming Democratic Congress won a landslide because the public is sick of Trump’s corruption and wars. It’s of paramount importance that Congress use its investigatory powers to shut down Trump’s racket.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120387.title: Sozialpolitik | Die AfD vertritt das Gegenteil
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120387.author: Sarah Yolanda Koss
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120387.text:
- Politik
- Sozialpolitik
Die AfD vertritt das Gegenteil
Um Stimmen unter Arbeitern zu sammeln, muss sich die AfD nicht für Umverteilung einsetzen. Es reicht, wenn diese keine glaubhafte Alternative sehen.
Parteien von rechts-außen sind überproportional erfolgreich unter Wähler*innen der »alten Arbeiterklasse«. Beispielsweise unter Personen, die in der Produktion beschäftigt sind. Dabei vertritt sie ökonomisch gesehen keine Arbeiter*inneninteressen, meint Floris Biskamp von der Eberhard Karls Universität Tübingen auf dem Herbstforum des Wirtschafts- und Sozialwissenschaftlichen Instituts der gewerkschaftsnahen Böckler-Stiftung. Das habe sie aber auch gar nicht nötig.
Es ist eine altbekannte These: Wenn Mitte-links und Mitte-rechts-Parteien ökonomisch liberaler werden, könnte die Lücke von rechts außen gefüllt werden. Zumindest ökonomisch und sozialpolitisch müssten diese dann nach links rutschen. Tatsächlich entscheiden sich AfD-Wähler*innen aber nicht wegen der wirtschafts- und sozialpolitischen Programmatik für die Partei, sondern aus anderen Gründen. »Das wissen die Politiker der AfD. Sie machen deshalb die Politik, die sie für richtig halten. Das ist dann eben eine marktliberale Politik«, sagt Biskamp. Gewisse Ausnahmen, wie bei Forderungen für die Rente, gebe es trotzdem, weil Kürzungen dort doch Stimmen kosten könnten.
Parteiprogramm gegen Umverteilung
Das zeigt sich im Wahlprogramm der AfD. Sie fordert, die Bezugsdauer des Arbeitslosengeldes stärker an den Vorbeschäftigungszeitraum zu knüpfen. Das bedeutet für die meisten Menschen einen kürzeren Bezug jener Gelder. Nach dem Auslaufen des Arbeitslosengelds fällt man in die Grundsicherung. Hier schlägt die AfD einen verpflichtenden Arbeitsdienst nach sechs Monaten vor – quasi einen Zwangsdienst.
Bei den Renten setzt sich die AfD zwar seit 2025 für ein höheres Niveau ein. Rentenkürzungen kommen unter Wähler*innen nicht gut an, weshalb eine Reform immer wieder verzögert wurde. Zugleich schreibt die Partei aber keinen zusätzlichen Schutz mehr für jene mit niedrigen Alterssicherungen in ihr Programm. So werden Ungleichheiten aus dem Erwerbsleben – sowohl was Klasse als auch was Geschlecht betrifft – im Alter fortgeschrieben.
Unübersehbar wird die Verteilungspolitik der AfD in Steuer- und Finanzfragen. Hier setzt sie sich für die Abschaffung der Erbschaftssteuer und die formale Abschaffung der Vermögensteuer ein. Die Vermögensteuer wird seit einem Entscheid des Bundesverfassungsgerichts in den 90ern nicht mehr erhoben.
Rechtsaußen in Europa
Im europäischen Vergleich unter Rechtsaußen-Parteien ist die AfD eine der marktliberalsten Kräfte. Wirtschaftspolitisch haben sie aber länderübergreifend einiges gemeinsam. Sie stehen für einen Wirtschaftsnationalismus, in dem das eigene Land gestärkt werden soll. Oft nicht zum Vorteil der Arbeiter*innen. Mit Blick auf Produktivität versuchen sie, »Faulheit« und Leistung gegeneinander auszuspielen. Als Leistung werten sie dabei zuweilen auch eine kluge Geldanlage. Dieses Narrativ zeigte sich in der Bundesrepublik beispielsweise in der Debatte um das Bürgergeld. Zudem stehen sie alle für einen Wohlfahrtsstaat, von dem jene, die nicht als einheimische Bevölkerung gesehen werden, nichts abhaben sollen.
Dass es dadurch mehr Umverteilung geben kann, ist allerdings ein häufiges Missverständnis, meint Biskamp. »Das heißt nicht unbedingt, dass der Wohlfahrtsstaat für die als einheimisch gesehene Bevölkerung gestärkt und für die anderen geschwächt werden soll«, so seine Erläuterung. Stattdessen könne ein allgemeiner Abbau wohlfahrtsstaatlicher Maßnahmen für die eigene Bevölkerung ein bisschen langsamer vorangehen.
Die arbeiter*innenfeindliche Politik der Rechtsparteien offenzulegen, reiche allerdings nicht für eine Entzauberung derselben, so Biskamp. Eben, weil Arbeiter*innen diese gar nicht aufgrund jener Programme wählen würden. Stattdessen brauche es erst ein progressives politisches Angebot, das glaubhaft vermitteln würde, es bringe Arbeiter*innen ökonomische Sicherheit. »Dann kann man sagen: Die AfD vertritt etwas anderes. Nämlich das Gegenteil.«
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-schools-t.text:
The city education department will review its hiring practices after learning that the man accused of killing a Brooklyn jogger last month was previously hired as a paraprofessional, despite a documented history of mental health concerns.
Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels announced Friday that the city’s Law Department will conduct the independent review and deliver recommendations.
“The safety of our students and staff is our highest priority. We can leave no stone unturned and no path unexplored when it comes to protecting that safety,” Samuels said in a statement.
Sayed Mohassib, 27, is accused of fatally stabbing Katie Suarez as she jogged on the Shore Parkway Greenway on Oct. 30. Mohassib worked as a paraprofessional at PS 200, which is only blocks from the greenway that passes under the Verrazzano Bridge. He has pleaded not guilty.
According to city records, Mohassib was first hired by the education department in 2019. He then left the school system and graduated from the NYPD’s police academy in 2022. He only worked for the NYPD for a month before being granted military leave to join the U.S. Marines. He was then discharged from the Marines due to psychiatric issues. He tried to rejoin the NYPD in 2023, but NYPD supervisors were so concerned by his behavior he was taken to Bellevue Hospital, officials said.
Nevertheless, Mohassib was rehired as a paraprofessional in 2024, payroll records show.
Parents and local officials have demanded to know why Mohassib was allowed to work closely with public school children after the NYPD, where he had also worked briefly as a police officer, raised serious concerns about his mental stability.
The majority of the city’s paraprofessionals work closely with students with disabilities who have individualized education programs, commonly known as IEPs.
New York City Council member Kayla Santosuosso had earlier this week called for a review of the education department’s personnel policies in light of the murder.
“I’m looking at what happened that led up to this person continuing to be employed by the DOE and in such an intimate way with students,” she said. “My concern is that there seem to be numerous red flags along the way that some system within the DOE should have caught.”
Santosuosso said school staff who had worked with Mohassib in the past had also reached out to her office this week to say they had raised concerns about his behavior. The education department did not respond to requests for comments about why he continued to be employed despite those concerns, or after the NYPD had rejected him.
The city has been struggling with a shortage of paraprofessionals for years. The United Federation of Teachers is suing the city over legislation to raise pay for paraprofessionals in order to recruit and retain more candidates.
According to the criminal complaint, Mohassib denied killing Suarez but told investigators that he was sitting on a bench along the path and became “covered in blood.”
Surveillance footage of Mohassib running from the scene of the murder, entering his apartment building and then walking out about 15 minutes later to throw items in the garbage, according to a complaint.
Jessica Battaglia, a former teacher at the High School of Telecommunication Arts and Technology, who said she knew Mohassib when he was in ninth grade, said it was shocking to learn that the “sweet” kid she taught could be arrested for murder.
She said Mohassib stood out for his kindness to classmates, especially students with disabilities. “He was one of our favorite students, that’s why we’re so shocked,” she said. She remembered him winning awards that year at an end-of-year ceremony, and said the person she knew more than a decade ago would have been a “perfect” candidate for a job working with children with disabilities.
She noted the news reports that indicated someone missed multiple signs of his deteriorating mental health. “Why didn’t anyone help him before he hurt someone else?” she asked.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/fa.title: Fake UK Artist Visas Are Being Offered for $132,000, New Investigation Finds
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/fa.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/fa.text:
Several companies have been helping migrants apply for UK visas under the government’s Global Talent program by creating fake art portfolios, complete with fake published art criticism and art news, according to a new investigation published by the BBC Friday.
Nigerian art critic Molara Wood told the publication that she had found her name attached to fake online reviews praising the works of two obscure artists, just one instance of the materials created.
“There is a real problem whereupon fake articles are being implanted onto newspaper websites using bylines of reputable culture journalists,” Wood told the BBC. Following the BBC’s investigation, two Nigerian men’s visas are in the process of being revoked, according to the Home Office. The two claimed to be fine art photographers in their visa applications.
One BBC reporter went undercover to research the companies offering packages through the Global Talent program. The firm said it could supply the reporter with artwork produced in China, as well as arrange exhibitions, media coverage and letters of recommendation. The reporter had been reassured that the “fully inclusive” would grant them a visa without refusal—the package was priced at more than £100,000 ($132,000). The Home Office told the BBC that the company the reporter had dug out was already under investigation. A spokesperson for the Home Office said that they “will not tolerate anyone cheating the UK immigration system” and the “home secretary will take whatever action is needed to stop it being abused.”
The government’s Global Talent program was launched in 2020 and was designed to attract creative workers, including scientists and artists. However, in recent years, it has become a way for companies to target wealthy migrants looking to move without going through the official route, which has become challenging in the UK following new immigration laws.
In another case, a woman said she worked with a company to help her secure a talent visa through the tech route. The company had used fabricated evidence for her application, including a fictitious mentoring award and materials falsely suggesting that she had been a keynote speaker at an event. In the end, her application was rejected.
The companies offering talent visas have been targeting all nationalities. The BBC found two companies in its investigation: iCareer Consultancy and its sister company, ADArt Global Ltd, based out of London’s corporate hub, Canary Wharf, offering fake artwork and immigration advice. During a call with an undercover BBC reporter, an iCareer consultant said that four of his clients obtained a visa this year and that they can supply the reporter with an employee to pose as a client and network for them at gallery openings. The company also said that for £28,000 ($37,000), they can offer a Chinese art award sponsored by Forbes magazine, boosting their chances of securing a visa.
iCareer told the BBC through its lawyers that it strongly denied “offering any visa services whatsoever” and that meeting with the consultant “was not authorized by iCareer.”
“We do not endorse the representations or purported services attributed to him,” the company said.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Governo venezuelano confirma ingresso de US$ 15 bilhões da venda de petróleo entre janeiro e novembro de 2026
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Leonardo Fernandes
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O governo venezuelano confirmou a incorporação de mais de US$ 15 bilhões procedentes da comercialização internacional de petróleo e outros recursos naturais à economia nacional. As informações públicas divulgadas na quinta-feira (12) pelo governo venezuelano no portal Transparência Soberana detalham os fluxos de ingressos e retiradas dos fundos nacionais até 12 de novembro de 2026. Até a quarta-feira (11), o portal informava apenas um repasse de US$ 300 milhões em março deste ano.
Do total de US$ 15,603 bilhões arrecadados no período, a venda de petróleo e derivados por empresas mistas representa a principal fonte de receita, somando US$ 15,148 bilhões, o equivalente a 97,1% do montante. O restante inclui US$ 336,6 milhões em outras commodities, US$ 77,6 milhões em combustível para aviação, US$ 25,3 milhões em gás e US$ 15,7 milhões em outras receitas.
Em relação às despesas, o portal registra um total de US$ 14,86 bilhões em retirada, sendo mais de 99% para o pagamento de salários, aposentadorias e pensões, e para a manutenção dos serviços públicos, correspondendo a US$ 14,71 bilhões. Apenas 1% do valor, somando US$ 150,5 milhões, vai para o funcionamento administrativo do governo.
Os gráficos do site também mostram variações mensais ao longo de 2026, com o pico de arrecadação e desembolso registrado no mês de outubro, quando entraram US$ 3,028 bilhões, dos quais foram aplicados US$ 2,437 bilhões.
A transferência desses recursos é um alívio para a economia venezuelana, que, há mais de uma década, sofre os impactos das sanções econômicas impostas pelos Estados Unidos para pressionar por uma mudança de regime. Mesmo sob assédio, a economia venezuelana tem tido um crescimento sustentado nos últimos anos, fechando acima dos 8% em 2025, e com projeção de incrementar em torno de 7,4% neste ano.
Contexto
A movimentação financeira ocorre sob o impacto da Ordem Executiva 14373, decretada pela administração estadunidense em 9 de janeiro de 2026, seis dias após a agressão militar que resultou no sequestro do presidente Nicolás Maduro e da primeira-dama e deputada, Cilia Flores. O mecanismo impôs o congelamento das receitas petrolíferas em contas no exterior sob controle de Washington.
Em julho de 2026, uma reportagem do jornal britânico Financial Times revelou que os Estados Unidos acumulavam cerca de US$ 13 bilhões em receitas venezuelanas sem repasse ao país, utilizando os recursos como forma de pressão política.
Diante das tentativas de ingerência externa, autoridades da Venezuela reafirmaram a gestão autônoma das divisas. Em julho de 2026, a presidenta encarregada, Delcy Rodríguez, anunciou a retomada da capacidade produtiva da indústria energética, alcançando a marca de 1,203 milhão de barris diários.
Em outubro, o presidente da Assembleia Nacional, Jorge Rodríguez, reiterou que o Estado venezuelano exerce o controle absoluto e soberano sobre os ingressos procedentes da venda de hidrocarbonetos, garantindo que o dinheiro entra diretamente na caixa fiscal da nação para atender às necessidades sociais.
“Os recursos ingressam no caixa fiscal sob a supervisão de instituições bancárias nacionais autorizadas, descartando qualquer tipo de fideicomisso externo ou a gestão de contas por terceiros alheios à estrutura institucional da nação”, disse o deputado, à época.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump-backed Maga firebrand Lauren Boebert defeated in Colorado congressional race
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Dara Kerr
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Lauren Boebert, the firebrand conservative Republican Colorado representative whose three terms in Congress have been marred by multiple controversies, was defeated in her re-election bid.
The gun rights advocate, born-again Christian and one-time QAnon fan lost to Democrat Eileen Laubacher by a less than 1% margin, according to the Associated Press.
“I’m honored by the trust the people of Colorado’s fourth district have placed in me. This campaign was never about party labels. It was about putting people first,” Laubacher said in a statement. “To those who voted for me, thank you, I will strive to make you proud. To those who didn’t, I’ll fight just as hard for you and hope to earn your support.”
This district, which spans the eastern plains of Colorado, is one of the state’s most conservative seats and has long been a Republican stronghold. Laubacher is a retired two-star navy rear admiral, who was deployed to Afghanistan and later worked on the national security council under the Biden administration.
Laubacher just became a registered Democrat in 2025, saying in a debate with Boebert the Republican party had become “nearly unrecognizable”. She focused her campaign on decades of military and national security service.
In a statement congratulating Laubacher, Suzan DelBene, chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, declared: “Lauren Boebert’s sideshow is over.”
Both Laubacher and Boebert moved to Colorado’s fourth congressional district in recent years. Boebert accused Laubacher of moving there and changing parties in order to run for Congress. Likewise, Boebert has been questioned for her move to the district in 2024 after barely eking out a win in the third district’s previous election.
Boebert said the move was because of “dark money” flowing from Hollywood to “steal” district three’s congressional seat: “It’s coming from Hollywood … when you have Barbra Streisand coming in and donating to the Democrat, when you have Ryan Reynolds coming in and donating to the Democrat … It shows you that Hollywood is trying to buy their way into Congress.”
Boebert’s tenure in Congress has been racked with controversy. She decried the 2020 presidential election as being rigged, demanded to carry a handgun on the House floor and was accused of helping incite the January 6 insurrection by tweeting “Today is 1776” the morning of the riots, among other actions. Boebert later condemned the attack on the Capitol.
She went viral in 2023 when she was filmed groping her date, vaping and being escorted out of a Beetlejuice musical in Denver in 2023. Initially, Boebert joked that she would “plead guilty to laughing and singing too loud”, but the incident later led to her publicly apologizing and divorcing her husband (who was not her date).
And just weeks before the election, she was hit by an ethics complaint over allegations she had sexual relationships with three staffers and had paid one to stay silent, allegations she has denied and called “politically motivated”.
Despite the dust-ups and being a Maga loyalist, Boebert did occasionally stand up to Trump. She was one of the most vocal members of Congress calling for the release of the Epstein files, even after the White House tried to persuade her to remove her name from a discharge petition for the documents.
This earned the ire of Trump, who has called Boebert a “carpetbagger” and “dumb”. The president’s first veto of his second term was for a bill sponsored by Boebert that would have funded a drinking water project in district four. The bill had passed the House and Senate unanimously.
“Nothing says ‘America First’ like denying clean drinking water to 50,000 people in south-east Colorado many of whom enthusiastically voted for him all three elections,” Boebert said in a statement at the time.
“But hey, if this administration wants to make its legacy blocking projects that deliver water to rural Americans; that’s on them.”

https://hyperallergic.com/botanical-arti.title: Botanical Artists Show Us What We Stand to Lose
https://hyperallergic.com/botanical-arti.author: Amy Levine-Kennedy
https://hyperallergic.com/botanical-arti.text:
Ascending to the third floor of NYC’s Society of Illustrators this fall is like entering a secret garden. The room is aglow with daylight and rare flora, not in situ, but in the 50 framed winners of its collaboration with the American Society of Botanical Artists’ 29th Annual International Exhibition. The works radiate with majesty, and the intricate sumptuousness is agonizing. Here, the threat of climate change looms.
With strong sun rays streaming in, the plant-potted upper patio of the Society of Illustrators is a jewel box of windowed light, a parade of watercolors on vellum or watercolor paper bask in the sunlight. Here is awe for Mother Earth and her plants — and these botanical artists — and for the meticulous, enchanting detail and outcry that cherish every bud, stem, leaf, petal, bark, seed, blade, stamen, and root.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/why-e.title: Why is Erdogan's son meeting Lebanon’s top leaders?
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/why-e.author: Ragip Soylu
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/why-e.text:
Why is Erdogan's son meeting Lebanon’s top leaders?
Necmettin Bilal Erdogan, the son of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, has raised eyebrows in the Middle East by meeting with top Lebanese officials over the past two days.
Erdogan holds no official role in the Turkish government, but is known for promoting traditional sports, humanitarian aid, and philanthropy worldwide.
"The visit is social and economic in nature," a senior Lebanese government official told Middle East Eye. "Erdogan brought with him Turkish businessmen and institutions, and came to send a message of support to Lebanon."
According to the official, the visit was coordinated with the Lebanese state.
The encounters have prompted questions about the purpose of his trip, as he held high-level meetings in Beirut during a time of heightened tensions in the region.

Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Some in the Middle East regard him as a potential successor to his father. But sources close to Erdogan told MEE that the visit was one of many trips he has made across the region and beyond in recent years, and carries no political significance.
Erdogan was in Tokyo earlier this month and also visited Syria earlier this year. He also travels to Europe, North Africa and South Asia on trips he arranges independently.
Erdogan made a point of including Selim Argun, president of the Yunus Emre Institute, in his delegation to highlight the cultural focus of his itinerary. The institute promotes the Turkish language, arts and cultural heritage through its branches around the world.
Invited by Deputy Prime Minister Tarek Mitri, who oversees Lebanon’s relations with Ankara and Damascus, Erdogan met senior Lebanese officials, including President Joseph Aoun.
The visit comes as Turkey seeks a larger role in Lebanon by deepening political ties, helping Syria repair its relations with Beirut and offering technical and economic assistance.
Reuters reported last month that Ankara had hosted talks aimed at defusing tensions between Hezbollah and the new Syrian government, which were on opposing sides of the Syrian civil war. Both the Turkish and Syrian governments denied the report.
What happened in the meetings?
In his meetings, Erdogan discussed joint projects between Turkish companies and institutions and Lebanese state bodies across several sectors, including transport, trade and exports, the official said.
"In every meeting he held, he warned of Israel and the danger it poses to Lebanon and Syria, and stressed Turkey's role in linking the two countries," the official added.
Another source involved in planning the trip told MEE it was purely aimed at building cultural bridges, with no political ambitions.
The source dismissed suggestions that Erdogan might be working behind closed doors to ease regional tensions, including those between Syria and Hezbollah.
“It's exploring Lebanon and visiting the key people and hearing from them - and friendship - and understanding the region,” the source said. “So far it's been well received from everyone.”
Translation: On the second day of his visit to Lebanon, Bilal Erdogan travelled to Tripoli, where members of the city’s Iman Scouting Association, carrying Turkish and Lebanese flags, saw him off.
Speaking on Friday at the Lebanon-Turkey Strategic Leadership Dialogue, hosted by the Lebanese economy ministry, Erdogan said his visit sought to reaffirm the deep-rooted ties between the two peoples, highlighting the historical and cultural dimensions of the relationship.
He said that, given the right conditions, Lebanon and Syria could experience economic growth similar to Turkey’s over the past 20 years. Stability in nearby countries, including Greece, Armenia, Lebanon and Syria, was in Turkey’s interest and would contribute to regional prosperity and peace, he added.
On Thursday, Erdogan held separate meetings with parliament speaker Nabih Berri, Future Movement Vice President Bahia Hariri, and Druze leader Walid Jumblatt, the former head of the Progressive Socialist Party.
He travelled to Tripoli on Friday, a Sunni stronghold, where footage showed crowds welcoming him with Turkish flags.
According to the Anadolu Agency, Erdogan was received by Tripoli's mufti, Sheikh Muhammad Imam, and the head of the Alawi Islamic Council, Sheikh Ali Qaddour.
He also met Muslim and Christian religious leaders in a mosque’s meeting hall. Those attending included the Maronite Archbishop of Tripoli, Youssef Soueif, and Greek Orthodox Archbishop Ephrem Kyriakos, the agency reported.
Erdogan told those gathered that Turkey and Lebanon needed to strengthen their fraternal ties, as did Lebanon and Syria, and Turkey and Syria.
He said Muslim countries and other nations in the region should prioritise the well-being of their immediate neighbours before looking further afield, stressing the importance of regional solidarity.
