https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Microsoft says services still returning amid widespread outage
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Microsoft says services still returning amid widespread outage
Governments, businesses, individuals disrupted as server failures stretch into second day.
Microsoft has said its popular email and other services were improving but not fully restored more than 24 hours after a mass outage disrupted communications worldwide.
The outage, which began around 16:00 GMT on Thursday and affected users in 74 countries, was caused by overloaded servers that became “unexpectedly available,” the company reported. There was no indication of a cyberattack or malicious activity, the tech giant said on Friday.
“We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure,” the company said in a statement.
Microsoft reported that “email queues [are] significantly reduced and approaching normal levels”.
The outage affected Microsoft 365 services used by global businesses, institutions and individuals, including Outlook, Teams and Copilot, its artificial intelligence (AI) tool. It was one of the longest in Microsoft’s history and the second disruption to its services this year.
While Microsoft has not said how many people were affected by the outage, the company announced in January that it had more than 450 million Microsoft 365 commercial subscribers. The United States-based tech giant is valued at more than $3.8 trillion.
Microsoft reported midday GMT that email delivery and 365 services were improving across Europe, North America and the Asia Pacific but acknowledged that some services remained spotty.
As the outage stretched into its second day, users scrambled to navigate the outages, which caused logistical headaches and forced some operations to stall or grind to a halt.
‘A communication risk’
The outage underscored how dependent institutions, businesses and people have become on a handful of tech companies providing services that power governments and global economies.
“What we do know so far is that this is first and foremost a communication risk,” said Walter Pasquarelli, a strategy adviser to governments on AI and affiliated researcher at the University of Cambridge. “It’s not just workers across businesses who cannot get access to it, but there’s lots of government services and lots of government infrastructure that actually relies on that.”
Foreign banks and financial institutions in Taiwan were hit especially hard, a trader told the news agency Reuters, as their data is emailed to overseas headquarters through Microsoft’s systems. Fax machines were used in Taipei while European exchange operator Euronext told companies to phone in their trades.
Norway’s parliament and several ministries lost access to email, while 80 to 90 Danish municipalities were reportedly affected. Rail operators in Germany, the United Kingdom and Canada said the outage impacted timetables and emailed tickets, and the UK’s massive National Health Service pivoted to using paper records.
In the United States, the House of Representatives and local governments were affected, Reuters reported.
The US Department of Defense, which relies heavily on Microsoft’s services, did not comment on whether it was affected. The Pentagon was slated to upgrade its Microsoft infrastructure starting in June in a $9.7bn deal that included access to Microsoft 365.
The server failures did not appear to shake Wall Street’s confidence in Microsoft, however, which said it would review the incident along with measures to prevent future disruptions. Microsoft’s stock was mostly flat in US market trading on Friday as the tech-heavy Nasdaq index fell slightly, led by the embattled AI company Nvidia.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Comment | Is art market regulation too much of a ‘good thing’?
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Alexander Herman
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Anyone who says the art market is unregulated probably has not spent much time in an auction house compliance department. At the big houses, such departments might consist of half a dozen full-time personnel tasked with ensuring that the business can digest what has become an expanding layer cake of government regulation in the art sector.
In the European Union (EU) and UK, this includes regulation around money-laundering, data protection, imports and exports, artist resale rights, a growing economic sanctions regime, endangered species, firearms and complex tax reporting. The UK has additional obligations around ivory and issuing annual “modern slavery” statements.
Focus on the goal
None of these areas of control seem objectionable at first glance. But a careful observer must consider two things. Does the imposition of regulation achieve the intended goal? And, if it does, does it need to apply across the board, both up and down the market, to all participants?
In 2015, the British Art Market Federation undertook an analysis that listed 167 laws and regulations impacting the UK art market. The organisation’s current chair, Tom Christopherson, tells me that the impact of laws and regulations has increased considerably since then. Sophisticated players, with their compliance teams and in-house lawyers, may be able to spot trends, change course and avoid falling foul of the many rules. But what about the small fish?
Consider anti-money laundering regulations, which were extended to the art market by the EU and the UK in 2020. Absolutely nobody wants ill-gotten gains to proliferate in the art market. But despite negative stereotypes and hearsay around “dodgy dealings”, I have yet to find convincing evidence of money laundering in the European art market that could have justified such an expansive regime.
Registration issues
In the UK, data from HMRC (the official tax, payments, and customs authority) shows that more than 200 art market participants have been fined for violating the rules from the date enforcement began in 2022 to September 2025. None of these infractions involved the actual laundering of money, merely the failure to register with HMRC or to report material changes. (One gallery failed on additional grounds relating to risk assessments, due diligence and staff training.) Many of those fined are small operations, such as a toy soldier shop in London that featured in a recent Financial Times story on this topic.
With registration and reporting obligations, the onus falls on market participants. The scope of an offence can extend well beyond laundering itself. With the art market now a “regulated sector”, failure to report suspicions around, for instance, activities that could conceivably be connected to the funding of terrorism is now a criminal offence. An east London art dealer was caught under this new “failure to report” offence in 2023 and sentenced to two-and-a-half years behind bars.
Another area involves sanctions, far less simple than checking customer names against a list of oligarchs. The Russia sanctions list continues to grow by the month; in the UK, it consists of nearly 2,000 individuals and 1,000 companies—with additional lists for countries including Belarus, Iran and Libya—often with a multitude of transliterated names.
Also in the UK, an offence exists that goes beyond dealing with listed sanctioned individuals to exporting or “making available” luxury goods (including art) to anyone “connected with Russia”. This offence was used recently to charge the gallery Hauser & Wirth, along with its shipping company. Judge Tony Baumgartner of Southwark Crown Court dismissed the case in July, having found that the prosecution had failed to make a case that the individual to whom the work had been shipped was indeed “connected with Russia”, as he was no longer ordinarily residing in that country.
We all understand the benefit of regulation when it comes to saving lives, protecting the environment and smothering criminality in high-risk markets. But whether every piece of regulation is justified for the art world remains to be seen—or, rather, proven.

https://taz.de/Tod-von-Lisa-T/!6224455/.title: Tod von Lisa T.: Der Feed ist voll und die Gedanken leer
https://taz.de/Tod-von-Lisa-T/!6224455/.author: Nora Belghaus
https://taz.de/Tod-von-Lisa-T/!6224455/.text:
Tod von Lisa T.: Der Feed ist voll und die Gedanken leer
Der Fall des toten Mädchens Lisa T. erschüttert das Land – und geht viral. Was macht es mit jungen Menschen, wenn sie solchen Content konsumieren?
Schon Minuten vor der eigentlichen Schweigeminute schweigen die Menschen. Es ist Dienstagabend, dunkel und kalt. Ein paar Dutzend dick eingepackter Gestalten drängt sich auf dem Vorplatz des Berliner S-Bahnhofs Lichtenberg um einen öffentlichen Wasserspender. Sie zünden Kerzen an, stellen sie zu dem gerahmten Foto, das gegen den Spender gelehnt ist. Sie legen Rosen nieder, schweigend, in Gedenken an das Mädchen, das auf dem Foto zu sehen ist.
Das Mädchen heißt Lisa. Ihr Verschwinden und später ihr Tod haben in den vergangenen anderthalb Wochen Nachrichtensendungen, Feeds und Timelines gefüllt. Lisa, 13 Jahre alt, war in Berlin-Marzahn am Dienstag, den 3. November, gegen 7.15 Uhr aus dem Haus gegangen, um zur Schule zu gehen. Doch sie kam nie dort an. Die Vermisstenmeldung ging viral. Eine groß angelegte Suche blieb erfolglos. Fünf Tage später wird sie gefunden: tot, in einem unbewohnten Einfamilienhaus in Brandenburg. Neben ihr ein 22-jähriger Mann mit schweren Schussverletzungen.
Ab hier setzt sich etwas in Gang. Eine Lawine der Berichterstattung. Im Fernsehen, auf Nachrichtenseiten – und vor allem in den sozialen Medien: Instagram, Youtube, Tiktok. Jede neue Bewegung in dem Fall, jedes Detail, jedes Gerücht wird in einem neuen Beitrag gepostet und gerepostet. Dass gegen den Tatverdächtigen zuvor wegen des Verdachts des Erwerbs und Besitzes kinderpornografischer Inhalte ermittelt worden war, dass am Tag ihres Verschwindens vor dem Einfamilienhaus in Brandenburg stundenlang ein Auto mit eingeschaltetem Warnblinker gestanden haben soll, dass Nachbarn Hilferufe gehört hätten, aber niemand etwas tat.
wochentaz
Dieser Text erschien zuerst in der wochentaz, unserer Wochenzeitung von links!
In der wochentaz geht es jede Woche um die Welt, wie sie ist – und wie sie sein könnte. Eine linke Wochenzeitung mit Stimme, Haltung und dem besonderen taz-Blick auf die Welt. Jeden Samstag neu am Kiosk und natürlich im Abo.
Der Strom des Contents reißt nicht ab, der Fall wird in eine allgemeine Bedrohungserzählung übertragen: Ein Influencer postet einen Warnhinweis vor einem angeblichen „pädophilen Amoklauf“. Momfluencerinnen sind alarmiert, warnen die Elternbubble in Reels, ihre Kinder nicht mehr aus den Augen zu lassen.
Was erklärt die enorme Aufmerksamkeit – und wie wirkt sie sich auf unsere Wahrnehmung von Gewalt aus? Und was macht es mit jungen Menschen, wenn ein Verbrechen nicht nur in den Nachrichten auftaucht, sondern in tausenden Reels und Clips immer wieder neu inszeniert, emotionalisiert, kommentiert und mitunter spekulativ ausgeschmückt wird?
Offene Falltür ins Rabbithole
Am Mittwochmorgen hängt der Hochnebel über der Stadt und umhüllt die oberen Stockwerke der Berliner Häuserzeilen. Die taz spricht mit zwei Schülerinnen, die gerade auf dem Weg zur Schule sind. Haben sie von Lisa T. gehört, dem vermissten Mädchen? Ja, eine Freundin hatte ihnen auf Tiktok einen Post geschickt. Wie sah ihr Tiktok-Feed in den Tagen nach der Meldung über ihren Tod aus? Alles voll von Lisa. Die eine Schülerin sagt, zwischendurch sei es ihr auch mal zu viel geworden und sie habe das Handy weggelegt. Zum Beispiel, als ein Video ein vermeintliches Phantombild und ein angebliches Foto des mutmaßlichen Täters zeigte.
Ein Blick auf Tiktok zeigt, wie schnell sich die Falltür zum Rabbithole öffnet. Wer einen Clip zu Lisas Fall zu Ende schaut, bekommt gleich den nächsten angezeigt. Suchvorschläge führen zu weiteren Videosammlungen. Viele Beiträge sind mit dramatischer Musik unterlegt, die Schnitte schnell, die kommentierenden Stimmen aufgeregt. Die Grenzen zwischen Nachricht, Kommentar und Unterhaltung verschwimmen hier. Eine Ofcom-Studie beobachtete, dass Kinder Nachrichteninhalte von Tiktok-Creators teilweise ungeprüft für glaubwürdig hielten. Auch die deutsche #UseTheNews-Studie stellte fest, dass vielen Jugendlichen das Wissen über die Arbeitsweisen des professionellen Journalismus fehlt.
Am Anfang der Lawine jedoch stand eine Meldung. Sie wurde aufgegriffen von Medienhäusern, Reporter:innen wurden losgeschickt, ein Videojournalist begleitete live die Suchaktion der Polizei. Der Fall erregt Aufmerksamkeit, bundesweit und auf allen Kanälen. Gleichzeitig wurden seit dem Verschwinden von Lisa zwei mutmaßliche Femizide begangen, in Hamburg und Baden-Württemberg. Ein Medienecho dieser Größe bleibt bisher aus. Warum ist das so?
Ein Anruf bei Medienforscher Thomas Hestermann von der Macromedia University. Seit 20 Jahren untersucht er, wie Medien über Gewaltkriminalität berichten. Sein Befund: Tötungsdelikte dominieren, die Opferseite kommt häufiger zu Wort als die der Tatverdächtigen, und kindliche Opfer sind stark überrepräsentiert. Seit den 2000er Jahren sei der Kampf um Auflagen, Quoten und Klicks härter geworden. Das führe zu einer stärkeren Emotionalisierung. Damit entstehe ein bestimmter Blick auf Opfer von Gewalt, sagt Hestermann. „Im Fokus steht ein idealisiertes Opfer, das einer Gesellschaft Anteilnahme wert ist.“ So ist im US-amerikanischen Diskurs vom „worthy victim“ die Rede: Dieses Opfer ist weiblich, jung, am ehesten ein Kind. Je unschuldiger, desto besser. So wie Lisa.
Zusammen mit dem Druck der Aufmerksamkeitsökonomie sieht Hestermann darin ein Problem: Wenn Medien vor allem auf starke Emotionen und Klicks setzen, droht die journalistische Einordnung verloren zu gehen. Die Idealisierung einzelner Opfer als besonders „wertvoll“ könne zudem ein verzerrtes, lebensfremd eindeutiges Bild von Gewalt erzeugen – hier der Täter, da das Opfer, schwarz und weiß. Redaktionen sollten darauf besonderes Augenmerk legen.
Auf Tiktok arbeiten Content Creators in der Regel nicht mit Redaktionen, die ihnen journalistisch-ethische Standards setzen. Sie sitzen allein zu Hause mit ihrem Handy und filmen sich selbst oder schneiden Videoschnipsel zusammen, die sie im Internet finden. Es wird emotionalisiert und inszeniert in Dauerschleife.
Die beiden Schülerinnen sprechen auf ihrem Weg zur Schule über ihre Angst. Ja, die sei stärker geworden seit dem Vorfall mit Lisa. Sie seien froh, dass sie immer zu zweit zur Schule und danach auch zusammen wieder nach Hause gingen. Ihre Mutter, sagt die eine, hätte ihr vor ein paar Tagen einen Schlüsselanhänger für den Notfall gegeben. Sie zieht ihren Schlüssel aus der Jackentasche, ein schwarzes Plastikteil baumelt daran, aus dem eine kurze Kordel hängt. Wenn sie daran ziehe, gehe ein Alarm los.
Die Angst ist reell geworden, obwohl es statistisch extrem unwahrscheinlich ist, dass sich eine Entführung wie die von Lisa in so kurzer Zeit wiederholt. Obwohl es im Gegenzug viel wahrscheinlicher ist, dass die Tochter auf dem Weg zur Bushaltestelle von einem Auto erfasst wird. Welche Rolle spielen die sozialen Medien für die Entstehung von Angst?
Ein Anruf bei André Ilcin. Er ist klinischer Psychologe und arbeitet mit Kindern und Jugendlichen in Berlin. Wie stark Gewaltvideos belasteten, hänge auch davon ab, wie häufig Jugendliche ihnen ausgesetzt seien. Wiederholte Konfrontation könne das Gefühl verstärken, der Gewalt ausgeliefert zu sein und die Kontrolle zu verlieren. „Wenn sich das über Tage hinweg wiederholt, kann die Umwelt irgendwann als unberechenbar und gefährlich wahrgenommen werden.“ Eine andere Reaktion sei, gegenüber Gewalt abzustumpfen.
Auch könne ein Teufelskreis entstehen, sagt Ilcin: „Ich habe Angst, setze mich aber trotzdem immer wieder aktiv dem aus, was mir Angst macht.“ Durch die Suche nach weiteren Informationen versuchten Jugendliche, Unsicherheit abzubauen und ein Gefühl der Kontrolle zurückzugewinnen – und konfrontierten sich dabei immer wieder mit denselben belastenden Inhalten.
Swipet man auf Tiktok durch die Clips zum Mord an Lisa, fallen einige Videos und Accounts besonders auf. Es sind Content Creators, meist jung, die oft in die Kamera sprechen. Sie legen ihr eigenes Bild über Ausschnitte aus der Fernsehberichterstattung oder beliebige andere Bilder. Ihre Videos sind versehen mit Hashtags wie #truecrime oder #crimetok. Sie berichten, was sie aus den Medien erfahren haben, manchmal unter Nennung der Quellen. Oft werfen sie auch Fragen auf, stellen Vermutungen an, spekulieren. „Klingt so, als hätte Lisa auf jeden Fall noch ein bisschen gelebt“, sagt etwa eine Sarah Kolumna in ihrem Video.
True Crime ohne Standards
True-Crime-Formate boomen bei Kindern und Jugendlichen. Auch eines der Schulmädchen erzählt, sie höre regelmäßig True-Crime-Podcasts, um sich abzulenken. Die Freiwillige Selbstkontrolle Fernsehen (FSF) hat in einer kleinen Studie mit Jugendlichen untersucht, was sie an solchen Formaten fasziniert und was sie ängstigt. Entscheidend sei nicht nur, dass die Geschichten tatsächlich passiert sind, sondern auch ihr gefühlter Realitätsbezug. Lebensnahe Fälle, etwa mit kindlichen Opfern, könnten besonders intensiv erlebt werden.
Doch nicht alles sei schlecht daran, sagt Claudia Mikat, Geschäftsführerin der FSF und Expertin für Jugendmedienschutz. True Crime könne Jugendliche über Verbrechen aufklären und ihr Wissen um Gefahren schärfen. Entscheidend sei, wie drastisch die Taten dargestellt und wie Originalmaterial eingesetzt werde – etwa ob Opfer erkennbar seien. Auch eine klassische Krimi-Dramaturgie, in der am Ende ein Fall aufgeklärt und Gerechtigkeit hergestellt werde, könne Jugendlichen helfen.
Claudia Mikat, Geschäftsführerin der Freien Selbstkontrolle Fernsehen (FSF)
Während professionelle True-Crime-Produktionen redaktionellen und rechtlichen Standards unterliegen, kann auf Tiktok praktisch jeder Inhalte über reale Verbrechen verbreiten – ohne journalistische Ausbildung, redaktionelle Kontrolle oder Rücksicht auf die Persönlichkeitsrechte der Betroffenen.
An der Verwertung von Lisas Fall in True-Crime-Videos kann man die Folgen der Unreguliertheit sehen: Ihr Foto ist in den meisten Fällen nicht verpixelt. Der Fall kann vorerst auch keiner Krimi-Dramaturgie folgen, da der mutmaßliche Täter auf der Intensivstation verstorben ist und die Aufklärung noch Monate dauern dürfte. Eine True- Crime-Content-Creatorin hat dennoch in drei Tagen sieben Videos zum Fall von Lisa gepostet. Das meistgeklickte hat 710 Tausend Aufrufe.
Was tun? Die Expertin Claudia Mikat appelliert für mehr Medienbildung: „Man sollte über die Machart von Medien sprechen: Was ist eine sachliche Nachricht und was ist eine gestaltete, effekthascherische Darstellung? Kinder müssen lernen, das zu erkennen und auch Manipulationsmechanismen zu durchschauen.“
Die Gedenkveranstaltung für Lisa am S-Bahnhof Lichtenberg ist nach zwei Stunden vorbei. Am Wasserspender bleiben die Kerzen, die Rosen, ein paar gebastelte Plakate und der Bilderrahmen zurück. Drei Teenager – zwei Mädchen und ein Junge – laufen vorbei, bleiben stehen, schauen herunter auf Lisas Bild. Ob sie von dem Fall gehört haben? Ja, auf Tiktok. Wie fühlen sie sich, wenn sie daran denken? Traurig, wütend, leer? Leer. Auf die Frage, ob sie auch True-Crime-Formate konsumierten, nickt eines der Mädchen. Und wie sie die finde? Sie lacht und sagt: „Die finden mich.“
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.humanite.fr/feminisme/femini.title: « Les vrais coupables sont ceux qui l’ont laissé faire » : le journaliste sportif Pierre Ménès face à la justice
https://www.humanite.fr/feminisme/femini.author: Mejdaline Mhiri
https://www.humanite.fr/feminisme/femini.text:
L’ancien journaliste de Canal + comparaît aujourd’hui devant le tribunal de Nanterre, visé par trois accusations de harcèlement et d’agressions sexuelles sur d’anciennes collègues. À la suite du documentaire de Marie Portolano, qui avait révélé le sexisme systémique dans les rédactions sportives, l’inspection du travail avait saisi le parquet.
Une véritable déflagration. Au printemps 2021, la diffusion sur Canal + du documentaire Je ne suis pas une salope, je suis une journaliste, réalisé par Marie Portolano et Guillaume Priou, fait l’effet d’une bombe. Dans un sondage réalisé à l’époque par Odoxa pour RTL, 39 % des Français.es déclaraient avoir vu ou entendu parler du film.
Durant 76 minutes, près d’une vingtaine de journalistes sportives, dont des figures bien connues comme Vanessa Le Moigne, racontent le sexisme subi dans l’exercice de leur métier, notamment de la part de collègues et de supérieurs hiérarchiques. Comme Tiffany Henne, sommée quotidiennement par son chef de révéler son orientation sexuelle, persuadé qu’elle est lesbienne. Jusqu’au jour où il l’enferme...

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: The End of Russell Brand's Rape Shtick
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Laurie Penny
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The End of Russell Brand’s Rape Shtick
The British celebrity kept reinventing his image to try to cloak his predations.
Foreign rapists are not, apparently, all created equal. Years of fearmongering about notional predators penetrating the US border don’t seem to count when the culprits are rich and famous and British. This week, born-again YouTube grifter and alleged comedian Russell Brand received a 10-year sentence in England for rape and sexual assault. Today, apex manosphere grifter Andrew Tate and his unimportant brother will appear in a Florida court pending extradition to the United Kingdom on rape and human-trafficking charges. These are men who got away with staggering feats of sexual violence not only in plain sight but also on large public platforms—getting away with it, in fact, was the gimmick. Performative misogyny wasn’t incidental to their appeal. It was their shtick from the start.
Everyone knew about Russell Brand. Not just everyone at the BBC in 2009 or everyone on liberal Twitter in 2012, but everyone who, at any point in the past several decades, watched him leering and groping and degrading women live on air. “Did Russell Brand go too far this time?” has been an open tab in British public discourse for my entire adult life. He swaggered around the BBC in a skinny scarf cackling about his conquests like some sort of sex pirate—an erotic swashbuckler who would never be square enough to ask before grabbing or take no for an answer. Everyone loves pirates; yes, they’re violent criminals, but that’s fine because they’re on the right side—namely the side where, to quote the leader of the nominally free world, “when you’re a star, they let you do it.”
How much violence and corruption should powerful men be allowed to perpetrate? How many rules do they get to break? How long do we let them laugh at the concept of individual and democratic consent? The moral questions shape our politics on a fundamental level. The #MeToo movement still casts a deep shadow over culture, and the misogyny of the modern right is not your mother’s misogyny. It’s new, reactive, and openly vengeful—after all, if women were allowed to take the rule of law into their own hands by asking men to stop raping them, men should get to overthrow the democratic consensus and wreck the global economy just to show us they still can.
That wounded, weaponized patriarchy is still in power—for now. Millennial and Gen Z men are in the unlucky position of having to foot the bill for a thousand years of male privilege that they never got to enjoy because they happened to hit adulthood just when the music stopped and the reckoning began. These men have proven easy marks for self-serving Gordon Gekkos of the attention economy like Brand and the Tates and the president of the United States.
But something has changed. We’re now in the backlash to the backlash to the backlash. It’s been a good few weeks of consequences for men who model that vengeful, nihilist masculinity, where power is its own reward and the rules only apply to losers. Russell Brand was one of the very first. In the early aughts men wanted to be him; women wanted to fix him; non-binary people wanted to know how he got his hair like that. All the while, he lapped up the attention, indulging his particular fetish for sexually degrading women live on air where they had to keep smiling. His personal aura has shifted through the whole spectrum of charismatic criminality from Jack Sparrow to, lately, David Koresh. He’s always been the patron saint of getting away with it—a wrong’un so devoid of integrity that he could and did relentlessly alter his personality so as to attach his coercive control circus to any movement that could offer him a moral alibi and an army of adoring fans. When it was cool to be anti-capitalist, he was suddenly a revolutionary figurehead, until those of us who actually went to the meetings started pointing out that he never did.
Brand first attempted to retcon his cheeky-neighborhood-crotch-grabber persona in the 2010s by identifying as a sex addict—as a sinner in need of saving, a sick boy in need of healing, rather than an adult man in charge of his own behavior. I remember him claiming to have been cured, as so many coercive men do, by “the love of a good woman”—as opposed, presumably, to the bad women who let him degrade them. The good woman in question, Jemima Khan, has spoken today about the abuse she suffered at his hands, and his ex-wife, Katy Perry, has only commented that Brand belongs in jail.
And yet Brand is clearly convinced that he is the victim here—a martyr to vile mind-virus #MeToo purity politics, which are of course very different from the down-home purity politics he’s pushing these days. His latest incarnation is as a born-again YouTube guru, complete with salt-and-pepper ponytail and linen shirt, taking the knee for God on stage for cash and applause at Turning Point USA. The alt-right is certainly a more welcoming place for professional sex pests. Among the lost boys of the manosphere, Brand, like the Tates, groomed an army of angry minions ready to rush to his aid as a brave free speech defender. Now that consequences have come calling, inevitably, wokes like me are being told that this is all our fault. We are the ones who somehow made him do it, along with every other outrage that dark-triad Svengalis perpetrate against public decency.
I will not waste energy arguing with this, having finally learned that when someone wants to fight a version of you they made up, it’s best to leave the room and let them get on with it.
More interesting is the insistence we are now seeing in the online blood-gutters where chemtrail-huffing tech moguls and their flying monkeys now control the discourse that this conviction represents a miscarriage of justice—mob rule that degrades the rule of law. In the maelstrom of #MeToo, this is what women were accused of doing when they denied wrongdoers their day in court, but now that those days are here, the same procedural outrage persists. The absolute importance of the rule of law, of course, is conveniently forgotten when it’s your own side that runs militantly afoul of it. The alleged journalist Michael Tracey has made it his business to reveal the identities of Brand’s accusers, just as he tried to expose Jane Doe in the ongoing frat-house rape cases at Cornell University. Feminist scholar Catherine MackInnon wrote that the crime of rape is defined not by women’s experience of violation but by the level of violence men consider acceptable. Here the question isn’t whether sexual violence happened but whether we consider it a crime.
At his trial, Brand didn’t dispute the events—but he still seems to believe he did nothing wrong, and millions of people agree with him. The fact is that a great many ordinary people seem to think that violence is the price women should expect to pay for casual sex, and that women who claim otherwise are the real villains. Brand and his online corps of enablers seem to think that if a young girl goes to a celebrity’s dressing room, he gets to do whatever he wants to her; that his reputation will always be more important than her dignity and safety. They seem to think that sex is disputed territory in a war between men and women—a violent, dirty thing men do to women who are foolish enough to let them.
Brand, the Tates and their ilk groomed millions of supporters for cash and cover stories. Their fans know whom they are defending, just as the millions of Americans knew what they were choosing, in 2016 and 2024, when they showed the world that they would rather elect a rapist than a woman. But persecution fantasies are part of the playbook of modern fascism. Brand has every incentive to position himself as a martyr, a figure unfairly punished for doing what every man would obviously do if he only had the balls.
This is, of course, nonsense. Most men and boys are not abusers-in-waiting, and most have far more in common with the victims of Brand and Trump and the Tates and every other professional wrong’un. But that’s the whole point of this weaponized, wounded patriarchy. It’s integral to the recruiting strategy of modern fascism to persuade millions of men that they are no more than temporarily embarrassed sex criminals, who owe their allegiance to the venal and shameless.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120386.title: Humanoider Roboter | Ein Phantom für den Untergrund von Gaza
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120386.author: Matthias Monroy
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120386.text:
- Politik
- Humanoider Roboter
Ein Phantom für den Untergrund von Gaza
Israel könnte Kampfroboter eines US-Startups in angeblich verbliebene Hamas-Tunnel schicken, so einer der Firmengründer. Ein Trump-Sohn ist Investor.
Israel hat laut einem UN-Bericht allein in den ersten zwei Kriegsjahren 200.000 Tonnen Sprengstoff und Munition im Gazastreifen eingesetzt, das entspricht der Zerstörungskraft von 13 Hiroshima-Bomben. Mindestens 80 Prozent der Gebäude im Gebiet halb so groß wie Hamburg sind zerstört – wohl auch die in unklarem Ausmaß existierenden Hamas-Tunnel, deren Vernichtung die Armee als Kriegsziel genannt hatte. Immer noch müssen sie aber als Begründung für weitere israelische Angriffe herhalten.
Bald könnten auch humanoide Roboter namens Phantom MK1 in diesem dubiosen Untergrund noch lebende Hamas-Mitglieder suchen. Die Roboter werden von Foundation Future Industries hergestellt, einem Start-up aus San Francisco. Mitgründer Mike LeBlanc erzählte im Interview mit der »Financial Times«, er führe Gespräche mit Israels Generalstabschef über den Verkauf von bis zu 1000 Robotern. Nach Angaben des britischen »Telegraph« kostet ein Exemplar rund 130.000 Euro.
Zusammen mit dem israelischen Militär und einem Phantom MK1 habe LeBlanc auch schon Hamas-Tunnel besichtigt. Nach der Veröffentlichung des Interviews ruderte ein Foundation-Firmensprecher jedoch zurück: Es gebe keinen Vertrag von Foundation mit Israel, die Gespräche seien »früh und sondierend« gewesen.
Den Roboter für militärische Zwecke präsentierte die Firma der Öffentlichkeit im Oktober 2025, ein Jahr nach ihrer Gründung. Er ist 1,75 Meter groß, mattschwarz und wiegt rund 80 Kilogramm. Anstelle eines Gesichts ziert eine Fläche mit Kameras den Kopf des Phantom MK1. Foundation-Chef Sankaet Pathak kündigte letztes Jahr an, bis Ende 2027 bis zu 50.000 Geräte bauen zu wollen.
Im Februar soll Foundation bereits zwei Phantom MK1 in die Ukraine geschickt haben, wo sie für Tests Munition und Nachschub zu Stellungen gebracht hätten. Wie der US-Sender CNBC berichtet, schwächelten die Geräte jedoch: Die Nutzlast von 20 Kilogramm erwies sich als für den Kriegseinsatz zu gering, der Akku als zu schwach für längere Einsätze, der Roboter außerdem als nicht wasserdicht. Angeblich kann der Humanoid nach einem Sturz auch nicht selbst aufstehen.
Das soll der Nachfolger namens Phantom MK2 beheben. Pathak attestiert ihm »übermenschliche Fähigkeiten« und die doppelte Traglast. Nach Firmenangaben soll er sechs Stunden laufen können. Foundation will auch Waffen für den Roboter entwickeln – mit Handgelenken, die das Schießen erleichtern.
Seit März ist der US-Präsidentensohn Eric Trump »Chefberater für Strategie« bei Foundation Future Industries und hält Anteile an der Firma. »Er liebt die Roboter«, sagt LeBlanc. Das könnte erklären, warum der Mitgründer den Phantom MK1 für Einsätze in vermeintlichen Hamas-Tunneln bewirbt: Vater Donald Trump hatte Anfang 2025 angekündigt, 2,1 Millionen Einwohner*innen von Gaza in andere arabische Staaten umsiedeln und den Küstenstreifen in eine »Riviera des Nahen Ostens« verwandeln zu wollen. Für Gazas Bevölkerung wäre in Trumps »Riviera« kein Platz mehr. Für das Roboterbusiness seines Sohnes schon.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://gothamist.com/news/engineers-que.title: Engineers question city-approved plans after Brooklyn building collapse
https://gothamist.com/news/engineers-que.author: David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/engineers-que.text:
City-approved excavation plans at the site of Wednesday’s fatal apartment building collapse in Brooklyn did not require construction crews to install additional bracing to support the adjacent structure, according to a review of building records.
The plans instead called for cutting into the soil at a 45-degree angle away from the three-story apartment building’s foundation to a depth of roughly 15 feet. Every other building around the perimeter of the construction site was required to have reinforcing steel buttresses known as rakers, according to the plans.
The collapse killed eight people and injured 18 more. The development team behind the property had previously ignored a stop-work order earlier in the year, city records show. The absence of the bracing raises further questions about the safety of the construction work.
Three structural engineers who reviewed the engineering documents, known as “support of excavation” plans, said they were surprised to see that the buildings department approved the measures without the additional structural support, which can help prevent adjoining buildings from collapsing when excavation work is done.
“That’s a recipe for disaster,” said Abi Agheyere, a structural engineer and a professor at Drexel University. “You have to have shoring.”
Agheyere said the extra precaution should have been taken due to the age of the 94-year-old building, which sat atop a rubble foundation. A preconstruction plan drafted by the engineering firm Quiver League and submitted to the Department of Buildings also described the building facade next to the construction site as in “poor condition with noticeable cracks.”
Quiver’s report notes that its inspectors lacked detailed information about the apartment building’s foundation and other structural features, and that they were only able to assess the building from the sidewalk and other adjoining properties.
Quiver engineer Sepehr Rezaeimalek prepared the report. He did not respond to a phone message Friday.
Chris Cerino, past president of the Structural Engineers Association of New York, said he would have expected to see additional bracing in the drawings, or “underpinning” to support the foundation of the collapsed apartment building.
“I would have anticipated a different detail on that side of the site,” Cerino said in a text message after reviewing the plans.
Department of Buildings spokesperson Andrew Rudansky said the support strategy depicted in the approved plans is “standard industry practice” and that “similar excavation designs have been safely performed at other work sites across the city for decades.”
Rudansky also said the project engineer — in this case, Jieming Wang of LMW Engineering — is responsible for making sure the plans are safe for construction before submitting them to the buildings department.
“Upon that confirmation by the design professional engineer, plans go through a full plan exam at the DOB,” he said.
Rudansky said the department completed the full exam and found the designs complied with city requirements. He said investigators are now conducting additional reviews, with a special focus on the project’s “geotechnical report,” which evaluated the soil and rock at the construction site before excavation work began. The engineer who prepared the report, Michael Karantinidis of International Geotechnical/Structural Laboratories Inc., did not immediately respond to a message left at his office.
Rudansky did not say what was supposed to support the building that collapsed between excavation and pouring a new foundation at the construction site.
Wang submitted the excavation plans for approval in December 2025. At the time, the owner of 2625 Bedford Ave., a limited liability company tied to Robert Fischman and Judy Swimer, sought to construct a three-story apartment building on the site. The development team later submitted a new plan in September to build a nine-story complex, but the Department of Buildings had not yet approved the revised project proposal.
A person who answered the phone at Wang’s office extension Friday immediately hung up.
Buildings records indicate that special inspector MD Islam was contracted to monitor excavation. Records updated Thursday said Islam had requested to withdraw from the project after the building collapsed.
Islam did not respond to requests for comment or emailed questions about the withdrawal.
In the immediate wake of the catastrophe, the city’s Department of Buildings issued a full stop work order. A comment on its online portal attributed the collapse “to unsafe construction operations.” The agency later deleted the comment, Crain’s reported Thursday.
The Department of Buildings is investigating the cause of the collapse alongside the city’s Department of Investigation and the Brooklyn District Attorney’s office. The city is also conducting sweep inspections at building sites across the city where the same contractors have conducted work. On Friday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the inquiry had expanded to 160 properties involving six different entities.
The edge of the now-collapsed building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. was the only location in the construction site where the engineering plans did not require steel supports.
Agheyere said the beams add another layer of protection against collapse.
“There's nothing that stops it from spreading right into the hole,” he said.
Another engineer who reviewed the plans said steel reinforcement is not always required to support an adjacent building if excavation is done properly.
“As long as you're not digging under the foundation, you don’t necessarily have to put up steel or additional measures,” said Eugene Gurevich, from the firm RAND Engineering & Architecture.
He likened the structure of a building to a ladder, with two parallel sides serving as feet and wooden joists, framing and floors as the handholds.
“One leg of the ladder was kicked out from under it and pulled the whole ladder down,” he said.
In an interview, Carpenter’s Union Executive Secretary-Treasurer Paul Capurso said construction crews may have dug too deeply to prepare for a potential nine-story building, rather than the three-story structure approved by the buildings department.
“There is potential they could have changed their design on the fly,” Concurso said.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/rh.title: Rhizome Announces Partnership With Electronic Arts Intermix Following Vimeo Censorship Concerns
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/rh.author: Lmiller
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/rh.text:
Earlier this week, Rhizome, the 30-year-old digital art nonprofit that has been affiliated with the New Museum since 2003, announced a pilot program with its internal video hosting platform video.rhizome.org, and Electronic Arts Intermix (EAI). Rhizome hopes to offer VRO, as it’s known, to other digital arts organizations and artists as an alternative to commercial video platforms like Vimeo.
“We think offering artists video hosting is something that could be meaningful for people in the community right now,” Michael Connor, Rhizome’s executive director, told ARTnews. “With the way that the web is going, it’s harder and harder to run a platform the way Vimeo operated a decade ago.”
Rhizome initially set up VRO in 2022, but their plans to offer the technology to others in the digital arts community kicked into high gear this summer following a breakdown in the relationship between Vimeo and EAI, a video and new media distributor with a collection of thousands of digital artworks by over 200 artists.
The trouble started in May, when EAI began receiving emails, which EAI executive director Rebecca Cleman believes were AI-generated, flagging their account for community guideline violations. Karl McCool, EAI’s distribution director, told ARTnews that the two works Vimeo initially flagged were Barbara Hammer’s 1970s films Dyketactics and Women I Love, two of EAI’s most requested films.
EAI wasn’t completely caught off guard by this, McCool explains. He’d heard from colleagues at similarly sized arts organizations, like Collectif Jeune Cinema, a French experimental film distributor, and Visual AIDS, which supports HIV+ artists, about issues they were having with Vimeo. And in December, Connor says he told Cleman to “watch out for Vimeo,” having also heard about problems with streaming controversial or explicit media.
Despite EAI’s repeated attempts to get in touch with Vimeo to explain the history and value of Hammer’s, and others’, artworks, neither McCool nor Cleman was ever able to speak with a real person at the company, and their account was shut down over Memorial Day weekend.
EAI finally connected with someone at Vimeo about a month later, and the account was temporarily reinstated—once they took down the videos that had been flagged by artists like Ellen Cantor, Carolee Schneemann, Peggy Ahwesh, and Alex Bag, in addition to Hammer.
ARTnews reached out to Vimeo, but did not receive a response about their policy for removing videos or suspending accounts by press time.
“One thing that struck us,” said McCool, “is that a lot of the videos were works by women. Because we know the catalogue inside and out, we know that there’s a lot of work by men that is arguably far more explicit. And those things weren’t flagged … I don’t know that they were deliberately targeting women, but it was really notable what they didn’t pick up on, like the two films of Bruce Nauman’s testicles, or the many films of Vito Acconci completely naked doing sexual sorts of things, or the two Lawrence Weiner films that are full of unsimulated sex.”
EAI proactively removed these videos as well, since their contact at Vimeo explained that the account would be reinstated only once. By this point, EAI was already working with Rhizome on the new platform and planned to transition away from Vimeo as soon as it was ready.
Cleman and McCool trace their recent issues with Vimeo to the company’s $1.38 billion acquisition by Bending Spoons, a tech conglomerate that also owns WeTransfer, Eventbrite, and Airtable, in the fall of 2025. It was then that Vimeo’s business model shifted significantly, Cleman wrote in an email to ARTnews, with a majority of their workforce being dismissed in favor of AI replacements. McCool explained that he and others at EAI reached out to contacts at Vimeo they had been in touch with as recently as a few weeks or months prior, and all had been let go.
McCool credits Rhizome with “heroic” efforts over the summer to build an alternative to Vimeo using PeerTube, an open-source video platform, that addressed all of EAI’s specific needs. “We couldn’t just use PeerTube like an alternative version of YouTube,” McCool explained. “We needed Rhizome’s help to build a version that was tailor-made for us. We had to ensure that videos could be embedded on our own website with certain digital rights management protections in place. We had to make sure these works aren’t easily copied or pirated. We had to have good captions in place. There were all these different considerations that we needed Rhizome’s help with.”
Rhizome delivered on building the service—pro bono, McCool notes—and EAI is now able to host their videos via VRO. Connor plans to continue advocating for the importance of independent infrastructure in keeping digital artwork reliably available online. “Rhizome is still a nonprofit,” Connor said. “We’re not trying to run a video-hosting business. But the work our developers did for EAI is really easily replicable if we have other institutions or artists that need their own channels. We see hosting artist videos as mission-aligned work.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Brasil deve investir em cooperação comercial e em ciência e tecnologia com a Ásia, diz analista internacional
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Lucas Krupacz
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) está nas Filipinas para participar do encontro da Associação de Nações do Sudeste Asiático (Asean), que reúne 11 países e acontece no sábado (14) e domingo (15), com o objetivo de ampliar a presença do Brasil no bloco. A viagem também marca os 80 anos de cooperação entre Brasil e Filipinas.
Ao Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, a analista internacional Ana Prestes avalia de forma muto positiva a presença de Lula no encontro, que é hoje o polo da economia do mundo. “Lula esteve algumas vezes na região durante seu mandato e a agenda mostra que a política externa brasileira vai continuar investindo nessas relações e aprofundando a cooperação”, explica.
O Brasil chega com diversas mesas de negociação já estabelecidas. Prestes destaca os resultados positivos do ano passado, quando o comércio bilateral entre o Brasil e a Asean alcançou US$ 38 bilhões em um cenário que estamos “enfrentando guerra comercial com o tarifaço e problemas na região com o Mercosul por causa das relações com a Argentina”.
“É muito importante que o Brasil diversifique as suas relações internacionais para a área do comércio, mas para outras áreas também, cooperação em ciência e tecnologia, cooperação para a transição energética, ou seja, é uma agenda muito ampla”, defende.
A analista afirma que há uma elevação do status do Brasil, que se articula para passar de parceiro setorial da Asean para parceiro de diálogo pleno, e destaca que, em Brasília, já há laços bastante estreitos entre o governo brasileiro e as representações diplomáticas desses países. “Eles reconhecem o papel do Brasil no Sul Global e como articulador latino-americano, e o Brasil é o contraponto hoje aos EUA”, conta.
Ana Prestes destaca também a urgência de o Brasil priorizar a reindustrialização nesses nossos acordos. “O Brasil precisa de desenvolvimento científico e tecnológico. A gente precisa fazer cooperação com transferência de tecnologia para dar valor agregado aos nossos produtos e nossas indústrias”, avalia.
Para ouvir e assistir
O jornal Conexão BdF vai ao ar em duas edições, de segunda a sexta-feira: a primeira às 12h e a segunda às 17h, na Rádio Brasil de Fato, 98.9 FM, na Grande São Paulo, com transmissão simultânea também pelo YouTube do Brasil de Fato.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US supreme court agrees to consider Trump’s ban on asylum at US-Mexico border
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The US supreme court agreed on Friday to consider Donald Trump’s ban on asylum at the US-Mexico border, a pillar of the Republican president’s far-reaching crackdown on immigration.
The Trump administration wants to overturn lower court decisions that found the executive order banning asylum applications is illegal.
Federal law gives people the right to seek asylum if they fear persecution in their home countries, no matter how they arrived in the US.
At the same time, it also allows the executive branch to decide whether people are granted asylum. The Trump administration argues it can categorically deny asylum to migrants covered by the order and should not have to accept applications destined to be rejected.
Federal attorneys say years-long processing times had previously contributed to an influx of migrants at the southern border as many were released into the country while awaiting a decision.
But immigration attorneys at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and National Immigrant Justice Center counter that border crossings were already falling before Trump took office.
They say his executive order is an attempt to unilaterally “eviscerate” legal protections aimed at protecting people fleeing danger in their home countries.
The executive branch does decide whether to grant asylum, which allows people to live and work legally in the US. But those decisions are supposed to be made on an individual basis and the law doesn’t allow the president to unilaterally stop people from even applying, those attorneys argue.
The asylum ban was one of a series of immigration restrictions Trump rolled out upon his return to office in 2025. It has remained in place during the litigation.
